en: The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, Volume One: The Precepts for the Bhikṣu Saṃgha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India, together with Faxian, during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

The Bhikṣu Saṃgha’s Code of Precepts, Part 1: The Four Pārājika Dharmas. Clarifying the First of the Four Pārājika Dharmas: The Precept Against Sexual Misconduct. If a faithful son of good family desires to obtain the five benefits, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
What are these five?
If a son of good family wishes to establish the Buddha-dharma, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
If he wishes to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those who do not wish to harbor doubts or regrets and must inquire of others should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those monks and nuns who, having committed an offense, feel fear and require a refuge should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those who wish to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
This is called a faithful son of good family receiving and upholding this Vinaya, which brings about five benefits.
If one can fully receive and uphold the precepts of regulated conduct,
there are five benefits and merits as taught by the World-Honored One.
Those who receive and uphold this Vinaya should listen well to its meaning.

If one can fully receive and uphold [the teachings], Mastering the discipline of the precepts, And establishing the instruction of the World-Honored One, Such a person is called a true son of the Buddha.
The Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time; One is able to practice the gift of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, they will give rise to neither doubt nor regret, and will seek instruction from others.
Whether as bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, they shall find refuge when committing offenses;
as they travel and transform beings in all directions, they will encounter no obstacles wherever they go.

The Bhagavat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having now accomplished that which he had cultivated since first resolving upon his aspiration, dwells in the city of Śrāvastī for the sake of delivering sentient beings; he is venerated, supported, honored, and praised by gods and men of the world, and his renown throughout the ten directions is supreme among all offerings.

For the sake of sentient beings seeking merit, he establishes them in merit; for those seeking fruits, he establishes them in fruits; he brings peace and security to those afflicted by suffering; and for the sake of devas and humans, he opens the gate of the Deathless (amṛta). Among the sixteen great nations, there are none who do not submit to him in reverence, as they recognize and perceive his self-awakening.

As for the dwelling of the Buddha: he dwells in the celestial abodes, he dwells in the Brahma abodes, he dwells in the abodes of the noble ones, he dwells in the most supreme abode, and he dwells in the mind of omniscience; having attained mastery to dwell wherever he pleases, the Tathāgata therefore dwells in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting alone in a quiet place in the full lotus posture, absorbed in samādhi.
Having emerged from samādhi, he reflected thus:
"By what causes and conditions does the Dharma not remain for long after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?"
“By what causes and conditions do the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, long endure after their parinirvāṇa?

Thereupon, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Śāriputra arose from samādhi and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Having sat to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While I was in a quiet place, I entered into samādhi; having emerged from that samādhi, I reflected thus:"
"For what causes and conditions do the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, not remain long after their parinirvāṇa?
And for what causes and conditions do the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, remain long after their parinirvāṇa?"
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are Tathāgatas who do not extensively expound for their disciples the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātakas, vaipulyas, and adbhutadharmas.”

Śāriputra! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not establish precepts for the sake of śrāvakas, nor do they institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa; therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata, the Dharma does not remain for long.

Śāriputra! It is like a garland-maker or a garland-maker’s apprentice who places flowers of various colors upon a table without stringing them together; if a wind from any of the four directions blows, they will scatter with the wind.
Why is this? Because there are no threads to connect them.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata does not extensively expound the ninefold Dharma for his disciples, nor does he establish precepts for the śrāvakas, nor does he institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa; therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Dharma will not endure for long.
Śāriputra!

Because the Tathāgata has extensively taught the ninefold Dharma for his disciples, established the precepts for the śrāvakas, and instituted the exposition of the Prātimokṣa, the teachings will long endure after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.

Śāriputra! It is like a garland-maker or a garland-maker’s apprentice who strings various colored flowers together with thread; even if winds blow from the four directions, they do not scatter with the wind.
Why is this? Because they are connected by a thread.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata extensively expounded the ninefold canon of scriptures and established the rules of training for the śrāvakas by instituting the teaching of the Prātimokṣa; it is because of this that the Dharma will endure for a long time after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra!
For these reasons, there are teachings that endure for a long time and those that do not endure for a long time.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively expound the ninefold canon,

skillfully establish the precepts for the śrāvakas, and institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa, so that the Dharma-teaching may endure for a long time and the gate of ambrosia may be opened for all gods and worldlings.”
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata does not establish precepts for his disciples or institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa based on causes and conditions that do not involve faults or afflictions.”
"Śāriputra!
For example, a wheel-turning sage king does not impose punishments upon brahmins or householders for offenses they have not committed.
It is just so, Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata is likewise; he does not establish precepts for his disciples or institute the Pratimokṣa rules in the absence of causes and conditions involving faults and afflictions.

However, Śāriputra, in the future there will be sons of good family with right faith who, within the Buddha-dharma, believe that the homeless life is superior to the home life and thus leave their homes to renounce the world; yet, some among them may have distracted and inverted minds, giving rise to perceptions of purity, and with the three poisons raging intensely, they commit various transgressions.
"Śāriputra!
At that time, the Tathāgata shall establish the precepts for his disciples and institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa.
Stop!"
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata himself knows the proper time.
Śāriputra said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata himself shall know the proper time.
At that moment, Śāriputra bared one shoulder and joined his palms in homage.
In accordance with the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, he requested the most excellent teaching.
He exhorted the World-Honored One:
"Now is precisely the right time; for the sake of the assembly of disciples, please extensively establish the rules of the Vinaya."
"May the Buddha’s True Dharma endure for a long night;
may you reveal the gate of ambrosia and transform the multitudes of devas and humans.
Having made this exhortation while dwelling in his final body, he passed away.
At that time, the Most Victorious One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"The disciples have committed no offense; the entire Saṅgha is completely pure.
Never has it been the case for the Buddhas to establish a precept for one who is without fault."
Just as the Lord of the World, a king who rules over his realm, would not impose punishments upon those who have committed no offense;
so too is it with this: the World-Honored One, the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
No precepts for disciples were established when no faults or afflictions existed;
only when such faults had arisen and some began to commit evil deeds did the Teacher of Gods and Humans establish the code of discipline for the sake of the assembly.
"In the past and future worlds, there is nothing the Buddha-eye does not see;
according to the gravity of each matter, he establishes precepts according to that gravity.
When this True Dharma was spoken, it was at the Jeta Grove.
Śāriputra made this request, and the World-Honored One answered thus.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!..."

Venerable Śāriputra, why is it that the Blessed One has prescribed the training rules and established the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Dharma even though the bhikṣus have as yet committed no transgressions?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“It was not only today that Śāriputra requested the establishment of a precept because there was no transgression; in the past, in a certain city or village where the people and householders had committed no offense, he once likewise requested me to establish various penal regulations.”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Did this already exist in times past?”
The Buddha said, "It is so.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
we wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.

At that time, the king was known as Mahāyaśas; he governed by means of the Dharma, had no enemies, practiced generosity and upheld the precepts, loved all beings universally, and skillfully cared for his kinsmen."

The Dharma King governed the world, and the population was vast and flourishing; it was wealthy, joyful, and abundant. Villages and hamlets were so densely settled that the chickens flew from one to the next. All the people of the nation respected and loved one another, enjoying themselves together with various kinds of performing arts.
At that time, there was a great minister named Tāli, who possessed many strategic insights. He reflected thus:

"Now this realm of the king is naturally wealthy and joyful, with a flourishing population; the cities and villages are so close together that the chickens of one flock fly into the next. All the people of the nation respect and love one another, and they enjoy themselves through various kinds of arts and performances."
Then that minister went to address the king, saying:

"Today the realm is naturally prosperous and happy, and the population is flourishing; from city to town and village, the roosters' cries reach one another. All the people of the kingdom respect and love one another, enjoying themselves with various kinds of music and entertainment."
"I pray that Your Majesty will establish punishments for these people, so that they do not give rise to transgressions in their extreme pleasure.
The King said, "Stop!"
Stop! These words are unacceptable. Why is this so?
"Before faults have even arisen, you wish to impose punishment.
The minister replied again to the king:
"You should guard against the future; do not allow Sukhāvatī to give rise to any faults or calamities."
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"This minister is now wise and resourceful, and having many partisans, he cannot be restrained abruptly; if I were to reprimand him now, it might give rise to trouble."
At that time, the king, wishing to offer a subtle admonition to his great minister, spoke this verse:
"One who possesses power and delights in anger is difficult to rebuke or restrain suddenly;
to recklessly create faults and calamities for others—this is most improper."
Great persons possess much compassion; though they know that others have committed actual transgressions, they still observe them closely before inflicting punishment out of pity.
Evil persons, however, delight in distressing others and do not examine whether their faults and crimes are truly established.
Yet if one inflicts punishments upon them, one’s own reputation for evil increases.
If a king delights in tyranny and wrath, unjustly harming the virtuous,
his ill repute will spread far and wide, and after death he shall fall into the evil realms.
Transforming the common people through the True Dharma, with body, speech, and mind pure;
practicing patience and the four immeasurables—this is called a king among men.
As a king, the highest among men, you ought to restrain the heart of anger:
"Be benevolent and merciful toward the guilty, And show compassion when inflicting punishment.
At that time, having heard what the king had said, the great minister was filled with great joy and spoke these verses:
"O most excellent King among men, May you forever provide shade for the common people!"
Through patience one tames oneself; through the transformation of the Way, even enemies submit.
When a king’s virtue extends beyond all frontiers, his reign flourishes eternally without end.
Governing the world through the Way, he shall forever be a king of devas and humans.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for that king Mahāyaśas at that time, was he anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
The minister Dāruka at that time was Śāriputra.
At that time, there were no transgressions or afflictions among the elders and householders of the cities and villages, yet they requested me to establish penal laws.
"Now, while these faults have not yet arisen among the bhikṣus, you have requested that I establish precepts for my disciples and institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed as long as he pleased in Śrāvastī, he traveled through the human settlements of Kośala with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus surrounding him in front and behind, proceeding toward the village of the plowman brāhmaṇas in the kingdom of Kośala.
Having arrived, he stayed in the Karṇa-śāṭaka forest.

Then, at the hour of late afternoon, the Blessed One arose from samādhi, surveyed all directions—above and below—and looking again toward the level ground before him, he smiled and walked back and forth in meditation.

At that time, Śāriputra saw the World-Honored One arise from samādhi, surveying all directions above and below, and again looking toward the level ground before him; he smiled and paced back and forth. Having seen this, he went to where the many bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Venerable Elders!..."
I have previously seen the Blessed One arise from samādhi, surveying the various directions, and even walking back and forth in meditation.
Venerable Elders!
A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not manifest a smile without a cause or condition.
"If we go to inquire, we shall surely hear him speak of past lives and events from long ago.
Today we should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this matter; as the Buddha explains it, we shall practice accordingly."

When the bhikṣus had heard what Śāriputra said, they immediately went together with him to the place where the World-Honored One was; having prostrated themselves at his feet, they followed the Buddha as he walked to and fro.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Just now, seeing the World-Honored One arise from samādhi, observing the various directions, and even coming and going while walking to and fro, I immediately went to where many bhikṣus were and said to them: 'Elders!'"
Just now, I saw the Blessed One arise from samādhi, surveying the various directions, and even walking back and forth in perambulation.
Venerable Elders, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not smile without a cause or condition.
"If we go to inquire, we shall surely hear him speak of matters from the distant past and our former lives.
Today we should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning; as the Buddha explains it, so shall we practice."
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did you manifest this smile?
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm, pointed toward the ground, and addressed Śāriputra:
"Do you see this ground?
Śāriputra replied,
"Indeed, I see it."
The Buddha said:

"This ground was the site of the old grove of Kāśyapa Buddha; this spot was the site of his vihāra; this spot was the place for walking meditation (caṅkrama); and this spot was the place for sitting meditation."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra took his saṃghāṭī robe, folded it into four layers, and spread it upon the ground.
Having spread it upon the ground, he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray, World-Honored One!”
"Sitting upon this seat, I shall cause this ground to become the place where two Buddhas sit.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted and sat down. After the Venerable Śāriputra had prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For how many reasons of benefit do the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha establish the precepts for his disciples and institute the teaching of the Prātimokṣa?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"For ten reasons of benefit, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have established precepts for their disciples and formulated the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma."
What are the ten?
First, for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha;
second, for the sake of thoroughly gathering the Saṃgha.
Third, it is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the Saṃgha;
fourth, it is for the sake of subduing those who lack a sense of shame;
fifth, it is so that those who possess a sense of shame and remorse may dwell in security.
Sixth, to cause those who lack faith to attain faith;
seventh, to increase the faith of those who already possess it;
eighth, to attain the exhaustion of outflows within this present life.
Ninth, because it prevents unarisen outflows from arising;
tenth, because it causes the True Dharma to endure for a long time, opening the gate of the gift of ambrosia for all devas and humans.
For these ten reasons, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has established the precepts for his disciples and formulated the Dharma of the Prātimokṣa.
At that time, Śāriputra, baring one shoulder and joining his palms,
in accordance with the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, questioned the Most Victorious One. Dwelling in his final body,
having thus joined his palms and questioned him, he remained there.
At that time, the Most Victorious One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"There are ten benefits and merits known and seen by the Tathāgata;
therefore, for the sake of his disciples, he has extensively established the regulations of the Vinaya."
Because it gathers the Saṃgha and gathers them thoroughly;
because it causes the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness;
and because it subdues those who lack a sense of shame.
Shame and remorse bring peace and security;
lack of faith leads one into faith,
and for those who already have faith, it causes them to increase in virtue.
In this very life, one attains the exhaustion of outflows;
outflows that have not yet arisen do not arise;
the True Dharma abides for a long time, and the gate of the gift of ambrosia is opened.
While this True Dharma was being spoken in the Kasiṭa forest,
Śāriputra requested an explanation, and the World-Honored One answered thus.
At that time, having stayed as long as he pleased in the village of Kasiṭa, the World-Honored One traveled from the country of Kośala toward the country of Vajji.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with five hundred bhikṣus, arrived at the city of Vaiśālī in the kingdom of Vṛji and stayed at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest Monastery.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, the people suffered from famine and the five grains did not ripen; white bones lay scattered about, and it was difficult to obtain almsfood.

In the city of Vaiśālī, there was the son of an elder named Yaśas, who, having faith that the homeless life is superior to the household life, left his home to renounce the world; as his father’s name was Kalandaka, all fellow practitioners of the holy life addressed him as the son of Kalandaka.
At that time, there was a famine and alms were difficult to obtain; consequently, whenever mealtime arrived, many would return home to eat. His mother said to Yaśas, "My son!

You undergo great suffering, having shaved off your hair and beard and donned these tattered hempen robes; you carry an alms bowl and beg for food, becoming a laughingstock to the people of the world."
"In this house there is now great wealth; the money of your parents and the remaining treasures of your ancestors are all at your disposal as you wish.
Furthermore, your beloved wife is still here; you should live together with her. Why do you subject yourself to such hardships?"
"You should return home to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, give freely in charity, cultivate various merits, and make offerings to the Triple Gem.
At that time, Yaśas said to his mother:
"I pray you, Mother, desist!"
"Stop!
I delight in practicing the holy life.
His mother urged him a second and a third time as she had before, and Yaśas answered her just as he had previously.
The mother spoke again:
"If you do not wish to remain at home, you must beg for my seed to continue the lineage, so that the family line is not severed and our property does not fall into the hands of the state."
Then Yaśas spoke to his mother, saying:
"If you now wish for me to leave my seed within this [womb], I shall obey your command.
His mother was immediately filled with joy; she quickly entered her daughter-in-law's chamber and said to the new bride:
"Quickly adorn yourself and put on the garments that Yaśas formerly loved and used for his own body;
go and meet him. The bride replied, "So be it."
He then adorned himself exactly as instructed.
At that time, Yaśas enjoyed himself with his wife according to worldly custom, whereupon she subsequently became pregnant and, when the months were full, gave birth to a son.
The family deliberated and said, "Since we originally sought seeds for this purpose, we shall now establish his name as 'Seeds-Continued' (Jùzhǒng).

At that time, everyone in the world called him Seeds-Continued; his father was called Seeds-Continued, his mother was called Seeds-Continued, his grandfather was called Seeds-Continued, and all his wealth and possessions were likewise called Seeds-Continued.
Such ill repute spread far and wide, heard by both monastics and laypeople alike.
When Yaśas heard this infamy, he felt profound shame before his father, who had continued the family lineage; mortified by what he had heard, he reflected:
"Among the Śramaṇas of the Śākya clan, I have never seen or heard of such a thing."
"Is this the Dharma?
Or is it not the Dharma?

I shall now report this matter in detail to the Venerable Śāriputra; Śāriputra shall then report this matter fully to the Blessed One, and I shall practice according to the Blessed One’s instructions."
Then Yaśas went quickly to where the Venerable Śāriputra was and related the preceding events in detail.
The Venerable Śāriputra, together with Yaśas, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Once they were seated, the Venerable Śāriputra related the aforementioned matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked Yaśas:
"Is it true that you have done such a thing?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"Yasa! This is a great transgression; such a thing has never occurred within the community of bhikṣus.
You foolish man!"
For the first time you have opened the gate to great transgressions; where previously no taints or afflictions existed, you have now given rise to them.
Māra, the Evil One, has constantly sought the faults of the bhikṣus but was unable to find them; yet you have now, for the first time, opened a path for Māra.
"You have now destroyed the banner of the True Dharma and raised the banner of Pāpīyān.
You foolish person!

It would be better for you to have your living body cut and severed by a sharp blade, or to place it in the mouth of a venomous snake, or in the mouth of a mad dog, or within a great fire, or amidst ashes and charcoal, than to engage in sexual desire with a woman."
"Yaśas! Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, rebuke sensual desire:
that desire leads to delusion and intoxication; that desire is like a great fire that burns away one's roots of goodness; and that desire is a great affliction?"
I have always, through various skillful means, praised the renunciation of desire, the abandonment of desire, and the transcendence of desire.
Why do you now commit such an unwholesome act? Yaśas!
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"

"How is it that this Bhikṣu Yaśas has never before been among the Saṃgha, yet he, Yaśas, first opens the door to offenses; where there was no prior affliction of outflows (āsrava), he gives rise to such afflictions?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that this person, within my Dharma, has given rise to outflows and afflictions where none previously existed.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Did this indeed happen in the past?
The Buddha said, “It was so.”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the past, at the time when this world was undergoing the dissolution of a kalpa, all sentient beings were born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. When this great earth had subsequently re-formed, those sentient beings returned from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to this place."

At that time, those sentient beings possessed wondrous radiance upon their bodies; they were masters of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and took the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) as their food. Whatever they required was provided according to their wishes.
The radiance from the bodies of these sentient beings illuminated one another; there were no sun, moon, or stars, nor were there days or nights, nor months, fortnights, seasons, or years.
At that time, this great earth produced a natural essence of earth (pṛthivī-rasa), fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor, no different from the nectar of the gods (amṛta).

Then, there was a certain restless and lustful sentient being who tasted this essence of earth and perceived its fragrant sweetness; he gradually began to eat it, and immediately a mind of attachment arose within him.
When the other sentient beings saw this, they followed one another’s example and all vied with one another to take and eat it.

Once the sentient beings had eaten the earth-flavor (*pṛthivī-rasa*), their bodies became heavy and their radiance immediately vanished; they became greedily attached to the five desires and fell away from their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*).

Thereafter, in the world, there appeared the sun, the moon, and the constellations, along with the cycles of darkness and light, the half-months and months, and the seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"As for those restless beings at that time, could they have been anyone else?"
This is none other than the bhikṣu Yaśas.
At that time, while the taints and afflictions had not yet arisen in other beings, Yaśas gave rise to them first;
today, once again within the pure Saṅgha, he has first opened the gateway for the taints.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Has this been so for the bhikṣu Yaśas since his previous lives?”
"How did his mother skillfully employ expedient means to seduce and deceive her son with carnal desire?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only today that Yaśas’s mother skillfully employed expedient means to seduce and deceive her son; in a past life as well, she once deceived him."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
has this indeed happened before?”
The Buddha said, "It is so.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
we wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.

At that time, the king of that land was known as Mahāyaśas; he was free from all enemies, practiced generosity and upheld the precepts, loved all people with universal compassion, governed according to the Dharma, and skillfully cared for his retinue.”

At that time, the king’s principal consort ascended a high tower at dawn to observe the stars and constellations; she saw a golden-colored deer king coming from the south, soaring through the void toward the north.
Upon seeing it, the lady immediately thought to herself:
"If I could obtain this golden deer skin to make a rug, my life would end without regret;
if I cannot, what use is there in being the wife of this king?"
He then thought to himself:
"If I were to tell people,
'I saw a golden deer king,' [they would not believe me]."
"Who would believe this?
He further thought:

That bhikṣu immediately felt doubt and remorse, and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!
Have you not heard that the Buddha has established a precept forbidding sexual intercourse?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I know the established precept, but she was a dead woman.
The Buddha said:
"Engaging in sexual intercourse with a dead woman also constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
There are three conditions under which a bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* by engaging in sexual intercourse.
What are these three?
“Death, sleep, and awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Have all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”

If a bhikṣu receives full ordination within a harmonious Saṃgha, and without returning his precepts or relinquishing them due to weakness of resolve, commits the act of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.
The first *pārājika* account concludes.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu": one who has received full ordination and is properly ordained;
one who is ordained according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma.
Being in harmony and not being disharmonious;
being praiseworthy and not being unpraiseworthy;
being twenty years of age and not being less than that—this is the meaning of the term "bhikṣu."

Regarding receiving the precepts within a harmonious Saṃgha: when a bhikṣu receives full ordination, he properly receives it through one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*), provided there are no obstructing factors, the Saṃgha is harmonious and not a divided assembly, and there are ten or more monks present. This constitutes a bhikṣu receiving the precepts within a harmonious Saṃgha.
Regarding "one who returns the precepts," this is intended first to clarify the act of returning the precepts.

As for returning the precepts: when a bhikṣu returns the precepts, if he is sorrowful and unhappy, his mind is firmly resolved to abandon the dharma of a śramaṇa; he takes no pleasure in performing the duties of a bhikṣu, nor does he take pleasure in being a son of the Śākyas, saying:
"I wish to become a śrāmaṇera; I wish to become a follower of an external path; I wish to become a layperson and experience the five original sensual desires."
If one says to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, an outsider, a renunciant, or a layperson:

"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training, I renounce the teaching, I renounce communal residence, I renounce communal profit, I renounce the sūtras and treatises, I renounce the bhikṣus, I renounce the śramaṇas, I renounce the Śākya clan; I am no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer of the Śākya clan; I am a śrāmaṇera, an outsider, or a layperson, and I shall now enjoy the five desires as I did before."
This is called returning the precepts.
What is meant by abandoning the Buddha?

To abandon the Buddha means to abandon the Perfectly Awakened One, to abandon the Most Supreme, to abandon the Body of All-Knowledge, to abandon all vision, to abandon the knowledge and vision that leaves nothing remaining, to abandon the Father of Rāhula, to abandon the golden-hued body, to abandon the halo of light, to abandon the thirty-two marks, and to abandon the eighty minor characteristics.
If one abandons the name of each and every Buddha, it is called abandoning the Buddhas; such abandonment of the Buddhas is called abandoning the precepts.
If one says:
"I abandon the Buddhas of the past and the future."
This does not constitute the abandonment of the precepts, but one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
However, if one does not say:
"I abandon the Buddhas of the past and the future," [it is not an abandonment].
To speak directly, saying,
"I renounce the Buddha," is called the abandonment of the precepts.
If one says,
"I renounce the state of a pratyekabuddha," this is called renouncing the precepts.
The Buddhas of the past and future are likewise like those who have relinquished [all attachments].
Furthermore, all the renunciants of the non-Buddhists and the disciples of the Six Teachers each say:
"There is a Buddha."
If a bhikṣu, while truly wishing to renounce this Buddha, falsely says,
"I renounce the Buddha of the non-Buddhists," this is not called a renunciation of the precepts; he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one abandons the Buddha in jest, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If spoken by mistake or due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
What is the abandonment of the Dharma?
The Dharma is not encompassed by the three periods of time; its characteristic is eternally abiding.
It is called unconditioned nirvana, which is free from all afflictions, wherein all suffering and calamity are forever exhausted without remainder.
If one says,
"I renounce this Dharma," it is called the relinquishing of the precepts.
If one says,
"I renounce past and future dharmas," this is not called renouncing the precepts; one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one does not refer to the past or the future, but simply says,
"I relinquish the Dharma," this is called relinquishing the precepts.
All non-Buddhists each have their own doctrines; if a bhikṣu truly intends to abandon this True Dharma but falsely says,
"I am abandoning those [non-Buddhist] doctrines," this is not called abandoning the precepts, yet he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one abandons the Dharma in jest, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If spoken by mistake or due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
What constitutes abandoning the Saṃgha?

The Sangha refers to the Sangha of the World-Honored One’s disciples: those who are rightly directed toward and rightly intent upon wisdom, who follow the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and who practice in conformity with the Dharma—namely, the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones. They are perfected in faith, perfected in virtue, perfected in learning, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are worthy of veneration and constitute the unsurpassed field of merit.
If a bhikṣu says,
"I renounce this Saṃgha," this is called the renunciation of the precepts.
If one says,
"I renounce the Sangha of the past and the future," this is not called renouncing the precepts; one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one does not refer to the past or the future, but speaks directly, saying,
"I renounce the Saṃgha," this is called the renunciation of the precepts.
It is the same for the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
If one says:
"I renounce the many bhikṣus."
This does not constitute the relinquishing of the precepts, but one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says:
"I relinquish the many bhikṣus of the past and the future," [it likewise does not constitute the relinquishing of the precepts].
This is not called relinquishing the precepts, yet one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one does not specify "I relinquish [the precepts before] many past and future bhikṣus," but simply says:
"I relinquish many bhikṣus."
This is not called relinquishing the precepts; one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
As it is for many bhikṣus, so it is for many bhikṣuṇīs.
If one says:
"I renounce one bhikṣu"—this is not called renouncing the precepts; one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one says:
"To renounce a past or future bhikṣu" does not constitute a renunciation of the precepts;
one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (a transgression requiring mental regret).
If one does not speak these words:
"I relinquish one bhikṣu from the past and the future," he said directly:
"I relinquish one bhikṣu."
This is not called relinquishing the precepts, yet one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
As it is for one bhikṣu, so it is for one bhikṣuṇī.
If one says:
"To relinquish the preceptor" is termed "relinquishing the precepts.
The distinctions are as explained in the section on relinquishing [the precepts] within the Sangha.
If one says,
"I renounce my preceptor," this is not termed a renunciation of the precepts; rather, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says,
"I renounce my past and future preceptors," this is not called renouncing the precepts;
it constitutes an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
If one does not refer to the past or the future, but simply says,
"I renounce the ācārya," this is not called a renunciation of the precepts; one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says "I renounce" in jest, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If spoken by mistake or due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
For example, if those non-Buddhists each call themselves a "Saṃgha," and a bhikṣu, truly wishing to renounce this Saṃgha, falsely says:
"To renounce the monastic community of non-Buddhists" does not constitute a forfeiture of the precepts, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says "I renounce the community" in jest, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one speaks erroneously or is deranged in mind, there is no offense.
What is the relinquishing of training?
There are three kinds of training:
There are the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
The training in higher virtue refers to the detailed and abbreviated explanations of the Prātimokṣa.
The training in higher mind refers to the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
The training in higher wisdom refers to the four noble truths.
These—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—are all collectively termed "training" (*śikṣā*).
If a bhikṣu says,
"I renounce this training," it is in all cases termed the renunciation of the precepts.

As previously explained in the section on "renouncing the Buddha," there are various forms of worldly training, such as those in crafts, writing, arithmetic, and technical skills; all of these are termed "training" (*śikṣā*). If a bhikṣu wishes to renounce this training, he might falsely say:
"I renounce that training."
This does not constitute the forfeiture of the precepts, but results in a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

It is like the various trainings that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) each have for themselves; if a bhikṣu wishes to renounce these trainings and falsely says, "I renounce the training of the non-Buddhists."
This is not called relinquishing the precepts; one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says in jest, "I relinquish the training," [it is likewise].
One incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
There is no offense if one speaks erroneously, is mentally deranged, or has relinquished the training.
What constitutes relinquishing the teaching?
There are three types of observances:
the fourteenth-day, the fifteenth-day, and the intermediate *poṣadha*. Regarding the fourteenth-day:
it refers to the third and seventh *poṣadhas* of winter, the third and seventh *poṣadhas* of spring, and the third and seventh *poṣadhas* of summer.
Within a year, these six *poṣadha* days on the fourteenth are called "fourteenth-day [observances].
The remaining eighteen *poṣadha* days are on the fifteenth; together, they constitute twenty-four *poṣadha* observances, which are termed "fourteenth- and fifteenth-day *poṣadhas*."
Regarding the intermediate *poṣadha*: when monks are performing the *poṣadha* and the Saṃgha is not in harmony, one monk proclaims within the assembly:
"When the Saṃgha is in harmony, we shall perform the *poṣadha*."
If not even one bhikṣu makes the proclamation, the entire saṃgha incurs an offense of violating the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If one bhikṣu makes the proclamation, the entire saṃgha is without offense.
If there is no assembly on the fifteenth day, the *poṣadha* should be held on the first day.
If there is no assembly on the first day, it should be held on the second day, and so on, up to the twelfth day.
If the twelfth day is not in harmony [with the lunar phase], one should perform the *poṣadha* on the thirteenth day.

If the fourteenth day is the proper time for the *poṣadha*, one should not perform an intermediate *poṣadha* on the thirteenth day; instead, one proceeds directly to the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day, which is both an intermediate *poṣadha* and is called the proper *poṣadha*.

If the month is long, one may perform the intermediate *poṣadha* on the thirteenth day provided the conditions coincide; if they do not coincide, one must not perform it on the fourteenth day, but should instead perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, which is also called the intermediate *poṣadha* and is also called the regular *poṣadha*.
Why is this? One must not perform the *poṣadha* on consecutive days; rather, one should perform the *poṣadha* on alternating days, which is called the "intermediate *poṣadha*.
Those who are to perform the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day must not let it be delayed until the fifteenth day.
Regarding those who should perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, they must not go against the fourteenth day.
If there is a valid cause or condition, one may perform the *poṣadha*.
Whether it be on the fourteenth day, the fifteenth day, or an intermediate *poṣadha*, all are termed "recitation" (*pravāraṇā*).
If one says, "I renounce this teaching," it is called the relinquishment of the precepts,
as explained previously in the section on relinquishing the Buddha.
Those various non-Buddhists also each have their own doctrines; if one truly intends to renounce these [Buddhist] teachings yet falsely claims,
"I am renouncing the teachings of the non-Buddhists," this is not called renouncing the precepts, and one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one discloses [the offense] in jest, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense of transgression).
If one discloses it by mistake or while insane, there is no offense.
What is the relinquishing of communal residence?
There are two kinds of communal residence (*sāṃvāsika*):
first, pure communal residence; second, semblance communal residence.
Regarding pure communal residence: when the entire assembly is pure and they perform the *poṣadha* together, this is called pure communal residence.

Regarding "living together in semblance": one who is impure manifests the appearance of being pure and performs the *poṣadha* together with those who are pure; this is called living together in semblance.
Whether it be pure co-residence or similar co-residence, all are termed "co-residence.
If one says:
"I renounce co-residence."
This is called abandoning the precepts, as explained in detail above regarding the abandonment of the Buddha.

Those non-Buddhist practitioners also have communal residence; if one truly intends to abandon this communal residence, yet falsely says, "I abandon that communal residence," [it constitutes an offense].
This does not constitute the relinquishment of the precepts, but one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says, in jest, "I relinquish communal residence," one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one relinquishes communal residence through mistake or due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
What is the relinquishing of shared benefits?
There are two kinds of shared benefits:
first, the benefit of the Dharma; second, the benefit of food and clothing.
The benefit of the Dharma refers to receiving, reciting, questioning, and answering.
The benefit of robes and food refers to receiving a single act of giving together.
Both the benefit of the Dharma and the benefit of robes and food are collectively termed "shared benefits."
If a bhikṣu says,
"I renounce this benefit," this is called the renunciation of the precepts; the rest is as explained in detail above in the section on the renunciation of the Buddha.
If one says,
"I renounce the Dharma and its benefits," this is called the renunciation of the precepts, as explained in detail above in the section on renouncing the Buddha.
If one merely says,
"I relinquish the benefits of food and clothing," this is not called relinquishing the precepts; it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says,
"I renounce past and future benefits of food and clothing," this is not called renouncing the precepts;
it constitutes an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
If one does not refer to the past or future, but speaks directly, saying:
"I relinquish the benefit of robes and food," this is not called relinquishing the precepts; rather, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Those non-Buddhists also have common interests; if one truly intends to renounce these common interests but falsely claims,
"I am renouncing those common interests," this is not called renouncing the precepts, yet it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one jokingly says that they renounce shared profits, they incur a *vyatikrama* offense.
If one speaks erroneously or renounces shared profits due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
What is meant by "renouncing the Sūtras and Śāstras"?
There are nine divisions of the sūtras and śāstras; if a bhikṣu says,
"I renounce these sūtras and śāstras," this is called the renunciation of the precepts.
If one says,
"I renounce the sūtras and śāstras of the past and future," this is not called renouncing the precepts; one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one does not refer to the past or the future, but simply says,
"I renounce the sutras and śāstras," this is called the abandonment of the precepts.
If, while performing music, one composes songs and verses based on the Buddha’s words and then says,
"I renounce these Buddha's words within this song," this is called abandoning the precepts.
Those non-Buddhists also have their own scriptures and treatises; if one truly intends to renounce these [Buddhist] scriptures and treatises, yet falsely claims,
"I am renouncing those [non-Buddhist] scriptures and treatises," this is not called renouncing the precepts, and one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one speaks jokingly of abandoning the sūtras and śāstras, it is not called abandoning the precepts, but one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one abandons the sūtras and śāstras through inadvertent speech or due to mental derangement, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu should say: "I abandon the Buddha; the Buddha abandons me.

I am separated from the Buddha; the Buddha is separated from me. I am distant from the Buddha; the Buddha is distant from me. I am weary of the Buddha; the Buddha is weary of me. I have ceased [association with] the Buddha; the Buddha has ceased [association with] me."

All such cases are termed "renouncing the precepts. This applies equally to the renunciation of various sūtras and treatises; this is called "returning the precepts" (*pratyāpanna-śīla*). Regarding those who do not return the precepts:

if one renounces them out of anger, or speaks abruptly, or speaks alone, or speaks unclearly, or speaks due to a dispute, or speaks while harboring a private thought, or speaks when the other person does not understand, or speaks toward someone who is sleeping, toward someone who is insane, toward someone who is suffering, toward an infant, toward a non-human (*amanuṣya*), or toward an animal—such declarations of returning the precepts are not termed "renouncing the precepts."
Regarding "one whose morality is weak," they think:
"It would be better for me to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, even to the point of abandoning all the sūtras and śāstras.
They further think:
"I shall become a śrāmaṇera, a layperson, or a follower of an external path.
He thinks this in his mind and speaks these words,
yet he has not definitively declared it to others.
This is called "weakness of the precepts" (śīla-kaśāya).
If one speaks of the matter of weakness of the precepts, for every word spoken, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, one forms a mental thought and utters it verbally:
"I had better abandon the Buddha," he thought,
and even went so far as to say,
"I had better become an ordinary layman once again."
Furthermore, he says:
"It would be better for me to abandon the Buddha... [and so on] ...it would be better for me to revert to my former status as a layperson.
This is called "weakness in morality" (śīla-kaśāya).
If one speaks of being weak in the precepts, for every word spoken, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; this is called "weakness in the precepts.

If one who is weak in the precepts practices the dharma of sexual intercourse—whereby "the dharma of sexual intercourse" refers to engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman in any of the three orifices while life remains, and experiencing pleasure at the beginning, middle, or end—this is called "practicing the dharma of sexual intercourse."
If a bhikṣu, while his precepts are weak, engages in sexual intercourse, he incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

Whether it be with a human female, whether she is alive or dead, if he engages in sexual intercourse in the three places and experiences pleasure at the beginning, middle, and end; or likewise with a non-human female, whether she is alive or dead, or with a female animal, whether she is alive or dead—if he engages in sexual intercourse in the three places and experiences pleasure during the three times, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

If a human male has life and dies, a non-human male has life and dies, and a male animal has life and dies—engaging in sexual intercourse with these two types of beings and experiencing pleasure at these three times—the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

If a human hermaphrodite has life and death, or a non-human hermaphrodite has life and death, or an animal hermaphrodite has life and death, and one experiences pleasure in two locations during the three periods of beginning, middle, and end, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "animals": from elephants and horses down to chickens, these are called animals.
If one commits an offense against such an animal, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Whether it be the large body of an elephant or the small body of a chicken, [if one kills it with intent], one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
If the elephant's body is small or even the chicken's body is large, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; therefore, it is said that even with an animal, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
"Pārājika" means that one has regressed from and fallen away from the knowledge of the Dharma, such that there is no longer any portion of the fruits of the path; this is called pārājika.

Likewise, regarding the knowledge of the unknown, conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising—one has regressed from and fallen away from these various knowledges, such that there is no longer any portion of the fruits of the path; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, *pārājika* refers to one who has fallen away from and descended from *nirvāṇa*, lacking the portion for realizing the fruits; this is called *pārājika*.
Furthermore, *pārājika* refers to one who has fallen away from and descended from the holy life (*brahmacarya*), lacking the portion for the fruits of the path; this is called *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding the *pārājika*: because the offense committed cannot be confessed and purified, it is called *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, desires to look at a woman, he incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression requiring mental repentance).
If one sees with the eyes or hears sounds [of such acts], one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If they touch each other while naked, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Even if it enters [the body] as little as a sesame seed, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If that body is large and one enters it without touching its edges, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Regarding sentient beings who have a single passage through which they eat, excrete, and pass urine—whether they are born there or die there—if one has sexual intercourse with such a being and experiences pleasure at the beginning, middle, or end, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If a woman’s body is split into two parts and one engages in sexual intercourse with each part individually, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If she is bound together and one engages in sexual intercourse [with her thus], it is a *pārājika*.
If a woman’s body is divided into three parts: if a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with her lower part, it is a pārājika offense;
if he engages in sexual intercourse with her middle part, it is a thullaccaya offense;
if he engages in sexual intercourse with her upper part, it is a pārājika offense.
If one commits sexual intercourse with a woman whose body is livid, bloated, and swollen, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if the body is decomposed and putrefied, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and if the body is completely withered and dried up, it is likewise a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that has been moistened and preserved from decay by being soaked in ghee, oil, or water, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If the form is decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a skeleton whose bones remain connected and which is smeared with pus and blood, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding a white bone or a withered corpse: it is a *vyatikrama-citta-kaukṛtya* (an offense requiring mental regret).
Regarding a woman made of stone or wood, or a painted woman, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu neither declares his renunciation of the precepts nor declares that he does not renounce them; or if his precepts have become weak, yet he neither declares their renunciation nor declares that they are not renounced, and he thus becomes a layperson—then he shall be punished according to the law in accordance with his transgression. The same applies if he becomes a follower of an external path.

If it is wrapped but not covered, or covered but not wrapped, or both covered and wrapped, or neither covered nor wrapped—even if it enters [the body] as small as a sesame seed—it is a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu does not return the precepts, or if his precepts have become weak but he does not manifest the signs [of renunciation], and he then assumes the appearance and dress of a layperson and commits an offense, he incurs the guilt corresponding to that which he has committed.
If a bhikṣu forcibly commits sexual intercourse with a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense;
if the bhikṣuṇī experiences pleasure, she also incurs a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī forcibly commits sexual intercourse with a bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense;
if the bhikṣu experiences pleasure, he also commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣu engage in sexual intercourse with one another, both commit a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī engage in sexual intercourse, both commit a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu and a śrāmaṇera engage in sexual intercourse with one another, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and the śrāmaṇera is expelled.

If a bhikṣu and a layperson engage in sexual intercourse with one another, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense, while the layperson does not commit an offense; this applies likewise even to non-Buddhist practitioners.
If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with three kinds of beings—humans, non-humans, and animals;
furthermore, with three kinds of persons—women, men, and eunuchs;
furthermore, with three kinds of orifices—the upper, middle, and lower paths; and furthermore, with three kinds [of conditions]:...
Whether awake, asleep, or dead, it is all *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu is asleep, his mind is deranged, or he has entered meditative absorption, and a woman forcibly approaches him to engage in sexual intercourse, if the bhikṣu experiences pleasure at the beginning, the middle, or the end while awake, it is *pārājika*.

If this bhikṣu is asleep or even in meditative absorption, and a woman forcibly engages in sexual intercourse with him, he experiences no pleasure at the beginning upon waking, but experiences pleasure in the middle and at the end; he too commits a pārājika offense.

If this bhikṣu, while sleeping or even in a state of meditative concentration, is forcibly approached for sexual intercourse by a woman, and upon waking he does not experience pleasure at first but experiences pleasure later, it constitutes a pārājika offense.

If this bhikṣu is asleep or even in meditative absorption, and a woman engages in sexual intercourse with him, provided that once the bhikṣu has awakened, he experiences no pleasure at the beginning, middle, or end, he is without offense.
What is called "experiencing pleasure"?
What is called "not experiencing pleasure"?
Regarding those who experience pleasure:
For example, just as a hungry person who obtains various kinds of fine food finds pleasure in that food;
or as a thirsty person who obtains various kinds of excellent drink finds pleasure in the sensation of drinking—
that which is called sensual pleasure is also like this.
One who does not experience pleasure is like a person of pure and refined character with various corpses tied around his neck;
or like one whose body is pierced by a boil or scorched by glowing red-hot iron—
one who does not experience pleasure is just like this.

If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse—whether with one obtained by purchase, obtained by hire, obtained through a bond of affection, obtained as an acquaintance, obtained through dalliance, obtained for the sake of testing, or obtained from one inexperienced in such matters—in all such cases, if he engages in sexual intercourse, it constitutes a pārājika offense.
If one's mind is deranged and they are not self-aware, there is no offense.

Therefore it is said: if a bhikṣu has received full ordination within a harmonious Saṃgha, and without returning the precepts or manifesting signs of weak resolve, commits the act of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

In the fifth year after the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood at the city of Vaiśālī, on the twelfth day of the fifth half-month of winter, following the midday meal, while sitting facing east when one and a half shadows remained, he established this precept for the Elder Yaśas, son of Kāḷaka.
"Once a rule has been established, one should practice in accordance with it; this is called 'conformity to the Dharma'.
The precept against sexual misconduct is concluded. Regarding the precept against stealing: the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the Elder Ghaṭīkāra, the potter’s son, exhorted others to establish a monastic dwelling. It was adorned in various ways, lofty and magnificent, with intricate carvings and engravings; its floor was smeared with fragrant oil, appearing the color of deep lapis lazuli, and it was constantly provided with various kinds of food and drink.
At that time, an elder bhikṣu came and asked Daṇḍaka,
"Elder, how many years have you been ordained? He replied:
"For that many years.
The visiting bhikṣu said, "You are junior; I should reside here."
Once Daṇḍaka had been assigned a room by the Elder, he further exhorted others to build a second room.
When another elder bhikṣu arrived, the rooms were assigned to him in the same sequence as before.
Furthermore, he was exhorted and inspired to build a third room; yet another elder bhikṣu arrived, and the situation was exactly as before.
At that time, Daṇḍaka thought to himself:
"I have undergone all manner of hardships to build this room, yet I am unable to dwell in it. Where else shall I find timber and labor to construct another dwelling?"

Constantly tormented by wind, rain, cold, heat, mosquitoes, and gadflies, one manages to complete this dwelling only for a bystander to seize it as soon as it is finished, like a cat waiting for a mouse; how can one ever hope to accomplish such a task?
He then thought to himself:
"I am skilled in crafts and possess physical strength; I shall construct a finished earthen house upon the black rock beside the hermitage cave."

At that time, after Daṇḍakin had formed this thought, he built a finished earthen house upon a black rock beside the hermitage cave. It was adorned with various carvings and provided with windows and doors; however, excluding the door-panels, the door-latches, and the clothing rack, everything else was completed in a single firing, its color a pure crimson like the *utpala* flower.

At that time, after the rains had ceased and the sky was clear, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth in meditation beside Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. With the Buddha-eye of a Tathāgata, there is nothing he does not see, nothing he does not hear, and nothing he does not know. For this reason, wishing to preach a sūtra so that the Vinaya might endure for a long time, he knowingly asked the bhikṣus:
"On the black rock by the side of the hermitage cave on Mount Ṛṣigiri, there is something the color of an udumbara flower; what is it?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

This bhikṣu Daṇḍaka first exhorted others to construct a monastic dwelling, adorning it with exquisite carvings and engravings until it was most beautifully decorated. Once completed, he took the seat of honor; then he did the same for a second and a third [monastery], in exactly the same manner.”

He then privately constructed a fired-brick house upon a black rock beside the cave of the Rishi Mountain; its color was exquisite and beautiful, like the udumbara flower, and it is this very one that stands today upon the black rock beside the cave of the Rishi Mountain.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda,
"Bring me my robe. Ānanda brought the robe and presented it to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having donned his robes, went to the Black Stone of the Seer’s Cave. The World-Honored One was perfected in the supreme deportments—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—in which he no longer required conscious effort to maintain these postures.

Why is this so? Because the merit of his karmic conduct is naturally sublime, surpassing that which can be attained by any of the devas or Brahmā kings, as is explained in detail in the *Vinaya-sūtra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his sublime deportment, proceeded to the place where the baked-brick house of Dāniya stood; the devas caused the door of the house to open of its own accord.
The lower part of the door was small, yet the Tathāgata entered it level; though low, it did not obstruct him, and though narrow, it did not constrain him.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had entered the house built by Daṇḍakin and burned it down, he stroked the walls with his golden hand—its fingers joined by webbing—and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Behold, monks, how this bhikṣu Daṇḍakin was skilled at adorning and constructing this fine house. Although this bhikṣu Daṇḍikin has gone forth as a renunciant, he is still unable to weary of what he formerly practiced; he has not yet abandoned his craftsmanship and technical skills, and moreover, he has burned and killed living beings."
Furthermore, this tile-roofed house is extremely cold when it is cold and extremely hot when it is hot; it can damage one's eyes and cause many illnesses.
It possesses these various afflictions. You should demolish this house so that future bhikṣus do not practice the way of this house.
In future generations, bhikṣus will say:
"When the World-Honored One was alive, each of the bhikṣus lived in houses they built for themselves.
For this reason, it is appropriate that [this house] be demolished.
Then the bhikṣus immediately demolished this house.
After the World-Honored One had demolished this house, he returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
At that time, the elder bhikṣu Daṇḍakin, returning from alms-gathering in the village, saw that the house had been demolished and spoke these words:
"Who has destroyed this house?
At that time, a bhikṣu said to Daṇḍaka,
"You have now gained a great and wholesome benefit."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata condescended to visit this house; you have received the merit of enjoying this house, and the World-Honored One, knowing the proper time, has now destroyed it.
When Daṇḍakin heard these words, he was filled with such supreme joy that for seven days he forgot both hunger and thirst.
After the seven days had passed, he thought to himself:
"Where else can I find timber to erect a dwelling?"
"King Bimbisāra’s carpenter-minister, Yaśoda, was my acquaintance in the past; he must certainly have timber.
He then put on his village-dweller’s robes, took up his bowl, went to Yaśoda’s house, and after exchanging greetings, said:
"May you be free from illness and long-lived!"
"I wish to erect a dwelling, but I have no timber. Would you be able to grant me some timber?
The minister replied, "There is no timber in my own house, and the timber of the King is also exhausted. However, if timber is brought here, I shall certainly provide it to you."
Dhanika spoke again:
"Do not say such a thing!
How can you say that the timber for the royal palace is exhausted?"
The minister spoke again:
"Venerable sir!
If you do not believe me, you may go and see for yourself."
Then Daṇḍakī immediately went to the place where the timber was being prepared; seeing five pieces of material for a ladder, he took two of them and carried them back to build his house.

According to the ancient laws of the former kings, every five days the ruler would go on inspection tours to view the treasuries, the stores of gold, silver, and precious treasures, the palace attendants on duty, and the elephant stables, horse pens, carriages, and military equipment.
Next, they proceeded to the Wood Workshop and saw that there were two pieces missing from the materials for the flight stairs;
they immediately asked Yaśodharā, "Why are there two pieces missing from the materials for the flight stairs?"
He replied, "Great King! They are all here;
it is not few."
In this manner, he inspected it a second and a third time.
He then asked Yaśodharā,
"Why are there so few materials for the ladder, lacking two pieces?"
He replied: "Great King, they are all present;
it is not a small number."
The king then spoke with anger:
"Did you not burn my timber?
Did you not give my timber to the enemy state?"
The officials then seized Yaśodharā and bound her.
Once she was seized, Yaśodharā thought to herself:
"Has the Venerable Daṇḍakin, who recently came to request timber, perhaps taken it away?"
He immediately sent a messenger to say to Dhanika:
"Venerable One!
Did you not previously come to request timber, and take these two pieces of ladder material away?"
He replied, "Bring it here.
He then sent a messenger to inform the Venerable One:
“Because I sat upon this flight of stairs and caused its destruction, I have been cast into prison.
Venerable One!
You should employ skillful means so that you yourself may remain free from fault while I am released early.”
Dhanika replied: "You should simply inform the King:
'The bhikṣu Dhanika previously requested timber from me; could he possibly have taken it away?'"
"I pray that you will issue an order to investigate this.
The King immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Daṇḍakin.
Daṇḍakin then went to the King's presence; the Elder Daṇḍakin was upright in person, his deportment was dignified and refined, and he was revered by both gods and men.
The king, seeing this, was filled with joy and asked,
"Venerable Daṇḍakin, did you not take my two pieces of ladder timber?
He replied:
"I shall take it.
The King said,
"Venerable One!"
"How is it that a renunciant takes what is not given?
Daṇḍakin replied, "Your Majesty previously gave it; it was not that he did not give."
The king asked,
"Who gave it?
and they replied:
"The King himself shall grant it.
The King said,
"Venerable One!"
"I am a king; although my affairs are many, I do not recall ever meeting you.
Why, then, do you speak of giving [me something]? Daṇḍakin said:

"Your Majesty, do you not remember when you first ascended the throne? At that time, the great ministers of the kingdom gathered all the waters of rivers, ponds, and springs, as well as all medicinal herbs and seeds, and soaked them in water; they then performed the consecration by pouring drops of this water from a white ivory tusk upon your head and installed you as king."
At that time, the king spoke these words himself:
"I am now the king; all the water, grass, and trees within my realm, I bestow as a gift upon the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
"Therefore, it was given by the King; it was not withheld.
The King said, "Venerable One!"
"I have given [the kingdom] to those who were without protection, not to those who already had protection.
How could I rely on your previous words and false claims to be thus slandered?
The king said:
"Release Yaśodharā and let her go.
All the brahmins in the kingdom, as well as the laymen and laywomen who held him in reverence and faith, spoke with joy:
"Excellent!"
The Venerable Daṇḍakin, through his skillful means and wisdom, gave a clever reply to the Great King, thereby escaping this transgression and ensuring that Yaśodharā was safely released.
At that time, those in Rājagṛha who did not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma all spoke with resentment, saying:

"How can this śramaṇa Daṇḍakin rely on false reasoning to deceive the King and merely escape punishment? We fear that from now on he will take away all the timber in our homes as well, claiming the King previously gave it to him. What are we to do!"
"What path can there be for one who ruins others in this way!
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call the bhikṣu Dhanika here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Daṇḍaka,
"Is it true that you took the timber for the royal flying staircase?
He replied:
“I actually took it.
The Buddha said, “How can you,
who have left the household life, take the property of another that was not given to you?”
Daṇḍakin said:
"World-Honored One!
It was the king who first saw it; it was not that he did not give it."
The Buddha said,
"How did the king give it? Dhanika replied:
"When the King first ascended the throne, he spoke these words himself:
'Whatever water, grass, and trees exist within the kingdom, I bestow them as gifts upon the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.'"
"Therefore, I said 'I give,' it was not that I did not give.
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
The king gives to those who are without protection, not to those who have protection.
Now, this King Canda has protection; why do you say he will give? Dhanika!
Have you not always heard the Buddha, through various causes and conditions, reprimanding the taking of what is not given, and in various ways praising the taking only after it has been given?
Why then do you now take what is not given?
“Dāniya! This is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya, and this is not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot increase wholesome qualities through such matters.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How was it that the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka first initiated the taking of what was not given?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Dhanika has not only committed this first offense of taking what was not given today; in a past life as well, he already once committed that first offense of taking what was not given.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, “Has it truly been so?”
The Buddha said, "It is so.
In a past age, when this world reached the end of its kalpa, all sentient beings were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven."

When the world had returned to formation, the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to the world. At that time, these gods moved, dwelt, and stood in mid-air; they took the joy of dhyāna as their food, lived happily and well-established wherever they wandered, and their own bodily radiance illuminated one another, such that they did not rely on the sun and moon for light.
At that time, sentient beings had no distinction between day and night, sun and moon, years, or seasons.
When the waters had receded, the "taste of the earth" (pṛthivī-rasa) emerged, like the nectar of the gods (amṛta).

At that time, there was a certain sentient being who was greedy for flavors and flighty; upon tasting the essence of this earth, he perceived its color, fragrance, and delicious taste, and his mind became attached to it.
The other beings followed his example and ate it, perceiving its excellence as well, and they all began to partake of it together.

Having eaten, his body became coarse and heavy; he fell away from his supernormal powers and his radiance was completely extinguished. Thereupon, the world came to have the sun and moon, with their cycles of darkness and light, as well as years, numbers, and seasons.

At that time, sentient beings were neither male nor female. After consuming the essence of the earth for a long period, their physical forms and complexions became diverse: those who ate much had coarse and ugly complexions, while those who ate little had upright and handsome complexions.
At that time, those who were handsome claimed superiority for themselves, while seeing those who were coarse and ugly, they looked down upon them as being inferior.

Because they relied on their physical beauty, pride arose; due to the transgression of that pride, the flavor of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) immediately vanished, and the "earth-skin" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) appeared, its taste like pure honey.
At that time, all sentient beings were struck with wonder and sighed, saying:
"How is it that the essence of the earth has suddenly vanished?
Thereupon, they again began to eat the crust of the earth together; those who ate much became coarse and ugly in appearance, while those who ate little remained upright and handsome in form.
Those who were handsome became increasingly arrogant; subsequently, the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-crust) vanished.

Once the earth-crust had disappeared, there next arose the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-vasā*), which tasted like rock honey. Those who ate much of it became ugly, while those who ate little remained beautiful, just as before.
Those who were handsome became twice as conceited, whereupon the earth-fat suddenly vanished again.

Once the earth-fat had disappeared, there spontaneously appeared wild rice; though they took it, it was never perceived to increase or decrease, appearing in the evening after being taken in the morning, and appearing in the morning after being taken in the evening.
"Monks, you should know that when the sentient beings of that time saw the *pṛthivī-vasā* (earth-fat) vanish, they were overcome with grief and distress, just as a man might be oppressed by sorrow.
Although those beings were anxious and fearful at heart, they did not recognize their own faults and transgressions."

At that time, sentient beings again ate that naturally produced non-glutinous rice; as they ate it for a long period, male and female forms gradually emerged, and they became mutually attached to one another. Their lustful desire grew increasingly intense, and they eventually formed the institution of husband and wife.
Other sentient beings, having seen this, became angry and struck them, saying:
"How is it that such unrighteousness has suddenly arisen in the world?
This assembly is not a gathering for rebirth in heaven; from this day forward, we shall cultivate wholesome dharmas so as to attain a heavenly assembly."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"At that time, there were sentient beings who practiced what was not the Dharma. Feeling shame and loathing for their defilement, they hid themselves away and did not come forth, sometimes for one day, two days, or even up to a month; they then built houses to shield themselves from view for the sake of their unrighteousness."
At that time, sentient beings thought to themselves:
"Why do we exhaust ourselves with toil throughout the entire day?
It would be better to gather enough non-glutinous rice in the morning for both today's meal and tomorrow's."
The next day, another sentient being came and invited him to go together to gather non-glutinous rice.
This sentient being replied, "I gathered it all yesterday. That sentient being said:
"This is a good dharma," they said, and they imitated one another, taking [the rice] until ten days, twenty days, a month, or two months had passed.
Because they stored it with greedy intent, the non-glutinous rice turned into husks and chaff; what was gathered in the morning would not grow again by evening.
At that time, the sentient beings gathered together; having gathered, they said to one another:
"In the past, we all flew through the air naturally, taking the joy of dhyāna as our food, living in happiness and peace.

When we began to eat the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa), those beings had not yet developed unwholesome dharmas; however, because unwholesome dharmas arose, the essence of the earth vanished and the crust of the earth (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) appeared.
