Once the crust of the earth had arisen, it was fragrant and delicious."
Subsequently, the earth-fat, and so forth, down to the non-glutinous rice, remained fragrant and delicious; we should now establish regulations and divide the rice-fields with boundaries.
He then sealed it, saying, "This portion belongs to me; that portion belongs to you.
At that time, a certain sentient being thought to himself:
"If I take my own portion myself, it will soon be exhausted. It would be better to take a small amount from the other's portion so that my own portion lasts longer."
When those beings see this being taking what was not given, they say to him:
"Why do you now take what was not given?
Do not do so again."
"Yet this sentient being still does not stop taking, even after being told up to three times.
When that sentient being sees this repeatedly, they say:
'How is it that this sentient being practices taking what is not given, even up to three times?'"
"From this day forward, if anyone takes what is not given, they shall be subjected to punishment.
He did not stop there; he immediately seized him and severely flogged him with whips and canes.
Having received the staff, he cried out loudly, saying:
"How can there be such an evil law in the world as to cause this sentient being to be struck with a staff?
At that moment, the striker threw the staff to the ground and also cried out loudly.
"How is it that such evil dharmas exist in the world? What kind of sentient beings take what is not given, speak falsely, and feel no shame?
Thereupon, these three evil dharmas appeared in the world.
What are the three?
First, taking what is not given;
second, speaking falsely.
"Third, striking others with a staff.
These are the first three unwholesome dharmas that have appeared.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The being who was the very first among sentient beings to take what was not given at that time—could he have been anyone else?
It was none other than the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin, the potter’s son.
Since the past, Daṇḍikin has been the very first to take what was not given, and now, within my True Dharma, he has again been the very first to take what was not given."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How was it that the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka, having received the grace of the World-Honored One and being clothed in the kāṣāya, was released by King Bimbisāra upon seeing him?"
The Buddha said, "So it is, monks!"
This bhikṣu Daṇḍakin is not only receiving my robe today to escape punishment; in a past life as well, he already received my grace by wearing my robe and thereby attained liberation.
In a past age, there was a śāmbalī tree on the shore of the great ocean, upon which lived a garuḍa.
This bird’s body was immense; the distance between its two wings spanned one hundred and fifty yojanas.
This is the nature of the garuḍa: it takes nāgas as its food.
When it wishes to eat a nāga, it first strikes the ocean with its two wings, causing the waters to part on both sides; the nāga’s body then appears, and it immediately seizes and devours it.
It is the constant law of the nāgas that they fear the garuḍa and always seek to place a *kāṣāya* robe upon the gate of their palace;
when the bird sees the *kāṣāya*, it conceives a heart of reverence and no longer advances to devour those nāgas.

At that time, the bird struck the sea with its wings and saw the dragon, intending to devour it; the dragon was greatly terrified and immediately took the *kāṣāya* robe, placed it upon its head, and fled along the shore.
At that time, the nāga transformed himself into the likeness of a human being, and the garuḍa transformed himself into the likeness of a brahmin; he pursued the nāga while uttering various insults:
"Why did you not release the kāṣāya robe sooner?"
"Terrified of death, this dragon seized the *kāṣāya* tightly, clinging to it until his death and refusing to let go.

At that time, there was a dwelling place for a *ṛṣi* by the seashore where flowers and fruits flourished; the dragon, in his terror and finding no one to rely upon, went and sought refuge at the ṛṣi’s dwelling."
The rishi possessed great majestic power, and the garuḍa did not dare to enter easily; from afar, it addressed the rishi in verse:
“This wretched and evil dragon, Having transformed himself into human form, Fearing death and seeking liberation, Has come to enter within this place.”
"By the power of the seer’s virtue, I shall endure hunger and thirst;
I would rather lose my own body and life than eat this dragon again.
At that time, the seer thought to himself:
"Who recited this verse?
he asked, and immediately rose to go and look.
He saw that this dragon was being pursued by a garuḍa, and he then spoke a verse in reply to the garuḍa, saying:
"I shall grant you long life, that you may always consume the nectar of the gods;
for the sake of your respectful heart toward me, I have endured hunger and refrained from eating the dragon."
At that time, the garuḍa was relieved of its hunger and thirst by the spiritual power of the rishi.
Then the rishi further addressed the garuḍa:

"Because you violated the precepts, you received this avian body; now, if you continue to practice killing, you shall fall into hell. He then spoke extensively on the ten non-virtuous actions up to wrong views.
In this way, each and every one of them shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
You should now, together with this nāga, mutually repent so that no further resentment remains hereafter.
They immediately repented; having repented, each returned to their original place.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was the seer at that time anyone else?"
I myself am that very person.
The garuḍa was King Bimbisāra,
and the nāga was the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin.
This bhikṣu Dhanika was previously protected by my kāṣāya and thereby escaped the peril of the garuḍa; now, once again protected by my kāṣāya, he has escaped the peril of the king.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"How was it that King Bimbisāra, seeing this bhikṣu Daṇḍakin wearing the kāṣāya, released him and set him free?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Not only today; it was already so in the past.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Has it been so before?
The Buddha said, “It has.”

In a past age there was a king who skillfully transformed both people and things, causing them to be free from all enemies. The five grains ripened in abundance and the people enjoyed much happiness; they were observant of integrity and righteousness, kind and benevolent, possessing the virtues of humanity, filial piety, and compassion, and practiced giving, upholding the precepts, and so forth.
At that time, there was an elephant hunter in that country whose family was impoverished and had many sons; each son begged for food and drink.
Then the hunter’s wife said to her husband, "Our household is so poor and suffering from such hunger and cold; why do you not apply yourself diligently to your work?"
The hunter asked his wife,
"What do you wish to do?
The wife said:
"Why do you not diligently cultivate the occupation of your ancestors?

At that time, the hunter immediately prepared provisions and took up his hunting gear, proceeding to the edge of the Snowy Mountains. There, a six-tusked white elephant was dwelling at the foot of the mountain.
Whenever an elephant is born with such wisdom, it reflects to itself:
"For what reason do people wish to kill me?
They wish to kill me because of my tusks."
At that time, when his grandfather elephant died, he took its tusks and stored them in one place;
when his father subsequently died, he again took his tusks and stored them in another place, then left the herd of elephants to wander and forage at will.

At that time, the hunter was wandering through the hunt in succession, traversing various mountains and forests until he reached the elephant's location. Seeing the hunter from afar, the elephant immediately thought to himself:
"Who is this man who has come even into this place? Could it not be a hunter wishing to come and kill me?"
He immediately raised his trunk to beckon the hunter; the hunter, who was well-versed in the methods of reading elephant signs, thought:
"If I do not go, I shall surely be killed."
He then went to where the elephant was, and the elephant immediately asked,
"What do you seek by coming here?
The hunter then explained his purpose for coming, and the elephant said:
"If you do not come again, I shall provide you with whatever you require.
The hunter replied,
"I have obtained something that I do not wish to leave the door for, much less come all this way."
At that time, the elephant immediately gave him the ancestral tusks he had previously hidden.
Having obtained them, the hunter returned to his country in great joy, thinking to himself:
"Before long after I bring these tusks home, my wife and children will have their food and clothing provided; for the time being, I shall eat them alone in a secluded place."
"If I remain strong and healthy, I shall have wives and children; but once I am gone, they will have neither me nor even the share of five coins.
He then took an ivory tusk and went to a tavern.
At that time, the wine-seller saw him coming from afar and thought to himself:
"From where have you come?
Today I shall surely obtain some small profit.

He then spread out a bed and mat, took over the ivory for him to carry, and invited him to sit. Taking advantage of his hunger and thirst, he gave him wine until he was intoxicated; once drunk, the man asked for more, so they drew up a contract together. The wine obtained was very little, yet the contract written on top was very extensive.
On a later day, having sobered from his intoxication, he again requested wine. The wine-seller said:
"Why do you request more?
It seems you have not yet settled the account; we shall calculate it together, and if there is money remaining, I shall give you more."
Having finished the calculation, not a single coin remained.
He then thought to himself:
"Where else can I obtain more wealth?"
"I shall go back into the mountains and kill that elephant.
He then entered the mountains and went to where the previous elephant was. When the elephant saw the hunter, it asked, "For what reason have you come back?"
The hunter explained his purpose to the elephant, who asked:
"Where is that which I previously gave to you?
He replied:
"It was due to a lack of wisdom that you exhausted it through negligence.
The elephant said,
"If you can refrain from being negligent again, I shall give it back to you."
The hunter replied, "I have already repented for my previous actions; why must you press me so?
If you can grant me yet another favor, I truly shall not leave this door."
The elephant again took his father’s tusks and gave them to him.
The hunter then took the elephant tusks and returned to his kingdom; yet as before, he exhausted them through improper use. He then thought to himself:
“I must kill that elephant, but if I go now, I shall not let it see me.”

That great elephant, during the month following spring when the weather was intensely hot, entered the pond to bathe; having finished his bath and emerged, he stood beneath a tree to rest in the shade before the assembly of elephants.
At that time, the hunter struck the great elephant with a poisoned arrow; it hit between its eyebrows, and blood flowed into its eyes.
The elephant raised its head to look toward where the arrow had come from, and upon seeing the hunter, it addressed him from afar:
"You base and wicked man, you have no sense of gratitude or reciprocity! Although I possess the strength to kill you right now, I do not kill you only because I revere the *kāṣāya*."
He immediately called out to the hunter,
"Come quickly and cut off my tusks!
He used his own body as a shield to protect the hunter from being harmed by other elephants.
At that time, there were various devas in the forest who spoke these verses:
“Internally not free from the garment of delusion, Externally relying on the wearing of the kāṣāya;
With a mind constantly harboring malice— The kāṣāya is not for such as you.”
"Samādhi is tranquil and signless; it eternally extinguishes the afflictions of suffering.
When the inner mind is always in a state of cessation, one should wear the kāṣāya robe.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, was the Great Elephant King anyone else?
He was none other than the present King Bimbisāra.
As for the hunter, he was the present bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta."
Since King Bimbisāra had previously shown reverence for the kāṣāya, he pardoned that hunter;
now, because Daṇḍakin was clad in a kāṣāya, the king did not inflict punishment upon him.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why was it that King Bimbisāra, seeing the dignified and composed deportment of Daṇḍakin, did not give rise to an evil thought?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that King Bimbisāra has delighted in majestic deportment and refrained from giving rise to evil thoughts.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
has it already been so?
The Buddha said:

"It is so! In times past there was a king who governed people and things with excellence, remaining free from all enemies. The five grains ripened in abundance and the people enjoyed much happiness; they were observant of integrity and righteousness, kind and benevolent, possessing the virtues of humanity, filial piety, and compassion, practicing giving and upholding the precepts while loving all beings universally."
The king possessed an elephant named Mahākāya, which was fierce and difficult to subdue, its majesty shaking both near and far.
At that time, none among the enemy nations could withstand it; wherever he led an expedition to punish, all were utterly crushed and defeated.
As for those who violated the king’s laws, he would command this elephant to trample them to death with its feet. Relying on this elephant, the king lived without fear.
The elephant stable collapsed, and the elephant fled to the vicinity of the vihāra. There he beheld the bhikṣus, whose deportment was dignified and composed.

Furthermore, he heard them reciting the sūtras, which spoke of how killing leads to suffering while abstaining from it brings merit. Upon hearing these words, the elephant’s mind immediately became gentle and subdued.

At that time, there was a criminal who had committed an offense deserving death; the king commanded an official to have an elephant trample him to death. However, the elephant sniffed at the criminal three times with its trunk and had no intention whatsoever to kill him.
The executioner immediately reported this to the king, saying:
"When the elephant saw the criminal, it merely sniffed him with its trunk and had no intention at all to kill him.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great sorrow and fear, and he spoke to those who had come:
"Is it truly so, elephant?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
The king summoned his ministers to deliberate on this matter.
Once the ministers had assembled, the king told them:
"I have now become a king whom none can defeat, relying solely upon this elephant; yet now it has suddenly met with such a fate—what should we do?"
At that time, the minister immediately called for the elephant keeper and asked him:
"Where has the elephant gone now that the stable has collapsed?
The elephant keeper replied:
"Go to the vihāra. The minister was wise and intelligent;
he foresaw that when this elephant saw the bhikṣus, it would surely hear the Dharma and its mind would become so gentle that it would have no desire to kill living beings.
He then instructed the elephant calf to stay near the elephant stable, saying: "Build a gambling house, a butcher's shop, and a prison here;
you must tether the elephant near these various buildings."
That elephant saw the gambler staring with wide eyes, waving his hands, and shouting at the top of his voice;
he saw the butcher slaughtering sentient beings;
and he also saw prisoners being subjected to torture and cruel suffering.
Having seen this, the elephant’s evil intent arose once more, and the king sent the criminal, whom the elephant immediately trampled to death.
At that time, the devas spoke these verses:
"The elephant saw the one of virtuous discipline, And heard the sounds of sin and merit; [The elephant] was filled with compassion and did not kill him."
The virtuous mind increases day and night, while evil conduct gradually comes to an end.
By associating with various evil deeds, the former mind arises once more;
only the person of clear wisdom advances straight on without turning back.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, was the elephant with the massive body anyone else?
He was none other than King Bimbisāra."

In a previous life, King Bimbisāra had once seen a bhikṣu whose deportment was dignified and composed; he felt love, joy, and delight. Now, seeing Daṇḍakī’s deportment likewise dignified and composed, he was filled with great joy and did not inquire as to his crime.
At that time, Daṇḍakī thought to himself:
"I built the first dwelling, yet the senior monk received it; he has driven me out.
He has likewise driven me out from the second and the third."
Subsequently, he built a house of fired bricks; the World-Honored One again commanded it to be demolished.

He then took timber from the royal household to build a dwelling; the World-Honored One again rebuked him in various ways, saying: "In vain do you toil yourself; what is the use of such excessive endeavor?"
"From this day forward, let us cease these painful tasks; follow the community of monks and act as you please regarding both pleasure and pain.

Thereupon, Daṇḍakī abandoned his worldly affairs and practiced with diligence day and night, devoting himself exclusively to the work of the Path. He attained the various *dhyānas*, accomplished the fruits of the Path, and gave rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), personally realizing and verifying them for himself.
At that time, Daṇḍakin was deeply moved by joy and consolation, and spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa, One should practice the Dharma of the śramaṇa;
Resting thus sustains body and life, Like a snake entering a mouse hole."
If you wish to attain the bliss of tranquility, you should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa;
clothing and food sustain the body and life, whether coarse or refined, according to what the community receives.
If you wish to attain the bliss of tranquility, you should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
"All should know contentment and exclusively cultivate the path to Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Rājagṛha assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu takes what is not given by means of theft, he commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with us.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, as explained in detail above.
At one time, a certain bhikṣu, when the hour had come, put on his village-entering robes and took up his bowl;

he entered the city to seek discarded rags (pāṃśukūla). He searched throughout Rājagṛha without success, then went to the cemetery and still found none, and finally sought along the waterways, yet again found nothing.
Finally, he went to the laundry place to search for it. At that time, the washerman had finished washing the clothes and was standing in another spot conversing with someone.
The bhikṣu went to where the clothes were, and a certain man said to the washerman, "That renunciant wishes to take your garment."
The owner of the robe asked,
"By which path have you gone forth?
He replied:
"A member of the Śākya clan has gone forth as a renunciant.
The washerman said, "Do not worry;
the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas do not take what is not given."
After a short while, the bhikṣu took the robe and, turning toward another man, spoke again to the washerman, saying,
"The śramaṇa has already taken your robe.
The washerman, however, still replied as before:
"There is no suffering; the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas do not take what is not given.
Then that bhikṣu tucked the robe under his arm and departed. The man spoke again to the washerman:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has already carried the robe away."
The owner of the robe then rose and looked at it, exclaiming: "Alas!
He has truly taken the robe away!"
He then pursued him, calling out:
"Venerable One! Venerable One!"
"This robe has been granted by the king’s ministers and granted by the elders; each has its own owner. I pray that you do not carry it away.
Yet the bhikṣu continued on his way and still would not give up the robe. The owner then reviled him, saying:
"You monk of ruined conduct! If you do not return my robe, I shall punish you in such and such a manner."
The bhikṣu took the robe and went to his dwelling; he opened the door, spread the robe upon the rope bed, closed the door, and sat down.

At that time, the washerman carrying five kinds of ash followed him into the Jeta Grove. There were other bhikṣus walking up and down between the gates of the Jeta Grove, and others sitting in meditation. The bhikṣu then said to the washerman:
"Why are you shouting so loudly?"
The laundryman said,
"Now that I have lost my clothes, why do you ask me with such a loud voice?
The bhikṣus said:
"Who took your robe away?
He replied,
"An ordained person."
He then asked,
"By which path did you go forth?
He replied:
“Son of the Śākya clan.
The bhikṣus asked,
“Where have you brought this?”
The laundryman said,
"Enter this room. The bhikṣus then went to that room,
tapped on the door with their fingers, and called out:
"Elder, open the door!

The monk remained silent and did not respond; a young monk of great strength then forced his way in by pushing the door open. The monk who had stolen the robes was immediately filled with great shame, lowered his head, and said nothing.
Then the young bhikṣu took the robes from the bed and went out; counting the collars, he said to the washerman, "Do the number of robes correspond [to what was given]?"
He replied, "It is appropriate.
Then the bhikṣus said to the laundryman:

"In this community of renunciants there are many different kinds of people; they are like the five fingers of one hand, which are not equal. How could those who have left the household life from various castes be of a single type?
You, O worthy one, should not speak of this widely to others; we ourselves shall report it to the World-Honored One."
Then the washerman said:

"The Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas possess the power of kings and the power of Brahmins and householders; previously I was only afraid that I would lose this garment entirely, but now that it has been returned, what more is there to say?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Summon that bhikṣu.
They immediately summoned him.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you have done this? He replied:
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has established the precept that one must not take what is not given?"
“World-Honored One!
I understood the established precept to refer to cities and villages, not to open spaces.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! What difference is there between not being given [alms] in a village and not being given in an open space?
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot serve to nourish wholesome qualities.”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
How is it that this washerman did not believe his neighbor and was deceived by that bhikṣu?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This washerman did not merely lack faith in this present life; in past lives as well, he was once without faith.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
has it already been so?
The Buddha said:
"It is so! In times past, there were two brahmins who went to South India to study the sūtras and śāstras of non-Buddhist paths; having completed their studies, they returned to their own country."
On his return journey, he traveled through a wilderness and passed by a cattle-pasture, where he saw two rams fighting one another in the path.
According to the nature of rams when they butt, as they stepped forward, they would then retreat again.
At that time, the one walking in front was particularly simple-minded and upright in his faith;

he said to his companion behind him, "Look at this ram, a four-legged beast, yet it deliberates and yields! It knows me to be a Brahmin who upholds the precepts and is learned, and so it repeatedly steps aside for me to clear the path."
The companion replied: "Brahmin!

Do not lightly believe that the sheep are deliberating. This is not out of mutual respect for opening a path or yielding to one another; rather, it is the nature of fighting sheep to advance and then retreat again."

The one walking in front did not believe his words; he was struck by the sheep and immediately fell prostrate, his two knees wounded and broken, and he lay on the ground in a swoon. His clothes, parasol, and canopy were all torn to shreds and scattered about.
At that time, a deva spoke these verses:
“His garments are torn and worn away; his body wounded, he lies prostrate on the ground.
This affliction is brought about by delusion; it arises from foolish faith.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was that brahmin who walked ahead at that time anyone else?
He is none other than this man whose robes were lost."
The brahmin who was walking behind at that time is this man who has now spoken to the stranger.
The ram at that time was the bhikṣu who took the robe.
The person who lost his robe had already lacked faith when he was beset by the ram; now, again lacking faith, he brought about the loss of his robe himself.
"Previously I did not believe the words of those who practice later; now, although they have spoken with sincerity, I still do not believe them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, in a village or an open space, takes what has not been given and it amounts to theft, he commits a pārājika offense;
he should not live in community with others. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 2 (3) *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
This is the third part of the Four Pārājika Dharmas, following the section on the precept against stealing. Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; the detailed exposition is as above.
In the time of King Bimbisāra’s ancestors, the law for punishing criminals was such that if someone committed theft, they were struck on the head with the hand as a severe admonition;
the thief felt such great shame that it was no different from death, and thereafter would never do it again.
During the time of King Zu, the method for punishing criminals was as follows: if there was a thief, they would surround him with ashes and release him after a short while;
the thief felt such profound shame that it was no different from death, and thereafter he never committed the act again.
During the time of his father, the King, the law for punishing criminals was as follows: if there were those who committed robbery, they were driven out of the city;
the robbers, feeling ashamed and considering it no different from death, would never commit such acts again.
According to the law of King Bimbisāra, any who committed robbery were to be driven out of the country; this was his instruction.
At that time, there was a thief who had been driven out seven times, yet he still returned to plunder and kill people in villages and cities.
At that time, someone captured this thief and bound him, delivering him to the king, and said to the king:
"This thief has been driven out seven times, yet he still returns to plunder and kill villages and cities; we pray that Your Majesty will punish him severely."
The king said to his ministers,
"Take this thief away and punish him according to the law.
The ministers replied:
"Stop! Stop!
Great King, do not punish the king's own transgressions by delegating them to his ministers."
"How could there be such a thing as a minister acting on his own authority by abandoning the King?
The commands of the Great King are respected at all times; they originate solely from the King, and thus the laws of governance shall endure for a long time.
The King said:
"As you depart, cut off his little finger.
At that time, the officials quickly and urgently cut off the criminal's finger, fearing that the king might regret his command.
The king then immediately tested it himself by biting his own finger; the pain was truly unbearable, and he at once sent a messenger with an edict to the great ministers, saying:
"Do not cut off his finger.
The minister replied to the king,
"I have already cut off his finger."
The king was deeply distressed and remorseful, thinking to himself:
"I am now the last of the Dharma-kings, not the first of those who act contrary to the Dharma.
As a ruler, one should be concerned for the people and all things; how could there be a human king who would wound or cut off another's finger?"

At that time, King Bimbisāra quickly ordered his carriage to be prepared and went to visit the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The law for punishing criminals established by my former ancestors consisted solely of striking them on the head with the hand.

From those successive kings down to myself, evil practices have daily increased while righteous governance has gradually thinned. Having mistakenly attained the throne as king, I have mutilated and severed human bodies; reflecting upon this lack of virtue, my shame and fear are indeed profound."
The Buddha asked:
"Great King, when you govern the kingdom, at what amount of theft does the crime merit the death penalty?
At what amount of theft should one be driven out of the country?"
“For stealing how many coins of Qi should one be subject to corporal punishment?
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Nineteen coins constitute one kārṣāpaṇa; this one kārṣāpaṇa is divided into four parts. If one steals one part, or something of the value of one part, the offense shall merit the death penalty.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to King Bimbisāra in accordance with his needs, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Once he had thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, the king’s distress was immediately dispelled; he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
Not long after the king had departed, the World-Honored One went to where a great number of bhikṣus were, sat upon a prepared seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just now, King Bimbisāra came to my dwelling, paid homage to me, sat to one side, and said to me:
'World-Honored One!'"

"In the past, my ancestors governed the punishment of criminals by striking their heads with their hands; this orthodox transformation has been handed down through generations until it reached my own person. I then asked:
"Great King!..."
"At what amount of stolen property does the offense become punishable by death, or even subject to fines?

The King replied, "Nineteen coins constitute one kārṣāpaṇa. If one divides a kārṣāpaṇa into four parts, then for stealing one part, or for property worth one part, the offense shall be punishable by death."
“I taught the Dharma to King Bimbisāra in accordance with his needs, and he departed with joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“From now on, you should know that nineteen *purāṇas* are called one *kārṣāpaṇa*. One *kārṣāpaṇa* is divided into four parts; if one steals one part, or what is equivalent to one part, one commits a *pārājika* offense.”
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that King Bimbisāra fears such a transgression so greatly?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This King Bimbisāra was not only thus fearful of transgression in this present life; he was also fearful of transgression in past lives.”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
has this indeed happened before?”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.”
At that time there was a king named Yaśas.

The people of the kingdom all sustained themselves through various arts and crafts; that is to say, they engaged in music, song, and chanting, or fashioned vessels of gold and silver, flower garlands, necklaces, and other ornaments for adornment, or trained elephants and horses and practiced various esoteric arts. There were no such diverse skills they did not master, and by these means they made their living.
One who lacks skillful arts and techniques is called foolish;
likewise, one who commits robbery is also termed foolish.
At that time, there was a man who committed robbery, and the people of the country bound him and brought him before the king, saying:
"Great King!
This man has committed a foolish act; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him.
The King said:
"Stop! Stop!
It is worldly people who lose their wealth and worldly people who commit theft; what use is there for me to join you in doing evil?"
The king then reflected:
"By what means may I conduct the affairs of state such that my ministers remain unaware and evil practices do not arise?
He reflected further:
"From time immemorial, there has been but one foolish person; until this foolish person completes the number of a thousand, I shall not pass away.
He then entrusted the foolish person to a high minister, saying:
"I require a thousand foolish persons for a great assembly; when the number is complete, inform me so that I may know."
The minister immediately seized the fool and bound him in one place.
The king then thought to himself:
"This foolish man might die of hunger."
He then addressed his ministers, saying:
"Bring that fool here.
He spoke to the ministers again, saying:
"Look well after this man and do not let him become emaciated; place him within my Aśoka Garden and provide him with the five desires, entertainments, and musical performances.
Having received these instructions, the minister immediately led the foolish man away according to the king's command.

At that time, there was another foolish man who, hearing that the king had captured a fool and provided him with music and entertainment while stationing him in the Aśoka Garden, went of his own accord to the minister’s residence.
He replied, "I am a foolish man!
Desiring to please the king's mind, the minister would bring them as soon as they arrived and send them away to the Aśoka Garden; in this way, before long, their number reached one thousand.
The minister said to the king:
"The number of fools has already reached one thousand; what more do you require?
You should have them prepared at once."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great sorrow and anxiety, thinking:
"In the vast expanse of time since the beginning, there was but one foolish person; how is it that now, before even a short time has passed, there are already thousands?"
"Will these evil dharmas increase in the final age?
The king then commanded his ministers to sweep and clean the Aśoka Garden, to burn incense and hang silk banners and canopies, and to prepare various kinds of delicacies, food, and drink.
The minister immediately prepared everything as commanded by the king.
At that time, the king went out on an excursion with his various ministers and eighteen assemblies to the Anupama Garden.
Once the king was seated, he asked his ministers, "Where is that foolish man now?"
"Summon them here.

When the fools had all arrived, the king saw that they had been in the garden for a long time, their garments soiled and greasy, their nails long and their hair disheveled. He immediately commanded his ministers:
"Take these fools away; have them bathe, put on fresh clothes, and trim their hair and nails, then bring them back."
"Once they have arrived, I shall provide them with various kinds of food and drink, and bestow upon them wealth and treasures to satisfy all their needs.
He then commanded the fools:
"Return home to support your parents, diligently attend to your household affairs, and do not commit robbery again."
At that time, the foolish man, hearing the king’s command, joyfully set out to carry it out.

Then the king of that country immediately transferred the royal throne to the crown prince and left the household life to enter the mountains to study the dharma of the rishis. At that moment, the king spoke these verses:
"I originally sought a thousand fools, Thinking such an assembly would be hard to find; Now that I have gathered them, they are all here, And I shall bestow upon them the wealth of the world."
How is it that in so short a time, the thousands have suddenly reached their full number?
As evil dharmas increase day and night, the Great Assembly has now ceased;
those who wish to leave behind the wicked people of the world should at once go forth into homelessness.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for that king named Yaśas at that time, could he have been anyone else?
He was none other than King Bimbisāra."
"King Bimbisāra has always feared the retribution for his transgressions since his previous lives; now that he is king, he continues to fear such retribution.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"How is it that King Bimbisāra, having issued a command, subsequently repented of it?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that King Bimbisāra, having issued a command, subsequently repented of it; in past ages as well, he once repented."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Has this happened before?
The Buddha said:
"So it is! the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a brāhmaṇa who had no wealth and lived by begging. This brāhmaṇa had a wife who did not bear sons; however, from a *nākulā* insect in his house, he finally begot one son."
At that time, because the brahmin had no son, he regarded the boy Nāḍakūla as his own child; likewise, Nāḍakūla regarded the brahmin as his father.
At that time, while the brahmin was at a gathering in another's house, he obtained some curd and cakes as well as meat; taking these back home, he gave them to Nākulā.
Later, the brahmin’s wife suddenly became pregnant, and when her months were complete and she gave birth to a son, she thought to herself:
"It is because of Nākulā that this auspicious son has been born, for she has enabled me to have a child."
At that time, as the brahmin was about to go out to beg for alms, he instructed his wife, saying:
"If you must go out, you should take the child with you; be careful not to leave him behind."
After the Brahmin’s wife had given food to her child, she went to a neighboring house to borrow a mortar for husking grain.
At that time, the young child was filled with the fragrance of ghee and curd; a venomous snake, drawn by that scent, arrived there, opened its mouth, and spat poison, intending to kill the child.
The Nāḷāgiri insect then thought to himself:
"My father has gone abroad and my mother is not at home; how can this venomous snake wish to kill my younger brother?
As it is said:
“The venomous snake Nāṅgula, the flying crow, the rabbit, and the owl;
the śramaṇa and the brāhmaṇa, the mother-in-law and the son-in-law—
these always harbor mutual hatred and jealousy, conceiving poison with the intent to harm one another.”
Then Nakula killed the venomous snake, cutting it into seven pieces, and thought to himself:
"I have now killed the snake so that my younger brother may live; when my parents learn of this, they will surely reward me."
Smearing her mouth with blood, she stood at the gate, wishing for her parents to see her and rejoice.
At that time, the Brahmin was returning from outside; seeing his wife from afar standing outside the house, he spoke with anger:
"I instructed you to take the child when you went out; why have you come alone?"
As the father was about to enter the gate, he saw blood in Naṅgula’s mouth and thought to himself:
"While my wife and I were away, could it be that Naṅgula has killed and eaten my son?"
Speaking with anger, he said,
"I have nourished this mere worm only to be harmed by it," and immediately stepped forward and struck Nākulī to death with a staff.

Having entered within the gate, he saw his own son sitting in the courtyard sucking his fingers and playing; he also saw a poisonous snake split into seven pieces upon the ground. Having witnessed these things, he was immediately filled with great sorrow and regret.
At that time, the brahmin reproached himself deeply, saying:
"That Nāṭakuṇḍala was kind-hearted and saved my son's life, yet I failed to examine him properly and killed him in haste."
"How pitiable!
How lamentable!
he cried, immediately falling to the ground in a swoon of distress.
At that time, a deity in the sky spoke this verse:
"One should observe with careful discernment; Do not act with sudden violence or rage.
To separate from a virtuous friend through affectionate ties, And to harm them unjustly—this wounds the good."
"It is like the brahmin who killed that Nākulī.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was the brahmin at that time anyone other than [myself]?"
"He is none other than King Bimbisāra himself.
Because he acted with rashness in the past and subsequently repented, he is likewise so now.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Let all the bhikṣus residing in Rājagṛha assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣu, in a village or an open space, takes what is not given.”
In accordance with the stolen object, the king may seize, kill, bind, or banish him, saying: "Ho! Man!"
"Are you a thief?
Are you a fool?
A bhikṣu who thus takes what is not given commits a pārājika offense; he should not live in community with others.

The second section on the origin of the precepts concerning the term "bhikṣu" is concluded. A bhikṣu is one who has received full ordination, properly received full ordination, through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*), in a harmonious assembly of ten or more members where no obstructing factors exist, and who is twenty years of age; such a person is called a bhikṣu.
Regarding "village" (*grāma*): a village is so called if it is surrounded by city walls, or if it is surrounded by water channels, moats, fences, or hedges.

Furthermore, a village may also be a settlement of herdsmen, a settlement of actors, a settlement of wagon-traders, or a settlement of cowherds; even four houses or a single stack of firewood is termed a village.

Regarding "open space" (*śūnyadeśa*): open space refers to the area outside of walls, fences, and courtyards; with the exception of the village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*), all other areas are termed open space.
As for the "village boundary": it is the area not far from the fence where the tracks of many people's footsteps reach; this is called the village boundary.
Thus, outside the water channels, ditches, moats, and fences, everything other than the village boundary is called open space (*śūnyadeśa*).
Regarding a village for grazing cattle, everything outside the outermost lanes and houses, other than the village boundary, is called open space.
Regarding a village of performers: outside the outermost edge of the wagons, excluding the village boundary, all that remains is designated as open space.
Regarding a village of traveling caravans: outside the outermost edge of the wagons, excluding the village boundary, all that remains is designated as open space.
Regarding the village of Gomayanikā: outside the house at the very edge, excluding the village boundary, all that remains is designated as open space (*akṛta*).
Regarding the village of Catuḥśālā and Ekakāṣṭhika: outside the house at the very edge, excluding the village boundary, all that remains is designated as open space.
"Without it being given" means that whether it be a man, a woman, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a layperson, or a monastic, there is no one who gives it, yet one takes it with a thieving mind.
Regarding the objects stolen, there are eight types of items:
first, food for the daytime;
second, food for the nighttime portion.
Third, seven-day medicines;
fourth, lifetime medicines;
fifth, miscellaneous items.
Sixth, heavy objects;
seventh, impure objects;
eighth, objects that are both pure and impure—these are called the eight.
"Taking" refers to grasping an object and moving it from its original location; this is what is meant by "taking.

Regarding "according to what was stolen": for example, there was a sixteen-fold supervisor who stole a single small coin from the royal treasury and bought a melon to eat, for which he was executed by the king.
Kings have no fixed law, acting according to their own whims; sometimes they kill for stealing a small amount, while others do not die even after stealing much.
This is as when the World-Honored One questioned King Bimbisāra regarding the law:
"Great King, in governing your kingdom, at what amount of stolen money does one deserve death?"
"How much shall be paid for driving him out?
How much shall be paid as a criminal fine?
King Bimbisāra replied to the Buddha:
" Nineteen coins constitute one kārṣāpaṇa; this kārṣāpaṇa is divided into four parts. Whether one takes one part or the value of one part, the offense shall merit death."
Now, the meaning of "theft" shall be determined according to this standard.
As for "a king," the term refers to those known as Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, householders, or laymen who have received their office and become kings.
"Seizing" means that the king causes his men to seize him, either by grasping his hand or other parts of his body;
this is called seizing. "Killing" means taking away his life; this is called killing.

As for "bondage," it refers to being bound by houses, or bound by cities, or bound by timber; or being fettered with chains and shackles, or being constrained by cangues and manacles—this is what is called bondage.
"Expulsion" means driving out from the village, driving out from the city, or driving out from the country;
this is called expulsion. "Ho! Man! [he says].
"You thief! You fool!
You ignorant one!"—these are words of reproach.
A bhikṣu who acts in such a manner commits a pārājika offense and should not live in communal association.
Regarding "pārājika": it means that one has receded from and fallen away from the knowledge of the Dharma; having no share in the fruits of the Path, this is called pārājika.

In this way, even up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), if one regresses from or falls away from those various knowledges such that there is no longer a portion of the fruit of the path, this is called a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, "pārājika" means to retreat from, sink back into, and fall away from nirvāṇa, such that one lacks the portion for realizing the fruit; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, "pārājika" means to depart from the dharma of non-stealing and to retreat from, sink back into, and fall away [from it]; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, regarding *pārājika*: because the offense committed cannot be confessed and purified, it is called *pārājika*.
"Medicine for the time" (*kālabhojana*) refers to all roots, all grains, and all meats.
Regarding roots:
the roots of medicinal herbs, lotus roots, *śālūka* roots, taro roots, radish roots, and scallion roots—these are called roots.
Regarding grains, there are seventeen kinds:
1. Rice; 2. Red rice; 3. Wheat; 4. Barley; 5. Small beans; 6. Peas; 7. Soybeans; 8. Lentils; 9. Millet; 10. Foxtail millet.

Eleven: *tila* (sesame seeds); twelve: *śṛṅgavera* (ginger); thirteen: *jāti*; fourteen: *pāṣāṇabhedaka*; fifteen: *śyāmāka* (millet); sixteen: *jīvantī*; seventeen: *kudrava*. These are called the seventeen kinds of grain.
"Meat" refers to the flesh of aquatic and terrestrial insects.
What are aquatic insects?
Aquatic insects include fish, tortoises, timi, timitimingila, asura, susura, susumara, and other such aquatic creatures that are edible; these are called aquatic insects.
What are terrestrial insects?
Terrestrial insects include those with two legs, four legs, no legs, or many legs; such as these are called terrestrial insects.
Likewise, food consisting of roots, grains, and meat are all termed "timely food" (*kālabhojana*).
Why is this? Because one may eat at the proper time, but may not eat outside of the proper time; this is called "timely food" (*kālabhojana*).
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches medicine for the proper time, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one moves that object, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is moved from its original location by a full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding medicines for the night-time: there are fourteen kinds of fermented liquors (*parisrut*).

1. Āmra juice, 2. Koli juice, 3. Pomegranate juice, 4. Tiṇḍuka juice, 5. Grape juice, 6. Parūṣaka juice, 7. Karkandhu juice, 8. Plantain juice, 9. Kāśmarī juice, 10. Kapittha juice, 11. Bilva juice, 12. Sugarcane juice, 13. Harītakī juice, 14. Khārjūra juice.

These various syrups may be received during the first watch of the night and drunk during the first watch; received during the middle watch and drunk during the middle watch; received during the last watch and drunk during the last watch; or received before a meal and drunk until the end of the first watch. For this reason, they are called "medicines for the watches of the night."
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches nocturnal medicine, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes it from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The seven-day medicines are: clarified butter (*sarpis*), oil, honey, rock sugar (*phāṇita*), fat, and fresh butter (*navanīta*).
As for clarified butter: it is the clarified butter of cows, water buffaloes, goats, rams, and camels.

Regarding "oil": sesame oil, mustard oil, safflower oil, *āḍhaka* oil, castor oil, *bilva* oil, *pīlu-maṇḍa* oil, *kālañjara* oil, *cāra* oil, *atimuktaka* oil, *maṇḍūka* oil, hempseed oil, and various other kinds of oils—these are what are called "oils."
Regarding honey: *kunda-madhu*, *pautika-madhu*, yellow honey, and black honey—these are called honey.
Regarding rock honey (*śarkarā*): *paṃśu-madhu*, *nala-madhu*, *mañja-madhu*, and *mahābīra-madhu*—these are called rock honey.

Regarding fats: fish fat, bear fat, brown bear fat, *śiśumāra* (crocodile) fat, and pig fat—these various fats that are boneless, fleshless, bloodless, odorless, and devoid of the scent of food may be accepted and consumed by a sick bhikṣu for seven days. This is called "fat."

Regarding "fresh butter" (*navanīta*): it refers to the fresh butter of cattle, sheep, and other such animals that has been purified by straining and washing so as to be free from any odor of food. It may be accepted all at once, and a sick bhikṣu is permitted to consume it for seven days.
Because these medicinal substances are pure and free from the odor of food, they may be accepted all at once and consumed for seven days; therefore, they are called "seven-day medicines."
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches seven-day medicine, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place, it is a *pārājika*.

Medicines for the duration of one's life (*yāvajjīvika*) are: *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, *pippalī*, black pepper, ginger, *āyuṣphala*, *ṛṣiphala*, *kṣīraphala*, *mudgaparṇī*, *pārūsaka*, *panasa*, the five minor roots, the five major roots, all types of salt, all ashes except for the eight kinds of ash, and all grounds except for the dregs of stone honey and the ground itself.
These medicinal substances, being devoid of any flavor for food, may be taken immediately by a sick bhikṣu for the rest of his life; they are called "lifetime medicines.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches a lifetime medicine, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding "removing from its original place to the full extent": this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

As for "accessories," these include: the three robes, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), the wound-covering cloth, the rain-bathing cloth, the bowl, the large alms-bowl case, the small alms-bowl case, the bowl pouch, the shoulder strap pouch, the water-strainer, the two types of waistbands, the knife, the copper spoon, the bowl-rest, the needle-case, the *kuṇḍikā* water flask, the oil-container leather bottle, the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), the leather sandals, the parasol, the fan, and other various items that ought to be kept; these are called accessories.
Furthermore, there are householders' belongings—such as military equipment, swords, staves, clothing, and various other items possessed by laypeople—which are also termed "belongings."
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches an object belonging to another, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
"Valuable items" refers to beds, bedding, and other heavy objects. Regarding beds and bedding:
these include sleeping beds, sitting benches, small cushions, large cushions, cotton-wool pillows, and other heavy objects such as all copperware, all woodenware, bambooware, and all ceramicware.
As for the names of copper vessels: copper jars, copper cauldrons, copper pots, copper ladles, and various other kinds of copper vessels—these are called copper vessels.

As for wooden and bamboo vessels: wooden mortars, wooden jars, wooden basins, wooden bowls, wooden ladles; bamboo baskets, bamboo mats, and even bamboo boxes, as well as all other various kinds of wooden and bamboo vessels—these are called bamboo and wooden vessels.
Earthenware refers to items ranging from large jars down to oil lamps; these are called earthenware.
Beds, bedding, and various other such items are called heavy objects.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches such a heavy object, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding "impure objects": these are money, gold, and silver; because a bhikṣu is not permitted to touch them, they are called impure objects.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches an impure object, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is moved from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding "pure and impure objects": these refer to pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and jade; because one may touch these various precious objects but not possess them, they are called pure and impure objects.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches this pure or impure object, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes it from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, there are sixteen kinds of things: earth and the things within the earth;

water and the things within the water; boats and the things within boats; vehicles and the things within vehicles; four-footed beings and the things upon four-footed beings; two-footed beings and the things upon two-footed beings; footless beings and the things upon footless beings; and space and the things within space.
What is called earth?
Gold ore, silver ore, red copper ore, lead and tin ore, white brass ore, azurite, realgar, bitumen, ochre, white clay, and even the soil taken by a potter—these are called earth.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches these various grounds, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those objects, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding objects within the earth: if a person hides items in the ground—namely, coins, gold, silver, crystal, conch shells, pearls, musaragalva, and agate;
jars of ghee, jars of oil, and jars of stone honey;
or various medicinal substances such as roots, stalks, branches, leaves, and fruits—even up to eight kinds of items hidden in the ground—these are called objects within the earth.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches an object within this ground, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding water, there are ten kinds:

river water, pond water, well water, water from dragon-pools, clear water, hot spring water, health-giving water, rainwater during floods, water in the sky, and flowing water. In some places water is precious and in others it is cheap; one might obtain four or five jars for a single coin, or conversely, obtain only one jar even with all one's possessions.
For example, if there is good water near a village or city, one may obtain five or six jars for a single coin.

There were merchants traveling on a long journey through a vast and remote wilderness, spanning five yojanas, ten, or even up to five hundred yojanas. As there was no water along the road, each of those merchants carried water with them; some used it for their own needs, while others sold it.
At that time, there was a merchant who had run short of water and was tormented by heat and thirst; he then thought to himself:
"If I survive, I shall naturally obtain money; but if I die of thirst, what use will money be?"
He spent all his money and goods to buy a single jar of water.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling with the merchants; the merchants had regularly supplied the bhikṣu with water, but before they reached their destination, the water was nearly exhausted.
Then the merchant said to the bhikṣu, “The road is still long and the water is nearly exhausted; let this much water suffice for the Venerable One, and I shall drink the remainder myself.”
Just as with the provisions given by a merchant, a bhikṣu should drink according to the proper measure. If he drinks more with a thieving mind and reaches the full amount, it is a pārājika offense;
if he does not reach the full amount, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
The merchant spoke again:
"I am now providing water for the Venerable One's drink; I pray that you do not give it to others.
At that time, there was an old man suffering from illness who, driven by the heat and thirst, came to beg the bhikṣu for water to drink.
With a mind of loving-kindness, the bhikṣu attended to that sick person and reflected:
"Although my master has spoken thus, that patient is pitiable; I shall now offer him water, and my master will surely not find fault or reproach me for it."
Because it was done with consent, there is no offense.

Suppose someone is traveling by boat carrying water, and a bhikṣu, driven by thirst, touches the water on that boat with the intent to steal; he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If he places the water in an alms-bowl or a *kaṇḍolaka* (water-vessel) while it has not yet left the boat, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one carries away water while both body and robes remain entirely on the boat, and it becomes full, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one pierces that water vessel, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if one uses a tube inserted into the hole to drink the water and it becomes full, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one drinks little by little and stops repeatedly, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for every sip.
If the water vessel already has a plugged hole and one removes the plug with a thieving mind, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If water is poured into a vessel, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the stream of water is interrupted and the vessel becomes full, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If the water flows continuously without interruption, yet one immediately gives rise to a mind of repentance, fearing the commission of a grave offense, and pours the water back into the original vessel, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one intends to steal by joining boats, and the stern of the boat being towed passes the bow of the other boat, it is a *pārājika*.
If the boat is towed in reverse, and the bow passes the stern, or if it is towed alongside from the right so that the left side passes over the right, it is a *pārājika*.
If he likewise pulls it from the left side, it is the same.
If it is a small boat that is easily moved and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, touches it, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that small boat, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the water is diverted from its original course by a full measure, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If there is a person who maintains an irrigation canal for flowing water, worth one *māṣaka* per night, or even two, three, four, or five *māṣakas*, and if a bhikṣu, whether for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, or for himself, with a thieving mind destroys that canal, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline);
if the water flows into the fields, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If it is full, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu does not intend to directly destroy the channel, but employs a stratagem such as pulling bricks or wood to cause the water to burst forth, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense at the time of pulling;
when the water flows into the field, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is full, it is a *pārājika* offense.
It is the same if one employs means to drive away cattle, sheep, camels, or to destroy a channel.
If a bhikṣu, out of a jealous mind, destroys a channel and discards the water, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu is traveling through a wilderness with merchants, and someone says,

"We shall reach water tomorrow," and at that time there are merchants carrying large loads of water along the way, the bhikṣu, being extremely thirsty, begs for water but does not receive it; he then speaks with anger, saying:
"You wicked man, why are you so miserly and greedy?
You carry much water along, yet you do not drink it yourself, nor do you give it to animals, nor do you give it to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"It shall soon be discarded; what use is there for water?
The bhikṣu then destroys that water vessel; because of his evil intention, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If water is stored in a vessel within a person's house, and the bhikṣu’s own kinsman or acquaintance is being burned by fire, if the bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, takes the water to extinguish the fire, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense if he touches it.
If one moves that water vessel, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one extinguishes a fire by pouring water over it until it is full, it is a *pārājika*.
If one thinks to oneself:
"One should return the water.
If one takes and uses it directly when it is given, there is no offense.
If that house has been set on fire, and one uses that water to assist in extinguishing the flames, there is no offense.

If, at a time when a drought has lasted for ten or twenty years, there is someone guarding the water of a pond or a well, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes a vessel and touches that water, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when he fills the vessel with water, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he carries the water away from the pond and it is full, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If there is a pond enclosed by a wall with its gate shut, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, holds a tube and drinks the water from a distance, if the water flows in an unbroken stream and fills [the vessel], it is a pārājika offense;
if he drinks and stops at each mouthful, for every mouthful there is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If it is well water, when a bhikṣu lowers the bucket with the intent to steal, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
when the water enters the vessel, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he carries the water away from the well and it becomes full, it is a *pārājika*.

There were certain followers of non-Buddhist sects who stored water in vessels; when their dwellings were set on fire, those non-Buddhists became terrified. At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves: "Just so, just so!
These evil and heterodox outsiders constantly envy the Buddha-dharma and revile the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya. Now we shall confront you!"
He then stepped forward and struck the water vessel with his staff, breaking it. Because he had maliciously destroyed another's property, he incurred a *vinayātikrama* offense.

There are various waters known by name: namely, the Ganges River in the kingdom of Campā; the hot springs at Rājagṛha; the Śoṇa River at Pāṭaliputra; the waters of the Buddha’s walking-pool at Vārāṇasī; the dark-flowing waters at Śrāvastī; the Puṇḍarīka waters at Śrāvastī; the Yāmuna River at Mathurā; and the honey-water at Saṃkāśya.

If there are noble persons who have sent messengers to take these waters and they are halted on the road, and a bhikṣu, driven by thirst, touches that water with a thieving mind, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if the water enters a vessel, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the flow of water is cut off and the vessel is full, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If the flow of water has not been cut off, and one gives rise to a mind of regret, fearing the commission of a grave offense, and pours the water back into its original vessel, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

There are certain nobles who, while sporting in a garden, create fragrant pools; if a bhikṣu takes that water with a thieving mind, even though the water itself is not worth money, one incurs an offense according to the value of the fragrance at that time. This refers to water.
Regarding "things in water": there are things that grow within the water, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *sugandhika*, lotus roots, and other various kinds of aquatic plants.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches any living creature within these waters, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that creature, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place by a full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If the value of a single flower reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*;
if it does not reach the full amount, each [flower] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
However, merely taking the flowers and placing them on the ground does not yet constitute a *pārājika*.
If a bouquet of flowers is so heavy that one cannot lift it, and although one drags it a great distance, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, once it is lifted off the ground, it is a *pārājika*.
This applies equally to all aquatic creatures.

If noble persons, within their pleasure-pools for bathing, have fashioned flowers of gold and silver, as well as various toy boats and diverse kinds of birds such as ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks—if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches those objects, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if he moves them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.

Furthermore, if there are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, conch shells, red gems, or other eight kinds of such items, and a person places these various objects in water, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches those objects, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
These are called watercraft.
As for vessels, they include the *vikuḷa* boat, the *kuhaṭa* boat, the *vajjuli* boat, the *viśiga* boat, the horse-faced boat, the elephant-faced boat, the fish-faced boat, and the sheep-faced boat;
those with one layer up to seven layers; those with walls or without walls; and boats for carrying elephants, horses, goods, earthenware, hides, iron implements, and even rafts made of woven reeds.
If a boat or raft is moored in one place, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, touches that boat, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that boat, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes it from its original location, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
Even if the rope has been cut but the boat has not yet left its original place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
even if it has left its place but the rope has not yet been cut, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the rope has been cut and the boat has left its original place, it is a *pārājika*.

If one originally intended to steal the boat and not the goods, but because of fear of being discovered took both the goods and the boat away, then although they have been moved from their original location, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, if after abandoning the goods the boat leaves its original location, it is a *pārājika*.
If one originally intended to steal goods but not the boat, yet boards and departs with the boat because of fear of being discovered by others, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, if one abandons the boat and carries away the goods, it is a *pārājika*.
If one intends to steal a boat or its cargo, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense when the boat has left its original place.
If one intends to carry it away from the bottom of the water, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense at the moment it is submerged.
If someone has moored a boat by the shore and is sitting in a secluded place, and a bhikṣu wishes to steal the boat, at that time another person says to the owner of the boat:
"There is a renunciant who wishes to steal your boat."
At that time, the boatman asked,
"By which path have you gone forth?
He replied:
"O śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas!
The boatman said,
"Do not worry!"
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, does not take what is not given.
At that time, when the bhikṣu touched the boat with his body, another person spoke again to the boat owner, saying:
"This bhikṣu has already taken your boat."
The boat owner then became suspicious,
thinking, "Could it be that this bhikṣu intends to steal my boat?
He immediately rose and asked:
“Venerable sir!
What do you wish to do?
At that time, the bhikṣu remained silent and did not respond; [the other] then used a pole to push the boat away and departed.
The boatman called out after him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Do not go by boat; this boat belongs to the king, or to a great minister, or to a brahmin, a householder, or a lay devotee. It is a boat for making merit, a boat for ferrying people across."
Furthermore, he terrified the bhikṣu, saying:
"You wicked man!
If you board my boat and depart, I shall later punish you severely."

"Even though this bhikṣu has traveled far by boat, if the boat owner does not form the thought that it is lost and the bhikṣu does not form the thought that he has acquired it, there is no pārājika offense;
however, if the boat owner forms the thought that it is lost and the bhikṣu forms the thought that he has acquired it, it is a pārājika offense."
If a boat owner moors his boat alongside the bank, a visiting bhikṣu comes and says to the boat owner:
"Long-lived one!
Lend me your boat so that I may cross."
The boatman replied, "I am all alone; how could I ferry you across?
The bhikṣu spoke again:
“Long-lived one!
My time for eating is approaching; do not cause me to miss my meal.
If you ferry me across now, it will be as if you have given me food, and it will be as if you have bestowed happiness upon me.”
"I shall now ferry you across both in this life and in future lives.
The boatman replied again,
"Since there is no payment for you either, how can you wish to cross for nothing?"
"Your feet are like those of a hungry crow, unable to stay still as you pace back and forth; who would ferry you across?
The bhikṣu again spoke with humble words and earnest entreaty, but the boatman replied once more:
"You may cross by yourself; since there is only one person here, Reverend Sir, how can we provide for your crossing?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Long-lived one!
You simply hold the rudder; I shall exert my own strength."
The boatman immediately consented and called for the Venerable One to board the vessel.
Once they reached the middle of the river, the bhikṣu took up his staff and struck the boatman, rebuking him, saying:
"You vile and wicked man, how dare you insult and humiliate a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas!"

Having finished reviling him, he strikes the boat owner’s arms, hands, feet, and calves, causing them to be wounded and bruised; having thus struck him, he casts him into the water, incurring a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the boat owner dies, the bhikṣu who previously harbored the intent to kill incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if he did not previously harbor the intent to kill, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, if a bhikṣu steals that boat or its equipment, if the value is fulfilled, it is a pārājika offense;
if not fulfilled, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a bhikṣu, with a malicious mind, sinks that boat, breaks that boat, or sets it adrift to flow away, because he has caused the destruction and loss of another's property, he incurs a vinayātikrama offense.
Suppose there is a person who, for the sake of merit, constantly ferries people across by boat.
If a bhikṣu wishes to cross, he should moor it to the bank so that others may cross afterward.
If the bhikṣu steals that boat, and the conditions for the offense are fulfilled, it constitutes a pārājika.
If [the raft] sinks in the water, or is broken, or is released to drift with the current, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.

When a bhikṣu has crossed to the other shore by means of a raft, he should pull the raft onto the bank and leave it in a visible place so that others may cross; he must not leave it in a secluded or hidden spot. This is called "boat property."

Regarding "objects on a ship": this refers to all items found upon a ship, namely gold, silver, pearls, money, amber, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, *śaṅkha-śilā*, red jewels, threads, *karpāsa* cotton, and even all clothing, grain, food, and the eight kinds of goods—whether they are covered or uncovered—if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches those various objects on the ship, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he moves them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Vehicles" refers to wheeled carriages, litters, palanquins, or hand-pulled carts, even down to children’s toy carts; these are what are called vehicles.
If one steals a two-wheeled vehicle, and by pulling it forward from behind, the value reaches the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If one pushes it backward from the front, and the value reaches the full measure at the rear, it is a *pārājika*.
If he pulls the left wheel aside so it passes the right wheel, or the right wheel so it passes the left wheel, and the value reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu destroys that vehicle and takes it bit by bit, or steals each individual piece of wood, and the value reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*;
if it does not reach the full amount, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the small vehicle can be entirely carried away, touching it constitutes a *vyatikrama* offense;
moving that vehicle constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is moved from its original location by the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
These are called vehicles.

As for the objects used to cover vehicles: whether covered with lion skins, tiger skins, or yellow *kambala* wool, or various other kinds of coverings—all such bedding materials and all decorative items for vehicles.

Regarding "riding upon all kinds of objects," this refers to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearl, conch shell, coral, amber, and red jewels, as well as clothing, bedding, food, drink, and the eight types of articles—whether they are covered or uncovered—if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches such an object, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves it, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes it from its original place to the full extent [of the value], it is a *pārājika*.
These are called "mounted objects.
Regarding "four-footed objects," they refer to elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, mules, sheep, and even weasels.
If a bhikṣu intends to steal an elephant, whether by pulling it, driving it, or lifting one foot up to three feet, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a four-footed animal is moved from its original place and the act is completed, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This applies equally to horses, camels, and even sheep.
If the animal is small enough to be carried entirely, touching it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If it is moved, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called "four-footed property."

Regarding "objects belonging to four-footed creatures": this refers to ornaments for elephants up to ornaments for weasels, as well as eight types of objects. Whether they are concealed or unconcealed, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches these various items, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those items, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
These are called four-footed superior objects.

As for two-footed objects, these refer to humans, birds, and the like. If a bhikṣu steals such a human—whether by luring them away or driving them off with weapons—he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense when one foot is lifted, and a pārājika offense when both feet are lifted.
If it is something that can be carried, touching it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense;
moving it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and if it is removed from its original place, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This applies even to birds.
These are the two-legged beings.
As for the most excellent among two-legged beings, these are the ornaments of women, the ornaments of men, and even the ornaments of parrots.

The ornaments of women include hairpins, bracelets, clothing, and so forth; the ornaments of men include garments, caps, necklaces, and so forth; even the ornaments of parrots include various beads and bells tied to their necks and feet, as well as eight other types of objects—whether concealed or unconcealed—if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches these items upon the two feet [of such creatures], he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those items, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
These are called the supreme among two-legged beings.
