As for those without legs, they are the snakes and pythons—those that eat flowers, eat fruits, eat flesh, or inhale breath, and so forth.

If a snake is placed in a bottle or in a basket, and there is a bhikṣu who was formerly a snake-handler and has since gone forth as a monk, and this bhikṣu wishes to steal that snake; if he intends to take the snake but fears its owner might wake up, and he lifts the basket and carries it away, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense.
However, if he takes the snake out and it leaves the basket, once the full measure is reached, it is a *pārājika*.

If one originally intended to steal the casket but not the snake, and because of fear that the owner might wake up, carries it away together with the snake, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, if one discards the snake and carries the casket away, and the value is fulfilled, it is a *pārājika*.
If one intends to steal a snake from its basket and carries it away, moving it more than a full arm-span’s distance from its original location, it is a *pārājika*.
If one steals a snake from a jar and the tail has not yet left the mouth of the jar, it is not a *pārājika*;
if both head and tail have completely left [the jar], it is a *pārājika*.
If, out of anger or resentment toward them, one reviles them by saying, "Evil person!
Why do you cage and bind sentient beings?
and then opens the jar to allow the snakes to escape, one commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, touches an object without feet, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
These are called "footless objects.

Regarding the most excellent of footless objects, they are gold, silver, pearls, musaragalva, amber, coral, conch shells, lapis lazuli, red gems, and so forth, up to the eight kinds of such items. Whether these footless objects are concealed or unconcealed, people fear them and no one dares to take them. If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches these most excellent footless objects, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is moved from its original place to the full extent [of the distance], it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "an object above the ground that is footless.

Regarding objects in space, these refer to the mango tree (*āmra*), the campaka tree, the jambu tree, the coconut tree, the *cīpala* tree, the nāgapuṣpa tree, the auspicious fruit tree (*śrīvṛkṣa*), and indeed all trees bearing flowers and fruits.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, steals these trees—if one tree reaches the full value—it is a pārājika offense;
if it does not reach the full value, for each tree he uproots and plants, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one uproots trees and piles them together in one place, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, once they are lifted off the ground by the full measure [of the required distance], it is a *pārājika*.
If one is unable to lift them due to their weight and drags them along without them leaving the ground, then even if the distance is great, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense.
If it is lifted off the ground, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches this object in space, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves it, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the fruit] is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called an "object in space.

Regarding objects in space, these refer to mangoes up to *śrīphala* fruits; if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, eats these various fruits, and if he eats even one fruit to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If it does not reach the full amount, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for every mouthful.
When a bhikṣu shakes a tree so that fruit falls to the ground, he has not yet committed a *pārājika* offense;
however, if he takes the fruit and carries it away until the full amount is reached, it is a *pārājika*.
If two people steal fruit—where one climbs the tree to drop the fruit and the other stands below to pick it up—it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, if the person in the tree descends from the tree and carries away enough fruit to reach the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
Taking all such fruits is likewise.

Whether it be the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, the assembly site of the Venerable Ānanda, the assembly site of Rāhula, or the assembly site of the Pañcavārṣika festival—at all these locations, rows of trees are planted. Each tree is adorned with various jewels and the eight kinds of objects, whether they are concealed or unconcealed.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches those various jewels, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those objects, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
These are called objects in mid-air.
These are the sixteen kinds of objects.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches such an object, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one moves that object, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is separated from its original place by the full measure, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, there are thirteen kinds of objects defined by their boundaries.
What are these thirteen?
First, the delimitation of objects;
second, the delimitation of locations;
3. The boundary of indefinite extent;
4. The boundary of enclosure walls;
5. The boundary of a cage.
Sixth, the section on designations;
seventh, the section on miscellaneous matters;
eighth, the section on banners.
9. The boundary of mutual dependence;
10. The boundary of the stake;
11. The boundary of the garden.
12. The limit regarding thieves;
13. The limit regarding taxes.
Regarding the limit of objects, there are eight kinds of objects.

What are the eight? First, medicines for the proper time; second, medicines for the night period; third, medicines for seven days; fourth, medicines for the duration of life; fifth, miscellaneous items; sixth, valuable items; seventh, impure items; eighth, items that are both pure and impure. These are called the categories of objects.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches these various objects, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those objects, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.

The limits of distribution (*pariccheda*) are as follows: the earth and things on the earth; water and things in the water; boats and things in boats; vehicles and things in vehicles; four-footed creatures and things upon them; two-footed beings and things upon them; legless creatures and things upon them; and space and things in space. These are called the limits of distribution.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches these various objects, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves those objects, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he removes them from their original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the indeterminate boundaries: as it has been taught, lying while knowing [the truth] is a *pāyattika*;
lying while not knowing [the truth] is also a *pāyattika*.
Or, lying while knowing [the truth] may be a *pārājika*.
If one speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Or, if one speaks falsely knowing [the truth], it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "speaking falsely knowing [the truth] is a *pārājika*": if a bhikṣu has not actually attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), yet says of himself, "I have attained arhatship."
"Knowing [the truth] yet speaking falsely is not a *pāyattika*, but is a *pārājika*.

Knowing [the truth] yet speaking falsely that constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense means: if a bhikṣu, with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, slanders a pure bhikṣu, this knowing yet speaking falsely is not a *pāyattika*, but is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
Regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya* for speaking falsely while knowing the truth:
if a bhikṣu says, "I am an arhat," this is a deliberate falsehood; it is not a *pāyattika*, but rather a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the offense of *vinayātikrama* for speaking falsely while knowing the truth:
if a bhikṣu says to himself, "Am I an arhat?",
this is a false statement made with full knowledge that does not constitute a *pāyattika* offense, but rather an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

"Speaking falsely while knowing [the truth] is a *pāyattika* offense" means: excluding the aforementioned matters, all other instances of speaking falsely constitute this *pāyattika* offense of speaking falsely while knowing [the truth].
Furthermore, there are cases of injuring or killing plants and trees that constitute a *pārājika* offense;
cases of injuring or killing plants and trees that constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and cases of injuring or killing plants and trees that constitute a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the *pārājika* offense of injuring or killing plants and trees: if there are trees, flowers, or fruits that have an owner who guards them, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, injures or kills such plants and trees, it is not a *pāyattika*; however, if the act is completed, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offense for injuring or killing plants and trees: if there are trees, flowers, or fruits that have an owner who guards them, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, if the value does not reach the full amount, it is not a *pāyattika*, but rather a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "injuring or killing plants and trees constitutes a *pāyattika*": injuring or killing any plant or tree constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, not all instances of eating at an improper time constitute a *pāyattika*;
there are cases where eating at an improper time constitutes a *pārājika*, cases where it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, and cases where it constitutes a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the *pārājika* offense of eating at an improper time: if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's food and eats it at an improper time, if the amount is full, it is not a *pāyattika*, but is a *pārājika*.

Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offense of eating at an improper time: if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's food and eats it at an improper time, if the amount is not sufficient [to constitute a full offense], it is not a *pāyattika*, but rather a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the *pāyattika* for eating at an improper time: if a bhikṣu obtains food through legitimate means and consumes it at an improper time, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, regarding the drinking of alcohol: not all instances of drinking alcohol constitute a *pāyattika*;
there are cases where drinking alcohol constitutes a *pārājika*, cases where it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*, and cases where it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pārājika* offense of drinking alcohol: if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's alcohol and drinks it in full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offense of drinking alcohol: if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's alcohol and drinks it but not in full measure, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the *pāyattika* for drinking alcohol: if a bhikṣu obtains alcohol through legitimate means and drinks it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu touches an object of uncertain value with the intent to steal, he incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense;
if he moves that object, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is moved from its original place and fills [the space], it is a *pārājika*.
This is called the "indefinite boundary.
As for the "enclosure boundary," it includes elephant stables, horse stables, camel stables, and pens for donkeys, cattle, and sheep.

In the case of a garden of radishes, a garden of vegetables, a garden of melons, or a garden of sugarcane, if a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes an elephant from there, and the elephant raises one foot up to four feet to pass through the stable gate, if any part of its body has not yet cleared the gate, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
once any part of its body has cleared the gate, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The same applies even down to a donkey.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another's sheep, drives the sheep away so that they flee in terror, or beats them to death out of anger, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu cuts flesh and throws it outside the fence, it does not constitute a pārājika offense;
however, if the bhikṣu goes outside the fence and carries the flesh away from the ground, once the full measure is reached, it is a pārājika offense.
If one eats meat from within a pen and the value reaches the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If two bhikṣus steal a sheep—one outside the fence and one inside—and they cut the meat and throw it outside the pen, it is not yet a *pārājika*;
once the person who was inside has gone out and lifted the meat off the ground, if the value reaches the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes radish roots—if he pulls out one root and the value reaches the full measure, it is a pārājika offense;
if it does not reach the full measure, for each root pulled out at that time, there is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one uproots a large mass of [grass or trees] but has not yet moved it beyond the boundary of the garden, it is not a *pārājika* offense;
once it is held and lifted out of the garden, it is a *pārājika*.
If one uproots a heavy bundle that cannot be lifted, and drags it away even a great distance, it is still not a *pārājika* offense.
If it is separated from the ground and the measure is full, it is a *pārājika*.
This applies to all vegetables, even including gourds.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes another’s sugarcane and eats one stalk, and the measure is full, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is not full, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each root [of the plant].
If it is cut and placed outside the fence, it is not yet a *pārājika*; it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is taken out of the garden and carried away, and the measure is full, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, employs craftiness and deception, tying sugarcane to his feet and dragging it away, he does not commit a pārājika offense as long as it has not yet reached its destination;
if it leaves the ground by the full measure [of the distance], it is a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu stands outside the orchard while another stands inside, and he throws sugarcane outside the orchard, it does not constitute a pārājika offense;
however, if after it has gone out, he lifts it so that it leaves the ground and the measure is full, it is a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu carries off sugarcane and, while the stalks and leaves have merely touched the garden enclosure but he has not yet left it, he has not committed a pārājika offense;
once he has left it, it is a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu touches these various items with a thieving mind, he incurs a vyatikrama-śikṣāpada offense.
If one moves that object, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is separated from its original place, it is a *pārājika* offense when the full measure is reached.
Regarding the "limit of the cage," this refers to various birds such as parrots and various beasts such as lions.

If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes those birds, there are two cases: if he intends to steal the birds and not the cage, yet carries them away together with the cage for fear of being discovered by others, he has not committed a pārājika offense;
if he abandons the cage and carries the birds away, and the value is fulfilled, it is a pārājika offense.
If one intends to steal the cage but not the bird, and because of the fear of being discovered, takes it away while keeping the bird inside, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
however, if one takes the bird out and carries the cage away, and the value is sufficient, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bird in a cage is subject to the offense of theft, and one takes it away from its original place, if the value is fulfilled, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes a bird and puts his hand inside the cage, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he pulls out one leg, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If both legs have emerged and wings are present, but the tail has not yet passed through the opening of the cage, it is not a *pārājika*;
once it has fully emerged, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes a lion from within its inner enclosure, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one leg has been pulled out, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
even if four legs have been pulled out but the tail has not yet left the enclosure, it is not a *pārājika*;
once it has left, it is a *pārājika*.
It is the same for all wild animals.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches an object within the boundary of such a cage, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is moved from its original place and the measure is full, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding "entrusting to a designated person": if a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), an instructor (*ācārya*), a disciple, or a friend entrusts items to one another—whether it be a bowl, robes, or other various objects—and the recipient thinks:
"The sender has gone far away; since the giver does not know [where the item is], I shall take this object for myself."

If, having conceived a thieving mind, one takes [the object]—moving it from the ground onto the knees, from the knees onto the ground, from the left shoulder onto the right shoulder, and so on, even down to moving it from the head onto the shoulders—and each successive movement completes the act, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu, having received a deposit, crosses a river, or a pond, or a flooded stream, or encounters rain, and fearing that the garment might get wet, goes out to look at it; seeing that the garment is fine, he thinks to himself:
"The person who deposited it has gone far away and does not know [of my presence]; I shall take this thing for myself."

If, having conceived a mind of theft, one takes [the object]—moving it from the ground onto one's knees, from the knees onto the ground, from the left shoulder onto the right shoulder, and so on up to moving it from the shoulder onto the head—and each such movement completes the act, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
As the bhikṣu who had received the deposit was traveling along the road, he saw another bhikṣu coming from the opposite direction and asked him:
"Venerable sir, where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from such-and-such a place. He asked:
"Do you know such-and-such a bhikṣu?
He replied, "I know him."
He asked again,
"Is that bhikṣu well?
They replied:
"He has already died, or entered parinirvāṇa.
These robes and requisites should belong to the *saṃgha* present there. However, if the monk to whom they were entrusted is known to be deceitful and unrighteous, he might think:
"Why should I share these with that monk?"
He silently departed from the other bhikṣu and,
having gone beyond the range of sight and hearing, spoke these words:
"If that bhikṣu passes away or enters parinirvāṇa, whatever robes, bowl, or other miscellaneous items he possesses should be divided among the monks present."
"Since there is no Saṃgha present before me, I should now accept [the offering].
Having accepted it, because that bhikṣu accepted it alone with a deceitful mind, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
While the bhikṣu who had accepted the deposit was boarding a boat to cross the water, another bhikṣu came across from the opposite bank; this bhikṣu asked him:
“From where have you come? He replied, “I have come from such-and-such a place.”
He asked again,
"Do you know that bhikṣu?
He replied:
"Śāriputra," he asked again,
"Is that bhikṣu well?"
He replied, "Whether he dies or enters parinirvāṇa.

At that time, these robes and articles should belong to the *saṃgha* present there; yet this bhikṣu, being knowledgeable in the Dharma yet full of deceit, even performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) with a deceptive mind, commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If a monk who has received a deposit is crossing a body of water by boat and is in midstream when another monk comes from the opposite direction to cross,
and they meet in midstream, this monk asks:
"Venerable sir, where have you come from?"
...up to the point of performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) with a deceitful mind, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).

If a bhikṣu who has received a deposit disembarks at the far shore, and another bhikṣu, having just arrived there, intends to board the ship, [and the former] performs a formal act with a deceitful mind, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
The monk who had been entrusted with the goods went ashore, and another monk came along that same path.
He asked,
"Venerable sir, where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from such-and-such a place.
Even by performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā) with a deceitful mind, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If that bhikṣu reflects:
"There are many who share this same name; how can I be certain? I must go to that place.
Having arrived there, he asks again:
"Is that bhikṣu at peace? He replied:
"He has either died or entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the robes and articles should belong to the *saṃgha* present there; however, this monk, being deceitful and well-versed in the Dharma, thought to himself:
"Why should these robes be shared among so many people?"
He secretly summoned a knowledgeable bhikṣu outside the boundary and said to him:
"If a certain bhikṣu passes away or enters parinirvāṇa, all his robes, bowl, and various miscellaneous belongings should be divided among the monks present."
"I am present here now; we should receive it.
Having accepted it, because of this formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed with a deceitful mind, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
If a bhikṣu should think thus:
"These robes and bowl originally did not say to me, 'Give them to the stūpa' or 'Give them to the Saṃgha.
If the one to whom they were given has already died or entered parinirvāṇa, there is no offense in taking these items and returning them to the original bhikṣu.
This is called "entrusted property.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches such entrusted property, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves it from its original place and the value reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the classification of miscellaneous items: it is like a herdsman who tends various kinds of livestock, namely elephants, horses, oxen, camels, donkeys, sheep, and so forth.
Regarding elephants: there are many kinds of elephants, such as those that are well-behaved, beautiful in color, or swift in gait.

If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes an elephant and, having mounted it, grasps the hook and leads it toward a certain direction—such as intending to go toward the east—but the elephant goes mad and runs toward the south, west, or north, he has not committed a *pārājika* offense.
If, with a thieving mind, he takes an elephant intending to go toward the south, but the elephant goes mad and runs toward the west, north, or east, he has not committed a *pārājika* offense.
The same applies to the northwest.
If one intends to steal an elephant toward the east, and the elephant goes toward the east, it is a *pārājika*;
the same applies to the south, west, and north.
If there was no fixed direction previously and he follows wherever it goes, then when the elephant lifts all four feet, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding horses: there are many kinds of horses—those that are well-behaved, those of good color, and those that are swift runners. If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, intends to take such a horse and, having mounted it, wishes to go toward the east, but the horse goes mad and runs toward the south, west, or north, it is not yet a *pārājika*;
the same applies to the south, west, and north.
The horse departs in a particular direction as previously described.
If it goes in any direction without a fixed course, and the horse lifts all four feet,
it is a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu steals a fine horse to ride away, and the owner notices it and immediately pursues him on the horse, if the owner does not form the thought that he has lost [the horse] and the bhikṣu does not form the thought that he has acquired it, there is no pārājika;
if the owner forms the thought that he has lost [the horse] and the bhikṣu does not form the thought that he has acquired it, there is no pārājika;
if the owner forms the thought that he has lost [the horse] and the bhikṣu forms the thought that he has acquired it, it is pārājika.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, lures away another’s horse by means of salt or grass and leads it to a place beyond the range of sight or hearing, he commits a pārājika offense.
As for oxen, there are many kinds: those that are well-behaved, those with soft hair, those of beautiful color, and those that are swift of foot.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes up a staff and drives cattle toward the east, whether he commits an offense or not is as explained in the section on elephants.

Even if the owner of the cattle awakens and pursues them, if the owner does not form the perception that they are lost and the bhikṣu does not form the perception that he has acquired them, it is not a pārājika offense;
however, if the owner forms the perception that they are lost and the bhikṣu forms the perception that he has acquired them, it is a pārājika offense.
If, with a thieving mind, one lures another's ox away by means of salt or grass, or drags it away with a long rope, such that it is beyond the range of sight or hearing, it is a *pārājika*.
As it is with cattle, so it is with other animals such as camels, donkeys, and sheep.
This constitutes the "mixed boundary.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches this mixed boundary, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
"Up to moving it from its original location; if it is full [of the measure], it is a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the dimensions of the banner: at the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained enlightenment, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, the great assembly of Ānanda, the great assembly of Rāhula, and the great assembly of the *pañcavārṣika*, these various sites of great assemblies are adorned in diverse ways, with silk streamers, banners, canopies, and many jeweled bells suspended there."
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, takes a banner and unties one end of the rope, it does not constitute a pārājika offense;
once both ends are untied and the value is complete, it is a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, falsely distributes various banners and takes them from here and there, it does not constitute a pārājika offense;
however, once he has taken them and carries them away, if the value is fulfilled, it is a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu steals a flower garland, as long as he has untied only one end, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense;
only when both ends have been untied and the full value is reached is it a *pārājika*.
If two bhikṣus steal a banner in a dark place without being aware of each other, each unties the rope from one end and gathers it up, meeting in the middle, where they ask one another:
"Who are you? Terrified, he abandoned his banner and fled, incurring a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
when these two bhikṣus questioned one another, each said:
"To steal the banner.
They then conspired together to steal it; if the full measure is reached, it is a *pārājika*.

If many banners of various colors are tied together on a single rope and are so heavy that each person loosens one end and it falls to the ground, and they drag it along from the ground because they cannot carry it, then even if the distance is great, it is not yet a *pārājika*.
When it is lifted off the ground, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If that bhikṣu thinks:
"This is property for the adornment of the stūpa; to take it is a grave sin," [he is not guilty].
"I require only one colored object.
If he then takes one colored object and it is full, it is a *pārājika*.
If he says:
"I must have half the color.
If he takes half the color and it does not reach the full measure, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it reaches the full measure, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If two bhikṣus were to steal a banner in a dark place without being aware of each other, each untying the rope from one end and gathering it up until they met in the middle, they would ask one another: "Who are you?"
Terrified, he abandoned the banner and fled, committing a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

There was a bhikṣu who, while circumambulating the stūpa early in the morning, saw this banner beneath it; he then took it away with the intent to steal. If the value is fulfilled, this bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense.

There were those who made offerings to the Bodhi tree, adorning it with the seven treasures—gold, silver, pearls, and various kinds of banners and flowers; with continuous golden cords and hanging bells from golden locks; and with the brilliant light of broad mountain-like gold used for their offerings.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, takes those various objects and the value reaches the full measure, it is a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, takes various silken fabrics offered as worship at the stūpas of non-Buddhists and the value reaches the full measure, it is a pārājika offense.
If the wind blows it down to the ground, one should not take it if one knows it was a ritual offering from atop a stupa;
however, if it has been blown to a distant place and is covered in dust, grime, and black filth, there is no offense in taking it with the thought that it is refuse.
If there are miscellaneous items or clothing within a temple belonging to the devas, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it constitutes a pārājika offense if the value is fulfilled.
If dust, grime, or black stains have been blown there by the wind and he takes them with the perception that they are discarded refuse (pāṃśukūla), there is no offense.
This is called the boundary of the banner.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches an object within this boundary of the banner, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is moved from its original place and the value is full [of the prescribed amount], it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the limits of the causal factors: for example, in the house of a householder, there may be articles left uncollected in another location, such as clothing, necklaces, and so forth.

At that time, a bhikṣu led a śrāmaṇera into a householder’s home. Then, with a thieving mind, the bhikṣu took the householder’s clothing and placed it inside a bag, instructing the śrāmaṇera to carry it away. At that moment, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when the śrāmaṇera carries it beyond the boundary of the monastic precinct, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he forms the perception of acquisition and the value is complete, it is a *pārājika*.
At that time, the host woke up and said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir! What are you doing?"
He replied,
"Long-lived one! It was my own hand that moved."
When one speaks these words, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one causes a layperson to carry it away, it is also as described above.
It is likewise when one carries an object away from among sheep with long wool.
If a bhikṣu enters the house of a householder and a calf, seeing the color of the bhikṣu’s robe, thinks it is its mother and approaches the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should drive it away.
If one entices that calf with salt or with grass, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if one leads it across the boundary but has not yet exited the territory, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
once it has exited the territory, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, while eating, takes the alms-bowl (*kaṇḍolaka*) of his neighbor with a thieving mind, places it in his own bowl, and has a disciple carry it away, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when the disciple crosses the boundary, it becomes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he forms the perception that he has acquired it, it is a *pārājika* offense.
When that bhikṣu had awakened, he immediately asked the elder,
"What are you doing? The elder replied:
"If I was merely joking," he says;
by making such a statement, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu is traveling together with merchants, and other merchants come from that direction and meet them midway, they stay overnight in the same place.

If a bhikṣu, during the night, gives rise to a thieving mind and seizes another’s carriage, tying it to another’s carriage; seizes another man, tying him to another man; seizes another woman, tying her to another woman; or seizes another child, tying them to another child—desiring that each be led away by the other—and employs such means, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline);
if he goes beyond the boundary of the monastery grounds, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);
if he forms the perception that the act is accomplished, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
This is called "an object defined by its characteristic marks.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches such an object defined by its characteristic marks, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the "boundary of the stakes": this refers to the places where the Buddha was born, where he attained enlightenment, where he turned the wheel of Dharma, the great assembly of Ānanda, the great assembly of Rāhula, and the great assembly of the *pañcavārṣika*; within these various monasteries, they are adorned and decorated, with stakes driven into the ground everywhere to hang various banners and canopies, and many kinds of precious jewels suspended upon those stakes.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, takes various treasures from this peg; if he lifts the treasures with his hand, although the treasures have been lifted, as long as the rope has not yet detached from the peg, it is not a pārājika offense;
once they have detached from the peg, it is a pārājika offense.
If the rope is stiff and strong, and when lifting the treasure the rope becomes detached from the peg, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one steals by means of the peg, at the moment the hand touches it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one moves that peg, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.

If a jar of ghee, a jar of oil, a jar of honey, or a bowl, or a ball of thread, is suspended on a peg, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes this jar of ghee: when he lifts it with his hand, if the rope is slack and the peg is upright, then although he has lifted it, it is not yet a *pārājika*;
once it is entirely detached from the peg, it is a *pārājika*.
If the rope is stiff and the stake is crooked, although it is lifted, it does not constitute a *pārājika*;
only when it has completely left the stake and descended is it a full *pārājika*.
If the rope is soft and the stake is crooked, although it is lifted, it does not constitute a *pārājika*.
If she has completely moved away from beneath the stake and it is full, it is a *pārājika*.
If the rope is taut and the stake is upright, lifting [the organ] constitutes a *pārājika*.
If she pierces a jar, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one uses a vessel to receive [liquor] from another vessel, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the flow has ceased and the vessel is full, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if the flow has not yet ceased and one, fearing the commission of a grave offense, repents and pours it back into the original vessel, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The same applies to oil jars and honey jars.
If a bhikṣu intends to steal a bowl, when he lifts it with his hand, if the cord is slack and the peg is upright, although he has lifted it, he has not yet committed a pārājika offense;
only when the bowl has moved away from the peg is it a pārājika offense.
If the rope is stiff and the stake is curved, although it is lifted, it does not constitute a *pārājika*;
once it has been separated from the stake, it is a *pārājika*.
If the rope is soft and the stake is curved, while it is being lifted and held, it does not constitute a *pārājika*.
Once it has been removed from the peg, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If the rope is taut and the peg is upright, lifting it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one steals a ball of thread, the case of the ball of thread, the rope, and the peg is as explained above.
Furthermore, if at the time of stealing the ball one thinks,
"I need a small amount of thread," and takes thread by winding it around a peg without breaking it, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense.
If the thread is completely severed, it is a *pārājika* offense.

While this bhikṣu is winding the thread, if the thread has not yet been severed and he immediately regrets his action, fearing the commission of a grave offense, and returns it to its original place, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the "boundary of the stake.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches an object within this boundary of the stake, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is moved from its original location to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the boundaries of a garden: there was once a householder whose family was very wealthy; a certain bhikṣu named Kulu used to frequently enter and leave his house.

When their parents were still alive, the brothers lived together as a household; however, after their parents passed away, discord arose within the family. The younger brother wished to divide the property, but the elder brother was unwilling, desiring instead to live together in accordance with righteousness.
The younger brother continued to demand his share without ceasing; the elder brother, unable to avoid the situation, granted him his request and spoke to him with words of righteousness:
"Who is capable of dividing the wealth?
He replied:
"The Ācārya Kulu is he whom our parents honored and supported while they were alive; he knows everything that is present or absent within the household.
They all said, "Excellent!"
Then the younger brother, being deceitful, went at once to Kuru to pay his respects and inquire after his well-being. Having finished his inquiries, he said:
"Ācārya, you are one whom my parents revere and my brothers honor; you know all that pertains to the affairs of our household."

"While my parents were still alive, my brothers and I lived together; now that my parents have passed away, there is discord within the household. Desiring to divide the property, I have come to submit this petition: after I have separated from them, I shall provide for the Ācārya, and with what remains after those offerings, I shall support myself."
"If the Ācārya, on the day of distributing the property, would grant me the best [items]," if a bhikṣu accepts such a proposal,
he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya);
if he retains the superior items, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
Once the distribution of the goods has been finalized, it is a *pārājika* offense.
While the goods are being distributed, a bhikṣu asks:
"What shall we distribute first?"
The host said, "First divide the bipeds and the quadrupeds.
The bhikṣu then first divided the bipeds; among the male and female slaves, those who were old, sickly, difficult to command, or untrustworthy were set aside as one portion.
Those that are young, free from illness, easy to manage, and trustworthy constitute one portion.

When dividing them into four groups, those among the herd that are weak, old, and lacking strength; coarse and poor in quality, difficult to use, and yielding little milk; or those that do calve but are difficult to milk—these form one portion.
Those that are young in age, robust, well-behaved, easy to manage, prolific in breeding, yielding much milk, excellent, and easy to milk—these further constitute one portion.

If rooms and houses are to be divided, those that are dilapidated and worn out shall constitute one portion, while those that are new and well-kept shall likewise constitute another portion; the same applies to multi-storied pavilions and shops.
Even down to the division of fields: he took the thin, poor, and weedy plots as one portion, and the fertile, excellent ones as another portion;
from among the gardens, he took those that were inferior with few flowers and fruits as one portion, and those where the flowers and fruits were lush and superior as another portion.
Furthermore, when they wished to divide the grain, rice, gold, silver, and wealth, the elder brother said to the bhikṣu:
"Ācārya, you were respected by my parents and esteemed by my brothers; how is it that you divide the property in such a manner?"
The Ācārya returned and reflected upon the Buddha’s words:
"If a bhikṣu, with such a thought, divides another's property, even if the owner has not given permission, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya."
After Kuru had returned, the brothers immediately discussed it further:
"Who else could there be who is held in high esteem by our parents?
An elder of great virtue, who knows the family's affairs, should be requested to divide the inheritance."
"If we do not divide it quickly, I fear that should the King hear of it, he might tax or seize it.
He then reflected, "The Great Virtuous One is blameless and superior even to Kuru; it would be appropriate to request him once more to divide this wealth."
The brothers, being united in brotherly duty, went to the Kuru country to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being. Sitting to one side, they addressed the Kuru, saying:
"Preceptor, you were highly esteemed by our parents; we wish to know whether there is anything in our household concerning which you have knowledge."
"Now I shall divide these goods for you.
At that time, Kuru regretted that he had not been granted a share previously, and said:
"You brothers are devoid of righteousness, full of suspicion, and lacking in faith; who could possibly bear to divide the property for you?"
The brothers said:
"Previously we were indeed hasty; we feel ashamed before the Ācārya.

Since the Ācārya has long been familiar with our household affairs, we now wish for you to divide this wealth for us. Should the King find out, he might perhaps tax or seize it; therefore, we wish to divide it quickly."
The bhikṣu replied,
"Do you truly intend to have me divide it?
They answered:
"It is indeed so,
Ācārya! that bhikṣu replied.
"If it must be so, we shall make a formal agreement: once the goods have been divided, you may take your share immediately; if there is no further dispute, we shall divide them for you.
Each of them replied, "We shall follow your instructions and dare not disobey again."

Once that bhikṣu has accepted the invitation, he should divide the land into equal portions. When they are measuring the land with a cord to divide it, if he measures with partiality even by the width of a single grain of barley, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Because the land is priceless, this is called the boundary of the garden.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches any object within this garden boundary, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if the value reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the "demarcation of thieves": there were bhikṣus traveling on a road who were plundered by bandits; the bandits were few and the bhikṣus were many.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Now these bandits are few and we are many; we should join our forces together to recover our original property."
They immediately seized bricks and stones together and pursued the thief, shouting insults from afar:
"You wretched, evil criminal! We may shave off our own hair and beards ourselves, but do you think you can shave off our hands and feet?"
At that time, the bandits, struck with terror, released the robes and bowls and fled in all directions.
If the bhikṣu had not yet formed the thought that they were lost, he incurs no offense in taking back his original belongings;

however, if he has already formed the thought that they are lost and then takes them back, he is effectively robbing the robbers of their plunder. If the conditions are fulfilled, it is a pārājika offense.
There were some bhikṣus traveling on the road who were robbed by bandits. Having lost their robes and bowls, the bhikṣus entered a forest to hide.
At that time, the bandits thought to themselves: "Our group is large while these goods are few; it would be better to give them back and seek a small amount [of wealth] elsewhere."
He immediately hid his robe and bowl, covering them in one place, and then continued along the road to rob others.
At that time, the bhikṣu saw those hidden items and, waiting until the thief had departed, took the robe and bowl.
If this bhikṣu did not previously form the thought that the item was lost and takes back his original property, he is without offense;
if he formed the thought that it was lost, he should not take it, and if he does take it, he is like a thief robbing another thief; if the value is complete, it is a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, while some bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they were robbed by bandits. The bandits seized the robes and bowls of the bhikṣus and departed along the path.

At that time, the bhikṣus followed behind, looking back from afar to see where the group of bandits had gone, pursuing them without ceasing until they drew near a village, at which point the bandits divided the loot.
The bhikṣu then said to the robbers:
"Long-lived ones!
We are renunciants who depend on others for our livelihood; you may beg from me my robes and bowl."
"What use have you for these robes and bowl?
If a bhikṣu obtains them in this manner, there is no offense.
If the thief should revile him, saying:
"You wicked śramaṇa, I have already granted you your life.
How dare you come again, wishing to take my robes and bowl?
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Since these bandits have already approached the village, they will certainly not harm me; I shall terrify them.
He then said to the bandits:
"Do you think that I have nothing to rely upon?"
"I shall inform the King and the various ministers that you are a thief.
If [the person] is obtained through intimidation, there is no offense.
The thief then speaks with anger:
“I shall never give it to you; you may go as you please.
If a bhikṣu informs the village headman, he should not report it if he subsequently seizes, binds, or kills various thieves.
If one speaks to the village headman using skillful means to obtain robes and a bowl, there is no offense.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who possesses many robes and bowls and has many disciples under his care, yet those disciples do not cultivate virtuous conduct; they might think to themselves:
"We should go to the room of our upādhyāya or ācārya and steal their various robes and bowls."
He also placed his own robes and bowl inside the teacher’s room, and they then made an agreement:
"Whichever of us obtains clothing or requisites shall share them with the other; likewise, if I obtain anything, it shall be shared with you."

If he enters the room and, at the clothes rack, takes the robes of his preceptor or teacher and moves them toward his own robes without removing them from the original rack, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he lifts the teacher’s robe from the rack and places it upon his own robes, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If the teacher’s robe belt, the corner of the robe, or the threads have not yet left the robe rack, it is not a *pārājika*;
once everything has left [the rack], it is a *pārājika*.
If that preceptor or instructor suspects that this disciple might steal his robes and bowl, he then hides his own robes and bowl and places them elsewhere.

A disciple then entered the darkness and mistakenly stole his own robe and bowl; because he did not distinguish them upon coming outside, if the full portion was on one side of the half-robe, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
There was an elder bhikṣu who had gone forth but was not skilled in the practice of the precepts.
Another bhikṣu said to him, "Elder, come, let us commit robbery together. The elder replied:
"I originally lived as a householder and never committed robbery; now that I have gone forth, how could I commit robbery?
That bhikṣu said, "If you do not wish to commit robbery, simply guard the gate, and we shall share the proceeds with you."
The mahallaka thought to himself, "I did not commit the theft; why should I share the portion with you? Why do you not leave?
He replied:
"Very well. They then went together and had the mahallaka guard the gate.
When that bhikṣu entered and touched an object with the intent to steal, both incurred an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
If one moves that object, both incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is moved from its original location by a full measure, both incur a *pārājika* offense.
Suppose a visiting bhikṣu comes and stays overnight in the dining hall or a meditation cell, and departs at dawn, perhaps forgetting his robes, bowl, or other belongings.

At that time, an elder monk named Māmāṭi was inspecting the dwellings and wished to know whether the visiting monks had departed. Upon seeing their robes and bowls, he immediately conceived a mind of theft; having taken them, he moved them to another location to conceal them, thereby committing a *pārājika* offense.

If another bhikṣu comes along and, seeing these same clothes and items, likewise gives rise to the intent to steal, takes them, and moves them to another location to conceal them, he also commits a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, if a third person likewise conceives the intent to steal and moves the object to another location to conceal it, this also constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Regardless of the number of people involved, if they conceive the intent to steal and successively move the object, all of them incur a *pārājika* offense.
Once the owner of those robes and belongings had gone far away, he returned because he remembered them; taking them back was without offense.

There was a bhikṣu who forgot his robe and bowl; another bhikṣu saw this and immediately conceived the intent to steal it, yet instead of taking it with his own hand, he spoke to an elder (mahallaka) bhikṣu and ordered him to take it.
The *mahallaka* bhikṣu, thinking it was his own robe and bowl, took them up.
At the moment of contact, the bhikṣu with the intent to steal incurs a *vinayātikrama*;
at the moment of movement, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is moved from its original location to the full extent [of the required distance], one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Because the *mahallaka* did not have the intention to steal, he is entirely without fault throughout the three stages [of the action].
If he had previously spoken to the *mahallaka*:
"Take these robes and bowl; we shall divide them together.
When the mahallaka touched them with a thieving mind, both committed a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when he moved them, both committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is moved from its original place to the full extent, both commit a *pārājika* offense.
If a *mahallaka*, having observed this, thinks:
"Why should I share it with him?"
"I shall take it alone.
Having spoken thus, he immediately took it away;
he incurs a *pārājika* offense, while that other bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣu acting as a *karmadāna* has no materials for a stūpa, but the Saṃgha does have materials, he should think:
"The reason devas and humans make offerings to the Saṃgha is that they all receive the grace of the Buddha; to make an offering to the Buddha is itself to make an offering to the Saṃgha."
If one takes property belonging to the Saṃgha to repair a stūpa, this *karmadāna* commits a *pārājika*.
If the stūpa has property but the Saṃgha has none, one should then think:
"Those who make offerings to the Saṃgha also make offerings to the Buddha, for he is included therein."
If one takes property belonging to a stūpa to make offerings to the Saṃgha, and the *karmadāna* (steward) uses it, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
If the stūpa has no property but the Saṃgha does, one may borrow and use it according to the Dharma, provided one clearly records in writing:
"It was borrowed at such-and-such a time; it shall be returned at such-and-such a time."
If the Sangha has no property but the stūpa does, it is likewise permissible to borrow and use [the stūpa's property] in accordance with the Dharma.

When that administrative officer (vaiyāvṛtyakara) transfers his duties, he must read out the formal statement (śāstra) within the Sangha and hand over the responsibilities clearly; if he does not read out the statement, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
This is called lending for use.

When two bhikṣus have shared property that ought to be divided, if one bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes it alone—excluding his own portion and taking what belongs to the other—if the amount is full [of the required measure], it is a pārājika offense;
if he takes it with the other's consent, there is no offense.
If one thinks,
"I am using this now, but shall repay it later," there is no offense.
There were two monks who were preceptors; they made a mutual agreement, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
From this day forward, whatever we may obtain, we shall share it equally between the two of us."
Later, when one person obtained a fine piece of cloth, he thought to himself,
"If I obtain another later, it will surely not equal this.
He then said to his companion:
"From this day forward, let us each take what we find for ourselves; if you find something, you take it yourself, and if I find something, I take it myself.
Because the items previously obtained violated the rule, regarding the division of these items into halves or wholes, [the offense] is a *pārājika*.
If this bhikṣu, having accepted the offering and performed the blessing, says to the donor,
"Set it aside for you; I shall take it later," and then returns to say to his companion:
"Elder! From this day forward, let us each manage our own acquisitions; if you obtain something, you may take it yourself, and if I obtain something, I shall take it myself.
When these words were spoken, he committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If this bhikṣu hears that someone intends to give robes, he speaks in advance to his companion, saying:
"Venerable sir!
From this day forward, let us each look after our own affairs; if you obtain [a robe], you take it yourself; if I obtain one, I take it myself."
When these words were spoken, he committed an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
There were two *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments, and the bhikṣus made a mutual agreement:
"From this day forward, if we obtain any *pāṃśukūla* garments, they shall be shared equally."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu obtained a fine paṃsukūla robe and thought to himself:
"This robe is truly excellent; even if I were to obtain another later, it would surely not equal this one."
He then said to his companion, "Elder!
From this day forward, let us each manage our own affairs; if you obtain anything, you take it yourself, and if I obtain anything, I take it myself."
Because this bhikṣu has violated his original vow, regarding the "half-full" [measure] therein, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If this bhikṣu obtains a fine rag (*pāṃśukūla*) but does not take it, instead covering it with grass, bricks, or stones, and then immediately returns to rescinding the vow as previously described, this bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If this bhikṣu, having seen a fine piece of discarded cloth, neither takes it nor covers it, and then immediately releases his commitment as previously described, that bhikṣu incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that among the property of the Saṃgha there is that which should be given and that which should not be given:
what should be given?
That which would cause loss or that which would bring benefit should be given.
What constitutes causing harm?

Suppose bandits come to a monastery seeking various kinds of food and drink; if one does not give them these, they may burn or plunder the monastery. Although one should not give such things, out of fear of causing harm, one should give according to what is available, however much or little it may be.
Who are those who should be benefited?

Those who repair the dwellings of the Saṃgha—whether as plasterers, carpenters, or painters—as well as those who manage the affairs and property of the Saṃgha, should be provided with food before and after meals, as well as oil for anointing the body, non-time-allowed drinks, and so forth. Furthermore, kings and those of great power should be given food and drink; these are called those to whom gifts should be given for their benefit.

If a bhikṣu loses his robes or bowl and has not yet formed the intention to relinquish them, and later discovers their location, he should seek them back; seeking them back in this case constitutes no offense.

If, however, he has already formed the intention to relinquish them, then even if he later discovers their location, he should not seek them back; if he does seek them and obtains them, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If one first forms the thought:
"Should I later discover where it is, I shall demand it back," then there is no offense in so demanding it.

There were two bhikṣus who established a restriction: "We shall together receive the sūtras and we shall together recite the sūtras; whoever afterwards does not receive or recite them shall incur a *vinayātikrama* offense."
This is called property belonging to thieves.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, touches this property belonging to thieves, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [the object] is moved from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the limit for tax exemption: there was a bhikṣu traveling on a road with some merchants. The bhikṣu had a large retinue, so the merchants said to one of the bhikṣus:
"When your master, the Venerable One, reaches the customs checkpoint, who would dare to inspect him?"
"You should carry this item for me and place it within your teacher’s robe-bag so that we may pass through this customs checkpoint.
The disciple immediately agreed, took the entrusted object and placed it in his teacher's bag; the disciple incurs a *vyatikrama* offense, while the teacher is innocent as he was unaware.
If they reach the customs checkpoint, the disciple incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, while the teacher does not commit an offense.
If they have already passed through the customs checkpoint, the disciple incurs a *pārājika* offense while the teacher does not.
If the merchant says to that teacher, "The Ācārya is a person of merit; while traveling with his retinue, who would dare to inspect him?"
"Please, for my sake, carry this small item and place it within the bag of an ācārya’s disciple as we pass through the customs post.
The teacher immediately agreed; at the moment he took it and placed it in the disciple's bag, he committed a *vyatikrama* offense, while the disciple was not guilty as he was unaware.
When they reached the customs post, the teacher committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense, while the disciple remained without guilt.
If they pass through a customs checkpoint, the teacher incurs a *pārājika* offense while the disciple is without fault.
If both speak together and both give their consent, both incur an offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*;
if they reach the customs checkpoint, both incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If they pass through a customs checkpoint together, both incur a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu is traveling along a road with merchants and, upon reaching the outskirts of a village, the bhikṣu washes his hands, the merchant asks him:
"Venerable sir, what do you intend to do?"
He replied,
"I wish to go out for alms.
The merchant said:
“Ācārya, do not beg for alms; I shall provide you with food.
He then gave the bhikṣu various kinds of fine food.
Having finished eating, he said to the bhikṣu:
"The Ācārya, please carry this small item for me past this customs checkpoint.
The bhikṣu said,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that forbids me from carrying taxable items past a customs post."
The merchant thought to himself:
"If I lose the government tax, it is a loss; if I give it to the bhikṣu, it is also a loss.
Since it is a loss in both cases, I shall give it to the bhikṣu so that I may obtain merit."
He then said to the bhikṣus, "Please stand in order; I wish to give alms.
The merchants immediately gave alms in order, filling each of their bowls with precious objects.
Having completed the almsgiving, he went out ahead of the caravan and stayed outside the pass to wait for the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus arrived shortly thereafter, the merchant prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣus and said:
"Venerable sirs, do you recognize me?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"Do you recognize me as the one who gave that gift just now?
He answered:
"I know. "If you know, why do I give alms?
He replied:
"You wish to create merit," the merchant said.
"It is indeed so!"
"But my wife must have food and clothing, and debts must be repaid; I wish to recover my property.
The bhikṣu should say to him:
"You wicked man!"
"If you dare to deceive me, having previously performed meritorious deeds, why do you now demand them back?
Having spoken these words, if the person still continues to demand them and the bhikṣu returns [the goods], he commits no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing in advance that it is not being given as a gift, returns from a place where customs duties are collected, he commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu travels together with merchants, even saying:
"The Buddha does not permit one to receive a consignment of taxable goods and carry them past a customs checkpoint."
The merchant said to the bhikṣu, “I will not have you carry this item through the customs post; please guard it for me while I go briefly to see the customs official, and I shall return in a moment.”
The bhikṣu accepted the deposit, and the merchant went straight out beyond the frontier gate to wait for him.
After the bhikṣu had stayed there for a long time, having nowhere to deliver the goods, he took them across the gate himself.
If one passes through a customs checkpoint [with such goods], it is a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu travels on the same road as merchants, even though the Buddha has not permitted a bhikṣu to accept a taxable item as a deposit and carry it across a checkpoint, the merchant says:
"I am not having the bhikṣu carry this item across the checkpoint; I am merely having him guard it for me."
"I wish to see the gatekeeper for a moment and shall return immediately.
The bhikṣu then acted as the gatekeeper and said to him,
"If you do not return, I shall leave your belongings and depart."
The merchant again thought to himself:
"Even though the bhikṣu has spoken these words, he will ultimately not leave my goods behind.
He then went outside the pass and waited there for the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu remained there for a long time, but since the merchant did not return, he left the goods behind, passed through the customs checkpoint,
and departed. The merchant said to the bhikṣu,
"Where are my goods?"
The bhikṣu spoke with anger:
"Do you dare to mock me?
Did I not say earlier:..."
"If you do not return for a short while, shall I abandon your belongings and leave?
"Your belongings are still in their original place; you may go and retrieve them yourself.
If a bhikṣu acts in this manner, he does not commit an offense.
A bhikṣu was traveling as a companion with some merchants; eventually, the Buddha did not permit a bhikṣu to accept a taxable item in trust and carry it past a customs post.
The merchants said to the bhikṣu, "We are not having you carry goods past the customs post; we simply ask you to guard them for us."
"I wish to see the gatekeeper for a moment and shall return immediately.
The bhikṣu acted as his guardian and said to him:
"If you do not return, I shall take your belongings and entrust them to the gatekeeper."
The merchant thought to himself,
"Even though the bhikṣu speaks thus, how could I possibly entrust my goods to a border guard?
He then went outside the pass and waited there for the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu stayed for a long time, but the merchant did not return. He then took the goods and entrusted them to the customs officer, saying:
"If a merchant arrives with such appearance and such a name, you shall take the tax from him and return the remainder."
When the bhikṣu emerged from the pass, the merchant asked him,
"Where are my goods?
The bhikṣu replied angrily:
"Do you dare to mock me?
Did I not say earlier:
'If you do not return for a moment, I shall entrust your belongings to the gatekeeper'?"
"Your goods are now with the gatekeeper; you may go and collect them yourself.
If a bhikṣu acts in this manner, he does not commit an offense.
When a bhikṣu’s monastery is near a main road and a bhikṣu is walking up and down along the roadside, a merchant says to the bhikṣu:
"I have goods subject to duty; I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will carry them into the city for me.

The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit us to carry goods subject to duty past a customs post. However, I shall now teach you a skillful means: you may go with me through a breach in a wall, or between a fence, or through a drainage ditch; furthermore, you may entrust them to the cart of one whose goods are already taxed, or entrust them to a vessel belonging to the royal household, or entrust them to a maidservant’s water jar, or entrust them within the wool of a ram."
If one points out the way for another to enter [a restricted area] as described above, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
It is the same whether one points it out while inside or when outside.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is subject to taxation, yet knowingly passes an object that should be taxed, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If these taxable goods exceed [the limit] and reach the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu knows that the goods exceed [the limit] and they reach the full measure, he incurs a *pārājika*.
Even if he does not know that these goods are subject to tax, if they exceed [the limit] and reach the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is subject to taxation and also knows that he has exceeded the tax limit, he commits a pārājika offense.
If the value of the objects exceeds the limit, it is a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣu does not know that an object is subject to taxation and does not know that he has exceeded the tax limit, he commits a pārājika offense; however, if he has exceeded the limit without such knowledge, he does not commit an offense.
What items should not be taxed?
What items should be taxed?
The property of the World-Honored One’s disciples—monks and nuns—as well as all renunciants of other paths, is called that which should not be taxed.
If those who buy or sell are required to pay tax, this is called the "limit of the tax portion.
If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, touches an object belonging to this tax portion, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if the value reaches the full amount, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, touches time-medicine, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he moves that object, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if it is moved from its original place by the full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If two, three, or even many bhikṣus, with a thieving mind, touch time-medicine, they incur a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if they take it to its full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu sends another bhikṣu with a thieving mind to touch a medicinal drug at the proper time, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if [the drug] reaches its full measure, it is a *pārājika*.
If he sends two, three, or even many bhikṣus with a thieving mind to touch a medicinal drug at the proper time, they incur *vinayātikrama* offenses.
If it reaches its full measure, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If one who has been sent to receive [the medicine] sends another monk, and likewise a second, a third, or even many monks, when they touch the medicine with a thieving mind, they incur a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when they move it, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is removed from its original place to the full extent, it is a *pārājika*.
This applies likewise to [the offenses] of the night, the seven-day period, and for life, as well as to the pure and the impure.
If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with five factors and commits taking what is not given, he incurs a pārājika offense. What are these five? They are:
[the object is] complete, it has an owner, he knows it has an owner, he conceives a thieving mind, and he removes it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are five factors that, when fully present, constitute the taking of what is not given; if these are complete, it is a *pārājika*.
What are the five?

The perception that the object was not given, the perception that it is not one's own, the perception that it has an owner, the perception that the owner did not consent, and the perception that it is not being taken for temporary use.
There are five factors that, when fully present, do not constitute an offense of pārājika.
What are these five?

The perception of [the object] as belonging to another, the perception of oneself [as not the owner], the perception of there being no owner, the perception of [the act] being with consent, and the perception of it being for temporary use. These are called the five factors by which a bhikṣu’s taking what is not given does not constitute a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu takes what is not given—whether he goes to the east, south, west, north, or wherever one dwells in the open air—it is a pārājika offense in all cases.

If a bhikṣu takes what is not given, whether by dispatching a slave, a laborer, a friend, or by testing [the owner], or by doing so for the first time, or if he does so without knowledge or shame while perceiving it as pure, he commits an offense.
There is no offense if one is insane or mentally deranged;

in such cases, there is no guilt. Therefore it is said: "If a bhikṣu takes what is not given from a village or an open space, according to the value of the stolen object, the king may seize him, or kill him, or bind him, or drive him away, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
“Are you a thief? Are you a fool?
Thus, for a bhikṣu who takes what is not given in this manner, it is a pārājika offense; he should not live in community.

The Blessed One, while at Rājagṛha, in the sixth year after his enlightenment, during the second fortnight of the winter season on the tenth day, sitting facing east after his meal when two and a half shadows remained, established this precept for the elder Kumbhakāra-putra Daṇḍaka, concerning King Bimbisāra and the bhikṣu who wears rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika).
Having established [the precept], one should practice in accordance with it; this is called "conformity to the Dharma.
The section on the precept against stealing is concluded.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle Three. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Part Four of the Explanation of the Four Pārājika Dharmas: The Precept Against Killing. The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu in Vaiśālī who had been afflicted by illness for a long duration and had not recovered despite receiving treatment.
The bhikṣu who was tending to the sick grew weary in mind and said to the sick bhikṣu: "Elder!
I have tended to you for a long time; I am unable to attend upon my upādhyāya or ācārya, nor can I receive, recite, or contemplate the sūtras, or practice the Path."
"Venerable sir, my illness has been long-standing and cannot be cured despite treatment; I too am weary and distressed.
The sick bhikṣu said, "What should be done about this?"
"I too am afflicted by this unbearable pain; it would be well if you could kill me.
That bhikṣu then killed him.
When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
“Summon that bhikṣu.
Once he had come, the Buddha questioned him extensively about the aforementioned matter:
“Bhikṣu!...”
"Did you truly do this? He replied,
"It is indeed so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“Foolish man!”

Have you not often heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise those who practice the holy life, saying that one should practice loving-kindness in body, speech, and mind toward them, and provide for them with whatever they require?
How can you now, with your own hands, sever the life-root of another?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; one cannot nurture wholesome dharmas through such an act.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu should personally take the life of another with his own hand, this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense; he should not live in community.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was a sick bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time and could not be cured despite medical treatment.
The bhikṣu who was nursing the patient became weary and dissatisfied, and said to the sick bhikṣu:

"Elder, I have been attending to your illness for a long time; I have been unable to serve my upādhyāya and ācārya, nor have I been able to receive or recite the sūtras, or to contemplate and practice the Path."
"The Elder has been ill for a long time; he cannot be cured by medical treatment, and I too am weary and distressed.
The sick bhikṣu said:
"What can be done? I too suffer from this unbearable pain; it would be well if you could kill me.
The bhikṣu said:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not take life with one’s own hand.
The sick bhikṣu said:
“If you cannot kill me with your own hand, you may seek out someone who carries a blade for me.”
At that time, the bhikṣu who was attending to the patient went to the heretic Mṛgāra and said:
"Long-lived one!
If you can kill such-and-such a bhikṣu, I shall give you my robe and bowl."
He then killed him exactly as instructed and took his robes and bowl.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣu who was tending to the sick here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the monk who was tending to the sick:
"Did you truly do this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Foolish man!"

Have you not often heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise those who practice the holy life, saying that one should act with loving-kindness in body, speech, and mind toward them, providing for and supplying all their necessities?
"Why do you now seek someone with a sword to sever another's life-root?
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot nurture wholesome dharmas through such an act."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu takes life with his own hand, or seeks out one who holds a blade to cause the taking of life, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not dwell in communion.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was a monk who had been long ill and another monk who was tending to him. [The caregiver] spoke to the long-ill monk, saying:

"I am unable to receive the scriptures, recite them, contemplate them, or practice the Path. Moreover, when I seek from others food, drink, and medicinal decoctions according to your illness, everyone grows weary of me, and I too am exhausted and distressed."
The sick bhikṣu said, “What should I do?
I too suffer from this unbearable pain; it would be well if you could kill me.”
That bhikṣu said,
"Have you not heard that the World-Honored One has established a precept stating that one must not kill a person with one's own hand?
The sick bhikṣu replied:
"If that is so, then call for a man with a sword to come to me.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"Have you not heard the precept established by the World-Honored One, that one must not seek out a man with a sword to have him kill someone?"
The sick bhikṣu said,
"What should be done now?
The bhikṣu who was nursing him replied:

"You merely seek to live for yourself and do not wish to die; yet if you wish to die, you already possess a blade with which you may kill yourself, or you may drink poison, hang yourself with a rope, throw yourself into a pit, leap into fire, or embrace a stone to sink into a deep pool—the methods for committing suicide are indeed numerous."
Having spoken these words of praise, he withdrew and went outside.
At that time, the sick bhikṣu subsequently committed suicide.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu who attended to the sick.
When he had come, the Buddha questioned him extensively on the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:

“Have you not often heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise those who practice the holy life, saying that one should practice loving-kindness in body, loving-kindness in speech, and loving-kindness in mind toward them, providing for and supplying whatever they require?”
Why do you now praise death and extol death?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha.
One cannot nurture wholesome dharmas by means of such matters.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
