"Assemble all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu takes life with his own hand, seeks out and provides a weapon to a killer, instructs another to die, or praises death, this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, after the non-Buddhist ascetic Māṭhara had killed a bhikṣu, he was overcome with great distress and thought to himself:
"How is it that I have now taken the life of one who practices the holy life and committed such an evil deed?"
"After my life ends, will I not fall into the evil realms and enter hell?
At that time, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, constantly employing skillful means to increase all manner of evils, spoke from the air to the non-Buddhist practitioner, saying:
"Do not be distressed or fearful of falling into the evil realms."
"Why is this? What you have now done is to liberate people from suffering and affliction, delivering those who have not yet been delivered; your merit is immeasurable.
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioner immediately thought to himself:
"I shall gain great merit by killing this bhikṣu, and I will cause the devas to rejoice and praise me for it.
Having formed this thought, he later took a sharp sword and went to the monastic quarters and the walking paths, shouting everywhere to the bhikṣus:
"Who wishes to be free from suffering?"
"Who seeks deliverance?
I am able to free them from suffering and enable them to cross over.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to the bhikṣus. Then, as the bhikṣus practiced this contemplation, they became weary of their bodies and afflicted by suffering; among them, many committed suicide by binding themselves with ropes, ingesting poison, stabbing themselves with knives, throwing themselves into pits, or leaping into fires.
Furthermore, those who were killed by the outsider Mṛgāra at various times were not merely one or two people, nor three, four, or five; they numbered ten, and even up to sixty.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, the World-Honored One sat amidst the Saṃgha, surrounded by his attendants, intending to perform the Poṣadha ceremony.
Observing that the assembly of monks was sparse, the World-Honored One looked around to his left and right and asked Ānanda:
"Why is the community of bhikṣus so thin this day? Why do we not see such-and-such bhikṣus?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you have previously taught the bhikṣus the contemplation of impurity and praised the merit of practicing this contemplation.”

These bhikṣus diligently practiced the meditation on impurity; having cultivated this meditation, they came to feel extreme revulsion toward their own bodies. Some took their own lives with blades, while others even allowed the non-Buddhist ascetic Mṛgaśṛṅga to end their lives. Within half a month, as many as sixty people had passed away, all of those who failed to attend being deceased.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will further expound other teachings, so as not to cause the bhikṣus to grow weary of their bodies and commit suicide, and so that the noble sages may remain long in this world to benefit devas and humans.
Thereupon the Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is another samādhi that enables the bhikṣus to practice with ease and joy, without becoming weary of the body.
What is this samādhi through which they practice with ease and joy, without becoming weary of the body?"
Regarding what is called mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*): Ānanda,
how does a bhikṣu practice mindfulness of breathing so as to realize it, achieve its perfection, and dwell in peace?

If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a town or village, when the time arrives, he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, and enters the town for alms. Restraining body, speech, and mind, he abides well in mindfulness of the body; his mind does not wander or become distracted, but he constantly practices right concentration, keeping the sense faculties restrained as he enters the town for alms.

Having finished his almsround, he returns to that secluded place and sits down in a composed posture—whether on open ground, in mountain ravines, in rocky caves, or among burial mounds—spreading out grass and sitting upright.

Having removed the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, and having extinguished all obstacles, one fixes the mind upon the breath with the clarity of mental wisdom:
when the breath enters, one knows the breath enters; when the breath exits, one knows the breath exits;
when the breath enters long, one knows the breath enters long; when the breath exits long, one knows the breath exits long.
When the exhalation is long, one knows the exhalation is long; when the inhalation is short, one knows the inhalation is short;
when the inhalation pervades the entire body, one knows the inhalation pervades the entire body; when the exhalation pervades the entire body, one knows the exhalation pervades the entire body;

when the inhalation brings about the relinquishing of bodily formations, one knows the inhalation brings about the relinquishing of bodily formations; [and so on] for the exhalation bringing about the relinquishing of bodily formations.

At the time of equanimity, he knows the equanimity of bodily formations during exhalation; at the time of joy during inhalation, he knows the joy of inhalation; at the time of joy during exhalation, he knows the joy of exhalation;
at the time of pleasure during inhalation, he knows the pleasure of inhalation; at the time of pleasure during exhalation, he knows the pleasure of exhalation;
at the time of mental formations during inhalation, he knows the mental formations of inhalation; and at the time of mental formations during exhalation, he knows the mental formations of exhalation.

At that time, when he knows the mental activity of exhaling, he knows the mental activity of exhaling; when he relinquishes the mental activity of inhaling, he knows he is relinquishing the mental activity of inhaling;
when he relinquishes the mental activity of exhaling, he knows he is relinquishing the mental activity of exhaling.

When he knows the mind while inhaling, he knows he is knowing the mind while inhaling; when he knows the mind while exhaling, he knows he is knowing the mind while exhaling. When the mind is gladdened while inhaling...
When the mind is gladdened during inhalation, one knows the mind is gladdened during inhalation; when the mind is gladdened during exhalation, one knows the mind is gladdened during exhalation.

When the mind is concentrated during inhalation, one knows the mind is concentrated during inhalation; when the mind is concentrated during exhalation, one knows the mind is concentrated during exhalation.
When the mind is liberated during inhalation, one knows the mind is liberated during inhalation; when the mind is liberated during exhalation, one knows the mind is liberated during exhalation.
With a mind at peace and liberated, when inhaling, he knows he is inhaling impermanently; when exhaling, he knows he is exhaling impermanently.
When the inhalation ceases, he knows the inhalation has ceased; when the exhalation ceases, he knows the exhalation has ceased.
When the inhalation is free from desire, he knows the inhalation is free from desire; when the exhalation is free from desire, he knows the exhalation is free from desire.

At that time, one knows the out-breath when it is free from desire; one knows the cessation of the in-breath when the in-breath ceases, and one knows the cessation of the out-breath when the out-breath ceases.
It is thus, Ānanda!

"One who forms such a thought is called one who is happy, well-trained, and not excessively weary of the body; such a person causes the noble ones to remain long in the world for the benefit of devas and humans.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu takes the life of a person with his own hand, seeks out and provides a weapon to a killer, instructs them to die, or praises death, saying:
"O man! What is the use of living such a wretched life?"
"Death is better than life.

With such an intention and such a thought, he employs means to praise death and intentionally causes that person to die, and not anyone else; this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in community with others.
"A bhikṣu" refers to one who has received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty; this is called a bhikṣu.
"With one's own hand" means by one's own body, by a part of the body, or by the power of the body.
"By one's own body" means: if one kills a person by crushing them with one's entire body, it is a *pārājika*;

this is called "by one's own body. "By a part of the body" means: if one kills a person with a hand, an elbow, a foot, a knee, or any other part of the body, it is a *pārājika*; this is called "a part of the body."
Regarding "the power of the body": if one kills a person by hurling from a distance a staff, a stone, or a brick, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense; this is called the power of the body.
Regarding "a person": it refers to a sentient being possessing life, categorized within the human realm (*manuṣyagati*).
"To take life" means to cause the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of another not to continue and for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to disperse; this is called taking life.
"To seek" means to seek out a person who holds a blade, whether they be male or female, large or small, a layperson or a monastic.
"Swords" refers to blades such as swords, halberds, long knives, short knives, spears, lances, iron wheels, and all other sharp instruments down to needles and the like.
"Praising death" means saying:
"What is the use of living this evil life?"
"To die is better than to live.
Such an intention is a murderous intention; such a thought is a murderous thought.
To praise the joy of death is to cause that person to die.
"No other" means that because of this [offense], the bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community.

A *pārājika* is one who has retreated, fallen away, and lost from the knowledge of the Dharma, having no share in the fruits of the path; likewise, up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), he has retreated, fallen away, and lost from these various knowledges, having no share in the fruits of the path—this is called a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, "pārājika" refers to falling away and descending from nirvāṇa, such that one lacks the portion for realizing the fruits [of the path]; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, "pārājika" refers to being separated from non-killing and falling away and descending; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, regarding *pārājika*: a transgression that cannot be confessed and purified is called *pārājika*.

A bhikṣu who kills a human being does so either by using a weapon, by poison, by applying a lethal substance, by inducing vomiting, by administering a purgative, by causing an abortion, by describing the victim's faults, or by praising death.
"Blades" refers to swords, large and small knives, and even needles and the like.
When one moves the body with the intent to kill, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
when one makes physical contact with the other's body, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If death results from this [act] and no other, it is a *pārājika* offense;
this is called killing by means of a blade.
Regarding killing by means of poison, there are three kinds of poisons:
There are natural poisons, there are prepared poisons, and there are sorcery poisons.

As for natural poisons, there are poisons produced by the soil of certain lands; for example, the *śṛṅgaka* poison produced in the country of Vīra, and the *kālakūṭa* poison produced in the country of Ujjayanī—these are called natural poisons.
Regarding "those who prepare poisonous drugs": it is like a hunter who prepares poisonous drugs by compounding roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves into a medicine;

this is called preparing poisonous drugs. Regarding "poisonous charms and drugs": these include snake venom, *nākulī* poison, cat poison, rat poison, dog poison, brown bear poison, human poison, and various other such poisons; these are called poisonous charms and drugs.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, takes these three kinds of medicine, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when it reaches the person's body, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the person dies because of this medicine, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called killing by poison.
Regarding killing by applying medicine: if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, takes poison in his hand, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if he applies it to the person's body, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If he dies because of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "killing by applying medicine.
As for "killing by inducing vomiting": if a bhikṣu, desiring to kill a person, prepares an emetic with the following thought:
"If I give this medicine to him with the intent that it shall cause him to vomit up the pus and blood within his internal organs," one incurs an offense of *pāyattika*;
if one gives the medicine to him [without such intent], one incurs an offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If, because of this medicine, the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "administering purgatives": when a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, prepares a purgative, he thinks:
"I shall give this medicine to him so that he may purge pus and blood, and purge his internal organs."
If she does so, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if she gives her that medicine, she commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if she dies as a result of that purgative medicine, she commits a *pārājika* offense.
This is called killing by means of inferior medicine.
Regarding "killing by causing an abortion": if a bhikṣu intends to kill a woman and the fetus is aborted, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he intends to cause an abortion and the mother dies, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one intends to kill one's mother and the mother dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one intends to cause an abortion and the fetus—whether as a part of the body or as a whole—is expelled, including the loss of its physical faculties and life-faculties, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If a person causes the miscarriage of an animal's fetus, they incur a *vyatikrama* offense.
This is called killing by causing an abortion.
As for the description of its characteristics: if a bhikṣu says to another person:
"I see now that you will certainly die; you may as well commit suicide—what is the use of living such a miserable life?
If, because of these words, the person dies, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, he said:
"As I have seen in my dream, you shall certainly die.
He spoke yet again:
"I have heard the cries of jackals, earth-owls, crows, and magpies; now I see that your facial complexion has changed and your nose is crooked—you are surely going to die.
You might as well commit suicide; what is the use of living in such misery?"
If this person dies as a result of this [act], that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Again, he asked:
"How many years old are you?"
He replied,
"I am so many years old.
He spoke again:
"I understand the nature of all life; you will certainly die this year. It would be better for you to commit suicide yourself—what is the use of living such a wretched life?
If, because of these words, the person dies, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Again he asked:
"To which lunar mansion do you belong?
He replied:
"I belong to such-and-such a star," he said.
Then [the other] replied:
"I know that star; you must surely die now, without a doubt."
"Why do you not commit suicide? What is the use of living in such suffering?
Because of these words, that person dies, and the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, he asks again:
"What is your name? He replied, "My name is so-and-so."
He spoke again:
"I understand all names; you shall certainly die.
He asked once more:
"What is your clan?
He replied, "My clan is so-and-so."
He spoke again:
"I understand all names and surnames; you shall surely die now.
He asked once more:
"What do you eat? He replied,
"I eat such food as this."
He then instructed him to vomit it up; once he had done so, he said:
"If you eat this food, you will certainly die, without a doubt.
He asked again:
"Where did you eat? He replied, "I ate at such-and-such a place."
He further instructed him to vomit it up; once he had done so, he said:
"There is poison in such-and-such a place; you will surely die now.
Why do you not kill yourself? What is the use of living in such suffering?"
If that person dies as a result of this, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, describes their physical characteristics, he incurs a vinayātikrama offense;
if the other person employs means to commit suicide, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one commits suicide, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
this is called "speaking of killing.
Regarding the praise of the killer and the fruit of giving and precepts for the donor, a bhikṣu asked:
"Do you practice giving? He replied, "I give."
The bhikṣu said:
"Since you have already performed meritorious deeds, you will certainly be reborn in a good realm.
Why do you not take your own life? What is the use of living in such suffering?"
This is called one who practices giving and precepts.
A bhikṣu asks a person:
"Do you uphold the precepts?"
He replied, “I maintain the precepts.
[The Buddha said,] “The World-Honored One has taught that maintaining the precepts leads to rebirth in two places:”
Whether among the gods or among humans, what is the use of such a miserable life?
This is called praising the fruit of upholding the precepts.
The bhikṣu said:

“You have already attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and shall not fall into the evil destinies; at most, you will come and go among gods and humans seven times before reaching the end of suffering and closing the gates to the evil destinies.”
"Why do you not commit suicide? What is the use of living in such suffering?
He further said, "You have already attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin; by returning to this world but once more, you shall bring an end to all suffering."
"Why do you not commit suicide? What is the use of living in such suffering?
He spoke again:
"You have already attained the stage of Anāgāmin; by not returning to this world, you shall bring an end to suffering."
"Why do you not commit suicide? What is the use of living in such suffering?
He replied again:
"I have already attained arhatship; lust, anger, and delusion are exhausted. I am no longer subject to the afflictions and have attained mastery over my mind."
"Why do you not commit suicide? What is the use of living in such suffering?
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill someone, praises the fruits of giving and precepts, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he employs means to encourage that person to commit suicide, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one has committed suicide, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Whether by walking [into danger], or by remaining alone and desisting [from life], or by the *vidyā-mantra*, or by medicinal powder, or by *umāntu*, or by falling into a pit, or by *apacīmantu*, or by showing the way [to a precipice], or by a river, or by a high official, or by a monastery, or by a tiger, or by a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).

Regarding walking: if ten or twenty people are traveling together along a road, and a bhikṣu harbors a prior grudge or resentment and intends to harm the person in front but mistakenly harms the person in the middle, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he intends to harm the person in the middle but mistakenly harms the person behind, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he intends to harm the person behind but mistakenly harms the person in the middle, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one intends to harm a middle person but mistakenly harms a person before them, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if one intends to harm a person before them and actually harms that person, it is a *pārājika*;
if one intends to harm a middle or a later person and actually harms that middle or later person, it is a *pārājika*.
If one possesses the intent to kill toward all beings, one incurs a *pārājika* offense according to the person harmed;
this is called "committing killing.
Regarding "laying a trap": if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, lays a trap, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline) at the moment he sets it along the path.
When that person experiences pain and suffering, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if that person dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "killing by solitary abandonment."
Regarding the *vidyā-mantra*: if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, performs a *vidyā-mantra*, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense at the moment he performs the spell with a harmful mind;
when he causes that person to experience terror, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if that person dies, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This is called killing by means of a *vīdara* spell.
Regarding killing by means of powdered medicine: if a bhikṣu, desiring to kill a person, prepares a medicinal powder while forming this thought:
"I shall use this medicine to kill that person."
If [the medicine] is applied to his body, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he dies, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called killing by means of powdered medicine.
Regarding *umantu*: if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, prepares *umantu* on the road, at the moment the bhikṣu acts with the murderous intent, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when that person experiences the pain, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called killing by means of a trap. Regarding killing by a pitfall:

if a bhikṣu, desiring to kill a person, constructs a pit in the middle of a path and places various sharp stakes within it, covering it over with grass and soil so that the victim falls into it and dies—when he performs this act with the intent to kill, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If the victim experiences pain, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if they die, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called killing by means of a pitfall.

Regarding "placing an *apacīman* [poison] to kill": if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill a person, places an *apacīman* on a path, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense at the moment he acts with the murderous intent;
if the victim experiences pain, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the victim dies, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This is called killing by means of a signal.
Regarding killing by showing the way: if a bhikṣu is walking up and down along a path, someone comes and asks the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir!..."
"I wish to go to such-and-such a village; where does the road lie?
A bhikkhu who previously harbored resentment toward that person then thought:
"I have now found my opportunity with this man; I shall show him the wrong path so that he dies, ensuring that not a single one survives."

If she points out evil paths—such as the dangers of kings, the dangers of lions, tigers, and wolves, or the dangers of venomous stings—and when she indicates these various evil paths, she incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if they suffer pain [as a result], she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if they die, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called killing by pointing out the way.
Regarding killing by a river: if a bhikṣu is walking up and down on the bank of a river, someone comes and asks him, "Venerable sir!..."
"I wish to go to such-and-such a place; by which ford should I cross?
That bhikṣu, having previously harbored resentment and ill-will toward that person, thought to himself:
"I have now found this man's vulnerability; I shall show him a place that is not a crossing, so that not even a single person may escape."

If she points out places that are not safe for crossing—such as whirlpools, submerged rocks, rapids, or places infested with *śiśumāra* crocodiles; or if she points out the path to the opposite bank where there is the danger of royal prohibition, the danger of bandits, or the danger of lions, tigers, wolves, poisonous insects, and the like—when she points out such unsafe places, she incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If he suffers pain [as a result], she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If he dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "killing by the river.

As for the "minister," it refers to a minister who is tyrannical and unrighteous, greedily seizing the property of others for his own sustenance, fearing neither punishment nor retribution, and indulging in self-indulgence and negligence while thinking to himself:
"I would rather be a crow today than a peacock tomorrow."
Upon hearing this, the king had him arrested and imprisoned, charging him with a crime;
out of fear of death, he offered all his wealth and possessions to ransom his life.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who frequented the man’s house and went to comfort him, inquiring after the family’s hardships and well-being.
His wife replied, "The master of the house has been imprisoned for some offense; how could he have any pleasure?

You should know, Ācārya, that our master now fears his crime will lead to death, so he has spent all his wealth to ransom his life. If his money is exhausted, we shall soon be destitute and have no means to support ourselves."
The bhikṣu said, "Do not be distressed;
I shall speak to your husband so that he will not spend the wealth.
He then went to the prison and comforted her, saying:
"Are you free from illness?
May you have a long life!
Seeing the bhikṣu approach, the minister was filled with great joy and said:
“Ācārya! What have you heard outside?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have heard that you are about to die, and I wish to take all my family wealth to ransom your life.
If you do so, your future wife and children will surely suffer poverty, hunger, and cold, and they will be forced to beg; furthermore, a foul reputation will spread throughout your household."
The minister replied,
"What should be done? The bhikṣu said:
"This king is unrighteous; even if you were to deliver all your wealth to him, he would still not let you live. Be careful not to give him anything.
You should simply leave it to his judgment."
If that minister agrees with his words, the bhikṣu incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama);
if the victim suffers pain, he incurs a thullaccaya offense;
if the victim dies, it is a pārājika offense.
If the minister hears those words of the bhikṣu, he replies:
"The ācārya is my friend, yet he begrudges his wealth and will not use it to save me."
"After my death, even if the sun and moon were not to rise, that would not be a cause for my concern, much less any other matter!
Ācārya, you may return; reflect upon the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, the good or the evil, of the Buddha's words, but do not involve yourself in matters concerning the Venerable One."
At that moment, he committed an offense against the Vinaya.
The minister immediately reflected:
"As the bhikṣu says, this king is unrighteous; even if I am given all the wealth, he will surely kill me."
Since I shall die in vain, my wife and children will have no means to survive from hunger and cold; the disgrace to our family is more painful than death itself.
I shall now bear this burden myself and will not give you any wealth.
Because he did not immediately follow the monk’s words, the person died; since the monk had previously employed such expedient means, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Suppose there is someone who violates the king’s law; a watchman captures him, binds him, and delivers him to the king. The king commands that he be taken away and punished according to his offense.
Then, the executioner adorns the offender’s head with *kapila* flowers, binds his two hands behind his back, beats a drum, blows a conch shell, and makes a proclamation as he parades him around.
Having made the proclamation, they led him out through the city gate toward the place of execution.

At that time, there was an elder (*mahallaka*) bhikṣu who did not well understand the characteristics of the precepts; out of compassion for the suffering of this criminal, he said to the executioner:
"This man is to be pitied; do not cause him further agony. Take your blade and make a single incision for him."
At that time, the executioner replied,
"As you command," and taking a sharp blade, he inflicted a single wound upon him.
This bhikṣu, the mahallaka, commits a pārājika offense.
If the executioner replies to the bhikṣu, saying:
"What is the use of your knowing this?"
"As the King has commanded, I shall carry it out myself; you may now return and contemplate the Buddha's words.
At that moment, he committed an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
The executioner then immediately reflected:
"He used the words of a bhikṣu to inflict a single wound.
Because he did not immediately follow the words of the bhikṣu, this mahallaka bhikṣu incurred a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called a great minister.
Regarding the monastery quarters: when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they should receive rooms in the proper order.
At that time, the bhikṣu in charge of the quarters had a prior grievance with the visiting bhikṣu, and he thought to himself:
"I have now found an opportunity against my son; I shall give him a ruined house so that he will surely die.

He then gave him a dilapidated house where the pillars and walls were collapsing, near the terrifying place of Vitatā, near the abode of the Pūtana malevolent spirits, and near the place of venomous snakes.
If she shows it to her at the time of giving, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
when she experiences the pain, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if she dies, it is a *pārājika*.

That visiting bhikṣu rose early in the morning and asked the resident bhikṣu for items to wash his hands. The resident bhikṣu took bees, scorpions, centipedes, vipers, and snakes, placed them in a jar, covered its mouth, and said to the visiting bhikṣu:
"In this jar are items for washing your hands; take and use them as you please."
When the visiting bhikṣu takes [the organ], he commits a *vinayātikrama*;
when it experiences pain, he commits a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it dies, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called "killing within the saṃghārāma.
As for the tiger: there was a place in the wilderness where tigers frequently harmed people. At one time, the community gathered in one location and held this discussion, saying:
"Venerable elders!..."
"In this araṇya dwelling, there is a tiger that fears it will harm people; who among you can subdue this tiger?
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who harbored a grudge against another bhikṣu and said to the crowd, "I can subdue the tiger."

At dusk, that bhikṣu took up his bow and arrows and went out; at that time, the bhikṣu who had been the object of his resentment, wearing yellow robes with a darkened face, came out to the place for defecation and urination.
If that bhikṣu, at that time, intending to kill a bhikṣu, kills a tiger, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if intending to kill a tiger, he kills a bhikṣu, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if intending to kill a bhikṣu, he kills a bhikṣu, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one intends to kill a tiger and kills a tiger, it is a *pāyattika*.

If there is the intent to kill both [a human and a tiger] and one harms them, one incurs an offense according to the being killed: for a bhikṣu, it is a *pārājika*; for the tiger, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is what is called a "tiger.

As for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there were those who worshipped the sun and moon; when an eclipse occurred, groups of Brahmins would pursue one another, carrying weapons and vessels in their hands, shouting loudly as they went to rescue the sun and moon. Passing by the side of a monastery, they saw the bhikṣus and spoke with anger:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are partisans of the asuras; we shall now kill them!"
When the bhikṣus heard these evil sounds, having heard them, they immediately struck the ghaṇṭā to assemble the saṃgha. Some bhikṣus said:
"Today we must make a pact together to subdue these wicked and heterodox outsiders, so that not a single one shall remain alive."
Because they have made an illegal agreement, the entire Saṃgha incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
if that person suffers pain, the entire Saṃgha incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he dies, the entire Saṃgha incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If they make a mutual agreement, saying:

"Do not cause him to die; let him only suffer pain so that he may reform his evil ways and contemplate the good," then by making such an agreement, the entire Saṃgha incurs an offense of Vinaya-transgression (vāittiya).
When he experiences the pain, the entire Saṃgha incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Elders!..."
"One should not harm others, nor should one inflict pain upon others.
As the Blessed One said:
'O Bhikṣus!'"

If enemies or bandits were to cut and mangle one's body with saws or knives, at that time one should not give rise to an evil mind, nor should one utter harsh words toward others; rather, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of altruism, and a mind of patience.

"O bhikṣus, you should together contemplate the World-Honored One’s *Sakalikasūtra*. By employing even a slight expedient, you can practice patience; thereafter, simply secure your doors firmly and raise your voices in a great shout to terrify those heretics."
“There is no offense.
Since the entire Saṃgha has collectively made a formal agreement and vow, the entire Saṃgha is without offense.
There was a bhikṣu who struck the son of a brāhmaṇa until he was on the verge of death, whereupon he thought to himself:
"If this man dies, he will destroy the Dharma of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; we must now seek a physician to treat him and cure him.
If another bhikṣu says this to that bhikṣu: "What are you doing?"
He replied, “I struck this brahmin until he was on the verge of death, and I thought to myself:
‘If he were to die, it would violate the law of the Śākya-sons; I now wish to seek a physician to treat him and restore him to health.’”
If another bhikṣu says,
"You go and seek a physician; I shall keep watch over him for you," and after that bhikṣu has departed,
the other bhikṣu subsequently brings about the end of his life.
Striking the bhikṣu first constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense;
killing the bhikṣu afterwards constitutes a pārājika offense.
This is called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of killing a person, takes up a knife, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if he touches that person's body, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If two, three, or even more persons, for the purpose of killing a human being, take up a blade, they incur a *vyatikrama* offense;
if [the victim] dies, they incur a *pārājika* offense.
If one bhikṣu dispatches another bhikṣu for the purpose of killing a person, when [the latter] takes up a blade, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
upon the death [of the victim], it is a *pārājika*.
If one dispatches two persons, three persons, or even many bhikṣus for the purpose of killing someone, at the moment they seize a knife, they incur a *vyatikrama* offense;
upon the victim's death, it is a *pārājika*.
If a monk who has been sent on a mission for the purpose of killing further dispatches another monk to seize a sword, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if [the victim] dies, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
In this manner, for the second and third times, and even when dispatching many bhikṣus to seize a sword, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if [the victim] dies, it is a *pārājika*.

The same applies to killing by poison, killing by applying [poisonous] ointments, killing by inducing vomiting or purging, killing by causing miscarriage, killing by describing [one's] characteristics, and killing by praising [the victim].
If one kills a person while possessing five factors, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
What are the five?
First, a person;
second, the perception of a person.
Third, the arousal of skillful means;
fourth, the intent to kill;
fifth, the severing of life.
These are called the five matters.

Whether one dispatches a slave to kill, or a servant, or a friend, or acts as a trial, or acts for the first time, if one lacks wisdom and shame and perceives it as pure, one commits an offense in all such cases.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged;
thus there is no guilt. Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu takes the life of a person with his own hand, seeks out and provides a knife to a killer, instructs them to die, or praises death..."
"Alas! What is the use of living such a wretched life?
Death is better than life."

If, forming such an intention and such a thought, one uses skillful means to praise death and intentionally causes that person to die, and no other, this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

In the city of Vaiśālī, on the ninth day of the third fortnight of winter in the sixth year after attaining Buddhahood, before the midday meal, the World-Honored One sat facing north when the shadow was one and a half man-lengths; for the sake of the many bhikṣus who were tending to the sick and because of the outsider Mṛgāra, he established this precept.
"Once a rule has been established, one should practice in accordance with it; this is called 'conformity to the Dharma' (*anulomika-dharma*).
The third precept is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, in a certain village, two groups were observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*). When one group had finished their retreat, they returned to Śrāvastī, paid their respects to the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side."
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monk,
from where have you come after your summer retreat?"
He replied,
"I am observing the rains retreat in a certain village.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Was your summer retreat pleasant?
Was almsfood easy to obtain?
Did you practice the Path in accordance with the Dharma?”
“Once the retreat has concluded, will you receive the robes for the retreat?
Will the lay devotees come and go frequently?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

We have spent the summer retreat in comfort and practiced the Path according to the Dharma; however, almsfood is difficult to obtain, robes and requisites are insufficient, and the lay devotees do not come and go frequently.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“How can those who have left the household life ever obtain worldly benefits?
Bhikṣus, you should know that the eight worldly dharmas always follow worldly people, and worldly people also always follow these eight worldly dharmas.”
What are the eight?
First, gain; second, loss; third, praise; fourth, blame; fifth, fame; sixth, infamy; seventh, pleasure; and eighth, suffering.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!
The foolish worldling has heard little and knows little; his mind is not disciplined within the True Dharma, and his mind has not yet attained understanding regarding the dharmas of the noble ones.
If worldly gain arises, one should not fail to observe that the arising of such worldly gain is itself a phenomenon subject to impermanence and decay.
If a phenomenon is truly impermanent and subject to decay, one should know that although this gain has arisen, it will quickly perish and remain no longer.
If one does not contemplate this true meaning, it constitutes the unsubstantial wisdom of ordinary beings that conforms to worldly dharmas.
Thus, regarding what is disadvantageous up to pleasure and pain, they likewise do not contemplate that although such pleasure arises, it is itself a phenomenon subject to impermanence and extinction.
If phenomena are truly impermanent and subject to decay, one should know that although pleasure and pain arise, they quickly perish and do not abide.
If one does not contemplate this true meaning, such a person is a worldling lacking genuine wisdom who merely conforms to worldly conventions.

Monks, you should know that because one does not contemplate these worldly phenomena, if worldly gain arises, attachment is produced; if gain does not arise, distress is produced. This is likewise true for pleasure and pain.

"Monks! In this way, the three feelings increase. When the three feelings have increased, the four clingings blaze up. Because the four clingings blaze up, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as well as mental agitation and madness. In this manner, the accumulation of the mass of suffering arises and expands."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that a noble disciple who is learned and wise is well-tamed in mind regarding the True Dharma and attains understanding and liberation through the noble teachings.”
Once worldly gain has arisen, one should skillfully observe that all such worldly gains which arise are of a nature that is impermanent and subject to decay and extinction.

If a phenomenon is truly impermanent and subject to decay and extinction, one should know that although this gain arises, it quickly perishes and does not abide; even pleasure and pain are entirely like this.

"Monks, you should know that for one who practices this contemplation, if worldly gain arises, no greed or attachment is produced; if worldly gain does not arise, the mind feels no sorrow or distress. This applies likewise even to pleasure and pain."

"When love and hatred do not arise, and all perceptions are compliant and free from sorrow and grief, even unto the cessation of the aggregate of suffering—the suffering of suffering—one attains Nirvāṇa.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Gain and loss, defamation and fame, Praise and blame, as well as pain and pleasure;..."
The eight worldly conditions constantly pursue one another, coming and going like a turning wheel.
These eight conditions are not solid; they are subject to decay and transformation.
Therefore, the noble disciple holds fast to the mirror of impermanence for illumination.
Contemplate the eight worldly dharmas: they do not pause for even a moment.
Amidst the four types of gain and pleasure, he is never moved;
yet when encountering defamation, disparagement, or slander, he does not let grief or distress enter his mind.
"One who is free from the eight worldly dharmas is called a wise person;
such a one can emerge from the river of desire and cross over the ocean of birth and death.
At that time, all the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were greatly rejoiced and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
It is marvelous how you have skillfully taught the eight worldly dharmas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses the threefold unimpeded penetration; his brilliance of wisdom is like the full moon. What is there to marvel at in his teaching on the eight worldly dharmas?”
"In a former time, while in the realm of animals, I was a parrot who could explain the eight worldly dharmas to other birds;
this is truly marvelous. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "Was it indeed so?"
The Buddha said: "It is so!
In a past age, there was a king who raised two parrots."
One was named Lada and the other was named Pāla; both understood human speech.
The king cherished them dearly, housing them in a golden cage and always eating from the same table as they did.

At that time, there was a high minister who presented a young monkey to the Great King. As human nature delights in novelty, the King immediately took affectionate interest in it, providing food and drink for its sustenance even more lavishly than he did for his parrot.
Then the young parrot Pārāvatika spoke these verses to Lāḍa:
“Formerly we ate together with the king, The finest delicacies in the world;
Now they have been seized by a monkey— It is fitting that we fly away together into the void.”
At that time, Raudrākṣa replied:
"All these things are likewise impermanent.
This monkey will, before long, lose this gain and honor as well."
He then spoke these verses for Pāra:
"Gain and loss, defamation and fame, Praise and blame, as well as suffering and pleasure— These are all impermanent phenomena;
Why should they cause you grief or joy?"
At that time, Pāra again spoke in verse:
"Whatever the eyes behold brings no joy; there is not a single sign of delight.
One hears only sounds of reproach; never is there praise."
"I harbor the aspirations of a soaring bird; why must I undergo such suffering?
This monkey, when young, had glossy fur and would leap and bound about, being a source of amusement for people.
Gradually, as it grew larger, its feathers became withered and ragged, making it loathsome for people to behold;
it stood on its hind legs, bared its teeth, and terrified small children. At that time, the young parrot Rāṣṭra spoke this verse to Pāla:
"With ears pricked and face gaping, It snarls to frighten the children."
"Sitting idly will only breed sin and trouble; before long, you will lose your gains and offerings.
As the monkey grew larger, the king’s affection for him gradually faded, and he immediately commanded his attendants to tie him to the pillar of the horse stall.
At that time, the prince was young; he took food and drink in his hands and went to where the monkey was.
The monkey sought food, but the prince would not give it to him. The monkey, filled with rage, tore at the prince’s face, wounding him, and rent his clothes to shreds.
The prince was struck with terror and raised his voice, crying out loudly.
The king asked those nearby,
"Why is my son weeping?"
The bystanders reported the matter to the king.
The king became greatly enraged and ordered his men to beat the bird to death, cast it into a ditch, and let Manda eat it.
At that time, the young parrot Pāla immediately spoke a verse to Rāva for him:
"You are a wise one who foresees what is yet to come;
whereas beasts, lacking knowledge, perish and become food for the mandārava."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, was that young male parrot Rāta anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
The young *pāla* parrot was none other than Ānanda.

When I was a parrot, I was able to explain to him that the eight worldly dharmas are impermanent, subject to change, and cannot be maintained for long; how much more so now that I have attained perfect enlightenment—what is there to marvel at in my explaining the eight worldly dharmas?
Then, when that second group had completed their *vassa* retreat, they immediately came to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
Knowing [the answer], the World-Honored One asked intentionally:
"Monks, from where have you come after your *vassa*?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One,
we are observing the rains retreat at such-and-such a place.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Was your summer retreat pleasant?
Were you weary from practicing the Path?"
Is almsfood easy to obtain?
Have you received the robes for the summer retreat at its conclusion?
Do the lay devotees come and go frequently?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

“We have spent the summer retreat in comfort; we have practiced the Path without fatigue; almsfood was easy to obtain; we received much clothing for the retreat; and many lay devotees (upāsakas) have come and gone.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:

"By what causes and conditions did two assemblies dwell together in dependence upon a single village for the rains retreat, yet one assembly alone received abundant offerings while the other did not?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By means of immeasurable skillful methods, we have praised the Three Jewels; we have also constantly praised the great disciples of the Buddha, such as the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as well as praising ourselves for the merits we have cultivated.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
“Is what you have praised truly so?
[He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"What I have praised regarding the Three Jewels and the Venerable Śāriputra and others is true; my self-praise is not true.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
This is an evil deed.
Why, for the sake of bodily gain and offerings, do you falsely and in vain praise yourself?

It would be better to consume ashes and charcoal, to swallow excrement and soil, or to have one's belly ripped open by a sharp blade, than to obtain offerings by falsely claiming superhuman attainments.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have always praised having few desires and being content; why do you have such great desire, being difficult to satisfy, seeking extensively without weariness?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas by means of this."
After the Blessed One had rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways,

while the bhikṣus were observing the rains retreat in that village, those who entered the village for alms and proclaimed their own virtues found it easy to obtain food, whereas those who did not proclaim themselves found it extremely difficult to obtain any at all.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who thought to himself:
"Why should I falsely praise myself and sustain my life by claiming to have attained superhuman states?"
"From this day forward, I shall no longer falsely praise myself.
In the morning, he put on his village-entering robes and took up his bowl to beg for alms. At that time, someone asked him:
"Venerable One!..."
"Have you attained any of the noble fruits?
That bhikṣu did not praise himself; immediately thereafter, as he went from place to place begging for alms, he received nothing.
As the time for his meal was passing and he became hungry, exhausted, and emaciated, he again praised himself, and immediately he obtained something.
Another bhikṣu, having heard that this elder spoke falsely at one moment and truthfully at another, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Why is it that this elder bhikṣu’s resolve is so weak and inconsistent, and his character so frivolous and flighty?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This elder was not only weak-willed, lacking constancy, and flighty today; in past lives as well, he was just the same."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Has this indeed happened before?”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
In a past age, it rained incessantly for seven days, both out of season and at the wrong time; consequently, the herdsmen did not go out for seven days."

At that time, there was a starving wolf who, wandering about in search of food, traveled through villages until he had passed through seven villages without obtaining anything at all. He then reproached himself, saying:
"How meager is my fortune, that I have traversed seven villages and found nothing?"
"It would be better for me now to remain observing the fast.
He then returned to the mountain forest and, within his cave, made this prayer:
"May all sentient beings attain peace and security."
Thereafter, he composed his body, sat upright, closed his eyes, and entered into contemplation.
On the days of the fast—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month—it is the custom for Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to mount the white elephant Airāvaṇa and descend to observe the world:

"Which sentient beings are filial toward their parents? Who makes offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas? Who practices giving, maintains the precepts, cultivates the holy life, and observes the eightfold fast?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra traveled about observing until he reached that mountain cave; seeing the wolf with eyes closed in contemplation, he thought to himself:
"Alas! How strange!"
"This wolf-beast is truly extraordinary; even among humans there is no such disposition, let alone in this wolf-beast!
I must test it to know whether its claims are true or false."
Śāriputra immediately transformed his body into that of a sheep and stood before the cave, calling out loudly to the flock.
When the wolf saw the sheep, he thought to himself:
"How strange! How marvelous!"

"The karmic retribution for this fast has suddenly arrived; while I was wandering through seven villages seeking alms, I obtained none, yet now, while I am temporarily observing the fast, these delicacies have come of their own accord.
The provisions for the kitchen have already arrived, so you should simply eat now; once you have eaten, you may then continue to observe the fast."
He immediately emerged from his den and went toward where the sheep was.
Upon seeing the wolf approaching, the sheep was startled and fled; the wolf then pursued it relentlessly.
Having chased it for a great distance, the sheep transformed into a dog with a square mouth and drooping ears, which turned back to pursue the wolf, barking at him with an urgent voice.
When the wolf saw the dog coming, it was terrified and fled; the dog pursued it urgently, and only with great difficulty did the wolf manage to escape.
Upon returning to its den, it thought to itself:
"I intended to eat him, but instead he wishes to devour me."
At that time, Śakra again stood before the wolf, mimicking the bleat of a lame sheep. The wolf thought to himself:
"The previous one was a dog; I was hungry and distressed, my vision blurred, and I took it for a sheep."
"What I see now is truly a sheep.
Observing it again with close attention, he saw that its ears, horns, hair, and tail were indeed those of a sheep, and so he went out toward it.

The sheep fled again in terror; as the wolf pursued it and was about to seize it, the sheep transformed back into a dog and turned to chase the wolf, just as before, saying: "I wished to eat him, yet he instead wishes to devour me."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately manifested before the wolf as a lamb, bleating and calling for its mother. The wolf then spoke with anger:
"If you were a piece of meat, I might still not let you go; how much less would I yield to being deceived by you in the form of a lamb?"
He returned once more to observe the fast and contemplate with a tranquil mind.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the wolf’s thoughts as he returned to his fast, intentionally manifested himself as a lamb and stood before the wolf.
Then the wolf spoke this verse:
"If you were truly a sheep, You still could not have escaped;
How much less so now that you act with falsehood, Terrifying me as before."
Seeing that I had returned from my fast, you came again to test me;
even if I were a mere piece of meat, I would still not have trusted you.
How much less so now that you act as a lamb’s fawn, falsely bleating "me-me"?
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there is a renunciant who, though upholding the precepts, has a fickle mind,
And cannot relinquish gain and honor— such a person is like a wolf observing the fast."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Was that wolf anyone else?
It was none other than this very bhikṣu."
"When he was a wolf, his resolve was unstable; now that he has left the household life, his mind remains fickle.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I command all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī to assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...as those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu, not yet knowing and not yet having realized, claims for himself that he has attained superhuman states, noble knowledge and vision, and excellence, saying, "I know thus; I see thus," that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, there were two bhikṣus dwelling in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*). One of the bhikṣus had temporarily perfected the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening; free from greed and anger, he said to the second bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, you are my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) whom I hold in high esteem; I now wish to speak a secret matter to you."
He asked, "What do you wish to say?
and then [the other] spoke.
“Venerable sir!
I have attained arhatship. He then replied:

“Venerable one! While the Blessed One was in the world, he personally received the Dharma teachings; by practicing with diligent effort, he attained the fruit of the Path—it is only fitting that he did so!

Later, as this bhikṣu wandered through various villages, he let his sense faculties run wild and neglected the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Consequently, afflictions arose, and delusive thoughts and craving were born within him. He then said to his companion:
"I originally thought there was something to be attained, yet I have certainly not attained it myself.
How do I know this?
Because I perceive within my own mind that afflictions still remain."
That bhikṣu said:
"Elder, you have falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states; you have committed a pārājika offense.
That bhikṣu replied:
“I did not speak falsely out of knowledge; I merely said it was so.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One:
“A certain bhikṣu spoke falsely, claiming to have attained superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).”
The Buddha said,
"Call him here!
When he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Is it true that you falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states?
“World-Honored One!
I did not falsely claim to have attained superhuman states; I thought I had attained them, and it was with such a thought that I spoke.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"By what causes and conditions do you speak thus?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While dwelling in a forest hermitage, I practiced the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening, and no afflictions arose.
Believing that I had attained arhatship, I spoke of my attainment to my companions.”
At another time, while wandering through a village, my faculties were not restrained and afflictions arose.
I immediately gave rise to doubt and regret, saying: "This bhikṣu is not speaking falsely."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu has not intentionally spoken falsely, claiming to have attained superhuman states; you should know that this bhikṣu is one of overweening pride."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"How is it that you have developed overweening pride (*adhimāna*) by abandoning the home for the homeless life within this True Dharma?
You should employ skillful means to eliminate this overweening pride, and then you may attain arhatship."

At that time, the bhikṣu felt great shame and remorse; he immediately applied himself with diligent effort before the Buddha to practice right contemplation, thereby eliminating his overweening pride and attaining the fruit of arhatship.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!

This bhikṣu, having received the compassionate grace of the Buddha, applied himself with diligence and skillful means to practice right contemplation; thus he eliminated his overweening pride and attained the fruit of arhatship."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It is not only today that this bhikṣu, by virtue of my grace, has diligently applied skillful means to cultivate right contemplation, thereby eliminating his overweening pride and attaining the fruit of arhatship."
"In a past life as well, he received my grace; through diligent effort without slackening, he has obtained this great fruit.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, "Has it truly been so?"
The Buddha said, "It is so.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a kingdom named Kāśi and a city named Vārāṇasī. At that time, the people within that country were prosperous and happy, yet the three poisons were raging intensely.
There was a poor brāhmaṇa who came from a neighboring village and entered the city."

On this day of the festival, the people within the city—some riding elephants, some riding horses, some riding chariots, and some riding in litters—bathed themselves, anointed with fragrant perfumes, and donned new garments; they indulged in the five desires and engaged in all manner of diversions and pleasures.
At that time, a thirst of craving arose in the brahmin's mind, and he asked the people:
"By what causes and conditions do these people obtain such happiness?
They replied:
“Brahmin, do you not know? He replied, “I do not know.”
At that time, the people said to the brahmin:
"These individuals attained this happiness because they cultivated meritorious deeds in previous lives and furthermore applied themselves diligently to their household affairs in this present life."
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:

"These people are no different from me in their hands, feet, four limbs, and entire bodies; I should now simply apply myself diligently to manual labor, for by so doing I can acquire wealth and enjoy happiness at my own pleasure, no differently than they."
He then returned home and said to his wife,
"I wish to travel far away to seek wealth through hired labor.
His wife replied:
"By begging for alms in the vicinity, you can easily obtain food and drink for your son;
what need is there to travel far? The Brahmin replied, "As things stand, I have no choice but to travel far."
His wife thought to herself,
"If he intends to go, what can I do?
and she said to the brahmin:
"Go or stay as you please; take good care of yourself.
The Brahmin then instructed his wife, saying, "Be prudent yourself and look well after your son."
Then the brahmin departed from there and went to a coastal village, where he saw a group of merchants gathered for a sacrifice. He made a proclamation throughout the lanes and alleys:
"Who is able to follow me into the sea to gather precious treasures together?"
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"I wish to enter the sea.
The merchant asked:
"What goods do you have?
He replied, "I have no goods;
I only wish to beg food from you and offer you blessings through my incantations."
At that time, all the merchants, for the sake of merit, urged him to board the ship; they immediately obtained a favorable wind and reached a village on a sea islet.

Thereupon, the brahmin entered the village to beg for food and exerted himself in his efforts to acquire wealth, obtaining thirty-two pieces of pure gold and fourteen mani-jewels, after which he returned to Jambudvīpa with his companions.
When the ship reached the shore, the Brahmin then boasted greatly to the merchants:
"What is so extraordinary about taking wealth there and returning with goods?"
"I originally went empty-handed and have now obtained this treasure; it may truly be called a marvel.
Overcome with joy, he took the treasure in his hands and played with it incessantly, whereupon he immediately lost the treasure, which fell into the waters of the sea.
At that time, the brahmin was filled with great distress and thought:
"I obtained these precious objects through extreme hardship; how is it that they have suddenly fallen into the water all at once?
I must drain the ocean to search for this treasure."
He immediately went ashore and obtained fine wood, which he took to a carpenter and said,
"I trouble you to fashion a wooden bowl for me.
After the carpenter had fashioned it, a turner turned it on a lathe, and an ironworker plated it with metal.
Having obtained the wooden ladle, he carried it to the seashore, bared his arms, and prepared to scoop up the ocean water.
At that time, a sea deity thought to himself:
"What does this brahmin intend to do?"
"I shall question him.
He immediately transformed himself into the form of a brahmin, went to that place, and asked in verse:
"With robes hitched up and arms bared, you seem in a great hurry, as if for urgent business;”
"I have therefore come to question you: what do you intend to do?
At that time, the brahmin replied in verse:
"This great ocean water is deep and vast, the lord of all streams;"
"I shall now employ skillful means, desiring to drain it until it is exhausted.
At that time, the Sea Deity spoke again in verse:
"O Lord of all flowing streams, what offense have you committed against me?"
"And yet you employ such expedients, wishing to drain it until it is entirely empty?
At that time, the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"I have endured great hardships and perils; having crossed the sea, I obtained precious jewels."
There are thirty-two measures of pure gold, and fourteen of mani-jewels.
Having abandoned the boat intending to reach the shore, my treasure-sack fell into the midst of the ocean;
for the sake of seeking those precious pearls, I shall bale out this great sea until it is empty.
Then the Sea God spoke again in verse:
“The great ocean is exceedingly deep and vast, The lord of the hundred rivers and myriad streams;
Even if one were to drain it for a hundred thousand years, It could never be exhausted.”
Then the brahmin replied with a verse:
"The sun and moon pass away forever without end; A wooden bowl and iron plates are difficult to destroy.
If one exerts effort with single-minded dedication without rest, Why worry that this ocean will not dry up?"
When the brahmin had spoken this verse, he began to bale out the ocean water and cast it onto the shore; yet as soon as he did so, the water flowed back into the sea.
At that time, the deity of the ocean observed the brahmin’s mind: was he becoming weary?
"Is he truly steadfast?
Having observed him, he saw that the Brahmin’s resolve was so single-minded that there would never be a time of retreat. At that moment, the sea deity thought to himself:
"Even if one were to bail out this ocean water for a hundred years, it could never be diminished by as much as a hair's breadth."
Moved by his single-minded devotion, the deity immediately returned the treasure.
At that time, the sea deity spoke this verse for the sake of the brahmin:
“The man of diligent skillful means, Whose will never rests;”
"By the power of single-minded devotion, though one may lose it, it is recovered again.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was the sea deity at that time anyone other than [myself]?"
I am that very person.
As for the brahmin, he is this bhikṣu.

In a past life, he already received a great fruit through my diligent skillful means; now again, through my diligent skillful means, he has cultivated right contemplation, eliminated his overweening pride, and attained arhatship.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu, not yet knowing and not yet having realized, claims for himself that he has attained a state superior to that of ordinary men—a noble knowledge and vision of excellence—saying, "I know thus; I see thus."
At a later time, whether he is examined or not, having committed an offense and desiring to seek purification, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sir!
I spoke of what I did not know as if I knew it, and I spoke of what I had not seen as if I saw it; these were empty, false, and unreal words."
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.
As for "bhikṣu," one who has reached the age of twenty and received full ordination is called a bhikṣu.
"Unknown" means due to a lack of wisdom.
"Uncomprehended" means not yet severed.
"Self-proclaimed" means claiming it for oneself.

Regarding "attaining the state beyond human dharmas": human dharmas refer to the five desires, the five lower fetters, the six destinies, the six roots of contention, the seven latent tendencies, the eightfold wrong path, the eight worldly conditions, the nine types of pride, the nine grounds for resentment, the ten courses of wholesome action, and the ten courses of unwholesome action.
Furthermore, regarding persons and phenomena, it is as when the various devaputras questioned the Buddha in verse:
"What kind of person proceeds toward goodness?
What kind of person is born in heaven?"
"What kind of person, day and night, cultivates virtuous merit?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the devaputra with these verses:
"One who digs fine wells along desolate roads, plants orchards and fruit trees as offerings,"
Providing shade and coolness with groves of trees, Building bridges and boats to ferry people across,
Practicing generosity and pure precepts, And using wisdom to abandon stinginess and greed—
One’s merit increases day and night, And one is constantly reborn among gods and humans.
These are the human dharmas.
Furthermore, being filial and obedient toward one's parents, making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and to those worthy of respect who practice the holy life—these are the human dharmas.

Regarding the qualities surpassing those of ordinary persons (*uttarimanussadhamma*): they are the ten knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*), conventional knowledge (*sammuti-ñāṇa*), knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, the knowledge of exhaustion (*khaya-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-ñāṇa*)—as well as the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), liberation, the superior wholesome mind, matured roots of goodness, the pure and impure liberations, the clear Dharma, the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the samādhis included therein; [these] they skillfully enter, emerge from, abide in, and realize through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
That is to say: śamatha and vipaśyanā; the three samādhis; the three vidyās; the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa);
the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda); the four dhyānas; the four immeasurables (apramāṇacitta); the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti);

the four noble paths (āryamārga); the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa); the four noble truths (āryasatya); the four fruits of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala); the five-limbed concentration (pañcāṅgasamādhi); and the five...
The faculties, the five powers, the five bases of liberation, the six unsurpassed qualities, the six noble qualities,
the six elements of deliverance, the six recollections, the six superknowledges, the seven riches, the seven qualities of non-attachment, the seven samādhis,
the seven powers of the destruction of the taints, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the eight bases of mastery, and the eight...
Liberation, the eightfold path leading to the tracks of the Dharma, the nine perceptions, the nine factors of joy, the fulfillment of the nine pure practices, the nine successive attainments,
the ten abodes of the noble ones, the ten totalities, the ten factors free from burning fever, the ten qualities of one beyond training,
and the ten powers of the exhaustion of outflows— these are called the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
Noble knowledge and vision refers to the knowledge and vision possessed by the Buddha and his disciples.

Some may claim to have knowledge but not vision; some may claim to have vision but not knowledge; some may claim to have both knowledge and vision; and some may claim to have neither knowledge nor vision.
One who knows but does not see says:
"I know suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path," but does not say:
"I possess the purified divine eye and see beings dying here and being reborn there—in happy realms or miserable realms, whether noble or lowly.
He does not say:
"I possess the divine ear, surpassing that of humans, by which I hear human and non-human voices, whether near or far."
Furthermore, he does not say:
"I know the minds of others, I possess the supernormal power of moving through the air, and I am cognizant of my own past lives.
This is called knowing, rather than seeing.
One who sees but does not know says of themselves:
"I have attained the pure divine eye, even unto the knowledge of my own past lives," but they do not say:
"I know the Four Noble Truths"—
this is called seeing, not knowing.
What is knowing and seeing?
To say:
"I know the Four Noble Truths, up to and including my own recollection of past lives"—
this is called knowledge and vision.
What is meant by "neither knowing nor seeing"?
It is also not saying:
"I know the Four Noble Truths," up to and including "I personally recognize my past lives."
This is called neither knowing nor seeing.
One who has attained excellence knows thus and sees thus.
Yet, not knowing, they claim to know; not seeing, they claim to see. Later, whether they are examined or not—if they are examined, someone may ask them:
“Venerable sir!
Have you attained the fruit of the noble path?
From which Dharma teacher did you learn to attain this fruit?”
"Where did you obtain it?
How was it obtained?
This is called investigation.

Regarding "not being examined": whether no one questions him or whether he is questioned, if he falsely claims for himself that he has attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), he commits a *pārājika* offense.
"Pārājika" refers to committing any one of the four pārājika offenses.
"Seeking purity" means desiring to attain purity, and thus saying:
"I did not know, yet I said I knew; I did not see, yet I said I saw."
"Empty" means void.
"Deceptive" means not according with reality.
"False speech" means speaking falsely of oneself.
"Excluding those with overweening pride" refers to those excluded by the Blessed One.
"Pārājika" is as explained above.
Furthermore, pārājika means to be separated from non-false speech, to retreat, to sink down, and to fall; this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, regarding those who have committed a *pārājika* offense: the transgression committed cannot be confessed or purified; this is called a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu says of himself:
"Do I possess the knowledge of the Dharma?"
One commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one says, "I possess knowledge of the Dharma," [one likewise commits an offense].
This is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says,
"I have attained the knowledge of dharmas," [it is likewise].
"An offense of defeat (pārājika).
Thus it is to be abandoned, thus it is to be cultivated, thus it is to be realized; in this manner each is explained in detail, until he says:
'Is this my power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya)?"'"
One incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one says,
"I have the power to exhaust the outflows," [one likewise incurs an offense].
One incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says,
"I have attained the power of the destruction of outflows," [one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense].
"Pārājika. The same applies to its abandonment, its cultivation, and its realization.
If a bhikṣu who is engaged in teaching goes to the house of a donor and speaks to a woman, saying:"
"Upāsikā! 'The bhikṣus observing the rains retreat at such-and-such a place are all not ordinary persons (pṛthagjana)'—
one who says this incurs an offense of Vinaya transgression."
If one says,
"I was also among them," one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
He asked:
"Venerable sir!
Have you attained this Dharma?"
He replied, “I have.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu says:
"Upāsikā! At such-and-such place, all the bhikṣus who completed the summer retreat have attained arhatship."
...up to saying:
"I have attained this Dharma," he commits a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu said:
"The bhikṣus at such-and-such a place have all attained the most excellent Dharma during their summer retreat," and so on,
up until he said:
"I have attained this Dharma," constitutes a *pārājika*.
If one says:
"It is the same for [the statement]: 'The bhikṣu of such-and-such a place has completed the summer retreat.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to an upāsaka or an upāsikā:
"In such-and-such a place, the bhikṣus who perform the *pravāraṇā* are all no ordinary persons; they are all arhats, all having attained the sublime Dharma.
... up to saying:
"I have attained this Dharma."
He commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu says: "Upāsikā!..."
"The bhikṣus residing within this monastery are all no ordinary persons; they are all arhats who have attained the wondrous and supreme Dharma.
... up to saying:
"I have attained this Dharma."
He commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu says to an upāsikā:
"The bhikṣus seated in that place are all not ordinary persons; they are all arhats, and have all attained the supreme and wondrous Dharma."
...and so on, until he asked:
"Elder, have you attained this Dharma?
He replied:
"I too have attained this Dharma.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
The same applies to the families of great kings, ministers, elders, and householders, as well as within cities and monasteries.
If a bhikṣu says:

"The bhikṣu who stays at your home, the bhikṣu who eats at your home, and the bhikṣu who recites the sūtras for your family members are all not ordinary persons; they are arhats who have attained the supreme and wondrous Dharma."
...up to "...I have attained this Dharma," he commits a *pārājika* offense.
If he says:

"Those who carry such bowls, wear such robes, eat such food, and who walk, stand, and lie down in such a manner are none other than Arhats who have attained the supreme and wondrous Dharma; they are not ordinary worldlings."
...up to "...I have personally attained this Dharma," he commits a *pārājika* offense.
If he says:
"These monks above have all attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
They then asked themselves:
"Do we possess the knowledge of phenomena?"
[If one says,] "I have attained the knowledge of the Dharma," one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
[If one says,] "I have [attained] the knowledge of the Dharma," it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says,
"I have attained the realization of the knowledge of dharmas,
though it is not real," it is a *pārājika* offense.
Thus one knows, thus one abandons, thus one cultivates, and thus one realizes; even up to the realization through the power of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it is likewise.
