If one acts before a eunuch, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one acts before a man, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one acts toward a *kiṃnara* woman or a female monkey, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one speaks [of such matters] to another female animal, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If it is toward a human woman, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is toward a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If [one acts] toward a man, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if toward a woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if toward a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If it is toward a man, it is a *vinayātikrama* with mental remorse (*cittavipratisāra*).
If it is toward a woman, it is a *vinayāpatti*.
If it is toward a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *vinayātikrama* with mental remorse.
If it is with respect to a male, there is no offense.
If it is with respect to a woman, it is a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense requiring mental regret).
If it is with respect to a *paṇḍaka* or a male, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind transformed by lustful desire, addresses a woman with coarse and wicked words, conforming to the ways of sexual desire as young men and women do, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The third precept is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Elder Udayin had an old acquaintance who was a brāhmaṇa; the brāhmaṇa said to Udayin, "I wish to travel elsewhere."
"Elder! Can you go back and forth from time to time to look after my wife and children?
Udāyin replied:
“Brahmin! Even if you had not entrusted me with this matter, you would still have intended to manage it; how much more so now that you have entrusted it to me!
Having said this, the brahmin departed on his way.

At that time, Udāyin, wearing his village-dweller’s robe and carrying his alms bowl, arrived at the house of a brahmin. When the brahmin’s wife saw the elder Udāyin approaching, she rose respectfully to welcome him, saying:
"Welcome, Ācārya!"
"It has been a long time since we last met; it is only now that you have deigned to visit us.
Please, be seated. He then took his seat. Udāyin said:
"I have come here for the first time; could you give me a small portion?
The Brahmin's wife replied, "I have various kinds of food and drink; whatever you command, I shall give it all to you."

Udāyin said, "These various foods and drinks can be obtained everywhere from households of faithful believers; however, that which is difficult for us renunciants to obtain—you have full control over it—so you should take it and give it to me."
The Brahmin’s wife said,
“I do not know what it is that is difficult for renunciants to obtain, such that I have gained mastery over it.
You should show me and tell me.”
"If there is something in my house, I shall take it and give it to you; if there is nothing in the house, I shall seek it from elsewhere and give it to you.
Udāyin said, "You surely know this matter; why do you not understand?"
"You are full of deceit and guile like a thief, possessing four eyes;
what is there that you do not know? The Brahmin’s wife replied, "I truly did not know; please inform me."
If there is something in the house, you should take it and give it to me;
if there is nothing in the house, you should seek to purchase it from elsewhere and give it to me.
What is it that you require?
Udāyin said: "You already know this matter;
why do you not recognize that this is the foremost form of offering?

That is to say, sexual intercourse. Just as I am a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, practices wholesome dharmas, and cultivates the holy life, to offer me this dharma-offering—namely, to comply with the practice of lust—is the highest honor."
At that time, among the Brahmin women, those who were young immediately felt ashamed and, with heads bowed, walked slowly back to their respective rooms.
Those of middle age likewise each stood there with heads bowed in shame.
An elder among them immediately rebuked him, saying:
"Ācārya Udāyin! This is not a good thing; you should not speak such improper words."
"This is a Brahmin family; how can they treat me according to the customs of a house of courtesans?
I shall report this matter to the bhikṣus. Udāyin said:
"Whether it be white or not white, it shall be as you wish.
Having spoken these words, he departed from that house.
Once he had left that house, he entered the quarters of various courtesans.
All the courtesans rose to meet him with reverence and greeted him, saying:
"Welcome, Ācārya Udāyin! It has been a long time since we last saw you; we are honored that you have deigned to visit us today."
He then invited him to take a seat, and Udāyin said, "It is rare for me to come here; can you give me something small?
The courtesans replied:
"There are various kinds of food and drink available according to whatever one requires; as for whatever you have been instructed to provide, you shall give it all to me.

Udāyin said, "Such food and drink can be obtained everywhere from households of faithful believers. However, that which is difficult for us renunciants to obtain—if you have the means to acquire it, it would be well if you were to bring it to me."
The courtesans said:
"We do not know now what it is that is difficult for a renunciant to obtain; please show us and tell us.
If there is something in our house, we shall take it and give it to you; if there is nothing in our house, we shall seek it from elsewhere and give it to you."
Udāyin said: "You already know this matter; why do you claim not to know?
You are full of deceit like a thief with four eyes; what is there that you do not know?"
Thus it was repeated up to three times,
yet the courtesans still said,
"We do not know."
Udāyin said: "You already know this matter;
why do you not recognize that this is the foremost offering?

That is to say, sexual intercourse—offering me, a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, practices wholesome dharmas, and cultivates the holy life, with this very dharma-offering, namely, the practice of lust."
At that time, among the courtesans, those who were young clapped their hands and laughed loudly.
Those who were middle-aged spoke these words:
"We rely solely on this to sustain our lives; if you are indeed a man, then come!"
Among them was an elderly man who spoke thus:
"Preceptor Udāyin, although I support myself in this way, do you not protect the Dharma of a śramaṇa?"
"I shall report this matter to the bhikṣus.
Udāyin said, "Whether you report it or not, it is up to your own will."
Having spoken these words, she departed.
The courtesans immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Call Udāyin here. When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned Udāyin extensively regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, "Udāyin! This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me, through various causes and conditions, rebuke sexual desire and, through various causes and conditions, praise the renunciation of desire?"
"How could you have committed such an evil and unwholesome deed? Udāyin!
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot serve to nourish wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, his mind transformed by lustful desire, speaks before a woman in praise of his own person for the sake of providing offerings, saying: "Sister!
As I am a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, practices the wholesome Dharma, and cultivates the holy life, you should provide offerings and offer praise through this method of sexual desire."
...so it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Lustful desire" refers to a defiled mind.
Regarding the "transformation of the mind": "transformation" refers to the cessation and transformation of past minds; this is also called "transformation.
However, the "transformation" mentioned here specifically refers to the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), awakenings (*bodhi*), and the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*).
"Mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"Women" refers to those who are relatives or non-relatives, whether they be old or young, or whether they be laywomen or ordained nuns.
"Praising one's own body for making offerings" means praising one's own person.
It says:
"Sisters!..."
"If one says, 'Just as I am a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, practices wholesome dharmas, and cultivates the holy life,
I offer sexual intercourse as the foremost form of veneration,' it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, speaks before a woman to that woman, saying:
"If you wish to obtain the foremost, supreme, and long-lasting sovereignty, great sovereignty, the peerless..."
Being peerless, one attains the most excellent state, the superior state, the state of liberation, the incomparable state, and the peerless state;
one is free from physical illness, free from illness for one’s mother, free from illness for one’s father, free from illness for one’s kinsmen, and free from illness for one’s retinue;
one possesses merit and renown, and is beloved by many people.
"Many will remember me, many will rejoice in me, and many will hold me in high esteem;
they shall obtain long life, beauty, happiness, power, a retinue, rebirth in the happy realms, birth among the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
the status of a queen of heaven, the divine eye, and pure, elongated ears— just as my śramaṇas maintain."
One should serve and attend upon those who observe the precepts, practice wholesome dharmas, and cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) by means of these qualities.

One should honor and respect them, support and provide for them with offerings, being unstinting in what is given, extending oneself fully, and receiving [their instructions] with compliant acceptance.
Among these, for each of the first thirty matters, one commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
for each of the next eight matters, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and for each of the final twelve matters, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a bhikṣu gives rise to a lustful mind, intending to go toward this person but goes toward another; intending to go toward another but goes toward this person; intending to go toward this person and goes toward this person; or intending to go toward another and goes toward another.

If a bhikṣu gives rise to a lustful mind toward a woman and speaks to a paṇḍaka about the first [category] up to "receiving in accordance with," for the first thirty matters, he commits an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (transgression requiring mental regret);
for the next eight matters, he commits an offense of *vyatikrama-āpatti*;
and for the final twelve matters, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu harbors lustful thoughts toward a eunuch and speaks to a woman regarding the first [category] up to the "conformable acceptance," for the first thirty matters he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
for the next eight matters, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and for the final twelve matters, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
It is the same for a woman with respect to another woman.

If a bhikṣu has a lustful mind toward a paṇḍaka and speaks to that paṇḍaka regarding the first [category] up to "receiving in accordance," for the first thirty matters, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance;
for the subsequent eight matters, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding the latter twelve matters, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of desire toward a woman, speaks to a man concerning the first [category] up to "consenting to comply," for the initial thirty matters as well as the subsequent eight matters, he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya requiring mental repentance (*vinayātikrama-cittavipratisāra*);
for the latter twelve matters, he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).

If a bhikṣu gives rise to a lustful mind toward a man and speaks to a woman regarding the first [category] up to "consenting to compliance," for the first thirty matters, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
for the next eight matters, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and for the final twelve matters, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
It is the same for a woman with respect to another woman.

If a bhikṣu arouses a lustful mind toward a man and speaks to that man about the first [category], up to "receiving in accordance," regarding the initial thirty matters and the subsequent eight matters, he commits an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense requiring mental regret);
regarding the final twelve matters, he commits an offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya* (an offense of transgression).
The four-line [formula] for a male *śaṇḍha* is also like this.
If one praises oneself before a woman regarding one's own service [to her], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding a *śaṇḍha*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
With a male human, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
With a *kiṃnara* female or a female monkey, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
With a female animal, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu [commits this act] with a woman, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
With a paṇḍaka, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
With a man, he commits a vinayātikrama offense.
If [the offense is committed] against a woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
against a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *vinayātikrama*;
against a man, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If [one acts] toward a woman, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
toward a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*);
toward a man, there is no offense.
If [the offense is committed] with respect to a woman, there is a violation of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance (*vitikkama-vinidhāya-citta*).
With respect to a eunuch or a male, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind corrupted by lust, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person for her support, saying: 'Sister!
As I am a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, practices the wholesome Dharma, and cultivates the holy life, you should honor and praise me with this method of sexual desire.'"
"whoever [does so], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The fourth precept is finished. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 5.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 6.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
This is the second part of the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* precepts. The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu named Kāla.
When the time arrived, he put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food from house to house until he reached a farming household.
The mistress of the house saw the Elder Kāla from afar; she rose to meet him, greeting him with reverence: "Welcome, Ācārya!
It has been a long time since we last met. Do not regard us as strangers; think of this as your own home."
"Please have him enter and sit," she said, and Kāla sat down immediately.
Then the mother, having prostrated at Kāla’s feet, stood to one side.
All the men and women of the household likewise came, and having prostrated at Kāla’s feet, they stood to one side.
At that time, an older son arrived later and, having prostrated at her feet, stood to one side.
Kāla asked him, "Whose son are you?
The mother replied:
"This is my son. Kāla asked,
"Has he been married yet?"
He replied, “I am unmarried. Kāla said:
"One should find him a wife so that he does not commit various transgressions while living abroad.
Kāla asked again,
"Is there anyone suitable?"
He replied, "There is a daughter in such-and-such a family; I sent a messenger to request her hand, but did not succeed. He asked:
"Why may it not be obtained?
He replied: "He spoke these words:"
"I wish to grant a son to one who has no son and a daughter to one who has no daughter; since he is like my own eye, being both my son and my son-in-law, I shall give her to him."
"What shall I do now?
For her sake, I shall release my son and let him go. Kāla said:
"As you have said, he is a fool.
Who would ever abandon their own son for the sake of a daughter?
As it is said: [The verse follows]"
"A woman's nature is to look outward; though born into a noble family, she must eventually depart according to the laws of marriage.
Just as you were originally from outside, so too shall you go forth."
"However, I also frequent that household; I shall seek out a husband for your son.
The woman replied, "Excellent, Ācārya!"
The bhikṣu Kāla immediately left that house and went to another house.
When the woman of that house saw Kāla approaching, she came out to meet him and respectfully greeted him, saying:
"Welcome, Ācārya!"
"It has been a long time since we last exchanged greetings; do not let it be thought that you have become estranged from our family as you might be from others. Now, consider our home as your own.
He invited him to sit; having sat down, he prostrated at Kāla’s feet and stood to one side.
The sons and daughters of the household also came forward to pay homage at his feet and stood to one side.
At that time, an eldest daughter arrived later to pay homage at his feet.
Kāla asked her:
"Whose daughter is she?
He replied, "My daughter."
He asked, "Are you married yet?
She replied:
"She is not yet married," Kāla said.
"You should settle this matter early; do not allow her to remain outside the home and inadvertently give rise to various transgressions."
Kāla asked again:
"Has anyone come to request [it]?
He replied:
“There is a certain family who once asked for [something] and was not given it. He asked:
“For what reason was it not given?”
He replied, "Ācārya!
I wish to have a son where there was none, and a daughter where there was none; furthermore, may he who has but one eye like mine also become my son-in-law."
"Just as my son came to my house, I shall give my daughter to him.
Why should I now abandon my daughter and let her go for the sake of another man?"
Kāla said: "How strange!
You are a fool! Have you never heard from the past that it is the man who goes to the woman when they marry?"
Just as you were originally, how could you come to depend on others?
As it is said:
"A woman’s heart is turned outward; though born into a royal family, she must still follow the laws of marriage and will inevitably depart from her home."
"However, that groom's family are my donors; if you marry your daughter to them, she will obtain wealth and happiness.
His mother replied, "Is this what you intend, Ācārya?"
He replied,
“I wish it to be so,” and he immediately gave his consent.
Kāla immediately returned to the groom’s family and said to the groom’s wife, “I have obtained the girl;
whatever needs to be done should be performed without delay.
At that time, both families were wealthy, and each sent wedding gifts to complete the marriage.
When the woman went to her husband's home, she was made to perform every kind of arduous labor, which eventually gave rise to exhaustion and illness;
she remained lying down until sunrise. Then her mother-in-law called out to her, saying, "Why do you not get up?"
"You do not know the etiquette of a wife; you ought to rise early in the morning to sweep and clean, perform your duties, and attend to guests.
Although he spoke thus two or three times, the wife still did not follow his instructions.
Her mother-in-law became extremely weary and disgusted, saying:
"It is because of this Kāla that I am given this suffering; he has brought me this handless and footless creature."
At that time, the daughter-in-law wept again and said, "It is because of this Kāla that I am subjected to such suffering; why does he cast me into this fiery pit?
When the mother heard this, she spoke with further indignation:
"My daughter was gentle, pleasant, and had few concerns while at home; now that she is in her husband's house, she has many tasks and endures hardship, weeping all day long.
Why, Kāla, have you settled my daughter in such a wretched and evil household?"
The bhikṣu Kāla was resented by both families.
For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One, who said:
"Summon the bhikṣu Kāla."
Having summoned him, the Buddha asked Kāla,
"Did you truly do this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Kāla! Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, reprove the practice of union with desire, and through countless skillful means, praise the practice of renouncing desire?”
"How can you now engage in the practice of sexual union?
This is an evil deed; because of you, I shall now establish a precept for all bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”

If a bhikṣu, acting as a messenger for another, brings about the union of a man and a woman—whether it be for the purpose of taking a wife or for illicit intercourse—even for a mere moment, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"A bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"A messenger" is one who accepts a mission.
"One who travels" refers to going and returning.
"Harmonious union" refers to the harmonious union of man and woman.
A "wife" is one who remains a wife for the duration of her life.
"Secret liaison" refers to a temporary sexual encounter.
"Even for as long as a moment," and "even if they are brought together so that they meet for a moment," also constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.

If she is an orphaned girl—having neither father nor mother, nor relatives; or being entirely destitute of both; or being self-reliant; or relying on another for support; or relying on her relatives for support; or relying on both.
"One who is motherless" refers to a girl who has no mother and lives depending on her father; this is called being motherless.
If a man wishes to seek such a girl as his wife and entrusts a bhikṣu to go and request her on his behalf, if the bhikṣu agrees, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he goes and speaks to the [father] regarding her, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When reporting back whether she has obtained it or not, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "an orphan girl without a father": this refers to a girl who has no father and lives depending on her mother; such is called an orphan girl without a father.
If there is a man who desires to seek this woman as his wife and entrusts a bhikṣu to go and seek her as a wife, the bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta* offense upon accepting the messenger's request;
he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense when going to speak to her;
and he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense when returning to report whether she was obtained or not.
The case of one who has neither kin nor husband is likewise.
As for "one who supports herself," she is one who lives independently without father, mother, or relatives.
If a man wishes to seek such a woman as his wife and hires a bhikṣu to go to her location to act as an intermediary, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one goes and speaks to the woman, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
when one returns with news—whether she has been reached or not—one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Standing by means of another" refers to a case where the woman has no relatives and stands supported by another.
If a man desires to take this woman as his wife and entrusts a bhikṣu with the mission, the bhikṣu commits a *vyatikrama* offense upon accepting the messenger's request;
he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense upon going to speak to her;
and he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense when he returns to report whether she was obtained or not.
The same applies to relying on one's parents or both.

If an orphan has no mother, no father, and no relatives—having neither self-reliance nor reliance on others, nor reliance on parents or both—and if this orphan, being motherless, lives by relying on his father, yet wishes to seek another woman as a wife and hires a bhikṣu to go as a messenger to receive her on his behalf, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he goes there and speaks to her on his behalf, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When the report of whether [the object] was obtained or not is delivered, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This applies likewise even when based on both [conditions].
If it concerns a household, a biological relative, a prior agreement, a fine, a king of the *kaṇṭaka* class, spinning thread, preparing food, drawing water, being childless, or regarding succession.
Regarding "within the household":
suppose there is someone who raises another's young child and instructs them until they have grown up; meanwhile, a daughter born into his own family has also reached maturity, whereupon he thinks:
"This daughter of mine is now grown; she should be given in marriage to another."
"This boy was raised by me today; now that he has grown up, why not give your daughter to him in marriage? He shall be like my own son, and also my son-in-law."
Being unable to speak for himself, he then requested a bhikṣu to speak on his behalf to the boy, saying:
"I raised you and taught you until you were accomplished; you have now reached full maturity."
"Now I have a daughter who is about to leave my home; I wish for you to become my son-in-law, just as my own son.
If a bhikṣu accepts such a message from that messenger, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he goes to the other party and conveys it, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If, upon returning to report whether she was obtained or not, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
it is likewise if that foster-father first desires to obtain his daughter himself and entrusts a bhikṣu to go and inform her father.

Regarding "a blood relative": if there is a deceased brother who is a blood relative, and one wishes to take his sister-in-law as a wife, he hires a bhikṣu to go and speak to that sister-in-law; when the bhikṣu returns to report whether she was obtained or not, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
First, as for the primary case: suppose there is a man who has an illicit affair with another's wife, and that wife says to the man:
"If my husband becomes angry and punishes me severely or drives me out of the house, you should take me."
He replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, that woman intentionally vexed her husband until he was filled with rage; she then subjected him to harsh treatment and drove him out.
Having heard this, the man was unable to go there himself; he instead requested a bhikṣu to go and tell the woman:
"Since you have already been harshly punished and driven out by your husband, you should come to me."
When a bhikṣu accepts such a mission and returns to report whether the task was accomplished or not, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Furthermore, if a woman desires a man but is unable to speak for herself, she may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to the man:
"I have already been harshly punished and driven out by my husband; now I wish to come to you to be your wife."
When a bhikṣu accepts a commission and, upon returning with or without success, reports back, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If this woman wishes to return to her original husband but is unable to speak for herself, she entrusts a bhikṣu to go and say to her husband:
"Return and live together; do not commit further transgressions."
When a bhikṣu accepts a mission and returns to report whether the task was accomplished or not, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, if the husband wishes to take his wife back but is unable to speak for himself, he may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to the original wife:
"I now permit you to return; do not commit such transgressions again."
When a bhikṣu accepts a mission and, upon returning to report whether the task was accomplished or not, commits an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "punishment": if a king wishes to take a woman from another's family but cannot speak for himself, he may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to her family:
"I can punish your family and take your daughter, but I do not wish to do so."
"If you provide my daughter with food and clothing, her ornaments will naturally never be lacking, and it will also bring benefit to your household.
If the bhikṣu accepts this commission and, whether he succeeds or fails in obtaining [the items], reports back to the donor, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The "King of the Thickets" is a marauder.
If this marauder wishes to seize another's daughter but cannot speak for himself, he commissions a bhikṣu to go to her family and say:
"I am the King of the Forest; I can do you no small harm."
"You should send your daughter to me; she may obtain food, clothing, and ornaments as she pleases, and you shall also have your household protected.
If a bhikṣu accepts such a mission and, upon reaching the destination or failing to reach it, reports back [to the sender], it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding those who spin thread: if there is a widow who supports herself by spinning and weaving, and a man desires her but cannot speak for himself, he may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to the widow:
"Become my wife."
The widow said:
"If I am unable to do other work for you, I can only spin thread; if you need it, I shall go.
When she has returned to report whether she obtained it or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "preparing food": if there is a widow and a man who desires her but cannot speak for himself, he may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to the widow:
"Come and live together."
The widow said, "I am only able to prepare food and nothing else; if you need it, you should come.
When she returned to report whether she had obtained it or not, it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding "one who takes a wife": if there is a widow and a man wishes to take her as his wife but cannot speak for himself, he may entrust a bhikṣu to go and say to the widow, "Come and live together."
The widow replied, "I am only able to fetch water and cannot do anything else; if you need it, I shall go.
When she returned to report whether she had obtained it or not, it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding those without children: suppose there is a man who has no offspring at all, and there is also a widow who likewise has no son. A man desires this widow but cannot speak for himself; he therefore entrusts a bhikṣu to go and say to the widow:
"Since we both have no children, come and live together."
When a bhikṣu accepts a mission and, upon returning to report whether the task was accomplished or not, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
It is likewise if that widow wishes to seek a man but is unable to speak for herself and hires a bhikṣu to go on her behalf.
Regarding succession: suppose there is a man and a woman who both have no offspring;

fearing that after their deaths they might fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) with no one to carry on their lineage, a man desires to take this widow as his wife but cannot speak for himself. He therefore entrusts a bhikṣu to go and say to the widow:
"Come and live together with me; if I should die first and fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, you must perform a sacrificial offering for me."
"If you die first, I shall perform a sacrifice for you.
When [the messenger] returns to report whether he has succeeded or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
It is the same if that widow wishes to seek out a man.

If there is a woman who is protected by her mother, protected by her father, protected by her brothers, protected by her sisters, protected by herself, protected by her clan, protected by wealth, or is a maiden, a widow, or another's wife.
Regarding "protected by the mother": suppose there is a woman who lives under her mother's protection, and someone wishing to obtain this woman sends a bhikṣu to speak to her mother, saying:
"I wish to take this woman as my wife."
...up to the point where, upon returning with the report of whether she was obtained or not, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The same applies to those protected by their father, those protected by their brothers, and those protected by their sisters.
Regarding "protecting oneself": there is a woman who has no parents or kinsmen and maintains her livelihood while observing the precepts to protect herself.

If a man desires this woman and hires a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf, then at the time when the messenger returns to report whether she was obtained or not, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "one of the same clan" (*gotra*): there is a woman who has no parents and lives in dependence on those of her own clan.
If a man wishes to seek this woman and entrusts a bhikṣu to go and speak to her kinsmen, then at the time when he returns to report whether he succeeded or failed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "protecting against debt": if a woman owes someone money that has not yet been paid in full, and a man wishes to obtain this woman, he may request a bhikṣu to go to her family and say:
"Give me this woman; I will pay the debt on your behalf."
...and so on, up to reporting back [to the donor], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
It is the same for a maiden, a widow, or the wife of another.
This also applies to a woman acquired by bartering grain, acquired by purchasing with money, or one who has paid a fee (*dāsī*), one who has paid half the fee, or one who has paid the full fee.
Whether staying for one month, or staying at will, or by plundering, or being given as a flower garland, or without seed, or for a brief moment.
Regarding those acquired by purchasing grain: if a woman has been purchased with grain, and a man desires this woman, he may request a bhikṣu to go and say to her:
"Become my wife."
...up to the point that when he returns to report whether he has obtained it or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The same applies to obtaining it by means of money.
Regarding "one who pays money": if there is someone who raises a girl and collects tax-money from her, taking everything except what is for her own maintenance.
If there is a man who wishes to seek out this woman and commissions a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf, up to and including the return of the report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
It is likewise if he pays half the fee or pays the full amount.
Regarding "staying for one month": if there is a widow and a man wishes to take her as his wife, he may request a bhikṣu to go and speak to the widow on his behalf.
The widow replies:
"I cannot stay for long; I can accompany you for one month, and if you require it further, I shall go."
...up to the point where he returns with the report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "living according to one's own will": there was a widow whom a man wished to take as his wife, so he requested a bhikṣu to go and speak to the widow.
The widow said, "I cannot stay for long; I shall remain for as long as I please, and if you have need, you must go.
She then returned and reported this.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa. Regarding "obtained by plunder":

if someone has plundered a woman after breaking into another's village, and a man wishing to seek out this woman hires a bhikṣu to go and speak with her, up to and including returning with a report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

Regarding those who carry flower garlands: according to the laws of certain countries, when a man wishes to seek a woman as his wife, he simply sends someone carrying a flower garland to the woman's family.
If she accepts the flower garland, it is known that she has been obtained as a wife; if she does not accept the flower garland, it is known that she has not been obtained.
If one then dispatches a bhikṣu to take the flower garland and deliver it to the girl's family, and [the messenger] returns with a report [of success], it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding "one without kin": if a man has neither a father nor a mother, and has no other relatives, and the woman is likewise;
if this man desires that woman and hires a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf, up to and including returning with a report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "for a moment": if a man commissions a bhikṣu to go and seek a beautiful woman for a momentary sexual encounter, and [the bhikṣu] returns to report this, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

A woman without children, a female slave, one who has left home, one who has been released, a prostitute, a procuress, an external prostitute, a procuress for an external prostitute, an abandoned girl, a beggar girl, a discarded girl, or a girl purchased with money.
Regarding a woman who has no son: if her family is wealthy, she may be married off while still a young child.
When the boy dies, this widow remains living with her mother-in-law in dependence upon her, until she reaches adulthood.
There was a man who wished to seek this woman and commissioned a bhikṣu to go and say to her:
"Since your son has passed away, I am now no different from your son."
"Give this woman to me; I shall provide her with food and clothing.
Upon returning with this report, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "a female slave": this refers to those living beings who are sold in various kingdoms.

If a man wishes to seek a woman as his wife but, fearing that he will be charged too much money if he says he is buying her to be his wife, he instead hires a bhikṣu to go and speak secretly to the woman, saying:
"I am now buying you to be my slave; in truth, I intend to take you as my wife."
...up to the point of returning with a report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding "one who has gone forth": if there is an attractive woman among those who have gone forth as an outsider, and a man desires to take this woman who has gone forth as his wife, he hires a bhikṣu to go and speak to her; up to the point of returning with a report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "releasing": there are two kinds of releasing—either selling or divorcing.
As for selling, according to the law of the country of Sphatika, a wife may be sold even for a minor grievance.

Regarding divorce, there is a law of the land: if a husband and wife do not find mutual pleasure, they may go before the king, pay three and a half coins and two pieces of *karpāsa* cloth, and seek a separation; the king shall then grant permission for them to divorce.
There may be a woman who has an illicit affair with another man, and they make a mutual agreement:
"If I divorce my husband, I shall become your wife. Answer:
“Very well. He then took the money and goods and obtained a divorce for her.
Upon hearing this, the man hired a bhikṣu to go and say to the woman:
"Since you have already divorced her, come and become my wife.
Upon returning with this report, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If that woman hires a bhikṣu to go and say to that man:
"I am already divorced; you should take me as your wife.
Upon returning with this report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding a "prostitute":
if a man hires a bhikṣu to speak to a prostitute, saying, "Have sexual relations with me," and so forth, upon returning with this report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"The procuress" refers to the courtesan's servant, which is also as explained above.
"External courtesans" refers to those courtesans who constantly remain in the fields seeking men.
If a man hires a bhikṣu to go and tell an outside courtesan, "I have had sexual intercourse with you," and so on, until he returns to report it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
It is likewise if an outside courtesan employs a messenger in the same manner.

Regarding "abandoning a girl": if a woman becomes pregnant through another man and subsequently leaves the household life to join the various non-Buddhist sects, and when her months are complete she gives birth to a daughter, she abandons the child at a crossroads.
If someone takes her in and raises her until she has grown to adulthood,
and a man desiring this girl hires a bhikṣu to go and speak to her, and that bhikṣu returns with a report [of his success], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding "begging for a girl": if there is a man who has many sons but no daughter, and he begs a girl from another to raise until she reaches adulthood;
and if a man desires her as a wife and hires a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf, up to and including the return of the report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "the woman who is sent away": if there is a woman who, before she has been married, has had illicit relations with another, and subsequently goes forth in marriage;
and the husband, knowing she is not a virgin, sends her back to her family and demands the original dowry.
When the man who had previously been common to her heard that she had been dismissed, he thought to himself:
"It was because of me that this woman was dismissed; I shall take her."
He commissioned a bhikṣu to go and speak to the girl’s parents, and upon the bhikṣu’s return with the report, it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding "the woman for whom money has been paid down": if a man has married a wife but has not yet finished paying the bride-price, and the girl’s parents demand more money than he can fulfill, he cannot obtain the wife; nor can the girl marry again.
There was another man who desired this woman and commissioned a bhikṣu to go and say to her parents:
"Give me this woman; I shall provide the money for her to return to her husband's family, and I will also give it to you."
...and so on, up to returning with a report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a man or a man’s messenger speaks to that bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, having heard it from the man or the man’s messenger, violates the Vinaya;
if he then goes and speaks to the other [person], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Whether she goes herself or sends a messenger, if she does not return with a report as to whether [the girl] was obtained or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The same applies if a solitary girl relies upon her maternal grandmother, her maternal grandfather, her maternal great-grandfather, her maternal uncle, her maternal aunt, or relies upon her paternal grandfather, her paternal grandmother, her paternal great-grandfather, her paternal uncle, or her paternal aunt; this is also as stated above.
Direct, indirect, through signs, by capability, regarding entry and exit, illness, the king, the faction of a Dharma-preacher, together, and mixed. Regarding "direct":
there is a man who wishes to solicit another's wife but cannot speak for himself; he therefore entrusts a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf.
If one receives the message, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if one speaks it to the other party, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the woman's family says:
"He is a kṣatriya, but I am a brāhmaṇa.
He is a vaiśya, but I am a brāhmaṇa.
He is a śūdra, but I am a brāhmaṇa."
Or some say:
"I am a kṣatriya and he is a brāhmaṇa;
I am a vaiśya and he is a brāhmaṇa."
"I am a śūdra and he is a brāhmaṇa," or again,
"He is a kṣatriya and I am a vaiśya."
"He is a kṣatriya, and I am a śūdra," or they say,
"He is a brāhmaṇa, and I too am a brāhmaṇa."
"He is a kṣatriya, and I am also a kṣatriya;
he is a vaiśya, and I am also a vaiśya;
he is a śūdra, and I am also a śūdra."
If one reports back whether she was obtained or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "indirectly": if a man wishes to seek another's daughter but cannot speak for himself, he entrusts a bhikṣu to go;
the bhikṣu says, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one may not act as a messenger."
If one does not consent verbally but agrees in one's heart, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if one goes and speaks to the other person, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and upon receiving or not receiving [the goods], if one returns to report it, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "gestures": if a man wishes to solicit another's daughter but cannot speak for himself, he entrusts a bhikṣu to go on his behalf.
The bhikṣu says:
"The Buddha has established a precept that one may not act as a messenger; however, I shall perform a gesture for you."
If you see me wearing soiled and greasy clothes, holding a broken, empty bowl, sitting on a low seat, and speaking words befitting a slave, you should know that it is not permitted.

If, however, you see me wearing fresh, clean clothes, holding a fine bowl, sitting on a great couch, and speaking of wife, children, and grandchildren while conversing with you, you should know that these are the signs of permission.
If one makes such a proposal and, whether the request is granted or not, reports back [to the donor], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding "one who is capable": if many bhikṣus go to a donor’s house for a meal, and after they have eaten, a female lay follower says to the bhikṣus, "I wish to take a daughter from such-and-such a family to be my son's wife; you should speak to them on my behalf."
The bhikṣus said: "Upāsikā!
The World-Honored One has established a precept that we may not send anyone on such an errand."
If one says, "Among them, there are two or three bhikṣus capable of practicing [the path]," one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
if one goes and speaks to them, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one returns [the request] and reports it, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding "entering and exiting": if a bhikṣu enters or exits another's household and receives offerings, and the host says, "I wish to seek a daughter from such-and-such a family to be my son's wife; Venerable Sir, please seek her for me."
The bhikṣu said:
"If you prepare food and drink for me, I shall seek [the means] for you.
The host replied:
"When my son has finished finding a wife, I shall prepare food and drink for you, Venerable Sir.
The bhikṣu said, "If I open my mouth, there is nothing I do not master; however, you should simply prepare the food."
If one then prepares food for them, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
One should go to that household and say:
"Do you know this?"
He asked, "What is it? and the bhikṣu replied:
"I wish to say something; those who follow my words should speak.
The host said, "Please speak."
The bhikṣu said,
"A man wishes to seek your daughter.
She asked, "Who is he?"
"Who is it? He replied,
"The son of such-and-such a family."
The host said angrily,
"I would rather place this girl in water, fire, or a dark place than give her to him!
The bhikṣu, struck with fear, fled, thereby committing a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a woman is unmarried, and a bhikṣu first flatters her with talk and then receives food or drink from her, yet she feels ashamed and returns to him saying she cannot give it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If that woman has either married or died, and one returns to report this, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Regarding the sick:
if a bhikṣu frequently enters and leaves a certain family, and the members of that family say to the bhikṣu, "I wish to seek a daughter from that family to be my wife; please seek her out for me."
If a bhikṣu accepts the message, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if he goes to deliver it to that person, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
That household says:
"My daughter is ill; do you know whether she will live or die?
If it is a man who is ill, he says:
"The son of that family is ill; do you know whether he will live or die?"
"But you gave her to him; if he were to die, it would leave my daughter a widow.
The bhikṣu replied again, "When people fall ill, must they all die?"
"Perhaps it will subside on its own!
You should simply give it to him.
At the moment he speaks these words, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one reports back whether she has been obtained or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding "the king": if a king wishes to obtain another's daughter, he says to the community of monks, "I now wish to seek the daughter of such-and-such a family; you should seek her for me."
If the entire Saṃgha grants permission, all incur an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
If the entire Saṃgha goes to seek [the object], all incur a serious offense (sthūlātyaya).
If they return without having obtained it, all the members of the Saṃgha commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If the Saṃgha sends a messenger to speak to that household, the entire Saṃgha incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
at the time of speaking, the entire Saṃgha incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
and when the report is received—whether it is successful or not—the entire Saṃgha incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If the one who has received the message reflects thus:
"If I return to the assembly and have everyone report it to the king, it would be better for me to go and report it to the king myself; the king will then recognize me."
If a bhikṣu who has been thus instructed returns with a report—whether he has obtained it or not—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
because it concerns the entire Saṃgha, there is first a sthūlātyaya offense.
Regarding the Dharma Master: there was a householder who wished to seek a daughter from another householder family.
That family did not wish to give her and said, "I would rather marry her to a heretic of wrong views than to a householder."
The groom’s family then thought to themselves:
“Who could bring about this union for us? Only the śramaṇas possess many skillful means; those who are able to preach the Dharma would surely be able to effect our reconciliation.”
He then went to the monastery and said to the Dharma Master,
"I sought the daughter of that family, but they were unwilling to give her to me.
The Dharma Master asked:
"What did he say? He replied,
"He spoke these words:"
"It would be better to give it to a heretic with wrong views than to this family.
If the Dharma Master explains the meaning of "fellow practitioners" to me so that they will give it to me,
and the bhikṣu consents to this, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one invites the Dharma master along with his retinue to depart, and they do so, the entire assembly incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, when the Dharma is being preached, members from both the male and female families come together to listen to the teaching.
At that time, the Dharma Master skillfully taught the Dharma, saying: "As the Buddha’s sūtra declares to the bhikṣus:

'All sentient beings associate according to their own natures and characteristics. Those who lack faith associate with those who lack faith as close friends; likewise, those who violate the precepts associate with those who violate the precepts; those lacking dignified deportment associate with those lacking dignified deportment; those lacking a sense of shame associate with those lacking a sense of shame; the indolent associate with the indolent; the distracted associate with the distracted; and the ignorant associate with the ignorant. Each follows its own kind, associating with one another as close friends.'"
All classes of sentient beings—those of the past, future, and present—are exactly like this.
It is just as foul, putrid, and impure things combine with one another; such, O bhikṣus, are these [bodies].

All classes of sentient beings, each according to their own nature, are deeply faithful and thus feel mutual affinity with those who are deeply faithful; likewise, those who observe the precepts are mutually affectionate with those who observe the precepts; those with dignified deportment with those of dignified deportment; those with a sense of shame with those who possess a sense of shame; those who are diligent with those who are diligent; those with concentrated minds with those with concentrated minds; and those with wisdom with those who possess wisdom.
All classes of sentient beings in the past, future, and present are exactly like this;
they are like white, pure objects perfumed with incense, whose own characteristics are naturally harmonized.
After the Dharma Master had finished preaching this teaching, he said to the girl's family,
"I have heard that your son wishes to seek your daughter.
He then replied to them:
"It would be better to give it to a heretic with wrong views than to that family.
"Have you not heard what the World-Honored One said: 'If there were a murderer or an enemy who, holding a sharp sword in hand, constantly watches for an opportunity to kill a person'?"
That son of an enemy would rather enter his own home than enter the house of a heretical outsider;
why do you now wish to give your daughter in marriage to a family of wrong views?
"One may see the upāsakas from time to time.
When the bhikṣus were observing the fast and maintaining the precepts, the woman's family said:
"Ācārya, do you wish for this?"
He replied, "I wish to do so.
The other said:
"If one says, 'I shall give it to the Dharma Master,' and at that time remains silent and does not speak, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the Dharma Master cannot endure this and speaks while seated, and the [offender] receives [the robe], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
Furthermore, if among the assembly of the Dharma-master, someone proclaims,
"I have attained it," that person also incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding "in common": there is receiving in common while speaking separately, receiving separately while speaking in common, receiving in common while speaking in common, and receiving separately while speaking separately.

As for "receiving in common while speaking separately": if bhikṣus, having each completed their summer retreat, travel through various villages and part from their acquaintances and hosts to journey toward other countries.
At that time, the upāsikās in the village said:
"I am seeking a wife for my son; I am seeking a wife for my brother; I am seeking a wife for my uncle."
In this manner, each of these various upāsikās recounted a single transgression of a bhikṣu,
to which he replied:
"It is acceptable."
One commits one *vinayātikrama*;
having gone to that place and each separately making a request, each commits a *sthūlātyaya*;
upon returning and reporting it individually, each commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding those who receive [the invitation] separately and speak together: if bhikṣus have each completed their summer retreat and are traveling through the countryside, they may wish to depart from their respective donors and travel to another land.
At that time, some upāsikās said to the bhikṣus,
"Seek a wife for our son.
Others said:
"If you seek a wife for my brother, and seek a wife for my uncle"—
if the bhikṣus each consent to this, they each commit an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
if they go to him and separately seek wives for each, they each separately commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Upon returning, he reports with a single word, saying:
"I have obtained it.
He commits one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Regarding "receiving and explaining together": it refers to when bhikṣus have each completed their summer retreat and are traveling through the countryside; they part from their various donors and wish to travel to another country.
If various upāsikās say to a bhikṣu,
"Seek a wife for my son," "Seek a wife for my brother," or "Seek a wife for my uncle," and the bhikṣu replies to them all at once:
"If it may be so," [one] commits one *vinayātikrama* offense;
if one goes to them and seeks [them] individually, one commits individual *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
Upon returning, he answered truthfully,
"I have obtained it.
He committed one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding the separate reception and separate explanation: if a bhikṣu, having completed the summer retreat, travels through the human world and encounters various donors, the upāsikās say to him:
"Seek a wife for my son; seek a wife for my brother; seek a wife for my uncle."
The bhikṣus each replied individually,
“So be it,” and each committed an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
When they went there, each acted separately for their own sake, and each committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
upon their return, each reported it separately, and each was found guilty of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "mixed": there was a bhikṣu with many acquaintances who, leading his followers, went to a certain household to request a meal.
After they had eaten, the mistress of the house said to the elder:
"I wish to seek a daughter from such-and-such a family for my son as a wife; you, Elder, should speak on my behalf."
At that time, the Elder, not being well-versed in the characteristics of the Vinaya, granted his permission; he thereby incurred an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
Since the members of his assembly had little knowledge of the precepts and feared they might corrupt the minds of others, they did not dare to admonish him.
Having left that house, he said to the elder,
"Why did you do this? The elder asked:
"What matter is this? He replied,
"Does the Elder not know that the World-Honored One has established a precept prohibiting the bringing together of men and women?"
The Elder replied,
"I do not know of an intermediate state.
The bhikṣu said:
If one says, "Venerable Elder, do not seek it yourself;
I shall seek it for you," he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Whether he succeeds in obtaining it or not, he must report back to the Sangha; [if he fails to do so], he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The Elder commits an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
If a laywoman (*upāsikā*) had previously said to that group of followers:
"I am seeking a daughter from such-and-such a family for my son; you should seek her for me."
At that time, the disciples, being ignorant of the Vinaya, replied,
"So be it," thereby committing an offense against the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
At that time, the Elder, having little knowledge of the Vinaya, feared he would corrupt the minds of others and did not immediately rebuke or stop them.
After leaving that house, he said to his followers:
"You have acted improperly by doing this."
He asked, "What kind of work did you do?
The Elder replied:
"Do you not know that the World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding one from sending [a messenger]?
He replied, "I do not know."
The Elder spoke again:
"Do not seek it for now; I shall seek it for you.
While the Elder was seeking it, he incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If she reports back whether it was obtained or not, she commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
her followers commit an offense of transgression against the *vinaya*.
If a laywoman (*upāsikā*) first informs the assembly and the assembly all agrees, everyone incurs an offense of transgression against the *vinaya*.
If all [the women] seek [him] together, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each;
when reporting back whether he was obtained or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for all.

If a man has many wives, some who are mindful [of him] and some who are not, and while a bhikṣu enters or leaves his house, a woman bows at the bhikṣu’s feet and, having respectfully inquired after his well-being, the bhikṣu asks her:
"Are you at peace and happy?
He replied immediately,
"Where could one find happiness?"
Question:
"For what reason?
The woman replied:
"This man always rises and lies down together with another person, while I alone am treated with such contempt by him; I am like a broken vessel, useless—how could I not suffer?"
The bhikṣu replied, “Do not grieve;
I shall speak for you so that things may be made equitable.
He then spoke to her husband:
"You know nothing; why do you imitate others by keeping many wives, being unable to treat them with impartiality, but instead sharing a bed and rising together exclusively with one person?
He replied, "What can I do about it?"
The bhikṣu said:
"We shall look after it with impartiality, making sure that it is distributed evenly.
He replied:
“I shall act according to the Teacher’s instruction.
At that moment, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a man has many wives yet still seeks another young girl, and being unable to speak for himself, he entrusts a bhikṣu to go and speak on his behalf; when the bhikṣu returns to report whether she was obtained or not, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a person’s husband and wife are quarreling, and a bhikṣu encourages them to reconcile, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

However, if those husband and wife are not in harmony, or if there is a dispute regarding matters of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, and the bhikṣu encourages reconciliation for the sake of performing meritorious deeds, there is no offense.
If there was a woman returning to her home and a bhikṣu went to her house, and all the men and women of that household paid him homage,
the bhikṣu saw that woman and said:
"Are you still living here?"
"You should not remain here for long; what would you do with the old coins your husband gave you?
You ought to return them to him.
When these words are spoken, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There was a man who kept many horses but had no fine breed to produce offspring. He requested a bhikṣu to say on his behalf:
"A certain family has a breeding mare; seek one for me.
The bhikṣu sought it for him and committed a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there were two mahallakas:
one mahallaka had left his wife and children to go forth, and another mahallaka had left his womenfolk to go forth.
Each of them wandered among the human world and returned to Śrāvastī, where they lived together in a single room.
The one who had abandoned his wife then thought to himself:
"I shall return home to see my former wife."
Having put on his village-dwelling robe, he went to his original home.
His wife saw Mahallaka approaching from afar and spoke with indignation:
"You, Mahallaka, are of meager merit and lacking in auspicious signs; you cannot even provide for your wife and children, and now you have fled far away from home to evade official service."
"The girl has grown up and cannot find a husband; what use is she to you now?
Return at once!
If you do not go, I shall break both your legs."
"Who would rejoice to see you?
At that time, the mahallaka returned to his original dwelling and lived there in sorrow and distress, like a merchant who has lost his wealth.
When those who had abandoned their wives and children to leave the household life returned home, it was likewise for them.
Living together in the same room, the one who had abandoned his son to go forth into homelessness possessed little wisdom; he said to the second mahallaka, "Elder!
Why do you dwell in such sorrow and distress?"
He replied,
"Elder! Why must you ask about this matter?"
He spoke again, saying:
"If you truly wish to know, why is it that we two share a single room, yet do not recognize one another's good or evil deeds?"
"If you will not tell it to me, to whom else should I speak?
That mahallaka then related the matter in detail and said to the mahallaka who had abandoned his son:
"Why should you grieve? What is there to be sad about?"
My family is likewise.
Do you know how to employ a skillful means now?
You may take your daughter to be my son's wife.
He replied, "Very well. At that time,
both mahallakas committed an offense of *vyatikrama*.
When the next day arrived and it was time, those mahallakas put on their village-dwelling robes and each returned to his own home.
He who had taken the girl spoke to his wife, saying,
"I have found a son-in-law for you."
The wife then asked,
"Whose son is he? He replied:
“Son of such-and-such a family.
When a man who has abandoned his male relatives and left the household life speaks thus to his wife:
“I have already found a daughter-in-law for you.”
He asked, "Whose daughter is she?
He replied:
When one says, "The daughter of such-and-such a family," both incur the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, while a boy and a girl were playing in the streets, a certain *mahallaka* said to the girl:
"This is your husband," said the second mahallaka to his son.
"This is your wife."
When these words were spoken, both incurred the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Then the two mahallakas, having arranged their marriage between them, each rejoiced as if a poor man had found treasure; they came to love and respect one another like elder and younger brothers.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One,
saying: "How is it, World-Honored One,
that these two mahallakas, having entered into marriage, are so full of joy and mutual respect?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These two mahallakas did not merely perform such an act today; they have done so even in past lives."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.
There was a brāhmaṇa who had some old masha beans that would not cook even after being boiled for a long time. He placed them on a stall, wishing to sell them to others, but no one would buy them."
At that time, there was a man who had a single, unruly donkey at home that he could not sell despite offering it in the market.
Then, the bean-seller thought to himself:
"I shall buy this donkey with my beans for use."
He then went to him and said,
"Could you trade this donkey for these beans?
The owner of the donkey thought again:
"What is the use of this obstinate donkey?
I shall take those beans. He then replied:
“Very well,” he replied,
and having obtained the donkey, he was filled with joy.
At that time, the owner of the beans thought to himself:
"Now I have obtained my son.
He then spoke this verse:
"The Brahmin’s dharma is a clever trade; He has been peddling old ice-beans for sixteen years."
"Though you exhaust your firewood, it will not boil; it shall break the large and small teeth of your household.
At that time, the owner of the donkey also spoke in verse:
"O Brahmin, what do you find so pleasing?"
"Though you have four legs and a fine woolly coat;
carry your burden along the road so that you may know it: even when pricked by needles or scorched by fire, you shall never move.
At that time, the owner of the bean field spoke again in verse:
"A single staff for a thousand autumns, with a four-inch needle at its head, can cure a donkey of its debauched ways;
what worry need there be that it cannot be subdued?"
At that time, the owner of the donkey became enraged and spoke this verse:
“Planting down your two front hooves, And springing up with your two rear ones— I shall break your front teeth; Only then will you know for yourself.”
The bean-owner spoke a verse to the donkey, saying:
"Though stung by mosquitoes, flies, and venomous insects, You rely solely on your tail for protection.
I shall cut off your tail and feet, To make you know the bitterness of hardship."
The donkey replied again:
"From my ancestors until now, I have practiced this obstinate way;
now I continue to follow it, and even unto death I shall never abandon it."
At that time, the owner of the beans, knowing that this wretched beast could not be reached with harsh words, began to praise him instead, reciting a verse:
“Your voice is clear and beautiful, Your face is as white as jade or snow;
I shall find a wife for you, And you shall roam together through the forests and marshes.”
Upon hearing these gentle and affectionate words, the donkey immediately spoke in verse:
"I can carry eight *droṇas*, And travel six hundred *li* in a day;
O Brahmin, you should know this, For I have heard my wife’s joyful words."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The two persons at that time were these two mahallakas now.
The donkey at that time was this mahallaka’s son now."
At that time, they had already deceived one another, and only after coming together did they rejoice;
now it is the same: they deceive one another, and only after coming together do they rejoice.
If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If he engages in sexual intercourse with a paṇḍaka, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he engages in sexual intercourse with a man or an animal, he incurs a vinayātikrama offense.
"To engage in sexual union with a Kinnarī woman or a monkey woman constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Therefore, this was said.
The Five Precepts are concluded. The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove (Kalandakanivāpa) in Rājagṛha; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus were constructing five hundred private dwellings in a wilderness area, each person begging for materials to build his own.
One bhikṣu, having dressed in his village-wearing robes in the morning, took up his bowl and entered a village in the wilderness to beg for materials for the construction of a dwelling.

Thus, there was a merchant who, holding a door-knob in his hand, came toward the marketplace to open his own shop. Seeing from afar that a bhikṣu was approaching in haste, the merchant thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu comes surely for the sake of begging for a dwelling; I have been here since early morning, yet my wares have not sold—whom could he possibly beg from?"
He then closed the shop door and returned home.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This merchant saw me and immediately closed his door to go home; I know it is because he does not wish to give to me as I come to beg."
He then went by another path, intercepted him in front, and asked,
"Long-lived one!
Where do you wish to go?"
"You must not abandon me; upon whom shall I rely to build my dwelling?
I shall rely precisely upon you who have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Since you know there are karmic fruits of virtuous and non-virtuous actions, yet do not wish to give to me, who else would give?"

Āyuṣman, you should know that as the Blessed One has said: one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness; for those who do not wish to hear, one should use skillful means to cause them to hear; for those who lack faith, one should teach them so that they may establish faith; even to the point of taking them by the head and forcefully exhorting them to practice giving.

The reason for this is that he shall, at the end of this life, certainly be reborn in the heavens, where his physical form, strength, lifespan, and retinue will be spontaneously provided; when he is later born among humans, he will likewise experience happiness, with his physical form, strength, lifespan, and retinue fully accomplished.
By practicing the Buddha-dharma, one increases merit and establishes the fruits of the Path.
Therefore, one attains longevity, as the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By performing meritorious deeds, one receives the retribution of happiness; Whatever one desires comes spontaneously."
Transcending the stream of birth and death, one attains the supreme tranquility of Nirvana.
If a person performs meritorious deeds, the celestial deities will naturally protect them;
all their aspirations will spontaneously be fulfilled, and no demons shall be able to destroy them.
Those of meager virtue encounter many afflictions, while merit can dispel all calamities;
when virtue and merit are firm and strong, one swiftly achieves steadfast stability.
One will experience joy upon rebirth in heaven, and likewise attain sovereignty among humans.
By virtue of these merits, wherever one goes, all things are spontaneous.
Through these skillful means of merit, one is forever freed from the suffering of birth and death;
attaining the Way and reaching Nirvana, one neither sinks nor is born again.
When the bhikṣu had spoken this verse, he further said:
"Long-lived one!
Assist me in building a dwelling; the merit thereof shall be greatest."
At that time, having heard the teaching of the Dharma, the merchants made some small offerings.
Then the merchants thought to themselves:

"If we enter the marketplace, there will be many beggars; we shall gain no further profit and will lose our capital. It would be better to stay at home and preserve our capital, for it is superior to losing both interest and principal in the market."
Having had this thought, he returned home and sat down.
The merchant’s wife spoke angrily to her husband:
“Why have you returned so quickly from the market? Being so lazy, how will you support our children and fulfill our official taxes and labor service?”
The merchant replied, "Do not be angry; listen!
This morning I went to the market stalls, and so forth, until I was afraid of losing my capital, and therefore returned home."
When his wife learned of this, she remained silent and said nothing.
Later, when the Venerable Śāriputra entered the village on his almsround, he arrived at her door and stood there.

At that time, the merchant’s wife was deeply faithful and reverent; upon seeing Śāriputra, she immediately took a clean vessel filled with food, brought it out and placed it into his bowl, and recognizing him, prostrated herself at his feet and respectfully inquired after his well-being.
Then Śāriputra comforted him, saying:
"How is it at home?
Is your livelihood well?"
His wife replied,
"All is well within the household, but our livelihood has suddenly fallen into ruin.
He asked:
"Why is this so? He then explained the preceding circumstances in detail to Śāriputra:
"Our household livelihood—food, drink, clothing, and the fulfillment of royal taxes and corvée labor—depends entirely upon our market stall."
"Currently, my husband resides at home; fearing that people might beg from him, he truly speaks when awake and truly sleeps when speaking.
This Ācārya is one whom our family honors, reveres, and respects; having nothing to conceal, I have thus declared this intention."
Then Śāriputra preached the Dharma in various ways to the merchant’s wife, causing her to attain a heart of joy.
She immediately returned to the vihāra and reported the preceding matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu who manages the monastery affairs.
Having summoned him, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu who managed the monastery affairs:
"Is it true that you begged for materials to build a dwelling and thereby troubled the donors, causing Śāriputra to speak of you with resentment?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This is an unwholesome practice; to privately beg for materials to build a dwelling is to trouble the donors.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not again trouble the donors for the sake of dwellings; wealth is difficult to obtain, and giving is likewise difficult.
Brahmins and householders must cut into their own resources to provide for śramaṇas—offering robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness; this too is exceedingly difficult."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu in charge of construction:
"In a past age, there was a bhikṣu named Bhaṭṭika who dwelt in a forest.
At that time, there were also śārmantaka birds that roosted in this forest; they would clamor noisily at dawn and dusk, disturbing that bhikṣu."
At that time, the bhikṣu Bakkula approached the Blessed One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣu in the forest, saying: "How is it?
Are you free from much illness and much affliction, and do you dwell happily in the forest?"
The bhikṣu in the forest addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have few ailments and little affliction, and I dwell happily within the forest; however, at dawn and dusk, I am disturbed by the clamor and cries of the śarabha birds, such that I am unable to engage in contemplation."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Do you wish for all the śiśumāra birds to not come at all?
He replied:
"May it be so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Monk! When the śārmantaka birds arrive at dusk, you should beg for a single feather from each of them; when they depart in the morning, you should do the same.”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
He immediately returned to the forest and sat in meditative contemplation.
When the sun was setting and birds gathered together, chirping in confusion, he spoke these words:
"O Śarabha, you birds, each of you beg for a single hair; I have need of them now."
At that time, the birds remained silent and still for a short while; having no other choice, they each plucked a feather and placed it on the ground.
When he went begging again at dawn, the birds immediately moved away to another place to stay for one night.
Not finding pleasure there, they soon returned.
At that time, the bhikṣu again asked for their feathers, and each bird gave them one.
The birds thought to themselves:

"This śramaṇa is most extraordinary and fond of begging; I fear that before long my feathers will be entirely gone, and with my body of flesh lying on the ground, I shall no longer be able to fly—what am I to do?"
They then deliberated together, saying:
"This bhikṣu always dwells in the forest; we should go and seek another place of residence, for it is no longer fitting to return.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Even birds and beasts find excessive seeking distasteful, let alone human beings.

You bhikṣus, do not engage in worldly affairs with many desires and much seeking, causing those faithful brāhmaṇas and householders to painfully give away their wealth and property to provide śramaṇas with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for illness."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that the bhikṣus in this grove are timid, easily disturbed, and afraid of the sounds of evil birds?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu in the forest was not only cowardly and inferior today; he was already fearful in the past.
The bhikṣus said:
"Has this happened before?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In a past age, there was an elephant-king dwelling in a secluded place within a forest. A great wind suddenly arose and blew down the trees; hearing the sound of the trees breaking, the elephant fled in terror."
His fear subsided slightly, but as he stood beneath a tree, that tree broke as well; he immediately fled again.
At that time, a deva saw the elephant running in terror and thought to himself:
"Why is this elephant running about so wildly and recklessly?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"When a violent wind suddenly arises, the trees are broken; the dragon-elephants are terrified and flee in wild panic.
Even if a great wind should blow across the whole world, where then could the dragon-elephants find refuge?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The elephant at that time was this very bhikṣu in the forest.
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣu in charge of affairs:
“In a past age, there were five hundred rishis dwelling in the Snowy Mountains.
One rishi lived in a separate location where there was a fine spring and an abundance of flowers and fruits.”
Not far from there was the Sāra River, in which a nāga resided.
Seeing the seer’s dignified and composed demeanor, the nāga conceived a feeling of affection for him.
