At that time, the river nāga came to visit the seer; it happened that the seer was sitting cross-legged in meditation, so the nāga immediately coiled its body around the seer seven times and remained with its head covering the seer’s crown. It did this every day, except during the time he ate.
Because the rishi had a dragon coiled around his body, he was unable to rest and sat upright day and night; consequently, his body became emaciated and he developed scabies.

At that time, there were people living nearby who provided offerings to the rishi. While wandering about, they came to the rishi’s dwelling and, seeing him so weak and afflicted with scabies, asked him:
"For what reason are you like this?"
The rishi recounted the preceding events in full detail.
He said to the rishi,
"Do you wish for this nāga never to come here again?"
He replied, "I wish to do so.
He then asked the seer again:
"Does this dragon have anything to which it is attached? He replied,
"There is only a precious jewel from a necklace upon its throat."
That person instructed him, saying:
"Simply ask the dragon for the pearl; the dragon’s nature is extremely stingy, so he will never give it to you. You must ensure that he does not come.
Having said this, he departed.
In a short while, the dragon arrived and immediately demanded the pearl.
Upon hearing the sound of the request for the pearl, the dragon’s heart was displeased, and it slowly departed.
The next day, before the dragon had even arrived, the rishi saw him from afar and spoke this verse:
“‘A radiant mani-jewel, adorning the body with necklaces;
if a nāga can bestow this upon me, he shall be my true and virtuous friend.’”
Then the dragon immediately replied with a verse:
"Fearing the loss of my mani-jewel, I was like one holding a staff to call a dog;
Since the precious jewel cannot be recovered, I shall not come to look upon you again."
Exquisite delicacies and various treasures—these can never be obtained by means of this honored maṇi; why then strive for them so earnestly?
To seek much leads to separation from loved ones, and because of this, they will not return again.
At that time, a deva in the midst of the void spoke these verses:
“The reason for the arising of weariness and disdain is entirely due to excessive seeking;
when the marks of greed appear in a brahmin, the nāga then hides in the abyss.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu in charge of affairs:
"Even nāgas, who are animals, find excessive seeking to be detestable; how much more so for human beings!

You bhikṣus must not engage in extensive management of affairs or seek widely without satiety, causing those faithful brāhmaṇas and householders to painfully relinquish their wealth to provide śramaṇas with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for the sick."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are ten qualities that cause one to be disliked by others.
What are these ten?"

Not associating with others; associating with them too lightly or too frequently; associating for the sake of profit; loving those who do not love one, and loving those whom one does not love; not accepting truthful speech; delighting in interfering in the affairs of others; desiring to overreach others despite lacking true majesty and virtue; delighting in private, secret conversation; and having many desires and cravings—these ten matters give rise to being disliked by others.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Summon all the bhikṣus residing in the wilderness. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a dwelling for his own use where there is no donor, he should build it according to the prescribed measure: it should be twelve sugata-span long and seven spans wide on the inside.
One should show the various bhikṣus the site for building a hut—a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu, for his own sake, solicits materials to build a hut on a site with difficulties or obstructions where there is no owner, and fails to show the various bhikṣus the site for building the hut, yet builds it in excess of the prescribed dimensions, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"A bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Begging for oneself" means going about begging for one's own sake, whether it be for one coin or two coins from house to house, up to a hundred thousand coins.
"A dwelling" refers to that which is permitted by the Buddha.
"One who builds" means either building it oneself or instructing others to build it.
"Without an owner" means there is no owner—whether male or female, layperson or monastic—who acts as the proprietor.
"One's own body" refers to oneself.
"It should be according to measure" means it should accord with the measure of the Dharma.
"Long" refers to the vertical measurement.
"Extensive" refers to horizontal measurement.
Regarding "twelve Sugata-spans": *Sugata* means "Well-Gone One.
A *hasta* (span) is two chi and four cun.

Regarding "seven cubits internally": the method for constructing a house involves both internal and external measurements; this refers to making the longitudinal and transverse dimensions within the walls.
As for the measurement of the house's height, the side walls shall be one zhang and two chi.
"Pointing out the site for the monks to build a hut" means indicating the ground.
"The monks" refers to either the Saṃgha itself or those sent by the Saṃgha.

The monk who is building the hut shall enter the midst of the Saṃgha and first perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) requesting permission; only thereafter shall he perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal motion followed by three proclamations) to request the site.
The *karmavācanā* is performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is personally seeking to have a dwelling built for himself; it has no owner and is for his own use. He wishes to request from the Saṃgha the assignment of a location."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant a place for the bhikṣu so-and-so to request from the Saṃgha the assignment of a dwelling.
"Venerable sirs of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so requests the assignment of a place; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
That bhikṣu enters the Saṃgha, kneels with his right knee on the ground, joins his palms, and speaks thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am personally soliciting materials to build a hut for my own use, without a patron."
"Now I beg the Saṃgha for instruction regarding my dwelling place; I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me instruction on the location.
Thus he begs three times.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, [name], has requested from the Saṃgha the assignment of a site for a dwelling to be built by himself, for his own use, as it is without an owner. He has already requested the Saṃgha to designate the location of the dwelling."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha designate a place for the monk so-and-so to build a dwelling.
Thus he makes the formal motion:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so is personally soliciting materials to build a hut for himself; as it has no owner, he has already requested from the Saṃgha that a site for the hut be assigned.
The Saṃgha now assigns a site for the hut for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
"Venerable sirs, please grant your consent for the assignment of a dwelling place for the bhikṣu so-and-so. Those who consent, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already granted its consent for the assignment of a dwelling place for the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

If there is no one among the entire Saṃgha who can perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā), the entire Saṃgha shall go to the site where the dwelling is to be built, and one bhikṣu shall announce within the assembly:
"The entire Saṃgha is designating the site for a dwelling for the sake of the bhikṣu so-and-so."
Thus it was said three times. Regarding the monk appointed as the messenger:

if the site for the building is distant, or if it is separated by water, or during extreme cold, extreme heat, heavy rain, or heavy snow; or if there are many elderly or infirm members in the Saṃgha such that not everyone can go—then that bhikṣu, having finished requesting instructions from the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should dispatch one, two, or three bhikṣus. Because a formal act (*karmavācanā*) cannot be performed with a larger group, the maximum is three persons. The one performing the formal act should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu is personally begging for materials to build a hut for his own use, as there is no donor. He has already requested from the Saṃgha that they designate a site for building the hut.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint such-and-such bhikṣus to designate the site for building the dwelling for this bhikṣu.
Thus he makes the motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has requested permission from the Saṃgha to build a dwelling for himself, as it is ownerless and for his own use. He has already requested from the Saṃgha the assignment of the site for building the dwelling."
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to designate the site for the construction of a dwelling for the bhikṣu so-and-so.

Venerable sirs, those who approve of the appointment of the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to designate the site for the construction of the dwelling should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to designate the site for the construction of the dwelling.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld as such."

When the dispatched bhikṣu goes to the site where the hut is to be built, he should inspect the location; if that site contains many insects, or trees bearing flowers and fruit, he should not tell them to remove them.
If there is no such matter, the observation is also as previously described.
One bhikṣu proclaims:
"The Saṃgha has designated the site for the construction of the hut."
Thus he spoke three times.
Regarding a place that is free from difficulties: it is a place where no trees bearing flowers or fruit grow, and where there are no insects or snakes. Regarding a place that is not obstructed:

on each of its four sides, there must be space sufficient for twelve ladders, with a space of one *vāmana* (a cubit measured by the span of a fist) between each ladder, so that those performing the work may come and go all around to plaster, repair, and thatch.
If a bhikṣu [builds] in a "difficult place," it is one where there are trees bearing flowers and fruit, as well as various insects and snakes.

A "hindering place" is one where, on all sides, there is no space to accommodate a twelve-rung ladder, such that those performing the work cannot move back and forth to cover, thatch, plaster, or repair.

If one begs for materials to build a hut for oneself when there is no donor, and does not have other bhikṣus designate the site, yet builds it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu himself solicits [materials] to build a dwelling, and there is a site that is problematic or obstructive, yet he does not have other bhikṣus point out the location, or if he builds it with dimensions less than the prescribed measure, or instructs another to do so—even until the time the work is finished—he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If he makes use of it, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
This applies likewise to two bhikṣus or a multitude of bhikṣus.

If a single bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a dwelling for his own sake where there is no donor, and if it is in a difficult location or an obstructed location, and he does not have other bhikṣus point out the site, yet builds it according to the prescribed measure or instructs others to build it, then at the moment the building of the dwelling is completed, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one uses it at that time, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
The same applies if two or more monks do so.

If a monk himself solicits materials to build a hut for his own use where there is no owner, and he builds it in a difficult location or an obstructed location, without having other monks designate the site, and he exceeds the prescribed measurements—whether he builds it himself or instructs others to build it—he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense when the hut is completed.
If one uses it [at such a place], one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The same applies if two or more people do so.

If a monk does not designate such a site, or if the Sangha of another boundary has designated it, or if it was previously designated in a prior year, or if it is in water, on ground that is not sandy, on ground that is not gravelly, on top of rocks, or on scorched ground; or if even one person among the Sangha does not build a hut there, or if two or three people do not build huts there—in all such cases, it is improper to designate it.
If there are many in the Saṃgha who do not construct rooms, it is permitted for one to act as a supervisor.
If a bhikṣu constructs a pure room (kappiyakuṭi) with the intention of using it himself, he should not do so.
If one constructs a pure room (śuddhāgāra), one should not construct it using materials intended for a firewood shed.
If one constructs a pure room, one should not construct it using materials intended for a well-house.
If one intends to construct a pure room (*śuci-kuṭī*), one must not use it as a bathhouse.

If a bhikṣu constructs a dwelling in a difficult location or an obstructed location without being instructed, or constructs it exceeding the prescribed dimensions, then at the time of construction, if he hands over bricks or lumps of clay, he incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline) for every such act.
If one piles bricks to establish the rows [of the foundation] and constructs a room, each monk incurs an offense of *vyatikrama*.
This continues until, once the doors and windows are completed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Up until the completion of the roof—if it is covered with bricks—when the very last brick is laid, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Whether it is covered with tiles, wood, planks, lime plaster, lumps of clay, or grass, up until the final handful of grass is laid, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one begins building a hut but stops before it is completed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When it is later finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If the builder, after the owner of the hut has settled into it, has another person build it, then at the moment the hut is completed, the bhikṣu who was the original builder incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If the householder has already established the dwelling and another person subsequently completes it, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu, in a difficult location or an obstructed location, constructs a dwelling exceeding the prescribed dimensions without having had the site assigned by other bhikṣus, and that householder-bhikṣu neither renounces the precepts nor dies nor surrenders [the dwelling] to the Saṃgha.

If there is a bhikṣu who, within this room, smokes his bowl, makes robes, receives instruction or recites the scriptures, or engages in any form of enjoyment while in meditation, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
the same applies if two or more persons construct such a room.

If a bhikṣu personally solicits materials to build a hut, provided it is not on a site that is difficult or obstructive, and he leads other bhikṣus to designate the location and builds it within the prescribed measurements—or if he instructs others to do so—then at the completion of the hut, this bhikṣu incurs no offense;
the one who uses it also incurs no offense.
This is likewise the case for two persons or many persons.

If a bhikṣu himself begs for materials to build a hut, provided it is not on a site with obstacles and is not a site that causes obstruction, and he directs other bhikṣus to supervise the work, having it built according to the prescribed measurements—whether he builds it himself or instructs others to do so—and even until the hut is completed, this bhikṣu incurs no offense;
there is no offense for those who use it;
and the same applies if two or more bhikṣus do so.

If a bhikṣu designates a site for a dwelling for other bhikṣus—provided it is not a site designated by the Saṃgha of another territory, nor one designated in a previous year; provided it is not on water, nor on sandy ground, nor on ground of broken stones, nor on large boulders, nor on ground that has been scorched; provided it is not a case where only one person among the Saṃgha does not build a dwelling, nor a case where two or three persons among the Saṅgha do not build a dwelling; and provided there are many who do not build dwellings—he is permitted to build with certainty. He is permitted to build a dwelling for residence, a pure dwelling, a well-house, or a bathhouse, provided these are built with certainty.

If a bhikṣu constructs a dwelling on a site that is free from difficulties, not obstructive, and not exceeding the prescribed measurements, and he shows the site for the construction to other bhikṣus, then if those bhikṣus assist by smoothing the clay lumps or by preparing and handing over the bricks, each of those assisting bhikṣus is without offense.
If he piles up one layer or two layers, even until the time of installing the doors and windows, this bhikṣu is without offense.
If he covers it with bricks, at the moment of the final brick, this bhikṣu is without offense.
If it is covered with tiles, wooden boards, grass, lime, or lumps of clay—when it is finally covered by the last lump of clay, there is no offense.
If one constructs only half of it, that bhikṣu is without offense.
If it subsequently becomes accomplished, that bhikṣu is without offense.
If he himself employs the means and causes another to accomplish it, that bhikṣu is without offense.
If he himself initiates the action and it is subsequently accomplished by another, that bhikṣu is without offense.

If a bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a hut, provided it is not on a site with obstacles and not in a place that causes obstruction, and he directs other bhikṣus to assist him in building it without exceeding the prescribed dimensions, then this bhikṣu has not abandoned the precepts, nor has he died, nor has he been expelled by the Saṃgha.
If the bhikṣus, while within [these sacred sites], fumigate their bowls, make robes, recite the sūtras, or engage in contemplation, all such uses are entirely without fault.

If a bhikṣu, at the place of the Buddha’s birth, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, or the place of the five-year great assembly—these venerable sites—wishes to construct a grass hut, a leaf hut, or a tent-canopy hut for the sake of making offerings, it is permitted to do so for temporary residence.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for materials to build a hut for his own use when there is no donor, and he builds it to an excessive size, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
The six precepts concluded. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī each built private rooms for themselves. At that time, there was no one who would build a room for the bhikṣu Chanda; the owner of the site where Chanda wished to build was named Abhaya.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda, having put on his robe for entering a village, went to that house.
When the host saw the bhikṣu approaching, he paid respectful homage at his feet and exchanged greetings with him.
Then the host said, "Ācārya!
I have heard that Kuśāmbī is constructing five hundred private rooms; is there perhaps anyone who will build a room for the Ācārya?"
He replied:
"It is indeed as I have heard; those who have owners all have houses built for them. I am of meager merit; being like a bald owl, I have no owner—whom can I expect to build one for me?"
The host replied,
"Ācārya! Do not be resentful!"
"I shall do it for you.
At that time, he immediately gave him five hundred gold coins and said, "Ācārya!"
"Take this and build a dwelling.

At that time, Chanda took the money and immediately went to a suitable location, intending to build a large house. He spent all five hundred gold coins, yet he had only managed to lay the foundation and erect a small portion of the walls before his funds were exhausted.
He went again to the householder’s home; the host prostrated at his feet, and after they had exchanged greetings and mutual inquiries of well-being, he asked:
"Has the Ācārya finished building the hut?
He replied:
"When the foundation of the house was first laid and a small portion of the walls had been built, the money and goods were exhausted.
At that time, the master gave him another five hundred gold coins.
Chanda took the five hundred gold coins and finished building the walls; he then installed doors and windows, and once again his money and goods were exhausted.
He went again to his host, and the host, having prostrated at his feet, asked again:
"Has the Ācārya finished with the cell?
He replied:
"When the walls and windows were finally completed, the money and goods were already exhausted.
At that time, the householder conceived a lack of faith and said to Channa, "Ācārya, you are a renunciant; why do you build such a large dwelling?"
"With a thousand pieces of gold, one could build a multi-storied pavilion; how could a single room not suffice?
Venerable sir, please return; I cannot give it to you.
At that time, Channa became sorrowful and distressed.
"How can this dwelling be constructed through skillful means?
There was a forest of sāla trees, so he cut them down and used them to build the house.
At that time, there were spirits dwelling in that forest who spoke to Channa, saying:
"Do not cut down this tree!
It would leave my weak children and grandchildren exposed to the wind and rain, with no place to rely upon.
Chanda replied:
"Evil spirit, depart at once! Do not remain here; who would delight in seeing you?
He then felled the tree.
At that moment, the spirit wailed loudly and, taking his sons with him, went to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing [the reason], asked intentionally:
"Why are you weeping? He replied:
“Bhagavān! The Venerable Channa has cut down the trees in my grove and used them to construct a dwelling.
Bhagavān!”
"I am a man or woman, weak and small, drifting and exposed by wind and rain; upon what shall I rely?

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of this spirit, preached the Dharma in accordance with its needs, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening it, so that its grief and suffering were immediately removed.
Not far from where the Buddha was, there was another grove of trees; the World-Honored One pointed it out, instructing them to take up residence there.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Call Cunda here."
He was immediately summoned; once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him extensively on the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Fool! This is an evil deed; do you not know?

Wherever the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has stayed for even a single night, that place and its surroundings—wherever there are trees reaching the height of a man—are treated as stūpas and shrines; therefore, the deities delight in coming to dwell therein.”
"How does a bhikṣu revile him with harsh words? Chanda!
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
How was it that the bhikṣu Chanda, by skillfully employing expedient means in managing affairs, obtained those one thousand old gold coins from the host?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is not skillful means. If one were truly skillful in means, one should be able to attain even more; why stop at only a thousand?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is indeed as the World-Honored One has said; you well know that this bhikṣu Chanda is unskilled in expedient means.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that I have known this bhikṣu to be unskilled in expedient means; in past ages as well, I already knew that the bhikṣu Chanda was unskilled in expedient means."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.
At that time, the king ruled the country with the Dharma, and the people lived in peace and happiness, free from all calamities and hardships."
At that time, the king had no son; his consort suddenly became pregnant and, after ten months, gave birth to a son who was without eyes or nose.
Seven days after the birth, a great assembly was convened, and all the ministers, physiognomists, and Daoist masters were gathered to bestow a name upon the child.
At that time, according to the customs of the kingdom, names were established based on auspicious marks, celestial constellations, or one's parents.
A Brahmin asked:
"What extraordinary marks are there upon the Prince’s body?"
The bystanders replied, "This prince’s face is perfectly flat; it is entirely devoid of eyes and a nose.
The brahmin said:
"Since this prince should be named Ādarśamukha (Mirror-Face), he shall be provided for and nurtured by four nurses:
one to rub, cleanse, and bathe him; one to remove and discard his impurities; one to hold and carry him; and one to suckle him with milk."
These four nurses attended him day and night, and he grew like a lotus flower increasing day by day.
When he reached adulthood, his father the king passed away, whereupon he was installed as the successor to the royal throne under the name King Mirror-Face.

However, this prince had planted the roots of virtue in past lives; thus, although he was born blind, he possessed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). His merit and power were such that he was fit to be a king, and when the people of the kingdom heard that Prince Ādarśamukha had become their monarch, there was none among them who was not filled with wonder.
At that time, there was a high minister who wished to test him but could find no opportunity.
It so happened that the king issued an edict commanding all his ministers to construct a new palace, adorned with intricate carvings, engravings, and various colorful paintings.
The minister thought to himself, "I have always wished to test the king; now is the very moment.

He took a monkey, dressed it in clothes, equipped it with various tools, placed it in a leather bag, slung it over his shoulder, and went before the king, saying: The minister thought to himself, "I have always wished to test the king; now is the very moment. He took a monkey, dressed it in clothes, equipped it with various tools, placed it in a leather bag, slung it over his shoulder, and went before the king, saying:
“Great King!
The command has been issued to erect the palace, and the master craftsmen have arrived; we pray that Your Majesty will instruct them on the methods for constructing the hall.
The king then thought to himself:
Thinking, "He will surely test me," he then spoke this verse:
"Observe these classes of sentient beings, With their flickering eyes and wrinkled faces; [They are like] those who have committed evil deeds."
Fickle by nature and volatile, they can destroy what has been accomplished;
such is the law of receiving one's portion—how could they build palaces?
They ravage flowers, fruits, and trees, and cannot draw near to human beings.
"How much less could he have built palaces?
He has been hurried back to the wild forests.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The King Mirror-Face at that time was none other than my current self.
The monkey at that time was the monk Channa.
At that time, I was born without eyes; having already known that he was incapable of giving, how much more so today?”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on the city of Kauśāmbī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, he should have other bhikṣus designate the site, ensuring it is a place free from difficulties and not a place of obstruction.
If a bhikṣu, in a difficult or obstructed location, builds for himself a structure with an owner, and does not have other bhikṣus point out the site, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Large" means exceeding the proper measure; this is what is called "large.
"Cottage" (layana) refers to that which has been permitted by the Blessed One.
"By the maker" means either making it oneself or instructing another to make it.
"Having an owner" means having a man or woman, whether lay or ordained, acting as the owner.
"To act for oneself" means to act for one's own sake and not for the Saṃgha.
"To direct the various bhikṣus to their respective places" refers to the Saṃgha or those sent by the Saṃgha, as explained above in the section on small huts.
"An unobjectionable site and a non-obstructed site" are as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, at an objectionable site or an obstructed site, does not have other bhikṣus designate the location for building a hut, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a single bhikṣu, in a place that is difficult or obstructed, constructs a large dwelling—whether building it himself or instructing others to do so—up until the time the dwelling is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one makes use of it, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is likewise true if two or many people do so.
With the exception of exceeding the prescribed dimensions, whether there is an offense or no offense in all other respects is exactly as explained above regarding the small hut.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, and does not have other bhikṣus point out the location, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
The seven precepts concluded. The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmadinnasuta, whom the Saṃgha appointed to oversee the nine matters of administrative duty.

The nine duties are: the official in charge of assigning beds and seats; the official in charge of appointing those to invitations for assemblies; the official in charge of distributing rooms and quarters; the official in charge of distributing clothing and utensils; the official in charge of distributing flowers and incense; the official in charge of distributing fruits and gourds; the official in charge of overseeing the provision of warm water; the official in charge of distributing various cakes and foods; and the official in charge of overseeing the selection of those capable of performing communal tasks. These are called the nine duties of the monk who serves as the presiding official.

When assigning the beds and seats, this elder shall assign them according to the order of seniority, using the little finger of his right hand to point out the lamp-light; this applies whether they are forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) or otherwise.

They dwell together with those who practice in the forest (*āraṇyaka*), with those who practice alms-gathering (*piṇḍapātika*), with those who wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*), with those who eat in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), with those who remain constantly seated (*naiṣadyika*), with those who sit in the open air (*abbhokāsika*), with those who sit on a layer of grass (*trṇasaṃstarika*), with those who recite the scriptures (*dharmabhāṇaka*), with those who are Dharma-teachers (*dharmakathika*), with those who study the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), with *srotāpannas* and other *srotāpannas*, with *sakṛdāgāmins* and other *sakṛdāgāmins*, with *anāgāmins* and other *anāgāmins*, with *arhats* and other *arhats*, with those possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*) and others possessing the three knowledges, with those possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and others possessing the six supernormal powers, and with those who lack formal deportment (*anairyāpathika*) and others who lack formal deportment.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra and the group of six bhikṣus came to request a dwelling.
Then the Venerable Dharmaruci replied:
"Wait a moment!"
"I shall wait until you have all been assigned to the lower-ranking rooms; next, I will assign a room to you.
When it came time for the assignment to the lower-ranking seats, he was given a room according to the sequence, but received an inferior one.

When the group of six bhikṣus saw that the beds, stools, bedding, and various articles within the dwelling were all worn out and decayed, and furthermore, that the food provided in the separate room was coarse and poor, they said to one another:
"The Elder Dabba Mallaputta treats us like enemies; he has given us this wretched room and such coarse, unpalatable food."
"If this elder has long been a practitioner of the holy life, he must cause us to constantly undergo manifold sufferings; we shall now slander him with a *pārājika* offense.
They then said to him: "Elder!..."
"You have committed a *pārājika* offense; I shall bring it to the assembly.
He replied, "I have committed no such offense."
He said: "Who else would call themselves a thief?
To say 'I am a thief'—you alone have committed a *pārājika* offense this day."
Having slandered him among a great multitude of people, they went further to the Saṅgha and slandered the Venerable Dharmaruci, claiming he had committed a pārājika offense.
Dharmaruci went to inform the Blessed One:
"The bhikṣu Maitrībala has slandered me with groundless charges of a pārājika offense."
The Buddha said,
"Do you have such a thing?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣu! The Tathāgata knows you to be pure; when others slander you, what should you do? Dabba replied:

“Although the World-Honored One knows that I am pure and without fault, I only pray that the World-Honored One will speak to him out of compassion so that he may give rise to faith, lest he suffer harm for a long night.”
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
Once they had been summoned, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you truly defame the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā’s son with groundless charges of a pārājika offense?
They replied, “It is true.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“For what reason?”
He replied,
"This elder gave me an old, dilapidated dwelling, even saying, 'If this elder remains long in the holy life, we shall constantly suffer distress.'"
He then slandered him with a *pārājika* offense.
The Buddha told the group of six bhikṣus:
“This is an evil deed. Do I not always say that toward those who practice the holy life (*brahmacārin*), one should arouse reverence and act with kindness through body, speech, and mind?”
Why do you now, with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, defame a bhikṣu who is blameless in the holy life?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth]... even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, resentment, and displeasure, slanders a pure and innocent bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense, desiring to cause that bhikṣu’s pure conduct to be ruined.
At a later time, whether he is investigated or not, he speaks thus:
"This matter is groundless; it was because I was dwelling in anger and resentment."
"One who speaks these words commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Angry" refers to the nine grounds for resentment and anger arising from improper causes.

The tenth resentment refers to those ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) who feel displeasure, as well as even Arhats who possess the unrooted [afflictions]; in these cases, the objective basis (*vastu-mūla*) does not manifest.
Furthermore, one has not seen that matter, not heard that matter, and does not suspect that matter.
Regarding "pārājika," it refers to each of the four pārājikas individually.
"Slander" means to speak falsely and groundlessly regarding something that does not exist.

It is the desire to destroy that pure practitioner, wishing to cause them to no longer be a bhikṣu, a śramaṇa, or a son of the Śākya; it is the wish to cause them to become a śrāmaṇera, a layperson, a gardener, or a follower of an external path.
At a later time, whether he is investigated or not investigated—
investigation means asking him:
"What did you see?"
Did you commit sexual misconduct?
Did you steal five coins?
Did you intentionally kill a human being?
Is it not a case of falsely claiming superhuman qualities?
How is this seen?
By what cause is it seen?
"Where was it seen?
This constitutes an investigation.
If one does not inquire in this manner, it is called a lack of investigation.
This matter was spoken because of groundless malice and resentment; one who makes such a statement commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, out of malice, slanders two who appear similar— one impure and one pure—
and says to the pure one, "Do you see me committing what offense?"
Is it one or two of the four matters?
Or is it one or two of the thirteen matters?
To slander [another] without having seen, heard, suspected, or reached a definitive conclusion regarding them.
Whether in a private place, among a great multitude, or within the Saṃgha:
"I have seen him commit a pārājika offense; I have heard that he has committed a pārājika offense; I suspect that he has committed a pārājika offense."

If one sees what is not real, the very basis of that seeing is unreal; if one hears what is not real, the very basis of that hearing is unreal; if one suspects what is not real, the very basis of that suspicion is unreal.

Having previously seen falsely, heard falsely, or suspected falsely, yet now claiming "it was not so seen," "it was not so heard," or "it was not so suspected," and thus slandering another face-to-face with open eyes—each such statement constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If this bhikṣu slanders [the Sangha] regarding each one of the four pārājikas, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If he slanders [the Sangha] regarding each one of the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one slanders [another] by charging them with each of the *pāyattika* offenses individually, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

If one slanders [another] regarding the *pratideśanīya*, the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, or the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*), one commits an offense of mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*) that constitutes a *vyatikrama-vinaya*.
If one slanders a bhikṣuṇī regarding the eight pārājikas or the nineteen saṃghāvaśeṣas, for each individual instance of such slander, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas and the one hundred forty-one pāyattikas, if one slanders her regarding each individual instance, one commits a vyatikrama offense.

Regarding the eight *pāṭidesanīyas*, the *śaikṣa* rules, and the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*), if one slanders each of them individually, one commits an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-kaṣāya* (transgression requiring mental remorse).
Regarding the eighteen matters for a trainee nun (*śikṣamāṇā*), if one slanders each of them by saying, "She should be given the training again," one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, if one slanders them one by one, saying that they should be ordained again, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Down to the five precepts of a layperson, if one slanders them one by one, one commits a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, speaks such words as these, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The Eight Precepts are concluded. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume Six.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
This concludes the remainder of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa precepts. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Dharmadinnaka (Dharmottara) was appointed by the community of monks to oversee the nine matters, as described above.
Even the group of six bhikṣus, having received inferior lodgings and coarse food, were constantly distressed in mind, even to the point of thinking:
"This Elder Dabba Mallaputta has long been a practitioner of the holy life, yet we are constantly subjected to such suffering."

Furthermore, the World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit one to slander another with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense; we must now seek out the root source of his transgressions.

Having spoken these words, he constantly followed the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—staying by his side until the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month.
When the bhikṣuṇīs came to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, the Venerable Dharmaruci was sitting to one side not far from the Buddha.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, they proceeded next to pay homage to the Venerable Dharmaruci.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who was a sister of Dharmaruci; as she was prostrating, the corner of her robe was blown by the wind and fell onto Dharmaruci’s lap, whereupon he immediately picked it up with his hand.
Then the group of six bhikṣus spoke thus:
"Venerable Dabba, you have committed a pārājika offense. Dabba said:
"I have no such thing.
The group of six bhikṣus spoke again:
"We have already seen the matter; what more is there to doubt?"
"Who else would act as a thief and yet call himself a thief?
He then spoke of this matter in private, among many people, and even within the Saṃgha.
At that time, Dharmapāla reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
They were immediately summoned.
The Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you indeed, without basis, slander Dabba Mallaputta with a charge of a *pārājika* offense? He replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
There truly is a root.
The Buddha said:
"What was the root cause?
The group of six bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"On a certain day of the Uposatha, several bhikṣuṇīs came to pay homage to the World-Honored One, and subsequently paid homage to the Elder Dabba."
At that time, the wind blew the nun’s robe, causing it to brush against Dharmapāla’s knee.
Thereupon, Dharmapāla took hold of the robe with his hand; this constitutes the root offense.
The Buddha said:
“Foolish men!
This is not a fundamental offense of pārājika; this is merely a minor matter within a different category.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the group of six bhikṣus.

“Have you not often heard how the World-Honored One, through various causes and conditions, has exhorted us to give rise to a heart of reverence toward our fellow practitioners of the holy life, and to maintain kindness in body, speech, and mind?

Why then do you now, for the sake of destroying the pure conduct of a pure and blameless bhikṣu, falsely accuse him with a pārājika offense—using a minor matter belonging to a different category that is not a pārājika—to slander a bhikṣu who is free from the pārājika transgression?”
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, because he is displeased, should defame a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense by charging him with a pārājika dharma based on a minor matter belonging to a different category, desiring to destroy that person's holy life (brahmacarya).
If, at a later time, whether he has been investigated or not, he speaks of a minor matter belonging to a different category because he harbors resentment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Regarding the bhikṣu who is resentful and displeased, it is as explained above.

As for 'a different category,' this excludes the four pārājikas and the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas; these minor matters of a different category consist of the *śaikṣa-dharmas* and the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*)."

If a monk who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense is slandered with a *pārājika* dharma—meaning he is slandered regarding any one of the four *pārājikas*—and he speaks of that non-existent matter with the intent to destroy the other’s holy life (*brahmacarya*), desiring to make him no longer a monk, no longer a *śramaṇa*, and no longer a son of the Śākya; desiring to make him a novice, a layman, a park-keeper, or a follower of a non-Buddhist path.
Later, whether he investigates or does not investigate—should he investigate, [he asks: "What do you see?
Is it sexual misconduct?"
Did you commit theft?
Did you intentionally kill a human being?
Or did you falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities?
How is it seen?
By what causes and conditions is it seen? Where is it seen?
This is called "investigation.
If one does not inquire in this manner, it is called "non-investigation.
If a pure and blameless bhikṣu, out of a sense of resentment, speaks based on a minor matter belonging to a different category [of offense], it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, out of malice, slanders two who appear similar:
namely, one who is pure and one who is impure.
The pure one asks:
"What offense do you see me committing?
All [the details] are as explained above regarding the groundless [accusations], up to the point of slandering a layperson, which constitutes a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu, out of malice and displeasure, on account of even a minor matter belonging to a different category, speaks [falsely] while abiding in malice, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; the details are as explained above.

At that time, Devadatta, desiring to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, applied himself with diligent expedients to maintain the causes for schism. Regarding the twelve sūtras—the preface to the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), the four *pārājika* rules, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, the two *aniyata* rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, the four *prātideśanīya* rules, the rules on miscellaneous training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), the seven rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), and the rules of conformity (*anudharmika*)—he established what had not been established and relaxed what had already been established. This extended even to the rules practiced in common by householders and renunciants, namely the ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-buddhavacana*).

Regarding the ninefold division of the scriptures—sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, jātaka, vaipulya, and adbhutadharma—they further produce different phrases, different syllables, different flavors, and different meanings for these nine types of sūtras, each explaining them with distinct terminology; they themselves recite, study, and uphold them, and likewise teach others to recite and uphold them.
Then the bhikṣus said to Devadatta:

"Do not employ means to destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha; do not persist in matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha. Do not exert yourself in employing means for the sake of destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, and do not engage in dispute by accepting matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha."
Elder, you should engage in the same affairs as the Saṃgha. Why is this?

Because when the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute, they train together as one, like water and milk blending; thus, teaching the Dharma according to the Dharma, they illuminate it and dwell in peace and happiness.
When he did not desist despite being admonished thus once, and likewise did not desist after being admonished a second and third time,
the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Devadatta, desiring to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, applied himself with diligent skillful means to uphold the matter of schism; from the preface of the precepts up to the ninefold division of the Dharma, he explained them with different phrases, different words, different nuances, and different meanings, using various distinct expressions for each, both reciting and practicing them himself and teaching them to others.
At that time, the bhikṣus admonished him once, but he did not desist; they admonished him a second and a third time, yet he still did not desist.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Devadatta is a foolish man!"

Desiring to break the harmonious Saṃgha, he diligently employs skillful means to maintain the act of schism, even to the point of treating the ninefold Dharma with different phrases, different syllables, different flavors, and different meanings, explaining each with distinct words and expressions.
Regarding "those who do not desist after three admonitions": you should go and admonish them in private three times, and in the midst of a group of many people three times;
then, in the midst of the Saṃgha, you should admonish them three times, causing them to relinquish this matter.
When a monk advises him in private, he should speak thus: "Devadatta!

Do you truly intend to break the harmonious Saṃgha by persisting in acts that cause schism—even down to the ninefold Dharma—using different phrases, different syllables, different expressions, different meanings, and different wording, both reciting and practicing them yourself and likewise teaching them to others?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
Then one should further say to Devadatta:
"Do not strive with skillful means for the sake of breaking the harmonious Saṃgha; do not persist in the matters that cause schism.
Venerable Devadatta!
To break the harmonious Saṃgha is the greatest evil and a grave offense; one shall fall into the evil realms and enter the hells, suffering retribution for kalpas."
Devadatta! Out of my compassionate desire to benefit you, you should accept my words.
One admonition has already passed; two remain. Will you relinquish this matter?
If he does not relinquish it, the second and third admonitions should be performed in the same manner.
Furthermore, three admonitions should likewise be performed before a large assembly.
If he still does not desist, he should be led before the Saṃgha, and a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) seeking his consent should be carried out.
The *karmavācanā* proponent speaks as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This Elder Devadatta, desiring to break the harmonious Saṃgha, has applied himself with diligent effort to maintain the causes for schism; regarding the twelve matters, up to the ninefold scriptures, he recites them himself and teaches others to do so, using different phrases, different syllables, different nuances, different meanings, and different wording."
Having already been admonished three times in private and three times before a group of many people, he still does not desist.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha shall now formally admonish him three times within the Saṃgha to cause him to desist.
The Saṃgha should ask Devadatta:

"Is it true that regarding the twelve dharmas, up to the ninefold scriptures, you have recited and retained them for yourself, and taught them to others, using different phrases, different words, different expressions, different meanings, and different terminology?"
“Monks, have you already admonished him three times in private and three times in the midst of a group, yet he still does not desist?
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
The Saṃgha should admonish him, saying: "O Devadatta!

Do not strive with skillful means for the sake of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha; do not persist in acts that cause schism, such as teaching the ninefold scriptures with different phrases, different words, different flavors, different meanings, and different expressions."

Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; to cause a schism in the Saṃgha is a great evil deed, a grave offense leading to rebirth in the evil realms and the hells, where one shall suffer punishment for kalpas.
Today, the Saṃgha has admonished you with a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of your benefit; you should accept the words of the Saṃgha.
One admonition has passed, and two remain; you should relinquish this matter.
"If he does not relinquish it, and after being thus admonished a second and third time, he still does not desist,
the bhikṣus again went to inform the Blessed One of this matter:
'This Devadatta has already been admonished three times in private, three times before a group of many, and three times before the Saṃgha, yet he still does not relinquish this matter.'"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This foolish Devadatta!

He has disrupted the harmony of the Saṃgha and diligently employed skillful means to maintain the act of schism. Although he has been formally admonished three times in private, three times before a group of many, and three times before the Saṃgha, he still does not relinquish this matter; therefore, the Saṃgha should perform the *karma* of formal censure against him."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
How is it that Devadatta, refusing to accept the admonitions of the bhikṣus, has brought suffering and affliction upon himself?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that he suffered distress by disbelieving the words of others; in past ages, too, he was just like this."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“Has this happened before?
The Buddha said:
"In this way, in times past, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.

At that time, there was a brahmin who constructed a charitable well in a wilderness. For those who were herding cattle, gathering firewood, or traveling along the road, all would come to the well to drink and bathe."
At that time, as the sun was setting, a pack of jackals came toward the well to drink the residual water remaining on the ground.
There was a leader of the jackals who did not drink the water on the ground, but instead thrust his head into the jar to drink the water.
Having finished drinking the water, he raised the jar high and smashed it; yet the rim of the jar remained pierced through his neck.
The other jackals said to their leader:
"If even damp tree leaves that are fit for use must always be protected, how much more so this jar, which benefits travelers?"
The jackal leader said, "I take pleasure in doing this;
I shall simply satisfy my own mind—why should I concern myself with the affairs of others?
Then the practitioner spoke to the brahmin:
"Your water jar at the well has broken.
He put another one on, yet it was broken by a jackal just as before;
this happened more than once, until fourteen jars had been broken.
The jackals repeatedly admonished him, yet he still would not accept their words.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Who is this person who is creating obstacles for my meritorious well? I shall go now to see."
Knowing the reason for this, he took a water jar and went to place it at the edge of the well, where he waited in concealment to observe.
He saw that although many passersby drank the water and departed, none of them broke the jar.
When evening approached, he saw a pack of jackals coming to drink the water remaining on the ground; only the leader of the jackals drank from the jar before smashing it to pieces.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"It is indeed a jackal that is creating obstacles for my merit-well.

He then fashioned a wooden bucket, sturdy and difficult to break, with a narrow opening at the top so that it was easy to put in but difficult to take out. Placing it by the side of the well, he took up his staff and waited for him in a concealed spot.

After the traveler had finished drinking, as evening approached, a pack of jackals gathered; they drank the water remaining on the ground as before, but when the leader of the jackals finished drinking the water from the jar, he threw it to the ground, yet was unable to break it.
At that time, the brahmin took up his staff, went out, and beat the jackal to death.
Then a deva in the air spoke this verse:
"The wise speak words of compassion, Yet the obstinate and cruel do not accept admonition; [They reject the counsel of those who wish them well. "
"By stubbornly persisting in his obstinacy, he invited this calamity and brought about the loss of his own life;
thus it was that the foolish jackal encountered such suffering from the wooden jar.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The jackal leader at that time was none other than Devadatta;
the pack of jackals were those bhikṣus who now admonish Devadatta."
"Monks, you should know that in the past, because he did not accept the gentle words of his spiritual friends, he lost his own life.
Now again, because he does not accept the admonitions of the bhikṣus, he shall fall into the evil realms and suffer for a long night."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”

If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of breaking a harmonious Saṃgha, exerts himself with skillful means, maintains the causes for breaking the Saṃgha, and engages in dispute, the other bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!..."
Do not strive with skillful means to uphold the causes for a schism in the Saṃgha, nor engage in disputes for the sake of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha;
rather, you should act in concert with the Saṃgha.

Why is this? Because when the Saṃgha is united, joyful, and free from dispute, they share a single training like water and milk blending together, teaching the Dharma according to the Dharma, illuminating it, and dwelling in peace and happiness.
"Venerable one, abandon this matter of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the monks thus admonish that bhikṣu, if he persists in that matter and does not abandon it, the monks should admonish him a second and a third time.
In order to relinquish this matter, it is good if one relinquishes it upon the second and third admonitions;
if one does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Monks" is as explained above. "A harmonious Saṃgha" means not being a separate group;

although the monks may quarrel and further incite one another, because they reside within a single boundary, a single assembly, and a single location, and perform the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* together, it is called a harmonious Saṃgha.
To what extent can it be said that one has exerted effort and maintained the act of schism so as to break the harmony of the Saṃgha?
If a bhikṣu, regarding the twelve matters— the introduction to the precepts, the four pārājikas,

the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas, the two aniyatas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas, the ninety-two pāyattikas, the four pratideśanīyas, the śaikṣa dharmas, the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha dharmas, and the anudharmas— should enact what has not been enacted or rescind what has been enacted, this is called the matter of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, to establish as an offense that which was not previously established among the five classes of offenses, or to relax that which has been established, is called an act that breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, to establish as an offense that which was not previously established among the four classes of offenses, or to relax that which has been established, is called an act that breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, regarding the offenses of the three groups, the two groups, and the one group, as well as the four *pārājikas*: to establish what was not previously established, or to relax what has been established, is called the act of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, there are six methods for the relinquishment of formal acts (*karmas*):

the act of subduing (*tarjanīya-karman*), the act of silence (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*), the act of reconciliation (*prasādanīya-karman*), the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the act of suspension (*utkṣepanīya-karman*), and the act of separate residence (*parivāsa-karman*). Regarding these six methods for the relinquishment of formal acts, to enact what has not been enacted, or to relax what has been enacted, is called the matter of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
A monk who causes a schism in the Saṃgha is, for example, Devadatta.
"The various monks" refers to whether there be one, two, many, or the entire community of monks.
Regarding the three admonitions: there are three admonitions in private, three admonitions in the midst of many people, and three admonitions before the Saṃgha.
As for the three admonitions in private, one asks:
"Venerable sir!..."

Is it true that you, for the purpose of breaking the Saṃgha, have diligently applied skillful means to maintain the act of schism—such as seeking to enact those twelve matters that have not yet been enacted, or to rescind those that have already been enacted?
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
that bhikṣu immediately admonished him, saying:

"Elder! Do not strive with skillful means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha by maintaining the causes for schism—namely, that which was not prescribed among the twelve matters, you prescribe; and that which was prescribed, you open up."
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha commits a grave offense, falling into the evil realms and entering the hells to suffer for a long night.
I now admonish you with a heart of compassion; for your benefit, please accept my words. One admonition has already passed, and two remain. Will you relinquish this matter?"
If they do not relinquish it, the second and third admonitions are to be performed in the same manner.
The same applies to the three prior admonitions before the assembly of many.
If they still do not desist, they should be brought before the Saṃgha, and a *jñapti-karman* (motion for formal authorization) should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been diligently applying means to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and has persistently maintained the matter of schism. Although he has already been admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of a group, he still does not desist."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, we shall now offer three admonitions within the Saṃgha to cause you to desist.
Within the Saṃgha, they further ask:
"Venerable One!..."

Is it true that you have diligently employed skillful means for the purpose of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, persisting in the act of schism, even to the point of abolishing what has not been established and opening what has been established?
If he replies,
“It is indeed so,” one should immediately admonish him, saying:
"Now, O Elder, the Sangha exhorts you:

do not strive with skillful means to maintain the act of schism for the purpose of breaking the harmonious Sangha, nor [insist that] what has not been prescribed be prescribed, or that what has been prescribed be set aside."
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha commits a most grievous and profound evil, and shall suffer for a long night within the miserable realms.
Today, the assembly of monks admonishes you with a compassionate heart; you should cease this matter."
"If he does not relinquish it, a second and third admonition shall likewise be made.
When thus admonished, if he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
When this bhikṣu is being admonished in private and does not desist after one admonition, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
The second and third times he was likewise admonished.
When he was admonished in the midst of a large assembly, if he did not desist after the first admonition, he committed an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
It was the same for the second and third admonitions.
When one reaches the midst of the Saṃgha for the first admonition, if the speech is not yet finished, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
when the speech is finished, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
During the second admonition, if the speech is not yet finished, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If the speech is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the third admonition is spoken but not finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the speech is finished, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Once a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has arisen, whether it be through admonition in private, admonition in the midst of many people, or admonition within the Saṃgha, all such offenses against the Vinaya and all *sthūlātyaya* offenses shall be combined entirely into one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one desists in the interim, they shall be punished according to the point at which they desist.
Therefore it is said:

"If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of breaking a harmonious Saṃgha, exerts himself with skillful means and persists in the act of schism, and even after being admonished three times does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The tenth precept is concluded. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, when the monks were performing the *karma* of formal accusation against Devadatta, no one raised an objection after the first *karma* was completed, nor did anyone raise an objection after the second *karma* was completed. During the third *karma*, Devadatta looked toward the faces of the group of six monks and said:
"O group of six monks!..."
"For a long night you have served me and worked together with me.
Now the Saṃgha has performed the *karma* of formal accusation against me; it has already reached the second proclamation, yet you remain silent."
Today you all have taken me from among the multitude like curd smeared on parched grain given to a crow;
like ghee smeared on a cake given to a *nākulī*;
like oil mixed with rice given to a jackal.
"The practitioners of the holy life are being oppressed by others, yet you sit and watch them.
The group of six bhikṣus then rose and spoke these words: "So it is!"
"So it is, Elder! This is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma, a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya."
Whatever this bhikṣu speaks of, all those things we wish to accept;
whatever this bhikṣu has seen and wishes to accept, we also wish to accept.
"This bhikṣu speaks with knowledge; he does not speak without knowledge.
At that time, many people obstructed the *karmavācanā* so that it was not accomplished. Then the bhikṣus said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not assist Devadatta in causing a schism in the Saṃgha by sharing his words and views; you should instead act in harmony with the Saṃgha.

May the entire Saṃgha be united, joyful, and free from dispute; may they train together as one, like water and milk blending, dwelling in peace and happiness while illuminating the Dharma according to the Dharma.
When they had thus admonished him once and he did not desist, and after a second and third admonition he still did not desist,
the bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“These six groups of bhikṣus, together with the foolish Devadatta, desire to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; they share the same speech and the same views, and have not desisted despite being admonished once, twice, and three times.”
"You must go and admonish him three times in private, three times before a group of many, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha, so that he may relinquish this matter.
The bhikṣu, having received these instructions, immediately questioned the group of six bhikṣus in private:
"Is it true that you, along with the foolish Devadatta, have broken the harmony of the Saṃgha, sharing the same words and views as his faction?"
“Monks, having already admonished them twice or thrice, have they still not desisted?
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
He then admonished them:
"You, group of six bhikṣus!

Do not share speech or views with Devadatta who has broken the harmony of the Saṃgha. You should act in concert with the Saṃgha; let the entire Saṃgha be harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute. Being of one training like water mixed with milk, you should dwell in peace and happiness, illuminating through the teaching of the Dharma according to the Dharma."
Venerable elders!
To cause a schism in the Saṃgha is the greatest offense; it leads to rebirth in the evil realms and the hells, where one suffers for a long night.
Out of compassion and with the desire to benefit you, I now admonish you: you should accept my words.
"One admonition has passed and two remain; you should relinquish this matter.
If he does not desist, the second and third [admonitions] are likewise spoken.
Furthermore, the threefold admonition before the assembly of many is conducted in the same manner.
If they still do not desist, the Saṃgha should perform the *jñapti-karman* for seeking permission:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These six groups of bhikṣus share the same speech and views as Devadatta in breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha; they have already been admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of a multitude, yet they still do not desist."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, you should admonish them three times within the assembly to cease [this conduct].
He then questioned the group of six bhikṣus in the midst of the Saṃgha:

"Is it true that you have spoken and held views in concert with Devadatta in order to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, and that after being admonished three times in private and three times before a multitude, you still do not desist?"
He replied, “It is indeed so. Thereupon,
he was admonished again, saying:
“O group of six bhikṣus!
Do not associate with Devadatta in speech or view to break the harmony of the Saṃgha.
To break the harmony of the Saṃgha is the most heinous of deeds; it leads to rebirth in the evil realms and the hells, where one suffers for a long night.”
"Now the Saṃgha exhorts you with a mind of loving-kindness for your benefit; you should accept the words of the Saṃgha.
One exhortation has already passed, and two remain. You must relinquish this matter.
If he does not desist, the second and third exhortations are likewise administered; yet he still does not relinquish it.
The bhikṣus again reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
They were immediately summoned.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:

"Is it true that you, along with the foolish Devadatta, have shared his speech and views in order to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; and that although the bhikṣus have already admonished you three times in private, three times in a group, and three times before the Saṃgha, you still do not relinquish this?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, "Monk! This is an evil deed.

Have you not constantly heard me, through various causes and conditions, rebuke those who are stubborn and difficult to admonish, and through various causes and conditions, praise those who are gentle and easy to admonish?"
"How is it that you are so stubborn and difficult to admonish?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot cultivate wholesome qualities by means of this."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Why do these six groups of bhikṣus, together with Devadatta, share the same speech and the same views, only to bring suffering upon themselves?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“These six groups of bhikṣus did not merely suffer in vain through their shared speech and shared views today; in past ages as well, they were already like this.”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Has this indeed happened before?
We only pray that you will explain it to us."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi. In a secluded place, five hundred monkeys were wandering through the forest when they came upon a nyagrodha tree."
Beneath the tree was a well, and within the well, the reflection of the moon appeared.
At that time, the monkey leader saw this reflection of the moon and said to his companions:
"The moon has died today and fallen into the well; we must go together and retrieve it, lest the world remain in the long night of darkness."
They deliberated together, saying,
"How can we get out?
Then the monkey leader said:
"I know the way out. I will grasp a branch of the tree; you must grasp my tail. By linking ourselves together in succession, we may escape.

Then the monkeys did as their leader said, grasping one another in turn. Before they had reached the water, the weight of the monkeys became too great for the weak branch, which snapped, and all the monkeys fell into the well water.
At that time, the tree deity spoke these verses:
"These are but foolish wild beasts, A crowd of deluded ones following one another;
Sitting here, they produce only suffering for themselves— How could they save the world?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The leader of the monkeys at that time was none other than Devadatta.
The other monkeys at that time were the six groups of bhikṣus."
"At that time, they already followed one another in experiencing various sufferings and afflictions; now it is likewise so.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Summon all the bhikṣus residing in Rājagṛha. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a monk, together with one, two, or many others who share his same speech and views, intends to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha,
and when the other monks admonish him, that monk who shares their views says:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not speak of this bhikṣu’s good or bad qualities.
Why? Because he is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya.
Whatever this bhikṣu speaks, all that we also desire to accept;
whatever this bhikṣu has seen and desires to accept, we also desire to accept.
"This bhikṣu speaks with knowledge; he does not speak without knowledge.
Then the bhikṣus admonished those bhikṣus who were in agreement with him, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not speak these words: "This bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma; this bhikṣu speaks according to the Vinaya.
Why is that? Because he is a bhikṣu who does not speak according to the Dharma, nor does he speak according to the Vinaya.
Venerable Elders!
Do not assist in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should joyfully assist in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha. Why is this?

The Saṅgha is harmonious and joyful, free from dispute; they train together as one, like water and milk mixed, teaching the Dharma according to the Dharma, illuminating it, and dwelling in peace and happiness.
Venerable Elders!
"You should relinquish this act of schism in the Saṃgha.

When the monks thus admonish that monk who agrees with [the schismatic], if he persists and does not relinquish it, the monks should admonish him a second and third time so that he may relinquish this matter.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, he abandons this matter, it is well;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"The bhikṣu" refers to Devadatta.
"Bhikṣus who share the same speech and the same views" refers to the group of six bhikṣus.

Whether there be one, two, or many such bhikṣus who share the same speech and the same views, there may be those who share the same speech but not the same views; those who share the same views but not the same speech; those who share both the same speech and the same views; or those who share neither the same speech nor the same views.
"Agreeing in speech but not in view" means that while one's words accord with and support another's, they do not share that person's view; this is called agreeing in speech but not in view.
"Agreeing in view but not in speech" means that while one shares the same view as another, one does not provide verbal support for it; this is called agreeing in view but not in speech.
Those who share the same speech and the same views assist others in their speech and accord with their views; this is called "sharing the same speech and sharing the same views.

Those who do not share the same speech and do not share the same views neither assist others in their speech nor accord with their views; this is called "not sharing the same speech and not sharing the same views."
Among these, those who share the same speech but not the same view, as well as those who share both the same speech and the same view, should be admonished and exhorted.
What is meant by "the dharma of sharing the same speech and the same view"?
Regarding the twelve matters, that which was not prohibited is prohibited, and that which was prohibited is then permitted; this is called the dharma of sharing the same speech and the same view.

Furthermore, regarding the five groups of offenses, those not previously prescribed are now prescribed, and those already prescribed are now opened [for amendment]. The same applies to the four groups, three groups, two groups, and one group of offenses: those not previously prescribed are now prescribed, and those already prescribed are now opened.

Furthermore, regarding the six methods of relinquishing [faults]: that which was not prescribed is prescribed, and that which was prescribed is then opened. This is called the method of identical speech and identical view.
The bhikṣus should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable one!..."
"Do not associate with those who strive through skillful means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha, nor share speech or views with them.
When the bhikṣus admonished these bhikṣus, those who stubbornly clung to this matter were the group of six bhikṣus.
"Various bhikṣus" refers to the Saṃgha, a group of many, or a single individual.
