"Three admonitions" refers to three admonitions in private, three admonitions in the midst of a group, and three admonitions in the midst of the Saṃgha.
One who admonishes in private asks:
"Venerable elders, do you truly share the same speech and views as those who are diligently applying expedient means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha?
They reply:
"It is truly so," he replied. He spoke again,
"Venerable sir!"
Do not associate with those who strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha, nor share their speech or views with them.
The schism of the Saṃgha is the greatest evil; such a person shall fall into the evil realms and suffer for a long night.
I now admonish you with a mind of loving-kindness: you should abandon this matter.
One admonition has already passed; two remain.
It would be well for you to abandon this matter.
If he does not relinquish it, the second and third admonitions are likewise to be spoken.
The same applies to the three admonitions before a group of many people.
Furthermore, if he still does not desist after the three formal acts (*karmavācanā*) have been performed in the Saṃgha, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
If this bhikṣu does not desist after being admonished once in private, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The same applies to the second and third admonitions.
The same applies to the three admonitions among a group of many people.
If one does not desist while the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) in the *saṃgha* is not yet concluded, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
once the recitation is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one does not desist before the second *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *vinayātikrama*;
once it is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Before the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
When the statement is finished, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Once the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has arisen, the three admonitions in private result in *vinayātikrama* offenses, the three admonitions before a group of many people result in *vinayātikrama* offenses, and the [offense] within the Saṃgha results in a *sthūlātyaya*; all these together constitute one single *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the intermediate suspension: one shall be punished according to the place where the suspension was carried out.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"If a bhikṣu consents to assist another, whether it be one, two, or many who speak with the same words and hold the same views, and they do not relinquish [the position] even after three admonitions, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The eleventh precept is concluded. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, the Elder Chanda was of a wicked nature and difficult to converse with. When the bhikṣus instructed him according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, he refused to converse with them and spoke thus:
"Venerable Elders!..."
"Do not speak to me of what is good or evil, nor shall I speak to you elders of what is good or evil.

Why is this? You are all of mixed castes, mere subjects and clerks of my household. It is like a crow or a bird that has gathered various kinds of bones together in one place; how can you teach me the matters of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha?"
"All these are my own. Since the Bodhisattva went forth from home, I have constantly attended upon him until this day.
May the Buddha instruct me; I shall receive and uphold his teachings."
Then the bhikṣus said to Chanda: "Venerable one!

The bhikṣus have rightly explained the matters concerning the transgressions within the Prātimokṣa; you must not make yourself one with whom others cannot speak, but you should make yourself one with whom others can speak."
"Elder! You should speak to the bhikṣus as is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; the bhikṣus, in turn, should speak to you as is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya."
Why is this? Because the assembly of the Tathāgata has grown in this way—namely, by engaging in mutual conversation, mutual discourse, mutual admonition, and emerging together from faults.
Venerable one, you have abandoned yourself and rendered yourself unfit for such conversation.
When he did not desist after the first admonition, and likewise did not stop after the second and third admonitions,
the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One:
"The Elder Channa has engaged in conduct that makes him unfit for communal discourse, yet he does not desist even after being admonished three times."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Chanda is self-willed and cannot be reasoned with; he did not desist even after being admonished three times.
If you go to a secluded place and admonish him three times and he still does not desist, you must then admonish him three times before a large assembly."
If they still do not desist, one should proceed to perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for seeking permission within the Saṃgha.
One should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

This Elder Chanda was of a wicked nature and difficult to speak with; although the bhikṣus spoke to him properly and well regarding the matters of the *prātimokṣa* he had transgressed, he made himself unavailable for conversation. Even after being admonished three times in private and three times before a large assembly, he still did not desist.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, we shall now offer three admonitions within the Saṃgha to cause him to desist from this matter.
He then admonished him within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Channa!..."

"You are indeed of such an evil nature that you are difficult to speak with; though the bhikṣus have spoken to you according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, you yourself act in a way that makes you unspeakable. Have you still not desisted, even after being admonished three times in private and three times before the assembly?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The monks should then admonish him within the Sangha, saying:

"Elder! Do not be ill-tempered and difficult to speak with. When the bhikṣus have spoken well and in accordance with the Dharma regarding the matters of the Prātimokṣa that you have transgressed, do not yourself act in such a way as to be unapproachable. Let the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata increase in this manner: namely, by speaking together, discussing together, admonishing together, and emerging together from offenses."
"The Saṃgha now admonishes you with a mind of loving-kindness for your benefit.
One admonition has already passed; two remain. You should desist from this matter.
If he does not relinquish it, a second and third admonition shall likewise be given in the same manner; yet he still does not desist.
The bhikṣus again went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said, "Call Chanda here.
They immediately called him.
The Buddha asked Chanda:
"Is it true that you are of such an evil nature that you are difficult to speak with, even to the point that you did not desist after the Sangha had admonished you three times?
He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said. "Chanda!"
This is an evil matter.
Have you not constantly heard me, through various causes and conditions, reprimanding self-will and praising the absence of self-will?
Why do you now act willfully and perversely?
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"How is it that the bhikṣu Chanda, following his own inclinations, speaks thus:
'There is only the word of the Buddha; I shall accept only the word of the Buddha'? "O bhikṣus!"
This bhikṣu Channa did not merely refuse the words of others today and rely solely on my own words;
in past lives as well, he was just like this.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Has this indeed happened before?
We would most gladly hear it."
The Buddha said: "It is so.
In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi."
At that time, there was a householder who had a slave named Amagyu, who was by nature fierce and evil.
At that time, the householder was sporting with several sons of brahmins in a garden, while his attendants all remained outside the garden gate.
At that time, Amagandha was beating the attendants outside the garden gate; those who were beaten each reported it to their masters, whereupon all the sons of the brahmins came out to rebuke him.
At that time, Amagandha did not accept their words and replied to the sons of the brahmins:
"I will not follow your words; when my master comes and rebukes me, I shall accept his words."
He continued to strike him without ceasing.
Thereupon, he went to inform his master, Āmāyudha.

Āmāyudha possessed the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); he observed that beneath the site of this quarrel there was a hidden treasure of gold and silver, and it was because the ground was inauspicious that they were fighting.
He immediately went to rebuke him, and at that moment the slave stopped.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was the elder at that time anyone other than [myself]?"
"I am that very person.
The one who was Āmāyus at that time is now the bhikṣu Channa.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that Chanda, relying on the World-Honored One as his protector, treats others with such contempt?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! This bhikṣu Chanda did not only today rely upon me to treat others with contempt; in past lives as well, he already relied upon me to treat others with contempt.”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“Has this happened before?
The Buddha said:
"It was thus.
In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.
At that time, there was a great Brahmin teacher named Bhāradvāja, who served as the preceptor to the king and constantly taught five hundred youths."
At that time, a slave was born into the Brahmin household named Kāla; he was constantly employed to serve the young boys.
According to the law of the Brahmins, members of other castes were not permitted to hear [the sacred teachings] indiscriminately.
Because this slave attended upon and made offerings to him, he was permitted to stay by his side and preach the Brahmanical dharma to the young boys.
This slave possessed sharp faculties; whenever he heard the words of the dharma being preached, he was able to memorize them all.
Once, this slave, having developed a slight resentment toward some other youths, fled to another country.
There he falsely claimed,
"I am the son of the brahmin Phalgu, named Yaññadatta."
He spoke thus to the king’s preceptor, the brahmin:
“I am the preceptor of the King of Vārāṇasī, the son of Bhṛgu.
I have come here with the desire to enter the service of the Great Master and study the brahminical dharma.”
The master replied, "So be it.
This slave was intelligent and had heard [the teachings] previously; hearing them again now, he was able to retain everything he heard.
The teacher was greatly pleased and immediately ordered him to instruct five hundred disciples.
The five hundred youths said,
"You shall teach in our stead, while we shall go back and forth between the royal palace."
This teacher, a brahmin, had no sons, only a daughter; he then thought to himself:
"May I now give my daughter to him as a wife?"
"If Yaśoda were always in my house, he would be like my own son.
He then said to him, "Yaśoda, you must follow my words."
He replied, "I shall follow your instructions.
The Buddha spoke to him again, saying:
"Do not return to Vārāṇasī; remain permanently in this kingdom, for I now give my daughter to you as a wife.
He replied, "I shall follow your instructions."
He gave it to her immediately.
While she was at home, she lived together with her husband like a child, and the household gradually became prosperous and happy.

However, Yaśodattā was difficult to please; whenever her husband prepared food for her, she was constantly filled with resentment, finding it neither sweet nor sour, neither salty nor bland, and neither raw nor cooked, such that it could never satisfy her palate.
The wife constantly thought to herself:
"If there should happen to be a traveler coming from Vārāṇasī, I shall receive from him the method for preparing food and drink, and only then will I make offerings to my husband."
When the brahmin Puluṣa heard all this, he thought to himself:
"My slave Kāla has fled to another country; I must go and seize him, for perhaps I may recover my slave."
He proceeded directly to that kingdom.
At that time, Yaśoda was with his disciples, having gone to the park for recreation; while on the road, he saw his former master from afar and was immediately struck with fear.
He whispered to his disciples: "Young men, you must all return and each continue your studies."
After the disciples had departed, he went before his master, prostrated himself with his head at the master's feet, and said to him:
"Having come to this country, I proclaimed that you, my lord, were my father, and I have thus taken you, the great national preceptor and eminent Brahmin, as my teacher."

"Because of my mastery of the great Vedic scriptures, my teacher, a Brahmin, has taken me as his wife; I pray that you, O Noble One, will not reveal this matter today, for I shall provide the price of a slave to be offered to the master."
The brahmin, being well-versed in worldly affairs, immediately replied:
"You are truly my son; what more need be said?
Simply employ some expedient means to have him sent away at once."
He then took him back home and told his family, "A dear friend of mine has arrived.

His wife was delighted and prepared various kinds of food and drink; once she had finished serving the meal, during a brief moment of leisure, she secretly prostrated at the feet of the brāhmaṇa and asked him:

"I serve my husband, Yaśoda, yet his food and drink offerings are never to my liking. I pray that you will now instruct me on what he used to eat when we were still at home, so that I may prepare food and drink according to those former ways."
The visiting brahmin immediately became incensed and thought to himself: "So it is! So it is!"
"You are tormenting your children.
He said to the woman:
"Simply dismiss me quickly. As I depart, I shall teach you a verse; when you recite this verse, it shall render your husband speechless."
The woman then said to her husband, "The venerable brahmin has come from afar; you should send him away at once.
Her husband then thought to himself:
"As my wife has said, you should send him away early and not let him stay long; if his words are leaked, the harm to me will not be small.
He then gave her a great amount of wealth, instructed her to prepare food, and went himself as the leader to seek companions.
After the wife had finished serving the food, she prostrated at his feet, took her leave, and requested the first verse.
He then instructed her to recite the verse, saying:
"Without kin, wandering to foreign lands, Deceiving the people of the world."
"Coarse food is the constant meal; why then should you find fault with eating it?
"I shall now give you this verse. If he becomes angry and complains that the food is bad, go to his side and recite it softly behind his back so that he may hear it."
Having given these instructions, he returned to his own country.
After Yaśodatta had sent his master away, whenever it was time for a meal, he would again fall into a fit of anger.
The wife then attempted to recite the verse in her husband's presence; upon hearing this verse, the husband’s mind was immediately displeased, and he thought to himself:
"Ah, this old woman has brought forth my own foulness!"
"From that time forth, he always spoke with gentle words, fearing that his wife might reveal their private matters to others.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was the brāhmaṇa Phalgu of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī someone else at that time? [It was none other than myself.]”
I am that very person.
As for the slave Kāraha at that time, he is now the bhikṣu Cchanda.
At that time, he already relied upon my power to treat others with contempt; now, once again, he relies upon my authority to treat others with contempt.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Kauśāmbī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu is obstinate and, when the other bhikṣus instruct him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he follows his own will and says:
"Do not speak to me of what is good or bad; I likewise shall not speak to you of what is good or bad."
The bhikṣus admonished that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable one!
The bhikṣus instruct you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; do not act according to your own will."
The bhikṣus should instruct you, and you should likewise instruct the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. Why is this?
Because when the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples instruct one another and admonish one another, they emerge together from their faults, and thus wholesome dharmas increase.
When the bhikṣus admonish this bhikṣu, he should relinquish that matter.
If he does not relinquish it, they should admonish him a second and a third time.
If he relinquishes it, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"The bhikṣu who uses perverse speech" refers to the bhikṣu Chanda.

"The bhikṣus who instruct according to the Dharma and the Vinaya" means they instruct one another by means of this Dharma and Vinaya: the introduction to the precepts, the four pārājikas, the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas, the two aniyatas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas, the ninety-two pāyattikas, the four pratideśanīyas, the dharmas of training (śaikṣa-dharmas), the seven adhikaraṇa-śamathas, and the dharmas that accord with the discipline.
Furthermore, there are offenses involving five groups, four groups, three groups, two groups, and one group.
Furthermore, there are six methods for relinquishing through formal acts, which involve instructing one another in succession.

Furthermore, regarding the *pārājika* rules, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *pāyattika*, and even down to the *vinayātikrama* offenses: if one speaks what is true rather than false, at the proper time rather than the improper time, for the benefit of others rather than their detriment, and with gentle words rather than harsh speech—doing so out of a compassionate heart and without seeking out faults—this is called instructing one another in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
"The bhikṣu" refers to Chanda.
"The bhikṣus" refers to one person, several persons, or the Saṃgha.
"Three admonitions" refers to three admonitions in private, three admonitions in the presence of several persons, and three admonitions in the midst of the Saṃgha.
In a private place, one should ask:
"Venerable sir!
Is it true that you yourself use perverse speech, and when the bhikṣus instruct you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, you yourself act so as to be beyond conversation?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
[the other] spoke in admonition:

"Elder! Do not be so obstinate in your speech. When the bhikṣus instruct you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, you should accept it. Do not make yourself unapproachable for conversation; rather, through mutual instruction, you shall attain the increase of wholesome qualities."
"I now instruct you with a heart of loving-kindness; you should abandon this matter. One admonition has passed, and two remain.
If he does not abandon it, the second and third admonitions are likewise to be given in this manner.
The same applies to the three admonitions in the midst of a large assembly.
If he still does not desist, the *saṃgha* shall perform the *jñapti-karman* for seeking permission.
The formal motion (*jñapti*) is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so uses perverse speech.

Although the bhikṣus have instructed him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he does not accept their words. He has already been admonished three times in private and three times before a multitude, yet he still does not desist."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, it should offer three admonitions within the assembly to cause him to desist from this matter.
Thereupon, the monks asked him within the assembly:

"Venerable sir, is it true that you persist in using perverse speech; that when the bhikṣus instruct you according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, you do not accept their words; and that even after being admonished three times in private and three times before a group of many, you still do not accept them?"
He replied, “It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the Saṃgha again admonished him, saying:
"Elder! Do not act according to your own whims. The bhikṣus instruct you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, even instructing one another in turn, so that wholesome qualities may increase."
Now the Sangha admonishes you with a mind of loving-kindness for your benefit; you should accept the words of the Sangha and relinquish this matter.
One admonition of the Sangha has already passed; two remain.
If he does not desist, and after a second and third admonition he abandons [the course], it is well;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu does not desist when admonished three times in private or when admonished three times in the midst of a group, for each instance of admonition he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
When he is being admonished in the midst of the Saṃgha, if the first admonition has not yet concluded, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense;
once the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is completed, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the second *karmavācanā* has not yet concluded, it is an offense of violating the *vinaya*;
once it is concluded, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the third *karmavācanā* has not yet concluded, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

When the explanation is finished, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Once the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has arisen, all offenses of *vinayātikrama*—whether admonished in private or within the Saṃgha—as well as all *sthūlātyaya* offenses, are all combined into a single *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the intermediate suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), one should punish the offense according to the specific point at which the suspension was halted.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"If a bhikkhu uses obstinate speech and does not relinquish it even after being admonished up to three times, it is a saṃghādisesa."
The twelve rules [of training] are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in various improper conducts at the village of Kāśi-Kṛṣṇagiri:
improper conduct of body, improper conduct of speech, and improper conduct of both body and speech.

Regarding "the body not being in a state of dignified deportment": this refers to running back and forth, leaping and jumping, crawling on all fours, clapping pots together in jest, carrying one another on the shoulders, and engaging in various such physical antics.

Regarding improper conduct of speech: one makes the cries of an elephant, a camel, an ox, or a sheep; one makes long sounds or short sounds; or one whispers into each other's ears; one engages in such various vocalizations for the sake of play and laughter.

Regarding those whose physical and verbal conduct lacks dignified decorum: they cause their bodies to become mottled or half-white, smear their faces black, dye their hair white, beat drums, play lutes, clap their hands, and engage in dancing and theatrical performances.

At that time, several upāsakas came to visit the bhikṣus, wishing to pay their respects and listen to the Dharma; seeing such a sight, they felt displeasure in their hearts and spoke these words: "Ācāryas!..."
The dharma of a śramaṇa consists of virtuous conduct that should cause those without faith to believe and increase the faith of those who already believe.
Yet what you are doing now is entirely contrary to the Dharma; it causes the lack of faith to grow and destroys the minds of those who do believe.
The group of six bhikṣus then spoke with anger:
"Do you consider yourself my teacher or my preceptor?
This is contrary to reason; I am the one who should instruct you, yet you instead instruct me."
His anger and hatred intensified, leading him to commit physical harm, verbal harm, and both physical and verbal harm. As for physical harm:

he entered their homes, dragged children about, beat and threw them down, smashed household vessels, broke the legs of calves, and pierced out the eyes of sheep. Furthermore, at the marketplaces, he mixed together various kinds of grain—rice, wheat, barley, salt, flour, ghee, oil, milk, and curd—until they were completely blended and could no longer be distinguished.

When sprouts grow in a field, one who requires water opens the channels to let it out, while for those that do not require water, one cuts them off so that the field remains full; to cut down and kill the living sprouts and burn the ripened grain—this is called physical violence and harm.
Viciousness of speech refers to going before a king to slander others and falsely accuse the virtuous; this is called viciousness of speech.
Viciousness of both body and speech refers to hiding one's person in a secluded place to terrify someone, or dragging and pulling an innocent person; this is called viciousness of body and speech.
All the upāsakas became incensed and said, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have committed such an unrighteous act; from this day forward, we shall no longer provide them with offerings.
At that time, when the bhikṣu went out to beg for food carrying his bowl, the householders saw him and still gave him food, though they were no longer very generous.
The lay devotees (upāsakas) further made this resolution:
"Since these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have committed such violent harm, we shall not allow them to enter our gates from this day forward.
Thereupon, that bhikṣu went to the houses of those who lacked faith to beg for alms; at first, they gave him food.
Later, he heard that the upāsaka had fasted and refused to give him anything, saying:
"He is certainly an evil man; why should I give him food?
Furthermore, he was not permitted to enter.
Thereafter, one engages in wrong livelihood of body, wrong livelihood of speech, and wrong livelihood of both body and speech.
Regarding wrong livelihood of body: it consists of making and selling water jars, wooden vessels, containers for clarified butter, leather bags, ropes, nets, and sewing garments.

Learning to make and sell cakes, learning to sell medicine, acting as a messenger for others—seeking food through various means such as these is called wrong livelihood of the body (*kāya-mithyājīva*).

Wrong livelihood of the mouth (*vāṅ-mithyājīva*) refers to reciting incantations and practicing arts, such as incantations for snakes and dragons, incantations for ghosts and diseases, and incantations for water and fire—seeking food through various means such as these is called wrong livelihood of the mouth.

Regarding wrong livelihood through body and speech: using one's hands to produce fire spontaneously, reciting incantations with the mouth, pouring clarified butter over one's hands, or scattering mustard seeds—seeking food through such various means is called wrong livelihood through body and speech.

At that time, the upāsakas from the village of Kālapabbata came to Sāvatthī to attend to official business. When their business was concluded, they went to the World-Honored One; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I am an upāsaka from the village of Kālapura. The group of six bhikṣus reside there, and they commit various unrighteous acts in that village.
[The rest is] as explained above in detail.
“I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will instruct him so that it may be well for those who do not dwell there.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the lay follower with a discourse appropriate to his needs, [the lay follower] prostrated at his feet and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go to the village of Kālaparvata and perform the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the group of six bhikṣus.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not dare to go.
The Buddha asked,
“For what reason?”
Ānanda replied:

"World-Honored One, the group of six bhikṣus are by nature restless and violent. If I were to go there, it would be like a man who has harvested sugarcane and is returning home in a carriage; along the way, some young boys come out from the village and seize the sugarcane, taking it at random and eating it on the spot."

Those six groups of bhikṣus are likewise; if they hear that I am coming, they will come out to the side of the road to perform unlawful acts, or perhaps even carry out a formal act of expulsion against me. For this reason, it is difficult for me to depart.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Go with a group of thirty people; you will be sufficient to subdue them.
At that time, Ānanda, surrounded by thirty people before and behind him, went to the village of Kālaparvata.
Furthermore, there were thirty bhikṣus who, hearing that the Venerable Ānanda had gone to the village of Kālapabbata, said to one another:
"We have never heard of a formal act of expulsion being performed; we shall follow Ānanda to that village to witness the performance of the act of expulsion."
Together with the previous thirty, there were sixty bhikṣus, and the great assembly departed.

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Venerable Ānanda was approaching with a retinue of sixty people to perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them, they were immediately seized by fear.
At that time, Suvandada and Mahīśadada went to the village of Rājavatī.
The elders Channa and Kālodāyin went one yojana to welcome the Venerable Ānanda, and immediately offered their repentance, saying: "Elder!..."
"What I have done was not good; I have committed various transgressions and evils. From this day forward, I dare not do so again.
At that time, the assembly of monks accepted his repentance.
When the Venerable Ānanda arrived at the village, those two men had already confessed their transgressions and the other two had already fled;
as for those who remained, he performed the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against them.

The World-Honored One did not permit the performance of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) by an assembly; rather, because the assembly performs the formal act, two or three persons may perform it for another.
The one performing the formal act should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
These bhikṣus, so-and-so by name, have repeatedly engaged in improper physical conduct in this village and have not desisted; this is known to both the monastics and the laity.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion) against these bhikṣus, so-and-so by name, on account of their improper physical conduct. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These elders, the bhikṣus [name], have behaved with a lack of decorum and have not desisted despite repeated admonitions; this is known to both the monastics and the laity. The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against these bhikṣus, [name]."

Venerable sirs, those who approve of the formal act of expulsion against the bhikṣus so-and-so and others for conduct unbecoming of their persons, remain silent; those who do not approve, speak. This first proclamation of the formal act is concluded.
The second and third [proclamations] were likewise spoken.
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of expulsion against the bhikṣus such as So-and-so for improper physical conduct; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
In this same way, improper conduct of speech and improper conduct of both body and speech are treated likewise;
bodily harm, verbal harm, and harm by both body and speech are treated likewise;

and wrong livelihood of body, wrong livelihood of speech, and wrong livelihood of both body and speech are treated likewise, as explained in the *śukla-tri-karmavācanā* (the white threefold formal act).
After the *karmavācanā* had been performed, those monks of the group of six who had been expelled said to the other monks:
"The monk Channa and the monk Kālodayin also practice what is contrary to the Dharma; why have we alone been expelled while they have not?"
The community of monks said to them:
"These two bhikṣus went to meet the Saṃgha for confession at a distance of one yojana;
the Saṃgha has already granted them absolution. Trivandhaka and Mahiṣaka have fled to the village of Rājamārga."
"Since you, sirs, have now neither welcomed the Sangha nor confessed your transgressions, nor have you departed, we shall therefore perform a formal act (karmavācanā) to expel you.
They replied: "Venerable ones!..."
"The Sangha is now acting out of favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion, for they are all committing the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣus admonished them again:
"Venerable ones!"

Do not slander the Saṃgha with what is unreasonable; the Saṃgha does not act out of affection, nor out of hatred, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion. It does not expel some who have committed the same offense while leaving others unexpelled.
When the bhikṣus had thus admonished them, they still did not desist.
A second and a third time they were admonished, yet they remained obstinate and would not stop.
Venerable Ānanda then preached the Dharma to the upāsakas in accordance with their needs, causing them to rejoice; they again made offerings to the Saṃgha as they had done before.
When the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly were about to return to Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Now that the Saṃgha is all returning, who shall be appointed to take charge of this monastery?"
Ānanda asked,
"Who should be appointed to oversee this?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable Channa should remain.
Ānanda spoke again:
"Channa has already committed transgressions in the past, causing others to lose faith; how can he be allowed to stay?"
Having thus arranged for other bhikṣus to take their places,
the Venerable Ānanda returned to the city of Śrāvastī and, having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, stood to one side.
Knowing [his thoughts], the World-Honored One intentionally asked:
“Ānanda! Have you already performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them in the village of Kṛṣṇagiri?
They replied:
"It has been done,
World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Chanda and the bhikṣu Kālodāyin went out one yojana to welcome the Saṃgha and repent."

Svāti and Mahāsvāti immediately went to the village of Rājagṛha; since the other bhikṣus neither came to confess their transgressions nor departed, the Saṃgha performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them.
Seeing that Chanda and Kālodayin had not been expelled, he slandered the Saṃgha with improper words, saying:
"The Saṃgha follows favoritism, follows hatred, follows fear, and follows delusion; there are those who have committed the same offense together, yet some are expelled while others are not."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“These six groups of bhikṣus have slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably, saying:
‘They act out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion; when there are those who have committed the same offense together, some are expelled while others are not.’”

"Regarding those who speak such words, you should go to a secluded place and admonish them three times, then admonish them three times in the midst of many people, and finally admonish them three times within the Saṃgha, so that they may cease this matter."
In a private place, he asked them:
"Is it true that because of the bhikṣus Chanda and Kālodāyin, you have unreasonably slandered the Saṅgha, saying:
'They act out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of delusion, and out of fear; they commit offenses together, yet some are expelled while others are not'?"
He replied, "It is truly so. Thereupon,
[the teacher] admonished him in a secluded place, saying:
"Elder! Do not slander the Saṅgha with what is unreasonable.
For what reason?

The Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion; thus, among those who have committed equal offenses, there are some who are expelled and others who are not.
"Do not, all of you, speak words that follow after desire, anger, fear, or delusion.
Venerable sirs!
I now admonish you with a mind of loving-kindness for your own benefit; you should abandon this matter."
"One admonition has already passed; two admonitions remain.
If he does not relinquish [the offense], he is to be admonished a second and third time in the same manner.
If he still does not desist after being admonished three times before a group of many, the *saṃgha* shall perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for seeking his consent.
The *karmakāraka* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These six groups of bhikṣus have slandered the Saṃgha with what is unreasonable; they have been admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of many people, yet they did not desist.
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, it should admonish this bhikṣu three times within the assembly to cease this matter.
He then asked that bhikṣu in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Is it true that you have groundlessly slandered the Saṃgha, and that after being admonished three times in private and three times in the presence of many people, you still did not desist?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Saṃgha should then admonish him, saying:
"Elder! Do not slander the Saṃgha with what is unreasonable.
For what reason?

The Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion; thus, there are those who commit the same offense yet are expelled, while others are not.
"Now the Saṃgha admonishes you with a mind of loving-kindness for your benefit; you should relinquish this matter.
One admonition has passed; two remain.
If he does not desist, a second and third admonition shall likewise be given, yet he still does not desist.
For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One:
"The group of six bhikṣus, having already been admonished three times in private and even three times in the midst of the Saṃgha, still do not desist."
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it true that you have slandered the Saṃgha in an irrational manner, and that you did not desist despite being admonished three times in private and even three times in the midst of the Saṃgha?
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the group of six bhikṣus:
"This is an evil matter. Have you not heard that the World-Honored One constantly praises those who are easy to admonish and reproves those who are difficult to admonish?"
Why do you now resist admonition and persist in holding to this without relinquishing it?
O group of six bhikṣus!
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Why do these six groups of bhikṣus, because Chanda and Kālodāyin have not been expelled, slander the Saṃgha unreasonably?”
The Buddha said:
"These six groups of bhikṣus have not only slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably today; in past lives as well, they have already slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Has this happened before?
The Buddha said:
"So it was. "I only wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.
At that time, the royal household kept two dogs, which were bound with chains of gold and silver and fed from precious vessels; at night, they were released to guard the gates."
At that time, the king suffered from a headache that persisted for twelve years without improvement through medical treatment; later, he gradually recovered.
While sleeping, the king heard the sound of a dog barking, whereupon he was startled awake and his headache intensified.
The king asked his attendant,
"What kind of sound was that?
He replied:
"A dog is barking.
The King immediately became enraged and commanded his attendants:
"Bring out the dog and drive it away!"
He was immediately driven out according to those instructions.
At that time, a dog asked the one who was driving him away,
"For what reason are you driving me away?"

The driver replied, "The King’s illness has slightly improved, but while sleeping he heard the sound of dogs barking; startled awake, his condition worsened, and for that reason I have driven you away.
The dog asked again:
"Have all the dogs been driven out?
He replied,
"They have all been driven out."
He asked again:
"Were the two dogs of the royal household also driven away?
He replied:
"The two dogs of the royal household are not driven away, while all the others are driven away.
The dogs then spoke with indignation:
"This king is unrighteous; he acts according to favoritism, according to hatred, according to fear, and according to delusion."
The dog then spoke in verse:
"If dogs were considered a nuisance, All should be driven out;
Yet you do not drive them all away— I know this king is without the Way."
“My own household raises two dogs, yet they do not drive them away alone; they drive me away.
You should know that this wicked king follows after craving, hatred, fear, and delusion.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The dog of the royal family at that time was none other than the bhikṣus Chanda and Kālodāyin now;
the other dogs were the six groups of bhikṣus now."
At that time, although he was expelled, because the two dogs were not expelled, he slandered [the community] unjustly.
Today, his expulsion is likewise; because the bhikṣus Chanda and Kālodāyin have not been expelled, he slanders the Saṃgha unjustly.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Why was it that when the multitude wished to appoint the bhikṣu Chanda to an administrative office, Ānanda would not permit it?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that this bhikṣu Chanda wished to return to his administrative duties and Ānanda did not permit it;
in a past life, he had already once sought to be appointed as king, and Ānanda did not permit it."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Has this indeed happened before?”
The Buddha said,
“It is so. [The interlocutor replied,] “I only wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said,
"In a past age, at the foot of the Snowy Mountains, amidst the folds of a winding mountain range, there was a warm place facing the sun where various kinds of birds gathered like clouds."
They then deliberated together, saying:
"Today we must elect one bird as king, so that the multitude will stand in awe and refrain from committing unrighteous acts.
The birds said:
"Excellent!
Who should be made king?
A certain bird said:
"One should consult the *cāṣa* and the *haṃsa*. A bird said, "That will not do!"
"Why is this? Because they have long legs and long necks; these birds might inadvertently peck at our brains. They all said:
"Yes," they replied. Then another bird said:
"We should elect the goose as king; his color is pure white and he is revered by all the birds."
The birds spoke again:
"This too is impossible!
Although its color is white, its neck is long and curved; since its own neck is not straight, how can it correct others?"
Again he said:
"There is indeed a peacock, its plumage adorned with variegated colors, which delights the eyes of all who behold it; it should be made king.
He spoke again:
"No! Why is this? Although their feathers are beautiful, they lack a sense of shame; whenever it is time to dance, their ugly forms appear. For this reason, it is not permissible."
A certain bird said:
"The bald owl should be king. Why is this? Because—"
"By day he remains tranquil, and by night he diligently watches over us; he is worthy to be our king.
The multitude all said, "So be it."
At that time, there was a parrot living in a certain place who possessed wisdom and thought to himself:
"It is the nature of birds to sleep at night for rest;
it is the nature of this bald owl, however, not to sleep at night."
Furthermore, these various birds attend upon me on all sides; they keep watch day and night and do not sleep, which is a source of great suffering for me.
If I were now to speak, they would surely become enraged and pluck out my feathers.

Just as he was about to remain silent, [he thought], "The various kinds of birds have suffered distress for a long night; it would be better for me to endure having my feathers plucked than to transgress the path of righteousness.
He then went before the birds, raised his wings in reverence, and addressed them, saying:
"I pray that you will listen as I recite a single verse."
Then the birds immediately replied with a verse:
"Wisdom and broad knowledge of meaning do not depend on advanced age;
though you are young in years, as a wise one, you should speak at this time."
At that time, having heard the verses spoken by the assembly of birds, the parrot immediately spoke these verses in reply:
"If you follow my counsel, do not choose the King of the Bald Owls;
even when his face is beheld in a moment of joy, he still causes terror among the birds."
"How much more so when he is angry, that his face cannot even be looked upon.
At that time, the birds all said,
"It is truly as you have said."
They immediately gathered to deliberate:
"This parrot is clever and wise; he is fit to be our king.
They then installed him as king.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who was the bald owl at that time is now the bhikṣu Chanda.
The one who was the parrot is now Ānanda."
"At that time, he had already forbidden him and would not allow him to be king;
now again he forbids him and will not allow him to hold office.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.

There are certain bhikṣus residing in cities or villages who defile families and engage in evil conduct; they are seen and heard to defile families, and they are seen and heard to engage in evil conduct.”
The monks should say to those monks:
"Venerable sirs!
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; that you have defiled families has been seen and heard by us, and that you have committed evil deeds has also been seen and heard by us."
"Elders! You should go out; you should not remain here.
Then that bhikṣu spoke to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
The Saṃgha follows affection, follows hatred, follows fear, and follows delusion. Why is this so?"
"There may be bhikṣus who have committed such an identical offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!..."

"You all must not speak thus: 'The Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, or out of delusion; for there are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.'"
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha does not follow affection, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion.
Venerable Elders!

"You have defiled families and practiced evil conduct; you have been seen and heard to defile families, and you have been seen and heard to practice evil conduct. You should depart; do not remain here."
"When these bhikṣus thus admonish him, if he persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should admonish him a second and a third time so that he may relinquish this matter."
"If, upon the second and third admonitions, he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding "the monks": this refers to the Saṃgha, or a group of many, or a single person.
Regarding those who dwell in dependence upon a city or a village: what does it mean to dwell in dependence upon a village?
If a bhikṣu obtains robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for the sick within that village, this is called dwelling in dependence.

Furthermore, if one does not obtain clothing, food, bedding, or medicinal decoctions for illness and debility, yet merely relies upon a village settlement to escape various hardships, this is also called "dwelling by reliance."
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu does not reside in a village for the sake of avoiding danger, but dwells depending on the boundary of a village, this is also called "dwelling by dependence.
Regarding "defiling another's family": other families refers to the families of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras; these are called "other families."
Regarding "defiling": if a bhikṣu engages in unchaste conduct, drinks alcohol, or eats at improper times within a village, this is not called "defiling a family.

If he causes those in the village who previously possessed faith—those who made offerings to the Saṃgha and established stūpas and monasteries—to fall away and lose their resolve, this is called "defiling a family."

One who practices evil conduct has non-restraint in body, non-restraint in speech, and non-restraint in both body and speech; there is violence in body, violence in speech, and violence in both body and speech; and there is wrong livelihood in body, wrong livelihood in speech, and wrong livelihood in both body and speech.
"Regarding one who defiles a family and commits evil deeds, both seen and heard": it means that while he performs various evil deeds, the people of the village also see and hear of them.
The monks say to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to defile families, and you have been seen and heard to commit evil deeds. Do not remain among us."
That bhikṣu speaks thus: "Venerable sirs!
The Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion; there are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not."
The bhikṣus spoke again to that bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable one! Do not speak such words.
The Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion; you must relinquish this matter."
Those monks who stubbornly persisted in their refusal to relinquish [their position] and unreasonably slandered the Saṃgha were the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika).
"The monks" refers to the Saṃgha, a large group, or a single individual.
Regarding the "three admonitions": these are the three admonitions in private, the three admonitions in the midst of many people, and the three admonitions before the Saṃgha.
As for the admonition in private, one asks in a secluded place: "O Elder!..."
In fact, he slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably, saying:
"Do you follow favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion, such that among bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not?"
He replied, “It is indeed so. Thereupon,
[the Buddha] rebuked him again, saying:
"Elder! Do not speak such words; you are unreasonably slandering the Saṃgha.
For what reason?

The Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion; thus, among those who have committed equal offenses, there are some who are expelled and some who are not.
"I now admonish you with a heart of loving-kindness for your benefit; you should desist from this matter. One admonition has passed, two remain.
If he does not desist, there shall be a second and third admonition.
If, after being admonished three times in the midst of a large group of people, one still does not desist, the *saṃgha* shall perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal act) for requesting permission.
One should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣu so-and-so has slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably; he has already been admonished three times in private and three times before a group of many, yet he still does not desist.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, we shall now admonish him three times within the Saṃgha to cause him to cease this matter.
The Sangha should ask him:
"Venerable sir!
Is it true that you have groundlessly slandered the Sangha by speaking these words?"
"The Sangha follows after desire, follows after hatred, follows after fear, and follows after delusion.
Even after being admonished three times in private and three times before a large assembly, do they still not desist?
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Sangha should then admonish him, saying:
"Elder! Are you not slandering the Saṃgha with what is unreasonable?
For what reason?"

The Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion; thus, regarding those who have committed equal offenses, some are expelled while others are not.
"Now the community of monks admonishes you with a mind of loving-kindness for your benefit. One admonition has passed; two remain. You should relinquish this matter.
If he does not relinquish it, there should be a second and third admonition; if he relinquishes it, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
When this bhikṣu is being admonished in private, if he does not desist after three admonitions, for each admonition he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
It is likewise when one is admonished three times before a large group of people.
Within the Saṃgha, if the initial statement is not yet finished, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
once the statement is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the second recitation is not yet finished, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense;
if the recitation is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the third recitation is not yet finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When the explanation is finished, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Once the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* has arisen—excluding the four *sthūlātyaya* offenses for groundless slander of the Saṃgha—all other offenses of *vinayātikrama* incurred during the three admonitions in private, the three admonitions in the midst of many people, and the three admonitions in the midst of the Saṃgha, as well as all *sthūlātyaya* offenses, are collectively merged into one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding intermediate cessation: one should punish the offense according to the specific point at which the monk ceases [the misconduct]. Therefore it is said:
"If there are bhikṣus who dwell in dependence on a city or a village, and when they are admonished for the second and third time, they relinquish [their conduct], that is good;..."
"If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The thirteen rules are concluded. **The Two Indeterminate Rules (Aniyata-dharma)** Regarding the first of the two indeterminate rules: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, there was a daughter of an old Brahmin acquaintance from the same village as the Elder Udāyin who had recently arrived at her husband’s home. She was distressed and unhappy, so she sent a messenger to tell her father:
"Please come to see me; if you cannot come yourself, tell the teacher Udāyin to come and see me."
Upon hearing this, her father went to Udāyin and said to him:
"My daughter has recently arrived at her husband’s home; she is distressed and unhappy, and she sent a messenger to summon me as well as you, O Ācārya."
"I am now a layperson with many affairs and cannot go; I pray that the Ācārya will go to visit me frequently.
Udāyin replied, "So be it!"
"If you had not entrusted me with this, I would still have wished to go and see; how much more so now that you have entrusted me?
On the following morning, the Elder Udāyin put on his village-dwelling robe and went to that house.
At that time, the woman sat with the door closed.
Udāyin called out from outside, "Is such-and-such there?"
The woman asked, "Who is this? He replied:
"I am Udāyin! The woman said, "Welcome, Preceptor! Please enter!"
"The Ācārya, please come in!
He then entered the room.
Once seated within the room, he engaged in conversation with him.
At that time, the mother-in-law Gopī Śakrā had thirty-two sons and also thirty-two grandsons; all her daughters-in-law were endowed with merit and auspicious marks.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, who was constantly instructing her sons and daughters-in-law and exhorting her parents and relatives, arrived at the door of this daughter’s room.
Being well-versed in propriety, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā did not enter the room abruptly, but paused hesitantly outside the door.

Through the opening of a door, he saw someone inside the room shaving their head and wearing dyed robes; observing their blinking eyes and soft speech, he knew they were a renunciant, yet he did not know whether they were a bhikṣu.
"Is this a bhikṣuṇī?
He then called out to the woman,
and she replied:
"Who is it? He replied, "It is I."
He said, "Mistress, come forward.
He asked:
"Whose wife are you to him?
She replied, "The Ācārya Udāyin!"
Udāyin said, "Upāsikā, why do you not go forward?
Mṛgāramātā then entered and spoke these words:
“Ācārya Udāyin! Are you sitting here? He replied:
"So be it," he replied, saying:
"O Ācārya, this seat is not a place of clarity; if there were good or evil, who would witness and know it?"
"You should speak of this matter to the bhikṣus.
Udāyin said, "What do you mean?"
Visākhā Migāramātā said,
"I saw Udāyin sitting together with a woman. Udāyin said:
"I shall also speak of you to the Buddha. Visākhā Migāramātā said,
"What would you wish to say?"
Udāyin said, "I saw Visākhā Migāramātā sitting together with another man.
Visākhā Migāramātā said:
"What kind of man? Udāyin said, "Am I not a man?"
Visākhā Migāramātā said, "Ācariya!
The Buddha has not prohibited me from sitting together with men; however, you are a renunciant and ought to protect the Dharma of the śramaṇas."
Udāyin said: "Alas! You have troubled me no small amount."
He then rose and departed, and again sat down in an open space with a woman.

After Visākhā Migāramātā had finished instructing her daughter-in-law and gone out, she saw Udāyin sitting and conversing with a woman in an open space; she went up to him and said to Udāyin, "This is unwholesome;
it is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa."
"What is it to sit with a woman in an exposed place?
You should report this matter to the bhikṣus. Udāyin said:
"What was said? Visākhā Mṛgāramātā replied,
"I saw Udāyin sitting alone with a woman in an exposed place."
She said to Udāyin,
"I too shall report your conduct to the Buddha.
Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā said:
"For what reason was this said? Udāyin replied,
"I saw Mṛgī sitting and conversing with a man in an exposed place."
Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ said,
"What kind of man?
She replied:
"Am I not a man? Viśākhā replied, "I am a laywoman;
for a man to sit with me is permitted by the Buddha's Dharma."
"Venerable sir, as a śramaṇa you ought to guard yourself;
why do you act thus? Udāyin replied, "You trouble me everywhere."
Having spoken these words, he immediately rose and departed.
Then Vimalā, the Mother of Viśākhā, reported this matter to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Buddha said:
"Summon Udāyin."
He was immediately summoned.
The Buddha asked Udāyin,
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Udāyin:
"This is an evil deed.
You foolish man!"
Laypeople still know that those who have left the household life ought to practice what is appropriate and avoid what is inappropriate;
yet you, who are renunciants, do not even know how to sit, stand, or speak, nor what should or should not be given.
Have you not often heard the World-Honored One, through various causes and conditions, reprimanding those who follow lustful desires and praising the renunciation of desire?
Why do you now commit such an evil deed?
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas by means of this.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Command all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī to assemble."

Once they had assembled, at that time the World-Honored One, for this reason and by means of various causes and conditions, extensively explained the matter of the faults and evils to the bhikṣus, censuring those faults and evils.
Having arisen, he taught the Dharma in accordance with the truth to the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons of benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has prescribed the precepts for his disciples and established the teaching of the Prātimokṣa."
What are the ten?
First, for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha;
second, for the sake of thoroughly gathering the Saṃgha.
Third, to bring peace and happiness to the Saṃgha;
fourth, to subdue those who lack a sense of shame;
fifth, so that those possessed of a sense of shame may dwell in peace and happiness.
Sixth, to cause those who lack faith to gain faith;
seventh, to increase the faith of those who already possess it;
eighth, to attain the exhaustion of outflows within this very life.
Ninth, because it causes unarisen outflows not to arise;
tenth, because it ensures the True Dharma abides for a long time by opening the gate of the gift of ambrosia for all gods and worldlings—these are called the ten.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has laid down the precepts for his disciples; those who have not heard them shall hear them, and those who have already heard them should hear them again.

If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a suitable spot for sexual intercourse, and a trustworthy upāsikā states one of three matters—whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika—[he is guilty].
If a bhikṣu says of himself,

"I sat in this place," he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma in accordance with each of the three categories of offenses— whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika— and he should be punished according to the Dharma based on what the trustworthy upāsikā has said.
This is the first *aniyata-dharma* for that bhikṣu:

"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded, private place where sexual intercourse is not possible, a trustworthy *upāsikā* may charge him with one of two dharmas: either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,

"I sat in this place," he should be dealt with according to the Dharma as prescribed for each of the two categories— either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or a pāyattika— according to what a trustworthy upāsikā has stated, and he should be dealt with according to the Dharma accordingly.
These two *aniyata-dharmas* concern the bhikṣu.

A bhikṣu is one who has received full ordination, properly received full ordination through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*), for whom there are no obstructing factors, who is in harmony and not in discord, who belongs to a quorum of ten or more, and who is twenty years of age or older and not less than twenty; such a person is called a bhikṣu.
"A woman" refers to one who is a mother, a sister, a relative, or a non-relative;
whether old or young, lay or ordained.
"A secluded place" refers to a dark location or a screened or concealed location.
A "place suitable for sexual intercourse" refers to a situation where a man and woman engage in sexual acts together without cause for shame.
"Alone" means one man and one woman with no other persons present.
Even if there are others present, if they are asleep, insane, infants, non-humans, or animals, it is likewise called being alone.
"Sitting together" means sitting in close proximity.
A "trustworthy female lay follower" (*upāsikā*) is one who has accomplished sixteen qualities; she is called a trustworthy female lay follower.
What are these sixteen?

Taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha; possessing unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha; enabling the Saṅgha to obtain what it has not yet obtained and causing what it has already obtained to increase; enabling the Saṅgha to achieve renown where it lacks it and swiftly extinguishing any ill repute it may have; being free from attachment, free from aversion, free from fear, and free from delusion; and being detached from desire while tending toward the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline—one who is endowed with these sixteen qualities is called "trustworthy."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,
"I know the affairs [of the Saṃgha], but I do not know how to sit," this matter should be dealt with.
If one says,
"I know how to sit, but I do not know the ritual," one should discipline them for their sitting.
If it is said,
"The administrator knows [the matter] and the one seated knows [it]," both should be disciplined.
If one says,

"I do not know the matter, nor do I know the offense," one should be dealt with according to the procedure for a *tassapāpiyasikā* (a formal act of searching for the offense), as explained by the upāsikā.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Woman" refers to one who is a mother, a sister, or one who is older or younger, whether she be a layperson or a renunciant.
"Solitary" means there is only one man and one woman, with no other persons present.
Even if there are others, such as those who are asleep, insane, infants, non-humans, or animals, this is also called being solitary.
An "exposed place" refers to an open space in the midst of daylight, devoid of any screens or enclosures; this is called an exposed place.
An "inappropriate place for sexual intercourse" refers to a location where the mutual acts of a man and a woman would be shameful.
"Sitting" means sitting in close proximity.
A trustworthy *upāsikā* is one who has accomplished the sixteen qualities as described above; she is thus called "trustworthy."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,
"I know the matter, but I do not know the seating," this matter should be dealt with.
If it is said,
"He knows the sitting, but does not know the matter," one should discipline this sitting.
If one says,
"I know the affairs and I know the seating," both should be disciplined.
If one says,

"I do not know the matter, nor do I know the seating," then one should act according to the statement of a trustworthy upāsikā and perform the *tassapāpiyasikā* (action for seeking the offense) kamma as a disciplinary measure.
Therefore it is said:

"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse, as reported by a trustworthy upāsikā, that bhikṣu is to be dealt with according to the Dharma; this is the first *aniyata-dharma*."

If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded place where sexual intercourse is possible, even if it is not a place where such acts are normally performed, according to what has been reported by a trustworthy upāsikā, that bhikṣu shall be dealt with according to the Dharma; these are the two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas).
The Two Indefinite Rules concluded. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll Seven.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Translated together with Faxian. 4.

The Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. 1. Exposition of the Beginning of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the elders Nanda and Upananda were traveling through various villages and had obtained so many robes and articles that they filled their carts and brought them back.
In the early morning, the World-Honored One heard the sound of heavy carts; knowing the reason, he intentionally asked the bhikṣus, "What is the sound of these carts?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!

These elders Nanda and Upananda have traveled through various villages and obtained a great quantity of clothing and goods, which they have brought back filling their carts; that is the sound of those carts.”
The World-Honored One immediately thought to himself:
"My disciples are thus so eager for robes and requisites.

Later, at one time during the winter, on the eighth night when it was bitterly cold and snowing, the World-Honored One put on a single robe during the first watch of the night and entered the *savitarka-savicāra* samādhi.
At the time of midnight, perceiving his body to be slightly cold, he put on a second garment.
At the time of the latter part of the night, perceiving his body to be cold again, he put on a third garment and then thought:

"For my disciples, these three garments are sufficient to ward off great cold and great heat, to protect against mosquitoes and gadflies, to cover and conceal one's sense of shame, and to prevent the destruction of the noble lineages."
"If one's constitution cannot endure the cold, I allow you to wear old clothes and to layer them as you wish with inner linings.
Then, when the night had passed and at dawn, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once, early in the morning, I heard the sound of heavy carts and asked the bhikṣus,
'What kind of cart sounds are these?'"
The bhikṣus said, “Elders Nanda and Upananda travel through various villages and obtain many robes and requisites; that is the sound of their carriage.”
I had this thought: "My disciples seek clothing and requisites excessively, giving rise to widespread attachment.
Furthermore, at one time during the eight nights of winter, I even layered on my three robes and then had this thought:

"My disciples, with these three robes, shall suffice to withstand great cold and great heat, to ward off mosquitoes and gadflies, to cover and conceal their sense of shame, and to preserve the noble lineage."
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to maintain a set of three robes.
If they obtain new ones, they shall make the saṃghāṭī double-layered, the uttarāsaṅga single-layered, and the antarvāsaka single-layered."
"If one's nature is unable to endure the cold, I permit you to wear old, worn-out clothes, or to add layers as you wish.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the detailed account is as explained above.
At that time, in a certain village, three mahallaka bhikṣus were living together.
One mahallaka died, leaving behind many articles of clothing and property, yet they did not know how to divide them.
One bhikṣu said,
"I need a saṃghāṭī.
A second one spoke again:
"I also must have it. In this way, they vied with one another for every single item, unable to relinquish their claims.
At that time, Upānanda was traveling through various villages and passed by their dwelling place; when those mahallakas saw him coming from afar, they thought to themselves:
"This son of the Śākya clan is handsome and excellent; having gone forth from the family of the Buddha, he shall surely settle this dispute for us. They then said:
"In our residence there are various robes and articles, which we all vie to take but cannot divide among ourselves."
"Venerable sir, today you have settled this dispute for me; I shall receive a share of the robes.
Upānanda replied, "If I were to divide the goods for you now, it would give rise to much resentment and ill-will."
The mahallaka said:
"If no one will divide it for us, who else shall?
We might as well go to the various non-Buddhist sects and ask them to divide the goods."
Upānanda spoke again:
"We must first make an agreement; if you follow my words, I shall divide [the property] for you.
He replied:
"Follow the instructions," he said,
"bring out all your belongings."
He then brought it out and immediately divided it into three portions.
At that time, the mahallaka thought to himself:
"I have only two people, yet this is being divided into three portions; surely he intends to take one portion for himself?"
"I would rather let you take one portion and cease my dispute.
Having divided it into three parts, he again asked the mahallaka, "Bring out all the goods; do not cause further disputes hereafter."
"If there is anyone who does not wish to come out, let the second person bring them out again.
He replied, "They are all gone."
At that time, Upānanda stood between the two groups, placing one portion between the two mahallakas,
and spoke these words:
"Listen as I recite the *karmavācanā*."
He replied, “Yes,” and then spoke these words:
"These two parts together with me—thus I have three;
you two together with one—thus you have three.
These three and those three—are these two threes not equal?"
These two mahallakas had already made an agreement beforehand; furthermore, because they feared the Śākyaputrīyas, they did not dare speak again.
Since these two mahallakas shared one portion together, they did not know how to divide it.
He spoke again, saying:
"Venerable sir!
How should I now divide this portion?"
At that time, Upānanda divided it into two portions, and the mahallaka took them both away.
Then the bhikṣus, on account of this matter, went to inform the Buddha, saying:
“How is this, World-Honored One?”
"Did Upānanda deceive that elder bhikṣu?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus, "It is not only today that Upānanda has deceived this bhikṣu; in a past life, he already deceived him."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Has this happened before?
He replied:
"In the past, in a land to the south, there was a river called Vimalā. In that river lived two otters:
one could dive deep, while the other dived only shallowly."
At that time, one who had entered deep water caught a carp fish, as explained in detail in the *Jātaka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, when the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, the detailed account is as above.
For five reasons of benefit, the Tathāgata would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days.
On one such occasion, the World-Honored One traveled through all the quarters and arrived at Nanda’s room, where he saw that many garments and belongings were stored within it.
Some were setting up racks to dry clothes; some were sewing garments; some were dyeing them; some were beating them; and some were performing the purification rites.
Nanda made such arrangements as if he were preparing for a great assembly to bestow all manner of monastic requisites upon the Sangha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, said to Nanda:
"Whose clothing and belongings are these? He replied:
"I permit it," the Buddha said.
"O bhikṣus!"
"These robes are too many," Nanda said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"First, you shall receive two layers of the saṃghāṭī:
one layer of the uttarāsaṅga and one layer of the antarvāsaka.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"This robe is very old.
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
I have robes for my fellow practitioners and those who rely upon me;
I shall each make two-layered saṃghāṭīs, one-layered uttarāsaṅgas, and one-layered antarvāsas, as well as robes for the śrāmaṇeras and others.
The Buddha said,
"This robe is still too much.
Again he addressed the World-Honored One:
“Since it is difficult for us renunciants to obtain [clothing] at the last moment, I have therefore washed, dyed, and finished these various garments and placed them in this container.
When a garment becomes worn out, you should take one of these to replace it.”
The Buddha told Nanda:
"This is an evil matter. You are one who has left the household life; why do you calculate things as permanent and remain greedily attached?
Have you not often heard the World-Honored One reprimand those with many requests and much desire who are difficult to satisfy, while praising those with few desires and contentment?"

"You now have many desires that are difficult to satisfy; you seek clothing and requisites extensively and hoard what remains in excess. This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities."
"How should one use extra robes?
From this day forward, if there are extra robes, it is permitted to keep them for one night.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that Nanda accumulates many robes and never knows contentment?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This Nanda is not only insatiable in his accumulation of many robes today; in past lives as well, he was already insatiable in his accumulation of many robes, as is explained in detail in the *Śakuntaka-jātaka*."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Kauśāmbī, where he was honored and provided for by gods and worldly people.
When the time arrived, the World-Honored One put on his robe for entering the village, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Kauśāmbī to go on his almsround.
At that time, the king’s consort, named Śamī, offered fifteen hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take these cotton garments and give them to the bhikṣus."
The Elder Ānanda immediately took it and gave it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not accept it and said to Ānanda,
"What is the use of this cotton cloth?"
"The washing and dyeing have not yet been completed, and it is already not according to the Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“From now on, if you obtain an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), it is permitted to keep it for up to ten days.
There were some bhikṣus who, when their extra robes reached ten days, took those robes and went to inform the World-Honored One:
“These robes have reached ten days; what should we do with them now?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you know a bhikṣu who is trustworthy, perform the rite of pure giving (viśuddhi-dāna) with him.
Furthermore, if you discard old [robes] to receive new ones, you may exchange them once every ten days."
Furthermore, when the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the people of Vaiśālī would annually provide meals for the Saṃgha and offer robes as alms; however, the bhikṣus did not accept them.
Various donors went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"Is there some expedient means by which the monks may be permitted to take and use robes, so that the donors may obtain merit and the recipients may receive benefit?"
The Buddha said:
"It is obtained.
As explained in detail above.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Have all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and has relinquished the kaṭhina privileges, and he obtains an extra robe, he may keep it for up to ten days.
