Should he keep it beyond ten days, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
"Regarding 'the robes being finished': when a bhikṣu’s three robes are completed, this is called 'the robes being finished.
Not having accepted the kaṭhina cloth is also called 'the robes being finished';
having already relinquished the kaṭhina cloth is also called 'the robes being finished.'"
When the washing and dyeing of the robes are finished, it is also called "the robes are completed.
As for "robes," they are: *kambala* robes, *kārpāsa* robes, *kṣauma* robes, *kauśeya* robes, *śāṇa* robes, *māñjiṣṭha* (hemp) robes, and *kṣaumika* (flaxen) robes.

Furthermore, there are robes known as the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antarvāsaka, the niṣīdana, the varṣāśāṭikā, the vraṇapaṭṭa, the paṃsukūla, the gahapatika, the pāṃsukūla, those that have been made or not yet made, those that are lawful or unlawful, those belonging to a kinsman, and the kaṭhina robe.
Regarding "having relinquished": there are ten ways in which the *kaṭhina* robe is relinquished:

relinquishment by receiving the robe; relinquishment by the completion of the robe-making; relinquishment by the expiration of the time limit; relinquishment by hearing [of the end of the season]; relinquishment by going away; relinquishment by loss; relinquishment by destruction; relinquishment by sending the robe away; relinquishment by the passing of the time; and relinquishment by completion.
"Ten days" means that the count reaches up to ten days.
"Extra robes" refers to robes other than those one is permitted to keep; if these exceed ten days, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this extra robe must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
To confess it without having relinquished it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.

*Pāyattika* means that which can cause one to fall into the evil realms; it is the designation of the name of an offense for the disclosure of an offense, the manifestation of an offense, and the raising of an offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains ten pieces of clothing on a single day, and does not perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification) until the tenth day, once the tenth day has passed, all constitute *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu obtains ten pieces of cloth on a single day, and he performs the ritual of *pariśuddha* (purification) for half of them while leaving the other half unpurified:
that which has been purified is in accordance with the rule of purification;
however, as for the half that remains unpurified, if ten days pass, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and performs the formal act of purification (kathina) on the second;
obtains another robe on the second day and performs the purification on the third;
and obtains yet another robe on the third day and performs the purification on the fourth; [he is not at fault].
On the fourth day he obtained another robe and performed the ritual purification on the fifth day;
on the fifth day he obtained another robe and performed the ritual purification on the sixth day;
on the sixth day he obtained another robe and performed the ritual purification on the seventh day.
On the seventh day he obtains another robe and performs the *viśuddhi* on the eighth;
on the eighth day he obtains another robe and performs the *viśuddhi* on the ninth;
on the ninth day he obtains another robe and performs the *viśuddhi* on the tenth.
If one obtains clothing on the tenth day and reaches the eleventh day, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for all [the garments], because they form an uninterrupted continuity.
If a bhikṣu obtains clothing on the first day and purifies it that same day, and continues in this manner until obtaining clothing on the tenth day and purifying it on the tenth day;
then, if he obtains clothing on the eleventh day and purifies it on the eleventh day, he commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense because there is no interval.
In this interval, if a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, he may keep it for an additional nine days;
if he obtains a robe on the second day, he may keep it for an additional eight days;
if he obtains a robe on the third day, he may keep it for an additional seven days.
If one obtains a robe on the fourth day, one may wait for six more days.
If one obtains a robe on the fifth day, one may wait for five more days.
If one obtains a robe on the sixth day, one may wait for four more days.
If one obtains a robe on the seventh day, one may wait for three more days.
If one obtains a robe on the eighth day, one may wait for two more days.
If one obtains a robe on the ninth day, one may wait for one more day.
If one obtains a robe on the tenth day, one may perform the *pariśuddhi* (purification) on that very tenth day.
If one obtains a robe on the eleventh day, it should not be accepted; this is called "intermediate.
If a bhikṣu first obtains many robes and later obtains few, by virtue of the power of the former robes, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu initially obtains a small amount of robe-cloth and subsequently obtains a large amount, by virtue of the power of the former robes, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has robes at the beginning and none in the interim, yet possesses them [at the end], it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has no previous robe but possesses one in the interim, if he possesses such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu has not received the *kaṭhina* cloth but has the perception that he has received it;

if he has relinquished the *kaṭhina* but does not have the perception that he has relinquished it; if he has not received a robe but has the perception that he has received it; if he has not performed the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) but has the perception that he has purified it; if he has not been given [the robe] but has the perception that the robe has been given to him; if he has not formally identified [the robe] but has the perception that he has identified it; or if he is deluded, acts with internal intent, or performs the purification in an improper place.

Regarding "not having received the kaṭhina robe, yet claiming to have received it": if a bhikṣu has not received the kaṭhina robe but claims to himself that he has, and an extra robe remains for more than ten days, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "having relinquished the kaṭhina robe while having the perception that one has not relinquished it": when a bhikṣu has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe but considers himself to have not relinquished it, and an extra robe exceeds ten days, he commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

"Regarding 'not having received the robe' while thinking one has received it: if a bhikṣu does not himself receive his three robes, yet thinks they have already been received, and fails to perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi) for ten days, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

Regarding "not having performed the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi) yet claiming one has": if a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe without performing the ritual of purification or giving it away as a gift, yet claims that he has already performed the ritual of purification, and ten days pass, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "that which was not given but perceived as given": if this robe was not given to a stūpa, not given to the Saṃgha, and not given to an individual, yet one claims it was given and keeps it for more than ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "not recognizing what should be recognized":
if a bhikṣu does not recognize them, yet says, "This is a *niṣīdana*, this is a *vraṇapaṭṭikā*, and this is a *varṣāśāṭikā*."
If one claims to have identified [the cloth] but does not perform the formal act of purification (*pariṣkāra*), and ten days pass, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
As for the "foolish," if a bhikṣu obtains a robe and, due to ignorance and delusion, does not perform the formal act of purification, and ten days pass, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Regarding "internal purity": if one declares internal purity within the mind but does not speak it with the mouth, this is called impure according to the Dharma; it constitutes an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one speaks it with the mouth, there is no offense.
Regarding what is improper: if a layperson, an animal, or one who is mindless performs the purification, it is not called "purified.
If ten days pass, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu must perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) for his extra robes (*atirekacīvara*). Toward what kind of person should he perform this purification?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"One should perform the purification (viśuddhi) in the presence of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs."
He asked again:
"If they are separated by a certain distance, may one perform the ritual of purification (viśuddhi) on their behalf?
The Buddha said:
“Within three yojanas, one can know their survival or demise.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If one has performed the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification) for an extra robe with a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and that novice subsequently receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), what should be done?
The Buddha said:
"One should perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* by invoking the name of a monk who has no seniority (*anuvatsara*)."
Upāli asked again:
"What should be done if this bhikṣu who has not completed his year of residence should die?
The Buddha said:
"One may keep [the meat] for ten days and perform the purification (pariśuddhi) before other acquaintances.
He asked again:
"To what extent should one perform the purification?"
“How much is not considered *parikamma* (purified)?
The Buddha said,
“One that is one cubit wide and two cubits long should be purified.”
If two bhikṣus share an object and have not yet divided it, there is no offense;
however, once it has been divided and received, they must perform the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite. If they do not perform the purification and ten days pass, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has been invited by a brahmin’s household to a meal for the Saṃgha along with the gift of robes and clothing, and a sick bhikṣu entrusts someone else to take his share of the robes, it is not an offense for that [other] bhikṣu to bring the share of robes even if he does not give it to him immediately; however, once it has been received, it must be made *pariśuddha* (purified).
If one does not perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) and ten days pass, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu hears that his teacher or disciple is sending a robe, even if he has not yet received it, there is no offense despite the passage of time;
however, once he has received it, he must perform the ritual of purification. If he does not perform the ritual of purification and ten days pass, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a weaver weave a robe for him, there is no offense for the bhikṣu even if the robe is finished and not yet given to him after a long time;
however, once he has obtained the robe, he must perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*). If he does not perform the purification and ten days pass, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu purchases a robe, even if the price has been settled, he commits no offense as long as he has not obtained it;
once he has obtained it, he must perform the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite. If he does not perform the purification rite and ten days pass, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha or the Saṃgha, seeks clothing and requisites and collects them in one place, even if he does not use them for a long time, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains a great amount of gifts of clothing and requisites at the Buddha’s birthplace, at the place where he attained enlightenment, at the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, at the place where Ānanda held a festival, at the place where Rāhula held a festival, or at the quinquennial assembly (pañcavārṣika), and these items are to be included in the final distribution to the Saṃgha, there is no offense even if they remain for a long time;

nor is there an offense if these items have already been distributed and many people together receive one portion, provided that among them is a person well-versed in the Vinaya who can, with the consent of the multitude, perform the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification). There is no fault.
If one does not perform the ritual of purification (*parikamma*) and ten days pass, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road in a place of fear, conceals his robe and departs, and then takes it back after ten days have passed, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If someone takes these robes and brings them to give to a bhikṣu, it is also a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, being pursued by bandits, abandons his robes and flees, and after ten days have passed someone obtains those robes and comes to return them to the bhikṣu, there is no offense.

If one does not lose [an item] but has the perception that it is lost; or if one loses [an item] but has the perception that it is not lost; or if one loses [an item] and has the perception that it is lost—in all these cases, there is no offense, and after ten days have passed, there is no guilt.
If one does not lose [an item] and has the perception that it is not lost, yet ten days pass, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has kept an extra robe for more than ten days and wishes to relinquish it, he should seek out a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya and is capable of performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā), and invite several learned bhikṣus to go outside the boundary.
If there is no boundary field, one should establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*). The officiant (*karmakāraka*) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karman*) within this area, extending one fathom (*vyāma*) outward from the edge of where the monks are seated."
Venerable sirs, listen!
Within one *vyāma* outside the area where the Saṃgha is seated here, the *karmavācanā* is performed therein.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding "a ground where the *karmavācanā* has not been performed": one may not carry out monastic affairs there; if one does so, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The *vinaya-dhara* should say to that bhikṣu:
"Relinquish this robe."
That bhikṣu should kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have possessed this extra robe for more than ten days and have thus committed an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. I now relinquish it before the Saṃgha."
The holder of the Vinaya asked again:
"Have you ever used this robe? If he says:
"Enjoy it. One should say:
"You have committed a pāyattika offense because you used an impure robe; for every instance of such use, you commit a vyatikrama offense."
If one says, "I will not partake," the other should say,
"You have committed a pāyattika offense."
That bhikṣu, kneeling with palms joined before the one who upholds the Vinaya, says:
"Venerable sir, please remember!
I, [name], have possessed this extra robe for more than ten days and have already relinquished it to the Saṃgha."
"In this matter, I have committed a *pāyattika* offense; I now repent before the Elder and dare not conceal it.
The Vinaya-holder asked, "Do you recognize your own offense?"
He replies, "I see it.
He should then be instructed:
"Do not do it again. He replied, "Yes."
In this manner, it was said a second and third time.
The recipient replied:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!"
I, bhikṣu [name], having kept an extra robe for more than ten days, have already relinquished it before the Saṃgha.
Regarding this matter, I have committed a pāyattika offense; furthermore, for every instance of using this impure robe, I incur a vyatikrama offense against the Vinaya.
"I now sincerely repent before the Elder for all these transgressions and dare not conceal them.
The Vinaya-holder asked,
"Do you recognize your own offenses?"
He replied, “I have seen it.
[The Buddha said,] “Do not do so again.”
He replied, "I shall receive it upon my head.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
The legal expert asked,
"Who among this assembly is your acquaintance?
He replied:
"Such-and-such a person," [the preceptor] says, as they sit in the order of seniority.
The *karmavācanā* should then be recited:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] has possessed an extra robe for more than ten days; he has already relinquished it to the Saṃgha and has performed the formal act in accordance with the Dharma.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha take this robe and give it to the bhikṣu [Name], his acquaintance. Thus is the motion.”
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has possessed an extra robe for more than ten days; he has already relinquished it to the Saṃgha and has performed the formal act in accordance with the Dharma.

The Saṃgha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so, a friend of his. Venerable sirs, those who consent to bestowing this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so, a friend of his, remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*."
Thus it was said a second and a third time.
"The Saṃgha has consented; the distribution of this robe to the bhikṣu [Name], a friend, is completed. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The knowledgeable bhikṣu should return that robe on that very day or the following day; he must not return it in the presence of the Saṃgha, nor may he delay its return for longer than fifteen days.

Once this bhikṣu has obtained the robes, if he intends to maintain them through formal possession (*dhāraṇa*) or perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*), but does not know how to maintain them or how to perform the purification, he should be instructed as follows:
"I, [Name], hereby accept and maintain without separation for one night these saṃghāṭī, these uttarāsaṅga, and these antaravāsaka."
Thus it is said three times.
If one is performing the purification (*viśuddhi*), one should instruct them to say:

"I, bhikṣu [Name], am purifying this extra robe by entrusting it to [Name]; [Name] shall not regard it as his own property toward me, but may use it as he wishes for any necessary occasion involving washing, dyeing, or sewing."
Thus it was said three times.

If a bhikṣu has finished his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been relinquished, he may keep extra robes for up to ten days; if he keeps them beyond ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. Therefore, this was spoken.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as related in detail above.
There was a brahmin who invited the community of monks for an overnight stay, providing them with offerings and gifts of robes and clothing.
When the bhikṣus heard of this invitation, each of them thought to themselves:
"At this time, it is temperate—neither cold nor hot; we shall go wearing only our upper and lower robes. If we receive a gift of robes there, we shall accept and maintain them as the three robes."
He immediately put on his upper and lower robes and departed.
At that time, for the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One went once every five days to visit the rooms of the bhikṣus; opening the door of one room, he saw many robes upon a rack.
The World-Honored One, knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"To whom do those many robes on the rack belong?
A sick bhikṣu replied to the World-Honored One:

"There was a brahmin who invited the bhikṣus to stay overnight and provided them with offerings of robes. Because the weather was warm, these bhikṣus left those robes behind and departed wearing only their upper and lower garments."
"If he receives a gift of robes, he should accept them and make them into the three robes.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the foremost among those who delight in happiness, has renounced the foremost happiness of household life; yet wherever he dwells, he always carries his three robes and holds his bowl while begging for food."
"Just as a bird's two wings are always present with its body,
you bhikṣus, how can you abandon your original clans and lineages to go forth out of faith?"
"It should be thus: wherever one goes, the Dharma robes must accompany one; one should not remain overnight apart from them.
Furthermore, after the summer retreat in Śrāvastī was concluded, the Buddha proceeded to Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had left the household life out of faith in the city of Rājagṛha. Having completed his rains retreat in another village, he heard that the World-Honored One had also finished his retreat and was traveling toward Rājagṛha, and thought:
"I shall now go to pay my respects to the World-Honored One!"
"I shall go with the Buddha to visit my relatives; as the weather is neither cold nor hot, I will leave behind one robe and go wearing only the upper and lower garments.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One reprimanded the bhikṣus in various ways according to the Dharma: "The Dharma robes and the alms bowl must always accompany the body, just as when a bird flies, its feathers follow it of their own accord; they should not be left overnight."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"For the sake of benefiting my kinsmen, I shall now go to the village of Nāla to observe the rains retreat; yet, I do not wish to be far removed from the World-Honored One."
"Because of our reverence, it is difficult for us to go and inform the Buddha.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I authorize the Sangha of the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha and the Sangha of the village of Senāna to establish a single *poṣadha* boundary together, so that Śāriputra may dwell in peace and happiness."
The officiant of the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
From this day forth, the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha and the village of Nāla shall constitute a single boundary for the *poṣadha*."

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now establish a single *poṣadha* boundary encompassing both Rājagṛha’s Bamboo Grove Monastery and the village of Nāla; this is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) once, and because the Saṃgha consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra entered the rains retreat in the village of Nāla; every day he went to the Veṇuvana Monastery to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Encountering seven days of continuous rain, he thought to himself:
"My body is now weak and this saṃghāṭī is heavy; if I wish to carry it away, it will become even heavier due to the rain.
If I do not carry it away, I might fail to return, which would result in the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"Stay here for now and wait until the rain has cleared; then we shall go to visit the World-Honored One.
On the way, they encountered various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) and engaged them in debate, as described in the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*.
Thereafter, he went to the World-Honored One,
paid his respects, and inquired after his well-being.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking for the sake of instruction, the Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, why have you not appeared for many days?
He then related the preceding events in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I establish the 'Boundary for Not Being Separated from One's Robes' (acelaka-sīmā) at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha and in the village of Nāla, so that the bhikṣus may dwell in peace and comfort."
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla—excluding the village itself and its surrounding boundary—I shall establish the rule for not losing one's robes (*acīvarāpanna-dharma*)."

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha proceed from Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla; excluding the village and its precincts, we shall establish the rule of not losing one's robe. This is the formal motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
From the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla, excluding the village itself and its surrounding boundary."
The Saṃgha shall now establish the *akalaka-cīvara* (non-forfeiture of robes) rule within this area.

Venerable sirs, those who consent to establishing the *akalaka-cīvara* rule from Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla—excluding the village itself and its surrounding boundary—should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.

“The Saṃgha has consented; from Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla, excluding the village and its precincts, the procedure for the ‘non-forfeiture of robes’ has been completed. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such.”
Having established the rule for not losing one's robe, the boundary for both sides of the road from this city of Rājagṛha to the village of Nāla shall be twenty-five cubits each.
If a robe is obtained on a road, one should place the robe twenty-five cubits to either side of the path.
If it is obtained in Rājagṛha, there is no offense in taking it as far as the village of Nāla; likewise, if it is placed in the village of Nāla, there is also no offense.
It was likewise at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha and at the village of Nāla;
and as it was with the circumstances concerning Śāriputra, so too were they with the circumstances concerning Maudgalyāyana.

Furthermore, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery. A certain bhikṣu, after his meal, wished to go to the Kaṇḍakavana forest to practice meditation, and he thought to himself:
"If I were to stay overnight there, I would lose my saṃghāṭī robe."
He then took his three robes and departed.
On the way, he encountered the World-Honored One. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"Why do you travel carrying so many robes?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I wish to go to the Kāṣṭhavāṭa forest to practice meditation; fearing that I might not return before evening and thus lose my saṃghāṭī robe, I am taking these three robes with me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, from the Jetavana Monastery to the Kāṣṭhavāṭa forest, the Eastern Monastery, the Western Monastery, the Eastern Grove Monastery, the Western Grove Monastery, the Royal Garden Monastery, and the Śalavana Monastery at the Gaṇḍaka Stūpa, the rule for not losing one's robes shall apply equally in all these places, so that the bhikṣus may dwell in peace and happiness."
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
From the Jeta Grove to the Āmrapālī Forest, from the Eastern Grove Monastery to the Voting-Staff Stūpa—within this area, excluding villages and village boundaries."
"If the time is ripe for the Sangha, let the Sangha proceed from the Jeta Grove, up to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) at the Staff-Receiving Stūpa, to establish the rule of 'not losing one's robe.
This is the motion (*jñapti*): "Venerable Sangha, listen!"
From the Jeta Grove to the Staff-Voting Stupa, excluding the villages and their surrounding boundaries, the Sangha now establishes the *acīvarāpatti* (the rule of not losing one's robe).

Venerable sirs, you who consent to establishing the *acīvarāpatti* from the Jeta Grove to the Āmrapālī Grove, and as far as the Staff-Voting Stupa, remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Saṃgha has consented; from the Jeta Grove to the Āpāṇa Grove, and as far as the Śalākā-stūpa, the procedure for the ‘not losing one’s robe’ (acīvarāpanna-dharma) has been completed.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, a fire broke out in the city.

At that time, the people of the city—including men, women, elephants, horses, and carriages—carried their clothing and belongings on their shoulders and fled the city. Many bhikṣus had left their robes with people inside the city; fearing their robes would be burned by the fire, they rushed toward the city in haste.
Those among the people in the city who did not believe in the Buddha all rebuked them, saying:
"We have been driven out of the city by fire to seek refuge, yet these śramaṇas run toward the city like moths flying into a flame; what urgent matter could they possibly have?"
At that time, someone said:

"Do not say that these śramaṇas do not follow correct principle; they wish to take the property of others, just as a thief watches for a person's negligence in storing goods, or like a physician who treats diseases to sustain his own livelihood."
"These śramaṇas are just like that; they wait for people to encounter misfortune and flee toward the city. What kind of path is there in such ruinous men!
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Having called him forth, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Why are you running toward the city, being censured by the people?
They replied, "Our clothing was previously in the city; because a fire broke out in the city and we feared it would burn us, we are running to retrieve them."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"How is it that you stay overnight apart from your robes without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā)?
They replied:
"Perform the *karmavācanā*.
He asked again:
"How is it performed?"
He replied,
"It encompasses the entire city of Śrāvastī.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"How is it that you have established a boundary for an *āraṇyaka* (forest-dwelling) area that extends into a village settlement?

From this day forward, it is not permitted to establish a boundary for an *āraṇyaka* area that extends into a village settlement; one should establish a boundary for an *āraṇyaka* area within an *āraṇyaka* area, and a boundary for a village settlement within a village settlement."

"If one formally demarcates an *āraṇyaka* (forest) area so that it extends into a village settlement, or formally demarcates a village settlement so that it extends into an *āraṇyaka* area, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu has finished his robes and has relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, and he stays apart from any one of his three robes in another location for even one night—unless by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Having finished with the robes" means that the three robes have been completed; this is called "having finished with the robes.
Not having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe is also called "having finished with the robes";
having relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe is also called "having finished with the robes."
When washing and dyeing are completed, it is also called "the robe is finished.

As for robes, they include: cotton cloth robes (*kārpāsa*), woolen robes (*kambala*), linen robes (*kṣauma*), silk robes (*kauśeya*), hemp robes (*śāṇa*), flax robes (*māṣī*), and *kumuda* grass robes.
There are ten matters regarding the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe: relinquishing from the time of receiving the robe up to its ultimate relinquishing.
"One night" refers to the period from before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light.
The three robes are the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka.
"Except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha" means that if the Saṃgha has not performed the formal act (karmavācanā), one is not permitted to stay overnight separated from one's robe.

If one performs a *karmavācanā*, but the motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the formal act (*karman*) is not accomplished, and the assembly (*saṃgha*) is not accomplished—should the formal act fail in any respect to accord with the Dharma, this is called "performing what is not performed."

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: when the proclamation is accomplished, the formal act is accomplished, the assembly is accomplished, and each individual formal act is performed according to the Dharma—this is called the Saṃgha performing a *karmavācanā*, which the World-Honored One has declared to be without fault.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
To confess it without having relinquished the robe constitutes a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.

"Boundary" (*sīma*) refers to the boundary for formal acts (*kamma-sīma*), the boundary for wandering (*cārika-sīma*), the boundary for dependence (*nissaya-sīma*), and the boundary of the seven *āmra* trees.
Regarding the *karmabhūmi* (boundary for formal acts): whether the village is extensive or concise, its name and boundary markers are designated according to the terrain and to avoid difficulties.
As for those that are extensive in all directions, such as the country of Mathurā, which has groves and monasteries.
To the east of Mathurā is the river Rāvaṇa; to the east of the river is the hermitage village monastery.
At that time, the bhikṣus of the Hermitage Village Monastery sent a messenger to the monks of the Forest Monastery, saying:
"We wish to establish a single *poṣadha* boundary together."
He asked, "For what reason? He replied:
"If there is excellent food and drink there, and one obtains separate room-clothing and robes for the rainy season retreat, that is why we wish to go together.
One should reply: "To come for the sake of clothing and food is not appropriate; you should simply remain where you are."
If one says:

"In the place where I reside, there are many young bhikṣus who are not skilled in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; they are not skilled in contemplating the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), sense bases (āyatanas), and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Therefore, I wish to come to the elders to study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and to contemplate the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination."
He should say to them:
"If you do not create obstacles when the Saṃgha later performs formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*), we shall act together with you.
You should tell all the bhikṣus to come; if any do not come, they must all go outside the boundary."
"If [the monk] has come or has gone beyond the boundary, the *karmavācanā* must be performed.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From now on, regarding these forest hermitages and hermitages in seers’ villages—whether they be internal boundaries, external boundaries, both internal and external boundaries, or intermediate boundaries—if it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha establish a single *poṣadha* boundary within these forest hermitages and hermitages in seers’ villages; this is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This forest vihāra and this hermitage village vihāra constitute the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the inner-and-outer boundary, and the intermediate boundary; the Saṃgha now collectively establishes them as a single poṣadha boundary.”

Venerable sirs, those who consent to making these two boundaries—the boundary of the forest monastery and the boundary of the hermitage village—into a single *poṣadha* boundary, please remain silent; if you do not consent, speak up.
“The Saṃgha has consented; the two boundaries of the Maṭhura Grove Monastery and the Ṛṣipatana Village Monastery have been established together as a single boundary for the Poṣadha ceremony.”
"Since the Saṃgha remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
If there is no river water between [the two sites], the *karmavācanā* should be performed at a single location.
Regarding those who have access to river water, the *karmavācanā* should be performed in three locations:
first, in the monastery at Mathurā;
second, within the water.
Third, the hermitage of Ṛṣipatana.
If there is an island within a river, one should perform the *karmavācanā* at five locations:
first, the monastery of Mathurā; [and so forth].
Second, in the water;
third, on the continent;
fourth, in the water.
5. The Village of the Rishis.
Just as on dry land, there are twenty-five cubits on each side of the path; it is the same in the water.

Once, during the summer floods, a bhikṣu who had received the *chanda* (consent) came to attend the *karmavācanā*. He was swept away by the waters and carried out beyond the boundary, nearly dying before he could escape.
He said to the bhikṣus:
"I was carrying the *chanda* (consent) when I was swept away by water; I barely escaped with my life. May we now establish the boundary extensively?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Very well; go and mark off three yojanas up and down the river, and come back having marked such things as trees, rocks, or mounds.”
The one who recites the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From the Maṭhura Vihāra to the Ṛṣipatana Vihāra, from this boundary limit onwards, there is the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the inner-and-outer boundary, the intermediate boundary, and the upper and lower waters."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha establish a single *karmavācanā* boundary for the Poṣadha ceremony, extending from the Mātula Monastery to the Rṣipatana Monastery, and including the area between the upper and lower limits of the river; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
The motion was made once, and so forth: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
On another occasion, one who held a proxy vote (*chanda*) came to attend the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and, having reached a boat, wished to cross over.
The boatman towed the boat upstream; only then was it to be crossed.
He said to the bhikṣu, "The boat is heavy and difficult to pull; you may go by foot and board it when you reach the proper crossing place."
Because that bhikṣu was holding the *chanda* (consent), he should not have stepped onto the shore.
Since stepping out of the boundary would have caused him to lose the *chanda*, he instead waded through the water from the bottom of the bank.
As the boat traveled swiftly, he consequently crossed beyond the boundary.
The bhikṣu should immediately swim directly toward the boat within the boundary; however, the water will again carry the boat downstream for three yojanas.
The bhikṣu must then abandon the boat and swim straight to the shore; having reached it, he should wade through the water and follow the bank upstream.
Upon reaching the entrance to the path and entering within the boundary, one then steps onto dry land; this is called the detailed explanation.
As for the abbreviated explanation, the *karmadāna* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
From the Māthura Monastery to the Rṣipatana Monastery, there are the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the intermediate boundary, and the middle boundary.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now, from the Māthura Monastery and the Rṣipatana Monastery, together establish a single *poṣadha* boundary; this is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
After performing the formal motion (*jñapti*) once, up to: "The Saṃgha consents, because it is silent.
This matter is thus maintained.
This is called the brief explanation of the boundary (*sīmā*).

Regarding the village boundary (*grāma-sīman*): for instance, in the case of the Maṇḍalakhī vihāra and the village vihāra, if one wishes to establish them as a single *poṣadha* boundary, one should recite their names and, within a range of three *yojanas*, perform a single *karmavācanā* for all the vihāras.
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be recited as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From this day forward, within the various monasteries—namely, the monastery of Tranquility (*Tianjing*), the monastery of Abandoning Carts (*Sheche*), the monastery of Victory (*Sheng*), the monastery of Non-confusion (*Buluan*), the monastery of the Worthy (*Xian*), the monastery of Sequential Precepts (*Jie-cidi*), the monastery of the Conch (*Luo*), the monastery of Curd Village (*Lao-cun*), and the monastery of Yellow (*Huang*)—there are the inner boundaries, the outer boundaries, the inner-and-outer boundaries, and the intermediate boundaries."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is ready, let the Saṃgha establish a single *poṣadha* boundary for all these monasteries; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
After the motion and the one *karmavācanā*, [the Buddha continued]: "...because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent."
"Maintain this matter thus.
This is called the village boundary (*grāma-sīman*).

Regarding the designation of the name boundary (*nāma-sīman*): if the *karmakāraka* bhikṣu does not know the names of the various monasteries (*vihāra*), he should have an elder bhikṣu who knows the names announce them within the Saṃgha. After the names of the various monasteries have been proclaimed, the *karmakāraka* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From this day forward, these names of monasteries spoken by the bhikṣu so-and-so—the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the inner-and-outer boundary, and the intermediate boundary—shall constitute a single *poṣadha* boundary for all these monasteries."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha establish a single *poṣadha* boundary for all the names of monasteries spoken by the monk [Name], as follows: this is the motion.
After the motion and one *karmavācanā*, up until: "The Saṃgha consents, because of its silence."
"Maintain this matter thus.
This is the boundary of naming.
As for the boundary of signs, one speaks as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From this day forth, we shall establish a single *poṣadha* boundary, using as its markers stones, mountains, wells, piers, trees, the inner boundary, the outer boundary, both the inner and outer boundaries, or the intermediate boundary."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is in agreement regarding a marker—whether a stone, a mountain, a well, or a tree—to collectively establish a single *poṣadha* boundary, it shall be announced as follows.
After performing the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) once, up until: "The Saṃgha consents, because it remains silent;
this matter is thus upheld.

If the person performing the *karman* does not know the boundary markers, he should first have an elder monk announce them within the assembly as above, reciting the names of the boundaries; this is called the "boundary of named markers" (*nāmāṅka-sīmā*).

Regarding those who follow curved boundaries: because there is a monastery at the edge of a village, it has fallen into disrepair; yet there are many offerings of bedding and requisites for the Saṃgha. [The residents] wish to establish a single *poṣadha* boundary together with the monks of the various monasteries, so as to repair the monastery and share these materials in common.
Among the bhikṣus at various locations, there are those who wish to join together and those who do not wish to join.
Those who wish to join should all assemble, or else go beyond the boundary;
as for those who do not wish to join, they should remain within the boundary of their own vihāra, having established markers.
When those who share the same desires have assembled in one place, the *karmadāna* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

From this day forth, at this single residence, [designated] by such-and-such a name, within the boundaries of the markers—namely the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the inner-and-outer boundary, and the intermediate boundary—we shall collectively establish a single *poṣadha* boundary."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha establish a single *poṣadha* boundary, from this dwelling place up to the dwelling place of the monk so-and-so, as marked by the boundary signs; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
After performing the formal motion once (*jñapti-ekakarma*), up to: "The Saṃgha consents, because it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
This is called the boundary of conformity (*anuvartana-sīmā*).

Regarding the boundary for seeking refuge: when the days of the preceding or subsequent *anvāyaṇa* (rainy-season retreat) have passed for the bhikṣus residing in a single location, and a difficult situation arises—whether it be the danger of bandits, the danger of the king, the threat to life, the violation of precepts, or an abundance of insects in the water such that it cannot be purified by straining—it may be necessary to go to another monastery to avoid these difficulties, provided the destination is within three *yojanas*.
If there is a bhikṣu there, whether he is summoned to come or has gone out of the boundary,
the one performing the *karmavācanā* speaks thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today, at this residence in such-and-such a village monastery, we shall establish a single *poṣadha* boundary encompassing the inner boundary, the outer boundary, the intermediate boundary, and the intermediate boundary between them.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha, from this day forward, establish a single *poṣadha* boundary for this residence and that monastery in such-and-such village; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
After performing the formal motion (*jñapti*) once, up until: "The Saṃgha consents, because it remains silent;
this matter is thus upheld.
If, having reached that place, one wishes to enter another monastery, one should relinquish the previous boundary and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

At this residence, where previously there was a separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa, if the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha [perform] at this residence, which was formerly [at] such-and-such a residence, a separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa; thus is the motion made."
Having performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) once, up until: "The Sangha consents, because of its silence.
This matter is thus maintained.
If the Sangha further wishes to proceed to a monastery (*vihāra*), they should again take an area within three *yojanas* and collectively establish it as a single *poṣadha* boundary.

If one wishes to proceed further, one should first release the boundary behind before establishing one in front; continuing in this manner until one seeks a dwelling place that is to one's satisfaction, thus establishing and releasing boundaries according to one's will—this is called the "boundary for avoiding difficulties" (*parihāra-sīmā*).

Regarding the "boundaries of all directions": if, during a bhikṣu’s summer retreat (*varṣā*), various difficulties arise—whether the difficulty of a king, the difficulty of bandits, the difficulty of threats to life, the difficulty of breaking the precepts, or the difficulty of water containing many insects such that it cannot be purified by straining—it is permitted to freely establish a boundary within three *yojanas* in each of the four directions, as explained above.
If a sudden emergency arises such that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) cannot be performed, one may depart without incurring guilt.
This is called "all directions.
This is what is meant by the *karmabhūmi* (ritual boundary).

Regarding the boundaries for wandering through realms: the boundary of a cluster of sixty households, the obstructed boundary, the boundary of a multi-storied pavilion, the boundary of two roads, the boundary of a well, the boundary of trees, the boundary of a garden, the boundary of creeping vines, the boundary of a temporary lodging, the boundary of a boat, the boundary within a house, and the combined boundary.

Regarding the boundary of a cluster of sixty households: for example, there are the great clusters of villages in the kingdom of Śākala, the great clusters of villages in the kingdom of Sumera, the great clusters of villages in the kingdom of Mathurā, and the great clusters of villages in Pāṭaliputra; in each of these clusters, houses are built separately.
If a bhikṣu leaves his robe in one room while he stays overnight in a third room, and he departs before sunset and returns by the time the dawn light appears, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one departs while the sunlight has not yet vanished and returns by the time the dawn light appears, there is no offense.
If one departs before the sunlight has vanished and returns before the dawn light appears, there is no offense.
If all the rooms within the dwelling are occupied by bhikṣus, there is no offense.
If one establishes a boundary, there is no offense.
If it is surrounded by a wall, there is no offense;
if it is surrounded by a moat, there is no offense.
If there is a moat of water surrounding [the dwelling], there is no offense;
if they share a single gate, there is no offense.

If one passes through a village, and the bhikṣu’s robe is on the left side of the road while his body is on the right side of the road, from the time before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it is also as explained above.
If a bhikṣu lies down on the road and uses his three robes as a pillow, such that the robes are separated from his head, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Because the robes cannot be cut [to fit], they must all be relinquished.
If a village is surrounded on all sides by a wall, or a moat, or a fence, and has but a single gate which is closed, there is no offense; this is called the "village boundary of sixty households."
The same applies to the boundary of a partitioned enclosure.

Regarding the boundary of a multi-storied pavilion: if it is outside the stairs or galleries, each side constitutes a boundary of twenty-five cubits. If a bhikṣu places his robe on the pavilion and, after it has passed the twenty-five cubits, departs before sunset and returns only when the dawn light appears, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If the sun has already set and the dawn light has appeared when he returns, there is no offense;
if the sun has not yet set and the dawn light has not yet appeared when he returns, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu stays atop a multi-storied pavilion and, fearing that bandits will attack the pavilion, takes his robe outside the pavilion beyond a distance of twenty-five cubits to store it, and then returns to stay overnight atop the pavilion, returning before the sun has set and until the dawn light appears, this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, as explained above.

If a bhikṣu goes for the purpose of relieving himself during the night and remains within twenty-five cubits of his robe, being in physical contact with it, there is no offense; this is called the "storey-boundary" (kūṭa-sīma).
As for the "two-way boundary," it refers to footpaths and carriage roads.
Regarding those who travel on foot: there are bhikṣus who, out of fear of the cold, go to various warm countries, or, out of fear of the heat, travel to various cool countries.
While traveling on the road, they journey together with their teachers and companions, engaging in discussion as they proceed.
The disciple followed behind carrying his robes and bowl, but did not catch up with his teacher.

When the sun had set, the teacher, fearing he would be separated from his robes while staying overnight, went outside the path to wait for him. The disciple, carrying his robes, passed straight by without seeing the teacher; it was not until dawn that they met and waited for one another.
If the teacher is at the place where the robe is kept and within twenty-five cubits of the path, and the robe is in contact with him, there is no offense;
if it is beyond twenty-five cubits, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a disciple carries the robe and walks ahead, and at sunset he thinks, "May I not cause my teacher to spend the night separated from his robe," he immediately stops by the side of the road to wait for the teacher to pass.
Even if he falls into a deep sleep and fails to notice the teacher passing, when dawn comes they inquire of one another; this is also as described above, and it is called the "walking path."

Regarding the carriage road: when a bhikṣu travels together with merchants on carriages, he places his robe upon the carriage; fearing that dust might soil it, he goes ahead. Upon reaching sunset, fearing the offense of staying apart from one's robe overnight, he should stop within twenty-five cubits off the road until the carriage has completely passed by; because he remains in conjunction with his robe, he commits no offense.

If a bhikṣu places his robe on a cart and follows behind it, such that by the time sunset arrives he does not know which cart is his own, the bhikṣu must, at that time, remain within twenty-five cubits of the cart and circumambulate it once; because he remains in contact with the robe, he does not commit an offense.

If a large carriage has one, two, or three steps of stairs, and a bhikṣu places his robe on the carriage while remaining below it, from the time the sunlight has not yet faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; this is also as explained above.
If one briefly places the hand inside the vehicle during the night, there is no offense.

However, if a bhikṣu sleeps in a vehicle and places his robes beneath it, or places the robes in front of the vehicle while he is behind it, or places them behind the vehicle while he is in front of it, or places them on the right side of the vehicle while he is on the left, or places them on the left side of the vehicle while he is on the right—from the time the sun has not yet set until the appearance of the dawn light—all such cases constitute a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu places his robe on a cart and stays overnight in a secluded place more than twenty-five cubits away from the cart, returning before sunset but by the time the dawn light appears, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, as explained above.

If a bhikṣu, out of fear of bandits, hides his robe outside a vehicle at a distance of more than twenty-five cubits and returns to sleep on the vehicle, from the time the sun has not yet set until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, as explained above.

If one rises in the middle of the night to attend to the needs of nature, provided one remains within twenty-five cubits of one’s robe and the robe remains in contact with oneself, there is no offense.

If, within a caravan camp, a long rope has been stretched crosswise for the purpose of tethering oxen, and a bhikṣu stands on one side of the rope while placing his robe on the other side, from the time the sunlight has not yet faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; this is also as explained above, and is termed the "boundary of two paths."

Regarding the boundary of a well: when a bhikṣu travels together with merchants and stays overnight by a well, the area within twenty-five cubits from the edge of the well-railing is called the boundary of the well.

If one places clothing upon a well-railing, and a bhikṣu goes more than twenty-five cubits from the well, and remains there from before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; this is also as explained above.

If, out of fear of thieves, one hides the robe outside the well at a distance exceeding twenty-five cubits and stays overnight by the well, returning when the sunlight has not yet faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one conceals a robe in a well or a half-cavity and stays overnight above the well, such that one departs before the sunlight has faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one stays overnight with the robe tied to the body by a cord, there is no offense.
If one places the robe at the bottom of the well and stays overnight above it, or places the robe above the well and stays overnight at the bottom, it is likewise.
If, during the night, one momentarily extends a hand or foot into the well such that it comes into contact with the robe, there is no offense; this is called the "well boundary."
Regarding the boundary of a tree (*vṛkṣa-sīman*): extending twenty-five *hasta* beyond all branches and leaves of a tree constitutes the tree boundary.
If a bhikṣu places his robe under a tree and goes more than twenty-five *hasta* away before sunset, he must act as previously described until the appearance of the dawn light.

If a bhikṣu, while staying under a tree, fears thieves and hides his robe outside the tree at a distance of more than twenty-five cubits, and then departs before sunset to return by the time the dawn light appears, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one returns before the sunlight has vanished and before the dawn light has appeared, there is no offense;
if one returns after the sunlight has vanished and the dawn light has appeared, there is no offense.
If one briefly reaches the place where the robe is during the night and remains in contact with the robe, there is no offense.

If one leaves one's robes on a tree while staying under a tree overnight, or leaves one's robes under a tree while staying on a tree overnight, and departs before the sunlight has faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (niḥsargika).
If a rope is tied to one's body, there is no offense; this is called the "tree boundary" (*vṛkṣa-sīmā*).
The "garden boundary" (*ārāma-sīmā*) is also like this.

Regarding the "creeper-boundary" (*latā-sīmā*): for grapevine arbors, unbroken vine arbors, *pūla* vine arbors, gourd vine arbors, or *mokṣaka* flower vine arbors—for all such vine arbors, an area extending twenty-five cubits outward from each is called the "creeper-boundary."

If a bhikṣu travels on a road together with merchants and stays overnight beneath a vine-creeper, and seeking a quiet place, he places his robe at the base of the vine-stand and goes beyond twenty-five cubits; if he departs before the sunlight has faded and returns when the dawn sign has appeared, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one returns before the sunlight has vanished and before the appearance of dawn has arisen, there is no offense;
if one returns before the sunlight has vanished and before the appearance of dawn has arisen, there is no offense.

If, out of fear of thieves, one hides the robe beyond twenty-five cubits and stays overnight at the base of a vine-trellis, from the time the sunlight has not yet vanished until the appearance of dawn arises, it is as explained above.
If, during the night, one goes briefly to the place where the robes are for the purpose of relieving oneself, there is no offense provided one remains in contact with the robes.
It is likewise if one hangs the robes on a rack and sleeps below them, or if one places the robes beneath oneself and sleeps above them.
If the body is connected by a rope, there is no offense;
this is called the "boundary connected by creepers.
Regarding the "boundary for temporary lodging," it refers to a guest house where various kinds of people reside, and a bhikṣu stays overnight therein.
The innkeeper said, "There is danger from bandits here; each of you must remain on guard.
The bhikṣu asked the innkeeper:
“Long-lived one! Where is it secure?
The innkeeper replied:
"Secure on the upper story," or "Secure on the lower story."

If a bhikṣu hides his robe in the lower story of a multi-storied building and sleeps in the upper story, or places his robe in the upper story and sleeps in the lower story, and departs before the sun has set to return only when the dawn light appears, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, as explained above.
If the path through the middle is accessible by means of a ladder or steps, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on the road, stays overnight in a temple, and the master of the temple says:
"There is danger here from thieves; each of you must keep watch."
The bhikṣu asked:
"Lord of the deva-shrine!
Where is it secure?"
The temple master said, "Whether the interior of the house is secure or the exterior of the house is secure.

The bhikṣu then placed his robe inside the house and lay down outside the house with his head toward the door. If he departs while the sunlight has not yet faded until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, as explained above.
If the door-bolt is on the side of the bhikṣu, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu traveling on the road stays overnight in an empty village, places his robe in the first room, and stays himself in the third room, [the rules regarding] departing before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light are as explained above.
If there are bhikṣus in all the rooms, there is no offense.
If a boundary has been established through formal ritual (karmavācanā), or if it is enclosed by a fence, a wall, or a ditch, or if it is surrounded by water, there is no offense.
This is called the "temporary lodging" boundary (*sāṃvāsika-sīmā*).
Regarding the "boat" boundary: if a bhikṣu is traveling upstream or downstream by boat, there are many places on the boat where one may stay.

Whether it be a bhikṣu’s dwelling or a non-Buddhist’s dwelling, because the bhikṣu’s dwelling is not secure or private, he may leave his robes with a non-Buddhist at their dwelling. If he departs before sunset and returns by the time the dawn light appears, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, as explained above.
If a non-Buddhist practitioner permits the leaving of clothing and belongings behind, there is no offense.

If a boat is moored at the shore, should a bhikṣu leave his robes on the boat and depart more than twenty-five cubits away, from the time the sun has not yet set until the appearance of the dawn light, it is as explained above.

If one is on a boat and fears pirates, one may take one's robe onto the shore and store it more than twenty-five cubits away, then return to the boat to stay overnight; if this is done from before the sun has set until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If, during the night, one goes briefly to the place where the robes are kept for the purpose of relieving oneself, there is no offense provided the robes remain with them.
If a bhikṣu washes his robes and dries them on a boat, and the wind blows all the robes outward so that they are separated from him overnight, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If the wind blows the robe briefly inside the boat during the night, there is no offense.

If, while drying the robe, half is inside the boat and half is outside, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; because it cannot be cut [to fit], it must be relinquished in its entirety. This is called the "boat boundary."
Regarding the "household boundary" (*gṛha-sīman*):

if two brothers live together in one house and have established separate internal divisions within that house, such that the elder brother does not permit the younger brother to enter his portion and the younger brother does not permit the elder brother to enter his, and if a bhikṣu is within the elder brother’s portion while his robe is within the younger brother’s portion, from the time before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it is as explained above.
If brothers say to a bhikṣu,
"The layperson has acted contrary to his own [customs], but he does not obstruct the Dharma;
you may stay as you please," then at that time, one may leave one's robes there according to one's wish without fault.
If a bhikṣu stays overnight at the house of a layperson and, out of fear of thieves, asks the layperson,
"Which place is secure?
and the latter replies:
"The interior of the dwelling is secure.
A bhikṣu places his robes inside the dwelling and stays overnight outside; from the time the sun has not yet set until the appearance of the dawn light, it is as explained above.
If one briefly inserts a single hand through a hole into the interior of the house at night, there is no offense. This is defined as being within the boundary of a householder's residence.
Regarding the case of contiguous boundaries:

if four village boundaries meet and a bhikṣu lies down with his head as a pillow, such that his head is in one boundary, each of his two hands is in a separate boundary, and his feet are in another boundary, while his robe is beneath his head—if the robe becomes separated from his head, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If, during the night, one’s hands or feet briefly reach the place where the robe is kept, there is no offense.

If a cart stands upon these four boundaries such that the yoke is on one boundary, the rear of the cart on another, the left wheel on another, and the right wheel on another; and if one leaves the robe in front of the cart and stays overnight behind it, or leaves the robe behind the cart and stays overnight in front of it, or leaves the robe to the left of the cart and stays overnight to its right, or leaves the robe to the right of the cart and stays overnight to its left—if one departs while the sunlight has not yet faded and returns by the time the dawn sign appears, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if one departs after the sunlight has already faded and returns by the time the dawn sign appears, there is no offense.
If one returns before the sunlight has vanished and before the dawn light has appeared, there is no offense.
This is called the "conjoined boundary" (*saṃsṛṣṭasīman*).
Regarding the "village boundary" (*grāmasīman*): if a bhikṣu enters a village wearing his upper and lower robes, and a host says to the bhikṣu:
"I wish to make offerings to the images tonight to cultivate merit; may the bhikṣu assist me in preparing them.
The bhikṣu then assisted in adorning the images, hanging silken banners and flower canopies, and arranging seats and couches. When sunset arrived, the bhikṣu informed the host, saying, "It is dusk;
let us return to the vihāra."

If the host earnestly invites the bhikṣu to stay overnight, and if there are bhikṣus at that residence who possess extra robes (*cīvara*), he should temporarily borrow them for the purpose of formal possession (*dhāraṇa*).
If there are none, he should borrow from whichever nearby residence has bhikṣus.
If there are no monks, one may also borrow from where bhikṣuṇīs reside.

If there are none there either, and if there is a layperson at that place who possesses robes and coverings, one should borrow them to perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi), provide them with ties, and then accept and maintain them.
If these circumstances do not arise and the city gates are opened during the latter part of the night, you should return quickly to the monastery and must not scale the walls to exit.
Upon reaching the vihāra, if the gate is still not open, you should request that it be opened.
If one cannot gain entry, one should stand at the base of the gatehouse.
If there is no gatehouse, one should insert one's hand into a hole.
There are two kinds of holes: either a door-hole or a drainage-hole.

If the door has no opening, one should insert either the hand or the foot through the opening in the drain; do not insert the hand or foot first. If there happens to be a snake or viper, one should first startle it with a staff, and only then insert the hand together with the robe.

If there is no waterway, one should enter by leaping over the walls; however, one should make a sign to let those inside recognize him, so as not to cause suspicion that he is a thief, which would lead to alarm and commotion.
If one cannot enter, one should quickly discard the robe; it is better to be without the robe and incur a *vyatikrama* offense than to exchange what is light for what is heavy.
If a bhikṣu washes a robe within the vihāra, he should hang it upon a wall or fence to dry.
If, at night, the wind blows it out so that it hangs over the outside of the wall, one commits a *naiḥsargika* offense.
If it remains inside, there is no offense; however, because it cannot be cut, it must be relinquished in its entirety.
If a bhikṣu takes off his robes outside the vihāra and, due to the heat, forgets them there;

if he remembers them at night and goes out to search for them but does not find them, and upon going out to look in the morning, finds the robes within twenty-five cubits of the path taken during the night's walk, there is no offense;
if they are beyond twenty-five cubits, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This is called the village boundary.
Regarding the boundary of seven *āmra* trees: when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a brahmin who was skilled at planting *āmra* trees.
When this brahmin heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was in Śrāvastī, fully endowed with all-knowing insight, and capable of answering whatever questions were asked, he thought to himself:

"I shall now go to ask him about the method for planting the *āmra* tree. How should one plant the *āmra* tree so that its roots and trunk become firm and solid, its branches and leaves grow luxuriantly, and its flowers and fruits reach full maturity, spreading out and flourishing without hindering one another?"
Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was, and after exchanging greetings with him, sat to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!..."

What skillful means are there for planting an *āmra* tree so that its roots and trunk become firm, its branches and leaves flourish, and its flowers and fruits reach fulfillment, growing luxuriantly without obstructing one another?
Then the World-Honored One said to the brahmin:

"Measure seven bows with a bow of five cubits and plant one tree at each interval. By planting in this manner, you will cause those trees to have firm roots and trunks, lush branches and leaves, and to flourish with abundant flowers and fruit, growing in fullness without obstructing one another."
At that time, the brahmin was filled with joy and spoke these words:
"Excellent! Śramaṇa Gautama, you know the methods of cultivation; you are truly omniscient."
He rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the brahmin had left, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This brahmin has now suffered a great loss; he failed to ask what should have been asked, and instead asked what should not have been asked."
If he had asked about the meaning of the origin of suffering, he would have attained the path.
Nevertheless, since this brahmin has now conceived a heart of joy toward me, he too shall gain great benefit.
At that time, Upāli, knowing the proper occasion, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have already heard the measurement of the *āmra* tree; I now ask further:”
If there is a location, city, village, or boundary that cannot be determined,
and one wishes to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā), to what extent must it be defined so that the ritual is considered properly performed?

"Is it permissible to perform a *karmavācanā* such that members of different assemblies see one another and thereby accomplish the ritual, without falling into the offense of performing it separately from the assembly?
The Buddha told Upāli:

"If one plants a mango tree every seven *dhanus*—where a *dhanu* is measured as five cubits—and performs the *karmavācanā* within the space defined by seven such mango trees, this is called a 'well-performed *karmavācanā*'."
"Although they see one another as distinct groups, there is no offense of being apart from the group; this is called the 'Seven Āmra-tree Boundary.
If a bhikṣu has stayed overnight separated from his robe, he should inform one who upholds the Vinaya and is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*, saying:
'Venerable One!'"
"I have stayed overnight separated from this robe; it must be relinquished.
Venerable sir, please perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for me."
The *karmavācanā* procedure is as explained above regarding robes kept for more than ten days.
Therefore it is said:

"If a bhikṣu’s robe-making is finished and the *kaṭhina* has been relinquished, if he stays overnight in another place separated from any one of his three robes, except by formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was staying by the banks of the Ajiravatī River. Having obtained a small piece of cloth, he went with a large number of bhikṣus to the banks of the Ajiravatī River and sprinkled water upon it to stretch and widen it.
At that time, the World-Honored One vanished from his own dwelling place and appeared on the banks of the Ajiravatī River.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking for the sake of instruction, he asked Anuruddha: "What are you doing?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
I have obtained a small piece of cloth that is insufficient in measurement; I wish to stretch it so that it becomes longer and wider."
The Buddha said to Aniruddha,
"Do you have any expectation of obtaining further robes?
He replied:
"It exists.
The World-Honored One asked,
"When can it be obtained?"
He replied, "One month.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I authorize those who lack sufficient robes but have expectations for obtaining them to wait until one month has passed, so that they may become fully supplied.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
If a bhikṣu has finished his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been relinquished,
and he obtains an out-of-season robe, the bhikṣu who needs a robe should take it and quickly make it into a robe for use.
If it is insufficient, one is permitted to keep it for one month in order to fulfill what is expected.
If one keeps it longer than that, whether it is sufficient or insufficient, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Having finished with the robes" means that the three robes have been completed, which is also called "having finished with the robes";
not having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe is also called "having finished with the robes";
and having already relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe is also called "having finished with the robes."
When the washing and dyeing are finished, it is also called "the robe is finished.
Regarding those who have relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe, there are ten ways of relinquishing it, as explained above.
As for "obtaining," it refers to obtaining a robe from the side of either a man or a woman, whether they be laypeople or monastics.
Regarding "out-of-season": if the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted, there are seven months which are called out-of-season;
if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been accepted, there are eleven months which are called out-of-season.
If one obtains a robe during this improper time, it is called an "improper-time robe.
Regarding the "robe," it is as described above.
Regarding "need," it means that the bhikṣu truly requires a robe.
If one takes [the robes] and they are quickly completed and received, but upon wearing them they are slightly insufficient, one may keep them for up to one month.
One month consists of thirty days; one should possess them until this time in order to seek their completion.
Regarding "one who has hope": this refers to a bhikṣu who actually hears that there is a place where robes can be obtained; he may wait for it to be fulfilled and keep the robe for up to one month.
If he keeps it beyond this one month, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and a *pāyattika* confession performed;
if one confesses without having relinquished it, one commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If, during the first ten days of the month, a bhikṣu obtains a robe that is expected, or one not expected, or a minor expectation for a robe, or an expectation lacking power, or a feeble expectation.
If, having given rise to an expectation, one cuts off that expectation and then gives rise to another expectation, all of these remain without a basis for cessation.
If, after obtaining this robe in full measure, one makes half of it *pariśuddha* (purified/cleansed) and half of it not *pariśuddha*, then that which is made *pariśuddha* is called "well-purified";
as for that which is not made *pariśuddha*, after ten days have passed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If, during the first ten days, a bhikṣu obtains a householder’s robe or a paṃsukūla robe, and neither makes it himself nor instructs another to do so, nor accepts it for storage, nor performs the ritual purification (pariśuddhi), then whether that robe has been made or not, once the ten-day period has elapsed, both the robe and any remaining materials constitute an offense of forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe during the first ten days—whether it be an old robe or a rag-robe—and having obtained it, he neither makes it himself nor instructs another to make it, such that it exceeds the first ten days, it is an offense of forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe within ten days, whether it has been dyed and purified or not yet purified, and that bhikṣu, having obtained this robe, neither makes it himself nor instructs another to make it, nor accepts it as his own, nor purifies it through ritual, then whether he makes it into a robe or does not, once ten days have passed with respect to the robe or the remnants of the robe material, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe within ten days, whether it be a robe that conforms to the Dharma or one that does not, and having taken possession of it, neither makes it himself nor instructs another to make it, until the tenth day has passed, it is an offense of forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu obtains cloth during the final ten days [of the robe season] and intends to make one robe out of it, but then wishes to make two robes, another bhikṣu should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Previously you intended to make one robe; why do you now make two?
You should now proceed as before and make only one.
