If that bhikṣu, having obtained the cloth, neither makes it himself nor instructs another to do so, until ten days have passed, it becomes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains cloth during the final ten days of the period and intends to make a small cut-and-sewn robe, yet instead makes a large cut-and-sewn robe, another bhikṣu should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Originally I intended to make a small *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe), but why now have I made a large *khaṇḍa-cīvara*?
It should be as originally intended.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe and neither makes it himself nor instructs another to do so, nor takes possession of it, nor performs the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), then whether he has finished making it or not, once ten days have passed from the time the robe or its remains were obtained, it becomes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe during the first ten days, he should make it immediately during those first ten days; if he obtains a robe during the middle ten days, he should make it immediately during those middle ten days; if he obtains a robe during the last ten days, he should make it immediately during those last ten days.
If a bhikṣu, during the first ten days— specifically within the latter five days— obtains a garment that he anticipates receiving;
or during the middle ten days— specifically within the first five days of those ten days— he should make a robe from it.

If a bhikṣu, during the middle ten days—having already passed the first five days and being entitled to expect a robe—he should, during the last five days of those middle ten days or the first five days of the subsequent ten days, make the robe within these ten days.
If a bhikṣu obtains the expectation of receiving a robe after five days have passed within the latter ten days, he should make the robe during these remaining five days.
If a bhikṣu obtains the expectation of receiving a robe after six days have passed within the latter ten days, he should make it during the remaining four days.
If the seven days have passed and one obtains the robe-cloth, it should be made within three days.
If the eight days have passed and one obtains the robe-cloth, it should be made within two days.
If the nine days have passed and one obtains the robe-cloth, it should be made within one day.
If one obtains robes on the tenth day, they must be made that very day.

When making the robes, others should provide assistance in washing, dyeing, cutting, stretching, pinning, sewing, cross-sewing, lengthwise-sewing, edging, attaching ties, boiling, dyeing, and purifying the cloth; once purified, it should be formally accepted and maintained.
If one fears that it will not be finished in a single day, one may conceal the coarse parts to complete it, and subsequently apply the fine details.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu’s robe is already finished and the kaṭhina privileges have been relinquished, whether the robe is sufficient or insufficient, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
The account concerning the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā should be told in full: at that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā gave a saṃkakṣikā to the Venerable Ānanda, and this garment was stained with grease and impure.
Ānanda took this robe, smeared it with mud, and dried it in the midday sun. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"Ānanda, what are you doing?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
This bhikṣuṇī Utpalā gave me this saṃkakṣikā; it was soiled and unclean, smeared with mud, and left out to dry.”
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Did you trade it for its fair value?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"One should engage in trade; women yield little profit.
Ānanda did not wish to give it, so the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Why do you not give it?"
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“What should be given?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Give him the cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) offered by King Prasenajit, which is sixteen cubits long and eight cubits wide.
Ānanda still did not give it to him, as is explained in detail in the *Karpāsa Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā, leading her retinue—all of whom were wearing tattered and worn-out robes—paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monks!
Who is this bhikṣuṇī who has come to me wearing such tattered and worn-out robes?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
This is the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is this bhikṣuṇī Śubhā not wearing [the robe] because she has obtained one,
or is it because she has no robe?"
The bhikṣus said, “We have indeed obtained it;
we have already taken it and given it to Udāyin.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, leading her retinue, all dressed in worn-out and tattered robes, came to the World-Honored One and prostrated with their heads at his feet.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣus:
"What kind of bhikṣuṇīs are these who come to me wearing such worn-out and tattered robes?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
this is the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
“As for this bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, did she not put on her robes because she had obtained them,
or did she not put them on because she had not obtained them?”
The bhikṣus said, “We have indeed obtained it;
we have already taken it and offered it to Ānanda.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Supriyā, leading her retinue—all of whom were wearing tattered and worn-out robes—approached the World-Honored One and prostrated with their heads at his feet.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣus:
"Who are these bhikṣuṇīs who have come to me wearing such tattered and worn-out robes?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
this is the bhikṣuṇī Subhaddā.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Did this bhikṣuṇī Subhaddā obtain the robe but not wear it,
or did she fail to obtain it?"
The bhikṣus said, “We may indeed receive it;
we shall take it and bestow it upon a bhikṣu who is skilled in interpretation.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
The bhikṣuṇī Śilavatī led her retinue, all wearing tattered and worn-out robes, to visit the World-Honored One, where they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
Knowing this, the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣus:
"Who are these bhikṣuṇīs who have come to me wearing such tattered and worn-out robes?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
This is the bhikṣuṇī Śilīmā.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"As for this bhikṣuṇī Śilīmā, did she obtain a robe but not wear it,
or did she fail to obtain a robe?"
The bhikṣus said, “We have indeed obtained it;
we have already taken it and offered it to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"If a relative bhikṣuṇī were wearing such tattered and worn-out robes, should that relative bhikṣu take those robes?
He replied, "He should not take them."
The World-Honored One asked again:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative has her own robes worn out, would she give clothing and articles to a bhikṣu who is a relative?
He replied: [Yes.]
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, monks, one should not accept a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange.
Thus the Buddha addressed the monks.
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
A "bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative" refers to one who is neither descended from the father’s lineage nor descended from the mother’s lineage; this is called a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.

Whether there is one relative and many non-relatives, many relatives and one non-relative, or if a śrāmaṇerī is a relative while the bhikṣuṇī is not a relative, or if a śrāmaṇerī is not a relative while the bhikṣuṇī is a relative—if one obtains a robe from among these, it constitutes an offense.
Apart from these two groups, there is no offense.
"Robes" refers to:

robes of *kambala* (wool), robes of *kappāsika* (cotton), robes of *kauśeya* (silk), robes of *kṣauma* (linen), robes of *śāṇa* (hemp), robes of *māñjiṣṭha* (flax), and robes of *bhojakaṭa* (coarse wool).
"To take" means to accept that gift.
"Except for trade": the Buddha taught that there is no offense if it is for trade.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika": this robe must be relinquished within the Saṃgha; as for the *pāyattika*, one must perform confession.
If one confesses [the offense] without having relinquished the robe, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

As for a non-relative bhikṣuṇī: [the robe] may be given by oneself and received by her; given by her and received by oneself; given by oneself and received by oneself; or given by her and received by her.
"Giving personally and receiving through a messenger" means that a bhikṣuṇī gives the robe with her own hand, while a bhikṣu receives it by dispatching a messenger.
"Giving through a messenger and receiving personally" means that a bhikṣuṇī dispatches a messenger to bring the robe to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu receives it personally.
"Giving by oneself and receiving by oneself" means that the bhikṣuṇī gives the robe herself, and the bhikṣu receives it himself.
"Sending another to give and sending another to receive" means that the bhikṣuṇī dispatches a messenger to bring the robe to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu dispatches a messenger to receive it.

If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, having agreed to an exchange, yet does not give it, does not instruct her to give it, does not speak for himself, does not instruct another to speak for him, returns the original robe, cuts the original robe, gives less than the full amount, gives a different object, or moves beyond the range of sight and hearing or beyond the boundary, that bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
"Not giving" means she does not give herself.
"Not instructing to give" means she does not instruct others to give.
"Not speaking for herself" means she does not speak to the bhikṣuṇī herself, saying:
"Later, after such a time, I shall give you a robe.
As for "not instructing," it means not having another person tell the bhikṣuṇī:
"Later, after such a time, I shall give you a robe."
"Returning the original garment" means returning the nun's previous garment; this should not be given back, but rather another garment should be given.
"Cutting" means cutting the original garment and returning it to her; this is not called an exchange.

Regarding "giving less": having received a full robe from them, if one gives a smaller robe in exchange, this is not considered giving; one should give a complete and sufficient robe. Regarding "giving different items":
having taken that robe, if one gives a bowl, a small bowl, or a *kañcaka* (a type of vessel), or gives food, drink, or other items, this is not considered an exchange; one should give a robe.

Regarding "leaving the range of sight and hearing": if a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and having taken it, does not pay for it, does not instruct someone to pay for it, does not speak of it himself, does not instruct someone to speak of it, and then departs and leaves the range of sight and hearing, it is a pāyattika offense.

Regarding "leaving the boundary": if a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and without paying its value, nor giving it himself, nor instructing another to give it; without speaking of it himself, nor instructing another to speak of it; he departs and goes beyond twenty-five cubits outside the boundary, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and does not pay for it, nor cause it to be paid for, nor instruct someone to pay for it; nor does he inform her himself, nor instruct someone else to inform her;
whether he sits, lies down, or enters meditative absorption, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative gives a robe to a śrāmaṇera she knows, saying: "Śrāmaṇera!
I give this robe to you."
"Take this robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu; you will thereby obtain merit.
If the bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
It is the same if a śrāmaṇerī, a śikṣamāṇā, an upāsaka, or even an upāsikā says: [the same applies].
"I give this robe to you.
By taking this robe and offering it to the Venerable [Name] Bhikṣu, you shall gain merit.
If the bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, please lend me this robe;
you may wear it as you please," the bhikṣu may wear it until it is worn out and returned; there is no offense.
If many bhikṣuṇīs give a robe to one bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should trade robes with each of those many bhikṣuṇīs individually; he may also give a single robe to the many bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Sisters!..."
"Exchange robes.
If one bhikṣuṇī gives robes separately to many bhikṣus, those many bhikṣus should each separately exchange robes with that one bhikṣuṇī; they may also give her a robe collectively, saying: "Sister!"
"This robe may be exchanged for a robe.
If many bhikṣuṇīs give robes to many bhikṣus, those many bhikṣus should return them to the many bhikṣuṇīs to exchange for robes.
If one bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to one bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should return it to the bhikṣuṇī in exchange for a robe.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives a bhikṣu an alms bowl, a small bowl, a cooking vessel, food or drink, or any other minor items, he may take them all without fault.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu receives a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll Eight.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India, together with Faxian, during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The second of the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Udāyin took a robe and gave it to the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, saying:
"Excellent, Gautamī!"
"Please wash, dye, and beat this robe for me.
Then Mahāprajāpatī immediately washed, dyed, and beat it, and having returned it, she said to Udāyin:
"This robe has been washed, dyed, and beaten; I now return it to you."
Udāyin then offered a blessing, saying,
"May you obtain happiness and freedom from illness," and escorted him into the room.
Then Mahāprajāpatī, having given the robe to Udāyin, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked her intentionally: "Gautamī!"
"Why is there dye on your hand?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I have dyed my hands with the color of the cloth because I was washing and dyeing the robe for Udāyī.
Not long after Gautamī had departed,
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"How is it, Udāyin, that you cause bhikṣuṇīs who are practicing the path to wash and dye robes, thereby obstructing and causing them to neglect their duties?

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the elder Ānanda, who was the former husband of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, failed to examine carefully and gave her an impure robe to wash, saying:
"Sister!"
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me.
Then, Sthūlanandā took the robe to the vihāra; spreading it out, she saw that it was stained with impurities from wearing.
She immediately showed the robe to the bhikṣuṇīs and said, "Look at these marks of a man upon this robe!"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to Thullanandā:
"How can you show to others such items that ought to be concealed?
If you wish to wash them, you should wash them; if you do not wish to wash them, you should store them away."
Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"What is there in this that is shameful for me to hide?
This is a man, with the marks of a man."
They further pointed this out to the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, standing not far from the bhikṣuṇīs, heard these words and clapped their hands, laughing loudly:
"How extraordinary!"
"What a strange thing!
Having heard these words, the bhikṣus immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:
“Call Ānanda here. Having summoned him, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
“Is it true that you have done this?”
He replied, "It is indeed so;
I gave it because I did not examine it carefully.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu who is a relative has such an impure robe, should it be given to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative to wash?
She replied, "I would not give it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Suppose a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative sees a relative bhikṣu commit an offense that ought to be concealed; should she disclose it to others?”
He replied, “I did not show it,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One should not even have a relative bhikṣuṇī wash an impure robe.
How much less should one have a non-relative bhikṣuṇī wash an old robe?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relatives" refers to those who are not descended from one's father nor descended from one's mother.
"Old robes" refers to anything that has been used for even a single pillow; this is what is meant by "old."
"Robe" is as explained above.
"Washing" means removing dirt and grease.
"Dyeing" refers to various types of dyeing, such as root-dye, bark-dye, leaf-dye, flower-dye, fruit-dye, and so forth.
"Striking" refers to even striking once with the hand.
"Naiḥsargika" means that this robe must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the pāyattika offense must be confessed.
To fail to relinquish [the robe] and instead feel regret constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above. [The four cases are:

receiving it oneself after having sent someone to fetch it; having someone receive it after one has sent them to fetch it; receiving it oneself after having fetched it oneself; and having someone receive it after having sent someone to fetch it.
"Given by oneself and received by a messenger": the bhikṣu gives it himself, while the bhikṣuṇī sends a messenger to receive it and washes it herself.
"Given by a messenger and received by oneself": the bhikṣu sends a messenger to deliver the robe, while the bhikṣuṇī receives it herself and washes it.
"Giving with one's own hands and receiving with one's own hands" means that a bhikṣu gives with his own hand, and a bhikṣuṇī receives it with her own hand and washes it herself.

"Sending a messenger to give and sending a messenger to receive" means that a bhikṣu sends a messenger to give, and a bhikṣuṇī sends a messenger to receive; if she then washes, dyes, and beats it herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu tells a [nun] to wash and she washes, tells her to dye and she dyes, or tells her to beat and she beats, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu causes a nun who is not a relative to wash a robe and she then dyes it, or instructs her to dye it and she then beats it, or instructs her to beat it and she then washes it;
or if he instructs her to do something and she does not do it, or does not instruct her to do something and she does it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If a bhikṣu tells a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash a robe, yet she dyes or beats it; or if he instructs her to dye it, yet she washes or beats it; or if he instructs her to beat it, yet she washes or dyes it; or if he instructs her to do something and she does not do it, or if he does not instruct her to do something and she does it—this constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a relative and has it washed by one who is not a relative;
or if he gives it to one who is not a relative and has it washed by a relative;
or if he gives it to a relative and has it washed by a relative.
If one gives [a robe] to a non-relative, or has a non-relative wash it;

or if one gives it to a relative, but a non-relative washes it: for example, if a bhikṣu’s mother or sister has gone forth as a nun, and the bhikṣu takes a robe and gives it to her to wash, and that bhikṣuṇī takes the robe back to the vihāra.
If this nun has a disciple nun who says, "The Ācāryā has some work to do;
I shall perform it," and then takes the robe and washes, dyes, and beats it, the bhikṣu is without offense. This is called "washing for a relative or a non-relative."

Regarding "washing for one who is not a relative or for a relative": if a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and instructs her to wash, dye, or beat it, and that bhikṣuṇī takes the robe back to the vihāra, and there is a bhikṣu whose mother or sister has gone forth, and she recognizes the robe, she asks that bhikṣuṇī:
"Whose robe is this?"
She replied,
"The robe of a certain bhikṣu.
Then that relative, the bhikṣuṇī, thought to herself:
"Such-and-such a person does not know the Vinaya; let this bhikṣu not incur the *naiḥsargika* offense.

She then takes the robe and washes it. This bhikṣu commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*); this is called "having a non-relative wash [a robe] with one who is a relative."
"Regarding 'with a relative' or 'a relative who washes': if a bhikṣu’s mother or sister has gone forth as a nun, and that bhikṣu takes a robe and gives it to her to wash, that bhikṣuṇī says:
'I am weak and ill.'"
The bhikṣu said, "If you have a disciple who is strong and healthy, you should have him wash it. He then instructed [the disciple] to wash it;
having instructed him to wash it, he brought it back himself. This bhikṣu incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one does not instruct her but she washes it herself, there is no offense; this is called "giving to a relative and having a relative wash it.

If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and that bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative washes, dyes, or beats it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; this is called "giving to one who is not a relative and having one who is not a relative wash it."
If a bhikṣu takes his robes and dye and entrusts them to a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra, then departs for another secluded place to observe the rains retreat,
and that bhikṣuṇī, after the summer retreat has ended, exceeds the limit by herself washing and dyeing robes and then proceeds to wash and dye robes for the bhikṣu.
When the bhikṣu had finished his summer retreat, he returned seeking his robe to wash and dye it.
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I have already washed and dyed it."
This bhikṣu does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu entrusts his robe with someone while thinking:
"He shall wash, dye, and beat it for me."
If, after [the robe] has been washed, dyed, and beaten, she [still] causes it to be forfeited, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu wears a soiled and greasy robe and goes to a bhikṣuṇī’s monastery, and a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative bows at the bhikṣu’s feet and asks:
“Why is your robe so soiled and greasy? Is there no one to wash and dye it?”
She replied, "No one has washed them.

Since this bhikṣuṇī was faithful, she immediately entered the room, took the robes, and gave them to the bhikṣu to wear; she kept these other robes for herself to wash, dye, and beat, and there was no offense.
At another time, that bhikṣu intentionally put on soiled and greasy clothes and went away, thinking:
"When the bhikṣuṇī sees them, she will surely wash them for me."
If one washes [the robe] with such an intention, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu enters a village and his robe becomes soiled by a mad elephant, a chariot, a horse, or splashing mud, and he immediately goes to a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra and has a bhikṣuṇī rinse it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; because it cannot be cut down, it must be relinquished entirely.
If a bhikṣuṇī pours water and a bhikṣu washes [the robes] himself, there is no offense.

If, while a bhikṣu is washing and dyeing robes in one place, a bhikṣuṇī happens to be traveling on the day of the Uposatha, passes by to pay respects at various vihāras, pays homage at the feet of the bhikṣus, and sees the bhikṣu washing the robes.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked,
"Preceptor, is there no one to wash your robes?
He replied:
"There is no one.
Out of faith, that bhikṣuṇī said to the bhikṣu:
"Stop! [Do not enter]."
"I shall wash it for you.
If the bhikṣu consents and allows him to wash it as he wishes, there is no offense.
However, if this bhikṣu intentionally washes his robes on a day of fasting (upoṣadha), thinking to himself:
"If a bhikṣuṇī will certainly come, she shall wash for me.
If one gives [clothing] to her to wash, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has many bhikṣuṇī disciples, although he may not have them wash, dye, or beat [the cloth], he may have them gather firewood, fetch water, boil the dye, take food, serve water, hold a fan to fan him, and collect the bowl after the meal; all such tasks may be performed.
If one instructs [a nun] to wash, dye, or beat [the robe], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one has a bhikṣuṇī wash a robe for the sake of one's upādhyāya or ācārya, it is a *vyatikrama* offense.
If it is for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha, there is no offense in having a bhikṣuṇī wash, dye, or beat [the robes].
Therefore, it is said:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, the multitude of people in the city all came out to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.

At that time, there was a man named Abhaya who, wearing two pieces of white cotton cloth, entered the Jetavana monastery and, having paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, proceeded to the dwelling of the Elder Upānanda and said: "Homage!"
"Ācārya," he replied,
"may you be free from illness and long-lived!"
Abhaya said, "I wish to inspect the various rooms.
At that time, Upānanda replied:
"Very well! Even if you did not wish to see it, I would have shown it to you; how much more so since you do wish to see it.
He then led them up to the second story of the multi-storied pavilion and said:
"Look at this elder’s [bed], carved and engraved with five kinds of colored paintings, set upon a floor of deep blue lapis lazuli, complete with mattresses and bedding.
Having looked, he replied,
"It is truly excellent!"
"Ācārya," said Upānanda,
"Long-lived one!"
"This cotton robe of yours is also excellent— long, wide, fine,
and delicate. At that time, Abhaya said,
"I wish to see other rooms as well."
Then Upānanda led him up to the third story of the upper pavilion to look at it, as described in detail above. Up to:
"Your robe is also excellent—long, wide, fine, and exquisite."
At that time, he thought to himself:

"This śramaṇa praises my robe; he must surely wish to have it. This bhikṣu is well-known to the king and the various high ministers and possesses great power and influence. If I do not give it to him, he may harbor resentment toward me."
Abhata said, "Ācārya, do you wish to have this robe?
He replied:
"I wish to receive it.
Abhaya said, "Ācārya, please follow me back; I shall give you another robe."
Upānanda said: “Alas! Long-lived one, why do you say this?”
"Give me another robe.

"I also have various other fine cotton cloths (*karpāsa*), but they do not match yours. The reason I wish to obtain this cloth of yours is that I desire to make a single garment so that it may be similar [to yours]."
He spoke again:
"If you intend to give, give me this very garment; I have no need for any other fine ones. Abhaya said:
"I must wear these robes when I go to visit the king and the elders, and to pay my respects to the World-Honored One;
this duty must not be neglected. Upānanda spoke again: "Why do you say:..."
"Give me another robe.
"You truly think I have no other fine cotton cloth.
If you wish to give, give me this very robe; as for the others that are fine, they are not what I require."
Avaṭa said: "If you must have this robe, follow me back; when we arrive at my home, I shall give it to you. Upānanda said:

"You do not understand skillful means and are unaware of the various difficulties within the household; if your parents, brothers, or sisters should be stingy and refuse to allow you to give this gift, I shall not receive these robes and you shall not achieve the merit of giving—both of us will suffer loss."
"Because of this difficulty, you should truly give me [your upper garment] here.

At that time, Abhaya, unable to refuse despite his earnest protests, immediately took off his upper garment and gave it to him, then departed wearing only his lower garment and headed toward Śrāvastī.
At that time, many people in the city came out to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
Then, Abhaya asked the crowd,
"Where are you all going now?"
He replied,
"I wish to go to the Jetavana.
[The other] said:
"Do not go. He asked,
"For what reason?"
He replied,
"The śramaṇa has robbed me.
He asked again:
"Did you forcibly seize people and things?
He replied,
"What more is there to ask?"
"You simply watch me as I go with two pieces of cotton cloth; right now, there is indeed one among them.
Those who did not believe the Buddha immediately returned to the city, and those who heard this were filled with doubt, wondering whether it was so or not.
He remained there, lost in reflection.
Those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma then thought: "This can never be."
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, do not take what is not given; how could they plunder others?
Perhaps they merely take [wealth] by means of skillful preaching of the Dharma.
For this reason, few people went to the Jetavana to pay their respects and visit the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are so few people coming today to enter the Jetavana?
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported the preceding matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Upānanda here. Having been summoned, the Buddha asked Upānanda:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu! This is an evil deed."
"How is it that a bhikṣu forcibly begs for robes from others?
Have you not always heard the World-Honored One praise few desires and reproach many desires and insatiability?
From this day forward, I do not permit you to beg for robes from laymen or laywomen who are not your relatives."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, sixty bhikṣus from the north came to Śrāvastī to pay their respects and visit the World-Honored One.
While on his way, he was robbed by bandits and lost his clothes; entering the Jeta Grove Monastery naked, he paid homage to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus asked him, "Who are you?"
He replied, “A renunciant.
He asked again:
"From what lineage did you go forth?
He replied,
"I went forth from the Śākya clan."
He asked again,
"Where is your robe that you are naked?
He replied:
"I encountered bandits on the road and lost my robes.
At that time, the various bhikṣus each gave him a robe; some gave him a saṃghāṭī, some an uttarāsaṅga, some an antarvāsaka, and some a niṣīdana.
Having put on his robes, that bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣus:
“From where have you come?”
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
We have come from the north.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Did you endure the hardship of begging for food without difficulty? Were you not exhausted by the journey?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!

We have endured hardship; begging for food was not difficult and we were not fatigued on the road. However, we encountered bandits along the way and lost our clothes, so we entered the Jeta Grove naked.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Is there no village or town along your path?
They replied:
“There is,” [the monk replied]. The Buddha said,
“Why did you not ask for it?”

The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “We have heard, World-Honored One, that the precepts have been established such that one may not beg for robes from those who are not relatives. Yet we have no relatives, nor is there any donor to give us alms. For this reason, we did not dare to beg for robes and have come here naked.”
The Buddha praised the upholder of the precepts, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O monks! You have gone forth in accordance with the straight path of true faith; even for the sake of losing your lives, you should not intentionally violate the precepts.
From this day forward, I permit you to beg for robes when you are deprived of them."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, except during the special time.
The "special time" refers to the occasion when one's robes have been lost; this is called the special time.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Non-relative" means not belonging to the paternal lineage nor the maternal lineage.
Even in the absence of a relative, there may be one relative among many non-relatives.
"Many relatives" refers to those who are kin; "one non-relative" refers to one who is not kin. One incurs an offense by being separated from these two groups.
A "householder" (gṛhapati) is the master of a household.
"Clothing" (cīvara) refers to robes made of *kambala* (wool), *kārpāsa* (cotton), *kṣauma* (linen), *kauśeya* (silk), *śāṇa* (hemp), *māñjiṣṭha* (flax), or *kṛmimaya* (silk).
Regarding "begging": whether one begs for oneself or causes another to beg, there is no offense in begging for robes except during the "exceptional times.
The exceptional times refer to the time when one's robes have been lost.
There are ten causes and conditions for the loss of robes:

If it is seized by the king, or seized by thieves, or consumed by fire, or blown away by wind, or carried off by water; or if a woman, having conceived a lustful desire, seizes it; or if parents or relatives seize it with the intent to cause one to abandon the religious life; or if one hides it oneself and later forgets where it is; or if the stored robe becomes moldy and rotten; or if, after a long period of time, it has decayed and can no longer be used—it is called the "ten exceptions to the remaining time," and the World-Honored One declared that there is no offense in these cases.

Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed; to confess it without having relinquished the robe constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu has a robe within three yojanas, and his saṃghāṭī is lost while his uttarāsaṅga remains, he should not beg for one.
If one loses the saṃghāṭī, but the uttarāsaṅga and antarvāsaka remain, one should not beg for them.
If one loses all three robes, but the āvaraṇaka-vastra (wound-covering cloth) remains, one should not beg for them.
If one has lost the three robes or the wound-covering robe, but the rain-bath robe remains, one should not beg for them.
If a bhikṣu has lost the three robes, the wound-covering robe, and the rain-bath robe, but the bedding and coverlets remain, he should not beg for them.

If a bhikṣu loses his three robes, his wound-covering cloth, his rain-bathing cloth, or his bedding coverlet, he may request [a replacement] provided that the robe intended for use is two cubits in length and one cubit in width; he should not request more than this.

Why is this? This bhikṣu should wear these lower robes and travel three yojanas to receive the previously offered robe; however, if there are various obstacles on the way such that he is unable to reach the robe, he may request a rain-cloth without incurring any offense.
If a bhikṣu begs for robes from one who is not a relative— whether begging for them himself, having another beg for them, begging through gestures, or begging by preaching the Dharma—
"begging for them himself" means going in person to beg.
"To cause someone to beg" means to send a person to go and beg.
"To beg by making signs" refers to making signs of cold or signs of heat.
What are signs of cold?

If, during the eight nights of winter when it is snowing or raining, a bhikṣu puts on worn-out, tattered robes and goes to the house of a donor (*dānapati*) to manifest the appearance of shivering from the cold,
the donor then prostrates at the bhikṣu’s feet and asks:
“Ācārya, do you have no seasonal robes?”
"Why is it so freezing cold?
He replied, "There is none."
"When your parents were alive, they always made seasonal robes for me; now that your parents have passed away, who will make them for me?
It is not only that your parents have died, but my own parents have also met with impermanence."
The donor then said,
"Ācārya, do not harbor resentment!
I shall provide you with seasonal robes."
This is called begging under the pretext of cold.
If one obtains a robe through this means, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
What is the pretext of heat?
If, during the great heat of five or six months, a bhikṣu wears a thick woolen robe (nāṃgalika) and, perspiring, visits the home of a donor (*dānapati*) displaying signs of being hot,
the donor then pays homage at the bhikṣu’s feet and asks:
“Does the Ācārya have no seasonal clothing?”
"Why is it that when you apply heat, you break into such profuse sweat?
He replied, "There is none."
"When your parents were alive, they always made seasonal robes for me; now that your parents have passed away, who will make them for me?
It is not only that your parents have died, but my own parents have also met with impermanence."
The donor then said:
"Ācārya, do not harbor resentment!
I shall provide you with seasonal robes."
This is called begging with signs of heat.
If one obtains a robe through this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
What is begging by means of preaching the Dharma?
For the sake of robes, this bhikṣu spoke a verse to a donor, saying:
"If a person gives robes as a gift, they shall be born in the most excellent place;
those who joyfully practice giving shall receive the reward of blessings among humans and devas."
"Born in heaven, one obtains exquisite form, adorned with celestial jewel crowns;
because of the gift of robes to a bhikṣu, in birth after birth, garments appear spontaneously.
This is called "begging by preaching the Dharma."
If one obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

However, there is no offense for begging for a water-strainer, a small patch for clothing, a headband, a bandage for a wound, a border for a robe, or a single strip from within a robe; for such items as these, one does not commit an offense.
If one begs for such items and the donor gives a complete object or a garment that has already been cut and sewn, the recipient does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"I shall ask only for small items, and the donor will surely give me a complete garment," [he commits an offense].
If she obtains it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she begs for the sake of her preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she begs for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha, there is no offense. Therefore, it is said:
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, except at other times.
'Other times' refers to the time when one's robes have been lost."

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Sixty bhikṣus were traveling from the north toward Śrāvastī when they were robbed by bandits on the road and lost their robes; they subsequently entered the Jetavana Monastery.
At that time, having seen this, Upānanda said to the monk who had lost his robe:
"Venerable sirs!
When the World-Honored One permitted monks to beg from those who are not relatives when they have lost their robes, why do you not beg?"
He replied, "The fellow practitioners of the holy life have already given me sufficient robes; therefore, I do not beg for them.
At that time, Upānanda said:
"If you do not ask for it now, you will lose this benefit in vain.
He replied, "I have already obtained the robe; whether I lose or do not lose this benefit, what difference does it make?"
Upānanda said to the monk who had lost his robe,
"If you are unable to beg for one, I shall beg for you. He replied:
"You know the time yourself. In the morning,
Upānanda put on his robes for entering the village, took paper and pen, entered the city of Śrāvastī, and said to the upāsakas,
"You all should assist me in begging for robes."
The upāsaka asked,
"For what purpose do you beg?
He replied:
"There is a bhikṣu who has come from the north; having encountered bandits on the road, he lost all his belongings.
It is for his sake that we beg for robes. The upāsaka said, "So be it."
He then proceeded to various shops in the marketplace to engage in exhortation and conversion.

At that time, many people had faith and respect; some obtained one piece, others two pieces, and in this manner he gradually acquired a great quantity of clothing and goods, which he carried away on a heavy load.
When he had finished begging from one-fourth of the households that had faith, and was about to beg from another,
the upāsaka said: "Ācārya!..."
"You may now return. Upānanda said, "Alas!"
"O Longevity, why is it so brief and hurried?
I have only just begun my alms-round; you should not return yet. Why is this?"
When many people give alms, many receive merit. We who have left the household life have fixed times for our meals, yet we do not wish to depart just yet.
You householders, on the other hand, eat whenever you encounter food without fearing the loss of the proper time; what urgent matter has caused you such haste that you wish to leave?
Thus he went on to beg for alms once more, and the upāsaka spoke again:
"Enough, Ācārya!"
Upānanda spoke again:
"It is still not enough.
The upāsaka said:
“How many people are there? He replied, “Many.”
He asked again,
"How many people are there?
and he drew out his voice, saying:
"There are sixty bhikṣus.
The upāsaka said, "Ācārya!"
"These robes are sufficient for five hundred bhikṣus, let alone sixty.
Why do you beg for them?
Do you wish to sit upon a cotton cloth stall?"
He immediately threw his paper and pen to the ground and said with indignation:
"Where have these people been born, who are so full of insatiable desire and lack all sense of contentment?
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who, having heard these words, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here.
He was immediately summoned.
The Buddha questioned him extensively about the aforementioned matter,
saying, "Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha then questioned Upānanda:
"For what purpose do you beg?
He replied,
"I beg for the sake of a bhikṣu who has lost his robes."
The Buddha immediately called for the monk who had lost his robe. Once he had come, the Buddha said:
"Monks, did you truly cause Upānanda to beg for a robe?"
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha again asked the monk who had lost his robe,
"Upānanda, for what reason did you speak such words?
The monk who had lost his robe then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Upānanda:
"This is an evil deed.
You foolish man!"
"You beg for what should not be begged for, and you do not beg for what should be begged for.
The Buddha said to Upānanda,
"Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, praise having few desires and disparage having many desires?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a bhikṣu loses his robes, he may beg for robes from a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative.

If a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative offers him robes of their own accord in great quantity, that bhikṣu may accept a set of upper and lower robes; if he accepts more than this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Monk" is as explained above.
There are ten matters regarding the loss of robes, as explained above.

"Robe" refers to a *kambala* robe, a cotton (*kārpāsa*) robe, a *kṣauma* (flax) robe, a *kauśeya* (silk) robe, a *śāṇa* (hemp) robe, a *māñjiṣṭha* (safflower-dyed) robe, or a *kṛmimita* (silkworm) robe.
"Non-relatives" refers to those who are not part of one's parental lineage; this is called "non-relative.
A "householder" is the head of a family.

Regarding "begging," it means either begging for oneself, having someone else beg, or exhorting others to do so. If a donor wishes to give freely, one may take upper and lower robes; "freely" means giving according to one's own will.
Regarding upper and lower robes: they are three cubits wide and five cubits long; one may take two such robes.
If one takes more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *niḥsargika* offense: this robe must be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one confesses without having relinquished it, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu has a robe within a distance of three *yojanas*, and he loses his *saṃghāṭī* while his *uttarāsaṅga* remains, he should not beg for one; this applies even as long as any robe remains, he should not beg for one.

Why is this? This bhikṣu should wear these lower robes and go three yojanas to receive his previously designated robe. If there are various obstacles on the way such that he is unable to go and retrieve the robe, he may beg for two robes without incurring any offense.
The characteristics of cold, heat, and preaching the Dharma are as explained above.
If a bhikṣu travels along a road together with merchants, and bandits follow from one direction, two directions, or three directions, he should flee far away from the bandits.
If enemies come from all four directions, one should not run away; rather, one should stand with the body upright and must not strike back at the enemy.
If the enemy says, "Bring me the saṃghāṭī," [one should give it].
He replied, "I give you long life!
In this manner, he gave each article of clothing as much as was requested; he must not shout loudly, call out in a great voice, or scold the bandits with anger.
Having given the object away, one should depart slowly, entering the forest grass to hide and observe from afar whether anything remains after the thieves have left;
whatever robes remain should be taken and kept.

If there are no other robes, and if among them there is a bhikṣu or one who has gone forth as a non-Buddhist ascetic who has been killed by bandits, one should take those robes and accept them for use.
If there is no death among the renunciants, but there is a death among the laity, one should take the clothing of the layperson, cut the threads to purify it, and then accept and wear it.
If there is no clothing from a deceased person, one should not take fine garments left behind by merchants; however, if they have discarded worn-out clothing, one may take it and accept it for use.

If a merchant returns and calls for the bhikṣu, saying, "I will give you this fine robe," he should accept it; having accepted it, he should cut the threads and dye it with cow dung to make it pure before taking formal possession of it.
If the merchant says to the bhikṣu, "I lend you this robe to wear;
when you reach your previous residence, return it to me without letting it be damaged or diminished."

That bhikṣu should take this robe, tuck the threads inside and stitch it so that the threads do not show; having performed the ritual purification (*śuddhi*) and accepted possession of it, he should return it upon reaching his residence.
If these things are not available, one should pluck tree leaves to cover the front and back before departing.

If even this is not possible, one must not walk along the road with arms flailing like the Nirgranthas; rather, one should use the hands to shield the front and conceal the body while walking on the side of the path. Do not enter deep thickets, lest bandits mistake you for a hunter or pursuer.

One should walk along the side of the road through shallow grass; while walking, if one encounters a person coming, one should immediately sit down in a small, visible spot within the shallow grass so that the passerby may see one.
If someone asks,
"Who are you? one should answer:
“Are you a renunciant?
“In what path have you gone forth?
He replied:
“The Śākyas have gone forth [into homelessness]. “Why are they naked?
He replied:
"If one has been robbed by thieves," if someone gives many robes of their own accord without being asked, there is no offense in taking them.
If they do not give of their own accord, one should ask for them; when asking, if they give many robes, one should take two robes, each three cubits wide and five cubits long.
If these conditions are not met, one should go to a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) dwelling; if one obtains robes there from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they should be accepted.
If there is no forest hermitage dwelling, one should go to a cemetery (śmaśāna).
If there is a guardian of the tomb, one should say to him:
"I wish to collect discarded garments.
If the guardian of the tomb instructs one to take them, having taken them, one should show them to me; one should take them and show them to me.
If one takes the clothes of a deceased woman while her body has not yet decomposed, one should go to the side of her head to take them.
If the body has already decomposed, one may take them as one pleases;
if it is the clothes of a deceased man, they may likewise be taken as one pleases.
If there is treasure within the clothing of a deceased person, one should step upon it with the foot to remove the treasure and then take the clothing away.

If one does not notice the presence of treasure and only discovers it after taking the clothing back home, one should entrust it to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to be used for medicinal decoctions.
If the guardian of the cemetery says to the bhikṣu,
"You may take an inferior robe; do not take one that is good," and that bhikṣu goes to the cemetery and,
not seeing any worn-out ones, finds many fine robes, he takes them back and says to the guardian of the cemetery:
"It is simply that these robes are of good quality.
The guardian of the tomb, having heard this, took them; but had he said, "These are excellent, I will not allow you to take them," [the monk would have been stopped].
The bhikṣu should return and seek another;
if that person says to the bhikṣu,
"Take one that is on the ground."
He then took the one that was on the ground.
If [the other] said,
"Take the one in the air," [he would have taken that].
"Regarding 'one should take that which is in the air':
if it is a fine robe with half on the ground and half in the air, one should cut off the half and take it.
If this is not possible, one should go into the village and inquire about the location of the bhikṣus' residence."
One should not enter a village during the day; one should wait until the cowherds have returned with their herds in the evening and then enter the village together with them.
One should not stay near the milch cows, but should instead move among the weak and young calves.
When seeing people, one sits in the full lotus posture;
if someone asks, "Who are you? one answers:
“A renunciant. “From which path have you gone forth?
“I have gone forth from the Śākya clan.”
"Where are your robes? He replied,
"They were lost entirely to bandits."
If they do not ask for it but give it of their own accord, one may take as much as desired.
If they do not give it, one should beg for it.
When begging, if they give much, one should accept two robes, each three cubits wide and five cubits long.
If, moreover, there is no such person, one should go to the monastery and ask the senior bhikṣus:
"Who here is the *karmadāna*?
Who is the person in charge of the bedding and mats?"
He replied, "It is so-and-so.
At that time, the bhikṣu should go to the place of the administrative bhikṣu and ask him:
"What kind of beds, mats, and bedding should a bhikṣu receive after so many years?
He replied,
"A bhikṣu [who has served] for so many years should receive such beds, mats, and bedding."
When this bhikṣu obtains such a mat, he should tear it apart and gather the wool fibers into one place; taking the outer and inner layers, he makes a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
If he obtains a pillow, he likewise tears it apart, gathers the wool fibers into one place, and taking the outer and inner layers, he makes a *saṃghāṭī-śākhā*.
Having received and put on the bedding, one should pay homage to the stūpa and to the senior monks (upādhyāya).
One should inquire after the junior monks (navaka) and say to them:
"I lost my robes while being robbed on the road; you should assist me in begging for new ones."
If an elder bhikṣu says:
"You are like a starving crow whose feet cannot remain steady; who would assist you?
It is truly the wine-sellers and the robbers who have seized you."
Or, having exchanged it for food, he says he has been robbed and asks for assistance in begging.
If that is the case, one should go to the upāsaka and say:
"Long-lived one!..."
"While traveling on the road, I was robbed by bandits and lost my robes; you should assist me in begging for new ones.
They replied, "So be it."
"Ācārya! Request them for me immediately.
If many robes are obtained, the bhikṣu should take two robes, each three cubits wide and five cubits long.
At that time, the upāsaka said to the bhikṣu:
"Is there a skillful means by which you might take all these robes for me?
He replied:
"You may exchange these two pieces of fine cotton cloth and bring them here.
If the upāsaka employs a skillful expedient, he leads the bhikṣu outside the boundary and says: "Ācārya!..."
"This robe is offered as a gift to the present Saṃgha; since there is no present Saṃgha, the Ācārya, being present, should accept it.
If the bhikṣu accepts it at that time, he commits no offense.
If an upāsaka offers a large piece of cotton cloth, one should cut it into two sections for robes.
He should ask:
"For what reason?"
He replied,
“The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one may properly take only two robes.
The upāsaka said:
"Ācārya, please just take the dye.
After the bhikṣu had taken the dye and returned it, the upāsaka said:

"When it was not yet dyed, it was a layperson's garment; I did not even desire it then. How much less now that it has been dyed into a monastic color? It is a garment for one who has left the household life, so I shall not take it back."
At that time, the bhikṣu may take them and use them as he wishes to make robes.

As for the outer and inner layers of the mat and pillow previously removed by this bhikṣu, which were used to make *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* and *kaṭhina* cloths, he shall wash them and restore them to their original state as mats, pillows, and bedding, returning them to the person in charge before departing.
If you wish to remain in this very place, you may do so as you please; however, you must not request [a robe] and then insist on staying.
Therefore it is said:
"When a bhikṣu has lost his robe, he may beg for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative."
If a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative offers many robes of their own accord, this bhikṣu may accept two robes, one for the upper body and one for the lower body.
To accept more than this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms; when the time arrived, he put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city.
Proceeding in order to beg for food, he came to a certain house.
The women of that household said to the bhikṣus,
"On such-and-such a day, we shall provide a meal for the Saṃgha and bestow robes as offerings.
The bhikṣus said:
“Excellent, sister!
May you establish the three firm things—body, life, and wealth—and may no obstacles arise in between.
Having said this, he departed.
After the bhikṣu had returned from begging for alms, he went to the heated hall and said to the bhikṣus,
"I have told the elders something good.
They replied:
"What good news is there?
"I have heard that a certain upāsikā intends to invite the Saṃgha for a meal and offer robes on such-and-such a day.
When Nanda and Upananda heard this, they immediately asked:
"Elder! Where is the location of that house and its lane?
What are his family name and given name?"
Having learned this, on the following morning at dawn, he put on his robes for entering a village and went to her house, saying:
"May you be free from illness, O upāsikā!"
The upāsikā said, “Homage to you, Ācārya!”
The bhikṣu said,
"I have heard good news. He asked:
"What news have you heard?
He replied,
"I have heard that you wish to invite the Sangha to provide offerings and bestow robes."
He replied, "I have this intention,
but I fear that various obstacles may arise along the way and prevent its fulfillment.
The bhikṣu said:
"You have invited the Saṃgha to provide offerings and donate robes, wishing to give fine and coarse robes to the elder bhikṣus.
If you were to give the coarse ones, they should properly be given to the śrāmaṇeras, the ārāmikas, or hung upon the robe racks."
If someone gives me something good, I shall present it to the noble and eminent members of the royal court and offer it to the Buddha.
Should anyone ask me about it, I shall say:
"A certain female lay follower of pure faith gave this to me."
"You may then be said to possess the merit of receiving the name and its enjoyment. He replied:
"There is nothing further; there is only this, which has already been granted to the Saṃgha."
"If there is anything [else], you should also give it separately.
The bhikṣu said,
"Whether you give it or not is up to your own will."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
The donor thought to himself:
"If he gives to him and not to the Saṃgha, [he misses out on this], for the Saṃgha is a fertile field of merit."
"If I do not give it to him but give it to the Saṃgha, he possesses royal power and could cause me harm.
Out of fear of him, she did not give it to the Saṃgha; and because he felt displeasure toward her, she gave it to neither.
The bhikṣus asked the bhikṣu who was begging for alms,
"There has been no news at all since you last heard from him.
The bhikṣu who was begging for alms replied:
"I know for certain that it will be tomorrow. At dawn the next day,
the bhikṣu who begs for alms put on his village-entering robes and went to her house, where he immediately asked the upāsikā,
"Why have you not prepared and set out various foods?"
He replied,
"Ācārya! It was because of Nanda and Upananda that my wholesome mind was destroyed."
He asked, “For what reason?
and the man then related the matter in full as described above.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu who had gone for alms told the other bhikṣus.
On account of this matter, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Call Nanda and Upananda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
“Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Foolish man!"
"This is an evil deed; you have committed two things that are not beneficial: the donor loses his merit, and the recipient loses his benefit.

The Buddha said, "Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, disparage great desire and praise few desires? Why did you not first invite him yourself, but instead go to urge him for the sake of something 'good'?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
For the sake of a bhikṣu, if a householder or a householder’s wife prepares the price for robes and says:
"I have prepared such-and-such a price for robes; I shall buy such-and-such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu."
"Before being invited by the householder, this bhikṣu, for the sake of its excellence, went to the householder's residence and spoke thus:
'Make such a robe for me, for the sake of its excellence.'"
"If he obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "for a bhikṣu," this refers to whether it is the Saṃgha, a group of many, or a single person.
"Householder" is as explained above.
"Robes" refers to robes made of *kambala* (wool), *kārpāsa* (cotton), *kṣauma* (linen), *kauśeya* (silk), *śāṇa* (hemp), *māñjiṣṭha* (flax), or *kṛmimaya* (silk).
"Price of robes" refers to gold, silver, precious objects, and so forth.

"To prepare" means: whether today, tomorrow, in half a month, or in a month, [someone] prepares such and such a price for robes, intending to buy such and such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu; this is called "preparing."
Regarding "previously not having been invited to the *pravāraṇā*": one who previously knew they had not been invited to the *pravāraṇā* then claims they were invited to the *pravāraṇā*;
and when others know they were invited to the *pravāraṇā*, those other monks likewise claim they were invited to the *pravāraṇā*.
I understand that when one is invited to a *pravāraṇā* (invitation to choose) and given other items, it is said that one has been invited to a *pravāraṇā* and given robes.
As for "going," it means arriving at a householder’s field, or arriving at their home, or entering inside their house.
Regarding "requesting": if one requests blue, yellow, red, black, or various madder-dyed colors;
or if one requests long, wide, or both long and wide; and whether the donor gives what was requested or gives something else instead, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding those who prefer [fine things], there is the preference for contentment, the preference for discontent, and the preference for coarse sufficiency.
What is the preference for contentment?
It is when, upon being given fine clothing, one says:
"I shall take what is coarse.
This is called being content with what one has obtained;
[if one obtains more than that], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
One who is discontented and fond of finery, when given coarse clothing, will say:
"If you give me coarse clothing, it is not fit to touch my feet."
"I am a person of high status; I ought to be given fine clothing.
This is called the offense of not being content with what one has received, for which a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* is incurred.
Regarding "being satisfied with coarse [clothing]," it means that when someone gives fine clothing, one says:
"I do not need these fine robes; I am an araṇyaka, like a deer in the forest, dwelling in an open space. Give me something coarse, sufficient to ward off the cold, heat, wind, and rain."
This is called "coarse and good.
If one obtains such [a robe], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe should be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense should be confessed.
If one does not relinquish [the offense] but merely regrets it, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣu, a householder or a householder’s wife, or even for the sake of excellence, should obtain a robe [for him], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. There was a bhikṣu who went for alms; when the time arrived, he put on his village-entering robe, took up his bowl, and entered the city to wander for alms in succession.
A householder’s wife spoke to a bhikṣu as described above.

This is recounted with reference to one householder; here, it differs only in that there are two householders involved. [The same applies] up until: "What has already been heard should be heard again."
For the sake of a bhikṣu, if two householders or two housewives each provide the price for a robe, saying:
"We have provided such and such a price for a robe; we shall buy such and such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu."
"Without having been previously invited to choose his own, that bhikṣu, for the sake of a fine robe, went to a householder and said:
'Prepare the price for such and such robes for me individually, and together make one robe for me, so that it may be fine.'"
If he obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
In this regard, it is as explained at length above concerning a single householder; the only difference here is that there are two householders.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. King Bimbisāra had two chief ministers:
one named Niti and the other named Varisa.
In the autumn, after the people had finished harvesting, they were transporting the grain into the city when the weather turned cold and snowy.
At that time, the two ministers thought to themselves:
"We have regularly invited the masters Nanda and Upananda year after year to provide them with food and robes; where might they be today?"
Someone said to him,
"They are in Śrāvastī. Thereupon,
the minister dispatched a messenger carrying a letter and eight hundred old coins as a gift for Nanda and Upananda.
The imperial messenger said, "You shall receive a reply.
The messenger proceeded toward the Jetavana Monastery; having arrived, he asked:
"Nanda, where is the room of Upānanda?
At that time, the bhikṣus pointed and said,
"This room is it."
The messenger immediately entered the room, and after paying his respects, asked:
"Is this Upānanda? He replied:
"Yes, why do you ask? He replied, "Nidhipāla,
a minister of King Bimbisāra, has sent me with a letter and eight hundred old coins as a gift for the Teacher, requesting a reply in return."
At that time, there was a lay follower named Fa Yu. Upānanda then said to the lay follower:
"Do you know how to calculate? Is the value of these robes consistent with what is written in the document?"
He then calculated and determined that it accorded with the letter, so he immediately sent a reply and dispatched a messenger.
At that time, the upāsaka Dharmapriya, wishing to depart, said:
"Venerable One!..."
"Where should this robe be placed?
He replied,
"It should be placed by your side."
He then took it away.
Having arrived home, he waited for one day, two days, and three days, but [Upānanda] did not come to retrieve it.

Because Upānanda was preoccupied with many affairs and had forgotten to go and fetch it, that lay follower’s household became short of supplies; he therefore borrowed and used the item, intending to repay it later.
On the very day they were used, Nanda told Upānanda to go and collect the price for the robes, and he went immediately to demand it.

The lay follower said, "I brought them here and waited for you for one day, two days, and three days, but you did not come to take them. My household was short of supplies, so I borrowed and used them; I must have them returned."
Upānanda then spoke with indignation:
"You are not someone to whom things can be entrusted; this is my property—how could you take it and use it without permission?
Nanda said to Upānanda:
"This object cannot simply be taken by request," he said,
and immediately told the officials to drag it away.
When the crowd saw this, they reviled the śramaṇa in various ways:

“The son of the Śākyas claims for himself that he is virtuous and good, yet even though his donor constantly provides him with all necessities, he can be so distressed and impoverished; how much more so would others be!
Having lost the dharma of a śramaṇa and practicing evil in such a manner, what path could he possibly possess?”
Having heard this, Upānanda felt ashamed and immediately let him go.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went to inform the World-Honored One, who said:
"Call Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Upānanda,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Upānanda:
"This is an evil matter.
Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, reprove excessive desire and praise few desires?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities."
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to go and seek [alms].
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the upāsaka Dharmapriya would regularly invite the bhikṣus to a meal in the proper order within the Saṃgha.
When it was time for the turn of the bhikṣu who was to receive food, he arrived at the house.
Dharmapāla asked him, "Why did Upānanda not come to collect the money?
When I had not yet received it, he came among the crowd and pressed me hard for it; yet now that I have obtained the payment, he does not come to collect it."
The bhikṣus said,
“The Buddha has established a precept that we may not come to solicit [alms]. Fayu said:
"If you do not permit me to seek [what I need], why have you come here in silence?
I know my own mind.
After that bhikṣu had finished eating, he returned and spoke to the other bhikṣus. When the bhikṣus heard this, they immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of the matter.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This lay follower Yü possesses such skillful means through his intelligence and wisdom.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to go and request [the goods] three times, and to remain silent for six periods.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
For the sake of a bhikṣu, if a king or a high minister sends a messenger to deliver the value of robes to that bhikṣu, the messenger arrives at the bhikṣu’s location and says:
"Venerable One!..."
"This garment price has been sent by a king or a high minister; Venerable One, please accept this garment price.
That bhikṣu should speak to the messenger thus:

"It is not in accordance with the Dharma for bhikṣus to accept garment prices. When I have need of a robe and obtain a pure robe, if I require it, I may accept it with my own hands and keep it as a bhikṣu's robe after having it made."
The messenger should say to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, do you have an attendant who regularly performs services for the bhikṣus?
That bhikṣu should point out an attendant to the messenger—whether it be a park-keeper (ārāmika), a monastery servant (ārāmika-vāsī), or a lay follower (upāsaka)—and should say to the messenger:
"These people are capable of serving as attendants for the bhikṣus.
He sent a messenger to the place where the attendants were, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Steward, purchase such-and-such clothing for such-and-such a price and give it to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
When that bhikṣu requires clothing, he shall come to receive it; you must then provide him with the garment."
Having either exhorted him himself or sent someone else to exhort him, the messenger returns to where the bhikṣu is and says:

"The official in charge whom the Venerable One pointed out, I have already exhorted him and the robe has been made. When the Venerable One requires a robe, please go and take it; I shall give the robe to the Venerable One."
A bhikṣu who needs robes should go to the person in charge of robes and request them, saying: "I need robes.
He should request them a second and a third time in this same manner.
If one obtains the robe, it is well;
if not, on the fourth, fifth, and sixth days, one should stand silently before the steward.
If one obtains the robe, it is well.
If he does not obtain [the robe], yet seeks beyond this limit for the sake of obtaining a robe, and if he should obtain that robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go himself or send a messenger to the place from which the price of the robe came, and say:
"The price of a robe was sent by you for the sake of a certain bhikṣu; however, that bhikṣu has ultimately not obtained it."
"You yourself must know your own wealth and ensure it is not lost; this is the natural order of things.
Here, "monks" refers to the Saṃgha, or a group of many, or a single individual.
Regarding the "king," it is as explained in the section on the precept against stealing.
Regarding "royal ministers," this includes even minor officials; anyone who leads and knows how to perform official duties is termed a minister.
Regarding "messengers," these may be male or female, senior or junior, whether they are laypeople or monastics.
"Robe" is as explained above.

"Price for a robe" refers to money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, amber, tridacna shell, agate, red gems, copper, iron, white tin, lead, and pewter; these are called the price for a robe.
A *ārāmika* (garden-attendant) is a person who provides service for the Saṃgha; this is called an *ārāmika*.

An *upāsaka* (lay follower) is one who takes the three refuges and practices this Dharma according to the one-part practice, the minor practice, the major practice, the complete practice, or the conforming practice; this is called an *upāsaka*.
Regarding "three requests": this does not refer to three requests within a single round of going and returning; rather, it means requesting up to three times over successive rounds.

If one remains silent for four, five, or six times, this refers to remaining silent during four, five, or six such rounds—not merely being silent once—and involves either going oneself to request once or sending a messenger while remaining silent for the other occasions.
1. Going oneself to request; 2. Sending a messenger and remaining silent;
1. Going oneself to request; 3. Sending a messenger and remaining silent;
1. Going oneself to request; 4. Sending a messenger and remaining silent.
First, one goes in person to request; fifth, one dispatches a messenger and stands silently.
First, one goes in person to request; sixth, one dispatches a messenger and stands silently.
Second, one goes in person to the gate to request; third, one goes in person to the gate to request—these are likewise.
First, one sends a messenger to request [the object]; second, one goes in person and remains silent;
third, one sends a messenger to request it and a second time goes in person and remains silent;
fourth, one sends a messenger to request it and a third time goes in person and remains silent.
1. Sending a messenger to request [it]; 4. Going there oneself and remaining silent; 1.
Sending a messenger to go and request [it]; 5. Going there oneself and remaining silent;
1. Sending a messenger to request [it]; 6. Going there oneself and remaining silent.
Second, sending a messenger to request the gate; third, sending a messenger to request the gate is likewise.
Going in person to request it; going in person and remaining silent—these three cases regarding the gate are likewise.
Sending a messenger to demand [the object] and sending a messenger to remain silent—these three modes are likewise applied.
When one goes to demand it three times and remains silent six times, there may be either a relaxed deadline or an urgent deadline.
What is meant by "slackness" and "urgency"?
If a bhikṣu goes to a donor's place to solicit robes and says:
"Long-lived one!..."
"Give me the price for the robe.
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Come back after one more month.
The bhikṣu goes to request it after exactly one month; if the donor says again, "Come back after another month," [he must wait].
If a bhikṣu goes again after one full month to request [the robe], and the donor says,
"Venerable sir, come again after another month," and the bhikṣu goes again after another full month to request it, he may not request it again once three months have passed.
If one says,
"I will come in half a month," and more than three half-months have passed, one may not request it again.
If one says:
"Ten days. Or if one says:
"Five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, or even a brief moment.
Once more than three brief moments have passed,
one may no longer request it.
The bhikṣu went there six times. Each time, the donor said, "I know the venerable one's intention to remain; please come back in one month.
When the bhikṣu had completed one month and went again, he remained in silence. Having gone and remained in silence in this manner for a full six months, he was not permitted to go any further.
If one says:
"Half a month.
Or if one says:
"Ten days, five days, four days, three days, two days, one day, or even for a brief moment.
Once more than six brief moments have passed, one must not go there again and remain in silence.
What is the measure for remaining silent?
It should be like the time it takes a person to enter a storehouse, take an object, place it upon their head, and depart; or like the time it takes to wrap an object in a cloth bundle.
If a bhikṣu employs such means to manifest his presence, carrying his robe, bowl, staff, and water flask past the person to whom he has entrusted his belongings, and if that person asks:
"Venerable sir, where do you wish to go?
He replied,
"I wish to go first to the owner of the goods and tell him to take note of this property so that it is not lost."
The person to whom the item was entrusted said, "I have already prepared the goods; there is no need to go again.
If the bhikṣu immediately takes the goods from that person, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one does not employ skillful means and the path lies ahead of that person, and if that person asks,
"Venerable sir, where are you going?
one should answer:
