"I intend to go; first send the items to the owner's side and tell him they are here so that he may know them himself, lest they be lost.
The person in charge of the deposit replied, "I have already prepared the items long ago; there is no need to go again."
If one gives the object immediately, the taker incurs no offense.
If the person who received the deposit says,
"Go as you please!"
"Even if you were able to destroy me as one destroys a tala tree, I would still not give you a single coin.
At that time, the bhikṣu should go to the owner of the goods and say, "Let him know for himself that this object must not be lost."
If the owner of the object says, "I previously gave this to the bhikṣu;
you may seek it back as you see fit," the bhikṣu may then proceed as before:
he may request it three times by speaking, or remain silent for six rounds.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"Whether it be a king or a high minister, they should ensure that the value of the robes is sent [to the recipient] and not lost; this matter ought to be handled in this way.
This concludes the first section (varga).
The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kukkuṭārāma in Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, all the bhikṣus were making their saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, antaravāsaka, and niṣīdana out of felt, with the sole exception of the water-strainer and the shoulder-bag, all of which were made entirely of felt.
The bhikṣus went about begging for wool everywhere to make felt robes; as they did so in great numbers, they became an object of resentment to the people of the world.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, having risen at dawn, put on his village-entering robe and entered Vaiśālī for the purpose of begging for wool.
There was a merchant who, holding a door-knob in his hand, came toward the marketplace to open his shop. Seeing from afar that a bhikṣu was approaching in haste, the merchant thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu must have come here at dawn specifically to beg for wool; since my goods have not yet been sold, who would be willing to give him this wool first?"
He then closed the shop door and returned to his own home.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This merchant saw me and closed his shop door to go back; it is because he does not wish to give me wool."
He then went to intercept him by another path, approached him, and asked:
"Long-lived one! Where are you going?"
"I cannot leave you; from whom else should I beg for hair?
It was precisely from you that I wished to beg.
You who have faith in the Buddha-dharma, knowing the existence of sin and merit, as well as the karmic retribution of actions—yet you do not give to me; who then would give to me?"
Āyuṣman, you should know!

As the Blessed One has said, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness; by skillful means, one should cause those who do not wish to hear to hear, and instruct those who lack faith so that they may establish it in faith, even to the point of grasping someone by the head with one's hand and strongly exhorting them to practice giving.
The reason for this is that he shall ultimately be reborn in the heavens, where his physical form, strength, lifespan, and retinue will be spontaneously provided.

When he is later born among humans, he will likewise experience happiness, with his physical form, strength, lifespan, and retinue fully accomplished. By practicing the Buddha-dharma, he will increase his merit and attain the fruit of ambrosia.
Therefore, Āyuṣmat!
The World-Honored One has said:
"By performing meritorious deeds, one receives the retribution of happiness; whatever is desired comes spontaneously."
Transcending the flow of birth and death, one attains the supreme tranquility of Nirvana.
If a person performs meritorious deeds, the celestial deities will naturally protect them;
all their aspirations will spontaneously be fulfilled, and no demons shall be able to destroy them.
Those with little merit suffer many afflictions; merit can eliminate all such troubles.
When merit is firm and strong, one swiftly achieves steadfast concentration.
One will experience happiness when born in heaven and possess sovereignty even among humans.
By virtue of these merits, wherever one goes, all things are spontaneous.
Through these skillful means of merit, one is forever freed from the suffering of birth and death;
attaining the Way and reaching Nirvana, one neither sinks nor is born again.
When the bhikṣu had spoken this verse, he further said:
"Long-lived one!
To give me wool brings the greatest merit."
At that time, having heard the teaching of the Dharma, the merchant immediately offered some wool.
Then the merchant thought to himself:

"If I enter the marketplace, I will beg for much more wool, and I shall no longer obtain profit; I will lose my capital. It would be better to stay at home and preserve my capital than to lose both interest and principal in the market."
Having had this thought, he returned home and sat down.
At that time, the merchant’s wife said angrily to her husband,
"Why have you gone to the market and returned so quickly?"
"If you are so indolent, by what means will you support your sons and daughters, or fulfill your official duties and corvée labor?
The merchant replied, "Do not be angry; listen for a moment!"
"This morning, I went to the market stalls and shops and spoke at length on the aforementioned matters, concluding that it would be better to return home and remain there.
Having heard this, his wife fell silent and desisted.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was begging for alms in succession and arrived at the house of a merchant, standing in the doorway.

At that moment, the merchant’s wife was deeply faithful and reverent; recognizing Śāriputra, she immediately took a vessel filled with food, stepped out of the door, and placed it into Śāriputra’s bowl. She then prostrated herself, touching her head to his feet, and respectfully inquired after his well-being.
Then Śāriputra also greeted her, asking:
"How is it at home? Is your livelihood well?
His wife replied:
"The household is entirely well, but our means of livelihood have suddenly fallen into ruin.
He asked, "For what reason?"
He then related the preceding circumstances in detail to Śāriputra:
"In our household life, for food, drink, clothing, and the payment of official taxes, we rely entirely upon the marketplace."
"Now my husband lives at home; fearing that people might beg for wool, he truly says he is walking when he is actually lying down, and truly says he is sleeping when he is actually awake.
You, Master, are now the one whom our family honors, reveres, and respects; we have nothing to hide from you."

Furthermore, this fur is highly precious; one may obtain one *liang* for a single coin, or even two, three, or four coins for one *liang*. Moreover, this fur is extremely fine and soft; it is exceedingly rare, as it does not cause tears to flow when it touches the eyes.
"Venerable Sir!
This wool comes from four great countries:
the country of Vaiśālī, the country of Vārāṇasī, the country of Dakṣiṇāpatha, and the country of Nandivardhana."
"Venerable Sir!
For the sake of seeking this hair, my husband and his kinsmen have sometimes returned and sometimes died without returning.
Because the hair is so difficult to obtain, it is therefore exceedingly precious."
"Furthermore, these bhikṣus come one after another to beg, destroying my household estate until I have reached utter poverty.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra extensively expounded the Dharma for him, causing him to give rise to joy, and then he returned to the vihāra.
After the meal, he reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here.
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
“Did you indeed make a felt robe by begging for wool, and even tell the merchant’s wife about it to Śāriputra?
He replied, “It is true.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Have you not often heard me, through countless skillful means, reprove excessive desire and praise few desires?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and does not accord with the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who rely on Vaiśālī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat out of pure black wool, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Pure" means not mixed with other types of wool; there are ten such kinds:

The *saṃtāna* sheep, the *chagala* sheep, the sheep of incomplete color, the *aja* sheep, the *pārāśara* sheep, the *urabhra* sheep, the *samāna* sheep, the *ravitṛ* sheep, the many-eared sheep, and the *kumuda* sheep.
"New" means that which has been recently completed.
"Bedding and seating" refers to woolen rugs.
"Makes" means either to make it oneself or to have another person make it.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bedding must be relinquished among the community of monks (*saṃgha*), and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one confesses the offense without relinquishing the item, it constitutes a *vinaya-ati-krama* (transgression of the discipline).
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
As for the "continuous sheep," there are six kinds of wool:
naturally blue, dyed blue, naturally black, dyed black, naturally blue-black, and dyed blue-black.
Whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, once it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
To use it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This applies even to wooden lotuses and sheep [skins], and so forth.
This bedding should be relinquished among the community of monks; the community of monks must not return it, nor may it be used for any other purpose.
It is only permissible to spread it upon the ground or to use it as a screen, curtain, blind, or canopy.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat from pure black wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī; the detailed explanation is as above.

At that time, the bhikṣus made all types of felt garments: the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antarvāsaka, and the niṣīdana; they made everything out of felt, with the sole exception of the water-strainer and the shoulder-bag.
Before the Buddha had established the precepts, at that time the bhikṣus wore felt robes and dwelt in comfort and security on open ground as if in huts.
After the precepts were established, because they no longer wore felt robes, they frequently fell ill and did not dwell in comfort.
He then spoke of this matter to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Before the Buddha had established the precepts, we wore felt robes and dwelt with as much security as if we were under a roof."
Since the Buddha has established the precepts, we can no longer obtain woolen robes; consequently, we suffer much from illness and lack peace and comfort.
Excellent, Ānanda!
You should report this in full to the World-Honored One, so that he may again grant permission for us to wear woolen robes.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and reported the foregoing matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"I permit the bhikṣus to return and wear woolen robes.
The Buddha said,
"I permit the bhikṣus to work with various materials [to make them]."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Vaiśālī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a new rug, he should use two parts of pure black wool from a ram, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior.
If a bhikṣu makes a new rug without using two parts of pure black wool from a ram, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.
“New” refers to one who has first made a bedding mat.
“Made of felt” means either made by oneself or caused to be made by another.
"Pure" means unmixed.
"Wool" refers to the ten types, as described above.

"Two parts" means using black wool predominantly while maintaining the perception of equality; if one uses [other materials] equally, one should perceive it as a reduction and increase [the black wool] accordingly.

Regarding the third part, the "white," one uses mostly white hair while forming the perception of it being equal [in quantity], and by forming the perception that it is less than equal, one adds more;
regarding the fourth part, the "inferior," one uses a small amount of inferior hair while forming the perception of it being equal—in this manner, one prepares a new bedding.
Whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, once it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one uses it, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bedding must be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
To repent without having relinquished [the wool] constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
The aforementioned four kinds of wool must be relinquished among the community of monks (*saṃgha*); the Saṃgha may not return them, nor may they be used for any other purpose.
It is proper to spread it on the ground and to use it as a screen, a curtain, or a canopy.
These latter six types are also to be relinquished among the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should not return them, but the Saṃgha may use them.
They must not be used as personal clothing; therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to make a woolen rug, but he had little sheep’s wool. The other bhikṣus asked him, “Have you finished making the rug?”
He replied,
“It has not yet been completed. He asked:
"Why is that? He replied,
"Because there is little wool."
The bhikṣus said to him,
"Do you wish for this felt to be made fine, soft,
and warm? He replied:
"I wish to do so.
The bhikṣus said to him,
"Go to the village of Vālukārāma and beg for *kocava* cloth, which you shall then combine with wool to make [a rug]."
He then went, just as he had said, to the village of Vālukṣa and approached the house of Kośika, saying:
"Long-lived one!
Give me some *kośika* cloth."
He replied, "Wait a moment;
wait until I have returned with the *koccha* grass, and I shall give it to you.
That bhikṣu waited outside for a short while and came back again to ask:
"Has it returned yet?
He replied, "It has just returned;
wait for me to rest a moment and finish boiling it, and I shall give it to you."
The family had a seat prepared for the bhikṣu, so he sat down and waited a short while. He rose again and inserted his finger into the cauldron to check whether the water was hot;
he then said, "The water is already hot; you may put in the cocoons."
The host, wishing to mock the bhikṣu, asked:
"Venerable sir, is this bath-water actually hot enough to be used?
He replied:
"It is indeed hot; you may take it.
The host immediately took the cocoons and placed them into the cauldron, where they made a sizzling sound.
The host spoke with displeasure:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, by means of countless skillful means, praises non-killing and censures those who kill.
How is it that a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, could intentionally kill a living being and thus lose the dharma of a śramaṇa?"
"What path could there be [in this]?
The host had no joyful heart and gave only a small amount.
Having received it, the bhikṣu immediately combined it with his own to make a bedding mat.
The bhikṣus asked again:
"Have you finished making your bedding?
He replied:
“It is finished;
however, in this undertaking there is little benefit and much fault.
The bhikṣus asked:
"What is meant by 'little benefit and many faults'?
He then related the aforementioned matter in full.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call this bhikṣu here.
Once he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
“This is an evil deed. Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, reprove the taking of life and praise its abstention?
Why have you now committed such an evil deed?”
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who rely on Vaiśālī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using *kauśeya* silk mixed with pure black wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "mixed with *koseyya* (silk)," there are two kinds of *koseyya*:
first, the natural (*jāta*), and second, the manufactured (*kata*).
The natural kind refers to fine thread.
The "maker" refers to the spinner.
The "wool" refers to the ten types, as described above.
"New" means recently produced.
"Bedding" refers to a woolen rug.
"Makes" means either to make it oneself or to have someone else make it.
Once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
To use it constitutes a violation of the Vinaya.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bedding must be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one does not relinquish [the robe] but merely regrets it, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If a bhikṣu makes a *saṃghāṭī* from *kauśeya* silk and an *uttarāsaṅga* from wool.
If one makes a *saṃghāṭī* from wool and an *uttarāsaṅga* from *koseyya* (silk), whether making it oneself or having another make it, once it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if one uses it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu makes his saṃghāṭī from kośeya silk and his antaravāsaka from wool;
or if he makes his saṃghāṭī from wool and his antaravāsaka from kośeya silk.
Whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if one uses it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If the warp is *koseyya* (silk) and the woof is wool, or if the warp is wool and the woof is *koseyya*, whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she uses it, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If the border is wool and the center is *koseyya* silk, or if the center is wool and the border is *koseyya* silk—whether she makes it herself or causes another to make it—if it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if she uses it, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If there is *koseyya* (silk) among the wool, or wool among the *koseyya*, it is also as explained above.

Whether the garment is made of wool with a border of *koseyya*, or the garment is made of wool with buttons and fastenings of *koseyya*, or the garment is made of wool with patches of *koseyya*, whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, all is as explained above.

This woolen robe is to be relinquished within the community of monks; the Sangha may not use it, nor should it be returned. It may be spread upon the ground or used to make screens, curtains, canopies, and hangings. Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.
For the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One would go on a tour of the monks' quarters once every five days.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was walking through the rooms, he saw old felt rugs scattered everywhere on the ground—in the refuse heaps, in ruined houses, and beneath the eaves—where crows and birds had built nests with them and mice had dragged them into their holes.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"What is this old felt that is strewn about everywhere?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
These bhikṣus have discarded their old felt rugs and, for the sake of something more attractive, have made new bedding.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, when making a new bedding or mat, it should be kept for six years.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, being old and sickly, carried a heavy woolen *saṃghāṭī*.
The bhikṣus said to him:
"If you carry this heavy saṃghāṭī, you will perish from exhaustion; you should discard this blanket and take up a light saṃghāṭī."
That bhikṣu replied:
"It has not been six years.
He spoke again:
"If you do not relinquish this robe, you will perish from want.
He replied,
"I would rather die than dare to violate the precepts."
The bhikṣus then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If an elderly or infirm bhikṣu develops an illness because he is wearing heavy woolen robes, the Saṃgha should perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the granting of woolen robes for him."
This bhikṣu should request it from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall grant him the *jñapti-karman* for seeking permission.
The one performing the *karman* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu is aged and ill; because his woolen robe is heavy, his illness has increased and he has become emaciated.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant permission for this bhikṣu to request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding a woolen robe.
Venerable sirs, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a woolen robe. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
This bhikṣu should request it from the Saṃgha; baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground, he should speak as follows:

"I, the bhikṣu [Name], am old and sickly; my woolen robe is heavy and causes me to become emaciated and my illness to increase. I now request the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a woolen robe from the Saṃgha; may the Saṃgha grant me the formal act for a woolen robe."
Thus he requests a second and a third time.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"Venerable sirs, this bhikṣu named [Name] is old and sick; his woolen robe is heavy, and he has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a woolen robe.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant the formal act for a woolen robe to this bhikṣu named [Name]. This is the motion."
Thus was the formal motion (jñapti) and the threefold proclamation (karmavācanā) made.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Has the formal authorization for the woolen robe for the aged and infirm bhikṣus already been granted?"
He replied,
"I have already given it.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"All those residing in Śrāvastī, assemble! For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, he must keep it for six years. If he makes a new bedding or mat before the six years have elapsed—whether or not he has disposed of his old bedding or mat—with the exception of a formal authorization by the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"New" means recently completed.
"Reclining mat" refers to a woolen rug (*kambala*).
"Whoever makes it" refers to either making it oneself or having another make it.

"Six years" refers to six summer retreats; during each four-month summer retreat, one must reside under a roof. For the sake of the woolen rug (*kaṭhina*), one should go out three times during the night, but one must not go out three times during the first watch of the night.
If she goes out during the first watch of the night but does not go out during the middle or last watches, she commits two offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
If she goes out during the middle watch but does not go out during the first or last watches, she likewise commits two offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
If one goes out during the last watch of the night but does not go out during the first or middle watches, there are likewise two offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
If one does not go out at all during the first, middle, or last watches of the night, there are three offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding the three times of going out during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, there is no offense.
"Less than six years" means not having completed six summer retreats.
"An old bedding set" refers to one that has been kept and used within the six-year period.
Whether one has discarded the old felt or not, if it is present before one and one discards it and makes [a new one], one commits an offense.

If it is present before one and one makes [a new one] without discarding it, one also commits an offense. If the old felt is not present before one and one discards it and makes [a new one], one also commits an offense.

Therefore, if one does not keep the old felt rug present before oneself and yet makes a new sitting rug—whether making it oneself or having another make it—the act of completion constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if one uses it, it is a *vinaya-āpatti*.

Regarding "for the sake of beauty": if one finds [the bedding] too small, too large, too light, too heavy, torn, too cold, or too hot; or if one thinks, "I have a donor," "someone has made it for me," "I have wool," or "I shall make a new bedding for myself"—if one acts for the sake of beauty, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding "excepting those for whom the Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā*": because the World-Honored One has permitted it, there is no offense.
The *karmavācanā* may be valid or invalid. As for the invalid:

if a bhikṣu is not physically frail, his complexion is not poor, his strength is not diminished, he can be satiated by coarse food, yet the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished, or the assembly is not accomplished—if such matters are not accomplished in this manner, it is called an unaccomplished *karmavācanā*.
If it concerns an elderly or sick bhikṣu whose body is frail, whose complexion is poor, whose strength has diminished, and who cannot be satiated even by fine food, let alone coarse food;

if the motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the formal act (*karman*) is not accomplished, or the assembly (*saṃgha*) is not accomplished—wherein such matters as these involve a failure—it is likewise called an unaccomplished formal act.

Regarding "accomplishment": if a bhikṣu is emaciated, his complexion is poor, his physical strength is diminished, he cannot be satiated by fine food, and there is accomplishment through the formal motion (*jñapti*) and accomplishment through the ritual act (*karmavācanā*), and if the assembly is accomplished—such that all these matters are without fault—it is called "accomplishment of the ritual act" (*karmasampad*).

Once this formal act (*karmavācanā*) has been performed for the aged and infirm bhikṣu, he should personally record it: first, he must note the year, month, and day on which he received his old rug; once his illness has been cured, he may again receive and use this old rug, provided that six full years have elapsed since the previous one.
If a bhikṣu recovers from illness but does not return the [robe] for six years, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what is called a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

Once it has been relinquished among the community of monks, the Sangha must not return it; the Sangha may use it for its own needs, but it must not be used as a personal possession. This is why it is said.
The Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest at Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.

Out of consideration for five benefits, the World-Honored One would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. There he saw old blankets scattered here and there—on the ground, among refuse, in ruined houses, and beneath eaves—where crows and birds had built nests with them, and rats had dragged them into their holes.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"What is this old felt that is strewn about everywhere?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
There are bhikṣus—some who have left the monastic life, some who have died, and some who are still present—who have discarded their old felt rugs, leaving them in disarray.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If the donor does not know how to calculate [the measurements], the recipient should calculate them.
When a bhikṣu receives a gift, he should use it and should not discard it.

From this day forward, if a bhikṣu makes a new rug or sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must attach a patch from his old rug measuring one Sugata-span in each direction, in order to destroy its fine appearance."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a bhikṣu makes a new rug or sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must attach a patch from an old rug measuring one Sugata-span in each direction, in order to destroy its fine appearance.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat or rug and does not attach a patch from an old sitting mat or rug measuring one span square, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“Bhikkhu” is as explained above.
“New” means just completed.
“Reclining equipment” refers to a woolen rug (*kambala*).
Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), it should be as permitted by the Buddha.
As for "making," it means either making it oneself or having another make it.
Regarding "an old sitting mat," it refers to one that has already been used for six years.
"Sugata" means the Perfectly Enlightened One.
A "span" (*vitasti*) is two feet and four inches in length.

When taking an old felt rug, one must not take it from those who have heard little, those who violate the precepts, those who lack learning, those who do not repair their dilapidated dwellings, those of ill repute, those with nihilistic views, those who distance themselves from their *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* and take no pleasure in inquiring after them, those unable to overcome Māra, or those who fail to discern the deeds of Māra; one should not take it from such persons.
One should receive it from a person who is learned and capable of discerning the works of Māra.

When taking an old felt rug from a designated area of one span (vitasti) of the Sugata’s measurement, one must not take a piece that is missing a corner, shaped like a barley grain, shaped like a pestle, or shaped like a cart; nor should it be hanging down, disordered, lifted up, or folded over.
"Chipped-cornered" means having no corners.
"Shaped like a grain of barley" means being broad in the middle and narrow at both ends.
"Shaped like a pestle" means being broad at both ends and narrow in the middle.
"Car-shaped" means one end is wide and the other end is narrow.
"Hanging down" means it is tucked up.
"Disordered" means it is not aligned properly.
"Raised" means protruding.
"Depressed" means concave on all four sides; if the seams are high and the center is low, it must not be worn in that manner.
When wearing it, ensure it is square or circular and perfectly aligned.
If it is torn or damaged, it should be mended; if it is soiled or greasy, it should be washed; it should be made by incorporating stray hairs into the weave.

If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and does not incorporate the old one, that *niṣīdana* must be relinquished before the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha should not return it; the Saṃgha may use it, but it must not be used as a personal cushion. Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest near Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was carrying a heavy load of wool, walking out of the city with his back bent, which caused people to criticize him:
"Look at the śramaṇa Udāyin! He is like a camel, like a donkey, or like a hired porter; he is carrying away this wool just like that."
"You have lost the dharma of a śramaṇa; what path do you possess?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said, "Call Udāyin here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Udāyin,
"Is it true that you were carrying heavy wool and were thus ridiculed by the people of the world?
He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an improper act; from this day forward, carrying [loads] is not permitted.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above, there were certain bhikṣus who traveled to the north and praised the Buddha, praised Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the elder bhikṣus, as well as the lay devotee Sudatta, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, the Jetavana Monastery, and the Āmrapālī Grove, and offered various praises for the bhikṣus.
Having heard this, sixty bhikṣus wished to come and pay their respects; they immediately asked the incoming bhikṣus:
"We wish to go there to offer a small measure of service to our fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin). What items should we bring so that they may suit his needs?"
He replied: "Elder!
All those bhikṣus are wearing woolen robes; except for their water-strainers and shoulder-bags, you may take the wool and go there."
At that time, there were sixty bhikṣus, each carrying a heavy load of wool, traveling from village to village and from city to city.
At that time, the people of the world criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"Look at these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, walking while carrying heavy burdens, like camels, like donkeys, like hired laborers, or like merchants—carrying such heavy loads."
Furthermore, some people said:
"Do you not know?
We buy low here and wish to sell high there."
"Having lost the dharma of a śramaṇa, what path could there be?
The bhikṣus gradually proceeded toward Śrāvastī; having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"From where have you come?
They replied:
“World-Honored One,
we have come from the north.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Are the roads not wearying, and is alms-seeking not difficult?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The journey was not exhausting and begging for alms was not difficult; it was only that, along the way, we were reviled by the people of the world.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "In what way were we reviled by the people of the world?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
We sixty people were all carrying wool, as described in detail above.”
The Buddha said:
"Monks! You should indeed be censured by the people of the world. From this day forward, I do not permit monks to carry wool themselves."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, finds wool and wishes to take it, that bhikṣu may take it with his own hands for a distance of up to three yojanas.
If he carries it beyond three yojanas, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"A bhikṣu" refers to one person, many persons, or the Saṃgha.
"One who travels on the road" refers to a distance of three yojanas, two yojanas, one yojana, half a yojana, or one krośa.
"Obtained" means obtained from a man or a woman, whether large or small, whether a householder or one who has gone forth.
"Wool" refers to the ten types, as described above.
"Those who wish to take [it] truly have need of it.
As for "carrying it oneself for three *yojanas*": five cubits (*hasta*) make one bow (*dhanus*); two thousand bows make one *krośa*;
four thousand bows make half a *yojana*.
Eight thousand bows make one *yojana*;
sixteen thousand bows make two *yojanas*;
twenty-four thousand bows constitute three *yojanas*.
"Three yojanas" means carrying it oneself for a distance of three yojanas; if it exceeds that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the wool must be relinquished among the community of monks, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one does not relinquish them but merely regrets [the action], it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

If a bhikṣu carries wool and travels along a road for one *yojana*, and having forgotten something, returns to retrieve it, and after retrieving it returns again to his original location, this constitutes a total distance of three *yojanas* and may not exceed that.
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one leaves for half a *yojana* and forgets an object, and it can be recovered, once it has been recovered, one must not go further.
If one goes beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one travels in a straight line for three *yojanas*, crossing over with one foot constitutes a *vinaya*-offense; crossing over with both feet constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If two people each carry a load, after they have traveled three *yojanas* together, if they exchange their loads, each may again travel another three *yojanas*; for three people, it is nine *yojanas*; for four people, it is twelve *yojanas*.
If there are many such people, the limit shall be set according to the number of persons; however, they must not carry a heavy load again.
As for those who have already carried it, whether by trade or by further acquisition, they may carry it again for up to three *yojanas*.
If a bhikṣu carries wool in his robe-sack, he may go from one house to another until he has traveled three yojanas; beyond that, he must not proceed.
If he carries wool in his alms-bowl sack while begging for food, going from one village to another, it is likewise.
If one carries wool in a bag while walking for meditation, it is likewise an offense.
If one carries it while circumambulating a stupa, it is likewise an offense.
Even if the object has not yet been completed, down to the amount of wool sufficient to fill a needle-case, it constitutes an offense.
If the object has already been completed—such as a woolen rug, a pillow, or a mattress—there is no offense.
If one carries camel hair or ox-hump hair, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one carries a yak’s tail, it is a *vinaya-āpatti*.
If it is provided with a handle, there is no offense.
If one carries a lion’s mane or pig bristles, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance.
If it is made into a vessel, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was formerly the husband of the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā. Then the Venerable Udāyin took some wool and gave it to the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā, saying:
"Excellent, sister!
"Please wash, dye, and beat this for me.

The bhikṣuṇī then took it away to her own quarters; having finished washing, dyeing, and beating it, she placed it in a chest, covered it with coarse hair from under her arms and coarse hair from her private parts, and sent a messenger to deliver it to Udāyin.
Having received it, Udāyin opened the box and saw that it was coarse wool; filled with joy, he showed it to the bhikṣus and said, "Look!
This elder bhikṣuṇī, though not a relative, has brought back a great quantity of wool for a small amount."
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to him, "This is something that should be concealed; why do you display it to others?
He then replied:
"What hidden object is there here?
I have come with a little hair and received much hair!
When the group of six bhikṣus heard this from afar, they clapped their hands and laughed loudly.
"How strange! How strange!
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Udāyin here. When he had come, the Buddha asked Udāyin:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said,
"This is an evil deed.
Then the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
"If it were one's own relative bhikṣuṇī, should items that ought to be concealed be shown to that relative bhikṣu? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Suppose a bhikṣu who is a relative obtains an item that should be concealed from a bhikṣuṇī who is also a relative; should he show it to others? “No.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin took some wool and gave it to the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, saying:
"Excellent, sister!"
"Please wash, dye, and beat this for me.

Then the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī immediately washed, dyed, and beat it; having finished, she returned it to Udāyin and went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrating herself at his feet and withdrawing to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Why is there dye on your hand?
He replied:
"I washed, dyed, and carded wool for the Venerable Udāyin.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"How could Udāyin have had a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, and card wool?"
The Buddha said,
"Call Udāyin here. When he had come, the Buddha asked Udāyin:
“Did you indeed cause the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī to wash, dye, and card the wool?
She replied, “It is true.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Udāyin!"
"How can you have a bhikṣuṇī who practices the path perform this?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The terms "bhikṣu," "non-relative," and "wool" are as explained above.
"Washing and dyeing" are as explained above in the fifth precept.
"Splitting" means analyzing [the fibers].
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this wool must be relinquished before the community of monks (*saṃgha*), and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
To fail to relinquish [the garment] and instead repent constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

In this context, there is one additional matter: excluding cases where one strikes [a nun], wears a soiled garment, or wears a greasy garment when going to a nunnery; the rest is as explained in detail in the fifth precept above.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Nine [continued] / Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Translated together with Faxian.
The third section on the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, the village headman of Cūḷa arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Yesterday, many great ministers, brahmins, householders, and elders gathered in the royal palace and engaged in this discussion, some of whom said:”
"Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, should possess gold and silver," some said; others said,
"They should not possess it."
"What is truthful speech, Dharma-speech, and speech that accords with the Dharma, which does not contradict the discourse regarding the present life?
The Buddha said, "A śramaṇa,
a son of the Śākyas, should not possess gold or silver."
If anyone should say, "One ought to possess gold and silver," this slanders me;
it is not true, not the Dharma, and not in accordance with it. In this present life, such a statement constitutes a perverse argument.
Why is this? If one were permitted to possess gold and silver, one should likewise be permitted to possess the five objects of desire.
What are these five?

"First, the eye discriminates forms and becomes stained by attachment, and so on until the body experiences contact and becomes stained by attachment; you should know that this is not the Dharma of the Śākya śramaṇas.
The village headman said:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"
"It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:
'A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not possess gold or silver.'"
"If one keeps gold and silver, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, nor is it the dharma of the Śākya clan.
For this reason, I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
"I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of the Buddha who abstains from taking life; may the World-Honored One bear witness to this.
Thus he spoke three times, up to and including the abstention from drinking intoxicants.
"Previously, I had this thought:"
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not keep gold or silver; if he keeps it, he is no different from one who indulges in the five desires.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the village headman in accordance with his needs, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Just as a clean cotton cloth easily takes on dye, he perceived the Four Noble Truths while still seated upon that very seat.
Having seen the Four Noble Truths, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Worldly people have many duties; I must now take my leave to return."
The Buddha said,
"You should know that now is the time.
He rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat, sat down, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just now, the village headman of Cūḍa came to me; as previously explained at length, he even circumambulated me to the right before departing."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should train yourselves thus: you must not possess gold or silver; I have no expedient means by which one may possess gold or silver."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
For the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One would go on inspection to the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days; on such an occasion, he visited the lodgings of Nanda and Upananda.

At that time, Nanda and Upananda were counting coins; soil was on their hands when they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha, knowing this, asked them intentionally:
"Why is there soil on your hands?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
Because I have been counting coins, there is dust on my hands.”
The Buddha said to Nanda:
"How is it that you yourselves take hold of living beings or those resembling them? From this day forward, I do not permit you to personally carry living beings or those resembling them."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest near Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.

At that time, when it was time for the meal, Udāyin put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of a mason; it was there that the family had just finished holding a festival.
His wife came out to meet him, paid her respects, and asked,
"Venerable sir,
why did you not come yesterday?"
"If you come, you shall receive fine food and drink.
He replied,
"Where were you yesterday and today?"
"If there is any fine food, you may bring it here.
He replied, "The fine food has already been exhausted; I shall now give the Venerable One some money, which you may exchange for fine food at the shop."
He replied,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit me to hold money with my own hands.
You may tie the money to the corner of my robe."
He then did exactly as he had said, tied up the money, and departed.
Upon reaching the marketplace, he called out:
"Long life to you!"
"Give me some cakes.
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Show me the money!
Udāyin said, "Just give me the cake;
I will not move from this spot, and I shall give you the money."
He said, "Venerable sir!
Please bring your alms bowl."
He immediately filled the bowl with various kinds of cakes and food, and having given it to him, said:
"Give me my money. He replied:
"Take it yourself from the corner of your robe.
Because the shopkeeper wished to mock him, he did not untie it for him, saying:
"Untie it yourself and give it to me."
He replied, "The Buddha does not permit me to handle raw or dyed materials; you take them yourself.
Having taken them, he immediately rebuked him, saying:

"How is it that these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim this is pure through such a minor expedient? We also do not constantly grasp it with our hands or place it in our mouths; nor do we tie it to the corners of our robes or inside bags and containers."
"This is a loss of the dharma of a śramaṇa; what path could there be [in this]?
At that time, Udāyin took the cakes to his own room, called other bhikṣus to eat with him, and the bhikṣus immediately asked:
"These cakes are excellent; where did you obtain them?"
"This is not a cake made at home.
He replied,
"Venerable Elders!"
"In this matter, there is little benefit and much fault.
The bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason is there much fault?"
He replied,
"It is because of such and such causes and conditions that I have many faults.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Udāyin here. When he had come, the Buddha asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “This is an evil matter.
From this day forward, I do not permit even the tying of robes.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in the city of Kapilavastu; the detailed account is as above.

Out of concern for five matters of benefit, the World-Honored One went from room to room among the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing a certain bhikṣu who was jaundiced, emaciated, and haggard, the Buddha, though already aware of the situation, asked him:
"Bhikṣu, can you endure your suffering? Are you dwelling in comfort?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
I am not at ease; I am suffering from illness."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Are you unable to seek out food appropriate for your illness and medicine appropriate for your illness?
He replied:

"I have heard that the World-Honored One has established a precept stating that one must not take hold of raw or processed gold with one's own hands, yet no one gives it to me; for this reason, I suffer distress."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick persons to have an attendant (kappiya-kāraka) look after them; do not be greedily attached.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all the bhikṣus residing in the city of Kapilavastu assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣu takes raw gold or silver in his own hand, or causes another to take it up for him, and is attached to it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"By one's own hand" means: either the body, a part of the body, or the continuity of the body.
"Body" refers to the entire body.
"Part of the body" refers to the hands, the feet, the elbows, or the knees.

Regarding the continuity of the body: if one is tied to a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, an antarvāsaka, a wound-covering cloth, a saṃkakṣikā, a rain-bathing robe, or if one is tied to an alms bowl, a small bowl, a water-strainer, or a bronze vessel—such things as these are called the continuity of the body.
"Born color" refers to gold.
"Resembling color" refers to silver.
"Both born and resembling color" refers to coins and other items used for commerce.
"To seize" means either to seize it oneself or to tell another to seize it.
"To lift up" means either to lift it up oneself or to instruct another to lift it up.
"To be greedily attached" means to form this thought:
"I shall use these things to obtain the five desires, namely form, sound, fragrance,
taste, and touch"— this is called attachment.
One who is without attachment is like a pure monk observing the precepts, who, when carrying his own provisions such as parched grain, roasted flour, rice, and wheat, reflects thus:
"I have no intention of eating this food through skillful means; rather, by conceiving the notion that this impure thing is pure, I shall consume it.
This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: gold, silver, and money must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one confesses the offense without having relinquished the object, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Regarding this gold, silver, or money—whether worked or unworked, much or little, pure or mixed, fashioned into vessels or not fashioned into vessels—and having relinquished it among the Saṃgha, it may not be returned; nor may that bhikṣu or the Saṃgha divide it up.
If there is an excess, it should be placed among the inexhaustible goods.
From the interest earned on these inexhaustible goods, one may provide clothing for the monastery quarters, but it must not be used for personal consumption.

Whenever a bhikṣu obtains money or, at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, receives the value of robes, he must not take it with his own hands; he should instead have a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) manage it.
If there is no *kappiyakāraka*, he should point to the ground by his feet and say:
"Know this [spot] as such."

Once it has been placed on the ground, one may personally take grass, leaves, bricks, tiles, or similar objects and throw them from a distance over it to cover it, waiting for a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) to arrive so that they may be informed.
If the *kappiya-kāraka* arrives and understands, he shall take it away;
if he is not to be trusted, one should instruct him to walk ahead, so that he may know to place it in a specific location.
If there is a trustworthy layperson (*śrāmaṇera* or *upāsaka*), one may direct them to place it in a certain spot.

When a bhikṣu knows that there is much gold, silver, or money for the sake of the Buddha or the Saṅgha and it must be lifted up: if it is on living soil (*jīvamṛttikā*), he should instruct a layperson to know [the procedure]; if it is on covered dead soil (*mṛtamṛttikā*), he may dig it up himself or have a junior bhikṣu dig it up.
If the attendant (karmadāna) is not to be trusted, one should blindfold them and have them circle three times; only then should they be made to know the location of the ground.
Once they know the ground, they should be made to know the interior of the money-pit, and then one should blindfold them again before sending them away.
If money falls onto the edge of a pit, one may take bricks or tiles and throw them into the pit to cause the money to fall inside; one may then fill the pit oneself.

When wishing to retrieve it later, if it is uncultivated ground (jāṅgalabhūmi), one must have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) know of it; if it is cultivated ground (marubhūmi), one may dig it up oneself, scooping out the earth until reaching the money.
If the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) is not to be trusted, wrap [the object] again, circumambulate it three times, and bring it here to take it.
If there is gold, silver, or money within the wrapping, do not grasp it yourself; you must have the attendant know of it.
If the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) is too small [to reach], one may lift them up so that they know how to take [the items].
When lifting them, one should say:
"I am lifting the attendant!"
"I shall raise the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who makes things permissible)! Having obtained the lower items, he should have them untied.
If he does not know how to untie them, he may take hold of the *kappiya-kāraka*'s hand and instruct him to untie them; once they are untied, he should instruct him on how to count them.
If one does not know how to count, one may take the hand of a pure person to count.
Once counted, the remainder should be returned and taught to be placed inside a bag.
If one does not know how to place them in the bag, one may take the hand of a pure person to teach them how to place them in the bag.
Once it has been placed inside the bag, he should instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) to tie it.
If [the monk] does not know how to tie it, he may have the *kappiya-kāraka* hold the bottom of the bag while the bhikṣu ties it himself.
Having tied it, one should place it back upon the stake; if a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) is too short to reach it, one may lift it by embracing it.
If items such as cages, boxes, chests, or baskets are on a rack or a stake, the procedure for taking them, lifting them, or covering them is likewise as described above.

If, while traveling on a road, a *kappiya-kāraka* (attendant) carries gold or silver, and if the attendant is small, one may lead them by the hand; if crossing a body of water, one may carry them across in one's arms, and should say:
"I am ferrying the *kappiya-kāraka*!"
"I am ferrying a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible)!
If a bhikṣu brings a *kappiya-kāraka* along, and if that *kappiya-kāraka* is small and unable to board the boat himself, he may take him up in his arms.
He should speak as follows:
"I have censured the lay attendant!
I have censured the lay attendant!
It was the same when they disembarked from the boat.
While this bhikṣu was traveling on the road, he ate and rested by a river, a well, or a pond.
After he had finished eating, a lay attendant forgot his bag and left. An elder bhikṣu, who was behind him, looked around to see if anyone had forgotten any belongings.
Seeing some items left behind, he thought to himself,
"These must certainly belong to a bhikṣu," and he immediately took them away.
Having set out with his companions, he asked his companions,
"By whom was this permitted? Someone said:
"This is the lay attendant's bag.
He should immediately place it on the ground, and the lay attendant should then take it away; he must not call out the name [of the monk].
If a bhikṣu travels on a journey and stays overnight in the same place as a lay attendant, when they set out at night, the lay attendant should hold the bhikṣu’s shoulder-cloth (*pātra-paṭṭaka*).

On the eighth day of the fourth month and during times of great assemblies for making offerings, monks must not take hold of gold or silver stūpas, images of Bodhisattvas, banners, flags, canopies, or any other offering implements that are plated with gold or silver with their own hands; they must have a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) hold them.
If one falls to the ground, one should grasp it where there is no gold or silver.
If the surface is entirely covered with gold or silver plating, one should grasp it by wrapping the hands in cloth, flowers, or similar items.
If there is no cloth to wrap the hands, one may grasp [the object] provided that on the image there are parts not yet smeared [with lacquer].
If the handles of incense burners, lamps, or fly-whisks are made of gold or silver, or if all such items are made of gold or silver, they must not be grasped if they have been smeared [with lacquer].

A bhikṣu may handle [objects] that assist [his practice], but he must not grasp them.
Where there is gold or silver, a bhikṣu must not first grasp it and then let go of it.

If it is not used in the country and does not possess the characteristics, and one holds it as copper or iron, there is no offense.

All such cases should be understood as follows:
if a bhikṣu who lives on alms has leftover flour and hires someone to repair his leather sandals while using impure speech, he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).

If a bhikṣu, while at a shop, appraises the price with impure speech and takes it with pure speech; or appraises the price with pure speech and takes it with impure speech; or appraises the price with impure speech and takes it with impure speech; or appraises the price with pure speech and takes it with pure speech.

one asks the person before them, "For how much is this item being sold?

If one distinguishes the value using impure speech and takes it using impure speech, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There is no offense for one who takes [an object] through pure speech that distinguishes its value.
