“Be careful and do not commit it again.
He replied:
"Receive it upon your head.

The person carrying the bowls should hold this bowl and present it to the senior monk (*sthavira*). If the senior monk accepts it, he should hold that bowl and present it to the second senior monk. In this manner, it should proceed in succession down to the monk who has not yet completed his full year of residence (*anupālika* or *anuvatsara*).
If no one at all takes it, it should be returned to its original owner.

If the bowl is very expensive, it should be sold and the proceeds divided such that ten parts are taken; nine parts of the value should enter the Sangha’s pure kitchen, and one part should be returned to the original owner.
One should say to him:
"You shall hold this bowl until it breaks; this is the bowl to be held and mended.
When a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food and has finished eating, he should undo the mending.
Whether using ash or earth, one should wash it clean. When washing, one must not use hard objects to poke holes into it or break it; rather, one should use a bird’s quill to pierce through it.

When washing the bowl, one must not use sand or ash to scrub it until its color fades; instead, one should use the juice of *mūlaka* (radish) without sand, or the juice of leaves, flowers, or fruits to wash it.
When washing, one must not do so on the edge of a pit or on any dangerous place; nor under a tree bearing ripe fruit, nor upon a stone or a brick. One should wash the bowl on level ground.
If the ground is muddy, covered with refuse, or lacks a place to sit, one should bend the body so that it remains one span (vitasti) above the ground.
After washing it, one should dry it in the sun and then return to join it back together with cord.
Once it has been sewn, place it in one location.

Do not place it on a dangerous spot such as the edge of a pit, under a mature *vibhitaka* tree, under a coconut tree, on a stone, on a brick, on a path where people walk, or at a place where doors open.
If it is placed inside a bowl-bag or set within a niche on a wall, one should cover its opening with an object.
If one is pressed by urgent business and unable to wash it thoroughly, one should wipe it with the juice of roots, leaves, or other such substances; once the task is finished, it must be washed.
Tomorrow, after washing it, you shall take it into the village for alms. Even if it takes an entire day to mend a crack so that it can be used, it must still be washed clean.
If you should intentionally break it, you will incur a pāyattika offense.
If the upādhyāya, ācārya, or a spiritual friend thinks:
"This virtuous bhikṣu, because of washing his bowl, is obstructing his sitting meditation, receiving the sūtras, or reciting them."
"If [a bowl] is broken or hidden away, there is no offense in begging for another once it is no longer seen.

If one begs and obtains a single bowl, one should accept and maintain it. If one begs and obtains two bowls, one should accept and maintain one bowl, while the other bowl should be placed in the clean kitchen of the Sangha.
In this manner, even up to obtaining ten bowls, one should personally accept and maintain one bowl, while the remaining nine bowls should be placed in the clean kitchen of the Sangha.
If a bhikṣu has no bowl and seeks one, obtaining the value of a single bowl, this is called "possessing a bowl.

If he begs for the value of two bowls, the value of one bowl must be placed in the community’s pure kitchen; likewise, up to the value of ten bowls, the value of nine bowls should be placed in the community’s pure kitchen. Therefore, it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

For the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. Upon seeing the dwelling of Nanda and Upananda, he observed that their jars were filled with ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar, and that medicinal roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits were overflowing.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monks,
whose dwelling place is this, where there are full jars of ghee, oil, honey, and so forth, overflowing everywhere in such a manner?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is the dwelling place of Nanda and Upananda.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said, "Wait until he arrives; then I shall question him.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest Monastery at Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.

When the time arrived, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Vaiśālī together with a large number of bhikṣus. There he saw Upānanda coming out of the city carrying a bowl full of honey.
Having seen it and knowing [the answer], he asked intentionally:
"What is in this bowl? He replied:
“World-Honored One,
it is honey.
He asked again:
"What do you wish to have made?
He replied,
"Nanda is ill and requires it."
The Buddha said,
"It is too much.
He replied:
"One must take it throughout the entire day.
The Buddha said,
"How can one store medicine and then consume it throughout the entire day?"
"From this day forward, you must not keep medicine for the purpose of taking it throughout the entire day.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery under the Nyagrodha tree in Kapilavastu,
the World-Honored One, for the sake of five benefits, would go on a tour of the monks' quarters once every five days.
What are the five?
First, do my śrāvaka disciples not cling to conditioned phenomena?
Second, do they not cling to worldly frivolous discourse?
Third, does he not become attached to sleep so as to hinder his progress on the path?
Fourth, is he one who tends to the sick bhikṣus?
Fifth, is he a young bhikṣu who has newly gone forth, seeing the Tathāgata’s majestic deportment and giving rise to a heart of joy?
These are the five matters.
On the fifth day, the Tathāgata went on inspection through the various quarters and saw a sick bhikṣu whose complexion was sallow and who was emaciated and weak.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
“Monk! Are you harmonious? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am suffering from illness; my physical elements are not in harmony.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣu! Are you not able to seek out food appropriate for your illness and medicine appropriate for your illness for treatment?
He replied:
“The Blessed One has prescribed the precept regarding the storage of medicine, stating that it may be taken at the proper time but must not be kept for long;
therefore, I suffer. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I permit a sick bhikṣu to keep medicine for one day.”
At that time, the Buddha asked Nanda:
"When you were in Śrāvastī, did you keep much butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar?
He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"How can you be so full of desire and never satisfied?
Having thus rebuked him in various ways, [the Buddha declared: "From this day forward, I do not permit the accumulation of many [possessions].
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Rṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, he spoke at length as above.
At that time, there were sixty sick bhikṣus. A physician who had left the household life to follow the Way was treating those sick bhikṣus.
This physician-bhikṣu came to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"Bhikṣu physician!
Are the sick bhikṣus recovering well?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
The sick bhikṣus are at ease, but I am weary and distressed."
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason are you weary and distressed? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
The city of Vārāṇasī is half a yojana from here; I travel back and forth every day to seek what I require, and because of this, I am exhausted and distressed.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
"I permit a sick bhikṣu to suspend his medicine for one day once his illness has passed.
The Buddha asked the physician, "Bhikṣu!"
"If one wishes to store medicine, for how many days can one remain at ease?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The duration of the medicinal potency can be known for seven days.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, I permit you to keep it for one additional day, making it six or seven days in total."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell in dependence on Vārāṇasī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If there are medicines appropriate for a sick bhikṣu to take—such as ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, or fat—the sick bhikṣu is permitted to keep them for seven days and consume them.
"If one consumes it after seven days have passed without discarding the remainder, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding those who are ill and ought to take medicine: ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, and fat, as described above in the section on the precept against stealing.

Regarding illnesses, there are four hundred and four types: one hundred and one wind-related illnesses, one hundred and one fire-related illnesses, one hundred and one water-related illnesses, and one hundred and one miscellaneous illnesses.
If one has a wind disorder, it should be treated with oil.
If one has a heat disorder, it should be treated with ghee.
If one has a water disorder, it should be treated with honey.
Regarding miscellaneous illnesses, one should treat them by employing all three types of medicine mentioned above.
Seven days is the maximum limit for counting.
As for "storing [medicine] for seven days," it means that once one has formally accepted it, one may consume it for up to seven days.
If one consumes it after seven days have passed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this medicine must be relinquished before the community of monks, and one must perform repentance for the *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not relinquish [the medicine] but merely regrets [taking it], one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu obtains ten kinds of medicines on a single day—namely, ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, and the five kinds of fats—and consumes them all without performing the ritual of purification (*pariṣkāra*), after seven days, they all become subject to forfeiture (*niḥsargika*).
If a bhikṣu obtains ten kinds of medicine on one day, and half has been made pure while half has not been made pure:
therein, that which has been made pure is in accordance with the Dharma;
that which has not been made pure becomes subject to the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense after seven days have passed.
If a bhikṣu obtains ten kinds of medicines on a single day, it is as explained in detail in the previous section on the rule concerning extra robes (atirekacīvara).
The only difference here is that these medicines are for a period of seven days; this applies even to cases where one has not formally designated them, yet perceives them as having been designated.

This does not refer to oil for lighting lamps, oil for anointing the feet, or oil for anointing the body; if one has not identified it as such and has not performed the ritual purification (*parikamma*), after seven days have passed, it is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

Regarding that which is not performed as a ritual purification (pariśuddhi) according to the Dharma: if one performs the purification in the presence of a person who lacks the requisite intention, and seven days pass, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika).
One should perform the purification in the presence of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a layperson, or even an animal.

The profit from stored medicine defiles the profit from stored medicine; the profit from stored medicine defiles the profit from unstored medicine; the profit from unstored medicine does not defile the profit from stored medicine; the profit from unstored medicine does not defile the profit from unstored medicine. Layperson’s profit defiles the monk’s profit; the monk’s profit defiles the layperson’s profit; layperson’s profit defiles layperson’s profit; the monk’s profit defiles the monk’s profit. The profit of a visiting monk defiles the profit of a resident monk; the profit of a resident monk defiles the profit of a visiting monk; the profit of a visiting monk defiles the profit of another visiting monk; the profit of a resident monk defiles the profit of another resident monk. The Sangha’s profit defiles the monk’s profit; the monk’s profit defiles the Sangha’s profit; the Sangha’s profit defiles the Sangha’s profit; the monk’s profit defiles the monk’s profit.

There is that which is an occasion for food but not an occasion for receiving; there is that which is an occasion for receiving but not an occasion for food; there is that which is both an occasion for food and an occasion for receiving; and there is that which is neither an occasion for food nor an occasion for receiving.
These include: a jar of stone honey, a lamp, a vessel of curd, and a vessel of ghee.

Regarding "storing medicinal requisites and being defiled by the storing of medicinal requisites": if a bhikṣu obtains rock honey mixed with other food before the mealtime and stores the remainder without performing the *pariṣkāra* (purification) rite, and later obtains more rock honey and again takes and stores it without performing the *pariṣkāra* rite, this is called "storing medicinal requisites and being defiled by the storing of medicinal requisites."

Regarding "the benefit of storing medicine defiled by the benefit of not storing medicine": this refers to a bhikṣu who, before the morning meal, receives stone honey and eats it mixed with other food without performing the ritual purification (*paribhoga-vidhi*). Later, he receives more stone honey, performs the ritual purification, and accepts it for storage. This is called "the benefit of storing medicine defiled by the benefit of not storing medicine."

"Regarding 'not storing medicine for the sake of storing medicine, nor being defiled by such storage': if a bhikṣu obtains rock honey before a meal and, having mixed it with food, makes it pure food, but later obtains more rock honey and accepts it without making it pure food, this is called 'not storing medicine for the sake of storing medicine, nor being defiled by such storage.'"

"Storing medicinal requisites without storing medicinal requisites, and not being defiled by the storing of medicinal requisites" means: if a bhikṣu obtains rock honey before a meal, and having not mixed it with food, he makes it pure (kappiya) and then later obtains more rock honey, which he also makes pure and accepts—it is called "storing medicinal requisites without storing medicinal requisites, and not being defiled by the storing of medicinal requisites."
What is it for a layperson’s gain to defile a bhikṣu’s gain?
Suppose there is an upāsaka who comes to pay homage at the feet of a bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu has some rock honey that he had kept for seven days, and he says to the upāsaka:
"Do you wish to drink honey-syrup?
He replied,
"I wish to drink it."
Then the lay follower took the rock honey and departed; he prostrated at the feet of the other bhikṣus and said to them:
"Venerable sirs, would you like to drink some rock honey syrup?"
He replied, "I wish to drink.
That day, the bhikṣu obtained rock honey; he took it without performing the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), which is called "a layperson’s benefit defiling a bhikṣu’s benefit."
What is the benefit for a householder through the benefit of a bhikṣu?
There was a certain upāsaka who, carrying rock honey, came by and prostrated at the feet of a bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu had rock honey from the seventh day and said to the upāsaka:
"Would you like to drink some honey syrup?
He replied, "I would like to drink some."
He immediately took the combined jars and departed.
There was another upāsaka who came carrying rock honey; they met on the road, and the first upāsaka asked the second upāsaka, "Where do you wish to go?"
He replied,
"I wish to take this rock honey and give it to a certain bhikṣu.
He then said to him:
"You may take this rock honey and go; give some also to such-and-such a bhikṣu.
He then accepted it and departed. This is called a bhikṣu taking advantage of the gains of a layperson.
What is the defilement of a layperson’s benefit by a layperson’s benefit?
It is precisely because the two are distinct from one another.
What is the defilement of a bhikṣu’s benefit by a bhikṣu’s benefit?
A bhikṣu had some rock honey from the seventh day and said to another bhikṣu,
"Would you like to drink some rock honey syrup?
He replied:
"I wish to drink.
On that very day, this bhikṣu obtained rock honey; he accepted it without performing the ritual purification (pariśuddhi), and this is called a bhikṣu defiling the gains of another bhikṣu.
How does a visiting bhikṣu defile the gains of a resident bhikṣu?
A visiting bhikṣu has some rock honey from the seventh day and says to a resident bhikṣu:
"Would you like to drink some rock-honey syrup?"
He replied, "I wish to drink.

On that very day, the resident bhikṣu obtained rock honey; he accepted it without performing the *pariśuddhi* (ritual purification), which is called "the benefit of a visiting bhikṣu defiling the benefit of a resident bhikṣu."
How does a resident bhikṣu defraud a visiting bhikṣu of his benefit?
Suppose a visiting bhikṣu arrives, and the resident bhikṣu has rock honey that has been kept for seven days;
he says to the visiting bhikṣu, "Would you like to drink some rock-honey syrup?"
He replied, "I wish to drink.

That visiting bhikṣu received the rock sugar on that very day and took it without performing the ritual purification (pariśuddhi); this is called "the benefit of an established bhikṣu defiling the benefit of a visiting bhikṣu."
What is the case where visiting bhikṣus defile the gains of visiting bhikṣus?

There were two groups of visiting bhikṣus who arrived; in one group there was rock honey for the seventh day. A bhikṣu from that group said to the bhikṣus of the second group, "Would you like to drink honey syrup?"
He replied, "I wish to drink.

On that very day, this visiting bhikṣu obtained rock honey; he accepted it without performing the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*). This is called "a visitor’s benefit defiling a visitor’s benefit."
What is it for an elder bhikṣu to corrupt another elder bhikṣu?
An elder bhikṣu has some rock honey from the seventh day and says to another elder bhikṣu:
"Would you like to drink some rock honey syrup?"
He replied, “I wish to drink.

This resident bhikṣu received rock honey on that very day; he accepted it without performing the ritual purification (pariśuddhi). This is called "a resident bhikṣu defiling his own benefit with a resident bhikṣu’s benefit."

What is it that defiles the benefit of the Saṃgha with the benefit of an individual bhikṣu? Suppose the Saṃgha possesses rock honey on the seventh day; it is divided into portions, and a bhikṣu receives a portion of that rock honey on that very day. If he accepts it without having performed the *pariśuddhi* (purification/ritual preparation), this is called defiling the benefit of the Saṃgha with the benefit of an individual bhikṣu.
What is it for a bhikṣu to defile the gains of the Saṃgha with his own gains?

Suppose a bhikṣu has some rock honey on the seventh day; he immediately takes it and offers it to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha receives the rock honey on that very day and takes it without performing the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification). This is called a bhikṣu defiling the gains of the Saṃgha with his own gains.
What is meant by "monastic benefit defiling monastic benefit"?

Suppose the Sangha has rock honey for the seventh-day meal and gives it to another Sangha; if that other Sangha receives the rock honey on that very day without performing the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), this is called "monastic benefit defiling monastic benefit."
What is the case of a monk who benefits another monk with a benefit?
A monk has some rock-honey on the seventh day; he says to another monk, "Would you like to drink some honey-mead?"
He replied, "It must be so.
If a bhikṣu obtains rock honey on that very day and accepts it without performing the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), this is called a bhikṣu defiling the property of another bhikṣu.
What is an interval of food but not an interval of formal undertaking?

If a bhikṣu consumes stone honey for seven days and then, without creating an interval, consumes it again on the eighth day, he incurs a *vibhinna-vinaya* offense because he failed to create an interval; he should instead create a one-day interval. This is called an interval of food but not an interval of formal undertaking.
What is meant by "receiving [food] at intervals but not eating at intervals"?

If a bhikṣu receives rock honey and does not eat for seven days, and on the eighth day receives rock honey again, this constitutes receiving it without an interval; he incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya.
If one undertakes the *ekāha* (one-day) observance, this is called undertaking the *antara* (interval) but not the *bhojana-antara* (food interval).
What is meant by undertaking both the *antara* and the *bhojana-antara*?
If a bhikṣu, having undertaken the consumption of stone honey for seven days, undertakes [the consumption of] further food on the eighth day, he incurs two *vinayātikrama* offenses.
What is meant by "neither between meals nor between snacks"?
If a bhikṣu suffers from chest pain and spits up blood due to reciting many sūtras, the physician says:
"For this illness, you should take rock honey as a long-term medicine."

"One may obtain *śarkarā* (stone honey) before a meal; after a meal, once purified by water, one may eat it. This is called 'neither an interval between receiving [alms] nor an interval between meals.
What is meant by a jar of *śarkarā* being like the country of Vula?"
When a person seeking full ordination had received it upon the boundary of the precept-field (sīmā), he offered a jar of stone-honey (śarkarā-madhu) to each member of the Sangha.
Out of faith and joy, desiring to perform a meritorious deed, the bhikṣus took the jars of stone-honey and presented them to the elders of the Sangha.
The Elder, having developed faith, said:
"The Sangha is a field of merit.
He then immediately made another offering to the Sangha.
If the bhikṣus have rock honey (śarkarā) from the seventh day, they may take this rock honey; this is called "contamination by appearance.
If a bhikṣu, while eating, obtains a large quantity of sugarcane, he may eat the remainder and press it to make juice, which may be accepted until the end of the night.
If one cannot finish drinking it, one may boil it down to make stone-honey (śarkarā) and consume it for seven days.
If the stone-honey is not finished, one may burn it to make ash and consume it for as long as one lives.
If there are circumstances that prevent one from pressing [the juice], one should purify it with water before midday, making this declaration:
"If pure things arise herein, I shall accept them.
If one receives many fruits at a meal and cannot finish eating them, one may press them to make a syrup and accept it during the middle watch of the night.
If there is a matter that prevents one from squeezing [the water], one should immediately say these words:
"Pure things have arisen herein; I shall receive them.
If the time passes, one should not do so.

Regarding the lighting of lamps: if a woman of firm faith offers food to the Sangha and also prepares cakes to be placed upon lamps as an offering to the Sangha, the monks should not accept them directly with their own hands; they should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) take them.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one should tell the attendant to set it down on the ground; only after the lamp has been extinguished may one receive it.
If, out of faith, a woman does not wish to extinguish the lamp, she may still be permitted to receive it provided she is earnest in her intention.
Having received it, one removes the impurities with a knife and then eats; this is called "the lamp.
Regarding the curd-jar: when one receives a large amount of curd at mealtime and cannot finish eating it, one may immediately boil it to make fresh butter (*navanīta*) and accept it for seven days.
If fresh butter (*navanīta*) remains in excess, it may be boiled to produce clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which may be accepted for seven days.

If a bhikṣu receives a large amount of butter while begging for alms, and he is a bhikṣu with few acquaintances, he may immediately strain the butter through fine cotton cloth to purify it; thus obtained, it may be accepted for seven days.
If there is a circumstance that prevents one from preparing it before midday, one should say:
"Pure substances have arisen here; I shall accept them as seven-day medicine."
If one mistakenly forgets to receive [the food] or fails to perform the ritual purification (*pariṣkāra*) when the time has passed, this is called impure.
If one receives a large amount of oil while begging for alms, it is as explained above regarding ghee.
If one receives a large amount of sesame seeds at a meal and obtains them as leftovers that cannot all be consumed, one may immediately press them to make oil and accept it for seven days.
If circumstances prevent this from being done, it is as explained above regarding the clarified butter (*sarpis*); this is called a "curd-jar" (*dadhi-ghaṭa*).

Regarding fats: among those used by the Saṃgha are fish fat, bear fat, brown bear fat, pig fat, and *śiśumāra* fat. A bhikṣu with few acquaintances may obtain them, filter them through fine cotton cloth, and accept them for seven days.
If the conditions for performing the ritual are not met, it is as explained above regarding the *sarpis* (clarified butter).

When the Saṃgha is dividing oil, whether one intends to make it into pure oil (*viśuddha-taila*), seven-day oil (*saptāha-taila*), lamp-oil, foot-ointment, or body-ointment, if the portion divided is insufficient and one collects it back into a single place, it is entirely impure (*aviśuddha*).
If pure oil is returned with pure oil, they shall be washed together in one place, made clean, and given to a pure person.
Likewise, if seven-day oil is returned with seven-day oil, they shall be washed together in one place, made clean, and given to a pure person.
In this manner, having received oil for lighting lamps or oil for anointing the feet, one should accept it.
If a bhikṣu wishes to consume ash or drink oil—the ash being a lifelong medicine and the oil being a seven-day medicine—he must not first consume the ash and afterwards consume the oil;
rather, he should first consume the oil, wash his hands and rinse his mouth until they are clean, and only then consume the ash.
If a bhikṣu suffers from an ailment of the lower parts of the body, he should first consume ghee.
Ghee is a seven-day medicine; having washed his hands and rinsed his mouth until they are clean, he may then eat it.

If a bhikṣu has an ailment in the upper part of his body and wishes to consume ghee as a medicinal food, since ghee is a seven-day medicine, he should wash his mouth and bathe his hands until they are clean after finishing the meal, and only then consume the ghee.

If a bhikṣu has finished consuming oil and there is leftover oil which he intends to use as lamp oil or for anointing his feet, and the upādhyāya or ācārya comes along and, seeing it, disapproves because it is too much, if the bhikṣu drinks it again, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu has eaten rock honey and wishes to drink *yāmika-pānaka* (night-time beverage), he should first rinse his mouth until it is clean and then drink the beverage.
If, after having drunk the beverage, he wishes to eat rock honey, it is likewise.
If a bhikṣu wishes to boil rock honey, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) boil it.

If a bhikṣu receives ghee himself, such as ghee touching ghee, ghee touching oil, ghee touching honey, ghee touching rock honey, ghee touching fresh butter, or ghee touching fat—it is the same for oil, honey, rock honey, fresh butter, and even fat touching ghee, fat touching oil, fat touching honey, fat touching fresh butter, fat touching rock honey, or fat touching fat; it is likewise in all these cases.

Regarding those mixed with [medicines] for the timely period, for the night period, for seven days, or for life-long use: that which is mixed with [medicines] for the timely period may be consumed during the timely period;
that which is mixed with [medicines] for the night period, for seven days, or for life-long use may be consumed during the night period.
Regarding those who may be used for seven days or for the duration of one's life: if they are combined, one may consume them for seven days.
If a bhikṣu with few acquaintances obtains red salt, purple salt, or the like while begging for alms, he should wash the salt clean and keep it for the duration of his life.
It is the same if one obtains *pippalī* or *citraka*.

If a bhikṣu with few acquaintances, while begging for alms, obtains black stone-honey (*khaṇḍa*) or white stone-honey, he should wash it thoroughly to remove the odor of food and accept it as a seven-day medicine; therefore, this is said.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Ten [continued] / Volume Eleven.
