The Four Rules on the *Nissaggiya Pācittiya* Dharmas Concerning Common Property, translated by Fa-xian. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, during the height of winter, the Elder Nanda and Upānanda were wearing thick woolen robes (*nāṃgutha*), spreading warm bedding and mattresses, wearing caps on their heads and boots on their feet, and lighting fires in braziers before them.

Two non-Buddhist practitioners, black-skinned with blue eyes and shivering from the cold, approached and stood before him. Upon seeing them, the practitioners felt a sense of delight and attachment, and spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"You who have left the household life obtain such pleasure as this."
At that time, the non-Buddhists, whose hearts were drawn to the Buddha’s Dharma, spoke thus:

"We too are called 'those who have left the home life,' yet we have encountered the teachings of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. We go naked, pluck out our hair, throw ourselves from cliffs, leap into ravines, scorch our bodies with the five heats, and beg for food; we undergo toil and hardship in vain, without any true joy."
The bhikṣu replied:
"If you delight in this Dharma, then come forth into homelessness; you too shall attain such a state of joyful dwelling as I have.
The outsider answered:
"I have no saṃghāṭī robe," [the monk] replied,
"Come here; I shall give one to you."
The non-Buddhist practitioner immediately came and was granted the going-forth and the full ordination. Having done so, [the teacher] said to him:
"Now that I have ordained you and granted you the full precepts, you must serve me in this manner: in the morning, you must rise early and inquire whether I slept well."
He shall take out the spittoon and the urinal and place them in their usual positions;

having washed his hands, he shall provide water for rinsing and a tooth-stick; holding the alms-bowl, he shall go to welcome the gruel; once the light meal is finished, he shall wash the bowl, dry it, and place it in its usual position;
if there is a place where he has been invited to eat, he shall go to welcome the food.
"When I wish to enter a village, you should take my village-entering robe and give it to me;
take my usual robe, fold it neatly, and place it back in its proper location."

"When I return from the village, you should prepare a small seat for me; when you give me water and offer me food made of tree leaves, fan the food with a fan; once it has been washed, dry the bowl and place it back in its usual position."
"When you have entered the village, roll up and secure your robes; then give me back the garment I usually wear.
After you have finished eating, you should gather firewood and grass, wash my robes, boil them for dyeing, thoroughly sweep the interior of the room, and grind fine lime to smear the floor."

"When I wish to enter the forest to practice meditation, you should carry my sitting mat and follow behind me; when we return, you should follow back as well and provide me with water for washing my hands.
After you have presented offerings of incense and flowers, you should spread out my seat and provide me with water for washing my feet."
Furthermore, he massages [the body] with oil, prepares bedding, places a spittoon and a urinal within, and lights lamps; in this manner, he provides various services.
Only after ensuring that I am at ease does he attend to his own affairs.
Then that bhikṣu replied to his teacher, saying:
"This is not the dharma of one who has left the household life; it is merely the work of a slave.
The teacher said:
"If you cannot do it, you must return my saṃghāṭī to me.
He immediately took off his robe, placed it on the ground, and departed.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda was the elder brother of Upānanda.
Then Upānanda said to his brother’s attendant disciple,
"I shall enter the village with you and give you something."
"If I should perform any act contrary to the rules of decorum, do not tell others that I am your paternal uncle.
He replied, "If I were to see my own father acting unlawfully, I would surely speak of it to others; how much more so in the case of my paternal uncle, Upānanda?"
He spoke again:
"If you act in this way, I shall cause you to know [the consequences].
He then led him to the home of a noble patron (*dānapati*) to be served a meal; intending not to give him food, he formed this thought:
"Considering the current time and date, if you go out for alms now, you will not be able to return in time.
He then said to him,
"Return to the vihāra."
He immediately returned; fearing he would miss the mealtime, he hurried along, watching the sun as he went.

Upon reaching the monastery, he saw that the bhikṣus had all finished eating and were walking up and down in front of the gate. Seeing him approaching from afar, they suspected there must be a reason for his haste, and so they asked him:
"Today you traveled everywhere with many well-known bhikṣus to teach and transform others; what kind of excellent food did you obtain that your lips are so glossy?"
He replied,
"I have already lost my meal today, much less one of such fine quality.
After Upānanda had sent him back, he later partook of various kinds of food and drink.
Having finished eating, fearing that the matter would be exposed, he returned quickly.
Seeing the bhikṣus gathered in a crowd in discussion, he thought to himself:
"Since these people have assembled for discussion, it must be that those bhikṣus have spoken of my faults and evils to their fellow practitioners of the holy life."
He then said to Nanda:
"Elder! Your disciple has just spoken of my faults and misdeeds to the fellow practitioners of the holy life."
He then spoke with anger to his disciple, saying:
"Why do you now speak of my younger brother's faults?
You must return my saṃghāṭī robe to me!"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said to one another, "This bhikṣu has encountered two kinds of suffering today:
first, the loss of food; second, the loss of robes."
When the Buddha had heard this, he knew the situation but intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"Which bhikṣu is this who speaks so loudly?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
This Nanda has taken the robe of his fellow disciple; that is why he is crying out so loudly.
The Buddha said:
“Call Nanda here. Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned Nanda at length:

“Is it true that for the sake of providing for yourself, you ordained a person and gave him a robe, causing your disciple to become angry and unable to perform his duties as a servant, even to the point of seizing the robe of your co-practitioner?”
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said to Nanda:
“How can you ordain people for the sake of renunciation and yet fail to teach them the Dharma and Vinaya, instead making them perform labor merely to provide for yourselves?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, you must not ordain others for the sake of providing for yourselves. Whoever does so shall incur an offense of violating the Vinaya.”
"One should form this thought:
'May that person, by virtue of being delivered by me, cultivate all wholesome dharmas and attain the fruit of the Path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, later becomes angry and displeased, and either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, saying:
"Bhikṣu!..."
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
If he takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Robes" refers to the seven kinds, as explained above.
"Malicious and displeased" refers to the nine grounds for resentment, as explained above.
"Seizes" means either seizing it oneself or causing another to seize it, speaking as follows:
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
If he obtains it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" is as explained above.

Either one takes by oneself or causes another to take; either one causes another to take or takes by oneself; either one takes by oneself or takes by oneself [after having given]; either one causes another to take or causes another to take [after having given]. There is taking collectively after giving collectively, taking collectively after giving separately, taking collectively after giving collectively, and taking separately after giving separately.
Regarding "giving together and taking away separately": after a bhikṣu has given three robes at one time, he takes them back separately, saying:
"Return my saṃghāṭī; return my uttarāsaṅga; return my antarvāsaka."
If one seizes them in this manner, one incurs numerous *pāyattis*.
This is called "giving collectively and seizing individually.
Regarding "giving individually and seizing collectively": a bhikṣu does not give the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka* at the same time, yet he seizes them all at once.
"Give me back my robe!
If one seizes it in this manner, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; this is called "giving separately and seizing together.
Regarding "giving together and seizing together": a bhikṣu gives a robe all at once, and later says:
"Give me back my robe in its entirety!
If one seizes it in this manner, one incurs one *pāyattika*.

Regarding seizing separately what was given separately: if a monk is not given the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka* all at once, but the monk seizes them gradually; [if he seizes them in this way, he incurs a *pāyattika*].
"Return my saṃghāṭī, return my uttarāsaṅga, return my antarvāsaka.
If one makes such a demand and obtains [the robes], it constitutes many pāyattikas.
If a bhikṣu, when giving a robe to another bhikṣu, says:
"If you stay by my side, I shall give you this robe," and then takes it back if the other does not stay, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu and says,
"I shall give it to you if you stay here," and then takes it back if the recipient does not stay, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu, thinking, "I give this to you because it suits my mind," he commits no offense if he takes it back when it does not suit his mind.
If he gives it to one who has received the scriptures, and takes it back from one who has not received the scriptures, he commits no offense.
If a bhikṣu has sold a robe but not yet received the payment, or if the price in money has not been settled, there is no offense if he takes the robe back.

If a bhikṣu has given a robe to a co-practitioner or a dependent disciple, and because the disciple cannot be instructed or corrected, he takes it away for the sake of disciplinary subjugation; if he returns it after the subjugation is complete, there is no offense.
To take away the robe of a bhikṣu is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
To take away the robe of a bhikṣuṇī is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To take away the robe of a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
"Even down to one who takes the robes of a layperson, there is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya requiring mental repentance; therefore, it is said.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and within twelve yojanas in each of the four directions, the Saṃgha was offered *varṣāśāṭikā* (rain-bathing robes), as explained in detail in the *Vaiśākhamātṛ-nidāna*.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala on a journey, there was a mahallaka bhikṣu who, wearing his rain-cloak underneath and his antarvāsaka robe on top, was sweeping the ground with a long-handled broom.
Having seen this, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this mahallaka?
How is it that he wears his robes in such a distorted manner?"
When that mahallaka had seen the Buddha, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
"Mahallaka, what kind of lower garment are you wearing?"
He replied,
"The rain-cloak.
[The other asked,] "What garment do you wear on top?"
He replied, "The *antarvāsa*.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣu! How is it that you have the upper robe underneath when it should be on top, and the lower robe on top?
Why do you now use the rain-cloak at all times?”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"When you wait for the Tathāgata to return from his journey through the country of Kośala to Śrāvastī, you should say to me:
'You ought to prescribe a rain-bathing robe for the bhikṣus.'"
After the Buddha had completed his tour of the Kosalā country and returned, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, while you were touring the Kosalā country, you spoke these words:
‘When the Tathāgata returns from his tour of the Kosalā country to Śrāvastī, you shall then say to me:’”
"It would be appropriate to establish a rain-bathing robe for the bhikṣus.
"Now is the very time; we pray that you will establish the rain-robe rule.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who dwell in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If there remains one month of the spring season, a bhikṣu should seek rain-clothing; he should have it finished within half a month and use it.
If a bhikṣu seeks rain-clothing before one month of the spring season has remained, or has it finished and uses it before the half-month period has elapsed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"One month remaining of spring" refers to the fifteenth day after the third month and the fifteenth day of the fourth month; this is called "one month remaining of spring.
"Rain robes" refers to those permitted by the World-Honored One.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as explained above.
Regarding "seeking," it means begging, soliciting, or exhorting for alms.

When seeking, one should not seek one or two feet of cloth from various small households; rather, one should seek from prosperous and large families. Whether obtained from a single person or from a group of many people, this is called "seeking."
Regarding "the remaining half-month": from the sixteenth day of the third month, one should perform washing, dyeing, and sewing; by the first day of the fourth month, it should be put into use.
If a bhikṣu has not yet approached a donor to request [materials], yet requests them before the sixteenth day of the third month and completes and uses them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
A monk who possesses five qualities should be appointed by the Saṃgha through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) as the person responsible for distributing the rain-cloths.
What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing gain and loss—these are called the five.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so has accomplished the five qualities. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of rain-cloths; this is the formal motion."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has accomplished the five qualities; the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of rain-cloths.
Venerable sirs, if you approve of this bhikṣu so-and-so being appointed as the distributor of rain-cloths, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak."
"The Sangha has consented; the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of rain-cloths is completed. Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Having performed the *karmavācanā*, one should announce in the midst of the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If there is a discrepancy in the size of the robes—whether they differ by four fingers or eight fingers—I shall set it aside as not being counted for distribution."
If one does not announce this, one incurs a *viniyatika* offense.

Once this person has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*), they must seek [robes] for the Saṃgha. When seeking them, one should not seek from small households here and there for a mere foot or two; rather, one should seek from wealthy and prominent families. Whether obtained from a single individual or from a group of many people—even down to obtaining a single rain-cloak—this is called "seeking."
If robes are brought after the sixteenth day of the third month, they should be divided.
One should ask the senior monk (*sthavira*) of the Sangha:
"Do you wish to take them now, or do you wish to wait for later?"
"Perhaps later there will be someone superior.
If the Elder says, "Take it now," [one may take it].
He then gave it to him.
If [the recipient] says,
"I will take it later," [he should give it].
"It shall be granted later.
If there is a visiting bhikṣu, one should ask:
"Where do you intend to observe the summer retreat?"
If he says, "In this place," one should grant it.
If one says,
"I wish to observe the rains retreat in another location, but I wish to receive my rain-cloak here," it should likewise be granted.
He says: "Do not take anything further from other places. If he says:
"I shall not take this here; I will wait until I reach my place of residence during the *varṣā* retreat before taking it.
This accords with his intention.
If a large quantity of rain-cloths is obtained, two should be given to each monk, and one should be given to a *śrāmaṇera*.

If there are those who were not fully included among the associates, when the distribution of robes occurs at the conclusion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should specifically provide them with the value of a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*). These robes may not be accepted [as ordinary property]; they must be treated as part of the three robes (*tricīvara*) and may not be given away through the ritual of formal dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
One must not put on a rain-cloak to enter a river or a pond to bathe, nor should one wear it during light rain.
Furthermore, one must not bathe naked; when bathing, one should wear a *saṃkakṣikā*.
If one has other old robes, one must not wear the rain-cloak for various activities; it should only be worn for bathing when there is heavy rain.
If the rain suddenly stops while one is still stained with grime, one may wear it to enter other water to bathe, and there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, while eating, wishes to smear oil upon his body;
or if he is ill; or if he is in a place frequented by many people, he may tie both ends [of the cloth] to create a screen.
This rain-bathing robe may be used for four and a half months; it must be relinquished by the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Regarding the relinquishing of the robe: one bhikṣu should make this proclamation in the midst of the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe."
Thus it was said three times.
If one discards [the robe] on the sixteenth day, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.

Once discarded, it may be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*); one may also perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) before a monk who is a *jñāti*, and one may enter other bodies of water to bathe; making various things from it involves no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda and Upānanda took thread and entered the house of a lay devotee, saying to the upāsikā:
"Give me some thread.
The laywomen thought to themselves,
"This bhikṣu wishes to buy thread."
Each person brought out a thread.
Upon seeing them, the bhikṣu immediately took one and compared it to his own, saying:
"I was precisely seeking a thread like this; now I have found its match."
If he sees something beautiful, he says:
"I wish to seek out its equal and obtain something even more excellent.
If he sees something coarse, he says:
"This thread, though coarse, can be made into something fine.
Because he brought the thread for this purpose, he could not escape his fate at all.
Carrying a heavy burden, he came to a narrow alley not far from the Jeta Grove Monastery; there, he established a weaving workshop and ordained a weaver as a monk to weave robes for him.
When the Venerable Ānanda arrived, he put on his village-entering robes, took up his alms bowl, and proceeded to beg for food until he reached the entrance of their house.
There he saw Nanda and Upananda holding balls of thread, together weaving a cotton cloth. Having seen them, he exchanged greetings with them, and Ānanda asked:
"Elders, what are you doing?"
He replied,
"I wish to weave robes.
The other then thought to himself:
"I have seen the attendant Ānanda today; he will surely speak to the World-Honored One, and I shall employ a skillful means.
He then took a ball of thread and gave it to the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Take this and sew my robe."
Ānanda did not accept it.
After the meal, he related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked Upānanda:
"Regarding the matter mentioned above, up until the point that Ānanda did not accept your thread—did you actually do this?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter.
Have you not heard me praise few desires through countless skillful means and censure many desires?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and it is contrary to the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread and has a weaver weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Those who beg for it themselves" refers to those who solicit through exhortation and persuasion, perhaps for one or two *liangs*.
"Threads" refers to the seven kinds of thread.
"Weavers" refers to the weavers of present-day Videha and Kośala.
If one has a robe woven, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread himself, it is a transgression of the Vinaya requiring mental remorse (*vyatikrama-citta-kaukṛtya*).
If she receives [the materials], she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she has them woven, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
According to the custom of the land of Kāśī, when a bhikṣu has finished his rainy season retreat, they provide him with thread and the wages for weaving.
When a bhikṣu wishes to have cotton cloth woven, he should speak to the weaver, saying:
"I give you this thread; weave cotton cloth for me.
The weaver replies:
"Venerable sir!
I do not understand these words.
One should then ask:
“What kind of work does your family do?
He replied,
“We weave cotton cloth.”
He should then say:
"May you weave this cotton cloth for me?

If the other person does not understand this phrasing, he should provide the thread to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) and have them know how to weave it; in no case may he speak of hiring someone to weave.
If a bhikṣu knows that another is weaving a waistband and wishes to have that bhikṣu weave it, he should provide the thread and say:
"Venerable sir,
please make a belt for me."
Thus it was said.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā would regularly invite the community of monks for a meal every day.
At that time, a bhikṣu arrived at her house for his meal and saw Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā holding thread and giving it to a weaver, saying:
"Weave this cotton cloth for me; I wish to offer it to the Venerable Nanda and Upānanda."
"That man is difficult to deal with; you should weave it well for him.
After the bhikṣu had finished eating, he returned to the vihāra and said to Nanda, "Elder!..."
"I wish to tell you something good news.
He asked, "What good news is there?"
He replied,
"I saw Visākhā Migāramātā wishing to give you a robe.
He answered:
"She will not give me a robe.
Why? Because this upāsikā intends to give [robes] only to the noble ones."
He spoke again: "It is not so;
I saw with my own eyes Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā giving thread to a weaver and saying to him:
'Give this thread to you; weave a fine cotton cloth for me, which I wish to offer to Nanda, for that man is difficult to please.'"
He asked, "Do you know where the weaver’s house is?
He replied:
“I know the place.
He then asked again,
“Where is that house located?”
Where are the streets and lanes?
In which direction do the gates face?
Show me the distinguishing signs.
Having thus inquired and learned his whereabouts, on the following day he put on his village-dweller’s robes and went to that man's house.
Seeing the weaver setting up the warp, he asked the weaver:
"Long-lived one!..."
"For whom are you setting up the cords? He replied,
"I am setting up the cords for Mṛgāramātṛ Viśākhā."
He asked again:
"Do you know? For whom was this made?"
He replied,
"I know it was for Nanda and Upananda.
He asked again:
"Do you know Nanda? He replied,
"I do not know him."
He then spoke these words:
"Nanda and Upananda, we are indeed those very people; you should weave well, making it long, wide, fine, and exquisite.
The weaver replied:
"The thread has its limits and its quantity is already fixed; how can I weave without warp-threads?
He then spoke again:
"Just do as I say and work well; that family is very wealthy and will surely provide you with more thread."
The weaver spoke again:
"That family gave me the thread; who then shall give me the wages for my work?
He then said:
“Simply weave well; I shall give you the wages for weaving.
The weaver said, “If the Venerable One gives me the wages for weaving and provides me with sufficient thread, I shall weave according to your instructions.”
The weaver then wove it well.
When the thread was exhausted, she went back to ask for more; she did so three times.
Visākhā Migāramātā thought to herself:
"This man has come only to seek thread and did not ask for it to be woven into cloth; why should I not give him the thread?
Having given him the thread, she had it woven into a fabric that was wide, long, fine, and beautiful, which she then sent to Mṛgāramātṛ.
Having taken it, Mṛgāramātā said:
"This is a fine cotton cloth; it should not be given to him, for this is a heavy offering.
Nevertheless, it was originally prepared for his sake."
He then sent it to him.
While the Nanda cotton cloth was still being made, Nanda went to the weaver’s house every day.
Once he had obtained the cloth, he would leave that house and walk through other alleys, like an old crow avoiding the direction from which arrows are shot.
The weaver had many tasks to attend to and was unable to come to collect his wages for the weaving.
Later, when the weaver’s guild officials gathered and arrived at Śrāvastī, the weaver then thought to himself:
"The people have not yet assembled; I should go now to collect my wages for the weaving."
He therefore went to the Jeta Grove; having arrived, he asked the bhikṣus, "Where do Nanda and Upananda reside?
The bhikṣus replied:
"It is in this room. He then entered the room;
having seen him, he prostrated at his feet and inquired after his well-being.
The other pretended not to recognize him, as if they had never met before.
He immediately asked,
"Venerable sir, have you obtained the cotton cloth?
To which [the other] replied in return:
"What kind of cotton cloth?
He replied,
"I am one who weaves for the mother of the deer."
He replied, “I have. He asked:
"Is this cotton cloth to the Venerable's liking?
He replied,
"It is quite acceptable."
He then said, "Ācārya,
you should give me the price for the weaving. He asked:
"What is the price for weaving?
He replied, "I shall provide whatever thread the laywoman requires; this is the fee I have agreed upon for the weaving."
He then spoke with anger: "So it is, so it is!
My son has given you grain; do you not recognize Nanda and Upananda?"
You wish to pluck out your own eyelashes to grasp smoke in empty space; you wish to scoop up pure water with your five fingers after having already washed the cauldron;
you, a naked ascetic, still hope to strip off two pieces of fine wool after having already been stripped bare; and you hope to strip five hundred catties of flesh from the feet of a dead, old crow.
If one were to scatter a handful of chaff into the swirling depths of the Ganges River and seek to retrieve such things from those places, how much less could you hope to recover my property!
He then said to his disciple, "Bring me my saṃghāṭī;
I wish to put it on and go to the royal palace to summon people to bind this man and deliver him to the authorities."
The weaver thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses great physical strength and frequently enters the royal palace; he will surely be able to do me harm."
"What is the use of practicing such honesty?
It will only serve to sustain my life.
Filled with fear, he retreated and went out through the door.
When he went among those gathered for the assembly, the people there complained, saying:
"We have each abandoned our household affairs to come here together to manage official business."
"Why do you now obstruct and hinder the assembly?
He replied, "Listen, Mother Deer,
give me the thread with which you weave the cotton cloth."
Nanda and Upananda came every day while the cotton cloth was still being woven.

Once they had obtained the cloth, they were like old crows that have moved far away from the direction of an arrow; they even reflected only upon how they might sustain their lives. As explained in detail above, it is for this reason that they arrived late.
The crowd immediately spoke with indignation:

"This bhikṣu treats us with contempt and refuses to pay us our wages; instead, he wishes to have men bound by the power of the king. Today we shall establish a restriction: henceforth we will no longer weave cotton cloth for śramaṇas."
Some people said:
"We should go to a secluded place and make a mutual agreement not to let anyone know.
We know the dimensions of the śramaṇas' robes: five cubits in length and three cubits in width, or five cubits in length and two cubits in width; we must not weave robes of such dimensions."

If that person should find out, this śramaṇa will have the power to compel the royal household to employ men by force, even to the point of performing acts of harm against him; therefore, do not let anyone know.
When the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrived, people brought thread to the weaver’s workshop, wishing to hire him to weave garments.
The weaver asked them,
“What size of robes do you wish to have made?”
He replied:
"Five cubits in length and three cubits in width; five cubits in length and two cubits in width."
The weaver thought to himself,
"This is the measurement for a śramaṇa’s robe," and he replied:
"I have already finished weaving for others and can no longer do more.
When he asked thus throughout the area, there was no one at all who could weave.

At that time, the wealthy and noble families took the finished cotton cloth from their own homes and gave it to the Saṃgha; however, the poor people, having no finished cloth themselves, had no clothing to give to the Saṃgha. Consequently, the Saṃgha received very few offerings of robes.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally: "Ānanda,
why has the Saṃgha received so few offerings of robes?"
Ānanda immediately reported these matters to the World-Honored One, including how the weaver had conceived a displeased mind and made a pact for his life,
and he presented them all in detail. The Buddha said, "Call Nanda here."
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned Nanda and Upananda in detail:
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me praise few desires and disparage many desires?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a householder or a householder’s wife employs a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu,
and that bhikṣu, having not been previously invited, goes to the weaver and encourages him,
saying: "Do you know?"
‘This robe is being made for me; you should weave it well, making it dense, long, and wide, and I shall give you money or the value of money, food or the value of food.
If a bhikṣu, having thus urged [the weaver] with money or the value of money, food or the value of food, obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"A householder" refers to the head of the household.
"A wife" refers to the head of the household's wife.
"For a bhikṣu" means for a saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual.
The weaver is as described above.
The robe is of ten kinds, as described above. "Not previously requested" means:

regarding what was not originally requested, one has the thought that it was requested; regarding a request for another person, one has the thought that it was for oneself; regarding a request for another object, one has the thought that it is for a robe.
"To go" means to go to the fields or to the house.
"To exhort" means to tell them to make [the work] fine and detailed, or long and wide.
"Money" refers to various kinds of currency.
"Value in money" refers to other goods.
"Food" refers to parched grain porridge, wheat porridge, and meat and fish.
"Value" refers to money and goods.
If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu says to a weaver:
"If you would weave it well for me—
firmly and tightly," when one speaks these words, there is an offense of *viniya*.
When the weaver applies his hand and beats the warp, for every beat, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a weaver, and the weaver stands listening with his hand supporting his chin, the bhikṣu says to the weaver:
"This should be heard with the ear; it should not be heard with the hand; the hands can be used for other tasks."
When one speaks these words, one incurs an offense of *viniya-āpatti*.
If a bhikṣu hears that robes are being made for him and goes to encourage [the donor] but does not permit a price, yet obtains the robes, he incurs an offense of *viniya-āpatti*.
If one hears [of the offer] and goes to encourage [the donor], and receives a robe even though [the donor] had already consented to give directly, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one goes to encourage [the donor] without having heard [of the offer], and receives a robe because [the donor] gives it personally, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one does not hear of it, does not encourage [the donor], and does not provide the funds, there is no offense for the one who receives the robe.
If a widow offers robes to the community of monks, and a bhikṣu is due to receive this robe according to the sequence within the saṃgha, the woman says to the bhikṣu:
"There is no one in my household; Venerable Sir, you may go to the weaver's place to have this robe prepared."
"Venerable sir, if you can go there yourself to manage the matter, it will be accomplished quickly and you may obtain what is excellent.
At that time, the bhikṣu went to the weaver's place and spoke these words:
"Long-lived one!"
"If you know how to weave quickly and know how to weave tightly," one who speaks these words incurs no offense.
Therefore, it is so said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a certain village. At the beginning of the retreat, in the morning, they put on their village-entry robes, took up paper and pens, and entered the village where they said to the lay followers (*upāsaka*):
"Provide us with the robes for our summer retreat in accordance with the communal agreement."
The upāsakas said:
"This is not the time to seek robes for the rainy season retreat; wait until the autumn grain is ripe.
At that time, people will have many joyful hearts and shall offer robes."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"You do not realize that there are many difficulties in the world, such as the perils of kings, water, fire, or bandits; or perhaps you were prevented by your parents from making this offering."
"You will not achieve success in merit, and I shall suffer loss.
The upāsaka said,
"Venerable One!"
"You merely point out my various difficulties, yet you do not see your own difficulties.
Venerable sir, having received the funds for the rainy season retreat, do you wish to abandon the path and go elsewhere?"
"Why do you have such great desire and greed for acquisition?
What kind of path is this?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus immediately reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you indeed, at the time of the first *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), solicit *varṣā-cīvara* robes from the *upāsakas*, and were you consequently rebuked by those *upāsakas*?
He replied, “It is true.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is an evil matter; to seek robes beforehand while the rains retreat has not yet concluded.
From this day forth, while the rains retreat has not yet concluded, one must not seek robes for the retreat beforehand."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was a minister of King Prasenajit named Mṛgāra, a Kṣatriya, who had rebelled. The king dispatched a high minister named Ṛṣidatta to go and suppress him.
As this minister was about to depart, he went to the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:
"The king's minister has rebelled, and the King now dispatches me to wage war against him. Facing such a powerful enemy, my life is in peril."

"Every year, after the summer retreat has concluded, I provide a meal for the Saṃgha and offer robes. However, I am currently being dispatched by the government and cannot wait for the proper time; I wish to offer the robes first.
If I return safely, I shall later provide the meal."
Venerable Ānanda then reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"How many days of the summer retreat remain for you?"
He replied, "Ten days.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I authorize you to accept ‘urgent offering robes’ up to ten days before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”

If, within the final ten days of the three-month summer retreat, a monk obtains an urgent offering of robes (ātyayika-cīvara), he may, if he requires it, take it with his own hand and keep it until the time for robes.
If he keeps it beyond that time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"The ten-day period" refers to the time from the sixth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month; this is called the ten-day period.
Regarding those who receive the "urgent robe-offering," they may be women or men, whether old or young, whether laypeople or monastics.
If one gives when setting out on a military expedition, when returning from an expedition, at the time of death, when a woman returns home, or when merchants depart, the donor says to the bhikṣu:
"If you do not take it today, there will be none tomorrow."
This is called "urgent giving of robes.
As for "robes," there are seven kinds, as explained above.
Regarding "one who wishes to take": if one requires these items, one should take them and keep them until the time for [receiving] robes arrives.
Regarding the time for robes: if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, one may keep them until the fifteenth day of the eighth month;
if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, one may keep them until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.
If one keeps [the robe] beyond the prescribed time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
A monk who is endowed with five qualities should be appointed by the Saṃgha as the person to solicit offerings and distribute the robes.
What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing gain and non-gain—these are called the five dharmas.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has accomplished the five qualities. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of robes through exhortation."
The motion is thus made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has accomplished five qualities; the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of robes through exhortation."
"Venerable sirs, if you approve of this bhikṣu so-and-so acting as the distributor of robes through solicitation for the Saṃgha, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.
"The Saṃgha has already approved the appointment of bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of robes through solicitation. Since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
Having received the *karmavācanā*, one should address the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
The measurements of the robes differ by four or eight finger-breadths; if these are permissible, I shall divide them."
If one divides [the property] without having made the formal announcement, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya.
After making the announcement as described above, one should then divide it.
From the sixteenth day of the third month, that bhikṣu should inform the various donors:

"Take up paper and brush, and record in full the names of all the dwellings: the lecture hall, the warm chamber, the meditation hall, the gatehouse, the kitchen, the water-purification house, the latrine, the firewood shed, the bathhouse, the places for sitting under trees, and the places for walking meditation."
One should announce within the Saṃgha:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At such-and-such a residence, there are this many beds and mats, this many robes for the rains retreat, this much food, this much food for the fast-day, and this much material for ritual blessings.”
In this residence, there are so many forest hermitages; as for the various monasteries nearby or those further away, one should distribute the rooms on the twelfth or thirteenth day.
"If this dwelling place cannot accommodate you, you may go to another location.
If there is a monastery near a village, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, one should distribute the details: "This room, bed, and bedding are for the Elder; I announce this to the Saṃgha:
'In such-and-such a dwelling, there are this many rooms, beds, and bedding; let the Elder take them as he pleases.'"
Having taken [the portion], he should next give it to the second, the third, and so on, down to the bhikṣu who has not yet completed his year of seniority.
The elder should speak thus:
"The dwellings are occupied in order of seniority; the gifts should be distributed equally."
At that time, one should follow the instructions of the senior monk (*sthavira*).
Once the senior monk has taken [the portion], it should be given in sequence to the second and third, and so on, down to the monk who has no years of seniority (*anupasaṃpanna*).
If there are many rooms, one person should be given two rooms. When giving two rooms, if they are unwilling to accept them, one should say:
"These are given for the purpose of managing affairs, not for personal enjoyment."
A *śrāmaṇera* shall not be given two rooms.
If there are few rooms, two persons shall share one room.
If the rooms are still insufficient, three persons, or four, five, or even up to ten persons shall share one room.
Whether it be a large hall, a warm chamber, a meditation hall, or a lecture hall, everyone shall enter therein together.
If one does not accept [a bed], the elder shall be given a couch for lying down, and the junior shall be given a bench for sitting.
If they still do not accept, the senior monk shall provide a sitting bench while the junior monks spread mats upon the floor.
If they still do not accept, the senior monk shall provide a grass mat while the junior monks sit in the full lotus posture.
If they still do not accept [the invitation], the senior monk should sit while the junior monks should stand.
If they still do not accept, the senior monk should stand and the junior monks should depart to a place such as beneath a tree or elsewhere.
After the sixteenth day of the sixth month, that bhikṣu should say to the donors:
"Long-lived ones!
Each of you should prepare robes."
At that time, if a donor offers [an item], one should say:
"Set this aside for you; we must wait for the proper time before giving it.

Whether it is offered when departing for a military campaign, upon returning from a campaign, at the time of death, when a merchant departs, or when a woman returns home—one should take it only if it is not taken today and there is none available tomorrow. At such a time, one should accept it.

After the fifth day of the seventh month, when these robes arrive, they should be gathered together in one place; if they are leaves or bark, they should be counted and recorded as follows: "So many robes for the [proper] season, so many robes for the improper season, and so many robes for urgent offerings."
There are three periods for robes: the period for timely robes, the period for untimely robes, and the period for robes offered in haste.
If the person distributing the robes has renounced the path or died, the robes shall not be distributed.
If the time has passed, the distribution of robes should be exchanged as follows:
the robe of a bhikṣuṇī should be given to a bhikṣu, and the robe of a bhikṣu should be given to a bhikṣuṇī.
If this cannot be done, the robe of a śrāmaṇera should be given to a bhikṣu, and the robe of a bhikṣu should be given to a śrāmaṇera.
If it is still not obtained, one should announce before the assembly of monks:
"Venerable sirs! The time for robes has passed;

the Sangha is in harmony. We shall prepare bedding and seating for the Saṃgha of the four directions. If you grant permission, we shall prepare bedding and seating for the Saṃgha of the four directions."
If someone should say, "We have lived here in peace during the summer retreat and have received this share of robes; why should they be used for the sake of the Saṃgha of the four directions?
one should say to that person:
"I shall give it to you when the time for robes arrives next year.
Thus it was said.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus were observing the summer rains retreat in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka).

When it was time for the bhikṣus to enter the village for alms, people who were tending cattle and sheep or gathering firewood and grass arrived carrying door-hooks; they opened the doors of the bhikṣus' rooms and stole their clothing and belongings.
At that time, because they feared theft, all the bhikṣus entered the village carrying their robes and requisites with them.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked them intentionally:
"Which bhikṣu here has brought these things along?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!

These bhikṣus had gone to dwell in retreats for the rains retreat and were away on their almsround. Later, someone took a door-bolt, opened the door from behind, and stole various garments and belongings; this is why they have been brought here.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, during times of fear and apprehension, it is permitted to entrust one or another of the three robes to someone within a village.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, a dispute arose among the Saṃgha during the summer retreat in the kingdom of Śāketa, which was settled in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"Go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and, together with the community of monks, resolve this dispute according to the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder Upāli declined and would not go. The Buddha asked Upāli:
"Why do you not leave? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"My saṃghāṭī is heavy; if it were to get wet by the rain, I could not bear its weight.
Yet, during this half-month of the rainy season retreat, if one leaves the robe behind, it constitutes a *niḥsargika* offense."
The Buddha asked Upāli,
“In how many days will you be able to return?
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Calculating two days for the journey there, two days for staying, and two days for the return, totaling six nights, we shall be able to complete the round trip.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you may keep extra robes for up to six nights.
Having arrived there, Upāli saw that this dispute was difficult to settle abruptly, so he immediately returned.
Having returned, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally: "Upāli!
Why have you returned so quickly? Has the dispute within the Saṃgha been settled?"
He replied, “It has not yet been extinguished,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason? He replied:

“The legal dispute is difficult to settle and cannot be resolved immediately; furthermore, I feared that the day would pass and I would commit an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*) due to losing my robes. For this reason, I have returned.
The Buddha said, “From this day forward, I permit you to stay away from your robes for one month without forfeiting them.”
The monks performing the *karmavācanā* should grant him the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the purpose of staying away from his robes for one month without them being lost.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Elder Upāli is now proceeding toward the country of Śrāvastī to settle a dispute for the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may Upāli request from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for one month’s exemption from the requirement of keeping one’s robes with oneself while traveling.
“Venerable sirs, listen!
Upāli requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one month’s *acīvarika-vāsa* (staying without the robe). Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”
One should request permission from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu Upāli, wish to go to the country of Śrāvastī to resolve a dispute for the sake of the Saṃgha."
"I only pray that the Venerable Saṃgha will grant me the *karmavācanā* for the practice of 'not losing the robe' for one month.
Thus he requests a second and third time.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The Elder Upāli wishes to go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to settle a dispute for the Saṃgha; he has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of a month-long *cīvara-anapahāra-saṃvāsa* (the permission to stay away from one's robes without forfeiture)."
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant Upāli the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of 'not losing the robe while staying overnight' for one month.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The Elder Upāli wishes to go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to settle a dispute for the Saṃgha; he has already requested from the Saṃgha the *māsa-cīvara-anapahāra* (one-month permission to stay away from one's robes).
The Saṃgha has now granted the Elder Upāli the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the one-month *anapahāra*.

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the *karmavācanā* for Upāli regarding the one-month *acīvaradhara-vihāra* (staying without the robe) remain silent; if you do not consent, speak now. This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already granted Upāli a month’s period for staying apart from his robes without them being lost. Since the Saṃgha remains silent, it consents; thus this matter is so upheld."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Have you already granted Upāli the *karmavācanā* for the month-long permission to dwell apart from his robes?
They replied:
"I have already granted it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

During the three months of summer that have not yet expired, if a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) experiences fear or apprehension, he may entrust one or another of his three robes to a lay household.
"If a bhikṣu has a matter for which there is a valid cause, he may stay [away from his robes] for up to six nights.
If he exceeds this, except by means of a formal authorization (saṃgha-kamma) of the Saṃgha, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
As for the three-month retreat (varṣā), it runs from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month."
"Before the time has elapsed" means before the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
A bhikṣu who has not yet reached the final month of the rainy retreat resides in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
An araṇya is defined as a place where, within a distance of five cubits or five hundred bows, there is no house belonging to a cattle-herder; this is called an araṇya.
"Terrified" refers to being killed or robbed.
"Suspicious" refers to having no intention of killing or robbing, yet harboring a suspicious mind that fears one might kill a person or seize their clothing at any moment.
If a bhikṣu knows such a place to be dangerous,
he may [leave] any one of his three robes— whether it be the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, or the antarvāsaka.
One must not entrust one’s *saṃghāṭī* or *antarvāsaka*; however, one may entrust one’s *uttarāsaṅga* to a household within a village.

Regarding those "insiders," one must not entrust it to laypeople; it should be entrusted to a trustworthy family who will return it. As for suspicious families, one should regard them as suspicious and think:
"These monks can no longer be relied upon at all; they must be fully on their guard."
If the bhikṣus have a legitimate reason—whether for the sake of the stūpa or for the affairs of the Saṃgha—they may stay away for up to six nights.
"Six nights" means a limit of six days and nights.
Regarding those exempted by a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*), the World-Honored One declared there is no offense.
If a formal monastic act is not accomplished, it is not called a *karman*.
An unaccomplished *karman* occurs when the assembly is incomplete, the proclamation (*jñapti*) is incomplete, or the formal act itself is incomplete.
If the motion (jñapti) is accomplished, the formal act (karman) is accomplished, and the assembly is accomplished, this is called the Saṃgha performing a karman.
Once the karman has been received within the Saṃgha, one must not remain for the sake of receiving offerings; one should depart immediately.
If the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed before a meal, one should depart after the meal.
If the *karmavācanā* is received after a meal, one should depart at dawn the following morning.
When departing, one must not take a detour to follow a donor; one should go by the direct route.

If there are obstacles on the direct path—such as the danger of lions, the danger of tigers and wolves, the danger of venomous insects, or the danger of losing one's life—at such a time, it is no offense to turn back and take another route.
Having arrived there, one must not delay while providing food and drink to the visiting bhikṣus.
If one arrives before the meal, one should assemble the Saṃgha after the meal to settle the matter of the dispute.
If one arrives after the meal, one should assemble the Saṃgha at dawn to settle the matter of the dispute.
If the legal case is concluded after the meal, he shall return at dawn.
If the legal case is concluded before the meal, he shall return after the meal; he must not remain to wait for the offerings of the visiting bhikṣus.
When returning, one must not take a circuitous route; one should return by the direct path.
If there are obstacles, it is as explained above.
When first traveling to that place, one must not recite sutras, fumigate the alms bowl, or dye robes.
If the legal case has been concluded, one may spend the remaining time reciting sutras or performing other tasks.
If the case is difficult to resolve, one may recite sutras or fumigate the alms bowl during the interval; furthermore, it is without fault to accept food and drink offered by visiting bhikṣus.

When settling a dispute, one must not arbitrarily take the side of another; rather, one should select from among the assembly those who are capable and possess authority, power, and influence. If a robe has been deposited at an āraṇyaka dwelling, it may be worn within a household for six nights.
If it exceeds six nights, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When this bhikṣu wishes to relinquish the robe, the proper procedure is to request a master of the Vinaya, as explained above in the first precept; therefore, this is stated.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. There was a certain bhikṣu who went for alms; when the time arrived, he put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to wander for alms in succession.
Arriving at a certain house, a woman said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
On a certain day, I shall provide offerings to the Saṃgha and bestow robes upon the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu said:
"Excellent, sisters!
You should quickly exchange these three non-firm things—body, life, and wealth—for the three firm things. Wealth is impermanent and beset by many difficulties."
Having spoken these words, he returned to the vihāra and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to tell you something good news.
The bhikṣus replied:
"What good news is there? He replied,
"I have heard that a certain upāsikā intends to provide a meal for the Saṃgha and bestow robes upon the Saṃgha."
When the group of six bhikṣus heard these words, they asked again,
"What did you say? He replied:
"I have heard that a certain female lay follower wishes to provide a meal for the Sangha and offer robes as a gift.
He asked, "Do you know the location of her house?"
"In which alley does it stand?
In which direction does its gate face?
Having asked these questions, he dressed in his village robes at dawn, went to that house, and upon seeing him, asked:
"Long life to you!
Are you at peace? He replied:
"Peaceful and well," he said, addressing the upāsikā:
"I have heard that you wish to provide the Saṃgha with meals and bestow robes upon the Saṃgha; is this truly so?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
I have this intention, but I fear there may be many obstacles along the way; do you know whether it will be accomplished or not?"
He then said:
"If you would give me a robe, I shall wear it when entering the royal court to pay my respects to the World-Honored One, or when visiting noble and eminent families."
If someone were to ask me,
"Where did you obtain this?
I would answer:
“I obtained it from a certain female lay follower (upāsikā) who possesses faith.
In this way, you will gain a good reputation and become well-known among the multitude.
The upāsikā said:
"I have nothing else in my house; what I intended to give to the Saṃgha, I shall now give to the Ācārya, for I have already promised it to the Saṃgha.
Had I possessed anything else, I would have given it separately both to the Ācārya and to the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu said,
"Whether you give it to me or not is up to your own will.
Having spoken these words, he departed.
After he had departed, the upāsikā thought to herself:
"If I were to give this to this bhikṣu alone and not to the Saṃgha, [I would miss out on the merit], for the Saṃgha is a field of excellent merit."
"If I do not give this to the bhikṣu, he will have power over the king and will be able to bring me harm.
For this reason, I will not give it to the Saṃgha; furthermore, because of my anger toward the bhikṣu, I will not give it to him either."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of the matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her extensively on the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; it is doubly improper, for it causes the donor to lose merit and the recipient to lose his robe."
The Buddha said to Nanda and Upananda:
"Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, praise few desires and censure many desires?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble, for the sake of ten benefits, so that I may establish a precept for the bhikṣus. Even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, yet diverts it to himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by himself or hearing it from another.

"Objects" refers to eight kinds of objects: those for a limited time, those for a night, those for seven days, those for life, objects that follow [the person], valuable objects, impure objects, pure objects, and objects that are both pure and impure.
"Directed toward" means having the intention to select items for the Saṃgha.
There are eight kinds of Saṃgha:
the bhikṣu-saṃgha, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, the guest saṃgha, the departing saṃgha, the resident saṃgha, the saṃgha in retreat, the harmonious saṃgha, and the discordant saṃgha.
If one appropriates for oneself, uses for oneself, or consumes for oneself, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This object must be relinquished within the Saṃgha, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
If one does not relinquish [the object] but instead regrets [the decision], one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
The term *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If someone comes wishing to make a gift and asks the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
I wish to practice giving; to whom should I give?
The bhikṣu should reply:
"Give it to whomever your heart honors.
The donor asked again,
"In whom does the fruit of the gift yield the greatest reward?"
He replied,
"The karmic fruit of giving to the Sangha is great.
The donor asked again:
"What is the Sangha that possesses the merit of pure observance of the precepts?
The bhikṣu should answer:
"In this Sangha, there is no one who has transgressed the precepts or is impure."
If a person brings an object to offer as a gift, the bhikṣu should say to them:
"One who gives to the Saṃgha obtains a great fruit of retribution. If they say:
"I have already given to the Saṃgha; now I wish to give specifically to the Venerable.
If the bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If someone asks the bhikṣu:
"I wish to give this object as a gift; where should I place it so that I may continue to see and enjoy its use?
At that time, one should say:
"The bhikṣu named So-and-so is a practitioner of meditation, a reciter of the sūtras, and one who upholds the precepts; if you give it to him, you will continue to see and enjoy its use."
If one knows that an object is intended for the Sangha and diverts it to oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one diverts it to another person, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one knows that an object is intended for this particular Sangha and diverts it to another Sangha, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one knows that an item was intended for this group of many people, yet redirects it to another group of many people, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one knows that an object was intended for this particular animal, yet redirects it to another animal, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If one knows that an object was intended for the Sangha, yet redirects it toward oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Sangha should not give back this object; the Sangha should instead utilize it. Therefore, this is said.
