The Ninety-two Dharmas of the *Pācittika*. Part 1: The First of the Ninety-two Dharmas of the *Pācittika*. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the community of monks gathered in one place, intending to perform a *karmavācanā*.
The Elder Śrīyava did not come, so they immediately sent a messenger to summon him, saying: "Elder!..."
The community of monks has assembled, intending to perform a formal ritual act (karmavācanā).
Śrīyāvatī thought to herself:
"This must surely be a formal act being performed against me."
Thereupon, fear and dread arose in his heart; unable to remain, he came.
Having arrived, the bhikṣus asked him:
"Elder!..."
“Have you committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense? He replied, “I have.”
His heart was filled with joy, and he thought:
"The fellow practitioners of the holy life have raised against me a matter that is capable of confession; it is not a matter beyond remedy."
He addressed the community of monks, saying:
"Please allow me to go out for a moment.
Afterward, the bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"This bhikṣu is fickle and unstable; having departed, he will likely speak falsely in a moment. You should question him three times to ascertain the truth.
After Śrīyāvat had left, he thought to himself:
"For what reason have I incurred this offense when I am innocent?"

"These bhikṣus constantly and repeatedly punish me for my offenses; I should not now accept these punishments. It would be better for me to lie to the Saṃgha, so that they may punish me for the offense of lying; though it is punished, it will be light."
The bhikṣus then called Śrīyāvatī in. Once she had entered, they asked her, "Have you committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
She replied:
"I did not commit an offense.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Why did you just now say that you had committed one?"
He replied, "The Sangha previously intended to cause me to commit an offense; that is why I answered that I had committed one. I do not now recall having any offense.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
“Call Śrīyāvatī here. Once she had arrived, he questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
“Is it true that you did this?”
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, rebuke false speech and praise truthful speech?"
How can you now speak falsely despite knowing the truth?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu speaks falsely while knowing [the truth], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means knowing through prior reflection.
"False" means that the matter is not as it appears.
"Speech" refers to verbal action.
*Pāyattika* (波夜提) is the designation for the offense established by the rules.
The noble ones speak on eight matters: speaking directly, falsehood and non-falsehood, doubt and non-doubt, certainty and non-certainty, and categorical speech.

Regarding the eight matters spoken by the noble ones: to say one has seen when one has seen; to say one has heard when one has heard; to say it is false when it is false; to say one has cognized when one has cognized; to say one has not seen when one has not seen; to say one has not heard when one has not heard; to say it is not false when it is not false; and to say one has not cognized when one has not cognized—these are called the eight matters of the noble ones' speech, which are blameless.

The eight matters that are not the speech of the noble ones (ārya) are: saying one has not seen when one has seen; saying one has not heard when one has heard; saying it is false when it is not false; saying one does not know when one knows; saying one has seen when one has not seen; saying one has heard when one has not heard; saying it is false when it is not false; and saying one knows when one does not know. These are called the eight matters that are not the speech of the noble ones, for which one incurs the offense of *pāyattika*.

Regarding "speaking directly": if one has seen, heard, known, or cognized something, yet says they have not seen, heard, known, or cognized it, this is called speaking directly [of what is false], and one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "lying": if one has seen what is falsely claimed to be not false, heard what is falsely claimed to be not false, known what is falsely claimed to be not false, or cognized what is falsely claimed to be not false, yet says they have not seen, heard, known, or cognized it—while the matter is indeed falsely claimed to be not false—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "not speaking falsely": if one has seen, heard, known, or cognized something, and does not falsely claim not to have seen, heard, known, or cognized it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Conversely, if one has not seen, heard, known, or cognized something, and does not falsely claim to have seen, heard, known, or cognized it, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding doubt: if one has seen, heard, known, or recognized something, yet says they do not doubt it; or if one has not seen, heard, known, or recognized something, yet says they do not doubt it, one incurs a pāyattika offense.

Regarding "not doubting": if one has seen, heard, known, or recognized something, yet does not doubt while claiming to doubt; or if one has not seen, heard, known, or recognized something, yet does not doubt while claiming to doubt—such a person incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "certainty": if one has seen, heard, known, or cognized something, yet declares with certainty what is uncertain; or if one has not seen, heard, known, or cognized something, yet declares with certainty that it is uncertain—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "uncertainty": if one has seen, heard, known, or cognized something, yet speaks with certainty about what is uncertain; or if one has not seen, heard, known, or cognized something, yet speaks with certainty about what is uncertain—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one who has seen, heard, known, or cognized something claims to have neither seen, nor heard, nor known, nor cognized it, they incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If one knows something exists but says it does not, speaking falsely despite knowing the truth, they incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If one knows that something does not exist but says it exists, knowing this yet speaking falsely, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one knows that something truly exists but says it does not, knowing this yet speaking falsely, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
To say "there is not" regarding what actually exists, speaking falsely with full knowledge, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
To say "there is not" regarding what actually exists and one perceives it as existing, speaking falsely with full knowledge, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one says there is "non-perception" when there is actually no non-perception, knowing it to be so, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one says there is "non-perception" when there actually is non-perception, knowing it to be so, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks of non-existence when there is actually no such perception, knowing it to be so yet speaking falsely, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
When five conditions are fulfilled, speaking falsely while knowing it to be so, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
What are the five?
Actual existence, perception, shifting the mind, contrary perception, and speaking with a different mouth—these are the five matters;
to speak falsely while knowing the truth is a pāyattika offense.
If one possesses four factors and speaks falsely with full knowledge, it is a *pāyattika*.
What are the four?
Having the perception [of the truth], having a perverted mind, having a contrary perception, and speaking with a different mouth—these are the four.
To speak falsely with full knowledge is a *pāyattika*.
When three conditions are fulfilled, speaking falsely with full knowledge is a *pāyattika*.
What are these three?
To turn the mind, to turn back the thought, and to speak with different words;
to speak falsely while knowing [the truth], this is a *pāyattika*.
When two factors are fulfilled—speaking falsely while knowing [the truth]—it is a *pāyattika*.
What are the two?
To turn away from one's thoughts and to speak otherwise;
to speak falsely while knowing the truth, which constitutes a pāyattika offense.
There is one dharma, the accomplishment of which constitutes lying with full knowledge:
a *pāyattika*. What is this one?
Speaking with a different mouth [from the mind].
To speak falsely while knowing the truth is a *pāyattika*; therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke with gentle words to entice and question the junior bhikṣus, saying:
“What is your name? What is your family clan?
What are the names of your father and mother?”
“What was the traditional occupation of your family?
The young bhikṣu, being honest by nature, answered truthfully:
“My family’s [occupation] was such-and-such; my name is such-and-such; and my occupation was such-and-such.”
Later, when those six groups of bhikṣus harbored resentment, they spoke as follows:
"You are of the most lowly and base caste; you are a caṇḍāla, a barber, a weaver, a potter, or a tanner."
When the young bhikṣu heard these words, he was overcome with extreme shame.
Upon hearing this, the other bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you used gentle words to entice and question the young bhikṣus, and later, out of resentment, spoke [of them] as far as saying they were potters or leather-workers?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed!
Six groups of bhikṣus!
How can you engage in speech that categorizes the physical forms of fellow practitioners of the holy life, as is explained in detail in the *Nandika-jātaka*?"
The Buddha then told the bhikṣus:
"Even animals revile and disparage one another; how much more so should humans!
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣu speaks of someone's lineage or physical appearance [in a disparaging way], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are seven matters concerning disparagement of lineage:
Lineage, karma, physical appearance, illness, offenses, verbal abuse, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding lineage, there are the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
As for the inferior: "You belong to the lineage of a *caṇḍāla*, a barber, a weaver, a potter, or a tanner."
If one speaks these words so as to cause the other to feel shame, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one says:
"Your parents are caṇḍālas, even down to being leather-workers," [one incurs a pāyattika offense].
To speak these words so as to cause another to feel shame constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*) are outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), even down to being leather-workers."
If he causes the other to feel shame and remorse, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If he says:
"Your friend and companion is a *caṇḍāla*, or even a leather-worker," [he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*].
By speaking these words to cause them shame, one commits a *vinaya*-transgression; this is called "low.
As for the "middling," one says:
"You are of intermediate caste."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause that person to feel shame, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says:
"Your parents are of intermediate caste."
One incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says:
"Your preceptor and preceptor-teacher are of intermediate caste."
If one intends to cause another to feel shame [by this], it is an offense against the Vinaya.
If one says:
"Your friend and acquaintance is of intermediate caste."
If one wishes to cause that person to feel shame so that they may incur a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (a transgression of the Vinaya involving mental regret), this is called the "intermediate" [level].
As for the "superior" [level], one says to the person:
"You are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
If one says:
"Your parents are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, one commits an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya.
If one says:
"Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*) are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause the other to feel shame, one commits a *vibhāṣā-vinaya* offense.
If one says:
"Your friends and acquaintances are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes."
"To cause that person who wishes to feel shame to undergo a transgression of the Vinaya through mental remorse—this is called 'lineage' (gotra).
As for 'action' (karman), there are the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
The inferior is as follows: if one says:"
"You are a butcher, a pork seller, a fisherman, a hunter, a bird-catcher, a snare-setter, a city guard, and an executioner."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause that person to feel shame, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
the same applies to one's parents.
If one says:
If one says, "Your preceptor or ācārya is a butcher,
even a professional executioner," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says:
"If your companion and friend is a butcher, even a professional executioner," one incurs an offense of *vibhinī*;
this is called inferior action (*hīnakarman*).
As for the middling [action], it says:
"If you are a perfume seller, a shopkeeper, a farmer, a vegetable grower, or a messenger"—
if one speaks such words with the intent to cause the other to feel shame, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
the same applies to [speaking thus of] one's parents.
If one says, "Your preceptor or preceptor-instructor," one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one says, "Your friend or spiritual companion," with the intent to cause them shame, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikramasamutthāpana*; this is called a middling action.
Regarding the "superior offender": if one says,
"You are a person who dwells in a shop selling gold, silver, mani-jewels,
or copper vessels," with the intent of making that person feel ashamed, one incurs a *vibhāṣā-āpatti* (an offense of transgression).
The same applies to one's parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), and teachers (ācārya).
If one says [they are] "companions or friends," one incurs a transgression of the Vinaya requiring mental remorse; this is called a superior offense.
Regarding physical appearance, there are three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
As for the inferior, it is as if one were to say:
"You are blind, hunchbacked, lame, with arms like bird wings, a pot-shaped head, and saw-like teeth."
If one speaks such words to cause another to feel shame, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
the same applies to one’s parents.
In the case of an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A fellow friend who transgresses the Vinaya is said to have the lower appearance.
As for the middle [appearance], you are very black, very white, very yellow, or very red.
If one speaks these words to cause another to feel shame or remorse, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
the same applies to one's parents.
Regarding an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*, they incur a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a fellow friend, having attained a transgression of the *vinaya*, confesses it with mental remorse, this is called the intermediate sign.
As for the superior [sign], one says:
"You possess the thirty-two marks and a halo of golden light."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*;
the same applies to one's parents, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), and teachers (*ācārya*).

Regarding a fellow practitioner or spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama* involving mental remorse (*cittavipratisāra*); this is called the superior characteristic.
Regarding illness, there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior; all illnesses are collectively termed "inferior. [The Buddha said:

"You who suffer from scabies, eczema, jaundice, leprosy, carbuncles, abscesses, hemorrhoids, incontinence, jaundice, malaria, emaciation from diabetes, epilepsy, insanity, and various other such ailments."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
the same applies to one's parents.
Regarding an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A fellow companion who commits a *vinaya*-offense—this is called "sickness.
Regarding offenses, there are none that are superior, middling, or inferior; all offenses are collectively termed "inferior":
"You have committed a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *vinayātikrama* offense."
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, it is a *pāyattika*;
the same applies to one's parents.
In the case of an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To transgress the Vinaya against a fellow friend is called an offense.
Regarding "reviling," there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior; all reviling is classified as inferior. It refers to worldly insults:
lewdness, filthiness, and all manner of evil abuse.
If one speaks these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame, it constitutes a *pāyattika*;
the same applies to parents.
For an upādhyāya or ācārya, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a fellow practitioner incurs an offense against the Vinaya, this is called "abusive speech.
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior; all fetters are collectively termed "inferior":
"You are a person who is foolish, dull-witted, and ignorant, just like a lump of clay."
"Like a sheep, a white crane, a horned owl, or an eagle.
To speak such various words with the intent to cause another to feel shame constitutes a *pāyattika*;
the same applies to one's parents.
If [a monk] reviles his Upādhyāya or Ācārya, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense;
if he reviles a fellow student or spiritual friend, he incurs a vyatikrama offense.
If a bhikṣu reviles others by means of the seven types of matters mentioned above, he commits a pāyattika offense.

to do so toward a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī incurs a vyatikrama offense.
Regarding those of similar status who are laypeople, they incur an offense of *vyatikrama* requiring mental repentance; therefore, it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used skillful means to entice and question various young bhikṣus:
"Do you know the name, parentage, lineage, and occupation of the bhikṣu so-and-so?
That young bhikṣu was upright by nature and answered according to the facts.
Later, when the group of six bhikṣus were filled with anger, they spoke these words:
"You are of the caste of outcasts, barbers, weavers, potters, or tanners."
Having spoken these words, he further said:
"I myself do not know; it was that bhikṣu, so-and-so, who spoke to you.
When the bhikṣu heard these words, he felt extreme shame.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you indeed entice and question the young bhikṣus, even to the point that the bhikṣus felt ashamed?
He replied, “It is true.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,

He replied,
“I do this for the sake of pleasure.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! This is an evil deed.
To engage in divisive speech toward those who lead the holy life is a painful matter, yet you speak of it as pleasure.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he explained the causal circumstances for them in detail, as extensively taught in the *Traṇamṛga-jātaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...as has been heard before, you should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Divisive speech" consists of seven matters.
What are the seven kinds? They are:
lineage, occupation, physical appearance, illness, transgression, verbal abuse, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding lineage, there are three types: inferior, middling, and superior.
The inferior ones are those such as you, the *caṇḍālas*, even down to the leather-workers.
Furthermore, he said:

"This is what so-and-so said.
Having formed this thought:

If he leaves her regardless of whether she has left him or not, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he says:
"Your parents are caṇḍālas, even down to leather-workers..."
He spoke again:

It was said by such-and-such a bhikṣu."
He forms this thought:
"I wish to separate them from one another and cause them to unite with me.
Whether they are separated or not separated, it is all a pāyattika offense.
If one says,
"Your preceptor or teacher is a candāla," or even "a leather-worker," it is also a pāyattika.
It is the same with friends and acquaintances.
This is called "inferior.
As for the "middling," it says:
“Elder! You are of the intermediate caste, the official-soldier caste, or the actor caste.
He spoke again:

If one forms this thought:

Whether she leaves or does not leave, it is all a *pāyattika*.
Whether it be her parents, preceptor (*upādhyāya*), teacher (*ācārya*), or close friends and acquaintances, it is all a *pāyattika*; this is called the "middle."
The superior [type] is one who says:
"Venerable sir!
You are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste."
He speaks again, saying:
"I do not know you; it was so-and-so who said that.
If he forms this thought:
"If one intends to separate them from another and cause them to turn toward oneself," whether they are separated or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Your parents, preceptors, teachers, and spiritual friends"—all these constitute a *pāyattika* offense; this is called "superior.
This is what is meant by "lineage."
"Occupation" refers to the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
The inferior is: "You are a butcher, even a public executioner.
He further says:
"I do not know you; it was merely someone else who said so!
If one has such a thought as:

Whether he leaves them or does not leave them, it is all a *pāyattika*.
Whether they be one's parents, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), or close friends and companions, it is all a *pāyattika*; this is called "low."
As for the middling [type]:
you are a person from a perfume shop, even down to a messenger.
Furthermore, he said:

"I wish to separate him from that person and cause him to turn toward myself."
Whether she leaves them or does not leave them, it is all a *pāyattika*.
Whether they be one’s parents, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), or close friends and companions, it is all a *pāyattika*; this is called the middle [offense].
"Superior one," he said, "you are a man of the gold and silver shops, even up to the copper shops.
He further said, "I do not know you; it was someone else who spoke thus!"
If one has this thought:
"I wish to separate them from each other and cause them to come toward me," whether they are separated or not, it is a pāyattika.

If [one commits this offense against] one's parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), or spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), it is a pāyattika; this is called "superior," and this is what is meant by "action" (karman).
As for its characteristics, there are the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
The lowest [offense] is, for example, to say:
"You are blind," or even "You have saw-like teeth," and then further say:
"I do not know you; it was merely so-and-so who said that! Or if one thinks:
"I wish to separate him from that person and cause him to turn toward myself."
If she leaves them, whether she actually departs or not, it is a pāyattika.
If it concerns her parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), or close friends and companions, it is likewise a pāyattika; this is termed "low."
Regarding "middling," it is as if one says:
"You are very black, very white, very yellow, or very red.
Furthermore, it says:
"I do not know you; it was merely so-and-so who said it!
Or if one thinks: "I wish to separate him from that person and cause him to turn toward me."
If she leaves them or does not leave them, it is a pāyattika.
This applies equally to parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), and close friends; in all these cases, it is a pāyattika. This is called the middle [offense].
The superior [type] is as follows: if one says,
"You possess the thirty-two marks and a halo of golden light," and further says:
"I do not know you; it was merely so-and-so who spoke!
If one thinks thus:
"I wish to cause him to be separated from that person and turn him toward myself."
If she leaves them or does not leave them, it is a pāyattika.
This applies equally to her parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), and close friends; all constitute a pāyattika. This is called the "superior" [case].
Regarding the sick, there are no categories of inferior, middling, or superior; all illnesses are termed "inferior.
If one says:
"You have scabies, or even madness.
He replied, "I do not know you; it was merely someone named So-and-so who said that!"
If one thinks, "I wish to separate him from others and bring him toward myself," whether he is separated or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one commits an offense against one's parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), or spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), it constitutes a pāyattika; this is termed "sickness.
Regarding offenses, there are no distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior; all offenses are termed "inferior."
If one says,
"You have committed a pārājika offense," or even "a vyatikrama-vinaya offense," and then further says:
"I do not know you; it was merely so-and-so who said that!
Thinking thus, [he intends]:
"I wish to separate him from her and bring her together with myself."
If she leaves them or does not leave them, it is a pāyattika.
This applies equally if they are her parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), or close friends; in all such cases, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "abusive speech": there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior; all forms of abuse are categorized as inferior.
This refers to committing worldly evil abuse, lewdness, or foul and ugly speech.
If one commits such abuse, whether the [offended] person is separated from it or not, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one says, "Your parents, preceptors, teachers, or fellow friends and associates—all are guilty of a *pāyattika* offense," this is called reviling.
As for the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior; all fetters are collectively termed "inferior."
"You are a foolish person, dull-witted and ignorant, like a clod of mud, and like cattle, sheep, white cranes, hornbills, and owls.
Thus he spoke in various such ways.
He further says:
"I do not know you; it was someone else who said this!
If he forms such a thought:
"If one desires to separate them from others and cause them to come to oneself," whether they are separated or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If this applies to parents, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), or close friends and acquaintances, it is likewise a *pāyattika*; this is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
To engage in divisive speech toward a bhikṣu is a pāyattika offense;
toward a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya offense;
toward a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a violation of the vinaya.
Regarding laypeople, there is a transgression of the Vinaya that requires mental regret; therefore, this is taught.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the Saṃgha had settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, spoke as follows:
"This matter is not settled; it must be further adjudicated.
After the group of six bhikṣus had spoken these words, the dispute arose once more, and they remained in discord.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you indeed, after knowing that the Saṃgha had settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, initiate it again?
He replied, “It is true.”
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason is this so?
He replied:
"I employ such skillful means as these for the sake of pleasure.
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
"To disturb those who practice the holy life is an evil deed.
How can this be considered pleasure?
The Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus:
“Have you not often heard me praise those who practice the holy life through countless skillful means, saying that they should constantly practice loving-kindness in body, speech, and mind?”
"You should always have shown respect.
Why do you now commit such an evil deed?
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a legal dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, should nevertheless reopen it and say:
"This formal act (kamma) was not concluded; it must be performed again."
"If the circumstances are not otherwise [than stated], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
The Sangha consists of eight types, as explained above.
Disputes are of four kinds:
disputes involving verbal accusations, disputes involving slander, disputes involving offenses, and disputes concerning routine matters.
Regarding the settling of disputes in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya: among the seven methods for settling disputes, each is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If, after a dispute has been settled, one raises it again based on the same circumstances without any change in the underlying cause, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
The "four disputes" are: disputes involving mutual verbal abuse, disputes involving slander, disputes involving offenses, and disputes concerning matters of constant practice.
Regarding disputes arising from mutual accusations, they are to be settled by means of each of the three *vinayas*.
What are these three?

They are settlement through the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*), settlement through the *vinaya* of searching for the truth (*tatsvabhāva-śodhana-vinaya*), and settlement through the *vinaya* of spreading grass (*tṛṇa-prastāraka-vinaya*).

Regarding the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling and disputing with one another; they lived together in discord, speaking words contrary to the Dharma, words contrary to the Vinaya, and words regarding what is not an offense, what is a grave offense, and what is a light offense; they spoke of what is curable and what is incurable; they performed formal acts (*karmans*) that were contrary to the Dharma—both those that were legitimate formal acts and those that were illegitimate formal acts—and they performed what should be done and what should not be done.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu in the assembly spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs! This is not the Dharma, it is not the Vinaya;

it is inconsistent with the Sūtras, inconsistent with the Vinaya, and inconsistent with the Upadeśas. It contradicts the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Upadeśas, and gives rise to all manner of defilements and outflows."

As I have taught, these are the Dharma, these are the Vinaya, and these are the Buddha’s teachings; they accord with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Upadeśas, and give rise to no defilements or outflows.
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sirs!
I am unable to settle this dispute.
I shall go to Śrāvastī to the place where the World-Honored One resides and inquire how this matter of the dispute is to be settled."
When that bhikṣu had arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are quarreling and disputing with one another; they dwell together in disharmony, contending over what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and so forth. Since I am unable to settle this dispute, I have come to the World-Honored One’s presence to inquire how this dispute may be settled.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will extinguish this dispute for the sake of the bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
“Go to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, extinguish this dispute.”
This refers to the settlement through *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of). Upāli!
Disputes arise from three sources:
Whether it be a single person, a group, or the Saṃgha, this dispute should likewise be settled in three ways, resolved in three ways, and extinguished in three ways. Upāli!
Go to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī and, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, settle this dispute through what is called the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties).
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many qualities must a bhikṣu possess to be able to extinguish such a dispute?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
“A bhikṣu who accomplishes five qualities is able to extinguish disputes.
What are these five?

One knows that this is real and not unreal, beneficial and not non-beneficial, that one has found companions and not failed to find companions, that one has found equal companions and not failed to find equal companions, and that one has found the right time and not failed to find the right time.
Upāli! If one settles matters at an improper time— whether it be a schism in the Saṃgha, a dispute within the Saṃgha, or a division of the Saṃgha—
and if one can extinguish the dispute when the proper time has arrived, then the Saṃgha will not be split, will not dispute, and will not be dispersed.
These are the five qualities by which a bhikṣu, having accomplished them, is able to extinguish disputes and is loved, remembered, and praised by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.

Now, go to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī and settle the matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching—namely, by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties).
At that time, the Venerable Upāli, having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, went to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī and said: "Elders!
Return to the place where that dispute arose; it should be settled there. Do not resolve the matter here."
"Why is this? Because the community of monks here is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; they dwell together in a single training. You should not disturb them.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī said to the Venerable Upāli:
"Venerable Sir!
If I were able to settle this matter of dispute there, I would not have come here.
I only pray that the Venerable One will go there for my sake and settle this dispute."
Upāli said: "If I were to go there, I would perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for those who require it, and I would impose punishment upon those who deserve it."

"You should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), the *prasādanīya-karman* (act of appeasement), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the *utkṣepanīya-karman* (act of suspension), the *parivāsa-karman* (act of probation), the *mānatva-karman* (act of penance), and the *ābhāṣaṇīya-karman* (act of rehabilitation). Should there be such-and-such faults, I shall treat you with such-and-such *karman*; at that time, you must not harbor dissatisfaction in your hearts."
The messenger bhikṣu said to the Venerable Upāli:
"If we have such faults, we shall accept such disciplinary measures; our minds will have no dissatisfaction."
Then the Venerable Upāli again went to the Buddha’s presence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one wishes to extinguish the dispute of those bhikṣus, how should one apply the mind?”
The Buddha told Upāli:

“One who wishes to extinguish a dispute should first deliberate upon their own physical strength, the power of merit, the power of eloquence, and the power of fearlessness; they must understand the causal origins of the matter. A bhikṣu should first reflect for himself whether he possesses such powers as these.”

Furthermore, since this matter of dispute has arisen but recently and this person’s mind is pliant and gentle, the dispute can be easily extinguished; at that time, this bhikṣu should effect the settlement of the dispute.

If one reflects upon one's own supreme powers and realizes that the dispute has already persisted for a long time and the person involved is so stubborn as to be impossible to subdue immediately, one should seek out a monk of great virtue to help resolve this matter together.
If there is no bhikṣu of great virtue, one should seek a bhikṣu of extensive learning;
if there is none of extensive learning, one should seek a bhikṣu who dwells in the forest (āraṇyaka);
if there is no bhikṣu who dwells in the forest, one should seek a lay follower (upāsaka) of great power.
When those quarreling bhikṣus see the upāsaka, they feel shame and remorse, and the matter of dispute is easily settled.

Furthermore, if such an upāsaka is not present, they should seek out a king or a powerful minister; when those quarreling bhikṣus see this person of influence and power, they feel awe and respect, and the matter of dispute is easily settled.

If this dispute is to be settled during the winter, it should be dealt with in a place that is sheltered from the wind, free from the cold, and warm; should visiting bhikṣus arrive, one should provide them with a brazier.
If it is during the spring season, one should provide a bed or seat beneath a tree in a cool place, serve cold water and thin gruel for drink, and fan them with a fan.
If it is during the summer season, one should provide a high and cool place and supply whatever is required at the appropriate times.

At that time, one capable bhikṣu should be appointed—one who is wise, understands the causes and conditions of affairs, is not timid, does not seek out the faults of others, and is not afraid of the assembly.
If a lay follower (upāsaka) comes, you should praise for him the merits of the harmonious Sangha.
Then speak to the lay follower:
"As the World-Honored One has said, there is one dharma that, when it appears in the world, causes suffering and distress for devas and humans, and causes devas and humans to lose their benefits."
What is called this one dharma? It is to cause dissension within the Saṃgha.
When the body perishes at the end of life, one enters directly into hell.
Furthermore, O upāsaka!
As the Blessed One has said, there is one dharma that, when it appears in the world, brings peace and happiness to gods and humans, and brings benefit to gods and humans.
That which is called this one dharma is the harmony of the Saṅgha.
Upon the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn in a good destination, among gods or humans.
"In this way, an upāsaka who wishes to attain great merit should bring the Saṃgha into harmony.
When the two groups speak these words, that bhikṣu should carefully examine the matter, taking up the meaning and flavor of their words, phrases, and syllables.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among those seated who was not a *tala-tāla* bhikṣu, yet he assumed the appearance of a *tala-tāla* bhikṣu and spoke these words:
"Listen, venerable sirs!"
When one speaks such words now that were not consistent with what was said previously,
if this person is by nature gentle and susceptible to being subdued, they should be addressed within the Saṃgha to cause them shame.
"You have acted improperly by engaging in discordant matters and holding discordant views.
It is for this reason that the Saṃgha has assembled here today.
If the person is wicked and of a harsh, violent disposition, and is likely to increase the dispute, one should speak to them with gentle words:
"Elder! The Saṃgha has assembled today for the purpose of settling this matter; I shall act as your companion, and together we shall harmoniously resolve this dispute."
When that bhikṣu’s mind has become supple, the monastic adjudicator shall say to the bhikṣu involved in the matter:
“Now, bring this matter forward.”
This bhikṣu speaks thus:
"I now bring this matter forward; I pray that the Saṃgha will grant me a judgment in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
At that time, one should reprimand this person to induce shame and should say:
"You are not well-versed; how could there be a legal or disciplinary decision made by the Saṃgha that is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya?
If that bhikṣu says:
"I have never spoken within the Saṃgha; I pray that the Saṃgha will instruct me in the proper procedures."
At that time, one should instruct him to say:
"I now emerge from the causes and conditions of this dispute; I shall follow and practice according to the Sangha's instructions.
If that bhikṣu does not comply with the Sangha’s words, one should further say to him:
"If you do not accept the Sangha's instruction, I shall cast a tally among the Sangha to expel you from the assembly.
If that bhikṣu still does not comply with these words, then an upāsaka should be sent at that time to ask the bhikṣu:
"Will you comply with the Sangha's instruction?"
"If you do not comply, I shall grant you the status of a layperson and expel you from the village and city.
Knowing the matter of dispute concerning this bhikṣu, if it is a minor dispute, the Saṃgha shall settle it in the presence of the upāsaka.

If it is a matter of base or defiling conduct, once the lay follower has been consoled and dismissed, the Saṃgha shall, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Sūtras, settle the case by applying the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement before the eyes) according to the facts of the matter.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Regarding what is called 'extinction through presence' (sammukhavinaya), why is it named 'extinction through presence'?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Regarding matters of dispute among bhikṣus: what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya; what is an offense and what is not an offense; what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; what is an offense that can be remedied and what is an offense that cannot be remedied; what is a formal act (kamma) in accordance with the Dharma and what is a formal act contrary to the Dharma; what is a formal act performed by a harmonious assembly and what is a formal act performed by a disharmonious assembly; and what formal acts ought to be performed and what formal acts ought not to be performed.”
Ānanda! If such a matter should arise, you should quickly assemble the Saṃgha.

Having quickly assembled the Saṃgha, investigate this matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Sūtra; then, in accordance with the facts of the case, apply the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face settlement) to resolve it.
If one accomplishes five kinds of illegal acts, the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) is not established.
What are the five?

Granting it without being present, not questioning [the accused], not accepting the transgression, not according with the Dharma, and granting it without concord—these are called the five illegal acts by which the *sammukhavinaya* is not established.
If five factors are accomplished according to the Dharma, the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) is established.
What are these five?

Granting in the presence, questioning, accepting the transgression, being in accordance with the Dharma, and granting through harmony—these are called the five factors that, when accomplished, establish the *saṃmukhavinaya*.
Thus it is, Ānanda!

When a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya*, if there are visiting bhikṣus, departing bhikṣus, bhikṣus who have given their consent, bhikṣus who saw [the assembly] but did not give their consent, newly ordained bhikṣus, or bhikṣus who were asleep during the sitting, and these bhikṣus say: "This is an improper *karmavācanā*;
it is separate from the Buddha, separate from the Dharma, and separate from the Saṃgha; it is like a herd of cattle or sheep; it is an unskillful *karmavācanā*, and the *karma* is not accomplished."
“Ānanda! To thus instigate [the matter] again constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; this is called a dispute by means of signs and words.

Regarding the settling of disputes through slander by means of the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*: if a bhikṣu has not seen, heard, or suspected that another bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *vinayātikrama*—yet slanders him with these five categories of offenses—this is called a dispute through slander.
Two *vinayas* are used for its settlement: namely, settlement by *smṛtivinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness) and settlement by *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict based on sanity).
Regarding *smṛtivinaya*: while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣuṇī Mādrī engaged in unchaste conduct and subsequently became pregnant.
He went to where the group of six bhikṣus were and said to them:
"I have engaged in unchaste conduct and am now pregnant.
With whom do you have a grievance? I can slander him."
The group of six replied:
"Excellent, sisters!
You wish to perform a beneficial service for us."
“Dabba Mallaputta is our enemy; he gave us a dilapidated dwelling, poor bedding and mats, and coarse, unwholesome food.
If this man remains a long-term practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya), we shall suffer for a long night.”
"Look at this bhikṣu who stands among the great assembly when the Dharma is being preached on the day of the fast; you should go into that crowd and slander him for practicing non-celibacy.
He replied, "I shall do as the Venerable One instructs."
When the great assembly preaches the Dharma on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the month, that bhikṣuṇī shall go before the assembly and say:
"Venerable ones!..."
"Prepare for me ghee, oil, non-glutinous rice, and various foods and drinks; thoroughly repair the dwelling; and seek out women to assist in childbirth, for the time of my delivery has arrived."
The Elder replied: "Sisters!
You know for yourselves that I have done no such thing."
The bhikṣuṇī spoke again:
“How extraordinary!
How extraordinary!”
"You are a man who departs in the morning and returns at night to engage in our business together;
yet now you say, 'I have done nothing of the sort. Do not speak further."
"However, you must prepare the ghee and other necessities for me, as my time for delivery has now arrived.
The Elder spoke again: "Sister!"
"You yourself know that I have no such thing.
Thus he spoke three times and departed.
At that time, those among the assembly who were faithless thought to themselves:
"Both of these men are young; there must certainly be such a matter.
Those who are loyal and faithful all gave rise to doubt as to whether it existed or not.
Those of superior faith then said:
"This Venerable One has already extinguished the three poisons; evil dharmas have been forever exhausted for him—such a thing could not happen.
At that time, however, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta engaged in unchaste conduct; his ill repute spread abroad, being heard in private places, heard by many people, and heard within the Saṅgha.
The bhikṣus reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus!
"This Dabba Mallaputta has engaged in un-Brahmin conduct, and his ill repute has spread.
You should question him three times in private, three times before a large group of people, and three times within the Saṃgha."
Regarding "questioning in private," one should ask as follows:
"Venerable Dharmaruci!
Does the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī know this matter regarding what she has said?"
Then the Elder said:
"I do not know that I did it, nor do I remember having done it.
Thus he was questioned a second and a third time.
Among the great multitude, he asked three times in the same manner.
Then, in the midst of the Saṃgha, he asked, saying:
"Venerable Elder Dabba Mallaputta!"
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrābhūmi said, "Do you know whether this was done?
She replied,
"I do not know that it was done, nor do I remember doing it."
The second and third inquiries were likewise made.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of this matter:
"Venerable Dabba Mallaputta has already been questioned three times in private, three times in the midst of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha."
He himself said:
"I do not know that I acted; I do not remember having acted.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Dabba Mallaputta is pure and blameless; it was the Bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā who confessed her own offense, and she should be expelled.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha were dissatisfied with the Blessed One and spoke thus:
"Look at this adjudication, which is unjust! Both have committed an offense; why is it that the bhikṣu is left alone while the bhikṣuṇī is expelled?"
"If both are guilty, they should both be expelled; if both are innocent, they should both be left as they are.
Why, World-Honored One, do you expel one and leave the other?
For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and summon the community of bhikṣuṇīs from Rājagṛha.
"So be it, World-Honored One! [he replied].
At that time, Ānanda went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said to them:
"Sisters! The World-Honored One calls for you."
Then the bhikṣuṇī said to the Venerable Ānanda, "I have no business or occasion with the World-Honored One; for what reason do you call me?
If there were a matter or occasion, I would go of my own accord without being called."
"The Venerable One has returned; I have no business that would allow me to go.
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:
"This is truly extraordinary! Having received the grace of the World-Honored One, I have been able to leave the household life to practice the Way."
"Why did he fail to give rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha and fail to follow his instructions?
At that time, Ānanda returned to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and say to the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha:
'You have committed an offense; the World-Honored One commands you to depart and not remain here.'"
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said to them:
"Sisters! You have committed an offense;
the World-Honored One has commanded you to depart and not remain here."
The bhikṣuṇī replied to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I have no business outside the city walls, so I am unable to go; furthermore, if I had any business, I would not wait for an order to go on my own."
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"How extraordinary!
By the grace of the World-Honored One, I have been able to leave the household life to pursue the Way."
"How can it be that he does not give rise to a heart of reverence for the Buddha?
When called to come, he does not come; when sent away, he does not go.
Ānanda immediately returned to the Buddha's presence, prostrated himself at his feet, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If, in a city or village, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha calls upon the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs and they do not come, or if he sends them away and they do not depart, the Tathāgata himself shall withdraw."
“Ānanda! Bring me my saṃghāṭī.

Then the Venerable Ānanda immediately handed over the saṃghāṭī, and at that time the World-Honored One did not speak to the community of bhikṣus, but took only Ānanda as he passed through the village of the Pañcābhijña-gahapati on his way toward Śrāvastī.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, having murdered his father the king, was deeply tormented by grief and distress; every day he went to the World-Honored One three times—to pay homage at dawn, at midday, and in the late afternoon—to repent.
Having performed his morning repentance, he returned at midday; not seeing the World-Honored One, he immediately asked the bhikṣus where the World-Honored One was.
The bhikṣus replied, "The World-Honored One has already departed."
The king spoke thus:
"Whenever the World-Honored One travels for a month or half a month, he always speaks to me; for what reason does he now depart in silence?"
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they immediately replied, "Great King!
The bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha do not follow the commands of the World-Honored One; when summoned, they do not come, and when sent away, they do not go."

Thus, Great King, you should know that if the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is told by the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in a city or village to come or not to come, or to depart or not to depart, the Tathāgata will simply withdraw of his own accord.
"Now the community of bhikṣuṇīs in Rājagṛha does not follow the Buddha's teaching; for this reason, the World-Honored One has departed in silence.
Upon hearing these words, the king became extremely incensed and commanded his ministers:
"All bhikṣuṇīs currently within my realm must be driven out!"
At that time, a wise minister immediately admonished the king, saying:
"It is not the case that all bhikṣuṇīs within the realm have committed offenses; rather, it is only the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha who have transgressed the instruction of the World-Honored One."
The king immediately followed the minister’s words and issued an edict to all the officials to expel the bhikṣuṇīs from Rājagṛha.

At that time, the officials all seized clubs, wooden staves, clods of earth, tiles, and stones, beating and hurling them at the bhikṣuṇīs as they drove them out of the city, rebuking them with these words:
“You wretched and evil women!”
"By the grace of the World-Honored One, I have been able to leave the household life to pursue the Way; yet you show me no respect and act in opposition to the Buddha's teachings.
Get out quickly and sit elsewhere!
You wretched old woman, you have prevented me from seeing the World-Honored One and hearing the True Dharma. All of you, get out at once; you may not remain here."
At that time, when the people of the streets and alleys saw this, they all cursed from afar, saying:
"Since you have even caused me not to see the World-Honored One nor hear the True Dharma, you must depart quickly; you may not remain here!"
At that time, Udāyin also took up his staff and drove the bhikṣuṇīs out, rebuking them as described above.
The King commanded his ministers:
"Observe the bhikṣuṇīs; if they follow behind the World-Honored One, you must provide them with protection so that they may travel in safety."
"If you go elsewhere, you may do as you please; there is no need for protection.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had left the city, they each said to one another:
"If we go to other regions, we shall be driven out wherever we go and will have nowhere to stay."
"We shall now follow behind the World-Honored One.
At dawn, the World-Honored One set out from his location, and by evening the bhikṣuṇīs arrived there.
In this manner, they were always one day behind him on the road.
At that time, wishing to convert and deliver them, the World-Honored One passed through the village of the Five-Supernormal-Powers Householder and headed toward Śrāvastī.

It was the constant custom of the Five-Supernormal-Powers Householder that whenever he heard that the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs was approaching from one yojana away, he would go out to welcome them and provide various kinds of offerings.

At that time, when the householder with five supernatural powers heard that these bhikṣuṇīs were coming, he immediately entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to observe them: for what cause and condition had the bhikṣuṇīs come?

Having observed them, he saw that all those bhikṣuṇīs were guilty of transgressions; they had all been expelled and punished, yet they had not attained liberation from their faults. They were not pure vessels and possessed no share in the noble Dharma.
Having made this observation, she did not go out to meet them or provide any offerings.
The bhikṣuṇīs, having inquired after one another, arrived at her door and said, "The bhikṣuṇīs from Rājagṛha are now outside the gate; let the laywoman know."

The householder immediately commanded his attendants to provide a dilapidated house and worn-out bedding, but he did not supply warm water for washing the feet nor oil for anointing them; he gave no non-time-appropriate drinks, nor did he inquire after him or offer words of comfort, and he did not light lamps at night.
At dawn the next day, they again failed to provide tooth-sticks and pure water; instead, they gave them coarse food and drink, and after they had eaten, sent them away in haste.
Once the bhikṣuṇīs had gone outside, they said to one another:
"We have heard that this layperson has always possessed faith and respectfully made offerings to the Saṃgha, yet judging by what we see now, he has neither faith nor respect."
Among them, a bhikṣuṇī said to the people,
"Stop! Stop!"
"Auntie! You should examine yourselves; we have exceeded our proper measure by receiving these offerings while contravening the World-Honored One’s instructions.
The bhikṣuṇīs gradually proceeded forward until they reached Śrāvastī, where they went to Ānanda, prostrated themselves at his feet, stood to one side, and said to Ānanda:

“We wish to see the World-Honored One to pay our respects, visit him, and inquire after his well-being. We pray that you will inform the World-Honored One on behalf of the community of bhikṣuṇīs, so that he may compassionately grant us permission.
Ānanda replied, “Excellent, sisters!”
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The community of bhikṣuṇīs from Rājagṛha wishes to come to pay their respects to the World-Honored One!”
"Let the listener be commanded to come forward.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not allow the community of bhikṣuṇīs from Rājagṛha to come and see me."
Ānanda said, “Excellent!
He prostrated to the Buddha and immediately returned; arriving at the place where the bhikṣuṇīs were, he told them:
"Sisters! The World-Honored One has given this instruction: 'I do not permit you to come before me.
A second and third time he spoke thus.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“For what reason are you so earnestly concerned for the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I do not form the notion that she is a bhikṣuṇī. Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One does not come when summoned and does not go when sent away,
there is a further principle in the World-Honored One’s words when he speaks of "the community of bhikṣuṇīs in Rājagṛha."
"Because it concerns the Saṅgha, I am therefore earnest.
The Buddha said,
"I permit [the assembly] to stand before the Bhikṣuṇī Saṅgha of Rājagṛha."
Ānanda immediately returned to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said to them:
"Sisters! You have gained a great benefit; the World-Honored One has permitted you to approach him."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they all exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!"
They immediately went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, and stood to one side. Addressing the Buddha, they said:
“World-Honored One!

We have been unskilled, like children who are foolish and ignorant; we did not recognize the field of merit, we did not know how to repay your nurturing kindness, and we did not accept the World-Honored One’s teaching.”
"I now recognize and see my transgression; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my confession.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha:
"You have acted improperly, like children who are foolish, ignorant of the field of merit, and unaware of the kindness shown to you."
The World-Honored One calls you but you do not come; he sends you away but you do not go. Now that you have seen your own fault, I grant you permission to repent.
In the Noble Dharma, those who are able to repent increase their roots of goodness.
"From this day forward, do not do so again.
If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha summons the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha according to the Dharma, the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha ought to come immediately in accordance with the Dharma.
If she does not come, she incurs an offense of *vibhinī*.
The community of bhikṣus should prohibit the community of bhikṣuṇīs from performing their *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*; if she arrives, they must not allow her to enter the gate.
If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha lawfully summons many Bhikṣuṇīs, or calls a single Bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise.
If the many Bhikṣus lawfully summon them, the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha should, according to the Dharma, come immediately.
If she does not come, one commits an offense of *vibhāṣā-vinaya*.
One should obstruct this bhikṣuṇī from participating in the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*; if she arrives, she must not be permitted to enter the gate.
If many bhikṣus summon many bhikṣuṇīs according to the Dharma, or summon a single bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise.

If a single bhikṣu summons the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, or many bhikṣuṇīs, or a single bhikṣuṇī according to the Dharma, the bhikṣuṇīs should come immediately; if they do not come, they incur an offense of violating the Vinaya (vibhāṣā-āpatti).
One should prohibit this bhikṣuṇī from participating in the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*; if she comes, one must not allow her to enter the gate.

Whether it be a community of bhikṣuṇīs, a group of many bhikṣuṇīs, or a single bhikṣuṇī, the method for confessing before a community of bhikṣus, a group of many bhikṣus, or a single bhikṣu is as explained in detail previously in the section on the method for confessing before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma in accordance with their needs for the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Then, one bhikṣuṇī attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You may now depart; return by the same path you came. If the lay follower Pañcābhijña has anything to say, you should receive and practice it."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha immediately returned to the village of Pañcābhijña.

Then the householder of Pañcābhijña entered meditative concentration and perceived through his vision that these bhikṣuṇīs had already repented before the Buddha and were all purified, having become accomplished vessels of the Dharma.

At that time, the householder with five supernatural powers, following his usual custom, drove a carriage drawn by a white stallion for one *yojana* to meet them. Seeing the community of bhikṣuṇīs from afar, he descended from the carriage and proceeded on foot; baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms, he said:
"Welcome, Ayyās!"
"Are you not exhausted from walking the path?
The householder then requested that the bhikṣuṇīs walk ahead while he followed behind them on their return.

Upon arriving at his home, he provided them with a fine new room, bedding, and requisites; he gave them warm water for washing their feet, oil for anointing their feet, and non-timely gruel. At dusk, he lit lamps and, greeting them with words of comfort, asked after their well-being, saying: [The text continues with the standard formula for the *pātimokkha* recitation.]
“Sister! May you dwell in peace.
The next morning, he provided her with a tooth-stick and water for rinsing, gave her various kinds of gruel, and at the proper time, offered her suitable food and drink.
Having finished eating, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed her, saying:

"I now invite you, Noble Lady, to observe the summer retreat. I shall provide all necessities of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for illness; I shall also teach you to receive instruction and recite the sūtras and verses, with the sole exception of the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* ceremonies."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:

"Today is already the twelfth day of the fourth month; the summer retreat is drawing near, and furthermore, the World-Honored One has commanded that we must accept the words of the householder Pañcābhijña."
Having reflected thus, she accepted the invitation for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Every day, the householder explained the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) to the bhikṣuṇīs. Having heard this Dharma, the bhikṣuṇīs practiced the Noble Path with diligence and without slackening during both the first and last watches of the night; they cultivated it until they achieved realization and attained its fruit.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had finished receiving the invitation for mutual admonition (pravāraṇā), they said:
"We should go to the World-Honored One to pay our respects, inquire after his well-being, and personally declare our fruits of realization.

Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇīs set out toward Śrāvastī and went to where Ānanda was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four foundations of mindfulness to us śrāvakas; we have practiced the Noble Path with diligence and without slackening during the first and last watches of the night, thereby achieving its cultivation and attaining realization.”
Having spoken these words, he returned to his dwelling.

Not long after the community of bhikṣuṇīs had departed, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then reported in full to the World-Honored One everything that the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha had said, up to their cultivation of the path and attainment of realization.
After the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What is the meaning of this?
I only pray that you will explain it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What these bhikṣuṇīs have said is true and without error. Why is this?

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are able to diligently practice the four foundations of mindfulness, they will all achieve and realize them, as explained in detail in the *Sūtra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness*.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do the bhikṣuṇīs of Rājagṛha fail to recognize the Buddha's kindness?"
They came to the city of Śrāvastī and went to where Ānanda was; not seeing the World-Honored One there, they had Udāyin seize their staffs and drive them away.
Venerable Ānanda earnestly entreated for their rescue, saying, "I only pray that you will explain this."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have not only failed to recognize my kindness today; when Udāyin seized his staff and drove them away, Ānanda earnestly pleaded for their rescue."
"In past ages it was already thus, as explained in detail in the *Nāgapūrvajanma-sūtra*.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
From the second part of the ninety-two matters concerning the *Pratideśanīya* offenses: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, there was in the city the house of a wealthy courtesan, which abounded in riches and treasures of every kind; its storehouses were overflowing and its defenses so secure that no external thief could find an opportunity to enter.
At that time, there was a leader of bandits who was skilled in employing expedient means. He sent a messenger to speak to the courtesan, saying:
"We wish to go to a certain pond and invite many courtesans to prepare various foods and drinks, so that we may enjoy ourselves to our heart's content."
"You must adorn yourself well before going to that pond; do not appear unattractive and risk being ridiculed by her.

With jealousy foremost in her heart, the woman adorned her body with famous garments, fine clothes, pearls, and necklaces. Arrayed in various ornaments that dazzled the eyes with their brilliance, she went to respond to the invitation.
Then this ringleader of the bandits used skillful means to lead them away to a secluded and deep hiding place.
There, the courtesan asked, "Where are the women you previously invited now?"
He replied, "She will arrive in a moment; for now, let us enjoy ourselves.
At that time, the courtesan thought to herself:
"I observe this person now and there is no doubt he is a thief.
How do I know this? This is not the place where we originally intended to meet."
Furthermore, none of the women came at all.
As the day drew toward evening, the courtesan said,
“I wish to return home.”
The leader of the bandits replied, "Enjoy yourself for a while; why such haste?
At that time, the woman reflected:
"This man is certainly acting as a thief and will surely be trapped by him.
I possess sixty-four kinds of marvelous arts; now is precisely the time for them.
If I do not employ them, how can he be saved?"
At that time, the woman feigned an alluring and affectionate appearance, clinking cups with the bandit as if drinking wine herself, and urged him to finish his.

She appeared outwardly diligent, flirtatious, and intimate, while inwardly remaining aloof; she caused the bandit’s mind to become infatuated and delighted, so that he no longer harbored any suspicion.
Then the bandit leader took the courtesan alone to a secluded place; the effects of the wine soon took hold, and she became so intoxicated that she was unconscious of her surroundings.
The woman slowly withdrew her body from the bandit, gathered up her bundle and finery, and set out for Śrāvastī.
The city gates were already closed, and as he turned toward the Jetavana, the monastery gates were likewise closed.
At that time, outside the gate, there was an elder bhikṣu named Kālu, who was not far from the entrance; sitting on a rope-bench in a secluded spot, his robes hung down to the four sides.
This courtesan, coming from a place of terror toward a place of safety, entered beneath the Elder’s bed.
At that time, Kāḷu had entered into samādhi and did not perceive her beneath the bed.
After midnight, the bandits awoke from their intoxication and wished to strip the courtesan, but though they searched for her, she was nowhere to be seen.
The bandit leader asked his companions,
"Did any of you see this woman?"
They all replied, "We do not see it.
Each took up a torch and searched, but they did not know its location at all; they then said to one another:
"If he cannot be found in this manner, one should seek his footprints.
He then followed the tracks to the gate of Śrāvastī.
The gate was closed, so he continued following the tracks until he reached the entrance of the Jeta Grove, where he lost the trail and did not know which way to go.
Although the bandits saw this bhikṣu, they harbored no suspicion.
At that time, dawn gradually broke; within the city of Śrāvastī, the morning drum had already been struck, and the sounds of elephants, horses, roosters, and dogs could be heard.
At that time, the bandit leader said to his companions, "We have now lost this woman and do not know her whereabouts.
As dawn is about to break, it is not fitting to remain here for long; we should return to our hiding places in the forest."
Having had this thought, he immediately returned to the forest.

At dawn, the city’s people—with their elephants, horses, and carriages—came out of the city, as did the various upāsakas. After they had paid homage to the World-Honored One and passed by to pay respects to the bhikṣu Kālu, they saw this courtesan emerge from beneath the bed. Upon seeing this, the crowd all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"This forest-dweller (āraṇyaka), who wears rag-robes and begs for alms, has spent the entire night engaged in affairs with a courtesan and only releases her at dawn!"
"He has lost the dharma of a śramaṇa;
what path does he possess?
At that time, the elder Bhikṣu Dharmaruci Kālo became notorious for his ugliness.
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they reported it in full to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus!
This bhikṣu Dharmadinnā has spread an ill repute regarding his non-celibate conduct."
"You should ask three times in a private place, three times among a group of many people, and three times within the Saṃgha.
As for asking in a private place, one should ask as follows:
"Venerable Dabba Mallaputta!"
When fellow practitioners of the holy life say, "Do you know of this matter?
he replies, "I do not know that I did it, nor do I remember having done it."
In this manner, the second and third times were likewise asked; among many people he asked three times, and among the Saṃgha he also asked three times.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

This bhikṣu, Dabba Mallaputta, has already been questioned three times in private, three times before a group of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha, yet he himself says that he does not know [the offense] and does not remember having committed it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta is pure and without fault; the Saṃgha should grant him the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) and he shall dwell together with the community in purity.”
Having performed the *jñapti-karman* for seeking permission, the one performing the *karman* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This is the Elder Dabba Mallaputta."
Fellow practitioners of the holy life have spoken thus, saying that they themselves do not know of having committed [an offense] and do not remember having committed it.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Elder Dabba Mallaputta request from the Saṃgha the settlement through the *paṭiññātakara-vinaya* (settlement by admission), so that he may dwell in purity.
Venerable sirs, listen!

This bhikṣu Dharmadinnaka wishes to request from the Saṃgha the settlement of a dispute through the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) so that he may dwell in purity. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the one who requests the formal act (*yācanaka*): the bhikṣu Dharmadatta shall bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and speak as follows:
"I, the bhikṣu Dharmadatta, have been addressed by my fellow practitioners of the holy life thus: 'I do not know that I have done it; I do not remember having done it.'"
I, Dabba Kāla, now request from the Saṅgha the settlement through *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) so that I may dwell in purity.
I only pray that the Saṅgha grant me the settlement through *sativinaya* so that I may dwell in purity.
In this manner, he requests a second and third time.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Elder Dabba Mallaputta, regarding whom fellow practitioners of the holy life have spoken thus, has declared himself that he neither knows nor remembers having committed [an offense].
He has already requested from the Saṅgha the *pātimokkha-thāpana* (suspension of the recitation) through the *sativinaya* (settlement by mindfulness), and he dwells in purity.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant the elder Dabba Mallaputta the *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) so that he may dwell in purity.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Regarding this Elder Dabba Mallaputta, his fellow practitioners of the holy life have said this: he himself says that he does not know of having committed [an offense] and does not recall having committed one.
He has already requested from the Saṅgha the *pātimokkha* procedure for the sake of recollection (*sativinaya*) to extinguish [the accusation], and he dwells in purity.
The Saṃgha now grants the elder Dabba Mallaputta the *paṭiññātakara-vinaya* for the purpose of settling the matter; he shall dwell in purity.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to granting the elder Dabba Mallaputta the *paṭiññātakara-vinaya* so that he may dwell in purity, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said for the second and third times.

"The Saṃgha has already granted the elder Dabba Mallaputta the *pātimokkha-thāpana* through the *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection) so that he may dwell in purity. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
“Have you already granted the *smṛtivinaya* to Dabba Mallaputta?
They replied: [“We have.”]
“It has already been granted.
The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu accomplishes five qualities, it is an illegal granting of the *smṛtivinaya*.”

What are the five? Giving while perceiving what is impure as pure; giving while perceiving what is pure as impure; not having first investigated; acting contrary to the Dharma; and acting without harmony. These are called the five unlawful ways of granting the *smṛtivinaya*.
There are five ways of legitimately granting the *smṛtivinaya*.

What are the five? Granting it when one is pure and perceives oneself as pure; granting it when one is impure and perceives oneself as impure; having first investigated the matter; acting in accordance with the Dharma; and acting in concord.
