These are called the five ways of legitimately granting the *smṛtivinaya*.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“How is it, World-Honored One,
that this lustful woman was pursued by bandits?”
The Buddha said, "It is not only today that he was pursued by bandits; in past lives as well, he was once pursued by them, as is explained in detail in the *Vairāṭyapūrvajanma-sūtra*."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is called the *smṛtivinaya*?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu slanders another bhikṣu regarding a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *vinayātikrama*, the Saṃgha should be assembled immediately."
Having quickly assembled the Saṃgha, he asks that bhikṣu’s preceptors, ācāryas, and fellow companions, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
You know that this certain bhikṣu previously lived among people; what was his conduct regarding the precepts like?"
"With whom do you have acquaintances?
Are those acquaintances good or evil? If he says:

"Such-and-such a person has previously maintained the precepts with pure conduct; though they committed minor offenses along with their virtuous friends and companions, they felt shame and remorse in their hearts and swiftly eliminated them through repentance."
"In such a case, the Saṃgha should grant the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of recollection).
If one says:

'I know that this bhikṣu’s previous conduct regarding the precepts was impure, and furthermore, he associated with evil companions; having committed an offense, he was unable to repent according to the Dharma.'"
"Ānanda! In such a case, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus should not grant the smṛtivinaya for the settlement of the dispute.
Thus it is, Ānanda!"

When a legal dispute has been settled through a *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, if there are visiting monks (*āgantuka*), departing monks (*prakrānta*), monks who have granted their consent (*chanda*), monks who saw [the act] but did not grant consent, monks who were asleep during the assembly, or newly ordained monks, and these monks say:

"This *karmavācanā* was performed unaccomplished, contrary to the Dharma, foolish, and lacking wisdom; it is separate from the Buddha, separate from the Dharma, and separate from the Saṃgha, just like the ill-performed and unaccomplished ritual of cattle and sheep."
If one initiates such [a claim] again, it is an offense of *pāyattika*; this is called the settlement of a dispute through denigration by means of the *smṛtivinaya*.
What is the settlement of a dispute through denigration by means of the *amūḍhavinaya*?
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
The Venerable Kapphiṇa had two co-practicing disciples:
one named Nandi and the other named Paṭinandika.
These two bhikṣus were formerly afflicted by madness; while they were ill, they committed various kinds of unrighteous acts.
Now that they have recovered, fellow practitioners of the holy life still continue to speak of what they did during their period of insanity.
When these two bhikṣus heard these words, they were filled with shame.
For this reason, they spoke of it to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Nandika and Upanandika were originally insane; while they were ill, they committed various kinds of unrighteous acts.
Now that their insanity has been cured, fellow practitioners of the holy life still speak of the things they did when they were insane."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should ask three times in private, three times before a group of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha.
As for asking in private, one should speak as follows:
“Venerable sir!
Do you know what these fellow practitioners of the holy life are saying?
He replied:
"I do not know that I have done it, nor do I remember having done it.
Thus, he was asked three times among many people, and likewise three times before the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, saying:

"He has been questioned three times in private, three times before a group of many, and three times before the Saṃgha, yet he himself says that he does not know [what he did] and does not remember having done it."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"These two bhikṣus were ignorant in the past, but they are not ignorant now. Regarding the conduct they engaged in during their former ignorance, those who practice the holy life say that they themselves do not know what they did and do not remember having done it."
The Saṃgha should grant him the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one who was not insane) as an act of reconciliation.
To perform this rite, one should carry out the *jñapti-karman* (motion for formal approval), announcing:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

These elders, Nandiya and Upanandiya, were formerly deluded but are no longer deluded now; those who practice the holy life speak of their former deluded conduct, and they themselves say they did not know what they did and do not remember having done it.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is ready, let the venerable ones listen! The bhikṣus Nandiya and Paṭinandiya wish to request from the Saṃgha the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of one who is no longer insane) for their own extinction of the offense.
May the venerable ones grant their attention!
"Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. Regarding the procedure for requesting [the *amūḍha-vinaya*]:
Nanda and Upananda, having bared their right shoulders, knelt on their right knees with palms joined, spoke as follows: "I, so-and-so, was formerly deluded but am now no longer deluded.
My fellow practitioners of the holy life have spoken of my former deluded conduct; I did not know that I had done it, nor do I remember having done it."
"I now request from the Saṃgha the *amūḍhavinaya* for my exoneration; I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me the *amūḍhavinaya* for my exoneration.
Thus he requests a second and a third time.
The Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:
"There is no one in the Saṃgha who speaks of your affairs.
Should anyone speak of your affairs, you ought to go and tell them not to speak of it again."
That bhikṣu should go to that bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable sir!
What I previously did while insane and deluded, I do not know I have done now, nor do I remember having done it; I pray that you no longer speak of what I did while insane."
If that bhikṣu ceases [the misconduct], it is well; if he does not cease, one should speak to his upādhyāya, ācārya, and fellow friends and associates, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."

"Your disciples, fellow students, or spiritual friends speak of what I did when I was formerly ignorant, saying that I did not know I was doing it and do not remember having done it; I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will rebuke them so that they shall not speak thus again."
The preceptor and ācārya should reprimand him, saying:
"It is not well that you do not know the characteristics of the precepts; have you not heard the World-Honored One say that there is no offense for one who is insane or whose mind is deranged?"
"If the person who reports the matter accepts it, that is well.
At that time, the Saṃgha should perform the *karmavācanā*. The one performing the *karmavācanā* shall proclaim as follows:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"

The elders Nandiya and Upanandiya were formerly deluded but are no longer deluded now; regarding their former deluded conduct, fellow practitioners of the holy life speak of it, yet they themselves say they did not know what they did and do not remember having done it.
He has already requested from the Saṃgha the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant the *amūḍhavinaya* to Nandiya and Paṭṭhanandiya.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This Nandika and Paṭinanda were formerly deluded but are no longer deluded now; fellow practitioners of the holy life have spoken of their former deluded conduct, and they themselves say they did not know what they did and do not remember having done it."
He has already requested from the Saṃgha the *amūḍhavinaya* (the discipline for one who is no longer insane) for his exoneration.
The Saṃgha now grants the *amūḍhavinaya* for the exoneration of [Name].
Venerable sirs, those of you who consent to granting the *amūḍhavinaya* for the exoneration of Nandiya and Paṭṭanandiya, remain silent; if you do not consent, please speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said for the second and third times.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the *amūḍhavinaya* to [Name] and [Name]; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Have you already granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of non-insanity) to Nandiya and Paṭanandiya?
They replied:
"It has been given,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"When five factors are fulfilled, it is an unlawful *adhiṭṭhāna* (formal act) of granting the *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane). What are the five?

Granting the *amūḷhavinaya* while perceiving the person as insane; not requesting that the matter be raised against the person so as to soften their mind; not begging the Saṃgha for the *amūḷhavinaya*; being unlawful; and being discordant. These are called the five unlawful factors that fulfill the granting of the *amūḷhavinaya*."
There are five factors for the formal granting of the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity) according to the Dharma.

What are these five? Granting it while the person is indeed sane and free from the perception of being insane; having requested the person who raised the charge to soften their heart; having petitioned the Saṃgha for the *amūḍhavinaya*; acting in accordance with the Dharma; and acting in harmony. These are called the five factors for the formal granting of the *amūḍhavinaya* according to the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called *amūḍha-vinaya*, why is it named *amūḍha-vinaya*?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is a bhikṣu who was formerly deluded but is no longer deluded now, and his fellow practitioners of the holy life speak of his former deluded conduct, at that time one should quickly assemble the Saṃgha."
Having assembled the Saṃgha, according to the Sūtras and according to the Vinaya, and in accordance with the facts of this bhikṣu’s case, grant him the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of non-insanity).
Thus it is, Ānanda!

If, after a dispute involving slander has been settled according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the instruction of the Blessed One by means of the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity), any visiting bhikṣu—even one who is foolish and lacking in wisdom—should again incite it like cattle or sheep, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
"This is called settling through the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-delusion).
Regarding the dispute over the offense of slandering: if a bhikṣu accuses another bhikṣu of a transgression, whether it be a *pārājika* or even a *vinayātikrama*.

This dispute regarding an offense is settled by two *vinayas*, namely, the *pratijñā-vinaya* (the *vinaya* of confession) and the *tatsvabhāva-aiṣīya-vinaya* (the *vinaya* of seeking the nature of the offense).
Regarding the *pratijñā-vinaya*:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At the time for the alms-round, the Venerable Āyuṣmat Rāhula put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī.
Next, he went out for alms and returned to the vihāra.
Having finished his meal, he placed his robes and bowl in their usual place, took up his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and proceeded toward the Indrasailaguhā forest, intending to practice dhyāna.
On the way, he saw a bhikṣu engaging in unchaste conduct with a woman.
Having seen this, the wicked bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If the Buddha’s son Rāhula sees me engaging in unchaste conduct, he will surely tell the World-Honored One."
"Before they have even spoken, I shall go to the World-Honored One and first report their transgressions.
At that time, the wicked bhikṣu went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I saw the Venerable Rāhula on the road leading to the Eye Grove engaging in unrighteous conduct with a woman.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was beneath a tree, absorbed in samādhi. Rising from his meditative concentration, he approached the World-Honored One; not recalling the matter of the wicked bhikṣu, he performed the customary salutation by bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Rāhula to remember a past event, immediately manifested the form of an evil bhikṣu before him. Upon seeing this, Rāhula’s original consciousness was awakened, and he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Just now, on the road through the forest, I saw this bhikṣu engaging in unchaste conduct with a woman."
The Buddha said,
“Rāhula! If that bhikṣu also speaks these words:”
"I saw Rāhula engaging in unchaste conduct along the road.
What do you think of this matter?
Venerable Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not possess such a dharma.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"If that bhikṣu also says,
'I do not possess this quality,' what should be said of this matter?"
Rāhula again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If it is thus, only the World-Honored One knows me."
The Buddha said:
"He further spoke thus:
'Only the World-Honored One knows me.'"
"What does this matter mean?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Let him settle the matter with me himself.
The Buddha again addressed Rāhula:
"If that bhikṣu should likewise say:"
"If one says, 'I pray that the World-Honored One grant me the *prātimokṣa* (self-confession),' what then should be done?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that is so, we pray that the World-Honored One grant both of us the *prātideśanīya* (confession) for our own words.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and having sat down, he explained the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
Having spoken thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu shall be settled through his own confession (*pratijñā-vinaya*). Why is this?"
"In future ages, there may be wicked bhikṣus who slander pure bhikṣus; they shall not be permitted to undergo self-accusation (svavāda), but shall instead be expelled.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are eight kinds of illegal [procedures] for granting self-accusation (svavāda-vinaya)."

What are the eight? To ask about a grave matter and state it as light, or for a light matter to be untrue—this is called "unlawful confession and adjudication. To ask about a light matter and state it as grave; to ask about a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and state it as non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

to ask about a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and state it as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; to ask about a light matter and state it as light; to ask about a grave matter and state it as grave; to ask about a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and state it as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; to ask about a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and state it as non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In each of these cases, if one does not speak of the actual offense, this is called "unlawful confession and adjudication."
There are eight ways in which the *pātimokkha* confession (*sappaṭiñña-pāṭidesanīya*) is accorded according to the Dharma. What are the eight?

To ask about a heavy offense while describing it as light—that is, when there is actually a light offense and one describes it as light—is called the *pāṭidesanīya* being accorded according to the Dharma.

If one asks about a light offense and answers with a heavy one; asks about a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and answers with a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; asks about a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and answers with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; asks about a heavy offense and answers with a heavy one; asks about a light offense and answers with a light one; asks about a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and answers with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; and asks about a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and answers with a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—if, in each of these cases, one speaks truthfully, this is called the eightfold "accordance with the Dharma" for granting the *pratijñākāraka* (atonement by confession).
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘extinction through one’s own admission’ (*pratijñākāraka-vinaya*), what is meant by ‘extinction through one’s own admission’?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a bhikṣu speaks of the transgressions of another bhikṣu’s characteristics, whether they be a pārājika offense down to a vyatikrama-vinaya offense,
Ānanda!...”
At that time, the Saṃgha should be assembled quickly.

Once the Saṃgha has been assembled quickly, according to the Sūtras, according to the Vinaya, and according to the instruction of the Blessed One, one should grant this bhikṣu the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya* (the discipline of confession) in accordance with the facts of the matter.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!

When a dispute has been settled by means of the *pāṭidesanīya* (confession) according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the instruction of the Blessed One, if a visiting bhikṣu or anyone else should again raise the matter, they incur a *pāyattika* offense. This is called settlement by means of *pāṭidesanīya*."
Regarding the *vinaya* for seeking out the basis of an offense during a dispute over an offense:

When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Śrīyāpuṣpa repeatedly committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. When the Saṃgha assembled, intending to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), Śrīyāpuṣpa did not come.
They immediately sent a messenger to summon him, saying: "Elder Śrīyāpuṣpa!"
"The assembly of monks has gathered, wishing to perform a formal ritual.
Śrīyāvatī thought to herself,
"This is surely being done as a formal act (karmavācanā) specifically against me."
Immediately, fear arose in his heart, and he came there out of necessity.
The bhikṣus asked him, "Elder!..."
"Does one commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He replied, "One commits it."
He gives rise to a heart of joy and thinks:
"The fellow practitioner has pointed out to me a matter that should be confessed; it is not a matter that cannot be remedied."
He addressed the community of monks, saying:
"Please allow me to go out for a moment.
Afterward, the bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"This bhikṣu is fickle and unstable; having departed, he will likely speak falsely in a moment.
You should question him three times to ascertain the truth, and only then perform the *karmavācanā*."
After Śrīyavat had emerged, he thought to himself:
"For what reason have I incurred this offense?
The bhikṣus have repeatedly punished me for my faults; I should not now continue to endure this punishment."
The bhikṣus then called Śrīyāvatī in; once she had entered, they asked her:
"Did you truly commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
She replied:
“I have not committed an offense.
The bhikṣus asked him,
“Why did you previously say in the midst of the Saṃgha that you had such an offense, and now say that you have not committed one?”
Śrīyāvatī said, "I do not recall this matter.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Call Śrīyāmba. When he had come, the Buddha questioned Śrīyāmba extensively on this matter:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“If Śrīyā, within the community of monks, having seen an offense, says she did not see it, or having not seen it, says she saw it, and speaks thus:
‘I do not remember,’ the Saṃgha should grant her the *tassapāpiyasika* (penance for one who persists in wrong-doing) *niḥsaraṇa*.”
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Śrīyava..."
If, within the Saṃgha, one who has seen an offense says they did not see it, or one who did not see it says they saw it, or one who says they do not remember it—
if the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha shall settle the case of the bhikṣu Śrīyabha by means of the *vinaya* procedure of searching for the characteristics of the offense (*mṛṣā-vinaya*).
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Sangha, listen! The bhikṣu Śrīyava..."
Within the Saṃgha, one who sees an offense says they do not see it; one who does not see it says they see it; and one who remembers says they do not remember.

The Saṃgha now grants the *tassapāpiyasika* (the rule for searching out the nature of the offense) to the bhikṣu Śrīyava by means of the *vinaya-niḥsaraṇa* (the method of settling through the Vinaya).

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the settlement of this *bhiṣaṇaka-vastu* (matter of seeking faults) for the bhikṣu Śrīyabha by means of the *vinaya-niḥsaraṇa* (settlement according to the discipline) should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were also spoken thus:

"The Saṃgha has already consented to the settlement of the *pāpikā-diṭṭhi* (faulty view) of the bhikṣu Śrīyapā by means of the *tassapāpiyasika-vinaya*. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Once this bhikṣu-saṃgha has performed the *vinaya-karman* for the purpose of seeking his offense (*mārgana-āpatti-lakṣaṇa*), that bhikṣu must practice eight rules for as long as he lives."

What are the eight? One must not ordain others; one must not confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon others; one must not accept dependence (*niśraya*) from others; one must not accept invitations in the order of seniority; one must not act as a messenger for the Saṃgha; one must not act as a Dharma-preacher for the Saṃgha; one must not act as a preacher of the Vinaya for the Saṃgha; one must not act as an officiant for the Saṃgha’s formal acts (*karmavācanā*). Once the Saṃgha has performed a formal act, this bhikṣu is forbidden to relinquish it for the rest of his life. These are called the eight dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
"Regarding what is called *tassapāpiyasikā* (the settling of an offense by finding fault), how is it defined as *tassapāpiyasikā*?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu, when seeing an offense within the Saṃgha, says he did not see it; or when not seeing one, says he saw it; or claims that he does not remember having committed it—this is obstinacy."

At that time, one should quickly assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, according to the Sūtra, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Dharma, the *pāpikā-ādhikaraṇa-vinaya* (the settlement by seeking out the offense) shall be granted to this bhikṣu, and the matter shall be extinguished.
The Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
You have not obtained any wholesome benefit."
"How is it that within the Saṃgha you say you see your offense when you do not, and say you see it when you do not; and you say of yourself, 'I do not recall having committed it'?
Because you have spoken these words within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha shall perform the *tassapāpiyasikā* (act of searching for the nature of the offense) against you."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!

Having settled a dispute according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the instruction of the Blessed One by means of the *vinaya-vastu* for seeking the characteristics of the offense (*mṛṣā-vādaka-vinaya*), if a visiting bhikṣu or anyone else should further incite it, he commits a *pāyattika* offense."
This concludes the settlement of the legal dispute concerning offenses through the *vinaya* of searching for the characteristics of the offense.
Regarding the legal dispute concerning accusations, it is settled by means of three *vinayas*.
The *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*) has already been explained previously.
Regarding the settling of disputes through formal investigation (*bahuśruta-vinaya*):
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in Kauśāmbī. At that time, there were two assemblies, each with its own teacher:
one named Viśuddhavādin and the other named Suviśuddhavādin.
He had a fellow disciple named Vajramukha; Śobhita had a fellow disciple named Stambhamukha.
His first attendant disciple was named Dhotaka, and his second attendant disciple was named Bhaddali.
His first lay disciple was named Dharmadinna, and his second lay disciple was named Anupama.
The first donor was King Udayana; the second donor was the householder Kuśika.
The first female lay disciple was Queen Śrīmātā; the second female lay disciple was Āmrapālī, daughter of Mrgadanta.
The first maidservant of the inner palace was Bhṛṅgimātā; the second maidservant of the inner palace was Pāṭaliputrakā.
Each group consisted of five hundred bhikṣus, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, five hundred upāsakas, and five hundred upāsikās.
When the leader of the first group had finished using the latrine and wished to use water, he saw insects in the water and placed a blade of grass across the vessel as a signal.
The second leader of the community entered the latrine later with his attendant disciple; seeing grass upon the water vessel, he spoke these words:
"Who is this shameless person?"
"Take this grass and place it upon the water vessel.
When the leader of the first group and his fellow disciples heard these words, they said to that man:
"How can you take the name of our preceptor, you shameless person?"
Because of this matter, the two divisions and the fourfold assembly subsequently gave rise to a great dispute.

At that time, throughout the city of Kauśāmbī, both inside and out, the sound of contention resounded; the inner and outer quarters were thrown into turmoil, like the waters surging with great waves when the King of the Golden-Winged Birds enters the sea to seize a dragon.

Such great disputes are merely quarreling over whether it is grass or not-grass. Therefore, monks engage in strife and discord while living together; they dispute what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, what is a grave offense and what is a light offense, what is curable and what is incurable, what is a legal formal act (dhamma-kamma) and what is a non-legal formal act, what is a harmonious formal act and what is a non-harmonious formal act, and what should be done and what should not be done.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among those seated who spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!

This is not the Dharma, it is not the Vinaya; it is inconsistent with the Sūtras, inconsistent with the Vinaya, and inconsistent with the Upadeśas. It contradicts the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Upadeśas, and serves only to give rise to various defilements and outflows."
As I understand it, this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Buddha’s teaching; it accords with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Upadeśas, and thus gives rise to no defilements or outflows.
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sirs!
I am unable to settle this dispute.
I shall go to the city of Śrāvastī to the place where the World-Honored One resides and inquire how this matter of the dispute is to be settled."
When that bhikṣu had arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are quarreling and disputing, speaking against one another and living together in disharmony; I have been unable to settle this matter of dispute, and I have come to inform the World-Honored One so that He may extinguish this dispute.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will extinguish this contentious dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Upāli:

"Go and, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, settle this dispute for the monks of Kauśāmbī by means of the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (the majority decision)."

"Upāli, when such matters involving the Śākyas, the Licchavis, and others cannot be settled immediately during a legal proceeding, they are also resolved through the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (the majority decision)."
Disputes arise in three places: among a single person, among a group of many, or within the Saṃgha;
they should likewise be relinquished in three places, accepted in three places, and extinguished in three places.

Upāli! Go to where the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are and, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, settle this dispute by means of what is called the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (settlement by majority), as explained in detail above in the section on the *saṃmukha-vinaya*.
Once the minds of these bhikṣus have become supple, the Saṃgha should distribute the śalākā.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, the Saṃgha should perform the *karmavācanā* and appoint him as the distributor of the śalākā.
"What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what is to be accepted and what is not.
The *karmadāna* (the officiant) should speak thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named [Name] has accomplished the five qualities and is capable of acting as the distributor of voting sticks for the community of monks.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint this bhikṣu named [Name] as the distributor of voting sticks."
The motion is thus stated.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has accomplished five qualities; the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks."
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to appoint this bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks (śalākā) should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, this bhikṣu should prepare two kinds of voting sticks (*śalākā*):
one black and one white.
He must not announce them by saying:
"Those who act contrary to the Dharma shall take black voting sticks; those who act in accordance with the Dharma shall take white voting sticks.
One should proclaim thus:
"Those who speak in this manner shall take the black voting sticks; those who speak in that manner shall take the white voting sticks."

When distributing voting tallies, those who distribute them should establish their minds within five principles before doing so; they should not act as unrighteous associates, but should act as righteous associates.
When the counting of the voting sticks is finished, if there are even one more illegal voting sticks than legal ones, the result should not be proclaimed.
If those who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous and those who act according to the Dharma are few, one should employ skillful means to dissolve the assembly.
If the time for the morning meal is approaching, one should announce that it is time for the morning meal.
If the time for the afternoon meal arrives, one should announce that it is time for the afternoon meal.
If the time for bathing arrives, one should announce that it is time for bathing.
When the time for preaching the Dharma approaches, one should announce that the time for preaching the Dharma has arrived.
When the time for preaching the Vinaya approaches, one should announce that the time for preaching the Vinaya has arrived.
If those who act contrary to the Dharma perceive this, they will say:
"We have achieved victory; the assembly has been dissolved for our sake.
We shall not rise now, but must resolve this matter right here on these very seats."
At that time, if there is a small hut near the vihāra that is free of insects, one should have a *karmadāna* set fire to it and shout:
"Fire! Fire!"
He should immediately disperse and go to extinguish the fire.
If he knows that there are those who act according to the Dharma in the vicinity, he should go and call them, saying:
"Elders, the distribution of voting tickets has already been completed; those acting contrary to the Dharma are many, while those acting according to the Dharma are few."

"Elder! You should go there for the sake of the Dharma, so that those who act according to the Dharma may obtain many voting-slips, the Buddha-Dharma may flourish, and you yourself may gain the merit of self-benefit.
If, upon hearing these words, he does not come, he incurs an offense of *vibhinī*.
Once they have arrived, the voting sticks (*śalākā*) should be distributed again.
After the sticks have been distributed, one should count them; if there is one extra white stick, one should not announce that there is "one extra," but should instead announce:
"Those who speak thus are many; those who speak thus are few."
Having made this proclamation, one should follow the majority.
Furthermore, there are five things that, if accomplished, render the distribution of voting tallies (śalākā) improper.
What are these five?

When those who speak according to the Dharma are few and those who speak contrary to the Dharma are many; when those who speak according to the Dharma hold different views and those who speak contrary to the Dharma hold the same view; and when they declare what is contrary to the Dharma to be the Dharma and what is the Dharma to be contrary to the Dharma—because of this, they cast voting sticks leading to the schism of the Saṃgha and its subsequent division. These are called the five unrighteous acts.
Reversing the previous [terms], this is called "the accomplishment of the five kinds of legal voting-slips.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding what is called settlement by means of *yadbhūyas-kārika-vinaya* (settlement by majority decision), why is it called settlement by means of *yadbhūyas-kārika-vinaya*?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When monks, within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the codes of decorum (*īryāpatha*), dispute and argue with one another, saying: 'This is an offense; this is not an offense; this is light; this is heavy; this is curable; this is incurable; this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; this is a non-*saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.'"

At that time, you should quickly assemble the Saṃgha and, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, deal with the matter according to its facts, resolving it in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If one is still unable to understand it, one should hear that in a certain place there is an elder bhikṣu who recites the Sūtras, recites the Vinaya, and recites the Mātṛkā.

In this way, if there is a bhikṣu of middle age or a bhikṣu of youth who recites the Sūtras, recites the Vinaya, or recites the Mātṛkā, one should quickly go to him to ask, or invite him to come; then, according to what that bhikṣu explains, the dispute should be settled by means of the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya*. Once the dispute has been thus extinguished, [the matter is concluded].
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If a visiting bhikṣu, or even a newly ordained bhikṣu, should initiate [a dispute] again, it is a pāyattika.
This is called a legal dispute arising from mutual recrimination, which is to be settled by the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (the rule of majority).
Regarding the settlement of disputes through verbal contention by the "grass-spreading" (*tṛṇastāraka*) method of discipline:

When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were disputing; they lived together in discord, claiming that what was Dharma was non-Dharma and what was Vinaya was non-Vinaya. Eventually, the Venerable Upāli spoke to those bhikṣus, saying:
"Elders!..."
"Once I have gone there, I shall perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); I shall perform various rituals to discipline and expel you all, so at that time do not let your hearts be displeased.
Then the messenger bhikṣu said, "I wish to go out for a short while."
Having departed, they thought:
"If we follow Venerable Upāli, he might severely punish us for our offense. We should now return alone to Kauśāmbī and settle this dispute among ourselves."
Having arrived at Kauśāmbī, they were still unable to settle the dispute. They spoke again, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
We ourselves are unable to settle this dispute; we shall now return to Śrāvastī to settle it."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went to the city of Śrāvastī and approached the Venerable Upāli, saying:
"Excellent, O Venerable One!"
"I shall settle this dispute for the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī.
Upāli said to those bhikṣus:

"Just as I previously told you, whatever matters arise there, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma in various ways; at that time, you must not be displeased in heart, but should follow along."
That bhikṣu replied,
"I dare not disobey again. Upāli said:
"Go back to where you came from and pass away; do not cause disorder among the Saṃgha here.
At that time, the bhikṣu of Kauśāmbī went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The monks of Kauśāmbī live together in discord and speak ill of one another; we pray that the World-Honored One will extinguish this dispute.
The Buddha told the monks of Kauśāmbī:
“Do not engage in strife or speak ill of one another, nor dwell together in discord.”
Why is this? In the distant past, there was a city named Kapilavastu and a king named Brahmadatta, as described in detail in the *Jātaka of King Dīrghāyu*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī: "Such was the case with him;
his kingdom was destroyed and his family perished, yet even when the crown prince Jīvaka failed to avenge his father’s enemy, they were still reconciled and harbored no ill will."
"How is it that you, having gone forth out of faith within the True Dharma, still engage in angry disputes and live together in disharmony?
The Buddha told Upāli:

"Go and, for the sake of the monks of Kauśāmbī, settle this dispute according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, by means of the *tṛṇastāraka-vinaya* (the 'grass-spreading' method of settling disputes)."
The Buddha again addressed Upāli:

"Disputes arise in three places; they are taken up in three places, relinquished in three places, and extinguished in three places. When such a dispute has been thus purified, it should be settled together with the lay followers (upāsakas)."

If it is an impure matter, one should expel the upāsaka by means of a simile; according to the facts of this bhikṣu’s case, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, one shall effect its settlement through the *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya* (the "spreading of grass" method).
The Buddha told Upāli:
"If a junior monk has committed an offense, he should go to where a senior monk is, prostrate at his feet with his head and face, and say:
'Venerable sir!'"
"I have committed unrighteous acts and transgressions through my offenses; I now repent and dare not do so again.
The Elder should then stroke his head with his hand, support him by raising him up and embracing him, and say:
"O Venerable One!
"I too have committed a fault; you should look upon me with kindness and forgive me.
If a senior monk has committed a fault, he should go to the junior monk, take him by the hand, and say:
"What I have done is contrary to the Dharma; I have offended you. I repent and shall not do it again."
The junior monk should rise, prostrate at the feet of the senior monk, and likewise perform the confession as above.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called the *tṛṇastāraka-vinaya*, why is it named the *tṛṇastāraka-vinaya*?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If a dispute arises among bhikṣus, they dwell together in disharmony; the two assemblies cannot endure it, and with malicious intent they speak to one another, each reciting dharmas that are not in accordance [with the truth], and thus an intolerable situation arises."

Ānanda! At that time, you should quickly assemble the Saṃgha according to the Dharma and the Vinaya. Within one group, there should be a senior monk who manages affairs, whose causal conditions and eloquence are clear, and who is unafraid when preaching the Dharma. He should praise the merits of the harmonious Saṃgha, rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and address the second group of monks, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"How is it that we, having gone forth out of faith within this same Dharma, give rise to disputes and dwell together in disharmony?

Both communities cannot endure this; each gives rise to an evil mind, engaging in mutual speech that does not accord with the Dharma. This arising of intolerance is entirely due to unwholesome reflection."
"In this life you will dwell in suffering, and in the future you will fall into the evil realms.
Venerable sirs!
You should each abandon these matters of dispute, spreading them out upon the ground like grass."
"I now confess before all the elders; let us each humble our minds and dwell together in harmony. Ānanda!
If the entire second assembly remains silent, then those among the second assembly who are long-standing, virtuous, intelligent, and eloquent should immediately rise and confess.
The method of confession is also as explained above. Ānanda!

When such a dispute arises within the Saṃgha, you should quickly assemble the community and, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, settle this dispute by means of the "spreading of grass upon the ground" (tṛṇastāraka).
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Regarding all these matters of dispute—such as mutual striking and punching, dragging [someone] out of the room, the class of divisive speech and groundless slander—all such offenses should be settled through the *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya* (the 'spreading of grass' discipline)."
In this manner, once it has been extinguished like grass spread upon the ground, if any guest bhikṣu, up to and including a newly ordained bhikṣu, should rekindle it, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding "disputes concerning customary affairs": if the affairs performed by the Saṃgha are conducted in accordance with the Dharma—being properly convened, properly concluded, properly dismissed, properly relinquished, and properly granted.

In this way, the immeasurable activities of the Blessed One’s community of bhikṣu disciples are all brought to cessation through the seven methods for settling disputes; each activity is thus extinguished. This is called the "dispute regarding constant activities," and it is for this reason that it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

At that time, when it was time for his almsround, the Venerable Udāyin put on his robes for entering the village, took up his bowl, and entered the city. As he proceeded on his almsround, he arrived at a certain house and preached the Dharma to a large number of women.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, while on his almsround, arrived at that house;
having seen him, he asked, "Elder, what are you doing? He replied:
"I shall preach the Dharma for these women.
Venerable Ānanda said to Udāyin:
"How can a bhikṣu preach the Dharma alone to a woman when no man capable of understanding is present?"

After Ānanda had finished his almsround, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
“Call Udāyin here.”
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Udāyin,
"Is it true that you did this?
He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter.
How could you teach the Dharma to a woman without a knowledgeable man present?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to teach the Dharma to a woman without a knowledgeable man present."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, when the time arrived, put on his robes for entering the village, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city. Proceeding on his almsround, he came to a certain house and taught the Dharma to a large group of women.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to that house while wandering for alms;
having seen him, he asked, "Elder, what are you doing? He replied:
"Preach the Dharma to women.
Ānanda said: "Venerable sir, have you not heard the words of the Blessed One:..."
"Is it that one cannot preach the Dharma to a woman unless a man is present?
He replied, "Ānanda!..."
"Do you not see these stone figures, wooden figures, straw figures, and painted figures?
One person would suffice, how much more so many?
After the Venerable Ānanda had finished his almsround, he reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Udāyin here. Once he had arrived,
the World-Honored One questioned Udāyin:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said,
"Udāyin! How can you preach the Dharma to a woman using a mindless man as a *puruṣadūta* (pure attendant)?"
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for a woman to teach the Dharma by employing a mindless man as a *pariṣad-vārika* (attendant).
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed account is as above.
At that time, Udāyin, when the hour had come, put on his village-entering robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī. He proceeded until he replied to the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Do you not see this small child being carried on [someone's] lap, this small child drinking milk, and this small child lying down?"
"One person would have been sufficient, how much more so many.
After the Venerable Ānanda had finished his almsround, he reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Call Udāyin here. When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Udāyin:
“Is it true that you have done so?”
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“Udāyin! How can you preach the Dharma to women while holding an infant as a ‘pure person’ (pariśuddha-pudgala)?
From this day forward, you must not preach the Dharma to women while holding an infant at the breast as if he were a man.”
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ was ill. Early in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda put on his village-wearing robes and went to inquire after her health, saying:
"O upāsikā, how is your illness?"
"Are you not greatly distressed?
He replied, "My ailment does not improve; it is unbearable. I pray that the Venerable One will preach the Dharma for me."
Ānanda replied,
“The World-Honored One does not permit a man who is not a *śramaṇa* to preach the Dharma to women.
The upāsikā said:
"If you cannot speak at length, may I ask you for five or six words?
Ānanda replied, "I do not know whether I shall receive them or not."
"I did not yet dare speak.
The upāsikā said,
"I pay homage to the ācārya."
Ānanda said, "May your ailment be swiftly removed.
Having spoken, he departed.
The Venerable Ānanda returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Knowing this, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
“Ānanda, from where have you come?”
Ānanda then reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā is a wise person, Ānanda!”
"If you were to speak five or six words for her, her illness would be cured and she would dwell in comfort.
From this day forward, it is permitted for a woman to speak five or six words to another woman when no man is present."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who dwell depending on the city of Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, without a pure person present, teaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six words, it is a pāyattika offense,
except when a man capable of understanding is present.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If there is no man who understands, whether he be blind or deaf, he is also called "lacking a pure person" (kappiya-kāraka).
However, if there is one blind man and one deaf man—these two persons together may serve as a single pure person.
Even if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), if he is asleep, it is still called "being without a man.
As for "women," this refers to whether they are one's mother, sister, elder, or younger, whether they are laypeople or monastics.
The Dharma consists of that which was spoken by the Buddha and that which was approved by the Buddha.
That which was spoken by the Buddha refers to what he spoke with his own mouth.
That which was approved by the Buddha refers to what was spoken by the Buddha’s disciples or others, and subsequently approved by the Buddha.
"Speaking" refers to teaching, reciting, and explaining.
Regarding "five or six words," there are two types:
long phrases and short phrases.
The long verse is: "Commit no evil whatsoever.
The short verse is: "The eye is impermanent.

Regarding the exception of a man who possesses knowledge: if one is less than seven years of age and does not understand the meaning and flavor of good or bad speech, he is called a man without knowledge.
Even if one has passed seven years of age, if they do not understand the meaning and flavor of good and bad speech, they are also called an ignorant man.
Whether seven years old or older, if one understands the meaning and flavor of good and bad speech, this is called a knowledgeable man.
Furthermore, there was a woman who came to pay homage at the stūpa early in the morning.
Having paid homage at the stūpa, she came to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu and said to him, "Venerable Sir, I wish to hear the Dharma; please speak it for me."
At that time, a bhikṣu may speak one and a half verses to her.
If that bhikṣu, having entered a village, speaks five or six words to the same woman again, it is a pāyattika.
The reason the World-Honored One established the rule of five or six words is that one may speak them within a single day.

Suppose a bhikṣu is dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) when a woman comes to pay homage at the stūpa; having paid homage at the stūpa, she then comes to pay homage at the bhikṣu’s feet and says:
“Venerable Sir, please preach the Dharma for me.”
The bhikṣu should say to that woman:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that one may not preach the Dharma to a woman unless a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) is present.
The woman then says to the bhikṣu:
"I know the Buddha's Dharma; as permitted by the World-Honored One, I pray that you will speak it for me.
At that time, a bhikṣu may recite one and a half verses for this woman, or two women together may receive up to three verses, and there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu enters a village to teach and many women come to listen to the Dharma, he may speak six sentences to each of them. He should say to the first woman:
"I shall speak six sentences for you."
Having finished speaking, he again said to the second girl:
"I shall speak six phrases for you.
Although he did this many times, there was no offense.
After the bhikṣu has departed, the women escort him out, prostrate at his feet, and take their leave; at that time, they may offer a blessing, saying:
"May you swiftly reach the end of suffering."
[If she says this,] she incurs a *pāyattika*. If she says:
"May you remain free from illness and dwell in peace," [there is no offense].
If [the woman] has no fault,

and after he has left, he goes again to another house to preach the Dharma, and the aforementioned woman follows him there again and listens from outside at a distance, the bhikṣu, having seen her, says:
"Have you come to listen again?"
He replied, "Yes. The bhikṣu said:
"If you deeply delight in the Dharma, you may listen.
If this bhikṣu commits this act, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
Even if he sees this woman and does not speak with her, but preaches the Dharma directly to other women, although the first woman hears it, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman, even though no pure person (kappiyakāraka) is present in the assembly, there is no offense provided that there are people passing by or resting who are walking, standing, or sitting, facing outward or inward, or on the upper or lower levels of a gallery, such that they can see or hear from afar.

If a layperson’s house faces a road and a bhikṣu is inside preaching the Dharma to women, even if there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), provided that travelers on the road pass by continuously so that they can see and hear him, there is no offense.
If there are no passersby on the road who can see or hear, one must not speak.
If a woman comes to pay homage to the stupa and, having finished her prostrations, says to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!"
"What kind of stupa is this?
I pray that you will tell me its name and location.
At that time, the bhikṣu was able to speak:
"The stupa at the place of birth, the stupa at the place of attaining the Way, the stupa at the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the stupa at the place of parinirvāṇa.
To answer each matter according to what is asked is without fault.
There are four types of pure persons:
those who have seen but not heard, those who have heard but not seen, those who have both seen and heard, and those who have neither seen nor heard.

Regarding "having seen but not heard": with the eye one sees from afar a bhikṣu and a woman, yet does not hear the sound of their voices; these four permutations are explained at length in this manner.
If one sees but does not hear, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If one hears but does not see, it is likewise.
If there is neither seeing nor hearing, it is a *pāyattika*.
To both see and hear [it] is without offense.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Kalandaka; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, there was a *karmadāna* bhikṣu who was teaching a group of many youths to recite the *pāramitās* word by word.
Then, a certain brāhmaṇa thought to himself:
"Where is there a truly excellent Dharma?"
"I shall go forth into homelessness under him.
Having formed this thought, he went to the Ārāma of the Wilderness, desiring to go forth.
He saw a bhikṣu teaching various youths to recite; it was like the sound of children in a schoolhouse receiving instruction and chanting. At that time, the brahmin had this thought:

"I now wish to seek the supreme Dharma and go forth from that [home], yet here there is only this constant clamor, like the sound of children reciting in a schoolroom; furthermore, I do not know who their teacher might be."
"Who is this disciple?
Having seen him, that person conceived a lack of respectful faith; failing to see the Buddha at all, he immediately returned home and no longer pursued the life of a renunciant.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣu in charge of affairs here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu in charge of affairs:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“This is an evil deed.”
"How can you teach those who have not received full ordination the method of reciting the verses?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to explain the method of reciting the verses to those who have not received full ordination.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in the city of Āṭavī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu teaches the dharma by verse to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "one who has not received full ordination," this excludes bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; even though bhikṣuṇīs have received full ordination, they may not be taught [the dharma by verse].
Regarding "phrase" (pada): it refers to the phrasing, the meaning, and the syllables, recited together as phrase, meaning, and syllables. Regarding "Dharma":
it refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha and that which was approved by the Buddha.
As for "spoken by the Buddha," it means that which the Buddha himself spoke.
That which is approved by the Buddha refers to the teachings spoken by the śrāvaka disciples and others that the Buddha has sanctioned.
All wholesome dharmas up to and including nirvāṇa are called the Dharma.
"Teaching" refers to speaking for the purpose of instruction.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu teaches a person who has not received full ordination, saying that the eye is impermanent, or that sound is raised at one time, lowered at another time, and cut off at another time, and that the combination of sounds constitutes pleasure without obstruction, it is a pāyattika offense.

The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the five aggregates (*skandha*), and the six elements (*dhātu*); and even all phenomena (*dharma*)—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—are likewise so.

If a bhikṣu is instructing a co-practitioner disciple or a dependent disciple regarding various sūtras such as the *Aṣṭavargika-sūtra*, the *Pārāyaṇa-sūtra*, the *Vigraha-vyāvartanī-sūtra*, the *Anavatapta-sūtra*, and the *Pratyekabuddha-sūtra*, and they are reciting, descending from recitation, or resolving doubts together, he should instruct the disciple, saying:
"Wait for me to finish my recitation and resolution, and then you shall recite."
If, when instructed in this manner, one does not accept the words, they may no longer be taught.
If that disciple should say:
"I pray that the Ācārya will grant me the sūtra once more," [he may be taught].
At that time, the teacher should say:
"If you do not recite together [with me] again, I shall grant you the transmission.
In this manner, such disciples—even including upāsakas and upāsikās—must not be granted it [if they fail to meet the condition].
If bhikṣus recite a sūtra together, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should recite aloud while the junior monk follows along silently in his mind.

If the senior monk’s recitation is not proficient, the junior monk should recite aloud while the senior monk follows along by silent mental recitation. This applies even to upāsikās in the same manner.
If, while verses are being recited within the Saṃgha, one must not recite the same verse as another; however, it is permissible for each person to simultaneously recite different verses.
Therefore, it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
As was explained in detail regarding each matter and its causal conditions within the fourth precept on false speech, here the distinction lies simply in speaking the truth;
even to the point where the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This is an evil deed."

For example, it is like a courtesan who sells her beauty to sustain herself; you are just the same, for you preach the subtle and true Dharma to others merely to sell your "beauty" for the sake of food and clothing, thereby sustaining your lives.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu claims for himself a superhuman state, saying, 'I know thus, I see thus,' and speaks the truth, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
To claim for oneself a state beyond the human; "a state beyond the human" is as explained above.
If one says of oneself:
"Do I possess the knowledge of the Dharma?"
"Having transgressed the Vinaya, one should repent in one's heart.
If one says:
'I possess the knowledge of the Dharma.'"
This constitutes an offense against the Vinaya.
If one says:
"I have attained the realization of the knowledge of the Dharma," [it is likewise an offense].
Pāyattika. Each phrase is explained at length as above, up to the ten qualities of one beyond training (*daśa-aśaikṣadharma*); if one speaks of these truthfully, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu says to a woman:
"If all the bhikṣus observing the summer retreat at such-and-such a place are not ordinary worldlings," one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti*.
It is asked: [What is the offense?]
“Is the Venerable One also among them?
He replied, “I am also among them.”
One incurs an offense of violating the Vinaya.
If a laywoman asks,
"Does the Venerable One also possess this dharma?"
He replied, "I have.
To speak thus according to the facts constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says to an upāsikā,
"The bhikṣus who have performed the *pravāraṇā* at such-and-such a place are not ordinary persons;
they are all arhats," he incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama* requiring mental regret.
The upāsikā asked,
“Does the Venerable One also perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony there?
He replied:
"So it is. One incurs an offense of violating the Vinaya.
He asked again:
“Has the Venerable One also attained arhatship? He replied, “I have.”
To speak the truth [in this regard] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if one says:
"In such-and-such a village, a bhikṣu has been reciting sūtras for you and your family members at the houses of kings, high ministers, elders, householders, and your own home."
The same applies to a bhikṣu’s walking, as well as his standing, sitting, and lying down; likewise to his wearing such robes, holding such an alms-bowl, and eating such food.

If one speaks the language of the central regions to those in the borderlands, or speaks the language of the borderlands to those in the central regions, or speaks the language of the central regions to those in the central regions, or speaks the language of the borderlands to those in the borderlands—yet speaks the meaning but not the phrasing—one commits an offense against the Vinaya.
If one speaks of the phrasing (*vyañjana*) but not the meaning (*artha*), there is a transgression of the Vinaya requiring mental remorse (*vairūpya-citta*).
If one speaks of the meaning and the phrasing, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks neither of the meaning nor of the phrasing, there is no offense.
If one writes a script, hand-seal, or seal-mark that manifests the meaning but not the flavor, one incurs an offense of *vibhinī*.
If it manifests the flavor but not the meaning, one incurs an offense of *vibhinī* requiring mental repentance.
If one manifests the meaning and manifests the flavor, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not manifest the meaning and does not manifest the flavor, there is no offense.
Even down to manifesting the appearance of an Arhat, it is a transgression of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance (*viniścaya-citta-kaukṛtya*).
Therefore it is said.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle Thirteenth.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle Fourteenth.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra from India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Regarding the third of the ninety-two matters of the *Prātimokṣa*: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, there was a householder who invited many bhikṣus he knew well. Among these bhikṣus was an elder bhikṣu who, while performing the *mānatva* penance, sat in the lower seats.
When the female lay devotee (upāsikā) saw this, she asked, "Venerable sir, your seat was previously up above; for what reason are you now sitting here in the middle?
He replied:
"Since you have found a seat, why must you ask?
The upāsikā said, "I know the Venerable One's seat; it should indeed be right here."
"I also know the seating places of all the venerable ones.
Then Nanda said to the upāsikā,
"For what reason did you call your ācārya to sit in the seat of the senior elder?"
"Your preceptor has not yet abandoned his childhood games.
Upon hearing this, the upāsikā was displeased and thought to herself:
"My preceptor must still be violating minor precepts; that is why he sits here in a lower seat."
He immediately seized the food basket and its contents, threw them on the ground, and departed, saying:
"Venerable sir, take your food from within this yourself.
Having spoken these words, he entered his room, closed one leaf of the door, and spoke this verse:
“Having long since gone forth and practiced the holy life, why do you not cease your childish play?
How can you accept the offerings of the faithful?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Nanda here. When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Nanda:
"This is an evil deed.

Having been negligent in the midst of your practice as a fellow practitioner of the Brahma-faring, you have now returned to practicing in accordance with the Dharma; why then do you mock and deride those who have not yet received full ordination by speaking of their gross offenses?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to speak of another's gross offense to one who has not yet received full ordination.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu seeking alms who, when the time had come, put on his village-entry robes and, carrying his bowl, entered the city.
Proceeding in order to beg for food, he arrived at a certain household. At that moment, the man spoke to the woman, saying:
"Give food to this renunciant."
The woman asked,
"By which path have you gone forth?
He replied:
"A member of the Śākya clan has gone forth as a renunciant.
The woman said,
"I will not give him food."
He asked, "Why did you not give it? He replied:
"This man is not one who practices the holy life; therefore, I will not give it to him.
The bhikṣu said to the woman: "Sister!"
"I am one who practices the holy life.
The woman said,
"Venerable Kālu Bhikṣu, even one of such great name and virtue as you cannot yet practice the holy life."
"How can you now say of yourself, 'I am one who practices the holy life'?
Hearing these harsh words, the bhikṣu was filled with grief and distress; he ceased begging for alms and returned immediately to the vihāra, fasting for a day.
Because he had fasted, his four elements were weakened; he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked him intentionally:
"For what reason are your four elements so weakened now?"
Having reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One,
the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu, why did you not say this to him?"
"Even if the bhikṣu Kālu were not one who practices the holy life (brahmacarya), what would that hinder my own practice of the holy life? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"

I am able to speak to him, but the Blessed One has established a precept that one must not disclose another's grave offense to a person who has not received full ordination; therefore, I do not speak of it.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you are indeed able not to violate the Buddha’s teachings and precepts for the sake of your life."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “This bhikṣu Kālu!
Both householders and renunciants know that he does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya). The Saṃgha should perform the formal act of ‘non-holy-life’ (abrahmacarya-karman) against him.”
The one performing the ritual should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Kālu is known by both householders and renunciants to be one who does not lead the holy life."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall declare that the bhikṣu Kālu has not practiced the holy life.
This is the motion.
Thus the formal act is performed with three proclamations (*jñapti-karman*).
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Have you already performed the formal act of declaring non-celibacy against the bhikṣu Kālu?
They replied:
"It has been done. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Gross offense" refers to the four matters and the thirteen matters.
Regarding "one who has not received full ordination," this excludes bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; even though a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination, one must not speak [of such offenses] to her.
"To speak" means to address others so that they may understand, except in the case of the *saṃgha-karman*. Regarding the *karman*:
if the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the assembly (*gaṇa*) is not accomplished, or the ritual procedure (*karman*) itself is not accomplished, it is not called a *karman*.
If the motion (jñapti) is accomplished, the assembly is accomplished, and the formal act (karman) is accomplished, this is called a karman.
The Blessed One has declared that there is no offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu knows of another’s grave offense (sthūlātyaya) and the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal ritual (karman), he must not disclose that grave offense.
If someone asks:
“Bhikṣu So-and-so has committed sexual misconduct and drunk alcohol,” [he may speak].
To this, one should reply:
"He himself shall know.
If the Saṃgha has already performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), one must not go through the alleys proclaiming it.
If someone should ask,
"That bhikṣu has committed sexual misconduct and drunk alcohol," the bhikṣu should question that person as follows:
"From where did you hear this?
He replied, "I heard it from such-and-such a place."
The bhikṣu should reply:
"I too heard it in such a place.
If a bhikṣu speaks to one who has not received full ordination regarding the four matters or the thirteen matters of a bhikṣu, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
To speak of the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules and the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules constitutes an offense against the Vinaya.

To speak of the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas and the rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*) regarding decorum constitutes an offense against the Vinaya requiring mental regret (*vinayātisāra-vinidhāya-citta*).
It is stated that for a bhikṣuṇī, [committing] the eight pārājikas or the nineteen saṃghāvaśeṣas constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense;
[committing] the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas or the one hundred and forty-one pāyattikas [constitutes a pāyattika offense].
Regarding the eight *pratideśanīya* rules and the *śaikṣa* precepts on dignified conduct, one incurs the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya* (transgression of the discipline) with mental regret.
Regarding the exposition of the ten precepts for *śrāmaṇera* and *śrāmaṇerī*, one incurs the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*.
Down to the five precepts for laypeople, one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (a transgression requiring mental repentance).
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Dharmaruci was the administrator of the nine matters concerning the *saṃgha-karman*, as explained in detail in the section on the thirteen matters.
At that time, there was a *śāṇa* rag-robe that could not be divided. Dharmaruci addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"This *śāṇa* rag-robe cannot be divided; may it be given to the Elder Mahākāśyapa?"
The bhikṣus all said,
“It may be given.
Fearing that there might later be disputes regarding this, Dharmadatta then made a formal proclamation before the Saṃgha:
"This rag-robe, *pāṃśukūla*, is for the Elder Mahākāśyapa.
Thus he proclaimed three times.
Having finished proclaiming this, the group of six bhikṣus rose from their seats and spoke as follows:
"Who said they gave it?
Did the group of six bhikṣus give it or not?
You have made this proclamation out of partiality; because you are privately fond of one another, you diverted the property of the Saṃgha to give to those bhikṣus."
For this reason, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
“This is an evil deed.”

For such fellow practitioners of the holy life, you should even give them your skin, flesh, blood, and marrow; how much more so these rag-robes that cannot be divided? Yet, after they were proclaimed and given within the Sangha, you have now withdrawn them.
Previously you were silent, which was like the manner of a person of noble status; now you have again obstructed [the assembly], which is like the manner of a person of lowly status.
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is about to distribute items, first consents to the distribution in harmony but later obstructs it, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
The "monks" are of eight kinds, as explained above.
The "objects" are of eight kinds:
from timely medicine up to pure and impure items.
Regarding "having first consented": having first agreed within the Saṃgha to divide and distribute items together in harmony,
if one later objects by saying, "Venerable sir,
you have given these Saṃgha items based on personal favoritism," it is a pāyattika offense.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.

If items are to be distributed among the Saṃgha—such as the saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, antaravāsaka, niṣīdana, wound-covering cloth, rain-bathing robe, waistband, knotted-string bowl, small bowl, copper vessel, fan, umbrella, oil-skin bag, knife, sandals, and water flask—all such items that are to be distributed should be taken in turn.
If one does not wish to take it, one may pass by without taking it.
If someone asks, "Why do you not take it? [one should explain].
One should respond, saying:
"This is not what I require; I wish to take other items.
If one takes them later when they are needed, there is no offense.
If the person distributing the items announces,
"Take as much as you wish according to your desire," the bhikṣus may then take as much as they require according to their own wishes; there is no offense.
There are three kinds of prohibitions:
prohibition after having already given, prohibition at the time of giving, and prohibition before giving.
Regarding prohibition after having already given, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one objects at the proper time, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vibhinī-āpatti).
If one objects before the proper time, one incurs an offense of transgression requiring mental remorse (vibhinī-cittavipratisāra-āpatti).
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus were reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month, they remained silent during the recitation of the four *pārājika* rules, became angry during the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, spoke out during the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, and rose up during the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, saying:
"Elders, who is able to uphold these precepts?"
"What is the purpose of reciting this?
The devas will be able to uphold these precepts and prevent the bhikṣus from giving rise to doubt or regret.
At that time, those who were reciting the Prātimokṣa felt ashamed and remorseful.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“This is an evil deed.”
Out of a desire to benefit them, the Tathāgata has established for his disciples the recitation of the Prātimokṣa every half-month.
How can you, within this context, disparage and obstruct its recitation?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All those residing in Śrāvastī, assemble! For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If, when a bhikṣu recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra during the half-monthly assembly, he should say:
"Venerable sirs, what is the use of reciting these minor precepts every half-month?"
"Causing the bhikṣus to give rise to doubt and regret.
To thus disparage and revile the precepts constitutes a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Half-month" refers to either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
"Prātimokṣa" refers to the ten sūtras.
"Recitation" means that the Saṃgha, being in harmony, recites them every half-month.
The miscellaneous minor precepts (*khuddakānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*) refer to those other than the four matters and the thirteen matters.
To cause the bhikṣus to give rise to doubt or regret regarding these constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
There are three kinds of disparagement:
disparagement before speaking, disparagement while speaking, and disparagement after having spoken.
Regarding "reproaching before it has been spoken": one first says these words:
"Venerable sir, do not speak of these minor precepts; I wish to finish quickly."
This is called "reproving before it has been spoken.
As for "reproving while it is being spoken," it refers to saying these words at the time of reciting the precepts:
"Venerable sir, what is the use of reciting these trivial rules?"
