This causes the bhikṣus to give rise to doubt and regret.
This is called "reproving while speaking.
As for "reproving after having spoken," it means that after one has finished speaking, one says these words:
"You have just spoken of these minor precepts; why do you explain them so extensively?
You have caused me to sit for so long that I am utterly exhausted and feel as if I am about to die.
This is called "reproaching after having spoken."
If one censures before it has been spoken, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one censures while it is being spoken, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one censures after it has already been spoken, there is an offense of *vinayātikramasātisāra*.
Therefore it is said:
False speech and its varieties, double-tongued speech and further incitement,
impurity and the violation of the rules of diction, and speaking of grave offenses to those beyond [the ordinary].
To treat the precepts with intimacy and to treat them with contempt—this concludes the first *varga*.
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Vihāra; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, a *karmadāna* bhikṣu cut down trees with his own hands, broke off branches and leaves, and plucked flowers and fruits himself. He was thus disparaged by the people of the world, who spoke these words: [text continues]

“Look at this śramaṇa Gautama! While he used countless skillful means to revile the taking of life and praise non-killing, he now cuts down trees with his own hands to gather flowers, thereby injuring and killing living beings.”
"You have lost the dharma of a śramaṇa; what path do you possess?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"Call the bhikṣu in charge of affairs here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"This is an evil matter.
Although there is no life within it, one should not cause people to give rise to evil thoughts.
You all may also perform fewer tasks and abandon various worldly affairs."
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to cut or break seeds with your own hands, thereby injuring the village of spirits.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell in dependence upon the wilderness assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu destroys seeds or breaks up a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Seeds" are of five kinds: [the root-seed, the stem-seed, the joint-seed, the node-seed, and the seed-seed].
Root-seeds, stem-seeds, heart-seeds, joint-seeds, and seed-seeds constitute the five kinds.
"Village of spirits" refers to trees and grasses.
"To destroy" means to cut down, fell, or injure.
To cut, fell, or injure [plants] is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above. Regarding "root-seeds":
ginger root, lotus root, taro root, radish root, onion root, and other such root-seeds—these are purified by fire or purified by splitting with a knife; these are called root-seeds.

Regarding stem-propagated seeds: the nyagrodha, bimbara, udumbara, and willow—such as these, which are propagated from stems, must be purified by fire or split apart with a knife; these are called stem-propagated seeds.

Regarding "propagation by joints," this refers to bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, and the like; these should be purified by fire, or purified by splitting them with a knife, or by removing the sprouts and eyes with the fingernails—this is called propagation by joints.
Regarding "seed from a plant": coriander, indigo, and others of this kind that grow from plants should be purified by fire or purified by manual rubbing; these are called seeds from plants.
Regarding seed-plants, there are seventeen kinds of grain as described in the second precept; these must be purified by fire or by peeling, and these are called seed-plants.

There are seeds enveloped by a husk, seeds enveloped by a skin, seeds enveloped by a shell, seeds enveloped by chaff, seeds enveloped by a pod, seeds pecked by parrots, those that emerge whole, those scorched by fire, seasonal seeds, non-seasonal seeds, aquatic seeds, terrestrial seeds, and seeds that regenerate from what was previously produced.

Regarding "fruits with seeds enclosed": these include the *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, and the sour jujube (*kharjūra*). Such fruits should be cleaned by removing the seeds with the fingernails before eating. If one wishes to eat the seeds together with the fruit, they must be purified by fire; these are called "fruits with seeds enclosed."

Regarding those seeds that are covered by a husk—such as the *bībhītaka*, the *udumbara*, the *liṅga*, and so forth—these seeds covered by a husk must undergo purification by fire. However, when they are ripe and fall from the tree of their own accord due to rotting, and upon falling touch wood, stone, or other objects such that their skin is damaged like the mark of a mosquito’s foot, they are then said to be purified.
One must not eat seeds while they are still enclosed in their husks; if one wishes to eat them, they must be purified by fire.
These are called "husk-enclosed seeds. Regarding "shell-enclosed seeds," such as coconuts, walnuts, and pomegranates—these shell-enclosed seeds must likewise be purified by fire.
If it is broken, this is called a seed enveloped in a husk (*tuṣa*).

Regarding seeds enveloped in chaff (*śūka*): for examples such as coriander and sesame, if they have no kernel, they are purified by being rubbed with the hands; if they do have a kernel, they are purified by fire. These are called seeds enveloped in chaff.

Regarding seeds wrapped in pods: these include large and small mung beans, mocha beans, and so forth. If such seeds have not yet formed into pods, they are purified by manual crushing; if the seeds have already formed into pods, they are purified by fire. These are called "seeds wrapped in pods."

Regarding "parrot-pecked": if a bird pecks at it until it breaks open and falls to the ground, leaving a wound as small as a mosquito's leg, it is then considered pure; one may remove the seed and eat it. However, if one wishes to eat the seeds themselves, they must be purified by fire; this is called "parrot-purified."

"Intact excrement" refers to that which has been consumed and then passed from within the feces—such as that which comes from the dung of oxen, horses, or monkeys; this is called "intact," and it is designated as pure.
Regarding "purified by fire": if the fruit of a tree is scorched by a wild fire and falls to the ground, it is immediately considered pure; this is called purification by fire.
Regarding "sown in season": when sowing grain at the time for grain and sowing barley at the time for barley, these seeds must be purified by fire.

If it is purified by removing the skin, it is like a heap of grain in the kingdom of Kuruṇṭi; fearing that non-humans might steal it, one circles it with ashes and fire on top as a mark—this constitutes purification.

It was as when Māmadēvī had grain in her granary that had not yet been purified; fearing that the junior bhikṣus did not know the Dharma, she had a *kappiya-kāraka* purify it by means of fire until the grain in the granary was exhausted.
A bhikṣu may always say:
"Having pounded [the grain], there is no offense.
This is called the "timely seed" (kālabīja).

Regarding seeds sown at the wrong time: when it is the season for grain but it is the season for wheat, or when it is the season for wheat but it is the season for grain; these must be purified by fire or purified by peeling the skin. This is called "seeds sown at the wrong time."

Regarding the water-element seeds: the *utpala* flower, the *kumuda* flower, the *saugandhika* flower, and others of this kind—whose roots should be purified by fire or split with a knife—are called water-element seeds.
Regarding "prepared first and grown later": this refers to items such as non-glutinous rice or radish roots that are split with a fire-purified blade; this is called "prepared first and grown later.
Regarding "land-grown seeds": this refers to the seventeen kinds of grain which, after being husked and purified or fire-purified, are called "land-grown seeds."

Whether one cuts oneself, or causes another to cut; whether one breaks oneself, or causes another to break; whether one crushes oneself, or causes another to crush; whether one burns oneself, or causes another to burn; whether one flays one's own skin, or causes another to flay one's skin.
Regarding "cutting oneself": if one cuts oneself by means of one's own methods and does not stop throughout the entire day, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
If one stops midway and cuts again later, for each instance of stopping and resuming, one incurs a separate *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "causing another to cut": this is a figurative expression meaning to cause another to cut on a single day; for doing so, one incurs one *pāyattika*.
If, during that time, one repeatedly says, "Cut quickly," one incurs a *pāyattika* for each such utterance.
In this same way, regarding all four matters—cutting, breaking, crushing, and burning, whether performed by oneself or caused to be done by another—it is likewise forbidden.
If one serves as an administrator for the Saṃgha, one must never say to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites):
"Cut this, break this, crush this, burn this, or peel this."
If that were so, there would be an offense.
In all such cases, one should say: "I know this; this is pure."
There is no offense.

However, if one throws a living being into a pond, a well, excrement or urine, or into a heap of refuse by means of the five ways [of throwing], one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya.
If the seeds are rotten or damaged, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, wishing to prevent grass from growing, walks back and forth upon it, he incurs a vyatikrama-śikṣāpada offense while walking.
If one injures grass even to the extent of a mosquito's leg, one incurs a pāyattika.
The same applies to standing, sitting, or lying down [if injury occurs].
If one scratches a tree with a needle and injures it even to the extent of a mosquito's leg, one incurs a pāyattika.
If moss grows upon a stone and a bhikṣu wishes to wash his robes, he must not remove it himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) do so before washing the robes.
If the moss has been dried by the sun and he removes it himself, there is no offense.
If timber has been left on the ground after rain, a bhikṣu must not lift it himself; one who lifts it incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If he damages even as much grass as the leg of a mosquito, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) first lifts [the items] and a bhikkhu subsequently assists, there is no offense.

If a bhikkhu has a saṅghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, antaravāsaka, sitting mat (nisīdana), pillow or bedding, sandals, or mold growing on his robes, he should have the lay attendant take note; once they have been placed in the sun to dry, he may then handle and repair them himself.
If mold has formed on a cake, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to make things permissible) know of it before one may eat it.
When beans, sesame, fruits, gourds, sugarcane, or similar items are being distributed among the Sangha, the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) should ask:
"Has this been purified (*kappiya-kata*)?"
If one says,
"It has not been prepared," one should cause it to be made pure (*kappiya*).
If one says,
"It has already been prepared," one should eat.
If there are many fruits within a single vessel, if one fruit is purified at its location, the others are also collectively considered purified.
If they are in separate vessels, one must purify each individual vessel separately.
If sugarcane has leaves, each stalk must be purified individually.
If it has no leaves, they may be tied together in a bundle; if it is fruit, it may be purified as a whole.

If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) ties two blades of grass together during the summer retreat because the growing grass covers the path and he fears losing his way, he commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If one ties it with another object to form a knot for the sake of identification before departing, and unties it upon returning, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu dwells in the mountains and, while the mud and rain make the ground slippery such that he is about to fall, he grasps at grass and pulls it until it breaks, and then grasps again—such cases as these involve no offense.
If one is being swept away by water and grasps at grass, which breaks off as it is pulled, there is no offense even though it is severed.
If, while working with mud, one becomes thirsty and wishes to drink water, and has mud on one's hands, one may drink from the hollow of a tree leaf.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who prepares what is permissible) to gather the leaves, one may drink from among the leaves growing on the tree; however, one must not pull them off so that they break.
If the leaves are too high to reach, one may shake the tree to collect dry fallen leaves, take water from them, and drink.
If a bhikṣu cuts newly grown, green, and tender leaves, it is a pāyattika.
If he cuts long-established, firm, and hard leaves, it is a pāyattika.
If he cuts leaves that have already withered and turned yellow, it is a violation of the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If the wind blows down the three kinds of leaves, one may take and use them without offense.
If a bhikṣu plucks raw fruit, it is a pāyattika.
If it is half-ripe, he incurs a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If one takes [the grass] after it has been thoroughly processed, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a journey and staying overnight, pulls up living grass with the thought that it is dry grass, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If he pulls up dry grass with the thought that it is living grass, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one perceives living grass as living grass, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one perceives dry grass as dry grass, there is no offense.
Within a city or a village, if people have offered branches and leaves to a sacred tree, they must not be broken off even if they are dry.
To break [a branch] constitutes an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
The four cases regarding trees are also as explained above in the section on growing grass.

If a bhikṣu requires water for the purpose of relieving himself or herself, he should go to a pond; if there is duckweed covering the surface of the water, and he wishes to take water for use, he must not clear it away with his hand to take the water.

One should seek out a place where cattle or horses have passed, or where snakes or frogs have crawled; if there are no such tracks, one should take a clod of earth and throw it upward, saying these words:
"Go up as far as the Brahma-heaven, or let this clod of stone fall back down."
At that time, if one uses a place where water has been drawn out, there is no offense.
If one turns over floating duckweed in the water, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If one seizes it and throws it onto the bank, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

When entering the water to bathe, if aquatic plants adhere to one's body, one should pour water over them to make them fall off while remaining in the water; if one cuts them like morning fungi, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense against the *vinaya*.
If one picks up dried cow dung that contains living grass, it is an offense of *pāyattika*.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the Saṃgha had assembled intending to perform a formal act (karmavācanā), but the Venerable Channa did not come. The Saṃgha sent a messenger to say to Channa:
"The Saṃgha has assembled intending to perform a formal act; Elder, please come."
Chanda thought to himself:
"That they have summoned me now must surely be because they wish to punish me for my offense;
there can be no other reason. He further reflected:
“Whom should I now disturb so that the entire Saṃgha is thrown into disorder and unable to perform the *karmavācanā*?
It would be proper to disturb the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; he is the one capable of accomplishing this task.”
However, Maudgalyāyana possesses great supernormal powers; though he may know me to be incapable, he might perhaps seize me and hurl me to another world-system—this matter is not possible.
He reflected further:

"If I were to disturb Mahākāśyapa, this matter might be accomplished; yet Mahākāśyapa possesses great majestic virtue, and he might perhaps humiliate me before the assembly—this matter is also not possible."
He further thought:

"The Venerable Śāriputra is gentle, upright, and easy to converse with; if I were to disturb him, it would cause the entire Saṃgha to be disturbed, so that they would not perform the *karmavācanā* against me."
After Cchanda had entered the midst of the Saṃgha, he spoke these words:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I wish to inquire about a certain matter."
Śāriputra said, "The community has been assembled for another matter; this is not the time to discuss the meaning of this doctrine.
Chandaka spoke again to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"Just as the True Dharma of the Buddha has no improper time, so too does it yield wholesome fruits within the present life that remove the fever of afflictions; all noble ones rejoice in this, without making any distinctions."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said,
"Listen to my question.
Chanda replied:
“The Blessed One has spoken of the four foundations of mindfulness; what are these four foundations of mindfulness?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra explained the four foundations of mindfulness to him, but Candana spoke again:
“I am not asking about the four foundations of mindfulness; I am asking about the four right efforts.”
"Elder, please explain the four right efforts for me.
Śāriputra said, "Listen,
if you wish to hear about the four right efforts."
He then taught him the four right efforts.
Chandaka spoke again:
"I asked about the four bases of psychic power."

"In this same manner, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path were each asked three times, as was done for the four foundations of mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus had been sitting for a long time and were weary; they dispersed one by one, and the Saṃgha was not in harmony, so the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call Channa here.
When he had come, the Buddha asked Channa:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said,
"Chanda! This is an evil deed."
"Have I not always, for your sake, used immeasurable skillful means to reproach you for disruptive speech and to praise you for compliant speech?
Why do you now engage in such disruptive behavior?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who rely on Kauśāmbī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu annoys another with discordant speech, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are eight matters regarding annoying another with discordant speech.
What are the eight?
First, when performing a formal ritual (karmavācanā);
second, when engaging in discourse in accordance with the Dharma; [and so forth].
Third, when discussing the Abhidharma;
fourth, when discussing the Vinaya;
fifth, when discussing without differentiation.
Sixth, speaking inconsistently with others;
seventh, interrupting the discourse;
eighth, distressing others by using different terminology.

"Performing formal acts" (*karmakaraṇa*) refers to when monks assemble in harmony to perform a *tarjanīyakarman* (act of censure), up to and including a *pārivāsikakarman* (act of temporary exclusion); this is called performing formal acts.
"Discourse in accordance with the Dharma" refers to teaching that there is neither permanence nor annihilation; this is called discourse in accordance with the Dharma.
The Abhidharma refers to the ninefold Sūtras; this is called the Abhidharma.
The Vinaya refers to the extensive and abbreviated Prātimokṣa; this is called the Vinaya.
Regarding "not deviating from the subject" (*ananyathā-vāda*): one must not depart from the original topic under discussion to discuss other matters;

this is called not deviating from the subject. Regarding "not deviating from the person" (*ananyathā-pudgala*): one must not depart from the person who first asked the question to ask another person; this is called not deviating from the person.
"Postponing the discussion" means that while the Dharma is being preached, one halts the speech with the intention to discuss it again later; this is called postponing the discussion.
"Harassing others with irrelevant speech" refers to how the Venerable Channa harassed others with irrelevant speech; these are the eight matters.
Among these, to speak differently with the intent to annoy another constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Apart from these eight matters, it is not a *pāyattika*.
If someone asks a bhikṣu:
“From where have you come?
He replied,
“I have come from the past.”
“Where has he gone? He replied,
“He has gone toward the future.”
“Where did you sleep? “I slept on a wooden beam.
“Where did you eat today?”
He replied,
“I eat with five fingers.
If one asks in this manner and answers incorrectly, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
If thieves enter the monastery and ask the bhikṣus,

"Show us the property of the Saṃgha," at that time the bhikṣus must not show precious treasures or other such items, nor should they speak falsely; rather, they should show them such things as rooms, beds, and seats.
If the robbers say,
"Show us the temple's property," one must not show the precious objects of the stupa,
nor should one speak falsely; rather, one should show the various ritual implements and utensils used for making offerings around the stupa.
If the robbers say,
"Show us a clean kitchen," the bhikṣu must not speak falsely,
nor may he point out the location of money or valuables; he should instead indicate the location of the cauldrons, pots, jars, and other such vessels.
If a beast belonging to a butcher runs away and asks a bhikṣu, "Have you seen it?
the bhikṣu must not speak falsely, nor may he indicate its location; he should say:
"Look at the finger! Look at the finger!
This refers to the case where a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) encounters a runaway prisoner who questions him; he answers as previously described in the section on animals.
If a bhikṣu, when questioned within the saṃgha, answers differently from what was asked, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he answers differently from what was asked before a group of many people, or before his upādhyāya, ācārya, or various elder bhikṣus, he commits a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, the people of the world possessed profound faith and reverence; many brought food and drink to make offerings to the World-Honored One, as well as to the assembly of monks, including the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Regarding those offerings made to the Buddha, the attendants collected them;
however, as for those given to the Sangha and to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, whether they were distributed or not, there was no one to manage them, so they remained putrid and foul-smelling.
At that time, the Venerable Dabba was still on the stage of training and thought to himself:
"When I have attained the state of one beyond training, I shall manage the affairs of the Saṅgha so that they may live in peace and happiness."

Having formed this thought, he practiced the Path with diligence during both the first and last watches of the night, immediately attaining arhatship. Having acquired the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, he thought:
"What need have I for conditioned activities?"
"I ought to cultivate delight in few desires and non-entanglement.
The Buddha said to Dhānañjāni:
"When you were formerly on the stage of training, you spoke these words:"
“Did you not speak these words: ‘If I attain the state of one beyond training, I shall attend to the affairs of the Saṃgha’?
He replied:
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Dabba!..."
"As you previously vowed, you should now act accordingly.
He replied, "I shall do as the World-Honored One has instructed."
At that time, the Saṃgha immediately appointed someone to oversee the nine matters as previously described.

Then, food was distributed according to suitability: if it was an elder or a senior monk (*sthavira*), he was given superior food; those in the middle seats were given middling food; and those in the lower seats were given coarse food.
The group of six bhikṣus, harboring resentment and malice, went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said to Dharmapāla:

"In the dharma of those who have left the household life, food should be distributed with equanimity. You should know that one should not feel insufficient when receiving little, nor feel weary when receiving much; whether one receives good or bad, one should remain impartial in all cases."
Thereupon, the Elder Dabba prepared three grades of food—excellent, mediocre, and coarse—in successive order, repeating the cycle again and again.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda rose early in the morning, put on their village-dwelling robes, took up their alms bowls, and went to the house where the meal was being served.
He said to the upāsikā,
"Give me some food.
The upāsikā replied:
“Venerable One!
The time for the meal has not yet arrived; I have not yet washed my face or cleaned the vessels, nor have I been able to prepare the food for the renunciant.

At that moment, the female donor, who was small of stature, rose up; as she bathed with her body exposed, the bhikṣu Nanda did not restrain his sense faculties and gazed lustfully at the woman’s form. The upāsikā then thought to herself:

"This bhikṣu is not one who follows the Vinaya, or perhaps he has given rise to faults and evils; it is not appropriate for him to remain here for long. Let us give him coarse food as a laborer and quickly send him away.
Having thought this, they immediately gave him coarse food as a laborer. Once the bhikṣu had received the food, he returned to the vihāra.

At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who, when the time had come, put on his village-entering robes and took up his bowl; with dignified and composed deportment, he went to a layperson's home for a meal, and the donor offered him various kinds of fine food, which he filled his bowl with and returned.
Then Nanda and Upananda, having seen this, spoke thus: "Venerable Dabba!
The World-Honored One has taught that food should be distributed equally; look at these two portions of food—is it not equal?"
Dabba said, "You arrived too early; it is not yet mealtime.

The next day, Nanda put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city; along the way, he watched elephants fighting and horses fighting, and listened to the conversations of the laypeople.
At that time, the upāsikā thought to herself, "The ācārya did not receive food when he came yesterday; today I should prepare it early.
Although the donor's family had prepared the meal for a long time, he did not arrive when the time came.
The upāsikā thought again:
"The Venerable One came early yesterday; for what reason does he not come today?
Perhaps there is a meal offering for the Saṃgha within the Jeta Grove Monastery, and that is why he has not come."
She then ate it all together with her husband and children.
At that time, Nanda arrived toward midday and said to the upāsikā,
"Give me some food."
The upāsikā said:

“I prepared the meal early, but waiting for the Venerable One not to arrive, I thought that someone in the Jeta Grove was providing food for the Saṃgha and that he had accepted an invitation there; thus, I have already finished eating this meal I prepared.”
Nanda said, "Are you now intending to cut off my food?

At that time, the upāsikā gave him the leftover food from the previous night prepared by the household servants. Having received it, he returned to the vihāra and related everything in detail as before.
Dharmapāla said,
"You arrived too late. Then,
for this reason, the Venerable Dharmapāla went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Nanda here. When he had come, the Buddha asked Nanda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me, through countless skillful means, censure excessive desire and praise few desires?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu reviles or reproaches [another], it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above. "Reviling or reproaching" means:
to bow to a person, to entrust someone with a bow, or to entrust someone with an entrusted bow.
One who performs the formal act of salutation (*abhivādana*) is like the Venerable Dabba; this is called "one who performs the salutation.

One who performs the formal act of entrustment (*anussāvana*) is like Dabba Mallaputta, who requested another person to manage the affairs of the Saṅgha; this is called "one who performs the entrustment."

Regarding "entrusting to one who has been entrusted": if the person whom one has requested to act on behalf of the Sangha further requests another person to manage the Sangha's affairs, this is called "entrusting to one who has been entrusted.
To harbor resentment toward or reprimand such a person constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If various kinds of cakes are being distributed among the Sangha, one should receive them in turn.
If one does not desire them in one's mind, one should let them pass. If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) asks:
"Why do you not take it?
He replied,
"I have no need for this."
If one wishes to take more of another [portion], there is no offense.

When rice gruel, curd gruel, sesame gruel, or fish-and-meat gruel is being served, or when various kinds of such gruels are being distributed, if a full ladle is offered to the *upādhyāya* (senior elder), the *upādhyāya* should not accept it immediately.
The Elder should say:
"Give equally.
If, when distributing the meat, more is given to the Elder than to others, the Elder should ask:
"Is it so for all? He replied,
"It is merely that there are more than with the Elder."
The Elder should say:
"Give equally.
If one does not require much, one should take a small amount; having taken a small amount, one should say to the others:
"Give equally. Thus, such excellent food should be distributed equally.
If, when a novice is serving the meal, he distributes it preferentially to his teacher, the administrator should say:
“Give it equally.
If the śrāmaṇera says,
“Why do you not give it yourself?”
The administrator should expel this śrāmaṇera and have another person serve the food.
If the one serving the food sees a person of great virtue among the saṃgha, they will give them much, while giving little to the others.
The administrator should say to the food distributor:
"In the Sangha there is no distinction of high or low; you must distribute it with equality.
There may be those who find fault but do not reprimand, those who reprimand but do not find fault, those who both find fault and reprimand, or those who neither find fault nor reprimand.
Those who were displeased and reproached him compared the food in his own bowl with the food in the bowls of those sitting beside him, saying: "Is this equal?"
This is called disliking without censuring.
These four permutations are explained in detail.
To dislike without censuring constitutes an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one reprimands without expressing disapproval, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If one both expresses disapproval and reprimands, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one neither expresses disapproval nor reprimands, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
While the Buddha was wandering among the people of the Vṛji country, he arrived with a community of bhikṣus at the bank of an old river.
At that time, some fishermen were casting nets to catch fish; having seen this, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This fisherman ought not to perform such deeds, yet he exerts himself in them.
After the bhikṣus had thus questioned him, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Having already obtained this body so difficult to find, why do you commit various evils?
Because of being defiled by craving and attachment to the body, at the end of life you will enter the evil realms.

At that time, the fishermen took a large net, weighted it with stones and buoyed it with gourds, and moving upstream, two hundred and fifty men on each side shouted as they pulled the net toward the shore.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
If this person exerts such diligence within the Buddha-dharma, he will obtain great benefit from the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, spoke in verse:
"What is called diligent exertion is not merely the pursuit of all desires;
it means being able to leave behind all evils and sustaining one's life through the Dharma."
This is as explained in detail in the *Kāpilavastu-jātaka*.
At that time, the multitude of fish fell into the net; among them was one great fish with a hundred heads, each head being distinct from the others.
When the World-Honored One saw him, he called him by his name, and he immediately responded to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Where is your mother?"
He replied,
"I am a worm living in a certain latrine.
The Buddha said:
"This great fish was a Tripiṭaka bhikṣu during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; because he used harsh speech, he received this retribution of having the heads of various creatures.
His mother, who had accepted his offerings, became a worm in a latrine."

When the Buddha had explained these causes and conditions, those five hundred people immediately ceased their fishing nets and left the household life to practice the Way; they all attained arhatship and dwelt by the banks of the Bāhukā River.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Prepare seats for these visiting bhikṣus. ...
[and so on] ... until Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“May the Buddha comfort the visiting bhikṣu.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You yourself do not know that I have already entered the fourth dhyāna to comfort the visiting bhikṣu.”

At that time, each of them had spread out their mats on the open ground, intending to go for alms. When the time arrived, these bhikṣus each used their supernormal powers; some went to Uttarakuru, some to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and some to the palaces of the nāga kings to beg for food. Their mats remained on the open ground, scorched by the sun, buffeted by the wind, and defiled by dust and filth. The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Wait for these bhikṣus to return."
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forth, because of you, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who rely on the Bhagīrathī River assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣu, at a monastery dwelling, having spread out or caused another to spread out a bed, chair, mat, or pillow on an open space, does not himself put it away or cause another to put it away when departing, it is a pāyattika.
"Monk" is as described above.
"The monastery grounds" refers to either a forest hermitage or a village residence.
"Sleeping and sitting beds" consist of fourteen types:

Round-legged reclining beds, round-legged sitting benches, lying mats, sitting mats, open-weave rattan reclining beds, open-weave rattan sitting benches, *uṇḍaka* (woven) reclining beds, *uṇḍaka* sitting benches, *tāmi* (cotton) reclining beds, and *tāmi* sitting benches.
Regarding mats: cotton-mats, wool-mats, felt-mats, Kāśī-mats, and grass-mats.
Regarding pillows: cotton-pillows, wool-pillows, felt-pillows, and Kāśī-pillows.
"Spreads" means either to spread it oneself or to cause another to spread it.
"Leaves" means to go elsewhere.
"Does not remove" means neither to remove it oneself nor to cause another to remove it; this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If one wishes to preach the Dharma in an open space, once one knows that the person who spread the bedding has finished spreading the bed and bedding, if one departs more than twenty-five cubits (*hasta*) without having entrusted the matter to them, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If two people share this knowledge, when one wishes to go out, he should entrust it to the second person.
When the second person wishes to go out, he should wait until the first person has returned and handed it back over before departing.
If, after one has finished spreading out a bed or mat, another person comes and sits upon it, the person who spread it may leave once they know of it; there is no offense.
If, during the spring months, one spreads bedding on an open space and a junior bhikṣu sits or lies down upon it, one should immediately entrust it to that bhikṣu.

If there is no bhikṣu on the bed, and a bhikṣu rises at night to attend to the needs of nature and touches the monastic bed—having touched it once and then departed—he incurs a pāyattika for each instance of contact.
If there is a bhikṣu on the bed, one may entrust it to that person and there is no offense.

However, if a monastic administrator (saṃgha-karmika), wishing to hand over the bedding, takes it outside and leaves it on the open ground at a distance of twenty-five cubits, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one has received a monastic bed or mat and leaves it in the sun to dry, departing at a distance of twenty-five cubits, it is also a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu is ill and sleeps in an open space, and his disciple comes to pay respects to the teacher;
if the teacher rises and departs, the disciple should lift the covering.

If there are two people sitting together on one bed, when the person of higher rank wishes to leave, they should entrust the bed to the person of lower rank; when the person of lower rank wishes to leave, they should inform the person of higher rank, saying:
"I wish to leave; where should this bed be moved?"
If the senior monk says,
"You go yourself; I shall lift this bed myself," and one then departs, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu spreads out a bed or mat for his upādhyāya or ācārya and then departs, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If the upādhyāya or ācārya knows that [the bed] has been spread for him, he should entrust it [to someone] when departing; if he departs without having entrusted it, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the measurement of twenty-five cubits: when extremely heavy rain falls, it does not penetrate because there are two layers of clothing.
If a bhikṣu places an image upon a bed belonging to the Saṃgha, and another bhikṣu comes to pay homage and touches it with his hand but does not lift it up, it is a pāyattika offense.
If many bhikṣus perform prostrations in succession, the hand-contact belongs to the last one.

There are cases where there is an entrustment but no belonging, cases where there is belonging but no entrustment, cases where there is both entrustment and belonging, and cases where there is neither entrustment nor belonging.
One who is entrusted but not dependent is a śrāmaṇera.
One who is dependent but not entrusted is a senior bhikṣu.
One who is both entrusted and dependent is a junior bhikṣu.
Regarding those who are neither entrusted nor assigned: these are laypeople.

If a virtuous bhikṣu has many disciples and they have spread out mats and bedding for him, and if the teacher knows that the bedding was spread for his sake, he should entrust someone to put it away when he departs; if he does not so entrust them, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If bedding belonging to the Saṃgha is spread out on an open space within a dwelling place of the Saṃgha, and one does not pick it up when departing, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If bedding belonging to the Saṃgha is spread out on an open space within a private dwelling, and one does not pick it up when departing, one commits a vyatikrama against the Vinaya.
If one’s own bedding or mat is spread upon the open ground belonging to the Saṃgha and is not removed when departing, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If one’s own bedding or mat is spread upon private open ground and is not removed when departing, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If a monastic’s bed or bedding is spread out in the home of a layperson and is not removed when departing, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If a layperson’s bed or bedding is spread out in an open space, one should inform them before leaving.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, there was a brahmin who had invited the community of monks for a meal and the gift of robes. The bhikṣus spread out the monastic sitting mats within the monastery cells and departed directly without putting them away.

Out of consideration for five benefits, the World-Honored One would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing that the bedding and furnishings within the bhikṣus’ rooms were defiled by insects, mouse droppings, filth, and dust, the Buddha, though already aware of the situation, intentionally questioned them. The bhikṣus then reported the matter to the World-Honored One in full detail.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You who have left the household life have no attendants to manage your affairs after death; why did you not lift [the body] when it was time to depart?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣu spreads out a bed or mat for himself in a private, enclosed place, or causes another to spread it, and upon departing neither lifts it up himself nor causes another to lift it up, it is a pāyattika.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Indoors" refers to a covered place.
"Beds and seats" are of fourteen kinds, as explained above.
Regarding pillows and bedding, it is as explained above.
As for spreading them out, one may either spread them oneself or have another person spread them.
As for departing, it means going to another location.
"Not lifting up oneself" means not lifting oneself up.
"Not causing another to lift up" means not causing others to lift [the bowl]; this is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu wishes to depart for another place, he should sprinkle water inside the dwelling and sweep the floor to make it clean, smear the ground with cow dung, and dry the bedding and pillows in the sun; then he should speak thus to the person in charge of the bedding:
"Venerable one!..."
"All these beds, mats, and pillows should be entrusted with instructions.
If one knows that the person in charge of the beds and mats is a junior monk, one should say to them:
"You must take care of these beds and mats."
He replied, “Yes.
If it was the senior monk who had entrusted him with the bedding and mat, he replied:
“If you do so,” [the Buddha said]. To depart without having informed [the resident monk] is a *pāyattika*.
If one departs without having informed him, and a monk has entered and is staying in the room, because it is not empty, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense against the Vinaya.
If one has already forgotten one's robes and bowl and returns to retrieve them and informs [the preceptor], there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu is traveling along a road and it becomes overcast and about to rain, and a junior bhikṣu goes ahead to the monastery to fetch a bed and mat for his upādhyāya or ācārya, he should inform [the preceptor] when the weather clears and he wishes to depart.
If one departs without having announced it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If many bhikṣus are staying overnight in a village monastery and have shared the use of the Sangha’s beds and bedding, each should form this thought:
"I shall entrust [the bedding] to such-and-such a person."

After they had departed, as they traveled along the road, they asked one another repeatedly, but there was no one at all to whom they had entrusted their belongings. The bhikṣus should have dispatched two people back to deliver the entrustment.

If bhikṣus were traveling on the road and stayed overnight at a monastery, and upon leaving did not entrust their bedding and mats, and after traveling a great distance they asked one another repeatedly, yet none at all had made an entrustment.
Meeting a bhikṣu on the road, he immediately asked him,
"Venerable sir, where are you going?
He replied:
"I wish to go to such-and-such a place.
That bhikṣu then said: "I stayed there last night;
when I left, I forgot to entrust my bedding and mats to you. Elder, when you arrive there, you should entrust them to me for me."
That bhikṣu spoke again:
"When I arrived, I also forgot to entrust [the robes] to you; Elder, please go to that monastery and entrust them for me.
When the two have thus entrusted one another in turn, even until they both enter the boundary of the monastery, it is termed "entrustment" (niyata).
If a bhikṣu stays overnight in a layperson’s house and receives beds, mats, or bedding, he should inform them of his departure when leaving.
If he has received a grass mat, he should say upon leaving:
"Where do you wish for this grass to be placed?"
One should arrange it according to the host's instructions.
If the donor says, "Just go;
I shall take care of it myself," [then one may leave].
The bhikṣu should gather one corner of the grass and depart.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, pulls up tangled grass to spread as a seat, he should gather it back together when leaving.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a visiting bhikṣu who came to the quarters of the group of six bhikṣus. The group of six bhikṣus said, "Welcome, Elder!"
Having spoken these words, he provided him with water for washing the feet, oil for anointing the feet, and non-time-appropriate beverages.
Once [the guest] had rested, he said to the visiting bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!..."
"Where do you wish to stay?
He replied,
"I shall stay in this room."
The group of six bhikṣus asked,
"Do you know whose room this is?
He replied:
"I know this is a dwelling for the Saṃgha.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"Although this is a dwelling for the Saṃgha, we, the group of six bhikṣus, have already been residing here first."
The visiting bhikṣu said:

"This is a dwelling for the Saṃgha from the four quarters; even if the group of sixteen bhikṣus had previously resided here, I would still take up residence according to my turn, let alone the group of six bhikṣus."
The group of six bhikṣus said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, if you wish to stay, then stay.
Once the visiting bhikṣu had settled in, the group of six bhikṣus each seized his hands and feet, or seized his head and lifted him up, intending to cast him out.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived through the air by means of his supernormal power; upon seeing the World-Honored One, the group of six bhikṣus prostrated themselves on the ground and departed.
The Buddha said to the visiting bhikṣu, "You simply remain in your room."

Furthermore, Venerable Nanda was the elder brother of Upānanda. When Nanda’s co-practitioner disciple [committed an offense] up to the point of being driven out of the room, once he had left the room, the disciple cried out loudly.
Hearing the sound, all the bhikṣus came out in alarm to look and spoke thus:
“This bhikṣu has today lost two kinds of benefit:”
"They have been deprived of food and their dwellings.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda and Upananda,
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How is it that you dwell in the monastic quarters belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions, yet you drag out visiting bhikṣus?"
This is an evil deed.

Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise and teach that one should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who practice the holy life—cultivating loving-kindness through bodily action, cultivating loving-kindness through verbal and mental action, and always providing for and supporting them?
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, while inside a monastic dwelling, either personally drags someone out or causes another to drag them out, even saying:
"Bhikṣu, you must leave!"
"One who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu drags another bhikṣu out, and that bhikṣu is either embracing a pillar, grasping a door, or leaning against a wall, for each instance of dragging him away from such a position, there is a separate *pāyattika* offense.
If one rebukes or scolds that bhikṣu with words and he departs from each respective location according to those words, there is a pāyattika for each instance.
If one uses expedient means to drive him directly out the door, one incurs one pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, drives away snakes or mice,
he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense. If he says,
"These are useless things," [he likewise commits an offense].
There is no offense in driving them out.
If camels, oxen, or horses are within a stūpa or monastery, there is no offense in driving them out for fear of defiling or damaging the stūpa or monastery.
If a bhikṣu drives another bhikṣu out, it is a pāyattika.
If one drives out a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one drives out a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, one incurs a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If one goes as far as driving a layperson out, it is a violation of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance.
Therefore, this is taught.
The Sixteen [Khandhakas] conclude. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 14.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The fourth of the ninety-two rules concerning the *pācittiya* offenses:

While the Buddha was wandering among the people in Kauśāmbī, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the śrāvakas during the first watch of the night. Having finished preaching the Dharma, the bhikṣus each returned to their respective quarters.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had been conversing elsewhere and returned after a long while; they knocked on the door of a room, and the person inside asked, "Who is it?
They replied:
"I am one of the group of six bhikṣus, and I wish to stay overnight here.
The bhikṣu in the room said,
"This room is already full."
The group of six bhikṣus again spoke with gentle words and entreated him earnestly:
"Give us a small portion, enough for one seat.
When they could not obtain it through such earnest entreaty, they went to other rooms, but there too they did not obtain it.

He then went to the quarters of the junior bhikṣus—whether it be a heated hall (*jantāghara*), a meditation chamber (*dhyāna-śālā*), or a lecture hall—and knocked on the door. The bhikṣu inside the hall asked, "Who is it?"
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"We wish to come here to stay overnight.
The bhikṣus inside the hall said:
"This hall is already full.

The group of six bhikṣus continued to press their request insistently without ceasing. The bhikṣus inside the hall then opened the doors for them; once they had entered the rooms, they threw themselves onto the beds in all directions and lay down, using their elbows and knees to shove and strike those beside them, and further saying:
"Venerable elders, make way so that we may have a single color!"
Having spoken these words, he immediately blew out the lamp.
He then called to his companions outside, saying, "Virtuous practitioners, please come inside.
Once they had entered, he kicked those in front on their knees and struck those behind on their elbows, emitting wind and playing in a lewd manner.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Who could remain in one place together with this person who lacks dignified decorum?
They immediately took their sitting mats (niṣīdana) and departed.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"Wait until I have returned from my journey through Kośala to Śrāvastī; then you may report this matter again, and I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

A visiting bhikṣu arrived and was assigned a room by the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika) to stay in for the night. Having closed the door, he fell asleep. At that time, because of their prior resentment toward him, the group of six bhikṣus secretly smeared slippery mud upon the lintel of the door and placed slippery mud, as well as bricks and stones, along the path where he would walk.
This bhikṣu went out at night and, stepping on a slippery spot, fell upon bricks and stones, whereupon he said:
"Venerable sirs!
The group of six bhikṣus has killed me; because they broke my neck, they have done such a thing wishing to disturb me. Who could live together with them?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

“The group of six bhikṣus has committed not only this one evil deed; while the World-Honored One was traveling through the country of Kośala, they disturbed the bhikṣus, even to the point that each of them took their own sitting mats (niṣīdana) and departed.”
The Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus,
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How could you know that another had previously prepared [the seat], only to come later and disturb it with the intent to make him leave?"
"This is an evil matter; it is not Dharma, not Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. One must not use this to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already spread out bedding and mats, comes later with the intent to cause disturbance and spreads them out, thinking:
"Those who do not wish for this shall leave of their own accord."
"If one creates such a pretext without it being otherwise, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Previously spread" refers to that which was spread first.
"Mats and bedding" are as previously described.
"Spreading later" means intending to cause disturbance so as to make the other person leave.
If one acts in such a manner without making an exception, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.

If the dwelling is small, a single bhikṣu should spread his bed, bedding, and *niṣīdana* within the space between two pillars; having covered them, he may then approach his *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* to pay homage, inquire after their well-being, or receive instruction and recitation before departing.
Later, another bhikṣu arrived, removed the first bhikṣu’s sitting mat, spread his own sitting mat, and having sat down, chanted with a low voice.
When the resident bhikṣu came and saw this, he thought to himself:
"Who is able to interrupt another's Dharma?"
If he then takes his own sitting mat (niṣīdana) and departs,
that bhikṣu commits a pāyattika offense.
The same applies when he is engaged in meditative concentration, reciting the sūtras, or is ill.
If one later comes and lies down upon another's bed, if that person is a senior elder (sthavira), one should say to them:
"Venerable sir, do you not know that the Blessed One has established the precepts?
If the monk who is lying down is a junior elder (navaka), one should reprove him.
"You do not properly understand the characteristics of the precepts; you do not know that the World-Honored One has established these rules. Why have you come later and slept upon another's bed?
If a bhikṣu is walking about in another place and sees a bhikṣu who arrived earlier, he should withdraw and leave.
If a bhikṣu, while sleeping at night, moves about or utters incoherent speech, provided he does not do so with the intention to cause disturbance, there is no offense.
To disturb a bhikṣu intentionally constitutes a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is an offense of violating the vinaya (vayyavatikā);
for a layperson, it is an offense of transgressing the vinaya through mental regret (vayyavatikā-cittāpatteḥ). It is for this reason that it is so stated.

The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Vihāra. There were two bhikṣus living together there: the senior monk stayed in the lower story and the junior monk in the upper story; the senior monk practiced meditation while the junior monk recited the sūtras.

When it was time for the senior elder (*sthavira*), he put on his village-entering robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the wilderness village to beg for food; he quickly obtained alms and returned swiftly.
Only after the junior elder had departed did the senior elder eat, wash his bowl, and set it aside in its usual place; then, having washed his feet, he sat down cross-legged.
The junior monk returned late after obtaining food; having returned, he placed his bowl in its usual spot on the upper story and uttered the sound "Hūḥ!
He then threw himself down with full force and sat upon the bed. The foot of the bed slipped out from underneath and struck the head of the senior monk, causing blood to flow from it.
The Elder spoke these words:
"Kill me! Kill me!"
Upon hearing the sound, the bhikṣus immediately gathered together and asked,
"For what reason is this so?
The Elder related the matter in detail, and the bhikṣus, for these reasons, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here. When he had come,
the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”

The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "How is it that you sat with force upon a bed with pointed legs spread out on the upper story? From this day forward, I do not permit sitting upon beds with pointed legs spread out on the upper story."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon the wilderness assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu places a bed with pointed legs on an upper story and sits or lies upon it, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "pavilion" (kūṭāgāra) refers to a second story.
A "house" (gṛha) is as permitted by the World-Honored One.
"Pointed legs" are like wooden stakes.
Regarding "beds," there are fourteen kinds, as explained above.
Whether sitting or lying down upon them, it is a *pāyattika*.
As for "a *pāyattika*," it is as explained above.

If the ground is made firm with mud and earth, or if it is constructed with planks so as to be tight, or if the legs are rounded, or if there is a railing around the edge, and no one sits beneath the railing, in all such cases there is no offense.
If one uses a bed or a chair with pointed legs made of loose materials, whether sitting or lying down upon it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits on such a bed with its legs turned inward, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If one sits on a cross-legged chair, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
If a chair has one pointed leg and three round legs, it is a pāyattika.
Likewise, if two, three, or four legs are pointed, it is a pāyattika.
If it has four legs and is round, there is no offense.
Therefore, it is said:

While the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, a monk in charge of construction affairs used water containing living beings to moisten grass and mud, and was consequently criticized by the people of the world.
“The ascetic Gautama uses countless skillful means to revile the taking of life and to praise abstaining from it.
Yet now this ascetic sprinkles water containing insects upon grass and mud; he is a man who ruins others—what kind of path does he have?”
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣu in charge of construction affairs here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; it should rightly be despised by the world.
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
"From this day forward, I do not permit the watering of grass or mud with water containing living beings.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside at the Āraṇyaka Vihāra assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings, yet pours it onto grass or mud, or causes another to pour it, he commits a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "knows," it means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Creeping creatures" refers to any living beings, down to the most minute.
"Water" consists of ten types, as described above.
"Grass" refers to reeds, awns, and the like.
"Mud" refers to mud made of grass, mud made of *śaṇa* hemp, mud made of the dung of elephants, horses, or oxen, and so forth.
"Sprinkling" means sprinkling it oneself or causing another person to sprinkle it.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings and, by means of some expedient, pours it out one breath at a time, it is a pāyattika offense.
For every breath, there is a separate pāyattika offense according to the number of breaths.
If one instructs another to pour water, it is a *pāyattika* for each such instruction.
If one further instructs them to pour quickly, it is a *pāyattika* for every such instruction.
If a bhikṣu requires water for the construction of a dwelling or a heated room—whether from a pond, a river, or a well—he must strain it, fill a vessel, and inspect it for insects before using it.
If there are still insects present, one should use a heavy cloth bag to strain the water and observe it closely.
If there are still insects present even after three layers [of straining],
one should construct a well again as before and observe it closely.
If there are still insects present, one should abandon the task at hand and go to another location.

As for the method of filtering water: one should set up three poles crosswise and tie their upper ends together; attach the water filter bag to them and place a vessel beneath it to catch the water. One should always keep a small amount of water in the filter bag before returning it to the well.

The arising of insects is impermanent; they may be absent at first and present now, or present now and absent later. Therefore, monks, you should examine them daily with close attention and use them only when no insects are found.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings, yet pours it onto grass or mud—whether he pours it himself or instructs another to do so—he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he uses water containing living beings to bathe his upādhyāya or ācārya, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one uses water from washing vessels, rice rinsings, any kind of gruel, or fermented grain-liquor that contains living organisms to pour over grass or mud, one commits a pāyattika offense.
Therefore, this is said.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Chanda exhorted [the laypeople] to construct a dwelling. Chanda then gathered materials for roofing, such as grass, wood, and bamboo;
having prepared them, he went to the roofers and said, "I have completed all the necessary preparations; now give me the roofing."
The person repairing the roof said,
"Ācārya, give me the price for my labor as food.
At that time, Chanda measured out and gave it to him according to its value.
Then the laborers went to the site of the house.
Chanda said to the laborers, "This is for covering the roof. The roofers replied:
"There are three ways to thatch a roof, differing in thickness; which kind do you wish to construct?
Chanda replied, "Why do you ask about the three types of thickness?"
"All the grass currently available must be used to cover it.
The person covering the roof said, "There should be a limit; how can it all be used?"
Thus it was repeated three times.
The house-builder spoke again:
"In all the world there are established norms; that which accords with these norms is praised by the world."
Chanda said, "Just use it all to cover [the robes]; what need is there for many words?

The teacher followed his advice and used it all to cover them. Because the layer of grass was so thick, the binding could not hold; when the seasonal rain began, they were all completely unraveled. As the flowers bloomed throughout the night under the rain, the robes and bowls became entirely soaked.
In the early morning, Chanda went to the roof-carpenter’s workshop and spoke these words:
"How is it that you have covered my roof to such an extent?
The roof-carpenter replied:
"Why is that? Chanda replied,
"It rained all night long, and my robes and bowl are completely soaked."
The person repairing the roof said:
"I did not previously inform the Ācārya that there are three types of roofing materials, differing in thickness; nevertheless, I shall provide everything exactly as you have requested."
Chanda said,
"You should cover it for me once more.
The man covering the roof replied:
"Give me more food as payment for its value.
Chanda replied,
"The value you have already received."
The house-builder said, "That which was previously obtained has already been completed; if you wish to have it built again, the price shall be three times the original.
Even so, Chanda, relying on the power of the king, forcibly compelled him to rebuild it without paying the fee; furthermore, Chanda walked around his own quarters, reproaching him with bitter words.
At that time, there was a traveler, and the master builder said to him:
"Look, people, at these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; relying on the power and influence of the king, they have forced me to work for them without giving me my wages."
The laborer then complained:
"How is it that these sons of the Śākyas, relying on the power of the king, compel people to work for them and yet do not pay them wages?
This is truly unacceptable."
"He circles his own hut like a horse on a training ring, trampling and killing the living grass; such a ruined man—what path could he have?
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, who said:
"Call Channa here."
Having summoned him immediately, the Buddha asked Chanda,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha told Chanda:
"This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Kauśāmbī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling and provides it with doors and windows, and the construction reaches three layers of roofing, he must reside within a plot of sparse grass; if he exceeds this limit, it is a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.
“Makes” means either makes it himself or causes another to make it.
“Large” means exceeding the prescribed measure.
A "room" (kūtāgāra) is that which was permitted by the World-Honored One.
A "door" (dvāra) is the place through which people enter and exit.
A "window" (vātāyana) is the place through which light is admitted.
The "manager" is one who instructs, speaks to, and gives directions.
There are ten kinds of "coverings":

that of grass, mud, wooden boards, lime, the covering of the country of Āpaṇa, the country of Magadha, the country of Kauśāmbī, the mountain country, the country of Gauragrīva, and the country of Kulūta.
Furthermore, "three" refers to no more than three; it does not mean five or six.
"A place with sparse grass" means a place where grass grows sparsely.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
When negotiating the price with a person hired to repair a roof, one must state the actual value without exaggerating or undervaluing it, and should say to the worker:
"If you perform the roofing in this manner, I shall give you such-and-such a price."
"If you do not acknowledge the concealment in this manner, we shall not give you such a price.
Thus it must be made clear.
After the three stages of adjudication are completed, the bhikṣu thinks:
"If one should employ a skillful means and take grass, wood, or bamboo to that place, thinking, 'If he sees me, he will quickly cover it well,' and the house-builder,
having seen this, judges it as either good or not good, [the offender] incurs a pāyattika."

Employing such expedient means with the desire that the house-builder might see him, he goes to pay homage to his preceptors and teachers, receives and recites the scriptures, practices walking meditation, or enters a village; thinking, "Once the house-builder has seen me, he will surely quickly and skillfully cover [the roof]."
Having seen it, whether it be good or not good, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
In all such cases where one employs the means [of concealment], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not employ the means, but having gone to see it, quickly covers it because it is good, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
Seeds and different speech, censuring and spreading on open ground,
spreading indoors and dragging out, and first spreading on an upper story.
[He] built a large dwelling with water containing insects.
The second *vagga* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in turn. Since Nanda and Upananda did not receive their turn to instruct, they said to one another:
"All the elder bhikṣus are instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in turn, yet we have not received our turn to instruct. We should now go there ourselves first to provide instruction."
He then thought to himself:
"Whom should I follow in succession?
Should I follow Mahāmaudgalyāyana in succession?"
That venerable one possesses great supernormal power; if he should find us unyielding, he might seize us and hurl us far away to another world-system.
Should we follow the Venerable Mahākāśyapa’s instructions and depart accordingly?
That venerable one possesses great majestic power; if he deems it inappropriate, he might humiliate us before the great assembly.
The Venerable Śāriputra is gentle, mild, and refined; we should follow his lead.
Having formed this thought, he immediately followed the proper sequence: at dawn, having put on his robes, he went to the bhikṣuṇī vihāra and spoke these words:
"Sisters, assemble together; we have come to provide you with instruction."

Then the bhikṣuṇīs immediately assembled the community; that bhikṣu Nanda, being learned, eloquent, and skilled in preaching the Dharma, then preached the Dharma for the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs according to their needs.

At that time, when it was the Venerable Śāriputra’s turn to give instruction, he put on his robes and went to stand beneath the porch of the bhikṣuṇīs’ quarters, where he heard the sound of them preaching the Dharma.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw the Venerable Śāriputra from afar, they did not rise to greet him out of respect for the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having witnessed this event, immediately thought to himself:
"I shall now return for the sake of not severing the Dharma.
He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked Śāriputra:
"Have you already instructed the bhikṣuṇīs?
He replied:
"He did not admonish him,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Why is that? Śāriputra related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Nanda and Upananda here."
Having summoned them immediately, the Buddha asked Nanda and Upananda,
"Is this truly so?
They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"How is it that you instruct bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha?
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture the wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu instructs and admonishes bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Without having been appointed" means that the Saṃgha has not performed the *karmavācanā*; this is called "not being appointed."
If the twelve matters are not accomplished, it is not called "dismissal.
If the assembly is not accomplished, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, or the ritual action (*karman*) is not accomplished, it is likewise called "non-dismissal."
"Instruction" refers to either the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu instructs bhikṣuṇīs without being appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika; therefore, this is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in turn. When it was the turn of the Venerable Nanda to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, he was unwilling to go.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The Venerable Nanda is next in line to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, yet he is unwilling to go. Who else should go?"
Having spoken these words, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
“Call Nanda here.”
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda:
"It is now your turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; why do you not go?
Nanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We have not yet been authorized by the Saṃgha through formal ritual action (karmavācanā); therefore, we do not go.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If twelve qualities are accomplished, the Saṃgha should appoint one as a monk to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
What are these twelve?
First, purity in maintaining the precepts;..."
2. One who has heard much of the Abhidharma;
3. One who has heard much of the Vinaya;
4. One who trains in the precepts.
Fifth, training in concentration;
sixth, training in wisdom;
seventh, being able to eliminate evil and deviant views for others.
8. Able to discipline oneself and able to discipline others;
9. Possessing eloquence in speech;
10. Not defiling the holy life (brahmacarya).
Eleventh, not violating the grave prohibitions of a bhikṣuṇī;
twelfth, having twenty years of seniority or more than twenty years of seniority.
These are the twelve dharmas.
The *karmavācanā* official should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Venerable Nanda has accomplished the twelve qualities. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint Nanda as the monk who instructs the bhikṣuṇīs."
Thus he makes the motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Venerable Nanda has accomplished the twelve dharmas; the Saṃgha now appoints Nanda to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."
"Venerable sirs, those who approve of appointing Nanda to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
"The Saṃgha has already approved the appointment of Nanda to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus settled."
At that time, the Venerable Nanda preached the Dharma extensively for the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset.
When the bhikṣuṇīs returned to the city at dusk, they were criticized by the people of the world, who said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have entertained themselves with these bhikṣuṇīs all day long; only at sunset do they send them back. Piteous are these women, lacking any autonomy."
"Even for such a person who is thus ruined and destroyed, what path can there be?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call Nanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda,
"Is it truly so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to Nanda.
