"This is an evil deed; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."
"One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, remains from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "appointed by the Saṃgha," it means the accomplishment of the twelve factors: the accomplishment of the assembly, the accomplishment of the formal motion (*jñapti*), and the accomplishment of the ritual procedure (*karman*).
Regarding "instruction," it refers either to the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
"Darkness" refers to the period from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light;
[to teach during this time constitutes] a *pāyattika*. A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If one teaches while the sun has set, yet perceives it as not having set, it is a *vinayātikrama*.
If the sun has not set, but one perceives it as having set, one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
If the sun has set, and one perceives it as having set, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the sun has not set, and one perceives it as not having set, there is no offense.
The four phrases regarding the appearance of light are also like this.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs one thinking they are a śikṣamāṇā, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā instructs one thinking they are a bhikṣuṇī, she incurs a vyatikrama offense.
If one instructs a śikṣamāṇā while perceiving her as a śikṣamāṇā, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs another while perceiving her as a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
The same fourfold application applies to śrāmaṇerikās, female renunciants of other sects, and upāsikās.
If a bhikṣuṇī bows at the feet of a bhikṣu at night, the bhikṣu says:
"May you reach the end of suffering and liberation."
If one says this, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Welcome!"...
There is no offense [if it is] as follows:

if the entire assembly of the fourfold community has been engaged in preaching the Dharma throughout the night, and a bhikṣu employs a stratagem with the intent to preach the *Mahāprajāpatī-vaiyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the *Kālī-gautamī-sūtra*, or the *Dharmadinnā-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* for a bhikṣuṇī, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one is correctly reciting this sutra and knows no other sutras, there is no offense in reciting them in succession.
If, at night, a bhikṣu is preaching the Dharma while seated on a high seat, he should speak thus:
"All you members of the assembly, listen attentively."
One who says this incurs a pāyattika.
If one speaks without having made such a statement, there is no offense.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in their proper order. Then the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The elder bhikṣus are instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in their proper order; we have not been permitted to do so."
"We should go ahead first to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Another said, "The World-Honored One has established a precept: unless the Saṃgha appoints one, one may not instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We know how to perform the formal act (karmavācanā).
They then went outside the boundary to perform the formal act; having taken turns bowing to one another, they immediately went to the bhikṣuṇī vihāra and spoke as follows:
"Sisters! When you have assembled as a harmonious Saṃgha, I shall instruct you.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs gathered very quickly.
At that time, those among the assembly who acted in accordance with the Dharma spoke thus:
"Who is able to receive the instructions of these people who do not follow the Vinaya?
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs gathered together, discussed worldly matters, and then departed.
Then, when the time had come, the Venerable Nanda dressed himself and went to the bhikṣuṇī vihāra, saying:
"All you bhikṣuṇīs, assemble; I shall instruct you."
At that time, the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs gathered together, but the group of six bhikṣuṇīs did not come.
Nanda asked, "Has the community of bhikṣuṇīs assembled?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Who has not come? He replied,
"The group of six bhikṣuṇīs have not come."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to summon them, but they did not come, saying:
"We have already received instruction from the group of six bhikṣus."
Nanda said, "If the bhikṣuṇīs are not in harmony, one may not provide them with instruction. Having spoken,
he returned to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Have you already instructed the bhikṣuṇīs?
Nanda then reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here. When they had arrived,
the Buddha questioned them thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said,
"Six Group Bhikṣus, how is it that you instruct bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha?
They replied:
“We have already received our assignments.
The Buddha said, “Fools!”
"Who appointed you?
They replied,
"We went outside the boundary and appointed one another in turn."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to go back and forth across the boundary to assign one another as attendants at a bhikṣuṇī monastery.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī fell ill. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to inquire after her health, speaking as follows:
"How is your physical strength?
Is your ailment abating,
and has it not increased?"
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
I am suffering, but it does not cause me harm."
"Excellent!
Venerable One, please teach me the Dharma.
Ānanda said:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept: one must not preach the Dharma to bhikṣuṇīs without having informed the bhikṣus within the boundary.
The bhikṣuṇī said, “I pay homage.”
The Venerable replied,
“I dwell in peace.
Having said this, he returned to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally; Ānanda then reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"If you had preached the Dharma for him, his illness would have been cured and his body would have attained peace and happiness."
"From this day forward, I permit you to preach the Dharma to sick bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu goes to the residence of bhikṣuṇīs with the intention of instructing them, but does not inform a virtuous bhikṣu, except at other times, it is a pāyattika.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Instructs" means to give instruction.
A "virtuous monk" is one who is present within the boundary (*sīmā*), not one who is merely present as a relative.
"Not having announced" means, for example,
saying: "I am entering the village at an improper time," or saying:
"To eat separately from those of the same meal" is not called "white.
As for what is "white," one should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please remember!
I announce my entry into the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma for the purpose of instructing them.
He should then say:
"Do not be negligent.
Except for other times; "other times" refers to when a bhikṣuṇī is ill, for which the World-Honored One has declared there is no offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), it is as explained above.
If two people are staying at a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka-vihāra) and one person wishes to enter a bhikṣuṇī’s monastery, he should inform the second person by saying:
"Venerable sir, please take note!"
"I shall enter the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma to give instruction. He should say:
"Do not be negligent."
He replied, "I accept it with the highest reverence.
If two people both wish to go, they should inform one another in turn.
If one person has already departed and another person subsequently wishes to depart, they should form this thought:
"If I see a bhikṣu on the road, I shall inform him; if I see one within the village, I shall inform him."
If one arrives at the gate of a bhikṣuṇī’s monastery, one must not enter immediately;
rather, one should ask: "Is there a bhikṣu inside?
If there is one, call him out and inform him; having informed him, one may then enter.
If one does not announce [one's arrival] and enters the gate with only one foot, one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*.
If both feet enter, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī invites a bhikṣu for a meal, the senior of the Saṃgha should make the following announcement:
"Go to the bhikṣuṇī quarters to provide instruction.
If the first elder is unable to respond, the second elder should announce [the matter].

If the Sangha has already taken their seats and a bhikṣuṇī asks a question, it is no offense for a junior bhikṣu among the assembly who possesses eloquence to respond and preach the Dharma in their presence.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while the dwelling place of the bhikṣus is joined by a shared wall, hears a bhikṣu chanting with a subtle and exquisite voice and asks from afar:
"Venerable One!..."
"Who can perform such a chant?
He replied, "I shall chant it."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"Venerable sir, you are able to perform such excellent chanting.
The bhikṣu said:
"Do you wish to hear more?
He replied,
"I wish to hear."
If a bhikṣu chants further [for her], it is an offense of pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī is ill and a bhikṣu chants for her, there is no offense.
If this bhikṣuṇī has already died, and the bhikṣuṇī’s disciple says to the bhikṣu:
"If the teacher has already died," the bhikṣu should immediately cease.
If he nevertheless performs a chant for impermanence, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī prostrates at the feet of a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu makes this benediction:
"May all your suffering be exhausted and you attain liberation," it is a pāyattika.
One should say:
"Welcome! Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes in the morning and stood at the gate of the Jeta Grove.
Then, a bhikṣu who was instructing the bhikṣuṇīs came out of the gate; having seen him, the group of six bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"You have now entered the city to indulge your sense faculties; you have gone for no other purpose than for fine food and drink.
At these words, the bhikṣuṇī who had been instructing them felt ashamed.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
He immediately called them.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; it is not Dharma, not Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching. It cannot serve to nurture the wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
You instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food."
" [This constitutes] a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "food," it refers to parched grain, flour, rice, fish, and meat.
Furthermore, there are foods consisting of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Instruction refers to either the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"I am now instructing the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika.
If one says,
"I instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of medicine," one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense against the Vinaya.
If a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī:
"That bhikṣu instructs you for the sake of food and drink," he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī:
"That bhikṣu instructs you for the sake of medicine," he commits a *vyatikrama* offense requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu,
"You are giving instruction to śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs for the sake of food and drink," he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one says,
"It is for medicine," one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* involving mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*).
Thus it is explained at length, even unto the upāsakas and upāsikās, who instruct you for the sake of food and drink;
[if you do so], you commit a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one says:
"I instruct you for the sake of medicine.
[If one says this,] one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression involving mental regret). Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin and the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā had previously been husband and wife.
The bhikṣuṇī Sujātā said to the Venerable Udāyin:
"I shall be on duty to guard the dwelling tomorrow; you may come and converse with me.

The next day, when the bhikṣuṇīs had each entered the village to beg for alms, Udāyin went to the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā’s quarters and crouched in a secluded place. Facing one another, they gave rise to mutual lustful thoughts; their bodies bristling with desire, they remained there gazing at each other.
At that time, there was an elderly and sick bhikṣuṇī who, upon encountering [the situation] while out walking, felt shame and remorse and immediately returned.
The sick bhikṣuṇī then reported this matter to the other bhikṣuṇīs, who said to the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā:
"How can you, as one who has left the household life, commit such an unrighteous act?"
"It is truly shameful!
The bhikṣuṇī Śailā then spoke with indignation:
"How extraordinary!"
"How wonderful!
This is my own kinsman, a bhikkhu who comes to visit me from time to time. If I do not entertain him with mutual delight, who else indeed should?"
"This is our family tradition; what is there to be surprised about?
Thus, each of the bhikṣuṇīs questioned her in turn, and the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā was able to answer each one with skillful eloquence.
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī in turn informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
“Call Udāyin here.”
He was immediately summoned.
The Buddha asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and revile sensual desire?
Why have you committed such an evil and unwholesome act?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu sits together with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded and private place, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"One" refers to one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī.
Although there may be persons who are insane, deluded, mentally deranged, asleep, non-human beings, or animals—even with such individuals present, it is therefore called "no person."
"An empty screened area" refers to a secluded place.
"Sitting together" means sitting in company.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī invites a bhikṣu to a meal, and one bhikṣuṇī sits together with the bhikṣu while another bhikṣuṇī comes and goes to serve him food,
then for every time the bhikṣu takes food while the serving bhikṣuṇī is away, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī is seated and a bhikṣu is to rise, he should not rise in silence, as this might cause the bhikṣuṇī to suspect that he intends to perform an improper act;
rather, he should say: "I wish to rise."
If a bhikṣuṇī asks,
"For what reason did you get up?
one should answer:
“The Blessed One has established a precept that one must not sit together with a bhikṣuṇī.
If a bhikṣuṇī says:
“Venerable sir, you simply sit; I shall rise.”
At that time, the bhikṣu who was sitting there commits no offense.

This applies even to śrāmaṇerīs. If [the structure] has a walkway with wooden steps or platforms, and he sits upon each step one by one as it is moved, then for each movement of a seat, the bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If it is a śrāmaṇerī who is less than seven years old, she likewise commits a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣu to sit alone in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.

If the door of the vihāra faces the road and passersby do not cease [their movement], all is as explained in detail in the section on preaching the Dharma to women: this is a transgression; it is a concealed place, not an open space; it is at night, or it is by day; it is with one person, not with many; it is nearby, not at a distance; for these reasons, it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were traveling along a road with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs. As evening fell and they were about to reach a village, they stopped by the edge of a pond to rest, seeking a place to stay for the night.
Then the bhikṣuṇī said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, please stay here; I shall enter the village to seek a place to stay.
She immediately entered the village to seek lodging and found a host who invited her to settle wherever she pleased.
Having found lodging, he went out to meet the group of six bhikṣus and said to them:
"Venerable sirs!
I have already secured a place to stay; please come in together for our mutual peace and security."
Having stayed there, the bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!
I wish to enter the village to exhort the people to provide me with food and drink tomorrow."
Arriving at the place where the women were, he spoke to them thus:

"The two assemblies of monks—the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—have both arrived as a saṃgha of those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya). You should prepare tomorrow’s meal, non-timely drinks, and oil for anointing the feet."

When the women heard this, some prepared offerings for one person, others for two; in this manner, everyone provided their own requisites. After they had eaten their fill, those with leftovers took them away. As they traveled along the road, they conversed, laughed, and flirted together, which was resented by the people of the world:
"Look at these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas! They are all young men who have shaved their heads together, appearing just like courtesans flirting with one another."
"These people ruin others; what path do they have?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
Having summoned them immediately, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
"From this day forward, I do not permit traveling together with bhikṣuṇīs by appointment along a road.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī and Vaiśālī, the various bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat, wished to come and pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they immediately asked the bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, you wish to go to pay homage to the World-Honored One; on what day will you depart?

The bhikṣus then told them the date of their departure. Because women are naturally inclined toward long-term planning, they calculated the days and went ahead to stay at a point along the road to wait for the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus saw her, they asked,
"Sister, where do you wish to go?
She replied:
"We wish to go to the Jeta Grove to pay our respects to the World-Honored One.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus, fearing they might violate the precepts, immediately departed in haste.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs were some who were young; they bunched up their robes and followed closely behind, pursuing them at a rapid pace.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, there were some who were frail and elderly; unable to keep pace with their companions, they were plundered by bandits.

The bhikṣuṇīs reported these circumstances to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. She then related the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying, "If the bhikṣus do not take care of the bhikṣuṇīs, who then shall take care of them?"
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to travel together on the road when there is danger.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu agrees to travel together with a bhikṣuṇī along a road, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to times of fear.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the appointment of a time: it may be today, tomorrow, half a month, or one month.
Regarding the distance: it may be three yojanas, two yojanas, one yojana, or one krośa.
"Except at other times" means that the Blessed One declared there is no offense during times of fear.
"Fear" refers to a momentary dread of losing one's life, of losing one's property, or of violating the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Although such a thing does not exist, if there is doubt that therein one’s life might be taken for a moment, property lost,
or the holy life (brahmacarya) ruined— *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī, there is one pāyattika for every village interval.
If it is open ground without villages, there is one pāyattika for every krośa.
If a bhikṣu travels together with his mother, sisters, or other female relatives in a caravan, and when the caravan stops or sets out, the bhikṣu calls to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Come quickly; do not let us fall behind the caravan."
One who speaks these words commits a pāyattika offense.
If one says:
"Go! [it is likewise].
"Go! Sister, do not let us lose our companionship.
There is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī is resting by the side of the road and a bhikṣu calls out to her, saying:
"Come! Come!"
"Sisters.
Once the appointment has been made, if she lifts one foot, she commits a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya);
if she lifts both feet, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
He said: "Go! Go!"
"If you do not allow [the merchant] to fall behind his companions," there is no offense.
When a bhikṣu travels along a road with merchants, and the merchants enter a village first while the bhikṣu does not know the way and asks for directions.
Seeing a bhikṣuṇī, he asked her, "Sister!
Show me the way."
This is called "making a mutual appointment.
If a bhikṣuṇī arrives and he lifts one foot, he commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya*;
if he lifts both feet, it is a *pāyattika*.
He can say: "Go! Go!"
If [one says], "Show me the way," there is no offense.
If a lay donor invites a bhikṣu to a meal within a village, and the bhikṣu does not know the location of the donor’s house, he may see a bhikṣuṇī and ask her:
"Do you know the location of the house of the donor so-and-so?
Show me the way there.
This is what is called making an appointment.
If one lifts one foot, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if both feet, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Go! Go! Sister, show us the location of our home."
There is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment but does not go, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she departs in silence without making an appointment, there is no offense.
If one makes an appointment to go together and then goes, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not make an appointment and does not go, there is no offense.
If one departs together but enters separately, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one enters together while departing separately, it is an offense against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If one departs and enters together, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one both departs and enters separately, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, on an auspicious day at dawn, men and women gathered on the banks of the Ajiravatī River to enjoy food, drink, music, and sightseeing.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rose early in the morning, put on their village-entering robes, and went to where the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were, asking them:
"Today is an auspicious day; do you have any food or drink?"
"We should go together to the riverbank to enjoy the sights.
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs said, "We shall do exactly that;
Venerable Ones, you may look for boats at the same time."

The group of six bhikṣus immediately went to the royal family’s boat station, requested a fine boat along with various ornaments, and placed their eating utensils upon it. They then traveled together with the bhikṣuṇīs up and down the river current, engaging in mocking conversation and frivolous laughter.
They were ridiculed by the people of the world, who said:
"Look at these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas! They are dissolute and lack the Way, behaving exactly like worldly people with whom they previously consorted."
"What path can there be for such a ruined and corrupt person?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
He immediately summoned them.
Once they had arrived, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an improper act; from this day forward, you must not agree to travel by boat with bhikṣuṇīs.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time, on the opposite bank of the Ajiravatī River, the two assemblies of monks and nuns were invited to cross over to accept the invitation.

At that time, it was not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to board the boat; yet the bhikṣus would sometimes have one person per boat, or two persons per boat, and so on through three or four boats, even when they were extremely light, without carrying any bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣus crossed over first, and only after they had done so did the bhikṣuṇīs cross.

Once the bhikṣuṇīs had finished crossing, they went to the place where the meal was being served; as they were to take their seats according to their seniority, the time for the midday meal passed, and they all remained without food.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having lost her meal, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side. Knowing this, the Buddha nevertheless asked: "Gautamī!"
"Why are you so extremely emaciated?
Mahāprajāpatī then reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to cross directly."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together on a boat upstream or downstream, except for crossing directly across, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "fixed time" refers to today, tomorrow, half a month, or one month.
With the exception of those who simply cross over, the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*:
as explained above, if a bhikṣu makes a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together in a vehicle, he incurs one *pāyattika* for every interval between villages passed.
If there is no village and it is open ground, [the distance] of one *krośa* constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī are traveling together by boat and they stop on the bank, and the bhikṣuṇī disembarks to attend to the needs of nature.
At that time, as the boat was about to depart, the bhikṣu called out to the bhikṣuṇī,
saying, "Sister, come! Having done so,
they had established an appointment.
If one raises one foot, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
if both feet, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one has made an appointment together [with others] but does not go, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one departs without having made an appointment, there is no offense.
If one makes an appointment and departs together [with others], it is a pāyattika.
If one does not make an appointment and does not depart, there is no offense.
The final four lines are also as above; therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a *varṣika* bhikṣu who, wearing a new, fine, dyed robe, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
After seven years had passed, he came into the presence of the World-Honored One wearing tattered and worn-out robes; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"You previously wore new, fine, dyed robes for many years; why do you now wear these worn-out, old garments?
She replied, "For seven years now, I have given my fine robes to the bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose a bhikṣu who is a relative were wearing such worn-out, tattered robes, and he were to give a fine robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is also a relative; should he take it?"
He replied, "I will not take it. [The other asked:
"Even if a relative bhikṣu were wearing such worn-out, old clothes, would you be able to give a fine robe to that relative bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied, "I will not give it.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, it is not permitted to give robes to a nun who is not a relative.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu from the south arrived carrying many robes and bowls. This bhikṣu had a sister who had gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma;
he then said to the Venerable Ānanda, “Please send me to visit my sister, the bhikṣuṇī.”
The Venerable Ānanda, having found a substitute, immediately delivered him to the gate of the bhikṣuṇī monastery and stood there, asking:
"Is the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so present? The bhikṣuṇī asked:
"Who is calling? He replied, "It is I,
Ānanda, and a certain bhikṣu."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Venerable sir, please wait a moment.
She then prepared the bedding for him, went inside, opened the door halfway, and called out:
"Venerable sir, please come in and sit.
Having entered and sat down, they exchanged greetings for a short while and then he departed.
At that time, the bhikkhu said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I have come from afar to see my sister, yet she does not come out to see me; for what reason is this?
Venerable Ānanda, being well-versed in the science of marks (lakṣaṇa-dharma), said to this bhikṣu:
"Do you not know the reason why your sister does not come out?"
He replied, "I do not know. Ānanda said:
"Your elder sister does not come out because her clothes are worn and she is ashamed; you have many garments, so why do you not give some to her?
The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not give robes to a bhikṣuṇī."
Ānanda said, "Simply give it to me;
I shall request permission from the Buddha on your behalf.
Ānanda then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
"Is it permitted to give robes to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative?
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, it is permitted to give robes to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative" and "a robe," these are all as explained above.
"Except for those involved in trade; the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
As with the thirty matters mentioned above, this is explained in detail within the section concerning the taking of a bhikṣuṇī’s robe; therefore, it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā, who had been the former wife of the Venerable Udāyin, took some clothing and wealth and gave them to Udāyin, saying:
"Venerable sir, please make a robe for me."

Udāyin immediately accepted the task and finished making the robe; he fashioned an image of a man and woman in union, and having completed it, he folded it and placed it in a chest to give to the bhikṣuṇī.
Having received it, the bhikṣuṇī carried it back to the vihāra; upon opening and seeing it, she was filled with joy and showed it to the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Venerable ladies, look! "
"This Venerable Udāyin is indeed skillful in his work," they said.
But the bhikṣuṇīs expressed their disapproval, saying, "This is something that should be concealed; why does he display it to others?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they went and informed Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went on account of these circumstances to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said: "Call Udāyin here."
Having summoned him immediately, the Buddha asked Udāyin,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"All those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī must assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu" and "non-relative bhikṣuṇī," it is as explained above.
Regarding the making of robes: whether one sews them oneself or causes another to sew them, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
One must not provide a robe for sewing to a nun who is not a relative; for every stitch, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If the needle is removed when the thread is exhausted, it is a pāyattika.
It is the same if one causes another person to remove it. Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a donor who had previously invited the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and others.
Only the Venerable Mahākāśyapa did not accept prior invitations.
When the time arrived the following day, he put on his robes for entering the village, took up his alms bowl, and went from house to house begging for food until he reached that door.
At that time, the laywoman, having seen them, was filled with joy; she immediately stepped forward, prostrated herself at their feet, and stood to one side, saying:
"Venerable Bhikṣus!..."
"Today all have gathered to accept my invitation; I pray that the Venerable One will also accept my invitation.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa thought:
"This is the present moment."
She immediately accepted the invitation and, without proceeding elsewhere, entered the house first and sat down.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, while begging for alms, arrived at that household. Seeing in the courtyard the female lay devotee sweeping the ground, washing the vessels, and preparing various offerings, she asked:
"Upāsikā, what are you doing?"
At that time, the woman was busy with her affairs and could not respond; thus she did not answer when asked a second and a third time.
Thullanandā then said: "This is truly strange!
You are so arrogant and self-important that you do not answer when called."
The woman replied, "Today I have invited the great virtuous śrāvakas, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others; because of this urgent business, I am unable to comply."
Thullanandā then said:
"What you have invited today is like not taking the great elephant from among a herd of elephants, but taking a small one;
or like not taking a peacock from among a flock of great birds, but taking an old crow."

As for those who are called "great elephants," they are Channa, Kālodāyin, Svāti, Mahāśramaṇa, Aśvajit, Pūrṇa, and the Venerable Ānanda, the attendant; if you were to ask me to invite them, I would indeed invite such great virtuous ones for you.
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa heard this, he cleared his throat with a loud cough. Having heard it, Thullanandā asked, "Whose voice is that?"
The woman replied,
"This is the Great Elder Mahākāśyapa.
The bhikṣuṇī then praised him, saying:
“You have gained great and wholesome benefit to invite such a great dragon-elephant as this; had I been invited, I too would have invited this Elder!
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa heard these words, his heart was not pleased, and he immediately asked:
“Sister, you just said:”
"This was but a small elephant, an old crow," he said;
yet now he speaks again, saying,
"This is a dragon-elephant of great virtue."
"If what was said previously is true, then what was said later is false;
if what was said later is true, then what was said previously is false.
Between these two statements, which one is the truth?"
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, possessing great majesty and dignity, rebuked the bhikṣuṇī with these two lines.
Terrified, the bhikṣuṇī fled and fell to the ground, injuring her body.
Having seen this, Chanda immediately asked the nun:
"Whom have you touched and disturbed such that your body is thus wounded and broken?
She replied:
"I have disturbed Mahākāśyapa," he said, and then added,
"You have touched that which should not be touched."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In this matter, even not praising [the practice] entails faults and calamities, let alone praising it."
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to accept food offered with the praise of a bhikṣuṇī.

Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda possessed merit and renown in the city of Śrāvastī; the World-Honored One declared him to be endowed with three qualities: noble lineage, a great retinue, and spiritual accomplishment.

Among those on the path of training, he was foremost in erudition and foremost in service. He caused the city of Śrāvastī to be filled with blessings, and whenever a new house was being built, they would invite Ānanda; whether entering a home, shaving one's hair, or piercing the ears, they would invariably invite Ānanda to all such occasions.
At that time, a householder invited the Venerable Ānanda to a feast for his new residence.
What was "new"? There was a new house, new beds, new utensils, new food, new ghee and oil, and a new son and wife wearing new clothes and holding new fans.
While Ānanda was eating, there was a bhikṣu seeking alms outside; Ānanda then said to the donor, "You may give food to the bhikṣu seeking alms who is outside."
Having heard Ānanda’s instruction, the donor joyfully filled his alms-bowl with various kinds of fine food and presented it to the mendicant bhikṣu.
Having received it, the mendicant bhikṣu stood waiting for Ānanda; once Ānanda had finished eating and offered his words of blessing, he departed.
When the mendicant bhikṣu saw Ānanda, he asked,
"Venerable sir, have you eaten yet?
He replied:
"I have eaten," [the Buddha said].
He then asked Ānanda again,
"Was the food to your liking?"
Ānanda asked, "For what reason do you not eat?
Why do you ask me whether my food is suitable or not?"
The bhikṣu who was begging for alms said,
"Venerable sir, the food you have eaten was praised by that bhikṣuṇī.
Ānanda said:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is so.”

Ānanda immediately used a bird’s wing to pick out the vomit; that day he missed his meal and became emaciated from hunger and weakness. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally: “Ānanda!”
"Why are your four elements so emaciated by hunger?
Ānanda then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you know [the reason]?"
He replied, “I do not know.
The Buddha said:
"This offense was committed knowingly, not unknowingly.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that this mendicant monk caused Ānanda to be unhappy?
The Buddha said, "It was not only today that he caused Ānanda to be unhappy; as is explained in detail in the *Śukasūtra* (The Discourse on the Birth of the Wise Bird)."

Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the elder bhikṣus, when the time had come, put on their robes for entering the village, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city to go on their almsround, moving with dignified and composed deportment in coming and going, bending and stretching.
At that time, there was an elder who spoke these words:
"Excellent, Great Virtue!
You have gained great and wholesome benefit in giving such clothing, food and drink, and medicines for the sick and weak to these renunciants."
He further thought to himself:
"If I possessed human power, I too would surely provide offerings to such renunciants as these.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī heard this and said to the elder:
"Long-lived one!
You need only provide the payment for the food; I shall prepare it for you.
The donor, filled with faith and joy, immediately gave the payment for the meal.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Long-lived one!
You should invite a bhikṣu."
She replied, “I do not know; please request it for me.
The bhikṣuṇī then prepared various kinds of food and drink and said to the donor:
“Long-lived one!
The meal is prepared; please go to the bhikṣu and inform him that the time has come.
Thus spoke the donor.
"I do not know [the time]; nun, please go and inform me when it is time.
The bhikṣuṇī immediately went and informed him that the time had arrived. When the bhikṣu entered the house of the donor and sat down, the bhikṣuṇī said to the donor:
"You may serve these various kinds of food yourself."
The donor said,
"Ayyā, please do it for me.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Is this food praised by the bhikṣuṇīs?
Having thus doubted, they immediately departed; in this manner, one person, two persons, and even the entire assembly all left.
The donor asked the bhikṣuṇīs,
“For what reason have all the venerable ones gone out and not yet returned?
The bhikṣuṇīs replied:
“I do not know; you should go to the World-Honored One and inquire about this matter in detail, and he will explain it for you.
Thereupon, that donor went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, stood to one side, and related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣus here. Once they had been called,
the Buddha questioned them in detail about the aforementioned matter.
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to dismiss former donors."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu knowingly eats food that has been praised by a bhikṣuṇī, except in the case of a long-standing donor, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knowingly" means either knowing it himself or hearing it from another.
"Praising" means extolling one's virtues.
"Food" consists of five kinds:
parched grain flour, noodles, rice, fish, and meat.
Regarding "excluding former donors," the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
As for the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

There is praising when announcing the equal distribution of offerings; praising at the very beginning of serving the food; praising while the food is first being prepared; praising once the food preparation is complete; and praising when invited to eat.

Regarding "praising when the *sādhukāra* is being proclaimed": when the distribution of food has been completed and the *sādhukāra* is being proclaimed, if another bhikṣu arrives, the bhikṣuṇī says to the upāsikā:
"Another bhikṣu has arrived."
The upāsikā said: "Excellent!
Since I could not even succeed in inviting you by sending a messenger out of joy, how much less so when you have come here in person?"
This is not called praise.
If a bhikṣuṇī says:
"This is forest-dwelling, alms-seeking, wearing rag-robes, sitting in the open air, and using grass mats."
If one praises the food received in this manner and then eats it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the time when the food is being served: if other bhikṣus arrive while the food is first being served, it is also as explained above.
Regarding "praising while it is being made": while it is first being made, another bhikṣu arrives, and she speaks to him in the same manner.
Regarding "praising when it is finished": once all the preparations for the offering have been completed, another bhikṣu arrives; the bhikṣuṇī says to the upāsikā, "Another bhikṣu has arrived."
The upāsikā said: "Excellent!
I sent someone specifically to invite you and yet could not succeed; how much more so now that you have come of your own accord?"
"This is not called praising.
The upāsikā said,
"One should give a large amount of parched grain, cakes, rice, and fine food, distributing them equally."
This is not called praising.
If the food and drink are meager, he further says to the donor:
"Prepare a handful of parched grain for me."
...so saying, it is a *pāyattika*.
To "invite" means to invite by mentioning one's name.
A bhikṣuṇī says to a donor:
"If such-and-such a disciple is learned and diligent, you should invite them all.
This is called "praising the food.
If one says:
"The leader of the community, so-and-so, is learned and diligent; for the sake of this bhikṣu, he has extended an invitation to twenty people.
This constitutes praise for one person, while for the others there is no offense.
If there are those who thus praise the food, one should trade food with them in turn and must not leave the meal unfinished.
If a neighbor sits nearby who is filthy and impure, and one does not wish to trade with him, one should form this thought:
"The food in this bowl was intended for me by such-and-such a bhikṣu; I shall eat it without fault."
If a bhikṣuṇī says to an upāsikā,
"Venerable so-and-so may be invited for long-term support," this is called praising [the donor].
If one says,
"Venerable So-and-so should always beg for food," this is not called praise.
Therefore it is said:
When the Saṃgha has not been appointed, when night falls, when there is no announcement for the sake of food,
sitting together, traveling on the same path, on a boat, and with regard to clothing.
The Praise for Making Robes and the Praise for Food.
The third *varga* is concluded.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll Fifteen.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The fifth of the ninety-two rules concerning the *pācittiya* offenses: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his rains retreat in a village, came toward Śrāvastī, desiring to pay homage to and visit the World-Honored One.
At that time, there was a lay devotee in a village who had built a hall for merit and offered a single meal to the Sangha from the four directions.
When this bhikṣu arrived, the lay devotee saw him and said with joy:
"Welcome, Venerable Sir!"

He immediately spread out mats and bedding, provided water for washing the feet, gave ointment for the feet and non-timely drinks, lit lamps at night, and prepared bedding so that [the guest] might sleep in peace and security.
At dawn, he was again provided with *yācī* (tooth-sticks) and pure water, and served food that was suitable for his body.
After the bhikṣu had eaten, he thought to himself:

"I have come from afar and am weary with hunger; today I have obtained such food that is suitable for my body. I shall stay here for a short while to rest my four great elements, and afterwards I shall go to pay homage to the World-Honored One."
Having reflected thus, he stayed in the forest hermitage during the day and returned to his home at night.
When the donor saw him, he rejoiced as before; this continued for three days.
The donor asked,
"Virtuous One!
Where did you eat today?"
He replied, “In this place.
He asked again:
"Where were you yesterday?
He replied, "Right here."
He asked again,
"Where were you the other day?
He spoke once more:
"This is our place," the donor said with displeasure.

"My family is poor and frugal; I have exerted myself to establish this as a place for providing a single meal to the Sangha from the four quarters. Venerable Sirs, you should not remain here for long."
"If my family were wealthy and prosperous, I would freely bestow gifts upon the entire Sangha.
The bhikṣu thought to himself, "The donor has uttered these words of regret; I shall depart."

Thereupon, he gradually proceeded forward to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and withdrew to stand to one side. Knowing [the answer] yet asking for the sake of instruction, the Buddha said:
"In what place have you been dwelling during the retreat?"
He replied, “In such-and-such a village.
[The other asked,] “How long has it been since you set out?”
He replied, "That many.
Then the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"For what reason have you come from such a short distance after so long a journey?
The bhikṣu then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"This is not permissible.
How can you, for the sake of body and speech, cause the donor to be displeased?
From this day forward, at a place where a single meal is offered, a bhikṣu must not exceed one meal."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat in a village, came to Śrāvastī desiring to pay homage to and visit the World-Honored One.
At that time, there was a donor who established a merit-house within a village to provide a single meal for the Sangha from the four quarters.
When this bhikṣu passed by this house, his needs were supplied as previously described.
Having finished his meal, the bhikṣu departed; however, a wind disorder was provoked, and he thought to himself:
"I am unable to walk. The World-Honored One has established a precept that at a place where one-meal alms are offered, one is not permitted to accept more than one meal."
"I shall remain here for now, but I will not accept his food.
Having thought this, he immediately returned to his dwelling. The donor provided him with all necessities as before, but the bhikṣu would not accept them.
When the next day arrived, he again offered him the same food as before, but [the monk] still did not accept it; thereupon, he departed, thinking to himself:
"When I reach such-and-such a village, I shall beg for alms."

When the bhikṣus arrived at the village, the time for their meal had already passed, and they consequently missed their food. Their four great elements were weakened by hunger; they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally questioned him; he then reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

Bhikṣu, you have followed the True Dharma and left the household life with faith; possessing few desires, you practice in accordance with it, not for the sake of livelihood, and you observe the precepts established by the World-Honored One without transgression.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, it is permitted for a sick bhikṣu within a house of merit to eat more than once.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a single meal, a bhikṣu who is not ill should eat only that one meal.
If he exceeds one meal, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the place where a single meal is given: this is permitted by the World-Honored One.
"Food" refers to the five kinds of food, as explained above.
"Not being ill" means that one's body is free from disease or ailment.
If one has a physical ailment and is unable to proceed on the journey, there is no offense in staying and eating.
If one who is not ill eats more than once [a day], it is a *pāyattika*.
As for what constitutes a *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If there are sixteen rooms and within one room there is a place where a family offers a single meal, if a bhikṣu stays overnight in my room, I shall provide him with food.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the Saṃgha, for the sake of the stūpa, or for his own sake, arrives at one of these rooms and stays overnight, after having taken one meal, if he wishes to attend to some business and that business is not yet finished, he should go to a second room; having stayed and eaten there, he should then depart.
If the matter is still not resolved, even after staying for food for up to sixteen intervals, one should depart once the matter is concluded.
If it is still not resolved, one must not eat further, but should instead go out to beg for alms.
When begging for food, one should beg at other places and must not return to beg from that same household.
Furthermore, if they were among those who assisted in building the house when it was originally constructed, one must also not beg from them.
Having gone to another village for alms, one should stay overnight in that very village; having stayed there, one should return to attend to the matter.
If the matter is not yet settled, one may again receive food as before within the sixteen intervals.
If the matter is not settled, he departs again; after staying away for one night, he returns to obtain the provisions and settle the affairs.
If that family sends a woman to welcome the bride into the new house, saying:
"I sent a messenger to invite the teacher and yet feared it would be difficult to find him, how much more so now that we see him and he wishes to depart!"
At that time, there is no offense for a bhikṣu who accepts an invitation to eat.
Therefore, it was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the monastery attendants provided meals for the Sangha every year when the rice, wheat, and other grains were newly harvested.
How was it that they were newly harvested each year?

When the rice was ripe, when the wheat was ripe, when the beans were ripe, and when the ghee, oil, and rock honey were ready, they would take a small portion from each and set them aside to provide for the community of monks.
Then the park-keeper said to the bhikṣus:
"Every year when the new grain ripens, I shall offer food to the Saṃgha.
If there are no donors at the Jetavana on any given day, I only pray that you will inform me; I shall then provide an offering so that the Saṃgha may eat to their heart's content."

At that time, the lay devotees offered various kinds of food and drink with faith; though there were few days when the morning or evening meals were lacking, on one occasion they encountered a day when nothing was provided. They then went to him and said, "Long-lived one!"
"Tomorrow there will be no offerings at Jetavana; since you previously wished to provide an offering, now is the time.
Having heard this, the park-keeper immediately went to Jetavana, prostrated himself at the feet of the Saṃgha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and said:
"I, the park-keeper [Name], shall provide an offering tomorrow and invite the entire Saṃgha; I pray that you will accept my invitation."
The Sangha accepted the invitation.

At that time, there was an elder who purchased two oxen for five hundred old coins; having acquired them, he wished to test them, so he yoked them to a cart and drove them back and forth for one *yojana*.
Because the carriage harness was too tight, one ox died immediately.
He became greatly distressed and dwelt in suffering and unhappiness, thinking:
"How is it that I have purchased this ox at such a high price, and it dies before I have even used it?"
A knowledgeable householder said to him,
"Why do you not take pleasure in such things?
The householder then related the aforementioned matters in detail, and the other immediately said:
"Why do you not practice the firm Dharma?
He asked, "What is the firm Dharma?"
He replied, “One who upholds the Dharma, you should go to the Jetavana, invite the Saṃgha, and offer this meat as a meal for the assembly.

Having heard this, that person immediately went to the Jetavana, entered among the monks, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
"I, [Name], shall invite the Sangha tomorrow to partake of a simple offering; I pray that you will accept my invitation.
An elder bhikṣu who was a former acquaintance immediately went to him and said:
"You do not understand the proper method of invitation; why did you not first inform me?"
"I shall instruct you on how to request the Saṃgha. He then replied, "Ācārya!"
"I purchased two oxen for five hundred old coins, and one ox has already died.
I now wish to prepare 'solid dharma' (khādanīya) from this beef.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Sangha has already accepted the invitation.
The donor said, "I have already prepared the food; what should I do now?"
The knowledgeable bhikṣu said:
"I shall now instruct you: go again and inform the Saṃgha, saying, 'I have invited the Saṃgha for the morning meal tomorrow.'"
If you are asked,
"What do you eat before a meal?
you should answer:
"Prepare barley rice and meat patties.
Having given these instructions, he immediately went to where the Sangha was, prostrated with his head at their feet, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and spoke as follows:
"I, [Name], invite the Sangha; tomorrow I shall provide the morning meal. I pray that you will accept my invitation."
The bhikṣu asked,
"What kind of pre-meal food did you prepare?
He replied:
He prepared barley rice and meat patties and said,
"Long-lived one!"
"Prepare everything early tomorrow morning at dawn.
He replied, "So be it!"
"I pray that the Venerable Ones will come early tomorrow morning.
He then returned home and spent the entire night boiling meat and preparing various kinds of food and drink.
At dawn, having spread out the bedding and filtered clean water, he went to inform the Saṃgha that the time had arrived. The monks put on their robes, took up their bowls, and came to his house.
Having sat down in order, the donor personally served various kinds of fine food until they were fully satisfied; they then returned to the monastery.
A monastery attendant thought to himself:
"The Ācārya is one who eats only once a day; he must eat his morning meal."
Throughout the night, he prepared various kinds of food and drink, arranged the beds and mats, and filtered the water.
Having done so, he went to the Jetavana, prostrated himself at the feet of the Saṃgha, knelt with palms joined, and said:
"The time has come."
At that time, because the bhikṣus were already full from their morning meal, although they saw the invitation arrive, it was as if they had not heard it.
Then the park-keeper thought to himself:
"How extraordinary!
"How extraordinary!
This is the practice of the ācāryas who eat but one meal a day; they should maintain the perception of hunger.
Now, hearing the invitation to a meal, it is as if they have not heard it at all."
"If non-Buddhists hear that you have been invited for a meal, they will immediately take up their triple-staffed walking sticks and water jars and go before you.

After he had praised them in this way a second and third time, the bhikṣus finally arose; they paced about, attended to their bodily needs, yawned and stretched, and adjusted their belts with dignified deportment. Proceeding calmly and composedly, they went to the house and sat down in order. The park-keeper served the food with his own hands, filling the ladle each time before giving it to them; however, when it was the turn of the senior monk, he raised his hand to signal that he would take only a small portion.
The park-keeper spoke again, saying:
"These Ācāryas are those who eat but one meal a day; they have no thought of craving for any of these various foods.
The park-keeper then had this thought:
"If the senior monk eats little, the junior monks should eat more.
Thus it was said a second and a third time, even down to the youngest, who spoke again:
"The Ācārya is one who observes the practice of eating only once a day; he has no desire for this food at all."
At that time, among those seated at the lower end, there was a junior elder (*mahallaka*) who spoke thus:
"We did not come today for the sake of food; we came for the sake of your intention. We have already finished eating our fill elsewhere."
"If you do not believe me, look at the meat broth on my feet.
Having heard this, the park attendant was displeased; he immediately set down his food vessel on the ground and spoke with resentment:
"The other Ācāryas accepted my invitation first; why then do they eat elsewhere?"
His resentment did not cease, so he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said to the Buddha:
"Why is it that the bhikṣus first accepted my invitation, yet ate elsewhere?"

The Buddha then preached the Dharma to the park-keeper in accordance with his needs, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having done so, the park-keeper addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Where should I place the leftover food from my offering to the Saṃgha?"
The Buddha said:
"Go to the bank of such-and-such a pond, sweep and clean the ground, and place the food there.
King Prasenajit has been defeated in battle by the Malla Kṣatriyas; his army is now retreating and will stay there. You may present this food to him."

The king came and entered the pool to bathe, then put on fresh clothes; he immediately took the various kinds of food and drink mentioned earlier and presented them to the Great King as well as his generals and soldiers.

Having come from a state of hunger and thirst, they obtained these various kinds of food and drink and were all filled with great joy; he then commanded that various precious jewels be bestowed as rewards, so that the gardeners immediately attained excellent benefits and immeasurable celebration.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu who ate [the food] here.
Having been summoned, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"How is it that you first accepted an invitation from one person, yet ate elsewhere?
Do you not know, monk,
that just as when someone serves the household deity or the tree deity, if they wish to travel elsewhere, they must first eat the host's food and only then depart?"
"You have not acted in accordance with the rule; having first accepted an invitation from one person, you ate elsewhere. From this day forward, I do not permit eating at various places.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
For five reasons, the Blessed One would go from house to house among the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing a sick bhikṣu, the Buddha, though already aware of it, asked: "Bhikṣu!..."
"What is your ailment, and has it increased or diminished?
He replied, "My suffering remains undiminished; previously, when I ate several times a day, my body enjoyed peace and comfort."
“Because the World-Honored One has established the precept that one must not eat repeatedly, my illness has not improved.
The Buddha said,
“From this day forward, I permit eating repeatedly when one is ill.”
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā annually invited the Saṃgha for a meal and offered them robes.
At that time, sixty sick bhikṣus from the Jetavana Monastery came to her home, and Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā said, "Ācāryas!"
"In the Jeta Grove Monastery there are five hundred monks; for what reason have exactly sixty bhikṣus come now?

The bhikṣus said to the upāsikā, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not eat at various places; he permits it only for those who are ill. For this reason, these sick bhikṣus have come."
Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ said,
“Ācārya! In the world,
people take the invitation for a meal as their limit.”
"If you eat my food, I shall give you a robe;
if you do not eat it, I will not give you a robe, Ācārya!"
"At this time when robes are being offered, you may go and inform the Buddha; perhaps there will be permission granted.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Visākhā Mṛgāramātā is wise and intelligent; from this day forward, I permit the time for offering robes."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the multitude exhorted and encouraged one another to organize a great assembly to provide food and drink as offerings to ninety-six kinds of renunciants.
There was one who went to a lay follower (upāsaka) to exhort him and solicit goods. The lay follower said:
"I wish to make a condition: if you allow my teachers to serve as the presiding elders (sthavira), I shall give you the goods."
He exhorted the people, saying:
"Listen! If there are those who have faith in the non-Buddhists, they too shall say:
'If you cause our teachers to become the presiding elders (sthavira), we shall give you these goods.'"
"How shall I gain the consent of everyone to be the presiding elder?

You need only give me your goods; on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, I shall go to the banks of the Ajiravatī River, adorn that place by erecting banners and streamers, arranging rows of jeweled trees, spreading exquisite seats of fine, soft, and pleasant materials, and providing various offerings and delicacies to hold this great assembly."
"Among those who have gone forth as renunciants, whoever arrives first shall be the senior elder (*sthavira*).
Because the lay devotees (*upāsaka*) regarded the Buddha and the Sangha as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), they immediately gave them their offerings.
Having given the objects to him, he went to the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated with his head at the Venerable’s feet, and reported the matter in detail:
“Venerable Sir!
By what means may the bhikṣus become the foremost, so that the followers of other paths will be put to shame?”

Venerable Ānanda immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:

"The various exhorters have prepared the food and invited ninety-six kinds of renunciants. They have further invited King Prasenajit, along with his ministers and crown prince, the village chiefs, the elder elders, and the caravan leaders, to all come to the site of the great assembly on the Ajiravatī River at a certain time to receive my offerings."
On the preceding day, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, “You should know that now is the time.

Venerable Maudgalyāyana immediately employed his supernormal powers to cause the river water to swell in a torrential flood until its foam reached the banks. Each of the non-Buddhist practitioners then spoke these words:
"I shall cross first and take the foremost seat.

Each of the non-Buddhist practitioners spent the entire night competing to bind rafts, all desiring to be the first to cross; however, as the current was violent and swift, just as they were about to reach the shore, they were swept back again.

Having endured exhaustion and suffering throughout the night, their raft was shattered and destroyed; submerged and frozen by the cold, they remained on the bank, crouching toward the sun, until mealtime passed without anyone being able to cross over.
At that time, there was someone at the Jeta Grove Monastery making offerings to the Sangha, and the Buddha remained there waiting for the proper time.
Among the bhikṣus, some who were young said to one another:
"Why has the World-Honored One come out so late?"
"Lest the various non-Buddhists should obtain the position of the Elder.

At that time, when the hour had come, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and with dignified and composed deportment, went together with the great assembly to the riverbank.
When the various non-Buddhists saw this, they said to one another:
"Throughout the entire night we devised all manner of expedients, yet no one has been able to cross over such suffering and affliction."
"How shall these shaven-headed śramaṇas cross over?
At that time, the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"You yourself know the proper time; cause the bhikṣus to cross over in safety."

At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately employed his supernormal powers to construct a bridge made of the seven precious gems, with railings fashioned from various miscellaneous jewels. Above it, he hung jeweled canopies interlaced with the seven precious gems, which covered the top; he rained down many famous flowers, performed various musical performances, and burned many famous incenses, the smoke of which rose like clouds.
When the various non-Buddhists saw this bridge, they were all greatly delighted and each said to themselves:
"These śramaṇas are coming slowly; we shall cross first and take the foremost seats."
They all immediately ran forward, vying with one another to reach the bridge, each desiring to be the first to cross.
As soon as their feet stepped upon the bridge, they all fell into the water;
the various items belonging to the non-Buddhists, such as their triple-pronged staffs and water jars (*kamaṇḍalu*), all fell into the water and were carried away by the current.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, no one died.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus proceeded with dignified and solemn deportment.
The Buddha walked at the very front, followed by the bhikṣus in succession, with Maudgalyāyana bringing up the rear; as they advanced, the jeweled bridge vanished from beneath their feet.
After the Buddha and the bhikṣus had crossed over, the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"You should cause the river to return to its former state, so that the various non-Buddhists may each cross by means of their own contrivances using rafts."
Once the Buddha had finished crossing, he turned his body toward everyone and spoke this verse:
"Having first ferried these beings from this shore, I have already crossed the ocean of birth and death;
No longer drifting with the worldly currents, Through right wisdom, I have reached the further shore."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, he sat down with composure; the bhikṣus also sat down in succession, while the non-Buddhists crossed over later and sat in a row below the bhikṣus.
At that time, the donor personally served various kinds of food and drink to provide for the World-Honored One and the assembly of disciples.
At that moment, the bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not eat at various places; how then shall we obtain food?"
He immediately rose and informed the Buddha, who said:
"I authorize you to perform the ritual for offering food.
You should speak as follows:
"I have obtained food today; I shall give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu, or even to a śrāmaṇerī, and they will not take account of me; I shall eat it myself.
Thus he says three times.
At that time, each of the donors thought to themselves,
"Who should offer the blessing? Some said:
"Nirgrantha," or he said, "Pūraṇa Kāśyapa."
In this manner, each of the non-Buddhists said,
"One should offer a blessing.
At that time, many people spoke as follows:
“The Elder Śramaṇa Gautama, it is the dharma that one should offer a blessing.
At that time, among the ninety-six kinds of paths, the World-Honored One did not exalt himself nor disparage others; he offered a blessing in accordance with the occasion.

As explained in detail in the *Jātaka-sūtra*, at that time the World-Honored One further extensively preached the Dharma for the multitude in accordance with their needs, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; they departed filled with joy.
The Buddha returned to the Jeta Grove and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on the city of Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu eats at various locations, except during the special times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The special times are: the time of illness and the time of [receiving] robes; these are called the special times.
"A bhikṣu" is as described above.
"Eating at various places" means eating repeatedly.
"Except at other times" refers to the time of illness.
Regarding "the sick": for those with diseases such as fever, wind, or cold, if they eat again after having already eaten and thereby attain physical ease, there is no offense for the one who eats.

Regarding "the time of [keeping] robes": during the month when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, or the five months when it has been spread, one may temporarily relinquish five precepts within that period of wearing the robe without offense;

namely: eating in a group apart from the community, eating at various places, departing from the place of common meals without informing others, keeping an extra robe, and staying overnight separated from one's robe.
Regarding "other times," the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

A bhikṣu must know the number of days for which food should be given; he must know the number of months since his ordination (*kappo*) and remember the robes he has received and maintains; and he must distinguish between eating in a separate group and whether one is ill or not.
If someone asks,
"What is the date today?
one must not respond by asking in return:
"Which day was yesterday?
One should know the first and second days of the month, and so on, up to the fourteenth and fifteenth days, as well as whether the month is large or small; all of this must be known.
In the early morning, a bhikṣu should form the intention to give food:
"Today, having obtained food, I shall give it to such-and-such a person; that person will not take account of me, and I shall eat."
Thus he spoke three times.
Day by day, he himself remembered his number of years since ordination (*varṣa*).

He should remember whether he was maintaining the three robes and whether he had not performed the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*) or the act of giving them away; he should also keep in mind the meal taken apart from the community (*pṛthag-bhaktika*).
Whether one is ill or not ill, what constitutes the meal of a bhikṣu?

If it is wheat porridge, three *bhaṭṭhālas*; or roasted flour, two *bhaṭṭhālas* or one *bhaṭṭhāla*; or rice cooked with fish or meat, one bowl or half a bowl—whichever of these one obtains, this is called the meal of a bhikṣu.

If food is being prepared within a monastery and it is not yet cooked, if a bhikṣu receives roasted flour and makes a drink from it, he commits the offense of eating at improper times and incurs a pāyattika.
If one is performing the ritual for offering food, or if one is ill, there is no offense.
If it is the time for robes, there is no offense in either case.
If there is an external invitation from a household, this is termed "a bhikṣu’s meal."

At that time, if a bhikṣu has requested someone to bring food, and before the food has arrived, the bhikṣu receives roasted flour and makes it into a flour-drink (saktu-pāna) to send as the meal; if the bhikṣu who brings the food knows the characteristics of the precepts, he should wait a short while.
One should wait until that bhikṣu has performed the ritual for giving food (*dāna-vidhi*) before handing over the meal.

If the bhikṣu delivering the food is unaware of the characteristics of the precepts and thus hastily hands over the food, not allowing time for the ritual of giving food to be performed, then at that moment, while food is still in his mouth, he should speak the ritual for giving food while holding the food in his mouth; this is because it is better to exchange the light for the heavy.
If a bhikṣu arrives at a house and the donor says to him:
"Ācārya! You shall take your meal at my home today."
"This is what is called a place for eating.
A bhikṣu then thinks:
"This food is not yet cooked; I now wish to go to another house."
At that time, one should depart only after having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
If one departs without making the announcement, it is an *pāyattika*.
If one obtains the five kinds of primary food (*bhojana*) or the five kinds of mixed primary food while there and eats them, it is two *pāyattikas*.
If one eats at various locations or at a place where eating is prohibited without having announced it, there is no offense provided one is ill or performing the ritual for giving food.
Regarding the time for robes, in both cases there is no offense.
If a donor should say this:
"Ācārya! If there is no food [available], please come to my home to eat."
The bhikṣu went to that house and said,
"Long-lived one!
I shall take my meal here today."
The upāsikā said, “Excellent!
I shall prepare it accordingly.”
If the food is not yet cooked and this bhikṣu wishes to go to another household, he should inform [the host] before departing.
