If he does not inform them, he incurs an offense as described above.
If a bhikṣu, while on his almsround in succession, arrives at a certain house, and the donor says:
"Today we have invited various bhikṣus to eat here; I pray that the Ācārya will also accept my invitation and not eat elsewhere."
If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation, that place is termed a "place of eating.
If a bhikṣu who lives on alms-food accepts an invitation, he should reflect:
"Who is capable of consuming this heavy gift of food offered out of faith?"
If one wishes to depart, one should inform [the community] before leaving.
If one departs without informing them, one incurs an offense as previously described.

If a bhikṣu of great merit and renown receives food brought by many people, and he accepts it all out of a desire to please the donors, those who accept such invitations and eat incur the offense of eating at various places (*anekāvasatha-bhojana*), which is a *pāyattika*.
If one performs the ritual for offering food, or if one is ill, there is no offense.
If it is during the time for robes, there is no offense for either.
There were two bhikṣus who each separately accepted an invitation from the head of a household; the first bhikṣu said to the second bhikṣu:
"Elder! Today let us go together to my donor's house for a meal.
The second bhikṣu should respond with "So be it" and then depart.
If one departs without having announced it, it is as explained above.
If a second bhikṣu makes the invitation, it is also the same.
Regarding the place where a bhikṣu eats: three *prastha* of wheat porridge, two *prastha* of parched grain flour, and one *prastha* of rice.
If one prepares rice, fish, or meat—whether it be a full bowl or half a bowl—and each individual portion within it is eaten by a single bhikṣu;
or if one household obtains three *sheng*, two *sheng*, one *sheng*, or half a *sheng*, and thus receives many such portions through begging, there is no offense.

If one household obtains three *pattha* of barley-gruel, two *pattha* of parched grain, or one *pattha*, or rice cooked as a meal, or fish and meat, whether one and a half *pattha* or one *pattha*, and one may not take more from other places—among these cases, which constitutes an offense?
What constitutes no offense?
If, when the gruel first emerges from the cauldron, it forms characters when drawn upon, it is an offense; if it does not form characters, it is no offense.

Regarding all vegetables, all parched grain flour, all cakes, and all fruits—provided they are not eaten in various places, not part of a separate group meal, and not a meal after one has finished eating—even if accumulated in great quantities in a *śālā*, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, there was a brahmin who invited the Saṃgha for a meal. Having prepared various kinds of food and drink, filtered pure water, and spread out mats and bedding, he had this thought:
"The Ācārya is one who eats but once a day; you must eat early.
He then went to the Jetavana, prostrated himself at the feet of the Saṃgha, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"I, [Name], have invited the Saṃgha for a meal. The provisions are prepared; may the Saṃgha know that it is time."

Then, when the time had come, the bhikṣu put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to that house. Having sat down in the proper order, the brahmin personally served him various kinds of food and drink until he was fully satisfied.
The brahmin again took food himself and followed them, urging them insistently.
All the bhikṣus said, "We have no need for more; we are full.
When the bhikṣus had finished eating, those who had no further business went straight back to the monastery, while those with business passed by the various donors.
Having seen him, the donor joyfully prostrated, inquired after his well-being, and said:
"Ācārya, do you require food before the midday meal?
Do you require fruits or melons?"
"Would you like some gruel?
If there is anything the Ācārya requires, I shall provide it.
The bhikṣu said:
"I have already eaten my fill at the house of such-and-such a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the donor, knowing that the bhikṣu’s mealtime had not yet expired, said this: "Ācārya!..."
"It is already early; you may take these cakes back to the vihāra to eat.
The bhikṣu then took the bowl and filled it with the cakes. Returning to the gate of the Jetavana, he sat down to eat them, and further called other bhikṣus to eat together with him.
When the brahmin had finished eating, he said to his wife, "Send some of the remaining food to our neighbors;
I wish to go to the place where the World-Honored One is to pay my respects, visit him, and inquire after his well-being."
Seeing from afar a bhikṣu sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove eating cakes with others, he went to a certain bhikṣu who was walking in meditation and asked,
"Is this a visiting bhikṣu?"
He replied, "No.
[The other asked,] "Is it a bhikṣu who intends to travel?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Is this a bhikṣu who eats from my household?
He replied, "Yes."
He asked again, "What are you doing?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Brahmin, do you not know? He replied, "I do not know."
"This bhikṣu has eaten little; let us provide more so that he may be satisfied.
At that time, the brahmin’s heart was immediately displeased, and he spoke these words:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are people who speak the truth, yet now they are not truthful."
"To speak of what is insufficient as sufficient, to use words that should not be used, and to claim fullness where there is no fullness—this is to ruin a person;
what path of cultivation could such a one possess?
Because of this resentment in his heart, he ultimately did not go to the Buddha, but instead returned home.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Monk!”
“How is it that you have risen after eating your fill, left your seat, and yet eat again?
From this day forward, I do not permit one who has eaten their fill to leave their seat and eat again.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus ate vegetables and said they were satisfied; they ate salt and said they were satisfied; after drinking water, they all declared themselves satisfied.
They did not eat anything further once they had left their seats, and consequently their bodies became emaciated.
For these reasons, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to eat the five kinds of primary foods and the five kinds of mixed primary foods; this is called 'sufficiency.'"
At that time, while the bhikṣus were at their seats, having received a small amount of food, they considered it sufficient and ate no more; nevertheless, they remained weak and emaciated.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Eating in a single sitting, the five kinds of primary foods, the five kinds of mixed primary foods, and eating as much as one desires—this is called 'sufficiency'."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there were sixty bhikṣus who were ill at the Jeta Grove Monastery. When the bhikṣus brought sixty portions of food for them, the sick bhikṣus did not finish eating it all; they discarded the remainder by the wall, where crows and birds gathered to eat it, fighting and making noise.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monks,
why is it that these birds are making such a great noise?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

“There were sixty bhikṣus who were ill; we brought food for them, but they could not finish it all. We discarded it by the wall, and because the birds are quarreling over this leftover food, they are making such a loud noise.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If a sick bhikṣu has not finished his meal, it is permitted for the attendant bhikṣu to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) ritual and then eat."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a monk who was nursing the sick performed the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-vidhi*). After he had eaten, there was still some remaining, and various birds began to quarrel over it, as described above.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"Why are the various birds quarreling?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:

"The bhikṣu who was tending to the sick performed the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-vidhi*), yet even after eating he could not finish it all; he discarded it by the wall, and for this reason the birds were quarreling over the food and making noise."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit one person to prepare *vighasa* (leftover food), and all others shall be allowed to eat it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, having finished eating and risen from his seat, eats food that he has not designated as leftover food (vighasa), it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are five kinds of food:
parched flour, boiled rice, barley meal, fish, and meat.
Furthermore, there are five types of mixed staple foods; these are called "food."
There are eight kinds of contentment:
first, contentment with self-indulgence;
second, contentment with few desires; [and so forth].
Third, feet that are filthy;
fourth, feet that are variegated;
fifth, feet that are unsuitable.
Sixth is the foot of guile;
seventh is the foot of abiding;
eighth is the foot of self.
Regarding "satisfying oneself at will": when a donor offers at will parched grain, rice, barley meal, fish, meat, or various other types of solid food, and encourages one to eat as much as desired,
the bhikṣu says, "I am already satisfied."

If one rises from one's seat in this manner and eats without performing the *kṛtāvaśeṣa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*; this is called being "content with what is offered.

Regarding being "content with little desire": if a donor offers five kinds of primary foods (*maulabhakta*) and five kinds of secondary primary foods (*vyañjana*), and a bhikṣu makes a gesture with his hand indicating he will take only a small amount, and having thus risen from his seat, eats without performing the *kṛtāvaśeṣa*, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called being "content with little desire."
Regarding "defiled feet": when one is eating, if the hands of the person serving food are defiled by scabies, sores, or other impurities, and a bhikṣu sees them defiled, he says:
"Do not serve me."
If one rises from one's seat and eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "defiled by foot.
Regarding "mixed with foot": a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) carries a vessel of milk or curd filled with flour-rice and goes about; when a bhikṣu sees this, he says maliciously:
"I do not want any of that."
If one rises from one's seat and eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "mixed with what is sufficient.
Regarding that which is not yet sufficient: when a layperson (*gṛhapati*) serves food, the bhikṣu asks, "What is this?"
He replied, "Flour. The bhikṣu said:
"If this wind disorder of mine is disturbed, I will not be able to go.
If, having risen from his seat for this reason, he eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*.
When the rice is being served, if a bhikṣu asks,
"Is it hard or soft?
he should answer:
"Hard. The bhikṣu said, "This hard rice is difficult to digest; I am not inclined to go."
If he says, "It is soft," the bhikṣu says:
"This is rotten and difficult to eat; I will not pass by.
When meat was being distributed, a bhikṣu asked, "What kind of meat is this?"
He replied, "Beef. The bhikṣu said:
“Beef is hot in nature; I cannot consume it.
If one says, “Water buffalo meat,” [one may eat it].
The bhikṣu said:
"Cold-natured [food] is difficult to digest and passes downward. If he says:
“Deer meat.
The bhikṣu said,
“This meat has a wind-nature that moves downward.”

This is called "not sitting properly. If, having risen from one's seat in this manner, one eats food without first performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*; this is what is meant by "not sitting properly."

Regarding "deceitful satiety": when a layperson offers the five kinds of pure food or the five kinds of mixed pure food, a bhikṣu, fearing that there will be too much, does not say with his mouth, "I am full," but instead manifests a sign with his hands—such as shaking his head or making a gesture by shrinking back his bowl—and rises from his seat without leaving any remainder of the food. If he eats [the remaining food], it is a pāyattika; this is called "deceitful satiety."
Regarding "stopping one's feet": when a lay follower (*upāsaka*) serves the five kinds of proper food or the five kinds of mixed proper food, the bhikṣu says:
"Long-lived one!
Do not place the rice balls too far forward for fear of touching your feet; you should first set down the vegetables, salt, and cold water."
If one has risen from one's seat in this manner and, without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), continues to eat, it is a *pāyattika*.

If, as the *vaiyyāvṛtyakara* (steward) or *karmadāna* (officer) on duty, one points out signs [of satiety] without having actually finished, this is not called "sufficient"; it is called "staying back" (*sthita-pātra*).
Regarding "being self-sufficient": a bhikṣu, having gone to a household for alms, sets aside his bag of parched grain in one place and asks the donor for water to drink.
The donor thinks to himself:
"This bhikṣu must surely need parched grain."
He then asked,
"Do you need some flour?
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This donor surely wishes to take some flour from his house to give me.
He replied, "I need it."
At that time, the donor immediately took the bhikṣu’s flour bag and handed it to him; however, because the bhikṣu was attached to his own flour, he said:
"Put it down! Put it down!"
When he has spoken thus, if he rises from his seat and eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it is a *pāyattika*. This is called "satisfying oneself.
Regarding "rising from one's seat," there are eight locations:
walking, standing, sitting, lying down, a long bed, a small stool, a boat, and a vehicle.
Regarding "staying": if a bhikṣu stands while eating during a *pravāraṇā* (invitation to eat freely) and is given food, he should remain standing in the middle [of his seat].

Whether walking, sitting, or lying down, all such actions are termed "leaving one's original place" (*sthānāntara*), for which the *vighasa* rule does not apply; if he eats in such a manner, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to walking, sitting, and lying down.

If a bhikṣu is sitting on a high bed and is freely offered food, when he sees a senior elder (*sthavira*), a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or a teacher (*ācārya*) approaching, he must not rise from his seat to avoid them; however, he may slide his body along the bed to move aside. If a leg of the bed breaks, this is considered leaving one's original place.
If one eats without having performed the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of not eating after the meal), it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "sitting on a long bed.
Regarding the "bed": if a bhikṣu sits upon a solitary bed and is offered food at will.
If, while sitting, one becomes aware that behind them there is a stupa, or a monk, or a preceptor (upādhyāya), or a teacher (ācārya), they should not leave their seat to turn around.
If it is raining, they should hold an umbrella over [the object] to cover it.

If there is no canopy, one may place the bed together with its frame and lift it to a covered location; however, if during the lifting it touches the ground, it is said to have left its original place.
If one eats without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "the sitting bed."

Regarding "on a boat": if a bhikṣu partakes of food while on a boat during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, whether the boat strikes the shore, touches wood or stone, or turns with the waves, if the bhikṣu’s body leaves its original position and he eats without performing the *atirikta-bhakta* (refusal of further food), it is a *pāyattika*.

Regarding "conveyance": if a bhikṣu is on a conveyance and is served food at his own will, whether the conveyance is ascending a slope, descending a slope, or turning over and leaving its original position, if he eats it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*. This is called "conveyance."
There are five improper cases that do not constitute the offense of *kṛtya-kṛta* (refusing food).
What are these five?
Being out of place, being out of the meal, being out of range, being out of arm’s reach, and being out of speech.

Regarding "leaving the place": if one prepares *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food) and gives it to a bhikṣu to eat while he is walking, or while he is standing, sitting, or lying down, and explains the rule for *kṛtapiṇḍa* at that time, this is not called "preparing [the food]."

Thus, when standing, sitting, or lying down, or while eating, walking, standing, or sitting, one explains the rule regarding leftover food (*vighasa*); this is called "leaving the place. Regarding "leaving the food":
if one does not give it as leftover food to be eaten, but instead explains [the rule] while giving it, it is not considered "made" [as such]; this is called "leaving the food."
Regarding "leaving the boundary": if one places food on the ground to leave it as a remnant, rather than within the reach of the hand, this is not called "making" [the act of leaving];

this is termed "leaving the boundary. Regarding "leaving the reach of the hand": if one leaves food as a remnant outside the range of an outstretched hand, rather than within the reach of an outstretched hand, this is not called "making"; this is termed "leaving the reach of the hand."
Regarding abstaining from speech:
one does not say with the mouth, "The food in my hand or in my bowl—I have no need for any of it now; give this leftover food to the Elder."

This is called "leaving off the speech," not "performing [the act]"; these are called the five unlawful ways, which do not constitute the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the formal distribution of food).
There are five lawful ways, which are called performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* in accordance with the Dharma.
What are the five?
Not being separated by place, not being separated by food, not being separated by the objective field, not being separated by the reach of the hand, and not being separated by speech.

Regarding "not being separated by place": if one prepares *khalupaścādbhaktika* (leftover food) and gives it to a bhikṣu while he is walking, and the method for leftover food is explained while he is still walking, this is called "preparation."
It is the same when standing, sitting, or lying down; this is called "not departing from one's place.
Regarding "not departing from food": having finished eating, one immediately gives the *vighasa-dharma* (the rule for leftover food); this is called "not departing from food."
"Not departing from the boundary" means that the leftover food is made within arm's reach and not on the ground; this is called "not departing from the boundary.

"Not departing from the reach of the hand" means that the leftover food is made within the reach of the extended hand and not outside the reach of the extended hand; this is called "not departing from the reach of the hand."
Regarding "not departing from speech," it means that after having eaten, one says these words:
"Whatever food there was in my hand and in my bowl, I now have no need for any of it; this leftover food is for you, Venerable One."
This is called "not departing from speech. These are the five ways of performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food) in accordance with the Dharma.
If one commits five unlawful acts, one shall not eat as *kṛtapiṇḍa* for the rest of one's life.
What are the five? They are:

unskillfulness regarding the dwelling, unskillfulness regarding food, unskillfulness regarding sensory objects, unskillfulness regarding reaching out the hand, and unskillfulness regarding prohibitions.

To be unskilled in one's conduct means not knowing that when walking one should eat enough for walking, when standing one should eat enough for standing, when sitting one should eat enough for sitting, and when lying down one should eat enough for lying down; this is called being unskilled in one's conduct.
Regarding "improper food": not knowing that the five types of primary food and the five types of mixed primary food are sufficient, while anything else is insufficient, is called improper food.
Regarding "improper objects": not knowing that what is in one's hand is sufficient, while what is on the ground is insufficient, is called improper objects.

Regarding "inappropriate extension of the hand": not knowing that within the extended hand there is sufficiency, and outside the extended hand there is insufficiency, is called inappropriate extension of the hand.
Regarding "inappropriate withholding": not knowing that withholding is sufficiency, and not withholding is insufficiency, is called inappropriate withholding.
If one accomplishes these five unrighteous [conditions], one is not permitted to consume *khalupaścitaka* food for the remainder of one's life.
If one accomplishes the five righteous [conditions], one is permitted to consume *khalupaścitaka* food for the remainder of one's life.
What are the five? They are:
a good location, good food, a good environment, skillful extension of the hand, and skillful restraint. Regarding "a good location":

it means knowing when to walk while eating so that walking is sufficient, knowing when to stand while eating so that standing is sufficient, knowing when to sit while eating so that sitting is sufficient, and knowing when to lie down while eating so that lying down is sufficient; this is called a good location.
Regarding "proper food": knowing that the five types of primary food and the five types of mixed primary food are sufficient, while anything else is not sufficient, is called proper food.
Regarding "proper circumstances": knowing that when food is in one's hand it is sufficient, whereas when it is on the ground it is not sufficient, is called proper circumstances.

One who is skilled at extending the hand knows that what is within the extended hand is the foot, and what is outside the extended hand is not the foot; this is called being skilled at extending the hand.
One who is skilled at withholding knows that what is withheld is the foot, and what is not withheld is not the foot; this is called being skilled at withholding.
Having accomplished these five dharmas, one may eat "leftover food" (vighasa) for the remainder of one's life.

If a bhikṣu brings food intending to make it leftover food, and makes it leftover while it is still in the bowl or the cup, it is only that which is in the cup which is properly termed "leftover food"; the food within the bowl is not so termed.
If the broth from a bowl flows into an alms-bowl, both may be designated as "leftover food" (vighasa).
If a bhikṣu seeks to make two bowls into leftover food while the person before him is eating from only one bowl, then only that single bowl may be made into leftover food.
If cakes or vegetables are placed across two bowls so as to cover them both, both are considered to have become *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover food); the same applies to various other types of vessels.
If a bhikṣu, having already finished his meal, goes to the house of a donor, and the host says:
"Ācārya! Would you be able to eat some cakes?"
He replied,
"I have had enough to eat.
The upāsaka who knew the Dharma spoke these words:
"If there is insufficient food at such-and-such a house, and if you require more, I shall go there and perform the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover-food) rite.
If the bhikṣu requires it, he should reply: "So be it."

The donor washed the vessel, filled it with various kinds of fine food, and the bhikṣu received it, wrapping it in a high-quality, fine cotton cloth so that no external dust or soil could enter. He placed it in the hands of a lay attendant (karmadāna) and spoke these words:
"Go, prepare it as *vighasa* (leftover food), and then bring it back."
The attendant, carrying the food, went to where the bhikṣu was and spoke these words:
“Venerable One!
In my home there is food, but it has not yet been eaten by a bhikṣu who has finished his meal; I pray that the Venerable One will perform the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover-food) rite for me.”
That bhikṣu should wash his hands thoroughly, and having received this food, say to the attendant:
"Stand near me within arm's reach."
After the bhikṣu has eaten one mouthful from that bowl, he speaks thus:
"Whatever food remains in this vessel in my hand, I have no further need for it; I give it to you as *vighasa* (leftover food)."
The attendant brings it and presents it to the bhikṣu; the bhikṣu may then eat it.
If there is further food remaining after [the bhikṣus] have had their fill, those who require it may also eat it together.

If there is a land where bhikṣus are few, and after the bhikṣus have finished eating, a great donor arrives bringing various kinds of food and drink, but the bhikṣus have already risen and departed—what should be done?

If there is a *karmadāna* (monastic administrator) on duty that month, or any other official who has not yet eaten their fill, one should perform the ritual of *vighasa* (leftover food) in the presence of that person.
If they have already eaten their fill, but the *sthavira* (senior monk) has not yet eaten his fill, one should perform the ritual of *vighasa* in the presence of the *sthavira*.

If the senior monk is modest and unable to do so among the people, they should rise together from their seats and go to a secluded place where the senior monk may perform the *kṛtānna* (leftover food) rite.
If the senior monk has already finished eating and a visiting bhikṣu arrives, he should ask:
"Venerable sir!"
"Is today's *pravāraṇā* complete?
If the visiting bhikṣus reply, "We have not yet completed our summer retreat; how could the *pravāraṇā* be complete?"
One should know that such a person does not understand the characteristics of the Vinaya and should be asked again:
"Have you eaten yet? If he says:
“I have eaten.
He asked again,
“Does the donor allow you to take as much as you wish?”
If one says:
"Venerable sir, where did you obtain this food for the *pravāraṇā*?
Even water and vegetables are insufficient, let alone other kinds of food."
"You should know that this is insufficient; you ought to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover-food) rite with that bhikṣu.
If he says, "I have been given food at my own donor's house as much as I wish," [then it is sufficient].
One should know that [the meal] is sufficient; the Saṃgha should employ skillful means and must not break the donor’s wholesome intention.

If there is a senior śrāmaṇera among the assembly, he should be brought to the boundary of the precepts (sīmā) and granted full ordination; once he has been instructed in the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-dharma), only then should they eat.
If a bhikṣu eats the five kinds of mixed proper food and sets aside the five proper foods as "leftover food" (vighasa), this is not considered a formal act of setting aside.
If the meal is insufficient and he eats more, there is no offense.
If one rises from one's seat and eats again, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.

If a bhikṣu eats the five types of primary foods (*bhojana*), setting aside the five types of secondary foods (*khādya*) as "leftover food" (*vighasa*), it does not constitute [the formal act of] making them "leftover."
If it is insufficient, there is no offense in eating more.
If one has eaten sufficiently and leaves the seat, yet eats again, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, apart from the five kinds of formal meals (*bhojana*) and apart from the five kinds of mixed formal meals, makes [food] into "leftover food" (*vighasa*), it is not called making it into "leftover food."
If one does not eat enough, there is no offense.
If, having eaten enough, one rises from the seat and eats again, one incurs a *vibhāṣā-āpatti* (an offense against the Vinaya).

If a bhikṣu makes the five types of formal meals (*bhojana*) or the five types of mixed formal meals into *vighasa* (leftover food), this is called making it into *vighasa* in accordance with the Dharma.
If one has not yet eaten enough, there is no offense in eating more.
If one has eaten enough and rises from the seat, there is an offense in eating again.
Among these cases, which constitutes an offense?
What constitutes no offense?

If all kinds of gruel have just come out of the cauldron and one cannot form characters with it; or if it concerns all kinds of fruit or vegetables; or if it is not a meal taken separately from the community, not a meal taken at various locations, and not a meal after having finished eating; or if there is a large accumulation inside a house—there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, Ānanda had two disciples who were his co-practitioners:
The first was named Pūrṇa and the second was named Abhaya.
They had two attendant disciples who traveled together with the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
the first was named Ajita and the second was named Śāradvatīputra; each of them spoke as follows:
“Who is the most learned?
Who possesses the greatest eloquence?

At that time, Ānanda’s co-practitioner was possessed of sharp faculties and great eloquence; however, Maudgalyāyana’s disciple excelled in debate and did not match him. Consequently, this disciple constantly followed Ānanda on his travels, remaining by his side whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, seeking out his faults.

On one occasion, two groups of disciples had accepted an invitation together. At that time, a disciple of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana received some cakes; he ate half and took the other half outside to speak with a disciple of Ānanda, saying:
"Elder!..."
"Do you wish to eat some cakes?
He asked, "Where did you obtain these cakes?"
He replied,
“I brought it from that place where the food was kept,” and he immediately took the food.
Having finished eating, he spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!
You have committed an offense."
He asked, "What kind of offense?
He replied:

“The World-Honored One has established the precept that it is not permitted for a bhikṣu, having finished eating and left his seat, to eat again without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite.
Ānanda’s disciple said:
“How can you wish to satisfy me while not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite, yet instruct me to eat?”
The disciple of Maudgalyāyana said, "When we were debating previously, why did you use your eloquence to so forcefully humiliate me?

Thereupon, they engaged in a dispute and went to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?

When I preach the ninefold Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas—namely, the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, and Adbhutadharma—have those śrāvakas, having heard this ninefold Dharma, done so with the desire to cause my disciples to engage in debate and contend over victory and defeat?"
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If it were not so, would I have taught these ninefold dharmas to the śrāvakas with the intention that the śrāvakas practice according to what has been taught?"
He replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
Then the two bhikṣus immediately confessed their transgressions before the World-Honored One, facing one another. The Buddha said:

"One must not rely on one's own knowledge of the Dharma to treat others with contempt, nor is it permitted for a bhikṣu who knows that another has already eaten enough to forcibly urge them to eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food)."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has already eaten his fill, encourages that person—who has left their seat and has not performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite—to eat more for the sake of causing annoyance, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Food" refers to the five types of primary food and the five types of mixed primary food.
"Sufficient" has eight kinds, as explained above.
"Leaving the original place" refers to the eight types mentioned above.
"Disturbing" means to provoke or annoy another person with the intent of making them unhappy.
"Not constituting leftover food" means that if five improper conditions are fulfilled, it is not designated as leftover food.
When five conditions are fulfilled, it is called "eating as leftover food" (vighasa) in accordance with the Dharma.
To eat by being pressured or urged to do so is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If five factors are fulfilled in an improper manner, a bhikṣu may not consume *vighasa* (leftover food) for the remainder of his life.
If five factors are fulfilled in a proper manner, he is permitted to consume *vighasa* for the remainder of his life; the detailed explanation of the intervening points is as stated above.
If one encourages another to eat while perceiving that they have not yet had enough, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one encourages another to eat while perceiving that they have already had enough, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one encourages another to eat while perceiving that they have had enough, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one encourages another to eat by saying "it is not enough, it is not enough," there is no offense.

In this regard, there is no transgression in the following cases: when the first portion of any gruel emerging from the cauldron does not form a character when drawn upon it; and in the case of all fruits and all vegetables. These are not offenses.
Therefore it was said:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha possessed everything made of discarded materials: a bowl of discarded materials, robes of discarded materials, food of discarded materials, and leather sandals of discarded materials.
What is a refuse-rag bowl?
When a bhikṣu’s broken bowl has been mended five times and is discarded, Aniruddha takes it, mends it further, and uses it; this is called a refuse-rag bowl.

Regarding the refuse-rag robe (*pāṃśukūla*): it refers to worn-out, discarded garments found in streets and alleys; having taken them, washed, mended, and dyed them, one accepts and wears them—this is called the refuse-rag robe.
Regarding refuse-food (*piṇḍapāta-pāṃśukūla*): if there is food abandoned by others after offerings to spirits or deities, and this elder takes and eats it himself, this is called refuse-food.

Regarding "cast-off leather sandals": these are leather sandals that have been discarded by various bhikṣus because they were torn or broken; having picked them up and repaired them further, one wears them—this is called cast-off leather sandals.

When it was time for the elder to go on his alms-round, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city. As he first entered the city gate, he saw a woman carrying a basket filled with rice and holding sacrificial implements—grass, cow dung, and fire—as she went out. Upon seeing this, the Venerable One thought:
"There is the possibility of obtaining food here; this would be pleasant for me, so I shall seek further."
He immediately departed and wandered from street to street, but found nothing at all.

Upon reaching the edge of a pond, he saw the same woman as before sprinkling water, sweeping, and smearing the ground; she had spread clean grass, arranged the sacrificial vessels, and completed her offerings.
He scattered rice around the four sides and spoke these words:
"Come, noble crow, to eat!
Come, noble crow, to eat!"
At that time, the Venerable One was standing beneath a tree; by the power of his majestic spiritual authority (*ṛddhibala*), none of the crows came to feed there.
When the woman saw the Venerable One, she spoke these words:
"You are like a blind crow, always following after people."
After the woman had finished her abuse, she returned immediately.

Then the Venerable One gathered up the sacrificial food and returned toward the monastery. When the bhikṣus saw him, they said to one another, "This Venerable One undergoes extreme hardship in seeking alms;
it is very difficult for him to obtain food."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Venerable sir, did you obtain food?
He replied:
"I have received it, but there are many faults within it;
I do not find it pleasing. He then asked, "What are the faults?"
He replied: "So it is! So it is!"
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, saying,
“How many offenses does one incur for reviling women?
The Buddha said:
"One incurs many offenses.
The bhikṣu asked again:
"To what extent is it considered 'many'?"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"For five hundred lifetimes, this woman has always been a blind crow; in all her future incarnations, she shall die of starvation.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Call Ānanda here. Having called him, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Is it truly so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha:
"Although you wish for few affairs, from this day forward, I do not permit you to take things with your own hands.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the World-Honored One had prohibited taking things with one's own hands. Having heard this, the bhikṣus received water and tooth-sticks from others; those who had attendants (kappiyakāraka) were able to obtain them, but those without attendants suffered and could not obtain them.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma for the great assembly, there was a bhikṣu who smelled a foul odor from his own mouth; he sat downwind from the crowd, not wishing the stench of his breath to permeate the other fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Monk, why are you sitting there like a person full of resentment?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, since the Blessed One has established the precept that one must not take anything unless it has been given, the bhikṣus receive all their water and tooth-sticks from others.”

If there is a *kappiya-kāraka*, one may obtain it; if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, it is difficult to obtain. Fearing that the foul odor from his mouth might offend his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), he stands downwind.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the exception of water and tooth-sticks.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣu takes what is not given and places it in his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Not given" means another person has not given it, nor has he received it from that person. "Places it in his mouth to eat" refers to food, excluding water and tooth-sticks.
There are ten kinds of water as previously described; if the water is turbid, it may be accepted.
If the nature of the water is yellow, there is no fault in drinking it.
There are two kinds of tooth-sticks:
First, the split; second, the ball.
If a bhikṣu develops sores from the heat in his mouth, the physician says:
"You should chew a tooth-stick and swallow the juice."
Regarding the phrase "one should accept," the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense except in the case of water and tooth-sticks.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
Receiving food on top of a tree, in a well, on a roof, in a clean kitchen, from a vessel or from what is not a vessel, on a bed, on a boat, on a vehicle, by mental intention, or on a road.

Regarding "upon food": at the time of eating, it refers to spreading out a bed, a long plank, a bundle of sugarcane, a bundle of radishes, or a sack of grain or beans, and then spreading various seats, couches, or rugs upon them.
When a bhikṣu is sitting, he should not move his body, nor should he ask questions.
If he moves or asks, "What is this?
[he commits an offense].
This is called impurity.
If, when a bhikṣu is eating, wind blows dust that falls upon the grass beneath his bowl but does not fall upon the food, he may eat; however, he must accept the grass leaves.
If dust, grass, or leaves fall upon one while eating, everything must be received again.
When a bhikṣu is eating, if dust from the hooves of cattle, camels, or similar animals comes and settles on him, he may eat provided it does not defile the food.
If dust or grass leaves fall [upon the food], one must receive it again.
If dust, grass leaves, or food [itself] falls [onto the bowl], all of it must be received again.
If dust from an animal shaking its body comes [into the bowl], if one receives it with intentional awareness, it is called "receiving."
If dust comes from flocks of birds, it is likewise.
If, when a bhikṣu is eating, a woman walks by with her garment trailing on the ground and dust rises up to sprinkle him, it is also like this.
If a layperson is carrying grass or leaves, the bhikṣu should say to them:
"Suspend it.
If they are carrying salt, fruit, or vegetables, he should say:
"Letting it hang down.
If a pure person (śrāmaṇera) places fruit on the grass and it immediately rolls away, this is not called "acceptance.
If it stops for even a short moment, it is called "acceptance."
If the fruit is firm, it may be taken and washed; if it is rotten, it should not be taken.
If a pure person shakes roasted flour from a vessel and some flour falls into one's own vessel, if one accepts it with intentional awareness, it is termed "received."
If one does not apply attention [to the food], it must be received again.

If a lay attendant (upāsaka) carries a vessel containing flour and the vessel falls into a bhikṣu’s bowl, if he brushes it away with his hand at the very moment it falls, the vessel is therefore considered pure.
If it remains for even a brief moment, it is then called impure.
If it is a copper vessel, one should wash it clean before using it.
If it is a wooden vessel and grease has entered within, it should be discarded.
If grease does not enter [the food], it may be scraped off and used.
When rice is being served, if grains of rice spring up into the air from the vessel as it is shaken, and a bhikṣu forms the intention to receive them, they are considered received.
If one has not formed the intention to receive [the food], one should receive it again.
The same applies when serving ghee, milk, curd, meat, vegetables, sauce, and so forth.

When holding a five-year great assembly, on the Buddha’s birthday, the day he attained enlightenment, the day he turned the wheel of Dharma, the assembly for Ānanda, or the assembly for Rāhula, if a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) is difficult to find, a bhikṣu should go to the edge of the vegetable garden and receive the vegetables; the same applies when serving salt, parched grain, or rice.
If a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) lifts [the object] but does not move it off the ground, this may still be termed "receiving," though it is not in accordance with proper decorum (iriyāpatha).
The bhikṣu should say to the lay attendant:
"Lift it off the ground and give it to me."
If the attendant (kappiyakāraka) is too small to lift [the vessel], one should say:
"Divide and give it to me little by little.
The same applies when receiving soup, cakes, or other food and drink.
When receiving a jar of ghee, if the rope touches the ground, one should say:
"Lift this rope.
If the attendant (karmadāna) is too small to lift it, one should instruct him:
"Give me a little less.
If, in such cases, one is unable to receive [the food] because the cauldron or pot is too hot, one should place two pieces of wood horizontally on the ground, step upon them with one's feet, and say:
"I receive it!"
"I accept!
This is called "receiving from above.
Regarding "from a tree": when a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) eats fruit from atop a tree, a bhikṣu says:
"Give me fruit.
The attendant then shook the tree so that fruit fell; that which fell into the bhikṣu’s vessel is termed "received," though it is not in accordance with proper decorum (*airyāpatha*).
In this way, whether with the foot, the hand, or the mouth, when lowering the fruit, if the fruit touches the branches or leaves, the bhikṣu should again give rise to the thought:
"I accept!"
"Receive!"—this is called "receiving.
If one is suspended by a rope and lets go of the rope with either foot or hand, and touches a branch or leaf, one should likewise say: [Receive!]"
"Feeling! Feeling!"—
this is what is called feeling.
If a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) is eating parched grain or beans and a bhikṣu desires them, he immediately asks for them, saying:
"Give me some parched grain or beans.
If the lay attendant does not wish to give them, the bhikṣu seizes the lay attendant's hand and pours the food into his own robe-sack, saying: [as before].
"Feeling! Feeling!"—
this is what is called feeling, yet it is not deportment.
A monkey was eating fruit on a tree; a bhikṣu, desiring some fruit, said to the monkey, "Give me some fruit.
The monkey shook the tree so that fruit fell down, which the bhikṣu caught in a vessel.
When it falls into the vessel, it is termed "receiving," though it is not [proper] deportment.
Likewise, when placing fruit in the hand, the foot, or the mouth, or when breaking off branches and leaves, one should further give rise to the thought:
"I receive!"
"Feeling!"—this is what is called "feeling," and this is what is meant by "upon the tree.
Regarding "in the well": if a bhikṣu is dwelling in a forest hermitage and the well is full of water, but there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare things for the Sangha).
A bhikṣu was drawing water from a well when another bhikṣu said, "It is time;
you may come out for food.
The bhikṣu in the well replied:
"If I go out, the water will fill up again.
I wish to eat here; please lower the food down.
The attendant should place the food and drink in a single vessel, tie it with a cord or knot, and lower it down.
At the time of eating, the monk at the bottom of the well should say to the attendant:
"Lower the rope and grasp it with your hand.
If there are living plants or grass growing along the sides of the well's interior, he should instruct him to avoid them.
Having reached the bottom of the well, the bhikṣu should pull up the rope with one hand while supporting it with the other, saying:
"Take! Take!"
This is called "receiving.
If the well water is clear, one may take it for drinking oneself.
If it is turbid, one says to a *karmadāna*:
"Hold a new, clean jar with its cord tied to the lower part of the water.
As explained above, this refers to [using water] from a well. Regarding "on the roof":
if a bhikṣu is dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), the bhikṣu covers the roof himself.
A bhikṣu said to a bhikṣu on the roof:
"The time for the meal has arrived; you may come down to eat.
The bhikṣu said:
"It is difficult to move things up and down while they are being discarded; if you wish to eat here, you may bring the food up.
He said to the attendant:
"Take the food and place it in a vessel to be brought up."
The bhikṣu lowers the long pole with its hook and says to the attendant:
"Place it upon this hook.
Having spoken these words:
"Feeling! Feeling!"—
this is called feeling.
Lowering the rope is also done in this manner; this is called "on the roof.

Regarding the clean kitchen: when constructing a new monastery (*saṃghārāma*), one should not build the kitchen in the eastern or northern wing, but should build the kitchen in the southern or western wing. One should provide ventilation and ensure that the water channels are clear and functional, allowing for the discharge of wash-water and drainage.
Within the kitchen, one should construct a food rack.
When preparing food, if the attendant (kappiyakāraka) is a minor, the bhikṣu may personally wash the copper cauldrons and pots; having placed water in them, he should say to the attendant:
"You know how to wash the rice."

If the attendant (kappiyakāraka) is too small [or weak] to perform the task, one may take him by the hand and instruct him; one may instruct him to wash, instruct him to pour out, or instruct him to scoop out the rice.
If the food vessel is not covered, one should tell him to cover it.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable), and if there are clean mats, clean woolen cloths, or clean boards, one may cover [the grain] oneself, provided it is hung over and placed above.
When drying grain, if a bhikṣu walks upon the grain, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* sweep away the dust from where his feet have trodden.
If pursued by lions, tigers, or wolves, or pursued by a woman driven by lust, a bhikṣu may flee without looking back; even if he tramples [the crops], there is no offense.
If rain falls upon a heap of grain, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) cover it.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one may cast a clean mat from a distance over [the items] to cover them, or take up a clean brick or stone and throw it down to weigh them down.

If a new monastery is being built and there are various items within the clean kitchen—such as pure oil, seven-day oil, or jars of flour, jars of lime, jars of salt, jars of grass chaff, jars of rock honey, jars of clay, bundles of sugarcane, bundles of bamboo, bundles of dried meat, and bundles of dyed tree bark—all gathered together in the clean house—a bhikkhu says to another bhikkhu:
"Go and fetch the seven-day oil."

If a bhikṣu mistakenly brings pure oil, and although the bhikṣu sees it from afar and knows it is pure oil, he must not speak out immediately, for fear that the person might be startled or terrified and thereby break the vessel.
When he had arrived, [the other] asked him:
"Venerable sir!
What kind of oil is this?"
He replied,
"Oil for seven days.
One should say:
"Set it aside!
Set it aside!
If one cannot obtain the name [of the precept], one may receive and maintain it for seven days.
If one says:
"Venerable sir!
Take some pure oil and come."
If a bhikṣu mistakenly brings seven-day oil and is unable to speak of it immediately, he should wait until it has been brought and then ask:
"Venerable sir,
what kind of oil is this?"
He replied, "Pure oil.
One should say:
"Set it aside!
Set it aside!"—
thus it is called "seven-day oil."
He spoke thus:
"Take the lime jar," but by mistake he took the flour jar.
He said,
"Take the powder jar," but by mistake he took the salt jar.
He said,
"Bring the jar of clay," but by mistake he brought the jar of rock honey.
He said,
"Bring a bundle of bamboo," but by mistake he brought a bundle of sugarcane.
He said,
"Bring a bundle of dyed tree bark.
By mistake, he brought a bundle of dried meat, as explained in detail above.
A bhikṣu said to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Go, examine the ash-pitcher thoroughly, and then bring it here."

This bhikṣu went there and reached his hand into the jar to grasp some flour; because he was merely looking into the jar, this was considered pure. However, if he had grasped the flour and placed it back into the jar, it would have been called impure.
The same applies to powdered vessels and clay vessels.
If one says:
"Having carefully inspected the bamboo, bring it here."
The bhikṣu went and pulled out the sugarcane; when he looked at it, it was still pure. However, if he returned it to the bundle and lifted the entire bundle, it would be impure.
The same applies to bundles of dried meat.
If the kitchen building is dilapidated, cracked, or leaking, one should say to the *kappiyakāraka*:
"Remove all items from within the kitchen.

Once they have been removed, one should block the mouse holes, sweep the floor, and apply a coating of clay mixed with cow dung. At the base of the walls, one should construct a foundation of bricks, placing the larger ones at the bottom and the smaller ones on top.

A bhikṣu may stand in the center and point out where the milk, curd, butter, oil, honey, rock sugar, and salt are to be placed; he must not see that the kitchen building is dilapidated and fail to repair it, but should attend to the matter according to the rules and regulations. This is called the "kitchen building."
Regarding vessels that are suitable or unsuitable for receiving [offerings]: among all leaves, those that are rolled up are suitable vessels, while those that are spread out are not.
If a bowl has a rim deep enough to submerge a grain of barley, it is called a suitable vessel.
Whether it be a bed or a sitting bench, if the cords are woven densely, it is a vessel; if they are woven sparsely, it is not a vessel.
As for a boat, when it is in the water it is not a vessel, but when it is on dry land it is a vessel.
If it is a cart, when yoked with oxen it is not a vessel; when there are no oxen, it is a vessel.

If a bhikṣu is begging for food and a shopkeeper gives him parched grain (*saktu*) measured with a bushel (*droṇa*), where the bushel is connected to various measures—such as five, four, three, two, or one *śoṇa* (measures)—the bhikṣu should then say to the donor:
"Untie the subsequent measures so they are separated, and then give them to me."

If the vessel is too small to be untied, the bhikṣu should request some leaves and have [the liquid] poured onto the leaves to receive it; this is called receiving with a vessel or receiving without a vessel.
Regarding "receiving on a bed": if a bhikṣu is sitting, meditating, or sleeping on a bed, and a lay attendant brings food and places it in his lap—if he awakens, it is termed "received."
If one was unaware [of the impurity] and wishes to eat when one becomes aware, one should receive it again from a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle food).
If one does not wish to eat, one should take hold of it oneself and hand it over to the *kappiyakāraka*.
It is the same when [the food] is placed upon a bed; it is likewise when it is suspended from the side of a bed.
If a bhikṣu, on a loft or gallery, has pure food or a robe and bowl, and when he takes up the robe and bowl he moves the pure substance, then everything becomes impure.
If it is firm and does not move, there is no offense.
If on a monk's robe rack there are jars of ghee or jars of oil, and when the monk takes his robe he moves them, it is likewise; this is called "the bed."

Regarding the boat: if seventeen kinds of grain are loaded onto a boat and straw mats or woven screens are spread over the grain as a covering, a bhikṣu may sit upon them; he should not [be considered] as having sat on the names [of the grain].
If it is merely a name, that is called impure.
If this boat is suddenly blown by the wind, or carried down by a current, or drifted onto the shore by a whirlpool, all of these are considered impure.
If the ropes or bamboo oars do not leave the water, it is pure; this is called a boat.

As for "riding," if seventeen kinds of grain are loaded onto a large cart, and straw mats are spread over the grain and covered above, and a bhikṣu sits upon them, he should not assign it a name; if he assigns it a name, it is impure.
If there are pure items, such as robes or alms bowls, upon a small carriage, and if a bhikṣu moves those pure items while taking up his robes or alms bowl, everything becomes impure.
He should say to the attendant:
"Take my robes and alms bowl for me."
One must not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) by means of an ox.
When ascending, a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) should ascend first, and only then may the bhikṣu ascend.
When descending, the bhikṣu should descend first, and the *kappiya-kāraka* afterwards.
If, when descending a slope, the cart overturns and becomes separated from the ground and the ox, everything is impure.
If, upon descending the slope or during an overturning, the ox’s body and its tethered tail do not separate from the cart, everything is pure; this is called "riding."

Regarding receiving by mental intimation: there was a man from the country of Dengqu who was a person of wrong views from a frontier region; because he was a wicked bhikṣu, they did not offer him food.
At that time, one should mark out the boundary of the *caṅkrama* (walking path) so that it is complete, and if the bowl is covered with leaves, one should say from afar:
"I receive!"
"Regarding 'receiving': if one is aware when [the food] descends but unaware when it falls into the bowl, it is termed 'received,' though it is not in accordance with proper decorum (*airyāpathika*).
If one is aware when it falls but unaware at the initial moment of descent, it is termed 'received,' though it is not in accordance with proper decorum."
When [the food] descends and one perceives it entirely as it falls into the bowl, this is called "properly receiving.

If, while a bhikṣu is begging for alms, a crow or bird causes a piece of meat to fall into his bowl, if he perceives it at the moment it descends rather than at the moment it falls, this is called "receiving," though it is not in accordance with proper decorum.
If one is aware at the time of falling [into the water] but not while descending, this is called "receiving" (acceptance), though it is not a formal act of deportment.
If one is aware both while descending and at the time of falling, this is called "wholesome receiving"; it is called "receiving through mental attention."
Regarding the road: if a bhikṣu wishes to travel with merchants, he says to the merchants, "Lend me a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person).
They reply:
"So be it. As they were about to depart, he said, "I have no attendants (kappiyakāraka), but I have oxen;
if the Venerable One requires them, you should take them."

"Have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) place various kinds of provisions in a large bag; calculate the portion for each day’s meal, tie it into a single bundle, fasten it onto the ox, and at the time of eating, have the *kappiya-kāraka* take it down."
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one person shall pull the cord while another receives it, saying aloud:
"I receive! I receive!"
This is called "receiving.

If the provisions within the bag are exhausted while the destination has not yet been reached, one should untie the bag, wash it clean, seek out further provisions to place inside, and tie the knot as before.
While traveling on the road, one should provide fodder for the oxen at appropriate times and in a cool place, ensuring they do not suffer.
Upon arrival, the oxen must be returned to their original owners.
If a bhikṣu is traveling along a road and passes by the side of a sugarcane grove...
He begged from the person guarding the sugarcane grove, speaking these words:
"Long-lived one!
Give me some sugarcane."
He replied,
"Venerable sir, take it yourself.
The bhikṣu said:
"Long-lived one!
I may not take it myself.
He spoke again:
"If you wish to eat, take it yourself; if you do not wish to eat, then depart.
At that time, the bhikṣu tied a good stalk of sugarcane with a cord to the ox's head and spoke these words:
"Know this, O sentient being."
"Beside the sugarcane grove there was a mass of fire; he immediately drove the ox past the fire so as not to let it be burned.
Once the sugarcane had been made pure, one person supported the ox's head while another untied the tether, saying:
'Receive it!'"
"Feeling!
This is what is called feeling.
It is the same with the root of a turnip.
When the ox was eating the turnip roots, the bhikṣu seized the ox by the head and rebuked it:
"Take it! Take it!"
This is termed "receiving," yet it is not proper deportment.

When a bhikṣu is traveling along the road and receives roasted grain from an attendant by holding the bag, if the rope has not yet left the ground, it is termed "receiving," yet it is not proper deportment.
When teaching, one should join the cord and hand it over;
therefore, this is said. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume Sixteen.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
This is the sixth section of the ninety-two rules concerning the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (Skt. / *Dun-ti* (Chn.). The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Because the Tathāgata takes but one meal, his body is light and agile, and he dwells in peace and happiness.
You, too, should take but one meal; by taking but one meal, your bodies will become light and agile, and you shall dwell in peace and happiness.”
At that time, the Venerable Bhadrika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I am unable to take even a single meal."
"Why is this? It is because I obtain peace and happiness by eating only once in the morning and once in the evening.
The Buddha told Bhadrika:

"If you are unable to eat in a single meal, you may rise early in the morning and enter the village with two bowls to beg for alms; since one bowl is for breakfast and one bowl is for the midday meal, these constitute two meals."
When he had thus instructed him a second and a third time, [Bhadrika] still said he was unable.
At that time, all the disciples received the World-Honored One’s instruction, with the sole exception of Bhadrika.
Out of shame and remorse, Bhadrika did not go to the Buddha’s presence for three months, as is explained in detail in the *Bhadrika-sūtra*.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus went begging for food at improper times, and were reviled by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, beg for food at improper times?"
"Having lost the fruit of the path, what path could there be?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“You who have left the household life, begging for food at an improper time is precisely what should lead to reproach from the people of the world.
From this day forward, begging for food at an improper time is not permitted.”
"In this regard, it should also be explained in detail as in the *Udāyi-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above."
At that time, the bhikṣus ate when night had fallen, and were criticized by the people of the world:
“How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas eat at night?
Even we householders do not eat at night.”
"These individuals have lost the Dharma of a śramaṇa; what path could they possibly possess?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Your eating at night is precisely what should be detested by the people of the world.
From this day forward, eating is permitted only during the first half of the day; when taking [the food], you should use either a foot-shadow or a water-clock.”
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the bhikṣus entered the village for alms before the meal, and after the meal, they went to various gardens, ponds, water-sides, and places where worldly people gathered for recreation to beg for food.
They were ridiculed by the worldly people: "Look at these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, begging in our own homes!"
"Now he has come to the edge of the pond and again begs from me.
He has ruined and lost the Way of the Dharma; what kind of Way does he possess?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"Call this bhikṣu here.
Having been summoned, the Buddha questioned him regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"What do you intend to do with the almsfood you have begged this morning?
He replied:
"Eat at the proper time.
He asked again,
"If you go begging after the meal, what else do you do?"
He replied,
"I have set it aside for tomorrow's meal.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"How is it that you eat food kept overnight?
From this day forward, eating at improper times is not permitted, nor is eating food that has been stored overnight.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, because the Venerable Bhadrika felt both shame and a sense of accomplishment, when he entered a village it was as if he were entering a military array.
At that time, he took two alms-bowls and entered the village to beg for food; having received it, he used one bowl for his meal on that day and the other bowl for his meal on the following day.
At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to enter a village to beg for alms, they called out to Bhadali, saying:
"Elder! Come, let us go together into the village to beg for alms."
He replied, "You may go yourselves; I cannot go.
The bhikṣus said:
“Elder! You have gained great benefit, for you were able to obtain two days of peace and security from a single meal.
He replied:
"I cannot remain at ease for two days on a single meal; because when I enter a village it is as if entering a battlefield, I therefore carry two alms bowls and beg for food for two days."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call Bhadali here.
Having been summoned, the Buddha questioned Bhadali:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"Although you wish to reduce the affairs of the community, from this day forward I do not permit you to eat at improper times, nor do I permit you to store food for later consumption."
This is as explained in detail in the *Bhadraśāli-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described at length above.

At that time, Aniruddha was on a black square stone at the fork of the Rṣi Mountain, drying some spoiled, rotten barley rice. The Buddha, by means of his supernormal power, went to that place; knowing [the situation] yet asking for the sake of instruction:
"What are you doing? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The śrāvaka disciples have faith and joy, and as they wish to rely [on you] tomorrow, they have not entered the village to beg for food.
The Buddha said:
"Although you wish to spare the community from various causes and conditions, from this day forward I do not permit you to eat at improper times or to store food to eat later."
By his supernormal power, the Buddha immediately returned to Śrāvastī.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on the city of Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu eats stored food, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
"Improper time" refers to when the time has passed by even as much as a hair's breadth or a moment, or by as much as a blade of grass or a leaf; this is called improper time.
"Food" refers to parched grain, boiled rice, wheat porridge, fish, and meat.
If one eats mixed food, it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
To "cease eating" means that the time has passed by a brief moment (*muhūrta*).

A "brief moment" consists of twenty *kṣaṇas*, which is called one "instant" (*tatkṣaṇa*); twenty instants make one "finger-snap" (*acchaṭā*); twenty finger-snaps make one "lāva"; and twenty lāvas make one *muhūrta*.

When the day is at its longest, it consists of eighteen muhūrtas; when the night is at its shortest, it consists of twelve muhūrtas. When the night is at its longest, it consists of eighteen muhūrtas; when the day is at its shortest, it consists of twelve muhūrtas.
Regarding "food," it refers to the five types of primary food and the five types of mixed primary food. If one stops eating after having partaken of even one of these, it is a *pāyattika*.
As for what constitutes a *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

Receiving at the proper time, receiving at the improper time, intentional receiving, unintentional receiving, receiving little, receiving much, receiving quickly, receiving slowly, and [receiving] snow and ice.
Regarding "eating at the proper time": if one eats at the proper time during the permitted hours, there is no offense.
If one eats after the time has passed—even by the duration of a hair's blink or the flick of a blade of grass—one commits a *pāyattika*.

If one sets aside food and eats it after a short interval has passed, one commits two *pāyattikas*: the offense of eating at an improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*) and the offense of eating stored food (*saṃnihita-bhojana*).
If one accepts food at an improper time, and then eats that food accepted at an improper time, one incurs one *pāyattika*.
If one eats after having set aside food for even a brief moment, one incurs two *pāyattikas*: eating at an improper time and eating food that has been set aside.
Such is the case whether the acceptance was intentional or unintentional, whether it was much or little, whether it was accepted quickly or slowly; there are various distinctions such as these.
Regarding the receiving of snow: if a bhikṣu wishes to eat snow, he should receive it from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant).
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he should wash his hands until they are clean and then take and eat it himself. The same applies to ice and hail; these are termed "ice and snow."

When a bhikṣu rises in the morning, he should wash his hands clean. He must not merely roughly wash the tips of his five fingers, nor should he wash up to the armpits; rather, he should ensure that the area from the wrist downward is clean. He must not wash in a coarse or violent manner, nor scrub until blood flows; instead, he should use the powder of *kurmaka* grass or ash and earth to wash his hands, rubbing them until they make a sound.
Once the hands have been washed clean, if they are rubbed against one another, they become impure and must be washed again.
If, after washing the bowl, one rubs and wipes it while it is still wet, it becomes impure; it should be set aside to dry.

Before a monk eats, he must keep his hands clean; if he touches his head, or grasps his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robe, leather sandals, or a leather bag for holding ghee or oil, he must wash them again as before.
If one has been holding the saṃghāṭī or the uttarāsaṅga, they should be washed again with water.
When a bhikṣu wishes to go out for alms, he should wash his hands thoroughly and put on the robes for entering the village.
Having put on the village-entering robe, he should again wash his hands and enter the village holding his alms-bowl.
If it is during the cold winter season, he should place the bowl inside a bag; when about to reach the edge of a village, or by a pond, or by a flowing stream, he should thoroughly wash his hands.
If there is no water, one should enter a village and go to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus to beg for water to wash one's hands.
If there is still none, one should go to the nunnery (bhikṣuṇī-ārāma) to seek water.
If there is still none, one should go to the home of a lay follower (upāsaka) who possesses faith to seek pure water.
If there is still none, one should open the bowl-bag, take out the bowl, hold it by one side while going for alms, and upon receiving food, return.

Upon leaving the village and arriving at a pond, a spring, or a flowing stream, one should place the bowl upon pure grass. Then, having washed one’s hands clean and washed the stone [for the meal], if there are grass leaves, one should wash them as well.

Having washed the rice that was touched by the finger of the bowl, one should pluck it off and discard it. Then, pour the rice onto the stone or onto the grass leaves. When pouring the rice, one must not pour it from the part of the hand that was held while it was impure.
After having vomited, one should wash the bowl clean again, place the vomit back into the bowl, and eat it.
If there is any food remaining after eating, one should pour it onto a heap of stones and depart.
The next day, the bhikṣu again entered the village to beg for food, but he obtained nothing at all and returned with an empty bowl.
Without making a conscious effort to return by his original path, he saw that the heap of rice on the stone was still there as before.
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food), one should have that person hand it over before eating.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, and there is a place where crows or birds feed, one may clear away [the impurity] by scraping it out and then take the food oneself.

If a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) holds food with impure hands and serves parched grain or rice to the Sangha, the portion received by the Elder (thera) is considered impure, while the remainder is designated as pure.
If a lay attendant holds pure parched grain and pours it onto impure parched grain, one may scoop off the top layer.
If one carries impure flour and pours it onto pure flour, all of it becomes impure.
If one carries pure flour and pours it into an impure vessel, one may scoop out the center; however, if one shakes the basket, all of it becomes impure.
If a bhikṣu, while eating parched grain flour, rubs his mouth with his hand, it is considered impure;
he must wash his hands again.
If he rubs both hands against each other, it is considered impure; he must wash them again.
If a bhikṣu is ill and requires gruel, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) cook it.
If he is in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) where a *kappiya-kāraka* is difficult to find, he may perform the purification himself.

Having washed [the vessel] so that it does not retain grease, and having placed water in a pot or cauldron, he may naturally ignite a fire to bring it to a boil, and then instruct the *kappiya-kāraka* to add the rice.
Once the rice has been placed on the fire, the bhikṣu must not light it himself; he should have a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) light it.
Once it has boiled, if the *kappiyakāraka* wishes to leave, the bhikṣu may take charge of it and cook it until it is thoroughly done. Once it is cooked, he should give it to the sick person.
If a bhikṣu has taken emetic or purgative medicine and the physician says,
"He should be given clear rice gruel; if he does not obtain it, he will die," what should be done?
At that time, one should use the rinsing water of washed rice, placing it in a trough to soak the sick bhikṣu.

If the patient cannot endure this, one should take unbroken grains of rice, millet, or wheat, wash them seven times until clean, place them in a bag with the opening tied shut, and boil them in a clean vessel.
One must not allow the heads of the rice grains to break; if they have broken, it should not be given to a sick bhikṣu.
If the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) at an araṇya dwelling falls ill, one should instead have that attendant cook the gruel and give it to him.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), once pure grain has been obtained, a bhikṣu may personally husk it and prepare gruel to give to the *kappiya-kāraka*.
If the *kappiya-kāraka* does not finish eating it, the bhikṣu must not eat it himself, nor may he give it to other bhikṣus.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, there was a householder who gave birth to a daughter; she was peerlessly beautiful, and her parents were filled with joy.
After the full moon festival had been held as an auspicious ceremony, her parents thought to themselves:
"This girl is so beautiful that she is a rarity in this world.
If the king hears of her, he might forcibly take her away."
"I shall give her an inauspicious name," he thought,
and thus named her "Blind.
As the girl gradually grew up, the king's diviners saw her and asked:
"Whose daughter is she? Someone replied,
"She is the daughter of a certain householder."
The king’s physiognomist thought to himself,
"By her physical marks, this woman should be the Great Queen of the King.
The physiognomist then addressed the king, saying:
"A certain person has a daughter whose noble status makes her a fitting consort for the Queen; you may take her as your wife.
The King immediately dispatched a messenger to inquire:
"What is this girl's name?"
He immediately replied,
"His name is 'Blind Eye,'" and then returned to report this to the king.
The king said, "These characters are inauspicious; they are not what I require.
Later, after someone had married her, her parents called her back to their home.
The husband sent a messenger to summon his wife, and her family replied,
"We shall send her.
They immediately prepared the requisites for sending off the daughter and made various kinds of cakes.
As the bhikṣu went on his alms round in succession and arrived at her house, the mother saw the bhikṣu and, with faith and joy, said:
"Venerable sir, do you require cakes?
He replied:
"Please do," [the donor] replied,
and immediately gave him various kinds of cakes, which the bhikṣu took away with his bowl full.
Having received these cakes, the bhikṣu returned to the vihāra and summoned his acquaintances, the other bhikṣus, to eat together.
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable one!
These cakes are excellent; where did you obtain them?"
He replied,
"It was obtained from the house of the blind woman.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to her house again and obtained [the items] as before.
In this manner, as she went to fetch each item one by one, all the provisions for sending off the daughter were exhausted.
On the second and third days, the husband again sent someone to summon her, and she spoke once more:
"Wait a moment."
