Having prepared the wedding gifts, the various bhikṣus went every day to beg for them until they were all exhausted. Because his wife had not yet returned, her husband became greatly enraged and said:
"I have now sent a messenger to summon her, yet she says the gifts are not ready and thus does not come; she must certainly have an outside heart."
He then sent her away and sought another girl.
When the blind mother heard that her daughter had been dismissed, she wept with great sorrow.
The daughter also sat there in distress; because the mother did not send her forth at the proper time, she was thus sent away.
The neighbors asked,
"For what reason are you so sorrowful and weeping?
They then answered them in full detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
The neighbors and their inhabitants rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you not first send away your daughter and separately prepare food and drink to offer to the bhikṣus?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"Call these bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, it is not permitted to accept food sent for the sake of a woman being given in marriage.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, as described in detail above, there was at that time a merchant leader in the city named Abhaya.
He wished to travel far with a caravan of merchants, and the merchant’s wife was preparing various provisions for the journey within her home.
The bhikṣus went from house to house on their almsround and arrived at that household.
When the merchant’s wife saw them, her heart was filled with faith and joy, and she asked,
"Venerable sirs, do you require parched grain?"
He replied, "I must.
He then distributed the provisions, filling his bowl to the brim and giving it to the bhikṣu.
Having received it, the bhikṣu took it back and entered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, where he summoned his acquaintances, the bhikṣus, to eat together.
The bhikṣus asked him:
"Where did you obtain such excellent food?"
He replied, "I obtained it from a merchant's house.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to that house; in this manner, each person went to beg for provisions until they were completely exhausted.

In this manner, on the second and third days they prepared provisions, but the bhikṣus came one after another and begged until everything was exhausted. By the fourth day, having finished preparing the provisions, they set out but could not keep pace with their companions; they were plundered by bandits, and all their wealth and goods were lost.
Upon hearing this, the merchant’s wife was filled with anxiety and grief, and she wept bitterly.
Her neighbors asked her, "Why are you like this?
She then related the aforementioned matter in detail to her neighbors.
A neighbor said, "Why did you not first prepare provisions and dispatch the messenger, and only afterwards separately make offerings to the bhikṣus?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Call these bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
“Is it true that you have done so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; the giver does not know moderation, yet the receiver ought to know moderation.
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching; it cannot serve to nourish wholesome qualities."
"From this day forward, begging for travel provisions is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Rājagṛha assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and is freely offered cakes or parched grain, he may accept two or three bowls and take them outside to eat together with bhikṣus who are not ill.
If he accepts more than that and takes them outside to eat without sharing them with bhikṣus who are not ill, it is a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikṣus” refers to one, two, or many.
“Lay families” refers to the families of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
At the *pravāraṇā*, one may offer either cakes (*piṇḍaka*) or parched grain flour (*saktu*).
As for cakes, these refer to various kinds such as those made of wheat, barley, rice, or beans.
As for parched grain flour, these refer to various kinds such as that made of wheat, barley, rice, or beans.
"Three bowls" means that at most one may accept three bowls.
"Carrying them out" means taking them wherever one intends to go.
"A bhikṣu who is not ill" refers to one who has the strength to travel to that person's house.
Regarding "eating together with a monk who is not ill": whatever food one has brought should be eaten together; if one does not eat together, it is a pāyattika.
A pāyattika is as explained above.
Sending provisions and travel rations, such as cakes and parched grain, does not constitute "sending provisions for a bhikṣu.
Regarding the giving of provisions during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, it is like the case of sending provisions for a blind woman, and so forth.
Provisions for the journey refer to those such as fearless caravan leaders and the like.
The cakes and parched grain are as described above.
"Not for the sake of a bhikṣu" means that it was originally prepared as travel provisions for other people.
Regarding "giving by one's own free will": it is like a blind woman and her blind mother giving by their own free will; it is like a merchant and his wife.
When a bhikkhu receives what has been given by one's own free will, he may accept up to three bowls. He should take them outside and eat them together with a bhikkhu who is not ill.
If a bhikṣu thinks,
"Who can perform many tasks?
and speaks thus to an upāsikā:
"Fill one bowl and place it in a vessel.
He then filled another bowl and placed it in a different vessel;
having taken a bowl for himself, he said to the woman, "If any bhikṣu comes, give him this bowl."
Furthermore, if another comes, give this second bowl to them.
If anyone else should come after that, do not give anything further.
If you were to give it, your merit would be meager.
Once the bhikṣu has taken the food out, if he encounters another bhikṣu on the way, he should say:
"There is food at such-and-such a house; you should take your portion yourself."
The second bhikṣu was likewise.
It was neither a gift of cakes for a bride nor provisions for a journey; it was not intended as sustenance for a bhikṣu, nor was it given at his own discretion.
"Not for the purpose of sending off a girl" means it is not like [a gift] sent off for a blind girl.
"Not as provisions for a journey" means it is not like [the goods] of fearless merchants and the like.
"For a bhikṣu" means it is prepared for a bhikṣu and not for anyone else.
Regarding "not for the purpose of sending provisions": apart from these two matters, if one acts on behalf of others, it is permissible to take [the items] without offense.
One may take them as they are given without restriction and carry them away. If a blind woman departs and her stepmother gives [the items] to her, it is permissible to take them; there is no offense.
If a woman has already arrived at her husband's house and gives [an item] to him, there is no offense in taking it.
If a merchant has already departed on his journey and his wife gives [an item] to him later, there is no offense in taking it.
If a merchant has arrived at his destination and [the goods] have been given to him for taking, there is no offense.
If, on a day when a family is giving a daughter in marriage, taking a wife, or holding a feast or festival, a bhikṣu goes to that house and the host says this:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I wish to send a messenger to invite him, yet I fear it may not be possible; how much more so for him to come of his own accord?
Having said this, he may take [the food] at his own pleasure without fault.
Therefore, it is so stated.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to a house of ghee to beg for ghee, a house of oil to beg for oil, a house of milk to beg for milk, a house of curd to beg for curd, a house of honey to beg for honey, a house of rock sugar to beg for rock sugar, a house of fish to beg for fish, and a house of meat to beg for meat. They were reviled by the people of the world, who spoke thus:

"The śramaṇa Gautama uses immeasurable skillful means to praise having few desires, contentment, being easy to support, and easy to satisfy; yet he censures having many desires, lack of satiety, being difficult to support, and being difficult to satisfy."
Now this śramaṇa is unable to beg for coarse food, yet he begs for ghee from a house of ghee, and even goes so far as to beg for meat from a house of meat.
This man of ruinous conduct—what path could he possibly possess?
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me praise few desires through immeasurable skillful means, and censure many desires?"
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teachings; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
From this day forward, I do not permit the begging for sumptuous food to be eaten.

Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Arāma monastery in the kingdom of Kapilavastu among the Śākyas. Out of a desire to benefit [the monks] in five ways, the Buddha would go on inspection of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days; there he saw a sick bhikṣu.
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"How is your illness?
Has it diminished or not?"
He replied, “It is not damaged.
The Buddha said:
“Are you not able to seek out food and medicine according to the illness?
He replied,
“I am able to beg for them, but because the World-Honored One has established a precept that forbids begging for delicacies, I do not dare to beg for them.”
"I have no donor; there is no one who gives [to me].
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to beg for choice food."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Kapilavastu assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If there are such fine foods in a household—namely, ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, milk, curd, fish, or meat—and a healthy monk seeks them for his own sake, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Household goods" are as described above.
Butter, oil, honey, rock sugar, curdled milk, fish, and meat are as described above in the second precept concerning theft; these are called "delicious foods."
Regarding the sick: the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense for those who are ill.

"The sick" refers to those suffering from jaundice and putrefaction, abscesses, hemorrhoids, incontinence, jaundice, malaria, coughing, emaciation from consumption, wind-swelling, or water-swelling; such various conditions as these are what is meant by "sickness."
"To provide for oneself" means to seek for one's own sake, whether seeking it oneself or causing another to seek it; as for "eating," it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu suffers from a fever and a physician says,
"This illness requires the consumption of ghee," he may beg for ghee,
but he must not go to the house of one who lacks faith to seek it.
Why is this? When begging, one should not disparage a bhikṣu; one may beg for ghee only because of a desire for fine flavors.
One should not go to beg from a bhikṣu whom one finds objectionable on account of their physical stature, whether tall or short.
When you go to the house of a faithful upāsaka to solicit [alms], once you have received them, you should deliberate for yourself.
If a bhikṣu suffers from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga) and the physician says,
"You should take oil," [you may accept it].
At that time, one may beg for oil, but one must not beg from an oil-presser, nor go to the house of one who lacks faith, as was explained regarding ghee.
If a bhikṣu suffers from a water-related illness and the physician says,
"This person should take honey," [he may do so].

At that time, he may also obtain honey by begging for it; however, he must not go to a house where honey is being harvested to beg for it, nor may he go to a household of those without faith to beg for it, as was explained regarding the ghee.
If a bhikṣu suffers from the disease of consumption and a physician says,
"This person should take rock honey," he must not go to a house where sugarcane is crushed to seek it, nor may he go to a house of those who lack faith to seek it, as was explained regarding ghee.
If a bhikṣu suffers from internal cold, and a physician says,
"One should take honey and curd, mixing these two together for consumption," he must not go to the house of one who lacks faith to seek them, as was explained regarding ghee.
If a bhikṣu suffers from a chronic ailment and a physician says,
"This person should take milk," he may then beg for milk from a cowherd; when he obtains it, he should measure it out with care.
If a bhikṣu wishes to induce vomiting or purging and takes emetic or purgative medicine, and the physician says,
"You should first take fish broth," at that time he may beg for fish broth;
however, he must not beg from a fisherman's household, nor may he go to the house of one who lacks faith to beg, as explained above.
If a bhikṣu wishes to have his head lanced to draw blood, or intends to take emetic or purgative medicine, and the physician says,
"He should take meat broth," at that time he may beg for meat broth; however, he must not go to a butcher's shop or to the home of an unbeliever to beg, as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu, while walking for alms, comes to the side of a person who measures out ghee, and that person says:
"Venerable sir!
What do you seek?"
He replied,
"I wish to beg for alms. He said:
"There is no other food; there is only this ghee. If you require it, I shall give it to you.
At that time, if a bhikṣu requires it, he may accept it until his bowl is full without fault.
If he has companions, he may encourage them to take it as well without fault.
The same applies to measuring oil, honey, rock sugar, and milk-curds.
If a bhikṣu, while begging for food, receives a bowl full of parched grain and rice but finds nothing in his cooking vessel, he may seek some broth from [the donor].
If a donor says, "There is no drink;
there is only meat broth, which I shall give to you if you need it," then one may take it at that time.
If, however, one should further ask:
"There is also meat; if you need it, I shall give it to you," then at that time, it is no offense to take enough to fill the bowl.
Furthermore, one may go to a sugarcane presser's house and ask for sugarcane juice;
if they say, "There is no sugarcane juice, but there is rock sugar; if you need it, we shall give it to you."
If a bhikṣu requires it, he may take a bowl full without fault, and he may also encourage his companions to do so.
He may also go to a house where oil is being pressed and beg for the dregs of the sesame; if the host says, "I have no dregs;
if you need oil, I shall give it to you," [he may accept].
If one needs it, one may take as much as fills a bowl without fault, and one may also encourage others to give to their companions.
One may beg for the clear liquid from the bottom of curdled milk;
if [the donor] says, "I have no clear liquid from the bottom of curdled milk, but I do have fresh milk and curds; if you need them, I shall give them," [one may accept].
A bhikṣu who requires it may take as much as fills his bowl without fault, and he may also encourage others to give to his companions.
He may beg for sugarcane, and he may beg for choice food for visiting bhikṣus or bhikṣus traveling from afar; furthermore, he may also beg while traveling on the road himself.
If a bhikṣu begs for eight kinds of fine food at one location and eats them separately, he incurs many pāyattikas.
If a bhikṣu begs for eight kinds of food at different locations and eats them at one location, he incurs one pāyattika.
If one begs at many locations and eats separately at each, one incurs numerous *pāyattis*.
If one solicits various kinds of food at a single location and eats them all together at once, one incurs a single *pāyatti*.
If one begs for food when not ill and eats it when ill, one commits a *vibhinī-āpatti*;
if one begs for food when ill and eats it when not ill, there is no offense;
if one begs for food when ill and eats it when ill, there is no offense.
If one begs for food when not ill and eats it when not ill, it is a pāyattika.
If one cooks according to the illness and eats according to the illness, there is no offense;
if one cooks according to the illness but eats what is not according to the illness, one incurs a vyatikrama-āpatti.
There is no offense in cooking according to the illness and eating according to the illness;
there is no offense in not cooking according to the illness and not eating according to the illness. Why is this?
Because the one who has gone forth depends on others for their livelihood, it is said:
"Wherever one gives a single meal, if the recipient is already satisfied, one should not urge them further."
Eating food that has not been formally offered; eating food set aside at an improper time;
taking two or three bowls of choice food; and eating separately from the community—these follow last.
The fourth *varga* concludes. In the Jeta Grove Monastery, the Sanskrit manuscript was damaged by insects and this precept regarding eating separately from the community is missing.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the people of the world were deeply faithful, respectful, and reverent, providing offerings of food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

At that time, there were also renunciant non-Buddhists in Śrāvastī, whom the people of the world did not honor, provide for, respect, or support with food, clothing, bedding, medical care for illness, or medicine.
At that time, there were many renunciant non-Buddhists gathered in the Hall of Discourse who made this argument:

"This śramaṇa Gautama resides at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove in Śrāvastī; the people of the world have deep faith in him, honoring and respecting him, and providing him with offerings of food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness."
"We have not obtained respectful offerings of clothing, food, bedding, or medicine for the sick and infirm.
Who could go forth from home into the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life?"
"Once we have studied and mastered those teachings, we shall return to our own Dharma; we will then teach one another in turn and likewise receive offerings, no different from them."
When the non-Buddhists had finished making this argument, they all said:
"Susīma is the foremost among our assembly; he should be sent to the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama to leave the household life and receive their discipline, and then return here."
Then that non-Buddhist spoke to Susīma, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama resides at the Jetavana Monastery; many people honor and support him, yet we have not obtained such benefits."

"You should now go forth in the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life. Once you have received and recited those sūtras, return to my Dharma and teach them to one another in turn; you shall likewise receive offerings no different from those he does."
Having heard these words, Susīma departed from the city of Śrāvastī and went to the Jetavana Monastery.

At the gate of the monastery, he saw various bhikṣus walking in meditation (caṅkrama) and practicing seated dhyāna. Susīma immediately approached the bhikṣus, exchanged greetings with them, and sat to one side, saying:
"I was originally a follower of external paths; now I wish to go forth and receive full ordination within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. What should be done in this regard?"
The bhikṣus replied:
"If one was originally a follower of an external path and wishes to go forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they should undergo a four-month probation."
"After four months have passed, if you have gained the consent of the bhikṣus, you shall grant her the going forth.
Then Susīma immediately accepted the instruction and acted accordingly; when the four months had passed and she had gained the consent of the bhikṣus, he then conferred the full ordination upon her.
Having received full ordination, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side, saying these words:
“We have realized [the goal]; our births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, and we shall not undergo further existence.”
Having spoken these words, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.
Not long after those bhikṣus had departed, Susīma prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and went to where those bhikṣus were, exchanging greetings with them.
Having exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side and asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Previously, in the presence of the Buddha, you said of yourselves:..."
"I have realized it for myself: birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence.
He replied, "So it is."
Then Susīma asked again:
"Venerable sir!

Knowing thus and seeing thus, one attains the purified divine eye and sees beings passing away from this life and being reborn there; those of beautiful form and those of ugly form, those in happy destinies and those in miserable destinies. One sees beings who have committed evil with their body, evil with their speech, and evil with their mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views themselves, and taught others to hold wrong views; at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the three miserable realms."

Furthermore, he sees sentient beings who practice wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; who themselves maintain right view and teach others to maintain right view; and who, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, are reborn in a favorable destination, among gods or humans.
"Venerable sir, have you attained such a supramundane, purified divine eye?
He replied, "I have not."
He asked again:
"Venerable One!

Having known thus and seen thus, you have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). Do you, Elder, know—having known one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, and even through the formation and dissolution of kalpas—their names, clans, and lineages; their death here and birth there, or death there and birth here; and all such matters of countless kalpas?"
He replied, "I do not know.
He asked again:
"Having transcended form and being free from form, one dwells, having personally realized and fully attained the peaceful liberation.
Elder, have you attained these liberations?
He replied:
"No," replied Susīma,
"regarding all the dharmas you previously asked about, you said: [that they do not exist]."
"That is not possible.
How can you speak thus before the Blessed One, saying:
"I have attained realization; my births are ended, the holy life is established, and I shall no longer undergo future existence"?
"Who would believe this?
The bhikṣus replied, "Elder!"
"I am one liberated through wisdom.
Susīma said, "What you have said is brief;
the meaning has not yet been fully revealed. You may explain it more extensively."
The bhikṣu said,
"Although the characteristics of the meaning have not yet manifested, I myself clearly know that I am one liberated by wisdom.
When Susīma heard the words of the bhikṣus, he thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the World-Honored One is to inquire about this matter; whatever the World-Honored One explains, I shall receive and uphold.

Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One:
"What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told Susīma:
"First is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), and afterwards is inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Susīma again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The teaching spoken by the Blessed One is concise and cryptic; I have not yet understood it.
The Buddha told Susīma:
“Although you have not yet understood it, there is nevertheless first the knowledge of the Dharma (dharmajñāna) and subsequently the inferential knowledge (anvayajñāna).”
Susīma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I have not yet understood; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this extensively for me.”
The Buddha said to Susīma:
“I shall question you in return; answer me according to your understanding. Susīma!”
"What do you think?
Is there old age and death because of dependent origination?
He replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Susīma!"
"What do you think?
Do the various formations arise conditioned by ignorance?
He replied:
"So it is," the Buddha said. "Excellent, Susīma!"
What do you think?
Is it because birth conditions cessation that old age and death cease?
And so on, up to: is it because ignorance conditions cessation that volitional formations cease?
He replied, "It is so. "Excellent, Susīma!"
The Buddha said to Susīma,
"If a bhikṣu correctly contemplates and correctly understands this Dharma, will he not attain everything that ought to be attained?
He replied:
"So it is. He then asked Susīma:
"Do you know that because of dependent origination there is old age and death?"
He replied, “It is so.
[The Buddha asked:
“Is it because of ignorance that there are volitional formations?”
He replied, "It is so.
He asked again:
“Because birth is conditioned by cessation, do old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair— the mass of suffering— cease? He replied, “It is so.”
“Is it because of the cessation of ignorance that volitional formations cease?
He replied, “It is so.”
The Buddha said to Susīma:
"If you know such a Dharma as this, have you attained the divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the various liberations?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Susīma:
"You yourself say that you know all such dharmas, yet you further say:
'I do not attain them.
Who would believe in these merits?"
Susīma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because I was bound and fettered by ignorance and evil views, such false views arose within me.”
"From the World-Honored One, I have extensively heard the True Dharma, which has extinguished my evil and false views, and I have attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Susīma then prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, I have gone forth with a thieving mind for the sake of stealing the Dharma.
O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, I only pray that you will accept my confession of transgression.
The Buddha said to Susīma:
"You are as foolish as a small child; within the True Dharma of the Buddha, you have gone forth with a thieving mind for the sake of stealing the Dharma.
I accept your confession.
The Buddha then addressed Susīma:

“Suppose, for example, there is a person who commits an offense against a king; the king orders his men to dismember his limbs, cut off his ears and nose, saw him apart and split him with knives, chop and hack him into pieces, have him trampled by elephants and horses, or subject him to such various tortures as poison to end his life.”
"You have left the home life with a thievish mind within the Buddha-dharma, for the sake of stealing the Dharma; therefore, your transgression is even greater than this.
I accept your confession of remorse, so that you may attain growth within the noble and holy Dharma. From this day forward, do not commit such acts again."

Because the World-Honored One had delivered Susīma, because the sandalwood bowl of Vaiśālī had subdued the non-Buddhists, and because Maudgalyāyana had performed his miraculous powers, the people’s reverence and faith doubled, and they obtained abundant offerings.
For this reason, various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) have groundlessly slandered the World-Honored One, as explained in detail in the *Sundarī-sūtra*.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the non-Buddhists received all manner of offerings; once the Buddha had appeared in the world, all non-Buddhists lost their gains and sustenance.
Why is this? It is because they know the profound and subtle nature of the Buddha-dharma, as explained in detail in the *Māyūra-jātaka-sūtra*.

At that time, the World-Honored One, weary of worldly offerings, returned toward the city of Śrāvastī. When the time arrived, he put on his robes for entering a village and, holding his alms bowl, entered Śrāvastī to go on his almsround.

Having finished his meal, he wandered about and practiced walking meditation; he gathered up his own bedding and mats without informing the assembly of monks or his attendant, and the Buddha traveled alone through the country of Kosala.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to Ānanda and said to him, "Venerable One!..."

After the World-Honored One had finished his meal and completed his walking meditation, he personally folded away his bedding and, without informing the assembly of monks or his attendant, traveled alone through the kingdom of Kośala.
Ānanda replied:
"Venerable sir!

If the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, after his meal, wanders for a walk and puts away his own bedding and seat without informing the bhikṣus or his attendants, traveling alone because he seeks solitude, the bhikṣus should not follow him."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having traveled from the kingdom of Kośala, arrived at the Pārileyyaka forest and stayed beneath a noble tree.

At that moment, a herd of five hundred elephants was roaming about; the elephant king always remained behind them, receiving only turbid water and leftover grass. Becoming weary of the crowd, he also came alone to this tree.

Once the Elephant King had arrived beneath the tree and beheld the Buddha, he immediately used his trunk to pull up grass and trample the ground to level it. He then filled his trunk with water and sprinkled it upon the earth to settle the dust. Furthermore, he gathered soft grass and spread it out to serve as a seat; kneeling down, he invited the Buddha to sit.
Seeing that the Buddha was seated, he immediately invited the Buddha to accept his offerings for three months.
Knowing the intention of the Elephant King, the Buddha accepted his invitation.
On account of this matter, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“Being solitary and free from sorrow, like an elephant in the open wilderness, one delights in the training of the precepts;
what need is there for companions?
At that time, the elephant king took a fine lotus root, washed it clean, and offered it to the World-Honored One. The Buddha remained for three months, receiving the offerings of the elephant king.
At that time, because they had not seen the Buddha for three months, five hundred bhikṣus went to the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: "Elder!
We have not seen the Buddha for a long time, nor have we heard the Dharma."
"We now wish to go and pay our respects to the World-Honored One and listen to his teachings.
Ānanda replied, "Venerable elders, please wait here for a moment; you must await my return."
He replied, “Excellent!
Ānanda then went to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and spoke these words:
"Elder! Five hundred bhikṣus have come to me and said:
'It has been a long time since we have seen the Buddha or heard the True Dharma; we wish to go to the Buddha to pay our respects, make offerings, and listen to his teachings.'"
"Elder! Observe where the Buddha is!
Maudgalyāyana immediately entered samādhi and surveyed all the worlds; he saw the Buddha beneath the noble tree in the Pāriyātra forest, receiving the offerings of the elephant king.
Having seen this, he spoke these verses to Ānanda:
"Leaving behind the lotus pond, His body is fresh and full;
Free from defilement and pure, He delights in solitude within the forest."
"Having attained the profound Dharma of the Deathless, With a body fully endowed with the marks and signs,
And a mind pure and free from stain, He has abandoned the multitude and dwells in the quiet forest.
After Maudgalyāyana had spoken this verse, he said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“The Blessed One is currently at the Pāriyātra forest beneath the tree of the noble one, receiving the offerings of the elephant king; if you wish to go, now is precisely the right time.”
The Venerable Ānanda returned to where the bhikṣus were and spoke to them thus:

"The World-honored One is currently at the Pāriyātra forest beneath the noble tree, receiving the offerings of the elephant king. Let us now go together to the World-honored One’s presence to pay our respects, behold him, and inquire after his well-being."
When the bhikṣus had heard Ānanda’s words, they immediately went together to the Pāriyātra forest, beneath the tree of the sages.
Not far from where the World-Honored One was, Ānanda said to the bhikṣus:
“Venerable Elders!”
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is staying in a forest hermitage; you should not go there directly.
Venerable ones, you may stay here for a moment while I go on ahead."
He replied, "Excellent, Ānanda!
and immediately went to visit the Buddha.
The Buddha saw Ānanda approaching from afar and spoke these words:
"Welcome, Ānanda!
It has been a long time since we last saw you."
Venerable Ānanda, having prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet, spoke these words:
“World-Honored One,
are you free from illness and affliction, and do you dwell in peace and comfort?”
The Buddha said,
"The Tathāgata has little illness and little affliction, and dwells in peace and happiness, having received the offerings of the elephant king.
He then asked Ānanda:
"Is the community of bhikṣus free from much illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace?
Are they not weary of seeking alms, and do they practice the Path according to the Dharma?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
The community of bhikṣus is free from much illness and affliction, dwelling in peace and happiness; they do not weary in seeking alms, and they practice the Path according to the Dharma.
He then spoke again, saying:
"Five hundred bhikṣus are currently outside the grove and wish to come to pay their respects; we only pray that you will grant them permission.
The Buddha said, "They may enter."
Ānanda immediately went to where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Venerable ones! You have gained a great and excellent benefit; the World-Honored One has granted you permission to enter."
The bhikṣus then followed Ānanda together to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu among those seated who had this thought:
"How does a bhikṣu, knowing thus and seeing thus, successively attain the destruction of the outflows?"
Having thought thus in silence, he did not dare to question the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, knowing what that bhikṣu was thinking in his mind, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"There is a bhikṣu in this assembly who has had such a thought."
"How does a bhikṣu, knowing thus and seeing thus, gradually attain the destruction of the outflows?
He thought this silently and did not dare to ask.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I have already taught the bhikṣus the contemplation of the aggregates (skandha), the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
If a bhikṣu knows thus and sees thus, he shall attain the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava)."
Having heard the words of the World-Honored One, that bhikṣu immediately thought to himself:
"Form is the self.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the bhikṣu’s mind, again addressed Ānanda:
"This bhikṣu forms this thought: 'Form is self.

Ānanda, you should know that if a bhikṣu contemplates form in this way—as being all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)—then through the contact of ignorance, feeling arises, and from that, craving is born."
Ānanda! What is the cause, what is the condition for craving?
From what does it arise?
How does it turn?
Ānanda, you should know this:
craving is the cause of feeling, the condition for feeling, born of feeling, and turns from feeling.
Ānanda, you should know this!
Feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its condition, arises from contact, and is transformed by contact.
Ānanda, you should know this!
Contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its condition, arises from the six sense bases, and evolves from the six sense bases.
Ānanda, you should know that the six sense bases are conditioned phenomena; they arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are subject to impermanence and cessation.
Contact is a conditioned phenomenon; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and is a dharma subject to impermanence and cessation.
Feeling is a conditioned phenomenon; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and is a dharma subject to impermanence and cessation.
Craving is a conditioned phenomenon; it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions and is a dharma subject to impermanence and cessation.
Volitional formations are conditioned phenomena; they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and are dharmas subject to impermanence and cessation.
Ignorance is a conditioned phenomenon; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions and is a dharma subject to impermanence and cessation.
It is thus, Ānanda!
If a bhikṣu knows and contemplates in this way, he will gradually attain the exhaustion of all outflows.
When that bhikṣu heard these words, he thought to himself:
"Form is not self; form belongs to me.
The Buddha, knowing what was in that bhikṣu’s mind, again addressed Ānanda:
"This bhikṣu thinks thus:
'Form is not self; form is mine.
Ānanda, you should know this!"
If a bhikṣu contemplates all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) regarding form in this way, he sees that craving arises from feeling born of contact with ignorance.
What is the cause, what is the condition, what is the origin, and what is the transformation of this craving?
Ānanda, you should know this:

craving is the cause of feeling, the condition for feeling, that from which feeling arises, and that by which feeling turns; and so on, down to ignorance and conditioned formations—these arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are phenomena subject to impermanence and cessation.
Having heard these words, that bhikṣu reflects thus:
“Form is not self, nor does it belong to a self;
form exists within me.”

The Buddha knew what was in that bhikṣu’s mind: that even ignorance and conditioned formations arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are subject to the law of impermanence and cessation.
Having heard these words, that bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Form is not self, nor does it belong to a self; nor is there form within me, nor am I within form."

The Buddha, having known what was in the mind of that bhikṣu, [taught] up to: ignorance and conditioned formations arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are impermanent and subject to destruction.
Having heard these words, that bhikṣu reflects:
"If form is not self, nor belongs to self, nor is there form within self, nor is there a self within form."
Feeling is the self; perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
If the five aggregates are not the self, nor belong to the self, nor does the self exist within the five aggregates, nor do the five aggregates exist within the self, how then could there be a self?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one contemplates the five aggregates and all conditioned phenomena in this way, craving arises from sensation born of contact with ignorance. Ānanda!"
Craving: what is its cause, what is its condition, from what does it arise, and how does it evolve?
Craving has feeling as its cause, feeling as its condition, arises from feeling, and evolves from feeling.
Ānanda, you should know this!
Feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its condition, arises from contact, and is transformed by contact.
Ānanda, you should know this!
Contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its condition, arises from the six sense bases, and is transformed by the six sense bases.
Ānanda, you should know this!

The six sense bases are conditioned formations; they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and are dharmas subject to impermanence and destruction. This extends even to ignorance as a conditioned formation; it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions and is a dharma subject to impermanence and destruction.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
If a bhikṣu knows thus and contemplates thus, he will gradually attain the exhaustion of the outflows.
Upon hearing these words, that bhikṣu attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣu further reflected deeply that all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent, being without self and without what belongs to a self.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When this bhikṣu reflected in this way, he did not grasp at any dharma; he attained the exhaustion of all outflows, and his mind achieved liberation.”
When the Buddha taught this Dharma to the bhikṣus, the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated, and they all became arhats.

At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling together with the bhikṣus. During the autumn months, there was unseasonable cold rain; the bhikṣus took a large log from the open air and lit a fire, but within the wood there was previously a large snake.
When the snake encountered the heat of the fire, it emerged with its head held high and pursued the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus spoke to one another in succession, crying out in loud voices:
"The snake has come out!"
"A snake has come out!
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Monks, for what reason are you shouting so loudly?"
He replied:

"It was an unseasonable cold rain, and some young bhikṣus were lighting fires with pieces of wood they had gathered from the air. There was a snake within the wood; because it became warm, it emerged and chased after the bhikṣus."
When the bhikṣus saw this, they spoke to one another, and for that reason there was a great noise.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When they had arrived, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are seven disadvantages to lighting a fire.
What are the seven?"

First, the eyes are impaired; second, the complexion is impaired; third, the body becomes emaciated; fourth, the robes become soiled and worn; fifth, the bedding and mats are ruined; sixth, it creates the conditions for violating the precepts; and seventh, it increases worldly discourse.
"Because of these seven faults, from this day forward, I do not permit the lighting of fires.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above, the World-Honored One, for the sake of five benefits, went on a tour of the bhikṣus' quarters every five days. There he saw a bhikṣu suffering from scabies.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Monk, are you comfortable?
Are you not suffering?"
He replied:
“I am suffering from scabies and find no pleasure; I obtain comfort by warming my body with fire.
However, because the World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding the lighting of fires, I find no pleasure.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to kindle fire.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, it was explained at length as above.

At that time, the Venerable Nandiya, Kimbila, and Bāhula, having completed their summer retreat at Gijjhakūṭa Hill, went to Sāvatthī to pay their respects to the World-Honored One; they were wearing rain-cloths that had been dyed and were worn out.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally: "Monks,
for what reason are you wearing this rain-cloak?"
He replied, “The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not kindle fire; therefore, we are unable to boil the dye or re-dye the cloth.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, except for when there is a specific cause.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble."
For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.
If a bhikṣu, being without illness, lights a fire for himself—whether of grass, wood, or cow dung—either lighting it himself or causing another to light it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"Except in cases of specific causes and conditions.
The term "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the "sick," there is no offense.
Regarding "the sick": if one suffers from conditions such as ringworm, scabies, eczema, jaundice, or wind-diseases causing sores, and requires fire for relief, it is permitted to kindle it.
Regarding "grass": this includes all types of grass, as well as reeds, rushes, bamboo, and the like.
"Wood" refers to all types of wood, whether split or whole.
"Cow dung" refers to whether one burns it oneself or causes another to burn it.
With the exception of such circumstances, the World-Honored One declared there is no offense.

Regarding the causal conditions: if one is on duty as the month’s supervisor, or is overseeing the preparation of food; if it is one's turn to light the fire, light the lamps, or light the fire in the warm bathhouse; or if one lights the fire for the sake of one's upādhyāya or ācārya; or if one lights the fire to warm water, to fumigate the alms bowl, or to dye robes—there is no offense in lighting the fire in these cases.
Except when there is a specific cause or condition, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If one takes firewood and places it upon fuel, grass, cow dung, wood chips, or refuse, it is a *pāyattika*.
In this manner, it is likewise even when one carries a fire of refuse onto wood, onto grass, onto cow dung, or onto wooden shavings.
If a bhikṣu approaches a fire among grass or wood—whether it has already been ignited or not—and stirs up a heap [of fuel], it is a pāyattika.
If one carries a firebrand that has not yet scorched the ground, it is an offense of *vibhinī*.
It is not an offense to carry an iron brick, a tile, or a potsherd containing a mass of fire.
If one whirls a firebrand to form a circle of light, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu tends the fire, and cuts grass to place into the fire, for each piece cut, it is a pāyattika.
If he burns grass or wood, it is a pāyattika.
If one burns a seed-stalk, one incurs two *pāyattikas*: the offense of burning fire and the offense of destroying seeds.
If the stalk is already broken, or has been purified by fire, or is burned for a specific necessary reason, there is no offense.
If there is grain in the straw sheaves, or if there is grain in the chaff, one incurs two *pāyattikas*: for lighting the fire and for destroying seeds. One should purify [the seeds] by means of fire;
if there is a valid reason [to light the fire], there is no offense.
If one burns human hair, horsehair, camel hair, or the like, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one burns leather, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one burns cakes, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one burns poisonous substances or charcoal, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If food is not digested, one may burn iron to cauterize the feet or the abdomen; there is no offense.
If one steps on a leather sandal over a fire, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Vihāra, as described in detail above.

At that time, a *karmadāna* bhikṣu hired laborers to make bricks and prepare mortar. These laborers sometimes stayed overnight in the monks’ dining hall, the meditation hall, or the heated bathhouse; they spit and expectorated impurities and defiled the place with excrement and urine here and there, thereby obstructing the bhikṣus from sitting in meditation and practicing the Path.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣu in charge of construction affairs here.
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
“Is it true that you hire laborers who defile various places and obstruct the bhikṣus from practicing dhyāna and walking the Path?
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
The Buddha asked, "Why is that? He replied:
"I wish to have my laborers begin work early and finish late, so that they may receive their full wages.
The Buddha said, "Even if this were so,
from this day forward you must not sleep in the same room as one who has not yet received full ordination."

Furthermore, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva living as a householder, his father, the king, cherished him deeply; fearing that the lineage of the Wheel-Turning King would perish, he grieved and wept, refusing to allow him to leave the household life. Because the Bodhisattva was carrying Rāhula in his womb, he then renounced the world and went forth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“No one could surpass the King, the Father, in providing comfort and ease for the Tathāgata; he constructed palaces for the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—as described at length in the *Ślakṣṇasūtra*, until the Tathāgata attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason did you undergo such ascetic practices for six years?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today; as is explained at length in the *Śakuntaka-jātaka*.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that Māra Pāpīyān constantly seeks to destroy and disturb the World-Honored One?
The Buddha said:
"Not only today; as is explained at length in the *Kūrma-jātaka*."

The meeting between father and son in the kingdom of Kapilavastu should be explained here in detail; likewise, the renunciation of Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and Rāhula should be explained here in detail.

For the sake of his kinsmen, the Buddha returned to the kingdom of Kapilavastu; the lay devotees built a latrine for the Buddha, and although he had no need for it, he accepted it out of consideration for worldly custom.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was sleeping in the open air. When the night wind and rain began, he went to the door of the Venerable Śāriputra’s cell and knocked.
He asked, "Who is there?"
He replied, "Upādhyāya! I am Rāhula."
He said, "You simply stay there.
Then he went again to the front of Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s cell and knocked on the door.
He asked, "Who are you?
and he replied:
"Ācārya! I am Rāhula," he said. The teacher replied:
"You may simply stay there.
Thus he went to another room after another, and each time they said,
"Stay in that place."
He immediately went to the World-Honored One’s latrine and lay down, propping himself against a wooden board.
During the night, there was a black snake that, fearing the wind and rain as well, wished to enter the latrine.

The Buddha constantly observed sentient beings; seeing this black snake about to enter the latrine, and fearing that the snake would disturb Rāhula, he immediately emitted a radiance and went to the latrine himself, saying: "Who are you?"
“World-Honored One! I am Rāhula.
The Buddha said:
"Rāhula, are you here? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already stayed in this place for too long.

The Buddha then took him by his golden, smooth, and supple hand and helped him up; having brushed the dust from his body, he led him into his own room and, pointing to a bed before him, said: "Dwell here."
At that time, the Tathāgata had already established the precepts for his disciples; therefore, they practiced these precepts accordingly.
Thus, the World-Honored One sat in the full lotus posture, and when he had finished his meal, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"Out of compassion, and because of Rāhula, I have enabled my disciples to dwell in peace and happiness. From this day forward, I permit those who have not yet received full ordination to stay in the same room for three nights; on the fourth night, they must stay separately."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did Rāhula remain in the womb for six years?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a rishi named Līpādu who went to the king seeking an audience.
The king replied to the rishi:"
"Stay for now in the Aśoka Garden; we shall meet in a moment.
Having given this instruction, he did not allow them to see him for six days.
The king at that time was Rāhula.
For this reason, he remained in the womb for six years,
as explained in detail in the *Jātaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Kapilavastu assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu stays in the same room with a person who has not received full ordination for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"One who has not received full ordination" refers to anyone other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Although a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination, she is not permitted to stay together [with a male] for more than three nights.
"Three nights" means the limit is exactly three nights.
"In the same room" means sharing one roof and one enclosure.
To stay overnight [in such a place] is a pāyattika offense.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If there is a separate door and a partition for a single room, there is no offense.
If they share a common door while being in separate rooms, it is a pāyattika.
If they share a single room and a single door, it is a pāyattika.
If they are in separate rooms and have separate doors, there is no offense.
If there is an obstruction and a concealment, it is a pāyattika offense.
If there is an obstruction and partial concealment, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If there is an obstruction but no concealment, there is no offense.
If it is concealed and obstructed, it is a pāyattika offense.
If it is concealed and half-obstructed, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If it is concealed but not obstructed, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination with half of that person’s body inside the room, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If one goes entirely outside, there is no offense.
If a person who has not received full ordination sleeps within the room and a bhikṣu also sleeps within the room, it is a pāyattika.
If a person who has not received full ordination sleeps within the room and the bhikṣu has half his body inside, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If they all go outside, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu is already lying down inside a room and an unordained person later enters and lies down, it is a pāyattika for each instance.

If a bhikṣu, or one who has not yet received full ordination, rises during the night to attend to the needs of nature, and having risen, returns to sleep, for each such instance it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If many persons who have not yet received full ordination fall asleep first, and a bhikṣu comes later and falls asleep, he commits one pāyattika offense.
If, in the interim, he rises to attend to the needs of nature and then lies down again, he commits a pāyattika offense for each instance of rising.
If one stays for three nights in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination, on the fourth night one must stay in a separate room or in the open air.
If it is very windy, snowy, or raining in the open air during cold weather, one should return to the room and sit there until the end of the night.
If a bhikṣu is old or ill and unable to sit upright, he should use a curtain as a screen.
Whether it reaches his head or his armpits, the lower edge of the curtain reaching the ground must be made of a thick, substantial material, such that even a kitten cannot pass through it.

If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, he may stay in the same room with a person who has not yet received full ordination for three nights; on the fourth night, he must stay elsewhere or stay in the open air.
When there is wind, rain, snow, or cold, one should enter a house; in such cases, one should spread out a canopy as described above to create a shelter.
If there is no canopy or shelter, one may sit until the ground is cleared.
If one is too old or ill to sit, or if there is a person who has not yet received full ordination but is trustworthy, one should say to them:
"You sleep; I shall sit."
When a bhikṣu wishes to sleep, he should call out to wake the other, saying:
"When I sleep, you shall sit; if you also sleep, you will have no merit.
If one continues to stay overnight with another whose offense regarding this rule of sleeping in the same room has not yet been confessed, his offense will increase further.
After having confessed their transgressions, they must stay in separate rooms; only then may they again sleep together.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā). Upānanda did not come, so they immediately sent a messenger to summon him, saying:
"Elder!..."
The Saṃgha has assembled intending to perform a formal act (karmavācanā); they call for the Elder.
Upānanda, knowing the characteristics of the Vinaya regarding formal acts, intended to perform the formal act with him.
Having so intended, he took his consent (chanda).
The bhikṣu said,
"After you have given your consent, do not speak further.
At that time, Upānanda’s co-practitioner disciple had a formal act of censure (*karma*) performed against him by the Saṃgha.
Having performed the *jñapti-karman* of formal accusation, he approaches the preceptor and says: "Preceptor!
Why did you grant this consent?"
The teacher asked:
"For what reason?
The disciple replied:
"The Sangha has performed the *karma* of formal censure against me.
The teacher said,
"I do not know."
Having heard these words, he spoke thus:
"Venerable sir!
I do not wish to give my consent; it is not good for me to do so. Since the *karmavācanā* would not be accomplished [otherwise], I shall not give my consent for this *karman*."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they felt ashamed and unhappy, and for this reason, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here."
After he had arrived, the Buddha spoke to him, saying:
"This is a wicked deed. How is it that after you have given your consent (*chanda*), you then say:
'The formal act (*karmavācanā*) is not accomplished because I did not give this consent'?"
"Why did you grant the *chanda* (consent) without first asking?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to grant *chanda* for a matter without having first asked.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, having already given his consent (*chanda*), later becomes angry and displeased, saying:
"I did not give my consent; it was improper. The *karmavācanā* is not accomplished; I did not give this consent."
"A *pāyattika*. Regarding the term "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
There are two kinds of giving consent (*chanda-dāna*): [the formal giving of consent and the informal giving of consent].
Whether one asks or does not ask.
To "ask" means to ask the person who intends to take [the robe]:
"What kind of work shall I do?"
He replied:
"Perform the *tarjanīya-karman* and grant the consent for the *tarjanīya-karman*. ... [and so on] ...
perform the *utksepanīya-karman* and grant the consent for the *utksepanīya-karman*."
In this manner, for each individual *karmavācanā*, after having asked [for permission], one gives the consent; this is called "giving after asking.
As for "giving without asking," one says: "I give my consent for the *karmavācanā*," and so states it three times.

In this way, one who has attained supernormal powers may grant their consent for all *karmavācanā* (formal acts), with the sole exception of the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*; this is called "granting consent without asking.
As for the latter, it refers to one who, after the *karmavācanā* has been completed, becomes angry and displeased.

Regarding "hatred and lack of joy": hatred refers to the nine grounds for malice (*navāghātasthānīyā dharmāḥ*) and the arising of anger toward inappropriate objects; the tenth, "anger," refers to the lack of joy experienced by those in training (*śaikṣa*), ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and even up to Arhats.
They speak thus: "I do not grant consent; it is not to my liking. The *karmavācanā* is not accomplished; I do not grant this consent."
...so it is said, "it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) has assembled and intends to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), everyone should come; however, if there is a valid reason—such as fumigating a bowl, dyeing robes, illness, matters concerning a stūpa, matters concerning the Saṃgha, or other such business—one should at that time grant one's consent (*chanda*).
Once one has given consent (*chanda*), one must not subsequently say:
"If I had heard this, I would not have acted in this manner.
If one has already given consent for the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one should thereafter express approval (*anumodana*).
If, having already given one's consent (*chanda*) within the Saṃgha, one subsequently violates it, it is a *pāyattika*.

If, among a large group, or before an elder bhikṣu, or before one’s upādhyāya or ācārya, one has given consent and subsequently violates it, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, Upānanda, who was the younger brother of Nanda, spoke thus to Nanda’s co-practicing disciple:
“Come with me into the village; once we arrive there, I shall provide you with fine food and drink.
If I should perform any act that is improper, do not speak of it to others, for I am your paternal uncle.”
In this regard, it should be explained in detail as in the "Thirty Matters.
It continues until [the Buddha] spoke to Nanda, saying:
"Where were your disciples when they spoke of my faults before those who practice the holy life?"
Nanda immediately reproached his disciple:
"You are a base person; how can you speak of my younger brother's faults in the presence of those who practice the holy life?
The bhikṣus, for this reason, went and informed the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Upānanda here. When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said to Upānanda:
"This is an evil deed; how could you speak to a bhikṣu in this way, saying:
'I will enter the village with you and give you fine food when we arrive there'?"
“Having arrived, why did you dismiss them and send them back?
From this day forward, I do not permit sending anyone back.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Let us enter the village together; when we arrive there, I shall give you food—either giving it myself or having someone else give it."
Later, wishing to drive him away, he said this: "Go!
I do not find pleasure in living or speaking with you; I find pleasure in living and speaking alone."
"If one acts according to these causes and conditions without deviation, the driver commits a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Village" is as explained above in the precept concerning theft.
Regarding "not giving later," it means that one does not give personally, nor does one cause another to give, saying:
"Venerable sir! Depart!"
"I do not find pleasure dwelling or conversing with you; I find pleasure dwelling and conversing alone.
To drive [her] away is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If one performs an improper act in the sexual organ while remaining within the monastery, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one performs an improper act in the sexual organ while being sent away on the road, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one performs an improper act within a village settlement, and is sent away from that settlement, it is a *pāyattika*.
One must not take [the person] back after having sent them away; however, if one lacks the strength to provide food for two people, they may be sent back, and there is no offense.
If one is able to obtain food for two people, they should eat together.
If one calls a physician to fetch medicine and then dispatches them, there is no offense.
If it is not possible to do so, they should be dispatched at the appropriate time.
If there is a place where one has been invited to eat, one should be sent to that place to eat.
If there is no such place where one has been invited, and there is food within the monastery, one should be sent back to the monastery to eat.
If there is no food obtained through an invitation or from within a vihāra, one should say:
"Venerable sir,
you must seek food for yourself."
If they perform improper conduct, such as looking about in a disreputable manner, there is no offense for one who dismisses them.
If they are engaged in activities such as fumigating bowls or dyeing robes, there is no offense for one who dismisses them.
To expel a bhikṣu is a pāyattika offense;
to expel a bhikṣuṇī is a sthūlātyaya offense;
to expel a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā is a vinayātikrama offense.
Down to ordinary laypeople, one commits a violation of the *vinaya* and must repent in one's heart.
Therefore, it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Ariṣṭa slandered the Sūtras, saying:
"I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; as for those things the World-Honored One has called 'obstructive dharmas,' practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the Path."
Then the bhikṣus spoke thus: "Venerable Ariṣṭa!
Do not misrepresent the sūtras;
this is a wrong view, an unwholesome view, which leads to the evil paths and entry into hell."
After being admonished once, twice, and thrice, he did not desist.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One:
"Ariṣṭa slanders the sūtras, saying:..."
"I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; regarding the dharmas spoken of by the Blessed One as obstacles to the path, I practice these dharmas and they do not obstruct the path.
Thus he persisted despite being admonished once, twice, and thrice.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“This Ariṣṭa slanders the sūtras, saying: ‘I understand and know the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
regarding the dharmas spoken of by the World-Honored One as obstructive to the path, practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the path.’”

"If [the offense] does not cease after one admonition, two admonitions, and three admonitions, you should admonish them three times in a private place, three times in the midst of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha."
Regarding "admonishing in private," one should ask him, saying these words:
"Venerable Ariṭṭha!
You have slandered the sūtras, saying this:"

"Does he still not desist after being admonished three times, saying: 'I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; as for the dharmas spoken of by the Blessed One as obstructing the path, practicing these dharmas does not obstruct the path'?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. At that time,
one should admonish him in a private place, saying these words:
"Āḷavaka! You misrepresent the sūtras;
this is an evil view, an unwholesome view, by which you shall fall into an evil destination and enter hell. Elder!"
I admonish you out of a heart of loving-kindness, desiring to benefit you; you should relinquish this matter.
One admonition has already passed, and two remain; you should relinquish this matter.
Ariṣṭa said: "This is a good view, a right view;
it is the very view that my parents and spiritual teachers have always maintained through our lineage. I cannot now abandon this view without first consulting my parents and spiritual teachers."

If, after being thus admonished a second and third time, he still does not desist, and even after being admonished three times before a group of many people he still does not desist, one should perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for seeking permission within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Ariṣṭa slandered the sūtras, saying: "I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
regarding the dharmas that the World-Honored One says obstruct the path, practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the path."
"Having already been admonished three times in private and three times before a group, he does not relinquish this matter.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now also admonish him three times within the assembly, so that he may relinquish this matter."
The assembly of monks should ask:
"Venerable Ariṣṭa!
Is it true that you have slandered the sūtras by making such a statement?"
"I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; regarding the obstructive dharmas spoken of by the Blessed One, I practice these dharmas and they do not obstruct the Path.
Have you been admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of a group of many people, yet still not relinquish this matter?
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Saṃgha should then offer him admonition.
The one who offers the admonition speaks thus:
"Āḷavaka! Do not misrepresent the sūtras;
those who misrepresent the sūtras fall into the evil paths and enter the hells."
"Elder! The Saṃgha desires to benefit you; you should accept the Saṃgha’s words.
One admonition has already passed, and two remain; you should relinquish this matter."
Ariṣṭa said: "This is a good view, a right view; my parents have inherited and maintained this view for generations, and I cannot abandon it without consulting them."
When he had been admonished thus a second and a third time, he still did not desist.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa slanders the sūtras, saying: ‘I understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
as for the dharmas that the World-Honored One says obstruct the path, practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the path.’”
"Having already admonished him three times in private, three times in the midst of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha, he does not relinquish this matter.
You should perform the *karma* of formal censure against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu should speak thus:
"Venerable sir!
I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One; regarding the dharmas taught by the Blessed One as obstructive to the path, I know that practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the path."
The bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable one!
Do not slander the Blessed One!"
"It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One does not speak such words.
The World-Honored One has declared that the dharmas which obstruct the path truly do obstruct the path.
You must abandon this evil deed."
If the bhikṣus admonish him and this bhikṣu still obstinately maintains his position and does not relinquish it,
and after a second and third admonition he still does not relinquish it— though it would be well if he did—
the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karma* of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*) against him; having done so, he incurs a *pāyattika*.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"World-Honored One" refers to the one who possesses all-knowledge and sees all things.
"Dharma" refers to that which was spoken by the World-Honored One and that which was approved by the World-Honored One.
"Spoken by the World-Honored One" means spoken by the World-Honored One himself.
"Authorized" means that while the disciples speak, the World-Honored One authorizes it.
"Spoken" means explained with detailed analysis for every single phrase.
"Knowing" refers to knowing through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

"Factors that obstruct the path" refers to the five desires: when the eye sees forms and conceives a longing for them, the mind becomes joyful and gives rise to desire and attachment; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and tactile sensations.
"Practicing" means performing these actions.

"Not being able to obstruct the Path" means they do not obstruct the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, nor the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat.
"Monks" refers to one individual, a group of many, or the Saṃgha.
"That monk" refers to the monk Ariṣṭa.
"Do not slander the World-Honored One" means do not grasp what is untrue or grasp it in an unfavorable manner.
Regarding the "three admonitions": it may be by one person, by many people, or by the Saṃgha.
As for the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
Up to the third admonition, if [the offense] is relinquished, that is well.
If he does not relinquish [the offense], the Saṃgha should perform the *karma* of formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against him, and he must confess a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, it is said.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The seventh of the ninety-two rules concerning the *pācittiya* offenses: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa did not relinquish his evil view; after the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against him, he went to where the Venerable Nanda and Upānanda were. Upon seeing them, he greeted them, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome!"

He immediately rose to welcome him, provided a small seat for him to sit upon, water for washing his feet, oil for anointing his feet, and non-timely medicinal gruel; he also gave him a dwelling, bedding, and requisites, and shared with him both the Dharma-food and the flavor-food.
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa went to the gate of the Jeta Grove Monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Have you performed the formal act of *karma* of suspension against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, thinking that there is no other place for him to stay?"

"I shall further obtain the company of fellow practitioners of the holy life who will provide me with dwellings, bedding, mattresses, and requisites, and share with me both the Dharma-food and the flavorful food.
If you lift me up quickly, you too shall soon obtain such an excellent dwelling place."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were filled with shame and displeasure, and immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and the others here."
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda, "Is it truly so?
They replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter.
How can you, knowing that the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), still partake together with them in the food of dharma and the food of flavor?
This is not Dharma, not Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed an evil view and does not relinquish it, and yet—whether the Saṃgha has already performed the *karma* of formal censure against him or has not yet performed it according to the Dharma—he eats with him or dwells in the same room as him, it is a pāyattika.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.
“Knows” means either knowing for oneself or hearing it from another.
“Holding wrong views” refers to those such as Ariṣṭa who slander the sūtras.
"One who has not yet acted according to the Dharma" refers to one for whom the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal act of *karma* for releasing a suspension or banishment.
"Eating together" means sharing both dharma-food and material food.
"Living together" means residing within the same boundary.
"Sharing a room" means sharing one roof and one enclosure.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If there is a bhikṣu who is disliked by his upādhyāya or ācārya, other bhikṣus must not entice him, saying:
"I shall provide you with robes and alms bowls, medicine for illnesses, and bedding and seating; you should dwell by my side, receive the scriptures, and recite them."
If, upon examining the circumstances of that bhikṣu, one determines that he will certainly abandon the precepts and return to secular life, he may be enticed away.
Having enticed him, one should instruct him, saying:
"You must recognize that the kindness of your upādhyāya and ācārya is exceedingly heavy and difficult to repay; you ought to return to live under their care."
There is no offense.
If one perceives that a fault has not been raised when it has actually been raised, yet lives and eats together with that person, there is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one perceives that a fault has been raised when it has not actually been raised, yet lives and eats together with that person, there is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one picks it up while perceiving that it is being picked up, it is a pāyattika.
