If one does not pick it up while perceiving that it is not being picked up, there is no offense.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera of Ariṣṭa, named Dharmadatta, spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I understand and know the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; yet the World-Honored One has said,
'Sensual desire is an obstacle to the Path,' yet practicing sensual desire does not obstruct the Path."
Then the bhikṣus said this: “Śrāmaṇera!
Do not slander the Blessed One!”
To slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome.
You have grasped this wrongly.
The World-Honored One has said:
"To practice the way of sexual misconduct is truly an obstacle to the Path.
Although he was admonished once, twice, and thrice, he did not desist.
On account of this matter, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This dharma [is for one who] speaks thus to a śrāmaṇera:
'I understand and know the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; the World-Honored One says:'"
"The practice of sexual misconduct obstructs the Path. [Yet you say,] "Practicing sexual misconduct cannot obstruct the Path.
You all should admonish him three times in private, three times before a group of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha, to cause him to abandon this matter.
In a private place, one should ask him:
"O śrāmaṇera, did you truly say these words?"
"I understand the Dharma as taught by the Tathāgata; the World-Honored One has said,
'Cultivating sexual desire is an obstacle to the Path,' yet cultivating sexual acts cannot obstruct the Path."
"Have you not ceased even after being admonished three times?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
At that time, one should admonish him in private:
"Novice! Do not slander the World-Honored One!"
To slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome.
You have grasped it incorrectly.
The World-Honored One has said:
"Engaging in sexual desire truly obstructs the Path.
I now admonish you with a heart of loving-kindness for the sake of your benefit; therefore, heed my words.
One admonition has passed, and two remain."
“Will you abandon this matter?
If he does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time in the same manner.
It is likewise when he is admonished three times in the midst of a large assembly.
If he does not relinquish it, the Sangha should perform a *jñapti-karman* (motion for formal authorization) within the assembly:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person has spoken thus to a śrāmaṇera:..."
"I understand and comprehend the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; yet the World-Honored One has said, 'Sensual desire is an obstacle to the Path.
However, practicing sensual desire cannot obstruct the Path."
"Having already been admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of the assembly, he still does not relinquish it.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should now also admonish him three times to cause him to relinquish this matter."
The Sangha should ask him: "Śrāmaṇera!
Did you truly speak these words?"
"I understand the Dharma as taught by the Tathāgata; yet the World-Honored One has said, 'Sensual desire is an obstacle to the Path.
However, practicing sensual desire cannot obstruct the Path."
"Did you indeed fail to relinquish [the offense] after being admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of a group?
He replied, "It is true."
The Saṃgha should offer this admonition:
"O śrāmaṇera! Do not slander the Blessed One!"
To slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome; you have grasped this unwholesomely. Sexual desire truly obstructs the Path.
The Sangha has admonished you with a heart of loving-kindness for your own benefit.
"You should accept the words of the Sangha.
One admonition has already passed, and two remain; you should relinquish this matter.
If he does not relinquish it, the second and third admonitions are to be performed in the same manner.
He still did not relinquish it.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
This person says to the śrāmaṇera:
"The World-Honored One has said:
'Sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.'"
"I understand that indulging in sexual desire cannot obstruct the Dharma.

If, after being admonished three times in private, three times in the midst of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha, he does not relinquish [his position], he should be expelled from the assembly.
Having driven them out, he went to where the group of six bhikṣus were; upon seeing them, he greeted them with "Welcome!
and provided them with non-timely drinks, lodgings, bedding and furniture, robes and bowls, and medicine for the sick and infirm.
Having received these various provisions, the śrāmaṇera went to the gate of the Jeta Grove and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, you expelled me from the community, saying that I could no longer find a place to stay."

I have now further obtained companions in the holy life with whom to dwell; they provide me with rooms, bedding, and furniture, share with me the food of the Dharma and the food of flavor, and give me robes, alms bowls, and medicine for sickness and weakness.
"Venerable Elders!
Had you expelled me earlier, I would have attained such a state of dwelling in happiness much sooner.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were displeased and immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here. When they had come,
the Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha told the group of six bhikṣus:
"This is an evil matter.

How is it that you know a śrāmaṇera has not abandoned his evil views and, though the Saṃgha has rightfully expelled him, you still dwell together with him, sharing both the food of the Dharma and the food of flavor?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a śrāmaṇera should speak thus:
"The Tathāgata has taught that sexual desire is an obstacle to the Path; yet I understand and know that practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path."
The bhikṣus should admonish the śrāmaṇera, saying:
"You, śrāmaṇera, must not slander the World-Honored One!
To slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome."
The World-Honored One has said:
"The habitual indulgence in sexual desire truly obstructs the Path.
You must abandon this evil view.
If the bhikṣus admonish this śrāmaṇera and he still does not relinquish [his position], they should admonish him thus a second and a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should say this:
"From this day forward, you, śrāmaṇera, must not say:..."
"The Buddha is my teacher.
Furthermore, you must not stay with the bhikṣus for more than three nights.
Depart; you may not remain here.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has not abandoned evil views, fails to expel him and instead entices, keeps, and supports him, eating with him and dwelling in the same room as him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Śrāmaṇera" refers to those who are equal to śrāmaṇeras according to the Dharma.
"World-Honored One" refers to the supreme field of merit for all, the one possessed of all-knowledge, and the one who sees all.
The Dharma is that which was spoken by the Buddha and that which was approved by the Buddha.
That which was spoken by the Buddha refers to what the Buddha himself spoke.
That which was approved refers to what was spoken by his disciples and subsequently approved by the Buddha.
"To explain" means to analyze and expound upon each sentence.
"To know" refers to knowing through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Regarding "dharmas that obstruct the Path," these are the five desires: when the eye sees forms and conceives a longing for them, the mind experiences joy and gives rise to desire and attachment.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and tactile objects.
"Practicing" means engaging in these activities.
"Not obstructing the path" means not obstructing the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, fourth dhyāna, or the four formless attainments.
It does not obstruct the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship.
As for "various bhikṣus," it refers to one person, many persons, or the Saṃgha.
This śrāmaṇera is one who, according to the Dharma, is equal to other śrāmaṇeras.
To slander the World-Honored One is to grasp what is untrue and to grasp it improperly.
Regarding the three admonitions: whether by a single person, by a group of many, or by the Saṃgha, if he relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, he should be expelled.
"A bhikṣu" is as described above.
"Knows" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Expels" means expelling from the saṃghārāma.
Regarding a *śrāmaṇera*: one who acts in accordance with the Dharma is equal to a *śrāmaṇera*.
One who has not yet acted in accordance with the Dharma is one who has not yet abandoned wrong views and has not been permitted by the Saṃgha to receive [the requisites].
To provide him with support means to provide him with robes, a bowl, and medicine for illness.
"Sharing food" refers to sharing both the dharma-food and the flavor-food.
"Living together" means residing together in a single saṃghārāma.
"Sharing a room" means being under one roof and within one enclosure.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a *śrāmaṇera* is disapproved of by his *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, a *bhikṣu* must not entice him to live with him, saying:
"I shall provide you with robes, alms-bowls, and medicine, and I shall teach you the sūtras."
If he recognizes that this is a śrāmaṇera and, for that reason, intends to return to lay life, one may entice him with gentle words.
Once he has been enticed, one should say to the śrāmaṇera:
"The kindness of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya is profound and difficult to repay; you should return to their presence."
If one expels someone while perceiving them as not to be expelled, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If one does not expel someone while perceiving them as to be expelled, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one expels someone while perceiving them as to be expelled, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not drive [the animal] and has no thought of driving it, there is no offense.
Therefore, it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus were wearing robes made of uncut strips of cloth, and the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) likewise wore robes made of uncut strips of cloth.

When a lay follower (upāsaka) wished to pay respects to a bhikṣu but instead paid respects to a non-Buddhist, it was only after hearing the latter’s blessing that he realized it was a non-Buddhist; the lay follower then felt shame and remorse in his heart.

A disciple of a non-Buddhist teacher intended to pay homage to his own teacher, but instead paid homage to a bhikṣu. Upon hearing the words of the blessing, he realized it was a bhikṣu, and the non-Buddhist disciple felt deep shame and remorse in his heart.
The bhikṣus, on account of these circumstances, went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall make separate garments by cutting the threads and dyeing them."
The bhikṣu then cut the threads and dyed them a different color.
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioners took red ochre to dye their robes for color, and they wore their hair in a topknot and carried triple-staffs to distinguish themselves.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, a wilderness-dwelling bhikṣu obtained a kauseya garment and, wishing to dye it, boiled some dye. The World-Honored One, traveling through the air by means of his supernormal power, went to where the bhikṣu was; knowing the situation, he asked him intentionally: "Bhikṣu!"
"What do you intend to do? He replied,
"I am boiling dye to color a *kauśeya* garment."
The Buddha said, “Kauśeya is soft and fine, while the dye is coarse and rough; it will damage this garment.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, there shall be two kinds of purification for *kauśeya* cloth:
purification by cutting the threads and purification by dyeing it blue.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī obtained some soft kṣauma cloth and, having boiled a dye, wished to color it.
The Buddha, by means of his supernormal power, went to their location; knowing [the situation], he asked them intentionally:
"Bhikṣus!..."
"What are you doing? He replied,
"I am boiling dye to color a *kambala* woolen cloth."
The Buddha said:
"The *kambala* is soft and fine, but the dyeing liquid is coarse and harsh; it will damage and tear the robe.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize two kinds of purification for *kambala* robes:
purification by cutting the threads and purification by dyeing blue.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, there was the Venerable Sundarananda, the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt and born of Mahāprajāpatī; he possessed thirty of the marks of a Great Man, lacking only the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows and the mark of the long-lobed ears.
Having finished his almsround, he departed from the city of Śrāvastī with Venerable Ānanda following behind him.
After the bhikṣus had eaten, they were walking and practicing meditation at the gateway of the Jeta Grove Monastery; seeing him approaching from afar, they thought it was the World-Honored One.
They all immediately rose to welcome him, joining their palms in reverence and saying:
"The World-Honored One has come!
The World-Honored One has come!"
Sundarananda also joined his palms together and said:
"Venerable elders!
I am Sundarananda; I am Sundarananda."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they each felt ashamed and remorseful. On account of this matter, they went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall dye your robes with a neutralizing color and make a mark upon them."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three kinds of discoloration:
either blue, black, or madder-brown.
If he uses it without applying one of these three kinds of discoloration, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Obtains" means obtaining from a man or a woman, whether they be laypeople or those who have gone forth.
"New robe" refers to a robe that has been newly made, such as a *kambala* robe, a *kārpāsa* robe, a *kṣauma* robe, a *kauśeya* robe, a *śāṇa* robe, a *māñjiṣṭha* robe, or a *kṛmivati* robe.
There are three types of dyed colors; if one uses each individual dyed color, they are:
blue, black, and mūlāṇa (wood-brown).
As for blue, it includes copper-green, *rājavarta*-green, and stone-blue.
Regarding "copper-green" (*tongqing*): when a copper vessel is placed upon a jar of fermented grain water (*kujiu*) and left there, that is called copper-green.
Regarding "growing-green" (*zhangyangqing*): this is the indigo-blue derived from *indigofera tinctoria*.
"Stone-blue" (śilānīla) refers to sky-blue (āpānīla).
One should use these for the purpose of purification by marking.
"Black" refers to both named clay and unnamed clay.
As for "named mud," it refers to *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, and *āmalaka* fruits placed together in a single iron vessel; this is called named mud.
As for "unnamed mud," it refers to actual mud, such as the mud from ponds or wells; all such things are included in this category.

*Mu-lan* refers to such things as *harītakī*, *bhallātaka*, and *āmalaka*; when these are ground upon raw iron and used to perform the purification by marking (*piṇḍa-śodhana*), it is called *mu-lan*.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe and uses it without performing the ritual of *pariśuddhi*, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If he obtains a new *saṃghāṭī*, it is good if he performs the *pariśuddhi*; if he does not perform the *pariśuddhi*, it is a *pāyattika*.

The same applies to the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, the rain-bathing robe, the wound-covering robe, and the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*): it is good if they are made pure; if they are not made pure, it is a *pāyattika*.
Kambala robes are purified in two ways:
by the purification of cutting the threads and by the purification of blue dots.
If one performs the purification of cutting the threads but does not perform the purification of blue dots, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one performs the purification by dyeing blue but does not perform the purification by cutting the threads, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one neither performs the purification by dyeing blue nor the purification by cutting the threads, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense and one offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one performs the purification by cutting the threads (*sūtra-cchedana-pariśuddhi*) or the purification by dyeing blue (*nīla-pariśuddhi*), there is no offense.
Folded robes undergo three types of purification:
purification by cutting the threads, purification by dyeing, and purification by dyeing blue.
If one performs the purification by cutting the threads and the purification by dyeing, but does not perform the purification by [removing] blue, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
If one performs the purification by [removing] blue, but does not perform the purification by cutting the threads nor the purification by dyeing, one incurs two *vinayātikrama* offenses.
If one does not perform the purification by cutting the threads, the purification by dyeing, or the purification by turning blue, one commits one *pāyattika* offense and two *vinayātikrama* offenses.
If one performs the three aforementioned purifications, there is no offense.
The three types of purification for robes made of *kusa* grass are the same as those for layered robes (*saṃghāṭī*).
The two types of purification for *kauśeya* silk are the same as those for *kambala* woolen robes.
The three types of purification for robes made of *śāṇa* hemp, *kṣauma* linen, and *kṛmimaya* silk-cotton are the same as those for layered robes.
The same applies to making it clean using blue, black, or madder dye.
When making it clean, it must be neither too large nor too small; at its largest, it should be the size of four fingers, and at its smallest, like a pea.

If one uses harītakī, āmalaka, or vibhītaka, one should grind them upon iron to extract the juice for the purpose of purification (pāriśuddhi). These should not be used simultaneously; rather, one may use one, three, five, seven, or nine fruits. One must not perform the purification by arranging them in the shape of a flower.
If mud falls upon a cloth while it is being washed, or if crows or birds with muddy feet step upon it, it is considered pure.
If one obtains many small, miscellaneous new items and joins them together to patch a single area, that single area is purified as a whole.
If each individual patch is replaced separately, one must perform the ritual of purification (*parikamma*) for each one.
If a new *saṃghāṭī* robe is being made, one should perform the purification at one corner.
If a single strip or even half a strip is patched, it likewise requires purification.
The *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, and all other robes—even those with new seams and patches—must be purified.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, on the fifteenth day when the moon was full, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, bathed, anointed his body, and donned fresh, clean robes; he was then in the main hall together with his various ministers.
Then the king said to a great minister:
"Today is the day of the full moon; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should we go, where we may be able to cultivate our roots of goodness?"
The minister replied:
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is in the city of Rājagṛha; he is a great śramaṇa who also has a large assembly. Your Majesty should go to him, for he can nurture your roots of goodness."
The king remained silent and did not answer.
Again, another minister said:
"This Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra is in the city of Rājagṛha; he is a great śramaṇa. You should go to him, for he can nurture your roots of goodness."
In this way, each of these ministers who were disciples of non-Buddhist teachers praised their respective masters, all saying:
"One should go to him; he is able to nurture one's roots of goodness."
At that time, the youth Jīrṇa was behind King Ajātaśatru, attending him while holding a parasol.
The king said to the youth, "Everyone is speaking; why do you remain silent and say nothing?"
"Now that the moon is full, to what place should I go so that my roots of goodness may grow?
The youth said to the king:
"The World-Honored One is currently staying in my Āmra Grove together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus."
"If one goes there, one may nurture one's roots of goodness.
The King approved of what was said and immediately addressed the elder youths:
"Quickly prepare five hundred female elephants, placing one lady upon each elephant."
Then the elder youth prepared the carriage exactly as instructed; having finished the preparations, he went to inform the king, saying, "The carriage is ready;
please know that it is now the proper time."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with five hundred ladies-in-waiting, took up torches and lamps at the hour of midnight; surrounded by them in front and behind, he departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to the Āmrapālī grove.
When they were about to reach the garden gate, all the bhikṣus were sitting in meditation; the king was immediately struck with awe and looked back at the youth, saying:
"You said there were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus in your garden."
"Why is this great assembly so silent and without sound?
Are you perhaps deceiving me?
The youth replied:
"I truly do not deceive the King; you should simply proceed straight ahead.
The youth then pointed out, saying:
"In this great hall, where the lamps are lit, the World-Honored One sits in the center. His majestic virtue is exceptionally sublime and peerless, like a bull king amidst a herd of cattle."
It was like a lion king among the beasts;
like a six-tusked white elephant king of the Snowy Mountains amidst a herd of elephants;
and just as the deep pool of the Ganges is clear, still, and silent, so too was the great assembly in profound silence.
"Furthermore, just as immeasurable waters flow into the great ocean, so too are the merits of the World-Honored One’s great assembly immeasurable.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru walked forward a short distance further, dismounted from his vehicle, and proceeded on foot to where the Buddha was. He circumambulated the Buddha and the great assembly three times and stood there, saying to the youth:
"The World-Honored One’s great assembly is tranquil, pure, and accomplished in merit; I pray that my son Udāyibhadra may also achieve such accomplishment in merit."
The Buddha told the Great King,
"Whatever you seek as a vow, you shall surely obtain it.
Thereupon, the king spread out a seat and invited the Buddha to sit.
The Buddha said, "Great King, please sit; the Buddha has his own seat.
Then the king prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet. Having paid homage at the Buddha's feet, he withdrew to sit to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"In this regard, can those of various crafts who have gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma attain the fruits of the śramaṇa in the present life?
This is explained in detail in the *Dṛṣṭadharmasrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*.
At that time, after the Dharma had been preached for a long duration, the ladies-in-waiting, because their precious necklaces were heavy, each untied them and placed them before their seats.

Then, because King Ajātaśatru bore the guilt of having killed his father, his mind was constantly filled with alarm and fear; hearing the sounds of drums, conchs, elephants, and horses within the city, the king became greatly terrified and immediately addressed the ladies:
"You should return to the city!"
"You may return to the city!
The lady departed in haste,
forgetting to take her necklace.
After returning to the palace, when the dawn of the following day arrived, the King’s Great Lady wished to put on her jeweled necklaces but could not find them.
The person who had dressed her said, "Yesterday, in our haste, I fear they were left there."
Thus all the ladies-in-waiting said, "We have forgotten such a great many necklaces; if we were to inform the King, he might perhaps reproach us.
At that time, a maidservant spoke to the King, saying:
"The ladies of the court returned late last night and have forgotten many of their necklaces.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin, the king's preceptor, who was seated with the king and addressed him, saying:
"If they were left behind there, all those śramaṇas must have hidden them; even if you go to search for them, you will certainly not find them."

At that time, the king dispatched a trustworthy person to investigate; he saw the Buddha and his great assembly sitting in solemn stillness, and he saw that all the ladies' necklaces were in their original places, brilliantly illuminated by the sunlight with a radiant and blazing glow.
He immediately collected them and returned, reporting everything in detail to the king.
The king was greatly delighted and said:

"The Buddha’s śramaṇas are truly excellent fields of merit; free from greed and desire, there is no group more worthy of trust than these. I pray that they may always remain within my kingdom; I shall provide for them with offerings as long as I live."
The king immediately addressed his queens:
"Take back each your own necklaces; do not scramble together to seize the finest ones.
When the bhikṣus heard these words spoken by the king and the non-Buddhist teacher, they went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If one does not take precious objects even when they are present before them, one already incurs the censure of people; how much more so for one who actually takes them?
From this day forward, taking precious objects is not permitted.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, the youth Licchavi, wearing a jeweled belt of various gems worth ten million pieces of gold, was riding out of the city in a carriage drawn by four horses for recreation; the precious belt, being heavy and smooth, he did not notice as it fell to the ground.
At that time, a bhikṣu came along from behind; seeing the jeweled girdle lying on the ground, he immediately called out:
"Young man! Young man!"
"I will take your jeweled belt.
Because of the sound of the carriage, the youth did not hear him.
Fearing that someone else might obtain it later, the bhikṣu stood waiting by the side.
As the youth was proceeding forward, he realized he had lost his belt; he immediately drove the carriage back. Seeing the bhikṣu from a distance, he asked him:
"Did you happen to see my belt as you were coming after me?"
The bhikṣu replied, "I saw one wearing a sash who called out to you from afar; it was you yourself who did not hear.
The youth then asked again:
"Where are you? He replied, "I am here."
The youth immediately stepped forward and took the belt.
Once it was fastened around his waist, he seized the bhikṣu and beat him severely on the hands and feet until they were bruised, reviling him in various ways, saying:
"If I do not give it back, you may keep the belt and take it with you!"
The bhikṣus, for these reasons, went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"If one does not grasp at that which has already arisen as a fault and affliction, how much less should one grasp at it?"
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.

At that time, some bhikṣus were on the banks of the Sū River, having removed their robes to bathe. There was then a Licchavi youth who also went to the river to bathe; he took off his earrings, covered them with his robe, and entered the water to wash.
Having finished bathing, he stepped onto the shore, put on his clothes, and departed, forgetting his earring behind him.
Later, when the bhikṣu came out and saw this earring, he immediately called out from a distance, saying:
"Young man!..."
"Child! Your earring is on the ground.
The child, being in a hurry, did not hear the call; as he walked further and further away, he realized his ear was without the ring and immediately turned back to search for it.
Calling out from afar, he asked the bhikṣu,
"Do you see my earrings?
The bhikṣu replied:
"The earrings are here; I saw them and immediately called out to you from afar, but because you were moving so swiftly, you did not hear my call.
Then the boy said, "Where are they now?"
He replied, "It is here.
The youth then took the earrings; having put them on, he seized the bhikṣu and beat him repeatedly and severely, reviling him as he did so.
“‘It is even so, my son; if I do not return, you should take this ring of mine and go.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If there is already trouble and affliction from not taking precious things, how much more so for those who actually take them!”
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove of the Śākyas, as described in detail above.

At that time, a son of the Śākyas was providing a meal for the bhikṣus; while eating together with his kinsmen, he found it inconvenient to eat because he was wearing heavy golden bracelets. He immediately removed the bracelets, placed them beside the feet of a bhikṣu, and said:
"Place these bracelets beside the feet of the ācārya."
After the bhikṣu had finished eating, he rose and departed; when another person saw him, they immediately took [the bracelet] and left.
Having completed his meal, the son of the Śākyas returned home, having forgotten to take the bracelet.
Having returned home, he realized the bracelet was missing; he went back to the original place to search for it but could not find it.
He then went to seek out the bhikṣu to whom he had entrusted it, and upon seeing him, said: "Ācārya!..."
"Return to me the bracelets I entrusted to you.
The bhikṣu replied, "I remember that you entrusted bracelets to me; they remain in their original place, for I did not take them."
The son of the Śākyas said,
"I could not find a place to deposit it and have thus lost this bracelet.
Feeling displeased in his heart, he went immediately to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I previously entrusted a bracelet to a certain bhikṣu, but he did not look after it and has now lost it.
The Buddha taught the sons of the Śākyas a Dharma discourse in accordance with their needs, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them; they departed with hearts full of joy.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had been summoned, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"If you receive a person's deposit, you should keep watch over it for them.
If you do not accept it, you should say that you have not accepted it."
"How can you accept another's entrusted property and fail to act as its custodian?
From this day forward, it is permitted within the monastery grounds to take up for oneself or have someone else take up whatever is precious or of great value."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Kapilavastu assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, whether it be actual treasure or what is considered treasure, takes it himself or causes another to take it within a monastery garden, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
As for "other times": if a bhikṣu, regarding a jewel or what is considered a jewel, takes it himself or causes another to take it, thinking:
"If there is an owner who comes seeking it, I shall give it back."
"This is called 'another occasion.
As for 'a bhikṣu,' it is as explained above.
'Within the garden' means within a stūpa garden or within a saṃgha garden."
"Jewels" refers to objects already fashioned into vessels, namely celestial crowns, jeweled canopies, necklaces, fly-whisk handles, and jeweled sandals—such are the vessels made of jewels.
"Jewels" refers to coins, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, amber, crystal, ruby, copper, bronze, lead, tin, white tin, iron, and so forth.
Regarding "taking": if one is pure, one may take it with one's own hand; if one is impure, one must have a pure person (pariśuddha-pudgala) take it.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: as explained above. Regarding "other times":

if within a stūpa garden or a saṃgha garden, if one sees treasure or what is considered treasure, if one is pure, one may take it oneself; if one is impure, one must have another person take it up and store it away.
One should form this thought:
"If there is an owner who seeks it, I shall give it.
One should not differ from such a thought.

If, at the time of the Buddha’s birth, at the time of a great assembly attaining the Path, at the time of turning the Wheel of Dharma, or during a great assembly involving Ānanda and Rāhula, people should forget their robes, ornaments, or various other items, or if a bhikṣu should forget his robe, bowl, or other belongings, and a bhikṣu sees them, he should take them up. Having taken them, he should make an announcement and ask:
"To whom do these belong?"
If the owner gives it back, that is well; if there is no one who recognizes it, one should hang it upon a pillar in a conspicuous place so that people may see it.
If someone should say, "This is my property," [one should inquire further].
One should ask:
"Where did you lose it?
If the answer is consistent [with the facts], one should give it back.
If there is no one who recognizes it, it should be kept until three months have passed.
If it is found within the precincts of a stūpa, it shall be used for the stūpa.
If it is found within the precincts of the Saṃgha, it shall be used as property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
If these are valuable items, such as precious necklaces, gold, or silver, they must not be displayed openly while proclaiming that one has obtained treasure.
The bhikṣu should carefully and minutely examine them to observe what characteristics they possess.
Only then did he raise it.
Suppose someone were to come and ask:
"I have forgotten a treasure; has anyone seen it?"
At that time, the bhikṣu should ask:
"Where did you forget it?
What are the characteristics of your treasure?"
If they are not suitable, one should say:
"This monastery is vast; you may seek a wider one.
If they are suitable, one should take out the treasure and show it, saying:
"Long-lived one! Is this your property? If he says:
"Yes. A bhikṣu must not confer it before a single person; he should assemble a large group and instruct them, saying:
"Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. If the World-Honored One had not established the precepts, you would not even have been able to look [at such things] with your own eyes."
If he says, "In addition to these jewels of mine, there are other things," one should say:
"Long-lived one! I have just obtained this and see no other object.
One should say to him:
"You are an evil person; you have already received more than enough with this alone. How can you now seek further goods and slander others?
Had the World-Honored One not established the precepts, you would not have seen these items."
If, despite this, they still do not understand, one should take them to the side of a lay follower (upāsaka) and say:
"I originally obtained these items in good faith and have returned them all; yet now I am being falsely accused."
At that time, the lay follower should rebuke him, saying:
"Just so, just so, my son!
You have already received more than enough of these goods, yet now you go so far as to slander the bhikṣu."
"You need only go!
I shall act as your counterpart to manage this matter.
If no one comes, then until the end of three years, it shall be used within its own boundary according to the place where it was obtained, as described above.
If a bhikṣu enters a village and sees an object left on the ground, he should not pick it up.
If someone picks it up and gives it to the bhikṣu, he may accept it; since the giver is the actual donor, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu enters a village and sees discarded clothing, or that which has been blown there by the wind, he must not take it; rather, he should take it with the thought that it is *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe material).

If he is on a desolate road where no people are present and sees clothing, he should take it. If he sees treasure upon the garment, he should step on it with his foot to break the connection, discard it, and then carry the garment away.
When departing, one should not conceal [the robe]; rather, one should hold it openly so that others may see it.
If there are stains upon the robe such that it would be held in contempt by others, one may cover it with something else while carrying it away.

If, at the time of taking it, one does not realize there is a precious object within the garment, and upon returning to the dwelling place one sees it, one should inform a pure attendant (śuddhakarman) and entrust him with it to manage as the value for medical requisites.

If, when departing from a village or while on the road, one sees a garment, and there is long-settled dust upon it, one should take it; having taken it, one must not conceal it, but should carry it away openly displayed.
If there is an owner pursuing a bhikṣu, he should say:
"Long-lived one!
Why are you running?"
He replied,
"I have lost my robe.
[The other] should say:
"Is this your robe? If he says, "It is."
The person should return and be instructed as follows:

"You should take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for if the World-Honored One had not established this precept, even if you had seen such a robe, you would not have been permitted to obtain it."

If one intentionally demolishes a monastery and, wishing to repair it, digs the ground to lay a foundation and discovers a treasure, and if a *kappiya-kāraka* (steward) cannot be trusted, one should inform the king. The king should say:
"This property should rightfully belong to me; I now bestow it upon the bhikṣu as a meritorious gift."
He is then called a donor.
If half has already been used and half remains, the king says:
"Why have you used my property?"
"If that which has already been used is finished, bring back what remains.
The bhikṣu should then return what remains.
If the king says:
"Why have you used my property?
Return it all!
If a bhikṣu has already used the property, he should return it using monastic property; if the Saṃgha has no property, he should beg for property to return it.
If one says,
"That which has already been used ceases; the merit belongs to me," then that is called "using for another."
If gold, silver, or precious objects are obtained while repairing an old stupa, if the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) is not to be trusted, one should inform the king;
if the *karmadāna* is trustworthy, one may take them and set them aside for three years.
After three years have passed, he should employ various materials for the construction of a stūpa.
If the royal household becomes aware of this, they will ask the bhikṣu:
"Did you find a treasure trove here?"
One should answer,
"I have obtained it.
If it has already been used, one should answer:
"Once obtained, it shall be used for this stūpa.
The king said, "Stop;
since it has already been made, this merit belongs to me."
If half has already been used and half remains, the king says:
"Cease using what has been used; that which remains shall be returned to me.
That which remains should be given to the king.
If the king says:
"Did you not know that the treasures within the earth should belong to me?
Why did you use them?"
"Return it all to me!
At that time, the bhikṣu should return the property of the stūpa.
If the stūpa has no property, he should beg for goods on behalf of the stūpa and return them.
If the king asks,
"What is said regarding the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya?
the bhikṣu should answer as follows:
"If an object is found within the grounds of a stūpa among the Buddha's teachings, it shall be used for the stūpa.
If an object is found within the grounds of the Saṃgha, it shall be used for the Saṃgha.
If the King says:
"One who acts for the sake of the Buddha-dharma incurs no offense.
If there is an iron seal with a name upon a treasure hoard, and that king asks:"
"Venerable sirs!
Do you see such a name and surname upon this treasure-vessel?
The bhikṣus should reply:
“Having seen it, I have already used it to complete a stūpa.
If he says, “This was an object belonging to my ancestors; why did you use it?”
"The user should return it to me.
If they say, "Since the stupa has already been completed, the merit belongs to me," [one should respond accordingly].
“There is no offense.
If half has already been used and half remains, return it to me.
At that time, the bhikṣu should indeed return what remains.
If one says:
"Why do you use the property of my family's ancestors?
Return it all to me!"
At that time, one should return it all; if the stūpa has property, one should use that to return it, and if there is none, one should beg for it to return it.
If they say, "This was the property of a former person; since that former person has died, this merit now belongs to them," [one should respond accordingly].
"There is no offense.
It is likewise when one receives goods from building a new monastery or building a new stūpa; therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha; the detailed exposition is as above.
In the city of Rājagṛha there were three hot springs:
the King’s Spring, the Bhikṣus’ Spring, and the Elephant’s Spring.
As for the King’s Spring, it was where the king, the ladies of the royal harem, the Buddha, and the bhikṣus would bathe.
The "Bhikṣu Hot Springs" is where the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus bathe.
The "Elephant Hot Springs" is where elephants and all people bathe.

At that time, the bhikṣus entered the King’s Hot Springs to bathe. Then the king, having anointed his body with oil, wished to enter the hot springs to bathe and asked the superintendent of the springs:
“Is the hot spring empty?
The superintendent of the springs replied, “The spring is not empty; there are bhikṣus bathing in it.”
The king said, "Let the bhikṣus bathe first; I shall go to the World-Honored One now and bathe later.
Having arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and then again questioned the superintendent:
"Is the pond empty? He replied,
"It is not yet empty."
When this had been said three times, there were still bhikṣus who did not stop bathing.
The king said, "Allow them to bathe; do not call for them to come out. I shall go back to the palace to bathe."
When the people heard this, they all spoke with reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are good and virtuous. "
"Thus, he has firmly blocked the pond so that the Great King cannot bathe.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Where is there a king who can endure all this?
From this day forward, bathing is not permitted.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept prohibiting bathing; because the bhikṣus were not permitted to bathe, their bodies became soiled with grime and emitted an odor.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma for the great assembly, the bhikṣus sat downwind, fearing that their foul odor might offend their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Buddha, knowing [the reason] yet asking on purpose: "Monks,
why are you sitting alone in one place, appearing as if you were resentful?"

The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, because the Blessed One has established the precept prohibiting bathing, our bodies have become soiled and foul-smelling. Fearing that we might offend fellow practitioners of the holy life, we have remained downwind.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit bathing once every half-month.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed account is as above.
At that time, during the heat of the spring months, the bhikṣus were unable to bathe, and their bodies became itchy and distressed.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit bathing during the two and a half months of the hot season: the last month and a half of spring and the first month of summer; this is called the 'two and a half months.'"

Furthermore, after the Buddha had completed his rains retreat while staying in Śrāvastī, he traveled through the human settlements of Kośala together with the bhikṣus. Along the way, the grasses and trees were dense; below, they were sucked by the hot vapors, and above, they were scorched by the sun, causing great suffering.
They ran toward the water like deer rushing to a pond.

The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally questioned them; the bhikṣus explained the preceding events in detail. Because of such suffering, the bhikṣus had vied with one another to run to the water. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to bathe while traveling."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
For five reasons of benefit, the World-Honored One would go on a round through the monks' quarters once every five days.
There was a bhikṣu suffering from scabies; the Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"Bhikṣu, are you at ease? He replied:
“I am not at ease; I have the itch of scabies and find pleasure in bathing frequently.
However, because the World-Honored One has established the precept that one must not bathe, I do not find pleasure.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to bathe.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, he spoke at length as above.
At that time, a bhikṣu in charge of construction affairs was carrying mud and bricks and performing various tasks; because he did not dare to bathe, he simply went to sleep as he was.
At dawn the next day, there were traces of mud upon his feet. The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"Why is there mud on your feet?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I was engaged in manual labor and my body was soiled with mud; fearing that I might violate the precepts, I did not dare to bathe, and for this reason my feet have dirt on them.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit you to bathe while working."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the bhikṣus encountered a great wind that raised clouds of dust which covered their bodies; they also encountered rain. Because the bhikṣus did not dare to bathe, they immediately went to bed.
The next morning at dawn, he went to inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being. Knowing [the reason], the Buddha nevertheless asked him:
"Bhikṣu, why is your body so stained and filthy?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Yesterday the wind blew dust onto my body, and subsequently it rained; because I did not dare to bathe, my body is now stained and filthy.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to bathe when there is a great wind.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, it was as explained in detail above.
At that time, the sky cleared and a few clouds arose; in a short while, a heavy rain fell. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the first auspicious rain of Jambudvīpa; you should bathe in it, for it can remove all diseases, sores, and scabs from within your bodies.
The bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not bathe; how then should we bathe?"
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit bathing during the rainy season.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"All bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī are to assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except during the special times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The special times are: the one month and a half following the end of spring, and the first month of summer—these two months and a half constitute the hot season;
as well as the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of travel. These are called the special times.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Half-month" means that if one bathes on the fifteenth day, when the count reaches the fifteenth day, one must bathe again.

Whether one bathes on the fourteenth, thirteenth, twelfth, eleventh, tenth, ninth, eighth, seventh, sixth, fifth, fourth, third, second, or first day, one must count from the day of bathing; it is only when the full fifteen days have been completed that one may bathe again.
Regarding "except at other times," the Blessed One stated that there is no offense.
As for "the hot season," this refers to the one month and a half following spring and the first month of summer; these two and a half months are called the hot season.
One must not take the periods before or after, but rather the present [season] itself.

Regarding "the time of illness": if a bhikṣu has ringworm, scabies, sores, carbuncles, or various other such ailments, and requires bathing for his comfort, he is permitted to bathe; this is called "the time of illness.
One should not consider the past or future, but rather take the present as the criterion.

Regarding "the time of work": if it is the time when the Saṃgha is engaged in all manner of labor—such as when a bhikṣu is plastering or repairing a dwelling, clearing drainage ditches, drawing water from a well, plastering a room, sweeping the ground, or bathing his upādhyāya or ācārya, even down to sweeping the courtyard of a stūpa or the monastery with five or six strokes of the broom—it is called "the time of work," and bathing at such times incurs no offense.
One must not take the time before or after; one should take the actual present moment.
Regarding the occasion of wind: if a bhikṣu’s body is covered with dust blown by the wind, he may bathe without incurring an offense;
he should not take into account what has already passed or what is yet to come, but should take into account the present moment.
Regarding the time of rain: if it rains from the heavens and one bathes, there is no offense;
one must not take the time before or after, but should take the actual time [of the rain].

Regarding the time of travel: within three *yojanas*, two *yojanas*, or even as little as one *krośa*, whether coming or going, this is called the time of travel; bathing during this time incurs no offense.
One must not take [the water] from before or after; one should take it from the present.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu has no other time available, he should follow the bathing method of potters: first wash both thighs and both feet, and afterwards wash the head, face, waist, back, arms, elbows, chest, and armpits. Therefore, this was said.
Kindling a fire for more than three nights; giving consent while entering a village;
slandering the Sūtras; expelling a co-resident; a novice monk’s three-colored robes;
taking precious objects; bathing once every half-month; the fifth *varga* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, while walking on his alms-round, became extremely thirsty. He entered a village and asked a woman for water, saying:
"Sister!..."
“Give me some water.
The woman then gave him some water.
Seeing insects in the water, Udāyin thought to himself:
"I shall drink only from this place where there are no insects.
As he drank, insects entered his mouth along with the water. Having finished drinking, doubt arose in his mind; for this reason, he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"How could you know that there were insects in the water and yet drink it?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not according to the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas."
"From this day forward, if you know that water contains insects,
you must not drink it. Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above,
there were two bhikṣus from the southern country of Pāṭaliputra who came together with companions to Śrāvastī to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the way, they were exhausted with thirst and lacked water; they came upon a well ahead.
One bhikṣu drew water and drank immediately, while another bhikṣu examined the water and saw insects, so he did not drink.
The bhikṣu who had drunk water asked his companion bhikṣu,
"Why do you not drink? He replied:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not drink water containing insects.
This water contains insects; therefore, it shall not be drunk.
The bhikṣu who was drinking the water urged him again, saying:
"Elder! Drink only water; do not let yourself die of thirst so that you fail to see the Buddha.
He replied:
"I would rather lose my life than violate the Buddha's precepts.
Having spoken these words, he subsequently died of thirst.
The monk who had drunk the water gradually made his way to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
from where have you come?"
He replied,
"I have come from the country of Pāṭaliputra.
The Buddha said:
“Monk! Do you have a companion? He replied:

"There were two of us traveling together as companions. Becoming thirsty and exhausted on the road with no water, we came upon a well. Although there were insects in the well water, I drank it immediately; by the strength derived from that water, I was able to come before and behold the World-Honored One."
"He maintained his precepts and did not drink, and thus he died of thirst.
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
"You do not see me, yet you think you have seen me; that deceased bhikṣu had already seen me previously.
If a bhikṣu is negligent and indolent, failing to restrain his sense faculties, then even though such a bhikṣu dwells in the same place as I, he remains far from me;
though he sees me, I do not see him."

If there is a bhikṣu on the other shore of the ocean who is able to be diligent and untiring without negligence, restraining his sense faculties, then although he is far from me, I always see him; he is always near me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. It cannot serve to nurture wholesome dharmas. From this day forward, if you know that water contains insects, you must not drink it."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...as has been heard before, it should be heard again."
"If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings and drinks it, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Creatures" refers not to fish, turtles, *śiśumāras*, and the like,
but rather to tiny, minute, and ephemeral insects, down to the most subtle forms visible to the eye.
"Water" refers to the ten kinds mentioned above.
"Drinking" means swallowing it into the stomach.
"Pāyattika" (an offense requiring expiation) is as defined previously.
As stated above:
once a bhikṣu has received full ordination, he must possess a water-strainer and perform ablutions in accordance with the Dharma.

When a bhikṣu travels, he should carry a water-strainer; if he does not have one, he should at least hold the corner of his uttarāsaṅga. When examining water, he should not do so by means of the divine eye.
Furthermore, one must not allow those with impaired vision to examine it; however, anyone who can see even the fine lines on the palm of their hand may be allowed to examine the water.

When examining the water, one must not be weary or distracted; one should examine it with a focused mind. It should neither be too fast nor too long—just for the duration of an elephant’s single turn or a bamboo cart’s single turn. If there are no insects, it may be used.
If there are insects present, one should strain the water before using it.
There are three grades of water: inferior, middling, and superior.
If the lower portion is free of insects while the middle and upper portions contain insects, one should take the insect-free water from the lower portion for use.
If there are no insects in the middle portion while there are insects in the upper and lower portions, one should take the water from the middle portion for use;
if there are no insects in the upper portion, one should take the water from the upper portion for use.
If there are insects in the upper portion [of the water], one should strike the water with the hand to cause the insects to sink to the bottom, and then take and use it.
If insects are present throughout all three portions, at that time one should strain the water before using it.
If there are extremely minute insects in the water, one must not use it for washing the hands or face, nor for the evacuation of excrement or urine.
When invited by a donor’s family to eat, one should ask at that time:
"Have you filtered the water?"
If it is said,
"It has not been strained," one should examine whether the person before them is trustworthy; if so, one should instruct them to strain the water.
If one cannot be trusted, one must not tell them to filter it, lest they harm or kill insects.
The bhikṣu should filter it himself for use; he should place the water containing insects into his own vessel and ask:
"From where did you take this water?"
He should return to the place from which he obtained it and pour the water containing insects back into it.
If the place where he first took the water was distant, and if he sees a pond whose water has not yet dried up within seven days, he may place the water with insects into that pond.
If there is no water in a pond, one should fill a vessel with water and bring it to nourish them.
If it rains heavily and there is a torrential flow, one should pour the insects into it and think:
"Go forth into the great ocean."
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on the road, becomes thirsty and requires water, he should examine it closely when reaching a well to draw water; if there are no insects, it may be used.
If there are insects, he should purify it by straining according to the aforementioned method before using it.
If one knows that there are insects in the water, one must not lend a water-drawing vessel, a rope, or any such implement to another person.
If it is pond water or stagnant water, one should inspect it before using it.
If one sees that there are insects, one must not shout out [to warn others].
"Elder! This water contains living beings; it contains living beings!
Thus he caused the man to give rise to doubt and lose his pleasure.
If someone asks,
"Are there insects in this water? one should reply:
"Venerable sir, please look for yourself.
If one knows that the person is a fellow preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), one should say:
"There are insects in this water; you should strain it before using it."
If there are no insects but one perceives them as such, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
If there are no insects but one perceives them as such, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya.
If there are insects and one perceives them as such, it is a pāyattika offense.
If there are no insects, and one perceives them as being without insects, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was fully endowed with an auspicious name, fully endowed with an auspicious nature, and fully endowed with an auspicious family;
for these three reasons, he was held in high esteem by the people of the world.
Whenever an auspicious day arrived—such as the moving into a new house, a wedding, or the piercing of ears—he would always first invite Ānanda.

On one occasion, when a certain family had invited the Venerable Ānanda for a meal, a non-Buddhist renunciant who was black-skinned, with blue eyes and a large belly, came to Ānanda’s place seeking food.
Ānanda immediately gave it to him.
Having taken it in his cupped hands and eaten it, he wiped his body with his hand and departed.
Then another non-Buddhist came and asked:
"From where did you obtain this food?
He replied,
"I obtained it from this shaven-headed householder."
Having heard these words, Ānanda was displeased in his heart; subsequently, he did not give to the beggars who came.
For this reason, Ānanda went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This person does not recognize the debt of gratitude; from this day forward, I do not permit one to give food with one's own hand to a naked ascetic who has left the household life."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the World-Honored One shaved his hair once every four months; because the people heard that the Buddha had shaved his hair, they sent various kinds of offerings.
At that time, there was a famine in the world, and five hundred people were constantly following the World-Honored One to beg for leftover food.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Is there any leftover food?"
He replied, "There is cake.
The Buddha said:
"Distribute them to the beggars.
Ānanda then gave one portion to each person; among them was a female renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect, to whom Ānanda took a cake and gave it.
Then the two portions were joined together.
Having obtained them, they sat down in one place to eat and said:
"This cake is truly exquisite and delicious; it is only a pity that it is so small, being but a single portion."
One who has received two turns says:
"I have received two turns.
One who has received one turn says:
“Ānanda, you ought to be his son-in-law; why then has he given you only two sets?
Having heard this, Ānanda was displeased and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to give food with your own hands to male or female naked ascetics (nirgrantha).
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is it that these non-Buddhists do not recognize as a debt of gratitude?
The Buddha said, “It is not only today that they fail to recognize a debt of gratitude; in past lives, too, they were already like this.”
"This has been explained in detail in the *Ṛṣimarka-jātaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male or female outsider who has gone forth without robes, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding those without robes: they may enter without robes and exit with robes; enter with robes and exit without robes; enter with robes and exit with robes; or enter without robes and exit without robes.
"Those who have left the household life" refers to those who have gone forth among the non-Buddhist sects, from Pūraṇa Kāśyapa down to the Nirgranthas.
"With one's own hand" means receiving it hand-to-hand or receiving it vessel-to-vessel.
"Food" refers to the five kinds of primary food and the five kinds of mixed primary food.
"To give" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu’s parents, brothers, or sisters have gone forth among the non-Buddhist sects, he must not give them food with his own hands; he should instead have a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) give it to them.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one should tell them to take the food themselves.
If one fears that the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) will eat it all, one should say: "Give it to me."
Having received it, one should take as much as desired according to one's wish; then, if it is placed upon a bed, a table, or on the ground, one should say:
"Take this food yourself.
If it is a relative or an outsider (tīrthika) who speaks with such resentment:
“You have now treated me like a *caṇḍāla*.
The bhikṣu should reply:
“You have no place in the renunciant order; such is the training rule established by the World-Honored One. If you wish to eat, then eat; if you do not wish to eat, it is as you please.”
If a bhikṣu has an outsider perform work for him, he must not give food with his own hands; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) give it.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he should give it according to the method described above.
If non-Buddhists come seeking rice gruel, soup, or fermented grain water, one must not give these with one's own hand.
If non-Buddhists beg for alms from within the community of monks, one must not give with one's own hand; rather, one should place it on the ground and give it to them.

If a non-Buddhist has faith and wishes to make an offering to a bhikṣu, at that time one must not give food or drink with one's own hand; rather, one may have the non-Buddhist prepare the food and drink and have them present it.
Having finished eating, he gave what remained; the method for giving was as explained above.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was living in the same village as a brahmin friend.
This brahmin’s daughter had married and was living in another village; she sent a messenger back to inform her father, saying:
"Please come to see me from time to time. If you, sir, are unable to come, I pray that you send the teacher Udāyin to see me from time to time."
As explained at length in the two previous cases of the undetermined offenses, up until the Buddha’s words: “Udāyin!
This is an evil deed.”
"Even householders know the proper conduct and laws of śramaṇas; how is it that you who have left the home life do not know where one should sit and where one should not?
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching; by this, one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu knowingly sits in a place of sexual intimacy at a house where food is being provided, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu knowingly sits in a secluded place at a house where food is being provided, it is a pāyattika.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing for oneself or hearing from another.
"Food" refers to parched grain, rice, wheat porridge, fish, meat, and various other such items; these are called food.

Furthermore, there are things called "food": when visual consciousness perceives forms, it gives rise to affectionate thoughts and produces desire and attachment; the same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, and body.

Furthermore, there are things called "food": a cauldron takes its lid as food, a mortar takes its pestle as food, and a winnowing basket takes its measure as food—all such things as these are called food.
Furthermore, there are names for foods: men are the food of women, and women are the food of men.
As for "families," they are the families of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
"A place of sexual intercourse" refers to a place where husband and wife engage in sexual desire.
"Sits" means to sit together in one place; [if this occurs], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"A family engaged in eating" is as described above.
"A secluded place" refers to a location where men and women may engage in sexual intercourse without shame.
Furthermore, there is that which is called a "secluded place," such as a dark interior or a closed door; all these are termed secluded places.
To sit together in one such place constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu sits in the same place as that couple, it is one *pāyattika*.
If another bhikṣu is at a distance and does not see them, it is two *pāyattikas*.
If one sits in a place suitable for sexual intercourse, in a secluded place, or with the door shut, and an outside monk does not see from afar, there are two *pāyattikas*.
If an outside monk sees, there is one *pāyattika*.
It is the same when sitting together within a gatehouse.
It is also the same if there is a screen made of a heap of sugarcane, a heap of grain, or a wall in the middle courtyard.
If there is a monk as a companion, there is no offense.
Even if there are many lay companions, there is still an offense.
If all are men, there is no offense; if all are women, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, a minister of Kośala named Mṛgāra, a kṣatriya, had rebelled. King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army, selected an auspicious day, and together with his ministers, struck the bells and drums, intending to go and suppress the rebellion.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda and Upānanda went before the army and stood there.
When the king saw them, he immediately withdrew his parasol, bowed low, and paid them respect from afar.
When the ministers saw this, they immediately expressed their disapproval, saying:
"Look at these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; they do not know the proper time. Now that the Great King wishes to campaign against the rebellious invaders, they stand right before the army."

Furthermore, they were displeased that the Great King, amidst his host of officers and soldiers, had sought an auspicious day for profit and, upon seeing a shaven-headed śramaṇa, had immediately removed his parasol and bowed his body from afar to pay him respect.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call Nanda and Upananda here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"How can all these kings possess such faith?
From this day forward, I do not permit you to enter military camps to meet them."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu observes an army setting out on an expedition, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
"An army setting out on an expedition" refers to one that takes up weapons and marches toward another country.
There are four kinds of military forces:
the elephant force, the cavalry, the chariot force, and the infantry.
As for the elephant force: four men protect the feet of each elephant; this is called the elephant force.
As for the cavalry, eight men protect each horse's hooves; this is called the cavalry.
As for the chariot force, sixteen men protect each chariot; this is called the chariot force.
As for the infantry, it consists of thirty-two men who carry weapons; this is called the infantry.
These constitute the fourfold army.
If a bhikṣu observes any one of these four types of troops, it is a pāyattika offense.

If a bhikṣu, wishing to view an army, goes from a village to a forest hermitage or from a forest hermitage to a village; from a low place to a high place or from a high place to a low place; from a covered place to an open place or from an open place to a covered place—whosoever goes to view it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, while on the road entering a village or town, encounters a military array and does not form the intention [to look], he is without offense.
If he forms the intention, raises his head or lowers it to peer out with the desire to see, and sees it, it is a pāyattika.

If the king goes out, or when a great elephant goes out, and the streets and alleys are so crowded that they are filled, it is no offense for a bhikṣu to remain in one place at that time without paying attention to what is happening.
If one intentionally intends to watch, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If a bhikṣu watches elephants, horses, oxen, and so forth fighting, even down to watching cocks fight, he incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If an army comes to the monastery, there is no offense if one does not intentionally look at it.
If one intentionally looks at it, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Even down to a verbal dispute among people, if one looks [at it], there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, there was a Kṣatriya minister in the kingdom of Kośala named Mṛṇāla, who had rebelled and was not submissive.
At that time, King Prasenajit dispatched the minister Daṇḍapāṇi, leading the fourfold army, intending to go on a punitive expedition.
Then, Daṇḍapāṇi sent a messenger to inform the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now setting out on this military campaign; I pray that you will send some bhikṣus to preach the sublime Dharma for me."
Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Go to the army and preach the Dharma to Daṭṭhāna.
Having arrived, the minister immediately provided him with various kinds of offerings.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that various offerings had been prepared for Ānanda, went to the army camp after their meal and visited the place where the troops were being inspected. Seeing those who were incapable, they spoke with disparagement:

"Your efforts at riding elephants are like those of a person mounted on a pig! Having consumed the King’s food and drink for this, if you enter the battle, you will surely lose your own lives and cause the King to lose his elephants."
If he sees one who is capable, he praises him, saying:
"You are skilled at riding elephants and expert at handling the hook; you are proficient in turning left and right and well-versed in the arts of combat; you ought to receive an official stipend."
"By entering the fray with this, one can save oneself and not lose the elephant.
If he observes someone riding a horse and sees that they are incompetent, he then disparages them, saying:
"You imitate others in riding a horse like one riding a donkey; you have wasted the King's food and drink."
"If you enter the fray with this, you will surely lose your life and also forfeit the king's horse.
But if he sees one who is skilled, he praises him, saying:
"You are truly adept at riding; your mastery of the reins is exquisite, and you possess the skillful means to turn left and right. You ought to receive the king's bounty."
"By entering the fray with this, you will surely be able to save yourself and not lose your horse.
If he observes someone riding a chariot and sees that they are incompetent, he disparages them, saying:
"You imitate others in riding a chariot as if it were mounting a bed; you have merely wasted the King's provisions."
"If one enters the ranks with this, they will surely lose their own life and also forfeit the King's chariot.
However, if he sees one who is capable, he praises them, saying:
"This artisan is skilled at holding the reins and proficient in advancing and retreating; his maneuvers to the left and right are most skillful, and he deserves the King's bounty."
"By entering the fray with this, you will surely be able to save yourself and not lose your chariot.
If he observes the infantry and sees those who cannot shoot, he disparages them, saying:
"You merely imitate others in grasping the bow, like one trying to spin wool; you consume the state's stipend in vain."
"Entering battle with this, one will surely lose their own life and forfeit the official bow.
Upon seeing a skilled archer, he praised him, saying:
"Your aim is level, upright, and perfect; you are truly a master archer and ought to receive official emoluments."
"Entering battle with these, one will surely save oneself and not lose one's bow.
Seeing those who held swords and shields, he would disparage them, saying:
"You imitate others in holding your shield; it is like grasping a cloth knife."
"If you enter the fray with this, you will surely lose your own life and forfeit your official weapons.
If he sees one who is skilled, he further praises him, saying:
"You are excellent at using the sword and shield; you are truly most clever and capable."
"By entering the battle with this, you will surely preserve your life and not lose the king's weapons.
Having thus disparaged and praised the four types of troops, those who had been disparaged each said in anger:
"Not only is the Malla Kṣatriya our enemy, but now this śramaṇa is also a thief; since he has insulted us, we shall kill him together."
Those who had received praise spoke to those who had been reviled, saying:

"These śramaṇas are all of royal lineage, or of great ministerial lineage, or of the kṣatriya caste; they have all practiced the arts of war from their youth and are well-versed in the deployment of battle arrays."
As it was said: "It would be a great folly for you to learn from his words and yet instead resent him.
