Having formed this thought, when the time arrived, he sent him back.
Fearing that he might miss his meal, he kept watch over the time and returned very quickly.

Once the assembly had finished eating, he went out through the gate of the Jetavana and paced back and forth as if wandering idly. Seeing him from afar approaching with parched lips, it appeared as though he had not received food.

If one intends to kill those who have already died, those who are dying at the present moment, or those who will die later, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If there are none at all who are to die, it is still a *pāyattika*; this is called "action" (*caryā*).

Regarding the *vidyā-mantra*: if a bhikṣu, for the purpose of killing an animal, recites a *vidyā-mantra* to raise a dead person, at the moment he chants the mantra, he commits a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline) with mental regret.
If one’s hair stands on end with terror, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*viniya-āpatti*).
If a person dies as a result of this, it is a *pāyattika* offense; this is called the *vidyā-mantra*.

Regarding "powdered incense" (*kṣema-ma*): if a bhikṣu, for the sake of killing an animal, prepares powdered incense and scatters it over the body of a living being, desiring to cause it to wither and die.
When employing the means, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya with mental regret.
If one touches their body, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If they die as a result, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding "snare": if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, sets a snare at a place where animals constantly roam, eat, or drink, he commits a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline) and incurs mental remorse.
If one touches their body, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
If they die as a result, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called a "snare.
As for a "trap": if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, [places a trap] at a place where animals constantly roam, eat, or drink.
When setting a snare, one commits a *vinayātikrama* through mental transgression.
If one touches the body [of the animal], it is a *vinaya*-offense.
If death results from this, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called a "snare."

Regarding "pits and ditches": if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, constructs a pit or ditch at a place where animals constantly roam, eat, or drink, and covers it over with grass and soil, at the time of its construction, he commits a *vyatikrama* (transgression) and incurs mental remorse (*citta-vipratisāra*).
When one falls into it, there is an offense of violating the Vinaya (*viniya-āpatti*).
If one dies as a result of this, it is a *pāyattika* offense; this is called a pit or trench.
Regarding the path: if a bhikṣu is walking at the edge of a path and sees a beast coming, having seen it, he thinks thus:
"Now I shall ensure that not a single one of these escapes.

Driven by this murderous intent toward a place of terror filled with lions, tigers, and wolves—or when driving them toward a king's hunting grounds—he commits a violation of the Vinaya and feels remorse in his heart.
If [the animal] suffers pain, it is a *vinaya-āpatti*.
If it dies as a result, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "on the path.
Regarding "a river": if a monastery is near a riverbank and a bhikṣu is walking up and down on the bank when a beast comes along, the bhikṣu, having seen it, forms this thought:
"Now I shall cause not a single one of these animals to survive.

With this murderous intent, he drives them toward a place where there is no rescue, or toward a place of swirling eddies and capsizing, or toward a place of *śiṃśumāra* crocodiles; or when driving them across to the other shore where there are lions, tigers, and wolves, or toward a place where the king hunts, he incurs a violation of the Vinaya through mental remorse.
When the victim experiences pain, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If the victim dies as a result, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called a "river.
When a monk seizes a knife with the intent to kill, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If [the victim] experiences pain and suffering, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If they die as a result of this, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to two bhikṣus or a multitude of bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of killing, gives a knife and sends a messenger—whether it be one person, two persons, or even many people—it is the same.
If the messenger further sends another messenger, and so on until many people are given the knife, there is a violation of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance (*vyatikrama-citta-kaukṛtya*).
If she experiences pain, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she dies as a result, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to [administering] medicine, poison, ointments, emetics, purgatives, or causing an abortion, as explained in detail in the section on "Swords."
If a bhikṣu, having fulfilled five conditions, takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
What are the five?
An animal, the perception of an animal, the intent to kill, the initiation of physical action, and the severing of the life-faculty—these are called the five conditions.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, wishing to cause the group of sixteen bhikṣus to feel doubt and regret, spoke as follows:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept: those who have reached twenty years of age are permitted to receive full ordination.
You have received full ordination before reaching twenty; therefore, you are not said to have received full ordination.”
Having heard these words, he immediately wept bitterly.
The Buddha, hearing the sound of his crying, knew the cause yet asked:
"What child is this whose voice cries out?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“It was the group of six bhikṣus who, wishing to cause the group of sixteen bhikṣus to fall into doubt and remorse, spoke these words:
‘The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must be twenty years of age to receive full ordination.’”
"You all received full ordination before you had completed twenty years of age; therefore, you have not truly received full ordination.
Having heard these words, they wept for this reason.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned them thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"Why is this so? He replied,
"Because I was seeking amusement."
The Buddha said:
"Foolish man! This is an evil deed;
you cause distress to those who practice the holy life while speaking of it as a source of playful amusement."
The Buddha said, "Do not despise him;
if he enters meditative concentration, by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he could hurl you to another world-system.
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities."
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to cause other bhikṣus to fall into doubt or regret.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to give rise to doubt or regret, such that for even a moment he is unhappy, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Formerly" means having previously performed the preparatory rites (*pūrvakṛta-upāya*).
"Doubt and regret" consist of seven matters:
birth, the formal act (*karmavācanā*), physical appearance, illness, offenses, verbal abuse, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
"One who has taken birth" refers to one who speaks thus:
"Venerable sir!"

The World-Honored One has established the precept that one who has reached the age of twenty may receive full ordination; since you have not reached twenty yet received full ordination, it does not count as having received full ordination.
Having spoken these words with the intent to cause doubt, whether the person before him becomes doubtful or not, it is all a *pāyattika*; this is called "arousing.
As for the formal act (*kamma*), one speaks as follows:

"Elder! The World-Honored One has established the precepts: the procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*) is a method free from obstruction. Your motion was not accomplished, your proclamation was not accomplished, and the assembly was not accomplished; since each of these was not accomplished in this way, you have not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), nor can you be said to have received full ordination."

Having spoken these words with the intent to cause another to feel doubt or regret, whether the other person subsequently feels doubt and regret or does not, it is a *pāyattika* offense; this is called a formal act (*kamma*).
Regarding physical characteristics, one should say:
"Venerable sir!

The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that only those whose bodies are fully formed are permitted to receive full ordination. You, however, have a hunched back, are lame, blind in one eye, have clubbed feet, a protruding head, saw-like teeth, or are otherwise physically incomplete; thus, even if you were to receive full ordination, it would not be called receiving full ordination."

Having spoken these words with the intent to cause another to feel doubt or regret—whether the other person subsequently feels doubt and regret or does not—the offense is a pāyattika; this is called "indication by physical appearance."
The sick person says:
"Venerable sir!
The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting the reception of full ordination for those who are not ill."
If you have scabies, eczema, jaundice, pustules, boils, or hemorrhoids—if you receive full ordination while afflicted by such various diseases—it is not called receiving full ordination.

Having spoken these words with the intent to cause doubt and remorse—if the other person feels doubt and remorse, or does not feel doubt and remorse—in either case it is a *pāyattika*. This is called the offense of "sickness.
Regarding the offense: one speaks as follows:
"Elder! The World-Honored One has established the precepts, decreeing that only those who are pure may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
You have committed offenses of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *vinayātikrama*; yet, having received full ordination, it cannot be said that you have truly received it."

Having spoken these words with the intent to cause doubt and regret—if the other person experiences doubt and regret, or does not experience doubt and regret—in either case it is a *pāyattika*; this is called an offense.
As for "reviling," it means speaking as follows:
"Elder! The Blessed One has established the precepts such that those who receive full ordination with joy are permitted to do so.
Since you received full ordination while being displeased, angry, and abusive, it cannot be called 'having received full ordination.'"

When one speaks these words with the intent to cause doubt or remorse—if the other person feels doubt or remorse, or does not feel doubt or remorse—it is all a *pāyattika* offense; this is called reviling.
The one who had taken the vow said this:
"Venerable sir!
The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting those who are wise and discerning to receive full ordination."
"You are foolish and lacking in wisdom, like a lump of clay, like a ram, a horned owl, or a white crane; though you have received full ordination, it shall not be called receiving full ordination.
When these words were spoken, he intended to cause doubt and regret.
Whether he feels doubt and regret or does not feel doubt and regret, it is all a *pāyattika* offense; this is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
If someone comes wishing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), if he is twenty years of age, one should grant him full ordination;
if he is not yet twenty, one should say to him:
"Wait! Wait until the twenty-year requirement is fulfilled.
If he should receive full ordination elsewhere and then come here, you must not speak to him in a way that would cause him doubt or regret.
To speak [thus] is an offense against the Vinaya.
If a bhikṣu is on the verge of receiving full ordination, but the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished, he should snap his fingers and say:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Your *karmavācanā* was not accomplished.
If one does not speak at that time, one must not later speak so as to cause doubt or regret by saying:
"When you received full ordination, the motion (*jñapti*) was not accomplished, the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished, and the assembly (*saṃgha*) was not accomplished."
If one speaks [of such a person], it is an offense against the Vinaya.
If a person is blind, hunchbacked, lame, or otherwise physically impaired, and has not yet received full ordination, one should say to them:
"Stay there for now."
If someone comes from another place having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one must not speak to them in a way that causes doubt or regret.
To do so constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
If a sick person comes wishing to receive full ordination, one should say:
"Stop for a moment.
If he then receives full ordination elsewhere and returns, one must not speak to him in a way that causes doubt or regret.
To speak in such a manner constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
If a bhikṣu harbors doubt or regret, it is a pāyattika;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a vinayātikrama offense.
If it is a layperson, there is transgression of the Vinaya and mental remorse.
Therefore, this is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus frequently changed their robes, wearing one garment before the meal and another after the meal.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked them intentionally:
"What kind of garments are these?"
He replied,
“This is a robe given as a pure gift by me.
The Buddha said:
“How is it that you give away a purified gift of robe-cloth to another, yet continue to use it as one of your three robes without relinquishing it?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to use a purified gift of robe-cloth without having relinquished it.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and later uses it without relinquishing his claim to it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"Monk" is as explained above.
"Gives" means to give through a formal act of purification (*pārisuddhi*) to one of five types of persons.
"Does not relinquish" means that he does not relinquish it later.
Regarding "use": to use [the robe] as one of the three robes constitutes a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu has many robes and, having forgotten them, does not recognize which are his, he should take all the robes, gather them in one place, and relinquish them by saying these words:
"This robe is given as a pure gift to [Name]; [Name] has no regard for me; I now relinquish it.
If it is one of the three robes, one should relinquish them individually:
"This is among my three robes; this saṃghāṭī was previously accepted and maintained, and I now relinquish it."
"This saṃghāṭī is among my three robes; I now accept and maintain it.
"This uttarāsaṅga is among my three robes; having previously accepted and maintained it, I now relinquish it."
"This *uttarāsaṅga* is among my three robes; I now accept and maintain it.
"This *antarvāsaka* is among my three robes; previously accepted and maintained, I now relinquish it."
"This *antarvāsa* is among my three robes; I now accept and maintain it.
"This is among my three robes; I accept and maintain it so as not to be separated from it overnight."
Any other robes with a length of two cubits and a width of one cubit or more must all be formally dedicated through the ritual of *viśuddha-dāna*.
As for the method of formal dedication, one should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I give this long robe to [Name]; [Name] shall not take it into account for me. When there is a necessary occasion for washing, dyeing, or sewing it, I shall relinquish it for use."
Having accepted and maintained them, and having purified them for offering, one should place them on the robe-rack and remember and keep them in mind every day.
If one should forget, one should say to the co-practitioner disciple or the dependent disciple:
"These are my three robes; you should assist me in remembering and identifying them every day."
If there is no disciple [to whom it may be given], one should write characters on the corner of the robe.
If one uses it oneself while facing [the donor] and having made a pure gift (pariṣkāra-deya) without relinquishing it, it is a pāyattika.
If one receives a pure gift (śuddha-dāna) while not in the presence of the donor and uses it without relinquishing it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one receives a pure gift in the presence of the donor and uses it without relinquishing it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if one does not relinquish the use [of the robe] in the presence of another person, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not recognize the robe, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one lacks the three robes, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one discards [the robe] at one time and accepts it at another, there is an offense of violating the Vinaya (viniya-āpatti).
If one does not discard it but uses it as one of the three robes, there is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not discard it but uses it for a stūpa, for the Saṃgha, or gives it to another person, there is an offense of violating the Vinaya.

"One must not perform the ritual of *śuddhika-dāna* (purification through giving) in the presence of the recipient; one should perform the *śuddhika-dāna* in the presence of another person. Thus it was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, before the meal, the group of six bhikṣus took another’s saṃghāṭī robe and took another’s bowl, hiding them in a different place.
When it was time for these bhikṣus to go begging for alms and they wished to enter the village, they could not find their saṃghāṭī robes.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who could not find his bowl. This bhikṣu asked the elder bhikṣus:
"Who has taken my saṃghāṭī?
He asked again:
"Who has taken my bowl?
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus laughed and said:
"Elder!..."
"This monastery is large; simply search for it.
He searched immediately, but after a long time he did not find it.
He spoke again:
"Elder! What do you wish to hire me for?
I shall assist you in seeking it."
Having heard these words, he knew it was his own store.
After the meal, he again hid away his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and needle case.
When the other monks had finished eating and wished to sit in meditation in the forest, they could not find their sitting mats and said:
"Elder! Who has taken my *niṣīdana*?
Another bhikṣu said:
"Who has taken my needle case?
The group of six bhikṣus laughed and said,
"Venerable sir!"
"This monastery is large; simply search everywhere.
He then searched, but after a long time he found nothing.
[The other] spoke to him again:
"What will you pay me?
I shall assist you in your search.
Having heard these words, he realized that this was his own hidden treasure.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha questioned them in detail about the aforementioned matter.
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason is this so?
He replied:
“For the sake of amusement.
The Buddha said,
“Foolish man!”

"This is an evil matter; to speak of playful amusement while causing distress to those who practice the holy life together is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit joking or laughing while hiding another's robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, or needle case.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu hides another’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—even in jest—it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Robes" refers to the seven kinds of robes.
"Alms bowls" refers to earthenware bowls and iron bowls.
There are three types of bowls: [earthenware, iron, and stone].
Superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), it is as permitted by the World-Honored One.
Regarding the needle case, it is a tube containing needles.
"Concealing" means whether one conceals it oneself or causes another to conceal it, even in jest, it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If one conceals any one of the three robes among the set of three robes, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one conceals the saṃkakṣikā or other such garments, it is a vinayātikrama offense.
If one conceals any one of the three types of bowls, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one hides keys, locks, or other implements, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
To hide a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is a *pāyattika*.
To hide other bedding or requisites is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding the needle case: if there are needles stored within it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If there are no needles, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If thread-needles are stored within it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one hides a needle without thread, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one hides a needle with thread, but merely removes the thread and conceals it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To hide a bhikṣu’s robe out of playful mockery is a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a vinayātikrama;
down to a layperson, it is a vinayātikrama with mental repentance.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rose from their meditation hall and stood in a secluded, dark place. With ears pricked up, faces contorted, eyes rolled back, and tongues protruding, they made whistling sounds to terrify the group of sixteen bhikṣus.
When the group of sixteen bhikṣus heard this, they were immediately seized with fear and cried out at the top of their voices.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"What is the sound of these children crying?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon the group of six bhikṣus."
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus,
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," [the Buddha said].
"For what reason is it so?"
He replied,
"For the sake of amusement.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! This is an evil deed;
to cause distress to those who practice the holy life for the sake of frivolous amusement.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Do not despise him; if he enters meditative absorption, he could use his supernormal power to hurl you to another world-system.
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot thereby cultivate wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on the city of Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Terrifies" means by means of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; [if he does so], it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.

"Form" refers to making a terrifying appearance by standing in a dark place with ears pricked up, face contorted, eyes rolled back, tongue protruded, or even by curling a single finger and making "u-u" sounds.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika* offense; this is called "form.

Regarding "sound": making the sound of an elephant, the sound of a horse, the sound of a donkey, or various other such sounds; or making a long sound suddenly stop, or a sudden sound drawn out long, even to the point of making a gesture with the ears to produce a terrifying appearance.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika*;
this is called "sound. Regarding "fragrance," one says:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Within this there is the scent of snakes, the scent of *pūtana* malevolent spirits, and the scent of scorpions.
By creating such various terrifying appearances, whether the person is afraid or not, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "scent."
Regarding "touch," it consists of heat and cold, lightness and heaviness, smoothness and roughness.

As for heat: if one uses fire, or if one uses the sun to heat a robe, an alms bowl, or a cooking vessel, and rubs a door-key against them to make them hot and then brings that touch to another's body, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Fire is breaking out!
Fire is breaking out!
Thus he created a terrifying spectacle.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "heat.
Regarding "cold": if one uses a fan or the wind from a garment, or sprinkles water, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Snow and rain!
Snow and rain!
Thus did he create these terrifying signs.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika* offense; this is called "cold.
Regarding "heavy": holding heavy bundles, grasping heavy woolen blankets, and pressing them down, one says:
"Venerable sir!..."
"The wall is collapsing!
The wall is collapsing!
Thus did he create a terrifying appearance.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "heavy.
As for "light":
covering [the body] with various light, fine garments and saying these words:
"Elder! Cloud-fall! Cloud-fall!"
If one creates such a terrifying appearance,
whether the other person is afraid or not,
it is a pāyattika.
This is called "light and smooth.
If the stalk of an *utpala* flower, the stalk of a *kumuda* flower, or the stalk of a *saugandhika* flower touches his body, he says:
"Venerable sir!..."
"It is a snake!
It is a snake!"—
thus he manifested a terrifying appearance.
Whether he fears it or does not fear it, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "smooth.
Regarding "rough": if one touches his body with the stalk of a *padma* flower or the stalk of a *puṇḍarīka* flower and says, "Venerable sir!..."
"This is a centipede.
Making such a terrifying gesture, whether the other person is afraid or not, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "roughness" (*khara*).
If a bhikṣu causes fear, it is a pāyattika;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a vinayātikrama offense.
Down to ordinary laypeople, they must confess their transgressions of the Vinaya with mental remorse.
Therefore, it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, where he was venerated by devas and humans, bringing benefit to many.
At that time, there were two sisters in the city of Śrāvastī who were pregnant but had not yet given birth; they were lay followers who had left the household life to practice the Path.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw the appearance of their bellies, they immediately drove them out. Because of this matter, [the sisters] went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "There is no fault for a laywoman who becomes pregnant.
Later, this bhikṣuṇī gave birth to a son whom she named Kāśyapa the Boy. When he reached the age of eight, he left the household life to follow the Way and became an arhat.

Together with a group of sixteen bhikṣus, each carrying a basin for washing, they went to the banks of the Ajiravatī River to bathe. Once they had entered the water, they floated about face-up and face-down, playing as they crossed back and forth, splashing the water and bathing themselves.
At that time, King Prasenajit was atop a multi-storied pavilion, looking out in all directions.
As the king had not yet placed his faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, upon witnessing this event, his lack of faith redoubled;
he immediately said to Queen Mallikā, “Look at the field of merit to which your family pays homage.”
The lady, possessing deep faith and free from doubt, did not look back but immediately replied:
"Great King!

Perhaps he is a youth who has recently left the household life and received full ordination, and thus does not yet know the precepts; or perhaps the World-Honored One has not yet established this rule. It is for these reasons that he acts thus."
The king said to the queen:
"It is just as when the head of a household speaks, his kinsmen follow;
or as when a preceptor or an ācārya speaks, his disciples follow."
Whenever the śramaṇa Gautama speaks, his disciples all say: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
"So it is, Sugata! Yet as I spoke with you,
you did not turn your head to look back."
At that time, the Venerable Elder Kāśyapa entered the fourth dhyāna at the crown of his head within the water; hearing the king’s voice with his divine ear, he spoke thus to his fellow bhikṣus:
"Elders!..."
The king’s lack of faith redoubled.
Mallikā felt displeasure arise in her heart and said, "I shall now cause him to give rise to a joyful mind.
They all replied: [as she commanded].
“Excellent!

Each of them immediately took up a basin, filled it with water, and placed it before him; then, sitting cross-legged and arranged in successive rows, they ascended into the void and passed through the air above the king’s palace.

At that time, Queen Mallikā was sitting in an open space; having seen the shadow of her own form, she looked up and beheld them seated in successive rows in the *paryaṅka* posture, all carrying water vessels and departing through the air like a king of geese.
Having seen this, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately said to the king:
"Behold, such is the divine virtue of the field of merit in my home.
When the king saw this, his heart was also filled with great joy, and he spoke these words:
“Excellent! I have gained a great benefit. I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will remain within my kingdom for the rest of their lives as a field of merit.
When the bhikṣus heard of the king’s displeasure, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of sixteen bhikṣus here. When they had arrived,
the Buddha questioned them thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"I now punish you; because of this, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu plays in water, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "water," there are ten kinds.
"Playing" refers to jumping, crossing over, returning across, submerging, emerging, splashing, patting, and splashing water.
This constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "a *pāyattika*," it is as explained above.
Regarding "jumping": if one jumps into the water for the sake of sport, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one falls into the water because the bank collapses while walking, or if one falls into the water because a moving boat strikes the shore or is jolted by wood or stones, there is no offense. This is called "jumping."
Regarding crossing: if one crosses water for the sake of sport, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one intends to cross, or is crossing objects, or if there is business concerning the Saṃgha or the stūpa on the opposite bank that requires frequent management, there is no offense. If one wishes to learn how to swim across, there is no offense.
If one returns to cross the water for the sake of play, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one returns to retrieve something that has been lost or forgotten for the sake of the object itself, there is no offense.
As for "submerging," if one submerges oneself in water for the sake of play, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bowl, a small bowl, a bronze vessel, or other utensils fall into the water and one retrieves them by submerging, there is no offense.
If one submerges oneself for the purpose of bathing, there is no offense.
Regarding entering and exiting [the water]: if one enters or exits the water for the sake of play, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is for the purpose of retrieving an object, there is no offense.
Regarding "pushing aside": if one pushes aside water for the sake of play, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the surface of the water is hot and one pushes aside the upper layer to take up the cooler water below, there is no offense.
Regarding "splashing": if one splashes water for the sake of play, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are *udakajantuka* insects on the surface of the water, there is no offense if one splashes them so they sink to the bottom in order to take up the insect-free water.
If one splashes water from the water onto the bank for the sake of play, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one splashes water from the bank into the water, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one pours water onto water, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one pours water onto land, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
However, if a bhikṣu is ill and faints from bloodletting on the head, or faints from a feverish illness, there is no offense in sprinkling him with cold water.
If a bhikṣu falls asleep while reciting the sūtras, it is no offense to sprinkle him with cold water.
If a śrāmaṇera causes a disturbance during a meal, and the administrator sprinkles water on him to prevent laypeople from losing faith, there is no offense; this is called "sprinkling water."
If one bathes an upādhyāya or ācārya and draws figures on their back with water, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of amusement at a meal, draws figures or writes characters on a bowl, a cooking pot, or any vessel with water, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya.
If, while pouring water on one’s feet, one draws lines on wood, or on jars, pots, or vases, for each instance there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one snaps one's fingers in the water to make a sound, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
To catch water by leaping into the air constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days—the days of the fast—bhikṣuṇīs came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and paid their respects.

At that time, sixteen groups of bhikṣus were sitting in one place not far from the Buddha; the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā and the śrāmaṇerī Tiṣyā also came to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being.

Having paid his respects and inquired after their well-being, he went to where the group of sixteen bhikṣus was; because they were of similar age and shared a mutual fondness for one another, he sat down among them.
Because he did not sit properly, they saw him, pointed at one another, and laughed.

At that time, there was a brahmin who was extremely ugly, with a hunched back and clubbed feet. He brought a young, beautiful wife to see the bhikṣus; after the bhikṣus had laughed, he thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas saw how ugly I am while bringing such a beautiful wife; they must surely be laughing at me."
He immediately spoke with anger, saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the rules of decorum;
they mock me with their expressions. The bhikṣus then replied:
"I am not laughing at you," the Brahmin said. "That is not so!"
"He is merely laughing at me.
Having spoken these words, he went to where the Buddha was and said:
"How extraordinary!"
"Gautama!
These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, do not know the rules of decorum; seeing that I am ugly, they have brought along their beautiful wives and are mocking my appearance.
The Buddha then gave a discourse to the brāhmaṇa in accordance with his needs, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; the brāhmaṇa departed with a joyful heart.
After they had departed, the Buddha said:
"Call the sixteen groups of bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
“There was a brahmin who was extremely ugly, yet he took a beautiful wife. When you saw this, did you not truly laugh?
He replied, “I did not laugh, O Brahmin.”
“Whom are you laughing at? He replied,
“World-Honored One!”

On this day of fasting, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā and the śrāmaṇerikā Tiṣyā came to where I was; because they were not sitting properly, I saw them and pointed them out to one another, which is why I smiled.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct was sitting improperly; you should have used skillful means to make her rise. Why did you laugh at her?
You shall now be punished, and because of this, I shall establish a precept for all my disciples."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu points with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
To point with one finger constitutes a pāyattika offense.
This applies even to a single finger;
for all fingers, it is a *pāyattika*. If one uses a clenched fist or fingers [to strike], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one points with a piece of wood or a bamboo stalk, it is a *vinaya*-offense.
If monks are quarreling and point at one another with their fingers, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the monk on duty or the administrator assigns food by pointing with his finger and saying:
"If you say, 'So-and-so, go,' it is a *pāyattika*.
If one points with a bamboo or wooden finger, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense."
One should say:
"So-and-so, it is your turn to eat; please go.
If a śrāmaṇera is asleep and one wishes to call him awake, one should snap one's fingers.
If they do not wake up, one must not poke them with a finger; rather, one should pull at their clothes to wake them.
If various bhikṣus are sitting in the home of a layperson and a mahallaka bhikṣu is sitting improperly, one should say to him:
"Sit properly."
If he does not perceive it, one should say:
"Straighten your robe.
If he still does not perceive it, one should say:
“Mahāra, cover your body.
If a bhikṣu sits within a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra, and after the bhikṣuṇīs have prostrated at the bhikṣu’s feet, they sit before him.
If one is sitting improperly, one must not speak to them to cause shame; rather, one should employ skillful means to have them rise and take up their belongings.

If one is sitting in the house of a donor (*dānapati*) and a woman comes to pay homage at the feet of a bhikṣu and sits before him improperly, one must not speak to her to cause shame; instead, one should employ skillful means to dismiss her so that she may take up her belongings.
If a lewd woman comes to test or provoke a bhikṣu and he does not sit upright on purpose, he must not speak to her; he should simply avoid her.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a man whose wife was disagreeable to him; in a fit of rage, he beat her severely and then departed.
The wife thought to herself:
"His anger does not subside; if he beats me again, I shall certainly die without a doubt. I must now flee and hide."
She then went out the door and saw a bhikṣu returning from begging for alms who was about to leave the city. The woman immediately asked him,
"Ācārya, where do you wish to go?"
He replied,
"I wish to go out of the city.
The woman said:
"I wish to follow the Venerable One.
The bhikṣu said: "Sister!
"This is the royal road; why do you ask?
He then followed after her.
Later, her husband had this thought:
"Perhaps my wife will flee after being beaten.
He entered, but did not see his wife, so he asked the others,
"Where has she gone?"
He replied, "I have just gone out following this path.
He then pursued him from behind and saw his wife following after the bhikṣu; immediately filled with rage, he uttered these insults:
"A wicked śramaṇa has seduced my wife and taken her away!
He then seized the bhikṣu and beat him severely, leading him before the judge and saying,
"This bhikṣu has seduced my wife and taken her away."
The judge said,
"Bring them one by one and interrogate them regarding the facts.
He then questioned the bhikṣu:
“You who have left the household life, how can you run away with another’s wife?
He replied, “It is not so.”
“By what cause did you follow me?
He replied, “I was returning from begging for alms and wished to leave the city; a woman asked me:”
"Where do you wish to go? I replied,
"I wish to go out of the city."
The woman said,
"I wish to go out with you. I replied:
"Sister! This is the royal road; why do you ask about it?
Such was the reality of the matter.
The adjudicator said:
"Lead the bhikṣu out and summon the woman.
He then questioned her, saying:
“Did this śramaṇa steal you away? She replied, “No.”
“For what reason did you follow her?
She replied, “My husband beat me; because his anger had not yet subsided and I feared he would beat me again, I fled out of dread for my life.”
Upon meeting a bhikṣu, he immediately asked him,
"Venerable sir, where are you going?
He replied:
"I wish to go out of the city.
I said, "I wish to follow Your Reverence."
The bhikṣu said:
"This is the royal road; why do you question me about it?
The facts are indeed as such; it was not stolen by him."
He immediately sent the woman out and called the bhikṣu back, asking him:
"You are a renunciant who has stolen another's wife.
How can you hope to escape by speaking such a lie?"
The woman just now said,
"You have indeed stolen.
Why do you say you did not?
The bhikṣu replied, “It is not so.
When he was questioned again, his response was as before.
He sent the bhikṣu away and called the woman back, questioning her:
"You wretched woman! You abandoned your husband and fled; do you hope to escape by lying and deceiving the authorities?"
The bhikṣu just now said:
"I truly stole from you.
Why did you say no?
He replied, "Indeed, it was not so.
Thus he was asked three times, and his answer remained as it was at first.

He immediately detained the woman and summoned the bhikṣu to confront them regarding the circumstances. Observing their facial expressions, he discerned the truth of the matter; however, the bhikṣu’s reply was the same as before.
The official asked the bhikṣu, “Why is your almsbowl broken?”
He replied,
“My ears were pierced.
[The other asked,] “Why is your robe torn and ruined?”
He replied,
“My ears were torn.
[The King asked,] “Why are your elbows and knees wounded and broken?”
He replied, "My ears are injured.
The wife’s anger toward her husband was not yet appeased; pitying the bhikṣu for suffering such pain without reporting it to the authorities, she immediately went to the officials and spoke of it.
Upon hearing this, the official became extremely enraged and spoke these words:
"You wicked sinner!
You yourself are the king; there is no one else!"
He immediately ordered his officials to attend to the bhikṣu, providing him with medicinal decoctions and returning his robes and bowl.
He then had that man seized and bound in prison, and confiscated his family’s property to be deposited in the state treasury.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In what place among all royal households can such faith be found?"
If such are the faults even when one does not make an appointment with her, how much more so when one does?
From this day forward, I forbid traveling on a road in company with a woman by prior appointment.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell in dependence upon the city of Vaiśālī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together on a road, even as far as the middle of a village, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Women" refers to one's mother, sister, elder, or younger relative, whether she be a laywoman or a nun.
"To make an appointment together" means to agree upon a time, whether for today, tomorrow, half a month, or a month.

Regarding "a path": if it is three yojanas, two yojanas, one yojana, half a yojana, one krośa, half a krośa, or even as far as the interval between villages, [to travel such a distance] constitutes a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: as explained above, if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together on a road, for every interval between villages traversed, there is one *pāyattika*.
If she returns, each instance is likewise a *pāyattika*.

The remainder is as explained at length in the ninety-second section, the third *vagga*, regarding traveling on a road with a bhikṣuṇī by appointment; here, the difference lies in the fact that it is a woman [who is the companion].
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha, having completed his summer retreat at Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata, returned to Śrāvastī to pay his respects and inquire after the health of the World-Honored One.
While traveling along the road, as darkness fell, he sought a place to stay for the night upon entering a village.
At that time, there was a woman in the village who, taking her daughter, was about to leave the village to fetch water; they met on the road.
When the woman saw that the bhikṣu’s countenance was upright and handsome and his deportment was composed and orderly, she immediately conceived a lustful thought.
As the bhikṣu entered the village, he searched everywhere for a place to stay but could find none; he then thought to himself:
"I shall return outside and sleep beneath a tree."
She immediately turned back and again encountered the mother and daughter.
At that time, the girl asked her mother,
"Where is this śramaṇa going as he heads toward the darkness?"
He replied, "I do not know.
The woman said:
“Mother, you may ask him. The mother then asked:
“Where is this śramaṇa going as he heads toward the darkness and leaves the village?”
He replied, "I entered the village seeking a place to stay but could not find one; I wish to go back outside to lodge under a tree.
The daughter said to her mother:
"You may take him back home and lend him a place to stay.
The mother then said,
"If the śramaṇa follows me home, I shall lend him a place to stay."
The bhikṣu followed him back to the house and was given a room, to which he said:
"Śramaṇa, you may stay here tonight.
The bhikṣu then spread out a mat of grass and sat down in the full lotus posture.
After the mother and son had finished eating, they returned to their sleeping place.

The bhikṣu, exhausted from his journey, lay down to rest. Once the girl observed that her mother was fast asleep, she rose quietly and stealthily, went to where the bhikṣu was, and pulled away his grass mat.
When the bhikṣu awoke, he sat up with his body straightened; the woman, being of a weak nature, immediately withdrew.
Having departed, the bhikṣu lay down again, and after a short while, this woman returned once more.
As the Blessed One has said, there are five kinds of people who do not sleep much at night. What are the five?

A woman does not sleep much at night because she gives rise to thoughts of desire and recollects a man; a man does not sleep much at night because he gives rise to thoughts of desire and recollects a woman; a thief with a mind for stealing does not sleep much at night; a king does not sleep much at night because he is anxious about the affairs of state; and a diligent bhikṣu practicing the path does not sleep much at night.
This woman could not sleep; she rose again in secret and pulled at her grass mat.
The bhikṣu, having awakened, sat up with his body straightened, and so it continued until the end of the night.
The next day, they went to where the Buddha was. Having seen them from afar, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked intentionally:
"Who has provoked you that your countenance is so displeased?
They then reported the preceding events in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "woman," she may be one's mother, sister, or someone senior or junior, whether she be a layperson or a renunciant.
"Room" means having a common enclosure and a common roof.
"Sleeping together" means sleeping in the same bed;
this constitutes a *pāyattika*. A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If one shares a room with a partition and a separate door, there is no offense.
If it is a different room without a partition, it is a pāyattika.
If it is the same room with a common partition, it is a pāyattika.
If they are in separate rooms or different doors, there is no offense.
If it is enclosed and obstructed, it is a pāyattika.
If it is enclosed and half-obstructed, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If there is concealment but no obstruction, there is no offense.
If there is both obstruction and concealment, it is a pāyattika.
If there is obstruction but only partial concealment, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If there is an obstruction and it is unobscured, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣu and a woman to be together inside a room, it is a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣu to be inside a room while half the body of a woman is within the house, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If the bhikṣu is inside the house and the woman is outside the house, there is no offense.
If both the woman and the bhikṣu are inside the house, it is a pāyattika.
If the woman is inside the house and half of the bhikṣu’s body is inside the house, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If women are inside the house and the bhikṣu is outside, there is no offense.

If there is a great assembly on the Buddha’s birthday, a great assembly on the day he attained enlightenment, a great assembly on the day he turned the wheel of Dharma, a great assembly for Rāhula, a great assembly for Ānanda, or a great assembly for the *pañcavārṣika*, or if the Dharma is being preached throughout the night, one should remain in the open air.
If it is windy, rainy, or snowy and one is suffering from the cold, one should enter a room and sit with the body upright.
If one is elderly or ill and unable to sit, one should provide a screen or partition.
One must not use porous materials for partitions; they should be as high as the shoulders and armpits.
If a bhikṣu travels on a road and stays overnight in a village, he should stay in a separate room and a separate enclosure.
If there is no roofed dwelling, one should sleep in the open air.
If there is wind, rain, cold, or snow, one should enter a room and sit with the body upright.
If one is elderly, ill, or physically infirm and unable to sit, one should construct a partition.
If there is no obstacle and the woman is trustworthy, one should say to her: "Upāsikā!
You sleep first; I shall sit."
When a bhikṣu wishes to sleep, he should say to the other, "I wish to sleep; you must not sleep.
For one who sleeps, there is no merit."
If a female elephant, or even a chicken, or a camel, ox, or donkey raises its head, there is no offense.
If one lies down with the head drooping, it is a pāyattika.
If a female dog stretches out its head, there is no offense; if it sleeps with its head tucked in, it is a pāyattika.
For a goose, a peacock, or a chicken, stretching out the head involves no offense;
tucking the head under the wings constitutes a pāyattika.
When an elephant stands upright, there is no offense.
When it leans against [the wall], it is a *pāyattika*.
If many bhikṣus are sleeping inside a room and a woman enters carrying her sleeping daughter in her arms, all the sleeping bhikṣus incur a *pāyattika*.
If the *karmadāna* or an administrator is present, they should say to the woman:
"Hold the child upright as you carry him in.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was with a Brahmin from the same village who was a close acquaintance.
A Brahmin woman, having married and gone to another village, sent a messenger to her father, saying:
"If you, O Ācārya, would come to see me from time to time.
This is explained in detail according to the circumstances in the section on the two *aniyata* dharmas.
The Buddha continued, “Udāyin, you foolish man!

Even a layperson at home knows what conduct is appropriate and what conduct is inappropriate for one who has gone forth; yet you, having left the household life out of faith, do not know the conduct appropriate for one who has gone forth?”
Is this not contrary to the Dharma?
Is it not contrary to the Vinaya?
Is it not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching? One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to sit alone with a woman in a secluded place.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded and quiet place, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Woman" refers to one who is a mother, a sister, or one who is older or younger, whether she be a layperson or an ordained nun.
"Alone" means being a single woman with no other person present.
Even if there were others, such as those who are asleep, insane, mentally deranged, in pain, infants, non-humans, or animals—despite the presence of such individuals—it is still called "alone."
"Empty and quiet" refers to a secluded place.
"Sits" means to sit together; [if one does so], it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu sits together with a woman for the entire day, it is one *pāyattika*.
If the bhikṣu and the woman rise from their seats and sit again, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has accepted an invitation and is seated at a donor’s house, and a woman, having served the food, sits before the bhikṣu and then rises again to add more food;
if she does this repeatedly, rising and sitting down each time, it constitutes a pāyattika offense for each instance.
When one woman is seated beside a bhikṣu and another woman comes and goes distributing food, the bhikṣu should rise when the women depart.
When rising, he must not do so abruptly, for fear that the woman might suspect him of improper thoughts;
he should first say: "Sister!"
"I wish to rise.
He asked, "For what reason do you wish to rise?"
He replied, “The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit sitting alone in a secluded place with a woman; for this reason, I have risen.
The woman said:
"If you, Venerable One, do not rise, I shall rise myself.
If [the nun] rises, there is no offense.

If a girl less than seven years of age sits upon a step or a wooden board, and having sat there, moves to sit upon a second board, and having sat there, moves again to sit upon a third board—if she moves from place to place in this manner and sits down each time, for each instance there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If household chores are being performed and lay attendants (kappiyakāraka) come and go without interruption, there is no offense.
If the door opens onto a road and people walking on that road pass by as frequently as a bhikkhu might beg for alms, they shall be considered lay attendants, and there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu and a woman sit together on an upper story, and a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) below sees the bhikṣu from afar, and the bhikṣu also sees the lay attendant, there is no offense.
Monks, when a woman is seated below a gallery and a person is likewise above the gallery,
there may be cases where one sees her but does not hear her, or hears her but does not see her, or both sees and hears her, or neither sees nor hears her.

Regarding "seeing but not hearing": if a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) sees from afar that a bhikṣu and a woman are sitting together but does not hear the sound of their voices, it is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression (*vai-ni-tsi*).
Regarding "hearing but not seeing": if one hears the sound of their voices but does not see the persons involved, it is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
Regarding "both seeing and hearing": if one sees [the person] sitting together and hears their voice, there is no offense.
Regarding "neither seeing nor hearing": it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is a blind *kappiya-kāraka*, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If the attendant is deaf, there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
If the attendant is both blind and deaf, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If the attendant is either blind or deaf, there is no offense.
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) is asleep, one must rouse them;

this constitutes an offense. This applies whether it is in a village or a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), whether it is the proper time or the improper time, whether it is by day or by night, whether it is in a secluded place or not an open space, whether it is a solitary and quiet place or a crowded one, and whether it is nearby or far away; for these reasons, it is so stated.
Therefore, seizing [another's] belongings and causing doubt or regret, failing to relinquish what one has hidden,
and harboring fear; playing in water, pointing fingers at one another, traveling together, and staying overnight in the same room—
the same applies to secluded and quiet places.
The seventh chapter concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā had made a long-term invitation for the Saṃgha of Jetavana to visit her house in succession. When it was time for the meal, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā prostrated herself at the feet of the monks.

Descending in order, she arrived at the place where the group of sixteen bhikṣus was. Seeing that they were young, their complexions were soft and supple, and yet they had been able to renounce the household life, she felt great compassion for them as if they were her own children.
Out of reverence for the Dharma as well, she immediately asked:
"When the Saṃgha at Jetavana has no offerings, where do you venerable ones obtain food?"
He replied, "The time has come;
I shall put on my robes, take up my bowl, and go from house to house for alms.
He then spoke to the Venerable One:
"If there is no time for offerings, come to my home to eat.
From this day forward, on any day when there are no offerings, I shall provide you with food.
Having heard these words, the young bhikṣu accepted the invitation; then, on a day when there were no offerings, he went to his home and ate.

When the Mother of the Deer had invited the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda went there every day for the purpose of requesting food. He saw sixteen groups of young bhikṣus eating in her house, and these youths spoke words of arrogance and insolence:
"Mother!..."
"This food is too much.
He replied, "Son, reduce it."
He spoke again, saying,
"It is too little.
He replied:
"You should add more.
Thus, they may find it too cold or hot, too hard or soft, too sweet, sour, salty, or bland; in such various ways, it is difficult to achieve a perfect balance.
The doe, possessing great faith and much compassion, replied, "Child,
take whatever you seek and I shall give it to you.
Having seen this, Ānanda thought to himself:
"If this is an unbelieving household, one will give rise to an evil mind.
For this reason, he went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I pray that from this day forward, you do not grant full ordination to children.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forth, if one has not reached the age of twenty, one must not be granted full ordination."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there were two householders, father and son, who were of faith and had left the home life to practice the Way; their son, a śrāmaṇera, provided service to five hundred bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus requested either tooth-sticks or tree leaves; as they were so numerous, he was unable to provide for them all.
At that time, the mahallaka thought to himself:
"I have but one son, yet I must provide for five hundred bhikṣus. Because their requests are so many, I am unable to provide for them."
In this way, before long, he will surely fall ill.
However, the World-Honored One has established a precept stating that one who is not yet twenty years of age should not be ordained with full ordination.
"Although I know it is improper, I shall nevertheless grant him the ordination so that he may be freed from his suffering.
He then led the bhikṣu out to the boundary of the precept-field (sīmā) and conferred the full ordination upon him.
Once he had received full ordination, the bhikṣus called out to him according to the former practice, saying:
"Śrāmaṇera, give us pure tooth-sticks and leaves from grass or trees.
He then replied:
"I have already received full ordination; why do you still call me a śrāmaṇera?
The bhikṣus said, "Who conferred it upon you?"
He replied, "My name is Vāhī.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call the mahallaka here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him in detail regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is a wicked deed! Mahallaka,
how could you knowingly confer full ordination upon one whose age is not yet twenty?"
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the conferral of full ordination upon those who have not reached the age of twenty.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu knowingly confers full ordination upon a person who is less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika offense.
The bhikṣus should reprove him, for this person is not said to have received full ordination.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Not full" means not having reached twenty years of age.
If one has less than twenty years of rain-retreats, this is called "not having completed twenty.
If one has less than twenty years of rain-retreats but has completed twenty years [of other requirements], this is called "not having completed twenty.
If one has less than twenty years of rain-retreats and has exceeded twenty years [of other requirements], this is called "not having completed twenty."
If one receives [the precepts] in winter after having been born in winter, and has not yet completed the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), this is called "incomplete.
If one receives [the precepts] in spring after having been born in spring, and has not yet completed the *varṣā*, this is called "incomplete."
If one receives the precepts during the earlier retreat (pūrvavārṣika) but has not yet completed the earlier retreat, this is called "incomplete.
If one receives the precepts during the later retreat (paścimavārṣika) but has not yet completed the later retreat, this is called "incomplete."
When this person is less than twenty years of age, half of those present consider him deficient and half consider him full.
For those who consider him deficient, it is a pāyattika offense.
For those who consider him full, there is no offense; this person is said to have received full ordination (upasampadā).

When this person is under twenty years of age, if everyone considers them to be less than full [twenty] and confers the full ordination upon them, it is a pāyattika offense for all; this person is not said to have received the full ordination.

When this person is less than twenty years of age, yet everyone considers them to be full [of years], and they are granted full ordination (*upasampadā*), there is no offense for anyone; this person is said to have received full ordination.
If one has completed twenty rains but is less than twenty years [of age], this is called "having completed twenty.
If one has completed twenty rains and is exactly twenty years [of age], this is called "having completed twenty."
To have completed twenty rains and passed twenty years is called "having completed twenty.
To be born during the winter season, to have completed the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat), and to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) is called "having completed twenty."
If one is born in the spring, completes the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), and receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), this is called being "twenty years old.
If one is born during the preceding *varṣā* period, completes the preceding *varṣā*, and receives full ordination, this is called being "twenty years old."
If one is born during the later retreat and completes the later retreat before receiving full ordination, this is called being "twenty years old.

When twenty rains have been completed, half of the people say he is full [of the required age] and half say he is not full; those who say he is not full commit a *vinaya* offense, while those who say he is full are without offense. Such a person is said to have received full ordination.

When one has completed twenty years of rain-retreats (*vassa*), if everyone says they have not completed them, all incur an offense against the Vinaya, and this person is not said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
When one has completed twenty years of rain-retreats, if everyone says they have completed them, all are without offense, and this person is said to have properly received full ordination.
If a bhikṣu knows that a person is less than twenty years of age and yet confers full ordination upon them, those bhikṣus should reprove him and then confess a pāyattika offense.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.

If someone comes wishing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), one who has completed the required months should be granted full ordination; one who has not completed them should be told to wait until they are complete.
If the person before you does not know [the answer], one should ask his parents or relatives.
If they still do not know, one should consult the birth-register (*janmapatra*).

If even that is unavailable, one should observe his facial features; in observing him, one must not look merely at his physical form, for a son of a noble or wealthy family may have a large physique despite being young in years.
One should examine whether his hands and feet are complete;
if, even after doing so, one still does not know, one should ask: "Which king?
In which year?"
Regarding the abundance or scarcity of lands and the seasons of drought or flood—for this reason it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a mutual grievance between the two kingdoms of Śrāvastī and Vaiśālī, and they raided and attacked one another every year.

Once, people from Vaiśālī came to Śrāvastī to plunder and rob the populace; having obtained their goods, they returned to their own territory, where they felt secure and set aside their weapons to rest.
King Śrāvastī thought to himself:
"As a king, I ought to repel neighboring enemies and bring peace to my people; why then do these bandits plunder the property and persons of others?
He immediately issued an order to his generals and soldiers:
“Look up and pursue him; you must capture him by all means. If he is not found, it will not do for you to return empty-handed.
The soldiers thought to themselves, “The King’s command is severe; this matter must be handled with speed.”
They immediately assembled their troops and pursued the tracks to launch a surprise attack.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī, having completed their summer retreat, were about to travel to Vaiśālī; the bhikṣus lost their way and fell into the midst of those bandits.
The bandits were struck with alarm and asked the bhikṣu, "Bhikṣu! Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a renunciant. [The other asked],
“In which path have you gone forth?”
He replied,
“I am one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan. He asked:
"Venerable sir!
Where do you wish to go?
He replied:
"I was heading toward Vaiśālī but lost my way and arrived here," he said,
whereupon [the bandits] showed him the path.
Then the bhikṣu asked the robbers:
“Long-lived one!
Where do you wish to go?
He replied:
"Head toward Vaiśālī.
The bhikṣu replied again,
"We should travel together as companions."
He replied, "We are bandits who plunder the property of others; we traverse thickets and travel by paths without choosing our way.
You are a virtuous person; why do you follow us?"
"This is the direct path; you may go by this way.
The bhikṣu requested again:
"I pray that you will take me with you!"
"Do not let me suffer this loss of the Way again.
The robber replied as before, and this was repeated three times. Before he had finished speaking, the pursuers arrived; they seized the bhikṣu together and brought him before the king, saying:
"Great King!"
"These are a band of thieves.
The king said,
"Bring the bhikṣu here first."
When he had arrived, the king said, "You are a renunciant; how can you act as a thief?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am not a thief.
"For what reason, then, did you follow us?
The bhikṣu related the matter in full to the king.
The king said,
"Send the bhikṣu away.
Bring this thief here."
Having arrived, he asked the robbers,
"Is this renunciant your companion?
They replied:
“Not his companions.
“Why, then, were they following him?
The thief related the aforementioned matter in detail to the king.
The king said,
"Take the thief away.
Summon the bhikṣu again."
When he had arrived, the king asked the bhikṣu:
"You are a renunciant; how can you act as a thief?
Do you hope to escape by lying and deceiving the officials?"
"The bandits claim that you are their accomplice; why do you say it is not so?
The bhikṣu answered as he had before.
The king immediately commanded the officials of the prison to release the bhikṣu, while the bandits were punished according to the law.

He then seized five hundred bandits, placed garlands of *kapila* flowers upon them, and went out through the crossroads beating drums and ringing bells, shouting as he led them forth intending to execute them; the bandits wailed loudly.
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣus!
What is this sound of so many people?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“World-Honored One!
These five hundred bandits have been ordered by the king to be executed.”
"It is merely a sound," the Buddha told Ānanda.
"Go and say this to the king:"
"You are a king of men; you ought to love your subjects as you would your own children. Why then do you intend to kill five hundred people all at once?
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to the king's location and related the Buddha’s words in full.
The King said, "Venerable Ānanda!
I know this matter: if killing one person brings such a vast retribution for the sin, how much more so for five hundred people?"

"However, these thieves come repeatedly to destroy my village and plunder its people; if the World-Honored One could cause these men to no longer commit such thievery, they may be released and allowed to live."
Ānanda immediately returned and reported in detail to the Buddha everything the king had said.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Go again and speak to the king:
"O King, simply release him; I can ensure that from this day forward he will never commit robbery again.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda went first to the place of execution and said to the executioners:
"These criminals have already been saved by the World-Honored One; you must not kill them yet."
He spoke again to the bandits, saying,
"Can you renounce the world?
The bandits replied:
“Venerable One!
Had I not left the household life in the past, I would not have encountered this suffering. Now I have a profound longing for it;
by what means could it be attained? Ānanda then went to the king’s presence and spoke these words:
The World-Honored One said to the king,
“I can cause this man not to commit robbery again from this day forward.
The king immediately issued an order to the supervising official:
"One may spare his life, but as he has not yet been released from his bonds, send him to the World-Honored One; the Buddha himself shall release him.

At that time, wishing to deliver that man, the World-Honored One sat in the open air. Seeing the Buddha from afar, the bandit’s bonds fell away of their own accord; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

The Buddha, observing their past karmic conditions, taught the Dharma accordingly: the retribution for the practices of generosity and maintaining the precepts, and the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that very moment, they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
He asked,
"Do you wish to leave the household life?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
Had we gone forth earlier, we would not have encountered this suffering. We only pray that you will now grant us ordination.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus!

As these words were spoken, the bodies and garments of the five hundred bandits were transformed into the three robes; they spontaneously possessed alms bowls, and their deportment became as dignified and orderly as that of bhikṣus with a century of seniority, all of whom had become Arhats.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that these five hundred bandits, having received the grace of the World-Honored One, were spontaneously liberated?”

The Buddha said, "It is not only today that you have received liberation from me; in past lives as well, you have already received it from me, as is explained in detail in the *Mārjāra-jātaka* (The Birth Story of the Monkey)."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a thief to travel together along a road, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
"Thief" refers to one who robs and steals.
"Period" refers to today, tomorrow, one month, or half a month.
"Distance" refers to three *yojanas*, two *yojanas*, one *yojana*, one *krośa*, half a *krośa*, or even as far as a village; [if one exceeds these limits], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
One must not travel on a road in agreement with thieves. If a bhikṣu wishes to travel, he should seek out companions by carriage or human companions.
The appearance of these thieves can be known by three things:
their scent, their color, and their adornments.
As for their scent, while in the wilderness they consume both cooked and raw meat.
As for their complexion, it is always one of terror.

As for their adornment, they are dressed in finery all day long, yet their faces are black and their hair is yellow; they are as fierce and evil as the attendants of Yama. These three types are known as the marks of a thief and should not be traveled with.
If bandits falsely claim to be good people, put on fine clothes, and go to a secluded place where they speak among themselves:
"Today we shall enter this village; we will break down walls and plunder wealth, taking everything without distinction between śramaṇas and brahmins."
"You should know that these are bandits; at such a time, you must not immediately abandon them, but rather follow along with them.
If you approach a village, find a skillful means to leave them behind."
If the thieves become aware of you, you should say:
"Long-lived ones! I have merely arrived here."
If one travels on a road with thieves by prior appointment, it is a pāyattika.
It is the same if one travels with female thieves.
If one travels with thieves who steal gold, it is a pāyattika.
"To travel together with a debtor who has fled his obligations constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, a bhikṣu in charge of construction personally dug the earth to build foundations, bricks, and mortar. He was criticized by worldly people:

"The śramaṇa Gautama employs countless skillful means to condemn killing and praise non-killing, yet now he personally digs the earth with his own hands to build foundations, bricks, and mortar; thus he injures and destroys the life of the roots."
"This man has ruined himself; what path can he have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣu in charge of affairs here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus.

"Although there is no life-principle (jīvitendriya) here, this is something those who have left the household life should not do. You should have few affairs and few duties; do not become objects of reproach by the world, nor lose the wholesome merit of others."
"From this day forward, you must not dig the earth with your own hands.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I command all the bhikṣus residing in the wilderness to assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus—those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or causes another to dig it, or points it out and instructs him to dig it, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"By one's own hand" refers to the body, the parts of the body, or bodily expedients. Regarding "the body":
if one leaps, bounds, runs forward, or runs backward with the entire body with the intent to damage the earth, it is a *pāyattika*; this is called "the body."
