"Body parts" refers to the hands, feet, knees, elbows, or fingernails; these are called body parts.

"Physical means" refers to using spades, pickaxes, axes, or chisels, or digging the earth with one's own hands using bamboo or wood; or if one hurls them from a distance with the intent to cause destruction, and destruction occurs, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Earth" (bhūmi) refers to "arising" (janman) and "action" (kriyā).
"Arising" means that the great earth is called arising.
"Action" refers to foundational action and superior action.
"Foundation work" refers to walls in an open space.
"Superstructure work" refers to covering the ground on top of a multi-storied building; this is called superstructure work.
"Digs oneself" means to dig by one's own hand.
If one causes another to dig, even down to saying,
"Dig this ground," it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If one digs extensively by one's own effort, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one stops in the middle of the process, for each instance [of digging], it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "causing another to do": if one causes another person to dig and that person digs more than the prescribed amount, it is a pāyattika.
Or, if one speaks with emphasis:
"Cause [him] to dig!"
"Dig quickly!"—
each such utterance constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu wishes to level the ground and employs means such as sweeping it, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If it is injured even as much as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pāyattika*.
If no preparatory effort was made, there is no offense.
If one makes a preparatory effort by pulling and dragging wood with the intent to cause the ground to break, at the moment of pulling, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one injures [the ground] as much as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not employ the means [of injury], there is no offense.
It is the same if one drives oxen or horses with the intent to break the ground.
If one does not employ skillful means, there is no offense.
If one wishes to level the ground for the purpose of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), the act of walking upon it constitutes an offense against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
If it is damaged even as much as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
It is the same when standing, sitting, or lying down; there is no offense if it was not intentional.
If a bhikṣu steps on the edge of a riverbank or a pit and causes someone to fall, for every step taken, it is a pāyattika.
If one walks along the edge of a pond or a ditch and the earth collapses, there is no offense.
If a clod of earth is too heavy for one person to lift and it breaks, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is broken because it is lighter than what one person can carry, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu picks up wood, stone, brick, tile, a spade, or a pickaxe and hurls them to the ground, there is no offense even if they are injured, provided it was not intentional.

If a bhikṣu engaged in monastic affairs possesses many items belonging to a stūpa or the Saṃgha and wishes to bury them in the earth: if they are in an open area on living soil, he may not dig himself but must employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant);
if they are in a covered place or on dead soil, he may dig and bury them himself.
If one strikes a stake into the ground, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one injures it even as much as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
When one extracts the stake, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If there is injury as small as a mosquito's leg, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu wishes to stretch out a felt or woolen rug and must stake its four corners, if he stakes them himself in a covered place where living beings have died, there is no offense;
if it is in an open place where living beings are born, he must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) do it.
When extracting [a nail], one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) oversee it.
If a monk drives a nail into a wall inside his room and thereby causes damage to the finished work, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If there was already an old hole, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu damages the ground outside [the monastery] even as much as a mosquito’s foot, it is a pāyattika offense.
If he intends to draw on the ground, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense;
if he damages it even as much as a mosquito’s foot, it is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense in painting on plastered walls.

If a *karmadāna* bhikṣu wishes to create a model, he should paint it upon a board, wood, or brick. If there are old or dilapidated rooms covered with mud-plaster that one wishes to demolish, one must not demolish them oneself; rather, one should have a *karmadāna* do so.

When wishing to demolish a wall, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) remove the plaster; thereafter, one may personally remove the bricks down to the foundation level, at which point one must have the *kappiya-kāraka* remove them.

If the wall is unplastered but has previously been rained upon, one should have the *kappiya-kāraka* remove two or three rows of bricks, and then one may personally remove them down to the ground level, after which one must again have the *kappiya-kāraka* remove them.

If a pile of bricks or tiles has been rained upon, one must not take them oneself; rather, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) take the top two or three layers first, and only then may one take them down to ground level, after which one should again have the *kappiya-kāraka* take them.
If it is covered above, one may take it oneself; once it reaches the surface of the ground, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) take it. The same applies to a heap of bricks.

If the clay has been rained upon, a bhikṣu must not take it himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* take it as far as the area saturated by the rain, and only thereafter may he take it himself without fault.
If rat-droppings have been rained upon and cannot be taken, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") take them.
After new rain has fallen, a bhikṣu must not draw water from a well himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* draw it.
If the attendant (kappiya-kāraka) is too small or incapable [of the task], one should first lower the attendant to stir the water until it becomes turbid, and only then draw it oneself.
If the water in a pond or a stream has been newly rained upon, a bhikṣu must not draw it himself.
If oxen or horses have already waded through it, one may draw water from it oneself.
If the mud has been rained upon, one must not take it oneself; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take it.
If the mud in a pond or a mire-pool has been newly rained upon, a bhikṣu must not take it himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* take it.
If there is water in a drainage ditch or a house gutter after a fresh rain, a bhikṣu must not drain it himself; he should have a *kappiyakāraka* (lay attendant) drain it.
If, while using water for the purposes of defecation or urination, one rubs the ground with the hand, it is a *pāyattika*.
One should use ash, soil, or bean flour.
If rain causes mudslides and the earth is pushed into a heap, a bhikṣu must not take it himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) take it.
If jars, bottles, or vessels have been left in the open air and rained upon, a bhikṣu must not take them himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* take them.

If wooden items for washing feet have been rained upon, one must not take them up oneself. Likewise, if various objects such as wood, stones, bricks, or tiles are left on open ground, a bhikṣu may not take them up himself after the rain; he should instead instruct a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) to do so.
To dig the earth is a pāyattika offense.
If it is half sand, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If it is pure sand, there is no offense.
The same applies to gravel, stone, excrement, and ashes.
Therefore it is said.

The ninth of the ninety-two rules concerning the *pācittiya* offenses. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, Mahānāma the Licchavi invited the Saṃgha to receive medicinal offerings.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that Mahānāma had invited the Saṃgha to offer medicinal provisions, and they intended to trouble him.
Rising early the next morning, they put on their village-entering robes and went to his house, where they exchanged greetings with him:
"We have heard that you, donor, have invited the Saṃgha to offer medicinal provisions; is this indeed true?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
“Venerable One!”
"Do you have anything you require? He replied,
"I need medicine."
"What medicine is required?
He replied, "I require this much ghee, this much oil, this much honey, this much rock sugar, and this much of root medicine, leaf medicine, flower medicine, and fruit medicine."
He said, "I am not yet fully prepared today; I must make the arrangements and shall give it to you.
The bhikṣu said:
“You should prepare the medicine first, and only then invite the Saṃgha.
To provide medicine for a single bhikṣu is like providing it for a great elephant; if I, as a single person, cannot even obtain medicine now, how much less so for such a multitude?”
"You merely seek reputation; you have no sincere heart.
He replied, "Venerable Sir!"
"The royal treasury does not even possess such a quantity of medicine, much less my own household;
however, I shall prepare it and give it to you.
The bhikṣu said:
"Whether I give it to you or not shall be up to your own judgment.
Having said this, he departed.
Subsequently, the donor prepared various medicines and went in person to say:
"The medicine you previously requested is now prepared; you may come and take it.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu laughed and said, "I was merely testing you before;
in truth, I have no need for the medicine."
He replied, "Why do you test me? Whatever I possess in my home,
I have no sense of scarcity or stinginess regarding it for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
The bhikṣu asked,
"Is the donor angry?
He replied:
"I was indeed angry.
[The other said: "If you were angry, I shall confess my transgression. He replied:
"I shall not accept your confession; you must confess directly to the Buddha.
The bhikṣu then confessed directly to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Why is that? He then reported the aforementioned matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! All that is dear and precious to the Licchavi Mahānāma’s family, he does not begrudge even to the Buddha and the bhikṣus.
Why do you disturb them?”
"From this day forward, I authorize you to accept separate invitations for a period of four months, excepting repeated invitations and extended invitations.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu accepts an individual invitation for the four-month period,
he should accept it; if he accepts beyond that, it is a pāyattika offense,
except in the case of repeated invitations, long-term invitations, or invitations for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
"A bhikṣu" is as described above.
"Four months" refers to either the four months of summer, the four months of winter, or the four months of spring.
"A private invitation" means an individual invitation.
"Exceeding" means exceeding four months.
"Except for renewed invitations" refers to those spoken of by the World-Honored One as being without offense.
"Except for long-term invitations" refers to invitations for as long as one's life lasts.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.
If a donor says to a bhikṣu:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Accept my invitation for the four months of the summer retreat.
If a bhikṣu accepts it, he must not let it extend beyond the sixteenth day of the eighth month.
To accept it beyond that limit constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one accepts an invitation for the winter, it is the same for an invitation for the spring.
A donor’s invitation is not fixed; it may be for four months, one month, or half a month. Once the stipulated period has expired, one must not accept further invitations.
If a donor says,
"Venerable sir, if you always reside here, I shall provide food for you continually," then if the bhikṣu stays away for even one night, he may not eat again [of that provision].
If a donor asks,
"Venerable sir, for what reason have you not come?
one should answer:
"You previously said that you would come to receive food only if you were staying here permanently; since I have already left my lodging, I have not come.
The donor said, "Whether you have left or not, from this day forward, simply come."
If one accepts in this manner, there is no offense.
The donor says:
"Venerable sir, please accept my invitation for food; consume all the grain in this granary."
When a bhikṣu receives it, he should repeatedly question the storekeeper.
If the keeper says,
"It has been eaten up," [he may take it].
"One must not eat again.
If a donor asks:
'Venerable sir, why did you not come?'"
He replied:
"I had previously accepted an invitation to consume all the grain in this granary; the grain is now exhausted, and for that reason I have not come.
If he says:
"Venerable One!
I do not mean this single granary; there are other granaries as well. From this day forward, you need only come [to those].
Accepting [the invitation] in this manner is without fault.
The same applies to being invited to eat ghee or sugarcane.
If a donor says:
"Venerable One!..."
"Accept my invitation to eat, and consume this cow's milk.
The bhikṣu accepted it, but he should repeatedly question the person milking the cow, asking: "Has the milking finished?
If she says, "The milking is over," [he may drink].
"One may not receive [the precepts] again.
If one asks,
"Why did you not come?"
He replied:
"I had previously accepted an invitation to consume this cow's milk; the milk is now exhausted, and for that reason I have not come.
If one says:
"I am not the only ox; there are other oxen as well. From this day forward, you may come [only for those others].
If one accepts [the invitation] in this manner, there is no offense.
If the donor says:
"If the Venerable One accepts my invitation for a meal, [considering that] the husband of this woman lives here," the bhikṣu should accept it.
If the husband has departed, he may not accept it again.
If one asks,
"Why have you not come?
the answer is:
"I had previously accepted an invitation and was staying with the husband of the maiden;
now that the husband has departed, this is why I have not come. If he says:
"Accept my invitation once more.
If one accepts in this manner, there is no offense.
If one says:
"Venerable sir, please accept my meal beforehand.
One must not request a subsequent meal.
If one requests a subsequent meal, one must not request a meal beforehand.
If invited to receive non-time food (vikālabhojana), one must not request medicine or other items;
if invited to receive oil for anointing the feet, one must not request non-time food;
if invited to receive medicine, one should request medicine from them, provided that they say:
"Venerable sir, please accept my invitation for as long as you live to receive food, clothing, bedding, and medicine.
At that time, it is without fault to request whatever one desires.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to Chanda:
"Elder, you should train yourself!"
"Do not commit the offenses of the five groups.
He replied, "I will not follow your words now; if I see another elder who is learned, upholds the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him."
"Whatever he may say, I shall accept and practice.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call this bhikṣu Chanda here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to Channa.
"This is an evil deed."
Have you not always heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise compliance and censure opposition? Why then do you act so stubbornly and willfully?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not according to the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on the kingdom of Kauśāmbī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If various bhikṣus instruct them, saying:
"You should train yourselves; do not commit the five classes of offenses," and if they speak these words:
"I shall not follow your words now; if I see another elder who is tranquil, learned, a keeper of the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him.
Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice."
"One who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika* offense.
A bhikṣu who desires to obtain the benefit of the Dharma should train accordingly, and should also inquire of other bhikṣus.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
The five classes of offenses are: pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, and vinayātikrama.
Regarding "do not transgress": this means instructing them to study the twelve matters. The twelve matters are:

the introduction to the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), the four *pārājika* offenses, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the two *aniyata* rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, the ninety-two *pāyattika* offenses, the four *prātideśanīya* offenses, the *saikṣa* training rules, and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
"You should train yourself in accordance with the Dharma and not transgress it.
When these words were spoken, he replied:
"I will not follow your instructions; if I see another elder who is tranquil, learned, a bearer of the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him."
"Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice.
One who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
“Elder! Among the five classes of offenses—*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *vinayātikrama*—you should train yourself not to commit them.”
When these words were spoken, he replied:
"I will not follow your advice; if you see another elder who is learned, upholds the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, you should consult him."
"Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice.
One who speaks these words commits a pāyattika offense.
In this way, there are offenses involving four groups, three groups, two groups, and one group.
One should train in the four *pārājikas* and not commit them.
When these words were spoken,
he replied:
"I will not follow your words."
"If you see another elder who is tranquil, of great learning, a holder of the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, you should consult him.
Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice.
To speak these words [with such a motive] constitutes a pāyattika offense.

If one speaks thus, the Elder has performed the six acts of relinquishment, namely: the act of subjugation (*tarjanīya-karman*), the act of silence (*pratisedha-karman*), the act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the act of reconciliation (*prasādanīya-karman*), the act of suspension (*utksepanīya-karman*), and the act of separate residence (*parivāsa-karman*).
"You should train yourself not to commit [such offenses].
When these words were spoken, he replied:
"I will not follow your instructions; if I see another elder who is tranquil, learned, a bearer of the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him."
"Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice.
One who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika*.
If one speaks thus:

"Elder, these six dharmas of relinquishment have already been subjected to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation). Having practiced the dharma of compliance and become subdued and pliant, you should thus relinquish them. This applies even to the *parivāsa-karman* (act of probation), which is likewise; you should train yourselves not to commit such offenses."
When these words were spoken, he replied:
"I will not follow your advice; if I see another elder who is learned, upholds the Dharma, and possesses deep understanding, I shall consult him."
"Whatever he says, I shall accept and practice.
One who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika*.
If one says:

“Elder! You should train in being virtuous, maintaining the precepts, and receiving and reciting the Dharma; you shall attain the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.”
When this instruction is given, one must not answer, "There is permanence; one should train thus.
One should instead answer:
"I have gone forth for this reason. Thus it was said.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, within the realm of Kauśāmbī, there was a malevolent dragon named Āmra, who could cause severe droughts and withhold rain, so that the crops failed to ripen and the people suffered from famine; such were the various calamities he brought about.
At that time, the Venerable Svāgata Bhikṣu went to subdue the evil dragon, as described in detail in the *Svāgata Bhikṣu Sūtra*.
Having subdued the evil dragon, the land became abundant and joyful, and the people were moved by his virtue; they recognized his kindness and repaid it.

There were five hundred great families who, for the sake of Svāgata, each erected permanent banners of alms-offering, prepared seats, and invited the Saṃgha to receive offerings; they separately invited the bhikṣu Svāgata, and in the houses they had prepared, they set out various kinds of fine food.
At that time, there was a family who, after offering food, gave him wine out of thirst because its color and flavor resembled water; having obtained it, he drank it and returned toward the vihāra.

At that moment, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly; the effects of the wine surged within him, and overcome by dizziness and exhaustion, he collapsed to the ground, lying prostrate with his legs stretched out before the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Which bhikṣu is lying here before the Tathāgata with his legs stretched out?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu! You have drunk too much wine, and for that reason you lie here intoxicated.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, “Did this ‘Welcome’ bhikṣu ever nap during the day before?”
"No, World-Honored One.
He then asked the bhikṣus again:
“Welcome! While you were not yet intoxicated, have you ever stretched out your legs and lain down before the Buddha?
“No, World-Honored One.”
He asked the bhikṣus again:
"If one has already drunk much alcohol, is it possible to prevent oneself from becoming intoxicated? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One!
He further asked the bhikṣus:

“Suppose a ‘Welcome’ (svāgata) bhikṣu were not to drink alcohol; if he heard the preaching of the subtle and wondrous Dharma of immortality, would he wish to lose this wholesome benefit by refusing to listen and receive it?”
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Could this *svāgata* bhikṣu, who was originally able to subdue evil dragons, now subdue a frog?
He replied, “I cannot.”
The Buddha said:
"If the Āmrapālī dragon were to hear this, he would become displeased.
From this day forward, drinking alcohol is not permitted."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Nāgita had consumed an excessive amount of honey-wine and returned to the monastery.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly, [a certain person], overcome by the intense effects of alcohol, fell to the ground in a stupor and lay down with his legs outstretched before the World-Honored One.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked intentionally:
"Which bhikṣu is lying here with his legs outstretched before the Tathāgata?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
That bhikṣu Nāgita drank an excessive amount of honey-wine; for this reason, he lies there intoxicated.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Did the bhikṣu Nāgita ever previously nap during the day? "No, he did not."
"World-Honored One!
he replied. The Buddha then asked the bhikṣu again, "Before Nāgī was intoxicated, had she ever stretched out her legs and lain down before the Buddha?"
"No, World-Honored One!
He then asked the bhikṣus again:
“If one has already drunk much alcohol, is it possible to prevent oneself from becoming intoxicated? “No,
World-Honored One.”
He asked the bhikṣu again:
"When Nādicī was not drinking alcohol, upon hearing such subtle and deathless Dharma being taught, would he have wished to lose this wholesome benefit by failing to listen and receive it?"
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, the drinking of stone-melodious wine (phāṇita-madya) is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who dwell in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣu drinks honey-wine, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Wine" consists of ten kinds:
Fermented, sweet, prepared, stirred, sour, pickled, yellow, powdered, sedimented, and clear. Regarding "fermented":

one takes rice powder and mold powder, mixes them with water in a vessel; thus, even a drop of grass or a drop of hair entering the mouth constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, let alone drinking from the vessel itself. This is called "fermented."
Regarding "sweet":
once the fermentation is complete, it begins to change and become naturally sweet; if one drinks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense. This is called "sweet. Regarding "accomplished":
when the flavor and aroma are fully developed; if one drinks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense. This is called "accomplished."
"Moving" refers to when the potency of the liquor has already deteriorated; for one who drinks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense—this is called "moving.
"Sour" refers to when the flavor of the liquor has deteriorated and turned sour; for one who drinks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense—this is called "sour."

"Steeping" (*tintika*) means: having washed a clean white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), one steeps it in wine, repeatedly removes it to dry it, and after drying it, steeps it again. When traveling through a remote wilderness, one steeps the cloth and wrings out the liquid; even if one drinks it, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*). This is called "steeping."
"Yellow" refers to turbid yellow liquid that is not yet clear; to drink it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense—this is called "yellow.
"Sediment" refers to the turbid sediment at the bottom of wine; to drink it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense—this is called "sediment."

"Clear" means that it is as clear above as the color of oil; thus, one must not allow even a drop of grass or a drop of hair to enter the mouth, much less drink from a vessel; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This is what is meant by "clear."
There are ten kinds of honey-wine (*śarkarā-madya*):
blended, sweet, fermented, stirred, sour, infused, yellow, granular, dregs, and clear. Regarding the "blended" type:

when honey and water are mixed together in a vessel, one must not allow even a drop of grass or a drop of hair to enter the mouth; how much less, then, should one drink from the vessel? [To do so constitutes] a *pāyattika* offense.
The other nine matters are as explained above.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above:
namely, fermented brews made from parched grain, fermented brews made from rice, fermented brews made from wheat, fermented brews made from *mudga* beans, and fermented brews made from flour.

Regarding "barley-beer liquor": when one ferments barley-beer water in a vessel, if even a drop of grass or a drop of hair enters the mouth, let alone drinking from the vessel itself, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding rice-mash: if one ferments rice-gruel with water in a vessel and drinks it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding barley-mash: if one ferments barley-gruel with water in a vessel and drinks it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "wood-grain mash": if one ferments wood-grain rice mixed with water in a vessel until it becomes a drinkable liquid, it is a *pāyattika*. Regarding "flour mash":
if one ferments flour mixed with water in a vessel, such that not even a drop from grass or a drop from hair may enter the mouth, let alone drinking it from the vessel itself, it is a *pāyattika*.
Drinking water after a meal is without offense.
Eating fermented yeast (maku) is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
To drink rice mixed with fermented yeast is a *pāyattika* offense.
Eating rock honey and drinking water incurs no offense.
Eating *kharjūra* fruit incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Drinking the three types [of honey] mixed together constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
To drink grain wine or stone-honey wine constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
To drink grape wine constitutes a *vyatikrama* offense against the Vinaya.
To drink *sīthu*, to drink *nandī*, or to consume dregs all constitute *vyatikrama* offenses against the Vinaya.
If one eats the fruit of the khajūra, the kapittha, the bilva, or the kola, these fruits cause intoxication in the eater; for so eating them, there is an offense of *vinaya*.
With the exception of fourteen kinds of fermented liquors—from *āmra* juice up to *jambū* fruit juice—if they have become clear and transparent, all are permitted to be drunk;
however, if they have changed into the color, taste, or fragrance of alcohol, none are permitted to be drunk.
One is not permitted to drink fermented grain vinegar that causes intoxication, with the exception of sugarcane-based vinegar, grape-based vinegar, and fermented grain vinegar.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Saṃgha was in harmony and wished to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā). The Venerable Chanda did not come, so a messenger was sent to summon him, saying to the bhikṣu Chanda:
"The Saṃgha is in harmony and wishes to perform a formal ritual; Elder, please come."
Yet he was unwilling to come.
The bhikṣus said, "Chanda is obstinate and perverse; even if you call him, he certainly will not come."
"If I say 'do not come,' there is still the possibility that he might come!
He then dispatched a messenger with these words:
"Elder, do not come."
He said: "Stop! Stop!"
"All of you go; tell me not to come.
He then entered among the monks, but when the bhikṣus told him to sit, he refused to sit.
The bhikṣus spoke to him again:
"Do not sit, Elder," he said;
they all sat down, yet he told them, "Do not sit."
He then sat down.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"Venerable one, you may now discuss this matter."
He replied, "I did not speak.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"Do not speak, Elder," he said; they replied,
"All of you speak, and tell me not to speak."
He continued speaking without ceasing, thereby obstructing and distracting the other monks.
The monks spoke to him again, saying,
"Venerable one, you should go outside for a moment."
But he refused to come out.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"Elder, do not come out."
He then departed immediately.
Consequently, the Saṃgha was not in harmony; everyone rose and left, so that the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) could not be performed.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣu Chanda here. When he had arrived,
the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter.
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said,
"This is an evil deed, Chanda!"

Have you not often heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise and speak words of gentle compliance while censuring obstinacy and perversity? Why then do you remain so obstinate and self-willed?
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on Kauśāmbī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so forth] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu treats another with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "a bhikṣu," it is as explained above.
Regarding "treats another with contempt," there are eight matters:
To speak when not invited to speak; to come when not invited to come; to sit when not invited to sit; to speak when not invited to speak; to go when not invited to go—each constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.

If the Bhikṣu Saṃgha assembles intending to perform a *tarjanīya-karman*, a *pratisāraṇīya-karman*, a *pravāsanīya-karman*, a *prasrabdhi-karman*, an *utkṣepanīya-karman*, or a *parivāsa-karman*, everyone must attend.
If one disregards another and they do not come, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu is engaged in matters concerning robes or bowls, or if they are unable to come due to the cause of illness, there is no offense in granting their consent (chanda).
If one says, "Do not come," and another person comes anyway out of disregard for that command, it is a *pāyattika*.
However, if there is a matter within the Saṃgha requiring the presence of the monks, and one informs the Saṃgha and requests permission to enter, there is no offense.
If one says,
"Venerable sir, sit," and then does not sit oneself out of contempt for the other, it is a pāyattika.
If there is an ulcer or abscess at the place where one is to sit, if one informs the Saṃgha and they grant permission, there is no offense in not sitting.
If one is told not to sit and yet sits lightly upon it out of disregard for others, it is a pāyattika.
If one is old, sick, or physically weak, and becomes extremely exhausted from standing for a long time, there is no offense in sitting down after having informed the Saṃgha.
If one commands another to speak and the other remains silent out of contempt, it is a pāyattika.

If one’s talent is inferior and one’s words are held lightly so that others do not respect or employ them, and if the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is consequently not accomplished and the Saṃgha is not in harmony, there is no offense in not addressing the Saṃgha for their permission.
If one says "do not speak" to someone who is speaking lightly, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one thinks:
"If I do not speak, the formal act (*kamma*) will not be accomplished and the Saṃgha will not be in harmony; the matter requires my speech."
If one speaks to the Saṃgha for permission, there is no offense.
If one says, "Go away," and the other person does not leave because they hold the other in low esteem, it is a pāyattika.
If one has this thought:
"If I were to leave, the *karmavācanā* performed herein would not be accomplished and the matter would remain unresolved.
If one informs the Saṃgha and they grant permission, there is no offense in not leaving.
If one says, "Do not go," while intending to send another away, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one thinks:
"If I do not go, the formal act (*kamma*) will not be accomplished and the matter will not be settled."
When one has informed the Saṃgha and it has granted permission, there is no offense in departing.
If, however, within the Saṃgha one says:

"Come," yet does not come; "Do not come," yet comes; "Sit," yet does not sit; "Do not sit," yet sits; "Speak," yet does not speak; "Do not speak," yet speaks; "Depart," yet does not depart; or "Do not depart," yet departs—[these constitute offenses].
In each such case, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If, among a multitude or within a group of teacher and disciples, one says "come" when they do not come, or even "go" when they do not go, for each instance one incurs a vyatikrama offense.
If the preceptor or the ācārya tells one to come and one does not come, or tells one to go and one does not go, for each such instance, one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, the bhikṣus were engaged in disputes and lived together in discord.

Then the group of six bhikṣus eavesdropped in private places; having heard these words, they told them to those people, and having heard those words, they told them to these people. Consequently, the disputes between those parties increased further, and they lived together in discord, claiming, "This is the Dharma, this is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, this is not the Vinaya," and so on, up to "this is a proper *karmavācanā*, this is an improper *karmavācanā*."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Summon those six group-of-six bhikṣus.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned them in detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu stands silently while the bhikṣus are engaged in a dispute, listening to those who speak with the intention, "I shall remember this so that I may use it as grounds for a claim," provided the circumstances are not otherwise, it is a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.

“Dispute” refers to [contentions over] what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, and so forth, up to what is a proper formal act (karmavācanā) and what is an improper formal act.

Regarding "standing to listen": if one stands to listen through a wall, or through a fence, or by a door, or through a curtain, or through a stone, or through grass, thinking, "If there is someone speaking, I shall remember and retain it," and if this cause and condition is not otherwise [than intended], it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If two bhikṣus are engaged in private conversation inside a hall, and a bhikṣu wishes to enter, he should snap his fingers or move his foot to make a sound. If the persons before him remain silent, he should withdraw;
if the persons before him continue speaking without ceasing, there is no offense in entering.

If a single bhikṣu is already seated inside the hall and two bhikṣus enter from outside engaged in private conversation, the bhikṣu inside must not remain silent; he should snap his fingers or move his foot to make a sound. If he remains silent, the bhikṣu inside should leave.
If a bhikṣu quarrels with another bhikṣu and harbors resentment, uttering such abuse as,
"I shall surely kill this wicked man," and then departs.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu said to that person:
"Venerable sir!
Be well-prepared; I have heard an evil sound."

When visiting bhikṣus arrived and were staying in the lecture hall, the warm bathhouse, or the meditation quarters, the *karmadāna* or the administrators went to visit the visiting bhikṣus and heard them say this:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"We shall steal such-and-such a storehouse, such-and-such temple property, such-and-such a monk’s pure kitchen, or such-and-such a bhikṣu’s robes and bowl.
Having heard these words, one should return in silence; having returned, one should announce among the community of monks:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Such-and-such a storehouse, such-and-such a stupa's property, such-and-such a monk’s pure kitchen, or such-and-such a bhikṣu’s robes and bowl must be guarded; I have heard an evil sound.
He should thus inform the person concerned.
If a bhikṣu has many disciples and, at dusk, comes secretly to inspect the various rooms to see whether they are living according to the Dharma,
and if he hears them engaged in worldly talk— such as speaking of kings or speaking of thieves— and hears such various kinds of conversation, he must not immediately enter and reprimand them.
Once they have arrived of their own accord, he then admonishes and rebukes them, saying:
"You have left the household life out of faith and eat the offerings of the faithful; you ought to practice meditation and recite the sutras."
"What is meant by discussing worldly and unrighteous matters?
These are not the practices of one who has gone forth that accord with wholesome dharmas.
If one hears discourses on the sūtras or their meanings, or engages in questions and answers, one must not immediately enter into praise.
Once they had gathered, he then praised them, saying:

"It is well that you are able to discuss the sūtras, explain their meanings, and discourse upon the matters of the Buddha-dharma together. As the World-Honored One has said, when bhikṣus assemble, two practices should be observed:
first, noble silence; second, the discussion of the dharma and its meaning."

If a bhikṣu enters a village and walks about speaking, and another bhikṣu arrives later, he must not remain silent; he should clear his throat or move his feet to make a sound. If the person ahead continues to speak intentionally, one may proceed accordingly without offense.
If a bhikṣu has gone ahead and a later bhikṣu comes along speaking, the bhikṣu who is ahead must not remain silent; he should clear his throat or move his feet to make a sound.
It is the same when a bhikṣu circumambulates a stūpa, or when, after a meal, he wishes to enter a forest to practice seated meditation.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform a formal act of censure (*karma*) against Upānanda’s fellow disciples and resident disciples.
When Upānanda heard that a formal act of censure was being performed against his disciples, he immediately rose and departed.
Later, when the bhikṣus saw that the seats were empty, they inquired:
"Who has come? Who has not come?"
"Whose seat is this?
The bhikṣu replied,
"This is the seat of Upānanda."
"In this way, the Saṃgha was not in harmony; each person rose and departed, and the *karmavācanā* could not be performed.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
'Summon Upānanda.'"
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him in detail regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to Upānanda. "This is a wrongful act.
How could you, when the Saṃgha was about to settle a matter, rise and depart in silence without informing the bhikṣus?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha intends to settle a matter, rises and departs in silence without informing the bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
When the Saṃgha intends to settle a matter, there are two kinds of methods:
first, expounding the Dharma and the Vinaya; second, performing acts of subjugation (nigarhaṇīya-karman) up to the act of separate residence (parivāsa-karman).
"To depart silently" means to rise from one's seat and leave.
"Without having informed" means that if one informs [the Sangha] of entering a village at an improper time, it does not count as having informed;
if one informs [the Sangha] of going to a nunnery for instruction, it does not count as having informed.
To announce one's departure from the place where food is being consumed is not called "announcing.
If the Sangha has assembled to recite the Dharma and the Vinaya, one should announce:
"I am departing from the seat of the Dharma discourse."
He replied, "Yes.

If the Saṃgha assembles to perform a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) or even a *pārivāsika-karman* (act of separate residence), one should announce it and grant one's consent (*chanda*).
If a bhikṣu departs from the assembly of monks present without having announced his departure, it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.

If the Saṃgha has assembled intending to perform a karma of subjugation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*) up to the karma of separate residence (*pārivāsika*), and a bhikṣu wishes to depart, he should announce his intention and grant his consent (*chanda*). If he departs without announcing his intention or granting his consent, it is a pāyattika.
If one announces [the matter] but does not grant consent (*chanda*), it is an offense of violating the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
If one neither announces nor grants consent, there is one *pāyattika* and one offense of violating the Vinaya.
If one both announces and grants consent, there is no offense.
If one intends to defecate or urinate and returns in a brief moment without neglecting the affairs of the Sangha, there is no offense.
However, if one thinks:
"I shall return late," [there is an offense].
One who says this should announce their departure and transmit their consent (*chanda*).
If one is preaching the Dharma or the Vinaya, they should announce their departure; if they depart without announcing it, they commit an offense against the Vinaya.
If a bhikṣu listens to many bhikṣus reciting the sūtras, he should inform them before departing; if he departs without informing them, he commits a vinaya offense.
If the reciters stop their recitation and speak of other matters, there is no offense for the one who departs.
If a bhikṣu listens to another bhikṣu receiving instruction on the sūtras, he should inform [the teacher] before departing; if he departs without informing him, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣu listens to another reciting the sūtras, he should inform [the reciter] before departing; if he departs without informing him, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, some bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages entered the villages at improper times, and were thus censured by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, dwell in forest hermitages yet enter villages at improper times?
What do they seek?
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
“How is it that you, while dwelling in an araṇya, enter a village at an improper time?
You are rightly subject to the censure of worldly people.
From this day forward, I do not permit those dwelling in an araṇya to enter a village at an improper time without having informed a bhikṣu.”
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus dwelling in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
Then, one bhikṣu, while plastering his cell, was bitten by a snake and said to his companion:
“Venerable sir!
I have been bitten by a snake.
He replied:
"Wait while I fetch my saṃghāṭī; I shall go and summon the physician Jīvaka.
While the teacher was in the midst of fetching the robe, he suddenly lost his voice. Once the other had taken the robe, he said:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have entered the village at an improper time.
At that time, the bhikṣu was unable to speak; thus it continued until he had spoken three times, saying:
"Venerable sir!"
"I have entered the village at an improper time.
Still, he did not speak.
He then thought to himself:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit a forest-dwelling bhikṣu to enter a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu. Since this bhikṣu did not report his departure, I shall bear the consequences of his actions; what else can be known?”
He then passed away.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If he were to call upon the names of the four great dragon kings with a mind of loving-kindness, he would not have died. Which four?
The Dragon King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Dragon King Elāpattra, the Dragon King Kālikasuta, and the Dragon King Śvetaka. I possess loving-kindness toward them."
I have loving-kindness for beings without feet; I have loving-kindness for two-footed beings; I have loving-kindness for four-footed beings; I have loving-kindness for many-footed beings.
May footless beings not harm me; may two-footed beings not harm me; may four-footed beings not harm me; may many-footed beings not harm me.
All sentient beings should attain the state of being free from outflows, and all worthy sages should regard one another with virtuous minds, never giving rise to evil intentions.
If a bhikṣu invokes the names of these four great dragon kings, he shall not meet with death.
"From this day forward, I permit [the use of footwear] except in times of urgency.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, except for special occasions, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding one who dwells in an araṇya: if one is five hundred bow-lengths away from a city or village—where each bow is five cubits long—and there is no human habitation within that interval, it is called an araṇya.
"Improper time" (*akāla*) means that after a meal has been finished; even if it is still early, it is nonetheless considered improper time.
"Village" (*grāma*) refers to a settlement enclosed by walls or fences, or even one where people dwell in a scattered manner.
Regarding "informal announcement" (jñapti): if one says,
"I inform you that I am leaving the household of a layperson," it is not called an informal announcement.
If one says,
"I shall go to the nuns' vihāra to instruct them," this is not called a formal announcement (jñapti).
If one says,
"The motion (jñapti) is separated from the place where the Dharma is preached," it is not called a motion.
One should say:
"Venerable sir,
I have entered the village at an improper time."
The other person said, “So be it.
Regarding the term “bhikṣu,” this refers to those present within the boundary, not merely the assembly of followers present.

Regarding "except at other times": if a bhikṣu suffers from various illnesses or is bitten by a snake, and for the purpose of summoning a physician, the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
If two bhikṣus are dwelling in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) and wish to travel together, they should inform one another in turn.
If one person has already set out first and another wishes to follow, they should inform the other bhikṣus.
If there are no other bhikṣus present, they should form this thought:
"Whether on the road, at a gate, in a village, or at a bhikṣuṇī-vihāra, when I see a bhikṣu, I shall inform him."
Having made this announcement, he may then enter a village at an improper time.
If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road and passes through a village, and there is a stūpa or a deva-temple along the roadside within that village, he should pass straight through along the path.
If one leaves by turning left or right on the lower path, it is a pāyattika offense.
However, if a fire breaks out or various predatory beasts come to pursue one, there is no offense in leaving as one pleases.
If a bhikṣu is traveling on a long road and, at sunset, wishes to enter a village to stay overnight, he must not carry a sack or bundle upon his shoulder while entering.

If there is water outside the village, he should halt and rest in the forest; he should first have two bhikṣus wash themselves thoroughly, put on their saṃghāṭī robes with their fastening ties adjusted, and have them announce themselves to one another before sending them into the village to seek a place to stay.
If he obtains a place to stay, he should ask the donor for whatever is suitable for his rest; then, upon returning from the village, he should say to the bhikṣus:
"I have found a place to stay."
At that time, the bhikṣus should wash their hands and feet thoroughly; those who wish to drink non-timely liquids (vikālabhojana) may do so right there.
If they enter a village, they must not allow people to criticize the śramaṇas for eating at night; they should distribute and take away their robes, bags, bundles, and vessels.
Having put on the saṃghāṭī and fastened its ties, and having taken up the staff and carrying the leather sandals, one should enter after announcing oneself to those present.
Once arrived at the lodging, if one wishes to go out again to fetch firewood, grass, or water, there is no offense in departing by the same path as before.
If one travels by another route, one should inform [the community]; if one departs without informing them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one wishes to seek oil for anointing the feet, non-timely gruel, or an invitation for a meal on the following day, one should depart after having informed [them].
If one departs without having informed [the community], it is a pāyattika offense.
However, if there is a monastery within the village, or if there are houses connected by a continuous roof along the road, there is no offense for departing.
One who departs by another path should inform [the others]; if one departs without informing them, it is a pāyattika.
Therefore it is said:
"Not being full [of a group], traveling with bandit companions, digging the earth, and the four-month invitation."
Not having trained, drinking alcohol, listening in silence while others speak,
rising in silence, and entering at an improper time.
The eighth chapter (varga) is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, the Venerable Upānanda rose early in the morning, put on his robes for entering a village, and went to the house of a donor. He said to the female lay follower:
"Ordinary people, when their lives end in death, mostly fall into the evil realms; you should listen to me preach the Dharma."

At that time, the upāsikā was occupied with her household affairs; being preoccupied with various urgent matters, she had no leisure to listen to the Dharma, and so she spoke disparagingly of the bhikṣu, saying:
"Let alone an ordinary person—if they die, they will fall into the evil realms. Ācārya, you should worry only for yourself; do not worry about others."
After he had finished eating, he instructed his disciple to wash the bowl and entered the house again as before, saying:
"Upāsikā! If an ordinary person dies and falls into the evil realms, you should listen to me preach the Dharma."
At that time, after the upāsikā had finished feeding her husband and son, she ate herself; she would not allow [the bhikṣu] to listen, and further complained of the bhikṣu, saying:
"Let ordinary people die and fall into evil realms; Ācārya, you should only worry about yourself and not worry about others."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him in detail regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"After you finished eating, what did you do?"
He replied,
“I have many affairs,
World-Honored One!”
"I wish to practice medicine to treat various illnesses.
The Buddha said,
"How can you go to other households before or after a meal without informing the bhikṣus while staying at the same place for eating?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to go to other households before or after a meal without having informed the bhikṣus at the place where one has eaten.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Tell the bhikṣus:
'The summer retreat has concluded; the various donors have offered robes for the retreat.'"
Ānanda then spoke to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus said:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts, forbidding us from eating in the same place, and not permitting us to go to other households before or after a meal without having informed the bhikṣus.”
"We eat and dwell together with our fellow practitioners of the holy life; because of our reverence and deference toward them, we did not dare to inform you frequently.
For this reason, Ānanda went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit [the wearing of] robes.
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu, while in a communal dining area, goes to another house before or after a meal without informing the other bhikṣus, except at the appropriate time, it is a pāyattika.
The "appropriate time" refers to the period for obtaining robes; this is called the appropriate time.
"Monk" is as explained above.

"Eating together" refers to either four *śī* of rice made into cooked rice or eight *śī* of roasted flour, or one *dōng* and two *shēng* of wheat porridge, or fish or meat in the amount of half a bowl or one full bowl; this is called eating together.
"Before eating" means not yet having eaten.
"After eating" means having already finished eating; although it may be early in the day, it is called "after eating.
"Going to other households" refers to the households of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

Regarding "informing" (*śrāvaṇa*): if one informs [the community] of entering a village at an improper time, or informs of going to a bhikṣuṇī monastery, or informs of leaving the place where the Dharma is being preached, these are not called "informing."
One should say:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:
I, [name], having departed from the practice of eating together, have gone to another household."
He replied, “Yes.
Regarding the phrase "except at other times," the Blessed One stated that there is no offense.
The "other times" refer to the robe season (*cīvarakāla*).
The robe season consists of one month when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, and five months when the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
During the interval of the robe season, one abandons five offenses:

There is no offense for eating apart from the community, eating at various locations, or consuming food separately without having informed others; likewise, there is no offense for keeping extra robes or staying overnight separated from one's robes.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation), it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu departs from his fellow monks while they are sharing a meal, he should inform them of his departure; if he departs without informing them, it is a pāyattika offense.
If he eats the five types of formal meals or the five types of mixed formal meals at another location, it is two pāyattika offenses.

If one eats at various places without informing others or leaving the community, there is no offense in either case if it is for the purpose of performing a ritual offering of food or during the distribution of robes.
If a bhikṣu’s residence has no food and someone invites him to eat, that very place is considered a "shared meal."
If one wishes to go elsewhere from that place, one should inform [the others] before departing; if one departs without informing them, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation within a village, that very place is termed "eating together."
If one intends to go elsewhere early in the morning, one should inform [the resident monks] upon passing by;
for one who goes without informing them, it is as explained above.
If the Sangha has been invited to a meal in a village, and a bhikṣu passes by their house, and the donor says:
"Venerable One!
Today I am providing a meal for the Saṃgha; may you, Venerable One, also accept my invitation.
If a bhikṣu accepts this, it is termed "eating together."
If it is still early in the day and the bhikṣu wishes to go elsewhere, he should announce his departure;
if he departs without announcing it, it is a pāyattika offense.
The rest is as explained above.
If a donor invites the Saṃgha for a meal, and a bhikṣu who is begging for alms happens to arrive at that house, the donor says:
"I have now invited the Saṃgha for a meal; may the Venerable One also accept my invitation."
If a bhikṣu accepts it, it is also called "eating together.
The bhikṣu then reflects to himself:
"The donor’s faith and generosity are profound; I cannot digest this. It would be better for me to go begging and obtain just enough to sustain my life."
If one wishes to depart, one should inform [the community] before leaving;
if one departs without informing them, it is a pāyattika offense.
The rest is as explained above.
If two bhikṣus, each having their own place for eating, travel together on the road toward a village and deliberate, saying:
"Today we shall first eat at one household, and afterwards we shall eat the afternoon meal together in succession at the remaining households."
"One bhikṣu should announce his departure;
if he departs without having announced it, it is a pāyattika.
If he arrives at a family where food has already been prepared and receives the five kinds of primary foods or the five kinds of mixed primary foods, it is two pāyattikas."
One is free from the offense of eating at improper times or eating at various locations, provided it is for the purpose of performing a ritual offering of food or during the distribution of robes;
in both cases, there is no fault. The same applies to a second person.
If a bhikṣu goes on almsround and receives one *śoṇa*, two *śoṇas*, or even up to one *droṇa* from each household, there is no fault in taking them.

If one household obtains four *sheng* of cooked rice, or eight *sheng* of flour, or one or two *sheng* of wheat cakes, or half a bowl or a full bowl of fish or meat, one must not seek further from other places.
Among these, what constitutes an offense and what does not?
All types of congee,
with the exception of congee made with fish or meat.
As for congee, it must be freshly drawn from the cauldron so that one cannot form characters by drawing on it.
All cakes, all parched grains, and all fruits are not "food for a separate assembly," not "food for various places," and not "satisfying food."
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
In this context, the story of Queen Mallikā should be told, as related in the *Madhyama Āgama*, up until the point where the elder bhikṣus entered the palace in succession to provide instruction.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin entered next to deliver his exhortation.
Meanwhile, Queen Mallikā was sitting within the palace, wearing fine garments of dyed silk and adorned with gold, silver, pearls, and jewels upon her clothes.

At that time, Udāyin entered the palace; when the lady saw him, a sense of reverence suddenly arose within her, and the heavy garments she had adorned with gold, silver, pearls, and gems slipped from her smooth body onto the ground.
The lady felt ashamed and immediately crouched down, while her attendants shielded her with their bodies.
Then Udāyin, having seen this, retreated and went out; returning to the vihāra, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones!
King Prasenajit has concealed a treasure vessel; I have now seen it."
The bhikṣus asked,
“What did you see? He replied:
"I have seen Lady Mallikā.
The bhikṣus said, "Elder!..."

When you, as one who has left the household life, enter a village, you should maintain the mindset of a forest-dweller (āraṇyaka); do not become attached to forms, seeing them as if you do not see and hearing them as if you do not hear.
He replied, "I truly saw it; how could I say that I did not see it?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for bhikṣus to enter the royal palace.
Because the bhikṣus did not enter the palace, the ladies said to Queen Mallikā:
"It is because of you that the bhikṣus no longer come here; we are unable to hear the Dharma or pay homage to the Saṃgha."
Queen Mallikā said:
"Why do you resent me?
You may seek the king for yourself."
The ladies-in-waiting then said to the king:
"Great King!
For what reason do the bhikṣus no longer enter the palace to provide instruction?"
At that time, having heard these words, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Bhikṣus, for what reason do you no longer enter the palace to provide instruction?
The Buddha said,
“Great King!”
"There is a fault therein; having seen it, the Tathāgata does not permit them to enter again.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying, "What fault or calamity is there in that place?"
“May I hear them?
The Buddha told the Great King:
“There are ten causes for transgression and harm such that a bhikṣu must not enter a royal palace.”
Regarding the ten matters, as stated in the *Madhyama Āgama Sūtra*: "A bhikṣu must not enter the royal palace.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha, having perceived the faults involved, prohibited bhikṣus from entering royal palaces.
When I myself had not yet given rise to faith, even my own right hand was still without faith; how much more so for a bhikṣu, for whom the Buddha has already established the precepts?
"You should simply comply.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu enters the palace of a kṣatriya consecrated king while the king’s wife and treasures have not yet been stored away, and he crosses the threshold, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "kings," this refers to those of the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Ugara royal lineage, the Śākya royal lineage, the Vṛjana royal lineage, and others of a similar kind; even if one is a king who is not of the Kṣatriya caste, there is no offense for one who enters.
If one is a king, a kṣatriya, but not consecrated, there is no offense in entering.
If one is a king, a kṣatriya, and consecrated, but has no territory, there is no offense in entering.
This king, this kṣatriya, this consecrated one who possesses a kingdom, may not enter.
To "enter the palace" means to enter the inner apartments.
"The king’s consort has not yet hidden her treasures" means that the king’s consort has not yet brought out her treasures.
"Regarding 'not yet concealed,' it means the royal treasure has not yet been brought out.
As for 'crossing the threshold,' it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
A pāyattika is as explained above."
If a king, having newly constructed a palace, speaks with faith and joy to a bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, please accept this for my sake and make use of it first," the bhikṣu should say:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not enter the palace.
The king spoke again:
“Venerable sir, is there perhaps some expedient means by which entry might be permitted?”
One should reply:
"The King’s consorts and treasures must all have gone out before one may enter.
If they have already gone out, one should enter.
Once the bhikṣu has entered, the king’s wife and her treasures follow in succession; the bhikṣu must not leave and go out. At that time, he may sit [there] without fault.
If the bhikṣu goes out in the interim for the sake of answering the calls of nature, he must not re-enter; should he re-enter, it is a pāyattika.

If the king frequently visits the ponds and groves for recreation and constructs a royal pleasure palace therein, and all the king’s ladies and treasures are brought out and placed within, and there are seven layers of gates—if one enters one gate, two, three, or even up to six gates, there is no offense.
In the seventh case, if one foot has entered [the palace], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if both feet have crossed the threshold, it is a *pāyattika*.

If the king has finished his excursion and the ladies-in-waiting and precious objects have all been removed, such that the pleasure palace is empty and people are entering, there is no offense for a bhikṣu to enter.
If a king, out of faith and with affection and respect, takes the bhikṣu by the hand and leads him in, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an ivory-worker named Dharmadatta. At that time, a bhikṣu went to his house and said, "Donor, please make a needle case for me."
He then fashioned one for him— neither too large nor too small, with a smooth and lustrous finish— and brought it back to his cell.
When the bhikṣus saw it, they asked, "Elder!..."
"Where did you obtain this, which is neither too large nor too small, and possesses such lustrous,
smooth color? He replied,
"A master ivory-carver named Dharmadatta made it for me."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they each went to seek [the ivory].
The ivory-worker thought to himself, "The bhikṣus will all surely need it.
He then thought again:
"The Sangha is a field of merit; I shall invite the Sangha to offer them needle-cases.
He then went to the Jeta Grove, prostrated at the feet of the monks, and said:
"I wish to invite the Sangha according to my custom to bestow needle-cases upon them."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they each went to take some; some took one, some took two or three, and so on up to ten, until the ivory was completely exhausted.
The donor said, "The teeth are already gone; now there are only bones. If you need them, I shall prepare them.
He replied:
“I need them all.
When the bones were exhausted, he spoke again:
“The bones are also gone; now there are only the horns. If you need them, I shall make them for you.”
He replied, "All are required.
As those who requested them were so numerous, there was nothing left with which to provide for their needs.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, when the hour had come, put on his village-dwelling robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, eventually arriving at that house.
At that time, Dharmadinnā, with a heart of faith and joy, took the food out to offer as alms; recognizing Śāriputra from before, she immediately prostrated herself at his feet and stood before him.
Śāriputra asked, “Sister! How is it at home?
Is your household business flourishing?”
He replied,
"The household is tolerable, but our business does not increase. He asked:
"Why? He replied, "Venerable Sir!"
My husband invited several bhikṣus and offered them needle cases.
Some bhikṣus took one, some took two or three, and others even took as many as ten.
"We have exhausted all the ivory for bone, and all the bone for horn; there are so many seekers that we have nothing left to provide for our livelihood.
Venerable One!
Our family depends on this for our living, to clothe and feed our children, and to pay our taxes and levies to the government."
"The Venerable One is my object of reverence; I was merely speaking thus!
For this reason, while my husband is present, I speak as if he were absent; while he is awake, I speak as if he were asleep.
At that time, after the Venerable Śāriputra had taught the Dharma to this woman in accordance with her needs and inspired her with joy, he returned to the monastery.
For these reasons, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned them thoroughly regarding the aforementioned events.
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the making of needle cases from ivory, bone, or horn.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from ivory, bone, or horn, having broken it [after use], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Ivory" refers to elephant ivory, fish tusks, makara tusks, pig tusks, and other such varieties of ivory.
"Bones" refers to the bones of elephants, horses, oxen, camels, and dragons, as well as other such bones.
"Horns" refers to the horns of cattle, water buffaloes, rhinoceroses, deer, and sheep, as well as other such horns.
Regarding the agent: whether one acts oneself or causes another to act, if [the object] is broken, one must confess a pāyattika offense;
if it is not broken and one confesses, it is a vinaya-offense of transgression (vyatikrama).
"Prāyaścittika" is as explained above.
At that time, the World-Honored One established a precept forbidding the making of needle cases from ivory, bone, or horn.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus instead made them from gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and precious jade. The Buddha said:

"One must not use gold, silver, or precious gems to make needle cases; rather, one should use copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, brass, white bronze, bamboo, wood, *kambala* wool, cotton cloth, or bird feathers—even down to the needle-cases attached to alms-bag straps."
Therefore it was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, on the fast days—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month—the people within the city went out to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
At that time, Prince Prasenajit also came to pay his respects; proceeding in order, he went to where Nanda and Upananda were, prostrated himself at their feet, and said:
"I wish to see [the Buddha]; I pray you show me the way."
He replied,
"Very well," and immediately led him up to the upper story of the pavilion, saying:
"O youth! Behold these pillars, beams, rafters, and ridgepoles; the capitals, brackets, and crossbeams; their various carvings and engravings, and their manifold painted decorations.

Next, he went to Nanda’s dwelling and saw a high, large bed upon a blue-colored floor-covering, provided with a heavy footstool and spread with a *kucīka* mat, with pillows placed at both ends. Having seen this, he immediately asked the Venerable One:
"Whose bed and bedding is this?
He replied, "It is mine."
The prince said, "This is grand and magnificent; it is not suitable for a bhikṣu.
He then asked again:
"If this is not suitable for me, who ought to possess it?
He replied,
"It is the kind of attire and ornamentation that should belong to a king or a prince."
The bhikṣu said: "Am I not a prince?
Had the World-Honored One not left the household life, I would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents; all of you would have been my subjects."

However, the World-Honored One does not delight in such places; he left the household life to attain Buddhahood and became a Wheel-Turning King of Dharma, and I am his son, a prince of the Wheel-Turning Dharma.
Even if my attire were to exceed this, it would still be appropriate, let alone these coarse garments!
Upon hearing this, the prince was filled with shame and remained silent.
The bhikṣus, having learned of these circumstances, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call Nanda and Upananda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Why have you decorated the beds and mats in such a way as to be ridiculed by the people of the world?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to make beds that exceed the prescribed measurements.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, the World-Honored One established a precept forbidding the making of beds that exceed the measurements.
After the bhikṣus had cut the wood down to the proper length, they used the discarded ends to prop up the legs of their beds.
At that time, on the fast days—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month—the people within the city went out to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
Prince Pasenadi also came to pay his respects, and subsequently went to where Nanda and Upananda were, saying to them:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Show me the place where you have been looking.
Eventually, he arrived at Nanda’s room; having seen it, he immediately asked, "For what reason did you cut off the legs of this bed?"
He replied,
"That which is cut short and above that size is permitted by the World-Honored One.
The prince said:
"If the Blessed One permits [beds] to be cut down to a certain height, yet they are now propped up again with supports, how is this different from the original state?
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bed legs must be measured according to the prescribed standard; the use of further supports is not permitted."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu makes bed legs, they should be made according to the prescribed measurement: eight finger-breadths of the Sugata’s measure in height, excluding the portion inserted into the frame.
If he makes them exceeding this measurement and then cuts them down, it is a pāyattika.
"Monk" is as explained above.
There are fourteen types of beds for lying down and fourteen types of seats for sitting, as explained above; among these, one commits an offense if they exceed the prescribed dimensions.
"Maker" means either making it oneself or having another make it.
"Sugata" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Eight fingers" refers to the eight fingers of the Buddha.
"Excessive" means exceeding the proper measure.
