"Entering the pivot-hole" means reaching as far as the bottom of the hole.
Having cut it [excessively], one commits a pāyattika offense and must perform repentance.
If one does not cut [the grass] and feels regret, it is a *vinaya-āpatti*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If one sits upon it oneself for the entire day, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one rises and then sits back down, for each instance of sitting, it is a *pāyattika*.
To sit upon another’s bed is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

A bed with raised legs must also be measured and made sturdy. When visiting bhikṣus arrive, the beds and bedding should be assigned in order. If one obtains a bed that exceeds the prescribed measure, one should inform the administrator (*karmadāna*).
“Lend me a saw! He asked,
“For what purpose?”
He replied, "This bed is of excessive size; I wish to cut it so that it conforms to the Dharma.
If the administrator said:
"Do not cut it!
If a donor sees this, they may become displeased.
If one does not intend to stay for long, one should dig into the ground and bury the feet, stopping at the appropriate measurement.
If one intends to stay for a long time, one should bury wooden tubes up to the level of the ground to hold the feet, so that they do not rot and decay.
If a bhikṣu enters a village and sits in the house of a donor, he must not sit with his feet dangling if the legs of the bed are high.
If one knows the person well, one should ask for a footstool to support the feet;
if one does not know the person well, one should ask for bricks or wood to support the feet while sitting. However, if one sits on a high seat within a house of merit, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, on the fast days—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month—the people of the city went out to pay their respects and visit the World-Honored One.
Prince Prasenajit also came out to pay his respects; next he went to where Nanda and Upananda were and said to them, "Bhikṣus!
Show me a place where I may look about."
He replied, "Very well!
and immediately led him up to the upper story, pointing it out and saying:
"Prince! Look at these pillars, beams, rafters, and ridgepoles; the capitals, brackets, and crossbeams; their various carvings and engravings, and their diverse painted decorations.
Next, he went to his own chamber and saw a blue-colored floor covering, a fine bed, spread with a cotton-wool mattress, with pillows placed at both ends and covered with white woolen cloth.
Having seen it, he immediately asked,
"To whom does this belong?
They replied:
"I grant you permission," the prince said.
"This is too grand and magnificent; it is not suitable for you, Venerable One."
He replied,
"If it is not suitable for me, who else should possess it?
The prince answered:
"The attire appropriate for a king, a prince, or a high minister.
He spoke again:
"Am I not a prince?"
"World-Honored One, had you not left the household life, you would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four quarters of the world, and all of us would have been your subjects.

However, the World-Honored One did not delight in that state; instead, he left home to attain Buddhahood and became a Dharma-Wheel King. I am a prince of the Dharma-Wheel King, so even if my attire were more magnificent than this, it would still be appropriate, let alone these coarse garments."
Upon hearing this, the prince was filled with shame and remained silent.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"Call Nanda and Upananda here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Why did you use a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton and fine linen, thereby being censured by the people of the world?"
"From this day forward, cotton-down and fine silk mattresses are not permitted.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu sits or lies down on a cotton-down or ramie-filled mattress, having pulled out [the filling], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding *tūla*: it refers to *agatūla*, *bakatūla*, *koṭaja-tūla*, *śṛṅga-tūla*, *trṇa-tūla*, *kāśi-tūla*, *puṣpa-tūla*, and all other such types of *tūla*; these are called *tūla*.
In this case, having pulled out the cotton-wool mattress, one must confess a *pāyattika* offense.

At the time of pulling it out, one should shake it until it is completely exhausted; if it is not exhausted, one should moisten the hands with water, rub and clean it, and only then [confess] the *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If one sits oneself for the entire day, it is one *pāyattika*.
Once having risen, if one sits again, for every instance of sitting, there is a separate *pāyattika*.
If one sits upon it when permission has not been granted, there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
If one uses a pillow made of ramie to support the head or the feet, there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
If one supports the head or the feet due to illness, there is no offense.
If one uses a pillow made of *tūla* cotton or animal hide, one incurs two *vinayātikrama* offenses: one for the hide and one for the *tūla*.
If a bhikṣu enters a village and the wind blows *tūla* onto his robe, and he sits down while still wearing the robe, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
One should brush it away before sitting.

If cotton-wool (*tūla*) has been carried in a vehicle, borne on the shoulder, or slung across the back, and the wind blows it onto a bhikṣu’s robe, if he sits with the robe as it is, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense; he should brush it away before sitting.
If grass or *tūla* cotton has been spread out, a bhikṣu must not sit upon it;
if a bhikṣu walks through a field of *tūla* cotton while wearing his robes, he must not sit down, but should brush them off;
if he walks through a field of grass or *puṣpa-tūla* (flower-cotton) while wearing his robes, he must not sit down, but should brush them off.
If one spreads grass, flowers, or cotton upon a seat, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one gathers grass, flowers, or cotton for a seat, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one does so while working in a field, it is likewise an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one prepares a lion throne for a Vinaya master or a Dharma master and scatters flowers upon it, one must not sit on it; however, there is no offense in brushing them away before sitting.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

For five reasons of benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would go from house to house among the bhikṣus once every five days. He saw that the beds, mattresses, and bedding of the bhikṣus were soiled, greasy, and impure, stained here and there like *mandārava* flowers left to dry in the midday sun.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Whose bedding and sitting mats are so filthy and impure?
They replied:
"These bhikṣus did not cover their bedding with any material; that is why it became soiled.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I allow you to make *niṣīdana* (sitting mats)."
Furthermore, after the Buddha had permitted the making of *niṣīdana* (sitting mats), the bhikṣus began sewing them from joined threads.

On five occasions for the sake of benefiting [the Sangha], the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha went on inspection through the various dwellings every five days. He saw that the sewn cotton cloths were soiled with grease and impurities, stained here and there like *mandārava* flowers left to dry in the midday sun.
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked intentionally:
"Who is this that has sewn threads together to make a *niṣīdana* that is so greasy and impure?
They replied:
“The Blessed One has permitted the making of *niṣīdana* (sitting mats), yet the bhikṣus are sewing them together from threads.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“How is it that you are sewing the *niṣīdana* together from threads?”
"From this day forward, you should make them according to measure: two Sugata-span long and one and a half spans wide.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were engaged in discussion in the lecture hall, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
The World-Honored One has prescribed the dimensions for the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat); yet when it is spread out as a seat, the two knees do not reach [the edge]."
"If I spread out both knees, there will be no room for me to sit.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Who is the senior elder (sthavira) in the Saṃgha?"
He replied, "Śāriputra. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Many fellow practitioners of the holy life have made this argument; why did you listen in silence?
You shall now be punished by standing in the midday sun.
Śāriputra accepted the punishment and immediately stood in the middle of the day.
Then the bhikṣus each came forward to repent their transgressions, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Venerable Śāriputra’s body is frail and weak; we pray that you will forgive his offense and not cause him distress."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“It is not that he does not wish to; it is because his body suffers from a cold wind disease that it finds relief only in the sun.
While the sun, moon, and stars in the void can still be turned back, Śāriputra’s mind, having received the Tathāgata’s reprimand, cannot be turned back.”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that the Venerable Śāriputra’s mind cannot be turned back?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today that his mind cannot be turned back; in past lives as well it was thus, as is explained in detail in the *Sarpajātaka-sūtra*."
"The serpent at that time was none other than Śāriputra; at that time, his mind was firm and could not be turned back.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

Out of consideration for five matters of benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would go from room to room among the bhikṣus once every five days. He saw that the center of the monastic mats and bedding was fresh and clean, while both edges were soiled and stained.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Monks, what kind of bedding is this?
The center is bright and fine, while both sides are soiled."
He replied, “World-Honored One, because the *niṣīdana* prescribed by you is small, it cannot cover the entire [seat]; thus, the area it covers is clean, while the area it does not cover is soiled.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit you to make [robes] in two layers. You must not haphazardly grow weary of your practice; when using small cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), you should make them in two layers.
If using *kambala* wool, you may make them in one layer, but for *kaijū* wool, you must make them in two layers."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it upon his shoulder, and paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One. Knowing this, the Buddha asked him on purpose:
"What is that which you carry upon your shoulder?"
He replied, "A small *niṣīdana*,
World-Honored One."
"This sitting mat is too small; we only pray that you will increase its size.
The Buddha asked, "By how much more must it be increased to be sufficient?"
He replied, "A span. The Buddha said:
“Listen; it shall be increased by one span.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
If a bhikṣu makes a niṣīdana, he should make it according to the prescribed measure: two sugata-spans in length and one and a half spans in width, with an additional span added.
"If one makes it exceeding [the prescribed measure], having cut it down, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Makes" means either to make it oneself or to cause another to make it.
The *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is that which was permitted by the Blessed One.
Regarding its measurements: it should be two Sugata-spans in length and one and a half spans in width;
"length" refers to the longitudinal dimension.
"Vipula" means broad.
"Sugata" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Vitasti" refers to the span of a Tathāgata’s hand, which measures two chi and four cun.
To increase it by one span means to add two or three layers, sewing them directly opposite one another.
If it exceeds the prescribed measure, one must cut it down and then perform the *pāyattika* confession;
if one confesses without having cut it down, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Regarding the *pāyattika*: as explained above, if one makes [a robe] that is of correct length but exceeds the prescribed width, whether making it oneself or having another make it, once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
To use [a robe] that exceeds the prescribed measurements constitutes an offense against the Vinaya:
namely, when it is wide within the proper measure but long beyond it;
or when it is of proper measure at the center but exceeds it at the edges.
If the edges are of the prescribed measurement but the center exceeds it, whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, upon its completion, it is a pāyattika offense.
To use it constitutes a vinaya-duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding cotton cloth, shrunken cloth, or cloth sprinkled with water, if one intends for it to expand once it has dried, and it is subsequently completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
To use it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
When making it, one must make it according to the prescribed measurements; it must not exceed those measurements.

A *niṣīdana* is a cloth for sitting upon; it may not be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be given away as a formal gift (*pariṣkāra-dāna*), nor may it be used to carry firewood, grass, or grain sacks—it may only be spread out for sitting.
If traveling on a road, one may obtain long cotton cloth (*dīrghakarpāsa*) and place it upon a robe-bag or carry it on one's shoulder.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

Out of his five ways of benefiting the world, the World-Honored One went on inspection of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days. He saw that a garment stained with pus, blood, and scabs was being dried in the sun.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked intentionally:
"What kind of garment is so impure as this?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
It is because the bhikṣus have the disease of scabies that their robes are soiled."
The Buddha said,
“From this day forward, I permit the making of wound-covering robes.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed account is as above.

At that time, after the Blessed One had permitted the making of wound-covering robes (*vastra*), the bhikṣus did not cut the threads but made them by joining the strands together. Because he wished to benefit them in five ways, the Blessed One went on a tour of the bhikṣus' quarters once every five days; there he saw wound-covering robes made of joined threads, stained with pus and blood and soiled with grime, being dried in the midday sun.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally:
"What kind of robe is this, made of such coarse thread and so impure?
They replied:
“The Blessed One has permitted the making of wound-covering robes, yet you monks have made them by spinning yarn together with pus, blood,
and filth. The Buddha said to the monks,
“How is it that you have made wound-covering robes by spinning yarn together [with such impurities]?”
"From this day forward, you should make wound-covering robes according to the prescribed measure.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering robe, it should be made according to the prescribed measure: four Sugata-spaṃs in length and two and a half spaṃs in width.
If he makes it exceeding these dimensions, he must cut it down; this constitutes a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikkhu” is as explained above.
“A cloth for covering sores” is that which was permitted by the Blessed One.
“Of measured dimensions, in length and breadth, of a Sugata’s span” is as explained above.
If it exceeds the proper measure, one must cut it down and then perform the *pāyattika* confession;
if one confesses without having cut it down, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If it is of proper length but exceeds the measure in width; or of proper width but exceeds the measure in length; or of proper measurement in the center but exceeds it at the edges; or of proper measurement at the edges but exceeds it in the center—whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it—and it is completed, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one uses it, there is an offense of *vinaya-duṣkṛta*.
If one bends the measure, contracts the measure, or sprinkles water on the measure with the intent that it shall grow larger once dry and be completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
To use it [in such a manner] constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.

It should be made as a standard-sized garment for covering sores or as a personal robe; it must not be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be given away as a formal gift (*pariṣkāra*), nor may firewood or grass be gathered within it to carry on a journey.

When about to enter a village, one should first put it on, and then don the saṃghāṭī with its fastening ties. Having left the village, one should remove the saṃghāṭī, shake out the folded cotton cloth, and place it back in its usual location.
When wearing the wound-covering cloth, do not allow it to dry out or peel away so that the blood from the wound flows out; rather, one should keep it moist when entering the water.
One must not enter the place where the Sangha regularly bathes, but should stay in a secluded spot, soaking it until it is saturated, and only then remove it to wash it clean.
Having bathed, one may take a cloth to wipe the body; on subsequent days, it shall be used in the same manner until the wound has healed.
Once healed, one may use it to make the three robes or give it as a pure gift for other purposes.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
It is as described at length in the *Vaiśākha Mṛgāramātṛ* section of the *Triṃśad-vastuka*.
Even within a distance of twelve *yojanas*, he gave *varṣāśāṭī* robes to the bhikṣus.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above, at that time the World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to make *varṣāśāṭī* robes; however, the bhikṣus did not cut the threads but instead joined them together to make them.

For the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. There he saw some cotton cloth made of spun threads that was soiled, stained, and impure, being dried in the midday sun.
Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked on purpose:
"What kind of garment is this, made of spun threads, that has become so impure?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
Although the Tathāgata permitted the making of rain-bathing robes, the bhikṣus have woven them from threads that are coarse, stained, and impure.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"How is it that you join threads together to make rain-bathing robes?
From this day forward, they should be made according to measure: six Sugata-spans in length and two and a half spans in width."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measurement: six Sugata-span hands in length and two and a half span hands in width.
If it exceeds the measurement, it must be cut down; [otherwise,] it is a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.
“Rain-bathing robe” is that which was permitted by the Blessed One.
“Of proper measure” means six Sugata-spans in length and two and a half spans in width.
"Long," "broad," "Sugata," and "span" are as explained above.
If it exceeds the prescribed measure, one must cut it down and then confess a *pāyattika* offense;
if one does not cut it down before confessing, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline).
Regarding the *pāyattika*: as explained above.

If it is long according to the measure but wide beyond the measure; or wide according to the measure but long beyond the measure; or the center according to the measure but the edges beyond the measure; or the edges according to the measure but the center beyond the measure—whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it—if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses [the robe] beyond the prescribed measure, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

Whether one bends the measurement, contracts the measurement, or sprinkles water upon it with the intent that it should grow larger after drying—if one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, and it is completed, it is a pāyattika.
To use it [in such a manner] constitutes an offense against the Vinaya.
A bhikṣu who has accomplished five qualities should be appointed by the Saṃgha as the distributor of rain-cloths (*varṣāśāṭī*).
What are these five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, and not following delusion, one knows what has been obtained and what has not been obtained.
The *karmavācanā* officiant should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"Venerable Sangha, listen! If the time has come for the Sangha, let the Sangha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to distribute the rain-bathing robes.
This is the motion. "Venerable Sangha, listen!"
"Monk so-and-so has accomplished five qualities; the Saṃgha now appoints monk so-and-so to distribute the *varṣāśāṭī* robes.
Venerable sirs, those who approve of appointing monk so-and-so to distribute the *varṣāśāṭī* robes, please remain silent; those who do not approve, please speak."
“The Sangha has already consented to the distribution of the *varṣāśāṭī* robe to the bhikṣu named So-and-so; because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed the *karmavācanā*, one should announce among the assembly of monks:
“Venerable sirs, in this distribution of items, there are discrepancies and differences—some being four finger-widths or eight finger-widths shorter—which cannot be calculated as equal.”
If one does not announce [the time], one incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
From the first day of the fourth month, one may obtain a rain-bathing robe; having received it according to the order of seniority starting from the *sthavira*, one is not permitted to bathe naked.
Furthermore, one must not wear a rain-bath robe; instead, one should wear other old garments.
There is no offense if one bathes naked in a secluded place or in deep water.

One must not wear a rain-bath robe while performing work for the Saṃgha, such as repairing halls and buildings, applying white lime, plastering with mud, roofing a house, or working on drainage channels and drawing water from wells; in these cases, one should wear other old garments.

This rain-bathing robe must not be used as one of the three formal robes, nor may it be given away as a pure gift (pariṣkāra); it must not be used for other purposes, such as carrying firewood, grass, or large grinding stones, nor may one wear it while entering a pool or a body of water to bathe.
One may wear [the robe] during heavy rain, but not during light rain.
If heavy rain has suddenly ceased and the stains have not yet been washed away, one may wear it to enter a pool or a large body of water to bathe.
If a bhikṣu, while ill, takes medicine that causes vomiting or purging, or draws blood from his head, or when eating in the open air, he may use it to construct a screen or shelter.
This rain-bathing robe is to be used for four and a half months; on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one should announce before the Saṃgha:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe.
Thus it is announced three times.
Once relinquished, it may be accepted and used as one of the three robes, or given as a pure gift (pariṣkāra), or used for other purposes.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, as described in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣus wore robes with loose threads, and the various non-Buddhists also wore robes with loose threads.

At that time, a lay follower (upāsaka) wishing to pay homage to a bhikṣu mistakenly paid homage to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). Upon hearing the different words of the blessing (svastyayana), he realized it was not a bhikṣu and immediately felt ashamed.
At that same time, a disciple of the non-Buddhists wishing to pay homage to his teacher mistakenly paid homage to a bhikṣu; such were their mutual confusions.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣus, robes should be made pure by cutting the threads and made pure by dyeing."

The non-Buddhists (tīrthika), wishing to distinguish themselves from the bhikṣus, left behind red ochre (*jūra*) and red stone to dye their robes, and they carried triple-jointed staffs and water flasks (*kuṇḍikā*).

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Bhikṣu Āraṇyaka obtained *kauśeya* cloth; he wished to boil a dye-liquid to color it, as described above among the three types of methods for dyeing robes.
Furthermore, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī and Vaiśālī, a bhikṣu obtained a *kambala* (woolen blanket), as described above.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, there was the Venerable Sundarananda, the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, who possessed thirty marks.
After the meal, he departed from Śrāvastī with Ānanda following behind, as was previously described regarding the three types of dyed robes.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the Venerable Arajunda made a robe according to the measurements of the Buddha’s robe and entered Śrāvastī wearing it.
This bhikṣu was short in stature, yet his robes were so long that they trailed on the ground as he walked, leading the people of the world to mock him, saying:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas walks with his robes trailing.
Others also rebuked him, saying:
"Do you not know? The robe of the śramaṇa Gautama was not made by his own parents; when it is worn out, he obtains another. That is why it is like this.
Because of these circumstances, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"Call Āraja Maṇḍa here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you shall make robes according to your own body measurements.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
If a bhikṣu makes a robe imitating the measurements of the Tathāgata’s robe, and it exceeds those measurements, he must cut it down; this constitutes a pāyattika offense.
The measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe is nine sugata-span lengths in length and six spans in width; this is called the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe.
"Monk" is as explained above.
As for the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe: it is nine Sugata-spans in length and six Sugata-spans in width.
"Householder" (gṛhapati) means one who is upright.
"Broad" (vistīrṇa) means horizontal.
"Sugata" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Regarding the span of a *vitasti*: the span of a Tathāgata measures two chi and four cun.
If it exceeds this, one must cut it down;
having done so, one commits a *pāyattika* offense and must perform repentance.
If one does not cut [the cloth] and confesses the offense, it is a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If the length is appropriate but the width exceeds the measure, whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses it, there is an offense of violating the Vinaya.

[This applies to] making it wide within the prescribed measure but long beyond the measure; or middle within the measure but edge beyond the measure; or edge within the measure but middle beyond the measure; or if it is made by bending the measure, contracting the measure, or using the "water-sprinkling" measure with the intent that it shall grow larger once dry—whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it—once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
To use [it] constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
When making it, one must reduce the measurements; it must not exceed the prescribed measure.
It should be made according to the size of one's own body.
There are three types of saṃghāṭī robes:
superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior one is five cubits in length and three cubits in width.
The medium size is five cubits long and three cubits one unextended hand wide;
the small size is four and a half cubits long and three cubits one unextended hand wide.
When putting on the robes, one should fashion the border-mark two finger-widths lower [than the edge].
There are three types of *uttarāsaṅga*:
superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior [type] is five cubits in length and three cubits in width.
The middling [type] is five cubits plus one unextended hand in length and three cubits plus one unextended hand in width.
The inferior [type] is four and a half cubits in length and three cubits plus one unextended hand in width.
There are also three types of *antarvāsaka* (inner robes):
superior, medium, and inferior.
The superior one is five cubits in length and three cubits in width.
The medium size is five cubits long and three cubits one unextended hand wide;
the small size is four and a half cubits long and three cubits one unextended hand wide.
Downward, it reaches as far as covering the three *maṇḍalas* to form the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
Therefore, it is said.
