The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, Volume Twenty-one.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The Tenth of the Ninety-Two Rules on the *Pācittiya* Dharmas. The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was appointed by the Saṅgha to oversee the nine matters, as described above.

Even down to Dharmaruci, who emitted light from his right little finger to illuminate the way, he assigned them to their respective quarters in order: those practicing in the forest (*āraṇyaka*) with those practicing in the forest; those who beg for alms (*piṇḍapātika*) with those who beg for alms; those who wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*) with those who wear rag-robes; those who eat in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*) with those who eat in a single sitting; those who always sit (*naiṣadyika*) with those who always sit; those who sit in the open air (*abhyavakāśika*) with those who sit in the open air; those who sleep on grass mats (*tṛṇasaṃstarika*) with those who sleep on grass mats; those who recite the scriptures (*dharmabhāṇaka*) with those who recite the scriptures; Dharma-teachers (*dharmakathika*) with Dharma-teachers; those who study the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) with those who study the Vinaya; Arhats with Arhats; those possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*) with those possessing the three knowledges; those possessing the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijña*) with those possessing the six supernormal powers; and those who do not observe formal decorum (*anairyāpathika*) with those who do not observe formal decorum.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to Dharmapāla:
"Venerable sir!
Please dwell in one place together with us six."
He replied, "Wait until the lowest-ranking member of your group receives the next room; then you may dwell together as you please.
At that time, the lowest-ranking member of the group received a dilapidated room, where the beds, stools, mattresses, pillows, and all other furnishings were worn out.
Furthermore, the food in the separate quarters was likewise coarse and poor, so they said to one another:
"The Elder Dabba Mallaputta treats us like enemies; he gives us inferior rooms and coarse food."
"O Elder! It is only because you have long dwelled in the holy life that you cause us such great distress.
However, since the World-Honored One has established the precept that one must not slander another with groundless *pārājika* charges, we shall now slander you with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
He immediately went to where he was and said,
"Venerable sir!
You have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
He replied,
"I have committed no such offense.
The other said:
"Who else is a thief that you would say, 'I am a thief'?
You have merely committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Thus he slandered the Bhikṣu Dharmadatta in private, slandered him among many people, and slandered him within the Saṃgha, claiming he had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhāvakī went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha asked, "Is this truly so? He replied:
"There is none," [the monk replied].
The Buddha said, "You have no such offense; the World-Honored One knows you to be pure."
Dhāvak said:

"Although the World-Honored One knows that I am without fault, I only pray that the World-Honored One will speak to those people so as to inspire faith in them, lest they slander me for a long night and fail to obtain what is beneficial."
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here. When they had arrived,
the Buddha questioned them thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter.
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"This is an evil matter.

Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, say that one should give rise to reverence toward those who practice the holy life, practicing kindness in body, kindness in speech, and kindness in mind?"
Why do you now slander [me] with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not according to the Buddha’s teaching; one cannot thereby cultivate wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, slanders another bhikṣu with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "anger" (*dveṣa*), it refers to the nine causes of resentment as well as anger arising from improper grounds.

Regarding the tenth, "resentment" (*upanāha*): if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a learner (*śaikṣa*) harbors displeasure—even toward an Arhat—regarding a matter that has no basis, and which they have neither seen, nor heard, nor suspected, yet they bring such a charge among the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, then for each individual accusation, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation), it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, out of malice, makes two kinds of similar accusations— namely, one that is pure and one that is impure—
the pure accusation is as follows:
"Do you see me committing any offense?
Regarding one or two of the thirteen matters, if he has not seen, heard, suspected, or ascertained [the offense], yet in private, in a group, or in the midst of the Saṃgha, he says:
"I see you committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa; I hear you committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa; I suspect you committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa."

If one hears what was not heard, the root of hearing is unreal; if one doubts what was not doubted, the root of doubt is unreal; or if one forgets having previously seen, heard, or doubted—yet claims, "I saw it not thus," "I heard it not thus," or "I doubted it not thus"—and slanders another face-to-face, eye to eye, with every word, it is a *pāyattika*.
To slander one who is pure by perceiving them as impure is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To desire to expel [one] is a *pāyattika*.
To slander one who is impure by perceiving them as pure is a *vinayātikrama*.
If one intends to expel [a monk] and does so, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one slanders a pure person while perceiving them as pure, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one intends to expel [a monk] and does so, it is a *pāyattika*.
To disparage one who is impure while perceiving them as impure is a *pāyattika*.
To slander a bhikṣu is a *pāyattika*.
To slander a bhikṣuṇī is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To slander a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To slander a layperson constitutes a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the time for almsround had arrived, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city. Proceeding in order to beg for food, he came to a certain household.
The woman said:
"Venerable Sir!
On a certain day, I shall provide a meal for the Saṃgha and bestow robes as an offering."
The bhikṣu replied:
“Excellent, upāsikā!
You should take this opportunity to cultivate the three enduring dharmas for the sake of your body, life, and wealth; practice them constantly and do not allow obstacles to arise.”
After the bhikṣu who had gone for alms returned to the monastery, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
I shall tell you something beneficial."
Question:
"What kind of wholesome deeds? Answer:
"I shall go to such-and-such a house on that day to provide a meal for the Sangha and bestow robes.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda were not far away; hearing the sound of these words, they immediately asked, "Where is that house located?"
"What are your family name and given name?
In which direction does your residence face?
Having thus inquired and gained this knowledge, he went to her house early the next morning and addressed the upāsikā:
"I have heard a pleasant sound.
"Venerable sir, what kind of sound did you hear?
"I heard that you intended to provide a meal for the Saṅgha and offer robes as a gift; is this indeed true?"
He replied, "The thought has just arisen; however, I fear there may be obstacles along the way.
Do you know whether it will bear fruit? Upānanda said to the upāsikā:
"You may take this robe and give it to Nanda.
He replied, "In my home there is no other property; I have only this robe, which I originally intended to offer to the Saṃgha, and I cannot now divert it."
Upānanda then spoke disparagingly:
"What is this so-called Saṃgha?
Even old crows are Saṃgha; even old vultures are Saṃgha."
The Sangha is like a hollowed-out mortar or a leaking trough; it can never be satisfied. What benefit does the Sangha bring you?
Can it give you sons or daughters to live, or can it go before the royal court to settle your legal disputes?
"Nanda can bring you much benefit; simply take this robe and give it to Nanda.
The laywoman replied with the same words as before.
At that time, Nanda again urged her to give it to Upānanda, as described above.
The upāsikā spoke again:
"My household has no other possessions; I was just about to offer them to you, Venerable Sir, but I have already promised them to the Saṃgha, so they cannot be diverted."
Upānanda said, "Whether you give it to him or not is up to your own will.
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
At that time, the upāsikā thought to herself:
"I intended to give this robe to Nanda, yet the Saṃgha is a field of supreme merit, so I now wish to offer it to the Saṃgha.
However, Nanda possesses great power and influence; I fear he might do me some harm."
Having reflected thus, he subsequently ceased giving.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call Upānanda here. When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! By committing these three evil deeds, the donor loses his merit, the recipient loses his benefit, and the Sangha is disparaged.
The Buddha said to Upānanda:
“Have you not often heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, praise few desires and censure many desires?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; one cannot nurture wholesome qualities by means of this.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, yet diverts it to another person, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by himself or hearing it from another.
As for "objects," there are eight kinds, ranging from pure to impure.
As for "direction," the distribution of the objects has already been determined.
As for "the Sangha," there are eight kinds, as explained above.
"To divert" means to transfer [the object] to another person;
this constitutes a *pāyattika*. A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If someone brings an object and asks a bhikṣu:
“Venerable One!
I wish to give these items as a gift; to whom should they be given?
He should say:
"Give it to him wherever his heart finds pleasure.
If he should further ask:
"Where can one obtain great karmic fruition?"
One should say:
"Giving to the Sangha yields great karmic fruit.
He asks again:
"Where are the monks who uphold the precepts?
I wish to give to them.
One should say:
"There are no monks who violate the precepts.
If he asks again,
"In what place do the bhikṣus diligently cultivate their practice, being able to protect the property and always residing here, so that I may see them constantly?"
He said, "A certain bhikṣu is diligently cultivating his practice and is able to protect things; he always resides here.
If you give [this] to that bhikṣu, you will be able to see it constantly."
If one says,
"I wish to give this object as a gift to the Venerable One," one should say:
"I give it to the Saṃgha.
If he says, "I have already given it to the Saṃgha; I wish to give it to you, Venerable Sir, please accept it for me," [one may accept it].
Taking it [in such a case] is without offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha and diverts it to himself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he diverts it to another person, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for one saṃgha, diverts it to another saṃgha, he commits a vinaya offense of *vyatikrama*.
If he diverts an object belonging to a group of many persons to another group of many persons, he commits a vinaya offense of *vyatikrama*.
Even down to animals, if one diverts [an offering] to give it to those animals, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense; one must repent with a sincere mind.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, when the six groups of bhikṣus were reciting the Prātimokṣa during the half-monthly assembly, they remained silent while the four pārājika rules were being recited; they became angry when the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules were being recited; they spoke out during the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules; and when the ninety-two pāyattika rules were being recited, they rose up and said:
"Elders!..."
"Was this spoken by the Blessed One?
Where did the Blessed One speak it?
Had I remained in the world for longer, I would have heard many more such matters; these are indeed the 'mothers of the Dharma,' from which further precepts arise and flourish."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they felt ashamed and, for this reason, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly about the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus,
"this is an evil deed."
The Tathāgata, wishing to bring benefit, has established the precepts for his disciples and recites the Prātimokṣa every half-month.
Why do you resent and obstruct this?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [and so on] ...even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If, when the *prātimokṣa* is being recited every half-month, a bhikṣu says:
"Only now do I know that this dharma is included in the *sūtra* and was recited within the *prātimokṣa* every half-month."
If the other bhikṣus know that bhikṣu’s background—that he has sat through the recitation of the Prātimokṣa two or three times, let alone more—then that bhikṣu cannot escape by claiming ignorance.
He must be dealt with according to the law for the offense he has committed and should be rebuked, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."

"You have lost a great benefit; when the *prātimokṣa* was recited during the half-month, you did not show respect, you did not attend with a single-minded focus, and you did not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears."
"Having rebuked [him], it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Half-month" refers to either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
The *Prātimokṣa* consists of the twelve *sūtras*.
To "expound" it means to speak these words:
"I have only now come to know this dharma, which is included within the fortnightly *Prātimokṣa*."
If that bhikṣu knows that [the other] has sat through two or three recitations of the Prātimokṣa, let alone more, that bhikṣu is not without offense simply because he was unaware.
According to the offense committed, one should deal with it in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
One should reprimand them, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."

"You have lost a great benefit; when the Prātimokṣa was recited during the half-month, you did not show respect, you did not attend with a single-minded focus, and you did not listen to the Dharma with an attentive ear."
Having rebuked him, he should confess the *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
Once the full ordination (*upasampadā*) has been received, one should recite the two divisions of the Vinaya.
If one cannot recite both divisions, one should recite one division.
If one cannot recite one division, one should extensively recite the precepts for the five groups of practitioners.
If one cannot do that, one should extensively recite the precepts for the four groups of practitioners.
If you are still unable to do that, you should extensively recite the precepts for the three assemblies.
If you are still unable to do that, you should extensively recite the precepts for two assemblies.
If you are still unable to do that, you should extensively recite the precepts for one assembly along with the verses.
If, at the time of the poṣadha, one recites the precepts for the five groups of practitioners in detail;
or if one is unable to do so, one should recite the precepts for the four groups in detail;
or if one is still unable to do so, one should recite the precepts for the three groups in detail.
If one is still unable to do that, one should extensively recite the precepts for the two assemblies.
If one is still unable to do that, one should extensively recite the precepts and verses for one assembly;
as for the remainder, it is what the Sangha hears regularly.
If one does not recite it, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Within the Saṃgha, one who is proficient in recitation should be made to speak it, while the others listen with single-minded attention.
The Buddha said:
"When the Prātimokṣa is being recited, other bhikṣus must not practice dhyāna or engage in other activities; they should all listen together with single-minded concentration.
If one listens to four matters but does not listen to thirteen matters, it constitutes a Vinaya offense.
If one permits the thirteen matters but does not permit the two *aniyata* dharmas, it is an offense of transgressing the *vinaya*.
If one permits the two *aniyata* dharmas but does not permit the thirty matters, it is an offense of transgressing the *vinaya*.
If thirty matters are permitted but ninety-two matters are not permitted, it is an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
If ninety-two matters are permitted but the four *pāyattika* offenses are not permitted, it is an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
If one permits the four *pāṭidesanīya* rules but does not permit the *śaikṣa* rules, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one permits the *śaikṣa* rules but does not permit the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one does not listen during the interval, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense for each instance.
If one does not listen at all, it is a *pāyattika*.

This offense cannot be confessed before an individual; it must be confessed before a member of the assembly who maintains the precepts, possesses majestic virtue, and is respected and esteemed by others.
The person before him should rebuke him, saying:
"Venerable sir!

You have lost a wholesome benefit; when the Prātimokṣa was recited during the half-monthly assembly, you did not show respect, you were not single-minded in mindfulness, and you did not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears."
Having rebuked him, he must confess a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore it is said:
Entering a layperson’s home, entering a royal palace, needle cases, beds, and two types of mattresses.
The sitting mat, the wound-covering cloth, the rain-cloak, and the Tathāgata’s robe;
the groundless slander as the tenth; the dedication [of merit] and the suspension of the *poṣadha*.
The ninth *varga* concludes. 6. The Four *Pratideśanīya* Offenses. Regarding the first *pratideśanīya*: The Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Śākya Monastery; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were staying in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), the parents, sisters, and kinsmen of the Śākya clan sent messengers with food and drink to deliver to the bhikṣus.
They brought food for people on the road, some eating half of it, some eating one-third of it, and others eating it all up.
Among those bhikṣus, there were some who returned home to visit;
their relatives asked them, "I previously sent various kinds of food and drink; did you eat them all?"
Among them, those who had arrived said,
"We have arrived," while those who were halfway there said:
"Half has arrived.
Regarding that which has arrived as one part out of three parts, it is said:
"One part has arrived."
Those who had not arrived said,
"We have not arrived.
When their relatives heard this, they immediately spoke with anger:
"You wretched dead man! You were sent by me to deliver food; how dare you take it for yourself?
He then whipped him.
The messenger, suffering great pain, cried out loudly:
"The śramaṇa sitting there caused me to be beaten.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"Call those bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "How can you dwell in an araṇya,
take food with your own hands, and eat it when you have not first informed those outside and they have not accepted what is inside?"

"From this day forward, I do not permit [monks] to dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka) where they do not first inform those outside, nor where those outside do not accept what is from within, nor where they take things with their own hands.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in Kapilavastu; the detailed account is as above.

For the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would go on a tour of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days. Seeing a bhikṣu who was weak and ill, his complexion withered and yellow, he knew of this yet asked intentionally:
"Bhikṣu, are you sufficiently strong?"
He replied, "I am suffering from illness,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Are you unable to take medicine according to your illness or food according to your illness?
He replied:

“World-Honored One, you have established the precepts and do not permit those dwelling in forest hermitages to take things with their own hands without first informing those outside and having those outside accept what is inside.
World-Honored One!”
“I am ill and unable to go outside; for this reason, I have become emaciated by the suffering of sickness.
The Buddha said, “From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to take [food] inside.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Kapilavastu assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) takes food with his own hands from outside and eats or consumes it without first informing another bhikṣu who is not ill, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before another bhikṣu.
He speaks thus:
"Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy offense; I repent of this offense."
"The first *pāṭidesanīya* rule.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"In a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka-sthāna*)" is as explained above.
Regarding "not having spoken beforehand," there are two kinds of speech:
that which involves a specific number and that which does not involve a specific number.
As for that which involves a specific number, one must speak beforehand:
"One should say, 'Please send such and such kinds of food and drink.
If one does not specify the quantity, one says directly,
'Please send food.'"
The number of types is not enumerated.
"Not receiving outside" means not [receiving] outside the monastery;
"receiving inside" means [receiving] within the monastery.

Regarding the sick person: those suffering from ailments such as diarrhea, cold-natured disorders, or wind-disorders, who are thus unable to go outside to fetch food—for them, the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
"Receiving with one's own hands" means receiving hand-to-hand or vessel-to-vessel.
"Chewing" refers to cakes, fruits, and the like.
"Eating" refers to the five types of formal meals.
If he chews it or eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now repent of this dharma."
The person before him should ask:
"Do you see your offense?
He should answer:
“I see it.
One should say:
“Be careful not to do it again.”
He replied, “I shall bear it upon my head.
Regarding *pāṭidesanīya*: this is a transgression that one confesses to another person without concealment.
If one sends food for this bhikṣu and informs another bhikṣu, and that other bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If one sends food for this bhikṣu and informs this very bhikṣu, and another bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If one sends food for this bhikṣu and addresses it to this bhikṣu, and this bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If one sends food for another bhikṣu and addresses it to that other bhikṣu, and that other bhikṣu accepts it, there is no offense.
If food is being sent, one should first say:
"Is there a fixed portion or no fixed portion?
If there is a fixed portion, the bhikṣu may remain inside; he should then recall the number of items and take those that correspond to his share, while returning those that do not correspond.
If there is a document sent, examine the document; if it is consistent [with the facts], accept it, and if it is inconsistent, send it back.
If there is a sealed letter sent, examine the seal; if it is intact, accept it, and if it is not intact, send it back.
If they arrive without having previously announced their arrival, one should receive them outside the gate of the vihāra.
If they suddenly enter the gate, one must not receive them.

If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), one should tell them to give it to the *kappiya-kāraka*. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should tell them to place it on the ground and wait for a *kappiya-kāraka* to come; once the *kappiya-kāraka* has arrived, one should say to them:
"Take this food outside.
Once he has gone outside, the bhikṣu should accept it.
If the bhikṣu is ill and unable to go outside, there is no offense in accepting it inside.
If a relative brings food and drink to a monastery garden, a pond, a forest, or a place for strolling and viewing, and offers it to a bhikṣu, he may accept it as he pleases without fault.
If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a journey, thinks to himself,
"I shall eat at such-and-such monastery," yet eats at another location instead, he should confess his transgression.
If one arrives at a certain monastery and encounters monks who have accepted an invitation, it is no offense to go along with them.
Therefore, this was said.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the detailed exposition is as above.
The account of the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā should be told in detail, up until the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvaka bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā is foremost in merit."
At that time, there was a famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain.
Then, when it was time, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā put on her village-entering robes, took her bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī to go on her almsround.
Seeing the bhikṣu, he immediately asked,
"Venerable sir,
have you obtained food?"
The bhikṣu immediately showed her his empty bowl.
Having seen this, the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"He whom I revere has failed to obtain any alms."
He then took the food from his own bowl and gave it to the bhikṣu.
Having received the food, the bhikṣu returned to the vihāra and called other bhikṣus to eat together with him.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Elder! Where did you obtain such excellent food?
He replied:
"I received it from the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they each went to seek it.
In this manner, one after another, all five hundred bhikṣus obtained food before seeking for themselves.
The time having passed and the meal lost, they returned to the monastery.
The next morning, the bhikṣus again donned their robes, took up their bowls, and stood at the gate of the bhikṣuṇī monastery.
Having seen this, the bhikṣuṇī immediately went inside and said to Śrīmā,
"The bhikṣus are now waiting outside the gate.
Upon hearing this, Śrīmā spoke to her disciple, saying:
"Bring my robe and bowl; I shall go for alms on behalf of the senior elders.
Having thus provided for the five hundred in succession, he then sought food for himself.
The time passed and they returned empty-handed;

on the third day it was likewise, until finally five hundred people had been provided for in succession, with only one person remaining unserved. This bhikṣu followed behind Śrīmā into a certain house; because he had missed his meals for three days, his body was so emaciated and weak that he fell to the ground in a faint.
When the women saw this, they rose in alarm and wished to support her, but the bhikṣuṇī said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Wait while I reflect: for what reason have I fallen to the ground?
He then recalled that, while begging for alms from the elders, he had lost his food and fainted from extreme exhaustion, falling to the ground.
Having risen and brushed away the dust from himself, and having properly adjusted his robes, he reflected:
"One who is able to practice giving possesses unsurpassed benefit.
Recalling this act of giving, he gave rise to a heart of joy.

Because of his joy, he attained the Samādhi of Purity; through this samādhi, he observed the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Adorned by generosity and with his mind tamed, he entered the Vajra-samādhi, exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), and realized the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*) within the Buddha-dharma.
After the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā had attained realization, a woman led her inside to bathe, spread out a mat for her to sit upon, and only then provided her with food.
That bhikṣu remained standing outside the door; seeing him, the woman stood by the doorway, fearing that he might come in again seeking food.
A bhikṣuṇī saw a door blocked and, a doubt arising in her mind, wondered, "Why is the door blocked?
She tilted her head and saw the corner of a bhikṣu’s robe, saying, "This is my venerable superior; he has not obtained alms."
He then said: "Venerable One,
please enter and take some food."
The woman said, "Ānanda, please eat; I shall seek more for you.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"In this world of famine and scarcity, where else could one find food?
she said, and again she took the food and gave it to him.
The woman spoke with resentment:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no heart of compassion; how can they, having lost their food for three days and being so utterly famished that their lives hang by a thread, still demand more food?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said, "Call those bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him in detail about the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said. "From this day forward,
I do not permit one to take food with one's own hand from a nun who is not a relative while inside a layperson's house."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Ariṣṭa had sores on his body and was loathed by others; people would not give him food.

Whenever he went out to beg for alms, if he had not yet entered a door, the door would be closed and he would not be allowed to proceed; if he had already entered, they would drive him out and give him nothing.

For the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha went on a tour of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days, and there he saw that Ariṣṭa’s body was covered with sores and wounds.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
is your physical strength harmonious and well-balanced?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
I am suffering only from the pain of hunger.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Are you unable to beg for alms?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to beg for food, but my body is covered in sores and wounds, which people loathe and despise.
Whenever I go to beg for alms, if I have not yet entered a gate, they close it and do not let me pass; if I manage to enter the gate, they drive me out and give me nothing.”
The Buddha asked,
“Are you unable to go to the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmā to beg for alms?
She replied:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not receive food with one’s own hands from a nun who is not a relative within a layperson’s home.
She is not my relative; therefore, I do not go.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to go.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who dwell depending on Vaiśālī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”

If a bhikṣu who is not ill receives food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative within a layperson’s house, and then eats or consumes it, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state; I repent for this offense.
This is called the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
"Bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relatives" refers to those who are neither one's father nor one's mother.

Regarding "the sick," the World-Honored One stated that there is no offense; this does not refer to minor ailments, but rather to conditions such as scabies, jaundice, festering sores, wounds, carbuncles, and pustules—those things which people loathe and despise. This is what is meant by "sickness."
"Within the home of a white-robed person" means within the home of a layperson.
"A bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) from among the two assemblies.
"Receiving with one's own hands" means receiving hand-to-hand or receiving vessel-to-vessel.
"Chewing" refers to cakes, fruits, and the like;
"eating" refers to the five kinds of formal meals.
This bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
“Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I repent of this dharma.
The person before him should ask:
"Do you see your fault?
He replied, "I see it."
One should say:
"Be careful not to do it again.
He replies:
"Uphold this upon your head.
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses to be confessed), it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu who is not ill receives food with his own hand from a non-relative bhikṣuṇī inside a layperson's house, at the moment he receives it, he commits a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline).
Regarding the offense of *deśanā-garhaṇīya* at the time of eating:
if one receives food from a person who is not a relative while perceiving them as not being a relative, one commits an offense of *deśanā-garhaṇīya*.
If one receives food from a person who is not a relative while suspecting them of not being a relative, one commits an offense of *deśanā-garhaṇīya*.
If one accepts food from a non-relative while perceiving them as a relative, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one accepts food from a relative while perceiving them as a non-relative, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one accepts food from a relative while harboring doubts about their status as a relative, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one accepts food from a relative while perceiving them as a relative, there is no offense.
If one accepts food on behalf of another person, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
The sick person is without fault; receiving food for the sick is without fault; eating the remains of the sick is without fault.
If a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī brings food, one should tell her to place it on the ground, and then receive it from another person; this is without fault.
If a bhikṣuṇī brings it herself and, having placed it on the ground, says,
"Venerable sir, please accept this for my sake," there is no offense for the one who accepts it.
If one receives [an offering] at a bhikṣuṇī’s residence, there is no offense.
Therefore, it is said.
The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā’s acquaintances invited the Saṃgha for a meal.
Standing before the group of six bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā pointed them out and said to the donor,
"Give rice to this bhikṣu, give soup to this bhikṣu, and give fish and meat to this bhikṣu."
Having heard this, the donor gave especially generous portions to the group of six bhikṣus.
The other bhikṣus spoke with disapproval, saying:
"How can the group of six bhikṣus accept specially instructed food from a bhikṣuṇī without rebuking her?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, “Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha questioned them regarding the aforementioned matter.
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said,
"How is it that you accepted the partial instruction of the bhikṣuṇī regarding the distribution of food without rebuking her?
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Rājagṛha assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, so that even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣu is invited to eat within the home of a layperson, and a bhikṣuṇī stands by pointing and saying,
"Give this rice; give this soup, fish,
or meat," the bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sisters! Wait a moment until the bhikṣus have finished their meal.
If not even a single bhikṣu among them says this to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sisters! Please wait a moment until the bhikṣus have finished their meal.
Those bhikṣus should confess their transgression before other bhikṣus, speaking as follows:
"Venerable one!
I have fallen into a blameworthy state; I confess this offense.
This is called a *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
“Bhikṣu” is as explained above.
“Lay family” refers to the household of a layperson.
“Invitation” means either today or tomorrow.
"Food" refers to the five types of primary food and the five types of mixed primary food.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who has received full ordination within the two assemblies.
"Gives" means providing this rice, giving this soup, or giving this fish and meat.
Regarding those who should speak to the bhikṣuṇīs, according to what they have seen, heard, or known, they should instruct them to say:
"Sisters! Wait a moment until the bhikṣus have finished their meal."
"If they stop, it is well; if they do not stop, one should speak a second and third time.
If one does not speak and yet accepts [the food], there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
As for the one who eats, they commit an offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*)."
That bhikṣu should confess before another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I confess this dharma."
The person before him should ask:
"Do you see this as an offense?
He should answer:
“I see it.
One should say:
“Be careful not to do it again.”
He replied,
"I shall bear it upon my head.
Regarding the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession), it is as explained above.
If one eats before the three-fold admonition has been completed, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one eats after the three-fold admonition has been completed and [the donor] still does not stop, there is no offense.
Once one person has finished their admonition, if everyone then eats, there is no offense.
If one neither sees nor hears [the donor], the eater incurs no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself acts as the *dānapati* (donor), there is no offense.

If the *dānapati* has never invited the Saṃgha and is ignorant of the ritual procedures, at that time the bhikṣuṇī may instruct them on how to arrange the images and teach the method for distributing the food; only after this should she sit down.
If one does not request [the food], or if it is not one of the five kinds of formal meals, there is no offense according to the teaching.
Therefore, it is said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
The story of the minister Viśākha should be told here in detail, up until the Śākya of Sāṃkāśyā.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The minister Viśākha gave away in alms to such an excess that his wealth was completely exhausted."
The Saṃgha should perform the *karmavācanā* for one who is a *śikṣādattaka*.
As for the method of the *karmavācanā*, it should be recited as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
The minister Viśākha has given away his wealth in excessive generosity until his funds are exhausted.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha perform the *kula-karma* (formal act regarding a family) for the minister Viśākha; this is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The minister Viśākha has given excessively in alms until his wealth is exhausted.
The Saṃgha now performs the *kula-karma* (formal act regarding a family) for the minister Viśākha."

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the minister Viśākha regarding his family being designated as a *śikṣādattaka* (a householder under training) should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first formal act.
The second and third [motions] were likewise.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the minister Viśākha; since the Saṃgha remains silent, it consents. Thus this matter is upheld."
When the minister Viśākha returned from the Śāṇḍilya Kṣatriyas, exhausted and covered in dust, he first asked his household:
"Have the various Ācāryas come here frequently?"
He replied,
“Come! However,
whenever there is something to be given, I do not accept anything at all.”

Having heard this, Viśākha felt displeasure in his heart; he did not bathe at all, but went to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Bhikṣus, for what reason do they not accept the offerings from my house?
The Buddha told Viśākha:

“Your giving has been excessive, and your wealth is exhausted. Because the Tathāgata wishes to benefit you, he has performed the *kula-karman* (formal act) of declaring your household a ‘householder under restriction’.”
"For this reason, the bhikṣus do not accept your offerings.
Viśākha then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"My household is now three times wealthier than it was in the past.
I only pray, World-Honored One,
that from this day forward you will permit the bhikṣus to accept the offerings of my family."
The Buddha told Viśākha:
"Today is the fifteenth day of the month; you should return home, bathe your body, put on fresh and clean clothes, and come with your kinsmen to visit the community of monks to request your wish."
Vijaya returned as instructed. Later, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Vijaya originally practiced giving to such an excess that the Saṃgha, wishing to benefit him, performed the *kula-karman* (formal act regarding a family)."

Vijaya has now declared that his household wealth and occupation have become three times more prosperous than before; he now wishes to request from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *śikṣādattaka-karman*, and the Saṃgha should grant him its revocation.
Viśākhā returned home, bathed her body, changed into new clothes, and together with her kinsmen, entered the monastery and related the aforementioned matter in detail.
At that time, the Saṃgha performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring a household as one from which alms should not be accepted) against them.
One should perform the *jñapti-karman* for seeking permission, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The minister Viśākha has given excessively in alms until his wealth is exhausted. Because the Saṃgha desires to benefit him, we shall perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring him a 'householder under training') for him."

"Now that his wealth and livelihood are abundant, if the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, for the sake of the minister Viśākha, grant him the *karmavācanā* for relinquishing the 'householder-status' (*śikṣādattaka*) within the Saṃgha.
"Venerable sirs of the Saṃgha, listen!
"Because the Saṃgha consented by remaining silent, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the dismissal of the householder status of the minister Viśākha is thus upheld.
At that time, the minister Viśākha came, entered the midst of the Saṃgha, prostrated with his head at their feet, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and spoke thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, Viśākha, was formerly wealthy but later became poor; out of compassion, the Saṃgha granted me the *kulapratisaṃvedin-karman*.

Now my livelihood is fully restored, even threefold more than before. I now beg the Saṃgha to revoke the *kulapratisaṃvedin-karman* for me; I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me the revocation of the *kulapratisaṃvedin-karman*.
Thus he requests three times.
At that time, the *vīja* should be placed in a location where it is visible but not audible. The officiant (*karmakāraka*) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This minister, Viśākha, gave away his wealth in excessive almsgiving until his resources were completely exhausted. Because the Saṃgha wished to benefit him, it performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring a family to be under training) for him.
Now, Viśākha himself declares that his household wealth is now three times what it was before; he has already requested from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *śikṣādattaka-karman*.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now perform the *karmavācanā* for Viśākha’s family to be designated as 'of diminished learning.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

The minister Viśākha gave away excessive alms until his wealth was completely exhausted; because the Saṃgha desired to benefit him, it performed the *kula-śikṣā-dattaka-karman* (the formal act of designating him as one whose family is under training) for him.

Viśākha now declares that his household affairs are fully restored and three times greater than before, and he has requested from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *kula-śikṣā-dattaka-karman*. The Saṃgha now grants Viśākha the revocation of the *kula-śikṣā-dattaka-karman*.
"Venerable sirs, if the Saṃgha approves of granting the *vaiśvāsika-śikṣāpada-karman* to [the householder], it shall remain silent; if it does not approve, then speak.
This is the first formal motion.
The second and third [motions] are stated in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the 'householder whose family is to be shunned' for Viśākha; since the Saṃgha remains silent, it consents, and this matter is thus upheld.
This formal act of shunning the householder's family requires the presence of the entire assembly; it is not merely the presence of the assembly.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

If there are monks who are householders under training (*śaikṣa*), and a monk goes to them without being invited and receives food with his own hands, whether he chews it or eats it, that monk should confess his transgression before other monks, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state; I confess this offense.
This is a *pāṭidesanīya* dharma. Regarding a "family of practitioners":
the wife is a *srotāpanna* and the husband is a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The wife is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the husband is a non-returner (anāgāmin);
the wife is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and the husband is a stream-enterer;
the wife is a once-returner and the husband is a non-returner.
The wife is an Anāgāmin and the husband is a Srotāpanna;
the wife is an Anāgāmin and the husband is a Sakṛdāgāmin;
the husband is a Srotāpanna and the wife is a Sakṛdāgāmin.
The husband is a srotāpanna and the wife is an anāgāmin;
the husband is a sakṛdāgāmin and the wife is a srotāpanna;
the husband is a sakṛdāgāmin and the wife is an anāgāmin.
The husband is an Anāgāmin and the wife is a Srotāpanna;
the husband is an Anāgāmin and the wife is a Sakṛdāgāmin;
both are Srotāpannas; both are Sakṛdāgāmins; or both are Anāgāmins.
"Households" refers to households of the four castes:
the Kṣatriya household, the Brāhmaṇa household, the Vaiśya household, and the Śūdra household.

Regarding "the bhikṣu was not previously invited": "not previously invited" means having the perception that one has been invited; "inviting another person" means having the perception that it is oneself.
As for going there, it may be to one's house, or to a garden, or to a field.
To take with one's own hand means to receive from hand to hand, or to receive from vessel to vessel.
"Chewable food" refers to cakes, fruits, and the like;
"edible food" refers to the five types of formal meals.
This bhikṣu should confess his transgression before another bhikṣu, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy offense; I confess this offense.
The person before him should ask:
"Do you see your own fault?
He replied, "I see it."
One should say:
"Do not commit this offense again.
He replies:
"Receive this upon your head.
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya*, it is as explained above.

If the Saṃgha has already performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding a family of practitioners, one must not cease visiting them entirely, like a bird avoiding an arrow; rather, one should go from time to time to see them, preach the Dharma to them, and discuss matters concerning the Dharma.
If a family of noble lineage (śaikṣa-kula) wishes to give a gift, one should say to them:
"Set this aside for yourself; I shall know the proper time.

If the Sangha has been invited beforehand and the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is subsequently performed, one must not accept items of high value or heavy substance; one may accept only small and light items.
If a family of practitioners should say, "Venerable sir, why do you not accept this offering? Do you consider us poor?
at that time, one should say:

“You are not poor. As the World-Honored One has said, a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) is the most wealthy among the śrāvakas because they have accomplished four qualities.
What are these four? ”
First, they give rise to a firm root of faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, or any other beings in the world.

Second, they give rise to a firm faculty of faith toward the Dharma; third, they give rise to a firm faculty of faith toward the Saṅgha; fourth, they give rise to a firm faculty of faith toward the precepts, which cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or worldly people.
This is called the accomplishment of four dharmas, by which a Tathāgata’s śrāvaka is not poor among his followers but is the most wealthy.

If anyone comes to the vihāra to provide a meal for the Saṃgha, to perform various offerings, or to offer non-timely beverages, one must not abandon them and depart; rather, one should assist in spreading out mats and bedding and providing articles of worship. Having accepted these for their use, one should extensively preach the Dharma for them.
Therefore it is said:
Dwelling in an araṇya, accepting food from a nun when not ill,
food assigned by a bhikṣuṇī, and food from a family under formal disciplinary action (karmavācanā).
The four rules for confession (prāyaścittika-dharma) are concluded.
7. The Rules of Training (śaikṣa-dharma). I. Regarding the beginning of the Rules of Training: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore their inner robes (antarvāsaka) in the following ways: they wore them low, they wore them high, they wore them unevenly, they wore them with a hundred folds, they wore them like a pomegranate flower, they wore them like a ball of barley meal, they wore them like a fish’s tail, they wore them like a tāla-leaf, and they wore them like an elephant’s trunk.
Those that are low reach the ankles;
those that are high reach the knees;
those that are uneven are not aligned straight.
"Having a hundred pleats" means that many pleats are made.
"Pomegranate flower" refers to a flower that covers one side.
"Wheat-rice ball" means the top of the head is shaped like a wheat-rice ball.
The "fish-tail" [style] has its two corners hanging down like a fish's tail.
The "tāla-leaf" [style] has ridges rising up like the leaves of a tāla tree.
The "elephant-trunk" [style] has one corner hanging down to one side.
Because of such faults, he was ridiculed by the people of the world:

"Look at the way these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, wear their robes; they are like those of princes, high ministers, or lustful men—so uneven in height and width as to even resemble an elephant's trunk."
"This man is ruined; what path could he possibly have?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here. When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Bhikṣus, is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“How is it that you wear your inner robe with such high and low folds, even like the trunk of an elephant, so as to be ridiculed by worldly people?
From this day forward, you are not permitted to wear the inner robe in such a manner.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble.
Once they had assembled, the Buddha put on his inner robe before the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus:
“You all should put on your inner robes in this manner, according to the practice of the Śuddhāvāsa devas: fold the right side and tuck in the left side when putting on the inner robe.
For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One should train in wearing the inner robe neatly.
When wearing the inner robe neatly, one must not wrap it like a roll; rather, one should grasp the right side and the upper corner of the left side, tuck them inside, and wear it neatly.
One must not, like a courtesan, sell one's beauty by looking here and there to see if it is attractive; rather, one should look at it so that it is worn properly and neatly.
If one indulges the sense faculties and does not wish to train in wearing the inner robe properly and neatly, one violates the rule of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to wear the inner robe neatly.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore their robes low, wore them high, wore them like the Brahmā-deva, and wore them like the Vasu-deva.
To wear them low means to have them reach the ankles.
One who wears the *kaṣāya* robe [with it] reaching to the knees.
As for one who wears the *brahmakāyika* robe, the garment is placed over the crown of the head and emerges from both armpits; this is called wearing the *brahmakāyika* robe.
Regarding the *vāsava-bandhana* robe: one places the robe over the back, passes it under both armpits, and draws it up over both shoulders; this is called the *vāsava-bandhana* robe.
Because of such transgressions, he was censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear their upper robes and lower robes so high, like kings, ministers, youths, or persons of noble rank and wealth?"
"What path does this ruinous man follow?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I do not permit you to wear your robes unevenly, even as far as the way of wearing them by the god Vasu; rather, you should wear your robes in a neat and orderly manner.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One should train in wearing the robe properly.

When wearing the robe properly, one must not wrap it like a roll of thread; rather, one should wear it over both shoulders with the fasteners closed, holding the two corners with the left hand. When holding them, the tips of the corners must not protrude from the hand like the ears of a sheep, nor should one act like a courtesan selling her beauty by looking left and right to see if it looks good or not.
One should look [at one's robes] so that they are in accordance with the Dharma, even and neither too high nor too low.
If, when applying clay, the hands can lift them up, yet one lets the faculties run wild and wears the robes improperly, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to wear the robe properly and neatly.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda were wearing fine, thin, coarse garments, so that their bodies were exposed.

Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus wore soiled, tattered clothes, leaving their waists, sides, backs, and elbows visible. They entered the homes of donors together and were disparaged by the people of the world:
"Look at these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya! They dress like kings or great ministers in fine, thin, coarse garments, with their bodies fully exposed."
Seeing one wearing tattered clothes, he said:
"Look at this śramaṇa son of the Śākyas! Wearing such garments, his body is exposed; he looks like a slave, a hired laborer, or a lowly man who has entered a house."
"What kind of path does this man who ruins others follow?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you should properly cover your bodies when entering the homes of others.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should train oneself to enter a house with the body well-covered.
If one makes an *antarvāsaka*, it should be made of a fine, dense material;
if the material is coarse, it should be made in two or three layers.
If the antaravāsaka is made of coarse material, the uttarāsaṅga should be made of fine material;
if the uttarāsaṅga is made of coarse material, the saṃghāṭī should be made of fine material.
If one enters a house with the sense faculties unrestrained and the body not properly covered, one violates the training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense if one is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to enter a house with the body properly covered."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople and watched elephants, horses, camels, birds, and the singing and dancing of performers. They were censured by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, look here and there like spies?"
He asked, "Venerable sir, what have you lost?
You look about to the left and right as if searching for something."
"One who has left the household life should look carefully before entering a house.
What kind of path can this person of ruin have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must look carefully when entering a house.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should train oneself to look attentively when entering a house.

When walking, one must not walk with the head bowed like a horse; one should walk looking straight ahead to avoid wild elephants, horses, or oxen, and should walk as one who carries a palanquin, without glancing here and there.
If one wishes to look, one should turn the body toward the place being looked at.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and does not train in looking attentively when entering a house, one violates the rule of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to look carefully when entering a house.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople while shouting and crying out loudly.
They were censured by the people of the world, who said:
"Venerable sirs, you are like merchants who have lost their caravan, or like herdsmen shouting and crying out loudly."
"You who have gone forth as renunciants should enter households with low voices.
What kind of path does this corrupt person possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,

"One should train oneself to enter a house with a low voice.
One must not enter a house shouting loudly; if one wishes to call out, one should snap one's fingers.
If the person in front does not hear, one should speak to the person sitting beside them.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and does not train in entering a household with a low voice, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train in entering a household with a low voice."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople together, engaging in playful banter and laughter, which drew the censure of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, enter [lay homes] together in playful banter and laughter like princes, ministers, or those who are licentious and dissolute?"
He asked, "Venerable sir, why do you expose your gums as if you wish to sell your teeth?
There are no performers here; for what reason are you smiling?"
"What kind of path does this ruinous man possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"How can you, within the Vinaya of the Noble Ones, show your gums and smile at one another in mutual jesting?
From this day forward, you must not enter a house while laughing or joking."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself not to laugh when entering a house.
One must not laugh; if there is something laughable, one must not show the gums and teeth by laughing "ha-ha," but should instead restrain and endure it.
One should give rise to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and contemplate the perception of death.
If these cannot stop [the mind], one should bite one's own tongue.
If one still cannot stop it, one should cover the mouth with the corner of one's robe and gradually suppress it.
If one enters a house while laughing boisterously with the sense faculties unrestrained, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house laughing."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople with their heads covered, and were reviled by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, enter houses with their heads covered like wanton courtesans, like thieves or spies, like new brides, or like honey-gatherers?"
He asked, “Venerable sir!
Are you suffering from eye pain?”
"Are you afraid of being scorched by the sun?
Why do you cover your head?
You are a ruined and degenerate man; what path of liberation can there be for you?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you have done so? He replied:

"From this day forward, you must not enter the homes of laypeople with your heads covered."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself not to enter a house with one's head covered.
Regarding "with one's head covered": this refers to covering it entirely, including both ears; one must not walk into the homes of laypeople with one's head covered.
If it is extremely cold, snowy, or if one suffers from a headwind, one may cover half the head and one ear.
However, if one covers the head while entering a house out of indulgence in the sense faculties, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house with the head covered.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople with their robes tucked up behind, drawing the reproach of the world:

"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act like princes, ministers, or lecherous women selling their beauty, entering people's houses with their robes tucked up and sitting down, exposing their elbows and ribs?"
He asked, "Venerable sir!
Do you wish to come and fight with me?"
"Why does he wear his robe slung over one shoulder and expose his side?
What kind of path can this degenerate man possibly possess?
For these reasons, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not enter a house with your robe tucked up behind.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who dwell depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One should train oneself not to enter a house with one's robe tucked back over the shoulders.
As for "tucking the robe," this refers to folding both edges back and placing them upon the shoulders.

One must not enter a house walking with the robe tucked back; however, in the event of wind or rain, it is permissible to tuck one side. If one is baring the right shoulder (*ekāṃśa*), one may tuck the left side; if one is covering both shoulders (*ubhaya-aṃsa*), one may tuck the right side. One must not allow the elbows to become visible.
When begging for food, if one fears that the robes will become soiled, it is permissible to fold them back over the shoulders; provided the elbows do not become visible, there is no offense.
If, however, one allows the sense faculties to run wild and enters a house with the robes folded back in such a manner, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter inside a house with one's robe tucked up over the shoulder.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople on their tiptoes, and were ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, walk like lecherous women who steal men, or like frogs?"
"What kind of path does this ruinous man have?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not enter the homes of laypeople walking on your toes.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter a house walking on one's toes.
When entering indoors where there is mud or water, one must not place the toes down first and the heels last; rather, one should place the heels down first and then the toes."
If there is a sore on the sole of the foot, one should walk with the foot turned to the side and fasten a covering for the sore; one should first place down the heel and then the toes.
If one gives rein to the sense faculties and does not train in walking with the feet level, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house walking on one's toes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople with their hands resting on their hips, drawing the reproach of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, enter people's houses with their hands on their hips like princes, ministers, or wrestlers?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an improper act; from this day forward, you must not enter the homes of laypeople with your hands placed upon your hips.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One must not enter a house with hands on the hips; this is how one should train.
Regarding "hands on the hips": it means placing both hands upon the hips.
One must not walk into a house with hands on the hips; however, if there is pain in the waist or spine, or if there is a wind-swelling (edema), one may place hands on the hips without fault.
If one has an abscess, ulcer, or scabies and applies medicine to it, there is no offense in crossing one's arms over the waist for fear of soiling one's robes.
However, if one allows the sense faculties to run wild and enters a house with arms crossed over the waist, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house with hands on the hips.
Wearing the inner robe and upper garment, one should enter well-covered and with eyes cast down.
One must not laugh with a low voice; nor cover the head, nor fold back the robes, nor point while walking, nor place hands on the hips.
The first *varga* of the *Śikṣāpada* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, enter houses swaying their bodies like princes, high ministers, or courtesans?"

"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house swaying the body.
There is no offense if one is old or sick and the body trembles, or if one trembles due to wind, rain, cold, or snow.
If one enters a house swaying the body out of indulgence of the sense faculties, one transgresses the training rule."
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house with the body swaying.

"What dharma of the Path can this man, who is so corrupt and ruined, possess?

However, there is no offense if one shakes the head due to being old, infirm, or ill, or if one has a headache, or is shivering from wind, rain, or cold."
If one enters a house with the sense faculties unrestrained and shaking the head, one transgresses the training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.

"What dharma of the Path can this degenerate man possess?

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter a house with arms swinging.
One must not enter a house walking with arms swinging. If there are those who were formerly princes or ministers whose former habits have not yet been eliminated, they should be instructed, saying:
'Now that you have gone forth, you should abandon these worldly customs and follow the Dharma of a bhikṣu.'"
If one wishes to call someone, one must not raise both hands simultaneously; rather, one should beckon with a single hand.
If, indulging the sense faculties, one enters a house with arms flailing, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to enter a house with arms swinging.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore soiled, tattered garments, exposing their elbows, waists, and ribs.
Nanda and Upānanda, however, wore fine, thin, and coarse garments that left their bodies exposed; they sat together with householders and were ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya wear fine, thin, and coarse garments like princes, high ministers, and nobles?"
Seeing one wearing tattered clothes, he spoke again:
"He looks like a slave, a hired laborer, or a lowly man, wearing ruined and soiled garments with his elbows and ribs exposed as he sits inside the house."
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should sit within a house with his body properly covered.
What kind of path or Dharma can there be in such a degenerate person?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:

"It is truly so."

"From this day forward, you should sit inside a house with your body properly covered.
