"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should learn to sit within a house with the body well-covered.
Regarding "with the body well-covered": one should use a fine material for the inner garment;
if a coarse material is used, it should be double or triple-layered.
If the inner robe (antarvāsaka) is coarse, the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) should be made of fine material;
if the upper robe is coarse, the outer robe (saṃghāṭī) should be made of fine material.
If the *saṃghāṭī* is coarse, one should use a fine material for the *uttarāsaṅga*.

When sitting, one must not sit directly upon the robe; rather, with one hand one should lift the robe and with the other hand one should press down upon the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and only then should one sit calmly and composedly.
If one is in a vihāra, in the presence of the preceptor, the teacher, or senior bhikṣus during a meal, one should sit with the body properly covered.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and does not train in sitting within a house with the body properly covered, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to sit within a house with the body well-covered.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople and sat there, watching the women and children as they came and went, ascending and descending the upper and lower galleries.
They were censured by the people of the world, who said: "How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit in the houses of others like lecherous men or like thieves, watching the women?"
He asked, “Venerable sir!
What have you lost that you are looking about here and there?”
"One who has gone forth should look closely at those who sit within their homes.
What path or Dharma can there be for such a person who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should carefully look around when sitting inside a house.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself to look attentively while sitting inside a house.

When sitting inside a house while looking attentively, one must not hold one's neck out like a horse and look downward; rather, one should look level forward, so as not to allow the donor—who may be carrying a hot vessel—to accidentally splash their hand or face with the hot liquid.
Whether in a vihāra during a meal, or when sitting before one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣu, one must not look left or right; one should sit with a level gaze.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and sits within a house without looking attentively, one violates the training rule.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to sit within a house while looking attentively."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, shout so loudly, like merchants who have lost their caravan, or like herdsmen calling out?"
He asked, "Venerable sir!
Why did you cry out so loudly?"
"One who has left the household life should sit with a low voice.
Why do you shout so loudly?
You are a person of ruin; what Dharma of the Path do you possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,

"From this day forward, you should sit with a low voice inside the house."

One must not sit inside a house calling out loudly; if one wishes to call someone, one should snap one's fingers.
If the person in front does not perceive it, one should speak to those nearby.
Whether eating in the vihāra, or sitting before the upādhyāya, the ācārya, or elder bhikṣus, one must not shout loudly.
When one wishes to speak, one should speak to the person sitting nearby; in this manner, it should be passed on successively to the second and third persons so that they may be informed.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and shouts loudly while sitting inside a house, one violates the rule of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to sit with a low voice within a house.

He asked, "Venerable sir!
What is there in this that is laughable?"
"Why do you bare your gums as if you wish to sell your teeth?
You are a ruined man; what Dharma do you possess?

"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.

From this day forward, you must not sit and laugh in the homes of laypeople."

"Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit laughing within a layperson's house.
One must not sit laughing within the home of a layperson; nor, while eating in a vihāra, may one sit laughing in the presence of one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus."
If there is anything laughable, one must not bare one's gums, show one's teeth, or laugh loudly; rather, one should endure it.
One should contemplate the notions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and cultivate the perception of death by biting one's own tongue.
If one still cannot stop, one must not laugh with exposed gums; rather, one should restrain oneself by covering the mouth with the corner of one's robe.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and laughs while sitting in the home of a layperson, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to sit laughing within a house.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

Are you suffering from a headache, or do you fear the sun scorching your head?"
"Why do you cover your heads?
You are a man fallen from ruin; what path or Dharma do you possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.

"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.

"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my head covered.
As for 'having the head covered,' it means covering the entire head along with both ears; one must not sit inside a house with the head covered."
If one is in a vihāra during a meal, or in the presence of one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus, one must not sit with the head covered.

However, in times of wind, cold, or rain, or when ill, or if suffering from a wind ailment in the head, one must not cover it entirely; rather, one should cover half of it so that one ear remains visible. When seeing an elder bhikṣu, one should pull it back.
If one is in a secluded place or a private room, there is no offense in covering the head.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and sits with the head covered inside a house, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to sit with one's head covered while inside a house.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat in the homes of laypeople with their robes tucked up, drawing the reproach of worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit inside the houses with their robes tucked up like princes, ministers, or lewd women who sell their beauty, exposing their elbows and ribs?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for such a person who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not sit inside a house with your robes tucked up.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus... [as before] ...and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One must not sit inside a house with one's robe tucked up; this is how one should train.
To "tuck up the robe" means to tuck it up on one side or on both sides; one must not sit inside a house with the robe tucked up.
When begging for food or when receiving food, one may lift up one's robe out of fear of soiling it; however, one must ensure that the elbow does not become visible, as there is no offense in this.
If sitting in a monastery during a meal, or in the presence of one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), or senior bhikṣu, one must not lift up the robe.
If one covers [the body], one may cover only one side, but not both sides.

If one has bared the shoulder, one should cover the left side; if one is wearing the robe over both shoulders, one may cover the right side. Upon seeing an elder bhikṣu, one should lower the robe again.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and sits inside a house with the robe tucked up behind the back, one violates the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One must train oneself not to sit inside a house with the robe tucked up behind the back."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat with their knees drawn up inside the house of a layperson, drawing the reproach of worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit with their knees drawn up like princes, high ministers, or arrogant laypeople?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not squat while inside a house.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with my knees tucked up while inside a house.
As for 'tucking up the knees,' it means tucking them up with one's hands or with one's robe; one must not sit with one's knees tucked up while inside a house."
Within a vihāra, when eating, or in the presence of one's upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus, one must not sit with the knees drawn up.
If one is ill, it is permissible to wrap them with a cloth; however, when wearing a meditation belt (dhyānabandhana), one must remove it upon seeing an elder bhikṣu.
If one is in a secluded place or a private room, one may sit with the knees drawn up; however, upon seeing an elder bhikṣu approaching, one must resume a formal sitting posture.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and sits with the knees drawn up inside a house, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to sit with knees tucked up inside a house.
Swaying the body, shaking the head, dangling the arms, and being overly preoccupied with covering the body—[these are to be avoided].
Gazing intently, speaking in a low voice, not laughing, sitting with the head covered,
and sitting with arms crossed over the knees.
The second *varga* is concluded.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Twenty-one (continued) / Volume Twenty-two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
The remaining portion of the *Śaikṣa-dharmas* translated by Fa-xian: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat with their legs crossed in the homes of laypeople, and were criticized by the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit with their legs crossed inside a house like princes or ministers?
These corrupting people—what path or Dharma do they possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not sit with your legs crossed inside a house.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself not to sit with legs crossed within a house.
To have the legs crossed means that the thighs rest upon the thighs, the knees rest upon the knees, the shins rest upon the lower legs, and the feet rest upon the tops of the feet.
One must not sit with legs crossed inside a house; rather, one should keep both feet straight.
Likewise, within a vihāra, during a meal, or in the presence of a preceptor (upādhyāya), a teacher (ācārya), or senior bhikṣus, one must not sit with legs crossed.
If one is ill, it is permissible to sit with legs crossed; however, upon seeing a senior elder approaching, one should straighten one's posture.
There is no offense in sitting with legs crossed while applying ointment to the feet or extracting a thorn.
If one sits with legs crossed within a house while indulging the sense faculties, one violates the training rule.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to sit with legs crossed inside a house.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat inside the house of a layperson with their hands on their hips, and they were criticized by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit inside a house with their hands on their hips like princes, high ministers, or wrestlers?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not sit with hands on your hips inside a house.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with hands on hips within a house.
As for 'hands on hips,' whether with one hand or both hands, one must not sit with hands on hips within a house."
Within a vihāra, when in the presence of those serving food, or before one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus, one must not sit with hands clasped around the waist.
However, if one is old or ill, or if there is pain in the lower back caused by wind-disorder (vāta), there is no offense in clasping the hands around the waist.

If one has an abscess, a boil, a carbuncle, or scabies and applies medicine to it, there is no offense in crossing one's arms over the waist for fear of soiling one's robes; however, if an elder (upādhyāya) is seen approaching, one should lower them.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and sits with arms crossed over the waist inside a house, one violates the rules of training (śikṣāpada).
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to sit with hands on the hips inside a house.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat in the homes of laypeople with their feet dangling, waving their hands, and even breaking the grass; they were censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit in a layperson's house like unrestrained performers, their hands and feet never still?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not move your hands or feet while sitting inside the homes of laypeople.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, which those who have already heard should hear again.”
"One should train oneself: 'While sitting inside a house, one must not move the hands or feet.

Regarding 'not moving the hands or feet while sitting inside a house,' this means one must not move the hands or feet, nor wave the hands or feet, nor sit while breaking off grass; rather, one should remain composed and tranquil."
If there is someone who asks a question, one should first protect the precepts and then answer in accordance with them.

If asked about the four stupas, it is without fault to point out that this is the place of birth, this is the place where the Way was attained, this is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and this is the place of parinirvāṇa.

If a donor wishes to have a bhikṣu construct a vihāra, the bhikṣu should observe the topography and configuration of the site and provide instructions accordingly, saying: "A vihāra may be built here; a lecture hall may be built here; a warm chamber may be built here; a monastic cell may be built here. To provide such instructions is without fault.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and moves the hands or feet while sitting inside a house, one violates the training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to move the hands or feet while sitting inside a house."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, a donor had prepared a meal in the vihāra to offer to the Saṃgha. While the food was being served, the group of six bhikṣus were just then asking for water to wash their hands and rinse their bowls. Upon hearing this, the donor immediately threw the basket of hot rice to the ground and spoke with resentment:

"I have abandoned my household duties to come to the monastery to provide this offering, hoping that the assembly of monks would partake of the midday meal together with a pure mind to cultivate merit."
"Now that we are about to receive food, you are asking for this and that.
One who has left the household life should receive food with single-minded focus; why do you ask for so many things at the meal?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should receive food with a single-minded focus.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself to receive food with a single-minded focus.

When receiving food with a single-minded focus, one must not place both hands on the bowl in front of one's feet; rather, one should first wash one's hands clean and rinse the bowl, and when the food is served, one should receive it with a single-minded focus.
If the person on duty or the food supervisor arrives later, it is not an offense to request water for washing the hands and rinsing the bowl.
However, if one allows the sense faculties to run wild and does not receive the food with a single-minded focus, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to receive food with a focused mind.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was an elder who provided a meal for the Saṃgha at a vihāra. The group of six bhikṣus first took much soup and then took rice.
Consequently, the contents of their bowls overflowed and fell to the ground. The donor spoke with displeasure, saying:
"I have deprived my wife and children of their portion to feed the Saṃgha, wishing for them to eat it all; yet now you cast it upon the ground."
"Does the Venerable One not know?
Within this single grain of rice there are a hundred merits.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall receive the soup, rice, and other foods.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Let all the bhikṣus residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One should train oneself in receiving soup and rice together.
Regarding "receiving soup and rice together": one must not take the soup first and the rice afterward; rather, one should first take the rice, press it down, and then take the soup.
If, according to the local customs of the country, soup is served first and rice afterwards, one should receive it using a *kaṃsī* bowl.
If none is available, one should use a leaf-bowl to receive it.

Furthermore, for those without leaves [to cover the bowl], one may receive the soup with the bowl; however, when receiving the rice, one should shield it with the hand and lower it slowly into the bowl so that it does not overflow.
If a bhikṣu is ill and requires much soup, he may take as much as needed without fault.
If, however, one indulges the sense faculties and receives food such as rice and soup without [proper moderation], he violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to receive soup and rice [in the proper manner].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, a lay devotee prepared a meal offering for the Sangha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus scooped out the food from the four edges and left the center, which drew the reproach of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act like dissolute people, scooping out the food from the perimeter and leaving the center?"
"What path or dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done this?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not eat by scooping out portions from one side.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let all those who reside in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should not eat by scooping out the center; this is how one should train.
Regarding "scooping out": one scoops out the four sides, leaving the center.
One should first receive the rice, press it toward one side, and then receive the soup to mix them together before eating.
If ghee or fat enters the rice, one must not scoop it out selectively for the sake of the soup; one should take it in regular order.
If one wishes to give some to another person, one may cut off half and give it.
If one indulges the sense faculties and carves and eats [the food] all around, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One must not carve and eat [the food] unevenly; this is how one should train."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within the vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus ate with their mouths turned back, and they were ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat like heedless people, like camels, oxen, or sheep, with their mouths turned back?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not eat by turning food around in your mouth.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should train oneself not to turn food around in the mouth while eating.
To "turn food around in the mouth" means to take a morsel of rice in the mouth and move it from one cheek to the other.
While chewing, one should swallow as one chews.
If a bhikṣu eats parched rice or non-glutinous rice, he commits no offense provided he rolls it with his tongue while chewing.
If he indulges his sense faculties by tossing the food around in his mouth before eating, he violates the training rule.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat by turning food around in the mouth.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, a householder prepared a meal for the Sangha within the vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus ate with their tongues lolling out, which drew the censure of the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat like those who are dissolute, like snakes, rats, dogs, or cats with their tongues lolling out?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for these people who bring ruin?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
“Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, you must not eat with your tongue protruding."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Let all those who reside depending on Śrāvastī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One shall not eat with the tongue protruding; this is how one should train.
To "eat with the tongue protruding" means to stick out the tongue and place food upon it before closing the mouth.

However, if the person on duty for the month or the supervisor of the meal wishes to know whether the food is raw or cooked, salty or bland, sweet or sour, they may place it in the palm of their hand and lick it with the tongue; there is no offense in this.
If one is ill, it is permissible to place salt in the palm of the hand and lick it; there is no offense.
If, however, one indulges the sense faculties by sticking out the tongue to eat, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore, it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat with the tongue protruding.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, a householder provided a meal offering for the Sangha at the monastery. On that occasion, the group of six bhikṣus ate their rice in large mouthfuls, which led them to be criticized by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat like heedless people, like oxen, sheep, camels, or like hungry prisoners in a jail eating large balls of rice?
What dharma of the Path can there be in such ruined and degenerate men?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned them:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not eat large mouthfuls of rice.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Summon everyone; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.
One must not eat a large mouthful of rice; this is how you should train."
"One must not eat too much nor too little; one should eat in such a way that it fits the mouth, like a woman of loose virtue who eats two or three grains at a time.
If a bhikṣu fills his mouth with non-glutinous rice while eating, there is no offense."
If one eats large mouthfuls of food while indulging the sense faculties, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat large mouthfuls of food."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within the vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus opened their mouths wide and waited for the food, drawing the reproach of the worldlings:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, be like heedless people, like turtles, tortoises, or frogs opening their mouths to wait for food?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked them:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not keep your mouths open while waiting for food.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Assemble all of you. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One should train oneself not to keep the mouth open while waiting for food.

Regarding "not keeping the mouth open while waiting for food": when a bhikṣu eats, he should follow the manner of eating of the Elephant King of the Snowy Mountains; once the food has entered the mouth, he should use his nose to mark the boundary behind the mouth.
After swallowing the preceding morsel, one should immediately take the subsequent ball of food into the mouth; one must not keep the mouth wide open while waiting for food.
However, if there is an ulcer in the mouth, it is permissible to have the mouth open in advance without fault.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and waits with the mouth open for food, one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to wait for food with the mouth open."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, when a householder was providing a meal offering to the Saṃgha within the vihāra, the group of six bhikṣus opened their mouths wide and tossed balls of food into them. They were censured by worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat by tossing balls of food like lecherous men?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not throw morsels of food.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather all of you together. For the sake of the ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall train oneself not to toss morsels of food into the mouth.
Regarding "tossing morsels of food": one must not take a ball of rice and toss it from a distance into the mouth.
However, there is no offense in picking up and tossing into the mouth various items such as jujubes, grapes, or even roasted beans.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and throws morsels of food [into the mouth], one transgresses the rules of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to throw morsels of food."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Sangha at a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus bit off half of their food and returned it to their bowls; they were ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, bite off half their food like unrestrained people?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins himself?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not bite off half a morsel of food.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Assemble all of you; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. Even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall not bite off half a morsel; this is how one should train.
One must not bite off half a morsel and place the other half back into the bowl; rather, one should eat it in portions that can be taken into the mouth.
If a ball of roasted flour is too large, one should divide it with the hand so that it can be taken into the mouth.
If one wishes to eat fruits, melons, sugarcane, or radish roots and the like, it is without offense to bite them.
If eating cakes, one should use one's hands to divide them into portions that are suitable for the mouth.
If one, being lax regarding the sense faculties, bites off half of a morsel while eating, one transgresses the rule of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel while eating."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Sangha at a monastery. On this occasion, the group of six bhikṣus spoke with food in their mouths, which drew the censure of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act like unrestrained people, like camels, oxen, sheep, or donkeys, speaking while chewing their food?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not speak with food in your mouth.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather all of you together. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall not speak while food is in the mouth; this is how one should train.

Regarding "one shall not speak while food is in the mouth": if the preceptor, the ācārya, or an elder bhikṣu calls out while one is eating, if one can respond without altering the sound of one's voice before finishing swallowing, that is permissible;
if one cannot do so, one must swallow first and then respond.
If the person before you is displeased, you should reply:
"There is food in my mouth; therefore, I cannot respond immediately.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and speaks while holding food in the mouth, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to speak with food in the mouth.
Sitting with legs crossed inside a house, resting hands on hips, or moving hands and feet [is prohibited].
Eating with focused intent, soup and rice in equal measure; scraping the bowl with one side of the mouth, turning the cheek to eat;
protruding the tongue, large mouthfuls; opening the mouth wide, tossing food from afar;
biting off half a morsel and speaking while food remains in the mouth.
The third chapter concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, there was a householder who prepared a meal offering at a vihāra for the Saṃgha. On that occasion, the group of six bhikṣus wiped their bowls with their fingers while eating, which drew the censure of the worldlings: [text continues]
“How is it that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat like small children, or like hungry prisoners in a jail? He asked,
“Venerable sir!”
"The food and drink are most abundant; for what reason, then, do they wipe their bowls?
These people who ruin themselves—what Dharma do they possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not wipe your alms bowl with your fingers while eating.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather everyone together; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. ... [as before] ... those who have already heard it should hear it again.
One must not eat by wiping the bowl with the fingers; this you should learn.”
"One must not wipe the bowl with the fingers while eating" means one must not bend the fingers to wipe the bowl.
If ghee, oil, or honey is stuck to the bowl, one must not bend the fingers to wipe it; rather, one should gather it together with the fingers and then take a mouthful to eat.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and uses the fingers to wipe the bowl while eating, one violates the rule of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to use the fingers to wipe the bowl while eating."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a lay devotee prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus licked their hands while eating, and were criticized by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat like small children, licking their hands after receiving food?"
He asked, "Venerable sir!
I have eaten my fill at will; for what reason are you licking your hands?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who ruins others?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not lick your hands while eating.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather all of you together; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall not eat while licking the hands; this is how one should train.

One must not repeatedly lick the hands while eating. If ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar has been placed on the hand, one should gather it together toward the edge of the bowl and place it in one spot, and only then take the food.
If one eats while licking the hands due to laxity of the sense faculties, one transgresses the training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat while licking the hands."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a householder who prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus sucked their fingers while eating, which drew the censure of worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat by sucking their fingers like small children?"
He asked, “Venerable sir!
I am freely bestowing food upon you; why do you lick your fingers while eating?”
"What dharma of the Path can this man who brings ruin possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not eat by sucking your fingers.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Assemble all of you. For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall not lick the fingers while eating; this is how one should train.

Regarding "one shall not lick the fingers while eating": if a bhikṣu is eating soup, stew, or sweet, oily foods that adhere to his fingers, he must not lick them. He should instead sweep them together into a single heap against the rim of the bowl, and only then take the food.
If honey, rock sugar, or salt is on the fingertips, one may lick them without offense.
However, if one allows the sense faculties to run wild and licks the fingers while eating, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat by licking the fingers.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a householder who prepared a meal in a vihāra to offer to the Saṃgha. Then the group of six bhikṣus ate with smacking sounds, and were rebuked by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat with sounds like pigs or rats?"
"What path or Dharma can there be for this man who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not eat making smacking sounds.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Assemble all of you! For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One should train oneself not to make smacking sounds while eating.
To make smacking sounds while eating, or to eat with the sense faculties unrestrained, constitutes a transgression of the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat making smacking sounds.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, a donor prepared a meal for the Sangha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus made slurping sounds while eating their rice, drawing the reproach of the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, eat by slurping like camels, oxen, or donkeys?"
"What kind of path or Dharma can there be for such a person who brings ruin?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not eat by making a slurping sound while inhaling.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather all of you together; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it shall hear it again.”
"One shall not slurp while eating; this is how one should train.
Whether eating thin gruel, milk, curd, soup, or rice, one must not make a sound by slurping, but should swallow slowly.
If one indulges the sense faculties while eating by making slurping sounds,
one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to make a slurping sound while eating.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal in a vihāra to offer to the Saṃgha. Then the group of six bhikṣus swallowed their food whole, making a gurgling sound, and were ridiculed by the people of the world: [text continues]
“How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat like oxen, donkeys, and camels, making gurgling sounds?
What path or Dharma can there be for such ruined people?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not swallow food whole.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather everyone together; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.
One must not swallow food whole; this is how you should train.”
One must not swallow food whole, causing it to make a gurgling sound.
If a bhikṣu has a disease of the throat, making such a sound is without offense.
If the throat is dry, one should moisten it with water before swallowing the food.
If one indulges the sense faculties and swallows food whole, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to swallow food whole."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

At that time, a lay devotee prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus dropped their food while eating—half entering their mouths and half falling to the ground—which drew the censure of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, drop their food like unrestrained people?"
He asked, "Venerable sir!
Do you mean that this food was made with unearned money?"
"I seized my wife and children to distribute as alms in pursuit of merit; it was calculated that this single grain was produced through a hundredfold labor. You ought to eat it all.
Why do you discard it on the ground?
This man is a ruinous person; what path or dharma does he possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you must not drop rice while eating."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all of you. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One shall train oneself not to let food fall while eating.
When receiving food, one must not allow even a single grain to fall to the ground; however, if it falls to the ground while a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) is pouring it out, there is no offense.
When placing food into the mouth, do not let it fall to the ground; however, there is no offense if it accidentally falls.
When eating fish, meat, fruits, melons, or sugarcane, one must not discard the skins, pits, pulp, or bones haphazardly on the ground; they should be gathered at the edge of one's feet.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild while eating fallen grains of rice, one violates the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat fallen rice."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a householder who prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus shook their hands while eating, soiling the robes of the bhikṣus sitting beside them.
The person sitting beside him immediately asked:
"Venerable sir!
Why are you shaking your hand?"
"Have you been stung by centipedes, bees, or scorpions?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you must not flap your hands while eating.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather all of you together; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"One shall train oneself not to shake one's hand while eating.
When shaking one's hand while eating, one must not shake it toward a fellow monk sitting nearby.
If food has adhered to the hand, one should shake the hand in front of oneself or shake it out over the alms bowl.
If one eats while shaking the hands and letting the sense faculties run wild, one transgresses the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense in the case of one who is insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to eat while shaking the hands."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha within the vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus looked at the bowls of those sitting beside them with a sense of dissatisfaction; seeing those who had little, they said:
"If you are chaste, pure, and self-restrained, and have no further need once you are full, you should give [the remainder] to us."
If he sees someone holding a large bowl, he says again:
"Ho! Ho!"
"This gluttonous man’s bowl is like a large cauldron.
The offerings provided by the donor will only just suffice to fill it; how then shall we others obtain any?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus felt ashamed and, for these reasons, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not look at the bowl of your neighbor with a mind of disparagement.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather everyone together; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.
One must not look at the alms bowl of a neighbor with a critical mind; this is how you should train.”
One must not look at the bowl of a fellow monk with a mind of resentment. However, if one is a supervisor of the meal, it is permissible to observe where food may be taken and where it may not;
looking in this manner carries no offense.
If a co-practitioner disciple or a dependent disciple is ill, one may check whether the food in their alms bowl is appropriate for their illness;
there is no offense in doing so.
One may also check whether those seated above or below have received [the proper portion].
There is no offense.
However, if one allows the sense faculties to run wild and looks at the bowl of a neighbor with a mind of resentment, one violates the training rule.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to look at the bowl of a fellow monk with a critical mind.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal offering for the Sangha within the vihāra. There was a bhikṣu who placed his bowl before him, turned his head back, and conversed with his neighbor while sitting.
The group of six bhikṣus took their bowls and placed them elsewhere. When it was their turn to receive food, they did not look at their bowls but felt about on the ground, soiling their hands.
When they asked the donor for water to wash their hands, the donor set down her food basket on the ground and spoke with resentment:
"I have abandoned my household duties to cultivate merit by providing this meal for the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha ought to assemble in order to receive the food."
Now, at the time of eating, you only seek water to wash your hands.
A person who has left the household life ought to maintain a composed mind while observing the alms bowl while eating; as for this man who ruins himself, what Dharma does he possess?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you must eat with a composed mind, observing the alms bowl."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all of you. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself to observe the alms-bowl with a composed mind.
Regarding "observing the alms-bowl with a composed mind": one must not leave the bowl set before oneself while conversing with those sitting nearby.
If there is a necessary reason to speak with those to one's left or right, one should rest the left hand upon the bowl.
When the person serving food reaches the third individual, one should first wash the bowl and hold it out in anticipation of its arrival.
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild and fails to train in upright mindfulness by observing the bowl while eating, one violates the rules of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself to eat from the bowl with a composed mind.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.
At that time, there was a householder who prepared a meal offering for the Sangha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus asked for rice and asked for soup, and were rebuked by the donor:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, ask for rice and ask for soup while the meal is being served?"
He asked, "Venerable sir!
I am freely offering you food; why do you call out and demand it?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to solicit food."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of five benefits, would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. There he saw a sick bhikṣu who was emaciated and withered.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
how is your illness?"
He replied,
"World-Honored One!
I am suffering from illness and feel unwell."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Are you unable to seek out food appropriate for your illness or medicine appropriate for your illness?
He replied:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding the solicitation of food.
The Buddha said,
“From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to solicit food.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on the city of Kapilavastu assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, such that those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One shall not, when not ill, seek food for oneself; this is how one should train.
One shall not, when not ill, seek soup or rice for oneself. However, if one is ill and requires much soup, it is no offense to seek it.
If one, being heedless of the sense faculties and not being ill, seeks food for oneself, one transgresses the rule of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense in the case of one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "A bhikṣu who is not ill shall not seek food for himself; this is how one should train."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a householder prepared a meal for the Saṃgha within a vihāra. Then the group of six bhikṣus first received a soup of fish and meat, and subsequently covered it over with rice.
When the food supervisor saw this, he immediately asked,
"Venerable sir,
did you receive the fish and meat soup?"
He replied:
"Long-lived one!
You know for yourself when you see forms."
"Why do you ask again?
The food supervisor asked the server:
"Why did you not give him the fish and meat soup from this bowl?"
He replied,
"Where could one not obtain it?
[The other said,] "I have not yet obtained it here."
He further said, "I have already given it; why do you say I did not receive it?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not cover the soup with rice in the hope of obtaining more.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Gather everyone together; for ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and those who have already heard it should hear it again.
One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more; this is how you should train.”
If the person sitting beside you is about to receive food and you fear it will soil your robe, you must not cover yourself entirely; you should leave one side exposed.
If you cover yourself completely, the person before you may ask:
"Have you received [your portion] yet?"
One should answer:
"I have already received it.
If, however, one indulges the sense faculties by covering the soup with rice in order to expect to receive more, one violates the rule of training.
There is no offense for one who is insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to cover the soup with rice in order to expect to receive more.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, a lay devotee was providing a meal offering for the Sangha within a vihāra. The group of six bhikṣus then grasped their drinking vessels with greasy hands, which made those sitting nearby feel disgusted and unwilling to accept them.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you must not hold a drinking vessel with greasy hands."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all of you. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One should train oneself not to receive a drinking vessel with greasy hands.

Regarding "not receiving a drinking vessel with greasy hands": when a bhikṣu is eating, he should protect his left hand so that it remains clean; he should receive the drinking vessel with his right hand and drink by holding it to his lips.

One must not hold the rim of the vessel deep within the mouth, nor allow the rim to touch the nose or forehead. One must not drink it all; rather, one should leave a small amount remaining, pour that out from the mouth, rinse it again with water, and then pass it on to the person seated below.
If the left hand has a sore or wound, one should use the right hand to reach over the rim of the bowl and skim off the oily residue from the pure water.
If it is not clean after washing, one may take it up with a leaf to drink, as previously explained.
If one, being lax regarding the sense faculties, holds a drinking vessel with greasy hands, one transgresses the training rule.
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself not to receive a drinking vessel with greasy hands."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

At that time, a householder prepared a meal in the vihāra to offer to the Saṃgha. Then the group of six bhikṣus rinsed the leftovers from their bowls and threw them on the ground. The donor complained, saying:
"Venerable sirs, do you consider this food to have been produced by 'childless money'?"
"I seized his wife and children for the sake of performing meritorious deeds; thus, one grain of rice represents a hundredfold labor. Why then does he pour it onto the ground?
This man of ruinous character—what Dharma does he possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you must not pour leftover food from your bowl onto the ground."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Gather all of you together. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"One shall train oneself not to discard leftover food from the alms bowl on the ground.
Regarding "not discarding leftover food from the alms bowl on the ground": when eating, one should take only as much as is appropriate for one's stomach and must not receive more than necessary.
If a lay attendant (upāsaka) suddenly gives too much, before it has been consumed, one should reduce the amount and give it to those sitting nearby.
If those sitting nearby do not take it, it should be given to the śrāmaṇeras and the gardeners (ārāmika).
When washing the bowl, one must not let even a single grain fall to the ground;
if any do fall, they should be gathered and placed upon a wooden board or on leaves.
If they are fine grains or flour that cannot be gathered, there is no offense.
If one, being lax with the sense faculties, pours the remnants of food from the alms bowl onto the ground, one violates the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for those who are insane, deluded, or mentally deranged.
Therefore it is said: "One must train oneself not to discard the remnants of food from the alms bowl on the ground."
Wiping the mouth, licking the lips, and making smacking sounds; swallowing whole, dropping grains,
shaking the hand over another’s bowl, seeking for oneself with a focused mind,
and covering the soup to discard the greasy hand.
The fourth *vagga* (chapter) is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda were standing while preaching the Dharma to a seated Licchavi youth, and they were censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, stand while preaching the Dharma to those who are seated, like performers?
What path or Dharma is there for such degenerate people?

Furthermore, this youth lacks a heart of reverence; when such subtle and wondrous Dharma is being preached, he should have been provided with a seat. Why does he sit and listen, causing him to preach while standing?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him about the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How can you stand and preach the Dharma to those who are seated and free from illness?"
"From this day forward, you must not stand while preaching the Dharma to those who are seated.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Let all those who reside depending on the city of Vaiśālī assemble. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, and even those who have already heard it shall hear it again."
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is seated and a bhikṣu is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
Regarding 'illness,' the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense."
"Exposition" refers to opening up and explaining the meaning for others through detailed analysis, with the desire that they practice according to what has been taught.
"Dharma" refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha and that which was authorized by the Buddha.
That which was spoken by the Buddha is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha spoke himself.
That which was approved by the Buddha refers to what was spoken by the śrāvakas, which the Buddha praised, saying:
"Excellent!"
This is called "authorization.
One must not stand while preaching the Dharma to a person who is seated, except when the person before one is ill;
in such a case, there is no offense. If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the stūpa or for the sake of the Saṃgha, approaches a king or a landowner, and that person says:
"A bhikṣu should preach the Dharma for me.
He must not say this so as to cause [the king] to rise, for fear that he might harbor doubts.
If there is someone standing nearby, he should direct his attention toward preaching the Dharma for that person; even though the king listens, the bhikṣu incurs no offense.
If one who has neglected the control of the sense faculties should preach the Dharma while seated to a person who is standing and free from illness, they transgress the training rule.
There is no offense in the case of those who are insane, deluded, or mentally disturbed.
Therefore it is said: "One should train oneself: when a person is seated and a bhikṣu is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda were sitting and preaching the Dharma to those who were reclining, which was criticized by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit and preach the Dharma to those who are reclining, like performers?"
What dharma of the Path can there be for this person who ruins himself?
This listener lacks a heart of reverence; hearing such a subtle and wondrous Dharma being preached, how could he listen while lying down?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Why did you sit and preach the Dharma to one who was lying down because he was not ill?"
"From this day forward, when a person is lying down and a bhikṣu is sitting, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Assemble all of you! For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus; even those who have already heard it should hear it again."

8. The *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Recitation) Rules, Part 1: Clarifying the First Section of the *Kṣudraka-vastu*. In the fifth year after the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, the community of bhikṣus was entirely pure. From that time onward, they gradually began to engage in improper conduct; accordingly, the World-Honored One established the precepts for each specific case and formulated the four kinds of complete methods for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*:
full ordination by self-attestation (*svayaṃ-saṃpanna*), full ordination by "come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*), full ordination by a group of ten, and full ordination by a group of five.

Regarding "self-perfection": when the World-Honored One sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained great enlightenment through his final moment of mind; having personally realized and perfectly fulfilled the sublime realization, as explained at length in the Sūtra on the Thread, this is called self-perfection.
"Welcome, O Perfected Ones. While the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata has everywhere delivered beings—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. You, too, should emulate the Tathāgata and extensively practice the deliverance of beings."

At that time, having heard the instruction of the World-Honored One, the bhikṣus traveled through various countries. When they saw faithful sons of good family who sought to leave the household life, the bhikṣus also imitated the Tathāgata and called out to them:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!"

Having ordained people for the homeless life, their deportment and movements, their glances to the left and right, and their manner of wearing robes and carrying the alms bowl were all contrary to the Dharma; they were thus ridiculed by worldly people, who said:

"The 'Come, O Bhikṣu' monks ordained by the World-Honored One have all their deportment and movements, their glances to the left and right, and their manner of wearing robes and carrying the alms bowl entirely in accordance with the Dharma."

Those whom the bhikṣus had ordained were also addressed as "Come, O Bhikṣu," yet their deportment and movements, their glances and looks to the left and right, and their manner of wearing robes and holding the alms-bowl were all contrary to the Dharma.
At that time, having heard these words, the Venerable Śāriputra sat cross-legged in a secluded place and reflected thus:

"Both are 'come hither' (svāgata); why is it that the 'come hither' bhikṣus ordained by the World-Honored One are all in accordance with the Dharma, whereas the 'come hither' bhikṣus ordained by other bhikṣus are all not in accordance with the Dharma?"

How can one cause the bhikṣus to ordain others and properly bestow full admission so that all are in accordance with the Dharma, sharing one precept, one conclusion, one dwelling, one meal, one training, and one recitation?

At the time of afternoon, Śāriputra arose from his meditation and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In seclusion, I reflected thus:
"Both are called 'Welcome' (svāgata); why is it that those ordained by the World-Honored One are all in accordance with the Dharma, while those ordained by the bhikṣus are not?"

How may I cause the bhikṣus to ordain others and properly confer full admission so that they are all entirely in accordance with the Dharma, sharing one precept, one boundary, one residence, one meal, one training, and one teaching?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this fully.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The five people, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, whom the Tathāgata has delivered, have come forth well into the homeless life and have properly received [the precepts].”

Being fully endowed with one precept, one conclusion, one dwelling, one meal, one training, and one teaching, he next ordained thirty people including Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; next, he ordained Subhadra of the city of Vārāṇasī;
next, he ordained the five hundred followers of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; and next, he ordained Nadī-Kāśyapa.
He first converted three hundred people; next, he converted two hundred people under Gayākāśyapa;
next, he converted two hundred and fifty people including Upasena and others; next, he converted you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, each with two hundred and fifty followers;
and finally, he converted Mahākāśyapa, Chanda, Kālodāyin, and Upāli.
Next, he ordained five hundred sons of the Śākya clan; next, he ordained five hundred people from the Vāṣpa family;
next, he ordained five hundred bandits; and next, he ordained the son of a householder, Svāgata.

In this manner, those bhikṣus who were well-come by the Tathāgata, having gone forth and properly received full ordination, shared one precept, one boundary, one residence, one meal, one training, and one recitation.

Śāriputra! Those people whom the bhikṣus may convert are also called "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu). They leave the household life and properly receive full ordination, even down to the single recitation; these are called those who receive full ordination as "Come hither" through the assembly of ten.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"From this day forward, I establish the method for receiving full ordination: when a group of ten is harmoniously assembled, performing one motion and three proclamations according to the unobstructed rule—this is called 'properly receiving full ordination.'"
When a person seeking full ordination first enters the Saṃgha, they should prostrate with their head at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha one by one. Having done so, they first seek an upādhyāya.
Baring the right shoulder, kneeling on the right knee and clasping the [upādhyāya’s] feet, they speak as follows:

When this has been repeated three times,
the preceptor should say:

either in brief or in detail.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, so-and-so, have received full ordination from the Upādhyāya so-and-so; the Ācārya so-and-so has already completed the interrogation with me in a secluded place."
I, [Name], with [Name] as my preceptor, now request the Saṃgha to grant me full ordination; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion for me, grant me full ordination!
Thus it was repeated three times.
The *karmavācanā* master should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so has already completed the instruction and interrogation in a secluded place, and he has already requested full ordination from the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha [listen]: So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor, wishes to have the obstructing factors interrogated before the Saṃgha.
Venerable sirs, listen!
So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor, wishes to inquire regarding the obstructing factors before the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld.
“Listen, son of good family!
Now is the time for sincerity; now is the time for truthful speech, before the devas, the world, the celestial Māras, the Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras.”
If one is not truthful, one deceives those within [the assembly], and furthermore deceives the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the community of śrāvakas; this is a great transgression.
Now the Sangha questions you: if it exists, say it exists; if it does not exist, say it does not exist.
Do your parents permit it?
Have you sought an upādhyāya?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
Are you a male?
Have you reached the age of twenty?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not a paṇḍaka?
What is your name?
If he says, "My name is So-and-so," [the preceptor asks],
"What is the name of your upādhyāya?"
He replied, "My name is so-and-so.
[The other asked,] "Have you not violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī?"
Are you not a thief living in concealment?
Are you not a runaway from military service?
Have you not gone forth [into homelessness] on your own accord?
Have you not killed your father? Have you not killed your mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
"Did you not intentionally draw blood from the body of a Buddha? Since the Buddha has long since entered parinirvāṇa, do you still rely on the old texts?
Have you previously received full ordination?
He replied:
"Has it been received?
"Have you not committed any of the four offenses? If he says:
"An offense.
One should say: "Go!"
"One shall not receive full ordination.
If one says: "I have not committed an offense."
Next, he asks about the thirteen matters:
"In each of these matters, is there an offense? If one says:
“An offense.
“Now that you have received full ordination, can you perform this offense according to the Dharma?
He replied:
"Yes. "Did you originally renounce the precepts?
He replied:
"Renounce [them].
"Are you not a slave?
Are you not a foster child?"
"Are you not indebted to others?
Are you not a subject of the king?
Do you not plot against the royal family?"
Are you a eunuch?
Are you not of dual gender? Are you a man?
Do you not have any such diseases as:

ringworm, scabies, jaundice with skin ulcers, leprosy, boils, hemorrhoids, incontinence, jaundice, malaria, coughing, consumption, insanity, fever, wind-swelling, water-swelling, abdominal swelling, or any other various ailments affecting the body?
He replies, “There is none.
The *karmavācanā* master should then speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so.

So-and-so has already completed the interrogation in a secluded place; So-and-so has already requested full ordination from the Saṃgha; his parents have given their permission; he has sought an upādhyāya; his three robes and bowl are complete; he is a male, twenty years of age, and declares himself pure and free from obstructing dharmas."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*).
After the threefold formal act (*karmavācanā*), [it continues]: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not yet completed his full term of residence (an-anvaya-bhikṣu), wearing a fine, new, clean, and dyed robe, who went to where the World-Honored One was to pay homage and inquire after his well-being.
At a later time, that bhikṣu, wearing soiled and tattered robes, went to where the World-Honored One was to pay homage and inquire after his well-being.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked him intentionally: "Bhikṣu!"
"You previously came to me wearing fine, new, clean, and dyed robes; why is it that the robes you are wearing now are so utterly worn out?
He replied, "These are indeed my former robes, but they have become so worn due to their long age."
The Buddha asked,
"Are you unable to repair it?
He replied to the Buddha:
"It can be mended, but there is no material available for patching.
The Buddha said,
"Can you not go into the alleys to pick up old, worn-out clothes, wash them clean, dye them, and patch them?"
