He said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!
The refuse-rag robes are impure; I find them utterly loathsome and am unable to accept and maintain them.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: “Stop! Stop!”
Do not speak such words.
Robes made of discarded rags require little effort to obtain, are pure and free from faults, accord with the dharma-robes of a śramaṇa, and it is upon these that one relies when going forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), sat down, and recounted the aforementioned matter in detail for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Out of a desire to bring benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has correctly proclaimed and established the first *prātimokṣa* within this assembly of śrāvakas."
"If a son of good family is capable of endurance and possesses direct faith, you should grant him full ordination;
if he is not capable of endurance, you should not grant it.

While the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery of Nyagrodha in Kapilavastu, for the sake of five benefits, he would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days.
What are the five?
Among my śrāvaka disciples, do they not take pleasure in worldly affairs?
Do they not delight in speaking useless words?
Do you not delight in or cling to sleep?
It is for the sake of the bhikṣu who tends to the sick, and so that faithful sons of good family may see the Tathāgata’s dignified and composed deportment and give rise to a heart of joy.
With these five matters in mind, he went from room to room among the bhikṣus.
He saw a bhikṣu who was ill, withered, pale, and emaciated. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally: "Bhikṣu!"
"Is your physical strength and composure harmonious?
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"I am afflicted by hunger and lack sufficient strength.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Are you unable to beg for food?"
He said: "World-Honored One!

In this kingdom of Kosala, one begs only for leftover food; one does not beg for that which is not leftover. This leftover food is impure, and I cannot eat it; for this reason, I have become emaciated."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: "Stop! Stop!"
"Do not speak such words.
Alms-food from leftovers is a minor matter and easy to obtain; it should be pure and free from faults. It is by relying on this that one leaves the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat, sat down, and explained the aforementioned matter in detail for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, for the sake of bringing benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall formally proclaim and establish a second reliance within the assembly of śrāvakas."
"If a son of good family who is patient, upright, and faithful is to be granted full ordination;
one who is not patient should not be granted it.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha went on his rounds among the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days. He saw a certain bhikṣu sitting beneath a tree and spoke these words:

"It is a hardship for a renunciant śramaṇa practicing the holy life to dwell beneath a tree; by day one is blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, and by night one is stung by mosquitoes and gadflies. I cannot endure it."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: “Stop! Stop!”
Do not speak such words.

Sitting beneath a tree involves few concerns and is easily attained; it is pure and free from faults, conforms to the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and is the basis upon which one goes forth into homelessness.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), sat down, and recounted the aforementioned matter in detail for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, for the sake of bringing benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall formally proclaim and establish the third reliance (niśraya) within the assembly of śrāvakas."
“If a son of good family who is patient and possesses a straightforward mind, you should grant him full ordination;
if he is not patient, you should not grant it.

While the Buddha was staying at the Śākya monastery of Nyagrodha in Kapilavastu, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha went to visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. There he saw a sick bhikṣu who was emaciated, wasted, and jaundiced.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monks,
is your physical strength harmonious and well?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
I am suffering from illness; my vital energies are unbalanced.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
“Are you unable to take medicine according to your illness or food according to your illness?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have neither the price for medicine nor anyone to give it to me; therefore, I suffer from illness.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Are you unable to take this discarded medicine?
He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"This discarded medicine is impure; I cannot take it.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "Stop!
Stop! Do not speak such words.
Discarded medicine is a minor matter and easy to obtain; it is pure, free from faults, conforms to the dharma of a śramaṇa, and is that upon which one relies when going forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat, sat down, and related the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, for the sake of bringing benefit, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall formally proclaim and establish the fourth reliance among the assembly of śrāvakas."
“If a son of good family who is patient and upright in mind is given the full ordination;
one who is not patient, he should not be given it.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a young brahmin in the village of Todeyya who, having requested the bhikkhus for ordination and received full admission (upasampadā), subsequently undertook the four reliances (cattāro nissayā).

“Pamsukūla robes require little effort and are easy to obtain; they are pure and free from faults, conforming to the dharma of a śramaṇa. By relying on these, one goes forth and receives full ordination.
Are you able to endure this for as long as life lasts?”
He replied,
"I cannot endure it. He asked:
"Why have you gone forth?
He replied, "I saw the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas wearing fine, light, and delicate robes; I became covetous of these robes, and for this reason I went forth."
The bhikṣus said:
"How could every single bhikṣu who has gone forth obtain such fine robes?
Then, a second reliance was granted:
"Leftover food is easy to obtain with little effort; it is pure and free from faults, conforming to the dharma of a śramaṇa. By relying on this, one goes forth and receives full ordination.
Within this, can you endure it for as long as life lasts?"
He replied, "I cannot endure it. He asked:
"Why have you gone forth?
He replied,
"I saw the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas eating white non-glutinous rice, various cakes, meats, and other foods."
"I have left the household life because I craved this fine food.
The bhikṣus said,
"How could every bhikṣu who leaves the household life obtain such fine food?"
Furthermore, he receives the third reliance:

"Sitting under a tree involves few concerns and is easy to obtain; it is pure and free from faults, conforms to the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and is the basis upon which one leaves the household life and receives full ordination."
"Can you endure this for as long as you live?
He replied,
"I cannot endure it."
The bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason have you gone forth?
He replied:
"I saw the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sitting in large dwellings and multi-storied pavilions; I coveted living in such dwellings, and for that reason I went forth.
The bhikṣus said, "Where can all bhikṣus who have gone forth obtain such excellent dwellings?"
Furthermore, one receives the fourth reliance:

"Medicines that are discarded, easily obtained with little effort, should be pure and free from faults, conforming to the Dharma of a śramaṇa; relying on these, one leaves the household life and receives full ordination."
"Can you endure this for as long as life lasts?
He replied,
"I cannot endure it."
He asked, "For what reason have you left the household life?
He replied:
"I saw that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, consume ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, and various other medicinal substances; I desired to take these medicines, and for this reason I went forth."
The bhikṣus asked,
"How is it that every single bhikṣu who has gone forth obtains such excellent medicine?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Why did you first confer the full ordination and only afterwards bestow the four reliances?

From this day forward, you must not first confer the full ordination and afterwards bestow the four reliances; rather, you should first bestow the four reliances, and only if they are able to endure them should you confer the full ordination."
If one says,
"I am not capable," one should not confer full ordination upon them.

If one first bestows full ordination (*upasampadā*) and subsequently bestows the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), it is considered that the full ordination has been received; however, the entire Saṃgha incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
When bestowing the four reliances, one should first perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) for seeking permission:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so. So-and-so has already completed the instruction and interrogation in a secluded place; he has requested full ordination before the Sangha; his parents have given their permission; he has sought out a preceptor and possesses the three robes and bowl; he is a male who has reached the age of twenty; and he declares himself to be pure and free from obstructing factors.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen: [Name], with [Name] as preceptor, wishes to declare the four reliances before the Saṃgha.
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!"
"Venerable [Name], with [Name] as your preceptor, you wish to declare the four reliances before the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
"Listen, son of good family!
This is because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desiring to benefit others, has correctly taught and established the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) among the assembly of śrāvakas.
If a son of good family is capable of endurance and possesses direct faith, one should grant him full ordination (*upasampadā*);
if he is not capable of endurance, one should not grant him the reliances.

The refuse-rag robe involves little effort and is easy to obtain; it is pure and free from faults, conforms to the dharma of a śramaṇa, and by relying upon it, one leaves the household life, receives full ordination, and becomes a bhikṣu.
"Within this, are you able to endure and maintain the practice of wearing rag-robes for as long as you live?
He replied, "I am able."
"If one obtains in excess a *kambala* robe, a cotton cloth robe, a *kṣauma* robe, a *kauśeya* robe, a *śāṇa* robe, a *māñjiṣṭha* robe, or a *kauravika* robe."

"Relying on the practice of begging for leftover food is a minor matter that is easy to obtain; it should be pure and free from faults, conforming to the Dharma of a śramaṇa. Relying upon this, one leaves the household life, receives full ordination, and becomes a bhikṣu."
"Among these, are you able to endure begging for alms for as long as you live?
He replied, "I am able."
“If one frequently obtains the Uposatha on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, as well as the distribution of voting tickets (*śalākā*) and invitations for meals;

if one relies on sitting under a tree, has few concerns, finds it easy to obtain requisites, remains pure and free from faults, and accords with the Dharma of a śramaṇa—by relying on these, one goes forth and receives full ordination, and may become a bhikṣu.”
"In this regard, can you endure sitting under a tree for as long as you live?
He replied, "I can."
"If one obtains a large house, a multi-storied building, a gabled house, a gatehouse, or a cave-dwelling;

if one relies on discarded medicine that requires little effort to obtain, is pure and free from faults, and accords with the dharma of a śramaṇa—by relying on these, one may go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu."
"Among these, are you able to endure taking discarded medicines for as long as you live?
He replied, "I am able."
"If one obtains in abundance ghee, oil, honey, molasses, fresh butter, and fat,
one should train in accordance with these four noble lineages.
The *karmavācanā* master should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so has already completed the interrogation in a secluded place, and So-and-so has already requested full ordination from the Saṃgha."

Having obtained the permission of his parents, having sought out a preceptor, and having been provided with the three robes and an alms bowl; being a male who has reached the age of twenty and has declared himself to be pure and free from obstructing conditions, he is capable of enduring the four reliances.
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
This is the formal announcement.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so has already completed the instruction and interrogation in a secluded place; So-and-so has already requested full ordination from the Saṃgha; his parents have given their permission; he has sought an upādhyāya and possesses the three robes and bowl; he is a male, twenty years of age, and has declared himself pure and free from obstructing factors; he is capable of enduring the four reliances.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.

Venerable sirs, may the Saṃgha grant its consent for the Saṃgha to confer the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor. Those who consent, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.
"Is this first *karmavācanā* accomplished?
The second and third [recitations] are spoken in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to grant full ordination to so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

“Good son! You have already received full ordination; you have properly received the full ordination through the legal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*) free from obstacles. The Saṃgha was harmonious and not discordant, consisting of ten members or more.”
You should now revere the Buddha, revere the Dharma, revere the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, revere your preceptor, and revere your ācārya.

You have already encountered this; do not let it be lost again. A human body is difficult to obtain, a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to meet, and hearing the Dharma is likewise difficult. It is difficult for the Saṃgha to be in harmony and for one's aspirations to be fulfilled. Having prostrated to the Lion of the Śākyas and the assembly of Śrāvakas who have attained full perfection—like the *anupama* flower free from dust and water—you should rely upon and cultivate the wholesome dharmas of Nirvāṇa.

Having already received full ordination, I shall now briefly explain to you the instruction regarding this sequence of the precepts: the four *pārājika* rules, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, the two *aniyata* rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, the four *prātideśanīya* rules, the *śaikṣa* rules of training, the seven rules for settling disputes, and the rules of conformity.
In this way, your preceptor and ācārya shall later explain it to you in detail.
This is called receiving the precepts through the tenfold assembly; as for receiving full ordination through the fivefold assembly:
The Buddha was staying in the Śītavana forest at Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a householder in the city named Ugga, a man of noble lineage and great power whose wealth was immeasurable. Hearing that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world and was residing in the Śītavana forest, he was filled with joy and exultation. Desiring to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to provide them with a meal, he adorned his house, sprinkled it with water, and smeared the floor with fresh cow dung.
At that time, there was a householder in the city of Śrāvastī named Anāthapiṇḍada, who had long been on intimate terms with Ugra.
He came to his home and, seeing him busily engaged in decorating and sweeping the grounds, asked:
"Householder! Why are you so busy?"
"For what reason are you in such a hurry?
Is it because you wish to give away a daughter in marriage or take a wife, or have you invited Brahmins, or the King and his ministers?
He replied:
"I have not given away my daughters in marriage nor taken brides for my sons, nor have I invited brahmins, kings, or great ministers.
Have you not heard that the Prince of the Śuddhodana clan has left the household life to attain Buddhahood, being designated as the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, appearing in this world?"
"I am currently at the Śītavana forest; I have now swept and adorned it, intending to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha, which is why I am in such a hurry.
Having heard this, Bhṛgu was greatly delighted and immediately asked, "I wish to pay my respects and visit; may I see him?"
He replied, "It can be seen!
The Buddha universally moistens all; there is nothing that he sees which does not bring benefit. You should know that now is the time."
Having heard these words, a heart of reverence arose within him, and he waited expectantly for the appearance of dawn.
The Buddha, perceiving his mind, emitted a brilliant light from the night that shone universally throughout the city.
When Poṇika saw the light, he thought it was dawn and immediately set out on his way; the gate opened of its own accord.
As he approached the city gate, the city gate opened again.
Having exited the gate, he saw a deva temple by the side of the road; wishing first to pay his respects there before proceeding to the Buddha, he entered.
As he turned toward the sacrificial gate, heaven and earth suddenly grew dark; he was seized with terror, bewildered as to whether to advance or retreat, and knew not where to go.
Then a deity in the air spoke to Bhṛtya, saying:
"Now is precisely the right time; proceed, and do not be afraid."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Hundred chariots drawn by oxen and horses, all adorned with the seven treasures—
if one were to give them all away as alms, even calculating that merit, [it would not equal the merit of this]."
Compared to your taking a single step, sixteen [of those merits] do not equal one.
Even if one were to take a hundred dragon-elephants from the Snowy Mountains,
adorned with the seven treasures, and use them to practice giving, the meritorious reward of that [giving]— [Your single step exceeds it.]
Compared to you taking a single step, sixteen [of those merits] do not equal one.
Even if one were to take celestial jade maidens of a hundred beauties, with bodies adorned with necklaces of the seven treasures,
and offer them as gifts in charity— if one were to calculate the karmic reward for that— [it would still not equal yours].
"Compared to your taking one step, sixteen [of my steps] do not equal even one.

At that time, having heard this verse, Anāthapiṇḍada’s reverence and faith redoubled; he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to return to the city of Śrāvastī to construct a vihāra and invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept my invitation.
Furthermore, I pray that the World-Honored One will dispatch a bhikṣu to oversee and adjudicate the matter.
As explained in detail in the *Pilā-sūtra*, up until the Buddha’s address to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"You all go there to observe the topography and terrain; according to where the monks reside, manage the arrangements and establish dwellings.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana received these instructions and immediately went to that place.

At that time, the householder Bhūti purchased the land for eighteen billion gold pieces, constructed monastic dwellings for eighteen billion gold pieces, and provided offerings to the assembly of monks with eighteen billion gold pieces, totaling fifty-four billion gold pieces.

Because this lay devotee was about to further increase his offerings, he dispatched Pūrṇa to the sea to gather treasures. Protected by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā Devānām-Indra guarded this man; thus, after seven round trips, he obtained a great abundance of rare jewels without encountering any obstacles.
Pūrṇa said to Bhāradvāja,
"I only pray that the householder will grant me permission to leave the home life.
The householder immediately granted his consent.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This man wishes to leave the household life; I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on him and deliver him.”
The Buddha then ordained him.
Once he had gone forth, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“I only pray that you will briefly grant me some instructions; I wish to go to the land of Suṇā and practice according to what you have taught.
The Buddha then gave him the appropriate instruction, as is explained at length in the Sūtra on the Thread (Sūtra on the Line).
Having received these instructions, Pūrṇa went to the country of Śūnapura.
In that country there was an elder named Ghaṭa, who built for him a chamber made of sandalwood.
In this regard, the causal narrative of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa should be told in detail, up until his request for ordination.
Pūrṇa took him as a novice and ordained him, yet for seven years he was unable to receive full ordination because the assembly of monks was difficult to assemble.

After seven years, the Gandharva had completed the sandalwood hall, adorned and decorated with exquisite craftsmanship; he then extensively invited the assembly of monks to provide offerings and bestowed the hall upon Pūrṇa.
At that time, there were ten monks among the assembly who were all upholders of the Vinaya. Because the Sangha had assembled, Pūrṇa conferred the full ordination upon Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Having received the full ordination, he immediately addressed his preceptor, saying:
"I wish to go to Śrāvastī to pay my respects and visit the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will grant me permission."
He replied, "As you wish!
Bear my name and inquire after the World-Honored One's well-being, and also request five boons on my behalf."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa received the instruction and proceeded to where the Buddha was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Prepare a bed and bedding for this visiting bhikṣu.”
"If he says to Ānanda to spread out the bedding, you should know that he intends to stay in the same room as the World-Honored One;
if he says to the Venerable Dharmaruci, you should know that he intends to be assigned a room according to seniority."
During the first watch of the night, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for the śrāvakas; during the middle watch, he returned to his room, where his halo remained constantly radiant.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "Do you recite the sūtras?"
He replied, “I am reciting.
[The other asked,] “Which sutra are you reciting?”
"Recite the *Aṣṭavargika-sūtra*.
The Buddha said,
"You may recite it."
Having recited it with a low voice, he was able to answer each and every question regarding the meaning of the verses.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
"Monk, as for the words, phrases, and meanings you have recited, they are exactly as I have previously taught.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The noble person does not delight in evil; The evil person does not delight in the noble."
"If one perceives the faults of the world, one resolves the mind to proceed toward Nirvana.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!"
"Among my disciples, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa is foremost in swift understanding and realization.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa immediately rose, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and, invoking the name of his preceptor, requested five boons from the Buddha.
Having heard these words, the Tathāgata rose early in the morning and went to where the many bhikṣus were; he spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and sat down.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Pūrṇa is in the country of Suvastu; he has sent Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa here to request five vows from me."
From this day forward, I permit the people of the country of Suvāstu five privileges.
What are the five?
First, the land of Suvāstu is naturally clean and they take pride in it; therefore, I permit them to bathe every day, whereas here [in our land] it is permitted only once every half-month.

Second, because the lands of the western regions abound with gravel, stones, clods of earth, and various thorny trees, they are permitted to wear double-layered leather sandals; here, however, single-layered ones are permitted.
Third, because the lands of the western regions have few bedding materials but many skins and leathers, they are permitted to use those skins and leathers as bedding; here, such use is not permitted.
Fourth, in the region of Aparāntaka, clothing is scarce and there are many garments of the deceased; they permit the wearing of such garments of the deceased, and this is also permitted here.

Fifth, in the region of Aparāntaka, monks are few; they permit the fivefold assembly to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), whereas here, full ordination is conferred by a tenfold assembly through self-ordination, by the "Come hither" (*ehi*) formula, or by a tenfold assembly through the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*).
"Receiving full ordination through the white-three-karmavācanā procedure among the five assemblies on the other shore is called the fourth way of receiving full ordination.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli had two śrāmaṇeras:
one named Dabaka and the other named Balaka.
These two śrāmaṇeras were raised from childhood, and when they reached the age of twenty and wished to receive full ordination, they thought to themselves:

"If one were to first confer the precepts upon one recipient, the latter would surely harbor resentment. Is it possible for them to receive full ordination simultaneously, under the same upādhyāya, the same saṃgha, and the same preceptor?"

Having formed this thought, Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is it permissible for one to receive the full ordination together with the same preceptor, the same preceptor of the precepts, and the same assembly?
The Buddha said,
"It is permissible."
"In this manner, two or three persons may also receive [the precepts] together, but they must not receive them as a group; this is called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If there is one person with two preceptors, one person with three preceptors, or one person with many preceptors, it is not called receiving full ordination."
If there is no *karmavācanā* master, it is not called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If two or three people share one *karmavācanā* master but have separate preceptors (*upādhyāya*), and receive it together with the same assembly, it is not called receiving full ordination.

Regarding two persons: if there are two persons performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for two others, or three persons performing the *karmavācanā* for three others, and they receive it together as one assembly while having separate preceptors, this is not called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Furthermore, there are cases that do not constitute the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*). If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is included among the ten persons required for the quorum, it does not constitute the conferral of full ordination. Likewise, if the person seeking ordination is used to complete the number of ten, or if a bhikṣuṇī is used to complete the number of ten, or if one who has granted their consent (*chanda*) is used to complete the number of ten, it does not constitute the conferral of full ordination.

If the name of the preceptor is not mentioned, the name of the person receiving full ordination is not mentioned, or the name of the Sangha is not mentioned, it is not called receiving full ordination.

If the preceptor recites the *karmavācanā*, the person receiving full ordination recites the *karmavācanā*, or a bhikṣuṇī recites the *karmavācanā*, in all such cases, it is not called receiving full ordination.
If the preceptor is in the air, the person receiving the precepts is in the air, the Sangha is in the air, and everyone is in the air, none of these cases are called the conferral of full ordination.
If half [of the body] is on the ground and half is in the air, it is not called receiving full ordination.
If there is an intervening obstruction, it is not called receiving full ordination.
If one half is in a covered place while the other half is separated by an intervening obstruction, it is not called receiving full ordination.
If the ground is half-covered and half-exposed, and one cannot reach another with an outstretched hand, it is not called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If sitting entirely in an open space, and body and hand do not reach one another, it is not called receiving full ordination. If sitting entirely in a covered place, one must not be outside the range of sight or hearing; if one is so removed, it is not called receiving full ordination.

Furthermore, one is not said to have received full ordination if, at the time of receiving it, they are asleep, ignorant, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by painful illness; in such cases, they are not said to have received full ordination.

Furthermore, one is not said to have received full ordination if, upon receiving it, the person does not speak, or if they do so only by mental reflection or by shouting loudly; in such cases, one is not said to have received full ordination.

Furthermore, one is not said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) if it is performed by means of a letter, a seal, raising the hand, or making gestures; these are not called receiving full ordination.

If the person is not present, if the person before whom the act is performed is not questioned, if there is no desire [to ordain], if it is contrary to the Dharma and lacks harmony, if the assembly is incomplete, if the motion (*jñapti*) is incomplete, or if the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is incomplete—if any one of these is incomplete, one is not said to have received full ordination.

Furthermore, those who are not called "fully ordained" include: one who has violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī; one who lives as a thief; one who has crossed over [to another sect]; one who has committed the five heinous crimes; the six types of eunuchs; one who is too young or too old; one whose hands have been severed, whose feet have been severed, whose hands and feet have both been severed, whose ears have been severed, whose nose has been severed, or whose ears and nose have both been severed; one who is blind, deaf, or both blind and deaf; one who is mute, lame, or both mute and lame; one with scars from whips or scars from branding; one whose tendons have been pulled or whose tendons have been cut; one with a hunched back; a king’s minister; one in debt; one who is ill; the child of a heretic; one who is a slave by body; one who is physically incomplete; one of ugly appearance; and one who has violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the Licchavi youth Ambaṣṭha violated the brahmacarya of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmapriyā’s disciple.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Dharmapriyā went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Licchavi youth has ruined the holy life of my disciple.
Having spoken these words, he paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take my saṃghāṭī robe and enter the city of Vaiśālī.
Ānanda immediately took the saṃghāṭī robe and presented it to the World-Honored One.
Since attaining Buddhahood, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has never entered a city or village after a meal.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Vaiśālī together with Ānanda. Then, five hundred Licchavis were assembled in the Hall of Debate, intending to discuss other matters.
Seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, they spoke to one another in succession:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata entered the city after his meal?
There must surely be a cause for this."

Then the Licchavis immediately rose, prepared a seat for the Buddha, and went out to welcome the World-Honored One. Kneeling with their right knees on the ground and joining their palms, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will sit upon this seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One spread out his sitting mat and sat down. The Licchavis prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said to the Licchavis:
"You should protect your retinues, just as you must protect my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs.

Should anyone violate them—whether they wish to do so or not—and thereby destroy their brahmacarya, according to my Dharma, such persons shall for the rest of their lives not speak with them, not dwell with them, and not eat with them."
The Licchavi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with the Dharma of the World-Honored One, those who have violated the holy life are not to be spoken to, not to be lived with, and not to share food with."
"In my worldly law, it is likewise: for the rest of one's life, one shall not converse with them, shall not dwell with them, and shall not eat together with them.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the Licchavis in accordance with their needs; having inspired in them a heart of joy, he departed.
Not long after he had departed, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmā approached the Licchavis and spoke these words:
"O householders!
The young Licchavi Ambaṣṭha has violated the holy life of my disciple; this is unwholesome and contrary to the Dharma."
Upon hearing this, the Licchavis said to one another,
"The teaching the World-Honored One has just given was precisely for this purpose.
They were immediately filled with great shame and spoke to the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"What kind of punishment do you wish us to inflict?
the bhikṣuṇī said:
"We shall change their family name and proclaim them as non-Śākyas; we shall turn their gate to face west, demolish their kitchen, and destroy their eaves by one cubit all around."
He replied, "I shall obey the instruction.
He then shouted the *phaliya* command, turned the gate to face west, and even destroyed its eaves.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat, sat down, and related this foregoing matter in detail to the bhikṣus:

"Regarding the violation of a bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct: whether she is an arhatī or an anāgaminī, if it occurs at the beginning, middle, or end, all such acts are termed the destruction of a bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct."

If a *srotāpannā*, a *sakṛdāgāminī*, or an ordinary nun who maintains the precepts experiences pleasure at the beginning [of the act], this is called the violation of a nun’s pure conduct; it is not called a violation during the middle or at the end.
At that time, there was a mahallaka who, while formerly a layman, had violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī; a doubt arose in his mind, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"When I was formerly a layman, I violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Mahāla himself says that he violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī; expel him."
The bhikṣus should immediately expel them.
If one has violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī, one should not grant him ordination;
if he has already been ordained, he should be expelled.
If one ordains her by granting the full precepts (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "corrupting the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding "stealing residence": when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed explanation is as above.

At that time, a donor provided a meal for the Sangha within the vihāra. Then, a man with black skin and a large belly came and sat in the seat of the presiding elder (sthavira). After a short while, the presiding elder of the Sangha arrived and asked:
"How many years of seniority (kappas) do you have?"
He replied, "We eat the same kind of rice wherever we sit; what is the use of troubling yourself by asking about my seniority?
The Elder, with a solemn and majestic bearing, said:
"Hey! Get down from here!
He then sat in the place of the second senior elder; after a short while, the second senior elder arrived and asked:
"How old are you?
He replied, "We eat the same food and sit in the same place; why ask such a troublesome question?"
In this manner, they passed the matter along until it reached the śrāmaṇeras, who pushed and prodded him, asking:
"Who is your upādhyāya? Who is your teacher?"
How many precepts does a śrāmaṇera have?
How many should a śrāmaṇera be counted as having?
What is the name of the first one?
First, all sentient beings depend upon food for sustenance.
Second, there are name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
Third, there are sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*).
4. The Four Noble Truths.
5. The Five Aggregates.
6. The Six Sense Bases.
7. The seven factors of enlightenment.
8. The eightfold noble path.
9. The nine abodes of sentient beings.
"10. The ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
The dharma of a śrāmaṇera should be counted in this manner.
He replied:
“I am Nanda and Upānanda, the foremost disciples.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Nanda and Upananda are not among the senior disciples; they are those who have gone forth on their own.
If such persons as these have never previously entered into the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, one may later grant them the going-forth and the full ordination provided they possess a virtuous mind.”

If one has previously participated in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, this is called "staying by theft" (*steyāśraya*), and they are not permitted to go forth or receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

However, if a prince or the son of a high minister puts on the *kāṣāya* robes for the sake of evading danger and has not yet participated in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, they may be granted the going forth.
"If one has previously participated in the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*, ordination is not permitted.
If a śrāmaṇera thinks to himself:
"What is being discussed during the recitation of the precepts?"
He immediately entered beneath the seat of the senior monk to eavesdrop.
If the śrāmaṇera is clever and perceives the beginning, middle, and end of the speech, he shall not later receive full ordination.
If one is dull-witted, or asleep, or if the mind is directed toward other thoughts such that the words at the beginning, middle, and end are not recorded, one may later receive full ordination.
If one has stolen residence [in the Sangha], they should not be granted leave from home;
if they have already left home, they should be expelled.
If one ordains another by conferring the full precepts (upasampadā), one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense; this is called "staying by theft" (*steyasaṃvāsa*).
Regarding "crossing over": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, it was explained at length as above.

At that time, there was a man who, before his meal, would don the insignia of a śramaṇa and enter a village with a black alms-bowl in hand to beg for food; after his meal, he would don the insignia of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) and, carrying a wooden bowl, follow people into forest groves, ponds, and gardens to beg for food. He was despised by the people of the world, who said:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, enter our villages to beg from our homes, and now, having come into the forest, they still cannot escape?"
Furthermore, some people said:
"Do you not know? This śramaṇa is deceitful;
for the sake of food and clothing, he enters both [the householder's and the monastic's] circles."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"This is called a 'transgressor' (tīrthika-pratyāpanna); he has abandoned the insignia of a śramaṇa and taken up the insignia of an outsider."

One who has discarded the insignia of a non-Buddhist and yet continues to hold the insignia of a śramaṇa—such a person who has transgressed the path of deliverance should not be granted ordination; if they have been ordained, they should be expelled.
"If one ordains them by granting the full precepts, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called 'one who has crossed over.
Regarding the five *ānantarya* [sins]: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above."
At that time, the brahmin Dūti, who was an old friend of Śāriputra, came to where Śāriputra was and said this:
"Venerable One!..."
"Let me go forth [into the religious life].
Śāriputra replied, "This is an excellent thing;
however, you Brahmins are constantly opposed to the śramaṇas—where could you possibly find faith?"
From whom did you hear the Dharma to give rise to such a heart of joy?
Was it from the World-Honored One,
or from the bhikṣus?
The brāhmaṇa said:
“I have no faith, nor do I have joy, nor have I heard it from another.
However, I killed my mother wishing to eliminate this sin; for that reason, I have gone forth.”
Śāriputra said, "Wait until I have returned after questioning the World-Honored One.
For this reason, Śāriputra went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"This person has committed the immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma) of killing his mother; he is a rotten and decayed seed who cannot produce the noble dharmas within the True Dharma, and therefore should not be granted ordination."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
The brahmin Dūti was an old friend of Ānanda; he went to where Ānanda was and said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
"I wish to leave the household life. Ānanda said,
"This is a good thing."
The Buddha continued speaking to Ānanda:

"This person has committed the immediate transgression of patricide; he is rotten and decayed, unable to produce the roots of the Path within the True Dharma. Even if the seven Buddhas were to appear in the world simultaneously to preach the Dharma for him, he would ultimately never produce goodness within the True Dharma."
It is like a *tāla* tree: once its head is severed, it will not grow again; it will no longer be green, nor can it be planted.
These five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) are likewise: within the True Dharma, they do not give rise to the seeds of the noble ones (*ārya*).
If one has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, they should not be granted ordination;
if they have already been granted ordination, they should be expelled.
If one ordains them and grants them full admission (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
The other three immediate offenses (*ānantarya*) are also like this; these are called the five immediate transgressions.
Regarding the six kinds of impotent persons (*ṣaḍ-ṣaṇḍha*): the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were sleeping in their quarters at night, someone came and groped their feet, their thighs and bellies, and then proceeded to inappropriate places.
When the bhikṣus tried to seize him, he simply ran away.
They went again to other places— the halls and the warm rooms— and it was the same everywhere.
The next day, the bhikṣus gathered at their place of residence and said to one another,
"Venerable elders!..."
"Last night while I was sleeping, someone came and groped about everywhere, even in improper places.
Just as I was about to seize them, they immediately ran away.
Another bhikṣu said:
"I am also like this," and so it was for many others as well. Then,
a certain bhikṣu had this thought:
"I shall lie in wait tonight to capture him.
When evening came, that bhikṣu went ahead and lay down to watch for him.
Once the other bhikṣus had fallen asleep, he returned as before to grope about, and immediately seized him, saying these words:
"Venerable elders!
Bring a lamp. When they had brought it, he asked:
"Who are you? She replied,
"I am the king's daughter."
He asked again,
"In what way is she a woman?
She replied:
“I am of two kinds; I am neither male nor female.
He asked again, “For what reason have you left the household life?”
She replied, "I have heard that śramaṇas have no wives; I have come wishing to be your wife.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"This is one who is not a male.
There are six kinds of those who are not males:
What are the six?
First, birth;
second, decay.
Third, cutting off;
fourth, depending on others;
fifth, jealousy.
Sixth, the "Half-Month" (ardhamāsa):
as for the "born" (jāta), one who is born as a eunuch is called "born.
As for the "crushed" (nirbhinna), when a wife or concubine gives birth to a child, they become mutually jealous; while the child is small, they crush it, and this is called "crushed."
Regarding "eunuchs who have been castrated": if a king or a high minister seizes a person and cuts off their male organ to serve as a gatekeeper, this is called a castrated eunuch.
Regarding "dependent on another": because of the touch of another person, the male organ arises;
this is called a dependent impotent. Regarding "jealous": seeing another engaged in sexual intercourse, the male organ subsequently arises; this is called a jealous impotent.
Regarding the "half-month eunuch": one who is potent for half a month and impotent for half a month is called a half-month eunuch.
Among these, there are those born as eunuchs, those castrated by others, and those whose organs were severed; these three types of eunuchs should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should be expelled.
The three types of impotent persons—those who are impotent by nature, those who are impotent through envy, and those who are impotent for half a month—should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled; however, if they later engage in sexual misconduct, they should be expelled.

These six types of impotent persons should not be granted ordination; if one grants them ordination and they receive full admission (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense. These are called the six types of impotent persons.
Regarding "the great and the small": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, various bhikṣus ordained young children. These children required assistance when lying down or rising; they soiled themselves with excrement and urine upon entering or leaving, defiling the monks' bedding and mats; and they cried out while sleeping or waking. Consequently, they were reviled by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain young children who do not yet know the proper conduct or how to distinguish between good and bad speech?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
Another person said: "Do you not know?
"These śramaṇas have no children of their own; they raise the small children of others, regarding them as their own offspring, to amuse themselves.
Furthermore, another person said:
"These śramaṇas only do not ordain two kinds of people:"
"First, there are those who are dead; second, the person before you does not wish to leave the household life.
If you do not ordain them, the community will not increase. For this reason, you should ordain many.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him in detail regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, one who is too young or too old should not be granted ordination.
Regarding those who are too young: whether they are less than seven years of age or exactly seven years of age, if they do not know what is good or evil, none of them should be granted ordination.
If one has reached seven years of age and is capable of discerning between good and evil, they should be granted ordination.
If a child has already been ordained previously, they should not be expelled.
To ordain such a person constitutes a *vinaya*-transgression; this is termed "too young."
Regarding "the very old": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, various bhikṣus ordained eighty or ninety people who were elderly—those with white hair, bent backs, and stooped spines; whose vital faculties were no longer restrained; some of whom, when urinating, had excrement leak out; and who required assistance for every movement and could not rise by themselves.

If, within a dwelling, a heated room, a place for washing feet, or a place for walking meditation, one gasps and coughs continuously, spitting and sputtering so as to splash and defile the Sangha’s pure grounds, one will be censured by worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain such an old man—his head white, his back bent, coughing and trembling, requiring others to assist him in rising and sitting?"
Those who have left the household life ought to be healthy so that they may practice seated meditation, recite the sutras, and cultivate various meritorious deeds.
As for this person who has brought ruin upon himself, what path could he possibly possess?
Again, some people said:
"Do you not know that the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, leave the household life without fathers? You should regard this old man as your father.
Still others said:
“Among these śramaṇas, there are only two kinds of people whom we do not ordain:
first, the dead; second, those who have no desire to leave the household life.
If we do not ordain them, the community will not increase.”
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Summon this bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, those who are too old should not be granted ordination."

"One who is too old" refers to one who is over seventy or less than seventy and is incapable of performing tasks, requiring assistance for rising and reclining; such a person is not permitted to go forth.
If one who has exceeded seventy years of age is still capable of performing [monastic duties], this is likewise not permitted.
However, if one has reached seventy and is healthy enough to cultivate various practices, permission is granted for them to go forth.
If one is too old, they should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them the going-forth and confers full ordination upon them, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called "excessively old.
Regarding "one whose hand has been severed": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, there was at that time a bhikṣu who ordained a man whose hand had been severed.
He was censured by the people of the world, [who said]: [text continues]
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain one who has violated the king’s law and had his hand cut off?
One who has left the household life should have a complete body; what path or dharma can there be for such a ruined person?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Summon this bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you have done this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, one who has had their hand cut off should not be granted ordination."

Regarding "one whose hand has been severed": whether it be the hand itself, the wrist, the little finger, or the thumb—if such a person has not yet gone forth, they should not be granted the going-forth;
if they have already gone forth, they should not be expelled.
If one ordains such a person by conferring full admission (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "cutting off the hands.
Regarding "cutting off the feet," the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a man whose feet had been severed. He was reviled by the people of the world, until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one whose feet have been severed should not be granted ordination."
Regarding those with severed feet: whether the foot has been severed, or the wrist, or the little toe, or the big toe, one should not grant them ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
...up to the point that one incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
This is called "cutting off the feet.
Regarding "cutting off hands and feet," the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a person whose hands and feet had been severed. He was censured by the people of the world, who said:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain a person who has violated the king's law and had his hands and feet cut off?"
"If one lacks even a single requisite, one cannot yet leave the household life, let alone two.
This man is ruined; what path could he possibly have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call this bhikṣu here.
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those who have had their hands or feet amputated should not be granted ordination.
Regarding those with amputated hands or feet: it refers to those whose right hand or left foot has been cut off.
If one has had the left hand and right foot amputated;
or if one has had the left hand and left foot amputated;
or if one has had the right hand and right foot amputated—one should not grant them the going forth.
If one has already gone forth, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them the going forth and the full ordination, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
This is called "cutting off hands and feet."
Regarding "one who has had their ears cut off": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a man whose ears had been cut off as a member of the Saṃgha. He was reviled by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain one who has violated the king’s law and had his ears cut off?"
The Buddha further said:
"From this day forward, those who have had their ears cut off should not be granted ordination.

Regarding those with cut ears: whether the earlobes have been severed, or the ear-rings have been cut, or the ears were previously pierced—if it is possible for them to be made to join back together, they may be granted ordination.
One who has had their ears cut off should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
If one ordains them and grants them full admission (*upasampadā*), it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called "cutting off the ears.
Regarding "cutting off the nose," the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣus ordained a person whose nose had been cut off, and they were censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain one who has violated the king’s law by having his nose cut off?
What path or Dharma can there be for such a ruined person?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha further said:
"From this day forward, those who have had their noses cut off should not be granted ordination.
As for "those with cut-off noses," whether the nose has been severed or the nostrils have been pierced, they should not be granted ordination; this is what is meant by "having one's nose cut off."
Regarding those who had their ears and noses cut off:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a person whose ears and nose had been cut off, and he was reviled by the people of the world: [text continues]
"How can these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, ordain those who have had their ears and noses cut off?
If one has been cut off, they may not even be ordained, let alone both.
What kind of path can there be for such a ruined person?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one who has had their ears or nose cut off should not be granted ordination."
...up to: this is called "cutting off ears and nose.

Regarding the blind: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, there was at that time a bhikṣu who ordained a blind man as a renunciant and led him along by pulling his arm, which drew the censure of the people of the world: [text continues].
“How can these śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, ordain a blind man?
Being unable to walk by himself, they must take him by the hand and lead him.
One who has left the household life ought to have all his faculties intact; for such a ruined person, what path could there be?”
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Summon that bhikṣu here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those who are blind should not be granted ordination. Regarding the blind:
one whose eyes do not see any forms at all, or one who can see the lines on the palm of the hand, or one with night-blindness (strabismus), shall not be granted ordination.
If one has already left the household life, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them the going-forth and the full ordination, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya.
This is called "blind."
Regarding the deaf: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a deaf person and allowed him to go forth, which drew the ridicule of worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain a deaf person and allow him to go forth?"
"If one does not hear words of good or evil, how can one listen to the Dharma?
This person is ruined; what path could he possibly have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, until the Buddha spoke these words:
"From this day forward, those who are deaf should not be granted ordination. Regarding the deaf:
one who does not hear any sound at all; however, if they can hear loud sounds, they may be granted ordination. This is what is meant by "deaf."
Regarding the blind and the deaf: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a blind and deaf person. He was censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain a blind and deaf person who cannot see or hear?"
"One who has left the household life ought to have all their faculties complete; even a blind person is not permitted [to ordain], let alone one who is both blind and deaf.
Such a ruined person—what path could they possibly possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those who are blind or deaf should not be granted ordination."
...up to: "This is called 'blind. Regarding the deaf-mute:
while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, at that time a bhikṣu ordained a mute person as a monk.
The man communicated by making gestures with his hands, and he was ridiculed by the people of the world."
“How can these śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, ordain a mute person?
He cannot speak and communicates only through hand gestures.
This is a ruined and degenerate person; what path could he possibly have?”
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one who is mute should not be granted ordination."
"One who is mute" refers to one who cannot speak and communicates by means of hand gestures; such a person should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled. This is what is meant by "mute."
Regarding the cripple: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a cripple and allowed him to go forth. He was reviled by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain a cripple who is unable to walk?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, a person who is lame should not be granted ordination."
Regarding the "crippled" (pangu): one who walks by grasping a wooden sandal with both hands and dragging their buttocks along should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled; this is what is meant by "crippled."
Regarding the mute and the lame: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed exposition is as above.

At that time, various bhikṣus ordained mute and lame persons, even granting them the going-forth and full ordination; this constitutes a violation of the Vinaya. This is called "the mute and the lame."
Regarding the "scars from whips": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the details are as explained above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a person with scars from whips and allowed him to leave the household life. He was censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas ordain a person who has violated the king’s law and bears scars from whips?"
"One who has left the household life ought to have a body that is pure and complete.
This man, being so ruined and decayed—what path could he possibly possess?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call this bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those with scars from whip lashes should not be ordained as monastics.

Regarding those with whip scars: whether they are raised or depressed, if the scars can be treated so that they become level again and are no different from the surrounding flesh, one may grant them ordination.
One who has scars from whip lashes should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them ordination and the full precepts, it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called a whip scar.

Regarding a seal scar: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, at that time a bhikṣu ordained a person with seal scars, and he was censured by the people of the world: [text continues].
"How can these śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, ordain those who have violated the king’s law and bear the scars of punishment?
Those who have left the household life ought to be complete and pure.
What path can there be for such a ruined person?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, a person with a scar from a seal-tattoo should not be granted ordination."

Regarding those with scars from branding: if one has cut the flesh and used peacock bile, copper sulfate, or similar substances to draw characters or various images of birds and beasts, such a person should not be granted ordination.
If one has already gone forth, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them the going forth and the full ordination, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya.
This is called "the scar of a seal."
Regarding those with severed tendons: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a man with severed tendons; the man walked by dragging his feet and was reviled by worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain a man with severed tendons?"
"He walks with his feet trailing; one who has left the household life should have his body fully intact.
For this ruined man, what path can there be?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha spoke as follows:
"From this day forward, a person who has their tendons cut should not be granted ordination. Regarding "one who has their tendons cut":
it refers to one who has the tendons of the heel cut; such a person should not be granted ordination, up to and including the offense of *vinayātikrama*. This is called "having the tendons cut."
Regarding the one whose tendons were pulled out: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a man whose tendons had been pulled out, and he was censured by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas ordain a man whose tendons have been pulled out?"
"One who has left the household life should have their body complete.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one who has had their tendons pulled out should not be granted ordination."

"Regarding 'pulling tendons': to pull [the tendons] from the heels up to the nape of the neck, or from the nape of the neck down to the heels; such a person should not be granted ordination, as it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense. This is called 'pulling tendons.'"
Regarding the hunchbacked person: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, a bhikṣu ordained a hunchbacked dwarf and allowed him to go forth. He was ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas ordain a hunchbacked person who was a mere plaything of the royal household?"
"One who has gone forth from the household life ought to keep the body straight and upright.
What path can there be for one such as this, a person so utterly ruined?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha spoke thus:
"From this day forward, those with hunched backs should not be granted ordination.
Those with hunched backs are those who are not upright.
Dwarfs are those whose upper bodies are long while their lower bodies are short, or whose upper bodies are short while their lower bodies are long.
One who is the shortest of all should not be granted ordination; otherwise, it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called a dwarf. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, fascicle twenty-three [and] fascicle twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

This is the second part of the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* on Miscellaneous Rules (*Kṣudraka-vastu*). Regarding the King and his Ministers: The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a royal minister and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*). When the official in charge of the prisons saw this, he seized the bhikṣu and delivered him to the magistrate, saying:
"This śramaṇa has privately ordained a royal minister."
The judge said: "Take the Upādhyāya and break three of his ribs;

take the Karmavācanā-ācārya and pull out his tongue; strike each member of the ten-member assembly with eight lashes of the whip; and as for those who received full ordination, punish them according to the strictest law."
At that time, a great multitude escorted him out of the city. Then, as King Bimbisāra was about to go to the World-Honored One, he saw this crowd and asked:
"Who are these people?"
He then reported the matter in full to the king.
Upon hearing it, the king became greatly incensed and immediately issued an edict:
"From this day forward, those who wish to leave the household life shall be permitted to receive ordination from their teachers as they see fit."
The king said,
"Summon the judicial officers.
When they had arrived, the king questioned them, saying:
"Who is the king in this country?
The minister replied,
"Your Majesty is the king."
He then asked,
"If I am the king, why do you punish people's crimes without first informing me?
The king immediately commanded his officials to seize the adjudicators, strip them of their official ranks, and confiscate all the wealth in their households for the state treasury.
The officials of the various departments immediately followed the King’s instructions, stripping him of his official rank and confiscating his family wealth to be deposited in the state treasury.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In what place do all kings have such faith?
From this day forward, kings and ministers shall not permit anyone to go forth [into the religious life]."
There are four kinds of ministers:
some have titles but no emoluments; some have emoluments but no titles; some have both emoluments and titles; and some have neither title nor emolument.

Among these, there are those who have no official title but hold a salary, and those who have both a title and a salary; such persons are not permitted to leave the household life in this country, nor are they permitted in other countries.
There are also those who hold a salary but have no official title; they are not permitted here, but are permitted elsewhere.
One who has no name and no salary may be ordained here and may also be ordained elsewhere.
A king’s minister should not grant ordination; if he does so, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense. This is what is meant by "a king’s minister."
Regarding the one who owes a debt: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a man who owed a debt. When the creditor came and saw him, he immediately seized him and took him before the judge, saying:
"This man owes me a debt but has not repaid it, and has instead gone forth as a monk."
The judge, having faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, said to that person:
"This man has renounced his wealth and entered the homeless life;
why then should he be indebted? He then released him.
The creditor spoke disparagingly:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain this debtor who has consumed my wealth?
This man is a ruined and corrupt person; what path could he possibly possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, those who owe debts should not be granted ordination."
If someone comes wishing to go forth, one should first ask:
"Do you not owe anyone a debt?
If they reply:
"If [the person] says, 'I am burdened; I have a wife and children at home, and I have fields, houses,
and wealth of my own to repay [my debts],' one should allow them to go forth."
If one says,
"I do not owe anything," they should be granted ordination.
Once he has gone forth, if creditors come, if the debt is small, he shall repay it with his robes and bowl.
If that is still insufficient, he shall personally repay it with his robes and bowl, or seek alms to assist in repaying it.
If one is unable to repay the debt, one should say:
"I previously asked you:
'Are you not a person who owes a debt?'"
"You yourself said,
'I do not owe you.
You must go yourself to beg for what is owed to repay it."
If a person who owes a debt should not be granted ordination.
If they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled; otherwise, it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense. This is called "being in debt."
Regarding the sick person: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a sick man who went to the physician Jīvaka and said to him:
“Jīvaka, treat my illness, and I shall pay you five hundred taels of gold and two pieces of fine cotton cloth.”
He replied, “I cannot;
I treat the illnesses of only two kinds of people:
first, the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; second, the king and the ladies of his inner palace.”
The sick person then went to the quarters of Nanda and Upananda;
having arrived, Nanda asked him, "Long-lived one, are your four great elements in harmony?"
He replied:
"My illness was not alleviated, so I went to Jīvaka’s place and hired him with five hundred taels of gold and two pieces of fine cotton cloth to treat it, but he refused to treat me, saying:
'I treat the illnesses of only two kinds of people:'"
"The Buddha, the Bhikṣu Saṃgha, the King, and the King’s harem ladies. Nanda said:
"Why would you discard five hundred taels of gold and two pieces of fine cotton cloth for that?"
"You need only relinquish two things:
first, your hair; second, your secular clothing.
The sick man said:
“Ācārya! Do you wish for me to go forth?
He replied:
"So be it! He was immediately ordained as a renunciant and received full ordination. Rising early in the morning, he put on his robes for entering the village and went to Jīvaka’s place, saying this:
"Young man!..."
"I have a fellow practitioner who is ill; please go and treat him for me.
He replied, "Very well, I shall take the medicine and go."
He immediately took the medicine and went there; upon seeing him, he recognized him and asked, "Venerable sir, have you already gone forth?
He replied:
"So be it," he replied, and praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
"I shall now treat you.
He immediately administered medicinal therapy; having finished the treatment, he gave him two pieces of fine cotton cloth and spoke these words:
"Venerable One!..."
"I shall practice the pure life (brahmacarya) within the Buddha-dharma.

Having accepted [the payment], he immediately abandoned the path, cast off his monastic robes (kāṣāya), and put on two fine cotton cloths (dukūla). Walking through the streets, he uttered these words of abuse:

"Jīvaka, the physician, son of a great man! I hired you for five hundred taels of gold and two fine cotton cloths, yet you were unwilling to treat me; but seeing that I had left the home-life, you then treated me, and in return, you even obtained the cotton cloths!"
Having heard this, Jīvaka felt deep regret; he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"This man, having been saved by me, has instead reviled and insulted me.
World-Honored One!
I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*). For the sake of increasing the Buddha-dharma, I pray that from this day forward, the World-Honored One will not permit the bhikṣus to ordain sick people as monks."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the youth Jīvaka in accordance with his needs, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Jīvaka prostrated at his feet and withdrew.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One went to where a great number of bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down; he then related the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one should not grant ordination to those who are ill.

As for the sick: those with ringworm, scabies, jaundice, leprosy, carbuncles, hemorrhoids, incontinence, jaundice, malaria, coughing, consumption, insanity, fever, wind-swelling, water-swelling, abdominal swelling, and even those who have not yet recovered from taking medicine—these should not be granted ordination.
If one has malaria that recurs every one, two, three, or four days, they may be granted ordination during the intervals when the fever does not manifest.
However, if the patient is suffering from such illness, they should not be granted ordination.
If one has already left the household life, they should not be expelled.
If one ordains them, grants them the going-forth, and confers the full precepts (upasampadā), it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense; this is called "sickness.
Regarding "heretics": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) as a renunciant. Having ordained him, he spoke of the faults of the non-Buddhists before him, saying:
"The non-Buddhists are faithless, hold wrong views, violate the precepts, and lack shame and remorse."
Thus he reviled the faults of the non-Buddhists.
Having heard this, they said:
"Venerable One!..."

Do not speak such words; there too there are those who are virtuous and good, and there too are those who maintain the precepts—in fact, there are all of them: srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, and arhats.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha questioned him in detail about the aforementioned matter.
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"Why did you grant ordination to a non-Buddhist without first testing him?
From this day forward, one must not grant ordination to a non-Buddhist without having tested them."

If a follower of another sect comes seeking to leave the household life, he should be made to dwell with the community for a trial period of four months; the bhikṣu to whom he has entrusted himself should inform the Saṃgha.
