Once he has informed the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should first perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for him to seek permission, and only then grant him leave to request ordination.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This outsider named [Name] wishes to go forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata."
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant that this outsider named So-and-so requests a four-month trial period within the Saṃgha.
"Listen, venerable sirs!
This outsider named So-and-so desires to request a four-month trial period within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
This person should request [permission] from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the outsider named so-and-so, wish to go forth and receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata."
"I, [Name], beg the Saṃgha for the trial period of four months' residence. May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the dharma of four months' residence.
Thus he begs three times.
The *karmakāra* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This outsider, so-and-so, desires to go forth and receive full ordination within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; he has already requested from the Saṃgha a four-month period of probation."
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now grant a four-month probationary residence to the outsider [named] So-and-so.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain outsider, desiring to go forth and receive full ordination within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, has already requested from the Saṃgha a four-month period of probation.
The Saṃgha now grants this four-month probationary residence to the outsider [Name].
Venerable sirs, the Sangha grants this probationary period of four months for the outsider [named] So-and-so. Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Sangha has completed granting this probationary period of four months to the outsider So-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, if he is able to perform the communal duties as a *śrāmaṇera*, he shall receive food in the order following the *śrāmaṇeras*.
If he is not able, one should tell him:
"Seek food for yourself."
"Every day, one should disparage the non-Buddhists before them, saying:
'They lack faith, hold wrong views, violate the precepts, and are without shame or remorse.
Having thus disparaged them in various ways, if they should say:"
"Elder! Do not speak such words.

There are also those who are virtuous and good there, and there are also those who maintain the precepts; indeed, all of them possess the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship."
One should say to him:
"Go back and seek arhatship there. If he says:
"It is truly as the Elder has said: we are followers of external paths with false views, lacking even a sense of shame or dread of blame, and performing the deeds that lead to hell.
Elder, we pray that you will deliver us."

If, after a trial period of four full months, his mind remains unshaken and does not waver, he should be granted ordination; if he attains the noble Dharma (āryadharma) during that interval, it is considered that the trial is complete.
If he discards the insignia of an outsider and comes wearing the robes of a layperson, he should be granted ordination.

If one who comes wearing the insignia of an outsider is granted ordination and the full precepts without a four-month probationary period, it constitutes a *vinaya*-transgression; such a person is termed an "outsider."

Regarding the boy: while the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery under the Nyagrodha tree in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, as described in detail above, at that time the Śākya youths were ordained and went forth into homelessness by the bhikṣus, even though their parents had not given them permission.
Later, when their parents instructed them, the sons spoke with resentment, saying:

"Even though the World-Honored One was on the verge of becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he still renounced his home and left the world; what have we to hold onto that we should not likewise leave the world?"
At that time, the Śākyas went to King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"Great King!
Although our son has not granted permission, these bhikṣus have nonetheless ordained him and caused him to leave the household life."
Other householders could not be instructed; even when they were taught, they harbored resentment and left the home life, saying:

"If even the World-Honored One renounced his position as a Wheel-Turning Sage King just before attaining it to go forth into homelessness, what do I have to be attached to that I should not go forth?"
"I only pray that Your Majesty will petition the World-Honored One on my behalf, requesting that my parents not release me so that I may not go forth into homelessness.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with many members of the Śākya clan, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The young Śākya novices among the bhikṣus had been permitted by their parents to go forth into homelessness;
however, those who remained at home, even when given instruction, harbored resentment and said upon going forth:
"Even though the World-Honored One was on the verge of attaining the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he nonetheless abandoned it to go forth."
"What is it that I have to be attached to that I would not go forth [into homelessness]?
World-Honored One!
My parents cherished their son with a love that pierced to the very marrow of my bones; I, too, have once been thus."
"During the seven years since the World-Honored One went forth, there has been no day that I have not wept while sitting, rising, eating, or drinking.
I only pray, World-Honored One!
That you will establish a rule for the bhikṣus: do not allow anyone to go forth who has not received permission from their parents."

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for King Śuddhodana in accordance with his needs, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy. The king prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.

Not long after the king had departed, the World-Honored One went to where many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down. He related the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, one who has not been permitted by his parents shall not be granted the going forth."
There are three kinds of children:
biological children, adopted children, and children who come of their own accord.
A biological child is one born of one’s own parents.
Regarding those who raise children: "adopted children" refers to those taken in through small-scale begging for adoption;
"children who come of their own accord" refers to those who come to depend on one as a child.
Among these, the children considered one's own kin are not permitted by this country, nor are they permitted by other countries.
Regarding the raising of children: if they are one's own biological children, this country does not permit [their ordination], whereas other countries do.
If the parents do not grant permission, one should not allow them to go forth;
however, if they have already gone forth, they should not be expelled.
If one grants [ordination] to such a person and confers the full precepts (upasampadā), it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called "a son.
Regarding "a slave": while the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery under the Nyagrodha tree in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he spoke extensively as above.
At that time, the Śākya clansmen did not release their slaves, yet the bhikṣus ordained them as renunciants.
Later, when the masters instructed these slaves on how to divide their labor and assign their tasks, they refused to comply. Full of resentment, they said:
"If even the Venerable Chanda has gone forth into homelessness, what do we have left to care for?"
"Having abandoned [the world] to go forth as a renunciant, he is now instead receiving prostrations, respect, and offerings.
Then the Śākyas went to King Śuddhodana and said to him:
"Great King!"
"We did not release our household slaves, yet the bhikṣus ordained them as renunciants. Now that the others cannot be employed in labor, they are full of resentment and say:
'If even the Venerable Chanda has gone forth as a renunciant, what do we have left to hold onto?'"
"Having abandoned our lives to leave home as renunciants, we are instead receiving prostrations, respect, and offerings.
"Great King!
We Śākyas have many servants; it is upon them that we rely for our labor."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will request a boon from the Buddha, so that this slave’s master will not release him to allow him to leave the home life.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with the Śākyas, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"From this day forward, I decree that no bhikṣus shall allow a slave to go forth into homelessness unless he has been released by his master.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to King Śuddhodana in accordance with his needs; once the king had given rise to a heart of joy, he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and withdrew.
Not long after the king had departed, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat, sat down, and related the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, one who is a slave and has not been released by his master should not be granted ordination. There are five kinds of slaves: [slaves by birth, slaves purchased with money, slaves won in war, slaves given as gifts, and slaves who have entered into servitude through their own labor].
Born in the household, purchased, captured, given by another, or come of her own accord.
"Born in the household" refers to those born to female slaves or concubines within the family.
"Purchased" refers to those acquired for the price paid.
"Seized" means captured from a neighboring state.
"Given by another" means bestowed by someone else.
"Coming of one's own accord" means coming voluntarily to become a slave.
Among these, the three types—born into the family, purchased with money, and obtained by seizure—are not permitted here, nor are they permitted elsewhere.
The two types—given by another and come of one's own accord—are not permitted here, but are permitted elsewhere.
If the master does not release the slave, one should not grant him ordination;
if he has already been ordained, he should not be expelled.
If one grants him ordination and bestows full admission (*upasampadā*), it is a *vinaya*-offense of transgression.
This is called a slave.

Regarding those whose physical features are not upright: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, at that time various bhikṣus ordained people who were deficient in their physical features in many ways, and they were reviled by the people of the world: [text continues].
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain those whose physical forms are not upright?
Those who have left the household life ought to have dignified and majestic bodies.
This person is ruined and decayed; what path can he possibly possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha questioned him in detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those whose physical features are not upright should not be granted ordination.
Those with physical features that are not upright include: the blind, the hunchbacked, the lame, those with clubbed feet, those with decayed teeth, and those with gourd-shaped heads.
If one has various such physical deformities and is not upright in appearance, they should not be granted ordination;
if they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
If one grants them ordination and confers the full precepts (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called having limbs that are not well-proportioned.
Regarding those of "ugly form": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, where he was venerated by gods and worldly people.

At that time, the bhikṣus ordained persons of deformed appearance—those who were too black, too white, too yellow, too red, too tall, too short, too coarse, or too thin—and were thus ridiculed by the people of the world:
"How can the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, ordain persons of such deformed appearance?"
"One who has left the household life should have a dignified and handsome appearance; this man is ugly and people do not like to look upon him.
This ruined person—what path or Dharma does he possess?
Furthermore, another person said:
"This śramaṇa has only two kinds of people whom he does not deliver:
first, the dead; second, those who have no desire for the homeless life.
If he does not deliver these, the assembly will not increase."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, those of unsightly appearance should not be granted ordination."
"Ugly form" refers to being too black, too white, too yellow, too red, too tall, too short, too coarse, or too thin.
Furthermore, people with such ugly forms are unpleasant even when they are not angry; how much more so when they are in a state of rage!
One with such a deformed appearance should not be ordained; if they have already been ordained, they should not be expelled.
If one ordains them and grants them full admission (*upasampadā*), it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called a deformed appearance;
this is said not to constitute the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
In this matter, one who is pure and in accordance with the Dharma is said to have received full ordination.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* and the matter of the *karmavācanā*: as for the *karmavācanā*, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a dispute arose among the monks of Campā, and they lived in discord; one monk censured another monk, two monks censured two monks, and many monks censured many monks.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit one person to censure another, nor even many people to censure many people."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, you should perform formal acts (karmavācanā).

As for formal acts: there are the fourfold act, the twofold act, the one-motion act, the three-motion act; there are formal acts performed by a group of four, five, ten, or twenty members; and there are cases where, having performed an illegal and discordant formal act characterized by five defects, one later regrets it, or having performed a legal and concordant formal act characterized by five qualities, one does not regret it.”

Regarding the four types of *karmas*: there is the illegal and harmonious *karman*, the legal and disharmonious *karman*, the legal and harmonious *karman*, and the illegal and disharmonious *karman*. These are called the four *karmas*.
Regarding the two types of *karmas*: the *poṣadha-karma* and the *gaurava-karma*; these are called the two *karmas*.
Regarding the *jñapti-ekakarma*, there are twenty-eight.
What are the twenty-eight? They are:
one who goes out on formal legal procedure (*karmavācanā*) without being separated from his robe; one who stays apart from his robe; one who points out the location for a dwelling;

one who points out the location for building a large dwelling; one who points out the location for building a preceding dwelling; the distributor of alms bowls; the distributor of voting sticks (*śalākā*); and the examiner of outsiders.
The Path; the keeper of the staff and the net-bag; the one in charge of beds and bedding; the one in charge of overseeing food;
the one in charge of determining the order of meals; the one in charge of assigning rooms; the one in charge of taking robes; the one in charge of managing robes;
the one in charge of distributing robes; the one in charge of taking cotton cloth; the one in charge of lifting cotton cloth; the one in charge of distributing cotton cloth; the one in charge of...
The distributor of flowers, the one in charge of distributing incense, the one in charge of distributing fruits, the one in charge of distributing warm water,
the one in charge of distributing various cakes, the one in charge of serving as requested, the one in charge of distributing rice gruel,
and the one in charge of distributing minor miscellaneous items— these are called the twenty-eight.
There are eight types of *jñapti-tri-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

What are the eight? First, subduing; second, silence; third, banishment; fourth, inspiring joy; fifth, formal accusation; sixth, separate residence (*parivāsa*); seventh, *mānatva*; eighth, *ābṛhaṇa*. These are called the *jñapti-tri-karman*.

Regarding the *karmas* of the fourfold assembly: the *poṣadha-karman* and all acts involving prostrations may be performed by a group of four persons; this is called the *karman* of the fourfold assembly. Regarding the *karmas* of the fivefold assembly:

the acceptance of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), the crossing of the boundary (*sīmā*), and the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*), as well as all matters concerning *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, may be performed by a group of five persons; this is called the *karman* of the fivefold assembly.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* of a group of ten: when a bhikṣu receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) or a bhikṣuṇī receives full ordination, it may be performed by a group of ten; this is called the *karmavācanā* of a group of ten.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* of a group of twenty: the *āpattipraticchādana* (rehabilitation) of a bhikṣu and the *āpattipraticchādana* of a bhikṣuṇī may be performed by a group of twenty; this is called the *karmavācanā* of a group of twenty.

Regarding the regret that arises after performing a *karmavācanā* through five kinds of illegitimate procedures: it is when people are not present, they are not questioned, and their faults are not cited; such is the illegitimate and discordant procedure. This is called the regret that arises after performing a *karmavācanā* through five kinds of illegitimate procedures.

Regarding the accomplishment of the five ways of performing a *karmavācanā* such that there is no regret thereafter: when people are present and question [the offender], and after being questioned, he himself admits his fault; if this is done in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony, this is called the accomplishment of the five ways of performing a *karmavācanā* such that there is no regret thereafter.
In this matter, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) should be performed by a community of twenty members; if performed by ten members, it is not accomplished.
A formal act should be performed by a community of ten members; if performed by five members, it is not accomplished.
A *karmavācanā* should be performed by a group of five; it is not accomplished if performed by a group of four.
A formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*) should be performed; it is not accomplished if only one proclamation is made.
A formal motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-eka-karman*) should be performed; it is not accomplished if only the single motion is made.
Where a *jñapti-karman* (a motion alone) should be performed, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) is performed; thus it is not accomplished.
Where a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* should be performed, a *jñapti-karman* is performed; thus it is accomplished.
Where a *jñapti-karman* should be performed, a *jñapti-ekavācika-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) is performed; thus it is accomplished.
One should perform a *jñapti-ekakarma* (a motion with one proclamation), which is accomplished by a *jñapti-trikarma* (a motion with three proclamations).
One should perform a *karma* for a group of four, which is accomplished by a group of five.
One should perform a *karma* for a group of five, which is accomplished by a group of ten.
It should be performed by a group of ten for a *karmavācanā*, and by a group of twenty for its accomplishment;

this is called *karma*. As for the matters of *karma*: the matter of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for a bhikṣu; the matter of the full ordination for a bhikṣuṇī; the matter of the completion of the required limbs; the matter of the purity regarding obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*); the matter of the purity regarding non-fulfillment; the matter of the non-arising of the precepts; the matter of the root of the offense; the matter of not relinquishing the root; the matter of relinquishing the root; and the matter of the root of harmony.

Regarding the formal procedure for a bhikṣu’s full ordination (*upasampadā-karman*): when a person seeking full ordination requests a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the preceptor provides him with a request for robes and a bowl, provides him with a request for the assembly, provides him with a request for a preceptor of the precepts (*śīlācārya*), and provides him with a request for a teacher in a secluded place (*ācārya*). These various matters give rise to the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the formal act (*karman*); both of these together are called the formal procedure for a bhikṣu’s full ordination.

Regarding the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for a bhikṣuṇī’s full ordination: once the bhikṣuṇī has already completed receiving the full ordination, she should be questioned by the Bhikṣu Saṃgha as follows:
"Are you pure and free from obstructing conditions?"
He replied, "It is pure.
These various matters can give rise to formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and motions (*jñapti-karman*); both of these are termed the formal acts for the full ordination (*upasampadā-karman*) of a bhikṣuṇī.

Regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for fulfilling the requirements: once a person has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they request an *upādhyāya*. The *upādhyāya* then provides them with a robe and bowl, provides them with a community (*saṃgha*), provides them with a preceptor (*śikṣācārya*), and provides them with a teacher for the secluded place (*pravrajyā-ācārya*). The teacher refers the candidate to the *saṃgha*, who then requests the full ordination from within the *saṃgha*. After inquiring whether there are any obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*), the four reliances (*niśraya*) are proclaimed.

These various matters can give rise to formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and formal acts consisting of a motion (*jñapti-karman*); these two together are called "the matter of the completion of the constituent parts of a formal act" (*aṅga-paripūrṇa-karma-vastu*).

Regarding the matter of purity within the prohibition of legal procedures (*pratikṣepa-dharma-viśuddhi-karma-vastu*): being pure within the prohibitions, these various matters can give rise to formal acts and formal acts consisting of a motion; these two together are called "purity within the prohibition."

Regarding the "incomplete and impure matters of *karmavācanā*": when the constituent factors (*aṅga*) are incomplete and impure, these various matters can give rise to both formal acts (*karman*) and motions (*jñapti-karman*); thus, both are termed "incomplete and impure matters of *karmavācanā*."

Regarding matters that do not give rise to the formal act of ordination (*karmavācanā*): defiling a bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct, stealing [the status of] residence, being a person who has crossed over [to another sect], committing one of the five ānantarya crimes, committing a pārājika offense, and a śrāmaṇera holding evil and false views—these various matters do not give rise to either the formal act (*karman*) or the motion (*jñapti*). Both of these are termed "matters that do not give rise to the formal act of ordination."
Regarding the matters of formal acts based on the roots of offenses:

there are five classes of offenses—*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *vinayātikrama*. These various matters can give rise to formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and motions (*jñapti-karman*); both of these are termed "matters of formal acts based on the roots of offenses."

Regarding the matter of the *karmavastu* of non-renunciation: when a bhikṣu has been admonished three times in private, three times in the midst of many people, and three times before the Saṃgha, yet does not renounce these matters, it gives rise to both formal acts (*karma*) and formal announcements (*jñapti-karma*). These two are both called the *karmavastu* of non-renunciation.

Regarding the formal act (*karmavastu*) based on relinquishment: there are three admonitions in private, three admonitions in the presence of many people, and three admonitions before the Saṃgha. When one relinquishes these matters, it can give rise to a formal act or a motion (*jñapti-karman*); both of these are termed "formal acts based on relinquishment."

Regarding the matters of the root of harmony in formal acts (*karmavastu*): when the community of bhikṣus assembles to distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*), those who do not attend provide their consent (*chanda*), and the harmony of the Saṃgha is proclaimed; these various matters can give rise to formal acts (*karman*) and motions (*jñapti-karman*). Both of these are termed the matters of the root of harmony in formal acts.
This is called a matter of *karmavācanā*.
Regarding the matter of the *tarjanīyakarman* (act of censure): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The monks of Campā were disputing and speaking to one another, dwelling in discord.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"You should perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him."
There are five matters concerning the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), which comprise all instances of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, what were these five that he prescribed?
First, engaging in the eight types of improper conduct.
2. Repeatedly committing offenses;
3. Entering too early and leaving too late at night, associating with evil friends and wicked companions, and frequenting unsuitable places;
4. Engaging in disputes and mutual accusations.
5. Honoring the Young:

Regarding the practice of the eight matters of intimacy. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra practiced intimacy through body, practiced intimacy through speech, and practiced intimacy through both body and speech.

Regarding "dwelling in physical intimacy": sitting on the same bed, sleeping on the same bed, eating from the same vessel, dressing in each other's clothes, and going out and coming in together—this is called dwelling in physical intimacy.

Regarding "habitual intimacy through speech": when one speaks with a defiled mind to another in mutual exchange, this is called habitual intimacy through speech. Regarding "habitual intimacy through body and speech":

sitting together on the same bed, sleeping together on the same bed, eating from the same vessel, mutually wearing each other's clothes, going out and coming in together, and speaking with one another while engaging in mutually defiled speech—this is called habitual intimacy through body and speech.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Venerable Bhikṣu Maitrībala!
Do not dwell in intimacy through body, do not dwell in intimacy through speech, and do not dwell in intimacy through both body and speech."
He did not desist despite being admonished once, nor even after being admonished up to three times.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:

"If this Bhikṣu Cīrṇabhūmi dwells in intimacy of body, intimacy of speech, and intimacy of both body and speech, and does not desist after being admonished three times, the Saṃgha should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him for dwelling in intimacy of body."
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Maitrībala dwells in close association with [the laity], and though he has been admonished three times, he does not desist."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against the bhikṣu Cidi for living in close association with him.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣu Maitrībala has lived in close physical association; though admonished three times, he did not desist.
The Saṃgha now performs a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against the bhikṣu Maitrībala for living in close physical association.
Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha grants the bhikṣu Maitrībhūmi the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* for living in close association with [others]. Those who consent to this remain silent; those who do not may speak.
"This is the first formal act (karmavācanā).
The second and third [acts] are also spoken in this manner.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* for the bhikṣu Maitrībala due to his physical intimacy; the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent. This matter is thus upheld."
The same is said regarding verbal intimacy and both bodily and verbal intimacy.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Udāyin lived in bodily intimacy, verbal intimacy, and both bodily and verbal intimacy with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā.
Physical intimacy (*kāyasaṃsarga*) refers to sitting together within arm’s reach or mutually wearing each other's clothing; this is called physical intimacy.
Verbal intimacy (*vāksaṃsarga*) refers to speech uttered with a mind of mutual defilement; this is called verbal intimacy.

Regarding "dwelling in close physical and verbal association": sitting together within arm's reach, mutually wearing each other’s clothes, conversing with one another, and speaking with defiled minds—this is called dwelling in close physical and verbal association.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Venerable Udāyin!
Do not dwell in physical intimacy with the bhikṣuṇī Bhaddā, nor in verbal intimacy, nor in both physical and verbal intimacy."
After being admonished once, twice, and three times, he did not desist.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If this Udāyin dwells in physical intimacy with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrajanman, dwells in verbal intimacy with her, and dwells in both physical and verbal intimacy with her, and does not desist despite three admonitions, the Saṃgha should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him for physical intimacy."
The *karmavācaka* (the person performing the formal act) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Udāyin has lived in close physical proximity with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrajanmanī; though he was admonished three times, he did not desist."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the *tarjanīya-karman* of censure for Udāyin regarding his physical intimacy.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
After the threefold proclamation (*jñapti-tri-karman*), [it continues]: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"Orally associating and dwelling together, and physically and orally associating and dwelling together, are also as explained above.
Furthermore, at that time, the bhikṣu Bhadrika associated with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrāśrī physically, orally, and both physically and orally, just as was explained in detail above regarding Udāyin."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣu Subhadra and the bhikṣuṇī Subhadrā lived in close physical proximity, close verbal proximity, and close physical and verbal proximity, as described in detail in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrajanmanī.

Furthermore, at that time, there was a bhikṣu who went into a householder’s home and dwelt in close physical proximity with the wife, in close verbal proximity, and in close physical and verbal proximity.

Regarding "dwelling in physical intimacy": sitting within arm's reach of a woman, exchanging incense, flowers, fruits, or melons with her, and acting as her messenger—this is called dwelling in physical intimacy.
Vocal habitual association refers to speech that occurs together with a defiled mind; this is called vocal habitual association.
Corporeal and vocal habitual association refers to when both of the aforementioned two matters occur together; this is called corporeal and vocal habitual association.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Do not dwell in physical intimacy with a woman, do not dwell in verbal intimacy, and do not dwell in both physical and verbal intimacy."
When he did not desist despite being admonished three times in this manner,
the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances,
as was explained in detail above in the case of Udāyin.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣu who lived in intimate association with a paṇḍaka through physical intimacy, verbal intimacy, and both physical and verbal intimacy.
Regarding physical intimacy: sitting within arm’s reach, going out and coming in together—this is called physical intimacy.
Regarding verbal intimacy: speaking with a defiled mind together—this is called verbal intimacy.

Regarding "dwelling in close association through body and speech": when both of the aforementioned two matters are present together, this is called dwelling in close association through body and speech.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"Do not associate with, dwell in proximity to, or engage in oral intimacy with one who is impotent, nor engage in both bodily and oral intimacy.
Even after being admonished three times, he did not desist.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, as was explained in detail above in the case of Udāyin.

Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Udāyin lived in close physical association, close verbal association, and close physical and verbal association with his co-practitioner disciple, as was explained in detail above in the section concerning the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra.

Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Chanda lived in close physical association with a youth, lived in close verbal association with him, and lived in close physical and verbal association with him, as was explained in detail above in the section concerning the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra.
These are called the eight matters of habitual association.
Regarding the one who repeatedly commits offenses: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣu Śrīyāva repeatedly committed each of the offenses within the five categories.
The bhikṣus admonished them, saying: "Elders!
Do not repeatedly commit each of these offenses among the five groups."
He did not desist after the first admonition, nor after the second, nor even after the third.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If this Śrīyapā has repeatedly committed each of these offenses among the five groups of transgressions, a *saṃvāsanīya-karman* (act of subduing for repeated offenses) shall be performed.
The person performing the *karman* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Śrīyava repeatedly commits offenses and does not desist despite being admonished three times.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Śrīyava for his repeated offenses.
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Śrīyava repeatedly commits offenses and does not desist despite being admonished three times."
The Saṃgha now performs the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the repeated offenses of the bhikṣu Śrīyabha.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *tarjanīya-karman* for the repeated offenses of the bhikṣu Śrīyabha, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this manner.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *tarjanīyakarman* of repeated offenses against the bhikṣu Śrīyava. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
This is called repeatedly committing offenses.

Entering too early, departing too late, having evil friends, having evil companions, and practicing in improper places: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣu Kālu entered the village too early, departed from the village too late, had evil friends, had evil companions, and practiced in improper places.
To enter too early means to enter a village for alms too early.
To emerge too late means to emerge from a village too late.
Bad friends refers to being intimately close with elephant trainers, horse trainers, thieves, bandits, gamblers, and those of such ilk.
"Evil companions" refers to evil friends.

"Practicing in improper places together" means practicing in such improper places as the homes of widows, the homes of unmarried girls, the homes of prostitutes, the homes of eunuchs, or with disreputable bhikṣuṇīs and disreputable śrāmaṇerīs. This is what is meant by practicing in improper places.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying: "Elder!
Do not enter too early or emerge too late, nor even go to the place where the shramanerika of ill repute stays."
He did not desist after the first admonition; he did not desist after the second admonition, nor after the third admonition.
The bhikṣus, on account of these circumstances, went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If this bhikṣu Kālu enters too early and leaves too late, and even acts in improper places, and does not desist despite being admonished three times, the Saṃgha should perform a *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of subjugation) for entering too early."
The *karmakāra* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Kālu entered the village too early and did not desist despite being admonished three times."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Kālu for entering a village too early.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
[The formal act is performed] through three proclamations (*tri-jñapti*), up until: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"In this way, emerging into great darkness, having evil friends and evil companions, and acting in an improper place, is also like this.

Regarding those who engage in disputes and mutual accusations: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit was arrogant and self-opinionated, engaging in disputes and mutual accusations."
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Venerable Bhikṣu Aśvajit!
Do not engage in dispute or mutual recrimination."
"Thus, he did not desist after one admonition, nor after two admonitions, nor after three admonitions.
The bhikṣus, for this reason, went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:"
"When five factors are present, one should know that disputes will arise again. What are these five factors?

Declaring an *karmavācanā* to be contrary to the Dharma when it is according to the Dharma; declaring an assembly to be contrary to the Dharma when it is according to the Dharma; declaring a formal accusation to be contrary to the Dharma when it is according to the Dharma; declaring a renunciation to be contrary to the Dharma when it is according to the Dharma; and declaring a bestowal to be contrary to the Dharma when it is according to the Dharma—these are called the five types of what is contrary to the Dharma."
The opposite of the aforementioned five matters is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Monks!
You should instruct the elder monks in this way: they must certainly accomplish these five qualities before entering the assembly.
What are the five?
One should enter the assembly with a low voice; having heard the *karmavācanā*, one should believe it; having believed it, one should practice accordingly.
If the *karmavācanā* is not in accordance with the Dharma and one cannot object to it, one should grant one's consent (*chanda*).
If one is unable to give consent (*chanda*), one should indicate to the person sitting beside them that one does not consent.
When the bhikṣu hears this instruction, he says:
"I am skilled in eloquent speech; why do I enter the assembly with such a low voice?
I am also widely learned; why must I place faith in the *karmavācanā* once it has been heard?
I am well-versed in the Dharma; why must I practice it once I have heard it?"
I am also skilled in the *karmavācanā*; why, upon hearing that a *karmavācanā* was not performed according to the Dharma, was I unable to object?
I should have granted my consent (*chanda*), and I would have gone there myself.
Why did I grant my consent to the one sitting beside me when I did not wish to do so?
"I shall restrain him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If five conditions are fulfilled such that a dispute arises again, the Saṃgha should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him."
What are the five?
First, self-exaltation;
second, a coarse, base, and violent disposition.
Third is meaningless speech;
fourth is untimely speech;
fifth is not associating with virtuous people.
"This is called the accomplishment of the five dharmas.
The Saṃgha should perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him.
The person performing the *karman* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
The bhikṣu Ma-suk has engaged in self-aggrandizing disputes and verbal quarrels, and though admonished three times, he did not desist.
If the time is right for the Sangha, the Sangha now performs the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against the bhikṣu Ma-suk for his self-aggrandizement."
[The motion] is thus stated.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Ma-suk has been self-exalting and engaged in disputes and mutual accusations; though admonished three times, he has not desisted."
The Saṃgha now intends to perform a *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of subordination) against the bhikṣu Aśvaka for his arrogance.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* against the bhikṣu Aśvaka for his arrogance should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are likewise spoken.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* for the monk Aśvaka due to his self-exaltation; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The latter four matters are also explained in the same manner. Regarding "showing respect to those who are younger": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.

At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda ordained a youth and personally attended to him, rising at dawn to inquire after his well-being. He provided him with the vessels for urination and defecation and the spittoon, placing them in their proper positions. He massaged his body, handed over his robes and bowl, and entered the village together with him, letting the youth walk ahead. When they reached the house of a donor, he had the youth sit in the place of honor and receive the offerings first.
Having made the offerings, he assists in collecting the bowls, washing them, and returning them to their usual place.

After the meal, he assists in dyeing the robes and fumigating the bowls. He assists in spreading out the bedding and mats. When evening falls, he assists in lighting the lamps and placing the spittoon and the vessels for the large and small calls of nature inside.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Elder! Do not provide for the young; the young should provide for the elder."
He replied: "It is as the Elder says;
however, this youth was formerly a person who delighted in pleasure, and for that reason I love, respect, and feel shame on his behalf, following him and providing for his needs."
When he did not desist after being admonished thus once, twice, and thrice,
the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call Channa here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! You have no affection, reverence, shame, or deference toward the Tathāgata, yet you instead feel affection, reverence, shame, and deference toward one who is young.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Regarding this bhikṣu Chanda, who is beloved by the young, the Saṃgha should perform for him the *karmavācanā* of 'subduing the beloved youth' (*piyaputrasamvartanīya-karma*)."
The *karmavācanā* official should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda is affectionately attached to, respects, and serves a youth; despite being admonished three times, he does not desist."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Chanda, who is affectionately providing for young men.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The monk Chanda was fond of and provided for a young man; despite being admonished three times, he did not desist.
The Saṃgha now performs the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against the monk Chanda for his fondness toward and support of that young man.

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s performance of the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Chanda for his affectionate support of young bhikṣus, please remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this manner.

"The Saṃgha has finished performing the *tarjanīyakarman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Chanda for his affectionate provision of service to a youth; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The same applies to the acts of *satkāra* (reverence), *hrī* (shame), and *apatrāpya* (moral dread); these are called the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of subduing).

Regarding the *asaṃbhāṣanīya-karman* (act of not speaking together): while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣu Aśvaka, after having been subjected to the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*, did not act in accordance with it; he did not perform the duties he ought to have performed, nor did he relinquish the things he ought to have relinquished.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:

"Since the bhikṣu Aśvaka, after the saṃgha has performed the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him, does not comply with it—failing to perform what he ought to do and failing to relinquish what he ought to relinquish—the saṃgha should perform the *asaṃbhāṣanīya-karman* (act of non-conversation) against him."
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Aśvaghoṣa, having been subjected to the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*, does not act in accordance with it; he does not perform the actions that ought to be performed, nor does he relinquish the matters that ought to be relinquished."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of *asaṃbhāṣya-karman* (the act of not speaking with) against the bhikṣu Maśuka.
This is the motion.
After the threefold proclamation of the *karman*, [it concludes]: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was at that time an elder who had gone forth; he repeatedly violated minor precepts: eating in a separate group, eating here and there, eating while storing food, eating from a common vessel, sleeping in the same room as a woman, staying for more than three nights, sleeping on the same bed, sitting on the same bed, eating impure fruit, accepting raw meat, accepting raw grain, and accepting gold and silver.
The bhikṣus admonished him, saying,
"Venerable sir, you should not do this.
He replied:
“Venerable sir, please speak to me; I shall receive and practice it.
The bhikṣus said, “This mahallaka has the intention to train.”
Later, he repeatedly committed minor and trivial offenses, ranging from eating in a separate group to accepting gold and silver.
The bhikṣus again admonished him, saying:
"Mahāla, you should not do such things."
He replied, "Venerable sir,
you should tell me [the precepts], and I shall receive and practice them.
Yet afterwards, he repeatedly committed offenses again.
The bhikṣus said:
"This mahallaka who has gone forth does not recognize kindness or instruction; he does not follow the teachings; he is sycophantic, dishonest, and unwilling to practice or study."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:

“This mahallaka has left the household life; he does not recognize kindness and instruction, nor does he comply with admonitions. The Saṃgha should perform the *asaṃbhāṣanīya-karman* (the formal act of not speaking with him) against him.”
The officiant of the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This mahallaka has gone forth [into homelessness] but does not recognize kindness or instruction, nor does he follow admonitions."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of *asaṃbhāṣya-karman* (the act of not speaking with) against Mahāra.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
[The formal act is performed] by three proclamations (*karmavācanā*) until: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."**
This is called the *kamma* of not speaking together (*asaṃvāsa-kamma*). Regarding the *kamma* of banishment (*pabbājana-kamma*): The Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī.

At that time, the group of six bhikkhus were living in the town of Kāsī. They engaged in improper conduct of body, improper conduct of speech, and improper conduct of both body and speech; they engaged in bodily harm, verbal harm, and harm of both body and speech; they engaged in bodily wrong livelihood, verbal wrong livelihood, and wrong livelihood of both body and speech. As extensively explained above in the Saṃghādisesa regarding the Black Mountain village, this is called the *kamma* of banishment.
Regarding the *karma* of "arousing joy": these refer to the laywoman Nandā, Śaṇakavāsinī, the fried fish eggs, Kāru, Mahānāman, and the group of six bhikṣus.

Regarding the laywoman Nandā: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Nanda traveled through various countries and returned to Śrāvastī. Then Nanda, wearing his village-entry robes and carrying his alms bowl, went to the house of the laywoman.
Having seen this, the laywoman Priyā was filled with joy and greeted him, saying:
"Welcome, Ācārya! For what purpose have you come?"
He immediately invited him to sit; once he was seated, Nanda said, "I travel rarely;
what do you wish to give me? He replied:
"Whatever you require shall be provided—whether it be food before the meal, food after the meal, gruel, cakes, or fruit; we shall prepare whatever is needed.
Nanda said, "I require food before the meal; please prepare it well."
He replied, "As you have instructed, I shall do so well; I only pray that you will come early tomorrow.
Having spoken these words, he departed.
Later, when the upāsikā rose at dawn, she prepared a fine morning meal, arranged the seats, and waited in anticipation.
Nanda was preoccupied with many affairs and consequently forgot to go.
Because the upāsikā had waited until the time for the meal had passed and he did not come, she set aside those items in the food that could be kept and ate those that could not.
In this way, when she did not come on the second or third day, he took all the food.
On the fourth day she finally arrived and asked,
"Are you free from illness, laywoman?"
The upāsikā spoke with displeasure:
"Ācārya, you accepted my invitation for a meal beforehand; why have you not come?
He replied:
“Is the upāsikā angry? She replied,
“She is angry.”
“If that is so, I repent my transgression.
The upāsikā said,
“Repent before the World-Honored One for what has passed.”
Nanda immediately repented before the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Why do you repent?"
Nanda reported all the aforementioned matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
"This upāsikā has no lack of generosity toward the Buddha, the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, and the Saṃgha; for what reason have you disturbed her?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This upāsikā is a person of profound faith while living at home; Nanda has disturbed her and caused her to lose her joy. The Saṃgha should now perform the *karma* of 'arousing joy' against Nanda."
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Nanda has disturbed laypeople, giving rise to feelings of displeasure."
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of causing the layman Nanda to experience joy.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Nanda has disturbed laypeople and caused them to lose their joy.
The Saṃgha now intends to perform the *karmavācanā* for Nanda regarding the loss of joy among laypeople.
Venerable sirs, if you approve of the Saṃgha performing this *karmavācanā* for Nanda regarding the loss of joy among laypeople, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] were likewise spoken.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *pārivāsika-prasādanīya-karman* for Nanda as a layperson. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
This is called the laywoman Nandā.
Regarding Śāṇakavāsin: when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the householder Citta invited the Saṃgha and offered them medicine.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard this, they said to one another, "The householder has invited the Saṃgha for medicine; we should go there to test him.
At the appointed time, they put on their village-entry robes and took up their bowls, went to his house, and exchanged greetings with one another.
Having exchanged greetings, he said:
"I have heard that you, householder, have invited the Saṃgha to receive medicine.
Is this indeed true?"
He replied,
“Yes! Ācārya, do you require anything?”
He replied,
"I require one load of śāṇa cloth.
The householder said:
"I must prepare it first; then I shall give it to you.
The bhikṣu said, "How strange!
You wish to invite the Saṃgha without having prepared the medicine beforehand."
Do you not know?
A single bhikṣu takes medicine equal in amount to what one great nāga-elephant of the Snowy Mountains would eat.
You do not practice giving, yet you seek only fame.
The householder said, "Ācārya!
Even the royal treasury has no stored medicine; how much less so my own home?"
"I shall wait for you to decide whether to give it or not. The bhikṣu said,
"Whether you give it or not is entirely up to your own will."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Later, the householder sent a man to the elephant village of Koṭikarṇa in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to fetch Śāṇakavāsin, who then informed the Ācārya:
"I have obtained Śāṇakavāsin; you may come to receive him."
Having heard these words, they looked at one another and smiled.
The householder spoke with reproach:
"Why do you look at one another and smile?"
"When I had not yet prepared it, you earnestly and painfully sought it; now that it is ready, you smile and will not take it.
Of all that belongs to my household, I have nothing I cherish more than the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. For what reason, Venerable One, do you test me thus?"
The bhikṣu asked,
"Householder, are you angry?
He replied:
"I was angry.
The bhikṣu said,
"If you were angry, I repent my transgression."
The householder said,
"I have already confessed my transgression to the World-Honored One," as is explained in detail in the case of the laywoman Nandā.
Regarding the matter of frying fish roe in oil: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the householder Citta invited the Saṃgha for a meal of a hundred flavors.
When the monks had finished eating, they returned to the vihāra.
The householder commanded the women and children of his household, saying:
"Prepare whatever food remains and give it to our neighbors;
I wish to go and pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were engaged in worldly conversation at the gate of the Jetavana.
When the householder saw them, he thought to himself:
"These are not people of the Vinaya; if I do not go to them, they may harbor resentment."
He immediately went to pay his respects with a bow.
The bhikṣu said, “Welcome, donor; you are like a great nāga-elephant.”
The householder asked,
"Venerable One,
will you take a meal at my home today?"
He replied,
“I am going to eat.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir,
was the food to your liking?
He replied:
“Excellent! But it lacks one element.
He asked:
"What is lacking?
The bhikṣu replied,
"If one obtains oil, salt, and fried fish roe, these constitute a 'named meal' (nāmika-bhojana), and the donor will gain a good reputation."
The householder said, "Venerable sir!
I did not know this before; had I known it, I would have made even more for you, giving each person a bowl."
The householder spoke again:
"Venerable Sir!
Listen as I tell you a parable."

In a past life, there was a flock of chickens living in a mango grove. A wild cat preyed upon the roosters until only the hens remained. Later, a crow came and sheltered one of them, and they together gave birth to a chick.
When the son made a sound, the father spoke this verse:
"This child is not mine; A wild father and a village mother Have united to produce this son, Neither a crow nor a chicken."
If one wishes to learn the cry of the father, it is born from a rooster;
if one wishes to learn the call of the mother, its father is a crow.
To learn the crow’s call like a rooster’s, and to learn the rooster’s sound as a crow’s—[this is the nature of such a being].
"The black chicken learns both [methods], yet neither of these two succeeds.
"In this way, O Venerable One, he is neither a layperson nor one who has gone forth."
The bhikṣu asked,
"Householder, are you angry?
He replied:
“I was angry.
The bhikṣu said,
“For my anger, I repent my transgression.”
The householder said,
"I have already confessed my transgression to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and confessed their transgressions before him.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason do you repent?
The group of six bhikṣus then reported the aforementioned matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Fool!
All these things belong to the householder Citta; he has no begrudging attachment toward the Buddha, the Bhikṣus, or the Saṅgha. For what reason have you caused such a disturbance?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This householder, through his supernormal power of recollecting past lives, saw that in a former existence the group of six bhikṣus had once been chickens and crows; for this reason, he spoke thus."
The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should perform the *pārihārika-karman* (the formal act of making one rejoice like a layperson) against the group of six bhikṣus.
This is as explained in detail in the section concerning the laywoman Nandā.

Regarding Kāla: while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms. When the time arrived, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, eventually arriving at the door of a certain house.
At that time, the husband was sitting in the middle courtyard and said to his wife,
"You should give food to the renunciants.
The wife replied:
"From what lineage did you go forth?
The man replied,
"I am of the Śākya clan who has gone forth."
The wife said,
"I will not give it.
The husband said:
"Why do you not give it?
The woman replied,
"This man does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
The bhikṣu said:
"Sisters! I am not one who does not practice the holy life."
The woman said, "Venerable Kālu cannot even practice the holy life; how much less can you?
Having heard these words, the bhikṣu was despondent and unhappy; he consequently ceased begging for alms and returned to sit in meditation.

Having arisen from meditation in the late afternoon, his body was extremely hungry and exhausted. He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
"Monk, why do you have such a hungry appearance?"
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“The food has been lost,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked,
"Are you unable to go for alms?
She then reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If this bhikṣu Kālu causes dissatisfaction among laypeople, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act (karmavācanā) of 'causing laypeople to rejoice' against him."
As explained in detail in the *Nandā Upāsikā*, this is called Kālu. Regarding Mahānāma:

while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan invited the Saṃgha to receive medicinal offerings. When Nanda and Upānanda heard of this, they said to one another, "We shall go and test him."
When the time arrived, he put on his village-dwelling robe and went to that house, where they exchanged greetings, saying:
"I have heard that the donor has invited the Sangha to provide medicine.
Is this indeed true?"
He replied, “Yes!
Venerable sir, do you require medicine?”
He replied:
"I require this much jar of ghee, this much jar of oil, this much jar of honey, this much jar of rock sugar, and this much of root medicine, leaf medicine, flower medicine, and fruit medicine."
He replied, "Venerable sir!
There is not that much medicine on this very day; we must prepare it before we can give it to you."
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"This is strange!
The donor did not previously stockpile medicine when he invited the community of bhikṣus."
"Do you not know?
A single bhikṣu takes medicine equal in amount to the food of a great nāga-elephant from the Snowy Mountains.
You do not wish to give it, but seek only fame."
He said, "Venerable sir!
Even in the royal treasury there is not such a quantity of medicine, much less in my own home."
"I must prepare it; I shall give it to you.
Nanda said, "Whether you give it or not is up to your own will."
Having spoken these words, he departed.
Later, when the householder had prepared the medicine, he said:
"Venerable Sir!"
"You may come now to take it.
Having heard this, they looked at one another and laughed.
The donor spoke with reproach:
"Why do you test me by looking at each other and laughing?
When I had not yet prepared it, you came with earnest entreaties; now that it is ready, you will not take it. Nanda said:
“Is the donor angry?
He replied, “He is angry.”
“If you were angry, I repent my fault.
He replied,
“I have already repented my fault before the World-Honored One.”
Nanda immediately went to where the Buddha was to repent his transgression.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason do you repent?"
He then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
"Everything belonging to the household of Śreṣṭhin Māna is at the disposal of the Buddha, the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, and nothing is withheld; for what reason, then, do you cause such disturbance?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Saṃgha should perform the *pravāraṇā-karman* (ceremony of reconciliation) for Nanda as a layperson."
As explained in detail in the *Nandā Upāsikā*, this is called Mahānāma. Regarding the group of six bhikṣus:

while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus were in the city of Kāśi. They were improper in body, improper in speech, and improper in both body and speech; they were harmful in body, harmful in speech, and harmful in both body and speech; they were wrong livelihood in body, wrong livelihood in speech, and wrong livelihood in both body and speech, to the point of causing displeasure among laypeople.
The Buddha addressed the community of bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *pravāraṇā-kuśala-karman* (the formal act of making a layperson express joy) against the group of six bhikṣus.
This is as explained in detail in the section concerning the laywoman Nandā; these are known as the group of six bhikṣus.
This is called the formal act (karmavācanā) for inspiring joy.
It is not termed "received" when it is incomplete;
when the constituent parts are full but impure, there is the formal act and the matter, as well as subjugation and non-conversing.
The *nissāraṇīya* (expulsion) brings forth joy.
The first *varga* is concluded.
Regarding the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*): the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the bhikṣu Channa committed each of the five classes of offenses. The bhikṣus said to him, "Venerable one!
Do you see these offenses?"
He replied, "I do not see it!
Why do you ask me whether I see it or not?"
The monks went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the monks:

"If this monk Channa has committed any one of the five classes of offenses and yet claims not to see it, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of one who does not acknowledge the offense."
The *karmadāna* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣu Chanda has committed each of these offenses among the five classes of offenses, yet he himself says that he does not see them."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of *karma* of charging the bhikṣu Chanda with not seeing his offense.

This bhikṣu Channa has committed each of the offenses among the five groups of transgressions, yet he himself says that he does not see them.

The second and third [acts] were likewise recited.
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense against the bhikṣu Chanda. Since the Saṃgha remains silent, it consents; thus this matter is so upheld."
Having performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension), he said to the bhikṣus:

I see this offense; I shall comply with whatever action is required. Out of compassion for me, please grant me the revocation of the *ukkhepanīyakamma* for not acknowledging the offense."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This bhikṣu Chanda has committed one or another of the five classes of offenses, yet he says he does not see them. Because the Saṃgha wishes to benefit him, it shall perform the formal act of *utkṣepanīya-karman* (suspension)."

"Having performed the actions he ought to perform in accordance with the rules, he himself confesses his offense; the Saṃgha should now carry out the formal act of *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (the act of reconciliation) for one who refuses to acknowledge an offense.
The person performing the *karman* should speak as follows:

This bhikṣu Chanda has committed one or another of the five classes of offenses, yet he says he does not see them.
Out of a desire to benefit him, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of *karma* for "not seeing an offense" (*adarśana-āpatti-utksepa*).
He has acted in accordance with what ought to be done and now acknowledges his own offense.

"Venerable sirs of the Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu Chanda wishes to request from the Saṃgha the revocation of the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-āpatti-sthāpana-karman*). Since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
This person should request [the formal act] from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu Chanda, have committed one or another of the five classes of offenses, yet I claim not to see them."
Because the Saṃgha, wishing to benefit me, performed the formal act of *karma* for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-āpatti-utkṣepa*).

I now beg the Saṃgha to revoke the formal act of *karma* for not acknowledging an offense; may the virtuous Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the revocation of the formal act of *karma* for not acknowledging an offense.

The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed each of the offenses among the five classes of transgressions, yet he himself says that he does not see them.

Having already acted in accordance with what was required, he now recognizes his own offense.
He requests from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karma* of suspension for not recognizing an offense.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha now grant the revocation of the *karma* of suspension for not recognizing an offense to the bhikṣu Chanda.
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed one or another of the five classes of offenses, yet he himself declares that he does not see them."
Because the Saṃgha desires to benefit him, it has performed the formal act of *karma* for charging him with a transgression for not seeing his offense.
He has already acted in accordance with what was required;
now he himself perceives his offense.
He has already requested from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karma* for suspension on account of not admitting an offense.
The Saṃgha now grants him the revocation of the *karma* for suspension on account of not admitting an offense.

Venerable sirs, if you approve of the Saṃgha granting the revocation of the *karma* for suspension on account of not admitting an offense to the bhikṣu Chanda, those who approve should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this manner.
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for the monk Chanda for his refusal to acknowledge an offense; because the Saṃgha is patient and silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Saṃgha has already completed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* for the suspension of one who does not acknowledge their offense. The bhikṣus said to him:
"Venerable sir, this offense must be dealt with according to the Dharma."
He replied:
"Why do you instruct me to act according to the Dharma?
I am unable to do so."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If this bhikṣu Chanda commits any one of the five categories of offenses and is unable to act in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karma* for one who has committed an offense and is unable to make amends."
The *karmakāraka* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed each of these five classes of offenses, yet he is unwilling to perform the appropriate remedial actions in accordance with the Dharma."

"If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha now grant the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of the bhikṣu Channa, who has committed an offense yet refuses to undergo the legal procedure according to the Dharma.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This Bhikṣu Chanda has committed each of the five classes of offenses, yet he is unwilling to act in accordance with the Dharma.
The Saṃgha now performs the *jñapti-karman* of formal censure against the Bhikṣu Chanda for having committed each of these offenses and being unwilling to act in accordance with the Dharma.

Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha now intends to perform the formal act of *karma* for the accusation of the bhikṣu Chanda, who has committed an offense yet refuses to act according to the Dharma. Those who consent should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] were likewise spoken.

"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* against the bhikṣu Chanda for having committed an offense yet refusing to act according to the Dharma; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"One admonition has already passed and two admonitions remain; will you relinquish this view?
He replied:
"This is a noble view, a virtuous view. It is a view handed down from my parents and former teachers; I cannot relinquish it."
When he did not desist despite being admonished thus a second and a third time,
the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu, such as Mālūkyaputra, gives rise to extreme views and does not desist after being admonished three times—both in private and in the midst of a large assembly—the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing extreme views (aniḥsargika-utkṣepaṇīya-karman) against him."
As stated above, this is called the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension).
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Śrīyāvat repeatedly committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Grant me the *mānāttā*.
The bhikṣus asked, "Elder!..."
"Why do you seek *saṃmānatta*?
He replied,
"I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
The bhikṣus, having previously known that he repeatedly committed saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, said to him:
"Venerable Śrīyapāla!
It is difficult for the Saṃgha to assemble and perform the karmavācanā; you must confess every offense you have committed, so that the karmavācanā may be performed all at once."
Thus, for a second and third time, he replied:
"I have indeed committed this offense.
After the *karmavācanā* had been performed, he thought to himself:
"Why should I perform the *karmavācanā* again?
All [the monks] should speak together and perform the *karmavācanā* at once.
He then said to the bhikṣus:
“Venerable sir!
Grant me the *mānatta* discipline.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Why do you seek *mānatta* again?
He replied,
"I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
The bhikṣus asked:
"Venerable sir!
When did you commit the offense?"
He replied,
"I committed it at that time.
The bhikṣus said:

"I have already told the Elder previously that it is difficult to perform a formal act (*kamma*) when the Saṃgha is assembled in harmony; therefore, you must confess everything you have committed all at once, and then we shall perform the formal act simultaneously."
"Why did you not speak at that time? He replied,
"Because of my sense of shame, I did not speak fully."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Śrīyāvatī here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Foolish man!"
If one felt no shame or remorse at the time of committing the offense, why feel shame now when seeking purification?
This is an evil matter; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching. One cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya grants another person absolution from an offense, he knows whether that person’s statement constitutes an offense or is without offense; he knows whether it was concealed or not concealed; he knows whether it has been confessed or not confessed; he knows whether parivāsa (probation) should be granted or should not be granted;

he knows whether parivāsa has been granted according to the Dharma or not according to the Dharma; he knows whether parivāsa has been correctly observed or incorrectly observed; he knows whether an offense occurred during the interval or no offense occurred during the interval; he knows whether the night has been interrupted or not interrupted; and he knows whether the conduct has been compliant or non-compliant.”

One should know when *mānāpya* should be granted; one should know when *mānāpya* should not be granted; one should know when *mānāpya* is granted in accordance with the Dharma; one should know when *mānāpya* is granted contrary to the Dharma; one should know when *mānāpya* is completed; one should know when *mānāpya* is not completed; one should know when there is an offense during the interim; one should know when there is no offense during the interim; one should know when the night is interrupted; one should know when the night is not interrupted; one should know when there is compliance with the practice; and one should know when there is non-compliance with the practice.

One should know when to grant the *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation); one should also know when not to grant it; one should know when the *ābhāṣaṇa* is granted according to the Dharma and when it is not; one should know cases of collective concealment and non-concealment; one should know cases of immeasurable concealment; one should also know the *vissa-ājāta* (the "open" offense). Furthermore, there are cases where an offense is combined with a non-night [concealment], cases where a night is combined with a non-offense, cases where both an offense and a night are combined, and cases where neither an offense nor a night is combined. There are also the original offenses (*mūlāpatti*) and the intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*).
A bhikṣu who accomplishes four dharmas is called one who upholds the Vinaya.
What are these four?
Knowing what constitutes an offense, knowing what is not an offense, knowing what is grave, and knowing what is light—these are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, one who accomplishes four dharmas is called an upholder of the Vinaya:
knowing what is an offense, knowing what is not an offense, not treating a grave offense as light, and not treating a light offense as grave—these are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, one accomplishes four dharmas:

knowing what is an offense, knowing what is not an offense, not saying that an innocent person has committed an offense, and not saying that a guilty person is innocent; these are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, one accomplishes four dharmas:
