If two administrative bhikṣus are in mutual agreement, they may share one roof with separate enclosures, separate roofs with a common enclosure, a common roof with a common enclosure, or separate roofs with separate enclosures.
"If two people do not get along with one another, they should construct [the dwelling] separately, covering it and enclosing it separately.
If one builds a house for the Saṃgha by encroaching upon an existing room, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

If one builds a room for the Saṃgha that creates an obstruction within [an existing space], it is likewise an offense of *vinayātikrama*. Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, monks erected a stūpa for a śrāvaka on a public thoroughfare. When various laypeople came wishing to pay homage to the World-Honored One, they saw it and spoke with displeasure:
"We have come wishing to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, yet before seeing the World-Honored One, we first see a tomb for the dead."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"How is it that you have erected a stūpa for a śrāvaka on ground frequented by many people without first performing the formal ritual (karman)?"

From this day forward, it is not permitted to erect a stūpa for a śrāvaka on ground where many people frequent without first performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā); one must first perform the ritual for seeking permission.
The *karmavācanā* official should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the bhikṣu so-and-so has passed away or entered parinirvāṇa, and if the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha erect a śrāvaka stūpa here for the bhikṣu so-and-so who has passed away or entered parinirvāṇa."
"Venerable sirs of the Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu named [Name] is erecting a śrāvaka stūpa at this location. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If they are not in harmony, one should say: "Elder!"

The World-Honored One has declared that four types of persons should have stupas erected for them, complete with tiered wheels and hung with banners and canopies: the Tathāgata, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Cakravartin King.
The monk Anitya, if he were a *srotāpanna*, should have spoken to those who are *srotāpannas*; if he were a *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*, he should have spoken to those who are *arhats*.
If one says,
"I am a holder of the Vinaya," or if one says:
“Dharma Master.
Or if one says:
“I am in charge of administrative affairs.”
The monk of virtue and renown should say:
"Venerable sir!
This person maintains the precepts with excellence and has made many offerings to the Saṃgha; having labored in service, he should be granted permission to erect a stūpa."
When these words have been spoken, one should erect a stūpa for him.

It shall be a stūpa for a śrāvaka; one must not see the stūpa before seeing the World-Honored One, but rather ensure that the World-Honored One is seen first and the stūpa afterwards. It must not be located where many people pass, but in a secluded place, and it must not be on a path where bhikṣus walk.
If one erects a stūpa for a śrāvaka at a place frequented by many people, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī— as explained in detail above—
at that time the Venerable Kālu was residing in the great city of Kāśi-Kilā.

At that time, an elder bhikṣu came to receive his room in the order of seniority, but [the other] was unwilling to give it to him. In a fit of anger, he seized a mattock and struck the room himself until it was broken.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, saying:
"What offense has this bhikṣu committed?"
The Buddha said:
"One incurs a sthūlātyaya by destroying six kinds [of things].
What are the six?
"Breaking the bowl, breaking the robe, breaking the stupa, breaking the dwelling, breaking the Saṃgha, and breaking the boundary.
Regarding "breaking the bowl," there are three kinds of bowls: superior, middling, and inferior.
If one intentionally breaks each individual bowl out of anger, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one intends to mend a broken bowl but accidentally drills through it and breaks it, there is no offense.
If one breaks a *kuṇḍika*, *pātra*, or *kañcaka* out of anger, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding "torn robes": if any one of the three robes is torn through anger, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one intends to exchange the edges for the center, the center for the edges, or sews them into two layers, there is no offense.
If one becomes angry and tears or breaks a *niṣīdana* or any other kind of robe, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
As for destroying a stūpa: if one destroys a stūpa of the World-Honored One out of anger, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, and the retribution for the karmic action is great.
If one wishes to repair it by making it better, there is no offense.
If one destroys a *nigaṇṭha* stūpa or the stūpas of other non-Buddhist sects out of anger, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Regarding "destroying a dwelling": if one destroys a monastic dwelling out of anger, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one intends to rebuild it better than before, there is no offense.
If one destroys the dwelling of non-Buddhist ascetics out of anger, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Regarding "causing a schism in the Saṃgha": if one, out of malice, causes a harmonious Saṃgha to split, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; the karmic retribution for this action is one kalpa in the hells.
Regarding "breaking the boundary": if, out of malice, one transgresses the boundary and performs an act that is not [validly] performed, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Having already relinquished the boundary (*sīmā*), to perform the ritual of demarcation (*karmavācanā*) once again is called the sixth type of *sthūlātyaya* offense involving a breach.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was wandering through the country of Vajjī and gradually arrived at the village of Bārāṇasīvana.
In that village, there was a householder who built a dwelling for Rāhula.
Having accepted it, Rāhula departed on his travels; the householder then gave this room to another bhikṣu.
When Rāhula returned, the matter was as explained in detail in the Sūtra on the Thread (Sūtram).
Finally, Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To whom should this room rightfully belong?”
The Buddha said to Rāhula:

"If a householder or a householder’s son, with faith and joy, builds a dwelling to give as a gift to the Saṃgha, yet after giving it to the Saṃgha, he subsequently transfers it to many people, this is an unrighteous gift and an unrighteous enjoyment."
If one has given to many people and then turns it over to give to a single person, this is an unrighteous gift and an unrighteous enjoyment.

If one has given to a single person and then turns it over to give to many people, or if one has given to many people and then turns it over to give to the Saṃgha, this is an unrighteous gift and an unrighteous enjoyment.

Having given to the Sangha, one does not transfer it to many individuals; having given to many individuals, one does not transfer it to a single person. This is called giving according to the Dharma and receiving and using according to the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"That which was given previously is a true gift; that which was given later is not.
This king resides upon the earth, and because he gave his gift first while dwelling therein, his merit increases day and night."
"Rāhula! You should receive a dwelling; those who come later should not.
This is called the rule for the saṃghārāma.
Regarding the rules for building dwellings: The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, as explained in detail above.
For instance, when the Venerable Daṇḍakīvaśi built a hut—as described in the second *pārājika*—he even uttered words of resentment, saying:
"I have worked with great hardship to build this hut; having built it while braving both cold and heat, as soon as it was finished, the Elder has seized it from me, like a cat watching for a mouse."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu who manages the construction has worked very hard; a formal act (karmavācanā) should be performed to grant this bhikṣu five years' residence."
The person performing the ritual (karmakāra) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to construct a dwelling for the Saṃgha."

"If the time has come for the Sangha, may the Sangha permit that the business-manager bhikṣu [Name], who is building a dwelling for the Sangha, requests from the Sangha permission to reside there for five years.

"Venerable sirs, listen: this business-manager bhikṣu [Name] wishes to request from the Sangha permission to reside for five years. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
That bhikṣu should beg [permission] by baring his right shoulder, kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, and speaking these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am building a dwelling for the Saṃgha; I now beg the Saṃgha for permission to remain for five years to oversee the construction."
Out of compassion!
I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me permission to stay for five years while attending to its affairs.
Thus he requested three times.
The *karmakāra* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so is building a dwelling for the Saṃgha and has already requested from the Saṃgha permission to reside there for five years while managing its affairs."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant a five-year period of administrative residence to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so has constructed a dwelling for the Saṃgha and has already requested from the Saṃgha five years' leave to manage its affairs.
The Saṃgha now grants the bhikṣu so-and-so five years' leave to manage its affairs.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha granting this bhikṣu permission to manage affairs and reside for five years should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
A second and third time, it was said in the same manner:
"The Sangha has completed granting the five-year *karmadāna* residence to the bhikṣu so-and-so; since the Sangha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
"Once the Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā* and granted him a five-year residence, he regains his own constructed cell and should also receive a Saṃgha cell in due order.
If an elder (*sthavira*) arrives, he should be given [the cell] according to the order of succession; however, it should not be given to one who obtained it through a formal act of the Saṃgha."
If one wishes to travel, these two rooms should be assigned to the Sangha for them to occupy in order, with the thought:
"When I return, I shall take them back.
When returning later, they should be filled from the first day of their arrival.

If a monastery cell has previously fallen into ruin and has been rebuilt with a changed orientation over two or three years, it should be granted for residence through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), according to the amount of labor expended.
If an empty room is unfit for habitation, the administrator should allow [the resident] to stay there for a single period.
If the beds, desks, pillows, or mattresses are soiled with grease or are torn and require washing, dyeing, or mending, the administrator should allow [the resident] to stay there for a single period.
If a monk in the midst [of the community] objects, he commits a *vinaya*-offense; this is called the rule for managing affairs.
Regarding the rule for beds and bedding: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, while the bhikṣus were in the midst of the rainy season retreat, the senior monk (upādhyāya) arrived and, following the established order, took possession of a room. The bhikṣu moved his belongings out of the room.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked the bhikṣu:
"Is this a visiting bhikṣu?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is this the bhikṣu who has departed?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Which bhikṣu is this who is carrying the palanquin?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
I took the rooms according to the sequence of seniority; that is why I have moved.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Why do you all rise in succession according to seniority at all times?
From this day forward, I do not permit rising in succession according to seniority at all times."
The Saṃgha should honor one who has accomplished these five qualities and knows how to assign rooms, beds, and bedding.
What are the five qualities?
Not following favoritism, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what is obtainable and what is unobtainable—these are called the five.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so has accomplished the five dharmas."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the official in charge of assigning rooms, beds, and bedding.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"Venerable sirs, this bhikṣu [Name] has accomplished five qualities; the Saṃgha now appoints him as the official in charge of assigning rooms, beds, and bedding.
Those of you, venerable sirs, who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] as the official in charge of assigning rooms, beds, and bedding, remain silent."
"If you do not approve, speak now.

"The Sangha has approved the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] as the official in charge of assigning rooms, beds, and bedding; because the Sangha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, from the sixteenth day of the third month onward, one should inform the *dānapati* to wash and repair the bedding and mats, the rooms, the meditation hall, the lecture hall, the warm bathhouse, the latrines, the gatehouse, the well-house, and all that belongs to the *saṃghārāma*, as well as the food and drink for the days of the fast; furthermore, the robes for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) should be listed item by item.
If a monastery in a city or village is far from the monastic residence, rooms should be assigned by the thirteenth day of the fourth month.
If one cannot find accommodation there, one may go elsewhere.
If the monasteries are situated near one another, rooms should be assigned every fifteen days, and this notice should be recited among the community of monks:
"In such-and-such monastery, there are so many rooms, so many beds and mats, so much food and drink for the fast days, and so much clothing."
The Elder should say:
"I assign a dwelling for a joint *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) offering.
Having spoken these words, he should assign a dwelling, but he must not give a room to a *śrāmaṇera*.
If the upādhyāya or ācārya says,
"Simply provide the dwelling; I shall take care of it myself," one may give it.
If there are many rooms, one person shall be given two rooms.
If they are unwilling to take two, saying,
"One room is sufficient for me," [then they shall take only one].
At that time, one should say:
"This is not given for the sake of personal enjoyment, but is given for the purpose of maintenance.
If there are many bhikṣus and few dwelling places, two or three should share a single room together.
If it is still insufficient, five or ten monks should share a single room together.
If there is only one large hall, all the bhikṣus should enter and reside within it.
The senior monk (sthavira) should be given a bed for lying down, while the others are given beds for sitting.
If there are still not enough, the senior monk shall give a bed for sitting, and the others shall spread out mats of grass.
If there is still not enough space, the senior monk shall spread out a mat of grass while the others sit cross-legged.
If there is still not enough space, the senior monk shall sit cross-legged while the others remain standing.
If there are still not enough [seats], the senior monk (sthavira) shall remain standing, while the others go outside under a tree or into an open space.

During the winter season, rooms and quarters may be assigned for the purpose of maintenance or for the purpose of use; when the senior monk arrives, they shall occupy them according to their respective order of seniority.

During the spring season, when assigning rooms, they are given for the purpose of maintenance and for the purpose of use; if a senior monk (*sthavira*) arrives, he shall stay according to the order of seniority.

During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), when assigning rooms, they are given for the purpose of maintenance and for the purpose of use; if a senior monk arrives, he should not stay according to the order of seniority.
If a bhikṣu does not know the Dharma and, during the rainy season retreat, requests a room in sequence but does not obtain one, he should not immediately show resentment;
rather, he should say: "Wait!
I must first consult the person in charge of the lodgings."
One should say to the person in charge of the rooms:
"Venerable sir!
An elder visiting bhikṣu has come and told me to get up."
The person in charge of the dwelling should reprimand him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
You do not properly understand the characteristics of the precepts."
"How can you cause another to leave during the retreat?
Do you not know that one may never,
at any time, drive another away?"
If it is winter or spring and a senior monk (*sthavira*) arrives, one should rise in due order; if one does not rise, there is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression (*viniyatikāpatti*).
If a bhikṣu does not properly understand the characteristics of the precepts and drives another person away during the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), there is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
This is called the rule for beds and bedding.

Regarding the rule of respectful conduct: while the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the śrāvakas during the first watch of the night, and returned to his own quarters during the middle watch.
At that time, among the bhikṣus, some had attendants who first took rooms for them; having listened to the Dharma, they each went to their rooms and slept.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had no attendants.
Having listened to the Dharma during the first watch of the night, he went to his room during the middle watch and knocked on the door,
asking, "Who is it?"
He replied, "It is Śāriputra.
[The other said,] "The room is already full."
"Great wisdom!
Again, there was a man named Nao who asked, "Who is this?"
He replied, "I am Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
[The other said,] "The rooms are already full."
"Great supernormal power!
Having failed to obtain rooms, one sat beneath the eaves and the other sat beneath a tree.
At that time, as it rained at night, the one sitting under the eaves spoke this verse:
"Sitting cross-legged beneath the eaves, with my two knees drenched by the leaking roof;
having attained this dwelling in peace and ease, I shall now sever this final body.
Thus spoke the one sitting under the tree.
"Knowing contentment beneath a tree, begging for food, and sitting on a grass mat—these two involve no greedy attachment; one shall thus end this final body.
At that time, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, rising early in the morning, wished to pay homage to the World-Honored One. Having seen him, he spoke with disdain:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, lack the dharma of respect, such that they do not provide a dwelling for one so greatly virtuous?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"This is precisely what should be detested by the people of the world.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Wait until I have finished my tour of the Kosalā country and returned to Śrāvastī; then tell me:
'You should establish a rule of respect for the bhikṣus.
Having returned, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Who should occupy the highest seat, take water first, and receive food first?
Who should receive salutations?”
"Who should rise to welcome him?
Who should join their palms and bow their heads in reverence? Some bhikṣus said:
"The sons of the Blessed One should receive it.
Another bhikṣu said:
"The kinsmen of the Blessed One should receive it."
Again, some said:
"The World-Honored One’s attendant should receive it. Others said:
"An Arhat should receive it.
The one who had gone forth from the Kṣatriya caste said:
"A Kṣatriya should receive it."
The one who had gone forth as a Brahmin said,
"A Brahmin should receive it.
The one who had gone forth as a Vaiśya said:
"The Vaiśya should receive it.
The one who had gone forth as a Śūdra said:
"The Śūdra should receive it."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you spoke these words out of excessive pride; to address the Son of the World-Honored One as being equal to even a śūdra is contrary to the dharma of humans."
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall explain the Dharma of persons for you,” as is extensively taught in the Sūtra on the Thread (Sūtram). ...
[and so on] until the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“From this day forward, the precepts are established: those who have gone forth earlier should receive salutations, rise to greet others, join their palms, and bow their heads with reverence; those who have gone forth earlier should serve as the senior seat (upādhyāya), and they should first accept invitations, sit first, take water first, and receive food first.”
The bhikṣus exclaimed,
“The World-Honored One is able to praise and speak in commendation of the veneration due to elders.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today that he was able to praise and honor the elders; in past lives as well, he did so.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "We wish to hear about this."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, long ago, there were three animals—a śṛgāla, a monkey, and an elephant—who lived together beneath a nyagrodha tree."
The elephants said:
"We three classes dwell together in this one place; among us, who is the greatest?
Who is worthy of receiving honor?"
The elephant said,
"I have once ridden past this tree.
The monkey said:
"I once urinated upon this tree.
The bird said, "I originally ate these fruits from beneath the Snowy Mountains and voided my excrement here; thus, this tree grew."
At that time, the bird was the largest; because the two animals showed respect to the bird, they were all reborn in a favorable realm upon their deaths.
At that time, the elephant was my own self.
You should show respect to the elders; in this way, the Vinaya will flourish.
This is called "reverence for the Dharma.
Regarding the first acceptance of an invitation: when someone comes to invite [a monk], one should first invite the senior elder (*sthavira*).
If the donor has not yet performed meritorious deeds and invites a junior bhikṣu, one should direct them to the place where the senior elder is; this is called the first acceptance of an invitation.

Regarding those who sit as senior elders (*sthavira*), when spreading out the seats, one must not allow the seats for the junior monks to be high while the seat for the senior elder is low; rather, the seat for the senior elder should be high and the seat for the junior monk should be low.
One should ensure that the sitting mats are even and straight; the superior ones should be given to the senior monks, and the inferior ones to the junior monks.
If a donor’s family requests that a monk they regard as a spiritual friend be provided with fine bedding and cushions, one must not dispute it, but should follow the host's intention.

If, at the time of a quinquennial assembly, the multitude is vast, the eight individuals from the lowest-ranking up to the *sthavira* (senior elder) should arrange the seats according to the Dharma; those seated below them may do so as is appropriate. This is called the seating protocol for the *sthaviras*.
Regarding "receiving food first": when the food is being distributed, it should first be given to the senior monk (*sthavira*).
If a donor has not yet provided for the merit of the assembly and instead gives first to those of junior rank, one should inform the senior monk's position, saying:
"When the rice is being distributed, you should take the best portion and give it to the senior monk."
"When practicing in this manner during all times of eating and drinking, one should instruct that the best portions be given to the senior monk (*sthavira*).
If a donor’s family invites one for a meal and distributes food with partiality, one should comply with the donor's intention and not engage in dispute."

If, during a quinquennial assembly, the multitude is vast, those from the senior-most seat down to the eighth should be given the superior portions, while those in the lower seats should be given what is appropriate according to the circumstances.
This is called "receiving food first.

Regarding those who prostrate, show respect, rise to welcome, or bow with palms joined: at that time, they were prostrating at the knees and the shins. For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should perform the prostration by touching his feet.
At that time, the bhikṣus sought out others' feet to perform the prostration, thereby disturbing those engaged in spiritual practice.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall perform the salutation of *vaṃdana* by means of speech."
At that time, a bhikṣu, out of playful mockery, spoke these words:
"Homage to the Venerable One!
Homage to the Venerable One!"
Furthermore, he disturbed others.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, there are three kinds of salutation (*praṇāma*):
of body, speech, and mind. Regarding the body:
if the person before one is either sitting or standing, one bows one's head to their feet; this is called salutation by body."
Regarding speech: if the person is at a great distance, one should join the palms, bow the head, and say "Vandana" (Homage); this is called speech. Regarding mind:
if one is turning away, one should join the palms as a mark of respect; this is called mental reverence.
"If one sees a senior elder approaching and does not rise to greet him with a respectful salutation (*vaṃdana*), it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called the rule for showing respect to senior elders.
Accusing others and administering punishment, Expulsion and living separately,
The Saṃgha adjudicates matters concerning fields and land; monks reside in monastic quarters for five years;
and bedding and mats are treated with reverence according to the Dharma.
These are called the three *vargyas*.
Regarding the *poṣadha* (confession) ritual: The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, as described in detail above.
At that time, practitioners of ninety-six types of religious orders all performed the *poṣadha*, yet the bhikṣus did not perform it. Consequently, they were censured by the people of the world:
"How is it that while practitioners of ninety-six types of religious orders all perform the *poṣadha*, the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not perform the *poṣadha*?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is only right that he should be censured by worldly people."
"From this day forward, the *poṣadha* should be observed.
This refers to: the verse; the fourteenth and fifteenth days; the demonstration of the *poṣadha*; the daytime *poṣadha*;
the hall; thieves; the king; Aniruddha; the two types of counting; disadvantage; and non-uniformity.
Cetiya, *anuloma* and *pratiloma*, wishing to hear the beginning, one who has not yet received full ordination,
speaking too early, a single residence, two assemblies, both already spoken and not yet spoken, giving consent (*chanda*),
receiving consent, giving much consent, equal consent, Ghoṣila, Mahāprajāpatī, Channa, and illness.
Aranya; giving what should not be given; the Āciravatī River; the eleven matters for which the transmission of consent (*chandadāna*) is not valid;
changing the transmission of consent; having stayed overnight; outside the boundary; a bhikṣuṇī; one who has not yet received full ordination; taking the transmission of consent and departing;
giving the transmission of consent and departing; having taken the transmission of consent and returning the precepts; having given the transmission of consent and returning the precepts; loss.

Regarding desire, the breaking of the assembly, the four *poṣadhas*, the four proclamations, the seven matters that should be spoken of as prohibitions, and the two matters that should be spoken of as prohibitions.
As for the verse, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Vipaśyin Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa for the Saṅgha of those seeking tranquility:
‘Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is praised by the Buddhas as foremost. One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.’”
The second Buddha, Śikhin, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a person with clear vision can avoid dangerous and evil paths,
so too does a wise person in this world remain far removed from all evils."
The third, the Buddha Vipaśyin, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Do not harm others, do not speak of their faults; act according to what is taught in the precepts;
know moderation in eating and drinking; always delight in dwelling in seclusion; with a pure mind, delight in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas."
The fourth Buddha, Krakucchanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, neither destroying its color nor its fragrance, but taking only its nectar and departing."

When a bhikṣu enters a village, he does not disrupt the affairs of others; he does not observe what they have done or left undone, but observes only his own bodily conduct, scrutinizing it for what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
The fifth Buddha, Konāgamana, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of those seeking tranquility, first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Those who desire a virtuous mind should not be negligent; they should diligently train in the wholesome dharmas of the noble ones.
If there is one who possesses wisdom, tranquility, and a unified mind, then they shall no longer have sorrow or affliction."
The sixth Buddha, Kāśyapa—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—first proclaimed the Prātimokṣa for the community of śramaṇas:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; cultivate fully all wholesome dharmas; purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
The seventh, Śākyamuni Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—preached the Prātimokṣa for the first time to the Saṅgha of the Silent Ones:
"It is good to guard the body; it is also good to guard the speech. It is good to guard the mind; it is good to guard all [the sense-faculties]."

When a bhikṣu guards all [three doors], he shall be freed from all suffering; when a bhikṣu restrains his speech and mind and his body commits no evil, these three paths of action are pure, and he attains the path realized by the noble ones.
This is called the Gāthā-poṣadha.
Regarding the fourteenth and fifteenth days: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, together with his attendant disciple, wished to perform the *mānatva* penance and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to go with my disciple to a small dwelling place in a village to perform the *mānatva* penance; it is now the fourteenth day.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"On this fourteenth day, the constellations are favorable, the season is favorable, and the assembly is favorable; one should perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and only then depart.
Regarding the "fourteenth day," these are the third and seventh *poṣadhas* of winter, the third and seventh of spring, and the third and seventh of summer.
The fifteenth day refers to the eighteen *poṣadha* days.
Within one year there are twenty-four *poṣadha* observances; the sixth, fourteenth, eighteenth, and fifteenth days are called the fourteenth and fifteenth day *poṣadha*.

Regarding the instruction on the *poṣadha*: When the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣus did not know the place for the *poṣadha*; consequently, some were able to perform the *poṣadha*, while others were not.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain shall be formally designated by *karmavācanā* as the place for performing the *poṣadha*."
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha from this day forth regularly perform the *poṣadha* at such-and-such a place on Vulture Peak."
[The motion] is thus stated.
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
At this location, the Sangha shall now regularly perform the *poṣadha* at a certain place on Vulture Peak."
"Venerable sirs, if you approve that the Uposatha shall always be performed at such-and-such a place, those who approve should remain silent; if you do not approve, please speak.
"The Sangha has approved that the Uposatha shall always be performed at such-and-such a place. Since the Sangha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
This is called indicating the place for the *poṣadha*.

Regarding the daytime *poṣadha*: when the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, at that time the bhikṣus performed the *poṣadha* at night; they had come from a very great distance, having fallen to the ground on a perilous path.
For this reason, he went to inform the World-Honored One, asking:
"May I receive the daytime uposatha?
The Buddha said:
"It is obtained.
If the *poṣadha* is held during the day, or if the Saṃgha is residing at a distance, one should announce:
"Venerable sirs!..."

Today is the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the fortnight; whether before or after the meal, so many people should assemble at a certain place—be it the lecture hall, the meditation hall, the warm room, or beneath a tree.
"If one does not chant [the precepts], it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called the daytime *poṣadha*. Regarding the hall:

when the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru constructed a *poṣadha* hall on Vulture Peak Mountain, adorned with various decorations and plates of golden lotus petals. After the monks had sat down, the World-Honored One took his seat.
All the bhikṣus entered [the assembly] intending to perform the poṣadha. A gold flower-slate fell to the ground, and a wicked bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, picked it up and tucked it under his arm.

The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus sat for a long time without performing the poṣadha. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The first watch of the night having passed, and the Saṅgha being weary from sitting for so long, [the monks] said, "We only pray that the World-Honored One will recite the Prātimokṣa for the bhikṣus to perform the uposatha.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Thus, from the middle watch until the last watch of the night, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The dawn has appeared and the assembly of monks has sat for a long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will recite the Prātimokṣa and perform the poṣadha."
The Buddha told Ānanda,
“The assembly is not pure.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had this thought:
"For whose sake has the World-Honored One declared that the assembly is not pure?
Maudgalyāyana immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived that this evil bhikṣu was sitting among the assembly with his body hunched over.
Having seen him, he immediately rose from his seat, went to where he was, seized him by the left hand and dragged him to the door, pushed him out with his right hand, and said these words:
"Evil bhikṣu!"
"From this day forward, you are no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a bhikṣu, and shall no longer remain within the community.
Having thus expelled him, the Buddha said:
"Henceforth, dragging people [by the hair] is not permitted."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall recite the Prātimokṣa. Why is this?"
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall not preach [the Dharma] to those whose assembly is not pure.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The Tathāgata’s discipline and law (vinaya-dharma) is like the great ocean, possessing eight marvelous qualities as extensively explained in the Sūtra on the Thread; having seen these, my disciples give rise to a heart of love and joy.”
This is called the "Hall. Regarding the "thief":

while the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the bhikṣus were performing the *poṣadha* ceremony and reciting the *Prātimokṣa*. When they reached the *pāyattika* section, after the *pāyattika* had been cut off, the *pāyattika* broken, and the *pāyattika* pulled out, as they were about to recite the *pāyattika* again, a thief arrived. The reciter remained silent; the thief stood there for a moment and then departed. They recited it once more, and this happened up to three times.
The thieves thought to themselves:
"This is an evil śramaṇa who makes such a statement:
'Once it has been cut, once it has been broken, and once it has been pulled out, it is a pāyattika.'"
"It is precisely to cut me, to shatter me, and to tear me apart!
He then entered and began beating the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus felt doubt and confusion in their minds.
"Did the thieves previously receive the recitation of the precepts?
For this reason, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Thieves are kings of the forest who can do us harm; it is permissible to speak of them.
Why do you all recite the same words as before?

From this day forward, when a bhikṣu is reciting the Prātimokṣa during the poṣadha ceremony, if a thief enters, he should immediately recite other sūtras, such as the *Pārāyaṇa*, the *Aṭṭhaka-vagga*, the *Munigāthā*, or the *Dhammapada*.”
If a thief knows the Dharma of the bhikṣus and says,

"I already know you, O śramaṇa; merely recite what you have previously memorized," at that time the bhikṣu should recite hurriedly so that the verses and phrases are indistinct, making it impossible for the thief to discern the beginning, middle, or end.
"If you recite the original words again, you will incur an offense against the Vinaya.
This is what is meant by "thief.
Regarding the "king": when the Buddha was staying at the Ambaṭṭha Park in Rājagaha, as explained in detail in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
Eventually, a bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, wondering,
"Is it permissible to recite the precepts in the presence of a king?
For this reason, he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"A king is one who can perform acts that are not beneficial.
As explained extensively above regarding thieves, this is what is meant by a "king."
Regarding Aniruddha: While the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, when the bhikṣus were performing the poṣadha karmavācanā, the Venerable Aniruddha did not come.
The bhikṣus sent a messenger to summon the Venerable Aniruddha, saying,
"The community of bhikṣus has assembled and wishes to perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of the poṣadha.
He replied:
“The Blessed One has said that purity is the *poṣadha*; as for me, I am one who is pure in this world, and I shall not go.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
The Buddha said,
"Go and summon him, but do not use your divine eye to come.
Because that elder had lost his physical eyes, he had traveled along perilous mountain paths with extreme hardship before finally arriving.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha:
"If you do not respect the poṣadha, who then shall respect it?
The Buddha continued:
"From this day forward, you must all come at the time of the *poṣadha*; if you do not come, or if you are ill and do not grant your consent (*chanda*), it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called Ānanda.
Regarding the two kinds of enumeration, the Buddha asked Upāli:
"Do you recite the Vinaya?
He replied:
“Recite them, but these miscellaneous minor phrases are difficult to maintain.
The Buddha said:
“You should recite them by counting with tally-sticks (*śalākā*).”
At that time, Upāli immediately performed the counting of the tally-sticks and recited them.
The Buddha again asked Upāli:
"Did you perform the counting of the tally-sticks and recite the Vinaya?"
He replied,
"Even with the counting of sticks for the miscellaneous fragments of verses, it is still difficult to maintain them through recitation.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, two types of counting sticks shall be made:
one set of five hundred and another set of seven hundred.

When you wish to recite [the scriptures], you must first wash your hands thoroughly; then, having taken up the counting sticks, even if you count down to only five, you must still wash your hands. If there are any [defilements], you should bathe the counting sticks with fragrant liquid. Anyone else who wishes to take up the counting sticks should do likewise.”
These are called the two types of enumeration.

Regarding "the unskilled": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a monk residing in a certain village. When the Saṃgha assembled and wished to perform the *poṣadha* ritual, they said to the elder:
"Recite the *Prātimokṣa*."
He replied, "I am not well.
Thus it was for the second and third [monks], and so on down to the junior-most monk, who likewise said the same.
The bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds and, for this reason, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, after receiving full ordination, one should recite the Vinaya of both divisions."
If one cannot recite both sections, one should recite one section;
if one still cannot, one should recite the Five-Line Sūtra;
if one still cannot, one should recite four, three, two, or even one.

During the *poṣadha*, one should recite the Five-Thread Sūtra (*pañca-vastuka-sūtra*) in full. If, due to certain circumstances, this is not possible, one should recite four, three, two, or even one; furthermore, the four *pārājika* rules and the remaining verses should be heard regularly by the Saṃgha.
If one performs the *poṣadha* without reciting [the precepts], it is an offense against the Vinaya.

If, in such circumstances, it would be disadvantageous for the entire assembly, one should have a senior elder (*sthavira*) go outside the boundary and perform the following mental reflection and verbal declaration:
"I am performing the *poṣadha*."
The other three perform the rite within the boundary, saying three times:
"We perform the *poṣadha*.
This constitutes a penalty for the *sthavira*.
This is called "not beneficial. Regarding "not beneficial for all":
the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu residing in a certain village. When the Saṃgha assembled and wished to perform the poṣadha ceremony, they said to the elder:
"Recite the Prātimokṣa."
He replied,
"I have gained one benefit.
He then spoke to the second elder, who replied:
"We shall recite two *khaṇḍas*.
Thus, they each recited one *khaṇḍa* in succession, and then recited them alternately.
Having performed the *poṣadha* together, doubt arose in their minds, and the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit communal recitation for the purpose of performing the *poṣadha*.
If there are those who act in such a manner, they should together instruct one person of keen intelligence to master it, and then have that person recite it."
"If one forgets [the text] while reciting, another person may provide the instruction; however, if they recite together to perform the *poṣadha*, it constitutes a *vinaya*-transgression.
This is called "not being beneficial for all."
Regarding "in direct and reverse order": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu living in a village where the Saṃgha had assembled for the poṣadha ceremony.

One bhikṣu recited the Prātimokṣa with skill, reciting it both in direct and reverse order: from the introduction (nidāna) down to the *dharmānudharma*, and from the *dharmānudharma* back up to the introduction.
After the *poṣadha* ceremony had concluded, a doubt and regret arose in his mind. The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to recite in reverse order; you should recite in the proper sequence."
"If one forgets anything while reciting, it may be recited again as a supplement.
To perform the *poṣadha* by reciting either in direct or reverse order constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is what is meant by "direct and reverse order."

Those who wish to hear the beginning [of this account]: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the community of bhikṣus gathered to perform the poṣadha ceremony, reciting the Prātimokṣa, up until the section on the "Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu came and said:
"Venerable sir!
I have been residing in a village, but I have never heard the Prātimokṣa recited in full. I pray that you, Venerable sir, will recite it for me in full."
The reciter then began again from the beginning of the precepts, up to the "Dharma that accords with the Dharma.
The bhikṣus were filled with doubt and, for these reasons, reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Why do you recite again for those who have already heard it from the beginning?
From this day forward, this is not permitted."

If the community of bhikṣus assembles to perform the poṣadha, reciting the Prātimokṣa and so forth up to the "Dharma in accordance with the Dharma," and visiting bhikṣus arrive and take their seats, it is then said that the poṣadha has been accomplished.
If a visiting bhikṣu says:
"I reside in a village where I have never heard the Prātimokṣa recited in full; I pray that you will recite it in full for me."
"Once you have waited until the Saṃgha has finished, only then should you recite with them.
If you recite while the Saṃgha has not yet finished, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called "desiring to hear at the beginning."

Regarding those who have not yet received full ordination: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣu explained the five classes of offenses—ranging from *pārājika* down to *vinayātikrama*—to persons who had not received full ordination.
Later, when a bhikṣu entered a village, a layperson said:
"Venerable sir!
You have committed an offense ranging from a pārājika down to a vyatikrama-vinaya."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus felt ashamed and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Why have you expounded the five categories of offenses of the Prātimokṣa to those who have not yet received full ordination?"
From this day forward, it is not permitted to speak [of these matters] to those who have not received full ordination; however, you may instruct them, saying:
"You must not engage in unchaste conduct, you must not steal, you must not kill living beings, and you must not speak falsely."
One may speak in such a manner to those who have received it.
However, if one speaks the names of the five categories of the Prātimokṣa to a person who has not yet received full ordination, it constitutes a Vinaya offense.
This is called a person who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Regarding "too early": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a certain bhikṣu living in a village. Having risen in the morning and finished the *poṣadha* ceremony, a visiting bhikṣu came and said to the resident bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!"
"Come, let us perform the poṣadha together.
He replied,
"I have already completed the poṣadha."
The visiting bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!
It is far too early to perform the poṣadha."
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should not perform the poṣadha ceremony too early."

If a single bhikṣu resides within a village, on the day of the poṣadha he should sweep the stūpa and the monastic quarters; if there are others present, he should sprinkle the ground with scented water, scatter flowers, and light lamps, waiting for visiting bhikṣus to arrive so that they may perform the poṣadha together.
If no visiting bhikṣus arrive, one who has committed an offense should reflect thus:
"If I obtain a pure bhikṣu, this offense shall be removed in accordance with the Dharma."
Having formed this thought, one should mentally reflect and verbally recite:
"Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the Poṣadha; I, bhikṣu [Name], am pure and shall receive the Poṣadha."
Thus he should say three times.
If, after the poṣadha has concluded, visiting bhikṣus arrive, they should express their sympathetic joy, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Having already performed the *poṣadha*, I, [Name], rejoice.
If one does not rejoice, one should go outside the boundary to perform the *poṣadha*.
If one performs the *poṣadha* at dawn, it is an offense against the *vinaya*.
This is called "too early.

Regarding "a single residence": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, the sky became overcast and dark; thinking it was dusk, they entered a village and went to a bhikṣu residence to perform the poṣadha ceremony.
After the poṣadha had been performed, the sky cleared and it was still early; the bhikṣus thought to themselves, "We should go on ahead.
Having departed, after a short while a second group arrived and performed the poṣadha at that same place.
He stayed overnight there and departed the following day, where he met the bhikṣu who had previously performed the poṣadha.
Having seen him, he said: "Elder!..."
"Where did you stay overnight yesterday?
He replied, "In such-and-such a place."
"Where is the poṣadha being held?
He replied, "At such-and-such a place."
“I also performed the *poṣadha* there.
The bhikṣus were filled with doubt and, for this reason, reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, one may not perform the *poṣadha* again in a single dwelling place.

If a bhikṣu is traveling on a journey and enters a village on the *poṣadha* day to reach the dwelling of other bhikṣus, once the *poṣadha* has been performed, he must not depart in silence; he should entrust the matter to a śrāmaṇera, a park-keeper, or a herdsman, saying:
‘If any bhikṣus come here, tell them that the *poṣadha* has already been performed here.’”

If there is no one present, one should write on the pillar, the door, or the leaf of the gate, or make a mark by scattering flowers. If anyone arrives later, they should be questioned and asked for such a mark; one must not perform the *poṣadha* arbitrarily.
"If the person before did not give instructions regarding the signs of non-performance, and the person behind neither inquired nor requested them, both incur an offense of *viniya-āpatti*.
This is called 'one dwelling place' (*ekavihāra*)."

Regarding the two assemblies: when two groups of visiting bhikṣus arrive—one group observing the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day and the other group observing the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day—from whom should [the resident community] follow?
Regarding those who enter first:
if the two assemblies enter simultaneously, they should follow the senior monk.
If there is no distinction of seniority, they should follow the one who upholds the Vinaya.
If both groups maintain the Vinaya, they should follow the one who first utters the voice.
Whether it be on the fourteenth day or the fifteenth day, they should follow the *poṣadha*.
These are called the two assemblies.

Regarding "two have already been explained and two have not yet been explained": when visiting bhikṣus arrive, the visiting bhikṣus perform the poṣadha on the fourteenth day, while the resident bhikṣus perform it on the fifteenth day.
The resident bhikṣus said to the visiting bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Come, let us perform the poṣadha together."
A visiting bhikṣu must not say,
"I have already performed the poṣadha," whether he intends to join the assembly or to go outside the boundary.
If the resident bhikṣus were on the fourteenth day and the visiting bhikṣus were on the fifteenth day,
the visiting bhikṣus said:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Come to perform the *poṣadha*.
The resident bhikṣu should say:
"I have already performed the *poṣadha*."
The visiting bhikṣu should express his approval, saying:
"Venerable one!
The poṣadha has been performed; I approve."
"If one does not rejoice [in the merit], one should go outside the boundary to perform the *poṣadha*.
These are called the two that have been explained and the two that have not yet been explained.
Regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*): when the Saṃgha has assembled for the *poṣadha*, there may be a bhikṣu who, due to matters concerning his robe or bowl, is unable to attend."
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the granting of consent (chanda)."
Regarding the method for granting consent (*chandadāna*), one should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, listen!
Today is the *poṣadha* of the Saṃgha, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day. I, the bhikṣu [name], grant my consent for the pure *poṣadha*; please declare it for me."
Thus it was said three times.
When conveying the *chanda* (consent), one must not go and give it to someone else; rather, it should be given to one capable of holding the *chanda* and entering the Saṃgha to announce it.
If, during the time for the robe and bowl matters or the *poṣadha*, one does not convey the *chanda*, it is a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "giving of consent" (*chanda*).

Regarding the one who receives consent: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the community of monks gathered to perform the *poṣadha* ritual. At that time, a monk who was ill gave his consent for the sake of his robe and bowl, but the [receiving] monk did not accept it.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you should receive the *chanda* (consent). When receiving the *chanda*, you should reflect for yourself: 'Am I able to transmit this consent?'"
One may not take the consent (*chanda*) of more than three people.
When giving the consent, one should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please remember!"
"Today the Saṃgha performs the Poṣadha; I, bhikṣu so-and-so, give my consent for the purity of the Poṣadha.
If one forgets the name, one should remember the number of years and say:
"A bhikṣu of such-and-such years."
If one is a visitor, one should say "I am a visitor," or if one is ill, one should say "I am ill," and then the bhikṣu may give the *poṣadha* purity and consent (*chanda*).
If one is ill and gives consent for the sake of matters concerning robes or bowls, yet the other does not accept it, it is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
This is called "giving consent regarding desire.

Regarding those who frequently give consent: when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony for the community of bhikṣus, there were many who gave their consent while few actually assembled.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted to perform the uposatha with many who have granted their consent (*chanda*) and few who are assembled. Whoever does so commits an offense against the Vinaya."
This is called "giving consent in excess.
Regarding "equal to those who give consent": when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the community of monks held the *poṣadha*.
At that time, a monk who had given his consent performed the *poṣadha* together with those who had assembled.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit the performance of the poṣadha by those who desire [to be absent] and so forth; rather, those who ought to assemble should be numerous."
"If you wish to perform the *poṣadha* [in such a manner], it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called "desiring [to act] equally" (*icchā-samāna*).

Regarding Kuśira: while the Buddha was staying at the Kuśira Garden in Kauśāmbī, the community of monks assembled to perform the *poṣadha*; during the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for settling matters, the sound of their voices was loud.

At that time, the householder Ghoṣila entered; the Saṃgha remained silent. After a short while he departed, and the Saṃgha resumed their business, speaking as loudly as before. This occurred up to three times.
The householder thought to himself:
"I shall enter in silence and leave with a loud voice.
Now, I shall enter and never leave again."
As was asked by Ghoṣila of the Venerable Ānanda, as explained in detail in the *Ṣaḍāyatanasūtra*.
At that time, the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and, for these reasons, reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said:

"If such a person of great virtue and excellence wishes to hear the community of monks adjudicate a matter, they may hear the adjudication; provided that there is someone in the assembly who is eloquent and capable of speaking so as to clarify the details of the case, let them speak."
"If an ordinary layperson interrupts while a matter is being decided, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called the householder Ghoṣila. Regarding Mahāprajāpatī:
when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī offered her consent (*chanda*), but the bhikṣus did not accept it.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"The bhikṣus do not accept my request; who then shall accept it?"
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma in accordance with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī’s disposition; having given rise to a heart of joy, she prostrated herself at his feet and withdrew.
The Buddha said, "Summon that bhikṣu to come."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs should receive the *chanda* (consent)."
If it is the senior monk (sthavira), he should say:
"I am the senior monk of the Saṃgha; I should not accept [this].
If it is the one who instructs the nuns or the one who recites the Prātimokṣa, each should speak for themselves accordingly.
"One should not accept it.
If the guardian of the dwelling or a sick person is present, one should say:
"I will not go into the midst of the Saṃgha; please give it to someone else."
If one says,
"I am a beggar for alms," "I am a forest-dweller," "I am a wearer of rag-robes," or "I am a person of great virtue," yet does not accept the formal consent (*chanda*),
it is an offense of violating the Vinaya.
If one says,
"I am the senior elder (sthavira), I am the instructor of nuns (bhikṣuṇī-śikṣamāṇā),
I am the reciter of the precepts (poṣadha-vācaka)," and does not accept [the invitation], there is no offense.
This is called Gopamā. Regarding Chanda:
while the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in Kauśāmbī, the Saṃgha assembled for the poṣadha ceremony.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda refused to come. The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
"What kind of offense is this?
The Buddha said,
"One incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
"If a bhikṣu who has been thus invited to the poṣadha refuses to come, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he does not come for the sake of his robes or bowl, nor gives his consent (chanda), he incurs a vinayātikrama offense."

Regarding the sick: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the community of bhikṣus had assembled, intending to perform the poṣadha ceremony. One bhikṣu was suffering from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga), and he spoke to a fellow in the adjacent room, saying: "Elder!..."
"I am afflicted by a wind disorder; I offer my pure desire [to serve].
The bhikṣu did not accept it.
He then went before the elder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
"I, [Name], am pure; may the Sangha remember and uphold this.
Having spoken thus three times, he departed.
The bhikṣus felt doubt and uncertainty, and for these reasons, they reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
"Is that so? The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"The formal act has already been performed according to the Dharma.
However, for those who do not accept the *chanda* (consent), there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called 'illness'."
Regarding the *āraṇyaka*: while the Buddha was staying in the village of Āraṇyaka near Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus would regularly perform the *poṣadha* together there.
At that time, the *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu entered the village, performed the *poṣadha*, and then departed.
Not long after they had departed, some visiting bhikṣus arrived and performed the poṣadha ceremony at that same place, staying there overnight.
When they met one another the following day, they asked:
"Elders!..."
"Where did you stay last night?
He replied,
"In this place."
“Where is the poṣadha being held?
He replied, “It is here.”
Having heard this, doubt arose in his mind, and for this reason he reported everything in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit a single dwelling place to perform the *poṣadha* twice."

Whether one is in a forest hermitage or entering a village for the *poṣadha*, one must not depart in silence; rather, one should entrust the matter to a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), a park-attendant, or a cowherd, saying:
"If any other bhikṣus arrive later, tell them that the *poṣadha* has already been performed here."
If there is no one present, one should write characters on a pillar, a door, or a leaf, or scatter flowers to form a sign.
A latercomer should inquire about and seek out these signs.
If the previous person departs without entrusting the matter or making a sign, and the latercomer neither inquires nor seeks out the sign, both commit an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called *āraṇyaka*. Regarding "giving what should not be given":

while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus would assemble at the proper time to give their *karmavācanā* consent, but they assembled at improper times to give their *pariśuddhi* (purity) consent.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, it is not permitted to grant a formal act (*karmavācanā*) when assembled at the proper time, nor to grant the desire for purity (*śuddhika-kāma*) when assembled at an improper time."

If the assembly gathers at an improper time, one should give the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) and the consent; if the assembly gathers at the proper time, one should give the consent for purity (*śuddhika*). Furthermore, when the assembly gathers at the proper time, one may also give both types of consent:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!"
If the Sangha now performs the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, I, the bhikṣu [Name], give my consent for the purity of the *poṣadha*; please communicate this to me.
Thus it is said three times.
To give the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) and the consent (*chanda*) is also to be stated three times.

If one gives the consent for purity when the assembly is not convened at the proper time, or gives the *karmavācanā* consent when the assembly is convened at the proper time, one commits an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called giving what should not be given.

Regarding the Ajiravatī River: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus went to the bank of the Ajiravatī River, spread out their *niṣīdana* mats, sat down, and recited the *Prātimokṣa*.

At that time, the water overflowed and gradually rose to his knees; thus it continued to rise until it reached his mouth. Having endured extreme suffering, he finally returned to the place where the Buddha was.
For these reasons, he reported everything in detail to the World-Honored One, asking:
"May I stand and perform the *poṣadha*?"
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted; one may perform the *poṣadha* while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

Regarding "while walking": if a bhikṣu travels together with merchants and on the day of the *poṣadha* there is danger or fear such that the merchants do not wait, it is permitted to perform the *poṣadha* while walking.

First, one should deliberate on how far it must extend so that the recitation of the precepts may be completed; whether it be a mountain or a rock, one should establish a marker such that arms can reach across, and then perform the *karmavācanā* to establish the boundary for the *poṣadha*.
After the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one then conducts the *poṣadha*; this is called "performing the *poṣadha*.

As for "staying [for the *poṣadha*]," when there are many bhikṣus and no beds or seats available, they perform the *poṣadha* while all standing with their arms extended so that they can reach one another; this is called "staying for the *poṣadha*."
Regarding "sitting": when one performs the *poṣadha* while seated on a bed or chair, this is called the "sitting *poṣadha*.

Regarding "lying down": when a bhikṣu is too old or ill to remain seated for long, he may perform the *poṣadha* while lying down with the corners of his beds joined together; this is called the "lying-down *poṣadha*."
This is called the Ajiravatī River.

Regarding the eleven matters that do not constitute the giving of consent or the transferring of consent: "I give my consent to the Elder; I previously received the consent of [so-and-so] and now give it as well."
This is called "transferring the *chanda*. Regarding "giving it in advance":
if the *poṣadha* is to be held tomorrow, one gives the *chanda* today; this is called "giving the *chanda* in advance.
Regarding "outside the boundary": one leaves the boundary to give the *chanda*; this is called "being outside the boundary."
A "bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who gives consent to a bhikṣuṇī; this is called a bhikṣuṇī.
One who has not received full ordination refers to one who gives consent to a person who has not received full ordination; this is called one who has not received full ordination.
"Taking the consent and departing" means that after taking the consent, one departs outside the boundary; this is called "taking the consent and departing.
"Giving the consent and departing" means that after giving the consent, one departs outside the boundary; this is called "giving the consent and departing."

"Having taken the *chanda* (consent) and then returning the precepts" means that after having taken the *chanda*, one returns the precepts and receives full ordination (*upasampadā*); this is called "having taken the *chanda* and then returning the precepts.

"Having given the *chanda* and then returning the precepts" means that after having given the *chanda* to another, one returns the precepts and receives full ordination; this is called "having given the *chanda* and then returning the precepts."

Regarding the loss of the *chanda* (consent): if a bhikṣu who is ill has given his consent and then hears the Dharma-master preaching the Dharma or a master of the Vinaya expounding the *Vinaya* within the Saṃgha, he exerts himself to go and listen; having sat for a long time and become weary, he previously gave his consent but then silently leaves his seat and departs—this is not called "having given consent," and he should give it again.
This is called the loss of the *chanda*.
Regarding "one who destroys the assembly": on the day of the *poṣadha*, when the community of monks has gathered, those monks who do not attend provide their *chanda* for purity.
If there is a violent storm, fire, or bandits, and all the monks are dispersed in alarm, it is not considered that the *chanda* was brought to the assembly.
If there is only one person present, this is called "reaching the Saṃgha.
This is called the eleventh [case], and it is not termed "granting consent" (*chanda*).
Regarding the four types of *poṣadha*: one person receives [the confession], two persons recite [it], three persons recite [it], and four persons chant it in full.

Regarding the one who receives [the instruction]: there was a bhikṣu living in a village who, on the day of the poṣadha, ought to sweep the stūpa and the monastery; if there were any [guests], he should sprinkle the ground with scented water, light lamps, scatter flowers, and wait for the visiting bhikṣus.
If no one comes, one who has committed an offense should reflect thus:
"When a pure bhikṣu is found, this offense shall be removed according to the Dharma.
Having reflected thus, one should kneel on the right knee with palms joined and speak these words aloud:
"If the Sangha now performs the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, I, bhikṣu [Name], am pure and shall receive the *poṣadha*.
Thus it is said three times; this is called "receiving by one person."

Regarding the two speakers: when two bhikṣus reside in a village, on the day of the poṣadha they should sweep the stūpa and the monastery; if there are materials available, they should sprinkle the ground with scented water, scatter flowers, and light lamps. If either has committed an offense, they should mutually confess it according to the Dharma and then, kneeling with palms joined, speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please take note!"
"If the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure.
Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind.
This is called "declaring."
The same applies to the three persons.
Regarding "extensive recitation": four persons should perform the extensive recitation of the Prātimokṣa; this is called "extensive recitation.
Regarding "fourfold proclamation": from the beginning of the *Nidāna* (Introduction) up to the end of the four *Pārājika* rules, the rest is the verse that the Saṃgha regularly hears recited.
Second, having completed the thirteen matters and the two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*), the rest of the Saṃgha regularly recites the verses.
Third, having completed the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, the rest of the Saṃgha regularly recites the verses.
Fourth, one enters the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, which should be recited in their entirety and in detail.
These are called the four recitations.
There are seven matters regarding the *poṣadha* that should be prohibited:
First, those who do not live in communal residence;
second, those living in isolation;
third, those who have not yet received full ordination.
4. The desire has not yet been expressed;
5. the śalākā has not yet been distributed;
6. for the sake of achieving concord.
Seventh, if the assembly has not yet reached consensus, this is called the seventh matter that should be prohibited.
Furthermore, there are two matters that should prohibit the *poṣadha*:
first, if those performing the *poṣadha* engage in quarreling and strife within the Saṃgha; [the second is if they engage in frivolous talk].
Second is the schism of the Saṃgha.
These two matters are to be prevented.
This concludes the rules for the Poṣadha ceremony, the procedure for granting consent (*chanda*), and the procedure for receiving consent.
Regarding the rules for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣus were wandering about during the rainy season and caused much injury to living beings, which led to the reproach of worldly people:
"The followers of the ninety-six other schools of renunciants still know how to observe the *varṣā*, remaining in their dwellings like birds in their nests."
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves excellence yet do not observe the rains retreat.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"It is indeed right that they should be censured by the world.
From this day forward, one should enter the rains retreat during the rainy season.

Regarding the method for entering the rains retreat: on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should bare the right shoulder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms together, and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please remember!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month rains retreat here at this monastery.
Thus it is said three times.

If a bhikṣu is traveling on the road and has not yet reached his dwelling place when the day for entering the rains retreat arrives, he should enter the retreat even by the side of the road, whether relying on a tree or a cart.

When the light of dawn appears, one should go to one's dwelling place; upon reaching the day of the later retreat (paścimikā varṣā), one should bare the right shoulder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and say these words:
"Venerable sir, please take note! [I am entering the later retreat]."
"I, bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the rains retreat for three months here in this saṃghārāma.
Thus he says three times.
If a bhikṣu travels on his alms-round and does not accept the rains retreat on the day of the *pūrvavarsa* (the first retreat), he commits one offense of *vinayātikrama*.

Upon arriving at their place of residence, if they do not undertake the rains retreat on the day for the later retreat, they commit two offenses of violating the Vinaya; such persons have broken the retreat and shall not receive the distribution of robes.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣu who was observing the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) in dependence upon a village. A donor (*dānapati*) was managing affairs for the Saṃgha and required water for irrigation; he requested the bhikṣu to petition the king to allow the passage of water.
At that time, the bhikṣu kept his robes and bowl close at hand and went repeatedly to the king’s gate, yet he was not granted an audience.
Since the road was not near, he feared he would lose the [proper time for] the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
Then the World-Honored One, seeing this and knowing it already, asked him intentionally:
“Are you a guest bhikṣu? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Are you the bhikṣu Gati? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Why do you carry your robe and bowl with you?
The bhikṣu reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, during the rains retreat, if one must attend to matters concerning a stūpa or matters concerning the Saṃgha, one should perform the formal act of seeking permission (*jñapti-karman*), saying:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"

"Venerable sirs, this bhikṣu named [Name] has entered the rains retreat here at this place. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha permit this bhikṣu named [Name], who has entered the rains retreat here, to go outside the boundary on account of matters concerning the stūpa or matters concerning the Saṃgha, and then return to stay here."

"Venerable sirs, listen: the bhikṣu so-and-so is departing from the boundary for the sake of stūpa affairs and saṃgha affairs, intending to return to this place for the rains retreat. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"If there are those who seek for the sake of a stūpa or for the sake of the Saṃgha in such a manner, they will certainly obtain something.
Whether it be robes, an alms bowl, a small bowl, a key, a lock, a waistband, or any other such thing, they shall certainly obtain at least one item."
If one does not obtain it, there is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
When such matters are concluded, one should return—whether after half a month, a month, or two months, or even until after the subsequent *pravāraṇā*.
If one does not return, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
However, if the road is dangerous and there is fear of bandits such that one's life might be lost, there is no offense in performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony there.
This is called the method for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).
As for the method for the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī;

the detailed account is as above. At that time, the bhikṣus were traveling together through the country of Kośala. They saw a grove by the side of the river Kalmāṣadā, in which there was a large *sāla* tree with a vast open space beneath it. Its shade was thick and dense, and the ground under the tree was level, even, and spacious. It was neither too far from nor too near to a village. They thought to themselves:
"This place is excellent; it is suitable for the rains retreat.
Thus did everyone who saw it, whether before or after, think to themselves.
On the day of the commencement of the retreat, a certain bhikṣu arrived first; he repaired an empty tree, arranged his robes and bowl, spread out some grass, and sat down.
After a short while, another bhikṣu arrived and asked,
"Elder, do you wish to observe the rains retreat here?"
He replied: "Yes! Excellent."
In this manner, the succession continued until there were sixty people.
The one who arrived first said to the monks who followed:
"Venerable ones!"
"Do you intend to remain in residence here for the entire summer retreat? He replied, "Yes."
"Excellent.
This tree provides sufficient space for my robes and bowl, and the area beneath it on all sides is enough for me to dwell in peace.
Having received the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) rules, he further spoke these words:
“Venerable elders!
What dharma should we practice so that we may dwell in peace and happiness? The others replied:
