"All afflictions and distresses arise from body and speech; since we have obtained this place of tranquility, it is fitting that we remain silent together. We should establish a rule of silence.

After they had established the rule of silence for three months, they returned to the city of Śrāvastī and went to the Blessed One’s presence. They prostrated with their heads at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Knowing [their thoughts], the Buddha asked them intentionally: "Monks, where did you spend your retreat?"
He replied, "In such-and-such a place.
The Buddha then asked the bhikṣu:
“Are you free from much illness and affliction? Is alms-seeking not difficult for you? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness, practicing the path in accordance with the Dharma?
He replied, “World-Honored One! [I am so.]”
"I have had little illness and little affliction; alms were easily obtained, and I have lived in silent joy for three months without speaking. I shall now depart.
The Buddha said, "This is an evil matter.
It is like dwelling with an enemy; according to the Dharma, one ought to speak with others."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.

Aniruddha and Kapphiṇa had completed their rains retreat at Mount Taṭaka and returned to Śrāvastī. They went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Knowing [the answer], the Buddha nevertheless asked:
“Where did you spend the rains retreat?”
He replied, "In such-and-such a place.
He asked again:
“Monk, are you free from much illness and affliction? Is it not difficult for you to beg for alms? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness, practicing the path according to the Dharma?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!”
“I have had little illness and few afflictions; alms were easily obtained;
I have dwelt in silence and joy for three months without speaking, and have now departed.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter, like dwelling together with an enemy.

From this day forward, I do not permit you to speak with one another. However, for the sake of convenience and to minimize affairs, you may remain silent for half a month; on the day of the *poṣadha*, you should speak together, exchange greetings, ask questions, and provide answers, and offer blessings. After the *poṣadha* day, you shall continue as before."
"If one does not speak with [another] out of pride or anger, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) procedure, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"From this day forth, I establish for my disciples the *pravāraṇā* procedure: after three months, with three utterances, once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is completed; in the place where one has stayed during the retreat, one performs the *pravāraṇā* there, beginning from the senior monk (*sthavira*) in harmony."
"Three months" refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
"The three statements" refer to what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
"The conclusion of the rains retreat" (varṣā) refers to the earlier retreat, which runs from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The later retreat (*paścimā vārṣikī*) lasts from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

If there is even one person among the assembly observing the retreat who is in the earlier retreat (*pūrvā vārṣikī*), then on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the entire assembly should perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) together with that one person. Once the invitation ceremony is concluded, they shall remain seated until the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
If all [monks] observe the later *varṣā*, they should all perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the eighth month; this is called the completion of the *varṣā*.

Regarding the place where one observes the *varṣā* and the place where one performs the *pravāraṇā*: if a bhikṣu is observing the *varṣā* within a village and hears that on the *pravāraṇā* day in the city there will be various offerings and Dharma discourses throughout the night, those who wish to go should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day and may then depart.
If one observes the rains retreat in this location but performs the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in another, one commits a *vinaya*-offense.
When proceeding from the senior monks (*sthavira*), one must not skip over them to establish the order; rather, the sequence should descend in regular order starting from the senior monk.
One must not proceed by placing people like the method of adding food; one must not skip over anyone; and one must not announce collectively, saying:
"Venerable sirs of the Sangha, please speak of any offenses you have seen, heard, or suspect regarding the *pravāraṇā*."
This is called [the procedure] from the elder.
One who has accomplished five qualities should be prostrated to as the person for the invitation (pravāraṇā), whether it be one or two, but not more than that.
The officiant (karmakāraka) should speak thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has accomplished the five qualities. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā*."

"Venerable sirs, listen! The monk so-and-so has been appointed as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the monk so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The person receiving the *karmavācanā* should say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"The time for the *pravāraṇā* has arrived. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the entire Saṃgha receive the *pravāraṇā*.
The motion is made thus.
The person performing the *pravāraṇā* should begin with the *sthavira* (senior monk).
The Elder should bare his right shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
“Venerable sir, please take note!

Today is the fifteenth day, the time for the Saṃgha’s invitation to admonition (*pravāraṇā*). I, the bhikṣu [Name], invite the Venerable One and the Saṃgha to admonish me. If you perceive, hear, or suspect any offense in me, please speak to me out of compassion.”
"If I know or see [a fault], I shall eliminate it in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus he spoke three times.
Next, he went to the second person.
If the second person is of lower rank, they should receive his feet and address him as "Venerable Sir" (*bhadanta*);
this is the distinction.

If two persons perform the *pravāraṇā*, one person shall receive the *pravāraṇā* from the senior monk (*sthavira*), while the other should stand before the junior monk; once the senior monk has spoken, the junior monk shall speak in turn.
In this manner, proceeding in succession down to one's own seat, one should receive the *pravāraṇā*. One must not wait until the *saṃgha* has completed its *pravāraṇā* before performing one's own.
Regarding those who are in harmony: one must not receive the *pravāraṇā* from those who are not in harmony, nor may one receive the *pravāraṇā* by proxy (*chanda*).
If a sick person should be brought [to the assembly], yet bringing them presents a danger to their life, the Saṃgha should go to where they are.

If there are many sick persons, they should be brought on stretchers; or the corners of their stretchers should be joined together. If bringing them on stretchers presents a danger to their lives, monks who are not ill should join their seats together in a continuous line.
If [the assembly] is not complete, the healthy bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*, while the sick bhikṣus perform the *pravāraṇā* within the boundary.

If the great assembly is large—whether ten thousand or twenty thousand—they should all gather in one place, whether in a lecture hall, a dining hall, or a bathhouse, to receive the *pravāraṇā*. The others should simultaneously chew tooth-sticks, attend to their bodily functions, and eat; thus, throughout the day and through the night, they must not leave their seats or move far away, performing the *pravāraṇā* therein until the first light of dawn has appeared.

If the great assembly consists of many—such as sixty thousand or eighty thousand—and one fears that the ceremony will not be completed, one should reduce the number and go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Alternatively, if there is only one person, they may receive the *pravāraṇā*; or if two, three, or four people, they may recite the *pravāraṇā* together.
Five persons perform the *pravāraṇā* extensively, while one person receives it.

If a single bhikṣu is observing the rains retreat within a village, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, he should sweep the stūpa and the monastery. If there are resources available, he should sprinkle the ground with scented water, scatter flowers, and light lamps. If he has committed an offense, he should form this thought:
"If a pure bhikṣu comes, I shall remove this offense according to the Dharma."
Having formed this thought, he knelt with his palms joined and spoke these words:
"Today is the fifteenth day of the month for the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure and accept the *pravāraṇā*."
Thus it was said three times.

When two persons have confessed their offenses and performed the mutual reconciliation according to the Dharma, they should bare their right shoulders, kneel with their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and say:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!"
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha holds the Pravāraṇā ceremony.
Venerable sirs, please perform the Pravāraṇā and speak to me if you see, hear, or suspect any offense. Out of compassion, inform me;
whether I know it or see it myself, I shall remove it according to the Dharma.
Thus it was said three times.
For three or four persons, it is likewise. For five persons, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed in full detail.
This is called the procedure for *pravāraṇā*.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Twenty-seven [and] Volume Twenty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Regarding the sixth section of the *Saṃyukta-bhāṇaka-vastu* translated by Fa-xian, concerning the *Kaṭhina-cīvara* rules: The Buddha was dwelling at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī, where he was venerated by gods and worldly people alike.
At that time, the queen of King Kausāmbī offered five hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take these pieces of cloth and give them to the bhikṣus."
The bhikṣus did not accept it and said to Ānanda, “The World-Honored One does not permit the keeping of extra robes; what is the use of this cotton cloth?
It is already improper as it has not yet been washed and dyed.”
Ānanda reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, it is permitted to keep an extra robe for ten days."
After ten days had passed, the bhikṣus took these extra robes and went to inform the World-Honored One, saying,
"These robes have now reached ten days.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe is permitted. Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe:

it is [accepted] by the Saṃgha, by a group of many, or by a single person; it possesses five benefits; it must be new, not previously accepted, not yet suspended, purified by cutting, purified by dyeing, purified by marking, or purified by the blade.
Regarding the "time": from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is called the time.
Regarding the "community of monks" (*saṃgha*): when the *saṃgha* prepares the *kaṭhina* robe, it may not be given to a large group of people, nor may it be given to a single individual.
When many people together make the *kaṭhina* robe, it may not be given to a single person.
Regarding the five benefits, one is freed from five offenses.
What are these five?

Eating apart from the community, eating at various locations, walking before or after meals, keeping extra robes without informing others, and staying overnight separated from one's robes—these are called the five benefits.
"New" refers to new cotton cloth.
"Not yet received" means it has never been received as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*).

"Not kept" means that after a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*) of cloth has been relinquished, one may make from it a *kaṭhina* robe, a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, an *antarvāsaka*, a wound-covering cloth, or a rain-bathing cloth; likewise, all such various cloths and even those with hooks and needles that have never been used may all be made into a *kaṭhina* robe.
"Cutting for purification" means cutting the threads to effect purification.
"Dyeing for purification" means dyeing it to effect purification.
"Marking for purification" means marking the corners to effect purification.

Regarding purification by the knife: leaving a space of four finger-widths from the tip of the corner, one cuts through three threads at a single spot with three strokes of the knife; this is called purification by the knife.
If a layperson offers the material for a *kaṭhina* robe to the Saṃgha, one must not accept it in silence.
The recipient should say:
"I now receive this material for the *saṃghāṭī* robe.
Having received it, he should go before the Saṃgha and hold up the cotton cloth; grasping it with his hands, letting it hang down long, and lifting it high, he should say as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has obtained this material for the kaṭhina-cloth. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha take this material for the kaṭhina-cloth.
This is the formal motion (jñapti)."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has obtained this wealth for the kaṭhina-cloth; the Saṃgha now takes this wealth for the kaṭhina-cloth.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to taking this wealth for the kaṭhina-cloth remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."
"The Sangha has finished taking the material for the kaṭhina robe; because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Among the members of the Sangha, there may be one, two, or three persons capable of managing the preparation of the kaṭhina robe.
The *karmakāra* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The Saṃgha has obtained these materials for the *kāṭhina* robe at this time. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha authorize [the names of] such-and-such a bhikṣu and others to prepare the Saṃgha’s *kāṭhina* robe."
The motion is thus made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has obtained these materials for kāṭhina-cloth at this time; the Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so and others to prepare the kāṭhina-cloth."
Venerable sirs, those who approve of [the robe] being made by this bhikṣu, that bhikṣu, and the other persons as the kaṭhina-cloth shall remain silent; those who do not approve shall speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to complete the *kaṭhina* robe; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
When one person among those performing the *karmavācanā* acts as the presiding officer to receive the cloth for the *kaṭhina*, he should speak as follows:
"I receive this cloth for the *kaṭhina*; the Saṃgha shall accept it."
Thus he says three times.
When washing it, he should say:
"I am washing this kaṭhina robe; the Saṃgha shall accept it."
Thus, when cutting, sewing, dyeing, or marking it for purification, one should act according to what has been explained above.
Regarding purification by means of a knife: leaving a space of four finger-widths from the tip of the corner, as one makes a single cut with the knife, one should say:
"This *kaṭhina* robe, the Saṃgha shall accept."
The second and third [times] should also be spoken in this manner.

At the time of performing the purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*), one must speak these words for each instance; if one performs the purification without speaking them, it is still called a *kaṭhina* robe, yet one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga-āpatti*).

If one speaks of each [robe] individually without performing the ritual purification (*kappiya-kamma*), it is not called a *kaṭhina* robe, and one incurs an offense of violating the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga-āpatti*).
If one gives rise to the intention for each one and performs the purification, it is named a *kaṭhina* robe, and there is no offense.
When the Sangha has obtained [the robe] and the robe has been made, all should assemble in harmony.
The person performing the *karmavācanā* should fold the robe, hold it with his hands so that the long ends hang down and lift it high, and should speak as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!..."
"The Sangha has obtained these robes at this time and has finished making them. If it is the proper time for the Sangha, may the Sangha accept these *kaṭhina* robes.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Sangha, listen!
The Sangha has finished making these robes from the cloth obtained at this time; the Sangha now accepts this *kaṭhina* robe.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to this *kaṭhina* robe remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Sangha has finished receiving the kaṭhina robe; because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
One should fold this robe and place it in a chest, scatter various flowers upon it, and proceed from the senior monk (sthavira) downward to recite words of rejoicing:
“Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!”

The Sangha accepts the kaṭhina robe at this dwelling place; I, the bhikṣu [name], rejoice in and accept it for the duration of four winter months, until the end of the period according to where we reside, at which time I shall relinquish it.
Thus it is said three times.

If the assembly consists of ten thousand or twenty thousand members and it is difficult for them to reach a consensus, many individuals may separately prepare the *kaṭhina* robe; everything is as for the large assembly, with the sole difference that "many" is substituted for "the assembly."
Four or more persons may not perform this separately.
If one person performs it alone, when taking [the robe], he should say:
"I now accept this *kaṭhina* cloth."
Thus it was said three times.
At the time of cutting, sewing, washing, dyeing, marking, and purifying with a blade—at the time of cutting—one should say:
"I shall accept this kaṭhina robe."
When sewing, washing, dyeing, marking, or performing the purification by cutting, it is as described above.
Once it has been completed, one should mentally reflect and verbally say:
"I, the bhikṣu [name], accept this kaṭhina robe."
Thus it was said three times.

Regarding those who receive the kaṭhina robe, there are those for whom there is the time of making but not the time of receiving; those for whom there is the time of receiving but not the time of making; those for whom there is both the time of making and the time of receiving; and those for whom there is neither the time of making nor the time of receiving.
Regarding "the time of action is not the time of reception": herein, there is that which encounters the time of action and receives it, even if it does not encounter the time of reception;

this is termed "reception. Regarding "the time of reception is not the time of action": encountering the time of reception and receiving it, even if it is not the time of action; this is termed "reception."

Regarding "one who acts at the time of acting and receives at the time of receiving": this refers to one who receives while encountering the time of acting and the time of receiving; this is called "acting at the time of acting and receiving at the time of receiving.
Regarding "neither acting at the time of acting nor receiving at the time of receiving": this refers to one who does not encounter the time of acting or the time of receiving when receiving;
such a person should express sympathetic joy, saying: "Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!"

The Sangha at this residence has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe; I, the bhikṣu [Name], rejoice in and accept it for the duration of the four winter months. When that residence reaches its full term, I shall relinquish it.
This is called the *kaṭhina* robe procedure.
Regarding that which is not a *kaṭhina* robe: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Sunda-ra-nanda made a *kaṭhina* robe out of coarse *tūla* cotton; the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to use *tūṇa* grass to make a *kaṭhina* robe.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda took *karpāsa* cotton to make a *kaṭhina* robe.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who made [a robe] using small pieces of material;
another bhikṣu made one using old materials;
and another bhikṣu made one using a woolen *kambala* from the land of Vaṅga.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who made robes from human hair;
there were bhikṣus who made robes from grass cloth;
and there were bhikṣus who made robes from leather.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who made robes from tree bark;
there were also bhikṣus who made robes from wooden boards.
The Buddha said:
"In all such cases, it should not be made;
it is not a robe, and thus is not called *kaṭhina*.

Furthermore, there are those which are not called *kaṭhina*: those made out of season, those not purified by cutting the threads, those not purified by dyeing, those not purified by marking, and those not purified by the knife—these are not called *kaṭhina*."
Regarding the procedure for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who frequently changed his robes; he wore one set before the meal and another after the meal. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"Your robes change so often; whose robes are these?"
He replied,
"World-Honored One,
it is my robe."
The Buddha asked, "Why so many?
They replied:
"I have received the kaṭhina robe.
The Buddha said,
"How can you receive the kaṭhina robe at all times?"
"From this day forward, you should abandon it.
There are ten matters regarding abandonment.
What are the ten?
1. Relinquishing after the robe-making is finished;
2. Relinquishing at the time of receiving it;
3. Relinquishing when the time limit has expired.
4. Relinquishment through hearing;
5. Relinquishment through sending away;
6. Relinquishment through destruction.
7. Abandonment through loss;
8. Abandonment through departure;
9. Abandonment through the lapse of time.
Tenth is relinquishment by completion.
Regarding relinquishment by the completion of the robe: when receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, one forms this thought:
"Once I have finished making the robe, I shall relinquish the *kaṭhina*."
Once the robe has been completed, it is termed "abandoned"; this is called "abandonment upon completion of the robe.
Regarding "abandonment at the time of receiving": one forms this thought:
"At the time of receiving this robe, I shall abandon the kaṭhina."
When one receives the robe-cloth, it is called "abandoned upon receipt"; this is termed "abandoned at the time of receipt.
Regarding "abandoned when the period has ended," one forms this thought:
"For such a length of time, I shall abandon the kaṭhina robe."
When the period has expired, it is termed "abandoned"; this is called "abandonment by the lapse of time.
Regarding "abandonment upon hearing," one forms this thought:
"When I hear that the Upādhyāya or Ācārya is abandoning the kaṭhina robe, I shall abandon it as well."
Later, he hears the Upādhyāya and Ācārya say, "Today the Saṃgha has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
At that moment, it is considered relinquished; this is called relinquishment by hearing.
Regarding "abandoning by sending": one forms this thought:
"Once I have given these robes to another, I shall relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe.
After the robes have been sent, it is then called "relinquished"; this is termed "abandoning by sending."
Regarding "abandonment through destruction": after having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, one says of one's own accord in the interim, "I now relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe.
At the moment these words are spoken, it is termed "relinquished"; this is called abandonment through destruction.
Regarding "loss through abandonment": one forms this thought:
"This robe has become worn out and ruined in the interim and is no longer visible; I shall abandon it.
Later, when the robe becomes worn out or is lost, that is called "abandonment"; this is termed "loss through abandonment."
Regarding "renouncing by going out": one forms this thought:
"While I am staying here, I shall renounce the *kaṭhina* robe when I go out.
If it is renounced at the very moment of going out, this is called the time of renunciation by going out.

Regarding "abandonment by lapse of time": if one does not abandon [the robe] on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, but abandons it on the sixteenth day, this is called abandonment by lapse of time; it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense of transgression (*viniyatikkama*), and is thus termed "abandonment by lapse of time."
Regarding the ultimate relinquishment: it should be relinquished on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. Within the assembly of monks, one person should make this proclamation:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
Today the Sangha relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe."
Thus it is said three times; this is called "final relinquishment.
These ten matters are known as the *kaṭhina* robe relinquishment rules (*kaṭhina-vastra-niḥsargadharma*). Regarding the rules for robes:

the robe before the end of the rainy season retreat, the robe at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, the robe during the retreat, fear for one's life, fear for the loss of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), out-of-season robes, in-season robes, and Kauśāmbī.
Regarding those whose *vassa* (rainy season retreat) has not yet concluded: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having completed their *vassa* in a village but before it had formally ended, went to the donors' residences and said this:
"Long-lived ones!..."
"Please accept this robe-offering for my *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Now is not the proper time; wait until the rains retreat has ended.
Once the harvest is completed, the people will be joyful and, mindful of his kindness, will give rise to the intention to offer alms; only then will there be any giving."
The bhikṣu said:
“Long-lived one!
You do not realize that the world is impermanent; whether by king, fire, water, or robbery, such as this, I shall suffer loss of profit and you shall suffer loss of merit.”
The donor said:
"Venerable One!
You merely point out impermanence to me, yet you do not see it yourself."
"Venerable One!
Do you wish to obtain the goods for the rains retreat quickly, so as to take them elsewhere?
Or do you intend to abandon the path, which is why you are in such a hurry?"
How strange! How marvelous!
Such great desire knows no satiety.
Having conceived a mind of displeasure, they departed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! Why have you requested the robe-offering for the rainy season retreat before the retreat has concluded?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to request the robe-offering for the rains retreat (*varṣāśāṭī*) until the retreat has concluded; [anyone who does so commits] a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called "the retreat not yet concluded."
Regarding "the conclusion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, after the various bhikṣus had completed their *varṣā* at the Jetavana Monastery, they distributed the *varṣā-cīvara* (robes obtained during the rainy season).
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having completed their rainy-season retreat elsewhere, came into the midst of the assembly and spoke as follows:
"Venerable sirs!

The World-Honored One has prescribed that once the rainy-season retreat is finished, one should receive the *varṣāśāṭī* robe; we too have finished our retreat and should receive the *varṣāśāṭī* robe. Give us our share of the *varṣāśāṭī* robes."
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"One who observes the rains retreat in another location shall not receive a share of the robes from this location; one receives a share according to the place where one has observed the retreat."
This is called the conclusion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Regarding those who observe the *varṣā*: the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, when the six groups of bhikṣus reached the period of the *varṣā*, after having received their lodgings, they placed leather sandals, dyeing equipment, and various other minor items inside the rooms, and then spoke these words:
"Venerable elders!
I am observing the rains retreat here; do not harbor further resentment toward me, for I know that you have always disliked me.
He then hired someone to take his share of the *kaṭhina* robes and proceeded to observe the retreat elsewhere.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"One must be in summer retreat at that location; it is there that one receives one's share of robes."
Regarding those who fear for their lives: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a great famine in Vaiśālī where alms were difficult to obtain; consequently, the bhikṣus went toward Śrāvastī, arriving just as the bhikṣus of Jetavana had finished their summer retreat and were distributing the robes.
While the Vaisali bhiksus were seated, a bhiksu from Jetavana asked them:
"Venerable sirs!

The World-honored One has established this rule: 'One who observes the rains retreat in a certain place shall receive a share of the robes from that place. In which place did you observe the rains retreat?"
He replied, "Elder!
I have come because I fear for my life; had I not come, I would have died of hunger."
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"If they have come for the sake of saving their lives, you should give them a share of the robes."
This is called "fearing the loss of life. Regarding "fearing the loss of the holy life":
at that time, there was a son of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who had gone forth as a monk in the city of Rājagṛha. His parents wished to make him desist from the religious life, so another person said:
"The śramaṇas observe the heavy *varṣā* retreat; during the retreat they certainly do not travel anywhere. You may make him desist at that time."
His elder sister, who had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma, said to her younger brother, "Your parents wish to make you abandon the Way; you should flee at once.
The younger brother immediately set out for Śrāvastī, where he encountered the monks of Jetavana concluding their summer retreat and distributing the robes.
While that bhikṣu was among the assembly, a bhikṣu from Jetavana asked him:
"Venerable sir!

The World-Honored One has prescribed that one must observe the rains retreat in this place and receive one's share of robes here; however, those who come fearing for their lives may still receive their share."
"How could you have replied, 'My parents wish to make me abandon the Path; if I do not come back, I shall lose my holy life'?
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"To one who comes fearing the loss of the holy life (brahmacarya), a share of the robes should be given.
This is called "fearing the loss of the holy life."
Regarding "out-of-season robes": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human realm who arrived with a cart fully loaded with robes.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Whose robe is this?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is my robe.
He asked again:
"Is this a robe for the proper season, or is it a robe for the improper season?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Is this an out-of-season robe?
"Has it been purified by the act of giving? He replied:
"No," the Buddha said.
"All these robes should be given to the community of monks."
This is called "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*).
Regarding the "in-season robe" (*kālacīvara*): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the countryside who arrived with a cart full of robes.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Whose robe is this?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is my robe.
He asked again:
"Is this robe for the proper season or for the improper season?
He replied, "It is for the proper season."
The Buddha said:
"These robes are too many; reduce them by half and give them to the Saṃgha.
This is called "timely robe" (kālacīvara).
Regarding Kauśāmbī: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

A raiding party from the kingdom of Kosala seized the village of Kauśāmbī and brought it to Śrāvastī; the bhikṣus who had previously entered the rains retreat in that village followed them there immediately.
At that time, monks from Jetavana arrived at this village seeking the offerings for the rainy season retreat robes.
The monks of Kauśāmbī said,
"Elders!..."
"I previously relied on this village for the rains retreat; therefore, I should be the first to request [a dwelling].
After the two had thus disputed, they went together to the place where the Buddha was and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"In this regard, regarding the rainy season retreat, one should seek [the site] first, and only then may others seek it;
if two people seek it together, they should share it."
"If a bhikṣu who is in the midst of the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) has not yet requested [permission], and another person requests it on his behalf, there is an offense of violating the Vinaya.

Furthermore, at that time, the Venerable Kapphiṇa had two co-practicing disciples who, out of some resentment, renounced the precepts; however, without breaking their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), they returned to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, when the bhikṣus of Jetavana had finished their summer retreat and were distributing the robes, they did not give him a share. He said this:
"Venerable sirs!
Because I had something to be dissatisfied with, I renounced the precepts; yet, without breaking my pure conduct, I have returned to receive full ordination again. You should give me a share."
They went together to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If one has abandoned the precepts due to some resentment, yet does not violate the holy life (brahmacarya), and returns to receive full ordination, one should be given an equal share of the distribution."
The Buddha said:
"There are five things that should not be given.
What are the five?
"Being suspended (ukkhepana), renouncing the path, death, breaking the rains retreat, and departing without having informed. Regarding "suspended":

among the three types of views, if one holds any one of them—namely, slandering the Sūtras, holding evil and heterodox views, or holding extreme views—and after being admonished, does not relinquish them, a formal act of suspension (ukkhepa-kamma) is performed; this is called "suspension."

Regarding those who have abandoned the path: one should not grant [the robe] to one who has forsaken the precepts. If, relying on the power of a king, or the power of a great minister, or the power of a band of thieves, someone makes this statement:
"If the śramaṇa does not give me my share, I shall do him harm."
"In such cases, although the person should not receive it, it ought to be given; this is called 'abandoning the path' (*pravrajyā-tyāga*).

Regarding 'death' (*anityatā*): one who has died should not receive a share. If the robes for the *varṣā* have already been collected but not yet distributed, and at the point of death one entrusts them to a certain person, they should be given to that person after the death; this is called 'death'."
Regarding one who has broken the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat): if a bhikṣu neither observes the early retreat nor the late retreat, he should not receive [the robe];

however, if it is due to the power of a king, a high minister, or bandits—[thinking], "If they do not give it to me, they shall do me harm"—then although such a person should not receive it, it should be given to him.
Regarding "departing without having made an announcement": if someone takes their share of the robes and departs without having announced their intention, one should not give it to them.
The person distributing the items should ask:
"Who took such-and-such a person's share?"
If there is anyone who takes [the items], one should ask:
"Did you take them as instructed when you left?
They should answer:
"Do not worry. One should say to them:
"Do not be anxious about this matter."
If he says, "I entrust it to you," one should examine the person before accepting.
If the person is trustworthy, one should give it to them; if they are not trustworthy, one should say:
"Do not worry about this matter.
If two people were previously in agreement and have always taken things for one another, one should give it to them.
These are called the five matters.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat, went to the village where he had been born. Because this bhikṣu had arrived, his kinsmen and relatives prepared extensive offerings and bestowed upon him robes and other requisites.
The resident monks who had previously entered the rains retreat in this village did not give this bhikṣu a share of the robes, as they were given after [the retreat] had concluded.
His relatives asked him,
"Did you receive a share of the robes?"
He replied, "I cannot.
His relatives said:
"I have prepared this offering for your sake; why may I not receive it?
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"A donor has prepared an offering for this bhikṣu; you should share it with him.
The Buddha said, "There are five kinds of giving by sound: [text continues]"

These are: giving robes to the community of monks who are in retreat; giving the value of robes to the community of monks who are in retreat; giving goods to the community of monks who are in retreat; giving the value of goods to the community of monks who are in retreat; and giving to those who are in retreat at a specific location. These are called the five.
If a donor wishes to give to other bhikṣus as well, it should be given according to the donor's intention.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of items that, by the donor’s word, should belong to the present Saṃgha.
What are the four?
My gift of robes, the price for robes, goods, and the price for goods—these are called the four kinds of items belonging to the *saṃmukha-saṃgha*.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds that should belong to the *saṃmukha-saṃgha*.
What are the ten? They are:

medicine for the daytime, medicine for the night-watch, medicine for seven days, medicine for the duration of life, the property of a deceased bhikṣu, gifts for the monastery, provisions for a great assembly, out-of-season robes, miscellaneous items, and invitations to meals.

Regarding "medicines for the proper time" (*kālabhaiṣajya*): these include food before the meal, food after the meal, and *tobhana*-food; these are to be received by the present Saṃgha, and are thus called medicines for the proper time.
Regarding "medicines for the night period" (*rātribhaiṣajya*): these refer to the fourteen kinds of syrups, which should be explained in detail; these are called medicines for the night period.
Regarding the seven-day medicines: ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, and ointments—these should be explained in detail—and these are called the seven-day medicines.
Regarding the lifetime medicines: harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalaka—as explained in detail in the second precept—and these are called the lifetime medicines.

Regarding the property of a deceased bhikṣu: when a bhikṣu dies, whatever robes, alms bowls, or miscellaneous items he possesses shall be obtained by the *saṃgha* present there; this is called the property of a deceased bhikṣu.

Regarding the gift of a dwelling place: if a donor has constructed a monastic cell or a vihāra and holds a great assembly, and then offers this dwelling place along with various other articles, the present community of monks (saṃgha) should receive them; this is called the gift of a dwelling place.

Regarding the great assemblies: the assembly for the Buddha’s birth, the assembly for enlightenment, the assembly for turning the wheel of Dharma, the assembly for Ānanda, the assembly for Rāhula, and the five-year assembly (pañcavārṣika). Among these, the items offered should be received by the *saṃgha* present.

Regarding "out-of-season robes": when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, it is for eleven months; when the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, it is for seven months. Any items offered during this period should be received by the *saṃgha* present before them; these are called out-of-season robes.

"Miscellaneous items" refers to alms bowls, bowl-rests, waist-bands, knives, needle-cases, leather sandals, oil-skin bags, water-flasks (*kuṇḍikā*), and ritual jars (*kamaṇḍalu*). When such miscellaneous items are offered as gifts, they shall be received by the *saṃgha* present; these are called "miscellaneous items."
Regarding "invited for a meal":
when a donor invites the *saṃgha* present before them to eat, one proceeds in due order; this is called "invited for a meal.
These are the ten matters that the *saṃgha* present before them should receive.

Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the bhikṣus did not cut threads when making robes; the full explanation is as given above in the section on the three kinds of discoloration for the pāyattika offenses.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Listen to me as I put on this one robe; it is to have few desires and few concerns.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"If you carry only the three robes, the water flask, and the alms bowl, that is itself having few desires and few concerns."
Again, another bhikṣu said:
"Allow me to wear the three robes.
Yet another bhikṣu said:
“Listen to me as I wear a *kambala* made of goat wool.
Another bhikṣu said:
“Listen to me as I wear a *kambala* made of hair.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
"Allow me to wear a horse-tail *kambala*.
Yet another bhikṣu said:
“Allow me to wear clothing made of grass,” said another bhikṣu. Yet another bhikṣu said:
“Allow me to wear clothing made of tree bark.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
"I request permission to wear leather garments.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, none of these robes should be worn.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:
"I request permission to go naked, for I have few desires and few concerns."
The Buddha said, “Monks! This is the dharma of the outsiders;
you should instead maintain the three robes, the water flask, and the alms bowl, which constitute having few desires and few affairs.”
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.
At that time, the bhikṣus wore robes of bright colors, which caused the people of the world to criticize them:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear robes of bright colors, no different from worldly people?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to wear garments of superior colors."

Regarding "superior colors": dyeing with *kukku*, *kāṃci*, *kubjaka*, *lākṣā*, *lodhra*, *cīnapiṣṭa* or saffron, madder, indigo, black, or the color of flowers—all such superior colors are not permitted.
One should employ dyes derived from roots, leaves, flowers, or tree bark, down to even dyeing with *kumuda* juice.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, he was walking back and forth before the cave of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, when he saw the rice fields of Magadha with their ridges and furrows clearly defined and properly aligned.
Having seen this, he said to the bhikṣus:
"The dharma of the robes of the past Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, ought indeed to be just like this."
"From this day forward, you shall use this method when making robes.
Furthermore, at that time, while the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was making a saṃghāṭī, the World-Honored One held it with his own hands and the Venerable Ānanda cut it.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who mended by patching, bhikṣus who stitched with short stitches, bhikṣus who stitched with long stitches, bhikṣus who stitched along the edges, and bhikṣus who attached fastenings and ties.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who made a robe by painting leaves on it. The Buddha said:
"Painting leaves is not permitted.
There was another bhikṣu who made leaves by folding [the cloth]. The Buddha said:
"One must not fold [the cloth] into layers; it should be cut into strips.
A bhikṣu sewed them together at the ends, and the Buddha said:
"Sewing at the ends is not permitted. One should make layers; the widest may be four finger-breadths, and the narrowest like a barley grain."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who made the leaf-seams facing in only one direction.
The Buddha said, "This is not permitted; they should face both ways.
There was another bhikṣu who made his robe with the horizontal leaf-seams meeting exactly at the center. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit it.

A five-strip robe should have one long and one short panel; a seven-strip robe up to a thirteen-strip robe should have two long and one short panel; and a fifteen-strip robe should have three long and one short panel."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who made a robe by sewing leaves so that they were attached to the garment; the Buddha said, "This is not permitted.
Later, the garment became loose and detached; the Buddha said:
"It should be made with horse-tooth [stitches].
A bhikṣu’s robe was torn at the top and bottom, and the Buddha said:
"It should be provided with a border."
There was a bhikṣu who made robes of four colors; the Buddha said, "This is not permitted;
they should be of a single color.
There was another bhikṣu who obtained a robe of superior color and wished to wash it to ruin its hue; the Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
“Monk! What do you wish to do? He replied:
“The World-Honored One has prohibited the wearing of dyed robes of superior colors; I wish to wash them to ruin their color.
The Buddha said:
“There is no need to wash them; I allow you to dye them with other colors to ruin their original appearance.”
There are seven kinds of robes:
first, the *kambala* robe;
second, the *kārpāsa* robe; [and so forth].
3. Kṣauma robes; 4. Kauśeya robes; 5. Śāṇa robes;
Sixth, the hempen garment;
seventh, the *kauravika* garment.
These are called the rules for robes.
The Poṣadha and the Karmavācanā, Giving consent and declaring purity,
The rains retreat and the Pravāraṇā, Accepting the kaṭhina robe and not accepting the kaṭhina robe, And relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
The distribution of robes at the conclusion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
The fourth *varga* concludes.
Regarding the rules for sick bhikṣus: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; the detailed account is as above.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Bring me the keys; the Tathāgata wishes to inspect the monks' quarters.
He replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One! he said,
and immediately taking the keys, he followed behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at a dilapidated room and saw a sick bhikṣu lying amidst excrement and filth, unable to rise by himself.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"How is your strength?"
"Is your ailment increasing or diminishing? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The affliction only increases and does not diminish.
He then asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you obtain food today?"
"No, World-Honored One! Did you obtain it yesterday?"
“No, World-Honored One.
“Did you receive it the day before yesterday?”
“No, World-Honored One!
It has already been seven days since I last received food.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you not eat because you had obtained [food],
or did you not eat because you had not obtained it?"
He replied,
“I cannot, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Do you have a preceptor here?
"I do not," he replied.
“World-Honored One!
Is there a preceptor? “There is none.”
“World-Honored One!
Is there an ācārya? “There is none.”
“World-Honored One!
‘Is there anyone who has been my preceptor?
‘There is none.’”
“World-Honored One!
Is there a bhikṣu named Anupama-śālā?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Because I am foul-smelling and filthy, they do not like me and have moved me away to another place.
I am solitary and suffering.”
"Bhagavān! I am alone. Sugata!"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
“Do not be distressed; I shall be your companion.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"Bring the robe; I shall wash it for you.
At that time, Ānanda said to the Buddha, "Let it be, World-Honored One!"
"This is the robe of the sick bhikṣu; I shall wash it for him.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You wash the robe, and I shall pour water."
Ānanda immediately washed [the bedding], and the World-Honored One poured water over it. Once washed, he dried it in the sun.

At that time, Ānanda took a sick bhikṣu and placed him on the open ground; he removed the excrement and filth, took out the mattresses and all the impure vessels, and sprinkled water inside the room. Having swept and thoroughly scrubbed the floor, he washed and aired the bedding, wove new corded mats, and spread them back in their original places.
Having bathed the sick bhikṣu, he was gently laid upon his bed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his golden, soft hand adorned with immeasurable merit, stroked the bhikṣu’s forehead and asked:
"Has your ailment increased or diminished?"
The bhikṣu said, “Having received the World-Honored One’s hand upon my forehead, all my sufferings have been entirely removed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught the Dharma in accordance with the needs of the sick bhikṣu and inspired a heart of joy, further expounded the Dharma for him, whereby he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

After the bhikṣu had been appointed, the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down. He recounted the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus and asked:
"Which bhikṣu was that from the neighboring room?"
He replied,
"It is I, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) are afflicted by illness, if you do not look after one another, who then shall look after them?

Each of you comes from different lineages and different families; having with faith left the home life for the homeless state, you all share the same lineage as Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya. If fellow practitioners of the holy life do not look after one another when ill, who then shall look after them?"

"Monks! It is just as, for example, when the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Sarayū, and the Mahī flow into the great ocean, they all lose their original names and merge into a single taste, which is called the great ocean."
In this way, you have each abandoned your original surnames and all share the same surname: the śramaṇas, sons of Śākya.
If you do not look after one another, who indeed shall look after you?

For example, it is like the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, who, though each belonging to different lineages, are all called "sea-merchants" once they have entered the great ocean together.
"Thus it is, bhikṣus!

You each come from different lineages and different families; having with faith left the home life for the homeless state and renounced your homes to go forth, you all share the same lineage as śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya. Since you do not look after one another, who indeed shall look after you?"
If a bhikṣu is ill, his preceptor (upādhyāya) should attend to him;
if there is no preceptor, those who share the same preceptor should attend to him.
If he does not attend to him, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If there is an ācārya, the ācārya should look after him;
if there is no ācārya, one who is like an ācārya should look after him;
if he does not look after him, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vibhinī-āpatti).
If there is a fellow resident, that fellow resident should look after it;
if there is no fellow resident, a neighboring room should look after it.
If one does not do so, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
If there is no attendant cell, the Saṃgha should appoint someone to look after the patient; as many people as are required according to the patient's needs should be provided.
If no one looks after them, all members of the Saṃgha commit an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
"Go back and look for the sick bhikṣu in his original cell.
Not far from where the Buddha was, the Buddha transformed himself into a sick śrāmaṇera and said:
“You have examined this sick śrāmaṇera; this shall be both a blessing and a punishment for you.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above, at that time two bhikṣus from the south came together to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the way, one bhikṣu fell ill. Another bhikṣu waited for him for two or three days and said to the sick bhikṣu, "I wish to go along with you to pay my respects to the World-Honored One!"
"You may come after you have recovered.
The sick bhikṣu said, "Elder!"
"Wait until I have dispatched [the others], and we shall go together. He replied, "Elder!"
"I have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time; I have yearned for him as one parched with thirst. I could not bear to wait, so you were sent back.
That bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Knowing this, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
"From where have you come?"
The bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus!...”
This is an evil matter.

If there is a bhikṣu whose mind harbors negligence, indolence, and a lack of diligence; who cannot restrain his sense faculties and runs wild after the six desires—though he may dwell near me, he does not see me, and I do not see him.
If there is a bhikṣu who can restrain his faculties and keep his mind from negligence, focusing his mindfulness on the Path, then even though he is far from me, he is seeing me, and I also see him.
Why is this? Because it accords with the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, because it destroys all evils, because it is free from desire, and because it cultivates tranquility.
You bhikṣus have likewise left the household life to practice the holy life; if you do not look after one another, who then shall?
"Go back and attend to the sick bhikṣu.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, there were at that time two bhikṣus from the country of Pārañjika who came together as companions to inquire after the World-Honored One's health. Upon arriving at the village of Bhr̥ṅgāra, one bhikṣu fell ill. The other bhikṣu waited for two or three days and then said to the sick bhikṣu:
"I wish to go together with you to inquire after the World-Honored One's health.
Once you have recovered, you may come slowly.
The sick bhikṣu said:
"Elder! Wait until I have recovered, and then we shall go together.
He replied:
"Elder! I have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time; my longing for him is like thirst, and I cannot endure waiting.
The sick bhikṣu said:
"If you must go, please convey my regards to the householder Citta-gahapati.
The bhikṣu then went to the householder's residence and spoke these words:
"Long-lived one!"
"The two of us have come from afar wishing to go and visit the Buddha; now one of us has fallen ill and wishes to remain here temporarily.
Long-life!
Please attend to our needs on our behalf, for we wish to proceed ahead to pay our respects to the World-Honored One."
The householder said, "Venerable sir!
You should stay here for a while so that we may look after one another; once you have recovered, we shall both depart together."
He replied, "Householder! It is not so;
it has been a long time since I have seen the Buddha, and I yearn for him as if parched with thirst."
The householder said, "Venerable sir, please depart;
the World-Honored One will surely send you back, so you will only weary yourself in vain.
Yet the bhikṣu continued on his way until he reached the Buddha's dwelling, where he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"From where have you come?
The bhikṣu then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Monks! This is an evil deed."

Each of you comes from a different clan; though you have faith in the homeless life, having left your homes to go forth, you now belong to the same Śākya lineage. Yet, when illness strikes, you do not look after one another—then who shall look after you?
“Go back and attend to the sick bhikṣu.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as related in detail above, there was at that time a bhikṣu coming from the north who wished to pay his respects to the World-Honored One. Upon hearing that there was a sick bhikṣu by the side of the road, he had this thought:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept that those who are ill must be attended to; if I were to see him, I would not be able to proceed.
He immediately turned back and departed, going to where the Buddha was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrawing to stand to one side.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally:
"From where have you come? He replied:
“World-Honored One, I have come from the north.
“By which path have you come?
He replied:
“From which path have you come?
The Buddha said,
“For what reason and by what conditions have you abandoned the direct path to come by a circuitous route?”
The bhikṣus reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣus!
"This is an evil deed; thus it continues until you must return and attend to the sick bhikṣu.

Regarding the rule for the attendant bhikṣu: if a bhikṣu falls ill while traveling with a caravan through a wilderness, his fellow bhikṣus may not abandon him. They should take him along, carry his robes and bowl on his behalf, and remain close by to support and assist him rather than leaving him behind.
If one is unable to proceed, one should borrow a vehicle or beast of burden from a merchant or trader, saying these words:
"Long-lived one!
This renunciant is ill and cannot keep pace with his companions; for my sake, carry me so that I may escape this hardship."
"If you obtain it, that is well.
If he says:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I am carrying a heavy load.
One should reply:
"Long-lived one!"
"I shall pay the price for the grain and fodder.
If he succeeds in obtaining them, he must not load them onto a cow-drawn cart or a female horse; rather, he should load them onto a bull-drawn cart or a stallion.
If one is so critically ill as to be unable to distinguish anything, there is no offense in using a vehicle.
If a vehicle cannot be obtained, one should leave behind a capable attendant—whether it be one person, two persons, or three persons—and say:
"You, my attendant, I shall go to the village to seek a vehicle and return to fetch you."
"One should leave provisions so that those staying behind do not suffer from lack.
If each says,
'Who can abandon body and life in the wilderness?'"

Since no one was willing to stay, he could not simply depart; instead, he built a hut, spread out a bed of grass, kindled a fire, and provided water and wood. He left behind *tatkṣaṇika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, and *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*, and said to the sick man:
"Venerable One!..."
"Settle your minds; when I reach the next village, I shall seek a vehicle to come and welcome you.
Upon arriving in the village, one must not circumambulate stupas or pay respects to one's preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya). Instead, one should say to the monks in the village:
"There is a sick monk in the wilderness; let us go together to welcome him back."
If one asks, "Where is it?
the answer is:
"At such-and-such a place. If one says:
"In that place there are many tigers and wolves; I fear they will devour them all, so that not even one in ten thousand will remain."
"Even upon hearing these words, one must not stop; one must certainly go to see for oneself.
Even if one sees crows and birds from afar, one must not simply turn back, but must reach that place."
If he has already died, one should make offerings to his remains. If he is still alive, one should bring him to a village and say to the resident bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
This is a sick bhikṣu from such-and-such a place; having made offerings to him in the wilderness, I have now come here, and it is next for the Venerables to attend to him."
If one does not look, it is a *vinaya-āpatti*.
If there is no bhikṣu present, one should say to the upāsaka:
"Long-lived one!"
"There is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness; please lend me a vehicle to go and fetch him.
The donor asked, "Where is he?"
In this manner, they should even escort them to the house of the donor and place them in a separate screened area.
If there are many people, two or three who are capable of nursing the patient should be selected to attend to them.
If the patient says,
"Many people must stay here for my comfort," then all should remain together to solicit offerings—

food before the meal, food after the meal, medicines taken at the proper time, medicines taken at night, seven-day medicines, and lifetime medicines— to provide for them so that they suffer no lack or exhaustion.
If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one must not immediately say:
"Venerable sir!
You must attend to the sick bhikṣu."
One should say,
"Welcome, Elder!
One should carry his robes and bowl for him, prepare a seat for him, and provide water for washing his feet as well as oil for anointing them.
If they arrive at the proper time, one should give them food for the morning or the afternoon; if they arrive at an improper time, one should give them non-time drink.
Once they have rested, one should say:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have been looking after this sick bhikṣu for a long time.
Venerable sir,
you should look after him next."
"If it is impermanent, one should make offerings to the relics.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī are traveling together with merchants, and the bhikṣuṇī falls ill, the bhikṣu must not abandon her and depart;
he should say: 'Go!'"
"Go! Sister, take her and receive her.
This should be understood as explained in the section concerning bhikṣus, with the sole exception of embracing and grasping.
If one requires massage or oil applied to the body, one should employ a woman to perform it.
If there is no permanent resident [monk], and the deceased has robes and a bowl, one should hire someone to cremate them; if there are none, one should depart.
A layperson remarked with disdain:
"Why do you leave this corpse here?
If one can conceive of it as being like the earth, one should carry it away to a distant place.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a virtuous bhikṣu who is ill, how should he be attended to?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
“When a bhikṣu of great virtue is ill, he must not be placed in a marginal, dilapidated, or small room, nor in a secluded or remote place; he should be placed in a well-exposed room.”

The co-practicing disciples and the resident disciples shall constantly attend upon him at his side, sweeping and sprinkling the room, grinding [incense] and smearing the floor, burning various famous incenses so that no foul odors remain, and arranging beds and seats.
If a bhikṣu comes to inquire after his illness, he should be given food before or after the midday meal; if he arrives at an improper time, he should be given non-time-appropriate gruel.
If there is a matter to be discussed, the patient should respond.
If the patient is too weak, the attendant should answer.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) comes to inquire after him, he should say:
"Welcome, long-lived one!"
He spoke, inviting him to take a seat and then preached the Dharma to him:
"You have gained great merit.
As the World-Honored One has said:"
“Look upon this sick bhikṣu who maintains the precepts as you look upon me, without any difference.
If there is an offering, he should accept it while reciting a prayer of blessing.
If the patient suffers from diarrhea, the visitor should not remain for long, but should quickly depart.
If the patient is unable to go out, one should keep three vessels for removing excrement:
one to be given to the patient, one to carry it out, and one to be washed and smeared with oil and dried in the sun; in this manner, they are used alternately.
One person should stand by the door so that no one enters abruptly;
another person should stay by the side of the sick person and, from time to time, preach the Dharma in accordance with their needs.
Thus it is, Upāli!
"A bhikṣu who is a *bhadanta* and is ill should be attended to in this manner.
Then the Venerable Upāli again asked the World-Honored One:
"How should a bhikṣu who is of minor virtue and is ill be attended to?"
The Buddha told Upāli:

"Regarding a sick bhikṣu of little virtue, one should not place him in a conspicuous location where his foul stench might permeate the outside; nor should he be placed in a secluded or private spot so that people would not know of his death when it occurs. He should instead be laid among the people."
If the sick person has a preceptor (upādhyāya), a teacher (ācārya), a co-practitioner disciple, or a dependent disciple, they should attend to him.
If there is no one [among these], the Saṃgha should appoint one, two, or three people to attend to the patient.
If the patient has funds for medicine and requisites outside of his robes and bowl, they should be taken and provided to him.
If he has none, the Sangha should provide them.
If the Sangha has none, and the patient possesses robes and a bowl of high value, these should be exchanged for items of lesser value to provide for the patient.
If a sick person is stingy, one should address the community of monks, saying: "Venerable Sangha!
This sick bhikṣu named So-and-so does not understand impermanence; he is miserly regarding his robes and bowl and refuses to exchange them."
Having made this announcement to the Saṃgha, he should speak with gentle words and teach the Dharma so that the person gains understanding; only then may they exchange goods.
If [the other party] still has nothing, he should beg for something and give it to them.
If he cannot obtain anything, he should take some of the best items from the communal food of the Saṃgha and give them.
If, moreover, there is none [to provide], the attendant should take two alms bowls into the village for alms; he should give the better one to the patient.
Upāli! This is called the rule for a monk attending to a sick monk of minor virtue.
"A patient who possesses five qualities is difficult to care for. What are the five? They are:

being unable to take medicine or food appropriate to the illness; not following the instructions of the caregiver; not knowing when the illness is worsening or improving; being unable to endure the pain of suffering; and being indolent and lacking wisdom. These are called the five qualities by which a patient is difficult to care for."
A patient who accomplishes five qualities is easy to care for. What are these five? They are:

being able to take medicine according to the illness and food according to the illness; following the instructions of the caregiver; informing others when asked about whether the illness is increasing or decreasing; being able to endure pain; and being diligent and wise. These are called the five qualities by which a patient is easy to care for.
There are five things that, when accomplished, prevent one from being able to tend to the sick. What are these five?

Being excessively defiled such that one cannot empty the vessels for excrement and urine, the spittoon, and so forth; failing to seek out medicine appropriate to the illness or food appropriate to the illness for the patient; failing to preach the Dharma in accordance with the patient's needs from time to time; and having a mind full of expectations while begrudging one’s own labor. These are called the five things that prevent one from tending to the sick.

There are five qualities by which one becomes a capable caregiver for the sick: being free from impurity in handling vessels for excrement and urine, spittoons, and the like; being able to procure medicine and food appropriate to the illness for the patient; being able to preach the Dharma to the patient appropriately from time to time; and having no expectation of reward while not begrudging one's own labor. These are called the five qualities of a capable caregiver for the sick.
If a patient possesses nine conditions, they will certainly die an untimely death even though their life span has not yet ended.
What are these nine?
First, knowing that food is not beneficial, yet greedily consuming it.
2. Not knowing how to exercise moderation;
3. Eating while the previous meal has not yet been digested;
4. Vomiting after food has not yet been digested.
5. Having digested [the previous meal], one continues to hold onto food that ought to be eliminated.
6. One does not eat food according to the illness.
7. While eating food according to the illness, one fails to exercise proper moderation.
8. Laziness. 9. Lack of wisdom.
These are called the nine factors by the accomplishment of which one will inevitably meet with an untimely death.
Furthermore, there are nine factors by the accomplishment of which one will never meet with an untimely death.
What are the nine?
First, knowing that food which is not beneficial, one eats little.
Second, one skillfully knows how to exercise moderation.
3. Eating after internal food has been digested;
4. Not forcing oneself to vomit;
5. Not forcing oneself to retain [undigested food].
Sixth, not eating food that does not accord with one's illness.
Seventh, when eating food that accords with one's illness, being able to exercise moderation.
Eighth, being free from indolence.
Ninth, possessing wisdom—these are called the nine dharmas through which one will ultimately never die an untimely death.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"There are three kinds of sick people."
What are the three?
There is a sick person who obtains medicine appropriate to the illness and food appropriate to the illness, and dies despite being nursed according to the Dharma.
Or there is a sick person who does not obtain medicine appropriate to the illness and food appropriate to the illness, yet lives despite being nursed according to the Dharma.

If a sick person obtains medicine suited to their illness and food suited to their illness, and obtains a nurse who attends to them in accordance with the Dharma, the illness will certainly be cured and they will not die. Upāli!

Among the sick bhikṣus, there are those who would die if they did not receive proper care, yet would live if they did; therefore, one should provide careful attention, striving to ensure they are settled in accordance with the Dharma, for this constitutes the gift of life.
"Therefore, tending to the sick brings great merit, as praised by all the Buddhas.
This is called the rule for those who tend to the sick. Regarding the rule for medicine:

while the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala, at that time the Venerable Śāriputra suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta). The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"What medicine do you require?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is *harītakī*.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to consume harītakī.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Wait until I have returned to Śrāvastī and inform me; I shall then establish the medicinal regulations for my disciples."
When the Buddha returned to Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
You should establish a rule for medicinal substances for the sake of your disciples; now is precisely the right time.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to take medicine. Regarding the rules for medicine:
there are roots that may be taken at the proper time and roots that may be taken at improper times; likewise for stalks, bark, leaves, fruits, and syrups.

Regarding "roots of the proper time" (*kāla-mūla*): radish roots, scallion roots, *kṣipra* roots, *āmlavetasa* roots, taro roots, *mudgara* roots, lotus root, and others of this kind that are suitable for food—these are called "roots of the proper time."

Regarding roots that are not for the proper time: the pāṭhā root, the pippalī root, the nyagrodha root, the kharjūra root, the sugandhaka root, and others of this kind that are not combined with food—these are called roots that are not for the proper time.
The same applies to the stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
As for "drinks," there are drinks permitted at the proper time (*kāla-pāna*) and drinks not permitted at the proper time (*akāla-pāna*).
Drinks permitted at the proper time include all rice gruel, steamed grain broth, and milk-curd drinks; these are called drinks permitted at the proper time.

Regarding "non-timely beverages" (vikāla-pāna): all beans, all grains, and all wheat whose husks have been soaked but not split; ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar—these are called non-timely beverages.
If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says,
"He will live if given this food, but he will die if not," one should wash the vessel seven times,
rinse the grain, place it in a tight sack and tie it shut, then boil it in the vessel so that the heads of the grain do not break, and only then give it to him to drink.
All grounds are both timely and untimely; with the exception of the eight kinds of ash, all other ashes are also both timely and untimely—this is called the dharma of medicinal substances.

Regarding the dharma for the preceptor (upādhyāya), the ācārya, the co-practicing disciple (sahacaryā-śiṣya), and the dependent disciple (niśraya-śiṣya): the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been ordained for one year, leading a disciple who had not yet completed a full year. Each carried a cloth bag upon his shoulders and wore them on his head; with his left hand he held an alms bowl and leather sandals, and with his right hand he carried a water flask and a leather oil-bag. Together they went to where the Buddha was and prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
The head-cloth and water-bag fell onto the World-Honored One’s lap; the World-Honored One set them aside himself and, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
“Whose are these? They replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is my co-resident disciple.
“How many years of seniority does he have?”
He replied, "One year. [The Buddha asked,] "How many years have you been a disciple?"
He replied, “There is no year.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"It is like attempting to rescue one who is drowning while you yourself are drowning; you have already been keeping disciples for years, though you yourself were but a year old when you began.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is impossible for one who cannot subdue oneself to subdue others."
It is impossible for one who cannot discipline oneself to wish to discipline others;
it is impossible for one who cannot cross over oneself to wish to deliver others.
"It is impossible for one who has not yet liberated oneself to liberate others; such a thing cannot be.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"It is possible for one who has already been able to subdue oneself to subdue others; such a thing can indeed occur."
It is possible for one who can discipline oneself to also discipline others;
it is possible for one who has already crossed over themselves to also cross over others;
it is possible for one who has already liberated themselves to also liberate others.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu who is less than ten years [of standing] to ordain others into homelessness and grant them full ordination.
Furthermore, the Buddha established a precept: it is not permitted to ordain others into homelessness and grant them full ordination if one has not yet reached ten years [of standing].

At that time, Nanda and Upananda had reached the age of ten; having received the full ordination after others were permitted to go forth, they failed to provide instruction. Like celestial bulls or celestial rams wearing horns and wandering wantonly, there was no one to restrain them. They were deficient in purity and deficient in dignified deportment. They did not know how to serve their preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), nor how to show deference to elder bhikṣus. They did not know the rules for entering villages, the rules for forest dwellers (āraṇyaka), the rules for entering assemblies, or the rules for wearing robes and carrying alms bowls.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if ten qualities are accomplished, I authorize you to ordain others, allowing them to leave the household life and receive full ordination."
What are the ten?
First, upholding the precepts;
second, being well-versed in the Abhidharma.
Third, being well-versed in the Vinaya;
fourth, training in the precepts;
fifth, training in meditative concentration.
Sixth, training in wisdom.
Seventh, being able to expiate one's own offenses and being able to cause others to expiate theirs.
Eighth, being able to tend to the sick and being able to cause others to tend to them.
9. When a disciple encounters difficulties, one is able to deliver them from those difficulties, or is able to send someone else to deliver them.
10. One has reached ten years of age.
These are called the ten matters by which it is permitted to ordain others, allowing them to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
