"Down to those who have reached ten years [of seniority] and know the two divisions of the Vinaya, it is likewise permitted.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, there was at that time a bhikṣu who passed away.
He had two co-resident disciples who, overcome with grief and affliction of mind, sat together beneath a tree like merchants who have lost their wealth.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"What kind of bhikṣus are these?
The bhikṣus then reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to request formal reliance (*niśraya*), honoring it as you would a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Regarding the ritual for requesting reliance: one should bare the right shoulder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, touch the feet [of the preceptor], and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please remember me!
I, [name], beg the Venerable sir for dependence; may the Venerable sir act as my preceptor for dependence, and I shall dwell in dependence upon the Venerable sir.
This is to be said a second and a third time.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu with one year of seniority who received dependence upon a bhikṣu with no years of seniority; likewise, up to a bhikṣu with nine years of seniority receiving dependence upon a bhikṣu with eight years of seniority.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for one who has fewer than ten years of seniority to receive dependence from another."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having reached ten years of seniority and received others as their dependents, failed to instruct or admonish them; they were like celestial oxen or celestial sheep, even to the point of not knowing the proper method for donning robes or carrying alms bowls.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those who have accomplished ten qualities are permitted to receive the formal reliance of others."
What are the ten?
Maintaining the precepts up to a full ten years [of ordination]—these are called the ten matters by which one may receive formal reliance (*niśraya*).
Even those who have reached a full ten years and know the two divisions of the Vinaya may likewise do so.
When wishing to request formal reliance (*niśraya*), one must not do so impulsively.
Only when five conditions are fulfilled may one then make the request.
What are these five?
1. Affectionate regard; 2. Reverence;
3. A sense of shame.
Fourth, shame.
Fifth, delighting in dwelling [in the Dharma]. These are called the five qualities by which one should request reliance upon an ācārya.
There are four types of ācāryas.
What are the four?
First, the preceptor; second, the Dharma-preacher from whom one receives the teachings.
Third, the preceptor (śikṣācārya).
Fourth, the instructor in secluded places.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of ācāryas.
What are the four?

There is an ācārya whom one may leave without asking; there is an ācārya whom one must ask before leaving; there is an ācārya under whom one should remain for as long as life lasts even if it is a difficult dwelling; and there is an ācārya under whom one should remain for as long as life lasts even if sent away, because it is a pleasant dwelling.

Regarding "departing without asking permission": there is a teacher upon whom one relies for residence, yet he provides no food, clothing, or medicinal decoctions for illness; furthermore, he is unable to explain the Dharma of the unsurpassed fruit of the śramaṇa—namely, the practice of the holy life and renunciation. In such a case, one may depart from that teacher without asking permission.

Regarding "asking and then departing": if there is an ācārya upon whom one relies and dwells, and although he provides food, clothing, and medicinal decoctions for illness, he is unable to explain the dharma of leaving the household life to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of the unsurpassed fruit of a śramaṇa—such a teacher must be asked for permission before departing.

Regarding dwelling in hardship: if one dwells in dependence upon an ācārya, even though there is a lack of clothing, food, and medicinal decoctions for illness, and that ācārya skillfully explains the Dharma of the unsurpassed fruit of the śramaṇa—namely, the practice of the holy life and renunciation—one should not leave such an ācārya with whom one dwells, even if the dwelling is difficult, until the end of one's life.

If there is one who dwells in happiness, relying upon an ācārya for his residence, and who can provide him with food, clothing, and medicinal decoctions for illness; and who skillfully explains the Dharma of renunciation, the cultivation of the holy life, and the unsurpassed fruits of the śramaṇa—then even if such an ācārya should expel him, he should not leave as long as his life lasts.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are another four kinds.
What are these four?

The Dharma-receiving preceptor relies upon the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion; therein he is able to skillfully teach the disciples the Dharma to eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion. Such an ācārya is most supreme and most excellent, just as from milk one obtains curd, from curd one obtains butter, and from butter one obtains ghee; of these, ghee is the most supreme and most excellent.
The Upādhyāya and the Ācārya should instruct their co-resident disciples and dependent disciples. Regarding the methods of instruction: they should prevent [disciples] from engaging in impurity;

they should forbid improper places of conduct and those subject to formal disciplinary acts (*karmavācanā*); they should personally dispel evil and false views or cause others to do so; they should personally undergo purification from offenses or cause others to do so; they should personally care for the sick or cause others to do so; and in the event of danger, whether from kings or bandits, they should either escort them themselves or cause others to escort them.

Regarding those impure matters that should be prohibited: if a disciple violates minor precepts, eats in a separate group, eats at various locations, stays in the same room as a woman, stays more than three nights with one who has not received full ordination, cuts living grass, or eats impure fruit, he should be instructed, saying: "Do not do this."
If he says: "Preceptor! Ācārya!
I shall not do it again."
If they say, "It is well," and then ask:
"Preceptor, Ācārya, you should only teach yourself; why do you teach others?"
"If it is thus, one should tell the person in charge of bedding to take away the bed and bedding, and tell the person in charge of food to cut off his meals.

If the former person is wicked and, relying on the power of the king or the power of a great minister, is able to cause harm, then if he is one's preceptor (upādhyāya), one should avoid him; if he is one's resident teacher (ācārya), one should take one's robes and bowl, leave the boundary for one night, and upon returning, immediately cease the relationship of dependence."
If a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple commits an impure act and the preceptor or instructor fails to admonish them, it is an offense against the Vinaya.
This is called "that which is impure and should be prohibited."

Regarding "non-appropriate places": the home of a young maiden, the home of a widow, a gambling house, a tavern, or the residences of a disreputable bhikṣuṇī or a disreputable śrāmaṇerī—if one frequents such places, the upādhyāya and ācārya should instruct them:
"Do not come and go to these places; they are not suitable locations for association."
If the recipient accepts it well, and [the preceptor] goes out of the boundary to stay for one night and then returns, this is termed "leaving the dependence.
If the co-resident disciple or the dependent disciple travels to and fro from a non-practicing area and the [preceptor] does not instruct them, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called an improper sphere of activity.

One who has been subjected to a formal act (*karmavācanā*) should resolve the matter; if the Saṃgha performs a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or *niḥśrayasamutthāpanīya-karman* (act of reconciliation through joy), and if among the three views—namely, the view of slandering the Sūtras, the view of evil and false doctrine, or the view of extremes—one should, upon admonition, not abandon such a view, and a *utkṣepanīya-karman* (act of suspension) shall be performed.
The Upādhyāya and Ācārya should apologize to all the people on behalf of the disciple, saying:
"Venerable elders!
This was originally a wrong view, but it has now been abandoned, and he practices in accordance with the Dharma."
"How could ordinary people, being ignorant and deluded, be without fault?
This child has studied for only a short time and truly possesses this fault; from this day forward, we shall instruct him so that he will never do it again."
Having gladdened the minds of the assembly, he requested the Saṃgha to revoke the *karmavācanā*.
If the co-resident disciples or the disciples who rely on him do not revoke the *karmavācanā* performed by the Saṃgha, they commit an offense of violating the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
This is called being subjected to the formal act (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding the arising of evil and wrong views and causing others to resolve them: if a disciple gives rise to evil and wrong views—whether it be slandering the *sūtras*, holding evil and wrong views, or holding extreme views—the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the instructor (*ācārya*) should instruct him:
"Do not give rise to such views; this is an evil matter that leads to falling into the evil realms and entering hell, where one suffers for a long night."
If, after being exhorted in these various ways, he abandons it, that is well;
if he does not abandon it, one should speak to his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as follows:
"Venerable sir, please speak to him so that he may abandon this evil view."
If one does not resolve it oneself nor causes another to resolve it, there is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
This is called "resolving a wrong view oneself or causing another to resolve it.

Regarding "purifying oneself from an offense or causing another to purify it": if a disciple commits a curable offense, such as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and conceals it, the teacher should personally grant him the *parivāsa* probation.
If one does not conceal [the offense], they should be granted *mānatta*.
As for offenses up to those involving the violation of the *vinaya*, they should be settled by oneself; if unable to do so, one should have another settle them.

If a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple commits an offense, and the preceptor neither personally grants them absolution nor causes another to grant it, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
This is called purifying one's own offenses while causing others to purify theirs.

Regarding "the sick person looking after themselves or causing others to look after them": if a disciple is ill, one should either look after them oneself or cause another to look after them; one must not merely cause another to look after them while failing to attend to the matter oneself. One should visit the patient three times a day and say to the caregiver:
"Do not grow weary or tired; looking after one another in turn is praised by the Buddha."
If a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple is ill and the teacher does not attend to them, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (viniya-āpatti).
This is called "attending to the sick oneself or having another attend to them."

If it is difficult to go, whether one sends oneself or sends another, if the disciple’s relatives wish to cause them to abandon the Path, the teacher should instruct them to avoid [those relatives] from afar. If the disciple has accomplished the merit of renunciation, the teacher should escort them himself; if he is old or ill, or if he knows that there are monastic affairs to attend to, he should entrust someone else to escort them. If he neither escorts them himself nor sends another to do so, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "difficult to initiate," whether one sends it oneself or sends someone else to do so.
Regarding "kings and thieves": if a disciple is arrested by the king, the teacher should not immediately abandon him; rather, he should wait outside for news.
If the royal household asks,
"Who are your preceptors and teachers?
at that time you should enter.
If the matter is unjust or wrongful, one should seek the testimony of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If it is necessary to pursue [the offender] for property, one should provide robes and alms-bowls; if these are lacking, one should beg for them and give them.
If a disciple is abducted by bandits and sold, or is located far away in another land, the preceptor should seek them out and redeem them.
If the upādhyāya or ācārya fails to rescue and redeem a disciple who has been seized by kings or bandits, they commit an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vibhinī-āpatti).

If the preceptor or the teacher has common-residence disciples or dependent disciples, they should likewise admonish them; they must not use harsh speech but should admonish the preceptor or teacher with gentle words according to the rules of instruction, saying:
"You should not do such a thing."
If one says:
"Son! I shall not do it again."
"If that is so, it is well.
Or if he says: "Stop!"
"Stop!
You are neither my preceptor nor my teacher; it is I who shall instruct you—how can you instruct me?
It would be like trying to pull back a bamboo joint against its grain."
"Do not speak further.
If it is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), one should abandon him and go far away.
If it is the resident teacher (*ācārya*), one should take one's robes and bowl, go beyond the boundary for one night, and then return to rely upon another person.
If the teacher possesses power and influence, one should depart from afar;
if one does not depart, one should rely upon a virtuous and eminent person. If the teacher engages in improper conduct, one should admonish him;

if he has been subjected to formal disciplinary action (*karmavācanā*), one should manage the situation for him. If he gives rise to evil views, one should resolve them oneself or request another to resolve them; one should personally undergo purification from offenses or request another to do so. Whether he is ill or healthy, one should provide for his needs; if the teacher encounters difficulties, one should escort him away; if he is seized by kings or bandits, one should pursue and rescue him.

If a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple does not admonish their teacher when he commits a minor offense, or fails to pursue and rescue him when he is seized by kings or thieves, it constitutes a *vinaya-āpatti*.
A co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple should perform these duties toward their preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya):

rising to greet them, responding to their speech, performing tasks for them—whether doing them oneself or assisting others in doing them—matters concerning robes and bowls, shaving one's own hair or assisting others in shaving, applying the razor, receiving items or taking them on their behalf, receiving scriptures or teaching them to others, giving consent or receiving consent, taking medicine, welcoming food or offering food to others, departing from the boundary, major offerings, and departing without asking permission.
Regarding rising to welcome: when a disciple sees his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) from afar, he should rise to welcome them.
If he is consuming one of the five types of formal meals, or if he is observing the practice of eating only a single meal a day and thus cannot rise, he should at least bow his head.
When receiving the practice of eating a single meal, one should inform the teacher; the teacher should ask:
"Are you able to observe the single-meal practice?
If one is able, one should accept it.
If they say,
"I am not capable," one should say:
"Do not accept.
If a disciple sees their teacher and does not rise, it is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
This is called "not rising in welcome."

Regarding responding to speech: when the preceptor (upādhyāya) or the teacher (ācārya) speaks together with one, the disciple should respond; if there is food in the mouth, one may respond provided that it does not cause the voice to change.
If you are unable [to respond], wait until you have swallowed and then report back.
The teacher said:
"Why did you not report back upon hearing my words?"
One should say:
"There is food in my mouth, disciple.
If the teacher speaks and one does not respond, it is a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "responding speech.
Regarding "performing tasks," when a preceptor or an ācārya instructs a disciple to perform a certain task, it should be performed in accordance with the Dharma.
If one says:
"Call her here; bring the wine.
One should respond with gentle words:
"I have heard that such unrighteous acts as these ought not to be committed."
If the teacher instructs one to perform a task in accordance with the Dharma and one does not do so, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called "performing a task.
Whether performing it oneself or having another perform it, if one wishes to do something, one should ask:
"I wish to perform this act together with such-and-such a person.
The preceptor should examine their characteristics; if that person does not maintain the precepts well, he should say:
"Do not engage in this matter with him."
If there is one who maintains the precepts well, one should tell them to perform the task together.

If it is one's turn to serve as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the month, one should inform one’s teacher, as explained in detail in the section on proper conduct (*īryāpatha*); this is called "performing it oneself" and "having another perform it."
Regarding matters concerning the robe and alms bowl: if one wishes to fumigate the bowl, or when taking the *kummāsa* clay furnace and during the fumigation itself, each step should be announced.
If one cannot announce each step individually, one should simply say:
"I wish to perform the task of fumigating the bowl."
Having thus made the formal announcement once,
when fumigating the bowl, one should ask the Upādhyāya and Ācārya:
"Do you wish for the bowl to be fumigated?"
If they say, "It perfumes," one should ask:
"Is it perfumed first and then perfumed later?
Or is it perfumed in a single location? If one says:
“One place. One should ask:
“Is it on top or on the bottom?”
One should act according to the teacher’s instructions.
When wishing to dye the robe-cloth, one should inform [the teacher]; likewise, one should inform him at each stage: when washing it, when sewing it, and when boiling it for dyeing.
If one is unable to do so, one should simply say:
"I wish to perform the task of dyeing the robes.
A single announcement suffices.
When dyeing the robes, one should first ask the upādhyāya or ācārya:
"Do you wish for the robe to be dyed? If they say:
Regarding the term "defiled," one should ask:
"Does the defilement occur first, does it occur later, or does it occur simultaneously?"
If one says,
"At once," they should first dye the robes of their preceptor and ācārya.
When sewing, dyeing, or lifting [the robes] in this manner, one must not use the teacher’s robe to wrap one’s own robe; rather, one should use one’s own robe to wrap the teacher’s robe.
If one performs tasks regarding robes or bowls without informing the teacher, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the matter of robes and alms bowls.
Regarding shaving one's own hair or having another shave it: when one wishes to shave one's hair, one should inform the teacher, and the teacher should ask:
"Who will shave you?"
He replied, "So-and-so.
[The Buddha asked,] "Does So-and-so know how to shave?"
He replied,
"This is a matter seen with one's own eyes.
The Master said:
"No. If one says: "I know!"
The preceptor should examine the person; if they do not maintain the precepts well, he should also say, "It is not permitted.
If they maintain the precepts well, he should say:
"Shave. If one wishes to shave another's hair, one should inform the teacher:
"I shall shave the hair of the bhikṣu so-and-so."
The preceptor should ask:
"Are you able?
He should answer:
"If this is a matter witnessed by the eye, why can it not [be proven]?
One should reply: "It cannot."
If he says, "I am able," one should examine the person before him;
if he is not well-versed in maintaining the precepts, one should say:
"No. One who maintains the precepts well should say:
"Be careful."
"If the preceptor or the ācārya has entered a village and a barber subsequently arrives intending to shave one's hair, one should inform another elder bhikṣu, saying:
'I wish to have my hair shaved.'"
The preceptor should then inform his teacher.
After the teacher has departed, if one obtains a barber to shave the hair, this is called shaving oneself and having another shave it.
Regarding medical treatment with a blade: when one wishes to have another person lanced an abscess, one should inform the teacher.
"Apply a poultice to the wound of such-and-such a bhikṣu.
The preceptor should ask:
"Are you able to do this?"
He replied, "This is something seen with one's own eyes; why should it not be possible?
The master said:
"No. If one says, "I can," [then proceed].
The preceptor should examine the candidate; if they do not maintain the precepts well, he should say:
"It is not permitted.
If they maintain the precepts well, he should ask:
"Where is the ailment?
If he says, "In the private parts," [one should respond accordingly].
To this, one should say:
"Stay four finger-widths away from the edge of the anus on both sides and do not touch it.
This should be done if one must pierce the head to draw blood or remove an abscess or similar growth.
If one wishes to break open a sore oneself, one should inform the teacher. The teacher should ask:
"Where is it? If [the student] says:
Regarding the phrase "in a secluded place," one should say:
"It is not permissible."
If, as described above, one undergoes treatment with a blade in another location, this is called "treatment by knife.
Regarding "giving": when one wishes to give an object to another, one should inform the teacher; the teacher should then ask:
"To whom do you wish to give it?"
If one says:
"Give [it] to widows, virgins, prostitutes, gamblers, wicked people, ill-reputed bhikṣuṇīs, ill-reputed śrāmaṇerīs, or bhikṣus who do not uphold the precepts."
One should say:
"One ought not to associate with such people.
If one's parents do not have faith in the Triple Gem, one should attend to them only slightly.
If there is one who has faith, they may receive as much as they desire without lack.
When wishing to take another's property, one should inform the teacher; the teacher should then ask:
"Who gave this to you?"
If it is said,
"A great maiden... or even a bhikṣu who does not properly maintain the precepts gave me [this]," one should say:
"Do not associate with such people as these.
If they say, "He is one who maintains the precepts well," [one should respond:]
One should say:
"Take it. Question:
"To what extent does 'taking what is not given without having informed' occur?
Half a thread [of cloth] or half a morsel of food—this is called taking what is not given without having informed.
When receiving food on behalf of another or receiving food for oneself, if one is commissioned by another to receive food, one should inform the teacher:
"Go to meet the food with such-and-such a bhikṣu.
The teacher should ask:
"Why does that bhikṣu not go?"
He replied, "In that place one eats bitterness; here one eats pleasure.
One should say:
"If you seek happiness, do not make requests on their behalf.
If one acts as the *karmadāna* (steward) or makes a request for a sick person, one should examine that individual; if they do not maintain the precepts well, one should say:
"It is not permissible."
If they say, "We shall go to meet you when it is our turn," one should say:
"Take that bowl, wash it thoroughly, join it with your own bowl, and carry them away.
If [the other] says,
"He maintains the precepts well," [then take them].
To this, one should say:
"I shall go to meet him.
If one wishes to invite someone to receive food, one should inform the teacher; the teacher should then ask:
"Why do you not go?
He replied, "In that place one eats bitterness; in this place one eats pleasure."
One should say:
"It is not permissible for you to do so for the sake of pleasure.
If he is serving as the *karmadāna* (steward) or is ill, one should ask him:
"Who shall go to meet him?
He replied, "So-and-so."
If he does not maintain the precepts well, one should say:
"It is not permissible. If he says:
"If he next offers me food to receive,
I should say:
'Please invite someone else.'"
If one’s own preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), or those who well maintain the precepts come to welcome him, this is called "welcoming food by oneself" and "welcoming food by another.
Regarding the receiving and bestowing of scriptures: when one wishes to bestow a scripture upon another, one should inform the teacher; the teacher should then ask:
"To whom will you bestow the scripture?"
He replied,
"I am teaching the scriptures to a certain bhikṣu.
[The other asked,] "Which scripture are you teaching?"
If they say, "The *Śālagukāyada*," one should say:
"It is not permitted; it is not authorized by the World-Honored One.
If one says:
"It is a mantra-sūtra."
One should say, "It may be done.
One should then instruct them as follows:
"Do not live by this. If one says, "The Āgamas," [then say: "Do not live by this."
The preceptor should examine that person; if they do not maintain the precepts well, he should say:
"It is not permitted.
If they maintain the precepts well, he should say: [it is permitted].
"Have you had a profitable journey? He replied, "I have not."
After the other has asked,
[the candidate] should say: "I shall receive it."
"No. If one says: "It is beneficial."
To this, one should say:
"I shall give it.
When one wishes to receive the sūtra oneself, one should also inform the teacher as described above; this is called "receiving for oneself and bestowing upon another."
Regarding "giving and receiving consent": when giving or receiving consent, one should inform the teacher as extensively explained above in the section on welcoming food.

Regarding "taking medicine": when wishing to take medicine, one should first inform the teacher. However, if one has already sat down and wishes to drink ghee first and then eat, there is no offense in taking it even without informing the teacher.

Regarding those who leave the precincts: upon exiting the gate of the saṃghārāma, one should announce one's departure after having gone twenty-five cubits; whether walking for meditation or sitting in dhyāna, one should announce it so that others may know one’s location.

When wishing to attend to the needs of nature, if one is in the presence of the teacher, one should depart with a bowed head and an attitude of respect; if not in the presence of the teacher, there is no fault in departing without such respect.
Regarding the performance of great giving, if one wishes to practice great giving, one should inform the teacher, saying:
"I wish to give away all that I possess."
The preceptor should say:
"One who has gone forth must possess the three robes, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a water strainer, and leather sandals.
The disciple says:
"I wish to give everything in alms, excluding only these.
The teacher should examine [the candidate]; if they do not maintain the precepts well, nor have received the recitations or practiced the path, he should say:
"Listen."
"If one maintains the precepts well and is able to receive, recite, study, and practice the Path, one should say:
'Generosity is not a permanent state; you should rely on these various goods to provide for medicinal requisites, so that you may sit in meditation, recite the sutras, and practice the Path.'"
If he says, "I have relatives who will provide me with clothing, food,
and medicine for illness," the teacher should say:
"If that is so, listen.
This is called the "Great Gift. Regarding the announcement of departure:

when one wishes to travel, one should announce it to the *upādhyāya* and the *ācārya*; one must not wait until the moment of departure to announce it. One should announce it in advance, one month or half a month prior:
"If a disciple wishes to go to a certain region or country,
the teacher should ask:
'For what purpose are you going?'"
If one says,
"The monastic community here performs its duties with hardship; it is difficult to receive and recite the scriptures," the Upādhyāya and Ācārya shall further say:
"Eat little, drink little, be alert, and sleep little.
"I shall dwell there in happiness.
The teacher should say:
"You have left the household life for this very purpose; how can you now refuse to endure hardship?
If he says, "My preceptor and ācārya are occupied with worldly affairs and do not teach me the sūtras; for this reason, I wish to depart."
If one is able to confer [the precepts], they should say:
"Do not leave.
If one is not able, there should be someone among the assembly who is well-versed in the precepts and proficient in recitation; they should say:
"Bestow it upon him.
If there is no one present, a learned and knowledgeable bhikṣu in that vicinity should entrust it by messenger.
If one departs without informing the upādhyāya or the ācārya on whom he depends, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (viniyatika).
Among these, the co-resident disciples and the dependent disciples should perform these duties toward their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya).
This is called "informing the preceptor and instructor and then departing."
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Twenty-eight [and] Volume Twenty-nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

[From] the *Sāṃghāṭī-vibhaṅga* translated by Fa-xian, Chapter Seven: Furthermore, while the Buddha was traveling through the country of Kośala, at that time the bhikṣus took up the robes and bowls of their preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*) and went ahead;
they stayed together within the boundary (*sīmā*) and sat waiting for their masters, fearing that they would lose their formal dependence (*niśraya*) if they were to go beyond the boundary.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"What kind of assembly of bhikṣus is this sitting here?
The bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This is not a case of being separated from one's formal reliance (niśraya). Wait until the Tathāgata has finished his tour of the Kośala country and returns to Śrāvastī; then I shall prescribe for my disciples the rule regarding the relinquishing of formal reliance."
The Buddha returned to Śrāvastī, and the bhikṣus reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One:
“Now is the very time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will establish for the bhikṣus the rule concerning the relinquishing of reliance.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If the preceptor passes away, one is separated from dependence; if one abandons the path, is suspended, or if the preceptor stays overnight outside the boundary, or if the co-resident disciple stays overnight outside the boundary—these are called being separated from dependence."

If one relies on a preceptor (ācārya), or if the preceptor passes away, renounces the path, is suspended, or stays overnight outside the boundary; or if the disciple who was relied upon stays overnight outside the boundary; or if five years have been completed and one is well-versed in the Dharma and well-versed in the Vinaya—one may become independent of reliance. This is called "abandoning reliance."

If a bhikṣu does not properly understand the Dharma, does not properly understand the Vinaya, cannot establish himself, and cannot establish others, such a bhikṣu must remain in dependence for as long as he lives.

If a bhikṣu has completed ten years [of seniority], is well-versed in the Dharma, is well-versed in the Vinaya, is able to establish himself and is also able to establish others—such a bhikṣu may receive the dependence of others.
This is called the rule for the co-resident disciple and the dependent disciple of a preceptor (upādhyāya) and an instructor (ācārya).

Regarding the rules for a novice (śrāmaṇera): the World-Honored One did not desire them; their parents loved and cherished them so much that they wept for them when they were about to renounce the world and leave the home-life to become a Wheel-Turning King, and so forth—the causes and conditions for the Venerable Rāhula’s renunciation should be explained in detail.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Go and ordain Rāhula as a renunciant.
Śāriputra said:
"How shall I cause Rāhula to go forth into homelessness?
The Buddha said:
"Go and instruct him, saying: [as follows]"
“I, Rāhula, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Thus he said three times.

“I, Rāhula, having completed taking refuge in the Buddha, having completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and having completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, shall not steal, shall not engage in sexual misconduct, shall not speak falsely, and shall not drink intoxicants.”
"The Buddha, the Blessed One, has gone forth; I, Rāhula, follow the Buddha in going forth.
Thus he spoke three times.

"The Buddha, the Blessed One, has gone forth; I, Rāhula, follow the Buddha in going forth. Casting off worldly garments and donning the saṃghāṭī robe, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life and observe the śrāmaṇera precepts."
To refrain from stealing for as long as life lasts is to uphold the śrāmaṇera precepts;
to refrain from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts is to uphold the śrāmaṇera precepts;
to refrain from false speech for as long as life lasts is to uphold the śrāmaṇera precepts.
To observe the śrāmaṇera precepts by not drinking alcohol for the rest of one's life;
to observe the śrāmaṇera precepts by not wearing flowers or perfumes for the rest of one's life;
and to observe the śrāmaṇera precepts by not watching or listening to singing, dancing, or musical performances for the rest of one's life.
One shall observe the śrāmaṇera precepts for as long as life lasts by not sitting or lying on high or wide beds;
one shall observe the śrāmaṇera precepts for as long as life lasts by not eating at improper times;
one shall observe the śrāmaṇera precepts for as long as life lasts by not handling gold, silver, or money.
"Thus you should remember and uphold this.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above, at that time the Venerable Ānanda had a lay supporter (*dānapati*) who was a close acquaintance.
The entire household had died of an epidemic, leaving behind only a small child who constantly lived by picking up grains from the front of a marketplace stall.

At that time, as the Venerable Ānanda was passing by, some children saw him and called out after him, "Grandfather! Ānanda did not hear them and continued on his way, which led the people of the world to criticize and disparage him, saying:

"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, when others have fathers, force themselves upon them like father and son, yet now that they see them in decline and loss, they do not look back or take care of them?"
The child called out after him incessantly; Ānanda looked back, recognized him, and called out, "Come, my son.
Thereupon, the child followed him into the Jeta Grove Monastery.
The Buddha, having already perceived this, asked intentionally:
"Whose child is this?
Ānanda then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
“Can this child go forth [into homelessness]?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What thought have you formed?”
He replied,
“With a mind of loving-kindness.
The Buddha said:
“May he go forth. “World-Honored One, how should he be granted the going forth?
This is explained in detail as in the account of Rāhula’s going forth.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as described in detail above.
At that time, there was an elder who had gone forth and, having completed his rains retreat in a village, wished to go to the World-Honored One to pay his respects; he took ten śrāmaṇeras with him.
At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting in the open air.
From afar, Mahallaka saw the World-Honored One and pointed him out, saying to the śrāmaṇeras:
"This is your grandfather.

At that time, the young novices vied with one another to approach the Buddha; some seized his seat, some pulled at his robes, some rubbed his feet, and some grasped his water pitcher. Knowing this, the Buddha asked intentionally:
"Which novice is this?"
He replied,
"It was my permission.
The Buddha said:
"How is it that you have ordained so many śrāmaṇeras?
From this day forward, you are not permitted to maintain a following.
If one maintains a following, it is permitted provided it does not exceed three; however, if a bhikṣu of great virtue is honored by many people, he should be told:
"Give it to another person.
He replied again:
"I know there are others, but I wish to receive the recitation of the Dharma under the Ācārya and increase my cultivation and study; therefore, I give it to the Ācārya."
One should speak thus:
"Give it to another person; you may then instruct him yourself.
If one keeps śrāmaṇeras as attendants, one commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was taking a śrāmaṇera back to visit his relatives. As they traveled through a wilderness, a non-human being manifested as a dragon along the way, circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, scattered flowers over him, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"You have gained great and wholesome benefit by leaving home for the homeless life and not handling gold, silver, or coins.
When the bhikṣu had visited his relatives and was about to return, the relative’s wife said:
"As you travel back now, the road is long and you will likely lack provisions; you may take this money and go to the market to exchange it for what you require."

The śrāmaṇera accepted the money, tied it to the hem of his robe, and departed. On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera carrying the money walking behind the bhikṣu; he then transformed himself into a dragon, came from the left to circle the śrāmaṇera, covered him with dust, and said these words:
"You have lost a great benefit! Having left the household life to practice the Way, you walk about clutching money."
The śrāmaṇera then wept.
The bhikṣu looked back and asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Why are you crying?"
The śrāmaṇera said, "I do not recall having committed any transgression; why am I being troubled without cause?
The teacher said:
"Do you have anything in your possession? He replied,
"I have brought this money."
The teacher said,
"Discard it. After it was discarded,
the non-human being again made offerings as before.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for śrāmaṇeras to hold gold, silver, or money."
If a bhikṣu causes a śrāmaṇera to be the first to take hold of gold, silver, or coins, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense against the Vinaya.
If he sees that the śrāmaṇera has already taken hold of them beforehand and subsequently causes him to take hold of them, there is no offense.
Furthermore, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, being honored by devas and humans, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with the novice Cūḍapanthaka, went after his meal to the Anavatapta Lake in Jambudvīpa and sat in meditation upon its shore.
At that time, the novice Saṃśaṭha saw golden sand along the edge of the pond and thought to himself:
"I should now take this sand and place it beneath the World-Honored One’s water-pitcher."
Venerable Maudgalyāyana arose from his meditation and, employing his supernormal powers, returned through the air.
At that time, the novice Sañjīva was possessed by a non-human spirit. Seeing him from afar, Maudgalyāyana called for the novice to come, but the novice replied, "I am unable to go."
Question:
"Do you have anything with you? He replied:
"Take this gold dust.
"You should discard it. Having discarded it, he immediately ascended into the void and departed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for śrāmaṇeras to handle gold, silver, or money."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery under a *nyagrodha* tree in Kāpiṭavastu.

When various donors prepared an offering of a meal for the Saṃgha, there was a śrāmaṇera among them who chased away the birds and drove off the flies, while simultaneously picking up leftover rice, bones, vegetables, fruits, and melons to eat.
At that time, there were some mothers who were naturally compassionate; having seen this, they spoke thus:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no heart of mercy; their eating is unjust, like a person raising a calf who first gives it milk and then milks it dry."
"Now these monks keep this young child, yet they eat alone and do not share with him.
This man is a corrupter; what path of the Dharma can he have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when monks eat, they should give equal portions.
This is the rule for śrāmaṇeras.
There are three grades of śrāmaṇeras:
first, those from the age of seven to thirteen are called *kākavāśika* (crow-scaring) śrāmaṇeras;
second, those from fourteen to nineteen are called *dharmārha* (fit for the Dharma) śrāmaṇeras.
Third, those from twenty years of age up to seventy are called *nāmadheya-śrāmaṇeras*.
These three categories are all termed *śrāmaṇeras*.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli, knowing the proper moment, questioned the World-Honored One:
"How should a śrāmaṇera share in the distribution of the rainy-season robes?
The Buddha said:
"If he has obtained the consent of the bhikṣus, he should be given either a half or a one-third share."
"One who understands the intention of the bhikṣus is capable of performing the purification rites regarding the precepts.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should one distribute non-seasonal robes to śrāmaṇeras?"
The Buddha said:
"Give them equally.
If a śrāmaṇera receives many robes and fears that taking them would constitute an improper act, one should give him half, or one-third.
If that preceptor or ācārya says,
"Give it equally," and the śrāmaṇera has no other [objection], he should give it according to the teacher's word.
The distribution of the deceased’s robes is also like this;
this is called the Dharma for śrāmaṇeras.

Regarding the Dharma for the alms bowl: not long after the Buddha had attained enlightenment while dwelling in the Śrīmālā Forest, there were two merchants, one named Tiṣya and the other named Bhallika.
This should be explained in detail until [the account of] carrying parched grain and honey to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then thought:
"Did the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past receive food with their hands, or did they receive it in vessels?"
Having formed this thought, the Four Great Heavenly Kings each brought a golden bowl to offer to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "One should not accept such silver bowls; bowls made of any precious substance whatsoever should not be accepted."
Each of them further brought a stone bowl; the Buddha again thought to himself:
"If I accept only one bowl, I fear the kings' hearts will not be pleased.

He immediately accepted the four bowls, stacking them in his left hand and pressing them together with his right hand so that they merged into a single bowl, yet allowing the four rims to remain visible.
After the Buddha had accepted the bowl, he received the parched grain and honey from the merchants and recited the extensive verses of blessing.
At that time, the merchants were filled with joy and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that you will grant us your hair and nails so that we may build a caitya."
The Buddha immediately trimmed his nails and shaved his hair for him and erected a stūpa for him.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the village of Śveta in the Sūrpāraka region, the deity of Sūrpāraka came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this regard, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past made use of earthenware bowls here; may the World-Honored One likewise permit the bhikṣus to make use of earthenware bowls.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, I permit the use of earthenware bowls.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣu went to the potter Dharmika and spoke as follows:
“Long-lived one!
Make a bowl for me.
At that time, he fashioned a well-made earthenware bowl, made its color like gold, and gave it to the bhikṣu. The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to make it gold-colored.
He then made it silver-colored, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to make it silver-colored."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Today is the day of the upoṣadha. Summon the upāsaka Dharmapriya; let him bathe, put on clean robes, and observe the poṣadha.
At that time, the upāsaka bathed, put on clean robes, and came to where the Buddha was. Having observed the poṣadha, the World-Honored One pointed out the site for the monastery.
“You should know that this clay is kneaded in such a way, struck in such a way, molded in such a way, fashioned in such a way, and fumigated in such a way to produce a bowl.
Once the fumigated bowl has been completed, three kinds of colors are applied:
first, a color like the throat of a peacock;”
"Second, it is like the color of a *viliṅga* bird;
third, it is like the color of a pigeon.
The Buddha said:
"When you are perfuming it, you must wait upon it to ensure it takes on such a color.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who came from the country of Upaviśā carrying an alms bowl and said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"Is it permitted to use this bowl?
The Buddha said,
"It is permitted."
In this manner, a bowl was brought from the country of Kācīya, and the Buddha said,
"Its use is permitted.
A monk from the north brought a red bowl and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it permitted to use this bowl?
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, for the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would go from house to house among the bhikṣus once every five days. He saw a bhikṣu with a hand ulcerated; knowing the cause, he nevertheless asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"Are you at ease? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"My hands were blistered, and I dropped my bowl to the ground; because the bowl was broken, I am unhappy.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to use iron bowls."
When using an iron bowl, one should fumigate it in a bowl-furnace; for fumigation, one should use the kernels of *āmalaka*, the kernels of *khadira*, *guggulu*, and bamboo roots.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru had completed a great new hall and thought to himself:
"Who is capable of pointing out the defects of this hall?"
"Only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who are clever and wise, are able to recognize this fault.
He further thought:
"I must not simply summon the bhikṣus to come and look at this hall; rather, while the assembly is being held, I shall station people in various places to listen secretly to what is said."
At that time, the bhikṣus entered, and one bhikṣu spoke thus:
"This hall is excellent, save for one corner which is deficient by the measure of a single grain of barley."
Furthermore, another bhikṣu spoke thus:

"This hall is excellent in every way, yet the lintels and doorframes on the upper gallery are too low; when the Kṣatriya king enters or exits with his ceremonial insignia, fans, and parasols, they cannot pass through straight."
At that time, there was an elder (*mahallaka*) bhikṣu who, seeing the head of a felled tree trunk on the ground, thought to himself:
"This is excellent; it can be made into a bowl.
After the bhikṣu had finished his meal and departed, the people each reported what they had heard to the king.
The king immediately summoned a skilled craftsman to measure it with a thread; finding it exactly as described and no different, he commanded the craftsman to alter it.
The king recalled the words of Mahāla: "The bhikṣus will still require bowls."
He immediately summoned a skilled craftsman to fashion wooden bowls on the spot, filling them with various kinds of food.
He further took earthenware and iron bowls, filled them with food, and sent people to deliver them as offerings to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"The use of wooden bowls is not permitted, for they retain grease and filth; furthermore, they are the insignia of non-Buddhists, and therefore may not be accepted.
In this regard, that which is pure the World-Honored One accepts, while that which is impure he does not accept.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru had not yet incurred the enmity of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī. At that time, a merchant from the southern country brought a piece of mani-jewel and presented it to the king.
Having received it, Ajātaśatru thought to himself,
"This treasure is what my maternal uncles require.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to deliver it to the Licchavis.
Having obtained it, the Licchavi thought,
"This treasure cannot be divided," and he immediately placed it within the maṇi-treasury.
The Licchavi later went to the various storehouses; having seen the maṇi, he thought, "This jewel is suitable for making a vessel to drink śākarasa.
He immediately summoned a maṇi-craftsman to fashion the vessel.
The vessel was finished with a shape somewhat resembling that of an alms bowl. A Licchavi thought to himself:
"This is a vessel for those who have left the household life; it is not suitable for a worldly person. It should be given to Satyaka Nirgranthīputra."
Again, some said:
"It should be given to the sister's son, Nyan. Others said:
"Why give this dregs-of-wine-eating donkey to him?
It should be given to the World-Honored One.
Thus, as the many people each held different opinions, they immediately cast lots to determine the recipient; those who wished to give it to the Buddha were in the majority.
The assembly deliberated, saying:
"We must not present our bowls empty to the Buddha; we ought to adorn and embellish them.
Thereupon, they filled their bowls with broken jewels and placed them within jeweled caskets.
He further took earthenware bowls and iron bowls filled with various kinds of food and offered them to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the Licchavis:
"This maṇi bowl should not be accepted; the broken jewels within it and the jeweled casket should likewise not be accepted."
"It is permitted to accept iron alms bowls and clay alms bowls, but it is not permitted to accept precious alms bowls.
One should accept what is pure; one should not accept what is impure.
The Licchavi then took the precious bowl and returned home. The assembly discussed this, saying:
"It should be given to my sister's son, the Nirgrantha.
Another person said:
"This is a donkey that eats wine dregs; it should not be given a jeweled cage or broken jewels. One should instead make a rope net-bag and give it an empty bowl to carry."
He immediately made a carrying-net, filled it with an empty bowl, and sent someone to deliver it.
At that time, there was a Licchavi who had faith in and respected the Nirgranthas; he went first and informed him of this matter:
"Be careful not to accept the bowl when it is brought by that person."
When the bowl arrived, the Nirgrantha said: "This is an empty bowl;
it should not be accepted. It is also made with a hempen rope for a carrying net; it should not be accepted.
Furthermore, because you gave it first to the śramaṇa Gautama and only later to me, it should not be accepted."
"I now accept only one thing: if you cut off the tongues of all these young Licchavis, fry them in salt and oil, and bring a full bowl to me, I shall accept it.
The messenger returned and reported this fully to the Licchavis.
The Licchavis said, "This is our nephew;
he speaks these words out of resentment and grief, but you should simply send him back.
They repeated this three times, and their words did not differ.
The Licchavis said, "This is a strange matter;
we have bestowed generous gifts upon him, yet he has instead conceived malice and poison.
They immediately dispatched men to go and seize him, beat him, and kill him.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying,
"How is it that Satyaka Nirgrantha harms his own body by sitting upon his tongue?
The Buddha said:

"It is not only today that one has harmed oneself by the tongue while sitting; as is explained in detail in the *Ujjitaka Jātaka*, as stated in the *Cūḷatāyaṇa Jātaka*, as stated in the *Kumma Jātaka*, and as stated in the *Suka Jātaka*."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who placed a partition inside his bowl to hold various kinds of food.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally: "Bhikṣu!"
"What is in your bowl? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"In this [vessel], rice is placed in one spot, soup in another, and meat and vegetables in another.
The Buddha said,
"Are you attached to various flavors?"
From this day forward, I do not permit the placing of a separator inside an alms bowl; if one places a separator therein, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
However, there is no offense if the separator consists of a cake or rice.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who vomited because he had eaten from a raw alms bowl. The Buddha said:
"It should be fumigated; one should use the kernels of *āmalaka*, the kernels of *khadira*, *guggulu*, and bamboo roots for fumigation."
At that time, the bases of the bhikṣus’ bowls were worn through.
The Buddha said, “A mandala-shaped plate should be fixed to the base.
At that time, the bhikṣus made them using gold, silver, and precious materials. The Buddha said:
"One should not use gold or silver to make them; rather, one should use red copper, white tin, lead, or pewter.
At that time, the bhikṣus covered their alms bowls entirely. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit covering them all over. The largest may have a four-finger-width border left uncovered, and the smallest should be like the leaf of a *śiṃśapā* tree."
The bhikṣus fashioned images of birds and beasts upon the maṇḍala. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the making of images of birds and beasts.
If one makes a bowl-cover (pātrabandhana), it may be either square or round."
Regarding the *maṇḍala* rule: if a bowl lacks a *maṇḍala*, it must not be placed on the ground.
Should it be placed on the ground, one incurs an offense of transgressing the *vinaya*.
It should instead be placed upon a bowl-rest, or upon leaves or grass.
If the bowl is placed upon a maṇḍala, there is no offense in setting it on the ground.
If the maṇḍala is made of mud, there is no offense in setting it on the ground.
At the very least, there is no offense in sprinkling water on the ground and placing the bowl there.
If one leaves the bowl unattended on the ground, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*. This is called the rule regarding the bowl (*pātra-dharma*).

Regarding the rule regarding rice gruel (*yavāgū-dharma*): The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Nandamātā and Utpalavarṇā-mātā within the city observed the *poṣadha* three times during the half-month—on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days. On these *poṣadha* days, they would prepare food, first serving the bhikṣus and then eating themselves. When the next day arrived, they again prepared *poṣadha* food; having cooked rice in a cauldron, they forced the rice broth up and drank it themselves. Immediately, they felt the internal winds in their bodies were dispelled and their indigestion cured. Feeling hungry and needing food, they had this thought:
“The Ācārya is one who eats but a single meal; he ought to have gruel.
Thus, taking a large amount of water and a small amount of rice, boil them together until two-thirds has evaporated, and then add black pepper and *pippalī*.
Once the gruel was cooked, he filled a jar to the brim and carried it to the Jetavana Monastery.
Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit the bhikṣus to eat gruel."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the eating of gruel.
On that day, there was a donor who provided a meal for the Saṃgha at the vihāra.
The bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not eat at various locations; how may we perform the ritual of purification (jīvakarman) so as to obtain food?
The Buddha said:

"If, when the gruel first comes out of the cauldron, it cannot form characters when drawn upon it, this is not 'eating here and there,' nor is it 'eating apart from the assembly,' nor is it 'satisfying food.

If, when the gruel first comes out of the cauldron, it can form characters when drawn upon it, it is called 'eating here and there,' and is also called 'eating apart from the assembly' and 'satisfying food.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses as a prayer of blessing:
"Pure in the observance of precepts, one is honored by all; Reverently offering congee at the proper time, One gains ten benefits that enrich the practitioner:
Vigorous appearance, strength, longevity, happiness, Eloquence, and clear speech."
It eliminates wind from undigested food and quells hunger and thirst; this is what the Buddha has taught as the true medicine.
Those who wish to be born among humans or devas and constantly experience happiness should offer rice gruel to the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala and gradually arrived at the brahmin village of Hatthigāma; this should be told in detail, until [it is said that] a brahmin followed the World-Honored One for six months, carrying in his chariot non-glutinous rice, beans, sesame, clarified butter, and rock honey, thinking: "I shall wait for a time when no one else is making offerings so that I may present my own offering."
While the Buddha was in the world, the people’s faith and joy were such that they provided abundant offerings; there was never a lack of food, whether before or after the meal.
When the World-Honored One returned to Śrāvastī, a messenger was sent from the house of a brāhmaṇa to summon him, saying, "The time for sowing has arrived; you ought to return quickly."
Then the brahmin asked the Venerable Ānanda,
"By which gate will the World-Honored One depart tomorrow morning for Śrāvastī?
Ānanda replied:
“Brāhmaṇa, why do you ask this?

The brāhmaṇa replied, “I have some rice and beans that I wish to scatter upon the road; I pray that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus will tread upon them as they pass, thereby accepting my offering.”
Ānanda said, "The brahmin wishes to question the Buddha. Thereupon,
the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda! Who has ever taught them so as to receive their offerings?"
He replied, "Venerable Śāriputra.
The Buddha then asked Śāriputra:
“Have you ever accepted offerings from him?
“World-Honored One!
I once accepted a single meal from him.”
The Buddha said, "You are the one who shall convert him; you may go and ask that brahmin, 'Would you be able to provide gruel for the Saṃgha tomorrow?'"
Śāriputra immediately went to preach the Dharma, and eventually asked, "Would you be able to provide gruel for the community of monks?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I actually intended to spread rice and beans upon the ground so that the Buddha and the Saṃgha might walk over them; why then would I not be able to provide gruel?"
That very night, he prepared various kinds of gruel:
ghee-gruel, milk-gruel, oil-gruel, curd-gruel, meat-gruel, and fish-gruel.
In the early morning, after the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, he personally served the gruel with his own hands. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked:
"Where have you placed the rice?
He replied,
"In this place."
“Where did you cook it?
He replied, “Right here.”
The Buddha said:
"Overnight storage is not permitted; cooking indoors is also not permitted.
Other kinds of pure congee are permitted, but this congee is not permitted."
Furthermore, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala and arrived at the village of Pāṣāṇa, formerly a settlement of brahmins.
At that time, there were two elder monks, father and son, who were former barbers and had left the household life to dwell in this village.
At that time, when the mahallaka heard that the World-Honored One was coming, he spoke to his son, saying:
"Take your shaving implements into the village and seek rice, beans, ghee, oil, and rock honey; when the World-Honored One arrives, we shall prepare various kinds of gruel."
The boy immediately entered the village, and the people asked him,
"Having shaved your hair, what do you wish to obtain?
He replied:
"I require rice, beans, ghee, oil, and rock honey.
[The other] asks, "What will you do with them? He replies:
"Tomorrow the World-Honored One will arrive; we shall prepare various kinds of congey.
When the householders heard this, their faith and joy redoubled, and they gave even more than before, which the monks then took back to their residence.

When the World-Honored One had arrived, the mahallaka himself prepared various kinds of porridge. When morning came and the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, the mahallaka washed his own hands and personally served the porridge. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"What kind of gruel is this?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"When I was formerly at home, I made offerings to the bhikṣus and constantly thought:
'When shall I be able to personally offer sustenance to the World-Honored One?
It is for this reason that I have now prepared this congee."
The Buddha asked,
"Where did you obtain the rice?
He replied:
“A child may earn a living by shaving hair.
The Buddha said:
“Overnight storage is not permitted; cooking inside [the monastery] is not permitted; cooking for oneself is not permitted; and earning a living by working as a hired laborer is also not permitted.”
"You may eat other pure rice porridges that have been prepared with pure ingredients.
Furthermore, as the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅguttarāpa, the brahmin Kaṇiya Jaṭila heard that the World-Honored One was coming and prepared various kinds of porridge:
ghee porridge, sesame porridge, milk porridge, curd porridge, oil porridge, and fish-meat porridge.
After the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had sat down, various kinds of gruel were served. The bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds, thinking:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not eat at various locations; how can we eat this so as to be pure?"
The Buddha said:
"If the rice gruel has just come out of the cauldron and one cannot form characters with it, it is permitted;
except for meat gruel and fish gruel, all other kinds of gruel are not 'food from every place,' not 'food for a separate group,' and not 'sufficient food.'"
If a bhikṣu begs for food and receives rice that is not yet cooked along with the rinsing water, and he presses them together to give it, there is no offense for one who eats it.
If, however, he takes only the rice and gives it, and the recipient eats it, this is called eating separately from the community, eating at various places, or eating to satiety.
This is called the rule regarding rice gruel.

As for the rule regarding cakes: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One shaved his hair once every four months. At the time of his shaving, people brought various kinds of cakes and food to visit and see the World-Honored One.
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa asked his wife,
"Do you have the ingredients for cakes in the house?
She replied:
"There are two *do* of non-glutinous rice and four *sheng* of oil.
What shall they be used for? He replied:

"The ascetic Gautama has shaved his hair today, and everyone is bringing cakes to him; you should quickly prepare some cakes, for I wish to join the company and make an offering to the ascetic Gautama."
He immediately prepared the cakes, placed them in a vessel, covered them with a clean cloth, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly; the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and the lords of the eighteen great villages were all present in the gathering.
This brahmin, filled with doubt and fear, did not dare to go forward; remaining alone in one place, he thought to himself:

"If the śramaṇa Gautama is all-knowing and all-seeing—one who constantly observes the world such that there is nothing unseen and nothing unknown—and if his illumination of the world extends to me as well, since I am also part of this world, he must surely know and see my mind."
The Buddha, having known the brahmin’s thoughts, immediately called out to him from afar.
When the brahmin had arrived, the Buddha, though already knowing the answer, asked him deliberately: "Brahmin!"
"What is in your vessel?
He replied, "It is a cake."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the brahmin, "Distribute this among the assembly of monks; give one *pātra* to each person."
He replied, “This assembly consists of five hundred people, yet the cakes are now very few; it will not be possible to provide for everyone.
The Buddha said:
"You simply go ahead.
The brāhmaṇa then distributed the cakes, giving one to each person; yet the cakes did not diminish. This continued for three rounds, and still they were not diminished.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power; even with such a small amount of cake, it has not diminished at all after the great assembly has partaken three times."

The Buddha, knowing that the brahmin’s heart was filled with joy, taught the Dharma in accordance with his disposition to instruct, benefit, and gladden him; the brahmin immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a brāhmaṇa obtains such a great fruit and retribution from a small cause?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today that one obtains a great fruit through a small cause;
it was already so in past lives, as recounted in the Jātaka-sūtras."

As for "cakes" (*piṇḍaka*): barley cakes, wheat cakes, small-grain cakes, rice cakes, bean cakes, oil cakes, ghee cakes, *mahura* cakes, *pāpalaka* cakes, "ox-ear" cakes, *pālisaka* cakes, *cutuka* cakes, *mandira* cakes, and *modaka* meat cakes—all such things as these are called cakes.
Except for meat cakes and *piṇḍa* cakes, all other cakes are not food for a separate group, not food for various places, and not food for satiety.
This is called the rule regarding cakes.
Regarding the method for cooking vegetables: When the Buddha was staying at the great city of Piṇḍola on the Southern Mountain, there were two female lay disciples (upāsikā):
one named Sābhikā and the other named Kapphā. They were able to cook vegetables so that they tasted like meat; having prepared these excellent vegetables, they offered them to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not eat at various locations; how then may we perform the ritual of purification (jñapti) so as to obtain food?
They reported these matters in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"All vegetables are not to be eaten at every place, nor as food apart from the community, nor as a meal that satisfies.
Regarding "vegetables": dried vegetables, radish greens, scallion greens, and gourd greens—such as these are called the rules for vegetables.

Regarding the category of parched grains: parched barley, parched wheat, parched *yava* grain, parched *makuṭa*, parched *masūra*, parched *kalāya*, parched *eranda*, and parched sesame; all such parched grains as these are not food for a separate group, not food for various places, and not food that brings satisfaction.
This is called the rule regarding flour-meal. Regarding the rule regarding fermented drinks:

while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the householder Ugga performed a great almsgiving, offering five hundred each of elephants, horses, and male and female slaves. Among the various gifts distributed, some fermented drinks had been kept for a long time; after drinking them, the bhikṣus became intoxicated and distressed. For this reason, they reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to drink spoiled fermented liquids.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the village of the Brahmin Piṇḍola on the Southern Mountain, the Brahmins and householders of that village were exchanging food and drink on the occasion of a festival.
At that time, when it was time, the World-Honored One put on his robe for entering the village and, taking his alms bowl, entered the village to beg for food.
Then Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has entered the village to beg for food; I shall go to the village first to delude the minds of the people so that they will not give him any food."
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a village to beg for alms but returned with his bowl empty, having received nothing at all;
he sat down beneath a tree. Then Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has gone begging throughout the village and received nothing; I shall now go there to disturb his mind."
He went immediately to where the Buddha was, stood to one side, and said:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
You should go to the village for alms; I shall ensure that upon entering the village you obtain various kinds of excellent food."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Pāpīyas:
"You have now lost all wholesome benefit because you have disturbed the Tathāgata;
you yourself shall incur immeasurable sin."
The Tathāgata has no suffering; having abandoned all afflictions, he always dwells in peace and bliss.
Sustained by the food of mindfulness of the Dharma and the joy of dhyāna, he is like the devas of Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that moment, Māra Pāpīyas suddenly vanished.

On that day, the World-Honored One lost his meal; when the bhikṣus heard this, those who had already begun eating regretted it, those who had eaten half stopped, and those who had not yet eaten did not eat at all.

At that time, when the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas heard that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had lost their meal, they immediately brought five hundred jars of stone honey to offer to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Purify it with water and receive it; bhikṣus who are ill and those who are not shall all be able to eat it."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Lohitya River, the bowl of the World-Honored One and the bowls of the bhikṣus were together in an open space. At that time, a monkey walking by saw ripe honey free of bees within a tree; it came to take the bowl of the World-Honored One, and the bhikṣus tried to stop it.
The Buddha said, "Do not stop him; he has no ill intent.
The monkey then took the bowl, gathered honey, and offered it; however, the World-Honored One did not accept it.
"One must wait for the water to be pure.
The monkey did not understand the Buddha's intention and thought he was calling it "contaminated with insects.
He then saw honey flowing along the edge of the bowl; he took it to the water's edge to wash the bowl, rinsed the bowl with water, and brought it back to offer to the Buddha, who then accepted it.
Having received [the honey], the monkey was filled with great joy; he retreated and danced, fell into a pit, and passed away.
At that time, the bhikṣus spoke these verses:
"The One of Ten Powers, the Hero of the World, was in the thicket forest; the Buddha’s bowl and the monks’ bowls were in the open air."
A wild beast, having cultivated virtue and possessing intelligence, saw that the honey was ripe and excellent;
it went straight forward and took the World-Honored One’s bowl. The bhikṣu wished to stop him, but the Buddha would not permit it.
Having obtained the bowl and filled it with honey, he came to offer it to the Buddha; out of compassion, the Tathāgata accepted it.
With a heart full of joy and delight, he danced backward; his foot slipped, he fell into a pit, and his life ended.
He was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and descending to earth, he left the household life and became an Arhat.

Furthermore, as the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅguttarāpa, the brahmin Kaṇikya, a conch-shell-crested ascetic, heard that the World-Honored One was coming and prepared various kinds of beverages to wait upon him.
When the World-Honored One arrived, [the donor] offered various kinds of fermented drinks to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus felt doubt in their hearts, thinking:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not drink fermented drinks."
"How can we drink it?
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to drink *pānaka* (beverages).
There are fourteen kinds of *pānaka*.
What are the fourteen?
First, mango juice; second, grape juice;
third, pomegranate juice.
4. Kharjūra juice; 5. Drākṣā juice; 6. Pāruṣaka juice.
7. Lodhra-wood syrup.
8. Plantain-fruit syrup. 9. Kāśmarī syrup.
10. *Kṣīrapāla* juice;
11. *Pālangu* juice; 12. *Phāṇita* juice.
13. Harītakī juice. 14. Kharjūra juice.
These are called the fourteen kinds.
If the fermented drink is clear and transparent, it is permitted for all to drink; however, if it changes its color, taste, or aroma to that of alcohol, it is not permitted for anyone to drink.
If someone brings fermented drink, it must be rendered pure (*kappiya*); if there is residual water remaining at the bottom of the vessel, it is considered purified;
if rain falls into it, it is likewise considered purified.
If there is residual water remaining in a vessel after it has been washed, it is also considered pure;
if stone honey is carried on a cart and is rained upon, it is immediately considered pure;
if water is carried in a boat and is splashed by rain, it is likewise designated as having undergone the purification process.
If water from washing the hands of a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) splashes onto [the food], it is also considered pure.
This is called the rule regarding fermented drinks (*pāna-dharma*).

Regarding *suvīra*: while the Buddha was wandering through the country of Kośala, the Venerable Śāriputra suffered from an ailment caused by wind (*vāta*). For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked,
"What medicine is required to treat this?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
We have *susvīra* juice.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, and take it to heart.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Wait until the Tathāgata has returned from his travels through the kingdom of Kośala to Śrāvastī and speaks to me; then I shall establish the rules for *sūvīra* juice for my disciples."
Having returned from his journey, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
When you previously commanded us to return to Śrāvastī, you said that you would then establish the rules for *suvīra* juice for the bhikṣus; now is precisely the time for this.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"As for the method of preparing *sūvīra* (sour gruel): take roasted barley, pound it lightly, remove the awns and dust, and ensure the grains do not break; then wash it thoroughly with water seven times and place it in a clean vessel."

When storing *sūvīra* (sour gruel), one must not place it toward the east or the north; it should be placed along the southern or western edge so as to leave a passage for air and prevent foul odors from entering. It must not be kept within the monastery courtyard nor in a prominent location, but should be kept in a screened place. One should place within it *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, black pepper, long pepper, and other such medicines to be used for life (*yāvajjīvika*). Cover it with a clean cotton cloth, tie it with a cord in the shape of a rooster’s foot, and place a wooden lid on top.
When receiving *suvīra* juice, one should dilute it with water according to the amount of the juice and then drink it.
If one drinks it without diluting it with water, it is an offense of violating the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga-āpatti*).
"If the tips of the barley grains are not broken, one may drink it at the proper time or at improper times.
If the tips of the barley grains are broken, one may drink it only at the proper time and not at improper times.
This is called the rule for *suvīra* juice.
The rules for medicine and the preceptor;
the rules for the co-resident ācārya and the dependent disciple;
the rules for śrāmaṇeras, the bowl, gruel, cakes and vegetables, parched grain flour, and various beverages.
The Method for *Suvīra* Liquor.
The fifth chapter concludes.

Regarding those who do not perform formal acts (*kamma*): The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the monks of Campā lived together in discord, litigating and disputing with one another. One monk censured another monk, saying:
"I have suspended an elder!
Two bhikṣus suspended two bhikṣus, and many bhikṣus suspended many bhikṣus.
For this reason, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
“The monks of Campā have acted contrary to the Dharma: how can one person suspend another, two persons suspend two others, and a multitude suspend a multitude?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are four types of karmavācanā. What are the four?

There is a formal act that is lawful but not in harmony; there is a formal act that is lawful and in harmony; there is a formal act that is unlawful but in harmony; and there is a formal act that is unlawful and not in harmony.
