Sundarananda; newly dyed robes; taking [an object] from one place and discarding it elsewhere; the Āmrapālī Grove; renunciant non-Buddhists; making an appointment; the perception of emptiness and stillness; the Sū River; the Sudharma Lecture Hall; the general Siṃhasena; a young man; the Licchavi youth; four men fighting; on the upper story of a pavilion; rolling a stone; hot springs; a courtesan; Trapuṣa; seeking oil; receiving food; nursing the sick; a piece of bird meat; a piece of thief’s meat; a piece of pork; kicking a woman; grinding flour; releasing a calf; abandoning his wife; the mahallaka; through a wall; the poṣadha; two kinds of *suvīra* juice; bricks; excrement; begging for alms; Ucchuṣma.

Regarding Sundarananda: when the Buddha was staying in the city of Vārāṇasī, at that time Sundarananda was at the Kiṭāgiri Sūkarakkha Monastery, practicing walking meditation and sitting in dhyāna during both the first and last watches of the night.
Having sat in the full lotus posture for a long time since rising at dawn, he arose with his body exposed as it had slumped over; he was unaware that he had been asleep.
At that time, there were two sisters who were courtesans in the city of Vārāṇasī:
one was named Kāśi and the other was named Upakāśi.
At night he went outside the city and, together with several youths in a grove, engaged in acts of lustful desire.
In the early morning, as he was returning and passing by on his way home, he saw the bhikṣu’s body erect;
seeing this, he said to his sister, "I wish to engage in this act of lust with the bhikṣu; sister, wait for me a moment."
He replied:
"This is an arhat who has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; he takes no pleasure in this matter.
Have you not heard how Sunda Nanda of the Śākya clan abandoned his beautiful and upright wife to leave the household life?"
He replied, "Not so; wait for me.
He then went up to her and performed the worldly rite.
The bhikṣu immediately woke up and kicked him down with his foot, wounding him in five places:
both elbows, both knees, and the forehead.
Upaka rose up, shook the dust from his robes, went to his sister’s place, and said to her:
"The bhikṣu has been thus humiliated.
The sister said,
"Did I not tell you before?"
"Now, whom do you resent?
The bhikṣu felt doubt in his heart and, for this reason, spoke to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said, "You have committed a pārājika offense."
He replied, "I am an arhat; I do not experience pleasure.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; he is an arhat and is without fault.
Thus the Vinaya rule was concluded; this is called the case of Sundarananda.
Regarding new dyed garments: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the time had come, put on his village-entering robes and, carrying his alms bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. As he proceeded from house to house, he came to a certain home where a woman was wearing a newly dyed garment; because she was not sitting properly, her body was exposed.
Having seen her, the bhikṣu immediately gave rise to lustful thoughts and said,
"Sister, you are too red.
She replied:
"Ācārya, this is newly dyed cloth.
This bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"With what state of mind? He replied,
"With a lustful mind."
The Buddha said,
"Send one bhikṣu to ask that woman whether she understands or not.
The bhikṣu then went and asked the sister:
"Has any bhikṣu come here? He replied, "There has."
He asked, "What did that bhikṣu say? He replied:
"I was sitting wearing newly dyed robes, and he said:
'It is a deep crimson. I said:"
"Just as the Ācārya said, the newly dyed color is exactly like that.
At that time, the bhikṣu reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"If one understands the meaning but not the phrasing, it is a thullaccaya.
If one understands the phrasing but not the meaning, it is a thullaccaya offense.
If one understands both the phrasing and the meaning, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If one does not understand the meaning and does not understand the flavor [of the offense], it is a *vinaya*-offense of transgression.
Thus concludes the *vinaya* rule; this is called "dyeing a new robe.

Regarding "being censured in another place": at that time, there was a bhikṣu living in one location. After the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of censure (*karma*) against him, he went to another community of monks and spoke as follows:
“Venerable sirs!

I have been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma*; I am now practicing in accordance with the Dharma, my mind is supple, and the Saṃgha should grant me the *pabbājanīyakamma* (the act of lifting the suspension).
The bhikṣus then performed the *pabbājanīyakamma* for him.
After the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the revocation of the suspension has been performed, he asks:
"Venerable one, for what reason were you suspended?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
The Sangha has already finished performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for my relinquishment of the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman*; why do you ask me again?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"As the bhikṣus have stated, when the Saṃgha is performing the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the removal of a suspension (*utkṣepa*), one should first ask [the offender]. If the suspension has already been removed without asking, one should not ask again."
"How is it that the Saṃgha in another location performs an act of formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), yet the Saṃgha here relinquishes it?
If the Saṃgha in another location performs an act of formal censure and the Saṃgha here relinquishes it, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga-āpatti*)."
If a bhikṣu who has been subject to a formal act of suspension goes to another place, he should speak thus:
"Venerable sir!
I have been subject to a formal act of suspension; I have practiced the conforming dharmas, my mind has become supple; please revoke it for me."
The Saṃgha should ask:
"Venerable one!
On account of what matter have you been suspended?"
If he says, "I have been accused without cause," one should say to him:
"Venerable one!
You have been censured without cause; let us partake together in the food of the Dharma and the food of flavors.
If he says:
"If a formal charge has been brought against you," the Saṃgha should say,
"Venerable one!..."
"You should return to that place and relinquish it within the Saṃgha.
If the monastery at that place is empty, or if the monks have passed away, or if they have left the path, or if they have gone elsewhere such that there is no Saṃgha at all, one should ask:
"On what grounds were you suspended?"
If he says, "I have been suspended for this matter," and his mind becomes supple,
he perceives his faults, and he practices in accordance with the Dharma, then the suspension should be lifted.
Thus the *vinaya* procedure is concluded; this is called the formal act of censure for another location. Regarding the Āñjana Grove:

at that time, the Blessed One had not yet prohibited bhikṣuṇīs from staying in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*). Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, was practicing meditation in the Āñjana Grove. They were all women of the Śākya, Malla, and Licchavi clans who had gone forth; these women were all young and beautiful.
While they were sitting in meditation during the first watch of the night, some lecherous youths came and sought to assault the bhikṣuṇīs; each bhikṣuṇī escaped by means of her supernormal powers.
In this manner, he sat again during the middle watch and the latter watch of the night, and the youths came once more.
Those who were not asleep and possessed sharp faculties departed by means of their supernormal powers;
those who were asleep and possessed dull faculties were then assailed and oppressed by them.
Doubt arose in her mind, and other bhikṣuṇīs said to this bhikṣuṇī,
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
She replied:
"I do not experience pleasure; thus, I do not know.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī then informed the Blessed One of these circumstances in detail.
The Buddha said:
"This is an arhatī who has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; she does not experience sensual pleasure and is without fault.
Thus the Vinaya was concluded; this is called the Grove of Opened Eyes.
Regarding those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist practitioners: The Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in Kapilavastu.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the time arrived, put on his village-entering robes and entered the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, there was a female renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect named Sundarī; she was young and of handsome appearance, wearing newly dyed robes, carrying a triple-jointed staff and holding a water flask in her hand as she walked before the marketplace.
Having seen her, a bhikṣu gave rise to a lustful mind and followed after her. There was a cow that had recently calved, which gored the bhikṣu with its horns and threw him onto the woman.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt doubt, and the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"What thoughts do you have? He replied:
"Desire. He asked the bhikṣu again:
"When the bull's horns were raised, what state of mind did you have?"
He replied, “A mind of fear.
The Buddha said:
"If there is no mind of lust when there is a mind of fear, or no mind of lust when there is a mind of fear," the Buddha said,
"if a mind of lust follows after a woman, one incurs a *vinaya*-offense at every step."
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called "one who has gone forth as an outsider.

Regarding "making a common appointment": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, when the time arrived, put on his village-entering robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for alms, proceeding from house to house until he reached a certain family.
A certain woman said to a bhikṣu,
"Come and do this thing.
He replied:
"I, a bhikṣu, may not do such a thing according to the Dharma.
The woman said:
"If you do not do this, I shall wound and break my own body and cry out loudly, saying:"
"The bhikṣu forcibly led me to engage in sexual desire.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall return once I have reached the monastery."
The woman said, "You Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not speak falsely; you must certainly come.
He replied:
"So it is," the bhikṣu said, reporting the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"This is an illegal discourse; what should not have been heard has been heard, and what should not have been permitted has been permitted.
You should go together with many bhikṣus. Having then gone with many bhikṣus, he spoke thus:
"Sisters!..."
"I have come," she said.
The woman replied,
"Homage to the Ācārya."
Thus concludes the Vinaya on this matter; this is called "making a mutual agreement.
Regarding the "perception of solitude": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣu who sat alone beneath a tree, cultivating the perception of solitude, and said:
"I have attained arhatship."
When this bhikṣu spoke these words, the other bhikṣus, having heard them, said: "Venerable one!
You have spoken falsely;
you claim to have attained superhuman states and have thus committed a pārājika offense."
He replied:
"Venerable sir!
I do not claim to have attained superhuman states."
"I sat alone beneath a tree, contemplating emptiness and stillness, and said to myself:
'I have attained the state of an Arhat.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you have not attained superhuman states, yet you claim to have attained superhuman states?
The bhikṣu replied:
“World-Honored One!
I do not claim for myself to have attained any state surpassing that of ordinary men. While sitting alone beneath a tree, I cultivated the perception of emptiness and stillness, thinking:
‘I have attained arhatship.’”
The Buddha said:
"If one claims to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) while harboring the thought that it is empty and still, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Thus concludes the Vinaya rule; this is called the "thought of emptiness and stillness."
Regarding the Sū River: While the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the community of bhikṣus gathered in one place.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke as follows:
"Elders!..."
"I have entered the formless attainments and heard the sound of the elephants and dragons by the Sū River shaking their ears after drinking.
The bhikṣus said, "This is impossible;
having entered the formless attainments and transcended all perceptions of form, how could one hear a sound?"
"You have spoken falsely and untruthfully; you should undergo the formal act of *karma* for accusation.
He then assembled the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha, traveling by means of his supernormal power, came through the air; knowing [the situation] yet asking the bhikṣus intentionally:

“What have you done? The bhikṣus reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, up until the point that they had performed the *jñapti-karman* of formal censure for false and unsubstantiated speech.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Maudgalyāyana has indeed attained the formless concentrations, yet he does not skillfully know the signs of entering and emerging from them; he hears [the sounds] upon emerging from concentration, not while entering it."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
“You should skillfully discern and understand.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called the Sūtra River.
Regarding the Dharma Hall: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus gathered in one place and engaged in this discussion:
"Does the pillar of the Dharma Hall support the beam?"
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said,
"The pillars and beams.
A bhikṣu who had not yet completed his first year of ordination said:
"Not supported.
"To what extent is it not supported?
"To the extent of a hair's breadth."
He immediately dispatched a bhikṣu with supernormal powers to go and see whether the pillar was supported or not.
Having returned after inspecting it, he said,
"It is not supported."
"To what extent is it not supported?
"It is not supported even by as much as a hair's breadth.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Since you do not know whether he is leaning against it or not, why do you say he is leaning against it?
Your speech is false and unsubstantiated; you should undergo the formal act of *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (the act of suspension).
Thereupon, they assembled the Saṃgha and performed the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman*.
The Buddha, possessing the supernormal power of the Buddha-vehicle, came through the air;
knowing [the situation], he asked intentionally: "Monks, what are you doing?
They replied:

“The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has committed an untruthful lie by claiming that which was not supported was supported; he intends to perform a formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*) against him.
The Buddha asked the monk who had no seniority:
“How do you know it was not supported?”
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Once, on one occasion, I was practicing dhyāna in the Sudharma Hall.”
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Why do you not examine it yourself?
You ought to verify it for yourself with thorough accuracy."
Thus the *vinaya* is concluded; this is called the Hall of the Good Dharma (*saddharmamaṇḍapa*).
Regarding General Siṃha: when the Buddha was staying in the city of Vaiśālī, King Ajātaśatru had a feud with the Licchavis of Vaiśālī.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru was leading the fourfold army, intending to attack the Licchavis. When the Licchavi general Siṃha heard that the king’s forces were approaching, he immediately went to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and asked:
"Venerable One!..."
Who has won?
Has the king won,
or have I won?
He replied,
“The King has won. He asked:
"What auspicious omen is there?
He replied, "I saw non-humans from the two kingdoms fighting together; the non-humans of the King's side were victorious, and thus the King shall also be victorious."
Having heard this, General Siṃha immediately recruited five hundred brave men from within the kingdom. General Siṃha said to them:
"Would we rather die as non-men, or live as men by entering a pit of fire?"
The people replied,
"It would be better to live as a man and thus provide for our kin.
When King Ajātaśatru heard Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s words, he became relaxed and free from fear, and slowly followed the Ganges upstream to cross the river.
At that time, General Siṃha suddenly attacked them before they were arrayed for battle and utterly defeated them.
King Ajātaśatru, unable to cross safely, narrowly escaped the danger and returned to his kingdom on horseback alone;
he immediately spoke with resentment, saying, "It is because of this Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana that my state affairs have been ruined."
At that time, after the Licchavi general Siṃha had defeated the army, he was filled with great joy and spoke these words:
"Maudgalyāyana has terrified me; because of this, I have gained a great benefit."
"Although these were untrue words, we have received this grace of your falsehood.
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that King Ajātaśatru was angry and the Licchavis were likewise resentful, they said:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, do you not know who has won and who has lost?"
He has spoken falsehoods that are untrue.
He then assembled the community of bhikṣus, intending to perform the formal act of *karma* for suspension (*ukṣepa*).
The Buddha, traveling by means of his supernormal power, arrived there; knowing the situation, he asked him intentionally:
“Monks! What do you wish to do?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
Mahāmaudgalyāyana has even, through false and unsubstantiated speech, sought to perform a *karma* of formal accusation.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
“You should examine this with careful discernment.”
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called the General Siṃha. Regarding the "son":
while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Mahāmaudgalyāyana had a lay supporter who was acquainted with him. The supporter’s wife was pregnant, and he asked:
“Ācārya! [What shall it be?]”
"Have I given birth to a boy? Or a girl?
She replied:
"A son has been born.
Thus he was asked three times, and so he said:
"A son has been born."
Later, when the time came for her to give birth, she gave birth to a girl. At that time, the mother woman spoke with resentment, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana has been telling lies throughout the long night; he said a boy was born, yet a girl has been born."
He spoke these words merely to please others.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they asked:
“How could the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana fail to discern properly and speak such a falsehood?”
"You should perform the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (the act of suspension).
He immediately assembled the community of monks.
The Buddha, traveling by means of his supernormal power, arrived and, though he already knew the answer, asked intentionally:
“Bhikṣu, what are you doing? He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana has gone so far as to speak falsely and untruthfully, desiring to perform the formal act of *karma* for censure.

The Buddha said, “Maudgalyāyana saw only the boy before him; he did not see that in the interim, the yakṣa Nimi had taken the girl from the family requiring a girl and given her to the family requiring a boy, and had taken the boy from the family requiring a boy and given him to the family requiring a girl.”
The Buddha said:
"Go and speak to that household, saying:
'The World-Honored One has declared:'"
"The woman is for you; the man is for me.
Having said this, they immediately went to have intercourse and exchanged [their goods].
Thus ends the Vinaya rule; this is called a "male child."

Regarding the Licchavi youth: while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the time having arrived, he put on his robe for entering the village, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī together with a great number of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a Licchavi youth on an upper terrace, enjoying himself with five hundred female musicians.
The Buddha saw him from afar and smiled.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do you smile?
The Buddha said:
"This person shall pass away seven days from now and enter hell.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Is there any cause or condition by which he might avoid entering it?"
The Buddha said,
"If this person were to go forth within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, he would not enter [the lower realms].
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Go and convert this person, exhorting him to leave the household life.
Ānanda immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction and went to exhort him; once he had left the household life, the Buddha told Ānanda:
“Tell the bhikṣus that they must protect this person, ensuring that he does not violate the precepts and incur grave offenses.”
Then the bhikṣus, having received these instructions, placed this bhikṣu in a single room and sealed its door from the outside.
This bhikṣu’s life came to an end; the "sword-wind" (śastravāyu) dissolved his physical form.
At that time, some bhikṣus had kinsmen come who, seeing that they had passed away, were filled with great sorrow and distress.
The Buddha spoke these verses for them:
"If a person, for a hundred thousand years, Makes offerings to a hundred arhats;..."
It is not equal to spending a single night Leaving the household life to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
By virtue of this merit, one shall escape Six hundred and sixty-six thousand years Of the suffering and affliction of the three miserable realms.
At that time, the monk who had closed the door felt doubt and regret, and for this reason he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the monk:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
It was with a mind of benefit; I feared that he might violate the precepts and incur grave retribution."
The Buddha said:
"Because you closed the door, you commit a *vinaya*-offense.
Thus the *vinaya* rule is concluded; this is called the Licchavi youth.
Regarding the four who abandoned their quarrel: while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, four men who had abandoned their dispute and desired to leave the household life entered Vaiśālī together.

Inside the city gate, they encountered their former enemies; at that time, the gatekeepers possessed bows and staves. One man immediately seized a bow, another drew it, another shot but did not kill, and the fourth shot and severed the life-faculty.
Among these, one person was shot dead and the other was shot but did not die; these two persons should not be ordained as monks, and those who have already been ordained should be expelled.

Among these, one person holds the bow and another strings it; these two persons should not be granted the going-forth into homelessness. Those who have already been granted the going-forth should be left as they are, but if they later commit evil deeds, they should be expelled.
Such evil persons should not be ordained; if they are ordained and receive full ordination, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the fourth case of abandoning strife.

Regarding "on the upper story": while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, there was at that time a bhikṣu who attained the contemplation of impurity; becoming weary of his own body, he threw himself down from the upper story.
At that time, there were two father and son working with bamboo on the upper story of the palace pavilion; the bamboo fell onto the father, and he died immediately.
The son then dragged the bhikṣu to the king’s presence and spoke these words:
“This bhikṣu killed my father.”
The king asked the bhikṣu, "Venerable one, you are a renunciant; how could you kill a person?
He replied:
"Great King!
I loathed my own body and threw myself down from the upper story, falling upon my father; such was indeed the reality.
The king said:
"Release the bhikṣu.
His son cried out in grievance:
"Great King!"
"How can one kill a person and yet not be held accountable for the crime?
The King, employing skillful means, wished to explain his intention:
"Go up to the upper terrace and have the bhikṣu remain below; then you yourself shall throw yourself upon him, killing that bhikṣu to avenge my father."
The man, cherishing his own life and regarding it as precious, was unable to throw himself down.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Because of weariness with the body," the Buddha said, "O Bhikṣu!"
"If you do not look down before throwing yourself, you shall incur an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya.
Thus the Vinaya rule was concluded; this is called "from atop a building.
Regarding "rolling stones": the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, an elder (*mahallaka*) and his son had both gone forth as monks and went together up Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
As the boy was walking ahead, there was a stone in the path, and he thought to himself:
"I shall clear the road to make it pure, so that Bharukaccha may come up without hindrance and in safety."
He then rolled down a stone,
which struck and killed the mahallaka.
His son was distressed and felt remorse, giving rise to doubt and regret:
"I have committed two harmful deeds:
killing a man and killing my father.
For this reason, he reported everything in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have cleared a path for my father so that he may obtain happiness.
The Buddha said:
"Rolling a stone while on the road constitutes a *vinaya*-offense of transgression (*vayittiya*).
Thus concludes the *vinaya* rule regarding rolling stones. Regarding the hot spring:

the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. At that time, a certain bhikṣu entered a hot spring to bathe; lustful thoughts arose within him, and as his body came into contact with the water, he discharged semen.
A mind of doubt and regret arose within him, and for this reason, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
it was a mind of desire.”
The Buddha said, "He commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called the Hot Springs.

Regarding the courtesan: while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, there was a bhikṣu who, when the time arrived, put on his robes for entering the village and, carrying his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food in sequence until he reached the house of a courtesan.
The courtesan said,
"The bhikṣu has come to do this thing with me.
The bhikṣu said:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not engage in [sexual intercourse]," the courtesan said.
"I know that the World-Honored One has established a precept against engaging in sexual intercourse; you simply come here, perform it inside, and discard it outside."
The bhikṣu then engaged in sexual intercourse with her and subsequently felt doubt and regret. For this reason, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

"If it is performed internally and discarded externally, or performed externally and discarded internally, or performed internally and discarded internally—if even a single joint, or as much as a sesame seed, enters [the body], one commits a pārājika offense."
Thus concludes the Vinaya; this is called the "prostitute" case. Regarding Pāva-ca:

while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, the Venerable Pilindavatsa was living in a village. When the time arrived, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went for alms in sequence. Having obtained food, he went to a cattle-herding household to eat.
The daughter of that family went to the side of the Venerable One and stood there weeping.
He immediately asked the girl, "For what reason are you weeping? She replied:
“Ācārya, today is the day of the festival when all the people gather for entertainment; I have no clothes and am the only one unable to go, so how could I not weep?”
Then the Venerable One immediately manifested various garments, jewels, necklaces, and ornaments adorned with gold and silver; having given them to her, he departed.
When the King heard of this, he summoned his daughter and asked:
"Where did you obtain these exquisite necklaces?"
He replied,
"Venerable Pilindavatsa gave it to me.
The king immediately summoned the bhikṣu and questioned him.
"Venerable sir, where did you obtain this fine gold?
It is not of this world.
The bhikṣu then took his staff and struck the wall and the bed; everything was transformed into gold, and he spoke these words:
"Where did the Śūdra obtain this gold?
This is it," the king said.
“The Ācārya possesses great supernormal power;
he has returned, and the cowherd girl has gone home.

When the bhikṣus heard this, they saw that Piṅgalavatsa had manifested such wonders, even to the point of seizing the cowherd girl. They realized that a *jñapti-karman* of formal censure should be performed, and they immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus.
The World-Honored One, traveling by means of his supernormal power, knew [what was happening] yet asked on purpose:
"What are you doing? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Piṅgalavatsa displayed such supernatural transformations that even a cowherd girl was seized.
The Buddha then questioned Piṅgalavatsa:
“Did you actually cause the cowherd girl to be seized?
He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"I did not intentionally manifest these transformations to cause the cowherd woman to be seized; it was solely out of my heart of compassion!
The Buddha said, "Because Pindola Bharadvaja possesses great supernormal power, he is without fault."
Thus ends the Vinaya rule.
Furthermore, the Venerable Pilindavatsa was dwelling in a village and was personally plastering his own dwelling.
At that time, King Bimbisāra came by, saw the Venerable one plastering and repairing his dwelling, and asked:
“Ācārya! What should be done? He replied:
“Śūdra, repair the dwelling. The King said, “Ācārya!”
"Is there no one to serve as an attendant?
I shall provide you with a park-keeper.
He replied:
"No need, Śūdra.
Thus he spoke up to three times, yet [the other] still would not accept it.
When the people of the village heard this, they came to his place and requested, saying:
"Ācārya! We pray that you will accept us as gardeners; we shall provide for you."
The bhikṣu said:
"If all of you are able to uphold the five precepts, I shall take you.
They replied:

"I can. Having accepted them, he fully received the five precepts, observed the fast, and cultivated virtue. Consequently, the village became prosperous and wealthy, which eventually attracted outside bandits who came to plunder it, seizing women and property.
A person from the village went to inform the teacher, saying, "Ācārya!
Thieves have come and plundered my children and wealth; everything has been exhausted this very day."
The Venerable Pilindavatsa entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and saw the bandits driving [the laborers] away; the bhikṣu then said to the bandits:
"Śūdras! Why do you plunder my laborers?"
He immediately manifested a great chasm, placing the park-keepers on this side and the bandits on the other side, and said:
"Śūdras, you go away!
When the bhikṣus heard this, they spoke as follows:
“Piliṅgavatsa has been robbed by robbers again; a formal act of *karma* for accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) should be performed.
Thereupon, the community of monks was assembled to investigate this matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived by means of his supernormal power; knowing [the situation] yet asking as if in ignorance:
"What are you doing? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
Pilindavatsa, who had been a bandit himself, was now being robbed by other bandits; they wished to perform the *jñapti-karman* against him.
The Buddha asked Pilindavatsa, "Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
I did not rob the thieves nor plunder them; rather, it was because the people of the village came weeping to inform me, and out of a heart of loving-kindness!”
The Buddha said, "This is a great supernormal power; it is without fault.
Thus the Vinaya rule is concluded.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Twenty-nine [and] Volume Thirty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

[This is] the eighth section on the *Kṣudraka-vastu* translated together with Fa-xian. Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the Venerable Pilindavatsa was residing in a village. Every day he would cross the Ganges River to beg for alms; having reached the riverbank, he spoke these words:
"Śūdra, stop! I wish to pass."
The water then stood still.
After [the time] had passed, it spoke these words:
"Śūdra, you may go."
Thus the flow of water remained as before.
The Water Deity was displeased and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Venerable Pilindavatsa spoke too harshly, saying:
"Stay away from the Śūdras! Go away from the Śūdras!
The Buddha said:
“Upāli, come here. When he had arrived, the Buddha said:
“Is it true that you did this?”
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"The River God thus detests you; you must repent before him.
Pilindavatsa said, "I repent, O Śūdra!"
The River Goddess said, "In the past you were a śūdra; now you are a śūdra. What difference is there that you should speak of repentance?
Piṅgalavatsa replied, "With the exception of the Buddha and his eight great śrāvakas, everyone else calls me a śūdra; even my upādhyāya, my ācārya, and all the elders call me a śūdra."
The bhikṣus said,
“Venerable Pilindavatsa, even your preceptors and ācāryas all call you a śūdra.
Is there truly only this one person who has gone forth as a brāhmaṇa?”

Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others like them were all renunciants from the Brahmin caste; they never spoke such words, and thus a formal act of censure (*karmavācanā*) should be performed against them.
He immediately assembled the community of monks.
At that time, Pilindavatsa was practicing meditation and did not come, so a messenger was sent to summon him.
The messenger then struck at the door and said:
"The Sangha has assembled; summon the Elder!

At that time, Pilindavatsa perceived that the community of bhikṣus had gathered intending to perform a *karma* of formal accusation against him. He immediately employed his supernormal powers to restrain the bhikṣus at the door, preventing them from leaving.
The community of monks wondered why the messenger had not returned for so long and sent another bhikṣu to summon him.

When the second bhikṣu arrived, he took the hand of the first messenger-bhikṣu and departed; as they came, the elder [the first bhikṣu] immediately became attached to him, and they could not part. In this manner, each successive messenger became attached to the one before, and none were able to leave.
The bhikṣus spoke with resentment, saying:
"Is this one person alone possessed of such great supernormal power (*mahā-ṛddhi*) among the assembly?
Does the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana not possess such power?"
"On the banks of the Qi River, they performed the *karmavācanā* for bestowing merit and inflicting punishment.
The Buddha, traveling through the air by means of his supernormal power, knew the reason but asked deliberately: "What are you doing?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
With the exception of the Tathāgata’s eight great śrāvakas, everyone else—from upādhyāyas and ācāryas down to all others—says:”
"Śūdra," he said, intending to perform the formal act of *karma* for suspension; however,
the Saṃgha had assembled, yet [he] did not come.

He sent a messenger to summon him, but the monk’s supernormal power restrained him, causing the messenger to become stuck so that he could not come; therefore, [the monks] wished to perform the *jīva-sīmā* (water-limit) *karma* of punishment.
The Buddha said, “Come.”
In the mere instant that Pilindavatsa gave rise to this thought, he stood before the Buddha, and the Buddha said to Pilindavatsa:
"You have used insulting language toward the Śūdras; the fellow practitioners of the holy life find fault with you."
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
What should I do?”
I am not arrogant, nor do I treat others with pride or contempt.
However, when I call upon my preceptors, teachers, or senior bhikṣus, as soon as I utter the sound, they become śūdras.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“This Pilindavatsa is not arrogant, nor does he look down upon others out of self-importance.
Having been born for five hundred lifetimes continuously in brahmin families, the habitual tendencies of speaking the language of the śūdras have not yet been exhausted.”
The Buddha said to Pindola Bharadvāja:

"Since the beginningless cycle of birth and death, you have been able to uproot even greed, hatred, and delusion forever, yet you cannot eliminate the habitual tendencies cultivated over five hundred lifetimes."
"From this day forward, do not speak the language of a śūdra.
Having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, out of reverence they never again did so.
Thus the Vinaya is concluded; this is called the Tripuṣkarasāṭaka.

Regarding the "one sheng of oil": after the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, there was an elder bhikṣu residing in Vaiśālī. At that time, a certain merchant invited the bhikṣuṇī Dharmaruci for a meal on the day of the *pravāraṇā*.
A bhikṣuṇī had a dependent disciple whom she constantly sent to fetch whatever she required.
At that time, the dependent disciple did not mention the teacher’s name, nor did she identify herself; she simply said directly:
“Oil is needed.”
The donor gave it immediately, and having received it, she used it herself.
Later, when the donor went to inspect the oil, he found that none had reached the teacher.
The disciple who was living with her felt doubt and regret, and spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs; the bhikṣuṇīs said:
"You have committed a *pārājika* offense.
The bhikṣuṇīs, not understanding this, went to ask the elder bhikṣus.
The elder bhikṣus said:
"Even though he took it by concealing it, because the donor had given it, he committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Thus ends the *vinaya* rule; this is called "one *droṇa* of oil.

Regarding "receiving food": at that time in Śrāvastī, there was a donor who provided a meal for the Saṃgha in the monastery. A certain bhikṣu, having eaten his own portion, further received an additional portion.
Yishishi asked him,
"Elder, for whom did you take this portion?
He replied:
"I have taken it.
"Whose portion is for the one who eats?
he asked again.
"I am my own portion.
Then the bhikṣu said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
The bhikṣus did not understand this and went to ask the elder bhikṣus.
The elder bhikṣus said:
"There was taking what should not have been taken; however, because there was a master who gave it, one incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya."
Thus the Vinaya rule is concluded; this is called "receiving food.

Regarding the one who tends to the sick: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a sick bhikṣu in the Jetavana Monastery who had quarreled with the bhikṣu who was tending to him. At that time, a donor (dānapati) was providing a meal for the Saṃgha within the monastery, and the sick bhikṣu thought to himself:
"How can that person possibly get food for me today?"
He then requested another bhikṣu to fetch food.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was nursing the patient thought to himself:
"Who will go to fetch food for him today?"
Then the two of them both took food. The person distributing the food asked the monk who was nursing the patient, "For whom did you take this food?
He replied:
"Such-and-such a patient has eaten.
He then asked the person who had been hired to fetch food:
"For whom did you take this food?"
He replied,
"It was eaten by a certain sick person.
The bhikṣus said:
"You have committed a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, the monks did not understand and went to ask the elder monks.
The elder monks said:
“There is no offense in this case of hiring someone to fetch food.
However, if a sick bhikṣu has a dispute with the attendant bhikṣu and, without informing the attendant, hires another person instead, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.”
"If a nurse, after quarreling with a fellow bhikṣu who is ill, does not inquire about him or offer him food, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
Thus ends the *vinaya* rule; this is called "nursing the sick."

Regarding the piece of bird meat: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the time had come, put on his village-entering robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, a bird dropped a piece of meat into a bhikṣu’s alms bowl; the bhikṣu took it back to the vihāra, cooked it, ate it himself, and shared some with the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said:
"Elder! Where did you obtain this meat?"
He then related the matter in detail as it had occurred. The bhikṣus said, "You have committed a pārājika offense.
As the bhikṣus could not reach a definitive conclusion, they went to consult the elder bhikṣus, and the elder bhikṣus said:
"Animals have no owner.
Thus concludes the *vinaya* [rule] regarding this; it is called the "meat-piece of a bird.
Regarding the "meat-piece of a thief": after the Parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One, elder bhikṣus resided in dependence upon Rājagṛha.

At that time, there were thieves who had stolen a cow; having slaughtered and eaten it in the Śītavana cemetery at night, they left some remains and said to a bhikṣu sitting in meditation in the forest:
"Venerable sir, do you require meat?"
He replied,
"I need some," and the other immediately gave him a full bowl.
The bhikṣu, having taken it, carried it back to the vihāra, ate some himself, and shared it with the other bhikṣus.
The other bhikṣus asked him,
"Venerable sir!..."
"Where did you obtain this meat?
[The monk] related the aforementioned matter in detail. The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable One!
If you take property from a thief worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The monks, not understanding this, went to ask the elder monks.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"For one who has left the household life, whether the person before them acts according to the Dharma or not, there is no offense in accepting a gift from a donor.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called the "meat-piece of a thief."
Regarding pork: at that time, in a village near Kausāmbī called Deva, some thieves stole pigs and ate them, leaving behind the heads and feet which they abandoned and departed with.
A bhikṣu, having seen this, took them back to the vihāra; after boiling them, he ate them himself and also distributed portions to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Where did you obtain this meat?
He then related the matter in detail as it had occurred, and the bhikṣus said:
"If it is worth exactly five māsakas, one incurs a pārājika offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not understand this and went to ask the elder bhikṣus.
The elder bhikṣus said:
"What thought did you have when you took it?
He replied, "I had the perception that there was no owner."
“There is no offense for taking [meat] with the perception that there is no owner.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called “pork.

Regarding the one who kicked a woman: at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, at the proper time, a certain bhikṣu put on his village-entering robes and, carrying his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food in sequence until he reached a certain household.
The woman said,
"A bhikṣu has come in to engage in such an act with me.
The bhikṣu said:
“The World-Honored One has established the precept that one must not engage in sexual misconduct.
The woman said, “If you do not comply with me,
I shall slander you in such and such a manner, claiming that you have forcibly dragged me [into this].”
Out of fear, that bhikṣu entered; having entered, the woman said to the maidservant guarding the door, "I wish to engage in sexual desire with the bhikṣu.
Once the woman had entered, her lustful mind became intensely inflamed and she lay down. The bhikṣu, having kicked her, departed.
The doorkeeper’s maidservant asked,
"Venerable sir, have you finished your work?
He replied:
“It is finished.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, so he went to consult an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"If you kick a woman with your foot, you commit a *sthūlātyaya*.
To claim that something was done when it was not done constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called "kicking a woman."

Regarding "grinding flour": at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu put on his village-entering robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to go on his almsround, arriving at a certain house.
He saw a woman crouching on the ground grinding flour, her clothes not covering her body; having seen this, the bhikṣu immediately gave rise to a lustful mind and said, "Sister!
I wish to eat some flour."
The woman then gave him flour.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, so he went to ask an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"With what state of mind? He replied,
"With a lustful mind."
He immediately sent a messenger to question the woman, who replied:
"I was crouching on the ground grinding flour when the bhikṣu begged for it; I gave it to him."
The messenger returned and answered as above.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"If one understands the meaning but does not understand the phrasing, it is a sthūlātyaya."
"Up to and including not understanding the meaning or the flavor [of the teaching], one incurs an offense of violating the Vinaya.
Thus ends the section on *piṣṭa* (ground flour). As for "the calf":
there was a man in the Vṛji country who, not far from a monastery, let loose a calf. The calf entered the monastery, trampled and ate the flowers and fruits, and butted against the sacred images.
The administrator said to the person tending the calf, "Look well after your calf; do not allow it to become unruly.
He spoke thus two or three times, yet [the calf] still did not stop.
The steward became angry, led the calf into the room, and instead of leaving it open, closed the door and entered the village to beg for food.
On the way, he thought to himself:
"There are many yakṣas in that room; could they not have killed this calf?"
He immediately returned to the vihāra; opening the door, he saw that the calf was already dead. Terrified, the bhikṣu placed it inside the monks' latrine and then departed.
The cowherd came and asked,
"Ācārya, have you seen my calf?
He replied:
“I did not see it.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and remorse, so he questioned the other bhikṣus, but they were unable to resolve his doubt. He went to question the elders, and the elders said:
"To lead a calf into a room and then close the door behind it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To place it inside a monastic latrine constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To see it and yet say one did not see it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called "releasing the calf.

Regarding the abandonment of a wife: in the great city of Kāśīgirika, there was once an old man (*mahallaka*) of handsome appearance who abandoned his wife to go forth as a monk. His wife followed him and remained outside the dwelling room spinning yarn.
The mahallaka said: "Go away!
I am an ordained person; I have no need for you."
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
What harm could there be in my doing this here?"
"I only wish to see the Venerable One from time to time; I cannot bear to be parted from him.
Because the Mahallaka spoke these words repeatedly, [the monk] still did not leave, so he took his robes and bowl and departed, abandoning him.
A woman saw him and said,
"Your husband has already left.
Upon hearing this, she immediately pursued him.
Having arrived, he immediately took hold of the master's robe and stood before him, saying:
"Preceptor, do not depart for my sake; I shall provide you with robes, bowls, and medicine for illnesses and ailments."
The mahallaka said, "I am an ordained monk;
according to the Dharma, this should not be done.
Even so, he still would not release it. The mahallaka became angry in his heart, set aside his robes and bowl in one place, beat him severely, and departed.
The mahallaka felt doubt and regret, and he related all that had occurred to the Vinaya-master Bhikṣu Yaśas.
Yaśas said, "One who strikes a woman out of anger commits a pārājika offense."
The bhikṣus said:
"This is not a proper resolution.
If you wish to resolve your doubt, you should go to Mount Cetiya and consult the Venerable Dharmadāsa, the master of the Vinaya; he will surely be able to provide a definitive answer."

Having heard this, he departed immediately. On the road leading to Kauśāmbī, he encountered a woman selling curd; seeing that the mahallaka was handsome, she conceived a lustful desire and said, "Come, Śramaṇa, let us engage in sexual intercourse."
The mahallaka thought to himself:
"I have already committed a pārājika offense; what else remains?
And so he engaged in sexual intercourse with her.
He went before the Vinaya-holder and reported the matter in detail.
The Vinaya-holder said,
"How can Yaśas establish the five *pārājika* rules?"
"Striking a woman in anger constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman selling curd constitutes a *pārājika*.
Thus concludes the Vinaya; this is called "abandoning a wife."
Regarding "the neighbor": there was a bhikṣu in the country of Vakkala who lived in a dwelling adjacent to a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra.
At that time, the bhikṣu gave rise to lustful thoughts and conversed with the bhikṣuṇī through the wall throughout the entire night.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, so he went to ask an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu said,
"What words did you speak with what intention?"
He replied, "A mind of desire. [The Buddha said,] "With such a mind of desire,
for every word spoken, one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya."
Thus the *vinaya* concludes; this is called "through the wall. Regarding the *poṣadha*:
the bhikṣus of the village of Vakkala performed the *poṣadha* together with the bhikṣus who were forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu residing in an araṇya dwelling named Pukkusāti, who possessed great virtue and renown; when the bhikṣus in the village saw him receiving offerings and gain, they conceived a mind of jealousy.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the uposatha, the Elder Pāṭali approached the village and said to the bhikṣus therein:
"Venerable sirs!
Come, let us perform the uposatha together."
He replied,
"I shall perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day.
The Puchiluo said:
"I know the number of days; today should be the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day.
He replied, "I will not do it;
the *poṣadha* shall be held on the fifteenth day."
When he had thus failed to comply for a third time, Vatsīputra departed.
After he had left, the bhikṣus in the village performed the poṣadha ceremony.
The next day, Vatsīputra came again, saying:
"Venerable sir, please come and perform the *poṣadha* together with us.
He replied,
"The *poṣadha* has already been completed."
The village monks said, "You have rebelled against the *poṣadha*;
we shall no longer share with you the food of the Dharma or the food of the taste.
At that time, Pukkusa came on the fourteenth day when it was the fourteenth, and on the fifteenth day when it was the fifteenth; thus, for twenty years, he did not obtain the *poṣadha* at all.
At that time, there was a benevolent spirit who held Vatsīputra in high esteem; he went to where the Venerable Śrīdatta was dwelling on Mount Citrakūṭa and spoke these words:
"Venerable One!..."
"It is unwholesome and contrary to the Dharma,
Venerable Sir!
While dwelling among the villages, monks commit such illegal acts as constantly harassing the Vṛji people."
“I only pray that the Venerable One will go there himself to attend to the matter.
Having heard this, the Venerable Jotika came immediately and thought to himself:
“If I arrive first at the forest hermitage, the monks in the village are fierce and wicked; upon hearing of my arrival, they will not share with me the food of the Dharma or the food of taste.”
Having had this thought, he went at once to where the bhikṣus were in the village.
Then the benevolent spirit said to the Venerable Pukkusa:
"The Venerable Sūtiṭṭha is now in the village; you may go there to pay him your respects."
Having heard this, he went at once to greet him, and after exchanging greetings, sat down to one side.
Jyotiṣka then asked: "Are you Pukkusāti?"
He replied, "Yes. "O Āyuṣmat!"
"Have you rebelled against the *poṣadha*? He replied,
"Whether I have rebelled against the *poṣadha* or not, you shall know it now."

For twenty years now, when there was a *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day, it has occurred on the fourteenth; when there was a *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, it has occurred on the fifteenth. Is this not a rebellion against the *poṣadha*?
"Did you break the Poṣadha?
Venerable sir, you know for yourself.
He replied:
“Āyuṣman! This accords with the Buddha-dharma.

However, the bhikṣus in the village do not follow it; for twenty years, their full ordination (upasampadā) is not called full ordination, and their formal ritual (karmavācanā) is not called a ritual.”
When the *vinaya* has been concluded in this manner, it is called the *poṣadha*.

Regarding the two kinds of drinks: at that time, in the kingdom of Ujjayinī, there was a person who had violated the king’s law; after his hands and feet were severed, he was placed in the *śītavana* (cemetery) near the dwelling of forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣus.
Winding his way, he came to where the bhikṣu was and said, "Ācārya!
I am suffering greatly from hunger; please grant me a little food."
He replied, "There is no food.
He spoke again:
“Ācārya! Have compassion for me.
I am suffering from two kinds of pain:”
"First, the suffering of having one's hands and feet cut off;
second, the suffering of hunger.
He replied:
"There is no food; there is only *sūvīra* juice.
Do you need some? He replied, "I do."
He then gave him the gruel.
Before he had finished eating, he drank it and died immediately.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and regret; he questioned the other bhikṣus, but they could not resolve the matter, so he went to question the elder bhikṣus.
The elder bhikṣu said,
"With what intention did you give it?
He replied:
"A mind of benefit.
"A mind of benefit is blameless.
Thus the Vinaya concludes.

Furthermore, in the kingdom of Ujjayinī, there was a person who violated the king’s law; having had his hands and feet cut off, he was placed in the Śītavana cemetery near the dwelling place of forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣus.
At that time, there was an elder (*mahallaka*) who had gone forth and was on duty guarding the dwellings. A person without hands or feet crawled toward him and said, "Preceptor!..."
"I am in such excruciating pain that it is unbearable; is there perhaps some small amount of medicine you could give me? I wish to die quickly.
He replied, "I am not a *caṇḍāla* or a murderous thief; why do you seek medicine from me?"
"No, Ācārya! My pain is difficult to bear.
Then the Mahallaka gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and thought to himself:
“There was once a bhikṣu who died after drinking *suvīra* juice.
He then asked him,
“Do you wish to drink *suvīra* juice?”
He replied, "I wish to drink.
He immediately gave him some gruel to drink; having drunk it, he died.
The mahallaka felt doubt and regret, so he went to ask an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu said,
"With what intention did you give it?"
He replied,
"With a mind of loving-kindness, I shall fulfill his wish.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"Although you possess a compassionate heart, you lack wisdom; by severing the life-faculty of another, you have committed a *pārājika* offense.
Thus the *vinaya* rule concludes; this is called the second [case of] fermented liquor.
Regarding the brick: at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu was building a dwelling when a park-keeper brought him a brick.
Because the bhikṣu did not hold it firmly, it fell onto the park-keeper’s head and shattered, whereby he died immediately.
The bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, so he went to ask an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu said,
"With what state of mind did you drop the brick?"
He replied,
"Because I did not grasp it firmly.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"One should grasp it firmly.
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called "brick.
Regarding "filth": at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, the refuse was cleared once every five days.

At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who took some excrement and threw it over the wall. A sick mahallaka (elderly monk) who had gone forth was defecating beneath the wall when the excrement fell directly upon him; he was unable to rise, and as more excrement continued to arrive, he died.
When Bhikṣu Dhammika was clearing away a high pile of refuse for fear that thieves might climb up it, he saw a dead bhikṣu.
A sense of doubt and remorse arose in his mind, so he went to consult an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu asked,
"With what state of mind did you clear away the refuse?
He replied:
“I will not look.
The elder bhikṣu said:
“If you do not look before throwing away the excrement, you commit an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.”
Thus the Vinaya concludes; this is called "refuse.
Regarding the *piṇḍapātika* bhikṣu: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various bhikṣus were residing at the Śākya vihāra in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having put on his village-entering robes and taken up his alms bowl, entered the city to walk for alms in succession.

At that moment, there was a woman of the Śākya clan who was beautiful; having finished bathing and put on fresh, clean clothes, she brought food to offer to the bhikṣu, and having made the offering, she prostrated herself with her head at his feet.
Having seen her, the bhikṣu’s lustful mind arose; unable to restrain himself, he discharged impurity which fell upon the woman's head.
The woman felt no resentment; she immediately took her robe, wiped it away, and said: "Ācārya!..."
"I have gained a great and wholesome benefit, for I possess such a desire as this: to cultivate the holy life within the Dharma of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt doubt and regret, so he went to consult an elder bhikṣu.
The elder bhikṣu asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"I see these preceding signs and my mind cannot restrain itself.
The elder bhikṣu said:
"You should carefully observe the signs and subdue your mind."
Thus concludes the Vinaya on this matter; this is called "begging for food.
As for *Utsūtra*: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, elder bhikṣus were staying at the Śākya Monastery under the Nyagrodha tree in Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Venerable Uruvela was acquainted with a member of the Śākya clan.
At that time, the Śākya was ill and had two sons by different mothers:
one son was the daughter of a Śākya woman, and the other son was the daughter of a woman of a different lineage.
When the Śākya was nearing his end, he entrusted the Venerable Uruvilvā, saying:
"Ācārya! After my passing, if either of these two sons should have a love for the Buddha-dharma and gain the heart of an Ācārya, show them this treasure hidden in the earth."
After his death, the daughter of the Śākya clan associated with evil friends; she took no pleasure in the Buddha-dharma, did not come to receive the scriptures, and had no interest in reciting them.

At that time, a daughter of another family associated with virtuous friends; she loved and delighted in the Buddha-dharma, came to Uruvilvā to receive instruction in the sutras and precepts, and won the heart of the Elder.
She then said: "When your father passed away, he entrusted me with this, saying: 'If among your children there is one who delights in the Dharma, you may show him this treasury.'"
He immediately showed her the place, where she obtained great quantities of gold, silver, and precious treasures, and her household became wealthy and happy.
Having heard this, the daughter of the Śākya clan said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ācārya!..."
"This is neither good nor appropriate.
Venerable Uttara, you have taken my father’s wealth and given it to the son of a mother from another clan.
According to our Śākya tradition, the daughters of the Śākyas should succeed to their father’s estate; all his property rightfully belongs to me."
Ānanda said, "This is an unlawful settlement;
I will not share in the dharma-food or the taste-food with you.
Then Rāhula came to the place where Ucchya was; since the two were of the same upādhyāya, he immediately spoke to Rāhula, saying:
"Do not share the same dharma-food or flavor-food as the Venerable Ānanda.
They asked, "For what reason?"
He related the preceding circumstances in detail:
"I have no need for it; Ānanda does not share with me the food of the Dharma or the food of flavor, whereas Rāhula, you share with me the food of the Dharma and the food of flavor."
When Ānanda heard that Rāhula was sharing both Dharma-food and material food with Ucchuṣma,
at that time Ānanda also did not share either Dharma-food or material food with Rāhula.
At that time, someone brought food to the Venerable Ānanda.
Ānanda said,
"Give it to Rāhula, the son of the World-Honored One."
In this way, whenever food was sent to Venerable Rāhula, Rāhula would say:
"Take this and give it to the World-Honored One’s attendant.
Thus, for seven years in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, they did not perform the Poṣadha or the Pravāraṇā ceremonies.
The Venerable Upāli was dwelling on Mount Cetiya. At that time, a son of the Śākya clan went to where the Venerable Upāli was staying and spoke to him thus:
"Preceptor!..."
"This is improper and not in accordance with the Dharma.
While the Ācārya is still alive, and since Kapilavastu is the birthplace of the World-Honored One, why have you not performed the Poṣadha and the Pravāraṇā for seven years?"
"I only pray that the Venerable One will go and bring about reconciliation.

Upāli immediately came and instructed the Śākyas to adorn the great hall, prepare excellent seats, scatter flowers, and burn incense, in order to provide a meal for the visiting bhikṣus and to invite the Venerable Ānanda.

First, he called Rāhula and placed him in a secluded spot; then, having a small child held by someone, he set the child down on the ground within the assembly. Once the Venerable Ānanda was seated, he saw the small child on the ground and said:
"Take [him]."
To this, one should say:
"I will not take it.
If you wish, Venerable Sir, to reconcile with Rāhula, then I shall take it."

After he had thus instructed them, the Venerable Upāli sat down, followed by the Venerable Ānanda; once all the bhikṣus were seated in order, a young woman of the Śākya clan, holding a child in her arms who was sucking fresh butter, let it fall onto the ground in the midst of the assembly, whereupon the child began to cry out.
Having seen this, Ānanda felt a sense of affection and said,
"Take this child. He replied:
"I will not accept it.
If the Venerable One is in harmony with Rāhula, I shall accept it; if he is not in harmony, I will not accept it.
Ānanda said:
"This is the dharma of a śramaṇa; it is not for you, a layperson, to do so—just hold the infant. He replied, "Not so."
Thus he spoke up to three times.
Ānanda said, "Call Rāhula here."
Having arrived, the Venerable Upāli said to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, suppose there is a donor who has instructed an elder in such and such a manner, saying:
'After my life comes to an end, may the elder bestow this upon me.'"
"What fault is there?
The Venerable Uruvela was likewise so.
Why, Ānanda, would you not harmonize this matter with Rāhula, the son of the World-Honored One?"
Thus the Vinaya is concluded; this is called *ucchāvana*, and this is called the Vinaya-dharma.
Regarding the dharma of obstacles and the dharma of non-obstacles: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, as explained in detail above.

At that time, the Venerable Nanda and Upānanda, having traveled through various countries, returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery; putting on their village-entry robes, they entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the home of the laywoman Priyā.
Having seen him, the upāsikā said, "Welcome, Ācārya! Why have you appeared so rarely?
She immediately invited him to sit, prostrated herself at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. After they had exchanged greetings, the bhikṣu said:
“Upāsikā! I am traveling on a rare occasion; what kind of fine food and drink can you provide for me?
The upāsikā replied:
"Following the instructions of the Ācārya, whether it be food before or after the meal, or cakes or meat, I shall prepare whatever is required.
He then invited him, saying:
"Venerable One, please accept my meal tomorrow; I pray that you will come early."
He immediately accepted the invitation.
The following day, the household prepared various kinds of food and drink, spread out seats, and waited for him.
However, due to many pressing matters, the bhikṣu forgot and did not come to attend.
When the time for the meal has passed, that which can be kept may be set aside; that which cannot be kept should be eaten immediately.
If, after two or three days have passed while waiting for him not to come, he still does not arrive, one should then eat all that remains.
When he finally arrived on the fourth day, the upāsikā was displeased upon seeing him and said:
"Ācārya! Why did you accept my invitation yet fail to come?"
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon Nanda and Upananda."
When she had arrived, the Buddha said:
"This laywoman Priyā has no attachment whatsoever toward the Buddha or the community of bhikṣus; for what reason does she cause such disturbance among them?"
"How can you accept an invitation unilaterally without disclosing the causes and conditions that constitute an obstacle?
As for the dharmas that constitute an obstacle:
if someone should say, "Venerable sir, please accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow morning."
If he requires it, he should say: "Yes.
He then says again:
"Venerable One!
You must certainly come.
One should say:
"There will be no obstacles in the interim; you shall come.
This applies likewise to meals after midday and to all invitations.
If a bhikṣu departs after completing the rainy season retreat, the donor says:
"Venerable sir!
Please come again later.
If he wishes to come, one should reply:
"Yes," the donor replied again,
"Venerable Sir!"
"He will certainly come.
One should reply:
"He will come provided there are no obstacles along the way."
If one says:
"Preceptor! I pay homage to the stūpa."
One must not say:
"There are no obstacles in between.
One should say:
"One should prostrate.
Or if one says:
"Venerable sir, please prostrate for me at the stūpa."
One should say: "If you remember, you should pay homage. If he says:
"Venerable One!
Pay homage to the elder bhikṣu.
One must not say:
If [the other] says, "There is no obstacle," one should say,
"I shall pay homage."
If he says, "Venerable sir, please pay homage for me to the elder bhikṣus," one should say:
"If you remember [this], you should pay homage.
Or if one says:
"Venerable sir, please receive this scripture, recite this scripture, uphold the precepts, or practice meditation."
One must not say:
"There are no obstacles in between; you should receive and recite the sutra.
One should instead say:
"I have gone forth for this reason.
Or if one says:
"I study for the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship."
One should not say:
"One should train so that there are no obstacles in between.
One should instead say:
"I have gone forth for this reason.
In this matter, if one fails to create an obstacle where one ought to do so, or creates an obstacle where one ought not to do so, in either case one commits an offense against the Vinaya.
These are called the dharmas that constitute obstacles and those that do not.
Regarding the *bhikṣuṇī-dharma*: The Buddha was staying at the Śākya vihāra in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred Śākya women, requested ordination from the Buddha. This is explained in detail in the *Sūtra on the Thread*, up until the point where the Buddha addressed the *bhikṣuṇīs*:
“From this day forth, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī shall be the senior of the community of bhikṣuṇīs; thus it shall be maintained.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Will we be able to hear in detail the Eight Rules of Respect established for bhikṣuṇīs?

The Buddha said, "Regarding those who have received the Eight Rules of Respect: even if a bhikṣuṇī has been ordained for a full hundred years, she must rise to welcome, show respect, and prostrate before a newly ordained bhikṣu."
One must not say:
"I will wait until I have reached one hundred years of seniority before I pay homage to a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts.
All bhikṣuṇīs should rise to welcome, show respect to, and pay homage to bhikṣus—whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or juniors.
When a bhikṣuṇī arrives at a bhikṣu’s monastery, she should prostrate with her head at the feet of every bhikṣu one by one.
If she is too old or ill to do so, she should prostrate according to her capacity; for those whom she cannot reach individually, she may prostrate collectively, saying:
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], prostrate with my head at the feet of the entire Saṃgha."
"When a bhikṣu arrives at a bhikṣuṇī's vihāra, all the bhikṣuṇīs should rise to welcome him and pay homage at his feet, as described above.

If a bhikṣuṇī makes such distinctions—thinking, 'This one has broken the precepts,' 'This one is a physician,' or 'This one is a mahallaka who knows nothing'—and fails to rise and pay homage out of pride and lack of respect, she violates the rule of reverence."

The first section on Reverence for the Dharma concludes. Regarding the second year of training: if a girl who has reached eighteen years of age wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the discipline of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya, the preceptor nun (*upādhyāyinī*) shall provide her with all necessary requisites and arrange the formal announcement to the Saṃgha.
The person capable of performing the *karmavācanā* among the community of nuns should speak as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This maiden so-and-so, eighteen years of age, desires to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata."
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha permits, [let it be known that] so-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts.
Venerable sirs, listen: so-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

"This woman shall enter the Saṃgha and pay homage at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha by bowing her head to the ground. Having paid homage at their feet, she shall kneel with palms joined and be instructed to speak as follows:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!'"
I, the maiden so-and-so, who am eighteen years of age, desire to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.
I now request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts; may the noble Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the two-year training in the precepts.
Thus it was said three times.
The *ni-karmācārya* should speak as follows:
"Listen, noble Saṃgha!
The girl so-and-so has reached the age of eighteen and has already requested from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant so-and-so the two-year training in the precepts.
The motion is thus made.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This girl, so-and-so, being eighteen years of age, has already requested from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts."
The Saṃgha now grants two years of training in the precepts to [Name].
Venerable Saṃgha, please grant two years of training in the precepts to [Name] with her Preceptor Nun [Name]; those who consent, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The first *karmavācanā* is concluded.
The second and third are likewise recited.
"The Sangha has already granted [the name] two years of training in the precepts; because the Sangha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
Once this śikṣamāṇā has completed her two years of training in the precepts, she should practice eighteen matters in accordance with the rules.
What are these eighteen?
She is to stand below all bhikṣuṇīs and above all śrāmaṇerīs.
What is impure for a *śikṣamāṇā* may be pure for a *bhikṣuṇī*, yet what is impure for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise impure for a *śikṣamāṇā*.
A *bhikṣuṇī* may stay with a *śikṣamāṇā* for three nights, and a *śikṣamāṇā* may stay with a *śrāmaṇerī* for three nights.
A *śikṣamāṇā* may receive food from a *bhikṣuṇī*, except for food that has not been purified by fire, the five kinds of living seeds, and the taking of gold, silver, or money.

Once a śrāmaṇerikā has received food, a bhikṣuṇī must not speak to her regarding offenses from pārājika down to those that violate the vinaya; she may only say such things as "do not engage in sexual misconduct," "do not steal," "do not kill," and "do not lie."
On the day of the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, the *śikṣamāṇā* enters the midst of the Saṃgha, kneels with her right knee on the ground and joins her palms, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha! I, so-and-so, am pure; may the Saṃgha bear this in mind."
Having spoken thus three times, he departed.
Regarding the subsequent four *pārājika* offenses, one must begin training anew;
for the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and below, if one commits any single one, one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession according to the specific offense committed.
If one violates the five precepts, one must retrain for as many days as the number of violations committed.
What are these five?
Eating at improper times, eating stored food, handling money, gold, or silver, drinking alcohol, and wearing flowers or perfumes.
These are called the eighteen matters.

When a śikṣamāṇā has completed two years of training in the precepts and wishes to receive full ordination within the discipline and teachings of the Tathāgata, the preceptor-nun (upādhyāyinī) should inform the Saṃgha and request the formal act (karmavācanā) for admitting a disciple.
The *ni-karmācārya* (nun preceptor) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Śikṣamāṇā [Name], having trained in the precepts for two years and being twenty years of age, wishes to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is in harmony, the preceptor-ni [named] So-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for maintaining a disciple.
Venerable Saṃgha, please listen: So-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the formal act for maintaining a following. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The preceptor nun should kneel with palms joined and speak as follows:
“Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!

This śikṣamāṇā has trained in the precepts for two years and is now twenty years of age; she desires to receive full ordination. I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of maintaining a disciple. I pray that the Saṃgha grant me the formal act of maintaining a disciple.”
When this has been repeated three times,
the person performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The śikṣamāṇā [Name] has studied the precepts for two years and is now twenty years of age; she wishes to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata. The nun [Name] has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for taking a disciple.
“If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the nun so-and-so to receive a disciple.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"This is the first formal act (*karmavācanā*).

"The Saṃgha has already consented to grant the formal act for [the nun] so-and-so to keep a disciple; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

If this śikṣamāṇā has trained in the precepts for two years and has reached twenty years of age, and wishes to receive full ordination within the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya, she shall enter the Saṃgha and first prostrate with her head at the feet of the Saṃgha.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, one first requests the Upādhyāyī, kneeling with palms joined, and speaks as follows:
"Venerable One, please take heed!
I, [Name], beg the Venerable One to be my Upādhyāya; may the Venerable One act as my Upādhyāya and grant me full ordination."
When this has been repeated three times, the preceptor nun should say:
"Generate a joyful mind.
The disciple says:
"I shall receive and uphold this.

The preceptor nun has already provided the candidate with a request for robes and a bowl, with a request for a community, with requests for two preceptors, and with a request for a teacher to instruct her in a secluded place; she now refers her to the Sangha.
The *karmavācanā* master should speak thus:
"Who among you here is able to act as the preceptor for [Name] in a secluded place?
They should reply:
"I am able. The *karmavācanā* master should speak thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
So-and-so, with Preceptor Nun so-and-so, has been appointed as the instructor in a secluded place by so-and-so; since the Sangha consents through silence, this matter shall be held thus.
The preceptor should lead the person seeking full ordination away from the assembly, neither too near nor too far, and instruct them in two ways: either briefly or extensively.
What is the brief method?
Within the assembly of monks, one should ask:
"If you have [it], you should say you have it; if you do not have it, you should say you do not have it.
