“Listen, virtuous woman!

Now is the time for sincerity; now is the time for truthful speech. Before the devas, the world, the Māras, the Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, and asuras—if you speak what is untrue, you will be deceiving them, and you will likewise be deceiving the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the community of śrāvaka nuns; this is a grave offense.”
"I shall now question you: if it exists, say it exists; if it does not exist, say it does not.

"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise recited.

The Sangha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so, acting as a messenger, to confer full ordination upon the Dharma-preceptor’s disciple, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Once this bhikṣu has completed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), he should immediately go to the nunnery.
The person receiving full ordination should entreat the messenger, kneeling with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!
I, [Name], have received full ordination from the preceptor nun [Name] and have already received full ordination within the community of bhikṣuṇīs; I am pure and free from obstructing dharmas.
If I were to leave this place, I would fear injury to my brahmacarya; therefore, I shall remain here.
I, [Name], with [Name] as my preceptor-ni, now request the Saṃgha to grant me full ordination; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me full ordination.
Thus it should be repeated up to three times.
The preceptor nun, together with the messenger, should go before the Saṃgha; the preceptor nun should then beg [for ordination], kneeling with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!

I am a nun belonging to our school; my disciple so-and-so wishes to receive full ordination. She has already received full ordination within the community of nuns and is pure, free from obstructing conditions. However, if she were to come here, I fear it would harm her holy life; therefore, she remains there.
"I, the disciple so-and-so, now request from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me full ordination.
Thus he requests three times.
The *karmakāraka* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

So-and-so has received full ordination from So-and-so; she has already received full ordination within the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, and is pure and free from obstructing conditions. However, if she were to come here, she would fear injury to her holy life (*brahmacarya*); therefore, she remains there."
The preceptor nun [Name] has already requested from the Sangha the conferral of full ordination.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as her preceptor nun.
"Thus it is announced.
After the one announcement and three *karmavācanās* have been completed, the preceptor nun, together with the messenger, returns to the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma and speaks as follows:
"Listen, virtuous daughter!

You have already received full ordination through one motion and three proclamations, in accordance with the rules of non-obstruction, by a quorum of more than ten members, and through the harmonious assembly of both orders.

Having completed the reception of full ordination, you should revere the Three Jewels; for you have encountered that which is difficult to obtain—a human body—and that which is difficult to meet—the appearance of a Buddha in the world—and that which is likewise difficult to hear—the Dharma.
This is called receiving full ordination within the two assemblies after two years of training in the precepts;
this is called the second rule of respect.
Regarding the disclosure of offenses: a bhikṣuṇī must not disclose a bhikṣu’s actual or non-actual offense.
A bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s actual offenses, but he must not speak of her non-actual offenses.

A bhikṣuṇī must not address a bhikṣu as a "physician," a "transgressor of the precepts," or an "old fool" (*mahallaka*). If he is a relative, she may admonish him with gentle words, but she must not revile him.
If they are young, one should say to them:
"Do you not study now, intending to study only when you are old?

In the future, you shall instruct and admonish your disciples; if you do not study, your disciples will likewise learn from you to commit evil. Therefore, you should study accordingly, receiving and reciting the sūtras."
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a bhikṣu’s faults, saying, "This bhikṣu is a physician," "this bhikṣu is a transgressor of the precepts," or "this bhikṣu is a mahallaka," she violates the rules of respect.
A bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s actual faults, but he must not revile her by calling her a "shaven-headed old woman," a "lecherous old woman," or a "Mahallikā (old crone)."
If a relative commits an unrighteous act, one may say to them, "Do not do this.
One must not scold or revile them,
but should instead admonish them with gentle words.
If they are young, one should say to them:
"Do you not study now, intending to study only when you are old?
In the future, you shall instruct your own disciples; if you do not study now, your disciples will later follow your example and practice evil. Therefore, you must receive and recite the scriptures."
If a bhikṣu reviles a bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Shaven-headed old woman! Licentious old woman! Mahallikā! You are unvirtuous and do not recognize kindness."
To do so constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This means that a bhikṣuṇī may not speak of a bhikṣu’s actual or non-actual offenses, whereas a bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s actual offenses.
This is called the third rule of respect.
Regarding "not receiving first": a bhikṣuṇī must not receive food, lodging, or bedding before a bhikṣu.
If someone invites a bhikṣuṇī for a meal, she should say:
"First, I invite the most venerable assembly.
If they say, "I have no respectful heart toward them; I wish instead to invite the bhikṣuṇīs," [one should respond accordingly].
To this, one should say: "I also do not accept. If he says:
"I have previously invited the Saṃgha for a meal before or after [the midday meal], and have already invited them together with others; however, I have never invited the bhikṣuṇīs.
If this is the case, they should accept.
As for the case where one has previously given a single morsel of food to the Saṃgha, if a bhikṣuṇī subsequently receives various kinds of excellent food,
she incurs no offense. If someone comes and says,
"I wish to build a dwelling for a bhikṣuṇī," [the same applies].
One should say:
"First perform it for the assembly of the most venerable ones. If [they] say:
If one says, "I have no respect for him; I simply wish to act as a preceptor for a bhikṣuṇī," one should say:
"I will not accept either."
If she says:

"I have previously built rooms, lecture halls, warm rooms, dining halls, gatehouses, well-houses, latrines, and foot-washing sheds for the Saṃgha; I have built them together with the multitude, but never for nuns."
"If that is the case, it should be accepted.
Even if one has previously given a single mosquito net to the Saṃgha, there is no offense for a bhikṣuṇī to subsequently accept a large room.
If someone comes to give a bed or bedding to a bhikṣuṇī, she should say:"
"First give it to the most venerable among the assembly.
If one says,
"I have no heart of respect for him," [one incurs an offense].
One should say:
"I, too, do not accept it.
If they say:
"If I have previously provided beds, mattresses, pillows, and bedding for the community of bhikṣus, but never for the bhikṣuṇīs,
then [the gift] may be accepted."
If she first gives a small bed to the community of bhikṣus, and the bhikṣuṇī subsequently receives a fine bed and bedding, there is no offense.
However, if a donor has never previously provided beds and bedding for the Saṃgha, and the bhikṣuṇī receives them first, she violates the rule of respect.
This is called the rule that a bhikṣuṇī must not use bedding or mats before having first received permission to do so.
This concludes the fourth rule of respect.

Regarding the *mānatva* for half a month: if a bhikṣuṇī violates a rule of respect, she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both assemblies (the assembly of bhikṣus and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs).

If one commits nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one should practice *mānatva* for half a month within both assemblies; while among the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, one should perform the practices of compliance and announce [one's status] daily to both assemblies. These are called the two assemblies.
This is called the bhikṣuṇī’s practice of *mānatva* for half a month within the two assemblies.
The fifth rule of respect is concluded.

Regarding the inquiry at the half-monthly *poṣadha* for requesting instruction: on the day of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣuṇīs—whether the entire community of nuns or those sent as messengers—having gone to the bhikṣus’ monastery to pay homage to the stūpas, shall go to a bhikṣu who is a spiritual friend and transmit their pure intention (*śuddhacitta*), speaking as follows:
"The entire community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, bows at the feet of the community of bhikṣus and requests instruction for the poṣadha.
Thus it is said three times.
At the time of the saṃgha’s poṣadha, the bhikṣu who recites the precepts should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Of the days until the next *poṣadha*, this many days have already passed, and this many days remain. Regarding the constant practices of the Buddha’s community of disciples (*śrāvakasaṃgha*), since the Venerable Ones have not come, the monks have declared their consent and purity (*chanda-śauca*). Who will receive the consent from the bhikṣuṇīs?"
The person receiving the *chanda* from the *bhikṣuṇī* sangha should go before the *sthavira*, baring the right shoulder, join their palms, and speak as follows:
“The *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha, being in harmony, pays homage at the feet of the *bhikṣu* saṃgha; they grant their *chanda* for purity and request the *poṣadha* and instruction.”
Thus it was said three times.
The one reciting the precepts should ask:
"Who will instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
If there was someone previously providing instruction, the subsequent person should ask:
"On what day did the nun come?
Where did she provide the instruction?"
The senior should say:
"I shall come on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a place.
If there is no one to give the instruction, she should first take the purity-entrustment (*śuddhikāmatā*) from the *bhikṣuṇī*.
The bhikṣu should say to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Since there is no one to instruct you, you should be careful and not be negligent."
"If a bhikṣu accomplishes twelve qualities, the Saṃgha should perform a formal act (karmavācanā) to appoint him as an instructor.
What are these twelve?
First, upholding the precepts;"
Second, being learned and not forgetting;
third, upholding the Vinaya in both its extensive and abbreviated forms;
fourth, possessing eloquence and the ability to teach.
5. Training in the precepts;
6. Training in concentration;
7. Training in wisdom;
Eighth, being able to eliminate evil and heterodoxy;
ninth, the purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
tenth, not defiling the pure conduct of bhikṣuṇīs.
Eleventh, patience;
twelfth, being twenty years of age or more.
This is called the accomplishment of the twelve dharmas.
The monk who is to serve as the instructor for the bhikṣuṇīs should prostrate.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
"Venerable Sangha, this bhikṣu [Name] has fulfilled the twelve requirements.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha appoint this bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
This is the formal motion."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so has fulfilled the twelve requirements; the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu named So-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
Venerable sirs, those who consent to this bhikṣu’s instruction of bhikṣuṇīs remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has already appointed the bhikṣu so-and-so as the instructor of bhikṣuṇīs; since the Saṃgha remains silent, it consents. Thus this matter is upheld."
Once that bhikṣu has received the formal authorization (*karmavācanā*), he should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the method of instruction, there are eight matters.
What are these eight?
First, the improper time;
second, the improper place;
third, the lapse of time.
4. The time has not yet arrived;
5. lack of harmony; 6. retinue.
7. Teaching the Dharma in verse;
8. Receiving instruction. Regarding "improper time":
from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, instruction is given; this is called improper time.
If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.

Regarding an improper place: he must not do so in a secluded or private place, nor in an exposed place; rather, he should do so in a place that is neither secluded nor exposed, such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree.
If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī at an improper time, he commits a vinaya offense; this is called "an improper place.
Regarding "the wrong time": the fourteenth and fifteenth days are called the wrong time.
Regarding "the time has not yet arrived": if it is the first, second, or third day of the month, this is called "the time has not yet arrived.
One should go to provide instruction from the fourth day until the thirteenth day.
If one instructs bhikṣuṇīs before the proper time has arrived, it is a violation of the Vinaya; this is called "the time not having arrived.
Regarding "lack of harmony": if the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs is not in harmony, one should not instruct them; only after they have become harmonious should one instruct them.
Once the instruction has been delivered, one should ask:
"Has the community of nuns reached consensus? If they say:
"Be assembled.
One should then dispatch a messenger to call out:
"Nuns, come to hear the instruction."
If one is unable to come due to old age, illness, taking medicine, or attending to matters concerning robes or alms bowls, one should give the *chanda* (consent).
One should speak thus:
"I, [Name], give the consent for the instruction."
Thus it was said three times.
If a bhikṣuṇī who instructs does so while the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs is not in harmony, she commits a *vinaya*-offense; this is called "not being in harmony. Regarding "retinue":
one must not instruct them in a partial manner; rather, all the bhikṣuṇīs must first be in harmony, and only then should they be instructed; this is called "retinue."
Regarding "speaking at length," it is as when the Venerable Nanda gave a long discourse of instruction to the nuns; one should speak thus:
"Commit no evil, practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
"Sisters!
This is the instruction; those who wish to listen may do so, and those who wish to leave may go as they please.
If a bhikṣu speaks at length when instructing bhikṣuṇīs, he commits a *vinaya*-offense. This is called "speaking the Dharma at length."

Regarding the method for welcoming the person who provides instruction: if a bhikṣuṇī residing in a city or village hears that the bhikṣu who provides instruction will arrive on a certain day, and if there is no one to provide offerings, she should hire some young bhikṣus to carry flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to go and welcome him.

If there are none, according to their number, one should at least join the palms in respectful salutation and assist in carrying the robes and bowl; or for a distance of one yojana, half a yojana, one krośa, or half a krośa; or at the very least, go outside the city or village to meet them.
If one does not go out to meet them, one commits a *vinaya*-offense.

Once they have arrived, one should exhort and inspire them to provide meals before and after [the meal], as well as non-timely drinks, making offerings with all one's heart; furthermore, for seven days, one must ensure that they and their retinue lack for nothing.
If there is nothing [to offer], one should take from among one's own robes and bowl whatever remains to provide as an offering.
If there is still nothing, one should at least join the palms in reverent salutation.
As for the method of instructing the nuns, it concerns either the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
The Abhidharma consists of the ninefold Sūtras.
The Vinaya consists of the detailed and abbreviated versions of the Prātimokṣa.
When instructing others or when a nun arrives, one must not remain with the head bowed; rather, one should observe her physical appearance and deportment.

If one sees someone with oil applied to their head, eyes adorned with makeup, wearing high-quality garments beaten smooth for luster, and a white sash tied around the waist—one such as this should be rebuked.
If she is young, one should say:
"Sister! Are you not learning now while you are young, intending to learn only when you have grown old?"

In the future, you shall instruct and admonish your disciples; if you do not study, your disciples will likewise learn from you to commit evil. Therefore, you should study and receive the sūtras in accordance with the Dharma, and recite them.
If there are laypeople present, she must not instruct [the woman], lest they give rise to unwholesome thoughts, saying:
"The śramaṇas are instructing women.
If she may not instruct her in such circumstances, she should ask another nun:
"Whose co-practitioner disciple is this?
Whose resident disciple is this?

Having asked this, one should instruct and admonish that preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), causing them to practice the Dharma in accordance with the rules and not to engage in improper conduct.

When a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī, he should regard her as a daughter; the bhikṣuṇī, for her part, should regard the instructor as the Buddha. This is called the fortnightly inquiry during the poṣadha for requesting instruction.
The sixth respect for the Dharma is concluded.

Regarding the rule that one may not dwell in the rains retreat without relying on a bhikṣu: if a relative wishes to invite a bhikṣuṇī to observe the rains retreat, the bhikṣuṇī should say to the donor, "Please invite the most venerable [bhikṣu] first."
If he says, "I have no respectful heart toward her; I simply wish to invite a bhikṣuṇī," the bhikṣuṇī should say:
"I shall not go either.

If one wishes to go for the sake of relatives, one should personally invite bhikṣus; having arrived there, one should provide them with morning meals, afternoon meals, non-timely drinks, and robes for the rainy season retreat, ensuring they lack for nothing.
If relatives do not provide [necessities], one should personally provide for them from the remainder of one's own robes and bowl.
If, during the *varṣā* retreat, a bhikṣu dies, renounces the path, or departs for another place, the bhikṣuṇī must not depart.
If there is a monastery within three *yojanas*, one should establish a common boundary and go every half-month to inquire about the *poṣadha*.

If there are obstacles such as bandits on the road, or if there is terror and fear of losing one's life or violating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and if such difficulties exist, one should go for the *pravāraṇā* at the end of the later retreat period.
If there should still be various difficulties, you should tell your relatives:
"Please invite a bhikṣu on my behalf.

Once he has arrived, provide him with all necessities—food before the meal, food after the meal, and non-timely drinks—ensuring he lacks for nothing. After he has finished his self-indulgent retreat (pravāraṇā), he should return to his original location.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to dwell in a place for the rainy season retreat (varṣā), she may not dwell there for the retreat if no bhikṣu is present.
If she should dwell there for the retreat, she violates the law of respect; this is called a "place where no bhikṣu resides," and a bhikṣuṇī may not observe the retreat there.
The seventh rule of respect is concluded.

Regarding the bhikṣuṇīs who, having completed their rainy season retreat, receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) within the assembly of the two divisions of the Saṃgha: once the bhikṣuṇīs have received the *pravāraṇā* on the day of the ceremony, they should all go to the assembly of the bhikṣus at dawn the following morning to receive the *pravāraṇā*.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, one who is capable of receiving the *pravāraṇā* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should be selected.
The person performing the ritual should speak as follows:
"Listen, O Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha!

"Such-and-such bhikṣuṇī is capable of acting as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the community of bhikṣuṇīs. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint such-and-such bhikṣuṇī as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the community of bhikṣuṇīs."

“May the community of bhikṣuṇīs listen: the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so shall act as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha. Since the saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
When both communities—the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs—are assembled in harmony, they should speak thus:
“The bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha is in harmony; the bhikṣu-saṃgha is in harmony and performs the *pravāraṇā*. If you see, hear, or suspect any offense, may the saṃgha speak to me out of compassion.”
"If there are offenses seen, heard, or suspected, they should be removed in accordance with the Dharma.
This should be said a second and a third time.
If the community of bhikṣus is in harmony and there are many bhikṣuṇīs, it should be said as follows:
“Many bhikṣuṇīs, the community of bhikṣus, and the community of bhikṣuṇīs shall perform the *pravāraṇā* together; if you see, hear, or suspect any offense, the Saṃgha should speak of it.
Out of compassion for me, if you know or see [any fault], you should remove it according to the Dharma.”
The second and third [invitations] should also be spoken in this manner.
If there is one bhikṣuṇī in a harmonious assembly of bhikṣus, she should speak thus:

"I, a bhikṣuṇī, invite the harmonious assembly of bhikṣus for the *pravāraṇā*. If you see, hear, or suspect any offense, may the Saṃgha speak to me out of compassion; having known or seen it, I shall remove it according to the Dharma."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
If a large number of bhikṣus or the community of bhikṣuṇīs are assembled, they should speak as follows: "The community of bhikṣuṇīs is harmonious;

may the Venerable Ones grant us the invitation to confess (pravāraṇā). If you have seen, heard, or suspect any offense, Venerable Ones, please speak to me out of compassion. Having known or seen it, I shall remove it according to the Dharma."
The second and third [times] should also be spoken in this manner.
If there are many bhikṣus or many bhikṣuṇīs, one should speak thus:
"Many bhikṣus and many bhikṣuṇīs, Venerable Ones, grant me the invitation to speak."
This was repeated for the second and third times as well.
Regarding the phrase "one bhikṣu... up to one bhikṣuṇī," it should be said as follows:

"I, a bhikṣu [or a bhikṣuṇī], request the venerable ones to perform the *pravāraṇā*. If you perceive, hear, or suspect any offense, please speak to me out of compassion; having known or seen it, I shall remove it in accordance with the Dharma."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
When a bhikṣuṇī has completed her rains retreat, she should receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) before both assemblies in this way.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not go to the assembly of bhikṣus on the sixteenth day to receive the *pravāraṇā*, but instead goes to receive it on the seventeenth day, she violates the rule of respect.
This is called the eighth *gurudharma* for bhikṣuṇīs. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 30.9.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 31.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Regarding the ninth section of the *Saṃyukta-vastu* translated by Fa-xian, concerning "storing overnight," "cooking indoors," and "cooking for oneself": The Buddha was dwelling at the Kalandaka-nivāpa (the Wild Deer Park) Monastery, which was venerated by devas and humans alike.
At that time, a kitchen was established within the monastery; the rinse-water from washing utensils and foul runoff flowed out into the street, causing the people of the world to resent it, saying:
"How is it that these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya do not separate their living quarters from their kitchen?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is only right that you are being censured by the people of the world. From this day forward, I do not permit the construction of an inner kitchen where the dregs of grain-water flow outside."
Regarding the method for preparing a clean kitchen (*kappiyakuṭī*): one should not prepare the clean kitchen in the east or the north; it should be prepared in the south or the west.
If a bhikṣu prepares the clean kitchen inside [the monastery] and the wash-water flows outside, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Furthermore, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Kosala and arrived at the brahmin village of Hatthigāma. As explained in detail above regarding the incident of the rice gruel, he even prohibited the practice of storing food overnight within the monastery and cooking within the monastery.
Furthermore, as the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala, he arrived at the brahmin village of Sthūṇā.

At that time, there were two elder monks, father and son, who had been barbers before they went forth. Hearing that the Buddha had arrived and intended to prepare rice gruel, the circumstances regarding the gruel—as explained in detail above—were recounted, up until the point where [the Buddha] prohibited storing food indoors, cooking indoors, or cooking for oneself.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was wandering through the country of Aṅguttarāpa, the brahmin Jñānika-jaṭila heard that the World-Honored One had arrived and was preparing a monastery and a clean kitchen; he then sent a messenger to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha told Upāli:
"You should go ahead and designate the kitchen for the Sangha’s meals; do not let the first watch of the night pass.
If it passes, that place shall be considered a dwelling of the Sangha and may no longer be used as a kitchen."
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it permissible to have a single roof but separate partitions?”
The Buddha said,
“He has attained it.
He asked again:
“Can one obtain supernormal powers through separation, distance, or concealment?
The Buddha said,
“One can.”
He asked again:
"Can one obtain the power of penetration through coverings and obstructions?
The Buddha said:
"Yes," he replied.
He asked again:
"Is it permissible to have separate and distinct coverings?"
The Buddha said,
“He has attained it.
He asked again:
“Can one attain the first side, the second side, the third side, and all of them completely?
The Buddha said, “One can.”
"Can one receive it across a path?
The Buddha said,
"One may."
“Can one go from the upper story to the lower story?
The Buddha said,
“One can.”
There may be a tree whose roots are in pure ground while its branches and leaves are in impure ground;
there may be a tree whose roots are in impure ground while its branches and leaves are in pure ground;
or there may be a tree whose roots and branches and leaves are both in impure ground.

If there is a tree whose roots, branches, and leaves are all situated on pure ground, and it is covered by one roof but partitioned separately, the Saṃgha may accept it and designate it as a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a house for pure goods). This applies even up to the case where it is partitioned separately and covered separately; the Saṃgha may accept it and designate it as a *kappiya-kuṭi*.
One side, two sides, or all three sides may entirely constitute a purified building (*pariśuddha-śālā*).

Regarding "separated by a path": if the two sides of the path are pure while the middle is impure, and one places a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta-kumbha*) or the like in the middle, one should pierce both sides so that it flows onto the pure ground; then its taking is permitted.
If bags of grain, wheat, or beans are placed across the middle of the path, one may untie both ends and take them.
If radishes, scallions, or sugarcane are on the road, one may cut off and take the clean portions.
Regarding "above the pavilion" and "below the pavilion": whether it is above or below the pavilion, one may receive [the produce] and designate it as a pure house (*śuci-veśman*).

If the roots of a tree are in pure ground while the branches and leaves are in impure ground—meaning the tree grows from pure ground but its branches and leaves shade impure ground—if fruit falls to the ground, it should be taken at the proper time and brought inside the pure house;
if it is not taken until after the first watch of the night has passed, it is then termed impure.

If the roots of a tree are in impure ground while the branches and leaves are in pure ground, the tree grows in impure ground but its branches and leaves shade the pure ground; if the fruit falls to the ground, it is then considered pure, and one may take it whenever desired.

Regarding that which is impure in both respects: it grows from impure ground, its branches and leaves also shade impure ground, yet the fruit falls and is taken at the proper time to be placed within a clean house;
if it is not taken at the proper time and remains until after the first watch of the night has passed, it is then termed impure.

Regarding "pure in both respects": when the tree grows on pure ground and its branches and leaves also shade pure ground, any fruit that falls is termed "pure. One may take it at any time as desired; this is called "pure in both respects."
If radishes, scallions, or vegetables grow on impure ground, they may be taken if taken at the proper time and placed inside a clean house;
if they are not taken at the proper time and the first watch of the night has passed, they are then termed impure.
If thieves come to steal fruits and vegetables and, having been discovered, become terrified and abandon them and depart, one should immediately take them and place them inside a clean room.
If they say, "We shall take them tomorrow," [one may keep them].
If it passes the first watch of the night, it is termed impure.

If one does not notice the time when it was discarded, and upon seeing it, one should take it inside a clean building; if one does not take it there and it passes the first watch of the night, it is termed impure.
If melons or gourds grow in an impure place, one should pick them up and place them inside a clean building at the proper time;
if they are not placed inside, once the first watch of the night has passed, they are termed impure.
If there is grain offered to the Sangha by a donor at a monastery site, and it is poured onto impure ground, it should be taken up and placed in a clean building immediately;
if it is not taken up and the first watch of the night has passed, it is then termed "impure."
If a layperson brings cakes, parched grain, or other provisions to stay overnight and gives them to a bhikṣu when departing the following day, they are considered pure.
If a bhikṣu thinks:
"He will certainly give these to me when he departs tomorrow," [it is also pure].
If it is given [at night], it is called impure.
The same applies to fruits and vegetables brought in and left overnight.

If grain and rice have been transported and the clean house or granary is full, if they are placed within a lecture hall, a warm chamber, a well-house, a firewood-house, in the courtyard, or on ground that is not pure, they should be moved at the appropriate time during the first, middle, or last watches of the night.
If it is not moved and the first watch of the night has passed, it is then termed impure.

If one wishes to construct a new dwelling place, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu should measure it out with a cord to establish the boundaries, determining that "this much shall be made into a pure house for the Saṃgha" and "this much shall be made into a residence for the Saṃgha. He should make this declaration:
"Within this area, this much shall be accepted as a pure house for the Saṃgha."
If it is not accepted, once the first watch of the night has passed, it is termed impure.

Depending on the specific case, the house is determined to be pure; once the house is determined to be pure, the same applies to dwellings, heated rooms, lecture halls, gatehouses, bathhouses, firewood sheds, and well-houses.
Regarding the fixed allocation of wells and houses:
if a donor says, "Do not make preliminary arrangements," one must wait until the meal has been prepared and offered to the Sangha; only then may the Sangha allocate them as they see fit.
Once it has been completed, one should say:
"The lower pavilion, the middle pavilion, and the upper pavilion are accepted as a pure dwelling for the Saṃgha.

Once accepted, it is immediately called "pure" and may be inhabited. Furthermore, even if it has not been formally accepted, it may be accepted at a time when the land is in turmoil and the king has not yet been established.
Furthermore, if one king has passed away and another king has not yet been enthroned by the people, at that time one may receive [the robes].
If one still does not receive them, after two years have elapsed while the residence and village remain abandoned, one may receive them.
Among these, there may be cases where the village has been abandoned but the residence has not;
or where the residence has been abandoned but the village has not;
or where both the village and the residence have been abandoned.
Or, it may be that the village has been abandoned and ceased to exist, or the dwelling place has been abandoned and ceased to exist;
in such cases, not receiving [the food] is called "impure.
If edible food is left overnight, this is called "storing overnight" (*antar-geha*) or "cooking overnight" (*antar-vāsa*).
Regarding cooking for oneself: a bhikṣu must not cook food himself. If he is ill, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) cook it.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, and he has a clean copper vessel that does not retain grease, he may wash it thoroughly and cook it himself until it boils; he should then have the *kappiya-kāraka* know when to add the rice.
Once the rice has been placed [in the pot], a bhikṣu must not ignite the fire himself; he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) ignite it.

When the water has boiled and the *kappiya-kāraka* wishes to leave, the bhikṣu may accept the vessel and cook it himself until it is done, but he must be careful not to let any food that has not been formally accepted fall into it.

In this manner, one must cook meat until it shrinks and vegetables until they wither; once received, one may cook them oneself until they are done. However, even for something as simple as boiling ginger water, one must not cook it oneself, but must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) cook it.
If one goes on almsround, there is no offense in warming cold food oneself.
If an attendant (kappiyakāraka) is ill, one should have another attendant cook the congee and give it to them.
If there is no attendant, one may cook the purified rice oneself.
If there is leftover gruel, one must not eat it oneself; this is called "storing overnight," "cooking indoors," and "cooking for oneself.

Regarding the acceptance of raw meat: while the Buddha was staying in the wilderness, at that time the group of six bhikṣus carried pieces of meat and raw fish, causing them to be disparaged by worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, unable to beg for food, carry pieces of meat and raw fish as they travel?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Bhikṣus!..."
“Is it truly so?
She replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I do not permit the acceptance of raw meat.”
"If a bhikṣu is ill, he may instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) to know how to boil and collect [medicinal herbs], and having received them, he may boil them himself until they are cooked.

If a bhikṣu is walking for exercise or practicing meditation in the forest and sees the remains of a dead deer or a gazelle beneath a tree, if he needs them, he must not take them himself; he should instead instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* to know how to handle them."
If one takes it oneself, one must not eat it oneself; it should be given to a park-attendant or to a śrāmaṇera.
It is the same if one sees it left over by a hawk.
If a bhikṣu obtains dried meat while begging for alms, he may accept it after roasting it over a fire.
There are sentient beings named Kūya who have no intestines or stomach; they swallow pieces of meat and expel them whole, so that those in need may receive them.
However, it is not permitted to accept raw grain.
Regarding grains: white rice, red rice, barley, and wheat are all prohibited from being accepted.

If one develops an abscess, carbuncle, or pustule that requires an application of wheat, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) perform the ritual purification (*kappiya*) so that one may take it oneself;
however, grinding it and using it for an application is not permitted.
If there are husks of grain or barley flour within a clean house, one may take them oneself if needed, but receiving them as a gift is not permitted.
If there are mung beans, mocha beans, soybeans, small red beans, or others of this kind, one may receive them if needed; this is called "receiving raw grain."
Regarding "taking for oneself and receiving further purification by peeling": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit had an Āmra grove where the fruit was flourishing.
The king asked the park-keepers, "Have any bhikṣus come to eat the fruit?"
The park keeper replied,
"Great King, since you did not invite us, how could we have come to eat?
The king said:
"You may go and invite the bhikṣus to come eat fruit.
He immediately went to where the Saṃgha was, prostrated at their feet with his head, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and said:
"The King invites the Saṃgha to eat fruit."
The bhikṣus then went to the grove to eat the fruit; they scattered it about on the ground or took some back with them, so that the grove-keeper could no longer deliver the fruit.
The king asked the grove-keeper:
"Why do you not deliver the fruit?"
The park-keeper immediately reported the matter in detail to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was displeased and spoke these words:
"The bhikṣus should simply eat the fruit; for what reason did they discard it on the ground and then take it away? To whom did they give it?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so. The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "You should simply eat the fruit;
for what reason did you discard it on the ground and then take it back again?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
I brought it here; having received it, I ate it further.”
The Buddha said:
"How is it that you take [food] yourself and then eat again after having already received it?
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, eating *āmra* fruits is not permitted.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the *Āmrapālī* Grove in the Elder’s Park near Rājagṛha, the Elder’s son asked a park attendant:
“Do the bhikṣus eat *āmra* fruits?”
He replied,
"The World-Honored One does not permit it.
When the elder youth heard these words, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The āmalaka is a fruit of the season; we pray that the World-Honored One will permit the bhikṣus to eat it.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to eat fruit after removing the peel.
At that time, the bhikṣus had their attendants (kappiyakāraka) completely remove the peels from the fruit before eating it.
The attendants complained, saying, "The fruit can be eaten with the peel; why do you have us remove all the peels?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"It is not necessary to remove all the skin; you should eat them after they have been cleaned with the fingernails."
One must not take food for oneself and then receive it later; rather, one should first have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) clean it with their fingernails before receiving it.
If a bhikṣu is walking in a grove and sees fallen fruit on the ground, he who requires it should have a *kappiya-kāraka* pick it up.
If one takes [fruit] oneself, one must not eat it oneself; it should be given to a park-attendant or a śrāmaṇera.
If fruit ripens and falls to the ground and becomes damaged or broken, it is termed "clean by fingernails" (nakhapariśuddha); it should be accepted, and once the pit is removed, it may be eaten.

If a bird has pecked at it, or if it is damaged or broken within a vessel—even down to the size of a mosquito's leg—it is called "pure by skin" (*taco-paṭalaka-śuddha*), and one may eat it after removing the seed-kernel.
If one wishes to eat the kernel itself, it is permitted to eat it once it has been purified by fire.
If one eats the kernel of a fruit that has been purified by peeling but not by fire-purification, it is a pāyattika.
If it has been purified by fire but not by peeling, both the peel and the kernel may be eaten.
If one eats that which has been neither purified by fire nor purified by peeling, there is one pāyattika and one vyatikrama.
"If both [parties] act together, there is no offense.
This is called "purification by taking oneself and subsequently receiving" (*pāṭidesanīya*).
This concludes the section on the settlement of legal matters (*vinayavastu*), concerning obstructions and non-obstructions.
A bhikṣuṇī staying overnight indoors, cooking indoors, or cooking for herself;
accepting raw meat or grain; taking [food] herself and then receiving it again;
purification by skinning and purification by fire.
The sixth *Bhadra* section concludes.

Regarding "heavy objects": while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus sold the beds and mats belonging to the Saṃgha, or lent them to others, or used them for private purposes.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣus to sell, lend out, or privately use the beds and mats belonging to the Saṃgha. Even when the entire Saṃgha is assembled, I do not permit them to be sold, lent out, or used privately.”
"If one sells it, lends it to another, or uses it privately, it is a *vyatikrama* offense.
What is meant by "valuable object"?
Beds, mattresses, iron vessels, earthenware, wooden vessels, and bamboo vessels—as explained in detail in the section on the precept against stealing—these are called valuable objects.

When a donor gives the Sangha items such as beds, mattresses, woolen blankets, pillows, cotton cloths, waistbands, knives, staffs, parasols, fans, leather sandals, needle-cases, nail-clippers, and water-pots: among these, heavy items such as beds, mattresses, pillows, and woolen blankets should be assigned to the Sangha of the Four Directions; the remaining light items should be divided.
If a donor says,
"Divide everything," one should divide it according to the donor's intention.
If it is said,
"All [this] is given to the Saṃgha of the four quarters," it should not be divided.

If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road and a layperson, seeing the bhikṣu, feels joy in their heart and offers various kinds of goods as a gift to the bhikṣu, and among these there are heavy items, he should give them to a nearby monastery and say to the donor:
"Give this bed and bedding to the bhikṣus of such-and-such a monastery."
If one says, "I have already resolved to give; why do you ask me again?
the bhikṣu says:
"One might also place this here to provide for visiting monks and thereby obtain merit," he replied,
"I cannot; I have already made my decision."
One should say:
"Long-lived one!
This is a heavy object that is difficult to transport; would it be possible to trade it for its value here and then have it made back there?"
If one says,
"It is up to your honor's discretion," one may trade and take the price.
Upon arriving at that dwelling, one should purchase beds for their value and trade bedding for its value; in this manner, everything should be traded according to its worth.
If they say, "Let us divide everything," [one should comply].
Regarding this, one should distribute it according to the donor's intention.
If he says: "I give everything to the Saṃgha of the four quarters," [then it should be distributed accordingly].
Regarding this, one should not divide [the offerings].
There are two kinds of invitations:
first, the sequential invitation for the Sangha; second, private invitations.

In that place, one may receive various kinds of miscellaneous offerings; items obtained through the monastic rotation (saṃghika) shall be entered into the Saṃgha, while items obtained from private invitations shall be entered into one's own possession.

If there are many beds and mats but few cauldrons and pots, one should inform the donor so that they may be made aware of the situation, and then the beds and mats may be exchanged for cauldrons and pots.
If there are many cauldrons or pots, trading them for beds or mats is likewise [permissible].
If one has a broken vessel that can be melted down to make something larger, this is called a "heavy object.
These are impermanent objects.
The Buddha was staying in the Āṭavī forest, while at that time the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was staying in Gṛhakūṭa.

There was a cowherd named Kuṇi whose wife’s name was Śivālī; when Kauṇḍinya reached the proper time, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village for alms. Having received food, he would regularly go to the cowherd’s house to eat.

At that time, the woman, with a heart of faith and joy, constantly provided him with milk, curd, fresh butter, and clarified butter. Having drunk them, she returned to her dwelling and thought to herself:
"What is the use of maintaining this vessel of suffering by remaining long in the world?"
"I am weary of this body.

He then set aside his robes and bowl in one place, and beneath the trees in the forest, he lay down on his right side with his head resting upon the elephant's dung, and with an undisturbed mind, he immediately entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Śivaka, knowing it was time for [the teacher] to arrive, prepared a seat, swept the ground, and set out milk, curd, and gruel to wait for him;
however, when the appointed time had passed and he had not come, Śivaka thought to himself:
"The Ācārya usually comes every day; why does he not come today?"
"Is he not ill?
Has he not been harmed by evil insects?
He then went at once to see him.
Seeing him lying beneath the tree, he thought to himself, "The Ācārya must still be asleep.
He stood silently listening, but heard no sound of breathing; he felt the master's heart with his hand and found that his body was already cold.
He then said:
"How extraordinary!
It has already become impermanent."
"I shall make offerings to the relics.

She then returned home and told her husband; he took an axe and split a pile of fine firewood, placing it in one spot, whereupon they performed the cremation of the relics, standing to one side to watch.
He saw four birds of various colors coming from the four directions; as soon as they reached his body, they turned white and departed.
At that time, the husband, Kanha, dwelt there in distress and unhappiness, thinking to himself:
"This bhikṣu’s robes and bowl must be surrendered to the king; the king’s law is difficult to fathom, and I fear he will demand further items."
He immediately took them and went to the king, saying:
"This bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya has passed away; these robes and bowl are to be offered to Your Majesty.
The king then assessed the value of these robes and bowl at five coins.
The official’s judgment stated:
“This śramaṇa has passed away; his robes and bowl shall be returned to the bhikṣus.
He then took them back and informed the Saṃgha, saying:
"The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya has passed away; here are his robes and bowl.
When the bhikṣus saw them, they recognized those robes and bowl and immediately asked, "Did you witness anything extraordinary?"
He replied, "I saw them!
When I was cremating [the body], I saw four birds of various colors."
Thereupon, the bhikṣu went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, asking,
"What is the meaning of this matter?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"These are the four Māra-devas who have come, wishing to observe his consciousness-spirit (vijñāna);
not seeing it, they turned white and departed.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To whom should these robes and bowl belong?
The Buddha said,
"They should belong to the Saṃgha."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a sick bhikṣu who said to another bhikṣu:
"Take care of me, and I shall give my robes and bowl to you, Venerable One."
At that time, the sick bhikṣu passed away. The community of bhikṣus assembled, intending to divide his robes and bowl.
The bhikṣu who had attended to him said:
"When this sick bhikṣu was still alive, he spoke to me, saying:"
"Look at me, and I shall give you my robe and bowl.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Has it been given,
or not? He replied,
"Not yet."
The Buddha said:
"If one gives it away and it subsequently becomes impermanent, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
That [object] should not have been given."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a sick bhikṣu who said to another bhikṣu:
"Take care of me, and I shall give my robes and bowl to you, Venerable Sir."
He then gave it to him.
Having received it, [the recipient] did not perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) and returned it to the side of the sick monk.
At that time, the sick monk passed away. Thereupon, the monks went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
"What is this matter?
The Buddha said, "Is it purified?
Or is it not purified?"
He replied, "I did not.
The Buddha said:
"One should not accept it.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a sick bhikṣu who said to another bhikṣu:
"Look after me, and I shall give my robes and bowl to you, Venerable Sir."
He then gave it to him; having received it, [the recipient] performed the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*) and returned it to the side of the sick bhikṣu.
Eventually, the Buddha asked:
"Was the ritual of purification performed?"
He replied, “I have. The Buddha said:
"It should be obtained.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a novice monk passed away.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha:
"To whom should these robes and bowl belong?
The Buddha said,
"They belong to the preceptor."
Furthermore, the bhikṣu who tended to the sick spoke with resentment, saying:
"In tending to the sick, I did not avoid cold or heat; I endured various hardships to seek out decoctions and medicines, even performing the task of emptying the vessels for excrement and urine."
"If this is indeed the case, who should receive it?
Do you say that the Saṃgha receives it?
For these reasons, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "The bhikṣu who nurses the sick undergoes great hardship; he should be given the three robes, an alms bowl, and any remaining medicine he has received.
Then the Venerable Upāli, knowing the proper time, asked:
“World-Honored One,
may a sick bhikṣu entrust his belongings to others?
The Buddha said:
“It is permitted.
He asked again,
“Is it also permitted to entrust [the medicine] to a physician?”
The Buddha said:
"It is permissible, provided that one gives instructions, saying:
'I will give it when I am not on a mission.'"
If he departs, it is called relinquishment.
If he entrusts [the robe] by saying, "I am going to that village; if I do not arrive, you should give it [to someone]," [it is also relinquishment].
If one has arrived, it is termed "abandonment.
If one says by way of entrustment:
"I am going away," [it is also abandonment].
"If it is impermanent, you should give it back.
To return it is called relinquishing.
If one makes a definitive entrustment, saying:
Regarding the statement, "Whether I die or live, my mind is resolved to give it," one should indeed give it.
If it was entrusted to many people, the last person among them should receive it.
"If it is given to many people, the one who was first [to arrive] should receive it.
If a bhikṣu passes away or enters parinirvāṇa, one should not immediately close his door.
If he has fellow disciples or resident disciples who maintain the precepts and are trustworthy, they may be given the door-key.

If they are not trustworthy, one should give the door-key to the monastery officials; after the offerings to the relics have been completed and the arrangements concluded, one may then take out his robes and belongings.
If there is a fellow traveler or a resident disciple who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy, he should be sent out;
if such a person is not trustworthy, a steward (karmadāna) should be sent out.
If a bhikṣu speaks as follows:

Regarding the statement, "I also have robes and a bowl here," one should observe the precept-keeping of the person before them; it should be given to one who is trustworthy, but not to one who is untrustworthy.
If there is a trustworthy person who can provide testimony, it should first be given to them, and only thereafter may the Saṃgha receive it.
There are three ways of receiving it:
formal reception through ritual action (*karmavācanā*), reception by portions, and reception by exchange of portions.
Regarding the formal act (*kamma*) for receiving [the items]: the person performing the formal act should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so has passed away or entered parinirvāṇa; whatever robes, bowl, and other miscellaneous belongings he possessed should be divided among the present Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Sangha, let the Sangha perform the formal act (karmavācanā) in the presence of the assembly to grant [the precepts] to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
The motion is as follows:
'Venerable Sangha, listen!'"
When this bhikṣu named [Name] passes away or enters parinirvāṇa, whatever robes, alms bowl, and other miscellaneous items he possesses shall be divided by the Saṃgha present before them.
The Saṃgha now, being present, holds these robes, alms bowl, and other miscellaneous items to bestow them upon the bhikṣu named [Name] who has received them.

"Venerable sirs, please consent to accept these robes, alms bowls, and other miscellaneous items for the sake of the bhikṣu so-and-so. If you consent, the Saṃgha remains silent; if you do not consent, please speak."

“The Sangha has already consented to bestow these robes, bowls, and other miscellaneous items upon the bhikṣu so-and-so; the acceptance is complete. Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”
This is called receiving through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
As for receiving by portions, once the portions have been made, one proclaims:
"Each person take their own portion."
This is called receiving by portions.
Regarding receiving through exchange: when they trade with one another, this is called receiving through exchange.
If four bhikṣus reside within a village and one bhikṣu passes away, the remaining three bhikṣus should receive [the inheritance].
It should be said thus:
"Venerable sirs!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having passed away or entered parinirvāṇa, has left behind these robes, bowl, and other miscellaneous items; the present Saṃgha should divide them."
"In this place there are no monks; we should divide [the property] here in our presence.
If three bhikṣus are residing there and one bhikṣu passes away, the two remaining bhikṣus should receive it.
It should be stated as follows, up to: "In this place there is no Saṃgha; I should receive [the property] in my presence.
If two bhikṣus are living together and one bhikṣu passes away, the other bhikṣu may receive it, and he should mentally reflect and speak these words:
"Bhikṣu So-and-so has passed away or entered parinirvāṇa; he possessed these robes and bowl, which the present Saṃgha should divide."
"Since there are no monks here, I should receive it in person.

If one wishes to give property to the monk who attended to the sick, one should distribute *śalākā* (voting sticks) to ascertain the number of people; once this is known, one should give the robes and bowl held by the deceased, as well as any remaining medicine he had received.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so has passed away or entered *nirvāṇa*; all his robes and bowl should be divided by the present Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha take these robes and bowl, as well as the remaining medicine received, and give them to the attendant bhikṣu, [Name].
This is the motion (*jñapti*).

[One *karmavācanā* is performed: "...The Saṃgha has already given the robes, bowl, and remaining medicine to the attendant bhikṣu, [Name]. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Regarding the attendant for the sick, what may or may not be received?
That which should not be received includes: receiving it merely for a short time, receiving it after recovery, receiving it out of a desire for merit, or receiving it through wrong livelihood.
"Temporary assignment" means to perform a task for a limited time and not do it thereafter; this is called temporary assignment.
"Appointed assignment" means to be assigned according to the order of the Saṃgha; this is called appointed assignment.
"Assignment out of a desire for merit" means to look after [the monastery] for the sake of one's own merit; this is called assignment out of a desire for merit.
Regarding "wrong livelihood": attending to the sick out of expectation for gain is called wrong livelihood.
Regarding "that which should be accepted," the Buddha said:
"If it is for the sake of providing benefit—even down to lighting a single lamp wick—with the desire to cause the patient to recover, it should be accepted."

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should measure the shadow. If any visiting bhikṣus arrive, one should ascertain whether they arrived before the *karmavācanā* or after it; whether they encountered death but not the *karmavācanā*, or encountered the *karmavācanā* but not death, or encountered both death and the *karmavācanā*, or encountered neither death nor the *karmavācanā*.
Among these, one who encounters the *karmavācanā* but does not encounter death, or one who encounters both death and the *karmavācanā*, should receive [the precepts];
among these, one who encounters death but does not encounter the *karmavācanā*, or one who encounters neither death nor the *karmavācanā*, should not receive them.
If one seeks medicine for a sick person, or departs for the sake of matters concerning a stūpa or the Saṅgha, [the property] should be given.
This is called the rule regarding impermanent items.
Regarding the rule on ignorance: while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the Elder Kapphiṇa had two co-practicing disciples.

One was named Nandi and the other was named Paṭṭanandi; they suffered from a delusional illness that would sometimes manifest and sometimes not. They brought about a schism in the Saṃgha through their formal acts (karmavācanā).
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"Nandi and Panthaka suffer from the disease of delusion; sometimes it manifests and sometimes it does not. If they perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that causes a schism in the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should carry out a formal act of delusion (*mūḍha-karman*) against them."
The *karmadāna* (the official performing the ritual) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Nanda and Pāṭananda suffer from a delusional illness; sometimes they come and sometimes they do not, yet they perform the formal act (*karma*) of schism."
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant the formal act of *karmavācanā* for the treatment of the delusional illness of Nandiya and Pāṭanandiya.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Nandi and Panthaka suffer from the disease of delusion; sometimes it manifests and sometimes it does not. They have disrupted the *saṃgha-karman*. The *saṃgha* now grants the *karman* for Nandi and Panthaka’s disease of delusion.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to the *karmavācanā* for the ignorant monk Nandika and Panthaka by remaining silent, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of *mūḍhaglāna-karman* for Nandi and Panthaka; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Once this *karmavācanā* has been performed, whether [the person] comes or does not come, the *karmavācanā* is not invalidated.
If the illness of delusion is cured and they regain their original mind, it is then termed "renunciation" (*pratyākhyāna*).
This is called the *mūḍha-karman* (the formal act of one who is deluded).

Regarding those who do not desire [the procedure]: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the monks of Campā were engaged in quarrels and mutual disputes; they lived together in discord, such that one monk would accuse another monk, two monks would accuse two monks, and many monks would accuse many monks.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the practice of expressing one's disapproval upon seeing [an offense]."
Regarding those who see [the action] as undesirable: if the Saṃgha performs an illegal *karmavācanā*, those who have the power should intervene and say:
"Venerable sirs!
This is neither legal nor in accordance with the Vinaya; it should not be done."
If the person before you is violent and powerful, and you fear that they might take your life or harm your practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), you should express your refusal by saying:
"This is an illegal *karmavācanā*; I cannot endure to grant it; I refuse."
Thus it is said three times.

When performing the *jñapticaturtha-karman* for the purpose of expressing one's refusal (*naiva-icchā*), one must not perform it in the presence of someone who is not present; rather, it should be performed in the presence of those who are in agreement.

One may not perform the expression of refusal before the entire assembly; however, it is permissible to perform it before two or three persons, while the remainder of the assembly should grant their formal consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma and then depart.

If one does not prevent an illegal adjudication of affairs within the Saṃgha, nor grants one's consent (*chanda*), nor expresses one's view or lack of desire [to participate], one commits a *vinaya*-transgression.
If one thinks thus:
"Just as the fire consumes the house according to its own course of action, I shall merely save myself; it suffices that my mind is protected and remains in accordance with the Dharma."
“There is no offense.
This is called ‘seeing what one does not desire.

Regarding the one who destroys the gift of faith: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the householder Mṛga invited the Saṃgha for a meal in turn. When it was Upānanda’s turn to go to his house, the householder asked him:”
"Do you wish to eat here, or do you wish to take it away?
He replied,
"I wish to take it away."
He immediately took the bowl and filled it with various kinds of food and drink.
Having received the food, Upānanda took it to the courtesan’s house and asked,
"Do you wish to have some food?"
He replied,
"I wish to obtain it.
[The other said,] "Bring your vessel here."
He immediately set out food and drink on a tray and offered it to him; however, the man begged to go again.
When the elder’s son had finished eating, he went to the courtesan’s house, where she said, "Master, would you like to eat?"
He replied, “Bring it here.
The man immediately took the tray and offered the food to him.
Having seen him, she recognized him and asked,
"Where did you obtain this food?
The woman replied:
“Everyone, just eat; why ask?
You can get it from the young men. “Not so!”
"I wish to know its location.
When his questioning did not cease, he said,
"The Ācārya Upānanda gave it to me."
The son of the householder spoke with reproach:
"I regard the Saṃgha as a field of supreme merit, yet Upānanda, on the contrary, regards a courtesan as a field of supreme merit."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, there was a caravan leader named Abhaya who offered two fine pieces of woolen cloth to the Saṃgha.

When Upānanda learned from within the Saṃgha that they had been received, he immediately took them and gave them to a courtesan. Having received them, the courtesan put them on and entered the marketplace.
Then the caravan leader Abhaya, having seen him, recognized him and asked:
"Where did you obtain this cotton cloth?
He replied:
"Why does everyone ask this?
You may obtain it from the young men.
He asked again:
"Not so! I wish to know it.
When his questioning did not cease, he spoke:
"Venerable Upānanda, please accept it.
At that time, the caravan leader spoke with resentment:
"I regard the Saṃgha as a supreme field of merit, yet Upānanda instead regards a courtesan as a supreme field of merit."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Upānanda,
“Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed; how could you destroy the offerings given out of faith?"
"From this day forward, I do not permit the destruction of objects given in faith.
Regarding "faith," it means giving with confidence or giving with joy.
There are eight kinds of such giving:
Regarding "eating at the proper time," "the night watch," and so forth, up to "pure" and "impure":

as for "breaking [the rule]," if one with a lustful mind gives [sexual favors] to a courtesan, a widow, a grown virgin, a eunuch, a woman of ill repute who is a bhikṣuṇī, or a woman of ill repute who is a śrāmaṇerī—even down to giving them to an animal with a lustful mind—one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If someone goes among the Sangha to beg for food and receives a single morsel, it should be divided equally if there are many people.
However, if the person before whom one stands has lustful thoughts, one should not give it to them.
If one's parents are poor and suffering but lack faith, one should give them a small amount;
if they possess faith, one may give as much as they desire.
There are two ways in which one should give:
There are those who benefit and those who cause harm.
As for those who benefit—such as donors or lay devotees (upāsaka)—if they perform work for a stūpa or for the Saṃgha, one should give to them.
As for those who cause harm—such as thieves, kings, or violent evildoers—if they do not give, they are capable of performing acts that are not beneficial; to such persons, one should give.
This is called violating the gift of faith.
Regarding the rule on leather sandals: while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Nanda and Upānanda were walking about wearing sandals adorned with gold, which drew the reproach of the people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear sandals adorned with gold like kings, ministers, or persons of high status?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to wear sandals made of gold or leather."

Furthermore, on an auspicious day for the people of the world, the group of six bhikṣus went out together to sightsee, some wearing leather sandals of various colors and others wearing single-layered leather sandals. They were censured by the people, who said:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear various kinds of leather sandals like kings and great ministers?"
Seeing those wearing such evil footwear, he spoke again, saying:
"How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya be like low-born men, wearing single-layered leather sandals?
These corrupt individuals—what path could they possibly possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the wearing of single-layered leather sandals."
Furthermore, the Buddha was staying at the Śītavana in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s body was slightly unwell. The Elder Kumāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have heard that the World-Honored One is unwell and may take purgative medicine.

Although the World-Honored One has no need for it, I pray that you will accept this medicine for the sake of all sentient beings, so that in future ages sentient beings may open their eyes to the light of the Dharma; let the sick receive the medicine and the donor obtain merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
The elder thought again:
"It would not be right to have the World-Honored One take medicine like an ordinary person; I should instead infuse the medicine into blue lotuses and present them to the World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One smelled it three times; the potency of the medicine caused eighteen bowel movements. Once he had finished, his radiant countenance was not pleased.
At that time, Ānanda said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"The World-Honored One has taken medicine; where is there food suitable for his illness?"
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately surveyed the kingdom of Campā and saw that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was daily cooking five hundred varieties of delicacies.

Then, by means of his supernormal powers, Maudgalyāyana arrived and stood before him. When Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa beheld the venerable Maudgalyāyana’s majestic deportment and spiritual virtue, his heart leaped with joy, and he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One is most wondrous and sublime, A mass of immeasurable merit;
If there is slight disharmony within his body, He should partake of food according to his ailment.”
You have now attained a sublime benefit and shall surely obtain a great fruit and reward.
Compared to the World-Honored One, all the śrāvaka disciples are like a single mustard seed set against Mount Sumeru.
At that time, having heard these verses, the son of the elder was filled with great joy and exclaimed:
"Excellent! Now I have obtained this benefit."
He immediately prepared a meal and invited Maudgalyāyana to stay and eat.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I have sought out food suitable for the World-Honored One’s ailment; it is not appropriate for me to eat first."
He then accepted the food and placed it in mid-air before eating it himself.
The youth Viśāṃpati said to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, "I wish for the World-Honored One to eat first and then I shall eat; how may this be known?"
Maudgalyāyana said, "These food vessels shall return in a moment; you will know for yourself when the meal is finished.
Then, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, Maudgalyāyana arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was and presented the food to him.
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, the vessel returned through the air.
At that time, the youth Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa saw the vessel returning from afar; he rose to meet it, received it upon the crown of his head, and honored it.
At that time, King Bimbisāra came to pay his respects to the World-Honored One; smelling the fragrance of the food, he asked, "What is this fragrance?
He replied:
"Eat the fragrance," the Buddha said to the Great King.
"Would you like to eat the remains of the Tathāgata's meal?"
He said, “I wish to eat,
World-Honored One!”
"I have gained a great and wholesome benefit, having obtained the remnants of the Tathāgata’s meal.
Having finished eating, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"World-Honored One, since I was born into the royal family, I have never before obtained such food as this.
Is this the food of devas, the food of nāgas, the food of those in Uttarakuru, or the food of ghosts and spirits?"
The Buddha said,
"This is not the food of devas, nor even the food of spirits or ghosts.
This is merely the food commonly eaten at the home of King Śūrasena’s son, the youth Viśvantara."
The World-Honored One then spoke to the king concerning the youth Śunaḥśepa, whose golden hair on the soles of his feet was four inches long and whose merit was such as this.
Having heard this, the king immediately wished to go and see him.
A minister addressed the king, saying: "How can this man be your subject?"
"You should summon him; it is not appropriate for you to go yourself.
He immediately sent a messenger to call him, saying to his parents, "The King wishes to see the boy."
The parents said, "The king summons us only because he wishes to find a pretext to fine us money; we would rather pay ten million coins than allow our son to go before the king."
He immediately loaded the gold, silver, and precious objects onto a carriage and went to the king's residence, saying to the king:
"The youth is delicate and weak; he cannot carry these things himself. All these rare treasures are now sent as an offering to Your Majesty."
The king said, "I already possess gold, silver, and precious objects; there is no need for these. I merely wish to see the boy's body.
The messenger returned and informed the king:
"The youth is a person from Sukhāvatī; he is so delicate and weak that he cannot endure a carriage.

The king said, "If that is the case, load him onto a ship and bring him here. If you reach a place where the boat cannot pass, dig a channel in the ground, fill it with mustard seeds, and pull him along."

He was immediately led to the mountain pass; the youth being delicate and tender, he spread his robe and bedding upon the ground and walked over it as he approached. Seeing from afar that the World-Honored One was sitting in the open air, upon seeing him, he immediately withdrew his robe and bedding and walked directly upon the bare ground.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One smiled.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason, World-Honored One, do you smile?"
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Do you see this boy?
They replied:
"Behold! The Buddha has said that for ninety-one kalpas this youth has never set foot upon the ground.
Now, seeing the Tathāgata, he shows such reverence; therefore, it is not that his merit is exhausted."

He proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha, in accordance with his needs, taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; he thereby attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The Buddhist youth said,
"If the King enters, I shall descend to the ground and sit cross-legged with my feet exposed.
When the King entered, the youth immediately descended to the ground and sat cross-legged with his feet exposed.
At that time, the king’s attendant immediately drew his sword and was about to strike him, but the king rebuked him.
When the youth saw this, fear arose in his heart, and he addressed the king, saying:
"Please allow me to leave the household life."
The king asked,
"In what way do you wish to leave the household life?
He replied:
"I wish to leave the household life to follow the Buddha-Dharma.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to say to his parents:
"Will you permit him to leave the household life?"
When his parents had granted their permission, he immediately sought ordination from the Buddha and received full precepts.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“By what causes and conditions did this youth’s feet not touch the ground for ninety-one kalpas?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world."
At that time, there were ninety sons of elders who invited the Buddha and an assembly of eighty thousand monks for a three-month *varṣā* retreat, each providing food for one day.

When it was the turn of the last son of an elder to provide offerings, he further spread white cotton cloth upon the ground as an offering to the community of monks. By the fruit of this merit, he was reborn in the heavens and among humans for ninety-one *kalpas*, never again treading upon the earth.
"The son of the elder at that time was none other than the youth Śuddhodana Viṃśatikoṭi, who is present here now.
After the youth had gone forth, he practiced walking meditation tirelessly in the Śītavana forest until his soles were wounded and bleeding onto the ground.
The Buddha, having already perceived this, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu!
Whose place of walking meditation is this, that blood has flowed to such an extent?"
The bhikṣus replied,
"This is the walking path of the youth Śūradatta Viṃśatikoṭi.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Even if this servant Śūradatta were to practice walking meditation with such diligence that Mount Sumeru were ground into fine dust, he could not attain the Way; how much less so when his skin is merely wounded!”
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went to a secluded place, sat down cross-legged, and reflected thus:
"Among the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, none is more diligent and untiring than I."
The World-Honored One then said:
"If you cannot attain the Way,
it would be better for you to relinquish the precepts and return home to perform various meritorious deeds in making offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, immediately traveled through the air by means of his supernormal power and sat before him.
