The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "I shall now question you; answer according to your own understanding."
"Can you play the lute? He replied, "I can."
“Can a musical note be produced when the strings are too tight? “No,
World-Honored One.”
He asked again:
"When the strings are loose, can they produce sound? "No, sir."
"World-Honored One!
he replied. The Buddha then asked the bhikṣu again:
"If the strings are neither too tight nor too loose, can they produce sound?"
He replied,
“Yes. The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"If diligence is too hurried, the mind gives rise to fetters; if diligence is too slack, the mind gives rise to fetters. When it is neither hurried nor slack, the mind becomes still and clear, penetrating all things, as explained at length in the *Ekottarika Āgama*."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“With a heart of faith, you renounced twenty koṭis to leave the household life; why then, within the True Dharma, have you given rise to overweening pride and brought suffering upon yourself?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It was because of you that I permitted the bhikṣus to wear leather sandals.
Then the youth Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Let it be permitted for the bhikṣus to wear leather sandals; I shall gradually train myself so that I may also wear leather sandals.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, it is permitted to wear single-layered leather sandals."

At that time, Ānandā Bhaginī, having heard that the Blessed One had permitted the bhikṣus to wear single-layered leather sandals, took five hundred pairs of leather sandals and went to where the Blessed One was. She prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the Blessed One [grant this]!”
"Accept these leather sandals.
The Buddha then spoke a verse as a prayer of blessing:
"With body, speech, and mind free from evil, you are a pure practitioner of the Brahma-faring life; with body, speech, and mind free from evil, you are a pure practitioner of the Brahma-faring life;"
Those who give leather sandals will enjoy happiness among humans and devas.
As various rewards for giving golden ground, they will adorn all their palaces;
attaining the divine power of *ṛddhi* at will, they shall be pure and free from obstruction.
"By giving a small amount, one gains great benefit, for it is a pure field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);
the wise person aspires to purity, and is thus able to obtain the fruit of the field of merit.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the World-Honored One went on an inspection tour of the monks' quarters once every five days and saw various leather sandals strewn about in disorder upon the ground.
Knowing [the answer], he asked intentionally: "Bhikkhu!
What kind of leather sandals are these, that they are so disheveled?"
The bhikṣu replied, “World-Honored One!
These leather sandals are worn out; fearing that they might become double-layered, I did not dare to repair them.”
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to mend it.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu from the south came to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
On the way, his leather sandals broke, and as his soles were worn through, he walked with his feet dragging while prostrating at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Why are you walking with your feet dragging?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
I wore a single-layered leather sandal that broke along the way; I did not dare wear a double-layered one, and for this reason my foot was injured.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the practice of making *nikkha* leather sandals. When wearing *pārupa* (undergarments), it is not permitted to cover the front; one should rather cover the back.

Regarding the rules for leather sandals: sandals made from the horns of rams or white sheep, sandals made of gold, sandals adorned with pearls, or sandals made of lapis lazuli, crystal, or agate—sandals of various such colors are not permitted to be worn."

If one obtains new, heavy leather sandals, it is not permitted to wear them; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) know how to put them on for five or six steps, and only after that may one wear them oneself.
If one wears them otherwise, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called the rule regarding leather sandals.

Regarding the rule for wooden clogs: the Buddha was staying at the Ambalaṭṭhikā Garden in the Jīrṇaśālavana near Rājagṛha. There, the Buddha preached the *Śramaṇaphala Sūtra* to King Ajātaśatru throughout the entire night.

At that time, Upānanda, having listened for a long while until he was utterly exhausted, returned to his own quarters to sleep. Rising during the final watch of the night, he put on his wooden sandals and approached, making a loud creaking sound. Upon hearing this, the elephants and horses were all startled and began to bray and neigh in competition. When the king heard it, he became terrified and immediately returned to the city.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Upānanda,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit the wearing of sandals."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, a bhikṣu was sitting in meditation beside a stone cave belonging to Śakra-devendra. At that time, another bhikṣu wearing sandals was walking back and forth in front of him; when the meditating bhikṣu heard the sound, his mind could not attain concentration.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the wearing of sandals.

As for sandals: gold sandals, silver sandals, maṇi-jewel sandals, ivory sandals, wooden sandals, leather sandals, horse-tail sandals, hemp sandals, kṣaumaka-cloth sandals, corded sandals, reed-grass sandals, and tree-bark sandals—all such sandals as these are forbidden to wear.
When wearing wooden clogs, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one wishes to wash one's feet, it is not an offense to place the clogs crosswise and step upon them.
When a bhikṣu puts on leather sandals, he should pull the heel-tab upward; if he does not pull it up, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance.
If one wears sandals that lack soles, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule regarding sandals.

Regarding the rule for bathing: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to the Ajiravatī River to bathe and used rubbing stones to scrub their bodies, which caused them to be criticized by the people of the world:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, rub their bodies with rubbing-stones like those in royal households, like wrestlers, or like athletes?
These ruined men—what path can they possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the use of rubbing stones to scrub the body."
Regarding "rubbing with a stone": [a tool] made of wood, or of stone, or of brick—none of these are permitted for use.
Furthermore, if there is a pillar in the water, one must not rub one's body against it.

When bathing, one should have another person rub one's body; while being rubbed, one must not raise both arms simultaneously, but should cover oneself with one arm and allow the rubbing to proceed in succession.
If there is no one else present, one should scrub oneself.
One must not bathe standing as laypeople do, but should remain seated.
Furthermore, one should wash the hands and arms in the proper sequence.
If there is grease or grime on the body, one must not rub it with the fist; rather, one should rub it by extending the hand.
If one uses a rubbing stone for bathing, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the method for bathing.
Regarding powdered incense: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Nanda and Upānanda took various kinds of powdered incense and went to the Añjiravatī River to bathe.
At that time, there were disciples of non-Buddhist sects who, having seen this, thought to themselves:
"We shall go together and disturb these śramaṇas and upāsakas.
They immediately went to their location and spoke as follows:
"Who is the teacher who has few desires and is content?
Then the lay follower said,
"My teacher has few desires and is content."
The disciple of the non-Buddhist sect spoke again:
"My teacher has few desires and is content.
The upāsaka said:
"Your teacher is shameless and lacks a sense of propriety, like a donkey eating wine dregs; my teacher has few desires, is content, and possesses a sense of shame and propriety.
The disciple of the non-Buddhist said:
"If your teacher has few desires and is content, we should wager something together."
He replied,
"What do you wish to wager?
The outsider answered:
"I wish to bet five hundred ancient coins.
The upāsaka said, "So be it."
They then deliberated together, saying,
"What test should we perform upon him?
Having prepared various kinds of powdered incense, they asked, "Whose teacher’s dwelling shall we visit first?"
The disciple of the non-Buddhist teacher said,
"I shall go first to my master," and immediately dispatched a messenger to inform his own teacher:
"I shall take these powdered incense offerings and go there; you should manifest an air of few desires and be careful not to accept them.
He immediately took them and went, saying:
"Out of compassion for us, O masters, please accept this powdered incense."
He replied, "I am an ordained monk, not a prince or a great minister; what use would I have for these aromatic powders?
Having refused them, he took them again and went to the Jetavana Monastery, saying these words:
"May the masters, out of compassion for me, accept these powdered incense.
Because the lay devotee was straightforward and had not previously informed them, the bhikṣus immediately struck the *gandī* bell to assemble the Saṃgha, intending to divide the powdered incense.
There were some who did not come, yet their disciples came forward to claim their shares, saying,
"Give us our share for our Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
Thus they vied with one another to demand their portions, their voices rising loudly.
Upon seeing this, the disciples of the non-Buddhists clapped their hands and laughed loudly, saying, "We have gained the advantage; today we have achieved victory.

At that time, the lay follower was filled with shame and remained silent. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and related the aforementioned events in detail, addressing the Buddha as follows:
“World-Honored One!
It is not that I am stingy with my wealth; rather, it is because the non-Buddhists have gained the upper hand that I feel ashamed.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma for the upāsaka, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Once his heart was filled with joy, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.
The World-Honored One went to where many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down; he then related the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the use of powdered incense is not permitted."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting [the community] in five ways, would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. There he saw a bhikṣu suffering from ringworm.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Monk,
are you dwelling in well-being and comfort?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
I have a scabies rash; if I bathe with powdered incense, it will be cured.”
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not use powdered incense; therefore, we dwell in hardship.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to use powdered incense."

Regarding "fragrant powders": powders made from human remains, horse-ear wood, the seven colors, *candana*, *kunta*, *amra*, *jambusiri*, *acuna*, or *kapila*—all such things as these are not permitted.
If a bhikṣu suffers from ringworm or scabies and requires powdered exfoliants for bathing to achieve a cure, he may use them without fault.
It is permitted to use *kāra* powder, *māṣa* powder, *māśūra* powder, and *saktu* powder as earth-based applications.
This is called the rule concerning powdered substances.

Regarding the rule concerning the staff and the bag: while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus—Nanda and Upānanda—carried a precious bag to hold their alms bowls.
Furthermore, there were those who carried black rope net-bags suspended from staffs over their shoulders as they walked, drawing the reproach of the people:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, carry precious net-bags containing their bowls upon their shoulders like kings and great ministers?"
Those who held him in contempt spoke again:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act like lowly servants, carrying their alms bowls in black net bags slung over their shoulders as they walk?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
Then the bhikṣus, for this reason, went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the keeping of staffs or pouches."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Tathāgata would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing a bhikṣu with a hand wound, he knew of it but asked nonetheless:
“Bhikṣu! [What happened?]”
"Are you dwelling in comfort and well-being?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Because my hand was injured, I broke my bowl; furthermore, the World-Honored One has prohibited the keeping of staffs and carrying-bags. For this reason, I do not find joy [in the community].
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, sick bhikṣus are permitted to request from the Saṃgha that they be allowed to keep staffs and carrying-bags."
The Saṃgha should perform the *karmavācanā* for him. The petitioner, having bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms, should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"I, [Name], having broken my bowl because my hands were injured, now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for keeping a staff and a carrying pouch. I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me this formal act.
The second and third requests are to be spoken in the same manner.
The *karmakāra* (the officiating monk) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has broken his bowl because his hand was injured; he has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karma*) for keeping a staff and a pouch."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for monk so-and-so to possess a staff and a pouch for it.
This is the motion.

After the single motion and the formal act, [it continues]: "The Saṃgha has already granted the formal act for monk so-and-so to possess a staff and a pouch for it. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
After the *karmavācanā* has been performed and one is about to set out, if one holds the staff and the carrying net in the hand, one must not lift them onto the shoulder while walking.
If one carries the staff in this manner, one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti*.
To carry a carrying-net bag constitutes a *vinayātikrama* with mental remorse.
To carry a staff, a carrying-net bag, and an alms-bowl together constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
When traveling on a road, one may tie a water-strainer to the head of a staff and walk while holding it in hand; it is not permitted to place it upon the shoulder.
If one carries a staff without having performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
Carrying a carrying-net (*śikya*) is likewise an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one carries both a staff and a carrying-net, one incurs two offenses of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the rule for carrying a staff and a water-strainer pouch.
Heavy objects, the robes of the deceased, those who are insane or seen as undesirable,
leather sandals offered out of faith that have been damaged, wearing wooden clogs, and rubbing the body on stones— these are the prohibitions.
[The rules on] incense powder, staffs, and bags.
The seventh *vagga* is concluded. Regarding the rule on garlic:

while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the householder Mṛgāra invited the Saṃgha to eat garlic. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to the garden to eat garlic; they scattered it about and threw it on the ground, and then took the remains back with them.
At that time, the householder went to inspect his garlic garden; having seen it, he immediately asked the gardeners, "Why is it like this?
The gardeners then explained the matter in detail as it had occurred.
The householder said, "Bhikṣu, you should simply eat; why do you discard it on the ground like this?
Furthermore, to whom would you take it and give it?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to eat garlic."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma to a great assembly.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who sat downwind after eating garlic, fearing that its odor would offend his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Buddha, knowing the situation, asked intentionally:
"Who is this bhikṣu sitting alone in one place like a person engaged in a dispute?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu eats garlic; fearing that its odor might offend his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he dwells alone downwind.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should know that if this bhikṣu does not eat garlic, would he wish to attain such ambrosial Dharma? He replied, "No."
The Buddha said:
"Because this bhikṣu consumed garlic, he lost such a deathless dharma.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"From this day forward, eating garlic is not permitted.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Monastery of the Śākyas in Kapilavastu, the Tathāgata went to visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days and saw that a bhikṣu was ill, emaciated, and jaundiced.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Monk, are you living in comfort and well-being?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!

My illness is not yet cured; when I was formerly a layman, it would have been alleviated by eating garlic. However, the World-Honored One has prohibited the eating of garlic, and for this reason I am unhappy.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to eat garlic, provided they act in accordance with the proper conduct.

Regarding garlic—whether it be cultivated or wild mountain garlic—and all similar varieties, as well as any other [types], whether raw or cooked, or in the form of leaves or skins, none of these shall be eaten."
If one has an abscess, a swelling, or a scabies sore, one may apply garlic as an ointment.
Once the garlic has been applied, one must not remain among the assembly, but should stay in a secluded place;
when cured, one should bathe thoroughly and return to the community of monks.
When he was ill, the physician said:
"Venerable sir!
This sick bhikṣu will recover if he consumes garlic; if he does not consume it, he will not recover."

If there is no other remedy, it is permitted to take [the medicine]. Having taken it, one should observe the *anuloma-dharma* (concordant practices) for seven days: staying in a small room at the edge [of the monastery], not lying upon the beds or bedding of the Saṃgha, not walking upon the places where the Saṃgha defecates or urinates, not washing one's feet in the place where the Saṃgha washes their feet, not entering the warm bathhouse, the lecture hall, or the refectory, not accepting invitations to meals assigned by the Saṃgha’s turn, not entering the Saṃgha’s dining area or the meditation hall, and not entering among the monks during the preaching of the Dharma or the *poṣadha*.
If there is an assembly of bhikṣus, one must not go to it, nor should one circumambulate the stūpa.
If the stūpa is located in the open air, one may perform a prostration from a distance downwind.
Having practiced the seven days of conforming conduct, on the eighth day, after bathing, washing one's robes, and fumigating them, one may enter among the saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill eats garlic, or one who is ill eats garlic but does not practice the prescribed method, both incur a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called the rule regarding garlic.
Regarding the rule for overturning the bowl (*pātra-nyāma*): When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a lay follower named Dharmapāla who regularly invited the Saṃgha for meals in turn.
When a bhikṣu arrived, he would interrogate him on the meaning of the teachings; if the visitor could explain them, he would be greatly pleased and personally provide him with various kinds of food.
If he could not answer, he would immediately disparage him and have his servants give him coarse food.

For this reason, when it was the turn of the senior monk in the assembly to depart, he did not go; everyone said he had passed his turn, and so it continued until even the youngest monks were unable to leave, whereupon they began to speak loudly and clamorously.
The Buddha, knowing [the reason], asked intentionally:
"For what reason are you speaking so loudly?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
The lay follower Dharmapāla constantly invites the Saṃgha for meals in turn; even when it was his duty to go, he did not go, and because of this, he raised his voice and spoke loudly.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Dharmapāla the upāsaka has shown contempt for the community of bhikṣus; you should perform the *pātra-nyubja* (inverted-bowl) karmavācanā against him.
There are eight matters concerning an upāsaka for which the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-nyubja* karmavācanā.”
What are the eight?
To revile a bhikṣu in his presence;
to rebuke a bhikṣu in his presence, speaking as follows:
"You are a practitioner of evil deeds," he said,
manifesting anger in the presence of the bhikṣu,
reviling him and cutting off his offerings and gains.
He takes no pleasure in working together with the bhikṣus;
he reviles the Buddha, reviles the Dharma, and reviles the Saṃgha.
These are called the eight matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-āvarta* (inverted-bowl) karmavācanā.
The *karmadāna* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This lay follower Dharmapāla has treated the bhikṣus with contempt. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa-karman* (the ritual of overturning the alms-bowl) against this lay follower Dharmapāla who treats the bhikṣus with contempt."
The motion is made as follows: "The motion is thus.

After the threefold proclamation of the *karmavācanā*, up to: "The Saṃgha has completed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa-karman* against the lay follower Dharmapāla for his contemptuous behavior toward the bhikṣus. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The upāsaka Dharmapāla would always eat his meal only after he had first fed the bhikṣus.

On that day, while waiting for the bhikṣus, the time passed and they did not arrive; he then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
“Bhikṣus, for what reason have they not come to eat?
The Buddha said,
“Because you treated the community of bhikṣus with contempt, yet desired to benefit them, I have performed the *pātra-nyubja* (inverted bowl) karmavācanā against you.”
At that time, there was an arhat not far from the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the upāsaka, "Go and ask this bhikṣu: 'What is meant by "salt"?"
“How many kinds of salt are there?
He then went to him and said,
“I pay homage to the Ācārya.”
The bhikṣu said,
"Welcome," and then asked:
“Venerable One!
What is called ‘salt’?
How many kinds of salt are there?”
The bhikṣu said:
"I already know; you are a *dhammika* upāsaka who has shown contempt for the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, and I have therefore performed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa-karman* against you."
"Is it because you have not had enough?
You who dwell happily here have come once more to trouble me; salt is indeed salt.
Having heard the bhikṣu’s words, his heart was filled with despondency, and he returned to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Regarding the meaning of salt that you have questioned, have you fully grasped its significance?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu has heard little and has not yet studied under a teacher; because he was asked about salt, he spoke of salt.
At that time, not far from the Buddha, there was another Dharma-preacher bhikṣu named Vakkula. The Buddha said to Phālguna:
"Go and ask that bhikṣu about the meaning of salt.
He immediately went to him and said,
"Venerable teacher, I pay homage to you."
He replied,
"Welcome, donor," and immediately told him to sit.
Although he had not yet asked about the meaning of the teaching, upon hearing the command to sit, he was filled with great joy and immediately took his seat.
He then asked:
"Venerable One!..."
"What is the meaning of 'salt'?
The bhikṣu replied, "This is a good question; I shall now explain it for you."
Regarding the meaning of "salt," there are two kinds: flavor and nature.
As for flavor, it is like the water of the ocean, which has the single taste of saltiness.
As for nature, there are black salt, red salt, Siṃhala salt, Vibhītaka salt, Bilva salt, Kacchaka salt, Sītā salt, and Pika salt.
"Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
that which is raw and that which is cooked; these are called 'salt'.
Having heard this, his heart was filled with joy. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu well understands and can skillfully analyze the meaning of salt, both in its broad and concise forms, and is able to answer according to both direct and reverse order.
The Buddha said:
"This is an ordinary person who has not yet tasted the flavor of the Dharma within my teaching.
The monk before you is an Arhat, yet out of arrogance you failed to distinguish the true from the false, thereby performing what is unbeneficial for a long night."
Thereupon, having heard the Buddha’s words, Dharmapāla was immediately struck with fear; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
I now repent.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will cause the bhikṣus to accept my offerings again from this day forward.

The Buddha said, "Return home, bathe, and put on new clothes; then, accompanied by your retinue, go to the Saṃgha and request the lifting of the *pātra-nyāya* (the bowl-covering rite). The Saṃgha shall grant you its lifting."
Having prepared as instructed, he returned home, bathed, put on new clean robes, and entered the midst of the Saṃgha. Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he spoke these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!

I, a lay follower (upāsaka), have been included among those who have treated the Saṅgha of bhikṣus with contempt; wishing to benefit them, I performed the *pātra-āvartana* (the ritual of overturning the bowl).
Now that I recognize my transgression and practice the conforming Dharma, my mind has become supple.
"I only pray that the Sangha, out of compassion, will grant me the *kaṭhina-utsarga* (removal) of the *pātra-praticchādana* (covered bowl) *karman*.

Having made this request three times, the Sangha should instruct him to remain within the boundary (*sīmā*). He should be placed according to the Dharma at a location where he is visible but cannot be heard. The *karman* is to be performed by the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the present Sangha), not merely by the assembly of monks present.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This lay follower, Dharma-preya, has shown contempt for the community of monks; desiring to benefit him, we first perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (the ritual of overturning the bowl) against him."
Having met with him today, his conduct has become compliant and his mind is now supple; he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-āvaraṇa-karman* (the formal act of covering the bowl).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant the Dhammika upāsaka the lifting of the *pātra-āvaraṇa-karman*.
"Thus it is announced.

After the threefold formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), up to: "The Sangha has completed the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa* (the ritual of overturning the bowl) against the lay follower Dharmapriya. Since the Sangha remains silent, it is approved; this matter is thus upheld."

Once the Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-āvartana* (turning-over of the bowl) karmavācanā against him, no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās shall be permitted to go there. One should take a *kāṣāya* robe and tie it upon the door of that house, and one should proclaim in the street:
"The *pātra-āvartana* karmavācanā has been performed against such-and-such a family."
If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one should say to him:
"The *pātra-nyāya* (the 'bowl-inversion' ritual) has been performed against such-and-such a family; you should not go there.
When performing the *pātra-nyāya*, one must not proceed to perform it for another [family] while it is still being carried out.
If they should say,
"It would be better if the śramaṇa did not enter my house," one should not act toward such a person in this way.
If there are those who possess a sense of shame and remorse, one should perform the rite for them.
If, having recognized their own faults, they act in accordance with the Dharma and their minds become supple, one should grant them the restoration of the bowl.
This is called the rite of overturning the bowl (*pātra-nyubja*).

Regarding the method for fastening the ties of the robe: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was once a bhikṣu on almsround who held his bowl in one hand and his *kuṇḍika* (water flask) in the other. A whirlwind arose and blew away his outer robe; he entered the Jeta Grove wearing only his undergarment.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
where is your robe?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One,
it was carried away by a whirlwind."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should attach fasteners and patches.
At that time, the bhikṣus used gold and silver to make the fasteners and patches for their robes. The Buddha said:

"It is not permitted to make knots, ties, or fastenings out of any gold, silver, or precious materials; one should instead use copper, iron, white wax, or wood and bamboo. Having prepared thread, one may attach knots and fastenings, but it is not permitted to enter a village without wearing these."
If there is no [button], one should sew it with a needle; if there is no needle, one should at least hold it with the hand.
If one enters a village wearing a robe that lacks a fastener, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
Likewise, if one enters a family [for alms], one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression through mental regret) as soon as one obtains [food].
If there is [food] but one does not partake of it, one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti*.
There is no offense if one enters a bhikṣuṇī’s monastery, a monastery of non-Buddhists, or if a donor announces:
"According to where it is comfortable," means there is no offense.
This is called the method for attaching and knotting garment fasteners.

Regarding the method for the waistband: When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, there was a bhikṣu on alms-round who held his bowl in one hand and his *kuṇḍika* (water flask) in the other. A whirlwind blew away his lower garment, and he entered the Jeta Grove Monastery wearing only his upper robe.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
where is your antaravāsaka?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One,
it was carried away by a whirlwind.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should wear a waistband.
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus made belts from loose threads, made them from knotted threads, or made them by weaving in the air, the Buddha said:
"Scattered threads or knotted threads are not permitted at all.
Those that are woven in the air should be joined by a central seam.
Whether they are made by weaving or by knitting, or if they are made in a circular shape, all such are permitted to wear."
When putting it on, one must not fasten it with four turns or even a single turn; it should be fastened with two turns up to three turns.

If a bhikṣu’s body is too supple to allow for such fastening, he should take it with him; when he reaches the vicinity of a village and intends to enter, he should fasten it, and upon leaving, he should unfasten it again.
If one enters a village without fastening the waistband, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one has it but does not fasten it, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If it is fastened with a single turn, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
"If it is wound twice or three times, there is no offense.
This is called the rule for waistbands.

Regarding the method for tying the band: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣu wore his headband without making a knot. As he walked before a shop, the band came undone and trailed on the ground as he went, which caused the people of the world to criticize him:
“How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, walk about trailing their entrails?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you should wear a headband with a knot.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who made a headband with a knot out of gold and silver.
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! It is not permitted to make a headband from any kind of precious material. Whether it be two or three knots, it is not permitted to make one knot or four knots; nor is it permitted to leave it entirely unknotted. To do so constitutes an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.”
This is called the rule regarding the wearing of the belt.
Regarding the rule concerning riding: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, on a day of a seasonal festival, the people went out to watch.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rode elephants, rode horses, and some rode donkeys, which caused them to be criticized by the worldlings.
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, travel mounted on elephants or horses like royal ministers?
Seeing some who were riding donkeys, they further said:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, travel mounted on donkeys like lowly servants."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit riding on donkeys or horses."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Ambaṭṭha Park Monastery in the Jīrṇakaśyapa’s Grove near Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata, for the sake of five benefits, would go on inspection of the monks’ quarters once every five days.
The Buddha saw a bhikṣu who was sickly, emaciated, and jaundiced; knowing [the situation], he asked him intentionally:
"Bhikṣu, is your illness increasing or decreasing? Is your breathing regular?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
I am suffering from illness; my breath is uneven."
The Buddha said,
"Are you unable to go to the elder physician to attend to the patient?
He replied:
“The World-Honored One has prohibited riding on vehicles; I am suffering from illness and cannot go there.
The Buddha said, “From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to ride on vehicles.”

Regarding "vehicles," these include elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, donkey-vehicles, camel-vehicles, boat-vehicles, ox-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and palanquin-vehicles—all such vehicles as these. One who is not ill is not permitted to ride them; however, one who is ill may do so. Furthermore, one is not permitted to ride a female vehicle; one should ride a male vehicle.
If one is seriously ill and does not distinguish [the circumstances], there is no offense in riding [a vehicle].
If there is a reason for traveling up or down [a slope], by water, or crossing directly across, one should form this thought:
"I have a matter of necessity."
At that time, one may ride a vehicle to cross over.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill rides a vehicle, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called "riding a vehicle."

Regarding the method of lying together on a bed: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus—two or three of them—lay together on a single bed, leaving the bedding worn out and torn upon the ground.

Out of five considerations for the benefit [of the Saṃgha], the Tathāgata would go on inspection to the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing a broken bed lying on the ground, he knew the reason but asked nonetheless:
"Bhikṣu!..."
"Whose bed has been broken and left in such a state of disarray upon the ground?
The bhikṣus then related the matter in detail as it had occurred.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, sleeping on the same bed is not permitted.
Regarding beds and bedding, as explained above, one person should sleep on one bed.
If one sits on a bed, two people may sleep joined together across three beds, provided that when extending their legs, they do not extend beyond the knees.
If using mats laid crosswise, it is permitted for three people to sleep lying crosswise.
If it is a square mat, two persons may sleep together using three mats joined, provided that when they extend their legs, they do not go beyond the knees.
If it is a grass mat, or if each person spreads their own *niṣīdana* sitting-cloth, there is no offense in lying down.

If it is cold, one may have a single covering that extends over both [the senior and junior], but they must not be too close; there should be a distance of one cubit between them, with the hands not extended.
Regarding the size of the bed, those who are three *saṃvatsara* (years of ordination) apart may sit together on the same bed, but they must not sleep together on the same bed.
If one sleeps on the same bed, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
This is called the rule regarding sharing a bed.

Regarding the rule regarding sitting together: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus—three or four of them at a time—sat together on a single seat, causing the seat to break.

For the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata would inspect the lodgings of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing that the beds were broken and lying in disarray upon the floor, the Buddha, though knowing the reason, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣus!"
"What kind of broken bed is this, that it lies so disheveled upon the ground?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, sitting together on the same bed is not permitted.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One said to Upāli:
“Do the bhikṣus receive and recite the Vinaya?”
He replied, "I do recite them,
but I have recited only a small portion.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"Why are there so few?

He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding sitting together on the same bed; each bhikṣu must occupy a bed alone. For this reason, those who receive and recite [the teachings] are few."
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit a bhikṣu of three years' standing to sit on the same seat as one who has been ordained for less than three years; a bhikṣu with no years of standing may sit with one of three years' standing; and so on, until a bhikṣu of seven years' standing may sit with one of ten years' standing."
If three people can sit on a bed where one person lies down, two people should share a sitting bed.
If the bed is one and a half cubits long, those who are three years junior may sit together with two others; if it is shorter than that, they should join the senior-most person (upādhyāya).
If a bed exceeds three cubits in length, one may sit together with a bhikṣu who has been ordained for four years or more; if it is shorter than that, one may not sit together.

If a great assembly gathers and there are few beds and seats, one may join the beds together by lashing them so they are connected; when tying them together, one must ensure they are secure so that the cushions do not shift, and then one may sit together.
If a square mat is three cubits long, one may sit together with a bhikṣu who has been ordained for four years; if it is less than that, one may not.
If grass is spread on the ground, there is no offense in sitting together.
This is called the rule for sitting together.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 31. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 32.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Regarding the tenth section of the *Prakīrṇaka-vastu*, the rules on "Eating Together": The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate together, which caused them to be criticized by the people of the world.
“How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat together like worldly libertines?
... [and so on] until the Buddha said:
“Call the group of six bhikṣus here.”
When he had arrived, the Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
“Is it true that you have done this? He replied:
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to eat together."
"To eat together" means to eat from a single vessel.
Regarding "food," there are the five types of primary foods (*bhojana*) and the five types of mixed primary foods; these should be eaten from separate vessels.
If one lacks a bowl, one should use a *kukkuṭapāda* (hook-bowl) or a *kaṇḍolaka* (basket).
If there is no [other person present], one should place a ball of rice in the left hand and eat with the right hand.
If one is still unable to do so, one should set the bowl down upon grass or leaves and take food from it alternately; both hands must not reach into the bowl at the same time.
Apart from the five types of formal meals and the five types of mixed formal meals—such as parched grain, cakes, fruits, or vegetables—there is no offense in eating together.
However, if one eats from the same vessel, it is a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
This is called the rule for communal eating.

Regarding the dining table: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Tathāgata, for the sake of five benefits, would visit the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing that the dining tables in the rooms of Nanda and Upananda were decorated with various colors, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"Whose dining tables are these, decorated with such various colors?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“This is Nanda and Upānanda’s food table.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, eating at a table is not permitted.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, he visited the quarters of the bhikṣus once every five days for the sake of the five benefits of a Tathāgata. There he saw a bhikṣu with a hand ulcerated by a carbuncle; knowing the situation, the Buddha asked him:
“Bhikṣu, are you well and at ease?”
He replied, “World-Honored One!
My hand was wounded and my bowl was broken; furthermore, the World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding eating from atop a table, and for these reasons, I did not enjoy it.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to eat from a table, but I do not permit various painted colors [on it].
If it is a communal dining table for the Saṃgha, there is no offense in having various painted colors."
If it is one's own private property, the use of a single color is permitted.
When a sick bhikṣu eats from a table, he should first establish a mental resolve; thus, its use is without offense.
If a bhikṣu is not ill, eating from a table is not permitted under any circumstances.
If one is aged or ill, has a wounded hand, or has bled from a head wound; or if the alms bowl is heavy, full, hot, or cold; or if one receives food on a table—there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill eats from a table, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule concerning tables.
[The rules on] eating garlic, covering the bowl, hooks and fasteners, and waistbands.
Riding together, sharing a bed, sitting together, eating from the same vessel,
and various colors at the dining table.
The eighth chapter (varga) concludes.
Regarding "one who kills": when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Nanda and Upananda were traveling and returned to Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was an old donor named Abhaya; when it was time for the meal, these bhikṣus put on their village-entering robes, took up their bowls, and entered his house. Upon seeing them, the donor spoke as follows:
“Ācārya! Why have you not been seen for so long?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Long-lived one!
I have come from afar; what kind of fine food do you wish to provide for me?
He replied:
"I shall prepare food for the ācārya tomorrow.
The bhikṣu said,
"Do not prepare food for a weaver."
He then asked,
"What is meant by 'the weaver's meal'?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Coarse rice with bean soup is what I have.
The donor said, "I will not give coarse rice and bean soup to the Ācārya; I shall give you meat instead."
The bhikṣu said,
"Do not give me cold meat.
He replied:
"I will not give cold meat to the ācārya; I shall cook it hot and give it to you.
The bhikṣu said, "When I spoke of 'hot,' I did not mean this kind of heat."
He asked, "What is this heat?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Freshly slaughtered warm meat.
The donor said, "If you desire such, come early tomorrow; you shall obtain it while still warm, having been slaughtered right before the Ācārya."
The bhikṣu replied, “So be it.
At dawn the next morning, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to that house; the donor then led forth the sheep, pigs, and chickens, lined them up before the bhikṣu, and slaughtered them.
After the meal was served and [the donor] had departed, the patron spoke with dissatisfaction:

"The śramaṇa Gautama uses countless skillful means to revile killing and praise non-killing; yet this śramaṇa instructs others to kill right before my eyes—how does this differ from killing it himself?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Monks! This is an evil deed.
Thus spoke the Buddha, and so forth.
"How can you directly instruct someone to kill?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to act for the sake of killing.
"For the sake of killing" means acting for the sake of killing a bhikṣu.
If a monk kills [an animal] for the sake of [another], then no bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, or upāsikā shall eat it at all.
In this manner, even if she is killed for the sake of an upāsikā, no bhikṣu shall eat it, nor shall the upāsikā herself eat it.
There are three grounds for this:
having seen, heard, or suspected [the killing].
"Seeing" means seeing with one's own eyes before one's face that [an animal] was killed for the purpose of slaughter; such food is not permitted to be eaten—this is called "seeing.
"Hearing" means hearing it oneself with one's ears, or hearing from another, that [an animal] was killed for the purpose of slaughter; such food is not permitted to be eaten.
If the person before one is untrustworthy and thus intends to cause confusion for the bhikṣu, one should not accept their words;
rather, one should ascertain the matter from a trustworthy person—this is called "hearing."

Regarding doubt: Suppose a bhikṣu frequently sees sheep at a donor’s house. Later, when he goes there, he sees only their heads and feet on the ground. Having seen this, doubt arises in his mind, and he should ask:
"Where are the sheep I saw previously?"
If it is said,
"The preceptor has already killed [the animal] for you," one should not eat it.
If one says:
"Venerable sir!
I killed [this animal] for the sake of a sacrifice to the gods; there is not enough to eat."
To obtain food [in this manner] is called "doubt.
In the same way, for all sentient beings, whether one sees them or hears of them, to harbor such doubt is likewise called "killing."
Regarding human flesh: when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time in the city of Śrāvastī an upāsaka named Gopikā, and his wife was also named Gopikā.
When a visiting bhikṣu arrived who also had the name Ācārya, the upāsaka, having heard this, thought to himself:
"The ācārya has the same name as mine; I shall go and invite him for a meal."

He immediately went to the monastery and invited [the Elder] to his home; having provided various kinds of food and drink as offerings, he prostrated himself at the Elder’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and said:
"Venerable One!..."
"I only wish that you would accept my invitation for the four requisites:
robes, food, bedding and seats, and medicinal decoctions for the sick.
The bhikṣu then accepted the invitation.
At that time, the husband wished to travel far away on business with a merchant caravan, and he instructed his wife, saying:
"I am going on a long journey; while you remain hereafter, you should provide excellent offerings to the ācārya and ensure that he lacks for nothing."
After she had departed, the bhikṣus were not in harmony and wished to take a purgative. They said to the upāsikā, "We wish to take a purgative;
can you prepare the food for us in the proper sequence at the appropriate times?"
He replied, "So be it.

After she had taken the medicine, he provided her with food according to the prescribed sequence for her illness: first clear rice gruel, then thick gruel, and next meat. He took a *kaṃsapātra* bowl and said to the maidservant:
"Take this and go buy some meat and bring it back.
The maidservant entered the market, but as it was the day of the fast, there were no slaughterers at all, and she could not return with any.
At that time, the upāsikā felt displeased and said:
"If the Ācārya takes medicine but does not receive food appropriate for his illness, it may cause his condition to worsen.
He then ground mustard seeds and soaked them in oil; entering his room, he immediately used a sharp knife to cut flesh from his thigh and said to a maidservant:
"Take this meat, wash it thoroughly with mustard-seed oil, prepare it as food, and give it to the Ācārya. Then ask the Ācārya what kind of food he will require for tomorrow."
The maidservant prepared the food as instructed and sent it off;
she then asked, "What food will you need for tomorrow? He replied:
"Stop! Do not send it any further.
At that time, the laywoman was lying down, afflicted by a sore, when her husband returned from his travels as a merchant and thought to himself:
"I always come back from my long journeys, and my wife would come out through the second or third gate to welcome me.
Why does she not come out today?
Entering the room, he saw his wife lying on the bed and spoke with indignation:
"Why do you disregard me and not come out?
His wife replied,
"What merit is there in this journey?"
He said, "I wish for you to come and meet me. He replied,
"I have traveled hundreds of thousands of millions of leagues to reach here."
His wife replied, "This is merely external wealth; what is so remarkable about it?
I shall cut flesh from my own body to provide for the ācārya."
Her husband asked, "Where did you cut it?
She immediately lifted her garment to show him; upon seeing this, the husband fell to the ground in a state of bewildered distress.
At that time, a spirit spoke to the bhikṣu.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu entered the samādhi of loving-kindness; through the power of his meditative concentration, the woman was restored to her former state.
His wife then said to her husband:
"Arise! Arise! Do not be afraid!"
"By the spiritual power of the Ācārya, my wound has already healed.
When her husband rose and saw that the wound was indeed healed, he was filled with great joy and went to the shop, saying these words:
"My wife is so diligent that she cut her own body to make this offering."
When the people heard this, they spoke with disdain, saying,
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat human flesh? The bhikṣus,
on account of this matter, went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here. When he had come,
the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
It is because I have not entered meditative concentration.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, eating human flesh is not permitted.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Rṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, there was a bhikṣu suffering from jaundice. A physician said:
“Venerable sir, you may recover by consuming human blood; if you do not consume it, you will die, for there is no other remedy.”

At that time, there was a person who had committed an offense against the king; his two hands were bound behind his back with a garland of *kapila* flowers, and he was led to the place of execution while drums were beaten and a proclamation was made.
When the bhikṣu arrived at the side of the executioner, he spoke these words:
"Long-lived one!"
"Give me human blood to drink.
The executioner said, "If you wish to eat flesh, I shall give it to you as well; how much more so blood?"
He then sat down beside the criminal on the ground, pierced the two carotid veins with a knife so that blood flowed out, and the bhikṣu caught the blood in both hands and drank it.
This was despised by the people of the world, who said: "This is no bhikṣu; he is a man-eating ghost."
He immediately threw tiles, stones, and clods of earth at him, but that bhikṣu was weak and managed to escape.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Monk!
This is an evil deed; you cherish your life to such an extent!”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, drinking human blood is not permitted; even consuming human marrow, all such things are forbidden.
If a bhikṣu develops a sore on his head and a physician says:
Regarding the statement, "One must apply human bone ash to recover," it is permissible to apply it.
Once applied, one must not remain among the assembly; one should stay in a small room at the edge. After recovery, one should bathe thoroughly and return to the assembly.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was a certain caste that ate the flesh of nāgas, and some bhikṣus also ate the flesh of nāgas; for this reason, many people killed them.
At that time, a nāga girl approached the World-Honored One’s bedside, stood there, and wept. Knowing the reason, the Buddha intentionally asked her, "Why are you weeping?
Then the nāga girl addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The people of Vaiśālī eat dragons, and the bhikṣus also eat them; for this reason, many are being killed.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will not allow the bhikṣus to eat dragons.”
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the dragon girl in accordance with her needs, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her before departing.
Then the World-Honored One went to where many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down; he then recounted the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of dragon flesh, dragon blood, dragon bones, dragon tendons, or dragon marrow; none of these are permitted to be eaten."
"If one has various external ailments of the body that require the application of bone ash, it is permissible to use it without fault.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra’s elephant died; there were some low-caste Caṇḍālas who ate its flesh, and among the bhikṣus, there were also those who ate it.
Then the Elder Youth went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
King Bimbisāra’s elephant has died, and various low-caste Caṇḍālas have been eating its flesh; some bhikṣus have also eaten it.”
"A bhikṣu is one who has left the household life and is respected by all people; we only pray that the World-Honored One will not cause him to eat elephant flesh.

The World-Honored One, for the sake of the youth, preached the Dharma in accordance with his needs, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him. The youth then prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew.
Then the World-Honored One went to where the many bhikṣus were, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), sat down, and explained the aforementioned matter in detail to the bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of elephant meat; even elephant marrow is not permitted to be eaten."
"It is permitted to make bowl-stands from ivory or bone; there is no offense in making fine knots for robes.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra’s horse died; the account is the same as that told regarding the elephant above.
If one has an external skin disease such as scabies or sores that requires the application of horse blood, there is no offense.
Having applied it, one must not remain within the assembly; one should instead stay in a small room at the edge.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, some bhikṣus ate dog meat; when they entered a village, they were chased by dogs who barked at them competitively.
On account of this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and so on, until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of dog meat, nor do I permit the eating of even dog marrow."
"If one is bitten by a dog, it is permissible to burn dog hair and apply it to the wound; there is no offense in doing so.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who ate crow meat. When this bhikṣu entered a village to beg for food, or while walking in meditation within the forest, flocks of crows would pursue him, cawing.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of crow meat; even crow marrow is not permitted to be eaten. However, if one requires wings or feathers for external use, there is no offense."

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ate the flesh of vultures. While the bhikṣu was walking in meditation near a forest grove, a flock of vultures pursued him, shrieking and calling out.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I do not permit the eating of vulture meat; even vulture marrow is not permitted to be eaten. However, if one requires the wings or feathers for external use, there is no offense."
1. Human flesh. 2. Dragon flesh.
3. Elephant flesh.
4. Horse meat. 5. Dog meat. 6. Crow meat.
7. Vulture meat. 8. Pork. 9. Monkey meat.
Tenth, regarding lion meat and garlic:
as for garlic, whether raw or cooked, including its skin and leaves, none of it is permitted to be eaten.
However, if it is required for external use, such as applying to a wound, its use is permitted.

If one has smeared oneself [with garlic], one must not remain within the assembly; one should instead stay in a small room at the edge. Once the period of exclusion has ended, one should bathe thoroughly and return to being permitted to join the assembly.
This is called the rule regarding meat-garlic.

Regarding the rule on hides: While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Nanda and Upananda went to a cowherd’s house and sat upon a bed. There was a newborn calf that, seeing the color of the bhikṣus’ robes resembled its mother, leaped about and rushed toward them.
The bhikṣu then rubbed his forehead with his hand; as it felt smooth and supple to the touch, he spoke these words:
"This hide is soft and fine; it would make an excellent sitting mat."
At that time, the cowherd thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu is known to the king’s high ministers and nobility; he possesses great power and influence, and for that reason he surely wishes to obtain this hide."
He then asked:
"Ācārya, do you require skin?
I shall give it to you."
The bhikṣu then said,
"Simply give me this calf-hide.
The cowherd replied:
"In my home there is the hide of a calf that died while still alive; it is soft and fine, and I shall have it tanned and treat it for you.
The bhikṣu said, "If you truly intend to give it to me, this alone will suffice; there is no need for anything else."
Then the cowherd thought to himself,
"This bhikṣu possesses great power and is capable of doing me harm. Out of fear and apprehension,
he immediately slaughtered the calf in front of the bhikṣu and flayed its skin to give to him.
At that time, the mother cow returned from grazing and, not seeing her calf, wandered along the fence lowing and calling for him.
A cowherd spoke with resentment, saying:
"The Śramaṇa sons of the Śākya lack a heart of compassion; if a śramaṇa were in the place of this mother cow, what would his state of mind be?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Monks! This is a wicked deed. How could you openly instruct someone to kill?
From this day forward, the use of skins is not permitted.”

Regarding skins: cowhide, oxhide, tiger skin, leopard skin, bear skin, and deer skin—all such skins are forbidden for sitting upon; only the woolen skins from the border regions of Śūrasena are permitted.
There are two kinds of sheepskins:
first, those of the black ram (*urabhraka*), and second, those of the hornless ewe (*ajinapada*).
Each of these—black rams and hornless ewes—has ten varieties, as described above.
If one sits upon a hide, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one sits upon a cushion stuffed with *tūla* fiber made of hide, it is two offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
If one sits upon a leather sandal, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one lies upon leather sandals above the knees, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense;
below the knees, there is no offense.
If it is a bed woven with leather, there is no offense in sitting upon it.
Regarding foot-rubbing implements: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Nanda and Upananda were using various kinds of foot-rubbing implements to wash their feet.
When the disciples of the non-Buddhists saw this, they thought to themselves, "We should go together and try to disturb these lay followers."
As explained in detail above regarding powdered substances, the Buddha further declared:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to scrub or wash the feet with various kinds of objects.
Regarding such scrubbing objects: whether square or round, carved with shapes like those of *māṣa* beans or *mudga* beans—none of these are permitted for use.
If the soles of the feet have dirt or cracks, it is permitted to use round grass, bricks, or tiles [for cleaning].
These are called foot-rubbing items.

Regarding eye medicine: when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at a time of worldly festival, men and women went out of the city to sightsee. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus adorned their eyes with *añjana* (antimony) and black substances, which caused them to be criticized by the people of the world.
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, adorn their eyes with *añjana* like noble youths?
Some who saw them adorned with black substances further said:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, walk about with eyes adorned by black substances like lowly servants."
"What path can there be for such a ruined person?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the adorning of the eyes."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at the Ambaṭṭha Park of the Elder Boy in Śrāvastī, some bhikṣus suffered from eye pain. The Elder Boy said:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
"You may apply this medicine to your eyes.
The bhikṣus said,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit applying it to the eyes."
The youth said,
"I shall go to the World-Honored One and beg for this vow.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bhikṣus are people who eat but one meal a day; the eyes are what people value most. We only pray that the World-Honored One will permit these bhikṣus to apply eye medicine.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the application of eye medicine is permitted, with the exception of *kṣauma* (azurite).
If a physician says:"
"Venerable Sir!
This eye pain can be cured by applying powdered *śūka-yantra* (empty-blue), and there is no other remedy.
"If that is so, you may apply it."

"Once you have applied it, you must not remain within the assembly; you should stay in a small room at the edge. After you have been appointed [to the task], you should wash yourself clean and may then return to the assembly.
This is called eye medicine.
Regarding the ointment tube: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus were using tree leaves to hold eye ointment.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked:
"Bhikṣus, what is this?"
He replied,
"It is eye medicine.
The Buddha said:
"Eye medicine is a precious substance; it should be kept in a tube.
At that time, the bhikṣus made tubes of gold and silver to store it in. The Buddha said:
"The use of gold, silver, and all kinds of jewels is not permitted."
"One should use copper, iron, white tin, bamboo or reed baskets, bird feathers, or even leather wrappings.
This is called a medicinal tube.

Regarding the eye-salve applicator: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who used bamboo to make an eye-salve applicator. The Buddha, knowing this, asked him about it intentionally.
“Bhikṣu, what is this? He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"This is an ointment stick.
The Buddha said, "The eye is a delicate organ; one should use a smooth object to make the stick."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who made [a bowl] out of gold and silver. The Buddha said:

"I do not permit the use of gold, silver, or any precious materials; one should instead use copper, iron, ivory, bone, sandalwood, or hard wood, smoothing it by rubbing until it is glossy, down to using even the tip of a finger."
This is called the rule regarding the ointment-stick. Regarding the rule on parasols:

while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, it was a day of public festival when men and women went out for recreation. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried various multicolored parasols, and some carried parasols made of tree bark. They were censured by the people of the world, who said:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, carry various multicolored parasols like princes and high ministers?"
Seeing one who was carrying a tree-leaf umbrella, he spoke again, saying:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, walk about carrying tree-leaf umbrellas like lowly servants?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to carry an umbrella."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, the Elder Aniruddha-Kimbila, having completed his rains retreat at Mount Gijjhakūṭa, returned to Śrāvastī to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu,
why is your robe so stained with salt?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit the carrying of umbrellas. While I was begging for alms, I was caught in the rain; that is why I acted thus.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the carrying of parasols.
Regarding parasols: those made of tree bark, tree leaves, or bamboo—such as these are permitted for use; however, various multi-colored parasols are not permitted.
This is called the rule regarding parasols.

As for the rule regarding fans: on days of worldly festivals when men and women go out to sightsee, the group of six bhikṣus carried fans adorned with mica, while some carried fans made of grass. They were censured by the people, who said:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, carry fans adorned with mica like princes and high ministers?"
Seeing someone carrying a grass fan, he spoke again:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, walk about carrying grass fans like low-born people?
These ruined men—what path do they possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the holding of fans.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣus in the meditation hall were troubled by mosquitoes and made noise with their robes as they fanned themselves.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Monks, what are you doing that makes a sound like an elephant shaking its ears?
The monks replied:
“The Blessed One has prescribed a rule that one must not hold a fan. The bhikṣus were troubled by mosquitoes; they used their robes to brush them away, which made a noise.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, I allow you to hold bamboo fans, reed fans, and leaf fans, with the exception of mica fans and fans decorated with various painted colors.”

If the Sangha’s fans are made of various colors, there is no offense; if one’s own fan is of a neutral color (bad-raga), or if someone brings a fan smeared with various fragrances as an offering, it is permitted to wash it and then use it.
This is called the rule regarding the fan. Regarding the rule for the whisk (*cāmara*):

while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, on a day of public festival, men and women went out for recreation. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried whisks made of white yak-tail hair with handles fashioned of gold and silver; some also carried whisks made of horsehair. They were censured by the people of the world, and consequently the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to hold a whisk."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, some bhikṣus in their meditation huts were troubled by mosquitoes; they brushed away the mosquitoes with tree leaves, which made a noise.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Bhikṣus, what is this sound?"
He replied, “The World-Honored One has established a precept prohibiting the holding of a fly-whisk; therefore, the bhikṣus have made a sound by using tree leaves as whisks to brush away mosquitoes.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the holding of whisks (*cāmara*).

As for whisks: those made of thread, split cotton cloth, *mṛdvīkā* grass, or tree bark; among these, with the exception of those made of the tails of white yaks or white horses, or those with handles of gold or silver, all others are permitted to be held."
If there is anything white, it must be dyed with a discolored hue before being permitted for use.
When holding the whisk (*cāmara*), one must not grasp it with the coquettish gestures or postures of a courtesan; this is called the method for using the whisk.
For killing; for eating human flesh; for eye medicine along with its tube and applicator stick;
for leather used for rubbing the feet; for umbrellas, fans, and fly-whisks.
The ninth chapter (varga) is concluded.
Regarding surgical treatment: While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu suffering from hemorrhoids who said to a physician, "Long-lived one!
Can you perform surgical treatment for me?"
He replied,
“Yes. The physician then thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas are clever and wise; once they see me governing, they will surely learn it for themselves and no longer seek me out.
Having thus sent away the bhikṣus, he wished to act contrary to the Dharma.
At that time, this bhikṣu immediately became suspicious and called out to the other bhikṣus, saying, "Elders, come here;
this physician wishes to perform an unlawful act.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus immediately entered, whereupon the physician, struck with fear, cast aside his knife and fled.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Monks! How is it that you treat the sensitive parts with a knife?
From this day forward, I do not permit the treatment of the sensitive parts with a knife.”
Regarding the "place of affection": it is four finger-widths away from the edge of the anus on either side.

If there is an abscess, boil, or carbuncle, it is permitted to chew barley or chicken dung and apply it to the area to bring it to suppuration; one should then have one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) pick it open.
If there are other ailments such as boils, carbuncles, or abscesses elsewhere on the body that require treatment with a blade, its use is permitted.
To treat a cherished part of the body with a blade constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called "treatment with a blade."
Regarding the irrigation tube: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī when there was a bhikṣu suffering from a wasting disease who said to a physician, "Long-lived one!
Can you administer an enema for my illness?"
He replied, "So be it," and then had this thought:
"These śramaṇas are clever and wise; seeing that I have poured [the water], they will not call me again," he thought, and so on, until he abandoned the tube and fled.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so forth, until the Buddha said:
“How is it that you use a tube to irrigate the illness?
From this day forward, the use of tubes is not permitted.
Regarding “tubes”: ox-hide tubes, buffalo-hide tubes, sheep-hide tubes—none of these are permitted for use in irrigation.
If a physician says,
"This illness requires an oil enema," one should place a board in the bathhouse to hold the oil, lift up one's garment and sit upon it, and hold a stalk of sugarcane in the mouth.
Furthermore, if one places cotton cloth, wool, or similar materials inside oil and presses them against the opening so that the oil flows in, there is no offense.
However, if one uses a tube to pour it in, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the method of pouring through a tube.

Regarding the method for shaving the hair: while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was a town named Mahāvana in a kingdom to the south, where at that time a merchant drove eight oxen toward the northern country of Kośala.
Furthermore, there was a merchant who was tending cattle together with others in a marsh.
At that time, a Licchavi captured a dragon to eat it;
he caught a female dragon who had observed the *poṣadha* vows and possessed a non-violent mind. She was able to cause people to pierce her nose so she could be led along by a rope.
Seeing that his physical appearance was upright and handsome, the merchant immediately conceived a heart of compassion and asked the Licchavi,
"What do you intend to do with this?
He replied:
"I wish to kill and eat you.
The merchant said,
"Do not kill me!"
"I will trade one ox with you to ransom it and release it to go its way.
The hunter was unwilling, and only when [the Bodhisattva] offered eight oxen did he finally say, "This meat is very delicious; for your sake, I shall now release it."
He immediately took eight oxen and released the dragon girl to go.
At that time, the merchant thought again:
"This is an evil man; I fear he will pursue her further to capture her once more."

He immediately followed him to see where he was going, and when they reached the edge of the pond, the nāga transformed into a human and said to the merchant, "The Celestial One has granted me my life;
I wish to repay his kindness. You may enter the palace with me, and I shall requite the favor of the Celestial One."
The merchant replied, "I cannot;
you nāgas are by nature impetuous and prone to sudden anger, and might perhaps kill me.
He answered:
"It is not so. Although that man bound me and I had the power to kill him, because I was observing the *poṣadha* precepts, I harbored no intent to kill at all.
How much less would I inflict harm upon you now that you have granted me my life?"
"If you will not depart, stay here for a moment; I shall first enter the palace of Piṅgala.
Having said this, he entered immediately.
At the gate of the nāga’s dwelling, he saw two nāgas bound together in one place. Upon seeing them, the merchant asked:
"For what reason have you been bound?

He replied, "This dragon girl observes the fast for three days during the half-month; we, her brothers, failed to guard her steadfastly and she was captured by the Licchavis. For this reason I am bound; I only pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and grant me leave to speak with them so they may release me."
If this dragon girl asks, "What kind of food do you wish to eat?

there are foods in the dragon palace that can only be digested over a lifetime, those that take twenty years to digest, and those that take seven years; there is also the food of Jambudvīpa. If she requests it, she should request the food of the human world in Jambudvīpa.
After the nāga girl had warded him off, she immediately called him in and seated him upon a jeweled couch and mattress.
The nāga girl said to him, "O Deva, what kind of food do you wish to eat now?"
"Do you wish to eat but a single meal for the rest of your life?
... until he replied, "I wish to eat the food of the human world in Jambudvīpa."
He then provided her with various kinds of food and drink and asked the nāga girl,
"For what reason has she been bound?"
The dragon girl said, “Heavenly One, simply eat; what is the use of asking? “It is not so!
[the Heavenly One replied.]
"I wish to know this.
As he questioned him incessantly, [the man] replied:
"This man has committed a transgression; I wish to kill him."
