The merchant said,
"Do not kill him.
[He replied,] "I will not!"
"You must kill him.
The merchant said,
"If you release him, I shall eat him."
He replied, "They may not be released so simply; they must be punished with six months of banishment among the people.
He was then punished with six months of banishment among the people.
The merchants saw the various precious objects and the adorned palace within the dragon’s abode, and they asked:
"Since you possess such splendor, what use have you for observing the poṣadha?"
He replied:
"In the dharma of us nāgas, there are five kinds of suffering.
What are these five?"
There are the dragons when born, the dragons when sleeping, the dragons when mating, the dragons when angry, and the dragons at death.
Within a single day, three times their skin and flesh fall to the ground, and their bodies are scorched by the hot sands.
He asked again,
"What is it that you seek? He replied:
"I wish to be born among human beings.
Why is this? Because there is suffering in the realm of animals due to their ignorance of the Dharma."
“I have already obtained a human body; what should I seek?
The dragon girl replied, “Leaving the household life is difficult to attain.”
He asked again:
"Under whom should you go forth?
He replied:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is now in Śrāvastī, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated; you may go forth into homelessness.”
He then said,
"I wish to return home.
The dragon girl immediately gave him eight gold coins and said:
"This is nāga-gold; it shall suffice for your parents and kinsmen to use throughout their entire lives.
He then said, "Close your eyes."
He then used his supernormal powers to transport them back to their own country.
His traveling companions arrived first and said to the family:
"They have entered the dragon palace."
The parents thought their child was dead, and their kinsmen and relatives gathered in one place, wailing and weeping.
At that time, some cowherds and wood-gatherers saw this and first returned to tell the family,
"So-and-so has come home."
Upon hearing this, the family members were filled with great joy; they went out to welcome him home, and once he had entered, they held a celebration for his birth.
During the celebration, they took eight gold *ping* and gave them to his parents, saying:
"This is dragon-gold; once it is cut, it grows back again. It shall last as long as your life and can never be exhausted."
"I only pray that my parents will grant me permission to leave the household life.
His parents would not release him, so he immediately fled to the Jetavana Monastery, where the bhikṣus ordained him as a renunciant.
The parents soon arrived at the gate of the vihāra and asked the bhikṣus,
"Do you recognize such-and-such a person?
They all replied:
"I neither see nor hear anything.
A bhikṣu said to him:
"Just stay here by this door; if there is anyone [coming], they will surely enter or exit in a moment."
He waited for a short while just as he had been told, and then saw the boy come out. He spoke these words of reproach:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya tell lies; they say they have not seen what they have seen, and they say they have not heard what they have heard."
The son said to his parents, "Do not do anything that is unbeneficial; who would ever know that I have gone forth as a renunciant here?

He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, he spoke to his parents, saying:
"We have truly been reborn; you who have now gone forth have gained great and wholesome benefit.
When the bhikṣus heard these words of reproach, they went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here.
Once he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:

"Why did you ordain a person for the homeless life without informing the assembly? From this day forward, it is not permitted to ordain a person for the homeless life without informing the Saṃgha; one should inform [the Saṃgha] before shaving the hair and entering the homeless life."

"Announcing" means announcing to the entire Saṃgha, down to announcing it to eight persons including the Elder; one should instruct them to announce it in accordance with the Dharma before shaving the hair. If one goes forth without such an announcement, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense;
if both [the candidate and the preceptor] have announced it, there is no offense for either.
If one does not announce the going forth (*pravrajyā*) and does not announce the shaving of the hair, there are two offenses of *vinayātikrama*;
if both are announced, there is no offense.
If one confers ordination while outside the boundary, there is no offense.
This is called shaving the hair.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata was ordaining people everywhere—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, elders, non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brahmins.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, you too shall ordain others, allowing them to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
At that time, the bhikṣus also followed the Tathāgata’s practice of saying “Come,” ordaining people so that they left the household life with their hair and beards still intact.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In what place did everyone obtain the Tathāgata’s fearless state such that their beards and hair fell off of their own accord?
From this day forward, you should shave your hair."
When shaving their hair, some bhikṣus shaved their hair but did not shave their beards, while other bhikṣus shaved their beards but did not shave their hair.
On account of this matter, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"One should shave everything.
Those who shave should first shave the beard and afterwards shave the hair.
If one who has shaved their head is difficult to converse with, there is no offense in shaving them first.
If one wishes for someone to newly go forth, one must not immediately speak of the joys of going forth; rather, one should speak of the hardships of going forth:
"Eating once, dwelling alone, sleeping alone, eating little, drinking little, staying awake much, and sleeping little—can you endure this for the rest of your life?"
If he says, "I can," one should grant him the tonsure.
If a bhikṣu first shaves his hair and afterwards shaves his beard, there is no offense.
This is called shaving the hair.
Regarding the implements for shaving the hair: while the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, he traveled through a village of brahmins named Po-lo-men (Brahma).
The Mahallakas, father and son, went forth as renunciants while carrying their shaving implements; consequently, the Buddha said:
"How is it that you allow those who have gone forth to carry their tools for shaving?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to provide shaving implements to one who seeks to go forth [into homelessness].
If a person who shaves hair brings their shaving implements and desires to go forth, one should say to them:
"Discard your shaving implements, and only then shall I grant you the going forth."
"After one has gone forth, if there is a need for something, it may be obtained by borrowing from them.
Likewise, blacksmiths, carpenters, goldsmiths and silversmiths, leather-workers, weavers, and other such artisans—these are not permitted to go forth as monastics while carrying their tools."
If one acts in accordance with the rules, it is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is called "preparing the implements.

Regarding "schism in the Saṃgha": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Blessed One has spoken of ‘schism in the Saṃgha. What is meant by ‘schism in the Saṃgha’?
The Buddha told Upāli:

“If there is a bhikṣu of great virtue who understands the profound principles according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, that bhikṣu should be saluted, revered, and followed in accordance with the teachings of the Dharma.”

If a bhikṣu says that what another bhikṣu has spoken is not the Dharma and does not act in accordance with it, this is a dispute within the Saṃgha but not a schism in the Saṃgha—provided they remain within a single boundary, reside together, recite the Prātimokṣa together, and perform formal acts (karmas) together.
"I have already established that within a single boundary and a single residence, performing separate *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* *karmas* is called 'schism' (*saṃghabheda*).
The Venerable Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of offense does one who causes a schism incur?"
The Buddha said:
"The retribution for a kalpa in hell.
This is called 'schism in the Saṃgha'."
Regarding the "harmonious Saṃgha": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "The World-Honored One has spoken of the harmonious Saṃgha."
"What is meant by 'harmonious assembly'?
The Buddha told Upāli:
"I have already established that a bhikṣu who is virtuous, who acts in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who well understands the profound principles, should be saluted and honored."

When the bhikṣus practice the Dharma in accordance with one another, dwelling together within a single boundary, performing the poṣadha and pravāraṇa together, and carrying out karmas together, this is called the harmony of the Saṃgha.
The Venerable Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What merit does the harmonious Saṃgha possess?”
The Buddha said:
"The wholesome retribution lasts for one kalpa;
this is called the harmonious Saṃgha."

Regarding the assembly of the Dharma-piṭaka by five hundred bhikṣus: The Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha. At that time, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, had a feud with Vaiśālī, as is explained in detail in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Eventually, the World-Honored One relinquished his life at the Śaraṇyamūla Stūpa in Vaiśālī, proceeded toward the city of Kuśinagara, and entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the Śālavana of the Malla birthplace on the banks of the Hiranyavatī River. He was cremated beside the Tiara Stūpa; however, the celestial beings caused the fire not to ignite, waiting for the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation within the Piṇḍava Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has already relinquished his life-force; where does he intend to enter parinirvāṇa?"
"Where is he now? Is he free from illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace?

Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the samādhi of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and, with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), surveyed all worlds. He saw the World-Honored One at the site of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara, by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River, within the Śāla Grove of the Sārathipura Forest, beside the Caitya of the Heavenly Crown, undergoing cremation until the fire would not ignite.
Having seen this, he was filled with sorrow and displeasure, and further thought to himself:
"Before the World-Honored One’s relics have been dispersed, I must go to pay my respects.
He then immediately added:
"I shall now go to see the World-Honored One in his final body; it is not fitting that I travel there by means of supernormal power, but rather I should proceed on foot.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable Elders!..."
"The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; let us each take our robes and bowls and go together to Kuśinagara to pay our respects and behold the World-Honored One.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they all said, "Excellent!"
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with a great multitude of bhikṣus, set out for Kuśinagara; on the way, they passed through a village.
In that village lived an elder bhikṣu who had previously resided there.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the mahallaka, "Bring your robe and bowl;
let us go together to the city of Kuśinagara to pay our respects to the World-Honored One."
The mahallaka said:
"Elder Mahākāśyapa!
Please wait until our morning meal and afternoon meal are finished; only then shall you depart."
Kāśyapa replied,
"It is not appropriate to wait for food.
Although the mahallaka insisted three times, Kāśyapa continued to say:
"It is not appropriate to wait.
At that time, the mahallaka spoke with anger:
"What urgent matter do you śramaṇas have that you are in such a great hurry?"
"A dead crow is not worth even a single coin; wait but a moment, and once you have finished eating, you may depart.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied again, "You should set aside your meal for now.
The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; before the cremation takes place, it is fitting that we go there with all haste."
At that time, having heard that the Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa, the mahallaka said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"I have now attained eternal liberation. Why is this? Because..."
"When that Arhat was alive, he constantly said:
'This should be practiced; this should not be practiced.
Now that he has entered Nirvana, what should be practiced and what should not be practiced is left to one's own will."
When Mahākāśyapa heard these words, he was deeply distressed and displeased; he then snapped his right finger, whereupon fire issued forth, and he stamped his right foot upon the ground.
Upon seeing this, the mahallaka was seized with great terror and fled.
When Mahākāśyapa went to where the Buddha was, the World-Honored One immediately manifested both feet, emerging from the coffin.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s feet, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa bared his right shoulder, prostrated with his head at the feet, and spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata’s ankles are full and rounded, The marks of the thousand-spoked wheels appear;”
The fingers are slender, long, and soft, Joined by the pattern of webbed membranes;
Therefore, on this day, I prostrate To the most excellent feet.
With those most excellent, supple feet, You once wandered throughout the world.
The Great Compassionate One who rescues all beings— From now on, we shall never meet again.
For this reason, today I bow my head At the feet of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata has rescued me; Through liberation, I have attained Arhatship.
This is my final sight of him; I shall never behold him again.
He who severed the world’s manifold doubts, the supreme among those free from desire, who benefits all beings—there is none who does not find joy.
Therefore, today I prostrate at the feet of the Most Victorious One.
Such are the virtues of the Buddha; he has skillfully answered and resolved the doubts of the assembly.
Now that the time has passed, the light of his compassion and wisdom will forever be extinguished.
"Therefore, on this day, I bow my head at the feet of the Most Victorious One.
Having realized the Four Noble Truths, I shall proclaim the jewel of the Buddha’s virtues.
Having finished praising and paying homage with these verses, he withdrew his two feet and entered.
The bhikṣus each deliberated, saying,
"Who should perform the cremation?
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said:
"I am the eldest son of the World-Honored One; I ought to perform the cremation.
At that time, the great assembly all said, "Excellent!"
He then performed the cremation.
Having cremated him, Kāśyapa recalled the words of the mahallaka bhikṣu from the village: “...if he wishes to go, he shall go; if he does not wish to go, he shall stay.”
He then spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
The relics of the World-Honored One are not our concern; they should be venerated by kings, elders, brahmins, householders, and those seeking merit."
"Regarding our task, we ought first to compile the Dharma-piṭaka so that the Buddha-dharma does not perish too quickly.
Thereupon, they further deliberated, saying:
"In what place should we compile the Dharma-piṭaka?"
At that time, some said, "To Śrāvastī," while others said:
"Head toward Śrāvastī.
Another said:
"Head toward Campā."
Some said, "Toward Vaiśālī. Others said:
"Head toward Kapilavastu.
Then Mahākāśyapa spoke these words:
"We should head toward Rājagṛha to compile the treasury of the Dharma."

Why is this? The World-Honored One has declared that among the śrāvaka upāsakas of Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, is foremost in rootless faith; furthermore, that king possesses five hundred sets of bedding and furnishings, so you ought to go there.
They all replied, "So it is.
Then the World-Honored One first addressed the Venerable Aniruddha, saying:
“When the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, you should protect his relics and not allow the devas to take them away.
Why is this? In the past, when the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the devas took the relics away; because of this, worldly people were unable to go there and lost all merit.”

"The devas are able to come to the human realm to make offerings, whereas worldly people cannot go there, except by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Therefore, you should protect [the relics] well.
The attendant Ānanda, however, did not depart because he wished to continue making offerings.

Then Mahākāśyapa, together with a thousand bhikṣus, went to the Kṣatriya Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha; there he prepared mats and bedding and adorned the seat for the World-Honored One.

To the left of the World-Honored One’s seat, a seat was prepared for the Venerable Śāriputra; to the right, a seat for the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; next, a seat for Mahākāśyapa. Having thus arranged the couches and bedding in this order and prepared the provisions for the four-month period, they severed all external ties in order to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.

When the great assembly had gathered, among them were those possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), whose power and virtue were sovereign; some had received and recited one section of the Vinaya directly from the World-Honored One’s presence, while others had received and recited one section of the Vinaya from a *śrāvaka*; some had received and recited two sections of the Vinaya directly from the World-Honored One’s presence, while others had received and recited two sections of the Vinaya from a *śrāvaka*. The assembly discussed together, saying:

"Among us, those who possess the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers and whose power and virtue are sovereign, and who have received and recited two sections of the Vinaya either directly from the World-Honored One’s presence or from a *śrāvaka*, should assemble here."
Having assembled, the number was short by two, falling short of five hundred.
They deliberated again, saying:
"We must reach five hundred."
The Elder Aniruddha arrived later, yet there was still one person missing.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was the first elder; the second elder was named Nadī-kāśyapa, and the third elder was named Upananda-kāśyapa.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa ascended his own seat; having left seats only for the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda, the bhikṣus each sat down according to their order of seniority.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Venerable Maudgalyāyana’s co-practitioner, the Elder Revata:
"Go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and summon the bhikṣu Svāti; the World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa, and the community of bhikṣus has assembled, desiring to compile the Dharma-piṭaka."
He immediately accepted the command and went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, saying:
"Venerable One!
The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; the community of bhikṣus has assembled and wishes to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, which is why they have come to summon you."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu was distressed and displeased, asking:
"Has the World-Honored One already entered parinirvāṇa?
He replied:
"Yes," he replied,
"I would go if the World-Honored One were still in Jambudvīpa; but the World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa, and the Eye of the World has been extinguished."
He immediately ascended into the air by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) to cremate himself.

Having witnessed this, he returned at once and entered among the community of monks, recounting the events in detail, up until the point where he said that [the monk] had entered the fire-light samādhi.

He was further sent to the Śirīṣa-wing palace in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to summon Gavāmpati; next, the Elder Sudarśana at Mount Gandhamādana, the Elder Pāṭaliputra at Mount Krīḍā, the Elder Bakula at Mount Campā, and also the Elder Uttara at Mount Śuddha; furthermore, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana’s disciple named Mahāprabha at Mount Prabhāsa, the Venerable Śāriputra’s disciple Mausuluka at Mount Mandara, and the Venerable Rādha at Mount Māla—all these, upon hearing the call, entered parinirvāṇa.
Again, a messenger was sent to the palace of Vaiśravaṇa to summon Śubhita. Once he had arrived, the messenger spoke these words:
"Venerable one!
The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; the community of bhikṣus has assembled and intends to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, and thus we have come to invite you."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu was distressed and displeased, saying:
"Has the World-Honored One already entered parinirvāṇa?
He replied:
"So be it," he replied.
Then he said, "While the World-Honored One is still in Jambudvīpa, I shall go to him; for after the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, the Eye of the World will be extinguished."
He immediately ascended into the void by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) to cremate himself, thereby entering parinirvāṇa.
The messenger returned to the community of monks and reported everything as it had occurred. Mahākāśyapa said:
"Venerable elders, stop for a moment!"

"Do not call for others again; those who hear the call shall immediately enter parinirvāṇa. If you call further, they too shall enter parinirvāṇa, and thus the world will become empty and devoid of fields of merit."
A certain bhikṣu said:
"Venerable elders!

The Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant; he has personally received the teachings of the Dharma. Furthermore, the World-Honored One has declared that Ānanda is foremost in three matters. It would be appropriate to summon him."
Mahākāśyapa said: "It is not so!
A learner such as this entering the assembly of those with the sovereign power of the virtues of one beyond learning is like a mangy jackal entering a pride of lions."
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having finished preparing the offerings, arrived at a certain village and said:
"I shall stay here tonight; tomorrow I shall go to Rājagṛha."
At that time, a deva came and said to Ānanda:
"Mahākāśyapa says:
'The Venerable One is a scabbed jackal.'"
Ānanda had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; I now wish to rely upon him.
Why does he treat me as a scabby jackal?"
His heart was displeased, and he further thought:
"This Mahākāśyapa surely knows the names and clans of my followers; he must have said this simply because my fetters are not yet exhausted."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda applied himself with diligent effort, walking in meditation without ceasing, desiring to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, being weary from the exertion of his practice and further distressed in mind by the sorrow over the Parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One, could no longer penetrate the teachings he had previously heard and retained. He then thought to himself:
"The Blessed One prophesied for me that, through non-negligence in this present life, I would exhaust all outflows; must I now undergo such extreme suffering?"

Without relinquishing his meditative concentration, he inclined his body as if about to lie down; before his head had even reached the pillow, he attained the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava). Possessing the three knowledges (vidyā) and six supernormal powers (abhijñā), with mastery over spiritual power, he immediately ascended into the air by means of his psychic power (ṛddhi) and departed.
Arriving outside the entrance of the Kṣatriya Cave, he spoke this verse:
"Ānanda, son of Gautama, who is learned and possesses eloquence, And who serves the World-Honored One, Now stands outside the door."
Because he did not open the door for him,
he further spoke this verse:
"One who is learned and possesses sharp eloquence, and who serves the World-Honored One— "
"Having already cast off the burden of the fetters, the son of Gautama stands outside.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke this verse:
"You have cast off the burden of afflictions, yet you say for yourself that you have attained realization."
“Before you were among the followers of the Gautama son; now you have come to join the followers of the Gautama son.
After Ānanda had entered, he paid homage to the seat of the World-Honored One, then paid homage to the senior monks in turn, and having reached his own seat, he sat down.
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"I do not speak thus out of self-exaltation, nor do I treat you with contempt;
rather, because your pursuit of the Way does not advance, I have spoken these words solely to urge you toward diligent effort so that you may exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*)."
Ānanda said: "I also know this;
however, because my fetters have not yet been exhausted, I wish to exert myself diligently to sever all outflows.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying:
"Now, which collection do you wish to assemble first?
The multitude all replied,
"We shall first assemble the Dharma-piṭaka."
He asked again:
"Who should assemble?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Venerable Ānanda. Ānanda replied, "No;
there are other elder bhikṣus besides him."
He further said, "Although there are other elder bhikṣus, the World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost among those of great learning; you should perform the compilation.
Ānanda replied:
"Venerable elders!
If I were to assemble you, those who act in accordance with the Dharma should rejoice, and those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma should be restrained.
If something is inappropriate, it should be restrained; do not fail to restrain it out of respect for me. Whether it be right or wrong, please speak to me."
The assembly all said:
"Venerable Ānanda! You need only compile the Dharma-piṭaka;
those who act in accordance with the Dharma shall rejoice, while those whose actions are not in accordance with the Dharma shall be known as such when the time comes."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda had this thought:
"How shall I now compile the Dharma-piṭaka?
Having reflected thus, he spoke the sūtra, saying:
“Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at the Bodhi-maṇḍala on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in Uruvilvā.
As soon as the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, five hundred Arhats who possessed mastery through the power of their merit ascended into the air and all uttered this sigh of admiration:
“We have seen the World-Honored One with our own eyes!”
"Now that you have already said you heard it," they all recited "Namo Buddha" and returned to their original seats.
At that time, Ānanda spoke this verse:
“Diligently practicing meditative absorption, One sees the arising and passing away of all phenomena;
Knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, One leaves ignorance behind and extinguishes afflictions.
Diligently practicing meditative absorption, One sees the arising and passing away of all phenomena.”
Knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, one realizes the extinction of all phenomena.
Diligently practicing meditative absorption, one perceives the arising and ceasing of all phenomena;
knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, one subdues the armies of Māra.
"By diligently practicing meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one perceives the arising and ceasing of all phenomena;
knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, one dispels all darkness like the sun.
Venerable Ānanda recited such treasuries of all dharmas; those whose prose and verses were long were compiled as the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Those with prose and verse were compiled as the *Madhyama Āgama*;

those with mixed prose and verse were compiled as the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, referring to what is called the "mixture of faculties," "mixture of powers," "mixture of awakening factors," and "mixture of the path"—such categories as these are termed "mixed.
Those consisting of one increase, two increases, three increases, up to a hundred increases, were compiled as the *Ekottara Āgama* according to their numerical categories and corresponding sequences.

The *Kṣudrakapiṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection) refers to the verses recited by Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats concerning their own past lives and causal conditions; such collections of similar verses are called the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda spoke these verses:
"All eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma, Such teachings as these were heard from the Buddha;
All eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma, Such teachings as these were heard from others."
"I have fully upheld such dharmas as these; these are the teachings of the Buddha leading to Nirvāṇa.
This is called the compilation of the treasury of all dharmas.
Next, the question was asked:
"Who else should be appointed to compile the Vinaya Piṭaka?
Some said, "The Elder Upāli."
Upāli said: "No;
there are other elder bhikṣus as well.
Someone else said:

"Although there are elder bhikṣus, the World-Honored One has declared that among those who have accomplished the fourteen dharmas, with the exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, this elder is foremost in upholding the Vinaya."
Upāli said: "Venerable elders!
If I am to compile [the teachings], those who act in accordance with the Dharma should rejoice, and those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma should be restrained."
"If it is not appropriate, it should be prohibited; do not show undue respect [to those who oppose]. We pray that you will instruct us on what is meaningful and what is not.
They all said:
"Venerable Upāli, simply convene the assembly; let those who act according to the Dharma rejoice, and those who act contrary to the Dharma shall be known as they arise."
Venerable Upāli then thought to himself:
"How shall I now compile the Vinaya Piṭaka?
Regarding the five pure practices (*pañca-avadāna*), those that accord with the Dharma and the Vinaya I shall approve; those that do not accord with the Dharma and the Vinaya I shall reject."
What are the five?
First, purity through restriction;
second, purity through method.
3. Purity of ethical conduct;
4. Purity of seniority;
5. Purity of local customs.

Regarding purification by restriction (*sīmā-bandha-pariśuddhi*): the monastics establish a restriction for their dwelling place, such that what accords with the four great teachings is used, while what does not accord is discarded; this is called purification by restriction.
Regarding purity of method: the nature of the land is such that one employs what accords with the four great teachings and discards what does not accord; this is called purity of method.

Regarding purity of conduct: I see a certain bhikṣu who upholds the precepts practicing this method; if it accords with the four great teachings, he employs it, and if it does not accord, he abandons it—this is called purity of conduct.

Regarding "purity through the elders": I have observed that when the elder bhikṣus, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, practice this Dharma, they employ what is consistent with the four great teachings and discard what is inconsistent; this is called purity through the elders.

Regarding "purity according to worldly custom": one must not eat at improper times, drink alcohol, or engage in sexual misconduct as permitted by one's original secular laws. All such practices are considered purity according to worldly custom; they are not the purity of the renunciant. This is called purity according to worldly custom.
"Thus it is, O Elders!
That which is in accordance with the Dharma should be rejoiced in; that which is not in accordance with the Dharma should be restrained.
The bhikṣus replied:
"If it is appropriate, it should be used; if it is not appropriate, it should be prohibited as the occasion demands.
Then the Venerable Upāli said to Ānanda, "Elder, you have committed an offense;
you should confess it before a pure assembly."
Ānanda asked,
"What kind of offense is there?
He replied:
“The Blessed One has prohibited the ordination of women as many as three times, yet you have requested it three times; this is an offense against the Vinaya.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa cast a tally onto the ground and said, “This is the first tally.”
Immediately, the trichiliocosm shook.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, he told Ānanda:
"The Stūpa of the Abandonment of Bow and Staff at Vaiśālī is delightful; if one has attained the four bases of psychic power, one may remain for an eon, or even longer than an eon."
"If the Buddha were in the world, people of the world would be able to see him.
You said: "It is so, World-Honored One!"
"So it is, Sugata!
"If you do not request the Buddha to remain in the world, you shall incur a *vinaya* offense.
Next, he cast the second tally.
"Furthermore, you stepped upon the seams of the World-Honored One’s saṃghāṭī robe with your right toe; did you not know that this saṃghāṭī is a stūpa for gods and humans, and should be revered?"
"This is an offense against the Vinaya.
Next, he cast down the third tally.
Furthermore, the Buddha told Ānanda, "Bring some water. This was repeated three times; since you did not provide the World-Honored One with water, this is an offense against the Vinaya.
He cast down the fourth tally.
Furthermore, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"When I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, you should speak to me; I shall then relinquish the minor precepts for the sake of the bhikṣus."
"Since you did not inform [the Sangha], you have committed an offense against the Vinaya.
The fifth tally is cast down.
"Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you showed the Buddha’s private male organ to a bhikṣuṇī; this is an offense against the Vinaya."
He cast down the sixth tally.

"Furthermore, after the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the various elderly women of the Mallas wept over the World-Honored One’s feet; their tears fell upon his feet, yet you did not prevent it as his attendant. This is an offense against the Vinaya."
The seventh tally was cast down.
At that time, Ānanda did not accept the two charges and spoke these words:
"Venerable Elder!..."
All Buddhas of the past had the fourfold assembly; for this reason, [the Buddha] requested three times that he ordain bhikṣuṇīs.

When the Buddha was in Vaiśālī, although he gave word three times, no one requested him to remain in the world. At that time, I was still a learner (śaikṣa) and was obscured by Māra; therefore, I did not request it.
In this matter, one commits five offenses of *vinayātikrama*.
Elder! Having acted in accordance with the Dharma, [it is concluded].
Then the Venerable Upāli spoke these words:
"Elders! These are the nine introductory points."
What are the nine? First, pārājika;
second, saṃghāvaśeṣa; [and so forth].
3. Two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas);
4. Thirty rules involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika-dharmas);
5. Ninety-two rules of expiation (pāyattika-dharmas).
Sixth, the four *pāṭidesanīya* rules;
seventh, the *śaikṣa* rules;
eighth, the seven methods for settling disputes.
9. The Dharma that accords with the Dharma.
[They ask: "In such-and-such a place, did the Blessed One establish this precept for a certain bhikṣu?
They all reply: [Yes.]
"Thus it is, Upāli! Thus it is, Upāli!
He spoke again:
“The Vinaya has five matters for recording.
What are the five? First, the Sūtra;”
2. Vinaya; 3. Meaning; 4. Teaching;
Fifth, regarding lightness and gravity:
the Sūtras refer to the five types of Sūtras;
the Vinaya refers to the brief and extensive versions of the two-part Vinaya.
"Meaning" refers to the fact that every sentence possesses meaning.
"Teaching" refers, for example, to the four teachings on the great elements as taught by the World-Honored One to the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and householders.
Regarding gravity and lightness: stealing an amount reaching five [units] is grave; otherwise, it is light.
If one omits five [factors], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called the five matters for recording the *vinaya*. Elder!
One should train in this way.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of Vinaya. What are the five?
First, the abbreviated Vinaya;
second, the extensive Vinaya;
third, the regional Vinaya.
Fourth is the *vinaya* of firmness;
fifth is the *vinaya* that accords with the Dharma.
The abbreviated *vinaya* consists of the five categories of precepts.
The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya* refers to the two divisions of the Vinaya.
The *Pradeśa-vinaya* refers to the five permissions granted to the frontier regions for the *śūdra*.

The *Sthira-vinaya* refers to receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, the relinquishing of the five offenses, eating separately from the community, and so forth, up to departing without informing others and eating apart from the community.

That which accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya refers herein to the *dharmakarma* (legal procedure according to the Dharma) and the *sāmagrīkarma* (procedure of harmony); these are called "accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya," while all others are not *karma*.
Thus the collection of the Vinaya Piṭaka was completed.
He summoned the thousand outside bhikṣus and said to them:
"Venerable elders!..."
"In this manner the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled; in this manner the Vinaya-piṭaka was compiled. A bhikṣu said:
"Venerable elders!"
The World-Honored One previously said to Ānanda:
"I wish to relinquish certain minor precepts for the sake of the bhikṣus.
Which ones does he intend to relinquish?
A bhikṣu said:
"If the World-Honored One were to relinquish the minor precepts, he would indeed be relinquishing his dignified deportment.
Another said:
"One should also abandon improper conduct and likewise abandon the minor rules of training (śaikṣa-dharmas).
Some say: "One should also abandon the four offenses entailing confession (prādeśanika-dharmas)."
Some said: "One should also abandon the ninety-two pāyattikas. Others said:
"One should also relinquish thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattikas*.
Some say: "One should also relinquish the two *aniyata-dharmas*."
Then the group of six bhikṣus said:
"Venerable elders!
If the World-Honored One were still present, we would have relinquished everything."
Mahākāśyapa, whose majestic power was as stern and formidable as that of the World-Honored One himself, spoke these words:
"Ho! Ho!"
"Do not make such a sound.
Immediately, everyone became silent.
Mahākāśyapa said:
“Venerable Elders!
If that which has already been established is then reopened, outsiders will say:
‘When Gautama was in the world, the rules of conduct were flourishing; today, now that he has entered Nirvana, the practice of the Dharma has fallen into ruin.’”
"Venerable elders!
Do not enact what has not been enacted; we shall train ourselves in accordance with that which has already been enacted.
From where was this Dharma heard?
I have heard from the Venerable Daoli the *Vinaya*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the *Ekottarikāgama*, the *Madhyamāgama*, and the *Dīrghāgama*.
From whom did you hear about the power of the Path?
I heard it from the Venerable Puṣyavat.
From whom did the Venerable Puṣyavat hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Dharmasreṣṭhin.
From whom did Dharmasreṣṭhin hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Saṃghadeva.
From whom did Saṃghadeva hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Nāgabodhi.
From whom did Nāgabodhi hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Dhammika.
From whom did Dhammika hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Tiṇṇaṅga.
From whom did Tiṇṇaka hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Dhammapāla.
From whom did Dhammapāla hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Jīvaka.
From whom did Jīvaka hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Pāṭieyya.
From whom did Pṭilā hear it?
From the Venerable Yaśas. From whom did Yaśas hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Khadira.
From whom did Khadira hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Āyupāla.
From whom did Āyupāla hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Suvīra.
From whom did Suvīra hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Gavāṃpati.
From whom did Gavāṃpati hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Ghoṣila.
From whom did Cūḷasāra hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita.
From whom did Mahākoṭṭhita hear it?
From the Venerable Mahānāma.
From whom did Mahānāma hear it?
From the Venerable Kaṅkhārevata.
From whom did you hear it that you are able to protect it?
From the Venerable Maudgalyāyana.
From whom did Maudgalyāyana hear it?
I heard it from the Venerable Khujjasobhita.
From whom did Khujjasobhita hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Dhammika.
From whom did Dharmottara hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Mūla.
From whom did Mūla hear it?
"I heard it from the Venerable Ghoṭamukha.
From whom did the Venerable Ghoṭamukha hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Sāḷha."
From whom did Jyotiṣka hear it?
He heard it from the Venerable Droṇa.
From whom did Droṇa hear it?
"I heard it from the Venerable Upāli.
"From whom did Upāli hear it?
"I heard it from the Buddha."
From whom did the Buddha hear [this]?
He attained self-awakening without a teacher and heard nothing from another.
The Buddha possesses immeasurable wisdom; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he bestowed it upon Upāli.
Upāli transmitted it to Dāsabala; Dāsabala transmitted it to Jotidāsa; Jotidāsa, and so on, until it was transmitted to the Venerable Mānava; Mānava transmitted it to me and others.
Following our teacher’s instruction, we have heard from the Unsurpassed Honored One;
having heard it, we uphold and recite the Vinaya, the Dharma practiced by the noble and holy ones.
We are the inner treasury of the World-Honored One, the successors to Śākyamuni.
Each and every one shall together protect and uphold [this], so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
This concludes the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka by the five hundred [elders].
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 32.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

The eleventh section on the rules for the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Recitations) concerning the Council of Seven Hundred: After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the elder bhikṣus were staying at the Sārandada Monastery in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the bhikṣus begged from the donors, making such piteous pleas:
"Long-lived one!
When the World-Honored One was present, we received offerings of food before and after the meal, as well as robes and other requisites."
"After the World-Honored One has entered *nirvāṇa*, we are orphans;
who will give to us? You may donate monastic property.

Thus they begged with piteous voices. At that time, some people gave one *kārsāpaṇa*, two *kārsāpaṇas*, or even up to ten *kārsāpaṇas*. When it was time for the *poṣadha*, these were placed in a jar and distributed in portions measured by a *kuḍuba* bowl in successive order.
At that time, Yaśas, who was an upholder of the Vinaya, arrived first; when it was his turn to receive a portion, he asked, "What is this?
and they replied:
"Next, you shall receive the value of medicinal supplies in kārṣāpaṇas.
Yaśas replied, "That is past."
He asked, "For what reason did you give alms to the Saṃgha in the past?
Yaśas replied:
"‘It is impure. The bhikṣus said: ‘You have slandered the Saṃgha by saying it is impure;
this case requires that the formal act of censure (karma-ud-dharaṇa) be performed against you.’”
He then performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (the act of suspension).
Once the *ukkhepanīyakamma* had been performed, the Venerable Dāsabala was in the kingdom of Mathurā; Yaśas went to him and spoke these words:
"Elder!..."
"I have been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) and am practicing in accordance with the Dharma. He asked,
"For what reason were you subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma*?"
He replied, "It is so, it is so; such is the matter. He said:
"You have been formally accused of no offense; let us, Venerable One, share the food of the Dharma and the food of taste together.
Having heard these words, Yaśas spoke thus:
"Venerable Elders!"
"We should further compile the Vinaya Piṭaka so that the Buddha-dharma does not fall into ruin.
They asked,
"Where do you wish to hold the council?"
He replied, "Return to the place where that matter arose.

At that time, in the city of Madhyadeśa, seven hundred monks had assembled from the Saṃghārāma in Mathurā and the Śākya monastery in Śrāvastī; among them were those who held one version of the Vinaya and those who held two versions of the Vinaya, as well as those who had received it directly from the World-Honored One and those who had received it from the Śrāvakas.

At that time, seven hundred monks—consisting of ordinary worldlings, those in training, and those beyond training—who had attained mastery over the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the powers, assembled at the Saṇḍa Monastery in Vaiśālī and prepared their seats and bedding with great care.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, Daḍhapaṭṭa, Upadaḍhapaṭṭa, and the Venerable Ānanda had all already entered parinirvāṇa.
Then the Venerable Yaśoda, the senior elder of the Saṃgha, asked:
"Who should compile the Vinaya Piṭaka?"
The bhikṣus said,
"Venerable Dāsabala should preside over the council. Dāsabala replied:
"Elder! There are other elder bhikṣus who should participate in the council.
The bhikṣus said:

"Although there are many senior elders, the World-Honored One has declared that the Elder Upāli, your preceptor, has accomplished fourteen qualities and is foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya; you have received it directly from his presence, and you should therefore perform the compilation."
Dāṣabala said: "If I am to perform the compilation, those who act in accordance with the Dharma should rejoice, while those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma should be restrained.
If something is inconsistent [with the Dharma], it should be restrained; do not show it respect. I pray that you will inform me whether this is meaningful or meaningless."
They all replied, "So it is.
At that time, the Venerable Dāsabala thought to himself:
"How shall I now compile the Vinaya Piṭaka?
There are five pure practices; those that accord with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be welcomed, while those that do not accord with the Dharma should be rejected."
"What are the five?
First is purification by restriction, up to purification by custom.
They speak as follows:"
“Venerable elders!
These are the nine introductory principles.
What are the nine?
From the four *pārājikas* up to the *dharmānudharma*, the Blessed One, at such-and-such places, established the precepts for such-and-such monks.
"I have heard from my preceptor that this precept was established for such reasons?
They all replied, "It is so!"
"So be it! The five matters concerning the recording of the Vinaya are explained at length as above, up until: "O Elders!..."

In this regard, those who need a bowl should seek a bowl; those who need robes should seek robes; and those who need medicine should seek medicine. There is no expedient means by which one may seek gold, silver, or money; thus, all you elders should train yourselves in accordance with this.
This is called the Seventh Hundred Council on the Vinaya Piṭaka.
To speak briefly regarding the Vinaya: when the Buddha was at the Śākya Monastery under the Nyagrodha tree in Kapilavastu, there were two bhikṣuṇīs:
one named Nandā and the other named Uttarā.
Having followed the Buddha for six months seeking instruction and admonition, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will briefly explain the Vinaya for me, so that I may attain understanding."
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇī:
“Lustful desire and a failure to understand dependent origination lead to mutual intimacy and the discussion of worldly matters, which increases the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
Excessive desire and a lack of contentment increase lustful desire, hatred, and delusion.”
Where there is contention and lack of harmony, there is neither tranquility, nor awakening, nor nirvāṇa.
One should know that such things are not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the Buddha’s teaching; one should understand it in this way.
Free from desire, one understands dependent origination; one does not associate with others, stays aloof from worldly discourse, and does not increase the aggregates of grasping.
Having few desires and being content, one is without greed, hatred, or delusion;
one leaves behind strife and seeks harmony, abiding in tranquility, awakening, and nirvāṇa.
"In this way, you should know: this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Buddha’s teaching.
This is called the brief exposition of the Vinaya.
[The following are] the treatment with a blade, the irrigation tube, shaving the hair, and the various implements.
On concord and discord, the five hundred and the seven hundred;
this concludes the brief exposition of the Vinaya,
ending with the tenth chapter (varga).
Regarding "slandering": while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus began to slander other bhikṣus in various ways.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here.
When they had arrived, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter. From this day forward, you are not permitted to disparage others.
To disparage means [to criticize] one's karma, region, clan, physical appearance, illness, offenses, verbal abuse, or fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding "those who explain": this refers to those who speak for themselves or those spoken for by others, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Within this [body] there are outcasts, bamboo-workers, tanners, potters, and even wardens and executioners."
This is called "speaking.
As for "understanding for oneself": "Venerable sir!
I am not a caṇḍāla, nor even an executioner or a jailer."
This is called "self-understanding.
As for "a person," it refers to those within this context who may be outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) or even wardens of hell;
this is called "a person."
The same applies to [criticizing] one's direction of origin, clan, physical appearance, illness, offenses, or fetters (*saṃyojana*).
To disparage another in these respects constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called "disparaging."

Regarding the performers of music: while the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, the group of six bhikṣus arrived first at the place where music was being performed and watched the performers as if they were bhikṣus practicing dhyāna.
Once the performers had assembled and were playing various musical instruments, the crowd was delighted and laughed with joy, while the bhikṣu remained silent.
After the crowd had finished laughing, the bhikṣu then clapped his hands and laughed loudly.
The crowd vied with one another to watch, so that the performers could not receive their wages. They complained, saying:
"It is because of this bhikṣu that we have been unable to obtain our wealth.
This man is a ruinous person; what kind of path does he follow?"
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; from this day forward, it is not permitted to watch performers.

As for "performers," this refers to those who beat drums, sing, dance, play the lute (*vīṇā*), gongs, or cymbals—various musical entertainments such as these—and even down to groups of four people playing games together; watching them is not permitted.

If a bhikṣu enters a city or village and sees celestial elephants emerging, or a king emerging with his retinue, accompanied by various kinds of musical performances, there is no offense in passing by and observing them.
If one watches while employing such means, it is an offense against the Vinaya.

However, at a great assembly for the Buddha’s birthday, a great assembly for the Bodhi tree, a great assembly for the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or a five-year assembly, one may perform various kinds of music as an offering to the Buddha.
If a donor says:
"Venerable sirs!
Join me in following and attending upon the World-Honored One."
At that time, one may remain seated together with the assembly.
However, if anyone among those seated develops a mind of attachment toward various kinds of music and performance, they should immediately rise and depart.
This is what is meant by "music and performance."

Regarding "incense and flowers": While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, on the day of a seasonal festival, the group of six bhikṣus—Nanda and Upananda—smeared their bodies with incense and wore garlands of *utpala* (blue lotus) and *campaka* flowers; some even wore garlands of grass flowers as they walked about, drawing the reproach of the world:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear *utpala* and *campaka* flower garlands?"
They are like princes or high ministers,
yet they are like lowly messengers wearing wreaths of grass flowers.
For such ruined persons, what path could there be?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to wear perfumes or flowers.
Regarding "perfumes": sandalwood, aloeswood, and all other such perfumes of this kind should not be worn at all.
If one has a fever and a physician says,
"One must apply sandalwood paste," then it is permissible to use the fragrant paste for application.
When wishing to apply [ointment], one should first make offerings at a stūpa of the Buddha’s clay relics, and only then apply it to the body.
Having applied it to the body, one must not remain among the assembly; one should stay in a secluded place.
Once the illness has been cured, one should wash oneself clean, bathe the body, and only then enter the assembly.
As for flowers, such as the *utpala*, *campaka*, and *sumana*—none of these flowers should be worn.
However, if a bhikṣu suffers from eye pain or a headache, and a physician instructs him, saying:
"You must bind a flower garland around your head for it to be cured," [he may do so].
Regarding the phrase "one obtains the binding":
if one wishes to perform the binding, one should first make offerings at a Buddha-stūpa, and only then may the binding be performed.
Once bound, one must not remain among the crowd; one should stay in a secluded place, and once the ritual is concluded, one should release it.
If one applies perfume but does not apply flowers, there is one *pācittiya* offense.
If one applies flowers but does not apply perfume, there is one *pācittiya* offense.
If one applies both, one commits two offenses.
If neither [of them] takes hold of it, there is no offense.
This is called the rule regarding incense and flowers.
Regarding the rule regarding the mirror: while the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, a donor provided a meal for the Saṃgha and struck the *gandī* gong.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda were looking at themselves in a mirror for a long time without arriving; they were resented by the *dānapati*, who said:
"I have abandoned my household affairs to come here to provide food for the Sangha, yet the bhikṣus do not assemble in a timely manner."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda and Upānanda here."
When they had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda and Upananda,
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to look into a mirror."
Regarding mirrors: whether in oil, in water, or in a mirror, one must not look at one's face to examine oneself for the sake of vanity.
If one is ill, one may look at one's face to see whether the illness has been cured or not.
If one has just shaved one's head, one may look at oneself in a mirror to see whether it is clean or not;
if there is a sore on the head or face, looking in the mirror incurs no offense.
To look in a mirror for the sake of vanity constitutes a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
This is called the "mirror-like dharma.
Regarding the "dharma of carrying," the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka-nivāpa (Wilderness) Monastery.
At that time, a monk in charge of construction work was carrying a yoke-pole laden with bricks, mud, and earth, and was derided by worldly people: [text continues].
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, resemble slaves, servants, or laborers carrying earth and mud?
These ruined men—what path could they possibly possess?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣu in charge of the construction work here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to carry [loads]."
"Carrying" refers to carrying in a rope bag or carrying in a basket.
If one carries a staff but does not carry a bag, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya, requiring mental repentance (*vyatikrama-citta-āpatti*).
If one carries a bag but does not carry a staff, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya, requiring mental repentance.
If one carries both [loads], it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If there are heavy stones, bamboo, or wood within the precincts of the monastery, they may be carried.
If one is performing duties in the order of the Saṃgha, jars and bottles may be carried by connecting them with ropes.
If one carries the robe-bag at both front and back, or carries the alms-bowl at both front and back, in each case it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If the long robe bag is slung over the shoulder, or the bowl is carried across the shoulder, there is no offense.
This is called "carrying the dharma.

Regarding those who wrap and tie their robes: while the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Vihāra, a monk in charge of construction affairs wrapped and tied his robe while carrying bricks, stones, mud, and earth. He was censured by worldly people:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, work like slaves or servants, wrapping and tying their robes as they labor?"
"This man is a ruin; what path can he have?
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the bhikṣu in charge of affairs here.
When he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, gathering and tying [the robes] is not permitted.
Regarding "gathering and tying": gathering and tying them on one side or on both sides is entirely forbidden.
However, if one is using mud to plaster a roof or a mud house, it is permissible to gather and tie an inner robe.
This is called the method of binding and tying.
Regarding "climbing a tree": the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One went to Uttarakuru to beg for food.
Then the bhikṣus had this thought:
"The World-Honored One, upon his return, will surely come by means of his supernormal power.
Some climbed trees, others climbed walls, to gaze afar for the World-Honored One.
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, the World-Honored One immediately made himself invisible and sat down upon his original seat.
The Buddha, knowing [the reason], asked intentionally:
"Where have the bhikṣus gone?
The bhikṣus then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, climbing trees is not permitted.
Regarding "trees," one must not climb any tree that is as high as a person.

If one holds a bodhi assembly and wishes to adorn the bodhi tree, yet climbs the tree with one foot while placing the other foot on a wall, it is a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression of mind).
If one climbs a tree with both feet, it is a *vinaya*-offense;
if one climbs a wall with both feet, there is no offense; the same applies to climbing a ladder.
If, while traveling on a road, one loses the way and becomes confused regarding the directions, there is no offense in climbing a tree to look about.
If one is threatened by tigers, wolves, lions, or similar creatures, there is no offense in climbing a tree;
this is called the rule regarding trees. Regarding the rule regarding fire:

while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the proper time, the World-Honored One put on his village-entering robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to walk for alms. Upon returning, he prepared his own bedding and, without informing his attendant or the community of monks, went to the Pārileyyaka forest in the kingdom of Kosala, beneath a noble tree, to accept the three-month供养 (dāna) of an elephant king. When unseasonable cold and snow arrived, the monks naturally kindled fires to warm themselves, which caused them to be criticized by the people of the world.

“The śramaṇa Gautama uses immeasurable skillful means to revile the taking of life and praise non-killing; yet now this bhikṣu burns the ground with fire and disturbs even a single blade of grass nearby.”
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to kindle fires.
Regarding fire: whether it be a fire of wood, grass, cow dung, husks, or splinters, one must not burn ground that has not yet been cleared.

Whether one is on duty in the warm room (*uṣṇāgāra*), serving as the monthly supervisor (*māsika*), or fumigating the alms bowl (*pātra*), one must first inform a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) before lighting the fire oneself; doing so incurs no offense.

If one carries a torch and wishes to shake it out, one must not do so over ground that has not yet been burned; rather, one should do so over ashes, or on a tile, or if the torch's flame falls to the ground of its own accord, one may shake it out directly upon that spot without offense.
If one lights a fire upon ground that has not been scorched, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule regarding fire.

Regarding the rule regarding the copper bowl: the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the householder Ugga made a great offering of five hundred elephants, five hundred horses, five hundred oxen, five hundred buffaloes, five hundred female slaves, and five hundred male slaves. Among these various offerings was a copper bowl.
The bhikṣus felt doubt in their minds and went to question the World-Honored One:
"Is this pure or impure?
Should it be accepted or not?"
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the acceptance of any copper bowls.
If one gives a pure vessel to the Saṃgha, it should be accepted after performing the ritual of dedication (paritta)."
"If one privately keeps a copper bowl, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Once it has been given to a person who is pure (*pariśuddha*), there is no fault in its use.
This is called the rule regarding the copper bowl.

Regarding dedication: While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the devas and people of the world, with hearts of faith and deep respect, brought various kinds of food and drink to make offerings to the Buddha, the community of bhikṣus, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the other bhikṣus.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus arrived at the entrance of the vihāra early in the morning and stood there. Seeing worldly people bringing food, they asked, "To whom is this food being given?"
He replied,
"To the World-Honored One. He then said:
"The World-Honored One should be honored with offerings.
He then asked:
"To whom, moreover, should these be given?"
He replied, "I shall give it to the Sangha.
He then spoke these words:
"The Sangha should receive offerings.
He then asked, "To whom,
then, should these be given?"
He replied,
"To the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
He then said:
"This person should be offered support.
He then asked:
"To whom else should this be given?"
He replied,
"I shall give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu," and then spoke these words:
“Such-and-such an elder is sick and cannot eat; simply discard your food for me.
You should offer it to me, and I shall recite a blessing for you so that you may obtain the merit of this meal.”
At that time, the people, believing him directly, gave it to him immediately.
However, those who were wise did not give it to him, saying:
"Why should I give to such a person devoid of shame and remorse?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, until the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
“Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to the group of six bhikṣus.
"This is an evil deed; how could you know that an object intended for another was diverted to yourself?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to knowingly divert property intended for another toward oneself.
'Property' refers to eight kinds:
from timely food up to pure and impure items, as explained in detail above."
If someone were to ask:
"Venerable sir!
I wish to practice giving; to whom should I give?"
He replied,
"I shall give it to the Saṃgha. If he asks again:
"If you ask, 'Where are there monks who maintain the precepts? you should say:
'There are no monks who violate the precepts; you should simply give.'"
If one asks:
"Where is there a bhikṣu who can constantly practice his religious duties in a single location, so that the object remains long-lasting and may be seen by me always?"
At that time, having received the instruction:
"A certain bhikṣu may be given [the item]," if one knows the object was intended for the Saṃgha but redirects it toward oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha and redirects it toward another individual, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one knows that an object is intended for a multitude of people and redirects it toward a multitude of people, or if one knows that an object is intended for a single person and redirects it toward a single person, it is a vyatikrama offense.
Down to the case of knowing that an object was intended for an animal and redirecting it toward another animal, there is a violation of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
This is called the method of redirection (*pariṇāmanā-dharma*).
[The following are: disparaging those who watch performers, [the rules concerning] flower garlands and mirrors, and the [rules concerning] the mirror-method.
Carrying and tying up robes; climbing trees; natural fire;
copper bowls; dedicating objects.
The eleventh *varga* is concluded.

Regarding "sentient beings": while the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, the householder Ugga gave away five hundred elephants and even five hundred male and female slaves as great alms. At that time, the bhikṣus felt doubt and regret, so they went to ask the Buddha, saying:
"Is this pure or impure?"
"Should they be accepted or not?
The Buddha said,
"No sentient being whatsoever is permitted to accept them."
As for "sentient beings," these include elephants, horses, oxen, water buffaloes, donkeys, sheep, deer, pigs, slaves, and servants; all such beings and others likewise should not be accepted.
If someone says,
"I give a female slave to the Sangha," it shall not be accepted.
If one says,
"I am giving this to the female servant of the monastery," it shall not be accepted.
If one says,
"I give this slave to the Sangha," it shall not be accepted.
If one says,
"I am giving this to the Saṃgha through an agent," it should not be accepted.
If one says,
"I shall provide a male lay attendant for the Saṃgha," it is permitted to accept.
If one is offered a female slave as a separate gift, it is not permitted to accept;
if a male slave, a servant, or a garden-keeper is offered, it is not permitted to accept;
however, if a pure attendant (kappiyakāraka) is offered for the purpose of managing the affairs of the Saṃgha, it may be accepted.
If a slave is offered to the community of nuns, it is not permitted to accept;
if a gardener is offered, it is not permitted to accept;
if a maidservant is offered, it is not permitted to accept.
If one says,
"I shall provide a nun or a female attendant," it is permitted to accept.
If a slave is offered to a single bhikṣuṇī, its acceptance is not permitted;
if a gardener is offered, its acceptance is not permitted;
however, if a pure woman is offered for the purpose of managing the affairs of the Saṃgha, she may be accepted.

If a donor holds a great assembly for the Buddha’s birthday, a Bodhi assembly, a Turning of the Wheel of Dharma assembly, a Rāhula assembly, an Ānanda assembly, or a five-year assembly, and with a heart of faith and joy, adorns elephants and horses to give as alms to the Saṃgha, [the monks] shall not accept them.
If a donor brings parrots, peacocks, chickens, sheep, deer, or gazelles to give as gifts, one must not accept them. If the donor says,
"If you do not accept them, I shall kill them," [one may accept].
One should say to them:
"You have already released yourselves.
One should provide them with water and food and protect them, so that no sentient beings may harm them.
One must not clip their wings or feathers, nor confine them in a cage; if they are able to fly or walk and can sustain themselves, one should release them and not restrain them.
If one accepts [a bird] from a sentient being [for such purposes], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the dharma of sentient beings.

Regarding the dharma of trees: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a donor planted an *āmra* tree in the monastery garden. A certain bhikṣu cut it down to build a room for a lay devotee. Once the room was completed, the donor provided beds and mats and invited the Saṃgha to receive offerings.
At that time, the donor who had planted the mango trees was also in the assembly; having seen this, he asked, "Venerable sir!
Whose room is this?"
The bhikṣu said,
"This is the room of the lay devotee so-and-so.
Then the donor said:
"Venerable sir!
Why have you taken my tree to build a hut for another?
This hut is my hut."

His mind remained unsatisfied, so he went to where the Buddha was staying, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him; he then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed with joy.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you have done so? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said,
"How could you cut down flowering and fruit trees to build a hut?"
"From this day forward, I do not permit the felling of flowering or fruit-bearing trees.

As for those who fell flowering or fruit-bearing trees—such as the *āmra* tree, the *jambu* tree, the *bilva* tree, the *kapittha* tree, the *panasa* tree, the coconut tree, the *aśoka* tree, the *campaka* tree, the *kṣīravṛkṣa* tree, the *atimuktaka* tree, and all other such flowering or fruit-bearing trees—I do not permit them to be cut down to make dwellings."
If the tree is old and bears no flowers or fruit, one should say to the donor:
"Long-lived one!
This tree is already old; furthermore, you must build a dwelling to house a bhikṣu so that you may obtain the merit of its use."
If the owner permits it, one may take it; if he does not permit it, one must not take it.
If wood is urgently required and it obstructs the ground, one should have a *karmadāna* (attendant) prick it with fish bones or pour lye upon it.
If the tree is already dead, one should say to the donor:
"This tree is already dry; if you require it, please take it.
If the donor consents, one may take and use it.
If a bhikṣu cuts down a tree that bears flowers or fruit, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule regarding trees.
Regarding the rule regarding firewood: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a monastery on the outskirts of a village where visiting bhikṣus came to cut and gather firewood.
The senior bhikṣus said:
"For what reason have you cut down and destroyed that which we labored so hard to plant?
You are but guests who come merely to sit in the shade; you cannot assist in its protection, yet you treat it with such wanton disorder as you please."
"Tomorrow we shall depart; we do not know of your suffering.
Having spoken thus, after the resident bhikṣus had gone out to beg for alms, the visiting bhikṣus split firewood while it was still dry, piled it up before the cell, and lit a fire.
When the resident bhikṣu returned from begging for alms and saw this, he immediately said:
"For what reason have you dried out living plants, stacked them up, and set them on fire?
The visiting bhikṣu replied:
"Why do you yourself take fire and kindle it, yet instead obstruct me?
After they had thus disputed, the two bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported the matter in full.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You must not take [firewood] for yourselves and prevent others from doing so; you should also protect it.
You must not chop dry or raw wood together, nor pile firewood in front of the dwellings."
"However, as for 'kindling,' there must be a standard:
so much may be kindled in the warm bathhouse;
so much may be kindled in the kitchen."
It is the same for that many bathhouses;
it is the same for that many separate rooms. One should take a portion according to the limit and must not take more than that.
If there is no fixed limit, then taking more is also without offense.
One must not cut down moist trees; one should take those that are dry.
Within the precincts of a monastery, trees that are particularly fine or beautiful may not be cut.
However, there is no offense in cutting trees in mountain forests that have no owner or guardian.
This is called the rule regarding firewood.

Regarding the rule regarding flowers: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a monastery on the outskirts of a village. At that time, visiting bhikṣus came to take flowers, and the resident bhikṣus said to them, "Why are you taking these flowers?"

We have labored with great hardship to plant, guard, irrigate, and nurture [this garden], yet you, a mere guest who has arrived here merely to seek the coolness, show no desire to tend to it; instead, you leave it in disarray to your heart's content.
Departing tomorrow, you take no account of our suffering.

After these words had been spoken, once the resident bhikṣus had departed on their almsround, the visiting bhikṣus—whether their flowers were prepared or not—broke and folded them together, leaving them in a disarray piled up before the hall.
When an elder bhikṣu returned from his almsround, he saw the heap of flowers and asked,
"Why have you taken these flowers?
The visiting bhikṣu replied:
"Why do you take [the robe] for yourself while simultaneously obstructing me?
After they had thus disputed, they went together to the Buddha and reported the matter in detail.
The Buddha said to the senior bhikṣu:
"You must not take [the bedding] yourself nor prevent others from doing so; you should protect it.
Furthermore, visiting bhikṣus must not form, break up, or pile up [bedding] in front of the room."
"If one possesses five qualities, they should be appointed as the distributor of flowers.
What are these five?
Not following favoritism, not following hatred, not following delusion, not following fear, and knowing what has been obtained and what has not been obtained—these are called the five qualities."
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so has accomplished the five dharmas."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of flowers.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having performed the one-motion-and-one-announcement (*jñapti-karman*), [the Buddha said]: "...Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Once that bhikṣu has received the formal ritual (karmavācanā), he should have a lay attendant (upāsaka) take charge of the flowers.
If the flowers are small, they should be divided by measure using a vessel, or otherwise estimated by hand.
If there are flowers such as the utpala, campaka, padma, or puṇḍarīka, these large flowers should be divided and counted accordingly.
If they are "Buddha-flowers," they should be offered to the Buddha.
If it is monastic flowers, one may offer them as one pleases or exchange them.
If there are many flowers, they may be given to a florist, saying:
"Give me this much of a garland every day; for the remainder, give me this much in payment."
Once it has been obtained, it may be used as a robe for a separate room.
If there is still a surplus after meals before or after [the midday meal], it should be placed within the inexhaustible treasury (*akṣayanīvi*).
This is called the dharma of flowers.
Regarding the fruit, it is as explained above concerning the flower.
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should inform a *karmadāna*.
If the fruit is small, it should be measured by weight; otherwise, the hand may serve as the limit.
If they are large, such as the tāla fruit, the bilva fruit, the coconut fruit, the snaśa fruit, or the āmra fruit, these should be divided by counting them individually.
If there is a surplus, it should be given to fruit vendors; one should tell them, "Give me this much fruit every day, and give me this much payment for the remainder.
Having received the payment, it should be placed among the food eaten before and after meals. If there is still a surplus, it should be placed within the inexhaustible wealth.
This is called the dharma of the fruit.
