Regarding the dharma of planting trees: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who planted an āmra tree in the monastery grounds. Once it had grown and matured into a tree, he took its fruit for himself and did not allow others to take them.
The bhikṣus said,
"For what reason do you take [the robe] for yourself while obstructing another?
He replied:
"I planted this tree and protected it so that it might grow large.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"This planting has merit; you shall be granted one tree for every year.
Regarding the rule of years: if a bhikṣu plants mango trees (*āmra*), rose-apple trees (*jambu*), or similar fruit trees on monastic land, he should be permitted to take [the fruit] after one year.
If one possesses many trees and does not wish to take them all at once, it is permitted to take one branch each year, ceasing when all branches have been taken.
If one has planted an entire grove of trees, one should be granted for one year;
however, if one says, "I wish to take one tree each year," [it should be granted].
This is also permitted.
If one plants turnips or scallions, such vegetables as these should be given after one cutting.
If one plants melons or gourds, they should be given after one ripening cycle.
This is called the method for planting trees.

Regarding the method for governing offenses: there are bodily actions, verbal actions, and both bodily and verbal actions; offenses committed due to lack of restraint in body, offenses committed due to lack of restraint in speech, and offenses committed due to lack of restraint in both body and speech; as well as acts performed by the body, acts performed by speech, and acts performed by both body and speech—these are called the nature of offenses.

To be without fault means to have no conduct of body, no conduct of speech, and no conduct of both body and speech; because the body is restrained one does not transgress, because speech is restrained one does not transgress, and because both body and speech are restrained one does not transgress.
Not acting with the body, not acting with the mouth, and not acting with both body and mouth—this is called non-offense.
Regarding the punishment for offenses: how should one punish a *pārājika* offense?
If one has become a layperson, or if one has been made to undergo training as a śrāmaṇera, or if one has been expelled from the Saṃgha—
how is the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense to be dealt with?
If it was not concealed, one should perform mānatva and āvarhaṇa.
For one who conceals [the offense], there is *parivāsa* (probation), *mānatva* (penance), and *āvarhaṇa* (rehabilitation).
How should one who has committed a *naiḥsargika* (offense involving forfeiture) be disciplined?

He should forfeit the object in question to the Saṃgha. Having forfeited it, if he is a senior (*sthavira*), he should prostrate with his head at the feet [of the monks]; if he is a junior (*navaka*), he should kneel on his right knee, join his palms, and speak as follows:
“Venerable Sir!
I have committed the offense of possessing an extra robe and have already relinquished it before the Sangha;
regarding this *pāyattika* offense, I now confess my transgression.”
One should ask:
"Do you see this as an offense?
He should reply:
If they say, "I saw it," one should tell them:
"Do not do it again."
He replied,
"I shall bear it upon my head.
The *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *vinayātikrama* offenses are likewise dealt with, though they differ only in their names.
This is called the method for adjudicating offenses.
Regarding sentient beings, as well as trees, stacks of firewood, flowers, and fruits:
planting and cultivation shall be permitted for one year; this is the method for adjudicating whether an act constitutes an offense or not.
The twelfth chapter (varga) concludes.
There are seven [types of] cessation.
What are the seven?

Saṃmukhavinaya (settlement in the presence), smṛtivinaya (settlement by recollection), amūḍhavinaya (settlement for one not insane), pratijñākāraka-vinaya (settlement by confession), tasya-pāpiyasikā-vinaya (settlement by finding fault with the offender), yadbhūya-sammativinaya (settlement by majority vote), and tiṇavatthāraka-vinaya (settlement like covering with grass)—these are called the methods of settling disputes.
"Disputes" refers to the four types of disputes.
What are the four?

Disputes arising from verbal quarrels, disputes arising from slander, disputes arising from offenses, and disputes arising from matters of customary practice; these are called the four ways of settling disputes.

"Subjugation" refers to the formal act of subduing (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of silence (*ābhāṣaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the formal act of reconciliation (*ārāvaṇīya-karman*), the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepanīya-karman*), and the formal act of separate residence (*parivāsa-karman*); these are called subjugation.
Regarding the matter of subduing, there are five classes of offenses:
*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *vinayātikrama*.
This is called the matter of subduing.
Regarding the listener of the Dharma: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"May I hear you build a thatched hut?
The Buddha said,
"I permit it."
“Is it permitted to construct walls, door panels, door lintels and frames, apply white plaster, and execute the five kinds of paintings?
The Buddha said, “It is permitted.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In a past age, there was a king named Kṣema who built a vihāra for Kāśyapa Buddha. It had one, two, and even up to seven stories, adorned with carved patterns, engravings, and various colorful paintings, with the sole exception of images depicting the union of men and women."
"Various" refers to the likeness of an elder bhikṣu, a grapevine, a makara fish, a swan, a corpse, and a mountain forest; all such things as these are called the five kinds of paintings.

The Buddha, while residing in Śrāvastī, permitted the construction of dwellings; in Vaiśālī, he permitted milk, curd, and ghee; and in the wilderness, he permitted fish and meat. All such permissions and all prohibitions were established within eight great cities:
first, Śrāvastī;
second, Śāketa; [and so forth].
Third, Campā; fourth, Vārāṇasī;
fifth, Kauśāmbī.
Sixth, Vaiśālī; seventh, Rājagṛha;
eighth, Kapilavastu.

Regarding these ninefold scriptures, if the location where they were spoken is forgotten, it suffices to cite one of the eight great cities; that place is what the World-Honored One has certified, and this is called "listening to the Dharma."
Regarding the matter of applying oil to the face: While the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, donors were providing a meal for the Saṃgha at the monastery.

At that time, Nanda and Upananda heard the *gaṇḍī* being struck, yet they were still applying oil to their faces and remained inside without coming out at the proper time; consequently, they incurred the displeasure of the donors.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, the smearing of oil on the face is not permitted."

Regarding "oil": sesame oil, hempseed oil, *ati-mukta* flower oil, *campaka* flower oil, and other such fragrant oils—if one applies them to the face for the sake of beautification, it is a *vinaya*-offense.
When bathing, one may use oil; likewise, when using soap powder or flour paste, or applying oil to the feet, it is permissible to place it on the hands and use it to wipe the face without fault.
This is called the rule regarding oil.

Regarding the rule on using face powder: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a donor had prepared a meal offering for the Saṃgha at the Jetavana Monastery. When the six groups of bhikṣus heard the gong being struck, they were still applying face powder and did not come out in a timely manner, which caused the donor to feel resentment.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣus to wipe their faces with powder."
"Powders" refers to such things as powdered mana-stone, lead, or tin.
If, for the sake of beauty, one applies even red earth to the face, it is an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression).
If there are sores, carbuncles, or swellings on the face, one may apply ointment without fault.
When applying it, one must not do so in the midst of a crowd, but rather in a secluded place.
This is called the rule for powders.

Regarding the method of brushing: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus brushed their heads; they remained there for too long without coming out, which caused resentment among the donors.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit bhikṣus to use brushes to brush their heads.
Regarding "brushes": this includes hair-brushes, grass-brushes, and root-brushes; likewise, even down to hand-brushes, if used for the sake of vanity, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If, after shaving the hair, one touches it with the hand, there is no offense;
this is called the method of brushing.
Regarding the method of combing: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One established a precept prohibiting the use of combs.

At that time, there was a donor providing a meal for the Sangha. Nanda and Upananda heard the gong being struck, yet they remained there combing their hair with a comb and did not emerge in a timely manner. They were resented by the donor, and eventually the Buddha said:
"The use of a comb is not permitted."

Regarding "combing": ivory combs, bone combs, horn combs, and wooden combs—all such combs are forbidden for use. Even down to combing one's hair with one's hand for the sake of appearance, it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called the rule regarding combs.

Regarding hairpins: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One established a precept prohibiting the use of combs. Subsequently, the group of six bhikṣus used hairpins to scratch their heads and could not emerge from their retreats in a timely manner, which caused resentment among the donors. Consequently, the Buddha said:
"The use of hairpins is not permitted."

Regarding hairpins: gold, silver, copper, iron, brass, ivory, bone, horn, bamboo, wood, and all such items are not permitted. Even using a boar-bristle brush for the sake of grooming the hair constitutes a *vinaya* offense.
If the hands are already clean but the head still itches, one may scratch it while holding an object;
this is called the rule for the hairpin (*śalākā-dharma*).
[The seven rules for settling disputes], together with the matters for settling them, and the subduing [of offenses], together with the matters for subduing them.
Listening to the Dharma while having one’s face smeared with oil, or while using powder, a brush, or a hairpin.
The thirteenth *vagga* is concluded.

Regarding the rules for stūpas: While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kosala on a journey, there was a brahmin plowing a field who saw the World-Honored One passing by; holding his ox-goad, he stood upon the ground and paid homage to the Buddha.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One broke into a smile. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?
We pray that you would grant us the opportunity to hear."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This brāhmaṇa is now paying homage to the two World-Honored Ones.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are these two Buddhas?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Bow to me; beneath this staff lies a stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“We wish to see the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Go and ask this brahmin for a clod of earth and some soil.
The bhikṣus immediately asked for them, and the brahmin gave them to them.
Having obtained it, at that time the World-Honored One immediately manifested the seven-jeweled stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha, one yojana in height and half a yojana in width on each side.
Upon seeing it, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"My surname is Kāśyapa; this is my Kāśyapa stūpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately constructed a stūpa for Kāśyapa Buddha at that very spot.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
may I receive the precepts?
The Buddha said:
"Receive the transmission.
He then immediately spoke these verses:
"Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of loads of pure gold and use them to practice giving,"
"It is not as good as taking a lump of clay and, with a reverent heart, repairing a Buddhist stūpa.

At that time, the World-Honored One himself rose up to the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha; he established its four-sided base, surrounded it with railings, raised two tiers of circular structure, added four square projections, and atop it placed a canopy, a long pole, and the mark of a wheel.
The Buddha said,
"The method for constructing a stūpa should be as follows.
Once the stūpa was completed, the World-Honored One, out of reverence for the Buddhas of the past, personally paid homage to it.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May we perform prostrations?”
The Buddha said,
“Yes. He then spoke this verse:
"Though one were to give away hundreds of thousands of gold pieces as an act of almsgiving,
it would not equal a single virtuous thought of reverently prostrating before a stūpa of the Buddha.
At that time, when the people of the world heard that the World-Honored One had built a stūpa, they brought incense and flowers to offer to the World-Honored One.
Out of reverence for the Buddhas of the past, the World-Honored One accepted the flowers and incense and carried them to offer as worship at the stūpa.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May we also receive offerings?"
The Buddha said, "It is so.
He then spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of carts filled with pure gold and use them to practice giving,
it would not equal a single virtuous mind that makes offerings of flowers and incense at a stūpa.
At that time, the great assembly gathered like clouds, and the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“You shall preach the Dharma for all these people.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“If one were to give as alms pure gold filling hundreds of thousands of Jambudvīpas, [the merit of preaching the Dharma would far exceed it].”
"It is not equal to a single gift of Dharma, which leads one to practice accordingly.
At that time, there were those among the assembly who had attained the Way; the Buddha then spoke these verses:
"If one were to fill hundreds of thousands of worlds with pure gold and give it as a gift,"
"It is not equal to a single gift of Dharma, which accords with the vision of the True Truth.
At that time, the brahmin attained indestructible faith and immediately offered a meal before the stupa for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

At that time, King Prasenajit, hearing that the World-Honored One was constructing a stūpa for Kāśyapa Buddha, immediately ordered seven hundred carts loaded with bricks and went to the Buddha’s location. Prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I wish to construct this stūpa on a grand scale; would that be permissible?
The Buddha said, "It is permissible."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In a past age, at the time when Kāśyapa Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Kṣema who wished to construct a stūpa made of the seven precious substances."
At that time, a minister addressed the king, saying:
"In future ages, there will appear those who do not act according to the Dharma; they shall destroy this stupa and incur grave offenses.
We pray only that Your Majesty may construct it with bricks and cover the top with gold and silver; if they take the gold and silver, the stupa will remain as it was, preserved in its entirety."

The king then acted according to the minister’s words, constructing it with bricks and covering the top with gold leaf; it was one yojana in height and half a yojana in width, with railings made of copper, and was completed after seven years, seven months, and seven days.
"Once it is completed, I shall offer incense and flowers as an offering to the community of bhikṣus.
King Prasenajit said to the Buddha, "That king possesses great merit and many rare treasures; I shall now act in a way that does not fall short of that king."
He then proceeded to construct it, completing it after seven months and seven days. Once finished, he made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

As for the method of constructing the stūpa: the lower foundation is square with a railing encircling it; above this, two circular tiers rise up, followed by four square projections, topped with a circular canopy, a long pillar, and the mark of a wheel.
If one says, "The World-Honored One has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; what is the use of this stupa?
one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense because the karmic retribution for such an act is grave.
This is called the dharma of stūpas.

Regarding the matter of stūpas: when establishing a saṃghārāma, one should first designate an excellent site in advance for the location of the stūpa. The stūpa must not be situated in the south nor in the west; it should be located in the east or in the north.
One must not encroach upon the land of the Saṃgha with the land of the Buddha, nor may the land of the Buddha encroach upon the land of the Saṃgha.
If a stūpa is near a cemetery, or if dogs bring in food scraps and defile the ground, one should construct a wall or fence around it.

One should construct the monastic quarters (saṃghārāma) to the west or the south; one must not allow water from the monastic grounds to flow into the Buddha’s grounds, nor allow water from the Buddha’s grounds to flow into the monastic grounds.

A stūpa should be constructed in a high and prominent location; one must not wash or dye clothes, sun clothes, wear leather sandals, cover the head, cover the shoulders, or spit on the ground within the stūpa courtyard.
If one says, "The World-Honored One has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; what use is there for this stupa?
one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense, and the karmic retribution is heavy.
This is called the matter of the stupa.
Regarding the niche of the stupa: at that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We have built a stupa for Kāśyapa Buddha; may we construct a niche within it?
The Buddha said, "You may."

In a past age, after the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, King Kṛkin erected a stūpa for the Buddha. He constructed niches on its four sides and decorated the top with various painted images of lions and elephants. He fashioned railings in front to serve as places for flowers, and within the niches he hung silk banners and canopies.
If someone says,

"The World-Honored One has already eliminated greed, hatred, and delusion; he merely adorns himself and experiences pleasure," one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the Vinaya, and the karmic retribution is grave.
This is called the rule for stūpa niches.
Regarding the rule for stūpa gardens: the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
"May I establish a garden for the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha?
The Buddha said, "You may do so."
In a past age, there was a king named Kṣema; after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, the king erected a stūpa for him and constructed various gardens and groves on its four sides.

Regarding the groves surrounding the stūpa: one should plant mango trees (*āmra*), jambu trees, *punnāga* trees, *campaka* trees, *atimuktaka* trees, *sumana* trees, nāgapuṣpa trees, and aśoka trees—all of which flower at all times; the flowers produced therein should be used to make offerings to the stūpa.
If a donor says: "Venerable One!
This is an offering from China for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
One should follow the words of the donor.
If there are many flowers, one may give them to a florist and say:
"Make a garland from this much flower and give it to me; for the remainder, give me such-and-such a price."

If one obtains money, it may be used directly to light lamps, purchase incense for making offerings to the Buddha, or for the restoration of stupas; if the amount is large, it may be placed among the Buddha’s inexhaustible assets.
If someone says, "The Buddha is free from lust, anger, and delusion; what use has he for these flower and fruit gardens?
they commit a *vyatikrama* offense, and the retribution is grave.
This is called the Dharma of the Stūpa Garden.
Regarding the Dharma of the Stūpa Pond: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and so forth, until the Buddha said to the Great King:

"In the past, after the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, King Kṛkin constructed ponds on the four sides of Kāśyapa Buddha’s stūpa and planted various kinds of flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka). Now, Your Majesty may likewise construct such ponds."

Regarding the rule for ponds: one may construct a pond on the four sides of a stūpa; the various kinds of flowers within the pond are to be used as offerings to the Buddha stūpa, while the remainder may be given to those who work with flower garlands. If there is no remainder, it may be placed among the inexhaustible goods (*akṣaya-nikṣepa*).
One must not wash clothes, bathe, wash hands or face, or wash the alms bowl at the lower end where the water flows out; however, it may be used as one pleases there without fault.
This is called the "Dharma for Stūpa Ponds."
Regarding the *caitya*: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and so forth, until the Buddha said to the Great King:
"You may construct a *caitya*.

After the Parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Kāśyapa, King Kṛkin built a precious *caitya* for the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha on all four sides, adorned with carvings, engravings, and various kinds of painted decorations."
"Now the King may also establish a *caitya*.
That which contains *śarīra* (relics) is called a *stūpa*; that which lacks *śarīra* is called a *caitya*.

Such sites as the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained the Way, the place where he turned the Wheel of Dharma, the place where he entered *parinirvāṇa*, images of Bodhisattvas, caves of Pratyekabuddhas, and the footprints of the Buddha—these various *caityas* may be provided with Buddhist canopies and articles of worship.
If anyone says, "The Buddha has already severed greed, hatred, and delusion; what is the use of making offerings with this vihāra?
they commit a *vinayātikrama* offense, and the karmic retribution for it is grave.
This is called a *caitya*.
Regarding the articles for offering: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
"May one obtain and use items for making offerings to a stūpa to worship the caitya?
The Buddha said,
"One may."

On the day of the Buddha’s birth, the day he attained enlightenment, the day he turned the wheel of Dharma, and on the day of the quinquennial assembly—on these occasions one may perform offerings; those of superior or middling capacity offer at the stūpas of the Buddha, while those of inferior capacity offer at the caityas.
If anyone says, "The Buddha has already exhausted lust, anger, and delusion; what is the use of making offerings with these banners and canopies?
they commit a *vinayātikrama* offense, and the karmic retribution is grave.
This is called the *Caitra* rite.

Regarding the offering of music and dance: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Is it permissible to perform music as an offering to a Buddhist stūpa?
The Buddha said,
“It is permissible.”
"After the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, King Kṛkin made offerings of all manner of song, dance, and music to the Buddha’s stūpa; now you, O King, have likewise obtained [this merit].
The Buddha said:

"Whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has entered Parinirvāṇa, all flowers, incense, music, various garments, food, and drink may be used for offerings. This is for the benefit of the world, so that all sentient beings may attain peace and happiness throughout the long night."
If anyone should say, "The World-Honored One is free from lust, anger, and delusion; what is the use of making offerings with such music and dance?
they commit an offense against the Vinaya, and the karmic retribution is grave.
This is called the method for musical performance.
Regarding the gathering of ritual implements: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!”
"May we receive branches to provide for our requisites?
The Buddha said, "You may."

"Collecting" means that on the Buddha's birthday, the day he attained enlightenment, the day he turned the wheel of Dharma, or during the quinquennial assembly, one produces many banners and canopies to make offerings at the caityas.
If a sudden storm arises, the entire community of monks should collect [the robes] together; no one should say:
"I am a senior elder," "I am a forest-dweller," "I am a beggar for alms," "I am a wearer of rag-robes," or "I am a venerable one."
"You who live depending on this [dwelling] should collect it yourselves.

If wind and rain should suddenly come, you should collect it together; it should be placed according to whichever room is nearest. You must not guard the room by saying, "It shall remain in its original place."
If it is damp, one should sun it; if it is covered in dust and dirt, one should shake it out, fold it, and put it away.
If one says:
"I am a senior elder (sthavira), I am a forest-dweller (āraṇyaka), I am an alms-collector (piṇḍapātika), I am a wearer of rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika), I am a venerable one (bhadanta)."
Whoever does so commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule for collecting requisites for offerings.

Regarding the difficult case: while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a crisis should arise concerning the property of a stūpa or the property of the Saṃgha, what should be done?
The Buddha said:
"If the external enemies are weak, you should seek fearlessness from the king.
If the king says:
'Venerable sir, simply remain here without fear; if my affairs later fail to be established, you may do as you please.'"

At that time, one should gauge the relative strength of the king's power. If the bandits are stronger, one should secretly dispatch a messenger to the leader of the bandits to request freedom from fear.
If the king says, "I am now afraid for my own survival; how can I grant you freedom from fear? [one should respond accordingly].
The Venerable One himself may go from among the bandits to seek protection and depart.

However, if the bandits hold wrong views, do not believe in the Buddha-dharma, and are not persons one can rely upon, he must not simply abandon the property and leave; rather, he should have trustworthy people hide the property belonging to the Buddha and the Sangha.
One should first scout and observe the bandits so as not to allow them to arrive suddenly and unexpectedly.

If the bandits approach urgently and there is no place to hide, one should use the property of the Buddha to adorn the Buddha image, spread out the sitting mats of the Saṃgha, and arrange various kinds of food and drink, so that the bandits may see these signs.

He should have a young bhikṣu wait in a secluded place to watch for the arrival of the robbers; when the robbers see the articles of worship, if they give rise to a heart of compassion, he should ask them:
"Is there any bhikṣu here?"
"Do not be afraid; you may come out.
At that time, the young bhikṣu should look after [the goods].
If bandits arrive suddenly and it is impossible to hide the items, he should say:
"Having said, 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,' he departed.
This is called a difficult teaching (*dūṣaṇīya-dharma*).
The rules for stūpas and matters concerning stūpas, stūpa niches and stūpa gardens,
stūpa ponds and caityas, musical instruments and offerings,
and the collection and preservation of incense and flowers.
The fourteenth *varga* is concluded.
[It contains] the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), the matter of suspension along with the *poṣadha*,
matters concerning the *vinaya* on the rules for the sick, heavy objects, and the eating of garlic.
On the matter of killing, cauterization with a blade, the reception of sentient beings through skillful means,
and the destruction of the *stūpa* dharma.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Scroll 33.
The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

9. The Dharma of Dignified Conduct (Ācāra-dharma) 1. Clarifying the First Part of the Dharma of Dignified Conduct: The Rules for Senior Monks (*Upasthāyaka-dharma*). The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the community of monks assembled, intending to perform the Poṣadha ceremony, and all the monks gathered together.
At that time, Nanda, who was the senior monk (*sthavira*) of the Saṃgha, did not attend.
A donor arrived bringing offerings; wishing to bestow them once the Saṃgha had assembled, he asked, "Has the Saṃgha gathered?"
He replied, "They have not yet assembled.
He asked again:
"Who has not come? He replied,
"The Sangha’s Elder has not come."
The donor complained, saying,
"I was waiting for the Sangha to assemble so that I might offer a gift, yet the Elder has not arrived.
After waiting for a long time, he then made his offering and departed.
The Elder arrived only at the close of day; he did not ultimately distribute the *śalākā*, nor did he announce:
"Do those monks who have not come declare their *chanda* and purity?
He simply briefly mentioned the four matters and departed.
A young bhikṣu asked,
"Has the Elder arrived yet?
He replied:
“The Elder came and has already departed.
A junior bhikṣu spoke with resentment, saying:
“How can it be that the Elder neither informed anyone when he arrived nor informed anyone when he left?”
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked Nanda,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, the senior monk of the Saṃgha should understand it in this way."
How is this to be known?
The Elder should know the proper procedure:

whether it is the fourteenth or fifteenth day for the *poṣadha*, and whether the intermediate *poṣadha* occurs by day or by night, one should know the location—whether it be a heated hall, a lecture hall, or within a grove—and should recite the five sections of the precepts in full, down to the four matters and the verses; as for the remainder, the Sangha has heard them regularly.
If there is a bhikṣu in a city or village, the elder should have someone announce:

"Today, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the fortnight, at such-and-such a time before or after the meal, the saṃgha will perform the poṣadha at such-and-such a location, where the shadow of a man is of this length."
"First, one should have someone sweep the ground, prepare it with mud, and scatter various flowers. Then, who should offer blessings, recite the precepts, and conduct the *śalākā* (lottery sticks)?
This should be known by the Elder (*sthavira*)."
When the time for the recitation of the precepts has arrived and the Saṃgha has not yet assembled, if a donor arrives, the Elder (upādhyāya) should preach the Dharma to them and exchange greetings.
If he is unable to do so, he should invite the second Elder to do so.
If the time for the Dharma master to preach the Dharma or for the *poṣadha* ceremony arrives, one should ask:
"Donor, do you wish to leave or stay? If he says:
Regarding "depart":
one should offer a blessing and dismiss them so that they leave.
Regarding "those who remain": once those who have departed have been sent out, one should perform the *poṣadha*.
Those present should wash the *śalākā* (counting sticks) with fragrant water before proceeding.

If there are those who prefer to sit, one person should distribute the sticks while another collects them. One must not walk about with the head covered or the shoulders covered while distributing the sticks; rather, one should remove one's leather sandals and bare the right shoulder while distributing the sticks, and the person receiving the sticks should do likewise.
First, distribute counting sticks for those who have already received full ordination; thereafter, distribute counting sticks for the śrāmaṇeras.
Having distributed them, one should announce:
"There are this many persons who have received full ordination, this many śrāmaṇeras; in total, there are this many persons."
The senior monk of the Saṃgha should recite the precepts.
If he is unable, the next senior monk should recite them.
If he too is unable, then whoever is able to recite them should do so.

When reciting, if it is near dusk, if the sky is overcast, if there is wind and rain, if there are elderly or sick persons who cannot endure sitting for long, if the dwelling is distant, or if there is danger from kings or bandits, at such times one may recite in an abbreviated manner.

If it is early in the day and no obstacles arise, one should recite extensively; whether the Elder recites himself or another person recites, the community may spend the entire night in harmony engaged in preaching the Dharma, discussion, question-and-answer sessions, and the chanting of auspicious verses.
The procedure for the *uposatha* of the senior monks (*sthavira*) should be as follows.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika-dharma*).
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the community of monks assembled intending to perform the *uposatha*. The first senior monk arrived, but the second senior monk did not arrive.
At that time, a donor brought offerings with the intention of giving them as alms and asked,
"Has the Sangha assembled yet?
They replied:
"Not yet assembled.
He asked, "Who has not come?"
He replied,
"The second senior elder has not come.
The donor expressed his displeasure, saying:
"I wish to give a small gift, but the second senior monk has not arrived.
Having waited for a long time without his arrival, he proceeded to give the gift and departed.
The second senior monk did not arrive until dusk; the senior monk spoke with reproach, saying:
“The World-Honored One rebuked me alone; why did the second senior elder not question him as well?
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call this bhikṣu here. Once he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, during the time of the *poṣadha*, the second senior monk (*sthavira*) should also know it in this way. How should he know it?
Everything is as explained at length regarding the senior monk.”
The only difference is that the second *sthavira* acts in his stead.
If the senior monk of the Saṃgha is unable [to perform the duties], the second *sthavira* should take cognizance of it.
If one does not act in this manner, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the community of bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform the poṣadha ceremony. The senior monk and the second senior monk arrived, but the others wandered about and did not assemble at the appointed time.
The Elder and the Second Elder spoke with resentment, saying:
"Does the World-Honored One restrict only us, and not others?
The bhikṣus, for this reason, went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Call these bhikṣus here.
When they had come, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, regarding the matter of the *poṣadha*, the entire Saṃgha should understand it in this way.
How should it be understood?

One should know the locations for the *poṣadha* on the first day, the second day, up to the fourteenth and fifteenth days, as well as during the intervals between *poṣadhas* and on the *poṣadha* days themselves.
If someone asks, "What day is it today? [one should respond accordingly].
One must not ask in opposition,
"What day was it yesterday?
but rather one must know for certain.

If one fears forgetting, one should prepare tally-sticks and string them together to hang before the lecture hall or the refectory; the administrative official serving as the "Month-Manager" shall place one tally-stick for each day that passes.
On the day of the Poṣadha, one recites the five groups of precepts at length, including even the four matters and the verses; the rest are as the Saṃgha regularly hears them.
Everything is as explained extensively in the section on the Elder (Upādhyāya), with the only difference being that [the roles] are all reversed.
If the Elder and the Second Elder are likewise unable, then all the others should know it.
If one does not act accordingly, one violates the rules of decorum.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a donor at the Jetavana Monastery prepared a meal offering for the community of bhikṣus; however, the foremost elder did not arrive, and the soup and rice had already grown cold.
The donor asked,
"Has the community of bhikṣus assembled yet?
He replied:
"Not yet assembled.
"Who has not come? He replied:
"The foremost Elder has not come.
The donor complained, saying,
"I have abandoned my household affairs and come here wishing to feed the Sangha, yet the bhikṣus have not assembled."
The elder arrived only when the time had come; he neither praised the food nor offered a blessing, but after eating in a hurried and disheveled manner, he departed.
The junior monks asked, "Has the elder arrived yet?"
He replied,
"I have already come, finished eating, and am now leaving.
The youth spoke with resentment, saying:
"The Elder comes without letting anyone know, and he departs without letting anyone know.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Nanda here.
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the Sangha’s senior elder (sthavira) should understand the meal in this way.
How should he understand it?"
Who is providing food today?
Is it for both divisions of the Sangha, or for one division?
Is it for a specific residence, or is it an invitation to the village?
If it is within a monastery, one should know this:

if someone invites the Sangha for a meal tomorrow, the Elder of the Sangha must not accept immediately. He should ascertain the name of the person who made the invitation, whether they are a newcomer or an old acquaintance, and their address or location, for fear that someone might be attempting to deceive or mock the bhikṣus; therefore, he should not accept at once.
If there is someone who recognizes the man or woman who has issued the invitation, they may accept it.

Having accepted the invitation, one must not depart immediately; rather, at dawn the following day, one should dispatch the officer of the month, a monastery attendant, or a novice to investigate whether they have encountered government officials, water or fire disasters, bandits, childbirth, or death, such that they are unable to prepare the meal.
If such an obstacle arises, the Sangha should provide the food themselves; if they have none, they should tell [the guest] to beg for it.
They should send someone to ask:
"Has the meal for the host been prepared?"
If one asks: "Who is this person?
What is this food?"
"You should know that they have deceived you.
If there is food in the monastery, you should prepare the regular meal; if there is none, you should announce:
'The community of bhikṣus has been deceived; each of you should go out for alms.'"
If the host says:
"Venerable sir!
I shall prepare it right now."
At that time, the senior monk (sthavira) should know the proper occasion.
If it is winter, they should all assemble together and depart; if it is spring or summer, they should depart one after another.
If they arrive at the invited household early in the morning and the meal has not yet been prepared, and they wish to go elsewhere, they should inform the bhikṣus:
"I wish to go to such-and-such a house; if the meal is prepared, do not wait for me.
Having departed, he should return early.
When entering the house of a donor, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should take note of the seating arrangements on both sides.
If a donor holds an auspicious assembly (*maṅgalika*), one should sit on the seat spread to the right.
If it is an assembly for hungry ghosts (*preta*), one should likewise sit on the seat spread to the left.
If a sitting mat for the *poṣadha* ceremony has been spread, those in haste should press it with their hands to loosen it, and then sit down slowly so as not to tear it.
If it is not urgent, one must not sit down abruptly; if there are objects beneath or a sleeping infant, one should first press down on the seat with one hand.
One must not place an oily bowl, cakes, or fruit upon it, nor use it to wipe one's hands.
"Elder, you should know who is inspecting the rooms and who is ill so that food may be provided to them.
If a donor is stingy, you should say to them:"
"Long-lived one!
It is the rule that the Dharma should be given;
it must not be withheld. If it is early in the day, he should put on his robes and go to fetch it; if it is late in the day, he should first take it and then dismiss him, sending him away.
The senior monk (*sthavira*) should ascertain what kind of gift the person before him has offered and should offer a timely blessing (*svastyayana*). If,
when the donor is distributing food, they give a large portion to the senior monk, the senior monk should ask:
"Does the entire Saṃgha all receive such [a portion]?
He replied,
"Only the Elder receives it."
One should say:
"I give everything equally. If he says:
"One who has finished receiving should accept it.
If one needs more and takes a small amount or lowers the vessel slightly, one should say:
"Give more."
If there are such fine foods as milk, curd, cakes, meat, or ghee, one should say to them all:
"Give equally.

According to the rule for the senior monks (*saṃghasthavira*), one must not eat immediately after those below; rather, one should wait until the distribution has been completed and it has been announced that the offerings are equal, only then may one eat.
The Elder should eat slowly according to the Dharma; he must not finish eating quickly and then remain watching so as to cause the juniors to eat in a state of distress and fail to be satisfied.

He should keep watch over them; he must not leave before them immediately after finishing his meal, but should wait until the pure water has been distributed and the verses of blessing have been recited, and only then depart.
If one is performing a meritorious offering for the deceased, one should not utter these auspicious praises:
“The virtuous and good have passed away; today is an auspicious day.
Having prepared various delicacies, we make offerings to this excellent field of merit.”
One should offer this prayer of aspiration:
"All classes of sentient beings, As long as they possess life, must return to death;
According to their deeds, whether good or evil, They shall themselves receive their retribution."
"Those who commit evil enter hell; those who do good are born in heaven.
If one can practice the Path, with outflows exhausted, one attains Nirvāṇa.
"If one establishes merit upon the birth of a son, one should not speak in such a manner:"
“The young boy was abandoned amidst the graves; Sucking his own finger, he lived for seven days, Unharmed by mosquitoes or gadflies— This was through the power of the young boy’s merit.”
"One should offer this blessing:
'The servant takes refuge in the Buddha:
The Tathāgata Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni,' "
Kāśyapa and Śākyamuni, the Great Holy Honored Ones of seven generations,
are like the parents of a person, who cherish their child with compassion and desire that they obtain every joy and necessity in the world.
"May your son receive all blessings, even more abundant than those [of others];
may all members of his household and kin likewise enjoy immeasurable happiness.
If one enters a new house to offer a meal, one must not speak these words:
"If, when a fire burns down a house, one can escape with whatever is within,
it will surely become one's own wealth and treasure, rather than being consumed by the flames."
One should offer this benediction:
"By the merit of this gift of a sheltering house, May all that is desired be obtained according to one's wish;
May the assembly of auspicious and noble sages Dwell within it and enjoy its use."
In this world, there are wise people who understand this point:
they observe the precepts and practice the holy life, cultivate merit by providing food and drink.
Because the Saṃgha recites blessings, the deities of the house are always joyful.
With a well-born mind protected, one dwells therein throughout the long night.
Whether entering a village or a wilderness,
whether by day or by night, the devas will always follow and protect them.
"In all directions, it is impossible to travel due to the threat of bandits;
now is precisely the time to leave the household life and practice the holy life."
One should speak thus:
"May all directions be peaceful and secure; may the auspiciousness of the devas be present.
Having heard this, may their hearts rejoice, and may they obtain everything they desire."
Those with two feet dwell in peace, and those with four feet likewise dwell in peace;
they find peace when departing and peace when returning.
They are at peace by night and at peace by day, for the devas always protect and assist them.
All companions are virtuous and good; all are entirely secure and at ease.
Healthy, virtuous, and excellent, with hands and feet free from ailment, throughout every part of the body, there is no place of sickness or suffering.
"If there is anything you desire, you shall attain your heart's wish.
"In the east there are seven stars that constantly protect the world so that it may have its wishes fulfilled:

the first is named Kṛttikā, the second Rohiṇī, the third Saṃjñā, the fourth Mṛgaśiras, the fifth Ārdrā, the sixth Punarvasu, and the seventh Aśleṣā. These are the seven stars in the east that constantly protect the world; they shall now protect you, granting you peace and prosperity and enabling you to return home early. All the lunar mansions shall likewise protect you."
Furthermore, in the eastern direction there are eight goddesses:

first is named Rākṣamati, second is named Śiṣamati, third is named Yaśas, fourth is named Yaśodharā, fifth is named Supratibhāna, sixth is named Varṣmā, seventh is named Varabuddhi, and eighth is named Abhihara. These are the eight goddesses who constantly protect the world in the eastern direction.

There is a Heavenly King named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with the Gandharva Kings and all the other devas, who shall constantly protect you, ensuring that you are everywhere secure, obtain benefit, and return home early.

In the east there is a deity named Dhanada, who constantly emits radiance and is venerated and made offerings to by the devas; this Deva of All Offerings shall protect you, enabling you to obtain wealth and profit, and to return safely and in peace.
“In the southern quarter there are seven stars that constantly protect the world:

the first is named Maghā; the second and third are both named Phalgunī; the fourth is named Ārdrā; the fifth is named Citrā; the sixth is named Svātī; and the seventh is named Viśākhā. These are called the seven stars, which reside in the south and constantly protect the world.”
Now I shall protect you so that you may be secure, obtain benefit, and return early; all the constellations shall likewise protect you.
In the southern direction there are eight goddesses:
first is Rākṣamati, second is Viśvamati, third is Yaśas, fourth is Yaśodharā, fifth is Suprabuddhā, sixth is Sugṛhā, seventh is Suvīryā, and eighth is Anupacchedā; these constantly protect the world.
There is a celestial king named Virūḍhaka, a king of the yakṣas, who together with you shall protect you so that you may obtain benefit and return early.
In the south is a region called Aparāntaka, which constantly emits radiance and is reverently honored and made offerings to by the devas.
"All the devas who worship the caityas shall constantly protect you all, ensuring your safety and well-being so that you may return home early with profit.
To the west there are seven stars that constantly protect the world:
the first is named Anihata, the second Vṛddha, the third Mūla, the fourth Dṛḍhavīrya, the fifth and sixth are both named Aṣāḍhā, and the seventh is named Abhijit; these are called the seven stars."
They constantly protect the world; they shall protect you so that you may obtain benefit and return early, and all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) shall likewise protect you.
To the west there are eight goddesses:
first is Āraṇubhā, second is Citrā, third is Aruṇā, fourth is Suprabhā, fifth is Ikādeśā, sixth is Navaśikha, seventh is Kṛśanī, and eighth is Śatadrū—these are known as the eight goddesses.

There is a celestial king named Virūpākṣa who constantly protects the world; there is a dragon king named Varuṇī, along with all the other dragons, who shall protect you all so that you may obtain benefit and return early.
In the west there is a mountain named Āvarta; the sun and moon abide therein, and whatever one seeks, one’s heart’s desire shall be fulfilled.
In the north there are seven stars that constantly protect the world:

the first is named Dhanisthā; the second and third are both named Śatabhiṣaj; the fourth is named Proṣṭhapadā; the fifth is named Revatī; the sixth is named Aśvinī; and the seventh is named Bharanī. These are called the seven stars that constantly protect the world; they shall protect you all so that you may obtain benefit and return early, and all the lunar mansions shall likewise protect you.
In the north there are eight goddesses:
first is Nīlatīvi, second is Suratīvi, third is Kuṭāvi, fourth is Padumā, fifth is Hani, sixth is Pali, seventh is Cālani, and eighth is Kāmā; these are called the eight goddesses.
There is a celestial king named Varuṇa who constantly protects the world; he shall protect you all so that you may obtain profit and return early.
To the north there is a mountain named Kīlasuva where spirits and deities (yakṣas) always dwell; all these spirits and deities shall protect you all so that you may obtain profit and return early.

The twenty-eight lunar mansions, the sun and moon, and the thirty-two goddesses, along with the Four Great Heavenly Kings who govern the world and possess renowned names: King Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, King Virūpākṣa in the west, King Virūḍhaka in the south, and King Vaiśravaṇa in the north.
The eight śramaṇas, the eight brahmins, the eight kṣatriyas of the great nations, and the eight daughters of Śakra shall protect you all, so that you may obtain benefit and return early.
"If one takes a wife as a gift, one should not say this:
'A dried-up river has no water; a kingdom empty of its king lacks protection.
A woman who has ten brothers is likewise said to have no protector.'"
"One should offer this prayer of aspiration:
'If a woman faithfully upholds the precepts, and her husband does likewise,
because of their shared faith, they are able to practice the giving of alms.'"
Both maintained the precepts and cultivated the practice of right view;
with joy, they together performed meritorious deeds.
The devas always rejoiced in them; such is the retribution of this karma—like traveling without provisions.
"If those who have left the household life practice giving, they must not say:
'May our descendants be numerous and flourishing; may our servants, slaves, wealth, cattle, sheep, and all six types of livestock increase and multiply.'"
One should offer this prayer of aspiration:
"Carrying the alms-bowl from house to house, one may encounter anger or meet with joy;
one should always act to protect their minds, for it is difficult to obtain offerings for one who has left the home life."
“The Sangha’s senior elder (sthavira) should know this; if he does not do so, he transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a donor provided a meal for the Sangha. Nanda sat down first as the senior elder, but Upānanda and the other bhikṣus did not assemble at the proper time. The senior elder complained, saying:
“Does the World-Honored One restrict these rules only to me, and not to others?”
...until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, everyone should assemble together for the meal.

The senior monk (upādhyāya) should act as previously described; however, in this case, the difference lies in [addressing] the second senior monk and the entire assembly, and so on, until one should leave a seat for the monk sitting beside oneself."
If the person distributing food passes by, one must not remain silent while watching the person sitting nearby;
one should say, "Give this to him.
One must not eat as soon as the food is received; rather, one must wait until it has been distributed to all before eating.
If the time is pressing, there is no offense in eating as one goes along.
The senior monk (upādhyāya) should offer a blessing; if he is unable to do so, the second senior monk shall offer the blessing.
If one is again unable [to perform this], it should be passed down; as for those who are able, they should offer blessings.
All such matters regarding the food on the seats of the elders (upādhyāya) should be known by the elder.
If one does not know this, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct (airyāpathika-dharma).

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Upānanda ordained people and granted them full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having granted them full ordination, he failed to instruct or admonish them; they were like celestial oxen or celestial sheep, lacking proper decorum (*īryāpatha*). They did not know the rules for serving their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), and senior monks (*sthavira-bhikṣu*); nor did they know the rules for entering villages or forest hermitages (*araṇya*), or the rules for entering the assembly, wearing robes, and carrying the alms bowl (*pātra*).
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call Upānanda here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, an upādhyāya should instruct his co-practicing disciple in this manner."
What is the instruction?
Having received full ordination, one should be instructed to recite the two divisions of the Vinaya;
if one is unable to do so, one should be instructed to recite one division.
If they are still unable, teach them to recite the five sections of the precepts extensively;
if they are still unable, teach them to recite four, three, two, or even down to four items.
Teach them three times a day: at dawn, at midday, and toward evening.
The "Teachings" (Dharma) refers to either the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
The Abhidharma consists of the ninefold scriptures.
The Vinaya consists of the brief and extensive versions of the Prātimokṣa.

If one is unable [to do so], one should instruct them to know the gravity of offenses, the meaning of the sūtras, the meaning of the vinaya, the meaning of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas), and the meaning of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); one should also instruct them in proper deportment and what constitutes improper deportment that ought to be avoided, as well as during the time of receiving the scriptures, reciting together, and practicing dhyāna—this is what is meant by "instruction."
If one does not receive the sūtras, recite them together, or practice seated meditation, one should at least instruct [the disciple] not to be negligent.
If a preceptor does not instruct their co-practicing disciple in this manner, they violate the rules of dignified conduct.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Upānanda’s co-practitioner disciple did not go to his preceptor frequently. Upānanda complained, saying:
“The World-Honored One restrains me alone, but does not restrain my disciple.”
"If my disciples come, I shall teach them; if they do not come, whom shall I teach?
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call this bhikṣu here.
When he had come, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, a co-practitioner disciple should serve the preceptor in this manner.
What is this service?

According to the dharma, a co-practitioner disciple should rise at dawn, enter the preceptor’s room first with his right foot, and having entered, prostrate with his head at the preceptor’s feet and inquire:”
"Are you sleeping peacefully?
Having received the scripture or finished inquiring about matters, one should depart.
One should place the small vessel for excrement and the spittoon in their usual places; first sprinkle water on the ground, then sweep it, and finally smear it with cow dung.
After they have washed their hands and finished with the water and tooth-sticks, one should take the bowl and go to welcome the rice gruel.
Once the gruel has been consumed, wash the vessel and set it back in its usual place.
If there is a place where one is invited to eat, one should go there to receive the food.
When about to enter a village, one should be given the "village-entering robe" (grāmāntika-cīvara), while the robes kept in the courtyard should be folded and placed in their usual location.
When entering the village, one should follow behind the teacher.
If one wishes to go for alms, one should inform the upādhyāya, and the upādhyāya should say:
"Practice according to the Dharma; do not be negligent.
If he returns first, he should prepare a seat for the Upādhyāya, fetch pure water, and arrange grass and leaves, waiting for the Upādhyāya.

Once the preceptor has returned, he should bestow the robes belonging to the monastery; he should take the robes for use in the village, shake them out, fold them, and place them in their usual location.
If it is hot, he should provide water for bathing; if it is cold, he should kindle a fire in the brazier.
If one obtains fine food, one should offer it to the preceptor; the preceptor, having looked at it, should ask:
"Where did you obtain this fine food?
If [the disciple] says:
"One may obtain [it] from the house of a courtesan, the house of a widow, the house of a young maiden, the house of a eunuch, or from a disreputable bhikṣuṇī or a disreputable śrāmaṇerikā."
The preceptor should say:
"This is not a proper place for alms; you should not take food from there.
If [the disciple] says:
If [the donor] says, "I have obtained it for the sake of preaching the Dharma," one should say:
"It is not permissible to accept food from others through wrong livelihood."

At the time of eating, one should provide water for washing the hands and serve the food; if it is hot weather, one should give cold water and fan them with a fan. When the meal is finished, one should collect the bowl, wash it with grass leaves, and place it back in its usual location.
When the Upādhyāya wishes to enter the forest to practice dhyāna, he should take his *niṣīdana* and place it upon his shoulder, holding a water jar above it and following behind.
Upon arrival, if he receives a scriptural discourse or inquires about its meaning, once he has received it, he should go to a secluded spot to cultivate it.
If one wishes to recite together with another, one should inform the upādhyāya, who should ask:
"With whom will you recite?
The disciple should reply:
"Recite together with so-and-so.
The preceptor should observe the person before him; if one who holds the Vinaya laxly, he should say:
"Do not go; you should not engage in reciprocal discourse with this person."
If there is one who is skilled in upholding the Vinaya,
he should say, "Recite it.
Upon returning, he should take his *niṣīdana* and place it on his shoulder, and carry the water jar while following back.
When the Upādhyāya wishes to pay homage to the stūpa, he should provide water for washing his hands and hand him flowers.
Once the homage to the stūpa is completed, he should provide a seat upon which to sit, water for washing his feet, and oil to anoint his feet.
When wishing to sleep, one should sweep and wipe the bedding, arrange the pillow, and provide a lamp, as well as a spittoon and a small vessel for excrement.
Once the preceptor has settled comfortably, one may then receive the scriptures and inquire about their meaning.
When it is one's turn to receive a room, one must first ask the preceptor before taking it.
If two people receive a room together, the preceptor should ask:
"With whom did you receive this dwelling?"
He should reply: "With so-and-so.
He should then observe the person before him; if that person's observance of the precepts is lax, he should say:
"Do not take it; it will give rise to calamities for living beings.
If a virtuous person says, "Take it," [then one may do so].
"If another elder comes later, you should likewise announce [his arrival] when he departs.
A disciple traveling together with his preceptor should act in this manner toward him; if he does not do so, he transgresses the rules of decorum."
"If there are many disciples, down to even one who sweeps the bed, this is called 'service'. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Nanda and Upānanda accepted people as their dependents but did not instruct or admonish them; they were like celestial oxen or celestial sheep. Each point is as explained extensively above regarding the *upādhyāya*, with the only difference being that these two acted as *ācāryas*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Nanda and Upananda were receiving formal reliance (*niśraya*) from others, yet their disciples did not come. The teachers complained, saying:
"The World-Honored One has restricted us alone, but has not restricted our disciples."
"If my disciple does not come, whom shall I instruct?
This is as explained at length above regarding the co-practicing disciples; the only difference here is that the focus is on the *niśraya-śiṣya* (dependent disciple).
The procedure for the *upadhivāra* (distribution of duties) by the senior monk is the same for all;
the rules regarding food at the head of the assembly are the same for all;
whatever the preceptor instructs, the co-practitioner should comply with.
Relying on the teachings that accord with the Dharma, the disciples should practice them accordingly.
The first chapter concludes.

The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. Every five days, the Tathāgata would go to visit the rooms of the bhikṣus. He saw that the beds were scattered here and there across the floor, buffeted by the wind, scorched by the sun, drenched by rain and dew, infested by insects, and covered with bird droppings.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu!
Whose bed is this?"
"Here and there they lie on the ground amidst the droppings of crows and birds.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should understand the use of beds and mats in this manner."
How is this known?

One cannot see the beds placed here and there on the ground, where they have been gnawed by insects, scorched by the sun, rained upon, drenched by dew, buffeted by the wind, or soiled by the droppings of crows and birds.

If they are scattered in various places, they should be collected and stored in one location; those that are tilted should be straightened; those weathered by the sun or blown about by wind and rain should be placed inside the room; those damaged by insects should have their legs propped up; and those soiled by the droppings of crows or birds should be shaken out and brought inside the room.
One must not fail to repair a dwelling that is leaking or dilapidated.

If it is thatched with grass, it should be patched with grass; if it is tiled, it should be patched with tiles; if it is plastered with lime, it should be patched with lime; and if it is plastered with mud, it should be patched with mud.
Where a wall is cracked, it should be repaired with mud and smeared with cow dung on the floor.

The bedding and mats of the Saṃgha must not be used haphazardly; they should be covered with a single layer of coarse cloth, and furthermore, two layers of *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) should be placed over them.
Regarding bedding, when sleeping, one should place an object between the body and the interior of the bed; it must not touch the skin.
If the mattress or woolen rug is thick, one must not fold it up while spreading it out, thereby damaging the property of the Sangha.
If mattresses, pillows, or handheld items are soiled or greasy, they should be washed; if torn, they should be mended so that they are restored to their original state.
One should maintain and care for the monastic beds, mattresses, and bedding in this manner; otherwise, one violates the rules of decorum.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus had not repaired their dwellings during the final month of spring.
For five reasons, the Tathāgata went on a tour of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days.
What are the five?
First, among my śrāvaka disciples, are they not attached to conditioned things?
Second, are they not attached to worldly discourse?
Third, is he not attached to sleep?
Fourth, it is for the sake of the monks who tend to the sick.
Fifth, it is so that young monks with faith, upon seeing the Tathāgata’s dignified and composed deportment, may give rise to joy.
These are called the five matters regarding sexual intercourse.
Seeing that a dwelling was dilapidated and not being repaired, the Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"What kind of dwelling is this, dilapidated and not being repaired?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“The bhikṣu who is observing the rains retreat should attend to the affairs himself.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, during the period of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), dwellings must be maintained in this manner.
How are they to be maintained?
When the time for the rains retreat approaches, one must not fail to inspect the dwellings and remain silent if they are dilapidated and unrepaired.”
"The person observing the rains retreat should repair it themselves.
If it is a thatched house, it should be re-thatched; likewise, if it is a mud house, it should be plastered and repaired, and any holes in the walls should be filled with mud.
One should block the mouse holes and plaster the floor; all items for use within the room should be gathered and placed in one location.
One who has accomplished these five qualities should be appointed as the person in charge of distributing rooms.
What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what is obtained and what is not obtained—these are called the five.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has accomplished the five qualities. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha appoint so-and-so as the assigner of rooms."
Thus he makes the motion.
After the motion and the single *karmavācanā*, up until: "Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Once that bhikṣu has received the *karma*, he should repair the cells, the heated rooms (*jantāghara*), the dining halls, the lecture halls, the bathhouses, the well-houses, the latrines, the gatehouses, the walking paths (*caṅkrama*), and the areas under trees, recording the number of each in detail. If it is a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) whose location is distant from other dwellings, on the twelfth or thirteenth day of the fourth month, the lodgings should be distributed; if one does not accept them, he should go elsewhere.

If there are many places where the *upavāsasthāna* (near-dwelling) is established, the rooms should be divided on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, and a formal announcement (*uddāna*) should be recited in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This certain vihāra has so many rooms, so many beds and mats, such an amount of food, such an amount of meals for the days of the fast, and such an amount of robes for the rainy season retreat."
The senior monk (sthavira) should speak regarding the distribution of the lodgings.
When there is a common gift, the lodgings should be divided; from the senior monk down to a bhikṣu who has not yet completed a year of standing, no room may be given to a śrāmaṇera.
If the preceptor or the ācārya says,
"Just give it; I shall attend to the matter," one should give it.
If there are many rooms, one person should be given two rooms; if they say,
"I do not need two, one will suffice," one should say to them:
"It is not given for the sake of personal enjoyment, but is given for the purpose of managing affairs.
If there are few rooms, two or three people shall share one room.
If they still do not accept this arrangement, five or six people shall share one.
If they still do not accept [the invitation], and there is a large hall, everyone shall enter the large hall together.
If they still do not accept, the senior monk (upādhyāya) shall spread out a large bed, and the junior monks shall spread out small beds.
If they still do not accept [the invitation], the senior monk shall sit on a small seat and the junior monk on a grass mat.
If they still do not accept, the senior monk shall sit on a grass mat and the junior monk should sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
If, however, he does not accept it, the senior monk should sit cross-legged while the junior monk should stand or move away from beneath the tree.
During the winter, rooms are assigned for the purpose of administrative maintenance as well as for personal use.
When the Elder comes to call him, he should immediately go.
It is the same when rooms are assigned during the spring.
During the summer, rooms are assigned for the purpose of managing affairs and for the purpose of personal use.
If a senior elder comes to summon him, he should not go.
A bhikṣu should repair his dwelling at the end of the spring month in this manner; if he does not do so, he violates the rules of decorum.

The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, for the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One went on inspection once every five days to the quarters of the bhikṣus. He saw that the dwellings were leaking and dilapidated yet unrepaired; rainwater pooled everywhere; drainage channels were blocked; doors and gates were eaten by insects; and the bedding and mats were moldy and green with mildew.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally: "Monks,
what kind of room is this?"
"One should not fail to repair leaks and damage in this manner.
...乃至... the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, during the summer retreat (varṣā), one should maintain the dwellings, beds, and mats in this way."
How should one thus perform repairs?
One must not see that a dwelling is leaking or ruined, nor that the bedding and mats are damaged, and fail to carry out the necessary repairs.
If it is covered with grass, it should be patched with grass; likewise, if it is covered with mud, it should be patched with mud, ensuring that the drainage channels and gutters remain clear.
If bedding or seats develop mildew while lying or sitting upon them, they should be sun-dried at midday.
If the interior of the room is damp, one should ensure that the furniture is kept away from the walls and its legs are supported on stands, so that insects do not eat it.
One should sweep away soot and cobwebs from the rooms; every half-month, one should smear the floor with cow dung.
If the floor is dry, it should be moistened with water before being smeared with cow dung; if it is already damp, it should be smeared directly with pure cow dung.
If the interior of the room is damp, one must not wash the hands, the feet, or the alms bowl, nor may one close the door.
One should open the door from time to time to allow air to enter, but one must not smoke inside it.
"If a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat, his dwelling must be maintained in this manner.
If he does not do so, he transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣu who had completed his retreat in a forest hermitage departed without leaving instructions. Subsequently, a wild fire came and burned the dwelling.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"When the bhikṣus have finished their summer retreat, the dwellings should be repaired in this manner."
What is the remedy?
If a bhikṣu has completed his rains retreat in an araṇya and, upon the arrival of winter, wishes to move to a warmer place, he must not depart entirely.
One should seek out two or three capable persons and have them stay there, providing them with food and drink so that they do not suffer from lack.
If they say, "We cannot; why should we remain here in this empty wilderness? [one should respond accordingly].

"If there is no place at all to stay, and if one possesses beds, pillows, mattresses, or copper and iron vessels, all should be deposited in a monastery within a village. The beds for lying down and sitting should be kept away from the walls, with their legs propped up by objects, so that insects do not eat them."
When the *varṣā* retreat has concluded, one must not depart without seeing that leaking rooms have been repaired;
if they are thatched with grass, they should be patched with grass, and likewise, if they are plastered with mud, they should be patched with mud.
One should plaster the rooms and make the walls white; having ensured that there is little fire around them, one should entrust them to the herders, saying:
"From time to time, look after them for me.
One should also attend to the dwellings within the village in this same manner, as well as the warm rooms, lecture halls, and dining halls, cleaning and sprinkling them when they become dirty.
If there is a donor (dānapati) for the monastery, one should speak to them and have it repaired, or appoint someone to repair it.
If there is no owner and no one is appointed to repair it, the entire Saṃgha should repair it.
When it is to be shared, each person shall receive one, two, or three cubits to cover the entire area.
If the beds for lying down or sitting down are loose or damaged, they should be re-woven to make them firm.
If mattresses, pillows, staffs, or bedding are soiled, they should be washed until clean.
If they are torn, they should be mended.
All items used within the room should be gathered and kept in one place.
"When a bhikṣu has completed the rainy season retreat, he should attend to his dwelling, bed, and bedding in this manner.
If he does not attend to them in this manner, he transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, on that occasion the World-Honored One, for five reasons of benefit, went once every five days to visit the rooms of the bhikṣus. He saw that the beds and stools were scattered about and lying askew on the floor everywhere. Knowing the situation, he nevertheless asked:
"What is this bed, so disarrayed and left unattended?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"These are the established residents, and I am a guest.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, a visiting bhikṣu should understand it in this way."
How is this known?
It is because one does not find beds for lying down or sitting left in disarray, infested by insects, and abandoned.

If they are in disarray, they should be gathered and placed in one location; if they are tilted, they should be set upright, and their legs should be propped up with objects so that insects do not eat them.
When a visiting bhikṣu arrives, he must not immediately place his belongings inside the room; rather, he should set his items aside in one place and seek out the resident bhikṣus.

Once he has obtained a room, if the floor is uneven, he should level it; if there are mouse holes, he should seal them with mud and repair them; if there is soot or cobwebs, he should sweep them away; and if the beds or chairs are loose, he should weave them tighter.
Mats, pillows, and handheld items should be shaken out inside the dwelling; the floor should be sprinkled with water, swept, and smeared with mud.
If there is a wooden rack for clothes, it should be wiped clean with a cloth.
If the bamboo is slippery, wipe it with your hand; you should examine whether it is sturdy and solid before suspending the bowl upon it.
If you are staying there until midnight, you should likewise finish preparing it before departing.
"If a visiting bhikṣu does not attend to these matters in such a manner, he transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, on that occasion, for the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata went from room to room among the bhikṣus every five days, until he said:
"World-Honored One!"
"This bedding has been prepared by a visiting bhikṣu, not by us resident bhikṣus.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, the resident bhikṣus should understand it in this way."
How is this known?
A senior bhikṣu must not allow bedding and mats to be discarded here and there, leaving them for insects to devour.
If they are scattered about in various places, he should gather them in one spot; if they have been eaten by insects, he should support the legs with some object.
According to the rules for senior bhikṣus, one may not occupy a fine room for oneself; one must leave the beds, mats, and pillows worn out, tattered, and greasy for visiting bhikṣus.
One should instead maintain and repair the well-kept items for the visiting bhikṣus.
