A senior bhikṣu should understand this; if he does not do so, he transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, for the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata would go on a tour of the bhikṣus’ quarters once every five days. On one such occasion, the Buddha saw [the situation] and, though he already knew it, asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"Whose bed and bedding is this?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"This bedding was already spread by the resident bhikṣus; it is only now that I have taken up residence.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, regarding beds and bedding, all bhikṣus should understand it in this way."
How is this known?
No bhikṣu shall allow beds or bedding to be exposed here and there to rain, dew, sun, or insects; if he sees them scattered on the ground, he should gather them and place them in one spot.

If it is exposed to rain, dew, or the scorching sun, it should be placed under cover; if it is being eaten by insects, the legs should be propped up; if the dwelling is leaking or dilapidated, it should be roofed over—whether with grass, one should repair it with more grass, or even if it is covered with mud, one should repair it with more mud—and if the walls are perforated or ruined, they should be repaired and the earthen floor treated.

If bedding, mattresses, or pillows are soiled, greasy, or damaged, one must not simply leave them as they are; they should be washed, dyed, and repaired. The inner cotton stuffing should be torn apart and re-distributed, and if the cords of the bed are loose, they should be woven tighter to make it firm and durable.
When the *gandī* is struck and it is time to repair the bedding and mats, one must not approach slowly; one should go quickly to assemble. Once assembled, you should work together.
Some should prepare the cords, while others should weave; you must perform these tasks collectively.
If it is to be divided, each person shall take their own portion.
When striking the *gandī* to repair beds and mats, one must not say:
"I am a forest-dweller," "I am an alms-collector," "I am of great virtue," or "I am a senior elder; I cannot do the repairs."
"In this matter, those who have made use of it shall repair it themselves; everyone shall gather together to repair it collectively.
Whether there be those with cord and thread, those who sew, or those who apply superior dye, the bhikṣu should have it repaired in all such ways."
"If it is not done in this manner, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus defecated here and there, causing the people of the world to criticize them:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are like oxen or donkeys?"
"Then go directly to the place of impermanence.
The bhikṣus, for these reasons, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should construct latrines. A latrine must not be situated in the east or the north; it should be in the south or the west, with a ventilation passage opened.

As for the method of construction: whether one makes a pit, relies on a high embankment, or if water wells up from the bottom of the pit, one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) first relieve themselves therein, and only then may a bhikṣu enter."
If there is flowing water at the bottom when one approaches the bank, one should place a wooden board so that the person first falls onto the board and only afterwards falls into the water.
One should make two or three holes; the diameter of each hole should be one span (a *muṣṭi*) and their length one and a half cubits (*hasta*).
"A partition should be installed within the chamber so that the two sides cannot see each other.
A toilet scraper should be placed at the edge, and a clothes rack should be installed beneath the structure.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu already inside the latrine when another bhikṣu arrived in haste and entered to relieve himself, intending to pass over the first bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu said,
"Venerable sir, do not defile me.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should know the proper method for using the latrine in this way. How should one know it?
[The following instructions follow...]"
One must not wait until the last moment before entering the latrine; rather, one should go as soon as the urge to defecate is felt.
Upon arriving, one must not enter in silence, but should snap one's fingers.
If there is someone inside, one should likewise snap the fingers in greeting.

If it is very urgent, one should crouch behind the person ahead and find a space to pass through; one must not come forward with one's robes already raised before arriving, but should lift them only as one proceeds.

One must not enter the restroom while wearing the monastic bedding; one must not chew toothwood, cover the head, or cover the right shoulder while on the toilet, but should instead expose the right shoulder.
One must not recite sutras, practice dhyāna, engage in the contemplation of impurity, or sleep therein, thereby obstructing others.
"When rising, one must not lift the robe high as one stands up and departs; rather, one should rise in accordance with its natural fall.
Furthermore, at that time, some bhikṣus used bamboo tally-sticks which injured and broke their bodies. On account of this matter, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the use of bamboo splinters, reed shavings, wood chips, or bone is not permitted.
One should instead use smooth objects that are round."

One must not dispose of [excrement] directly into a latrine; rather, it should be covered with earth and placed in one spot. If it is a deep pit or a high embankment, there is no offense in disposing of it therein.
When performing the great or small excretions, as well as spitting or expectorating, one should ensure they fall directly into the hole and do not soil the two sides.

If the aforementioned items have been defiled, they must be cleaned by scraping them with a wooden scraper until they are pure; one must not, after having relieved oneself, use the Sangha’s sitting mats, beds, or bedding without first using water to wash them.

One should install a water jar; if it is situated in a pit, one must not use the water therein, but if it is placed on a bank, its use is permitted. One should use wood, stone, or ceramic to make a lid for the jar.
The junior bhikṣus shall take turns adding water and wash the pitcher from time to time.
If it has a wooden lid, it must not be left out in the sun to dry, lest it break; if it is made of clay or stone, it may be placed in the sun to dry.
One should place ash, soil, and *kṛmijagdha* (insect-eaten wood) near the latrine.
If there are insects in the water vessel, one must not say:
"There are insects in this."
One should place grass across [the mouth of the vessel] to indicate the presence of insects.
One must not use excessive water, but should use it with moderation.

If the water in the jar is exhausted, one should inform the person in charge of the water to add more, or add it oneself; at the very least, one should ensure there is enough water in a single wash-basin for one person to use.
If one has hemorrhoids in the lower part of the body that cannot be washed, one should wipe with a soft material, such as cloth or tree leaves.
If there is no latrine building, one should do so behind the dwelling.

If one is near a wall, one should keep to the right; one must not chew on a tooth-stick while standing alongside others, nor cover the head or the shoulders, but should instead bared the right shoulder.
If one suffers from diarrhea at night, one should discard it in a vessel made of clay.
If there is no vessel available, one should go to the edge of a water channel, intending to wash away [the excrement] the next morning.
If one must suddenly void in a heated room or a lecture hall, one should exit immediately.

If one is in great haste and cannot leave, one should stay in one spot; one must not follow the movement of cattle and release [excrement] as they do. At dawn, one should remove it from the place where it was washed and apply oil down to the *goma* (cow dung) layer.
When circumambulating a stupa, if one suffers from abdominal pain or diarrhea, one should depart.
If the urgency is great, one should remain in one place; one must not leave like a cow that soils its own feet with dung.
Once finished, it should be removed; wash it with water and smear it with fragrant clay.
If there is no fragrant clay available in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), one should smear it with oil.
If one wishes to enter a village, one should first circumambulate it to the right before departing.
Once inside the village, if one is a male practitioner, one should go to the men’s latrine and must not enter the women’s latrine.
If it is not there, one should ask others for it and seek it out in whatever place it may be kept.
When asking, one must not question young women, as they will likely laugh upon hearing the request; rather, one should question those who are long-established in the community.
If there is no one else present, you should enter an empty house.
Upon entering, you must not stay in an exposed place, nor should you stay in a secluded spot where people might suspect you of being a thief.
If there is no such place, one should go by the side of the road or beneath a wall.
If there are companions, have them turn their backs toward the obstruction.
If traveling with merchants, when one must defecate, one should leave the path; do not cause an odor that offends others by being upwind, but remain downwind.
If one intends to pass by while the caravan is resting, one must not depart in silence; rather, one should inform the merchants, saying, "Do not call me a thief.
Furthermore, one should remain downwind and must not stay upwind.

If one travels upstream on a merchant ship and must defecate, one should go to a place suitable for excrement; there, one should place a wooden board beneath oneself so that the waste first falls onto the wood and only then into the water.
If there is no wood, one should even use a single blade of grass from a latrine as a receptacle.
If there is no grass from a latrine, one should place it in a ceramic vessel and then discard it.
If one sees impurities within a stūpa courtyard or a monastic compound, they should be removed.
If two people travel together and see [such a thing], the junior monk should remove it; if the junior monk is lax in his observance of the precepts, he should remove it himself.
If one is afflicted by poison, the physician says:
"One should consume the liquid from excrement."
"If one has already given one's consent, there is no need to receive it again; if another has given their consent, one should receive it.
This is how a bhikṣu should act while on the latrine.
If he does not act thus, he transgresses the rules of decorum."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus were urinating here and there, which caused the people of the world to despise them, saying:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, urinate here and there like oxen and donkeys?"
"This man is ruined; what path can he have?
The Buddha then said:
"From this day forward, you should construct a small restroom."
Regarding the method of construction: one must not [place it] in the north or the east; it should be in the south or the west so as to leave a passage for the wind.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had gone to relieve himself, and another bhikṣu came above him, wishing to urinate. The first bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!"
"Do not defile me.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should understand the method for urination as follows.
How is it to be understood?
One must not wait until one is in urgent distress before going; rather, when one perceives the urge to go, one should go immediately."
One should first snap one's fingers; if there is already someone present, one should likewise snap one's fingers in greeting.
If one is in a hurry, one should turn one's back to the person already present, who should then make room.
One must not cover one’s head or shoulders, nor chew a tooth-stick while entering; rather, one should bared the right shoulder.

When walking up, one must not occupy the upper position by practicing dhyāna, sleeping, reciting scriptures, or performing the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) to obstruct those who follow; one should depart as soon as the time has come.

If there is no place for urination, one should collect it in a jar; on top of the jar, one should place an inverted bowl with a perforated bottom, and pour the urine from another bowl into the opening of that bowl.
If there is no bowl, one should use a wooden ladle to pour it into [the jar].
One must not discharge excrement, urine, or spit into the midst [of the assembly], and young bhikṣus should dispose of it in succession.

When disposing of it, one should place it in a secluded spot; one must not discard it upstream within the precincts of a stūpa. After pouring it out, one should wash it away and cover the ground with water; if there is no water, one should seek out a vessel from each person.
If it is made of clay, wash it and place it on the ground; if it is made of wood, wash it and place it in the shade so that it does not crack.
One should provide strings for it, and at night, one should place it beneath the bed.
If there is no vessel available, one may urinate by the side of a drainage ditch, but one must not do so on top of a stupa where the water would flow over it.
If one wishes to urinate in a heated bathhouse or upon a lecture hall, one should go outside.

If one urgently needs to relieve oneself while traveling, one must not proceed. When one has lost control of the urine, one should stop in a single spot; once finished, one should wash with water, apply oil, and then apply *goma* (cow dung).

If one intends to urinate while circumambulating a stūpa, one should depart from the path. If it is urgent, one must not continue walking alongside others but should stop in a single spot; once finished, one should wash with water and apply fragrant ointment.
If there is no fragrant substance in an araṇya dwelling, one should use oil as an application.
If one wishes to enter a village, one should first urinate and then depart.
If one wishes to urinate within the village, one should do so in a secluded place.
If one is in haste and cannot reach a secluded place, one should face a wall; if there are companions, one should turn one's back toward a screen.
If traveling on a road with merchants and needing to urinate, one should do so downwind and not upwind.
If one must urinate while staying overnight, one should do so downwind.
Upon rising, one should inform others so that they do not mistake the person for a thief.
If traveling by boat, one should go to a place suitable for urination; if none is available, one should discharge it into a vessel and then discard it.
If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says,
"You should take urine," he must not take the first or the last; he should take the middle portion.
If one accepts it oneself, that is called "receiving.
If it is on the ground or if another person offers it, one should receive it; this is the proper method for urinating. If one does not act in this way, one violates the rules of decorum.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus chewed tooth-sticks that had not been trimmed, which caused the people of the world to criticize them, saying:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, like wicked men, chew tooth-sticks with their branches and twigs still attached?"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the use of tooth-sticks is not permitted."
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly. At that time, a certain bhikṣu had foul breath and stood downwind.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Which bhikṣu is staying alone in a secluded place like one who harbors resentment?
The bhikṣu replied:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit the chewing of tooth-sticks; fearing that one’s foul breath might offend fellow practitioners of the holy life, one should therefore remain downwind.
The Buddha said:
“The use of tooth-sticks is permitted; they should be used according to measure, with the longest being sixteen finger-widths in length.”
Furthermore, at that time, there was a donor who had planted trees in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*). A bhikṣu uprooted one and used it as a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
When the owner saw this, he became displeased and went to the Buddha’s presence to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha taught the Dharma in accordance with his disposition; having given rise to a heart of joy, he prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣu here."
When the bhikṣu had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," [the monk replied]. The Buddha said,
"Why did you take flowering and fruiting trees to make tooth-sticks?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to use trees that bear flowers or fruit as tooth-sticks.

When chewing them, one must not do so in a heated room, a lecture hall, a dining hall, or in the presence of the Sangha, nor before one's preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), a stūpa, or an image. One must not cover one’s head or shoulders; rather, one should bared the right shoulder and remain in a secluded place."

If one is inside a monastic dwelling, one should chew while holding it in a vessel; the remnants must not be placed back into the vessel, nor should they be discarded in the vicinity of a stūpa, within the monastic compound, or on regular pathways.
When scraping the tongue, one must not act like those driven by lust; having scraped it, one should wash it and place it in one spot.
If tooth-sticks are difficult to obtain, one should cut off the portion used for chewing and discard it, then wash the remainder and use it again the following day.

Furthermore, at that time, there was a bhikṣu who had nearly finished chewing his tooth-stick; seeing the World-Honored One approaching, he swallowed it out of reverence. However, because the small piece of wood remained stuck in his throat, he was distressed.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit chewing [betel] until it is completely finished; the longest shall be sixteen finger-widths, and the shortest shall be no less than four finger-widths."
When chewing, one should do so in a secluded place; first wash the hands thoroughly, and once the tooth-stick has been used, rinse it with water and discard it.
When using it, one must not act like those engaged in sexual desire; rather, it should be used for the purpose of removing foul odors and impurities from the mouth.
While chewing, one must not swallow the juice; however, if it is swallowed by mistake, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says:
"If you chew the tooth-stick and swallow [the juice], you shall recover."
Having accepted it, one should chew and swallow it.
If there is no tooth-stick, one should wash the mouth with ash, saline earth, brick-dust, gravel, grass, or wood, and then eat.
If one sees a used tooth-stick in a stūpa courtyard or a monastic courtyard, one should pick it up and discard it.
If two people see it together, the junior one should discard it.
If the junior person is lax in their observance of the precepts, they should pick it up and discard it themselves.
The method for using the tooth-stick should be as follows; if it is not so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
Regarding bedding and mats during the final month of spring, when the summer retreat has concluded, and for both visiting and resident bhikṣus—all cases are likewise thus.
Toilet houses for defecation and urination, and tooth-sticks—these two *varga*s.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. For the sake of five benefits, the Tathāgata went on a tour of the monks’ quarters once every five days. He saw that the monks were spreading their robes directly upon the ground while they mended them. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should use mats."

The method of application is as follows: one should use bamboo or reed matting ten cubits long and six cubits wide. When intending to sew robes, one should do so in the lecture hall, the warm chamber, or within the meditation hall. Having spread the matting, one should lay the robe upon it and sew it while sitting with the feet washed.
If it has not been washed, one should sit upon its back with the feet kept away from the surface.
One must not use it to dry grain, clothes, or dyed garments; nor should it be exposed to being scorched by the sun, or defiled by rain, dew, birds, or beasts.
When the sewing is finished, it should be kept inside where it is covered.
If there is no mat, one should sew upon the bed.
If even that is unavailable, one should smear the ground with cow dung in the heated chamber or the lecture hall and sew there.
"When sewing clothes, one should act in this manner; if one does not, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣu returned from sitting in meditation and used his cold feet to press against another bhikṣu, who became startled and felt uneasy.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must establish a partition."

As for the method of construction: one should use bamboo or cloth to erect four corners and provide curtains with cords for tying. When returning from sitting in meditation, one opens them; upon entering, one closes them again.
One must not close the door during the day while it should be raised, nor lower it at night.
Such is the proper method for partitioning off the space.
If one acts otherwise, one violates the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*).

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, for the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One went on inspection to the quarters of the bhikṣus every five days; he saw that the dwellings were leaking and dilapidated, yet remained unrepaired.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Why is this dwelling so leaky and dilapidated?
From this day forward, you should take care of dwellings in this manner."
How is this known?

It is because one has not heard that the rooms were leaking and ruined and left unrepaired; rather, if they were thatched with grass, the grass was patched, and so on, up to if they were plastered with mud, the mud was patched.
From time to time, one should sweep away the cobwebs and dust within the dwelling.
Any unevenness in the floor should be leveled; mouse holes should be filled with mud, and once every half-month, the floor should be smeared with cow dung.
If the ground is dry, it should be smeared with water; if it is damp, apply it directly.

If the ground of an upper story is made a deep blue color, one should wrap the legs of the bed with cloth. One must not light lamps therein, nor practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), nor wear leather sandals. One must not spit on the floor, but should instead use a spittoon.
If it is a middle-level dwelling, one may wash the feet, wash the hands, wash the face, and rinse the alms bowl.
If it is a lower-level dwelling, one may light a lamp, practice walking meditation, wash the hands, feet, and face, and rinse the alms bowl.
“Dwellings should be maintained in this manner; if they are not, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One went to inspect the rooms of the bhikṣus once every five days. Seeing that snot and spittle were dripping from the walls of the rooms and lecture halls onto the ground, the Buddha, though already aware of it, asked intentionally:
“What impure snot and spittle is this, that it has come to such a state?”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should understand the rules regarding spitting and expectoration in this way.
How should they be understood?
Once the mud-plaster on the walls has been applied but not yet fully dried, one must not spit.
If the ground has not been plastered, one should spit in a single spot and rub it with the foot; one must not defile the area everywhere.

If one uses it as a receptacle for earth, one should employ a spittoon; its bottom should be lined with sand, ash, or gravel. It must be discarded frequently so that foul odors or insects do not arise. Wash it clean with pure water, turn it upside down to dry, and one must not chew tooth-sticks inside it.
If one wishes to spit within a meditation hall, one should spit upon the sole of one's leather sandals and wipe the ground; if the floor is covered, one should use a spittoon.

If one wishes to spit while eating, one must not make a loud sound by spitting on the ground, causing fellow monks sitting nearby to feel revulsion; instead, one should spit between one's two feet and rub it away with the feet.
If saliva flows out in great quantity and does not stop, one should go outside to spit it and then return to sit.
If one wishes to spit in the presence of an upādhyāya or ācārya, one should go to a secluded place.
If one wishes to spit within a village settlement, one should spit at the edge of one's feet and rub it away with the feet.
If it is in the form of powder, there is no fault in spitting it out.
If one sees nasal mucus or saliva within a stūpa courtyard or a monastic courtyard, one should rub it away with the feet.
If two people see [the spittoon] together, the junior one should polish it.
If the junior one is lax in observing the precepts, he should polish it himself.
This is how a bhikṣu should act when spitting.
"If one does not act thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣu placed his bowl into a hole; a whirlwind blew it onto the ground where it immediately broke. Hearing the sound of the ghaṇṭā signaling the rice gruel, he went to retrieve the bowl, only to see a heap of broken shards.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you should understand the bowl in this manner."
How is this known?

One must not place it toward a hole, on a bank, or in a precarious location; one must not place it where a door-panel is open or where people pass back and forth; one must not wash it with ash to remove the color; rather, one should wash it with the juice of tree leaves or with coarse sand and water.
When washing, one must not do so on the bank, in a precarious place, on a stone, or on a brick; nor should one wash under a *tāla* tree, a *kapittha* tree, or a *nāri* tree.
When washing the alms bowl, one should sit in a squatting posture or kneel with the right knee on the ground, keeping the bowl at a distance of one span from the floor.
One should first wash the bowls of the upādhyāya and the ācārya, and only then wash one's own.

One must not pour the residual water from one’s own bowl into the bowl of the preceptor (upādhyāya) or the teacher (ācārya); rather, one should use the residual water from the bowl of the preceptor or the teacher to wash one’s own bowl.
When it is dry, one should first collect the bowls of the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya.
When filling them, one should fill the bowls of the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya first.
While filling them, one should sit in a squatting posture (*utkuṭuka*), hold the bowl-bag with a strap fastened around the arm, place it upon the knees, and fill it.
Whether one is lying on a bed or sitting on a bed, the alms-bowl bag should be made of two or three layers.
When wishing to hang the bowl, one should first shake and test whether the peg is firm.
Afterward, place it securely.

If there is no place to hang it, one should place it on a bed; if there is a screen or partition in the center of the room, it may be placed there; or if there is a niche for bowls, it may be placed there, taking care not to let them obstruct one another.
The bowl niche should be provided with a ledge.
One must not take up the bowl in the dark; one must not take it with impure hands; rather, one should wash the hands clean or pick it up by pinching it with leaves.
When taking up the bowl, one hand should grasp two [edges] and the other hand should grasp one; one must not grasp four.
When handing over the bowl, one must not release it abruptly, but should ask:
"Have you grasped it?"
If he says, "I have caught it," then one releases it.

One must not carry an alms bowl containing impure substances; nor should it be used to hold water for shaving the head, washing the hands, feet, or face, for use within the bathhouse, or for washing the private parts.
"One should protect one's bowl as one protects one's own eyes; it should be done in this manner.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus disparaged the gruel; if they saw it was thin, they spoke thus:
"This is not congee; this is the river Yāmunā.
If he sees thick congee, he says: "This is not congee;
it is rice that will break one's teeth."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this time forward, you should understand the gruel in this manner."
How is this known?
When one hears the sound of the gong for eating gruel being struck, one should know whether this is for the gruel of both divisions of the Saṃgha or for that of a single division.
Is this a group of teacher, disciples, and attendants?
Having recognized them, you should depart.
Upon arrival, you must not judge their status based on outward appearance; you should take what you receive according to order, and you must not bypass anyone to take [what is theirs].
When receiving [the food], one must not cover the head, cover the shoulders, or wear leather sandals; rather, one should remove the leather sandals and bare the right shoulder to receive it.
If the person distributing the gruel walks quickly, one may go as far as removing the base of the leather sandals.
If one cannot reach it to retrieve it, one should wait for the time of returning to take it, or have someone else fetch it, or if sitting, take it in successive order.
If the water is shallow, one should not say,
"It is too clear," just as when seeing the reflection of the moon in the remote Pūrṇā River.
If one is strong, one must not say,
"This rice will break my teeth";
one should take it as it is obtained.
"The method for preparing congee should be like this.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, a bhikṣu was practicing meditation on the side of Mount Śakrakoṭi. At that time, another bhikṣu stood before him, and the meditating bhikṣu’s mind could not attain concentration.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you should abide in this manner."

How should one stand in such a manner? One must not stand before a bhikṣu who is sitting in meditation; one must not stand directly in front of the Saṃgha; one must not stand directly in front of the seat of a group of disciples; one must not stand directly in front of one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus. Furthermore, one must not wear leather sandals, nor place hands on the hips, nor cover the head, nor let both arms hang down by the sides. However, there is no offense for one who is ill.
One must not stand before a prostitute, nor before gamblers, taverns, butchers, prisoners, or murderers; one must not stand or remain in secluded places.
"One should abide in the Dharma in this manner;
if one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Volume 34 [and] Volume 35.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;

Part Two of the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* on the Clarification of Dignified Conduct. The Buddha was dwelling at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a bhikṣu wearing a *tāla*-leaf sandal who walked back and forth (*caṅkrama*) in front of a bhikṣu engaged in seated meditation (*dhyāna*), causing the latter’s mind to fail to attain concentration.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣu here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you should perform walking meditation in this manner."

How is this so? One must not walk back and forth (caṅkrama) in front of a bhikṣu engaged in meditation, nor in front of the Saṃgha, nor in front of one’s own disciples, nor in front of an upādhyāya or ācārya, nor in front of an elder bhikṣu.
If one is ill and takes ghee or emetic or purgative medicines, one may walk in the *caṅkrama* (walking path) beforehand.
While walking, one must not turn one's back; rather, one should turn toward the right.
If walking together with one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), one must not go ahead nor walk side by side, but should follow behind.
When turning back, one must not turn first; one should turn last, facing toward the right.

One must not walk for meditation (caṅkrama) in front of a prostitute, in front of gamblers, in front of wine-sellers, in front of butcher shops, in front of prison guards, or in front of executioners.
One must not walk for meditation in deep places; one should walk for meditation in a place that is neither too deep nor too shallow.
"The method for walking meditation (caṅkrama) should be as follows.
If it is not so, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct (īryāpatha).
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus were performing the "camel-sitting" posture within their meditation cells.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said,
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, you must not sit in the camel posture; you should sit in the full lotus position."
If one sits for a long time until becoming exhausted, one should alternate in stretching out one leg at a time; one must not stretch out both legs at once.
When rising to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), one must not sit within the meditation hall with the head covered.
If one is aged or ill, it is permissible to cover half the head and one ear; if in a secluded place or under a tree, covering the head is without offense.
In the presence of an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or an elder (sthavira), a senior bhikṣu must not sit if they are standing.
One must not sit before a courtesan or in a secluded place; one should sit in a place that is neither too deep nor too shallow.
A bhikṣu should sit in this manner; if he does not, he transgresses the rules of decorum.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus lay prostrate, lay on their backs, or lay on their left sides.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call this bhikṣu here. When he had come,
the Buddha asked him:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should lie down in this manner.
How should one lie down?"
One must not lie down like a hungry ghost, nor lie down like an asura, nor lie down like a person of lustful desire. If one lies on one's back, it is the posture of an asura;
if one lies face down upon the ground, it is the posture of a hungry ghost; if one lies on one's left side, it is the posture of a person of lustful desire.

A bhikṣu should lie down with his body turned as a lion, the king of beasts, looks back; when spreading out [his bedding], he is not permitted to spread it on his left side, but should spread it on his right, with his head toward the robe-rack.
He must not point his feet toward his upādhyāya, ācārya, or elder bhikṣus.

One must not lie down at the beginning of the first watch of the night by merely sighing and exclaiming "Ah! in exhaustion; rather, one should dwell in right mindfulness of one's own karma until the middle watch, when one may lie down. One should lie on the right side like a lion king, with the two feet stacked, the mouth closed, the tongue pressed against the upper palate, the right hand used as a pillow, and the left hand extended along the body.

Without abandoning mindfulness and wisdom, one should maintain the perception of rising and not sleep until sunrise; when the latter part of the night arrives, one should rise and sit upright to contemplate one's own practice. However, there is no offense if one falls into a deep sleep at night and does not consciously perceive the turning of the body.
If one is old or ill, or if there is an ulcer or abscess on the right side, there is no offense.
This is the proper manner for a bhikṣu to lie down; if he does not act in this way, he transgresses the rules of decorum.
Robes, belts, curtains, and screens; Dwellings, as well as spittle and saliva;
Alms bowls, niches, gruel, walking, and staying; Sitting and lying down—these are the three *vargās*.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus closed the door of the monastery and sat together conversing. When visiting bhikṣus arrived and knocked on the door, they did not hear the call and thus leaped over the wall to enter.
An elder bhikṣu asked,
"Venerable one, from where have you entered?
He replied:
"He entered by leaping over the wall.
An elder bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason did you enter by leaping over the wall?"
The visiting bhikṣu said,
"Why did you close the door when I called out, yet not respond?
Thus they disputed with one another.
They went to inform the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not speak while the door is closed, nor may you enter by leaping over walls.
From this day forward, visiting bhikṣus should act in this manner, and resident bhikṣus should act in this manner."
How is this so? When a visiting bhikṣu travels, he should carry a door-bolt, a water-strainer, and a needle-case; if one companion possesses these, there is no offense for anyone.
As for the phrase "down to none at all," this refers to the entire assembly being culpable.
If there is a sick person on the road, one should carry their robes and bowl for them; one must not go far ahead, but should instead support and escort them along.
If one is unable to walk, one should borrow a vehicle to transport them.
If there is dew or moisture on the road, the younger person should go in front;
if there is fear of bandits, tigers, or wolves, the elder should remain in the center.
If one wishes to cause bandits to give rise to a mind of compassion, the elders should walk at the front.

If one encounters a caitya by the side of the road while passing through a village, one should proceed according to the usual path; one must not leave the road to circumambulate it to the left or right.

When wishing to stay overnight at dusk, one should first dispatch two young bhikṣus to go ahead and seek lodging, as well as non-timely drinks, oil for anointing the feet, food before the meal, and food after the meal.
One who is departing should fasten the hooks and ties of their robes and inform [the community] that they are entering the village at an improper time. Upon returning, they should report:
"I have reached my lodging.
If there is water from a pond or a well, one should bathe, fasten the ties of the robes, and enter after informing each other in turn.
If you wish to drink stone-honey syrup (*śarkarā-pāna*), you should drink it outside so as not to cause people to suspect that a renunciant is eating at an improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*).
You must not enter carrying it; rather, you should divide the contents among your robes and carry them in slowly together with the others.
If one has received permission by being told, "Enter as you see fit," then those who enter later without announcing themselves incur no offense.
One must not depart by another path; however, if there is a covered path along the way, there is no offense.
If there is a vihāra within a village, one should go there; if it is in an araṇya, one should likewise wash oneself in a nearby pond or well before entering.
One must not carry burdens; rather, one should share out the robes and remove sandals and staffs. If there is a caitya, one should circumambulate it to the right.
One must not enter with loud or boisterous speech.
Upon seeing an elder bhikṣu, one must not exclaim:
"Ho! Ho!"
"You remain here for this reason.
Born from within this very place, you die within this very place; you shall not escape being food for this jackal.
An elder bhikṣu must not say:
"Alas! Alas!
Like a prisoner who has been released from his shackles, he will not be seen again for four or five years."
The visiting bhikṣu must not say:
"How many years have you [been ordained]?
I ought to receive this room."
One must not ask:
"Who will provide the morning meal and the afternoon meal tomorrow? Will there be good food?
A senior bhikṣu must not speak while closing the door.
If one wishes to abandon the subsequent work of plastering or to perform other tasks, one should employ a monastery attendant, a novice, a *karmadāna*, a gatekeeper, or one who closes the gates.
A visiting bhikṣu must not enter by leaping over a wall; he should enter by opening the door with a door-hook.
Once he has been called in through the opened gate, the resident bhikṣus should ask:
"How many years of seniority do you have?"
One should answer,
"I am so many years old.
The senior bhikṣu says:
"If one has been [in the order] for such a number of years, one receives such a bed and bedding.
One should ask about the locations for the large and small excretions; one must not wait until the last moment to inquire.
Next, one should ask about the regulations of the Sangha, and the senior bhikṣus should say:

"The Sangha has established all these restrictions: do not go to the house of so-and-so because the *pātra-nikubjana* (turning-over-of-the-bowl) rite has been performed there; do not go to the house of so-and-so because their dogs are vicious;
do not go to the house of so-and-so because they are faithless. When a visiting bhikṣu rises early, he must not immediately depart to beg for alms;
rather, he should ask: "Are there meals before or after the midday meal available at this residence?"
The senior bhikṣu should say:
"Venerable one, do not go for alms; begging for food is wearying and may not be as you wish. Here, there is both morning and afternoon food."
If the traveling companions have already departed, one must not say:
"Venerable sir!
Since the merchants have already left, you can still catch up."
One should say:
"Venerable sir, please wait a moment; you shall have companions in a short while."
"If there is an urgent matter and one must certainly depart, one should provide provisions for the journey and entrust the traveling companion with instructions.
Such is the proper rule for both visiting and resident bhikṣus."
"If one does not act in this way, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus washed their feet and engaged in worldly conversation while playing with the water.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should wash your feet according to the method of Śāriputra."

The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. At that time, Śāriputra put on his robes for entering a village and, carrying his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food in due order. His deportment was dignified and composed as he came and went, looked about, bent and stretched, and lowered or raised himself; he wore his robes and held his bowl while guarding his sense faculties so that his mind was not distracted by external things, appearing like one who had attained the moistening grace of the sublime Dharma.
Having seen this, the brahmin thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, maintains his dignified deportment while in public, but once he reaches a secluded place, he will surely have no restraint; I shall follow him and observe."
"If you see me acting with negligence, you must strike my head with your hand.
He then followed behind him.
Thereupon, Śāriputra maintained his dignified deportment without change, whether in the village or in the forest hermitage (āraṇya).
Having arrived at his dwelling, he placed his alms bowl in one spot, shook out his saṃghāṭī robe, folded it, and set it in its usual place.

He spread out his sitting mat, took up his foot-washing board and water jar, and sat down near them. Then, taking his leather sandals, he shook them out and placed them on the ground; next, he took a cloth to wipe his calves, then picked up the sandals again, joined their soles together, and wiped them with the cloth.
Next, moisten a cloth with water and wipe the nose, the lacing loops, and the heel-strap of one sandal; next, wipe its sole.
Then, wipe the second sandal in the same manner.
Finally, wipe the area where the toes were grasped by the hand, and next wipe the area of the heel.
He wipes himself again, and does the same for the second time.
Next, he washes the towel, wrings it out, and hangs it up to dry;
then he washes his hands. Having washed his hands, he pours water with his right hand and washes his left thigh with his left hand, then his right thigh, and finally his feet.
Having seen this, the brahmin felt great joy and said:
"Venerable sir, since you are so pure, even this leftover water should be drinkable; the methods for purifying water followed by us brahmins do not equal this purity."
At that time, Śāriputra, taking advantage of the brahmin’s arising of a joyful mind, preached the Dharma for him, whereby he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"Excellent!
Because the Brahmin saw that Śāriputra’s deportment was pure as he washed his feet, he gave rise to a heart of joy, even to this extent.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"It is not only today that he rejoices; in past lives as well, it was just so, as explained at length in the *Jātaka-sūtra*.
At that time, the son of the elder was Śāriputra;
at that time, the thief was this present brahmin."
At that time, the devas, having seen this, spoke in verse:
"Pure and with excellent deportment, Through this one gains wholesome benefit;
Just as reflections appear in clear water, Training in deportment is most supreme."
"Coming with a malicious mind, yet rejoicing upon seeing [the host], one who does not train in virtuous deportment will surely be harmed by thieves.

"If a bhikṣu returns from a village, he should remove his village-wearing robes, shake them out, fold them, and place them in their usual spot. He should put on his park-wearing robes, arrange his sitting mat and foot-washing board, keep the water jar close at hand, and wipe the dust from his feet with a cloth."

Next, take the leather sandals and join their soles together; hold a cloth and wipe them. Next, dip the cloth and wipe the nose-strap and the lacing of one sandal; next, wipe the heel-base, and then wipe the second sandal in the same manner.
Then take back the first cloth you grasped; first wipe between the toes of the feet, next wipe the heels, and do the same for the second person.
Next, wash the cloth, wring it out, and hang it to dry so that dust does not settle upon it and insects do not eat it; only then wash your hands.

If the water vessel is on the right side, one should first wash the left thigh, then the right thigh, and finally the feet. One must not rub the feet with the hand holding the water; rather, one hand should pour the water while the other hand rubs them.
If there are two people, one shall pour and the other shall wash; they must not use excessive water and discard it, but should use it with careful consideration.
They must not cover their heads or their right shoulders, but should sit with the right shoulder bared.
While washing one's feet, one must not practice meditation, sleep, engage in the contemplation of impurity, or recite scriptures; once finished, one should withdraw and not obstruct others.
If one is the very last to wash, one may recite scriptures without fault.
If the water is exhausted, one must not leave it as it is in silence; one should inform the person in charge of the water to replenish it.
If that is not possible, one should even personally add the water of a single *kumbha* (bath-jar) so that at least one person may have the use of it.
"The method for washing the feet should be as follows.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus washed their feet, put on leather sandals while their feet were still wet, and then removed the dyed leather sandals to put them on their feet, thereby soiling the monastic beds and mats.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣus here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when washing your feet, you should act in this manner:
you must stand your sandals upright so that your feet may dry, and only then put on the sandals.
If many people are waiting, you should wring out the water with your hands and wipe them with a cloth before putting on the sandals."
One must not step with wet feet upon the clean and well-prepared ground of the Sangha; one should enter only after it has been dried.
If it is a place where only a single person washes, one should not wipe it dry, but rather wait until it is dry before putting on leather sandals.

One should protect against dust and soil; if one urgently wishes to sit in meditation, recite the sūtras, or practice walking meditation, one may even wipe away the dust with a handkerchief or a cloth before departing.
The method for washing the feet should be as follows.
"If it were not so, one would transgress the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the Saṃgha prepared a mandala of pure water. The bhikṣus took water from it to wash their feet, hands, and faces, and to rinse their bowls. Having finished using it, they tied a cord around the mouth of the jar, sealed the opening, and entered the village to beg for alms.
Later, a visiting bhikṣu arrived and spoke with resentment and displeasure, saying:
"Why did you seal the clean water and the hut with a seal before departing?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, during the spring months, water should be stored in this manner:
whether in large jars, small jars, or bottles, their mouths should be covered with clean materials and secured by tying them with rope."

If one makes a cover from tile, stone, or wood to place over it, one should place a water-scooping vessel inside; within that water, one should put *pāṭalī* flowers, *campaka* flowers, and *sumana* flowers, and so forth, to make the water fragrant and pleasant.
Regarding famous waters:

such as the Śoṇa River at Pāṭaliputra, the hot springs at Rājagṛha, the waters of the Buddha’s walking pool at Vārāṇasī, the Gaṅgā River in the kingdom of Campā, the honey-water at Śrāvastī, the cascading waterfall at Śāketa, the honey-water at Saṃkāśya, and the Pārāvatī River at Mathurā—one is not permitted to wash one's hands, feet, face, or alms bowl with such waters.
If one is ill and requires water, one should provide a full bowl.
If one intends to serve water during a meal, one should first purify oneself with water, wash one's hands, and rinse the vessel before serving the water.
The person receiving the water should protect their left hand to keep it clean while receiving the water; if the hand becomes soiled, they should wash it.
If they receive the water using a leaf as a vessel, they should also use the leaf to wipe away any grease from their mouth.
When drinking, one must not let the lips be submerged; one must not allow the rim of the vessel to touch the forehead; rather, one should drink while supporting the vessel against the lips.
When drinking, one must not drink it all at once; one should leave a small amount remaining, rinse it out, and then discard it from the opening of the mouth.

The person who distributes water should carefully protect the clean vessels. If he sees that the water has reached the lips or touched the forehead, he should set it aside in one place, marking it with grass so that others may know it is impure; if it can be purified by washing, he may distribute it again.

If one consumes food or drink at an improper time, the person serving the food or drink must first wash their hands and the vessel before serving; the person receiving it should likewise wash their hands before receiving it.
If they do not wash them, they should receive it by placing a leaf or a clean cloth beneath the bottom of the vessel as described above, until the point of the mouth, after which it is discarded.
If one drinks while in the bathhouse, one should hold a leaf beneath the vessel to support its base against the lips while drinking; the rest is as explained above.
When drinking while in the meditation hall, if the floor is covered, one should hold the vessel to receive the spilt liquid.
If they sit at a distance from one another, one person shall distribute the vessels and another shall distribute the water; the rest is as explained above.
This is called "excellent water"; it must not be used for washing hands, feet, or the face, nor for rinsing the bowl, nor should it be used for any other purpose or discarded.
If there is a need for robes or alms bowls, one may temporarily borrow them for use and must repay them.
If it is water, one may use it freely at will; taking it thus incurs no offense.
Water should be used in this manner; if not, one violates the rules of dignified conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dharma*).
The Buddha was staying at the Ambaṭṭha Grove of Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“I pray that you will allow the bhikṣus to bathe in a heated chamber; it can dispel cold and dampness, enabling them to dwell in peace and comfort.
The Buddha said, “I allow bathing in a heated chamber.”

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One permitted bathing in a heated hall. At that time, when the six group-of-six bhikṣus heard the gong signaling the bath, they entered the sauna first; having piled up firewood and charcoal, they closed the door and remained there to induce perspiration.
The outside bhikṣus asked for the door to be opened, but he refused to open it, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
Wait here until the fire has ignited."
He then used a great deal [of fuel].
When the firewood, charcoal, sawdust, and water were all exhausted, he finally opened the door and called out,
saying, "Venerable elders, you may enter."
After the bhikṣus had entered, they closed the door from the outside.
The bhikṣus, distressed by the heat, called out for the door to be opened, to which [the person inside] replied:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Stay here and take a sweat-bath; it will cure your scabies.
He then used up all the water and sand outside, covered the ground with a vessel, and only then opened the door, saying, "Venerable sir, you may come out."
Having emerged, he was distressed by the heat and sought water. The Buddha spoke to him again:
"Venerable one!
Use it sparingly; as the World-Honored One has taught, even water should be used with measured moderation."
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"The bathhouse should be constructed in this manner, and the method of bathing should be as follows."

The bathhouse should be constructed as either square or circular; it must be provided with a door facing a specific direction. According to the rules for orientation, the interior should be wider than the exterior. One or two openings should be installed to allow for the passage of smoke.

The interior of the house should have its floor paved with bricks or stones to form a hearth; this floor should be wide at the base and narrow at the top, situated half an elbow’s length above the ground, with a chimney for the passage of smoke and fire tongs placed alongside it.
If the hearth is on the right side, place the door leaf on the left;
if it is on the left side, place the door leaf on the right.
Make the door bolt short so that it may be easily opened and closed.
First, one should construct a robe-house, equipped with dragon-tooth pegs for hanging robes.
When intending to bathe, one should have a monastery attendant first sweep the dust and cobwebs from within the room, sprinkle it with water, and clean it thoroughly.

One should prepare firewood, charcoal, cauldrons, pots, jars, and basins; first place the firewood and charcoal, and then strike the *gandī* bell. One must not light the fire too early; rather, one should wait until the fire has burned down before striking the *gandī*.
When the *gandī* is struck, one should ascertain whether it is for the bathing of the entire Saṃgha, for the bathing of a group of disciples, or for a separate residence;
one should go according to the specific matter.
If it is for the bathing of the entire [Saṃgha], one should go in order, each person tying their robe with a waistband as a marker and placing it on the robe rack.
When entering, one must not enter with both arms swinging; rather, one should enter with one hand covering the front. One person enters while another exits.
If someone enters after others are already inside, those who entered first should yield their place to them.
One must not pass over vessels or above elder bhikṣus, but should enter slowly.
If one’s upādhyāya or ācārya is inside, one must not wait outside saying,
“When will you come out?”
"One should strip off one's clothes and enter to rub and wash [the body].
If one wishes to rub another person, one should inform the Upādhyāya or Ācārya; if one has informed them beforehand, there is no offense."
If the fire is intense, the youth should stay near it;
if the fire is weak, the elder should stay near it.
One must use water slowly and carefully, ensuring that no splashes soil those nearby.

When a disciple is massaging [the body], they must not raise both hands at once; rather, they should first have them massage one arm while covering the front with one hand, and once that is finished, proceed to massage the other arm.
Having drunk water internally, one should close the door and sit until the body perspires.
One should apply oil using either a small cup or the hand; the same applies to medicinal powders.
If a donor says,
"Give as much as you wish," one should calculate the amount of water needed, perhaps using a jar as a measure.
Regarding the division of usage, one should use only what corresponds to the vessel one has received and must not use an excess portion for others.
If it is said, "Each person shall provide their own water," [then one may do so].
Regarding this, those who have water may enter, while those who do not may not.
If a disciple should say:
"Preceptor, Ācārya, please enter alone; I shall provide the water."
One should also exercise due consideration when using it.
If a lay follower (upāsaka) or a park-keeper says, "Please enter;
I shall give you water," [one may do so].
"Even so, one should still use resources with moderation.
If one is near pond water, it is permitted to use it as one wishes without fault.
However, bathing naked in the open air is not allowed."
If the water reaches only to the waist or the armpits, one may use it without fault;
if one sits in the water up to the navel, that is also permissible.
Having emerged, one may take one's own clothes and put them on, or properly arrange another's clothes and depart.
If, after bathing, one wishes to depart immediately, one should inform the attendant of the monastery and have them lift up the bathing vessels.
If a bhikṣu arrives later and says, "Venerable sir, you may go;
I shall lift them myself," [one should comply].
Those [who have finished] should depart.
The latter should put away their belongings, lift up the items, and cover the fire.
The method for bathing should be as follows.
"If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the World-Honored One went to visit the monks' quarters once every five days. Seeing that the utensils for the clean kitchen were scattered in disorder everywhere, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"What are these utensils that are so disarrayed?"
The Buddha then said:
"From this day forward, you must not allow utensils to be left lying haphazardly like this.
Whether it be the *māmādi* (steward) or the month-steward (*māsika*), they shall have the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) or the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) clear them away."

If the *māmāte* (steward) or the month-keeper does not take personal initiative, they should instead have a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable) arrange them; whether they be copper, iron, cauldrons, pots, or pans, they should have the *kappiya-kāraka* wash them clean, coat them with clay, and place them inside a clean kitchen building; the same applies to earthenware cauldrons, pans, and pots.
Cover the ground with bricks and tiles to weigh it down; wooden basins and wooden ladles should likewise be washed clean before being lifted up.

If there are bamboo mats or sitting mats, they should be sun-dried and stored in a bamboo chest. Winnowing baskets and rice-strainers should also be hung up so that insects do not eat them. Rice boxes and rice scoops should be washed clean and hung up; bags, bundles, and water-strainers should also be hung up so that insects do not consume them.
The pestle and mortar used for pounding medicine must not be left on the ground; they should be washed clean and stored in their usual place.

One must not overlook holes or leaks in the kitchen or clean rooms where food is prepared; if they are thatched with grass, they should be patched with grass, and even if they are covered with mud, they should be repaired with mud.
Those that are worn through should be patched; they should be swept out regularly.

When burning firewood inside, it should be gathered and set aside in one place. The dyeing vessels and the basins used for holding dye must not be discarded after use; they should be thoroughly washed, repaired, and covered, then returned to their usual place.
When the wooden tub used for washing clothes has been finished with, it should also be thoroughly washed and placed back in its usual location.
As for the clothesline, one must not leave it lying on the ground in a tangled mess after use; rather, it should be wound up and placed in its usual location.

Chisels, axes, saws, chisels, spades, mattocks, ladders, and stools—these are the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters; having used them, one should put them away in their usual place so that those who need them later may find them easily and not be subjected to fatigue or hardship.
If it is required, it shall be given; if two people request it at the same time, it shall first be given to the senior monk (*upādhyāya*).
If the senior monk has used it for a long time while the junior monk has used it only briefly, it shall first be given to the junior monk.
If both persons have minor needs, one should first give [the items] to the senior monk (*upādhyāya*).
Such is the proper method for utensils.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were living together in a single room. Then, one bhikṣu took his own robe from a robe-rack, pulling another’s robe down to the ground. Later, other bhikṣus went out at night to relieve themselves and stepped upon the robes with their feet.
The owner of the robe sought it but could not find it; eventually, he found it on the ground.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, robes should be handled in this manner:
if many people reside together in a single room, each person should fold their robe and place leaves inside it."

If another's robe is on the rack, one should fasten it with a waist-cord; furthermore, one must not wrap one's own robe with the robes of one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), but rather cover the robes of the preceptor or teacher with one's own robe.
If there is much dust and soil during the spring, one should cover it with one's own robe.
If the ground is damp during the summer, one should place one's own robe underneath.
One must not allow dust and soil to remain in the room; one should frequently sprinkle water and smear the floor with cow dung.
One must not hold one's robes while grasping a spittoon, a vessel for excrement or urine, or leather sandals; nor should one store refuse or pick up cow dung.
If the robes become stained with grease or filth, they should be washed, dyed, and sewn frequently; when looking at one's robes, one should regard them as being like skin.
The rules for robes should be as follows; if not so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
Regarding visiting monks and resident monks, washing the feet and wiping the feet, the method for pure water and drinking, the warm bathhouse and bathing as well.
The Rules for the Clean Kitchen and Robes.
The fourth section concludes.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the village monks and the forest-dwelling monks shared a common almsgiving. The forest-dwelling monks used to arrive at the regular hour, but the village monks suddenly struck the *gandī* bell early and ate.
An araṇyaka bhikṣu arrived just as the time for the meal was approaching;
he asked, "Has the ghaṇṭā been struck yet?
They replied:
"We have finished eating.
Then the āraṇyaka departed; at dawn the next day, he returned early and took all the food with him.
When the village monks came to seek food, the attendants said:
"The forest-dwelling bhikṣus have already taken it all away.
The village-dwelling bhikṣus said,
"Elders, why did you get up so early and take all the food?"
The forest-dweller said,
"Why did you rise early to strike the *gandī* for the meal instead of waiting for me?
The two argued together and went to where the Buddha was, reporting the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, forest-dwelling bhikṣus should act in this way, and village-dwelling bhikṣus should act in this way.
In what way? [He continued:]..."

If forest-dwelling bhikṣus and village-dwelling bhikṣus share a common almsgiving, the village-dwelling bhikṣus must not rise early to strike the *gandī* for the morning meal, the afternoon meal, or meals offered by invitation; they should instead wait for the forest-dwellers.
An araṇya bhikṣu must not say, "I will go slowly; you should wait for me.
He should go first.
If someone is asked to invite a portion of food on behalf of others, or if they are instructed to reserve a seat, the bhikṣus from the village should ask:
"Has the forest-dwelling bhikṣu arrived yet?
If someone is asked to welcome food on their behalf, or if they are instructed to reserve a seat, they should indicate the location.
If a lay follower (upāsaka) invites the Saṃgha, the village monks should say to the forest-dwelling monks: "Venerable ones!
Please come early tomorrow; such-and-such a person has invited us for the meal before and after the noon meal; do not go begging for food elsewhere."

"Upon hearing this, the forest-dwelling bhikṣu should come early; once he has arrived, if the food is not yet cooked, he must not remain waiting, but should instead pay homage at the stūpa, recite the sūtras, and inquire about the Dharma."
The village-dwelling bhikṣus should first place water in the cauldron and light the fire; they should wait until it has boiled before adding the rice.
However, the forest-dwelling bhikṣus might not be able to come due to dangers from spirits, water, fire, or bandits, and thus the rice would be left behind.
If the food has already been prepared and the donor wishes to strike the *gandī* bell, one should say:
"Long-lived one!
The sun is still early; you may wait for the *āraṇyaka* to arrive."
If the time for the meal is approaching, one should strike the *ghanṭī*.
Those in the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) should use the shadow of a tree or a wall as a reference; thus they shall know whether it is early or late in the day and should come accordingly.
If one is to come from the future, one should leave a seat for them.
This should likewise be done if one is preparing food in an āraṇya (forest hermitage).
A bhikṣu of the āraṇya should not disparage a bhikṣu from a village by saying:
"You must have a tongue that lacks flavor and yet remain here.
One should praise him, saying:
"You dwell in the village, teaching and transforming through the Dharma, acting as a protector for the Dharma, and providing shelter and protection for us."
A monk living in a village should not disparage a forest-dweller by saying:
"You dwell in a forest hermitage because you hope for fame and profit; even deer and wild beasts dwell in forest hermitages."
"You have been in the forest hermitage from morning until evening for no more than a few years or months.
One should praise him, saying:

"You have left the villages and settlements to dwell in the forest hermitage, contemplating in solitude the supreme practice you revere. This is a place difficult to inhabit; that you can reside here and bring the mind and its faculties to rest is truly remarkable."
"An araṇyaka should act in this way, and a village-dwelling bhikṣu should act in this way.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time some resident bhikṣus were quarreling verbally when a visiting bhikṣu arrived and prostrated by touching their feet.
On a later day, a visiting bhikṣu came and again paid his respects, asking:
"How many days has it been since you arrived?
He replied:
"Four or five days," the senior bhikṣu said.
"You have been here for that many days; why did you not see me?"
He replied, "I have already paid my respects; it was because you elders were quarreling that you did not see me.
The senior bhikṣus said:
"Why do you prostrate toward me when you see me arguing with you?
He replied,
"Why do you not look at my prostration while you are arguing with me?"
The two then began to quarrel and went to where the Buddha was; eventually, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should pay homage in this manner, and you should exchange greetings in this manner."
What is meant by "prostrating in this manner" and "inquiring after one's health in this manner"?
When another person is engaged in a dispute or conversation, one must not prostrate; instead, one should simply lower the head in a slight gesture of respect.
If the other person stops [speaking], one should perform a formal prostration.

When building a house or performing plastering work, one should not pay homage. This applies to all such labors: when fumigating alms bowls, washing clothes, boiling dye, dying clothes, sewing clothes, bathing, anointing the body with oil, washing the feet, washing the hands and face, washing the bowl, paying homage at a stupa, eating, swallowing food, applying eye salve, reading scriptures, reciting scriptures, copying scriptures, walking in meditation (caṅkrama), ascending or descending from a terrace, using the toilet, not wearing robes, or wearing only a single *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*—in all these instances, one must not pay homage.

One should not perform prostrations in the dark; one should not perform prostrations while the scriptures are being bestowed; nor should one perform prostrations when wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, when putting on robes, or when walking quickly.

One must not perform prostrations while covering the head, covering the right shoulder, or wearing leather sandals; one must not prostrate to the knees, the feet, or the shins, but should instead perform prostrations by touching the feet.
If the person before you has sores on their feet, one should protect them from being stepped upon or touched.
The person receiving the prostration must not remain silent like a dumb sheep; they should exchange greetings with the other.
When inquiring after someone's well-being, one must not speak as follows:
"Where can one find much delicious food and drink?
One should instead ask:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you at ease and happy?
Have you not been fatigued or distressed by the journey?
The visiting bhikṣu should ask thus.
"Who is the senior monk of the Saṃgha?
Who are the second and third senior monks?
One should then pay homage by touching their feet.
The resident bhikṣu should ask:
"Venerable sir, how many years of seniority do you have?
If the visiting bhikṣu is junior, he should offer him a seat and have him sit.
If there are [such things], one should provide them with food before the meal, food after the meal, oil for anointing the feet, and non-timely beverages.
This should be done for both visiting bhikṣus and resident bhikṣus.
"If it is not done in this way, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus addressed one another with the secular titles of "uncle," "aunt," "elder brother," and "younger brother."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should address one another with greetings in this manner.
When speaking with an elder,
you must not address him as 'Uncle,' 'Father,' or 'Mahallaka.'"
One should say:
"Vāruḍatā. When speaking with one's mother, one must not say: [the following].
If she says, "Mother! Grandmother!", one should reply: "Paruhite."
When speaking with one's elder brother, one must not say,
"Elder brother"; rather,
one should say:
When speaking with one's sister,
one must not say, "Pabbā. Instead, one should say, "Bhaludā."
One should say:
"Vāruṇī. When speaking together with those of higher status, one must not say:
"Vatanda," one should say: "Upasanga."
When speaking with an ācārya, one must not say "baddhanta"; rather,
one should say:
“Ācārya. If there are many ācāryas, one should say: “Ācārya So-and-so.”
When conversing with those of equal or lower rank, one may address them by their given name, as "Gautama," or as "Vassaja.
When conversing with those of higher rank, one should address them as "Bhaddanta."
Whether it be an *āyuṣmat* or an *ācārya*,
if someone calls out, one must not respond by asking,
"Which path? (or "Whom do you call?").
"What is it? When the preceptor calls, one should respond: "Yes."
If the ācārya calls you, you should say:
"Yes. If an elder (sthavira) calls you, you should likewise say: [“Yes”].
"Very well.
When a junior calls out, one should respond:
"Why do you call?"
If a woman or a man calls out, one should say:
"Why do you call?
When someone asks:
"What are the names of your preceptor and preceptor-teacher?
One must not state the names of the preceptor and preceptor-teacher directly; rather, one should say:
"Because of the causal conditions of their meaning, their names are so-and-so."
"Speech regarding the Dharma should be like this.
If it is not like this, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a group of Kṣatriyas gathered, intending to discuss certain matters; Nanda and Upananda arrived first and took their seats.
At that time, the people complained, saying,
"We have gathered now wishing to discuss certain matters, yet this śramaṇa obstructs our deliberations.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and so on until the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you should enter the assembly of kṣatriyas in this manner.
How should one enter the assembly of kṣatriyas?
If there is a matter or occasion requiring you to go, you should first inform those of high rank therein of your purpose for coming.”
If it is said,
"You may come," one should go.
One must not enter carrying a parasol or wearing leather sandals; upon entering, one should remove them and place them in one spot.
One must not say:
"Are you enjoying yourself, sir?"
If he points out a seat, one should sit; however, one must not disparage or praise military formations or methods of combat.
If one sees excellent archery, one must not offer praise, but should instead say:
"The Kṣatriya caste is of noble lineage; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is always born into these two families."
In the families of kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas there are two kinds of wheels:
the wheel of the Dharma and the wheel of power. It is because those who have left the household life rely on the protection of the wheel of power that they are able to find peace for themselves.
"Once you have finished speaking on the matter of desire and existence, you should depart.
When entering an assembly of kṣatriyas, you should act in this manner.
If you do not act thus, you transgress the rules of dignified conduct."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a multitude of brahmins had gathered, and Nanda and Upananda arrived first and took their seats.
The brahmins spoke with resentment, saying, "We wish to engage in some discussion, yet these śramaṇas are obstructing and interrupting our business."
The Buddha continued, saying:
"From this day forward, you should enter the assembly of brahmins in this manner.
