If there is some business that requires you to go there, you must first inform the senior members of the situation; if they grant permission, you may proceed."
Before arriving, one should set aside the parasol and remove the leather sandals; one must not wait until having seen [the teacher] before withdrawing them.
Furthermore, one must not go there borrowing a parasol or leather sandals, nor should one say:
"Are you well?"

"O man! You must not disparage or praise the deva-temples, nor should you mock the Brahmins because of their great pride; otherwise, you shall be reborn among the six realms of existence—whether as a chicken, a pig, a dog, a jackal, a camel, an ass, or in hell."
One should say:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was born into two types of lineages: either a Kṣatriya family or a Brāhmaṇa family."
"If you wish to engage in discussion, you should depart after having finished speaking.
Such is the proper dharma for entering the assembly of brahmins.
If one does not act thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. ... [the text continues] until the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, when entering among the assembly of householders, if there is a reason for you to go, you should proceed as far as showing them a seat and sitting upon it.”
One must not say:
"You wash your hands and feet clean and sit in your shop, yet you deceive people with light scales and small measures; this is worse than being a thief."
One should say:
"There are two kinds of wheels:
the wheel of Dharma and the wheel of food. Only after obtaining the wheel of food does one turn the wheel of Dharma."
As the Blessed One said when addressing the bhikṣus:
“The brahmins and householders provide robes, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick; their benefit is very great, and this is a difficult task to perform.”
"I rely upon you all to practice the holy life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata and cross over the stream of birth and death; all of this is due to the grace of your faith.
Having said this, he departed as soon as he had finished speaking.
"One should enter among the assembly of laypeople in this manner.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and so forth, until the Buddha said:
"One should enter among the assemblies of non-Buddhists in this manner. How so?
Having been shown a seat, one should sit; one must not disparage or praise their views."
Furthermore, one must not disparage them by saying,
"You all hold wrong views, lack faith, and have no sense of shame or remorse.
Instead, one should praise their actual virtues:
"It is a most difficult matter for you to be able to leave the household life, to untie your bonds, to cast off secular attire, and to settle your minds in empty seclusion.
Thus one may speak of all such actual facts; one must not speak of their faults. If one wishes to discuss a matter, one should depart immediately after having spoken.
"When entering among the assemblies of non-Buddhists, the proper method should be as follows.
If one does not act thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and so forth, until the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, you should enter the assembly in this manner.
How should one enter the assembly?
If there is a matter to be discussed among the Sangha, it should be settled and resolved outside; one must not enter the midst of the Sangha to settle it.”
If a matter is difficult to resolve, one should inform the upādhyāya and ācārya.
If the matter does not require adjudication by the Saṃgha, one should tell them to desist.

If the matter must be brought before the Saṃgha and the person who raises it is trustworthy, one should explain to them the matters that are harmonious, in accordance with the Dharma, and in accordance with the Vinaya.
Once the Upādhyāya and Ācārya have granted their permission, you should go before the senior monks of the Saṃgha and say:
"I wish to say something; will you grant me leave?

The senior monk should examine the speech of the person [seeking permission], and so on, until the time of entering the assembly. You must not wear leather sandals, nor cover your head or your right shoulder; rather, you should remove your leather sandals, bare your right shoulder, and enter the assembly.
Entering the assembly, one should act in this manner.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
[Whether in] an araṇya or a village, one should pay homage at the feet and exchange greetings.
They call out to one another: the kṣatriyas, the brāhmaṇas, the householders, and the assemblies of outsiders, sages, and noble ones.
The fifth chapter (varga) is concluded.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having removed their inner robes within the monastery grounds, went naked to seek their inner robes in the village; and having come out from the village, they removed the inner robes they had obtained in the village and went naked to seek their inner robes within the monastery grounds.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"One should wear the robes in this manner.
How should one wear the robes in this manner?..."
When about to enter a village, one must not remove the inner garment worn within the monastery grounds and seek to enter the village while naked;
nor must one remove the inner garment worn for entering the village and seek the inner garment worn within the monastery grounds while naked.

When about to enter a village, one should first take the inner garment for entering villages and keep it close at hand; one must not put on the village-wearing robe and then remove the inner garment from beneath it in the park. One should put on one side of the garment while removing the other side accordingly.
When departing from a village, one should remove the inner garment worn for entering a village; the same applies when putting on the inner garment used while in a garden.
This is the proper method for wearing the inner garment.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wished to enter a village; they removed their park robes, put on a single inner garment, and sought out their village robes.
Upon returning from the village, they removed their village robes, put on a single inner garment, and sought out their park robes.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should wear your robes in this manner.

You must not remove your park robes to put on a single inner garment while seeking your village robe; rather, you should first take your village robe close to you, remove your park robe, fold it up, and place it in its usual location, and only then put on your village robe."
Having emerged from the village, one should take the park robes, place them close to oneself, shake out the village robes, and put them away in their usual place.
This is the proper method for putting on the park robes.
"If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Upānanda entered a village; he walked with his robes trailing, soiling them with mud, tearing them where they caught on hooks, and piercing them where they encountered thorns.
They passed through a narrow alleyway, jostling one another.
A disciple spoke with resentment, saying:
"We have worked hard to wash, dye, and sew these robes, yet they are not protected."
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when entering a village, you should wear your robes in this manner."
How is this so? It is because one must not allow one's robes to be dragged through a village until they become worn and torn.
If one leaves the village during the spring season, one should fold the robes and carry them on the shoulder.
Having approached the vicinity of the village, if there is a pool or a pond, he shall wash his hands and feet, put on his robes, fasten the ties, and enter.
If there is no water, he shall wipe the dust from his feet with tree leaves or grass, and then put them on and enter.
If it is winter, one should go wearing one's robes; if one encounters running elephants, horses, or carriages, one should remain upwind so as not to be defiled by dust, soil, or mud.
If one encounters hooks, thorns, or brambles, one must not pull them out or tear them away; if a road or alleyway is narrow, one must not brush against or jostle others to pass through.
If a gate is narrow, one should pass by leaning to the side; if it is low, one should pass by bending the body.
"The method for wearing robes when entering a village should be as follows.
If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Nanda and Upānanda sat down without having spread out their sitting mats; they placed rotten fruit and oily cakes in their robes, thereby defiling them.
The disciples spoke with resentment, saying:
"We have washed, dyed, and treated [the robes] with diligent effort, yet they are not protected.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, until the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, when entering the homes of laypeople, your undergarments should be worn in this manner.
What is meant by ‘in this manner’?
If the seat is covered in dust or is otherwise impure, you must not sit upon it unless you have spread a cloth over it.”
If one encounters an acquaintance, one should speak to them and ask them to spread out a seat. If they say,
"This śramaṇa is arrogant and difficult to serve," one should personally sweep and wipe the area,
spread out one's sitting mat, wash one's hands, and then sit down.
One must not use one's robe to catch any cakes, fruits, moist flowers, powdered substances, or mouth-wiping rags.
When sitting inside the home of a layperson, one should protect one's robe in this manner.
"If it is not thus, you will transgress the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Upānanda said to his co-practitioner disciple Nanda:
"I wish to enter a village with you to beg for alms. If I should act in an improper manner there, do not speak of it to anyone; I am your paternal uncle."
He replied,
"Even if my father and grandfather had acted improperly,
I would still have spoken [of it]," as explained at length above.
...until he replied,
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, the former śramaṇas should act thus, and the later śramaṇas should act thus.
What does it mean for the former and later śramaṇas to act thus?”
If the preceding śramaṇa succeeds in obtaining food, they shall eat together; if he does not succeed, they should send him back early to seek more food.

The following śramaṇas must not go so far ahead as to be out of sight of those before them, nor should they crowd too closely so that their heels tread upon one another; they should maintain a distance of at least one full arm’s span from each other.
If there are evil elephants, horses, or oxen ahead, one should say:
"Preceptor! Ācārya! There are dangerous creatures ahead;
we should move aside to another place."
If there is an elderly śramaṇa walking ahead, one should yield the way to him.
If someone is performing a prostration in front, one should say:
"So-and-so is prostrating."
If someone invites a monk to a meal, that monk should remember it; having returned to his residence, he should say:
"I was invited to such-and-such a house.
If the preceding monk was unable to offer a blessing, he should instruct one who is able to offer the blessing to do so.
One must not say:
"You sat down first, you took water first, and you ate first; why do you have me offer the blessing?
One should indeed offer the blessing.
"A former śramaṇa and a later śramaṇa should act in this manner.
If they do not act thus, they transgress the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣu asked another to go fetch food; having given him his bowl, he then abandoned him and departed.
A bhikṣu who had gone out to receive food brought it back, but though he searched for it, he could not find its location; he placed the bowl on top of the meditation hall and then departed.
When the next day arrived, another bhikṣu said to him:
"Will you not return my bowl to me?"
He replied,
"I have placed my bowl in the meditation hall.
He spoke again:
"Why did you take my bowl and leave it empty in the meditation hall?
He replied, "Why did you have me bring food and then abandon me and depart?"
The two of them disputed with one another and went to where the Buddha was, reporting the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when hiring someone to fetch food, it should be done in this manner; when giving someone food to fetch, it should be done in this manner."
How should one entrust another to fetch food or provide food for another?
One must not entrust another to fetch food and then depart, nor may one provide food for another and then leave the bowl empty upon the meditation hall and depart.
When receiving food from another, one should first say:
"Venerable sir!
I am now taking this food; do not go elsewhere, but prepare yourself and wait for me."
The person receiving the food should know the proper time; if the mealtime is imminent, they should bring it forward first.
If the time is still early, they should sit in order and take [the portions] in sequence.
When taking them, they must not mix them together; each should be kept in a separate place. Once they have finished eating themselves, they should bring [the remainder] back.
If the sun is about to set, one must not eat there; rather, one should take two portions of food and bring them back.
Upon returning, one should observe whether the day is still sufficient; those who arrive in time should come.
If you do not arrive in time, you should eat there yourself; do not cause both of you to miss the meal.
When requesting someone to fetch food, one must not say:
"I have already requested it."
Having departed, [the host] should first chew a tooth-stick, prepare water, arrange a seat, wash his hands, and wait.
He should frequently check the sun; if the time for the guest's arrival is drawing near, he should take a water jar and go out to welcome him.
If one encounters them on the road, they shall eat together; if those [monks] arrive early intentionally, they should wait until [the others] have arrived before eating.
If there is food remaining, it should be given to those who are taking food, and not to others;
however, if they do not require it, it may be given to others.
"The method for receiving food should be as follows.
If it is not so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms; they walked straight in with their heads bowed into the houses of laypeople, bumping into those ahead of them, which caused the people of the world to feel resentment and say:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are like rams; they charge straight ahead and butt people.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the method for begging for alms should be as follows.
What is meant by 'as follows'?
One must not go straight ahead like a head of a flock of sheep; nor should one stay too far away in a place where one cannot be seen; rather, one should remain in a place where one is visible."
One must not say,
"Give me food, and I shall obtain great merit.
One should stand in silence and must not look left or right, causing people to suspect one of being a thief or a spy.
One should restrain the six sense faculties and contemplate impermanence, nor should one remain for too long.
If there are women in the household engaged in tasks such as pounding grain, one may pause briefly until they have been observed.
If one sees her pounding [grain] again after having already pounded it, one should depart.
If one sees a woman spinning thread, having finished wrapping it yet spinning it again, there is no need for a mind of giving; one should depart.
If, upon seeing her, she enters the house empty-handed and leaves, one should depart.
However, if it is a wealthy household with many precious objects everywhere, one must not leave immediately;
one should wait for her to call out, and having seen her do so, then depart.
"The method for begging for alms should be like this.
If it is not like this, one violates the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Upānanda and his attendant disciple entered a village to beg for alms. When Upānanda returned from outside carrying the food, he sought his disciple but did not see him, and spoke with reproach:
"I brought food for you, yet you abandoned me and departed.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when begging for alms, a later monk should act in this manner. How so?

When an earlier monk is begging for alms, one must not stay too far away, nor too close by, looking on, such that it causes the householder to think: [‘Why does he watch him? Is he perhaps jealous?’]"
"Thinking, 'I cannot go begging for alms; I shall simply hope for the leftovers of others,' one should remain where one currently is.
If invited to a meal, one should eat; if not invited, one should beg for alms."
If one has finished eating by a well or a pond, there is no offense in washing the bowl and departing.
When eating, one should wait for others in this manner.
If one does not do so, it violates the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Undergarments, robes for entering villages,
robes for protecting lay households, The preceding śramaṇas and those following,
requesting to welcome and taking along, Begging for alms and waiting for others.
The sixth chapter concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, some bhikṣus fell to the ground while entering the meditation hall in the dark.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit the lighting of lamps.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, while on duty to light the lamps, extinguished them by blowing with their mouths, fanning them out with their hands, or waving them out with their robes; they even let loose drafts of air, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the method for lighting lamps should be as follows."

How is this so? One should proceed in order from the lowest rank upward. The person on duty should prepare a wooden drill and cow dung in advance within the dining hall for the maintenance of the perpetual fire; one must not light the lamp all at once, but should place the fire to one side and kindle it gradually.
When lighting lamps, one should first light those before the śarīra and the images; having performed prostrations, they should be extinguished.
Next, light the lamp in the latrine.
If the time for sitting meditation arrives, one should light a lamp within the meditation hall and should announce:
"Venerable sirs, may you recite blessings for the lamp and rejoice in it.
Next, light the lamps at the place where the monks walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*), and next, light the lamps at the head of the gallery.
If there is much oil, one should keep them burning throughout the night within the latrine building.
If the oil is low, when the person's movement ceases, it shall be extinguished.

Once extinguished, next the lamp at the end of the walking path (caṅkrama) shall be extinguished; next, the lamps at the ends of the galleries; and finally, the lamps within the meditation halls (dhyāna-kuṭī).
When extinguishing the lamps in the meditation hall, one must not extinguish them abruptly; rather, one should say:
"Venerable sirs, the mats have been spread, and I wish to extinguish the lamps.
Then, covering [the lamp] with one's hand, one should announce:
"The lamp is about to go out!
The lamp is about to go out!
One must not attempt to extinguish it by blowing with the mouth, fanning with the hand, or waving a cloth; rather, one should bend down and blow out the flame at its base until it is consumed.

When it is time for the latter part of the night, one should rise again; first light the latrine, next light the path for walking meditation, next light the head of the gallery, and finally light the meditation hall.
However, one must not enter the meditation hall abruptly at any time;
rather, one should announce: "Venerable sirs!
A lamp is about to enter!"
"Lamps, please enter!
Next, recite the verses.

When dawn is about to break and the lamps are to be extinguished, one should first extinguish the lamp at the head of the walkway, next the lamp in the walking area, next the lamp in the latrine building, and finally the lamp in the meditation hall.
"The method for lighting the lamp should be as follows.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct.
While the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, at that time some bhikṣus were practicing meditation in their meditation halls when they began to nod off and fall asleep.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should employ the meditation staff."
When the group of six bhikṣus were using their meditation staffs, they struck a bhikṣu on the ribs, whereupon he cried out in alarm, "Kill me!
Venerable sirs!"
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should practice the meditation staff in this manner."

Regarding the method for making a meditation staff (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*): it should be made of bamboo or rattan, eight cubits (*hasta*) in length, with both ends wrapped in cloth. It should be carried by the one seated at the lower end.
When walking, one must not cover the head, nor cover the right shoulder, nor wear leather sandals; rather, one should bared the right shoulder.

If there is someone sleeping, one must not call them awake abruptly, nor should one strike their ribs. One should instead place a staff against the front of the bed by leaning on its edge and shake it three times.
If they still do not wake, and if the sleeper is on the left side, one should press against the right knee; if on the right side, one should press against the left knee.
Having awakened, one should rise, take up one's staff, and proceed; one must not cover the head or the right shoulder, but should go with the right shoulder bared.
If many are asleep, one should not rise all at once like oxen, but rather two or three people should rise together.
When it is time for the youth to carry the staff, even if the preceptor (upādhyāya) or the teacher (ācārya) is sleeping, he should cause them to rise out of respect for the Dharma.
He should rise and take up the staff; the disciple must not give him the staff, but should carry it himself.
The person administering the staff must not seek out faults based on anger or attachment; they should instead restrain the six sense-faculties and contemplate with a single-minded focus.
If there is someone who is drowsy, they should give it to them; the person receiving the staff must not feel resentment, but should think:
"This person is now removing my hindrances for me; this benefits me no small amount."
Having reflected thus, one should arise and act; if there is anyone who is drowsy, one should give [the staff] to them.
Such is the method for practicing the meditation staff (dhyāna-yaṣṭi).
If one does not act in this way, it is a transgression of the rules of decorum (īryāpatha).
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus were using meditation sticks (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*), and because the weather was cold, their hands trembled.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should make them into pellets."
When the group of six bhikṣus were rolling balls, they threw them at their chests and faces; the bhikṣus cried out in alarm, "He is killing me!
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the method for making pellets and the method for throwing pellets should be as follows.
How so? [He continued:]..."
Regarding the method for making the balls: they should be made from thread, wool, or cotton; they must not be too hard, nor too soft.

When performing the rite, one should first give them to the person in the center. If there is anyone who is drowsy, one must not hastily throw them onto their head or face; rather, one should throw them in front of them.
Because the person before him reveres the Dharma, he should rise to receive [the medicine]; having received it, he returns to his seat.

If the preceptor or the ācārya is sleeping, one must not leave it there; one should also give them a pill. Because they revere the Dharma, they should rise, and the disciple should act as their representative by administering the pill.
He should return to his seat and must not harbor resentment or seek out faults.
One who receives the medicinal ball should form this thought:
"He has now removed my mental obscurations for me; the benefit he provides is no small matter."
"The method for walking with the *maṇḍala* (the ball) should be as follows.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus removed their leather sandals before the door of the meditation hall and entered while thumping the soles against each other like dragging dried fish, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus engaged in meditation.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when removing leather sandals within the meditation hall, you should do so in this manner."
How is this so? One is not permitted to thump leather sandals before the door of a meditation hall.
If the floor is covered, one should remove them and enter; one must not carry them like a bundle of dried fish.
One should enter while covering oneself with the lower robe tucked up; one should place it beneath the *niṣīdana* on the right side.
If the ground is not covered, one should enter slowly, remove the robe once inside, and then sit down.
"Inside the meditation hall, leather sandals should be worn in this manner.
If one does not do so, it violates the rules of dignified conduct.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stood inside the meditation hall, shaking their sitting mats (niṣīdana) until they made a noise, thereby disturbing the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the niṣīdana in the meditation hall should be used in this manner."

How is this so? One must not shake out one's *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) within the meditation hall; rather, one should fold it in the middle, place it over the left shoulder, and depart. Upon arrival, one should fold it again in the middle, spread it out, and sit.
Upon returning, one should likewise fold the garment and place it upon the shoulder.
If one wishes to store it in its usual place, one should fold it in half; when returning, one should unfold it slowly and sit down.
"In the meditation hall, the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) should be used in this manner.
If it is not done so, one transgresses the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*).
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made loud sounds by intentionally clearing their throats within the meditation hall, thereby disturbing the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when clearing one's throat within a meditation hall, one should do so in this manner."
How is this so? When one wishes to cough, one must not act with unrestrained license by making a loud sound; rather, one should cover the mouth and cough gently.
If it is too great to be restrained, one should rise and go outside; having gone out and finished coughing, one should return inside.
If they still do not stop, one should inform the person in charge and then depart.
Such is the proper method for clearing one's throat;
if one does not act thus, one violates the rules of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika-dharma*).

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus scattered grass roots, threads, and powders into their nostrils, causing them to sneeze repeatedly and making noise, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were engaged in meditative concentration.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when sneezing, you should act in this way. How should one do so?
[One should say: 'May you live long!'"
Within the meditation hall, one must not allow oneself to sneeze excessively. When a sneeze occurs, one should restrain it and cover the nose with the hand.
If it cannot be restrained, one should cover the nose with the hand while sneezing, ensuring that mucus or saliva does not splash onto those sitting nearby.
If someone sneezes, one must not speak.
If it is a senior monk (upādhyāya) who sneezes, one should say: "Vandana."
The junior monk remained silent.
This is the proper procedure for sneezing;
if one does not act accordingly, one violates the rules of decorum.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus yawned within the meditation hall, opening their mouths wide, stretching out their arms, and cracking their joints with loud sounds, thereby disturbing the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the method for yawning and stretching should be as follows."
How is this so? If, while sitting in the meditation hall, one feels the urge to yawn or stretch, one must not indulge in loud yawning or stretching; one should exercise self-restraint.
If one cannot restrain it, one should cover the mouth with the hand and yawn slowly; one must not disturb those sitting nearby.
When stretching, one should first raise one arm, and after lowering it, then raise the other arm.
The rules for yawning and stretching should be as follows.
If one does not act accordingly, one violates the rules of decorum.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus were sitting in a meditation hall; they scratched themselves, making a "ya-ya" sound that disturbed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so forth, until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should scratch in this manner.
How is it 'in this manner'? [The Buddha continued:]..."
One must not scratch with large handfuls so that it makes a rustling sound; one must not use fingernails or wooden handles to scratch.
If the itch is severe, one should rub it with the hand or scrape it with the fingertips.
"The method for scratching should be like this.
If it is not done thus, one transgresses the rules of decorum.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus were eating parched grain, chewing beans, and drinking much curd-milk. They sat in the four corners of the meditation hall, passing wind to one another with coarse and fine sounds, and said:
"Elder! Is this voice not most harmonious and excellent?
Having grasped his breath with his hand, he pressed it against the other's nose and said:
"Elder, do you smell it?
The bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, matters concerning lower winds should be conducted as follows.
What is meant by 'as follows'?
One must not intentionally consume flatulent foods for the purpose of making sport."
If a sudden draft of wind comes into the meditation hall, one should restrain it.
If it cannot be endured, one should sit lower down.
If there is a senior monk (*sthavira*) at the lower seat, one should return to the upper seat. When releasing air, one must not make a loud noise that disturbs those sitting nearby.
If flatulence arises while eating, one should sit downwind so as not to disturb those sitting nearby.
If it occurs in the presence of a preceptor (upādhyāya), an instructor (ācārya), or senior bhikṣus, one should move away to a position downwind so that the odor does not waft toward them.
If traveling on a road with merchants, one must not discharge wind (flatus) while in front of them.
If the wind arises and cannot be endured, one should step off the path and release it downwind.
The method for setting down the fan should be thus.
If it is not so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
Lighting a lamp while walking, using a meditation staff, throwing pellets, and carrying leather sandals [are likewise improper].
Coughing, sneezing, yawning, scratching, and passing wind.
The seventh chapter (varga) concludes.
What is proper conduct (*īryāpatha*) and what is improper conduct?
Proper conduct refers to practicing in accordance with the two divisions of the Vinaya; this is called proper conduct.
Not practicing in accordance [with them] is called improper conduct.

Regarding the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) and the training rules (*śaikṣa*): one should transcend evil thoughts; one should not intentionally touch a woman. If one does so with any intentional mind, it is a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline).
The section on decorum is concluded. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 35.
The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume Thirty-Six: The First [Section on] Bhikṣuṇīs.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

The Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya: The Eight Pārājika Dharmas Regarding the first [section], the Exposition of the Eight Pārājika Dharmas: The Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having fully accomplished all that was practiced from his original aspiration, resided at the Śākya Monastery in Kapilavastu, where he was honored and provided with offerings by gods and humans. The extensive account is as described above.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chāndakī, Chāndapālā, Chāndā, Chāndāmātṛ, and five hundred other Śākya women, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A Buddha’s appearance is difficult to encounter; it is difficult to hear the Dharma.”
"Now we have encountered the Tathāgata appearing in the world to proclaim the sublime Dharma of ambrosia, enabling all sentient beings to achieve the wondrous realization of nirvāṇa.
As explained in detail in the *Mahāprajāpatī Pravrajyā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, Mahāprajāpatī shall be the senior elder (*sthavirā*) of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha; remember this."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, since you have established these four grave rules involving defeat for the bhikṣus, may we also hear them in full?"
The Buddha said,
“It is permitted, Gautamī.”
If a faithful and virtuous woman desires to obtain five benefits, she should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
What are these five?
If a faithful and virtuous woman desires to establish the Buddha-dharma, she should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those who wish to cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those who do not wish to harbor doubts or regrets and instead seek instruction from others should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Any bhikṣuṇīs who have committed offenses and seek a refuge from their fear should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
Those who wish to travel and teach in various regions without hindrance should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
"This is called the five benefits for a faithful virtuous woman who upholds this Vinaya.
The remainder is as explained above in detail within the first five conditions concerning bhikṣus.

If a bhikṣuṇī does not return her precepts and, while her precepts are weak, does not renounce them, yet engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community.

A bhikṣuṇī is one who has received full ordination properly, through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tricarma*) free from impediments; who has been ordained in a harmonious assembly of both orders; who has done so according to the Dharma and not contrary to it; who has done so in a harmonious gathering and not in a discordant one; and who is twenty years of age and not less than twenty. This is called a bhikṣuṇī who has not returned the precepts.
Regarding "one who is weak in virtue but does not leave [the order]," this is explained in detail above in the section on bhikṣus.
"Receives" means to receive with a lustful mind.
"Sexual intercourse" refers to non-celibate conduct.
If a bhikṣuṇī [has sexual intercourse] with a human male—whether he is asleep, awake, or dead—and likewise with a non-human male or a male animal—whether they are asleep, awake, or dead.
Whether it be a human, a non-human, an animal, or a paṇḍaka; whether asleep, awake, or dead;
regarding the three orifices—whether the mouth, the urethra, or the anus—if one experiences pleasure in any one of them, this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community.
"Pārājika" means that one has fallen away from and lost the knowledge of the Dharma, having descended such that there is no longer any portion of the fruits of the Path; this is called pārājika.

Likewise, up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), if one falls away from and loses those various knowledges, such that there is no longer any portion of the fruits of the Path, this is called pārājika.
Furthermore, regarding *pārājika*: it is that which causes one to fall away from and sink back from *nirvāṇa*, falling into a state where there is no share in the fruits of the path;
this is called *pārājika*. Furthermore, regarding *pārājika*: it is that which causes one to fall away from and sink back from the holy life (*brahmacarya*); this is called *pārājika*.
Regarding *pārājika*: because the offense committed cannot be confessed and expiated, it is called *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, desires to look at a man, she commits a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline) requiring mental repentance.
If one sees with the eyes or hears the voice, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If they face each other naked, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Even if [the penetration] is as small as a sesame seed, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī neither declares her renunciation of the precepts nor declares that she does not renounce them, yet her precepts become weak and she becomes a layperson, she incurs an offense according to what she has transgressed; the same applies if she joins a non-Buddhist sect.

Whether it is wrapped but not covered, covered but not wrapped, both covered and wrapped, or neither covered nor wrapped—even if it enters [the body] as small as a sesame seed—it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī does not return her precepts and does not emerge from the state of weak precepts, but instead assumes the appearance and dress of a layperson and commits an offense, she incurs the guilt according to that offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī forcibly commits sexual intercourse with a bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; if the bhikṣu experiences pleasure, he also commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī engage in sexual intercourse together, both commit a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in sexual intercourse with a śrāmaṇera, the bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and the śrāmaṇera is expelled;
it is the same for a layperson.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in sexual intercourse with three kinds of beings:
humans, non-humans, and animals.
Furthermore, there are another three kinds:
There are three grades of paths: superior, middling, and inferior.
Furthermore, there are three states:
whether awake, asleep, or dead—[in all these cases], it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, while asleep, mentally deranged, or absorbed in meditative concentration, is approached for sexual intercourse by someone, and she becomes aware of it—if she experiences pleasure at the beginning, the middle, or the end—it constitutes a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī is asleep, mentally deranged, or in meditative absorption, and a person engages in sexual intercourse with her, even if she does not experience pleasure at the outset but experiences it during or after the act, she is likewise guilty of a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī is asleep, mentally deranged, or in meditative absorption, and a person engages in sexual intercourse with her, if she does not experience pleasure at the beginning or middle upon waking, but experiences pleasure later, she is also guilty of a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī is asleep, mentally deranged, or in meditative absorption, and a person engages in sexual intercourse with her, she incurs no offense provided she does not experience pleasure at the beginning, middle, or end once she has awakened.
What is experiencing pleasure?
What is not experiencing pleasure?
As for experiencing pleasure: it is like a person who, being hungry, obtains various kinds of fine food; that person takes pleasure in the food.
Furthermore, it is like a thirsty person who obtains various fine drinks and finds joy in drinking them;
those who experience sensual pleasures are just like this.
One who does not experience such pleasure is like a pure and clean person with various corpses tied around his neck.
Furthermore, it is just as when one suffers from a festering ulcer or has one's body cauterized with red-hot iron; likewise, there is no experience of pleasure [in such acts].

If a bhikṣuṇī engages in sexual intercourse—whether obtained by purchase, obtained by hire, obtained through favors or obligations, obtained through acquaintances, obtained through jesting, obtained through testing, or obtained from one who has not yet experienced it—in all such cases where she obtains and engages in sexual intercourse, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one's mind is deranged and they are unaware, there is no offense.
Therefore it is said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī does not return her precepts, or if her precepts have weakened and she does not renounce them, yet she engages in sexual conduct—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community."
The second, third, and fourth [formulations] are as explained in detail within the Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, in a village or an open space, takes what is not given, according to the value of the stolen object, the owner may seize her, kill her, bind her, or banish her."
"Hey! Woman! Are you a thief? Are you a fool?"
“If a bhikṣuṇī takes what is not given in this manner, it is a pārājika offense; she should not live in community.
“If a bhikṣuṇī takes the life of a human being with her own hand, or seeks out and gives a knife to a killer, or instructs another to die or praises death, saying:
‘Ho! [Why do you live?]’”
"What is the use of living a life of evil?
Death is better than life.

Holding such an intention and forming such a thought, she uses various means to praise the pleasure of death, and because of this, dies rather than for any other reason, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she should not live in communion.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, not knowing and not having understood, claims for herself that she has attained the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), a noble knowledge and vision (*ariyā ñāṇadassanavisesa*), saying 'I know thus, I see thus,' and if at a later time—whether she is examined or not examined—she commits an offense and, desiring to seek purification, speaks as follows:
'O Noble Lady!'"
"I claim to know what I do not know, and I claim to see what I have not seen; my words are empty, deceptive, and untrue.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this is called a *pārājika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī; she should not live in community with the others.
The Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery of the Nyagrodha Tree in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept prohibiting bhikṣuṇīs from dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka). Since there was no monastery yet in the village where the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrapālā lived, she resided in the house of a member of the Śākya clan and taught the sūtras to young Śākyas.

The bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrapālā was of upright and beautiful appearance yet had not yet abandoned desire; the youth was likewise of upright and beautiful appearance and had also not yet abandoned desire; thus, he came three times in a single day to receive the sūtras from her.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī, having seen him repeatedly, became obsessed with desire for him; she eventually fell ill, and her complexion grew pale and withered.
Other bhikṣuṇīs asked after her health, saying:
"Noble Lady!..."
"What is your ailment?
What medicine do you require?
Whether it be ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar, we shall provide them to you."
He replied, "There is no need; it shall naturally subside.
The same occurred when the upāsakas and upāsikās came to inquire after his health.
Then a young man of the Śākya clan asked,
"Noble lady, what ailment do you suffer from?
What medicine do you require?"
"I shall give it to you.
If there is something in my house, I will give it; if not, I shall seek it from elsewhere and give it to you.
He replied:
“Long-lived one!
Medicines such as these cannot cure it.
He asked again:
“Venerable One! Since this illness is not an illness of the body, you should know that it is merely an illness of the mind!
He replied:
"It is as you have said.
He asked again:
"How will this illness be cured?"
The bhikṣuṇī said,
“Do you wish for me to cure you?
She replied:
"I wish for you to recover," he said. He spoke again,
asking, "What do you require?"
"Now I seek to associate with you.
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"Come, let us do this together."
The youth replied, "I dare not.
I would not even entertain such a thought toward other renunciants who wear the *kāṣāya*, let alone toward my teacher, whom I hold in such high esteem."
He spoke again:
"If you cannot do that, simply embrace me, kiss and grasp me, and stroke me from head to foot.
He replied:
"If it is only that which you require, I can do it.
She then embraced him, suckled him, and grasped his two breasts, rubbing and stroking them up and down; having attained her pleasure, she did so repeatedly.
As the Blessed One said:
"One who recollects a form without forgetting it and gives rise to a defiled mind is like a woman remembering a man, or a man remembering a woman.
After this, [the thought] arose repeatedly and could not be stopped; other bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
“Noble lady! Do not do this; this cannot be allowed.
She replied:
"I find pleasure in doing this.
The bhikṣuṇī then reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and having heard it, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrā here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that with a lustful mind, you experienced pleasure by touching, below the shoulders and above the knees, a man who also had a lustful mind?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Rattha!
This is an evil deed.

Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, rebuke sensual desire? Desire leads to delusion and intoxication; desire is like a great fire that burns away one’s roots of goodness; desire is a great affliction.”
"I have always, through various skillful means, praised the renunciation of desire, the severance of desire, and the transcendence of desire.
How can you now commit such an evil deed?
This is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Kāśī gather together.
Once they had gathered, at that time the World-Honored One, for this reason and by way of these circumstances, extensively explained to the bhikṣuṇīs the arising of faults and calamities.
Having rebuked them through various causes and conditions regarding the arising of such faults and calamities, he taught the Dharma accordingly to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"There are ten benefits for which the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has established the precepts for his disciples and formulated the Pātimokkha rules."
What are the ten?
First, for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha;
second, for the sake of thoroughly gathering the Saṃgha.
Third, for the sake of ensuring the peace and happiness of the Saṃgha;
fourth, for the sake of subduing those who lack a sense of shame;
fifth, so that those who possess a sense of shame and modesty may dwell in security.
Sixth, to cause those who lack faith to attain faith;
seventh, to increase the faith of those who already possess it;
eighth, to attain the exhaustion of outflows within the present life.
Ninth, because it causes unarisen outflows (*āsrava*) not to arise;
tenth, because it ensures the True Dharma (*saddharma*) endures for a long time and opens the gate of the Deathless (*amṛta*) for all gods and worldlings—these are the ten.

For these ten reasons, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has established the precepts for his disciples and formulated the Dharma of the Prātimokṣa; thus, those who have not yet heard it shall hear it, and those who have already heard it shall hear it again.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows herself to be touched below the shoulders and above the knees by a man with a lustful mind, and she experiences pleasure from that contact, this bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense; she is not to live in community with the others.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"A man with a leaking mind" refers to one with lustful intent.
"Below the shoulder" means below the breasts.
"Above the knees" means from the thighs up to the navel.
"To touch and stroke" means to move the hand to rub and caress.
"To experience pleasure" means to perceive a sense of joy.
If she is stained by attachment, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding "pārājika," it is as explained above.
Regarding "not living together," it means that she may not live with the bhikṣuṇīs, nor may she share the food of the Dharma or the food of taste with them.
As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before.
Regarding the *pārājika* offense, one should not dwell together [with such a person].

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, and a man with a lustful mind, experience pleasure through touching from below the shoulders to above the knees, it is a *pārājika* offense, and she should not dwell together [with others].
In such cases, for a paṇḍaka or a woman, it is a sthūlātyaya offense;
if a bhikṣuṇī has a lustful mind while the man does not have a lustful mind, it is likewise a pārājika offense.
If it is with a person of indeterminate gender or a woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the bhikṣuṇī has a mind free from leakage (*anāsrava-citta*) while the man has a mind with leakage (*sāsrava-citta*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is with a person of indeterminate gender or a woman, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī has a mind free from outflows and a man has a mind free from outflows, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If it is a eunuch or a woman, it is a *vinayātikrama* with mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*).
If a bhikṣuṇī has a man shave her hair, two women must press firmly so that she feels the women but does not feel the man.
Likewise, when piercing the head to draw blood, or piercing the arm or the foot, she must have a woman hold her tightly so that she feels the woman but does not feel the man.
Above the shoulders and below the knees, if there is an abscess or ulcer, it is no offense for a woman to hold it while a man breaks it open.
This is not permitted in the private parts.
"Private parts" refers to the area below the shoulders and above the knees.
"If there is anyone who is ill in this place, one should have a woman treat them.
Thus it was said.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, where he was honored and provided for by gods and worldlings; the details are as explained above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrapālā taught the *Licchavikumāra-sūtra*, and even spoke thus:
"I would not even give rise to such a thought toward other renunciants who wear the saṃghāṭī, let alone toward one who is respected by my teacher."
The bhikṣuṇī said:

"If it were not so, he would have stayed near me, conversed with me, taken my hand, taken hold of my robe, come joyfully to invite me to sit, and leaned his body toward me to go on a journey together."
He replied, "If it is simply like this, then it may be so.
Having thus found satisfaction, he did not stop doing so repeatedly.
As the Blessed One has said:
"When mindfulness of form is not forgotten and a defiled mind arises, it is like a woman remembering a man, or a man remembering a woman.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of this matter, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the Blessed One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrapālā here. When she had come,
the Buddha questioned her thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matter:
"Did you truly do this? He replied,
"I truly did."
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed. How could you, with a corrupted mind, extend your hand into the presence of a man with a corrupted mind, or even make a mutual appointment?"
"From this day forward, I do not permit [a nun] to harbor lustful thoughts, to extend her hand toward a man with lustful thoughts, to remain within his reach, or even to make a mutual appointment.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Vaiśālī assemble; for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs."
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, stands within arm’s reach of a man with a lustful mind, converses with him, accepts his grasping of her hand or her robe, comes to greet him joyfully, invites him to sit, bends her body toward him, or makes an appointment to go away with him, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she is no longer to be lived with.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"A bhikṣuṇī with a defiled mind and a man with a defiled mind" means that both possess lustful intent.
"Standing within arm's reach" means at a distance reachable by the extended hand.
"Speaking" means whispering together.
"Taking the hand" means taking the hand, or taking the wrist, or taking the thumb, or taking the little finger.
"Taking the robe" refers to the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antarvāsaka, the saṃkakṣikā, or the rain-cloak.
Regarding "come with joy": welcome, be glad, and come frequently.
Regarding "please be seated": I have already spread out the bedding and mats;
you may sit. Regarding "bending the body": bowing the body, one approaches.
If she goes to a place where people are expected to leave—such as before a shop, in a garden or meadow, or on a frequented path—that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense;
she should not live in communion with the community.
Regarding the *pārājika*:

as explained above, if a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, converses within arm’s reach of a man who has a lustful mind, and consents to being taken by the hand or by the robe, or if he comes joyfully to invite her to sit, or they bend their bodies together to agree upon going away, this bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense and should not live in communion.
In the same way, if she does so with a eunuch or a woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī’s mind is free from desire while a man’s mind is not free from desire, it is also a pārājika offense;
if he is a eunuch or a woman, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī’s mind is free from desire while a man’s mind is not free from desire, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If [one acts with] a eunuch or a woman, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If both possess a mind free from outflows (*anāsrava-citta*), it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If [one acts with] a eunuch or a woman while possessing a mind free from outflows, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama-śaithilika* (requiring mental repentance).
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, stands within arm’s reach of a man with a lustful mind, or even makes an appointment to go [with him], it is a pārājika offense.
If she commits each of the eight matters in succession, it is a pārājika; if she commits them intermittently and they total eight, it is likewise a pārājika.
If one commits [the offense] once and immediately repents, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If, after repenting, one commits it again, up to the seventh time, it is a sthūlātyaya.
Upon reaching the eighth [repetition], it is a pārājika.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, as described in detail above.
At that time, a Licchavi had first fathered two sons and subsequently gave birth to a daughter, whom he considered inauspicious. He thought to himself:
"Who now shall take this ill-omened girl?
Someone said to him,
"Do you wish to keep this girl with you?"
She replied, “I wish to have one.
[The other] said, “If that is so, you may take this one and give it to the bhikṣuṇī Kālī; she shall raise it for you.”
She immediately summoned Kālī and said to her: "Noble Lady!

Since I have been born as this inauspicious woman whom no one will take as a wife, please raise me and grant me the going-forth into the religious life; I myself shall provide you with food and clothing."
The bhikṣuṇī then took her in to raise her and ordained her.
Her family sent food every day and provided clothing every year; once she had grown up, they taught her the precepts, after which she received full ordination (upasampadā).

It is the nature of women that lust is particularly prevalent; as their years advanced, their passionate desires also grew more intense, and being unable to restrain themselves, she said to her teacher:
"The fetters have arisen within me; I no longer delight in the life of renunciation and now wish to return to secular life."
The Master said:
"How strange!
The secular world is like a pit of fire; how could it be a source of joy?"
From that time forward, she gradually began to associate with laypeople and various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas), and subsequently became pregnant.
The bhikṣuṇī then expelled her and said to her preceptor,
"Do you not know that your disciple has been having illicit relations with laypeople and non-Buddhist practitioners?"

He replied, "I also knew this long ago; however, his family sends food every day and provides clothing every year. Had I informed the Sangha, they would have expelled him. Since I benefit from these two matters, I did not speak."
The bhikṣuṇī immediately informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went at once to report this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Summon Kālī."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed, Kālī! How could you,
knowing that a bhikṣuṇī had committed a grave offense, conceal it?"
"This is neither Dharma nor Vinaya; it cannot be used to nurture the wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"Summon all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Vaiśālī; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (pārājika) and does not disclose it to others, and after that bhikṣuṇī has moved away, died, or left the order, she later says:
"I previously knew this bhikṣuṇī had committed a grave offense, but I did not disclose it to others because I did not wish for others to know."
"Such a bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and should not live in community.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either knowing by herself or hearing it from another.
"Grave offenses" refers to committing any one of the eight *pārājika* rules.
"Not confessing to others" means not confessing before even a single person, nor before a group, nor within the Saṃgha.
"One who has left the community" refers to one who has been expelled.
"One who has died" means impermanence.
"One who has abandoned the path" refers to one who, having departed from this Dharma and Vinaya to become a layperson or a follower of an external path, subsequently says:
"If I previously knew that she had committed an offense, yet I did not wish for others to know," this bhikṣuṇī is guilty of a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
Regarding "pārājika," it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time when the dawn light appears, sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a grave offense (pārājika), and without the intention to conceal it, later forms the intention to conceal it by the time the sun rises and continues until the next dawn light appears, this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika; this is called the "two times."
In this manner, it continues up to the eighth watch, as explained in detail in the section on concealment for bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣuṇī commit a grave offense, she should speak of it to others.
If she sees a co-resident disciple or a dependent disciple commit a grave offense, she thinks to herself:
"If I were to tell anyone about this, the bhikṣuṇīs would surely expel them."
Out of affection, she concealed her offense and thereby committed a *pārājika*.
Upon hearing these words, that bhikṣuṇī said to a bhikṣuṇī who was a close friend:
"So-and-so has committed a grave offense; if I were to tell anyone, the community of bhikṣuṇīs would expel her. That is why I have concealed it."
Having heard this, that bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I report this, these two will both be expelled.
She then concealed it, and both committed a pārājika offense.
If all such instances of mutual concealment occur, they constitute a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees another commit a grave offense and says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"I saw so-and-so commit a grave offense."
That bhikṣuṇī then rebuked her, saying:
"You have now committed an evil deed; why do you speak to me?
Do not say such things again."
[If she does not speak of it,] she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a grave offense (*pārājika*), she ought to report it to others. However, if the offender is fierce and terrifying, possesses great power such that she fears for her life, or might harm her *brahmacarya*, she should form this thought:
"The karmic retribution for his deeds he himself must know; it is like a fire breaking out and burning a house—one should simply save oneself, for who knows another's affairs?"
"One who attains a mind of equanimity incurs no offense.
Therefore it is said:
The Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara in the Gośīrṣa Garden. At that time, among the five classes of offenses, Chanda committed either one or two. The bhikṣus said:"
“Elder Channa! Do you see this transgression?
He replied:
"What is the use of your asking me whether I see or do not see? I do not see.
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"If this Chanda, among the five classes of offenses, has committed any one of them and yet says he does not see it, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of one who denies his offense."
After the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension) against him for not acknowledging his offense, he went to the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra and said:
"Pāṭaliputra, the Saṃgha has performed the *ukkhepanīyakamma* against me; they do not share with me the food of the Dharma or the food of taste."
He immediately said,
"How strange!
Now I shall partake with you in the food of the Dharma and the food of flavor."
She then complied.
The bhikṣuṇī admonished her, saying:
"Mātā Cchandā!

"This Channa, the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension (ukṣepa-karman) against him in accordance with the Dharma; since it has not yet been performed in accordance with the Dharma, do not comply.
He replied:
"I am his mother, I am the one who gave birth to him; if I do not comply, who indeed would comply?"
The bhikṣuṇī immediately informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went at once to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:

“Since the bhikṣuṇī Mātṛcchandā has acquiesced to the formal act of *karma* of suspension carried out by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, you should admonish her three times in private, three times before a group of many people, and three times within the Saṃgha, to make her relinquish this matter.”
Regarding the admonition in private, one should ask:
"Do you truly know that Canda has followed the Saṃgha’s formal act of suspension (ukkhittakamma) carried out according to the Dharma?
He should answer:
"It is indeed so.
One should then admonish her, saying:
"Chandamātā!..."
The Saṃgha has performed the formal act of *karma* for suspension according to the Dharma; it has not yet performed it improperly. Do not comply with this.
I now admonish you out of a heart of loving-kindness, desiring to benefit you.
One admonition has passed, and two remain. Will you relinquish this matter?
In this manner, the second and third admonitions are likewise performed; the three admonitions before a large assembly are likewise performed.
If he does not relinquish [the matter], the saṃgha should perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion for permission) and should speak as follows:
“Listen, noble saṃgha!

The Saṃgha performed the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against Channa in accordance with the Dharma; however, as it had not yet been performed in accordance with the Dharma, Channa’s mother supported him. Although she was admonished three times in private and three times in the midst of a large assembly to relinquish this matter, she did not do so.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should now also formally admonish you three times to relinquish this matter.
Within the assembly, one should ask Chanda’s mother:

"Do you truly know that the harmonious Saṃgha has performed a formal act of censure against Chanda according to the Dharma, and that it has not yet been done improperly, yet you continue to comply with him? Have you already been admonished three times in private and three times before a large group to relinquish this matter, yet you still do not relinquish it?"
If they reply,
“It is indeed so,” one should immediately admonish them, saying:
“The Saṃgha, being in harmony, has performed the formal act of *karma* of suspension against Chanda in accordance with the Dharma; you must not comply with him.
Because the Saṃgha desires to benefit you, it exhorts you: you should comply with the words of the Saṃgha.”
"The first admonition has passed; the second admonition remains.
Will you relinquish it? He replied, "I will not relinquish it."
When she had been admonished thus a second and a third time, she still said,
"I will not relinquish it.
The bhikṣuṇī went because of these circumstances to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call him here. Once he had arrived, the Buddha asked him:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said,
"This is an evil deed.
Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, disparage those who are perverse and difficult to admonish, while praising those who are easy to admonish?"
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching; it cannot serve to nurture wholesome qualities.
How can you comply with a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal censure?
"From this day forward, I do not permit [you] to follow a monk who has been subject to formal suspension.
The Buddha said to Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Kauśāmbī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that the Saṃgha, being in harmony, has performed a formal act of censure (*karma*) against a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet she complies with him before the act has been performed in accordance with the Dharma,
the other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī,
saying: "Sister!..."
"This community of bhikṣus has performed a formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya; however, it was not carried out lawfully. Do not follow this bhikṣu.
When the bhikṣuṇīs were thus admonished, they spoke as follows:
"We do not follow him; who indeed would follow him?"
If the bhikṣuṇīs, having been thus admonished a second and third time, abandon this matter, it is well;
if they do not abandon it, that bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and should not live in community with the others.
“Bhikṣuṇī” is as explained above.
“Knows” means either she knows it herself or she hears it from another.
“In harmony” means not being a separate assembly.
Regarding those who act according to the Dharma and Vinaya: they do not perceive their offenses, they do not commit offenses, and they do not relinquish three views.
These three are: slandering the sūtras, wrong view, and extreme views.
One who has been subject to formal suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) does not dwell in communion.
One who has not yet performed what is in accordance with the Dharma is one who has not yet complied, nor has the Saṃgha yet lifted the suspension.
To comply means to share in the food of the Dharma and the food of flavor.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī who speaks thus: "Venerable lady!

This bhikṣu has been subjected to the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa-karman*) by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya; since the procedure was not performed in accordance with the Dharma, do not follow him in accepting food for the sake of the Dharma or food for the sake of flavors."
When being admonished, he says:
"I will not comply; who else should comply?
He should be admonished again and up to three times; if he relinquishes [the position], it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense.
Regarding "pārājika," it is as explained above.
If she relinquishes it after three admonitions in private, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, for each admonition she incurs a vyatikrama offense against the Vinaya.
It is the same among a great multitude of people.
Within the Saṃgha, at the time of the initial admonition, there is an offense of vinaya-transgression (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
When the admonition is finished, it is a sthūlātyaya.
At the first admonition during the second [stage], one commits a *vinayātikrama*;
when the admonition is finished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
At the first admonition during the third [stage], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the admonition is finished, it is a *pārājika*.
Whether in a private place, among a crowd, or within the Saṃgha, all instances of violating the *vinaya* constitute a single grave offense, a *sthūlātyaya*, which is termed a *pārājika*.
If one abandons [the training] in the interim, one is to be dealt with according to the specific offense.
Sexual misconduct, theft, taking human life, falsely claiming superhuman qualities,
[sexual contact] below the shoulders and above the knees, and the eight matters fulfilled by a mind of leakage.
The concealment of a grave offense and the following of a formal act of suspension are concluded.
The eight *pārājika* rules are finished.

2. The Nineteen *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* Dharmas: Part One, Explaining the First of the Nineteen *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* Dharmas—Sending a Messenger. This is explained in detail as in the section on the *bhikṣus*; therefore, the World-Honored One said:

“If a bhikṣuṇī, acting as a messenger, brings about the union of a man and a woman—whether it be for taking a wife or for illicit intercourse—even for a mere moment, this is an offense involving defeat (pārājika); it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.”
The two cases concerning groundless [accusations] are as explained in detail among the bhikṣus; therefore, the Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, malice, or displeasure, slanders a pure and blameless bhikṣuṇī with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣuṇī’s pure conduct."
At a later time, whether he is investigated or not, he speaks thus:
"This matter was groundless; I spoke these words because I was dwelling in malice and resentment."
"This is the first offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, resentment, or displeasure, intentionally uses a minor matter belonging to a different category to slander a bhikṣuṇī who has not committed a pārājika offense by charging her with a pārājika dharma, wishing to destroy her holy life (brahmacarya)."

If, at a later time, whether she has been investigated or not, she speaks on account of a minor matter belonging to another category, doing so out of malice, this is an offense involving defeat (pārājika). This is the first offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The walls separating the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma from the dwelling place of the non-Buddhist nuns collapsed.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said to the non-Buddhist nuns, "You should repair it;
you shameless people, your followers come and go, entering and exiting in the nude!"
"These virtuous and well-behaved members of my assembly possess a sense of shame; seeing you, they perceive that their fetters are increasing.
They replied, "Now is the rainy season, so it is impossible to work; we must wait until the rainy season has passed before we can do so."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"You must work quickly now; you may not wait for later.
He replied:
"I cannot do it. The bhikṣuṇī spoke with anger:
"You short-lived one!"
"You who eat wine dregs like a donkey, you dare not fail to do so!
Shameless and devoid of conscience, holding false views and lacking faith—you must be disciplined and expelled immediately!
Thus the outsider nun reviled her.
“Son of many people, fat-bellied nun! You have killed me; I will never work for you again.
The bhikṣuṇī then went to the magistrate and related the matter in detail:
“Long-lived one!”
"Order him to build a partition wall for me.
At that time, the magistrate, who had faith in the Buddha-dharma, immediately summoned the heretical nun. Once she had arrived, he spoke to her:
"You wicked and short-lived one, you donkey who eats wine dregs, you heretic of false views!"
"Why do you not build a wall for partition?
You are shameless, entering and exiting naked; you claim to be noble practitioners of the Brahma-faring life, yet if people were to see you, it would only increase their fetters and afflictions."
"You must work with haste; if you do not, I shall inflict punishment upon you.

The non-Buddhist nun then began to work, but having finished by day, it was ruined by the rain at night. In this manner, she was unable to complete the work throughout the three months of the summer retreat.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhists, feeling resentment and reproach, said to the lay devotees (upāsakas):
"Look at your field of merit! Relying on the power of the state, you have driven us to work as mud-brick makers for three months."
When the female lay followers heard this, they told the bhikṣuṇīs; the bhikṣuṇīs, having heard it, reported it to Mahāprajāpatī, who then informed the World-Honored One of these matters in detail.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked:
“Thullanandā! Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; why did you engage in mutual strife and verbal abuse?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Summon all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī. For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, so that those who have already heard it may hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī engages in quarreling, litigation, or mutual verbal abuse—whether with a layperson or one who has left the household—for even a brief moment during the day, or even fights and verbally abuses a park-attendant or a śrāmaṇera, this is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
“Bhikṣuṇī” is as explained above.
“Dispute” refers to verbal dispute.
“Layperson” refers to one who lives at home.
"Those who have gone forth" refers to those who have left the household life, ranging from non-Buddhist renunciants (tīrthika) to śākyaputrīyas.
"During the day" means until sunset.
"For even a moment" refers to a duration of even a brief instant, down to the level of a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) or a lay attendant (ārāmika).
Regarding the "first offense," it does not require three admonitions.
As for "saṃgha," it refers to the eight *pārājika* rules.
*Pāyattika* (or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*) means that this offense has a remainder; because the Saṃgha should administer a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to treat it, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, because this matter is confessed and repented within the Saṃgha, it is also called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the place of a royal official who adjudicates legal cases and engages in mutual dispute, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one speaks of it while on the way, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one speaks of it while at the house of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a family with faith, it is a *vinayātikrama*.
If one does so with a mind of resentment, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a royal household and engages in idle chatter, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she speaks with malice, she commits a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrā had a younger sister who had married into another village. Having fallen ill, she sent a messenger to summon Rāṣṭrā, saying:
"Come quickly to see me while I am not yet dead, so that we may meet."
He immediately went to see her, but before he could arrive, his sister had passed away.
Upon his arrival, her husband said to Rata:
"Your sister has died; who will now manage the household and look after the children?"
"I only wish that Ratha would manage affairs for me in place of my sister.
The bhikṣuṇī then thought to herself:
"This man has uttered such wicked words; perhaps he will forcibly violate me."
