Filled with fear, she feigned going outside and returned to Śrāvastī, where she said to the bhikṣuṇīs,
"How strange!
He is surely going to destroy my brahmacarya!"
The bhikṣuṇīs asked, "For what reason?
She then related the matter in detail as it had occurred above.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"How is it that you travel alone on the road?
From this day forward, traveling alone is not permitted.
Furthermore, while some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on the road, a certain young bhikṣuṇī left the path to relieve herself and fell behind.
When some merchants arrived and saw that the bhikṣuṇī was upright and beautiful, they immediately blocked her path and asked:
"You are young and beautiful; you ought to receive sensual pleasures. Why have you left the household life?"
"Please tell us the reason for this.
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I have left the household life; what need is there to ask me?"
He spoke again: “Not so!
There must surely be some meaning; tell it to me.”
The answer was the same as before.
After thus mocking her, he released her after a short while.
Having reached the village, she felt doubt and regret, and spoke of it to Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "If she did not wish to go, there is no offense.

Furthermore, while several bhikṣuṇīs were traveling together on a road, one bhikṣuṇī became ill and was unable to keep pace with her companions, remaining behind alone. Upon arriving, she felt doubt and regret, and reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then informed the World-Honored One of these events in detail.
The Buddha said,
"If it is due to illness, there is no offense.
The Buddha spoke to Mahāprajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels without a companion bhikṣuṇī, she must not go beyond the boundary of a village, except at other times.”
"Other times" refers to when one is unwilling or when one is ill; these are called "other times.
This is an offense of the first category, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Without a companion nun" means traveling alone on a road, as explained in detail above.
"Except at other times" refers to cases of incapacity or illness; the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense in such instances.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī is traveling on a road and has not yet crossed the boundary, there is no offense.

When she reaches the boundary of a village or town, they should remain within arm’s reach of one another; if they become separated beyond arm’s reach, when one foot has crossed [the boundary], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; when both feet have crossed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one person stands in the middle of the boundary, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Likewise, if other persons pass through, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. In Rājagṛha there was a man named Kalmāṣapāda who took a girl named Kalmāṣī as his wife.
She was exceptionally beautiful, with no peer, and she brought food to her husband.
When the World-Honored One arrived, he put on his robes for entering a village and, carrying his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food in sequence until he reached her house.
At that time, the woman thought to herself:
"If my husband sees the Buddha, he will surely rise to look at him, which would interfere with and disrupt our meal; I shall stand by the door."
Because she had a karmic connection with the Buddha, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a radiance that illuminated the interior of her house;
her husband looked out and saw the Buddha, whereupon he said to his wife:
"You have acted most unvirtuously; you seek only to bring me ruin."
His wife said, "It is not that I wish to harm you;
I only fear that once I have seen the World-Honored One, it will interfere with and cause me to neglect my meal.
Her husband spoke with anger:
"Women have shallow sentiments; though they may desire to provide a small benefit, the harm they cause is not slight.
The wife said to her husband, "Master, please listen to me and allow me to leave the household life."
The husband said to his wife,
"By what path do you wish to go forth into homelessness?
The wife replied:
"I am going forth into the Buddha-dharma," he said.
The husband replied,
"I grant you my consent."
He immediately went to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā to seek ordination; she then received him into the order and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

Through diligent and unremitting effort during both the first and last watches of the night, on the eighth day he exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). He realized for himself the realization of the three knowledges (*traividya*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), attaining mastery over his mind.
While she was sitting beneath a tree, Śakra Devānām Indra went to her place and spoke this verse:
"Surrounded by his celestial host, Śakra has descended To prostrate at your feet;
behold this woman Kalmāṣī, Who has been a renunciant for only eight days."
The bhikṣu Utpalavarṇa has exhausted his outflows and realized the six supernormal powers;
having accomplished what was to be done, he possesses the power of virtue and mastery of mind.
Having subdued all the sensory faculties, he sits with eyes closed beneath a tree.
"Therefore, I now bow my head to you, the excellent field of merit for the world.

This bhikṣuṇī possessed a beautiful, clear voice and was skilled at chanting praises. A lay devotee (upāsaka) invited her to go; after she had chanted, he felt great joy in his heart and immediately offered her a large, high-quality piece of fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
At that time, the devas in the midst of the void spoke in verse:
"Now you have attained a noble benefit; Your merit is most sublime.
All attachments are exhausted; You purely offer this robe."
Now, within the city of Rājagṛha, there are faithful men and women;
why do they not come to entreat you for the subtle and wondrous sound of the sublime Dharma?
To draw near to it enables one to leave suffering behind, yet if not requested, it shall not be spoken.
"Having heard this, if one practices accordingly, one will attain the supreme and wondrous state.
At that time, people from various households invited him to recite verses; having heard them with joy, he received great offerings.
The bhikṣuṇīs each gave rise to feelings of jealousy and said,
"This is a seductive song that deludes and confuses the minds of the multitude.
For this reason, the bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
“Did you actually compose these worldly songs?
He replied,
“I do not know the worldly songs.”
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣuṇī did not compose these worldly songs.
In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī, where a king named Kṛkin had seven daughters."
First is named Śramaṇa;
second is named Śramaṇamitra;
third is named Bhikṣuṇī.
The fourth was named Bhikṣuṇīdāsī;
the fifth was named Dharmā;
the sixth was named Sudharmā.
The seventh was named Bhikṣuṇī-Dāsī.
She had made a vow before Kāśyapa Buddha, as explained in detail in the *Saptabhaginī-sūtra*.

At that time, a bhikṣuṇī again took her away from the community to stay alone, and another bhikṣuṇī reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these events.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
Once she had come, he asked her:
"Is it true that you have indeed stayed alone, apart from the community?
He replied, "It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forth, it is not permitted to stay alone apart from the community.
Furthermore, the story of how King Virūḍhaka punished the kingdom of Kapilavastu should be told in detail.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs stayed overnight alone outside the city walls, except in cases of royal peril.

Furthermore, at that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on the road; being old or ill, they could not keep pace with their companions and stayed overnight alone. They felt doubt and regret, so they questioned Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then went and reported this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"If she does not wish to, there is no offense.
The Buddha then spoke to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī stays apart from other bhikṣuṇīs for one night, except during the [permitted] times."
"Other times" refers to when one is ill, or when a city is besieged by bandits or in a state of turmoil; these are called "other times. This constitutes the first offense for this rule.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"One night's stay" means from before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light.

"Except at other times" refers to when one does not wish to be separated from one's lodging, or when one is aged, infirm, or ill; or when besieged by bandits or rebels; or when one cannot exit the city or enter the city—these are called "other times."
This is an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category, which is the first offense [of its kind].
Regarding "saṃghāvaśeṣa," it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī stays apart from other bhikṣuṇīs from before sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
From sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, [if she remains there], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight in the same room within a saṃghārāma, they must remain within reach of one another’s outstretched hand; during the night, she must search for the other three times with her hand—not all three at once—but once in the first watch, once in the middle watch, and once in the last watch.
If one does not go to look for [the sick person] during the first watch of the night, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one does not go to look for them during the middle watch of the night, it is also a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one does not go to look for them during the last watch of the night, it is also a *vinayātikrama* offense.
It is not an offense to look [at them] at all times.
If one stays overnight in an upper or lower storied building, one should pass by three times during the night.
Likewise, if one stays overnight within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. In Rājagṛha there was an elder named Sudinna, who had a wife who was young and beautiful."
Her husband having passed away, the woman took no pleasure in men. Her younger brother-in-law desired to take her as his wife, so she spoke to the other women, saying:
"I take no pleasure in men, yet my brother-in-law wishes to take me as his wife."
The woman asked,
"Do you wish to be separated?
He replied:
"I wish to leave [the household life].
She then said to her:
"Go to Śrāvastī and approach the bhikṣuṇī Kālī; she shall ordain you and let you go forth."
This woman, appearing as if she were going out, went to Śrāvastī and asked people, "Which is the nunnery (bhikṣuṇī-saṃghārāma)?
They pointed out the location; having entered, she asked:
"Which is the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Kālī?
She pointed out the location of the room.
Having entered, he asked:
"Is this Āryā Kālī? She replied, "Yes."
"For what reason do you ask? He replied,
"I wish to leave the household life."
She was immediately ordained, leaving the household life and receiving full ordination.
Later, her uncle sought her but did not know her whereabouts;
someone said to him, "The bhikṣuṇī Kālī has already ordained her in Śrāvastī."
He then went to Śrāvastī and asked people,
"Which is the nuns' monastery?
They pointed out the location to him.
Having entered, she asked,
"Which is the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Kālī?
and they pointed out the location.
Having entered, he asked,
"Venerable lady, are you Kāli?
She replied:
"Yes! Why do you ask? he then said.
"I have not released my wife; for what reason have you ordained her and caused her to leave the household life?
The nun said, "Long-lived one!"
“From where have you come? He replied,
“I have come from Rājagṛha.”
The bhikṣuṇī reviled him, saying:
"You short-lived creature!
You are a thief!"
"The people of Rājagṛha constantly come here, delighting in spying and watching for the faults of the state's leaders.
He then said to his disciple:
"Bring my saṃghāṭī robe; bind this short-lived man and cast him into prison."
The man was immediately struck with fear and thought to himself:
"This person’s eyes are terrifying; perhaps he truly will do so.
He cast sidelong glances at him, gradually retreated, and once outside, spoke with indignation:
"This bhikṣuṇī has stolen my wife and ordained her, yet she now wishes to bind me!
When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, the Buddha asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said to Kālī:
"This is an evil deed. How could you ordain a person without the permission of her master?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to ordain anyone who has not been released by their master."
She then said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains one whose guardian has not given permission, this is an offense involving initial transgression, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If she does not obtain permission— where an unmarried girl must ask her parents, and one who is already married must ask her husband, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and younger brothers—
if she nonetheless goes forth and receives full ordination, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* is as explained above.
This rule constitutes an offense at its first commission.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains someone without the permission of their guardian, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one gives [the training] to one who is training in the precepts, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if to one who has received full ordination, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Therefore, the Blessed One said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the wife of a Malla from the village of Āmalaka was young and beautiful, and she had a secret affair with another man.
Her husband said to her: "Do not do this again; if you do, I shall punish you in such and such a manner."
His wife continued her misconduct despite his efforts to stop her. Her husband then waited for an opportunity, seized a man with whom she was consorting, and delivered him to the magistrate, saying:
"My wife has been having an affair with this man; I pray that Your Honor will punish them according to the law."
The one who metes out punishment according to the Dharma said:

"If a woman commits adultery with another, she shall be assembled before the two assemblies for seven days; once the seven days of assembly have passed, her body shall be torn asunder in the midst of the two assemblies."
The official then said to his wife, "You may return home for now;
if there is anything at home, you may go and prepare food and drink as an offering.
If there is nothing, do as you please."
"When seven days have passed, I shall tear your body asunder before the two assemblies.
She then returned home, prepared food and drink, and offered them to the two assemblies.
This woman wept in a secluded place, and the other women asked her:
"Why are you weeping? He replied, "How could I not weep?
After seven full days have passed, my body shall be split down the middle before the two assemblies."
The woman said,
"Do you wish to live?
He replied:
"So be it," she replied. He then said to her, "Go to the bhikṣuṇī Kālī in Śrāvastī and seek ordination there; you will be able to survive."
The people were intoxicated with wine; thereupon, the woman appeared as if she had briefly gone out and went straight to Śrāvastī, where she asked people, "Where is the nuns' monastery?"
Having been shown the location, she entered and asked the people there,
"Which is the room of the bhikṣuṇī Kālī?
They immediately pointed out the place to her.
Having entered, he said:
"Noble Lady! I wish to go forth into homelessness."
He asked, "Has your master given you permission?
He replied:
"How is it that she has permission?

The bhikṣuṇī replied, "If she is not yet married, her parents give permission; if she is already married, her paternal aunt, mother-in-law, husband, or uncle gives permission—this constitutes having permission."
She replied, “If that is so, you have already given your consent; my kinsmen and relatives all wish to tear my body apart and abandon me.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"If that is so, I shall release you with favor.
He immediately ordained him, granting him the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
The man sought him out, intending to punish him for his offense, but did not find him; he heard, however, that a bhikṣuṇī in Śrāvastī had already ordained him.
He immediately went to the city of Śrāvastī and asked people,
"Which is the bhikṣuṇī vihāra?
The people then pointed out the location to him.
Having entered, he asked,
"Which is the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Kālī?
and she pointed it out, saying:
"This is it. Having entered, she asked:
"Venerable lady, are you the bhikṣuṇī Kālī?"
He replied,
"For what reason do you ask?
The other said:
"I will not release my wife; why would she go forth into homelessness?
"Long-lived one! Where is your home?"
He replied,
"In the town of Āmalaka.
Then [the other] spoke to him:
“Short-lived one!
You are a thief; do you not know?
The people of Āmalaka frequently come here, seeking an opportunity to spy upon the kingdom.”
He then said to his disciple, "Bring me my robes; I shall inform the King that I am to be bound for this short life.
Having heard this, the man thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī has wide, staring eyes; she might be capable of doing evil.
Gradually retreating, he went outside and, filled with rage, reviled her:
"This śramaṇī has stolen my wife by ordaining her, yet now she wishes to bind me!"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Summon the bhikṣuṇī."
When she had arrived, the Buddha said:
"Kālī! This is an evil deed.
How could you, knowing that a person has committed an offense and that her relatives wish to punish her, ordain her as a renunciant?"
This is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching.
From this day forward, it is not permitted to ordain a woman who has committed an offense after she has been subjected to communal punishment for her transgression.
Furthermore, there was a woman in the village of Śākya-kaṇṭhī who, as described above, spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Ordain me and let me go forth."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "There was already a precedent; one who has committed such an offense is not permitted to go forth.
She then approached other bhikṣuṇīs, but none would ordain her. Consequently, she sought to go forth among the non-Buddhist sects.

The man wished to arrest her for punishment but did not know her whereabouts; he heard that she had gone outside the city of Śrāvastī and had already left home to join the non-Buddhist sect. Her husband thought to himself:
"This woman was originally the daughter of an upāsaka, yet now she has fallen into the false views of the non-Buddhists; this itself is sufficient punishment."
Thereupon, he no longer sought after them.

The various non-Buddhist teachings involve drinking rice-wash water and the rinsing water from cooking pots; they are shameless and naked, and furthermore, they commit boundless acts of sexual misconduct with their wives.
Her wife, weary and distressed, said,
"This is not the dharma of those who have left the home life.
She then departed for the bhikṣuṇī vihāra and spoke, saying:
"I have fallen into a deep pit with crumbling banks and am about to fall into hell; I only pray that you will lead me forth into the homeless life.
None of the bhikṣuṇīs dared to ordain her, so she went to Mahāprajāpatī and said, "Āryā!..."
"She is a woman of my own kin, a daughter of the Śākya clan; she has now fallen into a deep pit. I pray that you will deliver her and allow her to go forth.
Mahāprajāpatī then went and reported this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted; if she was previously ordained by non-Buddhists, you may later grant her permission to leave the household life.
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly ordains a woman who has committed an offense and whose relatives wish to punish her, except in other circumstances.”
"Other times" refers to when she was previously ordained by non-Buddhists; this is called "other times.
This constitutes an initial offense for a bhikṣuṇī.
The term "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Assembly" refers to two assemblies: the assembly of one's maternal kin and the assembly of one's husband's family.
"Relatives" refers to the Brahmin clans, the Kṣatriya clans, the Vaiśya clans, and the Śūdra clans.

As for the punishment of criminals, some are wrapped in thin cloth and burned; some have sandbags tied around their necks and submerged in water; some have their heads set on fire; some have their ears or noses cut off; some have their urethras cauterized with heated iron; or their bodies are split asunder—thus do the various national laws differ.
Except for those who previously went forth among the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika), the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
"Non-Buddhist ascetics" refers to the Nirgranthas, the Ājīvikas, the Kṣapaṇakas, and others such as these who belong to the non-Buddhist schools.
This is a primary offense, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, as explained in detail above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman who has committed an offense should be disciplined, nevertheless ordains her, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one [acts] with one who is training in the Dharma, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Therefore, the Blessed One said.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a large number of women were on the far bank of the Ajiravatī River, while the community of bhikṣuṇīs had assembled on this side.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā took off her robes, placed them on the ground, and swam across the current.
The women said to one another, "Look!
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā is coming across by swimming.
Having arrived, she sat down in an open space, and after a short while, she swam back across again.
The women spoke with resentment, saying, "How can this Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā be like a wicked person who, having crossed over, returns again?
When the Bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā here.
When she had arrived, the Buddha said:
"This is an evil act; how could you swim across alone at a boat-ferrying crossing?
From this day forward, you are not permitted to swim across alone at a boat-ferrying crossing."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī crosses a river alone at a ferry crossing, this is an offense involving initial transgression, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "crossing alone": if one leaves the boundary and reaches the other shore, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Kālī was wandering through a village; after she had departed, her dependent disciple was subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*).
When the teacher returned, the disciple said to him:
"The Sangha has performed the *karma* of formal accusation against me, and they no longer share with me the food of dharma or the food of flavor.
He then rebuked him, saying:
"Be silent for now; simply ensure that the Saṃgha assembles.
They immediately assembled the Saṃgha, and each of the bhikṣuṇīs thought to herself:
"This bhikṣuṇī returns from her journey and assembles the Saṃgha; she always delights in having gifts to distribute. What shall we receive today?"
They all gathered joyfully and quickly.
Having assembled, they immediately made this proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs has performed the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of [the nun] so-and-so.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant the revocation of the suspension of the *karma* for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has performed the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* against the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; the Saṃgha now grants the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the revocation of that *ukkhepanīyakamma*.”

Venerable sisters of the Saṃgha, those who consent to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the revocation of the formal act of suspension against the bhikṣuṇī [Name] remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
This is the first motion.
Thus, the formal motion was made three times.
Seeing that this bhikṣuṇī’s eyes were so terrifying, none of the other bhikṣuṇīs dared to stop her.
The bhikṣuṇīs then said to one another:
"What language is this?
they all said,
"We do not know this language either."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this to Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of these circumstances, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said. "This is a wicked deed.

How could you, knowing that the community of bhikṣuṇīs had performed a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet before you had practiced compliance or performed the act in accordance with the Dharma, first fail to inform the Saṃgha and yourself relinquish the formal act?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī saṃgha has performed a formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya, yet before the act has been rendered legal, she herself grants the relinquishment of that suspension without first informing the saṃgha, this is an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knows" means either she knows it herself or hears it from another.
"In harmony" means not being a separate assembly.
Regarding one who acts according to the Dharma and Vinaya: they do not perceive their offense, they do not confess it, and they do not relinquish their three views.
As for the formal act of suspension (*karmavācanā*): they are not to live in communion.
One who has not yet acted according to the Dharma has not yet practiced in accordance with the teaching, their mind is not yet subdued, and the Sangha has not yet granted them release.

Regarding "not having first informed": if one abandons [the matter] within the Saṃgha without having performed the formal act of seeking permission (*ñattikamma*) within the Saṃgha, this constitutes an initial offense, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is as explained above.
If the disciples have performed the formal act of suspension (*karmavācanā*) in concord, the preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*) or the teacher (*ācāryinī*) should go to the elder bhikṣuṇīs and say:
"Who is free from folly and constantly free from fault?"
"It was because wisdom was not present that this occurred; I shall never do it again.
Having spoken thus to all the people so as to soften their hearts, he then performed the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) before the Saṃgha to seek their permission.
It should be stated as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has been subject to the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) by the Saṃgha on account of such a matter; she has now acted in accordance [with the instructions], her mind has become supple, and she has relinquished [the offense]."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, the monk [Name] wishes to request from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karma* of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
Venerable sirs, please listen as this [Name] wishes to request from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karma* of suspension; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Thereafter, one should request [the formal act].
If anyone should obstruct it, the preceptor (upādhyāya) should speak with gentle words to cause them to desist.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha is in harmony and has performed a *karma* of suspension (*ukṣepa*) in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, should abandon it herself, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a householder who, with lustful intent, invited the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhā, providing her with robes, bowls, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions for illness, saying: "Āryā!..."
"Do you know for what reason I gave it?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I do."
He asked again,
"How do you know? He replied:
"Because of merit.
He spoke again:
"It is thus; thereafter, it is also for the sake of desire."
At that time, Śrīdattā was one who had transcended desire; upon hearing these words, her mind remained unperturbed. She did not take the matter to heart, yet she did not oppose it either.
The bhikṣuṇīs then reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went at once to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call Jyotiṣka here. Once he had arrived,
the Buddha questioned him thoroughly regarding the aforementioned matters:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
‘This is an evil matter. Do you not intend to set an example for future generations?’”
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Rājagṛha assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī, whether with a mind free from outflows or with a mind subject to outflows, receives robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness from a man, this is an offense entailing immediate confession; it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
“Bhikṣuṇī” refers to, for example, Bhikṣuṇī Jyotiṣkā.
“With a mind free from outflows” means with a mind free from desire.
“Alms bowl” refers to the superior, middling, or inferior types.
"Robes" refers to the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antaravāsaka, the saṃkakṣikā, and the varṣāśāṭī.
"Food and drink" refers to solid food (khādya) and soft food (bhojya).
Medicine refers to honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, and fat.
This constitutes an initial offense.
If a person gives robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness to a bhikṣuṇī, and says these words:
"If [the donor] says, 'I give this for that reason,' one should not accept it, but should say:
'I have no need of it; you may keep it yourself at another house.'"
If she accepts it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If she does not speak, but moves her hands or feet, blinks her eyes, waves her hand, snaps her fingers, or draws figures or letters on the ground—by such gestures indicating that she knows he has a lustful mind toward her—she should not accept it;
if she accepts it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one’s faith is pure and one’s senses are discerning, the recipient incurs no offense.
If a woman gives with a lustful mind—whether by moving her hands and feet or by winking—one should know that she possesses a lustful intent and should not accept [the gift].

If one accepts [the gift] while lacking faith, with impure intentions, and with unsteady faculties, it is an offense against the Vinaya. If, however, one accepts it with faithful confidence, pure intentions, and steady faculties, there is no offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume 36 [and] Volume 37.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhavarman of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

From the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), translated by Dharmakṣema, following the remainder of the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules: The Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha. At that time, the World-Honored One established a precept, forbidding one from receiving robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness from a man with lustful intent. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhā did not accept a robe offered by an elder.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said to Jyotiṣkā,
"Why do you not accept this man's gift?
Whether a man’s mind is defiled or undefiled— what concern is that of yours?"
"Only ensure that your mind is free from outflows (*anāsrava*), and having taken it up, employ it according to causes and conditions.
The bhikṣuṇīs then admonished this bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not speak such words:"
"What does it matter to worldly affairs whether this man’s mind is defiled or undefiled?
You need only ensure that your own mind is undefiled; you may accept this offering and use it according to the circumstances.
Thus he was admonished twice and thrice, yet he did not desist.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of it.
The Buddha said:
"Summon the bhikṣuṇī."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed; how could you encourage that person with a mind full of outflows to give?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"Command all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Rājagṛha to assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"You may accept this gift from this man; what does it matter to you whether he has lustful thoughts or not?"
"However, you must not let your mind stray; once you have accepted the gift, you may use it according to the circumstances.
The bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not speak such words:"
"You should accept this offering.
What business is it of yours whether a man has a mind of outflows or is free from outflows?
Provided that you yourself are free from outflows, you may accept the gift and use it according to the circumstances."
"In this manner, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
It is well if he relinquishes this matter; if he does not relinquish it, this constitutes the first offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
Regarding the bhikṣuṇī who speaks these words, she is like the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
Regarding the one who takes the gift, she is like the bhikṣuṇī Jyotiṣkā.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī to relinquish this matter, if she does not relinquish it, this rule involves up to three admonitions; it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; [the account of] the schism in the Saṃgha and the assistance rendered therein is as explained in detail among the bhikṣus.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī desires to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha and intentionally applies diligent means to maintain the matter of schism and engage in dispute,
the other bhikṣuṇīs should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
'Venerable sister!'"
Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not zealously employ skillful means to maintain the matter of schism or engage in disputes.
You should act in concert with the Saṃgha.
Why is this? When the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute, training together as one like water and milk mixed, they dwell in peace and happiness according to the Dharma.
If this bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If she relinquishes it, that is well; if she does not relinquish it, this rule constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense after the third admonition.
If several bhikṣuṇīs—whether one, two, or many—consent to assist one another, sharing the same words and the same views, with the intent to break up a harmonious Saṃgha.
When these bhikṣuṇīs are being admonished by other bhikṣuṇīs, those bhikṣuṇīs who side with them say:
"Venerable ladies!
Do not speak of this bhikṣuṇī’s good or bad qualities."
Why is this? Because these bhikṣuṇīs speak according to the Dharma and speak according to the Vinaya.
Whatever these bhikṣuṇīs have spoken is exactly what our hearts desire.
"Whatever matter this bhikṣuṇī has seen and approves of, we also approve of; this bhikṣuṇī speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge.
The other bhikṣuṇīs should then admonish those bhikṣuṇīs who agree with her, saying:
"Venerable ladies!..."
Do not speak these words:
“The bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Dharma; the bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Vinaya. Why is that?
This bhikṣuṇī speaks what is contrary to the Dharma; this bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Vinaya.
Noble Lady! Do not assist in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should instead joyfully assist in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha.
Why is this? "When the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute, practicing together in a single training like water mixed with milk, and dwelling in peace according to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, persists in her position and does not relinquish it, she should be admonished a second and a third time.
It is well if she relinquishes this matter; if she does not relinquish it, then for this offense, after up to three admonitions, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was involved in a dispute, and the Saṃgha performed a formal ritual (*karman*) against her in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
When the *karmavācanā* was concluded, he, out of malice, slandered the Saṃgha unreasonably, saying: "O Noble Saṃgha!
You follow desire, you follow hatred, you follow fear, and you follow delusion; the Saṃgha acts out of desire, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion; for this reason, you have censured me."
"This is an illegal adjudication of a case.
The other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Venerable lady!..."
Do not unjustly slander the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha does not follow favoritism, nor hatred, nor fear, nor delusion.
The Saṅgha does not settle legal matters in an unrighteous manner based on favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion.

At that time, the woman, with a heart of faith and joy, immediately gave the value for beds, mats, pillows, and bolsters; having received them, she used them to provide robes, bowls, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī went on her alms-round in due order and arrived at their house.
The women asked her, "Noble lady!
Have we yet provided the bed, bedding, coverlet, and pillow for the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā as promised?"
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"How could you do such a thing?
You should simply buy your own robes, bowl, food, drink, and medicinal requisites."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him:
"Is it true that you sought out bedding and requisites and used them for other purposes?
He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. Have you not constantly heard me, through immeasurable skillful means, disparage excessive desire and praise few desires?"
"How can you practice evil and unwholesome dharmas?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha; by this, one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas."
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to request bedding and mats for the purpose of converting them for other uses.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī solicits materials for a bed or bedding, yet uses them herself for robes, alms-bowls, food and drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“Bhikṣuṇī” is as explained above.
“Bedding, mattresses, pillows, and bolsters” are as explained in detail above in the section concerning bhikṣus.
“To beg” means to solicit through exhortation and persuasion.
If one subsequently uses it oneself for robes, alms bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this object must be relinquished before the Saṃgha, and one must confess the *pāyattika* offense.
If one repents without relinquishing [the object], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained in detail in the section on the *bhikṣus*.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* begs for bedding and mats, yet uses them herself for robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one makes a cord for this purpose, it must not be used for that purpose.
If one uses a cord intended for a bed to make a mattress, a cord intended for a mattress to make a pillow, or a cord intended for a pillow to make a binding strap, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If, through exhortation and conversion, one obtains a large amount of funds for beds, mats, and pillows, one should point each item out to the person and record them, saying: "This is the value for the bed; this is the value for the mat; this is the value for the pillow; this is the value for the bolster."
If one does not do so, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama* for each instance.
One may borrow items for the purpose of repairing dwellings or for using pots and pans, provided it is done in accordance with the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu requests bedding and mats, yet uses them for other purposes, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
It is permissible to borrow and use [items] in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, it is said.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was going on her alms-round wearing a garment that was soiled, greasy, tattered, and full of holes. Upon seeing her, a woman spoke to her, saying:
“Venerable One! I have given the price for the robe; please accept the robe.
Another person said:
"I have given the price for a bowl, knowing that I would obtain a bowl.
Having received it, she used it only for food and drink until it was exhausted, rather than making a robe or a bowl.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who was begging for alms, and a woman asked her:
“Thullanandā, have I not already given you the price for a robe and bowl?
She replied, “I have only used it for food and drink; how could I have made a robe and bowl?”
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇī informed Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of these circumstances, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed! Have you not heard me praise few desires and censure many desires through immeasurable skillful means?
How could you take the value of robes and alms bowls and put them to other uses?"
“From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī receives something from someone for one purpose, yet uses it for another, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "giving it away": this refers to giving the value of the robe or the alms bowl.
Regarding "using it for other purposes": this refers to using it for food, drink, or medicinal decoctions.
This constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; one must relinquish this object to the Saṃgha and perform confession for the *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī is given the price for a robe, the price for a bowl, the price for ghee, or the price for oil, she should recognize the price for a robe as a robe, the price for a bowl as a bowl, the price for ghee as ghee, and the price for oil as oil.
If one uses it for a different purpose, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a donor says,
"Use it as you please," [there is no offense].
There is no offense if there is no specific purpose for which it was intended, or if one acts according to what was done.

If a bhikṣu receives the price for a robe, the price for a bowl, the price for ghee, the price for oil, or the price for a robe, he should use them for their respective purposes—down to the case of the price for ghee, which should be known as ghee. If he uses them for another purpose, it is a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If one uses [the food] according to one's own discretion, there is no offense; if one does not intend to do anything with it, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā incited others to prepare food, saying to a woman:
“Upāsikā! I wish to prepare food for the Saṃgha.
The upāsikās, with faith and joy, gave the price for the food and spoke these words:
“Noble Lady! When it is the day for preparing food, please tell me, and I shall come to receive the meal.
Having received this, the bhikṣuṇī prepared food herself and purchased robes and bowls, while using the remainder to make coarse food.
On that day, he came in person to distribute the food; having seen it, he asked, "Venerable One!
Previously I gave you a large amount for the cost of food; why is your meal so coarse?"
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Where can one obtain fine food?
One should simply make robes and bowls for oneself and eat what one has."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to report these matters to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed."
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; let those who have already heard this hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for food and uses it to make robes, bowls, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions for her own enjoyment, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Regarding 'for food,' it means preparing food for the Saṃgha.
Regarding 'begging,' it means soliciting through exhortation and seeking.
Regarding 'misappropriating the use,' it means using robes or bowls for one's own food or drink; this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having solicited food for the Saṃgha, instead purchases clothing, a bowl, or food and drink for herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one who is to perform a task according to their original intention diverts food intended for a later meal to a previous meal, or diverts food intended for a previous meal to a later meal, they commit a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If one diverts the value of food to make bedding or mattresses, or if one divides it between summer, spring, or winter clothing, or between portions of food—using it according to one's own prior inclination rather than in accordance with the donor’s original intention—the offense is a *vinayātikrama*.
If a bhikṣuṇī has obtained food through solicitation on behalf of the Saṃgha, she should consume it all. If there is any surplus food, drink, ghee, or oil, she should point it out to the donor.
If the donor takes it away, she should remain silent; if the donor says, "I give this to you, Āryā," [she may accept it].
One should say:
"Give it to the Saṃgha.
Then he says again:
"I have already given it to the Saṃgha myself; this is for you, Venerable One.
Taking it in this manner is without fault.
Therefore, it is said.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, some visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrived and were due to receive rooms in the prescribed order. A bhikṣuṇī who had resided there previously and held a low seat said: "Āryā!..."
"I will wait until I have moved my bowl.
When the next day arrived, he asked,
"Have you finished moving the bowl?"
She replied,
"I have not yet finished moving my bowl.
The visiting bhikṣuṇī said:
"Do you wish to take these bowls and go to the pottery workshop?
What use have you for so many bowls?
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, the Buddha asked her:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"How is it that you keep an extra bowl?
From this day forward, keeping an extra bowl is not permitted."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above. Regarding "keeping an extra bowl":
a bowl refers to a *śrīvatsa* bowl, an *upashrīvatsa* bowl, an *ukkoṭana* bowl, or a *vakkali* bowl; such items made of iron, clay, and so forth, are called bowls.

There are bowls categorized as superior, middling, and inferior; there are surplus bowls, deficient bowls, and corresponding bowls. To possess them [in excess] constitutes an offense of forfeiture and confession (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
A bhikṣuṇī may possess sixteen bowls: one for personal use, three for designated giving (pariṣkāra-datta), four surplus bowls, four deficient bowls, and four corresponding bowls.
If one keeps [an extra bowl] beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" is as explained above.
For a bhikṣuṇī, there is a fixed limit to keeping an extra bowl; however, for a bhikṣu, there is no offense in keeping many bowls for the purpose of pure use (*pariśuddha-paribhoga*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke.
As previously described at length, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, and so forth, until he said:
"Do you wish to dwell in a clothing shop?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How is it that you keep extra robes?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to keep extra robes.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Robe" refers to a *kambala* robe, a *kārpāsa* robe, a *kauśeya* robe, a *kṣauma* robe, a *śāṇa* robe, a *māñjiṣṭha* robe, or a *kṛmivati* robe.
"Keeps" means to keep beyond the limit; this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
A bhikṣuṇī is permitted to keep twenty robes.
One may accept and keep five robes, or, having performed the formal act of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) for fifteen robes, one may use them.
If one keeps more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, there is no limit; if he uses robes after performing the formal act of dedication, he is without fault.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā’s saṃghāṭī robe was torn; she neither washed, dyed, nor mended it, but cast it down beneath a wall, saying:
"Whoever wishes to take it, let them take it."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhā was wearing a tattered robe, and the other bhikṣuṇīs said to her: "Āryā!
You may take this robe, wash it, dye it, mend it, and make use of it."
She immediately took it, mended it, washed and dyed it,
and put it on. The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said,
"Give me back my robe!"
She said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Look at this strange thing! These clothes and belongings must not be placed on the ground for even a moment; have you finished filling your rooms?"
She immediately seized the saṃghāṭī.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went at once to report this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
Once she had come, the Buddha asked her:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, "This is an evil deed. ... [and so on] ...
until the Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while staying at her residence, discards an old saṃghāṭī and proclaims:
‘Whoever wishes to take it, let them take it.’”
"If she later takes it back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Residence" refers to within the vihāra.
"To discard" means to cast it away upon the ground.
If, after another person has taken it, one seizes it back, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī has discarded an object and someone takes it for use, she may not reclaim it;
however, if no one takes it and she later takes it because she requires it, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, within a vihāra, discards his robe, bowl, leather sandals, or other minor belongings, and someone else takes them, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense if he later seizes them back.
If no one takes it, and one later retrieves it, there is no offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣuṇī who had a soiled saṃghāṭī robe; having unfolded it, she spread it out to dry in the midday sun, and a wind arose and blew it away.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“Why is it that after you have torn apart your old saṃghāṭī robe, you neither sew it yourself nor have anyone else sew it?”
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to pick up and wash your robes.

Furthermore, at that time there was a woman of the Śākya clan, a Malla woman who had originally been a musician; she had a saṃghāṭī robe that was so thick and heavy it was difficult to wash. She spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit [the observance] for five or six days.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.

If a bhikṣuṇī has an old saṃghāṭī robe, whether she tears it herself or causes another to tear it, and if more than five or six days pass without her sewing it herself or causing another to sew it—except in the case of illness—it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.”
"Regarding the term 'bhikṣuṇī,' it is as explained above.

Regarding the saṃghāṭī robe: if she wishes to wash it, whether she tears it herself or causes another to tear it, and for five or six days—limited to six days—if she does not return it to sew it herself nor cause another to sew it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī washes an old *saṃghāṭī* robe, she is not permitted to remove the padding if it is light and thin; however, if it is thick and heavy, she is permitted to remove it. Having removed it, she must wash it. After washing, she should spread it out on a mat or a straw mat, weigh down its four corners with stones, and once it is dry, she should call her co-resident disciples (*sahacaryā-śiṣya*), dependent disciples (*niśraya-śiṣya*), fellow preceptors (*upādhyāya*), fellow instructors (*ācārya*), and all her acquaintances so that the bhikṣuṇīs may quickly join together to complete the work.
If one is old or ill and has no one to assist them, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a trainee nun (śikṣamāṇā) said to Thullanandā:
“Noble Lady! Grant me the full ordination.
Thullanandā replied:
"If you give me your robe, I shall grant you full ordination.
She then gave him the robe, but afterwards did not grant her full ordination.
The śikṣamāṇā said:
"Grant me full ordination.
Thus it continued for a long time.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke of this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these events.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked her:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said, "This is an evil deed. ... [and so on] ...
until the Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā:
‘Give me a robe, and I shall grant you full ordination.’”
"Having taken the robe, if one does not give it to one who has received full ordination, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Śikṣamāṇā" refers to one who is training in the precepts.
"Robe" refers to the seven kinds of robes as described above.
Furthermore, there are robes ranging from the *saṃghāṭī* down to the rain-bathing robe.
If one has consented to grant full ordination (*upasampadā*), yet subsequently neither grants it oneself nor causes another to grant it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes a śikṣamāṇā’s robe with the intention of granting her full ordination (*upasampadā*), she must subsequently grant that ordination.
If one who is old or ill lacks the strength to receive [the precepts], one should say to another person:
"Take this robe and confer full ordination upon him.
If the former person does not wish to receive them and asks for the robe back, it should be returned.
If a bhikṣu promises a śrāmaṇera [to ordain him] but does not grant him full ordination (upasampadā), he commits a vinaya offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was a merchant from the north who was traveling about selling expensive, high-quality kambalas.
Someone asked,
"How much is this rope worth?
He replied:
"One hundred thousand.
At that time, the king, the prince, the ministers, and other great merchant lords all considered the price too high and did not purchase it; they sat in the shop, filled with sorrow and anxiety.
A person asked,
"For what reason do you have such a sorrowful expression? He replied:
"I am selling this *kambala* cloth; it is of great value and carries a heavy tax. Yet now, though I sell it, I cannot find a buyer, and for this reason I am unhappy."
The man asked,
"Do you wish to sell it?
He replied:
"I wish to sell it.
He then said, "You may take this to the śramaṇī Bhadrā; she will buy it from you."
She then took it and went to ask people, saying:
"Which of these is the bhikṣuṇī vihāra?
After the people had pointed out the location, she asked:
"Which is the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā?
When the people had pointed out the location, he asked, "Who is Bhadrā?"
The bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā replied,
"For what reason do you ask?
He answered:
"Do you wish to buy this *kambala*?
He asked, "For how much do you ask for it?"
He replied,
"A hundred thousand.
Without raising or lowering the price, he then said to his disciples:
"Go and tell the shopkeeper Varuḍa: 'Take a hundred thousand [coins] and give it to him.
Someone asked him:
"Have you sold the *kambala* yet?"
He replied,
"It has already been sold. He asked:
"Who took it?
He replied, "The śramaṇī Bhadrā."
That person immediately expressed his resentment, saying, "Those who have left the household life still harbor such desires for pleasure.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they spoke of it to Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇī:
"Will you not set an example for future generations?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to purchase heavy robes for more than four kārṣāpaṇas."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Summon all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on the city of Vaiśālī; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī purchases a heavy robe for more than four kārṣāpaṇas, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Four *kārṣāpaṇas* refers to four times forty-nine old coins.
A 'heavy robe' refers to a *kambala* garment.
'To purchase' means to knowingly take."
If one takes more than nineteen coins of old currency, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding what constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī does not purchase heavy robes for more than nineteen coins of old currency, there is no offense, even if they are of high value, provided she did not solicit them and they were given to her of their own accord.
For bhikṣuṇīs there is a limit, but for bhikṣus there is no limit; even if it is of high value, if one knows how to take and use it, there is no offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was at that time a merchant from the south who brought fine cotton cloth with the pattern of a swan’s markings. Someone asked him:
“How much do you ask for this robe?
He replied,
“A hundred thousand.”

Because the price was so high, the royal household did not purchase it, nor did any of the great ministers or merchant lords; since no one bought it, he sat dejectedly upon his shop, filled with sorrow.
Someone asked him,
"Why do you have such a sorrowful expression? He replied:
"I purchased this garment at a high price and paid much in taxes; yet now it cannot be sold.
He asked, "Do you wish for it to be sold?"
He replied,
"I wish to sell it.
[The other] said:
"You may take this and go to the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā; she will buy it from you.
He then went and asked people, "Where is the residence of the bhikṣuṇīs?"
Having learned this, she entered and asked, "Which is the dwelling of the śramaṇī Bhadrā?
The person immediately pointed out the location; having arrived there, she said:
"Salutations! Noble Lady! Are you Bhadrā?"
He replied, "It is so.
Why do you ask?"
He replied, "I have this swan-patterned cotton cloth; would you like to buy it? He asked:
“How much do you ask for? He replied,
“I ask for one hundred thousand.”
The bhikṣuṇī also did not seek to reduce the amount, but immediately said to her disciple:
"Go and tell them at the Pāruḥi shop to take a hundred thousand [coins] and give it to me."
Someone asked him,
"Have you been able to sell it?
He replied:
"It has been sold.
He asked, "Who took it?"
She replied,
"The śramaṇī Bhadrā took it.
Someone spoke with resentment, saying:
“How can those who have gone forth take such delight in this?
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇī told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on until the Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā:
“Will you not set an example for future generations?”
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to purchase fine, light clothing for more than two and a half *kārsāpaṇas*.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī purchases a fine, light garment for more than two and a half kārṣāpaṇas, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Two and a half kārṣāpaṇas" refers to forty-six old coins.
"The market price" means knowing the rate at which they are taken.
If [the value] exceeds this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī purchases fine, light clothing, she should acquire it for no more than two and a half *kārṣāpaṇas*; she must not exceed this amount.
If one gives it oneself without asking for it, even if one obtains a fine garment of high value, there is no offense in using it.
A bhikṣu incurs no offense in purchasing a garment of high value for his own use.
One may ask for bedding and mats for one's own use; however, the funds intended for robes and alms bowls must not be used for other purposes.
Reducing one’s own use for the sake of the community; keeping an extra bowl and keeping extra robes;
taking back robes after having discarded them; receiving full ordination while wearing disarrayed robes;
heavy robes and fine, light robes.
The second *vagga* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a wood-carrier driving a cart passed by a shop, and a merchant asked him:
"How much is this for sale?"
He replied, "One kārṣāpaṇa.
The merchant said to him:
“Load this firewood onto your cart and take it to my house to unload it; when you return and pass by here, I shall give you the payment.
When the wood-seller drove his cart past the nunnery where the bhikṣuṇīs resided, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā asked him, “Long-lived one!”
"Does your firewood have an owner who has purchased it yet?
He replied, "It already has."
“How much did you get?
He replied, “One kārṣāpaṇa.”
He immediately said,
"I will give you two kārṣāpaṇas.
Because the owner was greedy for profit, he gave them to him at once.
After the man had finished stacking the firewood and was returning, he passed by the merchant's shop.
The merchant said to him, "Take this for free. He replied:
"I have already sold it to another person.
He asked, "For how much was it sold?"
He replied,
"I obtained two kārṣāpaṇas. He asked:
"Who took it? She replied,
"The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā."
The merchants rebuked her, saying,
"How can this śramaṇī possess so much money? When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this,
they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
“Did you indeed know that he had already purchased it, yet take it by increasing the price?
He replied, “It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil deed. How could you, knowing that another had purchased it at the market, snatch it away?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome qualities."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has purchased something at market, buys it up [to preempt it], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Obtaining through purchase" refers, for example, to a merchant in a shop.

If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to purchase an item, and she knows that another has already purchased it, she must not snatch it away; she should wait until the previous person does not take it, at which point she may take it.
One should also ask the person in question:
"Did you take it intentionally? If they say:
"Therefore, one wishes to take it.
To make this firm, one should not take it.
If one says:
"I shall not take it again.
If one takes it, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī purchases a robe or bowl and then later takes it back from another, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If, within the Saṃgha, one takes an item of high value, there is no offense except in the case of the Upādhyāya or the Ācārya.
If a bhikṣu buys goods and then intercepts another's purchase, it is an offense of Vinaya-transgression (vibhaṅga-āpatti); therefore, this is said.
A long alms-bowl with fewer than five mends; the seven-day rule; taking back a robe out of anger;
selling gold and begging for thread; fine weaving and urgent offerings;
pilfering from the market and misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha.
The third chapter (varga) concludes.

Taking robes from a bhikṣuṇī, as well as washing, dyeing, pure black, the three parts, white *kocava* wool, the six-year-old *niṣīdana*, the three-yojana transport of wool, the rain-bathing robe, and the forest dwelling—these eleven matters should have been excluded [from the list], yet they were not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are eleven matters that should be included within the *Cīvaravastu* (Chapter on Robes) from the beginning of the *Bhikṣuvastu* (Chapter on Monks).

These emerge from the initial *Bhikṣuvastu*: taking the robes of a bhikṣuṇī, handling gold and silver, and supplementing [the rules] by including the washing of old robes and their subsequent sale or purchase.

Later, in the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga*, it is stated that one may use rain-clothing to supplement what has been sold for gold, or use items from a marketplace to supplement what was obtained in a forest hermitage; in these cases, whether one *varga* or two *vargas* are involved, the numerical requirement is not diminished.
Regarding the *niḥsargika* (offenses involving forfeiture), the World-Honored One has finished expounding the thirty matters for bhikṣuṇīs:
false speech and its varieties, malicious speech further incited,
[the offense of] releasing life, the rules regarding the recitation of the Dharma, and claiming superhuman qualities for oneself.
It is not sufficient to speak of grave offenses, nor to grant a suspension for slighting the precepts;
thus ends the first chapter (Bāḍhaka).
[The section on] censuring the spreading of bedding in the open air, and forcibly dragging someone out from a covered place.
First, spreading out beds with pointed legs; using water containing insects to moisten grass and mud;
causing remorse and regret so that one finds no joy—this concludes the second *varga*.
Eating at one time and eating at various times; receiving robes and not relinquishing them for use.
Not urging [others] regarding leftover food; not accepting food at improper times;
storing food after two or three bowls have been set aside; and eating separately from the community.
The third chapter (varga) is concluded.
Kindling a fire for more than three nights; giving consent and later becoming angry;
entering a village and sending [the monk] back; obstructing the Path while seeing [the offense] and not relinquishing it;
the three types of dyed robes for śrāmaṇeras; taking treasure and frightening others.
The fourth section concludes.
[Regarding] drinking water containing insects, a non-Buddhist, sitting in a secluded place where sexual misconduct occurs,
observing an army for more than three nights, a tooth-banner, and fighting one another.
Playing with knives in water; the fifth *vagga* is concluded.

Pointing fingers at one another, pointing at a thief’s companion, digging the earth, the four-month invitation, not following the training, drinking alcohol, and listening in silence while belittling others.
Not listening when adjudicating matters; the sixth *varga* is concluded. [The following offenses are:
eating apart from one's companions, [entering] the royal palace, needle cases exceeding eight finger-breadths, *tūla* cotton, sitting mats, covering sores, and imitating the Tathāgata.
The Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense of slandering [another] regarding the redirection [of offerings]; the seventh *varga* is concluded.
This is explained in detail within the Bhikṣu Precepts.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilī entered a village wearing her saṃghāṭī without having informed her resident disciple.
A bhikṣuṇī called out, saying:
"So-and-so, go and fetch some almsfood!
She replied:
“Venerable One! Wait while I fetch my saṃghāṭī.
He then searched for his robe, but could not find it.
The teacher’s robe was there, and he thought:
"The teacher will surely go wearing my robe.
Then this thought arose:
"The teacher may wear my robe, but I may not wear the teacher's robe.
He said, "You may go, but I cannot go."
"Why is that? He replied, "I have no clothes."
He then said,
"Come wearing your teacher’s robe.
He replied:
"I hold this in high esteem and dare not wear it; you may take it yourself.
One day she lost her meal.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to report this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked her:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “This is a wicked deed. Why did you not speak before putting on another’s robe?”
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence upon Vaiśālī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī wears another's robe without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
It is not permitted to wear a disciple’s saṃghāṭī without informing them; if one wishes to wear it, one should inform them.
"I shall wear your robe; if you go out, you may wear my saṃghāṭī.
In this manner, regarding all robes—if one wishes to wash, dye, or sew a robe, or has some business requiring one to wear the disciple's robe—one should say:
"Stay here; I shall bring food for you."
"If a bhikṣu puts on another's robe without informing them, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, Volume 37.
The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, Scroll Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India, together with Faxian, during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

The second part of the one hundred and forty-one *pāyattika* rules. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a man named Ghaṭīkāra who had gone forth among the non-Buddhists, while his parents had gone forth within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Ghaṭīkāra was living in the midst of severe cold without any clothing; he went to his mother’s place and stayed there like a wild beast.
His mother then thought with compassion:
"I have a newly washed, dyed, and purified *uttarāsaṅga* robe."
He then took it off and gave it to him; having received it, the man immediately put it on and went into a tavern to sit there, where he was reviled by the people of the world who said:
"This donkey who eats wine dregs and holds such wrong views has donned the insignia of a holy man."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wicked deed; why did you take this robe and give it to a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to give robes with one's own hand to those of external paths.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives clothing with her own hands to a layperson or a śramaṇa of a non-Buddhist sect, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Layperson" refers to one who lives at home.
"Heretics" refers to those who have left the household life as heretics.
"Giving with one's own hand" means receiving from hand to hand.
"The robes of a śramaṇa" are the insignia of the noble and holy ones.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.
One must not give robes with one's own hands to laypeople, non-Buddhist ascetics (*tīrthika*), or śramaṇas.

If a bhikṣuṇī possesses virtuous precepts and a woman or a child wishes to beg for a piece of torn cloth to ward off calamities, she must not give it with her own hands; she should instead have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) or a woman give it.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe with his own hands to a layperson or a non-Buddhist ascetic (śramaṇa), he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If there is a bhikṣu endowed with preceptual virtue and someone requests a piece of a tattered *kāṣāya* to ward off calamities, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) give it; he must not give a large piece, but should give a small one.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke:
"The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who wore her robes like a laywoman, and she was censured by the people of the world:
'How can a bhikṣuṇī wear long robes with trailing threads as she walks?'"
"Just like a worldly woman—this person is ruined; what path can she have?
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇī spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to make robes by joining threads together; they must be made according to the prescribed measurements.
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes an antarvāsa, it must be made according to the proper measurements: four sugata-span lengths in length and two spans in width.”
"If one exceeds [the prescribed length] and cuts it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Antarvāsaka" is that which was permitted by the Blessed One.
"Who makes it" means either making it oneself or having another make it.
"Of measured size" means four Sugata-span in length.
"Sugata" means the Well-Gone One (Sugata).
