The width shall be two vitastis.
If it is made exceeding this measure, one must cut it down and confess a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the term "pāyattika," it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes [a robe] that is of proper length but exceeds the prescribed width, and it is completed, it is a pāyattika offense.
To use it constitutes a vinayātikrama offense.
Likewise if it is of proper width but exceeds the prescribed length; [the same applies to other combinations].
Likewise, if the edges are of the proper measure while the middle exceeds it;
or if the middle is of the proper measure while the edges exceed it;
or likewise if it is folded, wrinkled, or sprinkled with water, and one desires it to become long and wide once it has dried, it is a *pāyattika*.
To use [it] constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣuṇī who was young and beautiful; she was walking along the road wearing her robes.
At that time, her two breasts became visible, and when the man saw them, he laughed at her.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to report the matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs should make saṃkakṣikās.
Furthermore, at that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who left threads hanging while making a saṃkakṣikā that was long and wide; [the Buddha] spoke thus until he said:
"From this day forward, when cutting threads, they should be made according to the prescribed measure.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a saṃkakṣikā, it should be made according to the prescribed measurements: four Sugata-spaṣṭas in length and two spaṣṭas in width.
If she makes it exceeding these measurements and then cuts it down, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Pāyattika," as explained in detail above in the section on the *antarvāsaka*.

The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā was bathing in the Sū River. Then five Licchavi youths were watching her from the riverbank; having seen her, they conceived lustful thoughts.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Long-lived one! Go!"
She replied, "I will not go;
I wish to see the physical form of the Noble One (āryā).
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Why do you gaze upon this foul, putrid body with its nine apertures?
He replied again, "Not so!"
"I very much wish to see him.
After a long while, he did not leave.
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"This person is a foolish and shallow commoner.
He then covered his front and back with his hands and walked out; upon seeing this, the man fell to the ground in a faint, and blood gushed from his mouth.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
Eventually, the bhikṣuṇīs asked the Buddha:
"How is it that these five Licchavi youths, overcome by lustful desire, fainted and fell to the ground in such a manner?"
The Buddha said, "It is not only today that she has had this lustful mind; in past lives as well, it was already thus.
The bhikṣuṇīs addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“In the distant past, there was at that time a heavenly maiden of exquisite and peerless beauty, and there were five sons of gods.
The first is named Śakrā, the second Mātali, the third Saṃjayanta, the fourth Vijayantī, and the fifth Māṭhara.
Having seen her, each gave rise to a lustful mind and thought:
"This is not something to be shared; it shall be given to whichever of us has the weightiest desire. Each said:
"So be it. Thereupon, Śikhāra spoke in verse:
"When I recall the time of lustful desire, I sit and lie down, yet find no peace."
"Even when falling asleep, one only finds peace when about to fall away from desire.
Mātali spoke again in verse:
"O Śākyamuni, even when you sleep, there is still a momentary tranquility."
"When I recall the time of sensual desire, it is like the sound of a battle drum.
Sañjayin further spoke in verse:
"The analogy of the mṛdaṅga drum still leaves some interval; [the mind] is not yet entirely free from it."
"When my mind is stained by desire, it is like a piece of wood drifting in a swift current.
Viśvantara spoke again in verse:
"Your metaphor of the floating wood may at times be held back; [but my mind is not so]."
"When I recall my thoughts of desire, they are like a fly that does not blink.
Thereupon, Māṭhara spoke again in verse:
"All that you have said is entirely a perception of pleasure; [it is not so]."
"When I was addicted to sensual desires, I was unaware of death and birth.
Thereupon, the sons of the gods said:
"You are the most grievous of all."
"Then he gave them all to her.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"The five sons of heaven at that time were these five Licchavis."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the Buddha:

“What karmic deeds did this bhikṣuṇī perform such that she is so beautiful, born into a great family, and having left the household life out of faith, has attained the realization of the outflows-free state?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī. There was a householder’s family who had recently taken a new wife, and they regularly provided food and drink to a hairdresser."

At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha named Xuanchi who came to the gate to beg for food; seeing that he was not particularly dignified in appearance, his wife felt no sense of reverence, so she neither gave him food nor spoke to him as he departed.
Having seen this, the hairdresser said to the bride,
"You should give her some food.
She replied:
"He is ugly and unattractive; I cannot give him [the food].
He then said, "Please grant me my portion of food; I wish to give it to him."
He replied, "As you wish;
it may also be discarded into the water.
Upon receiving the food, the man immediately gave it away as alms.
The Pratyekabuddha then accepted the food and departed through the air.
Seeing him fly away, [the man] was filled with great joy in his heart and immediately made this vow:
"May I, in my future life, be born into a family of great standing, with a handsome and upright body; may I see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and exhaust all outflows."

Thereupon, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the heavens; among hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, he excelled in five matters: lifespan, physical beauty and strength, renown, and eloquence.
When her life in the heavens came to an end, she was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Vārāṇasī during the appearance of Kāśyapa Buddha in the world.

At that time, her parents had gone out for a stroll, and the girl remained at home. As Kāśyapa Buddha entered the city to beg for alms, he arrived at her house; because of the virtue she had cultivated in previous lives, she beheld him with great joy. Having washed a copper platter clean, she filled it with various kinds of excellent food and a garment of *koseyya* silk, and offered them to the World-Honored One.
He then spoke in verse:
"I now offer food and clothing, The most supreme among all gifts;
Now making this offering to the Honored Muni, May he realize the exhaustion of all fetters and habitual tendencies."
"May I likewise realize the exhaustion of outflows in this way.
Later, this woman married into a brahmin family; her mother-in-law was stern and cruel, making tasks difficult to perform, until she thought: "What is the use of me living like this?"
"It would be better to commit suicide.
She then took her necklaces, body-unguents, and a rope for hanging herself, intending to take her own life.
As she passed by, she saw a stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha; she immediately used her ornaments to make an offering to the stūpa, and only then did she hang herself.
After his life ended, he was immediately reborn into a brahmin family, and even spoke these verses himself:
“With necklaces, garments, incense, and flowers, I faithfully made offerings at Kāśyapa’s stūpa;
By virtue of this meritorious retribution, I now pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should make bathing robes; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a rain-bathing robe, she should make it according to the prescribed measurements: four Sugata-spaṃs in length and two spaṃs in width."
"If one exceeds [the prescribed length] and cuts it, it is a pāyattika.
This is explained in detail above in the section on the saṃkakṣikā.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; at that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs said to Thullanandā:
“Are you able to request the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha?
He replied, “I am able.”
He immediately went to the house of one who lacked faith and said,
"O you of great merit!
Are you able to offer a *kaṭhina* robe to the Saṃgha?"
He replied, "I can.
After the Saṃgha had performed the *pravāraṇā*, he said to Thullanandā:
"Have you obtained the kaṭhina robe?
He replied, "I know."
He went immediately to that person's house and said,
"Long-lived one!
Has the kaṭhina robe been prepared?"
She replied, "I know.
She then went back to ask for it again, and the bhikṣuṇī spoke once more:
"I know. Thus, when the time for robes had already passed, the bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, the Buddha asked:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"Why have you gone to the house of one unable to provide robes to solicit *kaṭhina* cloth for the Saṃgha?
From this day forward, this is not permitted."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a family that is unable to provide clothing and begs for a kāṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Lacking faith" means being powerless and dwelling in a state of weak hope.
"Clothing" refers to garments such as those made of *kambala* wool, cotton cloth, and even *kṣaumaka* silk.
"To beg" means to seek a *kaṭhina* robe on behalf of the Saṃgha.
If the time for the robe has passed and it has not been obtained, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī is able to seek a kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha, she should seek it with great care and diligence. She must not go to the homes of those who lack faith to seek it; rather, she should beg from those families who have faith and many relatives.
If the person before you says,
"I know it myself," you should further say to them:
"Will you definitely give it?
Do not let the time for the distribution of robes pass.
One should also observe the person; if they will certainly be unable to provide it, one should seek it from another place.
One should also reflect for oneself; if one is unable to provide it, one should not request it from the Saṃgha.

If one has already promised to request robes for the Saṃgha, yet does not personally strive to seek them, nor employs others to seek them, and furthermore does not inform the Saṃgha so that the time for the robes passes by, it is a pāyattika.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu goes to the house of one who lacks faith to seek *kaṭhina* cloth for the Saṃgha, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī, having put on her upper and lower robes, came to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; subsequently, a fire broke out and burned her robes.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"Why is it that the robes you have received and maintained do not accompany you?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to receive and maintain robes that are not carried on one's person.

Furthermore, at that time there were two bhikṣuṇīs, a Śākya woman and a Malla woman, who had previously been performers before they went forth. Because their saṃghāṭī was heavy, they were unable to bear its weight and found it to be a great hardship.
The Buddha then said:
"From this day forward, I permit [the use of footwear] when one is ill.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, does not keep the robes she has received upon her person, it is a pāyattika.”
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Robes received" refers to the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antarvāsaka, the saṃkakṣikā, and the varṣāśāṭī.
Regarding the sick, the World-Honored One has declared there is no offense.
To not follow along [with the prescribed conduct] constitutes a *pāyattika*.
As for what a *pāyattika* is, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill does not carry the robes she has been assigned to wear, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if she is at a stūpa for worship, or engaged in walking meditation, or within the boundary of her daytime sitting-meditation place.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

"The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the house of the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā would regularly provide him with food. Having received it, she would further simmer it, roast it, and season it. When her brothers, uncles, and cousins came and saw this, they said:
'We wish to eat.'"
He replied, "So be it.
He immediately took and ate it, but perceiving that its flavor was extraordinary, he asked:
"Where did you obtain this fine food?
He replied,
"It was simply what my family sent from home."
He immediately spoke in anger:
"In my house, we have always prepared food only to waste our wealth; we never obtain good food.
He then returned home, whipped his servants and slaves, and reviled them.
"Money and goods have been wasted in vain and cannot even be eaten.
The man, filled with anger, said:
"It is because of this bhikṣuṇī that I have come to such suffering and distress."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wrongful act. From this day forward, you are not permitted to boil or fry [food] yourself."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there were at that time certain bhikṣuṇīs who were daughters of the Śākya clan and daughters of the Malla clan. While wandering for alms, they obtained stale rice, stale soup, and stale vegetables; after eating them, they vomited.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One:
"May we be permitted to warm our food?
The Buddha said:
“It is so. The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Vaiśālī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains *khādaniya* food or *bhojaniya* food, and she herself cooks it again, has someone else cook it; or she herself roasts it again, has someone else roast it; or she herself fries it again, has someone else fry it; and then an unill bhikṣuṇī eats it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Khadaniya" refers to the five kinds of solid foods.
"Bhojaniya" refers to the five kinds of soft foods.
"Cooking again" means either cooking it oneself or having someone else cook it.
"To boil" means either to boil it oneself or to have another boil it.
"To fry" means either to fry it oneself or to have another fry it.
Regarding the sick, the World-Honored One has declared that there is no offense.
What constitutes being ill?
Being afflicted by old age and illness, emaciated and weak, or suffering from cold food, vomiting, or a lack of appetite.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill cooks food for herself to eat, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
One is not permitted to re-fry or re-boil for the sake of making food more delicious; nor is one permitted to heat what is cold, nor to cook within a cauldron or a pot.
If one uses a copper bowl, a hook-bowl, or a *kian-ts'ie* (a type of vessel) to warm [the food],
and if a bhikṣu, for the sake of making it more delicious, reheats, roasts, or fries it himself, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) is made aware [of the transgression], there is no offense; if, while begging for alms, one warms cold food again, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time there were two people, husband and wife, who had gone forth from among the Śākyas.
At that time, while the husband Mahāla was eating, a bhikṣuṇī stood by his side pouring water and fanning him with a fan.
As Mahāla recounted events from the past, the bhikṣuṇī became angry; she immediately splashed water on his face and struck his head with the fan.
She rebuked her, saying:
"Because you do not recognize kindness and righteousness, you speak of past events; you have spoken what should not have been spoken.
Having seen this, the bhikṣuṇī said:
“Venerable One! This assembly of elders cannot be treated in such a manner.
He spoke again:
"This mahallaka is unwholesome and ignorant of gratitude and righteousness; he speaks now that which should not be spoken.
The bhikṣuṇīs told this to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here. When she had come,
he questioned her, saying:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter. How can you, as bhikṣus, provide food with water and fans?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not according to the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas."
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all those who reside in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī provides water or a fan while a bhikṣu is eating, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"A bhikṣu eating" refers to the five types of formal meals and the five types of mixed formal meals.
Regarding "water and fan": if a bhikṣuṇī carries a water jar to distribute water and uses a fan to fan [the recipient], it is a pāyattika.
A pāyattika is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī carries a water jar but does not carry a fan, it is a vinayātikrama offense.
To hold a fan but not hold water, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To hold both, it is a *pāyattika*.
To hold neither, there is no offense.
This offense applies to one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī;
if there are many bhikṣus, there is no offense for those who provide water or fans.
If there is a father or elder brother among the assembly, there is no offense in fanning him with a fan.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a garlic merchant named Paṃcaka who invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs to provide them with garlic.
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs went to the garden to eat the garlic, trampling it into a mess.
At that time, a merchant came to trade garlic; seeing this mess, he immediately asked the gardener, "Why has it come to such a state?
He replied:
"Previously, when I invited the bhikṣuṇīs for garlic, they either ate it on the spot or took some away, only to trample upon it like this.
The merchant spoke with resentment:
"I invited them and gave them garlic; they should have simply eaten it. Why did they take it away and trample it like this?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One, until he replied: “Is it truly so? [They answered:
“It is indeed so.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"This is an evil matter. From this day forward, eating garlic is not permitted; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Garlic" refers to cultivated garlic and mountain garlic.
In this manner, all types of garlic are prohibited from being eaten; it is not permitted whether raw or cooked, nor is it permitted if boiled repeatedly, nor is it permitted even if burned to ashes.

If one has a sore on the body, it is permitted to apply ointment; having applied it, one should remain in a secluded place. Once the sore has healed and one has washed oneself clean, entry is permitted.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said:
"The robes of others, the robes of non-Buddhists, the saṃkakṣikā, and the antaravāsaka."
Bathing robes, *kaṭhina*, Carrying robes without wearing them, Re-cooking, holding water, and fans, Eating garlic—the eight *varga*s. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the sister of Rāṣṭrapāla passed away, and he begged for various kinds of food and drink to give to his sister’s son. He was thus censured by the people of the world:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī accept the faithful offerings of others and give them to laypeople?
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī then reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, you are not permitted to give food with your own hands to laypeople.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a son of the Kṣāntivāda heretics went to his mother. When she saw him coming, she filled his bowl with various kinds of food and drink and gave it to him. Having received it, the son immediately took it to a tavern and ate it himself, and also gave some to others.
Someone asked,
"Where did you obtain this fine food? He replied:
“Be silent! The world regards śramaṇīs as fields of merit, and śramaṇīs in turn regard me as a field of merit.
Thus she was censured by the people:
“How can a śramaṇī take the faithful offerings of others and give them to one who does not increase merit?”
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wicked deed; how could you give food with your own hands to a non-Buddhist?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to give food with one's own hand to those of external paths.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī accepts food with her own hands from a layperson or a non-Buddhist, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," it is as explained above.
Regarding "layperson," it refers to a householder.
"Heretics" refers to those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist practitioners.
"With one's own hands" means receiving with hand-to-hand or vessel-to-vessel contact.
"Food" refers to *khādaniya* (solid food) and *bhojaniya* (soft food).
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a relative comes to a bhikṣuṇī wishing to give her food, she must not give it with her own hand; she should have a pure woman (*kappiyakārī*) give it to her.
If there are no pure women present, one should say:
"Take food with your own hands from within this [container].
If one fears taking too much, one should say:
"Take this much to receive; set the rest aside.
Having received it, place it on the ground and let them take it themselves.
If non-Buddhists (tīrthika) come, do not allow them to take it with their own hands; rather, have a pure woman give it to them.
If there is no pure woman present, one should say:
"Take food from within this [container] yourself.
If one fears that too much might be taken, one should say:
"Take this much," he said,
setting aside the remainder;
he placed what was in his hand on the ground and gave it to him.
If a relative should speak with resentment,
saying, "Do you treat me as a caṇḍāla?",
one should say:
"The place where you have gone forth is not good; the World-Honored One has established a precept that we may not give [to such as you].
However, one may allow an outsider to prepare the food, saying:
"Give this to me; eat the remainder yourself."
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus:

While the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Chāndamātṛ was skilled in treating diseases. Carrying medicinal roots, leaves, and fruits, she entered the homes of kings, ministers, and householders to treat various ailments of women, such as disorders of pregnancy, eye diseases, vomiting, and diarrhea; she administered fumigations for the throat, nasal irrigations, and used needles and knives, after which she applied these various medicines as ointments.
Because she gained great offerings by treating illnesses, the bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"This is not the dharma of one who has left the household life; this is merely that of a physician."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of this matter, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. From this day forward, you are not permitted to make a living as a physician."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Kauśāmbī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes her living as a physician, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Physician" refers to one who treats illnesses using medicines derived from roots, leaves, or fruits.

Furthermore, if there is one who, like the mother of Chanda, makes her living by means of medical incantations for poison, incantations for snakes, and even incantations for fire, the stars, the sun, and the moon, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
A bhikṣuṇī must not make her living as a physician; however, if there is a sick person, she may instruct them on the method of treatment.
If a bhikṣu makes his living as a physician, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
For this reason, the Blessed One spoke.

While the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī, the Blessed One had established the precept that one must not make a living as a physician. At that time, someone called upon Chanda-mātā to treat an illness, and the bhikṣuṇī said:
“The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit it.
He spoke again:
“If you do not permit it, then grant me the medical prescriptions.”
She then bestowed upon laypeople and non-Buddhist practitioners medical prescriptions.
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"Merely reciting medical prescriptions is not the dharma of those who have left the household life."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit the teaching of medical arts to laypeople or followers of external paths."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Kauśāmbī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī bestows medical prescriptions upon laypeople or followers of external paths, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Layperson" refers to a householder.
"Non-Buddhists" refers to those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist renunciants.
"To administer medical formulas" means to recite incantations for snakes, poisons, or even for fire, the stars, and the sun and moon; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
A bhikṣuṇī must not bestow medical prescriptions upon laypeople or followers of external paths, nor must she instruct them in such matters.
If a bhikṣuṇī bestows medical prescriptions upon laypeople or followers of external paths, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus:
The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī. At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā invited the Saṃgha of both divisions. Then, in the early morning, the bhikṣuṇīs went to her house and said to the upāsikā:
"Today you have invited the Saṃgha of both divisions."
"What should we do to repay her?
The doe said, "Noble Lady!..."
"Simply reciting the sutras and practicing the Way is itself repaying your kindness.
He replied, "Truly so."
"Nevertheless, let us repay you with another service.

They then went up to the upper chamber together to fetch some cotton (*karpāsa*). Some began to split it, some to card it, and others to spin it. Once they had finished the balls of thread, they said to him:
"That which we wished to repay you for is now complete."
The upāsikā said: “This matter is not a repayment;
one who wishes to repay [her kindness] should sit in meditation after eating, receive the scriptures, and recite them—this is what constitutes repayment.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. From this day forward, I do not permit [monastics] to perform worldly labor in the homes of laypeople."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs work for a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," it is as explained above.
Regarding "layperson," it refers to the household of a white-robed person.
If one performs work for a layperson—such as splitting cotton, carding cotton, or spinning it;
or threshing, grinding, or washing clothes—any such work performed for a lay household constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.
A bhikṣuṇī must not perform work for a layperson. However, if a donor (*dānapati*), desiring to make an offering to the Buddha, says:
"Noble Lady (*āryā*)!..."
Regarding the instruction, "Assist me in preparing the requisites for offering":
at that time, one may assist in binding flower garlands or assist in grinding incense.
If a bhikṣu assists a layperson in such work, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there were a husband and wife who, at midday, intended to engage in sexual intercourse within their own house in a place they thought was unobserved.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā entered abruptly without prior announcement; her husband saw her and became enraged, thinking, "She has interrupted my sexual pleasure."
Her body still stirred as she rose without ceasing, immediately pursuing [him] to seize the bhikṣuṇī.
Terrified of him, she ran back quickly to her dwelling and said to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"Today, he nearly ruined my brahmacarya."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked him,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wicked act. How could you enter a family where food is being served without first speaking to them?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she has entered a household where food is being served without first having announced her presence, commits this offense, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by herself or hearing it from another.
As for "food": women are the food of men, and men are the food of women.
As for "families": the families of the kṣatriyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras.
Regarding those who have not previously announced their arrival: if one enters without having first announced it, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī has not previously announced her arrival, she must not enter; if she wishes to enter, she should speak to the gatekeeper:
"I wish to enter.
If the gatekeeper has been informed and says "enter," one may then enter; if the gatekeeper does not respond, one must not enter.
If one hears voices from within the room, one should snap one's fingers or move one's foot to make a sound.
If he remains silent, one may not enter; if he comes out to meet [the visitor], one may enter.
If a bhikṣu enters without first speaking [to the resident], it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vibhaṅga-āpatti).
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī ordained a third-generation Licchavi girl and allowed her to live in close association with laypeople and non-Buddhists.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call the bhikṣuṇī here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked the bhikṣuṇī,
“Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; from this day forward, I do not permit [monks] to dwell in close association with nuns.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī associates closely with a layperson or a follower of another path, whether for an entire day or for a brief moment—even down to a park-attendant or a śrāmaṇera—it is a pāyattika offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Layperson" refers to a householder.
"Heretic" refers to one who has left the home life [but follows] non-Buddhist paths.
"During the day" means until sunset.
"Even for a moment" means for a brief interval.
"To dwell in close association" means to dwell in close association by way of body, to dwell in close association by way of speech, and to dwell in close association by way of both body and speech.
If [a nun] associates closely with those as low as a lay attendant (*ārāmika*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī habitually dwells in close association [with such persons], it is a *pāyattika*.
If bhikṣuṇīs live in close proximity and take pleasure in dwelling together with one another, their upādhyāyinī and ācāryinī should separate them and send them to different places.
If a bhikṣu associates closely with such a person, he commits a vinaya offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā quarreled with another bhikṣuṇī and then made a mutual oath of cursing, saying:
“Namo Buddhāya. He points to the Buddha and takes an oath; he points to the ācārya and takes an oath; he points to the edge of the *kāṣāya* and takes an oath:

“If I do this, may I not die within the *kāṣāya*, and may I not attain the end of suffering. May I incur the sin of killing my father and mother, the sin of ingratitude, and the sin of slandering the noble ones; may I enter hell, fall among the hungry ghosts, and fall among the animals.”
"If I am such as you say, I shall enter these various realms of existence;
if you are such as you say, you too shall enter these various realms of existence.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter. How can you, who have gone forth from the household life, make such a vow?
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities."
"Up to and including those who have already heard it, they should hear it again:
If a bhikṣuṇī curses herself or curses another, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding the self-imposed oath: "Namo Buddha. This invokes the Buddha as witness and invokes the Ācārya as witness:

"If I should do so, may I incur a transgression equal to that of Devadatta; may I incur the transgression of lying; may I incur the transgression of ingratitude; may I incur the transgression of double-tongued speech."
If I am such as you say, my holy life would not have been perfected, nor would I have died wearing the saffron robe; rather, I would have entered hell, fallen among animals, or become a hungry ghost.
If you slander me, you too shall incur this same fault.
"One who makes such a vow commits a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu makes such a vow, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has spoken thus."

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, after Thullanandā had engaged in a quarrel with several bhikṣuṇīs, she struck herself out of anger, scratched herself, and wept loudly with tears streaming forth.
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did so?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said. "Why did you,
out of anger, strike yourself and weep until tears flowed?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; it cannot be used to nurture wholesome qualities.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī beats herself and weeps with tears, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," it is as explained above.
"Beats herself" means: whether by striking with the hand, or punching with the fist, or with a staff, or a clod of earth, or a whip—if a bhikṣuṇī thus beats herself and weeps, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī strikes herself but does not weep, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If she weeps but does not strike herself, she likewise commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one strikes oneself and weeps, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not strike oneself and does not weep, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu strikes himself and weeps, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā went to the house of a layperson and proclaimed:

"The bhikṣuṇī Cūḍapanthaka is virtuous, maintains the precepts, and is diligent; her deportment is so dignified and orderly that she looks to the left and right with composure; she puts on her robes and carries her bowl with careful deliberation and tranquility, and is sparing in speech; she is honored by devas and humans."
When the donor saw this, he conceived a heart of reverence and provided him with robes, alms bowls, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions for illness.

However, because Sthūlanandā’s deportment was not complete—wearing tattered, filthy clothes, with her large belly, breasts, and ribs exposed, and behaving with sudden violence and excessive talk—the donor conceived a lack of respect and did not invite her to accept robes, alms bowls, food and drink, or medicinal decoctions for illness.
He then spoke these words:
"I praised Jyotiṣka at the householder's home, and it was because of that that I received this offering.
Yet Jyotiṣka spoke only of my faults, and for that reason, I did not receive an offering."
Jyotiṣka said: "Venerable One!
I do not speak ill; why then would I speak of your faults?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. Why did you not examine the situation with careful scrutiny before censuring him?"
"This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; one cannot thereby nurture wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not, without having heard the matter with careful scrutiny, harbor resentment or reproach others."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī: "Venerable lady!
Let us go together to such-and-such a house."
"If, subsequently, she cannot endure that [person], and the bhikṣuṇī, without cause and without having heard the matter clearly and accurately, reviles him, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
"Families" refers to the Kṣatriya family, the Brāhmaṇa family, the Vaiśya family, and the Śūdra family.
"Not enduring it later" is, for example, like the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhikā.
Regarding "unbearable matters," this refers to the tenth [offense]: giving rise to anger toward the nine grounds for resentment in an inappropriate situation.
Regarding "without cause or condition," it means to harbor resentment and reproach after not having listened with careful discernment; this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, without having heard the matter clearly and accurately, expresses resentment or reproach, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, without having heard the matter clearly and accurately, utters a rebuke, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, when the time had come, put on her robes, took her bowl, and went to stand before the gate of a great household.
A bhikṣu came to beg for alms and spoke thus:
"Venerable ones, please enter; this family is preparing food for the Venerables.
After giving them food, he then ate himself.
If a bhikṣuṇī comes and says again, "Noble Lady,
please enter; the donor has prepared food for you," she should eat after the donor has finished giving the food, and only then eat herself.
Or they may say:
"Other families also have food; why must we stay together here?
In this way, all such non-Buddhist mendicants protect their patron households with hearts of stinginess and jealousy.
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
“It is true,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter. Why do you protect other families with a mind of stinginess and envy?
From this day forward, it is not permitted."
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of stinginess and envy, guards a family, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Family" refers to families of the four castes.
Regarding those with a mind of stinginess and envy, it is like the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
As for the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
A bhikṣuṇī must not, with a mind of stinginess and envy, guard a family [for her own benefit].
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī asks, one should speak the truth;
however, if a follower of an external path asks, there is no offense in rebuking them if one fears they might become attached to the false views of that external path.
If a bhikṣu, out of a mind of stinginess and envy, begrudges another family [of patrons], he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said:
"Handing food to a physician, Prescribing remedies, assisting the laity in their work,"
Not speaking, entering, associating, self-cursing, self-beating,
weeping, reproaching, and protecting families.
The ninth chapter (varga) is concluded.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there were a husband and wife who had both gone forth as monastics. Once, the husband, a mahallaka (elderly monk), came to give food and stood by the side.
He spoke of the woman’s past misdeeds; having heard this, she was displeased and said:
"Short-lived mahallaka!"
"You do not recognize kindness or righteousness; you speak that which should not be spoken.
The bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying: "Āryā!..."
"One may not revile such a venerable assembly as this.
He then said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"This short-lived mahallaka does not understand gratitude or righteousness; he speaks what should not be spoken."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:
"Call her here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to revile or scold bhikṣus face-to-face."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu face-to-face, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Face-to-face" means their four eyes meet.
As for reviling, it means saying:
"Short-lived mahallaka!
You are unvirtuous and do not recognize kindness or righteousness."
"Pañcātika. As for 'pañcātika,' it is as explained above.

A bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu face-to-face. Even if he is a brother or a relative who has gone forth, even if that person does not maintain the precepts, she must not revile him; rather, she should instruct and admonish him with gentle words."
If they are young, one should say:
"Sālohita! Do not do this."
"If you do not train now, when will you ever train?
Your future disciples will also learn from you to perform unwholesome deeds.
If they are elders, one should say:
“Śāradvatīputra!
If you do not train now, will you wait until the time of old age and death to train?
A bhikṣu must likewise not revile a bhikṣuṇī face-to-face, saying:
“Shaven-headed women, lewd women,” and so on,
up to saying: “Mahāli!”
"You are unwholesome; you do not know gratitude or righteousness.
One may address them with gentle words as explained above.
If a bhikṣu reviles a bhikṣuṇī face-to-face, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus: "The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, bhikṣuṇīs who had been ordained for one year, two years, or three years were taking on disciples; yet they did not know how to instruct or admonish them. They were as unrestrained as celestial sheep or celestial oxen. They were incomplete in pure precepts, incomplete in dignified deportment, ignorant of how to respectfully serve their upādhyāyī and ācāryā, ignorant of how to honor senior bhikṣuṇīs, ignorant of the proper conduct for entering villages or forest hermitages (āraṇya), ignorant of the proper conduct for entering the saṃgha, and ignorant of how to wear robes and carry the alms bowl."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣuṇī here.
When she had come, he asked her:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to keep a disciple who has fewer than twelve years of rain-retreat.
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple when she has fewer than twelve years of standing, it is a pāyattika.”
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Less than twelve rains" means less than twelve years; this is called "less than twelve rains.
A bhikṣuṇī who has less than twelve rains but has completed twelve years [of training] is also called "less than twelve rains."
If a bhikṣuṇī has less than twelve rains (varṣa) but has passed twelve years, she is also said to have "less than twelve rains.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives full ordination during the winter season and counts that winter as the twelfth, yet the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has not yet been performed, this is called "having less than twelve rains."
If one receives full ordination during the spring season and counts twelve such springs, yet has not yet undergone the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, this is called "less than twelve rains.
If one receives full ordination at the time of the first *varṣā* retreat and has not yet undergone the *pravāraṇā* ceremony following that first retreat, this is called "less than twelve rains."

If one receives full ordination during the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*) and has not yet completed the later retreat before undergoing the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), this is called "less than twelve rains.
If a bhikṣuṇī has completed twelve rains but less than twelve years, this is called "full twelve rains."
A bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve rains and twelve years—
having thus passed twelve years— is said to have completed twelve rains.

A bhikṣuṇī who receives full ordination during the winter season, completes the rainy-season retreat (*vassa*), and performs the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) is said to have completed twelve rains.
If one receives full ordination during the spring season and undergoes the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the conclusion of the rains retreat;
or likewise, if after receiving full ordination during the first rains retreat, one undergoes the *pravāraṇā* at its conclusion;
or if one receives full ordination during the later rains retreat and undergoes the *pravāraṇā* at its conclusion—this is called being "full twelve years of rain."
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps one who has received full ordination [without authorization], it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains someone when she is less than twelve years [of standing], it is a vinaya-offense of transgression.
If one confers full ordination [upon such a person], it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu who has fewer than twelve years of seniority confers full ordination upon another, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept stating that one must not keep a disciple if one has fewer than twelve years of seniority (*vassa*).

Then, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and other bhikṣuṇīs, though having reached twelve years of seniority, were incomplete in the ten qualities; yet they kept disciples and failed to instruct or admonish them, behaving like celestial oxen or celestial sheep, even to the point of not knowing how to put on their robes or hold their alms bowls.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
"It is true, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, it is not permitted to keep a disciple without being endowed with the ten qualities.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years of rain-retreats keeps a disciple while not being fully endowed with the ten dharmas, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"One who has completed twelve rains" is as explained above.
"Not possessing the ten dharmas" means the ten dharmas are not accomplished.
What are these ten?
First, upholding the precepts;
second, extensive learning of the Abhidharma;
third, the Vinaya.
4. Training in the precepts;
5. Training in concentration;
6. Training in wisdom.
Seventh, he is able to purify his own transgressions and is able to cause others to purify theirs;
eighth, when a disciple’s relatives wish for them to leave the path, he is able to escort them himself or send someone else to escort them to another region;
ninth, he is able to attend to a disciple’s illness or send someone else to attend to it.
Tenth: having completed twelve rains or more.
These are called the ten dharmas.
If one ordains a disciple without fulfilling these ten dharmas, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one confers full ordination [upon someone who lacks the required qualifications], it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu ordains another person while not being fully endowed with the ten dharmas, it is a vinayātikrama offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has said this.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept: "Only after twelve rains [of seniority] and the fulfillment of the ten dharmas may one keep a disciple.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī who had completed twelve rains and fulfilled the ten dharmas kept a disciple.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"Even though you have completed twelve years of rain-retreats and are endowed with the ten dharmas, who can truly know you?
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters, and so on, until he replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, one who wishes to keep a disciple must perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion for formal authorization); only then may one request the *karman* for keeping a disciple.
The *karman* should be recited as follows:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the Sangha deems it the right time, this bhikṣuṇī [Name], who has fulfilled ten qualities, wishes to request from the Sangha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the permission to keep a disciple.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has accomplished the ten qualities and wishes to request from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for keeping a disciple.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
This bhikṣuṇī should request it from the Saṃgha, kneeling on her right knee with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, [Name], have completed twelve years of rain-retreat and am accomplished in the ten dharmas. I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karma*) for maintaining a disciple; may the Saṃgha grant me the formal act for maintaining a disciple."
Thus he requests three times.
The officiant of the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has completed twelve years of rain-retreat and is accomplished in the ten dharmas; she has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for taking a disciple.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant the formal act for taking a disciple to this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, who is accomplished in the ten dharmas.
Thus it was announced:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has completed twelve years since her full ordination, is endowed with the ten qualities, and has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for taking on a disciple."
The Sangha now grants the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the nun so-and-so to maintain a disciple.
Noble Sangha, please grant the formal act for the nun so-and-so to maintain a disciple; those who consent remain silent, and those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.
The Saṃgha has completed the *karmavācanā* for the nun so-and-so to maintain a disciple; because the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, though not having fulfilled the ten dharmas, keeps a disciple without performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding the "one who is endowed with ten qualities," it is as explained above.
"Not performing *karmavācanā*" means not performing a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) within the Saṃgha; one who is not endowed with the ten qualities is also said to be "not performing *karmavācanā*."

Even if a *karmavācanā* is performed, if the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not accomplished, the assembly is not accomplished, or the *karmavācanā* itself is not accomplished, it is likewise termed "non-*karman*.
Regarding the keeping of disciples: for one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), to grant full ordination to another without performing the *karman* constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

"When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī ordained a third-generation daughter of the Licchavis. After she had received the rules of training, she took a door-bolt to open the doors of others' rooms and lived together with laypeople and non-Buddhists."
The bhikṣuṇīs reproached her, saying:
"This woman has violated the precepts; she opened the door of another's room with a door-bolt and lived together with a man.
How could you confer full ordination upon her?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Summon Kālī."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.

"This is an evil deed. How could you, knowing that he had violated the precepts, having opened the doors of others' rooms by seizing the door-bolts, and living together with non-Buddhists, confer full ordination upon him?"
"From this day forward, it shall not be permitted to confer full ordination upon one who has violated the precepts.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Vaiśālī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has violated the precepts, opens the door of another’s room by taking the door-bolt and allows her to dwell together with a man, and then confers full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"One who violates the precepts" refers to one whose precepts are incomplete or who has transgressed them.
"Taking the door-bolt to open a room" means opening the door of another's room.
"A man" refers to a layperson or an ordained member of a non-Buddhist sect.
"Living together" means dwelling in close proximity.
"To confer full ordination [upon him]" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
*Pāyattika*, as explained above.
If one dwells in close association with laypeople or non-Buddhists, it is not permitted to grant them full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If, however, one can ensure that this person’s holy life (*brahmacarya*) remains intact, they should first be separated from such associates and only then granted full ordination.

If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has violated the precepts and dwells in close association with women, yet does not require him to undergo renunciation again before conferring full ordination upon him, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, bhikṣuṇīs were ordaining girls who were ten or twelve years old, allowing them to leave the household life and bestowing upon them full ordination."

At that time, the girl was weak and unable to endure arduous tasks; she was not complete in her purity, nor was she complete in her deportment. She did not know how to serve her preceptor nun (upādhyāyinī) or her instructor nun (ācāryinī); she did not know how to enter a village, nor did she know about forest retreats (āraṇya), nor how to enter the assembly, nor how to wear her robes or carry her alms bowl.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī [reported it] to the Buddha, who said:
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here. Once she had come, he asked her:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to confer full ordination upon a girl who is less than twenty years of age.
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence upon Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a girl less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika."
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Less than twenty rains" means less than twenty years; this is called "less than twenty rains.
A maiden who is less than twenty rains but has completed twenty years [of age] is also called "less than twenty rains."
A girl who has reached twenty years of age but is less than twenty *vassa* (rains) is also called "less than twenty *vassa*.
One born in winter who counts the current winter as the twentieth year, yet has not yet undergone the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, is called "less than twenty *vassa*."
The same applies to one born during the spring season.
If one is born during the preceding *varṣā* (rains retreat) and counts twenty preceding *varṣās* without having yet undergone the *pravāraṇā* ceremony;
or if one is born during the subsequent *varṣā* and counts twenty subsequent *varṣās* without having yet undergone the *pravāraṇā* ceremony—these are also called "less than twenty rains."
If a girl is less than twenty years of age, and those who confer full ordination upon her all perceive her as being less than twenty years of age, they all commit a pāyattika offense.
This person is not said to have received full ordination.
If one is less than twenty years of age, and half of those present perceive them as being less while the other half perceive them as being full, yet they are granted full ordination:
for those who perceived them as being less, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one perceives [the candidate] as being of full age, there is no offense.
This person is said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If a girl who is less than twenty years of age is perceived by all as being of full age and is granted full ordination, there is no offense for any of them; this person is said to have received full ordination.
To have completed twenty rains while being less than twenty years old is called "having completed twenty rains.
For a maiden, to have completed twenty rains while being exactly twenty years old,
or to have completed twenty rains while being more than twenty years old, is called "having completed twenty rains."
If a girl is born in winter, having completed the *vassa* (rainy season retreat) and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, she is twenty years old; she may then receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
It is the same if she was born in spring.
If she was born during the earlier *vassa*, she must wait until the earlier *vassa* has concluded and the *pravāraṇā* has been performed.

Regarding a girl born during the later retreat who has completed the later retreat and performed the *pravāraṇā*, if she is twenty years old but half of those present have the perception that she is less than twenty and half have the perception that she is full twenty:
for those with the perception that she is less, there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*;
for those with the perception that she is full, there is no offense, and this person is said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If a girl who has completed twenty years of age is given full ordination while everyone perceives her as being less than that age, all involved commit an offense of violating the Vinaya; this person is not said to have received full ordination.
If one perceives everyone as being fully ordained and everyone as being without fault, this person is said to have properly received full ordination.
Regarding a maiden: if one grants full ordination to her while her celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has not yet been impaired, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a maiden wishes to receive full ordination within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, she should be asked:
"When were you born?
If she does not know, one should consult the register of birth years.
If there is no one [to ask], one should question one's parents or relatives;
if they too do not know, one should ask:
"In the time of which king?"
"Is it a time of great abundance or a time of great scarcity?

If one still does not know, they cannot be judged by outward appearance; if she is the daughter of a wealthy family, though young in years, her form may appear large, so one must examine the bones and joints of her hands and feet.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One established a precept, not permitting a girl who has not reached twenty years of age to receive full ordination."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon a girl who was twenty years old.
The other bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"Whether she is exactly twenty years old or not yet twenty, who can know for certain?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the Blessed One of this matter. ... [as before] ... until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when eighteen-year-old girls wish to receive full ordination within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they should request two years of training in the precepts from the Saṃgha."
Having first performed the *jñapti-karman* (motion for permission), one may then request [the formal act].
The person performing the *karman* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This maiden, so-and-so, aged eighteen, wishes to receive full ordination within the discipline and teachings of the Tathāgata.
If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate, this maiden, so-and-so, wishes to request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This maiden so-and-so, being eighteen years of age, wishes to request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts. Since the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus upheld.
This woman should request [ordination] from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
I, so-and-so, an eighteen-year-old girl, wish to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata."
"I now request from the Saṃgha two years of training in the precepts; I only pray that the Saṃgha, out of compassion, will grant me two years of training in the precepts.
Thus he should say up to three times.
The *karmavācanā* official should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This maiden named [Name], who is eighteen years of age, desires to receive full ordination within the discipline and doctrine of the Tathāgata; she now requests from the Saṃgha two years of training in the precepts."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of granting two years of training in the precepts to [Name].
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This maiden of eighteen years wishes to receive full ordination within the discipline and law of the Tathāgata; she has already requested from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, and the Saṃgha now grants this maiden the two-year training in the precepts.
Venerable Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant two years of training in the precepts to [Name]. Those who consent, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Sangha has already granted the two-year training in the precepts to so-and-so; because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a girl who has reached twenty years of age without having her train in the precepts, it is a pāyattika.
"Having reached twenty years" means having completed twenty rains;
even if she has completed twenty rains but is less than twenty years [of age], she is still said to have completed twenty rains.

If one is born as late as the time of the later *anvārambhaṇa* (post-summer retreat), and having received the *pravāraṇā* at the later *anvārambhaṇa*, the count reaches twenty, this is called "complete.
"Not having been granted the training rules" means that although the *karmavācanā* was performed for them, they were not granted the training rules; this is called "not having been granted."
If ten factors are not fulfilled, it is also called "not granting the training precepts.

Even if the *karmavācanā* has been performed, if the assembly is incomplete, the motion (*jñapti*) is incomplete, or the formal act (*karman*) is incomplete—and if it is incomplete in any one of these respects—to grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī conferred the śikṣamāṇā precepts upon a woman, but before she had completed the training, she conferred the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) upon her. [The rest] up to "what has already been heard should be heard again" is as before.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has received the training precepts (śikṣamāṇā) confers full ordination (upasampadā) upon someone before the training period is completed, it is a pāyattika.
"Receiving the training precepts" means being granted the status of a śikṣamāṇā.

When ten factors are fulfilled, the assembly is accomplished, the formal announcement (jñapti) is accomplished, and the ritual act (karman) is accomplished—if each of these is accomplished, it is called "bestowing the training precepts."
For one who has not yet completed the training in the precepts, once she has received the training precepts, she must follow and train in eighteen matters for two years.
What are these eighteen?
She is to be ranked below all bhikṣuṇīs and above all śrāmaṇerīs.
What is impure for laypeople is pure for bhikṣuṇīs;
what is impure for bhikṣuṇīs is likewise impure for them.
They may stay in the same room as a bhikṣuṇī for three nights, and the same limit of three nights applies to staying with a śrāmaṇerikā.
One may receive food from a bhikṣuṇī, provided that the five types of cultivated seeds have been purified by fire;
one may receive food from a śrāmaṇerikā;
however, one must not recite the Prātimokṣa to them, nor speak concerning offenses from the pārājika down to the vyatikrama-vinaya. One may, however, say:
"One must not engage in sexual misconduct, one must not steal, and one must not kill.
Having received such instruction, one may not attend the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.
On the day of the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, one should go before the *sthavira*, prostrate oneself by touching one's head to the feet of the Sangha, and speak as follows:
"I, [Name], am pure; I remember and maintain this.
Having spoken thus three times, one should step back and depart.
Should one subsequently commit any of the four *pārājika* offenses, one must undergo the formal training (*śikṣā*) again on that very day.
If one commits any of the offenses from the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down, one must confess them all as *duṣkṛta*.
If one violates the five precepts—what are these five?
Eating at improper times, eating stored food, accepting gold, silver, or money, drinking alcohol, and wearing perfumes and flowers.
According to the number of days one has committed an offense, the period of training from the beginning is completed.
If it is less than two rains of training, this is called "incomplete training.
To grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) to one who has incomplete training constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One established a precept, not permitting the conferral of full ordination upon one who had not completed the training.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī conferred full ordination upon a girl of eighteen years who had completed the training in the precepts."
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with resentment, saying:
"Whether your training in the precepts is complete or not—who can know that?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until the Buddha said:

"From now on, a girl who has completed twenty years of training in the precepts and wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) as a bhikṣuṇī within the discipline and teachings of the Tathāgata must first perform the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for seeking permission."
“‘So be it. Thereafter, she should request from the Sangha the *karmavācanā* for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon completion of the training in the precepts.
The officiant of the *karmavācanā* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This maiden so-and-so, twenty years of age, has completed her training in the precepts and wishes to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may this maiden so-and-so request from the Saṃgha the full ordination upon completion of her training."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen: such-and-such a girl of twenty years, having completed her training in the precepts and desiring to request from the Saṃgha the full ordination of one whose training is complete—since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
One should request [permission] from the Saṃgha, kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, so-and-so, a twenty-year-old girl who has completed the training in the precepts, wish to receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata."

"I now request from the Saṃgha the full ordination upon completion of the training period; I only pray that the Saṃgha, out of compassion, will grant me the full ordination upon completion of the training.
Thus he requests three times.
The *karmadāna* should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This girl named [Name], having reached twenty years of age and completed her training in the precepts, desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata to become a bhikṣuṇī; she has already requested from the Saṃgha the full ordination upon completion of her training."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of conferring full ordination upon [Name], whose training is complete.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This girl so-and-so has completed twenty years of age; her training in the precepts is complete, and she desires to receive full ordination as a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata. She has already requested from the Saṃgha that, her training being complete, she be granted full ordination.

The Saṃgha now grants full ordination to [Name], whose period of training is complete. Those of you, Venerable Saṃgha, who consent to granting full ordination to [Name], whose period of training is complete, remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are spoken in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *karmavācanā* for the fulfillment of training for so-and-so; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī has completed her training in the precepts, yet the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is not performed to grant her full ordination (upasampadā), it is a pāyattika offense.
"Having completed the training in the precepts" means having practiced the eighteen matters in accordance with the two rainy-season retreats.
"One who does not perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) means one who fails to carry out the *karmavācanā*.
To grant full ordination [in such a case] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense is as explained above."
Therefore, the World-Honored One said.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 38.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 39.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

This is the third part of the one hundred forty-one *pāyattika* rules. The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī. At that time, there were women of the Śākya clan, the Koliya clan, the Malla clan, and the Licchavi clan who had previously been married and then left the household life; because they had endured hardships, they possessed wisdom.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
May a married woman who is less than twenty years of age receive full ordination?"
The Buddha said, "It is permitted.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī conferred full ordination upon a girl who had previously been married and was eight or nine years old; she was too small and frail to endure the hardships of monastic life.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter; [the Buddha said: "Even those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has married another woman grants full ordination when she is less than twelve years [of standing], it is a pāyattika.
'Less than twelve years' is as explained in detail in the section on being less than twenty years [of standing]."
To have sexual relations with another's wife is to destroy the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
To confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon such a person constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If a woman who has married another wishes to receive full ordination within the discipline of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya, she must first be questioned and even examined as far as her hands, feet, bones, and joints.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept, prohibiting the conferral of full ordination upon a woman who had married into another family if she was less than twelve years since her marriage.
At that time, there were bhikṣuṇīs who conferred full ordination upon a woman who had married into another family and was exactly twelve years since her marriage.
