The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"You have been married for twelve years; whether it has been twelve years or not, who knows?
The bhikṣuṇīs told this to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the Blessed One. ... [and so on] ... until the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, when a woman who has completed twelve years of rain-retreats marries another’s wife, she shall be granted two years of training in the precepts.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has married another woman and reached twelve years of seniority does not grant her training in the precepts before she receives full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
This is as explained above regarding the unmarried girl who does not train in the precepts.
Abusing others face-to-face yet not being fully ordained; lacking the ten factors of qualification;
maintaining a retinue without performing the *karmavācanā*; having violated the precepts or being less than twenty years of age;
not having trained or not having completed the training; or having completed the training but not having performed the *karmavācanā*.
Excluding twelve [cases], there is no training.
The tenth chapter concludes.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī ordained the wife of the royal minister Sudinna, granting her the training precepts. She had been pregnant while still a laywoman, and her belly grew larger and larger.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"Since she has already received the training precepts (śikṣamāṇā) yet is pregnant, she should be expelled.
She replied:
"Since I went forth, I have not known this Dharma.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of these circumstances, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Since he has been a renunciant, he has not known this Dharma; these were matters from his time as a householder.
If there are such cases as these, one should not yet confer full ordination upon him."
Once she has given birth, if it is a girl, she shall be granted full ordination after leaving the grass mat;
if it is a boy, she shall be granted full ordination once the child is able to wean.
If a relative or sister says,
"Bring this child here; I myself will nourish and raise him," then one should grant him full ordination.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having received the training precepts as a woman already married to another, grants full ordination before the training period is completed, it is a pāyattika.
This is explained in detail, as above, regarding the case of a maiden who has not completed her training in the precepts.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One established a precept, forbidding those who had not reached twelve years of age from marrying a woman, and forbidding those who had not completed two years of training in the precepts from receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī gave full ordination to a woman who had married another after she had completed two years of training in the precepts. The other bhikṣuṇīs complained, saying:
"Whether your training in the precepts was complete or incomplete—who can know?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One of these events. Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; let those who have already heard this hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a woman who has already been married and has completed the training in the precepts, without having performed the *karmavācanā*, it is a pāyattika.
This is as explained at length above regarding the case of a maiden without the *karmavācanā*.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, many bhikṣuṇīs kept numerous disciples but failed to instruct or admonish them; they were like wild oxen or wild sheep, lacking purity and lacking proper deportment. They did not know how to serve their upādhyāyas and ācāryas, nor how to serve elder bhikṣuṇīs. They did not know the rules for entering villages or the rules for forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka), nor did they know the rules for wearing robes and carrying the alms bowl.
The bhikṣuṇī told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; how can you ordain people without providing them with instruction?
From this day forward, you must provide instruction for two years.
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence on Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having conferred full ordination upon a disciple, does not instruct her for two years, it is a pāyattika.”
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Disciple" refers to a co-resident disciple.
"Two years" refers to two periods of the rainy season.
Instruction consists of either the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
The Abhidharma refers to the ninefold sūtras.
The Vinaya refers to the extensive and concise versions of the Prātimokṣa.
One should instruct them in proper deportment and restrain them from improper deportment.
If one fails to provide such instruction and admonition, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a disciple is incorrigible and unwilling to learn, they should be expelled.
If a bhikṣu does not instruct a co-resident disciple, he commits a vinaya offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣuṇī ordained a disciple; once the disciple had received full ordination, she abandoned her teacher and departed for another place.
At that time, the preceptor nun spoke with resentment, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts that one must instruct one's disciples; yet my disciple has abandoned me and left. Whom shall I now instruct?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; how could you go elsewhere after having received full ordination?"
"She should serve as a preceptor for two years.
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī, after having received full ordination, does not provide service and follow her preceptor nun (upādhyāyinī) for two years, it is a pāyattika offense.
"One who has received full ordination" refers to a co-resident disciple.
"Two years" refers to two periods of the rainy season.
"To provide for" means to provide for the preceptor nun.
Regarding those who should be followed, one must not abandon them.
If one fails to provide for or follow such a person, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the preceptor nun does not maintain the precepts well and has no desire to train, the disciple should think as follows:
"If my preceptor nun were to walk in a place that is not in accordance with the rules of decorum, and I were to follow her, it might harm my brahmacarya.
For the sake of preserving the purity of my conduct, it is no offense to leave her."
If a bhikṣu does not provide for his upādhyāya or attend upon him, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣuṇī year after year ordained disciples to receive full admission (*upasampadā*); doubt arose in her mind as to whether she had obtained it or not.
She immediately questioned Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others year after year; you must observe an interval."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple every year, it is a pāyattika.
'Every year' means during each rainy season.
'Keeps a disciple' means to confer full ordination."
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
It is not permitted to keep a disciple year after year; one should do so for the duration of a single rainy season.

If a bhikṣuṇī possesses merit and virtue, she may provide instruction on the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā*) for one year and grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) for the second year; even if she does this year after year, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
The Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Jyotiṣkī wished to confer full ordination upon her disciple and spoke to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, saying: "Āryā!..."
"Please the Saṃgha of monks on my behalf to confer full ordination upon my disciples; afterwards, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha shall confer full ordination upon them.
Thus, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā requested the six groups of bhikṣus.
Jyotiṣka asked,
"Have you obtained the Sangha's consent for my sake?
He replied:
"I have obtained it. "Obtained what?
He replied:
"I have obtained the group of six bhikṣus," he said,
"but I do not need them; tomorrow I shall invite virtuous bhikṣus to receive full ordination."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the Blessed One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said to Jyotiṣka.
"This is an evil deed. How could you, after the assembly had already completed its overnight stay and been purified, confer full ordination while again showing contempt for the community?"
"From this day forward, I do not permit a single assembly of pure nuns to stay overnight and confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), nor do I permit them to hold the assembly in contempt.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Rājagṛha assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī undergoes full ordination while staying overnight in a pure assembly, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"In a pure assembly" means undergoing full ordination within the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding "staying overnight": if one arrives at the assembly of bhikṣus on the following day to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is a *pāyattika*.

A *pāyattika* is as explained above. One is not permitted to stay overnight with a pure assembly to receive full ordination; nor is one permitted to disregard the assembly; nor may one request an assembly of wicked bhikṣus to confer full ordination; rather, one should first seek out virtuous bhikṣus.
If it cannot be obtained, one should seek half; if more than half is granted, one may perform the *karmavācanā*.
If it cannot be obtained due to difficulties such as kings or bandits, there is no offense in staying overnight.
A bhikṣu must not also slight the assembly.
He should receive half; if he performs a *karmavācanā* with more than half [of the assembly], one who slights the assembly incurs an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī ordained the third daughter born to a Licchavi family and allowed her to live in close association with laypeople and non-Buddhists.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the bhikṣuṇī Kālī:
"Do you know that this disciple lives in close association with laypeople and followers of external paths? Why do you not separate her and send her to another region?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī about this matter, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of it.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. How could you know that your disciples were living in close association with householders and non-Buddhists, yet did not separate themselves from them?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in dependence upon Vaiśālī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī has taken a disciple as a follower and, when an issue arises, neither sends her herself nor dispatches someone else to send her, even for a distance of five or six yojanas, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"One who ordains others" refers to the precept-mother (upādhyāyinī).
"Disciple" refers to the co-practitioner disciple (sahacāriṇī).

Regarding those with affairs: it may be that a disciple wishes to abandon the Way, or that parents or relatives wish to cause them to abandon the Way, or that a son-in-law or an uncle wishes to cause them to abandon the Way.
As for seeing them off: one should neither see them off oneself nor send someone else to see them off.
As for those who go as far as five or six *yojanas*, the maximum limit is six.
If a disciple is accustomed to living nearby, he should be sent on a journey; if he is old or ill and unable to go, he should entrust himself to someone else, who should instruct him:

"You may travel abroad, for there are many merits in doing so: you shall pay homage to various stupas and monasteries, see excellent assemblies of practitioners, and gain much learning and insight. Had I not been old, I too would have wished to go."
"If a bhikṣu has a co-resident disciple with business to attend to, and he neither sends him off himself nor sends someone else to send him, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus."

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, not having fulfilled the ten requirements, ordained a disciple and failed to instruct or admonish her; she was like a celestial ox or a celestial sheep.
Eventually, the bhikṣuṇīs said to her: "Āryā!..."
"You lack ten qualities; why do you ordain disciples and yet fail to instruct them so that they act according to the Dharma?
Thullanandā replied, "You are jealous that I ordain disciples, and so you reproach me."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:
“Call that bhikṣuṇī here.”
When she had arrived, he asked her,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter. How could you, lacking the ten qualities yourself, ordain a disciple and fail to instruct or admonish them, yet instead find fault with and reproach another?"
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to disparage others.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī: "Venerable lady!
One who has not fulfilled the ten dharmas should still ordain a disciple and provide her with instruction."
"If one, on the contrary, finds fault with or reproaches [her], it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding "a bhikṣuṇī," this refers to whether she belongs to the Saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual.
"This bhikṣuṇī" refers, for example, to the bhikṣuṇī Steunlananda.
One who lacks ten factors does not accomplish the ten factors.
To ordain a disciple means to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one expresses resentment or reproach while this admonition is being given, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.
For a bhikṣu to act in such a manner constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a śikṣamāṇā said to Thullanandā, “Āryā!
My training period is complete; please grant me full ordination.”
She replied, "So be it.
Later, the novice nun who was studying the precepts said:
“Venerable One! My training in the precepts is complete; please grant me full ordination.
Having heard these words, he neither conferred the ordination himself, nor did he cause another to confer it, nor did he dismiss him.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "You previously promised to grant her full ordination; why do you not grant it now?
Despite hearing these words, she still did not grant it.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Summon that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said, "This is an evil deed.
Why did you permit another to receive full ordination and yet fail to confer it upon them?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā,
"When you have completed the training in the precepts,
I shall confer full ordination upon you," yet later neither confers it herself, nor causes another to confer it, nor sends her away, it is a pāyattika.
“Bhikṣuṇī” is as explained above.
“Śikṣamāṇā” refers to one who practices the eighteen matters in accordance with the rules and trains for two years.
One who speaks these words is like the bhikṣuṇī Steunlananda.
If she has promised to grant full ordination (*upasampadā*) but later neither grants it herself nor causes another to grant it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā:
"I shall confer full ordination upon you.

If later one lacks the capacity [to do so], one should have another person confer it. If one neither confers it oneself nor has another confer it, one should tell them to depart and receive full ordination elsewhere.
If a bhikṣuṇī permits a śikṣamāṇā to receive full ordination and subsequently does not grant it, she commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu permits a śrāmaṇera to receive full ordination and subsequently does not grant it, he incurs a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kāpilāyanī traveled to her relatives' home riding in a fine carriage. She was censured by the people of the world:
"How can a female renunciant of the Śramaṇa order ride in a fine carriage just like a worldly person? Is her desire so great?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they told Mahāprajāpatī; Mahāprajāpatī then reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil matter; from this day forward, it is not permitted."

Furthermore, at that time, a Śākya woman who was a bhikṣuṇī was traveling on a road; being weak, old, and ill, she could not keep pace with her companions and was subsequently robbed by bandits. ... [The Buddha] then addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble. ... [and] let those who have already heard this hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill rides in a vehicle, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Ill" refers to one who is aged, infirm, or diseased, or one who is a person of leisure unable to walk; regarding these, the World-Honored One has declared there is no offense.
Regarding "vehicles," there are eight kinds, including even boat-vehicles; these are called the eight kinds.
Regarding "carrying," it is a *pāyattika* offense.

It is not permitted for a healthy bhikṣuṇī to be carried in a vehicle; however, one who is ill may not be carried on a bull-drawn carriage, but she may be carried in a cart drawn by a cow or on the back of a mare or a camel.
If one is ill and does not perceive whether it is male or female, there is no offense; if one crosses by boat directly, there is no offense.
If traveling upstream or downstream for a specific purpose, one may go after having formally undertaken the necessary observances.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill mounts a vehicle, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"Without being ordained, without the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), without a preceptor, and without instruction."
The disciple does not follow; year after year he keeps disciples;
he stays overnight and receives full ordination; when there is business, he is not sent away;
though censured for his faults, he is permitted to receive full ordination; when riding in a carriage, he is always at the very rear.
The eleventh chapter is concluded.

The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kāpileyī went to the home of her relatives carrying a parasol and wearing leather sandals; she was censured by the people of the world:
"How is it that a śramaṇī, like a worldly person, is so full of desire?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit the carrying of parasols or leather sandals."

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a woman of the Śākya clan named Mālā who had previously been a musician. While traveling on the road after having gone forth, it was then an extremely hot day and she was greatly exhausted and suffering.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit [this practice] during times of illness."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, carries a parasol or wears leather sandals, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "the sick," this refers to those who are aged, emaciated, ill, or physically weak; for them, the World-Honored One has declared there is no offense.
Regarding "parasols," these include canopies made of tree bark, *tāla* leaves, bamboo, *mālū* leaves, tree leaves, or cotton cloth; such items and other similar types of canopies are included.
Regarding leather sandals, they may be single-layered or double-layered.
To possess them for personal use constitutes a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
To carry a parasol without carrying leather sandals is an offense against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
To carry leather sandals without carrying a parasol is likewise an offense against the Vinaya.
To carry both is a pāyattika.
If one holds neither of the two, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu carries an ornamental parasol or double-layered leather sandals, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said this.

The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā Kāpileyī went to the home of her relatives and prepared a high-legged *khadira* bed with two or three layers of bedding upon it. She then climbed onto it, which caused the people of the world and the non-Buddhists to feel resentment, saying:
"How is it that a female renunciant, a śramaṇī, is like a worldly person with such great desire?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," [the monk replied]. The Buddha said,
"Why did you sit upon a couch made of *khadira* wood that exceeded the prescribed dimensions?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Vaiśālī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits or lies down on a couch or bed with a stuffed mattress (*kaṭhalla*) that exceeds the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Excessive" means exceeding eight finger-breadths.
Regarding "kāṣṭhila beds and mattresses," there are fourteen types of kāṣṭhila, ranging up to *bhaṅguraka*.
If one sits or lies down on a *kāṣṭhila* or *bhaṅguraka* bed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If one sits for the entire day, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one rises and then sits again, one incurs a *pāyattika* for each instance of sitting.
If a bed is of excessive size, one may sit upon it with the legs buried underneath.
If a bhikṣu sits on a couch (khaṭvā) of excessive height, he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has said this.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs slept together on a single bed with a single bedding cover; their pillows and mattresses were torn, and the bed itself broke apart.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī [reported it] to the Buddha, who said:
"Call those bhikṣuṇīs here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you have done this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed."
The Buddha then addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; let those who have already heard this hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī lies down to sleep on a bed or mat shared with another, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "shared": sharing one covering, one sheet, and one bed.
As for "bed," there are fourteen kinds, including even a *cilimilika* (grass-mat) bed; [if she does so], it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense, it is as explained above.

One must not lie down on the same bed; one person shall sleep on one bed. On a three-seated couch, two persons may sleep, provided that when stretching out their legs, they do not extend beyond the knees.
If it is a square mat, three mats may accommodate two people lying down; however, they must not stretch their legs beyond their knees.

If it is spread upon the ground, one must not occupy too much space; rather, one should leave a distance of one unextended hand between each other, spreading out one's own sitting mat before lying down.
If it is cold, one may have a superior blanket cover those below; provided each person is covered separately, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu lies on the same bed, it is an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus:

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kāli, having received a monastic cell from the Saṃgha, closed the door and departed. Later, an incoming bhikṣuṇī who was a senior elder arrived and was assigned a cell in due order; seeing the door closed, she immediately expressed her displeasure, saying:
"Why has this monastic cell been left with the door closed?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on until the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here. Once she had come, he questioned her, saying:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
The Buddha said:
"This is a wicked matter... how could you leave the monastic quarters without closing the door and depart?
From this day forward, this is not permitted."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"Have all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī leaves the monastic quarters without putting away her bedding, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Monastic bedding" refers to sitting benches, beds, pillows, mattresses, and bolsters.
Regarding "not relinquishing": if one departs for another place without returning [the bedding] and without informing [the keeper], it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to travel, she must relinquish her bed and bedding to the person in charge of the bedding before departing.
If one does not leave after having vacated it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the room is not empty and someone else immediately occupies it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Ghaṭāyā’s mother entered the room of the bhikṣu Ghaṭāyā’s father without prior announcement; she suddenly went in and rubbed his back. He immediately turned around to look at her, and having seen her, he said: “Hey!...”
"Hey! Keep away from me!
the bhikṣuṇī said.
"I have always bathed you in the past; why is it painful for you now that I touch you?
He replied, "I was originally a layman, but today I have gone forth into homelessness; I cannot be as I was before."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately went to report this matter to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wicked deed. How could you enter the bhikṣu’s vihāra without first announcing yourself?"
From this day forward, it is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again:
if a bhikṣuṇī enters a bhikṣu monastery without first having announced her presence, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Bhikṣu-saṃghārāma" refers to even a dwelling place where only a single bhikṣu resides.
"Without having first informed" means not having previously spoken to or summoned [the resident].
As for "entering," it is as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Gheṭāvatī, for which there is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the term "pāyattika," it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to enter the dwelling place of bhikṣus, she must go to the gatehouse and first announce her presence.
"Vandana! The bhikṣuṇī announces her arrival; we pray that you will grant us leave.
The bhikṣus should deliberate upon this.
If a bhikṣuṇī is virtuous and has no business to enter while wearing her robes, she is permitted to enter.
If she has business, or is engaged in mud-work, or is naked, one should say to her:
"Sister! [Wait until you have finished]."
"Wait a moment.
He should then announce:
"Venerable Elders!..."
"If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to enter, each should put on her own robe.
If a bhikṣuṇī is unskilled or lacks dignified decorum, one should say to her:
"Do not enter; there is business at hand."
If one enters first without having been informed beforehand, it is a *pāyattika*.
Those who arrive later are without offense.
For one who enters without having announced themselves, if they raise even one foot [inside], it is an offense of transgressing the *vinaya*.
If one places both feet [inside], it is a pāyattika offense.
If one returns and leaves, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
If a bhikṣu enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs without first having announced his arrival, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
"One should stand beneath the porch of a gatehouse and have a *kappiya-kārī* woman speak for one.
For this reason, the Blessed One spoke.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on a road. At dusk, they arrived at a village seeking a place to stay. They went to a certain house and said to a woman:
"Please lend me a place to stay.
The woman said, "My husband has gone away; he may perhaps return this evening."
The bhikṣuṇī repeated her request once more, saying, "I must indeed come;
you may let me stay for one night.
He then gave her a place to stay.
When her husband returned in the evening, driven by his bonds, he engaged in sexual intercourse with his wife.

The bhikṣuṇī, who had not yet abandoned desire, was displeased upon hearing the sound; after he had returned, she told the other bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, until the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
Having arrived, he asked:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," [the Buddha said].
"How did you know that you were staying overnight at a place of sexual misconduct in a family home?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on a road. When evening came, they reached a village; though they searched everywhere for a household with no men present, they could find none, and so they stayed overnight by the side of an alleyway.
One night, when a violent storm arose, several young men came to harass them and violated their holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The bhikṣuṇīs reported these circumstances to Mahāprajāpatī, and so forth, until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, except for other times, even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight at a place of sexual intercourse in a household where food is being consumed, except during other times, it is a pāyattika.
"Other times" refers to times of wind, times of rain, times when life is threatened, or times when the holy life (brahmacarya) is endangered; these are called "other times."
"Regarding the term 'bhikṣuṇī,' it is as explained above.
'Knows' means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
'Food' means that women are food for men, and men are food for women."
"A household" refers to a family of one of the four castes.
"A place for sexual intercourse" refers to the bedchamber of a married couple.
Except at other times, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
On other occasions, the Blessed One declared that there is no offense.
These "other occasions" are: during a windstorm, during a rainstorm, when life is at stake, or when one suspects a man might violate one's celibacy. This is what is meant by "other occasions."

One must not knowingly stay overnight at a place where food is being provided for sexual purposes; however, if one suspects that there are dissolute men in the village and stays out of fear, there is no offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs of Vaiśālī, having completed their rainy-season retreat, wished to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage to the World-Honored One; they arrived at the bhikṣus’ monastery and said, “We offer our salutations!”
"I have heard that the Venerable One intends to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage to the World-Honored One;
is this indeed so? He replied, "Why do you ask?"
"I wish to go along with you.
The bhikṣu said,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not travel on the same road as a bhikṣuṇī."
He asked again,
"When will you set out?
He replied:
"On such-and-such a day.
He then noted that date and waited by the side of the road, having already taken up his robes and bowl.
When the day arrived, the bhikṣu ate his meal and departed; seeing the bhikṣuṇīs, they spoke to one another:
"This bhikṣuṇī wishes to follow us; we must run with swift steps!
So saying, the young bhikṣuṇīs ran and pursued her, but the elderly and those who were ill or infirm could not catch up, and she was subsequently stripped of her belongings by bandits.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of this matter, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One, until [the Buddha said], "Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How could you travel toward another country through a desolate wilderness without the company of merchant companions?"
"From this day forward, it is not permitted.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this shall hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels toward another country without a merchant companion, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Without a companion" means without a merchant companion.
"Other countries" refers to the territories of different kings.
To go [there] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to travel, she must first seek out a caravan of merchants as companions.
If the person ahead says: "Venerable One!
Just come; I shall take care of it so that you may go."
One should examine the person.
If their speech is excellent but their gaze is unseemly, one should not follow them; rather, one should seek out a virtuous man who will take the woman with him and go together.

If, while departing, one does not suddenly perceive [the danger] and only realizes it upon reaching a remote place, one must not simply abandon [the object] and leave; rather, one should wait until near a village and then skillfully abandon it and depart.
If someone asks,
"Where do you wish to go?
one should say:
"I am merely seeking alms.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels without a merchant as a companion, she incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
Upon reaching her destination, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu travels through a desolate wilderness without the company of fellow merchants, he commits a *viniya-āpatti*.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time, bhikṣuṇīs went together with women to gardens and ponds to look about.
While several women were eating and drinking by the water’s edge, a bhikṣuṇī went to an old village house to look around.
At that time, some youths emerged from the forest and disturbed the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until: "What has already been heard should be heard again.
If a bhikṣuṇī, within her own territory, inspects gardens, groves, or old ruins, it is a pāyattika."
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Within the boundary" means within the king's own territory.
"Garden" refers to mango groves, up to and including *atimuktaka* groves.
"A forest" refers to various kinds of groves and trees.
"An old ruin" refers to within an empty house or dwelling.
To observe and look [at these] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to look at a garden, a grove, or a deserted dwelling, she incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense when she departs;
once she arrives there, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a female lay devotee invites him to go together with her, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to a desolate garden or grove for the sake of sightseeing and pleasure, it is an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣuṇī Sujātā was formerly the wife of Udāyin.
She spoke to Udāyin, saying:
“Venerable One! I shall guard the dwelling tomorrow; you may come to look.

At that time, all the bhikṣuṇīs had entered the village to beg for food. Then Udāyin, having adjusted his robes and taken up his bowl, entered the bhikṣuṇī vihāra. The two of them were together behind the dwelling; each drew back their bodies to sit in a squatting posture facing one another, looking at each other with lustful intent.

At that time, there was an elderly and sick bhikṣuṇī who went out to relieve herself; having seen [the Buddha], she felt ashamed and retreated. Because of this incident, she spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on until the Buddha said:
"Call that bhikṣuṇī here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter... as has already been heard, it shall be heard again.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits with a single bhikṣu in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika."
"First, it is 'one' because one is together with a single bhikṣu and there is no other person.
Even if there were another person, they might be asleep, intoxicated, insane, deluded, mentally disturbed, in pain, an infant, a non-human, or an animal; for these reasons, it is called 'one'."
"An empty and quiet place" refers to a secluded spot where no one is present.
"Sitting together" means sitting in company [with a monk];
this constitutes a *pāyattika*. A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits together with a bhikṣu for the entire day, it is one pāyattika.
If she rises in the interim and sits again, for each instance of sitting, there is a separate pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī is sitting alone in her room and a bhikṣu suddenly enters and sits down, the bhikṣuṇī should rise quickly.
When she wishes to rise, she should speak first so as not to cause the bhikṣu to feel suspicious.
If one asks,
"For what reason does it arise?
one should say:
“The World-Honored One has established the precept that I must not sit alone with a bhikṣu.
What if it is a boy less than seven years old? Does this also constitute an offense?
To what extent of time does the term “sitting” refer?
For example, while a renunciant is out begging for food,
if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who prepares what is permissible) moving about, coming and going, or entering and exiting without interruption,
there is no offense. Likewise, if a room door faces a path where people are passing by, and they do not cease their movement, there is no offense.
If a practitioner cuts [the tree], it is a *pāyattika*.

When the attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) is asleep, one should snap one's fingers to wake him; if he is on the upper story of a multi-storied building and someone sees him from below, or if he is on the ground floor and someone sees him from above, there is no offense provided that these three persons see one another in succession.
There are cases where one sees but does not hear, cases where one hears but does not see, cases where one both sees and hears, and cases where one neither sees nor hears.
Regarding seeing but not hearing: it is when one sees from afar a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī sitting, yet does not hear the sound of their speech.
"To hear but not see" means to hear the sound of speech without seeing [the speaker].
This is explained in detail as follows.
"To see but not hear" constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To hear but not see also constitutes a *vinaya* offense.
To both see and hear, there is no offense.
To neither see nor hear constitutes a *pāyattika*.

This offense occurs in a village as well as in the wilderness; by day as well as by night; at the proper time as well as at the improper time; in a concealed place rather than an exposed one; involving a single person rather than many; and in a nearby location rather than a distant one.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā went to the house of her relatives and sat in a secluded place with her brothers, sisters, and children. A bhikṣuṇī, disapproving, said:
"How can one who has left the household life sit in a private place with laypeople, acting just like a worldly person?"
For these reasons, she spoke to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to sit in a secluded place with a man; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place with a man, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the term "pāyattika," it is explained in detail as above in the section on the bhikṣus.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
Holding an umbrella, using a couch made of *khajjūra* wood, sharing a bed without relinquishing it,
staying overnight in a place of sexual misconduct without informing others, visiting a deserted ruin without a companion,
and a bhikṣu sitting in a secluded place with a man— the same applies to these cases as well.
The twelfth *varga* is concluded.

The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā went to the house of her relatives and stood within arm’s reach of her brothers, sisters, and nephews, whispering in their ears. The male and female servants spoke with resentment, saying:
"These renunciants are whispering; they must surely be speaking of our faults."
When the bhikṣuṇīs had heard this, they said to Mahāprajāpatī:
“Gautamī! Even those who have already heard it should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands within arm's reach of a man or whispers with him, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Within arm's reach" means standing together within the range of one's outstretched arms.
"Whispering" means speaking together by the ear; this is a *pāyattika*.
A bhikṣuṇī must not stand within arm's reach of a man to converse with him or whisper to him. If she wishes to converse, she should remain outside of arm's reach.
If one wishes to discuss secret matters, one should do so with a fence, a wall, a tree, or a curtain as a barrier.
For a bhikṣuṇī to do so [without such a barrier] is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu stands within arm’s reach of a woman and converses with her by whispering in her ear, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vyatikrama-vinayātikrama).
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

"When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā went to the home of her relatives. She entered suddenly and unexpectedly into a dark place without a lamp, where she was with her brothers, sisters, and children; at that time, the relatives were filled with shame and embarrassment."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
"It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"How do you know that there is a man in the darkness and enter without a lamp?
From this day forward, it is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a man sitting in the dark, enters without a lamp, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," it is as explained above.
"A man who sits" refers to one who usually sleeps or lies down.
"A dark place" refers to a place where they cannot see one another.
"Without a lamp" means there is no oil lamp or any other kind of lamp.
To enter [there] is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
One must not enter the place where men sit in a dark area; however, if there is a necessary reason to enter, one should do so upon hearing the loud voices of those inside.
If they do not hear your words, you should first send someone to speak to them, or snap your fingers, or manifest a sign by lighting a lamp; if someone calls you to enter, you should enter.
If one enters without speaking, without snapping fingers, or without providing a light, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu enters without speaking, it is a vyatikrama-vinaya offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:

When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣuṇīs went first to a place where musicians were performing and reserved seats. While the performers were playing, they laughed loudly, and the crowd followed suit by laughing.
When the people laughed, she would immediately fall silent, appearing like one sitting in meditation;
as soon as the laughter ceased, she would again clap her hands and laugh loudly.
Thereupon, the crowd abandoned the performers to watch the bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the performers, not receiving their wages, became angry and resentful, saying:
"It is because of this śramaṇī that we have lost our wages.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is a wicked deed; how could you watch theatrical performances?"
From this day forward, watching performances and music is not permitted.
Even those who have already heard this shall hear it again:
if a bhikṣuṇī goes to watch performances and music, it is a pāyattika offense.
“Bhikṣuṇī” is as explained above.
“Performances” refers to dance performers, singers, cymbal players, drummers, and so forth—all such things—even down to four people playing together; for one who watches this, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

One must not watch performances of music and dance. However, if a bhikṣuṇī, while begging for alms, happens to encounter a king, a queen, or a celestial image being paraded out accompanied by music and dance, there is no offense in seeing them by chance.
If one goes from a lower place to a higher one, intentionally peering out or watching after [the procession], it is a *pāyattika*.
If a donor wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, performing various musical performances, grinding incense, or weaving garlands, and says to a bhikṣuṇī: "Āryā!..."
"Assist me in preparing the requisites for offering.
At that time, one may assist in the work.
If, during that interval, one hears music and feels a mind of attachment arise, one should depart.
If a bhikṣu watches performances of music and dance, he commits an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
For this reason, the Blessed One spoke.

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were quarreling and living in discord. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the leader of the community, was unable to extinguish disputes that had already arisen among the monks, nor could she prevent those that had not yet arisen from arising.
The bhikṣuṇīs, on account of these circumstances, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Call Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī here."
When she had arrived, the Buddha said to Gautamī,
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is truly so," the Buddha said.
"How is it that you do not resolve disputes when they arise, and fail to employ skillful means to prevent those that have not yet arisen from arising?"
"From this day forward, whenever a dispute arises, it shall be settled and extinguished.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī quarrels and remains in discord, and the leader of the community does not attend to the matter to settle and extinguish it, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Dispute" refers to verbal dispute. "Quarreling" refers to taking turns to seek victory and not dwelling in harmony, [arguing]:

"This is Dharma, this is non-Dharma; this is Vinaya, this is non-Vinaya; this is an offense, this is no offense; this is light, this is heavy; this is curable, this is incurable; this has a remainder, this has no remainder; this is a formal act in accordance with the Dharma, this is a formal act contrary to the Dharma; this is a formal act of concord, this is a formal act of discord; this is a formal act that should be performed, this is a formal act that should not be performed; this is a formal act in the proper place, this is a formal act in the improper place."
Regarding the "leader of the community": he is the preeminent figure of the assembly and acts according to his own will.
As for "not managing [the matter] so as to bring it to cessation": neither extinguishing it himself nor causing another to extinguish it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*, it is as explained above.

If bhikṣuṇīs are quarreling and living in discord, one must not simply ignore them; rather, one should manage the situation to resolve and extinguish the conflict, causing them to repent of their faults one after another.
If the matter is not ceased and requires a formal ritual (karmavācanā), the Saṃgha should be assembled to handle it.
If one is unable to do so oneself, one should request other virtuous bhikṣuṇīs, bhikṣus, upāsakas, or upāsikās from the assembly to extinguish it.
If a dispute is difficult to resolve, one should reflect thus:
"The karmic actions of sentient beings depend upon time; once they have reached maturity, they will naturally cease.
One who acts in this manner incurs no fault.
If a monk engages in quarreling and the leader of the community does not attend to it to extinguish the dispute, he commits a *vinaya*-offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Bhadrā who went to the home of her relatives to visit and bathe. The women there said:
"I shall rub the body of the Noble One so that I may gain merit.
Because this bhikṣuṇī was beautiful, other women, wishing to see her body, permitted her to rub it and thus applied various kinds of fragrant oils to her body.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"Those who have left the household life still possess much desire.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“How is it that you allow the women of lay families to rub and massage your bodies?
From this day forward, this is not permitted.
Even those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī causes a laywoman to apply fragrant oils, rub her body, or bathe her, except during times of illness, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Householder women" refers to daughters from the four types of families.
"Anointing and bathing" means anointing and bathing with various kinds of fragrant oils.
There is no offense if [the woman] is old or ill.
If one rubs, massages, or bathes when not ill, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If there are sores or scabs on the body, one may apply medicinal ointments and rub or bathe [with them].
If one has a feverish illness, one may apply a paste of māyā-powder;
if one has a wind-related illness, one may apply a paste of wheat powder; and if one has a combined illness, one may apply a paste of various medicines without fault.
Having applied the ointment, one must not remain among the assembly; one should stay in a peripheral room and enter only after the illness has been cured and one has washed.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill causes a layperson to rub or massage him, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya (vyatikrama).
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the World-Honored One then established a precept, prohibiting laywomen from massaging or scrubbing [monks] during their baths.

At that time, Bhadrā the bhikṣuṇī had a bhikṣuṇī massage her body. The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances... [and so forth] ...up until: "What has already been heard should be heard again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, causes another bhikṣuṇī to rub, massage, or bathe her, it is a pāyattika.
If she rubs her but does not massage her, it is a vyatikrama offense."
To rub without scrubbing also constitutes a *vibhinī* offense.
To do both constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, when not ill, causes another bhikṣu to scrub or massage him, it is a *vibhinī* offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The śrāmaṇerikā is also like this.
[This applies] up to: "Those who have already heard it should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, causes a śrāmaṇerī to rub or massage her, it is a pāyattika.
A śrāmaṇerī is one who has followed the Buddha into the homeless life and received the ten precepts.
Regarding the act of rubbing and massaging, it is as explained in the section on the bhikṣuṇīs.
It is the same for the śikṣamāṇā.
This shall be heard again, even by those who have already heard it.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill causes a śikṣamāṇā to rub or massage her, it is a pāyattika.
A śikṣamāṇā is one who practices the eighteen matters in accordance with the rules and trains in the precepts for two years.
Regarding those who rub and massage [the body], it is as explained above in the section concerning the bhikṣuṇīs.
It is the same for laywomen.
This applies even to those who have already heard this; they should hear it again.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill causes a laywoman to rub or massage her, it is a pāyattika.
A 'laywoman' refers to a woman from one of the four castes."
The rubbing and massaging are as explained in the section concerning the bhikṣuṇīs.

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs assembled, intending to perform the *poṣadha* ritual. The bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī did not come, so the Saṃgha sent a messenger to summon her, saying: "Āryā!..."
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs has assembled and intends to perform the poṣadha; you should come.
Jyotiṣkā replied, "The World-Honored One has established the precepts that only those who are pure in the world may perform the poṣadha. I am indeed pure, and therefore I cannot go."
Mahāprajāpatī reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, until she replied:
"It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter... up to: if you do not show respect for the *poṣadha*, who indeed shall show respect?
...up to: those who have already heard this should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not show respect when the half-monthly pure *poṣadha* is held, it is a *pāyattika*."
Regarding the pure *poṣadha*: on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, if a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill does not come to respectfully attend the *poṣadha*, it is a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the sick: those who are aged and infirm, those taking medicine, those having bloodletting from the head, or those consuming clarified butter (ghṛta) should be given the *śuddhaka-chanda* (the formal expression of consent).
If one who is not ill does not come, or if one who is ill is not granted the *śuddhaka-chanda*, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not come for the poṣadha, and being ill, does not grant her *śuddhika-icchā* (the desire for purity), it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu does not come for the poṣadha, and being ill, does not grant his *icchā*, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore the World-Honored One said:
"Within arm's reach there is no lamp; The master of music does not extinguish it;
Scented oil for the bhikṣuṇī; And the śrāmaṇerī training in the precepts."
Women do not observe the *poṣadha*.
The thirteenth *varga* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; at that time, the elder bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus did not receive their turn for instruction, they spoke thus:
"We shall go to give instruction.
They spoke again:
“The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit us to instruct or admonish [the nuns] without being formally appointed.
We shall go outside the boundary, pay our respects to one another in turn, and then depart.
Having thus gone outside the boundary and paid their respects to one another in turn, they put on their robes in the morning and went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs, saying to them:
“Sisters, assemble all; I shall instruct you.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs assembled immediately, but the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs did not come, and they said:
“We cannot receive instruction from those who do not abide by the Vinaya.”
At that time, after the group of six bhikṣus had engaged in worldly conversation with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, they departed in a short while.
Then the Venerable Nanda, having dressed and taken his bowl, came to the vihāra and said, "Sisters, assemble; I wish to instruct you."
Thereupon, the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs all assembled, but the group of six bhikṣuṇīs did not come.
The Elder asked,
"Has the community of bhikṣuṇīs assembled?"
He replied, "They have not assembled. [The Buddha asked,] "Who has not assembled?"
He replied,
"The group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
He then immediately sent a messenger to summon them.
"Sisters, come!
I wish to instruct you.
They replied:
"I did not go, for I have already received the instructions from the group of six preceptors.
Then the Elder said,
"The nuns are not in harmony."
He immediately rose and departed.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked:
"Why did you finish your instruction so quickly?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!

When the time arrived, I put on my robes and went intending to provide instruction. All the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs had assembled, but only the group of six bhikṣuṇīs did not come; because the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha was not in harmony, I was unable to provide instruction.”
The Buddha said,
"Call the bhikṣuṇīs of the group of six here.
When they had come, he questioned them, saying:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
...and so on, up to: "Those who have already heard this should hear it again:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha provides instruction every half-month, does not show respect or does not attend, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Half-month" refers to the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
"Monastic instruction" (saṃgha-ovāda) means the instruction of bhikṣuṇīs.
If one does not show respect or does not come, it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" is as explained above.
If one is old, weak, ill, taking medicine, having bloodletting performed on the head, or consuming clarified butter (sarpis), one should give their consent (*chanda*) by speaking as follows:
"I, [Name], give my consent for the instruction.
Thus one should say three times.
If one who is not ill does not go, or if one who is ill does not give their consent, it is a pāyattika offense.
When the day of the *poṣadha* arrives, a bhikṣuṇī should be appointed to convey the consent (*chanda*) to the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony; with their heads bowed at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha, they inquire after the *poṣadha* and request instruction."
Thus it was said three times.
If there is a monk among the community of bhikṣus who is authorized to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, he should say:
"Sisters, you must stop."
"If there is a bhikṣu who is endowed with twelve qualities, he should be appointed through *karmavācanā* to instruct and admonish them.
If there is no such person, one should say:
'There is no one to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; do not be negligent!'"
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.

While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the nun Jyotiṣkā developed an abscess on her private parts. While the bhikṣuṇīs had entered the village to beg for food, a physician who treated abscesses arrived.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Long-lived one!
Give me this abscess to be lanced."
He replied,
"So be it," and immediately lanced the ulcerous sore; having applied the medicinal ointment, he departed.
When the bhikṣuṇīs returned from their almsround, they saw pus and blood on the ground and asked,
"What is this pus and blood?
They replied:
"I am lancing a carbuncle.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with disapproval, saying:
"How could you have a carbuncle in a private part and lance it without informing a virtuous bhikṣuṇī?"
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"Why did you break open a carbuncle between the knees and the shoulders without first informing me and seeking my permission?
From this day forward, this is not permitted."
...up to: those who have already heard this should hear it again.

If a bhikṣuṇī has an abscess or ulcer in a concealed area above the knees and below the shoulders, and a man breaks it open and washes it without her having first informed and obtained permission, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Above the knees" means above the thighs.
"Below the shoulders" means below the breasts.
Regarding "not having previously informed": this means not having informed a virtuous bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding "not having sought permission from the Saṃgha": this refers to not performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of seeking permission within the Saṃgha.
If there is an abscess in a private part that one wishes to lance, one should first perform the formal act of seeking permission within the Saṃgha.
The *karmakāra* (the officiant) should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has an abscess in her private parts. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the *karman* for the lancing of an abscess."

Venerable Saṃgha, listen: this bhikṣuṇī so-and-so wishes to request from the Saṃgha the *karman* for the lancing of an abscess. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

If there is an abscess in a private part, one should have a trustworthy person, or a dependent disciple, or a fellow preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), break it open with a needle or a fingernail and apply medicinal ointment.
If a man causes a boil to be lanced, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.

If there is a boil or ulcer above the shoulder or below the knee, and one wishes to lance the head to draw blood or wishes to lance the arm, he should have a woman press down firmly; if the man then lances it, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 39;
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Fascicle 40.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

This is the remainder of the one hundred forty-one *pāyattika* rules. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī, having accepted bedding and mats from the Saṃgha during the rainy season retreat, abandoned them and went wandering.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, who replied,
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
“How is it that you travel during the rainy season retreat?
From this day forward, it is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels during the rainy season retreat, it is a pāyattika.
'Rainy season retreat' refers to the earlier retreat or the later retreat.
'Travels' means, at the very least, staying overnight in a village; [if she does so], it is a pāyattika."
*Pāyattika* is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), stays apart from her boundary for even one night, it is a *pāyattika*.

However, if there is danger from a king, or if bandits from another region have arrived, or if there is fear of losing one's life, or fear of losing one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there is no offense in departing.

During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), a bhikṣuṇī may not wander about for the sake of the Saṃgha’s affairs regarding a stūpa without having requested permission through the formal procedure of a *karmavācanā*; therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, having completed their rainy season retreat at Śrāvastī, came to Vaiśālī.
She went to the home of the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā’s relatives, and the family members asked,
"Where did you spend the rainy season retreat?
She replied:
“Śrāvastī. He asked, “What is Śrāvastī like?”
"Is it not good? The bhikṣuṇī said:

"The Jeta Grove has flourishing flowers and fruits; the pond water is cool and refreshing. The vihāra is like this; the dwelling place of the World-Honored One is like this; the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana are like this; and the lay devotee Sudatta is like this."
The donor said, "This is a true renunciant.
[Bhadra replied,] "As for me, Bhadra, born here and raised here, I am like one without hands or feet; at first, I was not willing to go out."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so on, until they replied:
"It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
“How is it that you have completed the rainy season retreat yet do not go on tour?
From this day forward, this is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy season retreat, does not go on a journey, it is a pāyattika.
'Having completed the retreat' means the three months are finished.
'Does not go on a journey' means that she does not even leave the village to travel; this constitutes a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: as explained above, from the completion of the rains retreat until one has not left the boundary for even a single night’s journey, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one is weak, old, or ill and thus unable to travel, there is no offense.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Thullanandā said to Sthūlanandā, "Observe the rains retreat here."
She immediately went to the house of the donor and praised her, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇī Śuddhā is virtuous and maintains the precepts; you should provide for her.

Seeing that Śuddhā’s deportment was composed and her every movement and gaze conformed to the rules of propriety, the donor felt joy in her heart. However, later on, she came to feel resentment, reproach, and vexation toward her.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so on, until they replied,
“It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; even those who have already heard it should hear it again.
If a bhikṣuṇī says this to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Āryā!'"
"Stay here for the rains retreat.
If she later complains, scolds, or causes distress, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī says:
"Residing here for the rains retreat.
During the rains retreat, one causes disturbance or offense.
Regarding "causing disturbance or offense": whether by means of one's own body or speech, or by commanding another person to act through body or speech, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the person in question does not uphold the precepts and fears committing an unrighteous act, there is no offense in expelling them.
However, if it concerns a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it constitutes a vinayātikrama offense.
"Even for a layperson, this constitutes a violation of the Vinaya requiring mental repentance.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke thus:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī departed on a journey when the time for the rainy season retreat (varṣā) approached; having entered the retreat, she returned."
Once the distribution of the dwellings was completed, [a person] arrived and demanded, saying:
"This is my dwelling; give it back to me!
The resident said:
"I have already accepted it; it cannot be obtained.
Thus they quarreled.
A virtuous bhikṣuṇī called out to them, saying:
"Noble one, you may stay in this room.
Having entered, he gathered a large quantity of *kṛmuka* wood and piled it up inside the room. The former resident said:
“Venerable One! This is a useless thing; there is no need to place it here.
He then said:
“Venerable one,
have you purchased this dwelling?
He replied:
"I shall next obtain this monastic cell; if it is a monastic cell, why should I not dwell in it?
Thereupon, she disturbed [the community] through her body and speech.
For this reason, the bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One, and so on, until he replied:
"It is truly so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed. How could you, knowing that others had already entered the summer retreat, come later to cause them disturbance?"
From this day forward, it is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again:
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has already entered the rainy season retreat, subsequently arrives and either personally disturbs her or causes others to disturb her, it is a pāyattika.
"Knowing the prior *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat)" refers to the earlier or later *varṣā*.
"Disturbing" means disturbing by means of one's own body or speech, or causing another to disturb through their body or speech; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one disturbs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense.
If it is a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a vyatikrama offense.
Even if it is a layperson, it is a vyatikrama offense requiring mental repentance.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, without first looking outside the wall, threw away her excrement and urine."
At that time, there was a brahmin who had just bathed and was walking through an alleyway wearing fresh, clean robes when [the fruit] fell directly onto his head.
The brahmin, filled with anger, reviled her, saying:
"You śramaṇī, daughter of many men! You have defiled me in such a way."
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the Buddha, and so on, until he replied:
"It is true,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, "This is an evil deed. Why did you discard the impurity without careful examination?
From this day forward, it is not permitted."
"Even those who have already heard this should hear it again:
If a bhikṣuṇī, without looking over a wall, throws away impure substances, it is a pāyattika.
"Over a wall" means across a fence or a wall.
"Throwing impure things" refers to throwing away feces, urine, mucus, saliva, refuse, water used for washing hands and feet, hair, or fingernails.
"Without observing" means throwing them away without first looking [at the place].
When one wishes to discard an object, one should first examine it carefully; if many people are passing by, one should wait until they have cleared the way before discarding it;
if few people are passing by, one should snap one's fingers before discarding it.
If one throws [it] without looking and without snapping one's fingers, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu throws [it] without looking, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit’s Eastern Garden Pond did not prohibit the entry of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

Then, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs went into that garden and engaged in worldly conversation; they voided excrement, urine, mucus, and spittle upon the living grass, and furthermore, they wrapped filth in lotus leaves and threw them into the pond water.
At dawn the next day, King Prasenajit went with the ladies of the harem to a garden pond for sightseeing.

Having been confined within the deep palace for a long time without venturing out, the women were now finally able to go abroad for recreation; they were joyful, cheerful, and eager, each vying with the others to claim the living grass, saying, "This is mine!"
He went to seize it, which smeared his hands with mud. Going to the water to wash them, he again saw a bundle upon the surface of the water and thought to himself:
"When these young men heard that we had gone out, they must have wrapped up various incenses to await us."
He immediately went to seize it, which defiled his hands;
he then went to inform the king, saying, "What is this thing that is so impure?
The king then summoned the gardener and questioned him.
"Who defiled this garden?
She replied, "There was no one else;
yesterday, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs stayed within it like laypeople, speaking and joking before they departed."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter... [as before] ...those who have already heard it should hear it again."
If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine in water, it is a pāyattika.
"Regarding 'a bhikṣuṇī,' it is as explained above.
Regarding 'grass,' it refers to all types of grass. To discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva upon them constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If, during the rainy season, the ground is covered with growing grass, one should walk where there is no grass."
If there is no empty space, one should place it upon a tile or brick, dry grass or wood, cow or horse dung, or a path frequented by people.
If even these are unavailable, one should go down to a single wooden branch, ensuring that it first falls onto the branch and subsequently onto the grass.
If there is grass on the walking path (*caṅkrama*), one should place a spittoon at the head of the walking path.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs, it is as previously stated."
There are ten kinds of water, as described above.
If one voids excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or spits into water, it is a *pāyattika*.
If water overflows during the rainy season, one should void excrement and urine in a high place.
If there is no such thing, one should do so upon tiles, stones, dry grass, wood, or the dung of oxen and horses.
If even that is unavailable, one should catch it with a branch of grass or wood, causing it to fall first onto the branch and subsequently into the water.
If water emerges from beneath a latrine after it has been dug out, one must not first void excrement or urine therein; first, let a layperson go, and only then may a bhikṣuṇī proceed.
If there is flowing water beneath the latrine, one should place wooden planks so that [the waste] first falls onto the planks and only afterwards into the water.
If there is a latrine while traveling by boat, one should install wooden planks to receive it, ensuring that it falls onto the planks and only afterwards into the water.
If there is no board, one should support it with a wooden branch so that it falls first onto the branch and subsequently into the water.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were traveling about to proselytize, and they said to women:
"Give me some goods; I wish to prepare food for the bhikṣus.
The woman immediately gave them and said:
"Tell me on the day the food is prepared, and I shall distribute it."

At that time, he invited the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Revata, Kapphiṇa, and the Venerable Rāhula; he further invited the group of six bhikṣus and prepared two seats—one for the elder bhikṣu and one for the group of six bhikṣus.

At that time, the elder bhikṣus, when the hour had come, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house where they sat in order. To the Venerable Śāriputra, they served white rice, mung-bean soup, ghee, milk, and curd; then, in this manner, they served coarse food to the others.

Venerable Maudgalyāyana was given coarse rice, masha-bean soup, oil, and milk; other bhikṣus were given red rice and masha-bean soup, some receiving rice but no soup, and others receiving soup but no rice; even Venerable Rāhula was given red rice, hemp chaff, and vegetable soup.
Then the women brought various kinds of fine food and asked, "For whom is this?
The bhikṣuṇī then used her body to shield the elder bhikṣu and pointed out the group of six bhikṣus, giving them white rice, fine soup, ghee, milk, and curd, providing as much as they desired.
After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they departed.
The Buddha, knowing this, intentionally asked: "Śāriputra!"
"Did you obtain good food and eat your fill?
He replied,
"I have already eaten."
"World-Honored One!
Thus he asked three times, and the answer was likewise each time.
In this manner, he questioned each of the elder bhikṣus one by one, and all answered in the same way.
He even went so far as to ask Rāhula:
"Why is your physical strength insufficient?
Are you able to eat your fill of good food?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
By eating oil one gains strength; by eating ghee one gains a fine complexion; but by eating sesame chaff and vegetables, one lacks both complexion and strength.”
He asked the group of six bhikṣus,
"Did you obtain good food?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
