I have obtained white rice, excellent soup, ghee, curd, and various kinds of fine food.
All of these are due to the power of the sister’s faith and kindness.”
The Buddha asked,
"Who is the senior elder?
He replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra," the Buddha asked Śāriputra,
"is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"This is not a lawful meal.
Why did you look upon this disturbance of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and enter into a state of equanimity?"
Śāriputra said: “If the World-Honored One says,
‘This is not a lawful meal,’ [then how can it be so]?”
"Even in one kalpa, or more than one kalpa, it could not be digested.
Thereupon, he immediately took a bird's feather and prodded [his throat] until he vomited it up.
The Buddha said:
"Call the group of six bhikṣuṇīs here.
When they had arrived, he asked them:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"This is an evil matter; how could you know to divert the benefits intended for the entire Saṃgha to give them to a single group?
From this day forward, this is not permitted.
Furthermore, those who have already heard this should hear it again."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that it is the property of the community, diverts it to one specific group, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing it herself or hearing it from another.
“Assembly” refers to the assembly of bhikṣus and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.
“Benefit” refers to eight kinds: timely medicine, nighttime medicine, seven-day medicine, lifetime medicine, personal belongings, heavy items, impure items, and pure-impure items.
"Regarding 'to divert': when the selection of an object and its intended recipient have already been determined, but one diverts it to another group, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is as explained above.
If someone comes and asks:"
"If I wish to practice giving, to whom should I give?
One should reply:
"Give to whomever your heart desires."
If one asks,
"In what place is merit great?
one should say:
"Give it to the Sangha.
If asked, "Where are there good monks who uphold the precepts? [one should reply: "In such-and-such a place."
One should say:
"There is no sangha that has transgressed the precepts.
If one says:
"Where are there bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who maintain few concerns, practice seated meditation and recite the sūtras, and do not travel extensively, so that I may constantly behold such individuals?"
If she says, "Give it to so-and-so," and a bhikṣuṇī,
knowing that the object was intended for the Saṃgha, diverts it to herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one dedicates [the merit] to another person, it is a pāyattika.
If one community dedicates [it] to another community, it is a pāyattika.
If a retinue dedicates [it] to another retinue, it is likewise a pāyattika.
To dedicate an item belonging to one person to another person constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
To dedicate communal property belonging to a *saṃgha* to another *saṃgha* constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
Instruction regarding abscesses in private parts; departing overnight and not traveling;
censuring after the end of the rains retreat; arriving after the rains retreat has ended;
discarding impurities over a wall; and dedicating grass and water to the Saṃgha.
The fourteenth *varga* is concluded.
There are seventy rules on shared precepts for bhikṣus and seventy-one rules on non-shared precepts.
The exposition of the one hundred forty-one *pāyattika* sūtras is finished.
The Exposition of the Eight Dharmas of Confession (Pāṭidesanīya-dharma). First: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
"Once, when the Tathāgata was in Śrāvastī..."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs went to the butter market to beg for butter, the oil market to beg for oil, the honey market to beg for honey, the rock-sugar market to beg for rock-sugar, the meat market to beg for meat, the fish market to beg for fish, the milk market to beg for milk, and the curd market to beg for curd; they then ate them and were reviled by the people of the world:
"How can the śramaṇa Gautama praise having few desires while disparaging those with many desires?"
"As was explained at length for the bhikṣus in the context of the *nidāna*,
so too should the bhikṣuṇī Gautamī train in this way. Gautamī!"
At one time I was staying at the Śākya vihāra in Kapilavastu, where I heard that a sick bhikṣuṇī was requesting choice food.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Let all the bhikṣuṇīs residing in Śrāvastī assemble; even those who have already heard this should hear it again."

If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, for her own sake begs for ghee from a layperson’s house, or causes another to beg for it, and then eats or consumes it, that bhikṣuṇī should confess her transgression to other bhikṣuṇīs, speaking thus:
“Āryā! [I have committed a fault].”
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I confess this dharma.
This is a *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
Thus there are two [cases] for oil, three for honey, four for rock sugar, five for milk, six for curd, seven for fish, and eight for meat.
Regarding "for one's own sake," it means for the benefit of oneself.
Regarding "one who is ill," the Blessed One has declared that there is no offense.
What constitutes being ill?
The elderly and infirm, those suffering from illness, those who have taken emetic or purgative medicines, those who have had bloodletting from the head—such are the types of illnesses.
"Family" refers to families of the four castes.
"Ghee" refers to cow ghee, buffalo ghee, or sheep ghee.
Regarding "begging," it means either begging for oneself or causing another to beg.
Regarding "chewing" or "eating," that bhikṣuṇī should confess her transgression to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Āryā!..."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy offense; I repent of this offense.
The person before him should ask:
"Do you see this transgression?"
He replied, “I have seen it.
[The Buddha said,] “Do not do it again.”
“I shall receive and uphold this upon my head.
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses requiring confession): these offenses must be disclosed; this is called repentance.

If a bhikṣuṇī suffers from a feverish illness and requires clarified butter (*sarpis*), she may beg for it, but she must not go to the house of one who lacks faith to beg; she should go instead to the house of one who has faith.
If, while begging for alms, one sees someone measuring ghee, one should say:
"Long-lived one!
May you be free from illness."
He replied, "Noble Lady!
What do you wish to obtain?"
He replied,
“I am begging for alms.
The host said:
"I have no food, but I do have ghee; I shall give it to whoever needs ghee.
One may take as much as fills one's bowl and may also encourage others to take some.
The same applies to measuring oil.
If a wind-related illness arises, one may also beg for oil; however, one must not solicit it from an oil-presser’s house, but should instead solicit it from a household of faith.
If, while begging for food, one encounters an oil-measurer, one should say:
"I am without illness, long-lived one!"
He said, "Noble Lady! What do you require?"
He replied, "I am begging for food.
[The other] said, "I have no food; I have only oil."
"If one needs it, one should give it.
It is without fault to take as much as fills one's bowl.
At that time, one may also encourage others to give to their companions.

Regarding honey: if one has a water-related illness, one may beg for honey, but one must not go to a honey-gatherer’s house to solicit it. One should instead beg at the house of a person of integrity; even if they are persuaded to give it, it should be given to a companion in this manner—this applies even to rock-honey.
If one is ill and a physician says,
"One should take stone honey (śarkarā)," one may beg for stone honey;
however, one must not go to a house where stone honey is kept to beg for it, but should instead go to a house of those who are trustworthy.
If, while begging for alms, one sees someone weighing rock honey (śarkarā-madhu), one may even encourage them to give it to their companion.
If one is ill and the physician says,
"You should consume milk," [one may accept it].
One may beg for milk.
When begging for food, if one sees a cowherd’s household milking a cow, one should say:
"Long-lived one!..."
"I am free from illness. He said, "Noble Lady!"
"What do you wish to obtain?
He replied,
"I am begging for food."
He replied, "I have no food; I have only milk.
Whoever needs it may take it.
If one asks for curd-milk and says,
"There is no curd-milk, there is only milk," one may take it.
If one is ill and a physician says,
"You must have curd," one may beg for curd.
If, while begging for alms, one sees a person measuring curd, one should say:
"Long-lived one!
May you be free from illness."
He asked, "Venerable One!
What do you wish to obtain?"
He replied,
"I am begging for alms.
If [the other] says:
"If I have no food, but there is curd," one may take it,
and one may also encourage others to give it to their companions.
If one begs for curd and receives it with a clear liquid poured underneath, it may be taken.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes emetic medicine and the physician says,
"Fish broth is required," she may beg for it.
If, while begging for alms, one requests curd-milk and obtains fish, it may be accepted.
If one draws blood from the head, and the physician says,
"Meat is required," one may beg for it.
"One must not go to the house of a butcher to beg; one should go to the house of those who have faith to beg.
When begging for food, one may request vegetable broth;
if they say, 'There is no vegetable broth, there is only meat broth,'"
"Those who need it may take it.
If one knows for oneself:
'I am prone to a certain illness that frequently breaks out; at such times, medicine will certainly be difficult to obtain,' [one may take it]."
It is without offense to receive [food] when one has not yet become ill.
If one requests food while not ill and eats it while ill, there is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
There is no offense if one requests food while ill and eats it while not ill; there is no offense if one requests food while ill and eats it while ill.
If one begs for food when not ill and eats it when not ill, it is a *pratideśanīya* offense.
There is no offense if one cooks according to the illness and eats according to the illness.
If one cooks according to the illness but eats what is not according to the illness, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
There is no offense in cooking according to the illness and eating according to the illness.

There is no offense for a renunciant who lives by depending on others to cook what is not suited to the illness or to eat what is not suited to the illness; for this reason, the World-Honored One has spoken thus.
Ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, milk, curd, meat, and fish—these are the eight.
The *Bhikṣuṇī Pātideśanīya Dharmas* are concluded.
The rules of training for the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharmas*) are explained in detail as they are for the bhikṣus;
the only exceptions are that the group of six bhikṣuṇīs may void excrement or urine upon living grass or in water, whereas all other matters are identical.
The seven methods for settling disputes:

*sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane), *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by confession), *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement by searching for the nature of the offense), *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement by the majority), and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by covering with grass).
The Dharma that accords with the Dharma is explained in detail above in the section on the bhikṣus.
The analysis of the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa is concluded.

Now begins the first chapter of the Miscellaneous Section (Kṣudraka-vastu): The Rules for Sitting. While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣuṇī sat in the full-lotus posture during the first and last watches of the night; then a snake came and entered her vaginal opening.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and on account of this, Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"One should give such-and-such medicine to [Name]."
The snake did not die but emerged; he then gave it the medicine and it came out.
The Buddha said:
"Why were you sitting cross-legged?"
From this day forward, it is not permitted.
Regarding the method of sitting: one should bend one leg and cover the private parts with the heel of the other leg.
If a bhikṣuṇī sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Regarding the rule on bamboo mats: While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣuṇī spread out a bamboo mat to sew her robes; the bamboo splinters injured her urethra, and blood flowed out.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to sit on bamboo mats."
When sewing robes, whether in a lecture hall or a warm chamber, one should first smear the ground with cow dung and then sew the robe.
If such a surface is not available, one should spread [the robe] upon a bed or upon one's knees and sew it.
"If one sits upon a bamboo mat or a reed mat, it is an offense of *vinaya-ati-krama*.
This is called the rule regarding mats.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the nun Thullanandā went with many women to the Ajiravatī River to bathe after undressing. The bhikṣuṇīs emerged first; [Thullanandā] took the women's waist ornaments and wrapped them around her own waist, then said to the women:
"Do you find me attractive?
The women replied,
"We desire that men wrap their waists with food to make them slender, so that our husbands will love and cherish us."
"What is the purpose of this, Noble Lady?
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇī reported the matter in detail to Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until she replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"This is an improper act; from this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to wrap their waists.
If one wraps the waist with a woman's waist-wrapping cloth, it constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense."
"If there is an abscess or ulcer, there is no offense in wrapping it around the waist.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā went with many women to the bank of the Ajiravatī River; they took off their clothes, placed them in one spot, and entered the water to bathe.
First, he stepped onto the shore, put on a woman’s bodice, and said to the women,
"Do you think this looks suitable for me?
The women replied:
"I am a laywoman; having put this on, I wish to cause my husband to love and cherish me. Why do you wear it?
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and [the woman] replied, "It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, wearing *brea*-garments is not permitted. Regarding *brea*-garments:

it is not permitted to wear garments for the private parts adorned with such things as conch shells, mother-of-pearl, lapis lazuli, pearls, jade, gold, silver, or *maṇi* gems; even down to making the appearance of a garment for the private parts by tying threads together constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
If there is an ulcer or sore upon the body, wrapping it incurs no offense.
This is called a "tunic" (*bōyī*).

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, [a nun] emerged first from her bath and put on women's ornamental clothing. For this reason, the bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One, and so forth, until he replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit you to wear women's ornamental garments."

As for women’s attire: gilded forehead ornaments on the head, earrings, bells, necklaces, finger-rings, armlets, anklets, and all such like articles of female adornment and dress are not permitted to be worn.
If she wears them, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she has an ulcer or sore on her body and applies medicine or wraps it with a bandage, there is no offense.
This is called the ornamented attire of women.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained daughters of the Śākya clan, daughters of the Malla clan, daughters of the Licchavi clan, and daughters of wealthy families, ordaining them while they were still fully adorned with ornaments and fine clothing.

At that time, when the daughters of poor families went out their doors, or on festival days when people were traveling about, they all borrowed and hired [robes], which was criticized by the people of the world:
"These people who hire clothes are not following the Dharma of those who have left the household life."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so on, until they replied:
“It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to ordain women who are adorned with finery; they must be made to discard such things before being ordained.
As for "discarding": if a woman comes wishing to go forth, she should be made to discard the articles used by laypeople for adorning the body.
If one should think:
"At some time grain may be expensive and alms difficult to obtain; or when old or sick, one will require medicinal decoctions; women are seldom able to acquire things."
"One should place her in a household.
If a woman comes wearing worldly ornaments and finery, yet she is ordained as one who has gone forth in accordance with the rules, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
This is called 'going forth while wearing ornaments and finery.'"

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, women of the Śākya clan, the Malla clan, the Licchavi clan, and the families of nobles took female attendants into the religious life; these attendants were beautiful, and they were made to consort with outsiders for their own livelihood, which led them to be reviled by the people of the world:
"These are not those who have left the household life; they are merely courtesans."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances, and so on, until they replied,
“It is truly so.
The Buddha said:
“How can you maintain a courtesan to support your livelihood?
From this day forward, maintaining a courtesan for the sake of one's livelihood is not permitted; if anyone maintains one, it is an offense of violation of the Vinaya.”
This is what is meant by a "prostitute.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One established a precept forbidding the keeping of prostitutes.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs privately kept courtesans who engaged in debauchery outside [the monastery] to earn their livelihood, and were consequently reviled by the people of the world:
"This is not the Dharma of one who has gone forth; she is merely a courtesan.
On account of this, the bhikṣuṇī went to inform the World-Honored One, and so on, until he replied:
"It is indeed so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to privately keep the daughters of gardeners or the daughters of servants and employ them as prostitutes to sustain your livelihood.
Should anyone do so, they commit a *vinayātikrama* offense."
This is what is meant by "the daughter of a gardener.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a young bhikṣuṇī who was beautiful, yet her breasts protruded; whenever people saw her, they all laughed.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and so on, until they replied,
“It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall wear the saṃkakṣikā.
The procedure for the formal act is as explained above; one should first put on the breast-covering garment, and only thereafter put on the other robes.
If one does not keep a saṃkakṣikā, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (vinayātikrama).
If one possesses one but does not wear it, it is likewise an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the rule regarding the saṃkakṣikā.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. As explained in detail in the account concerning the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā, the Buddha said:
"Bathing naked is not permitted; one should use a bathing robe."
One must not enter a river or a pool of water to bathe naked; one should wear a rain-cloak.
If one bathes naked, it is a *vinaya*-offense (*vibhaṅga-dosa*).
However, if one bathes naked in a secluded place where no people are present, there is no offense.
This is called the rule for the bathing robe (*snānaśāṭī*).
Regarding the sitting mat and the bamboo mat, the waist-wrap and the covering garment,
the wearing of secular ornaments, and the crossing over while wearing ornaments— these are the rules.
[The rules concerning] the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-cloth) and the bathing robe for female lay followers are concluded at the beginning of the *Vinayakṣudraka*.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs was separated from that of the laypeople by only a single wall. A desire arose in a bhikṣuṇī, and she struck her own vulva with her hand.
At that time, the husband heard the sound and immediately said to his wife, "What is this sound?
She replied:
"Why do you make this sound? her husband asked.
He replied, "This renunciant is practicing the holy life;
his lustful mind has arisen and he cannot control himself, so he is merely making the sound of slapping his private parts!"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they went to report it on these grounds, until the Buddha asked:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"From this day forward, I do not permit the slapping of the private parts."

"Clapping" refers to clapping with the hands, or clapping with a *kumbha* (a small gong), or clapping with a *kaṃsī* (a bronze cymbal). To do this for the purpose of quelling lustful thoughts constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
This is called "clapping with the hands."

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī, having given rise to lustful thoughts, fashioned a phallus out of lacquer and attached it to the leg of her bed. Later, when a fire broke out, she removed it for fear that it would burn the bedding.
At that time, the worldly people saw the fire break out and wondered, "Which places are being burned?
Which places are not being burned?
Having seen this, they reviled and censured [the monks].
"How can those who have left the household life commit such evil deeds?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to [the Buddha], and so on, until he replied:
"It is indeed so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, making phallic-shaped objects out of hujiao resin is not permitted.

Regarding "phallic-shaped objects": whether made of hujiao resin, or copper, lead, tin, white brass, ivory, or wax and honey—if one fashions such a thing to represent the male organ in order to quench lustful thoughts, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the "shape of lac.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side. Then Mahāprajāpatī said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, the bodies of women have a foul odor; may they be permitted to wash?"
The Buddha said, "You may wash it.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī washed the exterior, yet the interior remained foul-smelling as before. For this reason, she went to inform [the Buddha], saying:
“May one wash the interior?
The Buddha said,
“One may wash it.”
Regarding the method of washing: it may be washed up to the first joint of a finger, but it must not exceed that.
If one exceeds this limit in washing for the purpose of quelling lustful thoughts, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the method of washing.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī had her menstrual period and soiled her bedding and mats. Mahāprajāpatī went to the Buddha’s presence and said to him:
“World-Honored One, may we make a garment for menstrual impurity?”
The Buddha said:
"It may be obtained.
It should be made from old cloth; it must not be made from stiff materials."
Furthermore, one must not insert anything deeply while forming the thought of sexual desire; rather, one should use a soft object to block the urinary passage.
If one uses a hard object and inserts it deeply to quench the desire for lust, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the rule for the menstrual cloth (*māsi-kāṣāya*).
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a bhikṣuṇī went to a women’s bathing place to wash her menstrual cloth. A woman complained, saying:
“These śramaṇikās have defiled this water until it is so red!”
The bhikṣuṇīs went and reported this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted for women to wash menstrual cloths at bathing places."
If she washes it, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule for women washing menstrual garments.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the World-Honored One had established a precept forbidding women from washing menstrual garments in places where men wash; yet they went instead to places where men wash to do so. [The Buddha continued] until: "If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a place where men wash to wash [her garments], she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense."
This is called the dharma of men.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the World-Honored One established a precept, forbidding women from washing menstrual cloths in places where men bathe.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī went to a guest laundry to wash her clothes, and so forth... "It is not permitted to wash menstrual raiment at a guest laundry.
She should take it in a basin or another earthenware vessel and wash it in a secluded place.
When washing, one must not sprinkle water on the ground; it should be poured into a drainage ditch in a place where no one can see. The clothes should be dried in the sun, and later used when needed.
If a bhikṣuṇī washes menstrual raiment at a public laundry, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called a "public laundry.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣuṇī gave rise to lustful thoughts; she placed her urinary tract against a falling stream of water, whereby she discharged impurity. She then became filled with doubt and remorse.
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to use the urinary tract as a receptacle for a suspended stream [of water]."
"Regarding 'pouring down': water pours down from above.
If a bhikṣuṇī bathes in water that is pouring down, she must hold her robes to shield herself.
If she uses the urinary tract to receive pouring water or leaks from a roof eave in order to quench lustful desire, it is a sthūlātyaya."
If one bathes under a cascading stream or a leak from a roof eave, one must not turn one’s body toward the water; rather, one should have one’s back to it.
If one turns one’s body toward the water in order to quench lustful thoughts, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called "suspended water.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time some bhikṣuṇīs were bathing in a rapid stream; lust arose in them, and as they went against the current, they emitted impurity.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to report this matter, and so on, until: "From this day forward, it is not permitted to touch the urinary tract against the current in a swift-flowing stream."
Regarding "flowing water": whether it be mountain water, rapid currents, or flowing water, if one faces the current or goes against the flow to quench lustful desires, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When washing in rapid currents, one must not face the flow; one should turn one's back to it.
If one directs it toward a flowing stream, it is a *vinaya*-offense of transgression.
This is called "flowing water.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣuṇī emitted semen through various bodily contacts; she did so by inserting radish roots, onion roots, or various other roots into her urinary tract.

The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform [the Buddha] of these circumstances, and so on, until: "From this day forward, it is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to insert radish roots or scallion roots into the urinary passage to emit semen in order to quench lustful desire; [if she does so, it is] a sthūlātyaya offense."
These are called the "roots":
the female organ, the male organ, the anus, the mouth, and the joints;
the menstrual cloth, washing at a woman’s bathing place, and likewise washing at a man’s bathing place.
Washing clothes at a guest-washing place, pouring from above,
and the various types of seminal emissions.
The second *vagga* is concluded.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus gathered but did not know how to perform the formal act of *karma* for suspension (*ukṣepa*). They therefore had a bhikṣuṇī perform it; subsequently, the bhikṣuṇī felt doubt and regret, and reported the matter to Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī then went to inform the World-Honored One of these events.
The Buddha said:
"This is a most venerable assembly; how could you perform an *ukkhepanīyakamma* against them?
From this day forward, it is not permitted to perform an *ukkhepanīyakamma* against a bhikkhu."
If among the bhikṣus there is no one at all capable [of performing the rite], one may receive the transmission and have another recite it.
If one cannot find anyone when the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is being performed, there is no offense in transmitting it from a distance.
If a bhikṣuṇī performs the *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣu, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
"A bhikṣu may perform a *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣuṇī without fault.
This is called a *karmavācanā*. The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā, wearing a garment of *kauśeya* silk, went to the home of her relatives. On the road she encountered a heavy rainstorm; her body became as visible as crystal, and a crowd gathered around, wishing to see her. Thereupon, she crouched on the ground, while her attendant disciple stood by her side to shield her.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform [the Buddha] of these circumstances, and so on, until he replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs are not permitted to wear kauseya garments.
There are two kinds of kauseya: [silk produced from] wild silkworms and [silk produced from] domestic silkworms.
The first is birth; the second is making.
Birth refers to the fine thread;
making refers to spinning the thread.
To wear fine silk *kauseya* is a *vinaya*-offense.
To wear spun silk is a *vinaya*-offense requiring mental regret (*vibhāṣā-citta-kaukṛtya*).
For a bhikṣu, wearing it is without offense.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had large breasts; she put on a single saṃkakṣikā and was walking up and down on an upper terrace. Seeing her from afar, some laypeople said to one another, "Look at her!
She looks like a gourd floating on the water."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must wear a shoulder-covering garment (saṃkakṣikā).
A shoulder-covering garment is to be folded and draped over the shoulders."
If one does not do so or does not wear it [properly], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
It is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to wear a single-layered saṃghāṭī while walking in meditation on an elevated place.
If she wears a single-layered saṃghāṭī in a secluded place, there is no offense.
This is called the *saṃkakṣikā*.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, daughters of the Śākya clan, Malla clan, Licchavi clan, and families of noble birth went forth as nuns. Being skilled in adornment, whenever there were weddings—whether for giving away a daughter or taking a bride—they would all borrow ornaments from them to beautify themselves. They also received fine food and drink, which led to them being ridiculed by the people of the world:
"These are not women who have gone forth; they are merely people who hire out their beauty."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and so on until the Buddha said:
"From now on, the adornment of women is not permitted. Regarding "adornment":
combing the hair, adorning the eyes, powdering the face, reddening the lips, and wearing ornate clothing for the purpose of making a living—this constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If one has a headache or eye pain, there is no offense in applying ground medicinal paste.
This is called the "Method of Adornment.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time, women from the Śākya clan, the Malla clan, and families of great lineage went forth as nuns; they grew *utpala* flowers and sold them, which led them to be criticized by the people of the world:
"This is not one who has gone forth; she is merely a woman selling flowers!
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the World-Honored One, and so on, until he replied:
"It is truly so."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the planting of flowers for sale in order to sustain one's livelihood.
If a bhikṣuṇī plants utpala flowers to sustain her livelihood, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense."
"There is no offense for planting it for the sake of a stūpa or as an offering to the Buddha.
This refers to the *utpala* flower.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a bhikṣuṇī planted *sumanā* flowers; [the same applies] up to: "There is no offense for planting them for the sake of a stūpa or as an offering to the Buddha."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the World-Honored One had established a precept prohibiting the planting of flowering trees.

Then, women of the Śākya clan and women of the Malla clan went forth into homelessness; they tied together flower garlands and sold them to support themselves, which led them to be ridiculed by the people of the world:
"These are not those who have gone forth; these are merely women selling flower garlands!"
The bhikṣuṇīs went to inform [the Buddha] of these circumstances, and so on until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the binding of flower garlands.
As for 'garlands,' they are those made of *utpala* flowers, *mallika* flowers, and *sumanā* flowers.
If one ties flowers into garlands and sells them for a livelihood, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

However, during the Great Assembly on the Buddha’s birthday, the Great Assembly at Bodhi, the Great Assembly of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the Great Assembly for Ānanda, the Great Assembly for Rāhula, or the Five-Yearly Assembly, if a donor says:
"Venerable One!..."
"Help me tie this garland.
At that time, it is without offense to tie various kinds of garlands.
This is called the method for tying garlands.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, women of the Śākya clan, the Malla clan, and the Licchavi clan had gone forth into homelessness; they spun thread and sold it, which drew the reproach of the world:
"These are not those who have left the household life; these are merely sellers of thread."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, spinning thread is not permitted.
As for "spinning thread," it refers to cotton thread, kusa-grass thread, kauseya-silk thread, śāna-hemp thread, and spun thread.
To sell that which provides one's livelihood constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
However, if one intends to make a water-strainer or a waist-belt and spins [the thread] for that purpose, there is no offense.
This is called the rule regarding spinning thread.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Sudinna had died and his wife had gone forth as a nun. Her uncle constantly sought to cause her to abandon the religious life.
Once, when a bhikṣuṇī entered a village to beg for food, the uncle encountered her and immediately tried to seize her; she then fled into the house of a prominent family and said to a woman there:
"How strange! I nearly ruined my brahmacarya!"
Question:
"For what reason?
Answer: [He] replied:
"The elder brother wishes to stop me on my way.
The woman said, "Do not fear; I shall protect you."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I wish to go to my upādhyāyī.
The woman said:
"If you wish to depart, you must don secular clothing and assume a different appearance before you can escape.
He immediately put on armlets, earrings, and the attire of a layman, and departed with four or five attendants.
Her uncle saw her outside and thought to himself, "This is not a bhikṣuṇī; she is merely a laywoman.
When he arrived at the residence, the bhikṣuṇīs rebuked him, saying:
"Why are you wearing this? He replied, "My uncle wishes to take me;
I am merely wearing it as a pretext to protect myself through skillful means."
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and Mahāprajāpatī immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
“Summon the bhikṣuṇī.”
When he had arrived, the Buddha asked,
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"How did you violate the rules of decorum?"
From this day forward, you are not permitted to violate the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*).
If one definitively violates the rules of decorum, she is no longer a *bhikṣuṇī*.
If one violates the rules of decorum for the sake of protecting oneself through skillful means, it constitutes an offense against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore she is called a bhikṣuṇī.
If a bhikṣuṇī deliberately violates her dignified deportment, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If she employs skillful means to protect herself, there is no offense.
The *karmavācanā* and *kauśeya*, the *saṃkakṣikā* and ornaments for guests,
planting flowers and *sumanā* jasmine, making garlands and spinning thread;
the violation of dignified deportment is the last.
The third chapter concludes.

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā went to a prominent household while begging for alms. There was a woman there who had suffered a miscarriage, and she said to her, "Discard this for me."
He replied, "I cannot.
He was requested again:
"I shall provide you with such an amount of goods.
Having said this, he took [the food] and placed it in his bowl before departing.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa always maintained this thought while begging for alms: "When I first obtain food, I shall give it to a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī."
Having seen this bhikṣuṇī, he said to her,
"Bring me your bowl.
She immediately turned it over and did not show it to him.
He called out again, but [the woman] still did not show herself.
Mahākāśyapa, being by nature majestic and imposing, called out with a stern voice; she immediately trembled with fear and showed herself.
Having seen her, he said:
"Hey! Why do you commit such an evil act?
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs, on account of this matter, went to inform the World-Honored One, until he replied:
"It is indeed so," the Buddha said.
"This is an evil deed and contrary to the Dharma."
"How do you cover your bowl?
From this day forward, covering the bowl is not permitted, nor is it permitted to hold it uncovered; once you have received food, you should cover it.
When you see a bhikṣu, you should lift the cover and show it to him."
"If one carries the bowl while exposed to view, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
If one sees a bhikṣu and does not show [the bowl] to him, it is likewise an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
This is called the matter concerning the bowl.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a high minister who had violated the king’s law; all the wealth and property of his household were to be confiscated by the state, so the king immediately dispatched men to guard it.
At that time, as the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was on her almsround, she arrived at that house.
The woman said to her, "Noble Lady!
My family has incurred an offense against the king punishable by death; our property shall be confiscated by the state. I wish to entrust you with some precious objects and ornaments."
"If I am released, I shall look back at you; if I die, I shall take this and give it to you.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī placed various jewels inside the bowl, covered it, and departed.
At that time, the gatekeeper saw him and asked, "What is in your bowl? He did not show it to him;
however, when the gatekeeper shouted at him again, he showed it out of fear.
Having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs went and reported it, until [the Buddha] replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is not permitted to conceal precious objects in one's bowl.

If there is someone who has committed an offense against the state but has not yet been arrested, nor has their property been confiscated, then one may take what has been entrusted to them at that time."
If the king seizes [the person] and also confiscates their wealth, one should say:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that this may not be accepted. If he says:
"If [the donor] says, 'I give it to you, to the stūpa, and to the Saṃgha,' one may take it.
Having received it, one must not depart while covering it; one should carry it away openly."
If anyone asks, you should say:
"It is property of the stupa, property of the Sangha, or my own property.
If they permit you to go, it is well; if they do not permit it, you should return.
This is called the rite of overturning the alms-bowl.
While the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇīs constructed latrines and covered them with objects.
Women would place dead fetuses inside them. Later, some low-caste Caṇḍālas came to baste the latrines; having seen this, they said:
"This śramaṇī herself caused an abortion and threw it into [the latrine].
The bhikṣuṇīs went to report this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to have a covered latrine; it must be made with an open mouth."
"If one closes the mouth while doing so, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
This is called the rule for the latrine.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a woman of the Śākya clan and a woman of the Malla clan were bathing in a bathhouse; then a young man entered therein and violated their celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
The bhikṣuṇīs told Mahāprajāpatī, and so on, until: "From this day forward, it is not permitted to enter the bathhouse.
However, those who are ill may light a fire inside their rooms, apply oil, and rub themselves with it.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a bathhouse to bathe, she commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.
This is called the rule regarding bathhouses.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; at that time, the precept had not yet been established, and there were no residences for bhikṣuṇīs either in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*) or within villages.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, with Mahāprajāpatī at their head, were residing in the King’s Garden.

There were young women of the Śākya clan and Malla clans who were beautiful; some young men, seeking an opportunity during the first watch of the night, wished to seize the bhikṣuṇīs, but upon seeing them, they flew away through the air.
They come again at midnight in the same manner.

They come again during the latter part of the night; among them, those who are of dull faculties, who do not enter meditative concentration at the proper time, or who fall asleep, cannot immediately depart and are thus plundered by them.
Mahāprajāpatī went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka). However, they may stay if the fourfold assembly has gathered and is preaching the Dharma throughout the night; even then, they must not remain in secluded places."
"If a bhikṣuṇī dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage), she commits a vinaya offense.
This is what is meant by "araṇya.
A bhikṣu may receive the kaṭhina robe, but a bhikṣuṇī may not.
A bhikṣuṇī receives the kaṭhina robe, but it is not for a bhikṣu;
a bhikṣu relinquishes it, but it is not for a bhikṣuṇī;
a bhikṣuṇī relinquishes it, but it is not for a bhikṣu.
A bhikṣu who has transgressed is not a bhikṣu;
a bhikṣuṇī who has transgressed is not a bhikṣuṇī.
Turning over the alms bowl and the precious bowl; opening the latrine and entering the bathhouse;
dwelling in an araṇya; a bhikṣu receiving a kaṭhina robe;
this does not apply to a bhikṣuṇī; a bhikṣu relinquishing a kaṭhina robe.
She is not a bhikṣuṇī.
The fourth section (varga) concludes.
Regarding food: what is impure for a bhikṣu is pure for a bhikṣuṇī; what is impure for a bhikṣuṇī is pure for a bhikṣu.
A bhikṣu may have a bhikṣuṇī serve him food, with the exception of gold, silver, money, and the five kinds of cultivated seeds that have not been purified by fire.
A bhikṣuṇī may receive food from a bhikṣu, with the exception of gold, silver, money, and the five kinds of cultivated seeds that have not been purified by fire.
There are three causes and conditions by which one is no longer a bhikṣu.
What are the three?

A firm resolve in the mind to renounce the precepts; being expelled from the Saṃgha for a factual offense; and the transformation of one's physical form into that of a woman. These are called the three cases of no longer being a bhikṣu.
One should be sent to the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra; one must not share the same enclosure with the bhikṣuṇīs, but should reside separately.
If he later regains his male organ, he shall return to the community of bhikṣus; thus he is called "fully ordained" (upasampanna), and his seniority is restored to its original state.
There are three causes and conditions by which one is no longer a bhikṣuṇī.
What are these three?
The mind is definitively corrupted; she possesses actual grounds for being expelled by the Saṃgha; or she undergoes a change of gender to become male.
As it is said in the section concerning the bhikṣus:
for bhikṣuṇīs, there is no *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leftover food); they may eat as much as they desire in a single sitting.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, on the far bank of the Ajiravatī River, the two communities of monks were invited to a meal.
When both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs wished to cross together, the bhikṣus said, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that we may not travel in the same boat.

Two or three bhikṣus then crossed in a light boat; once all the bhikṣus had finished crossing, the bhikṣuṇīs crossed. Having finished, they asked for their seniority (years since ordination), but the time for the alms-round had already passed.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, having lost her appetite and being emaciated from hunger, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Knowing the reason, the Buddha nevertheless asked:
"Why do you have such a look of hunger?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, eight senior monks shall sit in order according to the Dharma; the rest shall sit as they arrive."
If many people assemble for the five-year great assembly, eight senior bhikṣuṇīs shall sit in their proper order, while the rest may sit as they please.
If these eight do not sit according to the proper order, they commit a *vinayātikrama* offense.
Therefore the World-Honored One said:
"The purification of the two assemblies differs;
three are not the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, and three are not the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha; there are no parivāsa offenses for the eight elders."
The fifth *vagga* is concluded.

Within the *bhikṣu-vibhaṅga-vagga*, nine matters—separate residence, garlic, umbrellas, vehicles, cauterization with a blade, leather sandals, lying or sitting on the same bed, and musical performances—are omitted from the recitation; the remaining thirteen *vaggas* are distinct for the bhikṣuṇīs.

Within the fifth miscellaneous section on the rules of decorum (*vinaya*), the matters concerning forest dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), the bathhouse, latrines, and the sewing of robes and mats should have been set forth but were not; all other points are the same as for the bhikṣuṇīs.

The two divisions of the Sūtras and the training in the five hundred precepts were expounded by the World-Honored One in detail: the Preface to the Precepts, the eight pārājikas, the nineteen saṃghāvaśeṣas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas, the one hundred forty-one pāyattikas, the eight pratideśanīyas, the sixty-four śaikṣas, and the seven adhikaraṇa-śamathas; with the verses on the Dharma following the Dharma at the end, the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya is concluded.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* Private Notes: In ancient times in Central India, there was once a wicked king who ruled the world.
The śramaṇas fled in all directions to escape him, and the bhikṣus who had mastered the Tripiṭaka dispersed like stars.
When the wicked king had died, there was another virtuous king who again invited the śramaṇas back to his kingdom to provide them with offerings.

At that time, there were five hundred monks in the city of Pāṭaliputra; they wished to settle legal matters, yet they lacked a master of the Vinaya, nor did they have the Vinaya texts upon which to rely for guidance.
He immediately dispatched a person to the Jetavana Vihāra, where he obtained a copy of the Vinaya text that is still transmitted and esteemed today.
Faxian, meanwhile, at the Deva Vihāra south of the Aśoka Stūpa in Pāṭaliputra, in the kingdom of Magadha, obtained a Sanskrit manuscript which he brought back to Yangzhou.

In the eleventh month of the year Bingchen, the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, it was brought forth at Douchang Temple; by the end of the second month of the fourteenth year, the work was fully completed.
The Master Gong translated the Sanskrit text into the Qin language; therefore, this is recorded here.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa compiled the Vinaya Piṭaka as the foundation of the Great Teacher’s doctrine, fully upholding the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries.

After the Great Kāśyapa had passed away, next the Venerable Ānanda also fully upheld the eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas; next the Venerable Madhyāntika also fully upheld the eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas; next the Venerable Śāṇavāsa also fully upheld the eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas; and next the Venerable Upagupta, whom the World-Honored One prophesied as a Buddha Without Marks—as described in the account of the subduing of Māra—was likewise able to fully uphold the eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas.
Thereupon, five schools consequently came into existence:
first, the Dharmaguptaka became one school; next, the Mahīśāsaka became another school; next, the Kāśyapīya became yet another school; and finally, the Sarvāstivāda.
*Sarvāstivāda* means, in the Jin language, "Proponents of the Existence of All.
It is called "All Exists" because the tenets and doctrines of the various schools mentioned above differ from one another.

The *Sarvāstivādins* maintain that the past, the future, the present, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, they are named "Proponents of the Existence of All."
Thereupon, the five schools were established simultaneously, arising in contention and each asserting its own doctrine to be correct.
At that time, King Aśoka said:
"How can I now discern which is right and which is wrong?"
Thereupon he asked the Saṃgha:
"How does the Buddha-dharma settle legal matters?
They all replied:
"The Dharma should follow the majority.
The King said, "If that is so,
we shall cast lots to determine which side is more numerous."
Thereupon, voting sticks were distributed.
Those who took the original voting stick were very numerous; because they were so numerous, they were called the Mahāsāṃghika.
"Mahāsāṃghika" is a name for the Great Assembly.

The Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating the Precepts, as Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana arose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
There is a doubt in my mind that I now wish to inquire about; I only pray that you will grant me leave."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“I grant you leave to ask; I shall explain it for you.
Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī lacks a sense of shame and dread, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), as well as the prādeśanika, pāyattika, sthūlātyaya, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and pārājika offenses—how many unwholesome transgressions does such a person incur?”
“I only pray that you will explain this.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana,
“Listen attentively!”
Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you.

If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, being shameless and lacking a sense of propriety, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharmas), they will fall into the Niraya hell for a lifespan equal to five hundred years as reckoned by the Four Heavenly Kings; in human reckoning, this is nine hundred thousand years.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"If one is without shame or remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pāratideśanīya* offense, they will fall into the Niraya hell for a lifespan equal to one thousand years as reckoned among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, which corresponds to three hundred and sixty million years by human calculation."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and arrogance, commits a pāyattika offense. Such a person shall fall into the Niraya hell for a lifespan of two thousand years as measured by the Yāma devas, which corresponds to twenty-four billion years by human reckoning."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and arrogance, commits a sthūlātyaya offense. Such a person will fall into the Nirarbuda hell for the lifespan of four thousand years as measured in the Tuṣita Heaven, which corresponds to fifty billion and sixty thousand years by human reckoning."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Such a person falls into the Nirarbuda hell for a lifespan equal to eight thousand years of the Tuṣita devas, which, by human reckoning, is two hundred and thirty billion and forty thousand years."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and commits a *pārājika* offense, shall fall into the Avīci hell for a lifespan of sixteen thousand years as measured by the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; in human reckoning, this equals nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years."
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
"Because of the cause of contempt, At the end of life one falls into the evil realms."
Those who cultivate goodness through causes and conditions will, upon death, be reborn in the heavens.
By virtue of this cultivation of meritorious deeds, they leave evil behind and attain liberation;
yet those who do not skillfully contemplate causes and conditions fall into the evil realms when the body perishes.
